Let $P$ be the projection plane in an oriented $3$-sphere and let $n$ be the
unit viewing normal pointing toward the viewer. Orient $P$ so that $(u,v)$ is
a positive basis exactly when $(n,u,v)$ is a positive ambient basis. A
**crossing code** has a
finite set $C$ of crossing labels and a finite set $D$ of **darts**, where a
dart is one directed half-edge incident to a crossing. A fixed-point-free
involution $\alpha:D\to D$ pairs the two ends of each edge: $\alpha^2=\mathrm{id}$
and $\alpha(d)\ne d$. A vertex map $v:D\to C$ records the crossing incident to
each dart. A **rotation system** is the permutation $\sigma$ whose cycles give
the clockwise order of darts at each crossing. Each crossing has four darts;
the two over-strand darts and the two under-strand darts are opposite in that
cyclic order. An arrow on each dart records whether its edge is directed into
or out of its incident crossing. The pairing $\alpha$ must join one incoming
end to one outgoing end. At a crossing, each opposite pair has one incoming
and one outgoing dart, so following an edge and then the opposite dart defines
the oriented link components. A code is **connected** when the graph with
vertices $C$ and edges the $\alpha$-pairs is connected.

The sign of an oriented crossing is $+1$ or $-1$ according as
$\det(v_{\rm over},v_{\rm under})$ is positive or negative, where the two
tangent vectors follow the oriented over- and under-strands. This item fixes
the local cyclic-order convention as follows. Starting with the outgoing
over-dart and reading counterclockwise, a positive crossing has order
$(O_{\rm out},U_{\rm out},O_{\rm in},U_{\rm in})$; a negative crossing has
order $(O_{\rm out},U_{\rm in},O_{\rm in},U_{\rm out})$. The stored crossing
sign and cyclic order must agree. This is the page's explicit sign convention.
It agrees with the current KT-03 supplier: reversing its positive
counterclockwise order from outgoing over gives the clockwise record
$(O_{\rm out},U_{\rm in},O_{\rm in},U_{\rm out})$.

For a nonempty connected crossing graph, let $V=|C|$, $E=|D|/2$, and let
$F$ be the number of cycles of the face permutation $\phi=\alpha\circ\sigma$.
A **spherical code** is a code satisfying $V-E+F=2$. A spherical code becomes a
**plane code** by distinguishing one face as the outer face and deleting a
point in that face from the sphere. The crossingless one-component code is a separate case: its Gauss data are one empty component word, its DT pairing and crossing-sign vector are empty at $c=0$, and its PD data are the single loop `Loop[1]`; every format also carries an orientation marker, `ccw` or `cw`, for the unit circle $S^1=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:x^2+y^2=1\}$ in the oriented plane, and the outer-face marker is `outside`. Thus the crossingless code records which direction orients its circle. It has no crossing graph or face-permutation test. Disconnected crossing graphs and disconnected crossingless links are outside this code class.

A **normalized planar-diagram code** with $c>0$ has crossing labels
$C=\{1,\ldots,c\}$ and four dart positions $0,1,2,3$ at each crossing, in
clockwise order beginning with the outgoing over-dart. The opposite pair
$(0,2)$ is over and $(1,3)$ is under. For sign $+1$, the clockwise record is
$(O_{\rm out},U_{\rm in},O_{\rm in},U_{\rm out})$; for sign $-1$ it is
$(O_{\rm out},U_{\rm out},O_{\rm in},U_{\rm in})$. Edge labels are assigned
by scanning crossings in increasing order and their four dart positions in
order, giving the next positive integer to the pair containing the first
not-yet-labelled dart. The outer face is recorded by its least dart in its
face cycle. These rules remove arbitrary edge-name and face-name choices;
different crossing labelings may still represent the same diagram. At $c=0$
a normalized code is the crossingless record with one of the two orientation
markers above.

A **Gauss code** for an oriented diagram records, in traversal order on each
oriented component, a signed crossing label: $+j$ means the component passes
over at crossing $j$, and $-j$ means it passes under. For a knot there is one
cyclic word; for a link there is one cyclic word per component. Each crossing
label must occur exactly twice in total, once positively and once negatively.
When $c>0$, every listed component word is nonempty; a separate crossingless
component is not part of this code class. The zero-crossing case is only the
one-component code specified above.
The code also carries a separate algebraic crossing-sign vector
$\varepsilon_j\in\{+1,-1\}$, one entry for each label. Choosing a basepoint
turns the knot's cyclic word into a based word; changing the basepoint
cyclically shifts the word, and relabeling crossings changes only their names.
The visit order, over/under signs, and crossing-sign vector determine the
crossing rotation system; it is realizable in the sphere only when the
resulting code is spherical. A plane Gauss code also carries an identifier of
one cycle of its face permutation to designate the outer face.

A **signed Dowker–Thistlethwaite code**, in this page's convention, encodes a
based oriented knot with $c$ crossings by numbering its $2c$ visits
$1,\ldots,2c$ in traversal order. For each odd visit $2j-1$, record the even
visit $2k$ paired with it as $d_j=+2k$ when the odd visit is over and
$d_j=-2k$ when it is under; also record the algebraic crossing sign
$\varepsilon_j\in\{+1,-1\}$ for crossing label $j$, the pair containing odd
visit $2j-1$. Its parity conditions are that
$|d_1|,\ldots,|d_c|$ are exactly the even numbers $2,4,\ldots,2c$, each once,
and each paired crossing has one over-visit and one under-visit. The separate
$\varepsilon_j$ records the crossing sign; signed DT conventions elsewhere
may encode signs differently. The associated cyclic traversal and crossing
signs determine a rotation system, which must pass the same spherical
realizability test. A plane DT code also carries an identifier of one cycle
of its face permutation to designate the outer face.

An **oriented planar-diagram code** labels each edge segment by an integer and
lists its two incident darts at crossing records. Each crossing record lists
its four directed edge ends in clockwise order, beginning with the outgoing
over-dart, and records which opposite pair is over, the orientation of each
strand, and the crossing sign. Every edge label occurs exactly twice, once as
an incoming end and once as an outgoing end. The code must satisfy the local
crossing-order rule above; its crossing graph must be connected when nonempty;
and its rotation system must satisfy $V-E+F=2$. The record also carries an
identifier of one cycle of its face permutation as the outer face. Thus an
arbitrary word in labels, even when each label occurs twice, is not declared
realizable until all incidence, orientation, crossing, connectedness, and
face-count tests pass.

**Input:** A finite tagged Gauss code, signed Dowker–Thistlethwaite code, or
oriented planar-diagram code in the conventions of this page. The crossing
count $c$ is a nonnegative integer. When $c>0$, the code includes the finite
crossing labels, edge-end incidences, strand arrows, over/under data, crossing
signs, and a distinguished outer face. When $c=0$, the only admissible input
for this procedure is the one-component crossingless code specified in the
code definition.

**Output:** Either `Invalid(reason, witness)`, where `reason` is the first
failed check below and `witness` identifies the offending field, label, or
crossing, or `Valid(diagram, components, faces, outerFace)`. Here `diagram` is
a finite gluing record consisting of one crossing disk per vertex, one
rectangular edge band for each pair of darts under $\alpha$, and one cap disk
per cycle of the face permutation. Each band is attached at its recorded dart ports, and each
crossing disk records its clockwise order, strand orientations, over/under
pair, and sign. `components` lists the oriented link cycles, `faces` lists the
face-permutation cycles, and `outerFace` is the selected cycle. The gluing
record represents a polygonal spherical diagram; deleting a point in its
selected face gives the plane model. The procedure tests realizability of
this code only; it does not compare the represented link with another code.

**Instructions:**

1. Read the tag and crossing count. If the tag is unknown or $c$ is not a
   nonnegative integer, return `invalid-header` with that field.

2. If $c=0$, accept only one empty Gauss component word, the empty signed-DT
   code, or the single `Loop[1]` PD record, each with exactly one orientation
   marker, `ccw` or `cw`. Return
   `invalid-crossingless-code` otherwise. For an accepted input return the
   standard circle with the marked orientation, one component, its two sphere
   faces, and the `outside` face selector. Do not run crossing-graph tests.

3. For a Gauss code with $c>0$, reject an empty component word. Check that
   every label lies in $\{1,\ldots,c\}$, occurs exactly twice in total, and
   occurs once with each over/under sign. Check that its separate crossing-sign
   vector has length $c$ and entries in $\{+1,-1\}$. Return
   `invalid-crossing-label` for the first out-of-range label,
   `invalid-crossing-visit-count` with the label and its over/under counts for
   any visit failure, or `invalid-crossing-sign-vector` with the first bad
   position. Turn successive visits on each component word into directed edge
   labels, including each cyclic last-to-first edge, numbering these segments
   in the listed component order and then in traversal order, and form the
   crossing records from the over/under visits and the stored crossing signs.

4. For a signed DT code, check that its pairing list and sign vector each have
   length $c$, each pairing value has absolute value in
   $\{2,4,\ldots,2c\}$, every such absolute value occurs once, and every sign
   is $+1$ or $-1$. Return `invalid-dt-pairing` with the first bad index for a
   pairing failure, or `invalid-crossing-sign-vector` with the first bad
   position for a sign failure. The odd visit $2j-1$ is crossing $j$; if
   $d_j>0$ it is the over-visit and if $d_j<0$ it is the under-visit. At the
   even visit paired with $2j-1$, use crossing label $j$ and the opposite
   over/under sign. Decode visits in order $1,\ldots,2c$ into the corresponding
   signed Gauss word and continue with step 3.

5. For a PD code, check that there are exactly $c$ crossing records and four
   dart occurrences at each record. Return `invalid-crossing-record` with the
   first bad record otherwise. Use the edge labels and arrows in the records
   to form the paired-dart involution, crossing rotations, over/under pairs,
   and crossing signs.

6. In every nonempty encoding, check that each edge label has exactly two
   occurrences, one incoming and one outgoing; each crossing has exactly four
   incident darts; the opposite pairs are exactly one over-strand and one
   under-strand; each strand has one incoming and one outgoing end; and the
   cyclic order matches the stored crossing sign. Return, in that order,
   `invalid-edge-incidence`, `invalid-crossing-valence`,
   `invalid-over-under-pair`, `invalid-strand-orientation`, or
   `invalid-crossing-sign-order`, with the first offending label or crossing.

7. Starting at each as-yet unvisited outgoing dart, cross its edge by $\alpha$
   to the incoming dart at the other endpoint and continue through the
   opposite dart of that same strand. Stop only when the starting outgoing
   dart is reached. If an end is missing, a dart repeats before that return, or
   any dart remains uncovered after all cycles are traced, return
   `invalid-component-closure` with the first such dart. Then test the crossing
   graph for connectedness; if it is disconnected, return
   `disconnected-crossing-graph`.

8. Compute $\phi=\alpha\circ\sigma$ on all darts by finite table lookup and
   list its cycles. Put $V=c$, $E=|D|/2$, and $F=$ the number of cycles. If
   $V-E+F\ne2$, return `non-spherical-face-count` with $(V,E,F)$. If the
   supplied outer-face identifier is not one of these cycles, return
   `invalid-outer-face` with that identifier.

9. For a passing code, choose the lexicographically first spanning tree in the
   finite edge ordering. Root it at the least crossing label and attach its
   tree bands in increasing distance from that root, using the recorded cyclic
   gaps. Then attach the remaining edge bands in increasing edge-label order.
   Use the distinguished face for the plane projection, replace each crossing
   disk by its prescribed transverse crossing, attach one cap disk along each
   face cycle, and lift the over-strand above the under-strand. Return this
   finite gluing record, the directed components, the face cycles, and the
   outer-face identifier.

For every finite input in the three code formats, the validation and
reconstruction procedure terminates. It returns an invalid-code reason
exactly when the first failed syntax, incidence, orientation, component,
connectedness, face-count, or outer-face condition in its stated order occurs;
otherwise it returns the crossing-disk/edge-band model of the represented
oriented diagram, its oriented components, its face cycles, and its selected
outer face.

For an odd prime $p$, let $\mathbb F_p=\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z$ and define
$a*b=2b-a$. Then $(\mathbb F_p,*)$ is a quandle.

An **oriented Reidemeister move** is one of the following local replacements of
a regular oriented link diagram ([[def-regular-oriented-link-diagram]]),
performed inside a small closed disk while the diagram outside the disk is left
unchanged, and understood up to planar isotopy outside the disk
([[def-planar-isotopy-of-link-diagrams]]). All sign and orientation variants of
each local picture are included.

**(R1) Kink creation and deletion.** A single strand is replaced by a small
kink: two arcs crossing once and otherwise disjoint from the strand, with the
over/under datum of the new crossing as in the picture. The move is allowed in
both directions (create or delete the kink) and with both signs of the kink,
the sign being the sign of the crossing created. The orientations of the two
strands of the kink are the two possible consistent orientations through the
crossing, and all of them occur in the move list.

**(R2) Slide of two strands.** Two local arcs belonging to two strands are
replaced so that the number of crossings between those strands changes by two
of opposite signs: the standard picture slides one strand over or under the
other, creating or deleting the pair of crossings, with the two crossings being
the two possible signs in either order. All four orientation patterns of the
two strands at the two crossings are included.

**(R3) Sliding a strand past a crossing.** One strand is moved across an
existing crossing of two other strands, so that the crossing of the two other
strands passes from one side of the moving strand to the other; the three
crossings of the local picture keep their signs and the over/under data are
preserved. The three strands must have a consistent strict height order:
one is above both others, one below both, and the remaining strand is between
them. The cyclic over/under pattern is excluded. Every orientation pattern
and all six height orders of this standard local picture are included.

A local R2 or R3 picture is **braid-like** when, after a local coordinate
change and deformation, all participating strands run in the same positive
longitudinal direction. This is a local condition and does not require a
globally chosen braid axis. R1 is kept as a separate kink move.

The strands keep their orientations throughout every move. The union of the
three move types, together with planar isotopy, generates the equivalence
relation on diagrams used in the Reidemeister equivalence theorem below; the
moves are sometimes called R1, R2, R3 as above. Since every move changes the
diagram only inside a disk, it has a type and a finite list of local
orientation/sign variants, and each variant is realized by an ambient isotopy
as the next items show. The complete list of variants is required because the
Markov and Alexander constructions below act on oriented diagrams and count
signed crossings.

derivations.claim: For fixed $b\in\mathbb F_p$, define $R_b(a)=a*b=2b-a$. Then $R_b(R_b(a))=2b-(2b-a)=a$, so $R_b^{-1}=R_b$. Also $a*a=2a-a=a$. Thus both the forward and reverse crossing rules use the same involution, and an arc's color is uniquely recoverable across one underpass.

In an R1 disk, the coloring relation on the kinked side is either $y=x*x$ or $x=y*x$, where $x$ is the unchanged boundary color and $y$ is the color of the new interior underarc. In the first case $y=x$ by idempotency; in the second, $R_x(y)=x$ has the unique solution $y=R_x(x)=x$ because $R_x$ is bijective. Deleting the kink is the inverse restriction map. The two formulas cover both strand directions because the inverse operation equals the operation by step 1.1.

In an R2 disk, fix the color $b$ of the strand passing over the other strand and the incoming underarc color $a$. The first crossing changes the underarc color to $R_b(a)$, and the second changes it by $R_b^{-1}$; their composition is $R_b^{-1}(R_b(a))=a$. Therefore every boundary coloring extends uniquely across the two-crossing side, and the reverse R2 move gives the inverse bijection. Other orientation variants replace one of these maps by its inverse, which is the same map by step 1.1.

For a braid-like R3 orientation, start with boundary colors $a,b,c$. Propagating through the two sides gives respectively $(c,b*c,(a*b)*c)$ and $(c,b*c,(a*c)*(b*c))$. The last coordinates agree by right self-distributivity in [F2], so every boundary coloring on either side has a unique matching extension on the other. Reversing a crossing replaces a right translation by its inverse; step 1.1 makes that the same map, and relabeling the three strands gives every height-order and orientation variant in [F3].

If $D$ is empty, its unique empty coloring is carried to itself by planar isotopy, and no Reidemeister move is supported on the empty diagram. If $D$ is nonempty, planar isotopy carries every arc and local crossing relation bijectively to its image, while steps 2.1, 2.2, and 2.3 give explicit coloring bijections for every local move. Composing the finitely many bijections along any finite move sequence preserves the coloring count. These constructions act on finite arc labels and use no choice principle.

Let $D$ be a nonempty finite regular oriented link diagram: a projection of a finite union of oriented circles with finitely many transverse double points, no triple points, and one overpassing branch specified at each double point. Let $c(D)$ be its number of crossings and $m(D)$ its number of components. An arc is a connected strand segment cut at each undercrossing; each component with no undercrossings contributes one closed arc. Write $a(D)$ for the number of arcs. If $q(D)$ components have no undercrossings, then $a(D)=c(D)+q(D)$ and $0\le q(D)\le m(D)$.

A supplied finite code for $D$ has code length $L$, the total number of bits in that literal code, including its tags, signs, labels, and separators. The length depends on the chosen encoding. In particular, for one of the tagged Gauss, signed Dowker–Thistlethwaite, or oriented planar-diagram formats, $L$ is the bit length of the supplied valid code in that format. The procedures in this page take typed mathematical diagrams or valid codes as stated; no string parser or malformed-code behavior is included in any operation count.

These exponents are distinct, so its coefficient l1 norm is $\sum_{k=0}^r\binom{r}{k}=2^r$; multiplication by the monomial $A^{a(S)-b(S)}$ only shifts the exponents.

Since $a(S)+b(S)=c$, one has $|a(S)-b(S)|\le c$. The exponents in $\delta^r$ lie between $-2r$ and $2r$. Using $r\le m+c-1$, every exponent in every state term, and thus in the sum, has absolute value at most $c+2(m+c-1)=3c+2m-2$.

Put $q=c+m+1\ge2$. Represent a crossing endpoint by an integer from $1$ to $4c$, grouped into four successive ports at each crossing, and write $\alpha$ for the supplied edge-pairing involution. For a state, let $\beta$ pair the two top and two bottom ports for A, or the two left and two right ports for B. The multigraph on the $4c$ endpoints with one $\alpha$-edge and one $\beta$-edge at every vertex is two-regular, allowing parallel edges. Each connected component follows one smoothed circle, and the $u$ supplied crossingless components add $u$ further circles. Thus a traversal marking a vertex when first queued computes $|S|$ exactly. The same traversal, with the opposite ports paired instead of smoothing ports, computes the original component count $m$; perform it once initially and then compute $q$ for allocation. statement.

> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$.

The input is a finite regular oriented link diagram together with its declared
components. If it does not have exactly two components, return
`invalid-input`. For a two-component diagram $D$, initialize $s:=0$ and make
one pass over its finite crossing list. At each crossing whose branches lie on
different components, add
$$\operatorname{sgn}\det_P(v_{\rm over},v_{\rm under})$$
to $s$, where the determinant is taken in the oriented projection plane; ignore
self-crossings. Return $s/2$. The even-sum lemma establishes that this output is
an integer and is the diagram's linking number.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. On every finite regular oriented diagram
with exactly two components, the crossing-scan algorithm halts after one
iteration per crossing and returns the integer half-sum of the mixed crossing
signs. On an input with any other number of components it returns
`invalid-input` after the finite component-count check.

of a two-component oriented link in $S^3$, with components $K_1,K_2$. Write
$$S(D):=\sum_{c\text{ between }K_1\text{ and }K_2}\operatorname{sgn}(c).$$
Then $S(D)$ is even, and
$$\operatorname{lk}_D(K_1,K_2):=\frac{S(D)}2\in\mathbb Z$$
is unchanged by planar isotopy and by each oriented Reidemeister move of types
I, II, and III. Thus it has the same value on any two regular diagrams of
ambient-isotopic oriented links. It is symmetric in $K_1,K_2$; reversing exactly
one component changes its sign, and reversing both components leaves it
unchanged.

Input a finite regular oriented link diagram $D$ with $a$ arcs and $c$ crossings,
fixed finite orderings of its arcs and crossings, and an odd prime $p$. The algorithm returns the full set
$\operatorname{Col}_p(D)$ of assignments of residues in $\mathbb F_p$ to the
arcs satisfying the Fox crossing equations, together with
$|\operatorname{Col}_p(D)|$.

1. Create one variable $x_j$ for each arc in the supplied order, and process
   crossings in the supplied order.
2. At each crossing with overarc $o$ and the two underarcs $i$ and $j$, append
   the homogeneous linear equation $2x_o-x_i-x_j=0$ over $\mathbb F_p$.
   At a crossing, add the coefficients of any repeated arc in that row.
3. Starting with the first column and first unused row, scan columns from left
   to right. In a column with a nonzero entry in an unused row, choose the
   first such row, swap it into the next pivot row, divide it by its nonzero
   pivot, and add multiples of it to every other row to clear that column.
   Advance the pivot row by one. If the column has no such entry, leave it
   free and continue to the next column.

   independently any value in $\mathbb F_p$ and solve the reduced equations

   number returned.

returns $p^f$ colorings. It uses at most $a$ pivot steps and at most $ca$

obtained from $D$ by a finite sequence of planar isotopies and oriented
Reidemeister moves R1, R2, R3.

derivations.claim: The linking scan performs one visit per element of the finite crossing list by [F2]. On a two-component input each visit makes at most one component-membership test and, for a mixed crossing, one integer addition, so there are at most $c$ tests and $c$ additions after the constant-size component-count check. Each added term is $+1$ or $-1$, hence the absolute value of the sum is at most $c$ and the returned half-sum has absolute value at most $c/2$. The result is an integer and is the diagram's linking number by [F3] and [F4].

For each of the $c$ crossings, [F5] contributes three coefficients to a row. If arc labels repeat, combining at most three contributions requires at most two field additions for that row, so setup uses at most $2c$ additions; initializing the dense $c\times a$ matrix writes $ca$ zeros. There are $a$ columns, and each pivot search checks at most $c$ rows, for at most $ca$ entry tests.

Let $r$ be the number of pivots, so $r\le\min(c,a)$ and $f=a-r$. Normalizing each pivot row divides at most $a$ entries by its nonzero pivot, for at most $ra$ divisions. Clearing a pivot column from each of at most $c-1$ other rows updates at most $a$ entries, with at most one multiplication and one addition per entry. The row-reduction arithmetic count is therefore at most $ra+2r(c-1)a$. These loops are finite because there are at most $a$ columns and $c$ rows.

There are exactly $p^f$ assignments to the $f$ free variables by [F6]. For each assignment, each of the $a-f$ pivot variables is a linear combination of at most $f$ free variables; computing it uses at most $f$ multiplications and $f$ additions/subtractions, including the final negation. Writing the full solution uses $a$ output entries. Thus listing every coloring uses at most $p^f(2f(a-f)+a)$ field arithmetic and output-write operations. The loop is finite, including $f=0$, when there is one solution and only the $a$ entries are written.

For $f=0$, the count is $1$ without multiplication. For $f\ge1$, binary repeated squaring computes $p^f$ with at most $2\lceil\log_2(f+1)\rceil$ integer multiplications. Since $f\le a$, the magnitude bit length is at most $f\lceil\log_2p\rceil+1$. This count-only postprocessing does not enumerate the solution set and does not change the full-list cost in step 3.1.

The diagram-by-diagram scan, matrix construction, row reduction, and finite solution enumeration above use no choice principle. By [F7], the Fox coloring count is preserved along every finite sequence of planar isotopies and oriented Reidemeister moves; by [A1] and [F8], ambient-isotopic oriented links admit such a sequence. By [F4], the linking-number half-sum has the same move invariance. Thus ACω is used only for the ambient-isotopy interpretations, not for any finite operation count.

v_{\rm under})$ from the oriented projected tangents and set
$\operatorname{wr}(D)=\sum_c\operatorname{sgn}(c)$. At each crossing use the
local source chart in which the over-strand runs southwest to northeast; the
A-smoothing joins the top endpoints and the bottom endpoints with weight $A$,
and the B-smoothing joins the left endpoints and the right endpoints with
weight $A^{-1}$. Labels are transported by orientation-preserving changes of
local coordinates. Let $C(D)$ be the finite crossing set. A state is a map
$S:C(D)\to\{A,B\}$; let $a(S)$ and $b(S)$ count its A- and B-smoothings, and
let $|S|$ be the number of circles after all crossings are smoothed. Set
$$\langle D\rangle=
\sum_{S:C(D)\to\{A,B\}}A^{a(S)-b(S)}(-A^2-A^{-2})^{|S|-1}.$$
Define
$$f_D(A)=(-A^3)^{-\operatorname{wr}(D)}\langle D\rangle,$$
where $\operatorname{wr}(D)$ is the sum of the determinant signs of its
oriented crossings. If two such diagrams represent ambient-isotopic
oriented links, their $f_D(A)$ values are equal. Thus $f_D$ defines an
invariant of nonempty oriented links.

The writhe is the sum of one sign from each of the $c$ crossings by [F5], so a direct scan computes it in one pass. These finite operations use no choice principle.

Each crossing sign is $+1$ or $-1$, so $|\operatorname{wr}(D)|\le c$. Multiplication by $(-A^3)^{-\operatorname{wr}(D)}$ shifts every Laurent exponent of the raw bracket by $-3\operatorname{wr}(D)$ and multiplies coefficients only by a sign. Thus the absolute degree increases by at most $3c$, giving $6c+2m-2$ by [F4], while coefficient-bit size is unchanged and remains at most $m+2c+1$. For $m=1$ both bounds are linear in $c+1$.

Put $q=c+m+1$. By [F4], compute the raw bracket in $O(2^cq^4)$ bit steps in the specified representation. Summing the supplied sign bits uses an $O(\log(q+1))$-bit signed counter and $O(c\log(q+1))$ bit steps, rather than unit-cost unbounded arithmetic. The factor $(-A^3)^{-\operatorname{wr}(D)}$ has sign $(-1)^{\operatorname{wr}(D)}$ and exponent $-3\operatorname{wr}(D)$. Allocate a dense output array with exponents from $-6q$ to $6q$ and the same $O(q)$-bit signed coefficient slots as in [F4]. For each raw slot, copy its value to the position shifted by $-3\operatorname{wr}(D)$ and toggle the sign when necessary. There are $O(q)$ slots. Linear lookup or writing scans at most $O(q^2)$ tape cells per slot, including binary index counters, so even this naive normalization costs $O(q^3)$ bit steps. Step 1.2 ensures every shifted exponent and coefficient fits the array. This cost is absorbed in $O(2^cq^4)$, and for $m=1$ it is $O(2^c(c+1)^4)$. Under [A1], [F5] identifies the normalized output with an invariant of the ambient-isotopy class of the oriented link. The state count, writhe pass, degree shift, coefficient estimate, and specified bit implementation in steps 1.1, 1.2, and 2.1 remain choice-free. The running-time estimate is exponential in the crossing count, and makes no polynomial-time Jones evaluation claim.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

**Input:** A valid normalized oriented planar-diagram code $C$ for a connected one-component knot diagram, with $c$ crossings. A positive-crossing-count code records its finite crossing labels, four darts at each crossing, edge pairings, clockwise rotations, strand orientations, over/under pairs, crossing signs, and one outer face. A crossingless code records one oriented circle and its outer face.

**Output:** A finite ordered list of pairs $(E,\mu)$, where $E$ is a valid normalized one-component knot code and $\mu$ records either the finite crossing/edge relabeling identifying the unchanged planar-isotopy class or a local disk boundary, move type, and orientation/sign variant witnessing one oriented R1, R2, or R3 move from $C$ to $E$. Different labelings of the same candidate may appear more than once.

**Finite comparison rules:** Two normalized codes represent the same code class when some bijection of their finite crossing labels and edge labels carries all dart incidences, crossing rotations, orientations, signs, component cycles, and outer-face data of one code to the other. To test whether two codes differ by one move, enumerate all finite choices of local edge intervals and crossing subrecords of sizes allowed by R1, R2, or R3; test that the codes agree outside the chosen disk boundary and that the two local records are one of the standard orientation/sign variants of that move. The local-site test uses the exact variants in the oriented Reidemeister-move definition.

**Instructions:**

1. Validate $C$ with the planar-code validation procedure. If it is invalid, return its first invalid-code result.
2. Set $N:=c+2$ and run the bounded normalized-diagram enumerator with bound $N$. It returns a finite list of reconstructed one-component knot-diagram candidates.
3. For each candidate, form the finite set of normalized code representatives obtained by assigning crossing labels and edge labels in every permitted order and applying the code's normalization rule.
4. For each representative $E$, apply the finite comparison rules. Append $E$ with a relabeling certificate if it is the same code class as $C$, or with the successful local-site certificate if a comparison certifies one R1, R2, or R3 move between them. Preserve the enumerator order and retain duplicates.
5. Return the accumulated list.

The bound $c+2$ includes every one-move result because R1 changes crossing count by one, R2 by two, and R3 by zero. This procedure lists candidates one move away; it does not decide whether two arbitrary codes are related by any number of moves.

**Input:** A nonnegative integer crossing bound $N$.

**Output:** A finite ordered list of reconstructed knot-diagram candidates. A
candidate is a `Valid` output of the planar-code validation procedure whose
code is a normalized planar-diagram code with one oriented component and at
most $N$ crossings. Repeated candidates up to crossing relabeling or planar
isotopy are allowed; the list is not a list of knot types.

**Instructions:**

1. If $N$ is not a nonnegative integer, return `invalid-bound`.
2. Initialize the output list empty. Pass the two normalized crossingless
   one-component codes, with `ccw` and `cw` orientation markers in that order,
   through the validator and append both outputs first.
3. For each $c=1,\ldots,N$ in increasing order, use crossing labels
   $\{1,\ldots,c\}$ and the four normalized dart positions at each crossing.
   Enumerate every crossing-sign vector in lexicographic order, with
   $-1<+1$. The sign determines the incoming and outgoing positions at each
   crossing by the normalized-code convention.
4. For each sign vector, enumerate every bijection from the set of its
   $2c$ outgoing darts to its $2c$ incoming darts in lexicographic order.
   Pair each outgoing dart with its image to obtain the edge involution, and
   assign edge labels by the normalized-code rule.
5. Compute the cycles of $\phi=\alpha\circ\sigma$ for each pairing. For each
   cycle, in increasing order of its least dart, select that cycle in turn as
   the outer face and form the corresponding normalized PD code.
6. Pass each code through the planar-code validation procedure. Append its
   reconstructed output if and only if the validator returns `Valid` and the
   directed component tracing has exactly one cycle. Return the list after
   the finite loops end.

This procedure enumerates normalized finite codes and reconstructed diagrams;
it neither identifies equivalent codes nor decides whether two candidates
represent isotopic knots.

For every nonnegative integer $N$, the bounded enumeration procedure
terminates and returns exactly the reconstructed candidates represented by
normalized connected one-component planar-diagram codes with at most $N$
crossings. Each returned candidate has a valid spherical face structure and a
selected outer face. The procedure does not identify candidates that represent
the same knot type.

For every finite input in the three code formats, the validation and
reconstruction procedure terminates. It returns an invalid-code reason
exactly when the first failed syntax, incidence, orientation, component,
connectedness, face-count, or outer-face condition in its stated order occurs;
otherwise it returns the crossing-disk/edge-band model of the represented
oriented diagram, its oriented components, its face cycles, and its selected
outer face.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. For every valid connected one-component
oriented code with a selected outer face, the reconstruction procedure
produces a regular oriented diagram representing that code. Any two such
diagrams with the same code differ only by crossing and edge relabeling and
are planar isotopic. The normalized planar-diagram code of a diagram with $c$
crossings appears among the candidates enumerated at bound $c$. This statement
concerns diagrams and their finite codes; it does not identify distinct codes
that may represent the same knot type. The finite realization and enumeration
claims are choice-free; $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is assumed only for the smooth
ambient-isotopy uniqueness clause.

**Input:** Two valid normalized oriented planar-diagram codes $C_0,C_1$ for connected one-component knot diagrams.

**Output:** The algorithm returns Found(path) only if it has a finite sequence of code classes from $C_0$ to $C_1$, with a finite local-move certificate for each adjacent pair. It has no negative-output branch. It may run forever if the target code class is never reached.

**Instructions:**

1. Validate both input codes using the planar-code validation procedure. If either is invalid, return that first invalid-code result. For each valid code, form its canonical representative by checking all bijections of its finite crossing labels and edge labels, recomputing the prescribed edge normalization, and selecting the lexicographically least resulting code.
2. Set the initial frontier to the singleton containing the canonical representative of $C_0$. Initialize a discovered-code set with that representative and an empty predecessor record.
3. At the beginning of each breadth layer, test every code in the current frontier against the canonical representative of $C_1$. If one matches, follow its stored predecessor records back to $C_0$, reverse the resulting finite list, and return the path with its move certificates.
4. Otherwise, for each code $C$ in the current frontier, call the Reidemeister-neighbor algorithm. For each returned pair $(E,\mu)$, canonicalize $E$ by the finite relabeling procedure in step 1. If its canonical representative has not been discovered, add it to the next frontier and store $(C,\mu)$ as its predecessor record.
5. Replace the current frontier by the next frontier and repeat from step 3. If a layer is empty, continue with empty layers; do not return “inequivalent.”

Code equality in this procedure means equality of canonical representatives under the finite crossing/edge relabelings of the normalized code convention. Every loop in one layer is finite; the number of layers has no fixed bound.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $D$ and $D'$ be regular oriented link diagrams.
Then $D$ and $D'$ represent equivalent oriented links if and only if $D'$ can be
obtained from $D$ by a finite sequence of planar isotopies and oriented
Reidemeister moves R1, R2, R3.

derivations.claim: Fix a code $C$ with $c$ crossings. The neighbor procedure uses bound $c+2$. By [F2] and [F3], this yields a finite candidate list containing every normalized connected one-component code with at most $c+2$ crossings. Each candidate has finitely many crossing labels, edge labels, and local edge intervals; the number of relabelings, subsets of at most three local crossings, boundary orders, and move variants is finite. Each candidate validation terminates by [F4]. Thus the neighbor list is finite and its local comparisons terminate.

If the neighbor procedure returns $(E,\mu)$, its certificate $\mu$ records either a code relabeling or a local code replacement matching one of the oriented Reidemeister variants, so [F4] and [F5] identify the represented diagrams up to planar isotopy and that one local move. Conversely, any single R1, R2, or R3 move changes the crossing count by at most two. Its result therefore appears among the candidates bounded by $c+2$ by [F3]. The move disk has two, four, or six boundary endpoints and at most three local crossing records; these are among the finite sites and variants checked by [F1]. Relabeling its finite code data is also among the finite bijections tested. Hence every one-move neighbor is returned.

The initial breadth frontier is a singleton. If a frontier is finite, [F1] and step 1.1 give a finite neighbor list for each of its members; a finite union of finite lists is finite. By induction every layer is finite and is processed in finite time, including an empty layer, which the algorithm repeats without returning a negative answer.

If the search returns a path, every adjacent pair has a certificate from [F1]. By step 2.1 each such pair differs by planar isotopy or one oriented Reidemeister move; concatenating the finitely many certificates gives a finite move sequence between the input diagrams. The easy direction of [F7] therefore gives ambient isotopy.

If the represented oriented knots are ambient-isotopic, [A1] and [F7] give a finite sequence of planar isotopies and oriented Reidemeister moves. By [F5], each intermediate diagram has a valid normalized code class. By step 2.1, the code class after each move appears in the corresponding neighbor list. Induction on the finite path length therefore places the target code class in a finite breadth layer; by step 2.2 that layer finishes, and [F6] returns the path.

The algorithm has no negative-output branch by [F6]. If no finite move path exists, it never returns Found(path); any finite-depth run that has not found the target establishes only that no path of that bounded length was found. The finite enumeration proves no decision or complexity-class conclusion. Finite neighbor generation and breadth-layer processing are choice-free; $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is used only in [F5] and [F7] to interpret code and ambient-isotopy equivalence.

Let $A$ be an indeterminate and let $D$ be a typed nonempty unoriented regular
link diagram with finite crossing set $C(D)$. At each crossing use the chart
with the over-strand southwest-to-northeast: A joins the top endpoints and the
bottom endpoints with weight $A$, while B joins the left endpoints and right
endpoints with weight $A^{-1}$. The Kauffman bracket state-sum algorithm
terminates after exactly $2^{|C(D)|}$ state visits and returns
$$\sum_{S:C(D)\to\{A,B\}}A^{a(S)-b(S)}(-A^2-A^{-2})^{|S|-1},$$
where $a(S)$ and $b(S)$ count the two smoothing types and $|S|$ counts the
circles in the smoothed diagram. The algorithm takes a mathematical diagram
as input and makes no claim about parsing strings or rejecting malformed
encodings.

Input a finite regular oriented link diagram $D$ with $a$ arcs and $c$ crossings,
fixed finite orderings of its arcs and crossings, and an odd prime $p$. The algorithm returns the full set
$\operatorname{Col}_p(D)$ of assignments of residues in $\mathbb F_p$ to the
arcs satisfying the Fox crossing equations, together with
$|\operatorname{Col}_p(D)|$.

1. Create one variable $x_j$ for each arc in the supplied order, and process
   crossings in the supplied order.
2. At each crossing with overarc $o$ and the two underarcs $i$ and $j$, append
   the homogeneous linear equation $2x_o-x_i-x_j=0$ over $\mathbb F_p$.
   At a crossing, add the coefficients of any repeated arc in that row.
3. Starting with the first column and first unused row, scan columns from left
   to right. In a column with a nonzero entry in an unused row, choose the
   first such row, swap it into the next pivot row, divide it by its nonzero
   pivot, and add multiples of it to every other row to clear that column.
   Advance the pivot row by one. If the column has no such entry, leave it
   free and continue to the next column.
4. After all columns have been processed, assign every free variable
   independently any value in $\mathbb F_p$ and solve the reduced equations
   for the pivot variables. Return each resulting assignment once and the
   number returned.

For every odd prime $p$ and every finite regular oriented link diagram $D$,
the algorithm in the Definition terminates and returns exactly
$\operatorname{Col}_p(D)$. If its reduced system has $f$ free variables, it
returns $p^f$ colorings. It uses at most $a$ pivot steps and at most $ca$
row-entry elimination scans for a diagram with $a$ arcs and $c$ crossings.

Let $p$ be an odd prime. A Fox $p$-coloring of a finite regular oriented link diagram $D$ assigns an element of $\mathbb F_p$ to each arc and satisfies $2x_o=x_i+x_j$ at every crossing, where $x_o$ is the overarc color and $x_i,x_j$ are the two underarc colors. If $D'$ is obtained from $D$ by planar isotopy or one oriented Reidemeister move of type R1, R2, or R3, restriction outside the move disk gives a bijection from the Fox $p$-colorings of $D$ to those of $D'$. Consequently the number of Fox $p$-colorings is unchanged along every finite sequence of such moves. The local bijections use no choice principle.

Then $D$ and $D'$ represent equivalent oriented links if and only if $D'$ can be
obtained from $D$ by a finite sequence of planar isotopies and oriented
Reidemeister moves R1, R2, R3.

statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most

derivations.claim: With $c=8$, the state-count formula in [F1] gives $2^8=256$ visits.

The stated incidences and [F3] give the equations $2x_1-x_2-x_3=0$, $2x_2-x_3-x_1=0$, and $2x_3-x_1-x_2=0$. In $\mathbb F_3$, $-1=2$, so all three rows are $(2,2,2)$. Row reduction leaves one nonzero row and two zero rows, hence one pivot and two free variables. By [F4], the algorithm returns $3^2=9$ trefoil colorings.
The crossingless unknot has one arc and no crossing equations, so its matrix has one column and zero rows, rank zero, and one free variable. By [F4], it has $3^1=3$ colorings.

The crossing equation $2x_o=x_i+x_j$ is symmetric in the two underarc colors and independent of strand arrows, so reversing a component orientation does not change its Fox coloring set. If the trefoil and unknot were ambient-isotopic as unoriented knots, choose their orientations so the equivalence preserves orientation. By [A1] and [F6] the oriented diagrams would then be joined by a finite Reidemeister sequence, and [F5] would force equal coloring counts. The computed values $9$ and $3$ contradict this, so the underlying knot types are distinct.

An **oriented Reidemeister move** is one of the following local replacements of
a regular oriented link diagram ([[def-regular-oriented-link-diagram]]),
performed inside a small closed disk while the diagram outside the disk is left
unchanged, and understood up to planar isotopy outside the disk
([[def-planar-isotopy-of-link-diagrams]]). All sign and orientation variants of
each local picture are included.

**(R1) Kink creation and deletion.** A single strand is replaced by a small
kink: two arcs crossing once and otherwise disjoint from the strand, with the
over/under datum of the new crossing as in the picture. The move is allowed in
both directions (create or delete the kink) and with both signs of the kink,
the sign being the sign of the crossing created. The orientations of the two
strands of the kink are the two possible consistent orientations through the
crossing, and all of them occur in the move list.

**(R2) Slide of two strands.** Two local arcs belonging to two strands are
replaced so that the number of crossings between those strands changes by two
of opposite signs: the standard picture slides one strand over or under the
other, creating or deleting the pair of crossings, with the two crossings being
the two possible signs in either order. All four orientation patterns of the
two strands at the two crossings are included.

**(R3) Sliding a strand past a crossing.** One strand is moved across an
existing crossing of two other strands, so that the crossing of the two other
strands passes from one side of the moving strand to the other; the three
crossings of the local picture keep their signs and the over/under data are
preserved. The three strands must have a consistent strict height order:
one is above both others, one below both, and the remaining strand is between
them. The cyclic over/under pattern is excluded. Every orientation pattern
and all six height orders of this standard local picture are included.

A local R2 or R3 picture is **braid-like** when, after a local coordinate
change and deformation, all participating strands run in the same positive
longitudinal direction. This is a local condition and does not require a
globally chosen braid axis. R1 is kept as a separate kink move.

The strands keep their orientations throughout every move. The union of the
three move types, together with planar isotopy, generates the equivalence
relation on diagrams used in the Reidemeister equivalence theorem below; the
moves are sometimes called R1, R2, R3 as above. Since every move changes the
diagram only inside a disk, it has a type and a finite list of local
orientation/sign variants, and each variant is realized by an ambient isotopy
as the next items show. The complete list of variants is required because the
Markov and Alexander constructions below act on oriented diagrams and count
signed crossings.

**Input:** Two valid normalized oriented planar-diagram codes $C_0,C_1$ for connected one-component knot diagrams.

**Output:** The algorithm returns Found(path) only if it has a finite sequence of code classes from $C_0$ to $C_1$, with a finite local-move certificate for each adjacent pair. It has no negative-output branch. It may run forever if the target code class is never reached.

**Instructions:**

1. Validate both input codes using the planar-code validation procedure. If either is invalid, return that first invalid-code result. For each valid code, form its canonical representative by checking all bijections of its finite crossing labels and edge labels, recomputing the prescribed edge normalization, and selecting the lexicographically least resulting code.
2. Set the initial frontier to the singleton containing the canonical representative of $C_0$. Initialize a discovered-code set with that representative and an empty predecessor record.
3. At the beginning of each breadth layer, test every code in the current frontier against the canonical representative of $C_1$. If one matches, follow its stored predecessor records back to $C_0$, reverse the resulting finite list, and return the path with its move certificates.
4. Otherwise, for each code $C$ in the current frontier, call the Reidemeister-neighbor algorithm. For each returned pair $(E,\mu)$, canonicalize $E$ by the finite relabeling procedure in step 1. If its canonical representative has not been discovered, add it to the next frontier and store $(C,\mu)$ as its predecessor record.
5. Replace the current frontier by the next frontier and repeat from step 3. If a layer is empty, continue with empty layers; do not return “inequivalent.”

Code equality in this procedure means equality of canonical representatives under the finite crossing/edge relabelings of the normalized code convention. Every loop in one layer is finite; the number of layers has no fixed bound.

Let $P$ be the projection plane in an oriented $3$-sphere and let $n$ be the
unit viewing normal pointing toward the viewer. Orient $P$ so that $(u,v)$ is
a positive basis exactly when $(n,u,v)$ is a positive ambient basis. A
**crossing code** has a
finite set $C$ of crossing labels and a finite set $D$ of **darts**, where a
dart is one directed half-edge incident to a crossing. A fixed-point-free
involution $\alpha:D\to D$ pairs the two ends of each edge: $\alpha^2=\mathrm{id}$
and $\alpha(d)\ne d$. A vertex map $v:D\to C$ records the crossing incident to
each dart. A **rotation system** is the permutation $\sigma$ whose cycles give
the clockwise order of darts at each crossing. Each crossing has four darts;
the two over-strand darts and the two under-strand darts are opposite in that
cyclic order. An arrow on each dart records whether its edge is directed into
or out of its incident crossing. The pairing $\alpha$ must join one incoming
end to one outgoing end. At a crossing, each opposite pair has one incoming
and one outgoing dart, so following an edge and then the opposite dart defines
the oriented link components. A code is **connected** when the graph with
vertices $C$ and edges the $\alpha$-pairs is connected.

The sign of an oriented crossing is $+1$ or $-1$ according as
$\det(v_{\rm over},v_{\rm under})$ is positive or negative, where the two
tangent vectors follow the oriented over- and under-strands. This item fixes
the local cyclic-order convention as follows. Starting with the outgoing
over-dart and reading counterclockwise, a positive crossing has order
$(O_{\rm out},U_{\rm out},O_{\rm in},U_{\rm in})$; a negative crossing has
order $(O_{\rm out},U_{\rm in},O_{\rm in},U_{\rm out})$. The stored crossing
sign and cyclic order must agree. This is the page's explicit sign convention.
It agrees with the current KT-03 supplier: reversing its positive
counterclockwise order from outgoing over gives the clockwise record
$(O_{\rm out},U_{\rm in},O_{\rm in},U_{\rm out})$.

For a nonempty connected crossing graph, let $V=|C|$, $E=|D|/2$, and let
$F$ be the number of cycles of the face permutation $\phi=\alpha\circ\sigma$.
A **spherical code** is a code satisfying $V-E+F=2$. A spherical code becomes a
**plane code** by distinguishing one face as the outer face and deleting a
point in that face from the sphere. The crossingless one-component code is a separate case: its Gauss data are one empty component word, its DT pairing and crossing-sign vector are empty at $c=0$, and its PD data are the single loop `Loop[1]`; every format also carries an orientation marker, `ccw` or `cw`, for the unit circle $S^1=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:x^2+y^2=1\}$ in the oriented plane, and the outer-face marker is `outside`. Thus the crossingless code records which direction orients its circle. It has no crossing graph or face-permutation test. Disconnected crossing graphs and disconnected crossingless links are outside this code class.

A **normalized planar-diagram code** with $c>0$ has crossing labels
$C=\{1,\ldots,c\}$ and four dart positions $0,1,2,3$ at each crossing, in
clockwise order beginning with the outgoing over-dart. The opposite pair
$(0,2)$ is over and $(1,3)$ is under. For sign $+1$, the clockwise record is
$(O_{\rm out},U_{\rm in},O_{\rm in},U_{\rm out})$; for sign $-1$ it is
$(O_{\rm out},U_{\rm out},O_{\rm in},U_{\rm in})$. Edge labels are assigned
by scanning crossings in increasing order and their four dart positions in
order, giving the next positive integer to the pair containing the first
not-yet-labelled dart. The outer face is recorded by its least dart in its
face cycle. These rules remove arbitrary edge-name and face-name choices;
different crossing labelings may still represent the same diagram. At $c=0$
a normalized code is the crossingless record with one of the two orientation
markers above.

A **Gauss code** for an oriented diagram records, in traversal order on each
oriented component, a signed crossing label: $+j$ means the component passes
over at crossing $j$, and $-j$ means it passes under. For a knot there is one
cyclic word; for a link there is one cyclic word per component. Each crossing
label must occur exactly twice in total, once positively and once negatively.
When $c>0$, every listed component word is nonempty; a separate crossingless
component is not part of this code class. The zero-crossing case is only the
one-component code specified above.
The code also carries a separate algebraic crossing-sign vector
$\varepsilon_j\in\{+1,-1\}$, one entry for each label. Choosing a basepoint
turns the knot's cyclic word into a based word; changing the basepoint
cyclically shifts the word, and relabeling crossings changes only their names.
The visit order, over/under signs, and crossing-sign vector determine the
crossing rotation system; it is realizable in the sphere only when the
resulting code is spherical. A plane Gauss code also carries an identifier of
one cycle of its face permutation to designate the outer face.

A **signed Dowker–Thistlethwaite code**, in this page's convention, encodes a
based oriented knot with $c$ crossings by numbering its $2c$ visits
$1,\ldots,2c$ in traversal order. For each odd visit $2j-1$, record the even
visit $2k$ paired with it as $d_j=+2k$ when the odd visit is over and
$d_j=-2k$ when it is under; also record the algebraic crossing sign
$\varepsilon_j\in\{+1,-1\}$ for crossing label $j$, the pair containing odd
visit $2j-1$. Its parity conditions are that
$|d_1|,\ldots,|d_c|$ are exactly the even numbers $2,4,\ldots,2c$, each once,
and each paired crossing has one over-visit and one under-visit. The separate
$\varepsilon_j$ records the crossing sign; signed DT conventions elsewhere
may encode signs differently. The associated cyclic traversal and crossing
signs determine a rotation system, which must pass the same spherical
realizability test. A plane DT code also carries an identifier of one cycle
of its face permutation to designate the outer face.

An **oriented planar-diagram code** labels each edge segment by an integer and
lists its two incident darts at crossing records. Each crossing record lists
its four directed edge ends in clockwise order, beginning with the outgoing
over-dart, and records which opposite pair is over, the orientation of each
strand, and the crossing sign. Every edge label occurs exactly twice, once as
an incoming end and once as an outgoing end. The code must satisfy the local
crossing-order rule above; its crossing graph must be connected when nonempty;
and its rotation system must satisfy $V-E+F=2$. The record also carries an
identifier of one cycle of its face permutation as the outer face. Thus an
arbitrary word in labels, even when each label occurs twice, is not declared
realizable until all incidence, orientation, crossing, connectedness, and
face-count tests pass.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. For every valid connected one-component
oriented code with a selected outer face, the reconstruction procedure
produces a regular oriented diagram representing that code. Any two such
diagrams with the same code differ only by crossing and edge relabeling and
are planar isotopic. The normalized planar-diagram code of a diagram with $c$
crossings appears among the candidates enumerated at bound $c$. This statement
concerns diagrams and their finite codes; it does not identify distinct codes
that may represent the same knot type. The finite realization and enumeration
claims are choice-free; $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is assumed only for the smooth
ambient-isotopy uniqueness clause.

Input a finite regular oriented link diagram $D$ with $a$ arcs and $c$ crossings,
fixed finite orderings of its arcs and crossings, and an odd prime $p$. The algorithm returns the full set
$\operatorname{Col}_p(D)$ of assignments of residues in $\mathbb F_p$ to the
arcs satisfying the Fox crossing equations, together with
$|\operatorname{Col}_p(D)|$.

1. Create one variable $x_j$ for each arc in the supplied order, and process
   crossings in the supplied order.
2. At each crossing with overarc $o$ and the two underarcs $i$ and $j$, append
   the homogeneous linear equation $2x_o-x_i-x_j=0$ over $\mathbb F_p$.
   At a crossing, add the coefficients of any repeated arc in that row.
3. Starting with the first column and first unused row, scan columns from left
   to right. In a column with a nonzero entry in an unused row, choose the
   first such row, swap it into the next pivot row, divide it by its nonzero
   pivot, and add multiples of it to every other row to clear that column.
   Advance the pivot row by one. If the column has no such entry, leave it
   free and continue to the next column.
4. After all columns have been processed, assign every free variable
   independently any value in $\mathbb F_p$ and solve the reduced equations
   for the pivot variables. Return each resulting assignment once and the
   number returned.

For every odd prime $p$ and every finite regular oriented link diagram $D$,
the algorithm in the Definition terminates and returns exactly
$\operatorname{Col}_p(D)$. If its reduced system has $f$ free variables, it
returns $p^f$ colorings. It uses at most $a$ pivot steps and at most $ca$
row-entry elimination scans for a diagram with $a$ arcs and $c$ crossings.

Let $p$ be an odd prime. A Fox $p$-coloring of a finite regular oriented link diagram $D$ assigns an element of $\mathbb F_p$ to each arc and satisfies $2x_o=x_i+x_j$ at every crossing, where $x_o$ is the overarc color and $x_i,x_j$ are the two underarc colors. If $D'$ is obtained from $D$ by planar isotopy or one oriented Reidemeister move of type R1, R2, or R3, restriction outside the move disk gives a bijection from the Fox $p$-colorings of $D$ to those of $D'$. Consequently the number of Fox $p$-colorings is unchanged along every finite sequence of such moves. The local bijections use no choice principle.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $D$ and $D'$ be regular oriented link diagrams.
Then $D$ and $D'$ represent equivalent oriented links if and only if $D'$ can be
obtained from $D$ by a finite sequence of planar isotopies and oriented
Reidemeister moves R1, R2, R3.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Starting with $U_0$, insert $2N+1$ disjoint type-I kinks, one at a time, to form a diagram $U_N$. Each insertion is one R1 move, so deleting the kinks gives an explicit sequence of $2N+1$ moves from $U_N$ to $U_0$. Both diagrams are regular one-component knot diagrams; their normalized codes are valid and occur among the enumerated candidates at their crossing bounds by [F3] and [F4]. By [A1] and [F9], the finite move sequence makes the represented oriented knots equivalent.

The crossing count difference is $c(U_N)-c(U_0)=2N+1$. By [F1], any single Reidemeister move changes crossing count by at most two. A path of at most $N$ moves could therefore change the crossing count by at most $2N$, so no such path connects these two diagrams. The search through depth $N$ completes its finite layers by [F2] without finding a path, although the diagrams are equivalent by step 1.1. This refutes the statement.

The crossingless unknot has one arc and no crossing equations, so [F5]–[F7] give $3^1=3$ Fox 3-colorings. For the standard trefoil with arcs $x_1,x_2,x_3$, the crossing equations are $2x_1-x_2-x_3=0$, $2x_2-x_3-x_1=0$, and $2x_3-x_1-x_2=0$. In $\mathbb F_3$, $-1=2$, so all rows are $(2,2,2)$; the matrix has rank one and two free variables, giving $3^2=9$ colorings by [F6] and [F7]. These equations do not use strand arrows, so reversing either orientation leaves the count unchanged. If the underlying unoriented knots were ambient-isotopic, orient them compatibly; [A1] and [F9] give a finite oriented move sequence, and [F8] forces the counts to agree, contradicting $3\ne9$. Thus the Fox count is an actual distinction, while a finite failed search alone is not one.

Work in the smooth category ([[def-smooth-manifold]]). Fix once and for all the
three-sphere as the one-point compactification

$$S^3:=\mathbb R^3\cup\{\infty\}$$

of Euclidean three-space, carrying its standard smooth structure, and fix the
standard orientation of $S^3$: the orientation induced by the standard
orientation of $\mathbb R^3$ under the one-point compactification, so that the
charts of the standard atlas away from $\infty$ are orientation-preserving and
the orientation is that of a connected oriented $3$-manifold in the sense of
[[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]]. For $r>0$ write
$\overline B_r:=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:\lVert x\rVert_2\le r\}$, the closed ball of
[[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]] with the following restriction convention. Smoothness on a closed ball means
local extension to a smooth map on an open neighborhood in Euclidean space;
smoothness on $M\times I$, for a smooth manifold $M$ without boundary, means
local extension across $t=0,1$ in $M\times\mathbb R$. Thus these closed domains
are not asserted to be manifolds without boundary in the cited definition.

**Links.** The **standard oriented circle** is the circle
$S^1=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ with its standard counterclockwise orientation,
regarded as a smooth $1$-manifold; a
**finite disjoint union of oriented circles** is a smooth manifold
$C=S^1\sqcup\dots\sqcup S^1$ ($k$ summands, $k\in\mathbb N$)
diffeomorphic to the disjoint union of $k$ standard oriented circles. An
**oriented link** (with $k$ components) is a smooth embedding

$$L\colon C\longrightarrow S^3$$

of such a disjoint union in the sense of [[def-smooth-embedding]]. So $L$ is
injective, is an immersion, and is a homeomorphism onto its image with the
subspace topology, and its image $L(C)$ is a finite disjoint union of smoothly
embedded circles. Thus every link considered here is finite and tame: the
smoothness of $L$ is exactly the standing convention, and no polygonal or other
tame model is used. The **components** of $L$ are the images of the individual
summands, and the number of components is $k$.

**Ambient isotopy.** Let $I=[0,1]$. An **ambient isotopy** of $S^3$ is a smooth
map

$$H\colon S^3\times I\longrightarrow S^3$$

such that $H_0=\mathrm{id}_{S^3}$, each $H_t\colon S^3\to S^3$,
$H_t(x):=H(x,t)$, is a diffeomorphism ([[def-diffeomorphism-and-local-diffeomorphism-of-manifolds]]),
and each $H_t$ is orientation-preserving with respect to the fixed orientation.
The last clause is in fact automatic: $t\mapsto H_t$ is continuous in the
$C^\infty$ topology of the diffeomorphism group, the orientation sign is locally
constant in $t$, and $H_0=\mathrm{id}$ is orientation-preserving, so it is kept
only for emphasis.

**Equivalence of links.** Two oriented links $L_0\colon C_0\to S^3$ and
$L_1\colon C_1\to S^3$ are **equivalent** (written $L_0\sim L_1$), or
**ambient isotopic**, when there are an ambient isotopy $H$ and an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism $f:C_0\to C_1$ with
$H_1\circ L_0=L_1\circ f$. Thus parametrizations and component labels are
irrelevant, while the induced orientation of each image component is preserved. The relation is an equivalence relation on links:
it is reflexive with $H=\mathrm{id}$, transitive by composing isotopies, and
symmetric because a smooth family of diffeomorphisms has a smooth family of
inverses. An equivalence class is an **(oriented) link type**.

**Moving off $\infty$.** Because the definition of equivalence allows the
isotopy to move a link through $\infty$, the standard practice of this page is
to first apply an ambient isotopy that carries a given link into the open ball,
and only then to project; every projection and every Reidemeister move below is
read after moving the link off $\infty$ into $\mathbb R^3$ in this way. The
orientation-preserving clause in the definition of ambient isotopy is exactly
what the oriented Reidemeister moves and the oriented closure construction must
respect. The unoriented theory uses the same ambient isotopies but forgets
the orientations of the link components.

**Links in the three-sphere versus links in $\mathbb R^3$.** A link contained in
$\mathbb R^3\subset S^3$ is a link in $S^3$; conversely every link may be
assumed after isotopy to lie in $\mathbb R^3$, by choosing a point outside the compact one-dimensional image and moving that
point to $\infty$ by a smooth rotation of the standard sphere. When comparing
links already in $\mathbb R^3$, an isotopy can also be arranged to avoid
$\infty$ throughout; the track-avoidance argument is given in
[[thm-oriented-reidemeister-equivalence-theorem]].

For an open cover $X=U\cup V$, the sequence
$$\cdots\to H_n(U\cap V;G)\to H_n(U;G)\oplus H_n(V;G)\to H_n(X;G)\xrightarrow{\delta}H_{n-1}(U\cap V;G)\to\cdots$$
is exact, with middle map $(u,v)\mapsto u+v$.

For $X=U\cup V$ open, there is a short exact sequence
$$0\to C_\bullet(U\cap V;G)\xrightarrow{i}(C_\bullet(U;G)\oplus C_\bullet(V;G))\xrightarrow{j}C_\bullet^{\{U,V\}}(X;G)\to0,$$
where $i(c)=(c,-c)$ and $j(u,v)=u+v$.

For $n\ge1$, $\widetilde H_k(S^n;G)$ is $G$ for $k=n$ and $0$ otherwise.
For $S^0$, $\widetilde H_0(S^0;G)\cong G$ and all other reduced groups vanish.
Thus $H_0(S^n;G)\cong G$ for $n\ge1$, whereas
$H_0(S^0;G)\cong G\oplus G$.

For every CW complex $X$, abelian group $G$, and $n\geq0$, the cellular complex has an
isomorphism $H_n^{\mathrm{cell}}(X;G)\cong H_n(X;G)$, natural with respect to
cellular maps.

Let $X$ be a CW complex, $G$ an abelian group, and $n\geq0$.
The **cellular homology** of $X$ with coefficients in $G$ is
$H_n^{\mathrm{cell}}(X;G)=\ker d_n/\operatorname{im}d_{n+1}$ for the cellular
groups of [[def-oriented-cellular-chain-group]], with differentials defined in
[[def-cellular-boundary-from-three-consecutive-skeleta]].  These maps form a
chain complex by [[lem-the-cellular-boundary-squares-to-zero]].

Let $X$ be a CW complex. For $n\geq1$, in the integral cellular chain groups with the chosen cell orientations,
$$d_ne^n_\alpha=\sum_\beta[e^n_\alpha:e^{n-1}_\beta]e^{n-1}_\beta.$$

If $f:X\to Y$ is a homotopy equivalence, then for every $n\geq 0$ and every
abelian group $G$ the induced map
$$H_n(f_\#):H_n^{\mathrm{sing}}(X;G)\to H_n^{\mathrm{sing}}(Y;G)$$
is an isomorphism.

derivations.claim: Give $S^1$ its one-vertex, one-edge CW structure. By the oriented-knot convention [F1], the core circle has the specified positive orientation used for the section generator. The solid tube $S^1\times D^2$ retracts radially to the core circle, whose cellular boundary is zero, so $H_1(S^1\times D^2;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$. The product torus $T=S^1\times S^1$ has one $0$-cell, two $1$-cells and one $2$-cell; the two endpoint incidences cancel in degree $1$, and the attaching commutator of the $2$-cell has total signed incidence zero on each $1$-cell. Thus $H_1(T;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z^2$, with basis the fibre class $[\mu]$ and section class $[\sigma]$. The projection to the first $S^1$ sends $[\mu]$ to $0$ and $[\sigma]$ to $1$.

Set $U=\Phi(S^1\times\{|z|<3\epsilon/2\})$ and $V=S^3\setminus\Phi(S^1\times D^2_{\epsilon/2})$. They are open and cover $S^3$. Radial contraction in the disk coordinate retracts $U$ to the core circle and $U\cap V$ to $T$. The homotopy $r_t(r)=(1-t)r+t\epsilon$ for $\epsilon/2<r<\epsilon$, fixed for $r\ge\epsilon$, retracts $V$ onto $E$. The intersection map in the Mayer–Vietoris sequence is therefore the map $H_1(T)\to H_1(S^1)\oplus H_1(E)$ given by $x\mapsto(p_*x,-i_*x)$, where $p$ is product projection.

By exactness and [F3], this intersection map is an isomorphism. Its restriction to $\ker p_*=\mathbb Z[\mu]$ is an isomorphism onto $0\oplus H_1(E)$: injectivity follows from the isomorphism, and any $(0,y)$ has a preimage $x$ with $p_*x=0$. Hence $H_1(E)\cong\mathbb Z$, generated up to sign by $i_*[\mu]$.

Write $i_*[\sigma]=c\,i_*[\mu]$ for the unique integer $c$, and define $[\lambda]=[\sigma]-c[\mu]$. Then $i_*[\lambda]=0$ and its product projection is $1$. Every class in $\ker i_*$ has the form $a[\mu]+b[\sigma]$ and satisfies $a+bc=0$, so it is exactly $b[\lambda]$; the projection condition forces $b=1$. The change-of-basis matrix from $([\mu],[\sigma])$ to $([\mu],[\lambda])$ has determinant $1$, so the latter pair is a basis. All choices were the supplied finite product data and integer operations; no choice axiom was used.

derivations.claim: Give $T$ the one-vertex square cellulation with product generators $a=S^1\times\{1\}$ and $b=\{1\}\times S^1$. The cellular boundary of the square is the commutator $aba^{-1}b^{-1}$, whose signed incidence on each 1-cell is zero; the 1-cell boundary is also zero. Thus $H_1(T;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z[a]\oplus\mathbb Z[b]$, and the two product projections read the two coordinates. For a PL loop $c:S^1\to S^1$, lift its finitely many arcs successively to the covering line $\mathbb R\to S^1$; the endpoint displacement is an integer, its degree. A degree-zero lift closes and contracts linearly, so $c$ is null-homotopic; conversely a null-homotopy lifts over a finite subdivision and keeps the integer displacement zero. Applying this to both coordinate projections shows that if $C$ is not null-homotopic, at least one homology coordinate of $[C]$ is nonzero. If $C$ separated $T$, the closure of either complementary component would be an oriented PL surface with boundary $C$; its finite oriented triangulation gives a $2$-chain with boundary $C$, so $[C]=0$. Hence $C$ is nonseparating, and cutting along it leaves a connected compact surface with two boundary copies.

Choose a vertex $p$ of a triangulation of $C$, and let $p_+$ and $p_-$ be its two copies on the boundary of the cut surface. A shortest edge path joining these corresponding copies has no repeated vertices; push its interior off any intermediate boundary edges to obtain a properly embedded PL arc. After gluing the boundary copies back, its endpoints become the same point $p$ and the arc crosses $C$ transversely exactly once. Orient the resulting simple closed PL curve $D$ arbitrarily; its signed intersection with $C$ is $+1$ or $-1$.

For oriented transverse PL loops on an oriented torus, the signed crossing count is invariant under replacing either loop by a homologous cycle: across the boundary of each oriented triangle, the intersections with a closed transverse loop enter and leave with opposite signs. It is additive in each cycle. The product basis loops $a=S^1\times\{1\}$ and $b=\{1\}\times S^1$ meet once, while parallel copies of each are disjoint, so for classes $(p,q)$ and $(r,s)$ the pairing is $ps-qr$ up to the global orientation convention. Since $C\cdot D=\pm1$, this determinant is $\pm1$.

If an integer $k$ with $|k|>1$ divided both $p$ and $q$, it would divide $ps-qr$, contradicting its value $\pm1$. Thus $\gcd(|p|,|q|)=1$, which says exactly that $[C]$ is primitive. Its nonzero status was established in step 1.1.
