derivations.claim: If the JT search accepts, its vector is an admissible normal vector passing the candidate tests by [F1]. The vector is primitive on an extreme ray, hence fundamental: a sum of two nonzero cone vectors on an extreme ray would have each summand on that ray, and the primitive integer generator cannot split into two positive integer multiples. If $E$ contains an essential disk, [F3] supplies such a disk whose vector lies on a primitive extreme ray. By [F2], each coordinate is at most $2^{7t-1}$ and therefore has at most $7t$ bits. citations.quote: For every finite input code and either selected mode, the Haken–Jaco–Tollefson procedure terminates. It returns the prescribed first validation error for an invalid code, returns **not-a-knot** for a valid multi-component code, and for a valid one-component knot code returns either a finite normal-coordinate disk-candidate certificate or **no-candidate** after exhaustive search.

For a valid one-component knot code, the Haken finite-box search accepts if and only if the triangulated exterior contains a properly embedded disk with non-null-homotopic boundary. On acceptance it returns a normal-coordinate vector for such a disk; after exhaustive rejection, no such disk exists.

For a valid one-component knot code, the JT primitive extreme-ray search accepts if and only if the triangulated exterior contains a properly embedded disk with non-null-homotopic boundary. It examines at most $2^{7t}$ support subsets for a $t$-tetrahedron exterior, each candidate coordinate has $O(t)$ bits, and its sequential Turing space is $O(t^2\log(t+2))$ bits.

Assume countable choice. Let $K:S^1\to S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot with a supplied product tubular neighborhood, and let $E_K$ be its compact exterior with peripheral torus $T_K$, fibre meridian $\mu$, and the unique degree-one generator $[\lambda]$ of the kernel of $H_1(T_K;\mathbb Z)\to H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$ supplied by the product-tube Mayer–Vietoris calculation. Then $K$ is ambient isotopic in the smooth category to the standard unknot if and only if $E_K$ contains a properly embedded piecewise-linear disk $D$ whose boundary is not null-homotopic in $T_K$. Every such disk has $[\partial D]=[\lambda]$ or $-[\lambda]$ and has odd mod-two intersection with the original marked meridian $\mu$.

Assume countable choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot with a finite regular projection diagram $D$ having $n$ crossings and a supplied product tube. There is a polygonal knot $P$ inside that tube with the same crossing code as $D$ and a smooth rounding $K^\sharp$ of $P$ such that $K^\sharp$ is smoothly ambient isotopic to $K$. The compact exterior of this same $P$ has a good triangulation with at most $C(n+1)$ tetrahedra and a marked path for the original meridian with at most $C(n+1)$ boundary edges, for one universal constant $C$. The peripheral-preserving exterior homeomorphism transfers this model to $K^\sharp$.

Let $T$ be a finite tetrahedral triangulation of a compact piecewise-linear $3$-manifold with $t\ge1$ tetrahedra. A nonzero nonnegative integer vector in $\mathbb Z^{7t}$ is the normal-coordinate vector of a normal surface exactly when it satisfies every face-matching equation and at most one quadrilateral type is nonzero in each tetrahedron. Every primitive integer generator of an extreme ray of the Haken cone has each coordinate at most $2^{7t-1}$. Every fundamental normal-surface vector has each coordinate at most $t\,2^{7t+2}$.

Let $n\ge1$, and let $A$ be an integer matrix with at most $n$ rows and at most $n$ columns, all entries in $\{-1,0,1\}$. If $A$ has $b\ge1$ columns and rational rank $b-1$, a primitive integer generator of its one-dimensional rational kernel is computable within those bounds, with either choice of its overall sign. For the prism over $b_0b_1$, write $a_i^0=(a_i,b_0)$ and $a_i^1=(a_i,b_1)$. Use the staircase tetrahedra
$$T_1=[a_0^0,a_1^0,a_2^0,a_2^1],\qquad T_2=[a_0^0,a_1^0,a_1^1,a_2^1],\qquad T_3=[a_0^0,a_0^1,a_1^1,a_2^1].$$
Their common faces are triangulated by the same ordered diagonals, so the three tetrahedra form the triangular-prism block; repeating this order on the three-cycle of $S^1$ gives the product triangulation in [F2].

The level disk at the midpoint of the product edge separates the bottom vertices $a_i^0$ from the top vertices $a_i^1$. In $T_1$ it cuts off the single top vertex $a_2^1$, giving one triangle; in $T_2$ it separates the pair $\{a_0^0,a_1^0\}$ from $\{a_1^1,a_2^1\}$, giving one quadrilateral; in $T_3$ it cuts off the single bottom vertex $a_0^0$, giving one triangle. It misses all tetrahedra in the other two prism blocks. Its intersections on shared faces agree because they are the same level section of the product, so the matching equations hold. Only one quadrilateral coordinate is nonzero, so [F1] gives an admissible normal disk vector.

The geometric surface is exactly $D^2\times\{s_*\}$, hence is a connected disk. Its boundary is $\partial D^2\times\{s_*\}$, which is nonempty and has $\chi=1$. The marked meridian $\{a_0\}\times S^1$ passes through exactly one point of this boundary at $(a_0,s_*)$, in the interior of the chosen fiber edge; the intersection is transverse and has parity $1$.
Thus the explicit vector satisfies the matching, quadrilateral, connectedness, boundary, Euler-characteristic and mod-two meridian checks claimed in the statement.

derivations.claim: The link $Lk_E(v)$ of a boundary vertex in a triangulated $3$-manifold is a closed disk: its local link is a $2$-ball. In each tetrahedron containing $v$ the link meets that tetrahedron in the small triangle parallel to the opposite face; it misses tetrahedra not containing $v$. Across each shared face these triangles have matching normal arcs, so [F1] makes the link a normal surface. Its boundary is $Lk_T(v)$, a simple closed curve in the small boundary-star disk of $v$, hence contractible in $T$. The local half-ball star shows the disk is boundary-parallel.

The link disk is connected, has nonempty boundary, and has Euler characteristic one. Its boundary is null-homotopic, so its projection to the product-circle factor has degree zero. After a transverse PL perturbation, the parity of intersections with a fibre meridian equals the parity of preimages of a regular point under that projection; a lift with zero net degree crosses the level an even number of times. Hence the intersection parity is zero.

The disk therefore passes the first three tests in [F2] but fails the odd-intersection test, so the filter rejects this candidate. This conclusion concerns this boundary-parallel disk only; it does not rule out any other normal essential disk in $E$ and therefore does not classify the knot.

Let $K$ be finite and $f:K\to\mathbb R^q$ a whole-star smooth immersion in the
sense of [[def-relative-smooth-triangulation-and-projection-preserving-fitting]].
There is $\delta>0$ such that every strong piecewise $C^1$
$\delta$-approximation $g:K'\to\mathbb R^q$, on any finite subdivision $K'$,
is a whole-star immersion. If $f$ is also an embedding, $\delta$ may be chosen
so that $g$ is an embedding. The subdivision need not have a mesh or shape
bound.

Let $K$ be a finite geometric complex and $f:K\to\mathbb R^q$ piecewise smooth in
the sense of [[def-relative-smooth-triangulation-and-projection-preserving-fitting]].
There are subdivisions $K_m$ agreeing on every original face, with mesh
tending to zero and a single lower thickness bound $\theta>0$ for every
positive-dimensional simplex, whose secant maps $S_m$, defined by affine
interpolation of the values of $f$ at vertices, converge strongly in piecewise
$C^1$ to $f$.

If $L\subset K$ is a subcomplex and $U$ an open neighbourhood of $|L|$, the
approximation can instead be chosen pointwise equal to $f$ on a neighbourhood
of $|L|$ and equal to a secant map outside $U$, on shape-controlled
subdivisions; subdivision of $L$ is permitted and does not alter $f$ there, and
every affine target-plane constraint already satisfied by $f$ on original
simplices is preserved.

There is also a local extension statement: given a finite subcomplex
$A\subset K$, a sufficiently small strong approximation $g$ to $f|_A$ on any
subdivision extends to a prescribed small strong approximation $G$ to $f$ on a
subdivision of $K$, with $G=f$ and with the original simplices unchanged
outside the closed star of $A$. The permitted error of $g$ depends on the
requested error and the finite original simplices, not on the shape of the
subdivision of $A$. If $p$ is an affine target map and $p(g)=p(f)$ on $A$, then $p(G)=p(f)$
everywhere; equivalently, the linear part of $p$ annihilates each correction. This last extension does not assert a shape bound on its
coned simplices.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice-principle-for-foliation-pair]]). Let $S$ be an oriented Hausdorff $C^2$ surface without boundary, possibly disconnected. Then:

1. Every compact subset $K\subset S$ lies in the interior of a compact finitely cellulated $C^2$ subsurface $N$. If $K$ is contained in one connected component of $S$, $N$ can be chosen connected. A specified finite embedded regular $C^2$ graph contained in $\operatorname{Int}N$ can be included in its one-skeleton.
2. Every connected closed compact subsurface has an oriented genus normal form: the sphere for $g=0$, or the polygon word $\prod_{i=1}^g a_i b_i a_i^{-1}b_i^{-1}$ for $g\ge1$, with $\chi=2-2g$. A connected compact subsurface with $b>0$ boundary circles has a free fundamental group; capping its boundaries defines genus $g$ and gives $\chi=2-2g-b$ and free rank $2g+b-1$.
3. The fundamental group of every connected component of $S$ is torsion-free.
4. Every regular embedded $C^2$ nullhomotopic circle $c$ bounds an embedded compact disk region in $S$. Here a disk region is a compact subsurface homeomorphic to the closed disk, with boundary exactly $c$; its inherited surface structure and boundary are $C^2$. It is unique unless the **connected component containing $c$** is a sphere; in that component the two complementary disk regions are the two possibilities.

The normal forms in clause 2 are homeomorphism normal forms. No general differentiable smoothing theorem or arbitrary-surface triangulation-existence theorem is a premise of this item.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. A compact $C^2$ surface, with regular $C^2$ boundary allowed, is $C^2$ diffeomorphic to a compact smooth surface with smooth boundary. For a compact cooriented embedded surface in a smooth three-manifold, the diffeomorphism can be obtained by arbitrarily small local ambient displacements. This also applies to a compact intrinsic subsurface of a $C^2$ leaf: compactness is in the leaf topology, and its boundary is regular in that topology.

A connected oriented closed such surface with Euler characteristic zero is $C^2$ diffeomorphic to $T^2$. A compact regular surface region homeomorphic to a closed disk is $C^2$ diffeomorphic to $D^2$, and any prescribed $C^2$ diffeomorphism of its boundary circle can be realized by the disk parametrization.

Two disjoint regular closed disk regions in a $C^2$ sphere can simultaneously be carried to the standard two disk windows by a $C^2$ diffeomorphism, with compatible prescribed boundary parametrizations. A $C^2$ scalar function defined on a neighborhood of a compact set in $\mathbb R^2$ admits smooth approximations uniformly with its derivatives through order two on that compact set.

Finally let $L$ be a $C^2$ surface and $u:D^2\to L$ an **intrinsically continuous** map which is $C^2$ on an open boundary collar. On any smaller closed boundary collar contained in that open collar, $u$ has arbitrarily close $C^2$ approximations agreeing with $u$ on a neighborhood of the smaller collar, and a homotopy to each approximation fixed there. Closeness is uniform for any fixed compatible metric on $L$. No injectivity or immersion of the cap map is required.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Subdivide along the boundaries of finitely many smaller coordinate neighborhoods as necessary. Compactness and finiteness give positive separation between disjoint closed simplices away from their common stars, and between a sufficiently small replacement neighborhood and the closed complement of the prescribed neighborhood. Thus it suffices to smooth the finitely many unprotected vertices and edge portions inside these neighborhoods. All other points are already in smooth face interiors.

At an unprotected vertex use an ambient smooth chart centered at its image and affine coordinates on its finitely many incident triangles centered at the vertex. Write their common map as $f(x)=A(x)+R(x)$, where $A$ is the piecewise linear differential fan. On a sufficiently small star, $|R(x)|=o(|x|)$ and $\|DR(x)\|=o(1)$, uniformly over those triangles. Let $\eta$ be a radial cutoff equal to one on a smaller star and zero outside a slightly larger star of radius $\epsilon$, with derivative bounded by $C/\epsilon$. Replacing $f$ by $f-\eta R$ changes its derivative by $o(1)$, because $|R|\,|D\eta|=o(\epsilon)/\epsilon=o(1)$. Apply [F1] to keep it an embedding. This makes the surface exactly its linear cone near the vertex, with the original map retained outside the larger star. The vertices have disjoint neighborhoods, so these finite replacements do not interfere. The link of the resulting cone on a small round sphere is a simple closed piecewise smooth curve: the surface vertex link is a circle and the differential fan is injective.

Smooth an open edge portion away from the vertex centers. Its two incident smooth half-surfaces have distinct tangent half-planes meeting along their common edge. In a small tubular coordinate box their union is a graph $z=h(s,u)$ over a plane, with the edge at $u=0$ and $h$ smooth for each sign of $u$. For unit transverse rays $v_+$ and $v_-$ pointing out from the edge into the two half-surfaces, whole-star injectivity gives $v_+\ne v_-$. The linear functional $\ell(w)=\langle v_+-v_-,w\rangle$ has $\ell(v_+)>0$ and $\ell(v_-)<0$. Projection onto the plane consisting of the edge direction and this signed transverse coordinate therefore gives the required graph, and remains regular on a smaller box by continuity. Replace $h$ near $u=0$ by convolution in $(s,u)$, using a cutoff supported in that box and equal to one near a smaller edge core. The new graph is smooth at its core, remains an embedded graph, and agrees with the old surface outside the box. Where the cutoff changes the old graph is already smooth, so the interpolation is smooth there. Use arbitrarily small value errors and the finite separation margins to prevent collisions with the rest of the surface. Covering each remaining compact edge portion by finitely many such boxes and retaining earlier smooth cores completes the open-edge smoothing.

In the linear conical neighborhoods of step 2.1 choose the edge rounding radially: round the finitely many corners of the link curve on the unit sphere in disjoint spherical graph charts, and take rays over this rounded link. A radial cutoff joins this choice to the open-edge graph choices farther out. On the overlap the chosen graph projection is still injective, so graph interpolation joins them without intersections. After this operation the only unsmoothed point in each vertex neighborhood is its center, and on an annulus about that center the surface is $r\gamma(s)$, where $\gamma:S^1\to S^2$ is a smooth embedded circle. These operations are fixed near the protected set.

By [F2], $\gamma$ bounds a smoothly parametrized disk region $e:D^2\to S^2$. The circles $s\mapsto e(\rho s)$, with $\rho$ decreasing from $1$ to a small positive number, give a smooth isotopy of embedded circles. In a small chart about $e(0)$, choose a fixed small $r>0$ and use the expression $E(trs)/t$, continued at $t=0$ by $r\,dE_0(s)$; these circles remain inside that chart and are smooth and embedded for sufficiently small $r$: its derivative is uniformly close to the injective linear map, and projection onto its image plane gives injectivity by integration on segments. Deform the final linear ellipse to a round circle by its positive Gram square root, and carry it back through a spherical chart. This gives an isotopy $\gamma_t$ of smooth embedded spherical circles from $\gamma$ to a small latitude circle. Flatten its time parameter near both endpoints. No extension to a diffeomorphism of $S^2$ or of a three-ball is used.

In a smaller conical annulus replace $r\gamma(s)$ by $r\gamma_{\tau(r)}(s)$, where $\tau$ goes from zero on its outer collar to one on its inner collar. This is an embedded smooth annulus: different radial levels lie on disjoint round spheres, and at each fixed level the curve is embedded; its radial derivative has nonzero radial component, while its circle derivative is tangent to that sphere. Near the inner collar it is a circular cone. Close that cone by a surface of revolution lying inside the inner sphere: in coordinates around its axis, replace the conical graph $z=a\varrho$ near $\varrho=0$ by $z=a\psi(\varrho)$, where $\psi$ is smooth and even near zero, agrees with $\varrho$ near the outer radius and is positive at zero. Choose its modification supported in a much smaller radius so its graph lies strictly inside the inner sphere; a smooth convex rounding of the graph of $|\varrho|$ has these properties. This gives a smooth disk cap, unchanged on the annular seam. The cap replaces a conical disk by a disk with the same boundary, hence preserves the surface's homeomorphism type relative to everything outside the vertex neighborhood.

Apply step 6.1 in each of the disjoint vertex neighborhoods. The result is smooth on the face interiors, the edge cores, the connecting annuli and the caps, with identical maps on open seam collars. It is embedded by the graph, radial-level and separation arguments, and is unchanged on the protected smooth neighborhood. Replacing finitely many disks and edge strips by disks and strips with the same attaching collars gives a homeomorphism from the original surface to the result fixed there. All changes fit inside the prescribed neighborhood by step 1.1.

Finally, a surface PL in the specified compatible triangulation becomes a subcomplex after a common finite subdivision. Each restricted ambient simplex map is smooth and its differential fan is injective on the ambient star, hence on the surface's substar. Thus it has exactly the piecewise smooth whole-star data used in steps 1.1–4.1. The argument requires only this supplied compatibility and the stated countable choice, proving all clauses.

citations.quote:
Let $K$ be finite and $f:K\to\mathbb R^q$ a whole-star smooth immersion in the
sense of [[def-relative-smooth-triangulation-and-projection-preserving-fitting]].
There is $\delta>0$ such that every strong piecewise $C^1$
$\delta$-approximation $g:K'\to\mathbb R^q$, on any finite subdivision $K'$,
is a whole-star immersion. If $f$ is also an embedding, $\delta$ may be chosen
so that $g$ is an embedding. The subdivision need not have a mesh or shape
bound.

Let $K$ be a finite geometric complex and $f:K\to\mathbb R^q$ piecewise smooth in
the sense of [[def-relative-smooth-triangulation-and-projection-preserving-fitting]].
There are subdivisions $K_m$ agreeing on every original face, with mesh
tending to zero and a single lower thickness bound $\theta>0$ for every
positive-dimensional simplex, whose secant maps $S_m$, defined by affine
interpolation of the values of $f$ at vertices, converge strongly in piecewise
$C^1$ to $f$.

If $L\subset K$ is a subcomplex and $U$ an open neighbourhood of $|L|$, the
approximation can instead be chosen pointwise equal to $f$ on a neighbourhood
of $|L|$ and equal to a secant map outside $U$, on shape-controlled
subdivisions; subdivision of $L$ is permitted and does not alter $f$ there, and
every affine target-plane constraint already satisfied by $f$ on original
simplices is preserved.

There is also a local extension statement: given a finite subcomplex
$A\subset K$, a sufficiently small strong approximation $g$ to $f|_A$ on any
subdivision extends to a prescribed small strong approximation $G$ to $f$ on a
subdivision of $K$, with $G=f$ and with the original simplices unchanged
outside the closed star of $A$. The permitted error of $g$ depends on the
requested error and the finite original simplices, not on the shape of the
subdivision of $A$. If $p$ is an affine target map and $p(g)=p(f)$ on $A$, then $p(G)=p(f)$
everywhere; equivalently, the linear part of $p$ annihilates each correction. This last extension does not assert a shape bound on its
coned simplices.

Let $m\ge0$, $n\ge1$, and $r\ge1$ be integers, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$
be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be a $C^r$ map with

$$ r>\max\{m-n,0\}. $$

Then the critical value set of $f$ is a null subset of $\mathbb R^n$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice as an ambient hypothesis; the finite construction and
the ODE interfaces below use no additional choice, so this hypothesis is
dispensable. A smooth manifold with corners here is Hausdorff and second
countable, with charts in relatively open subsets of $[0,\infty)^c\times\mathbb R^{n-c}$
and transition maps smoothly extendible with invertible derivative at corner
points; transitions preserve the local depth and its face germs. Let $M$ be
compact. Then $M$ has a finite corner-adapted whole-star smooth triangulation.
Corner faces are locally subpolyhedra, and any specified finite union of
closed faces is a subpolyhedron.

If the total boundary already has a finite piecewise smooth triangulation
$f:L\to\partial M$ compatible on all local face intersections, with its
differential fan giving a homeomorphism onto the union of boundary faces of the
tangent orthant at each point, the triangulation extends to $M$, pointwise
preserving $f$ with compatible subdivisions allowed. In the resulting finite
union construction all intersections may be made full subcomplexes. The same
relative conclusion applies to a fixed corner-adapted triangulated closed neighbourhood piece
whose smaller protected subcomplex lies in its relative interior: fitting is
performed away from that protected subcomplex. No extension of arbitrary
incompatible boundary data is asserted.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: After a small smooth perturbation, keep $e$ proper and transverse to $\partial M$ and make it transverse to the finite strata of $h(T)$, avoiding the vertices. Here the elementary finite parameter argument suffices: in each of finitely many ambient chart cores add small coordinate translations multiplied by a bump equal to one on the core. Evaluation on that core is a submersion in the translation parameters, so the regular values of the projection of the corresponding inverse-image stratum give transverse perturbations by [F2]. At boundary points use the tangential chart translations on $\partial M$ and their product extensions in its collar. Choose the finitely many perturbations successively small enough to retain already obtained transversality and the disk's embedding and proper collar. Compact transverse intersections with the edge strata are finite; intersections with face interiors are compact regular arcs and circles after adding those edge endpoints, hence a finite embedded graph. There are no intersections with vertex strata.

Cut the disk along the finite inverse-image graph. Regard repeated slit sides as separate boundary copies before regluing. The pieces are compact smooth surfaces with corners: face-intersection arcs have nonzero differential; at an edge intersection their incident tangent directions are distinct, since the disk plane is transverse to that edge, so the two bounding equations in each sector give a corner chart by the inverse theorem. Supply each common boundary arc with one smooth regular parametrization, subdivided identically on its two copies. These are admissible boundary data in [F2], because the two corner rays are independent. Apply its finite relative whole-star construction to the pieces and reglue their identical boundary subdivisions. This gives a finite piecewise smooth whole-star triangulation of the disk with each simplex mapping into one ambient simplex. The inverse of $h$ on that simplex is smooth up to its indicated faces by the full-rank extension and inverse theorem. Consequently $g=h^{-1}e$ on this finite source complex is piecewise smooth. Its differential fan is injective: the ambient differential fan of $h$ is a homeomorphism onto the tangent half-space or space, and the disk differential is injective, so taking its inverse on the subdivided tangent sectors is injective. Thus $g$ is a whole-star embedding into a Euclidean realization of $|T|$.

Apply the shape-controlled secants of [F1] to $g$. Every refined simplex maps by affine interpolation of its vertex values into the same convex ambient simplex as its original carrier. Adjacent source simplices have identical interpolants on their common face. Thus these secants define a PL map into $|T|$, and sufficiently small strong error makes it an embedding by [F1]. They send boundary into the boundary subcomplex, since all the vertices of a boundary source simplex lie in its one boundary ambient face and the interpolant preserves that face.

Properness is retained as well. In a smooth disk collar the inward boundary defining coordinate of $M$ has strictly positive inward derivative, uniformly after a finite shrink, by the given transversality. Cellulate that collar as strips with its boundary as the only zero-coordinate face. In each ambient half-space simplex the corresponding affine boundary coordinate is nonnegative and positive on the vertices off that boundary face. Its affine interpolant is therefore zero precisely on the source boundary face. The derivative lower bound ensures these are precisely the collar sectors, even after a finer shape-controlled subdivision. Away from the collar the compact disk has a positive distance from $\partial M$, and a sufficiently small value error retains that separation. Hence the PL disk meets $\partial M$ exactly in its own boundary.

Along the original boundary, the secant curve lies in an arbitrarily small annular neighborhood and is transverse to its interval fibres: its tangential derivative is close to the nonzero derivative of the original parametrized curve in each of the finitely many sectors. Projection to the original circle is therefore a degree-one local homeomorphism, hence a homeomorphism. The new boundary is a graph in that annulus; interpolating its graph coordinate with zero gives an isotopy to the original boundary. Thus its nullhomotopy class, including its essentiality, is unchanged. The image under $h$ of the secant disk is the required properly embedded PL disk in the supplied compatible structure.

citations.quote: Let $T=S^1\times S^1$ be the standard oriented product torus. If $C\subset T$ is an embedded piecewise-linear simple closed curve that is not null-homotopic, then its class $[C]\in H_1(T;\mathbb Z)$ is nonzero and primitive, meaning that it is not $k x$ for any $x\in H_1(T;\mathbb Z)$ and integer $|k|>1$.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice-principle-for-foliation-pair]]). Let $S$ be an oriented Hausdorff $C^2$ surface without boundary, possibly disconnected. Then:

1. Every compact subset $K\subset S$ lies in the interior of a compact finitely cellulated $C^2$ subsurface $N$. If $K$ is contained in one connected component of $S$, $N$ can be chosen connected. A specified finite embedded regular $C^2$ graph contained in $\operatorname{Int}N$ can be included in its one-skeleton.
2. Every connected closed compact subsurface has an oriented genus normal form: the sphere for $g=0$, or the polygon word $\prod_{i=1}^g a_i b_i a_i^{-1}b_i^{-1}$ for $g\ge1$, with $\chi=2-2g$. A connected compact subsurface with $b>0$ boundary circles has a free fundamental group; capping its boundaries defines genus $g$ and gives $\chi=2-2g-b$ and free rank $2g+b-1$.
3. The fundamental group of every connected component of $S$ is torsion-free.
4. Every regular embedded $C^2$ nullhomotopic circle $c$ bounds an embedded compact disk region in $S$. Here a disk region is a compact subsurface homeomorphic to the closed disk, with boundary exactly $c$; its inherited surface structure and boundary are $C^2$. It is unique unless the **connected component containing $c$** is a sphere; in that component the two complementary disk regions are the two possibilities.

The normal forms in clause 2 are homeomorphism normal forms. No general differentiable smoothing theorem or arbitrary-surface triangulation-existence theorem is a premise of this item.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. A compact $C^2$ surface, with regular $C^2$ boundary allowed, is $C^2$ diffeomorphic to a compact smooth surface with smooth boundary. For a compact cooriented embedded surface in a smooth three-manifold, the diffeomorphism can be obtained by arbitrarily small local ambient displacements. This also applies to a compact intrinsic subsurface of a $C^2$ leaf: compactness is in the leaf topology, and its boundary is regular in that topology.

A connected oriented closed such surface with Euler characteristic zero is $C^2$ diffeomorphic to $T^2$. A compact regular surface region homeomorphic to a closed disk is $C^2$ diffeomorphic to $D^2$, and any prescribed $C^2$ diffeomorphism of its boundary circle can be realized by the disk parametrization.

Two disjoint regular closed disk regions in a $C^2$ sphere can simultaneously be carried to the standard two disk windows by a $C^2$ diffeomorphism, with compatible prescribed boundary parametrizations. A $C^2$ scalar function defined on a neighborhood of a compact set in $\mathbb R^2$ admits smooth approximations uniformly with its derivatives through order two on that compact set.

Finally let $L$ be a $C^2$ surface and $u:D^2\to L$ an **intrinsically continuous** map which is $C^2$ on an open boundary collar. On any smaller closed boundary collar contained in that open collar, $u$ has arbitrarily close $C^2$ approximations agreeing with $u$ on a neighborhood of the smaller collar, and a homotopy to each approximation fixed there. Closeness is uniform for any fixed compatible metric on $L$. No injectivity or immersion of the cap map is required.

statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

derivations.claim: Reverse the parametrization of $C$ if necessary so its class is $(1,q)$. Round its finitely many corners in disjoint torus coordinate disks, using a coordinate in which the two incident arcs are graphs and replacing the graph corner by a smooth arc fixed near its endpoints. Each change is an isotopy of simple curves supported in that disk: interpolate graph values, which preserves the graph projection. Thus $C$ has an isotopy through finite piecewise smooth embedded curves to a smooth curve $C_0$ in the same class. Write $L_q(s)=(s,\exp(2\pi iqs))$. This is a simple smooth curve in that class.

Put $C_0$ transverse to $L_q$ by an arbitrarily small finite graph perturbation. The shear $(s,z)\mapsto(s,z\exp(-2\pi iqs))$ is a torus diffeomorphism carrying $L_q$ to a product section, so cutting the torus along $L_q$ gives an explicit annulus. The cut pieces of $C_0$ are finitely many properly embedded arcs. A returning arc, whose endpoints are on the same boundary circle, cuts off a disk with a subarc of that boundary. One elementary way to verify this familiar annulus fact is to cut the annulus to a rectangle along a spanning arc, lift the returning arc to its strip of translated rectangles, and choose an outermost lifted arc: its union with the interval between its endpoints on the same strip boundary bounds a polygonal disk. If a translate or another arc enters this disk, choose an innermost such arc instead. Finiteness of the intersections gives a disk with embedded interior in the annulus. Equivalently the finite disk-and-band reductions in [F2] give the same disk. Choose an innermost returning arc among the cut pieces; its disk interior misses the other cut pieces. Sliding it across that disk and a little beyond is an isotopy supported in the disk's collar and removes two intersections of $C_0$ with $L_q$. For smooth curves use smooth graph slides, stationary near the endpoints of the time interval.

Repeat the preceding removal while a returning arc remains. There are strictly fewer intersection points at each removal. If intersections remain when no returning arc is left, all cut arcs span the annulus. Traversing the connected oriented curve then meets $L_q$ always with the same crossing sign: after a spanning arc one arrives at the opposite copy of the cut circle, and gluing crosses it in the same direction as at the preceding crossing. Hence its algebraic intersection with $L_q$ is nonzero. This contradicts [F1], because both classes are $(1,q)$ and their determinant is zero. Thus the finite sequence ends with a smooth curve disjoint from $L_q$. The two curves bound an annulus: cutting along $L_q$ places the other essential circle in the interior of an annulus; cutting along it gives two annuli, as is seen by the same finite surface normal form [F2], or by lifting to a strip and taking the region between adjacent lifts. Sliding through that annulus supplies an isotopy to $L_q$. Concatenate with step 1.1 to obtain a finite piecewise smooth isotopy of simple curves from $C$ to $L_q$, smooth after the initial corner rounding.

Put the isotopy of step 3.1 into a radial collar of the tube. More precisely choose a strictly decreasing smooth radius $r(t)$ from $1$ to $1/2$ and map $(s,t)$ to $(u_t(s),r(t)z_t(s))$, where $(u_t(s),z_t(s))$ parametrizes the curve isotopy on the boundary torus. Distinct $t$ give distinct radii, so this is an embedded annulus irrespective of overlaps between different curve images on the torus. On each smooth piece its circle derivative is nonzero and tangent to the radius torus, whereas its time derivative has nonzero radial component, so it is regular. Make the isotopy constant near its final time; its inner collar is then the product collar of the radius-$1/2$ copy of $L_q$.

Continue inward by $(s,r)\mapsto(s,r\exp(2\pi iqs))$ for $0\le r\le1/2$. This is an embedded smooth annulus including its core boundary $r=0$: the first coordinate separates distinct $s$, and the $r$ derivative is a nonzero normal vector even at zero. Its outer collar agrees with the preceding annulus after the chosen radial reparametrization. The joined annulus meets the boundary torus only in $C$ and has the smooth core as its other boundary. Its interior lies on the tube side of that torus, while a proper exterior disk lies on the exterior side, so their union is an embedded disk, with a smooth product collar at the core. This proves the statement.

citations.quote:
If $P\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ is a polygon, then $\mathbb R^2\setminus P$ has exactly two regions, one bounded and one unbounded, and

$$\operatorname{Fr}(U)=P$$

for each of them. Regions and frontiers are from [[def-plane-region-and-frontier]]. The proof uses the finite simple edge cycle of [[def-polygonal-arc-and-polygon]] and polygonal crossing parity from [[lem-polygonal-crossing-parity-is-locally-constant]].
Every simple polygon admits a triangulation.

derivations.claim: Put $D$ in finite PL general position: it misses vertices, meets edges transversely in finitely many points, and meets faces in finitely many arcs and circles. This is obtained by finite subdivision and small generic vertex displacements, choosing each displacement outside finitely many forbidden affine planes and lines. Preserve its proper boundary in the boundary faces. Every component $P$ of its intersection with a tetrahedron is a compact planar surface, because it is a subsurface of a disk. Components have nonempty boundary; an entire closed component in a tetrahedron would be a closed component of $D$. Put $w(D)=|D\cap T^{(1)}|$ and $\lambda(D)=\sum_P(1-\chi(P))$. A connected planar piece with $b\ge1$ boundary curves has $1-\chi(P)=b-1\ge0$, as is seen by cutting it along $b-1$ disjoint connecting arcs to a disk and counting the cuts. Thus $(w,\lambda)$ is a pair of nonnegative integers.

We first record the permitted disk replacement inside a tetrahedron. Whenever a new cap is disjoint from the other pieces, a disk piece may be replaced, fixing its boundary and a smaller attaching collar, by that cap just inside its chosen boundary disk region. This preserves the topology of the entire surface: two disk parametrizations with the same boundary identification are homeomorphic relative to that boundary, extending the circle map radially. It is enough to choose the new cap disjoint from the other pieces. If all the pieces in question are disks, choose a point away from their boundary curves and take the disk side not containing that point for each curve. These disks are nested or disjoint by [F1]. Put the caps at successively deeper levels for successively larger nested regions, rounding their finite collar corners PL. This realizes all those disk pieces by disjoint caps. The same construction works in a boundary disk region containing only boundary curves of disk pieces, with other pieces kept outside its collar. The chosen depth intervals can be arbitrarily small. Boundary curves, edge intersections and the planar Euler deficits are unchanged. No assertion that the old disk is isotopic to the cap in the tetrahedron is needed.

If $\lambda>0$, select in some tetrahedron a boundary circle $c$ of a non-disk piece $P$ that is innermost among such boundary circles, using either fixed planar diagram of the boundary sphere. All boundary circles in its inner disk region are boundaries of disk pieces. Move those disk pieces to nested boundary-parallel caps as in step 2.1, at shallower collar depths. A copy of the inner boundary disk placed deeper than those caps, with boundary on a curve just inside the collar of $c$ in $P$, is then an embedded compressing disk disjoint from all other pieces. Its boundary is essential in $P$, since $P$ is planar with at least two boundary circles. Compress along it. Locally this splits off a disk and replaces $P$ by a planar piece with one fewer boundary circle, so $\lambda$ decreases by one, while $w$ is unchanged. Globally compression of a disk along an interior simple circle gives a disk with the original boundary and a sphere. Keep the disk and discard the sphere; discarding pieces cannot increase $w$ or $\lambda$. The boundary of the retained disk is still essential.

Repeat step 3.1 until $\lambda=0$ unless a preceding sphere discard has already decreased $w$; in that event restart with the smaller weight. At $\lambda=0$ every tetrahedral intersection piece is a disk. We may rearrange these disk pieces as boundary-parallel caps by step 2.1, without changing $w$ or $\lambda$. This rearrangement is only preparation for the next simplifying move, so it introduces no infinite sequence of equal-complexity moves.

Suppose some disk boundary meets a tetrahedral edge $e$ more than once. The finite disjoint boundary circles on the tetrahedral sphere then admit an edge-return interval $\beta\subset e$ with endpoints on the same boundary circle and interior disjoint from all the boundary circles. To verify this, the complementary regions of finitely many disjoint circles on a sphere have a tree as their incidence graph: each added circle separates one region into two, by [F1]. The edge $e$ traces a walk in that tree. Crossing one circle more than once repeats a tree edge; any such walk has an immediate backtrack. The two consecutive crossings of that backtrack are the required endpoints of $\beta$. Choose the cap side of its disk piece containing $\beta$ and use the compatible nested cap arrangement of step 2.1. The strip between $\beta$ and its parallel arc $\alpha$ on this cap is a disk $E$ with $E\cap D=\alpha$, $\partial E=\alpha\cup\beta$, and interior disjoint from all pieces: inner caps miss $\beta$ and outer caps lie deeper. This is an actual embedded edge-compressing disk.

If $e$ is an interior edge of $M$, slide the strip of $D$ adjacent to $\alpha$ across $E$ and beyond $\beta$ into the other sectors of the edge star. In the local product of an edge interval and a normal disk this is the elementary removal of a bigon; it removes precisely the two intersections at the ends of $\beta$ and creates no new edge intersections. It is an isotopy supported in that edge star and preserves the global boundary. Hence $w$ decreases. The new disk may have a larger local Euler deficit, which does not matter because the first complexity coordinate has decreased.

If $e\subset\partial M$, the same disk $E$ gives a boundary compression. Cutting the global disk along the proper arc $\alpha$ and adding the two parallel copies of $E$ gives two proper disks. At least one has essential boundary. Indeed, after choosing a base point and whiskers in $\partial M$, the old boundary loop is the product of the two new boundary loops, with one conjugated by the connecting arc $\beta$. If both new loops were nullhomotopic, so would be the old one. Keep an essential-boundary disk. The total edge intersection number of the two new disks is smaller than the old one by two, so the retained disk has strictly smaller $w$. Again any increase of $\lambda$ is permitted.

The boundary is thus a triangle or quadrilateral normal curve. Replace the finitely many disk pieces by standard parallel normal disks with those same boundary matchings; disjoint boundary curves permit only one quadrilateral type in a tetrahedron. Their finite gluing has exactly the same abstract surface topology and boundary essentiality as the retained disk. It is the required normal disk. If the two types are equal, their two path edge sets are the same nonempty complementary sets $U,V$. Pairing $U$ with $V$ in each output recovers the original word twice. Pairing $U$ with $U$ and $V$ with $V$ repeats every edge in the corresponding nonempty set, so [F2] excludes that pairing. The remaining two paths concatenate in the order $(AC,AD,BD,BC)$, giving the same quadrilateral. The other pairing joins the two copies of $\{AC,AD\}$ in one output, repeating both edges, and is excluded.

The other common-face pairs are $ABC,ACD$ and $ABD,ACD$, whose common edges $AC,AD$ are crossed by the quadrilateral. Interchanging $C,D$ identifies these two cases, so consider $ABC,ACD$. derivations.claim: Move the finitely many edge-intersection points of $Y$ slightly along their edges, preserving their order on each edge, to avoid those of $X$. The normal side matchings for $Y$ are retained. For each triangular face, replace every arc of each family by its straight chord between the corresponding endpoints. Each family remains embedded by [F2]. Choose the point displacements generically so no two chords overlap or are tangent where they meet: equality of their supporting lines is one nontrivial determinant equation in finitely many edge parameters, and can be avoided by successively choosing parameters outside finitely many forbidden values, with arbitrarily small displacements and the prescribed orders. Since each family is disjoint, a point lies on at most one chord from each, so there are no triple points.

The new boundary curves of the disk pieces on every tetrahedral sphere retain their individual normal boundary types and side matchings. Each family separately is a finite disjoint family of those curves. Realize it by the nested disjoint caps [F1], leaving its boundary exactly the chosen straight face chords. Do this for both colors. It gives two embedded proper normal surfaces with the original coordinate vectors. Their abstract disk-side gluing data are unchanged, so their abstract surfaces are homeomorphic to the originals: map each old disk to its new disk with the prescribed boundary correspondence, extending its boundary parametrization over a disk by coning a finite polygonal subdivision. For boundary components, moving endpoints along their edges and replacing a face arc by its chord gives a homotopy within the convex boundary faces, and these homotopies concatenate around each boundary circle.

Keep the first family of boundary-parallel caps fixed. Put the interiors of the second family into finite PL transverse position relative to it, while keeping all boundaries fixed. Subdivide finitely and displace second-family interior vertices by successively sufficiently small generic amounts. The excluded affine coincidences form finitely many proper planes, lines and determinant-zero conditions; avoiding them makes the sheet intersections one-dimensional with no tangencies. Smallness preserves each family's embedding and avoids all tetrahedral edges. Near boundary crossings, use fixed half-plane product charts extending the already transverse chord intersections. Consequently the intersection in each tetrahedron is a finite disjoint union of proper arcs and circles, with every endpoint a crossing of one straight chord from each family in a face.

No proper intersection arc has both endpoints in the same face. Its two branches lie in a fixed disk of each family, since pieces of the same family are disjoint. Each of those normal disks meets a given face in at most one arc. Two endpoints in that face would therefore be two intersections of the same two straight chords, contradicting [F2]. Thus all proper intersection arcs join distinct faces. Moreover, a fixed pair of normal pieces has at most one crossing in each of their common faces by [F2]. A triangle meets only three faces, so at most two endpoints, hence at most one arc, can occur for a pair containing a triangle. Two quadrilaterals have at most four endpoints, hence at most two arcs. These counts remain valid after circle removal, which changes no face arc or proper intersection arc.

Suppose an intersection circle remains in some tetrahedron. Choose a circle $c$ innermost on one disk $P$ of the first family, and let $E\subset P$ be the disk it bounds. Its interior misses the entire second family. There is no circle there by innermost choice. Nor can a proper intersection arc lie inside $E$: its endpoints would be on $\partial P$, outside $E$, while it cannot cross the disjoint intersection circle $c$. Thus $E$ is an actual disk with interior disjoint from the second family. It lies in the interior of the tetrahedron.

The circle $c$ lies on a disk $Q$ of the second family and bounds an interior subdisk $Q_0\subset Q$. Remove $Q_0$ and replace it by a nearby parallel copy of $E$, joining it to $Q\setminus\operatorname{int}Q_0$ in a small transverse collar of $c$. Choose the copy on the side of $P$ occupied by that outside collar of $Q$. The needed product coordinates are explicit for this $E$: the first-family disk $P$ is still the fixed boundary-parallel cap from step 2.1. Its graph in the boundary collar has the product coordinates supplied in [F1]; restrict them to the compact interior subdisk $E$ and take sufficiently small levels on its two sides. Thus no regular-neighborhood theorem for an arbitrary PL disk is needed. Compactness away from the attaching collar permits its interior to miss the entire second family. It also misses every first-family disk, since $E$ lies in one of their mutually disjoint disks and the push is to one side of that disk. Therefore the replacement is embedded, preserves the second family's embedding and leaves its tetrahedral boundary unchanged. It removes $c$ and every intersection circle inside $Q_0$, creates no new intersections, and changes no proper intersection arc. For the last assertion, a proper arc cannot enter $Q_0$ without crossing its boundary circle $c$, which is already a distinct intersection component. The disk $Q$ remains a disk with exactly its previous boundary type.

Reapply step 5.1 to a remaining circle, if any, and step 6.1 to remove it. The finite number of intersection circles strictly decreases, while no new one is created. This ends with no tetrahedral intersection circles. Edge points and straight face chords have not changed, so step 4.1 still excludes same-face arc endpoints. Every replacement changed only an interior subdisk of one piece, preserving the abstract surface and its boundary. Gluing across the faces now gives the asserted finite global double-curve system, since the local intersection arcs match at the fixed transverse face crossings and have endpoints only on boundary faces. The boundary homotopies from step 2.1 preserve null-homotopy or its failure. All operations were finite in the original triangulation.

The spokes $Aa,Bb,Cc$ divide the region outside it into three convex quadrilaterals, one along each original edge. All original arc endpoints lie in the relative interiors of the outer strip edges.

For each type, designate one of its two original endpoint edges, using a fixed ordering of the three edges. Order that type's combined $\mathcal X$ and $\mathcal Y$ chords by the order of their corresponding original endpoints away from the common vertex on the designated edge. Assign their colors and individual labels in that order. By [F1], this order respects the order within each original family on both endpoint edges. The central chords therefore impose compatible same-color orders on their two central strip gates. On a central gate the two incident types occupy their separate canonical corner blocks.

In every strip join each original endpoint to the gate endpoint of its labeled central chord by the straight wire in the rectangular parametrization. For either color separately, its wire order at the outer edge equals its wire order at the gate: order within a type agrees by step 2.1, and the two types have the same separate corner blocks by [F1]. Thus wires of the same color do not cross by [F2]. A wire from the other color crosses it at most once. Distinct crossings cannot coincide, since that would make two same-color wires meet. All intersections are consequently transverse double points. Join the wires to their central chords. Each resulting arc has exactly one central chord and one wire in each of two distinct strips, so is embedded and has its original type.

Two original arcs of different types share only one strip, so intersect at most once. Two original arcs of the same type share two strips, but on that type's designated strip their combined endpoint and gate orders coincide, by step 2.1. They cannot intersect there, so can intersect only once in their other strip. This proves the first assertion, including the original pairwise bound.

At a wire crossing, choose the uncrossing that reconnects each incoming wire from the outer side to the other outgoing wire toward the gate. In a small rectangle this is the reconnection by two horizontal-monotone strands. The other uncrossing joins the two outer-side branches to one another and the two gate-side branches to one another. After any subset of the chosen reconnections, every parametrizing strand within a strip is still strictly monotone in its horizontal coordinate: following it from an outer endpoint always goes toward a gate, and conversely. It cannot form a circle or self-intersect, and no component can have both ends on the same side of that strip. All strips still have the same gate endpoints, and the central chords have not changed. Hence each full parametrizing component has exactly one central chord and wires in its two distinct strips. It is an embedded normal arc. No remaining crossing can be a self-crossing of such a component: it lies inside one strip, where that component has exactly one monotone wire. The central chords count its type, so all type counts are unchanged.

To check the local characterization, the two crossing arcs share the strip's original edge $e$. The chosen uncrossing pairs each outer branch, whose endpoint is on $e$, with one gate branch. The other endpoint of that gate branch lies on a different original edge, determined by its unchanged central chord. This recovers the original unordered pair of types. The alternative joins the two outer branches and therefore has both endpoints on $e$, an edge-return arc. Thus exactly one uncrossing preserves the two normal types. Since the preceding argument worked for any subset of crossings, all assertions follow without altering the original face or its edge endpoints.

citations.quote: Let $T$ be a finite tetrahedral triangulation of a compact piecewise-linear $3$-manifold with $t\ge1$ tetrahedra. A nonzero nonnegative integer vector in $\mathbb Z^{7t}$ is the normal-coordinate vector of a normal surface exactly when it satisfies every face-matching equation and at most one quadrilateral type is nonzero in each tetrahedron. Every primitive integer generator of an extreme ray of the Haken cone has each coordinate at most $2^{7t-1}$. Every fundamental normal-surface vector has each coordinate at most $t\,2^{7t+2}$.

Let $f$ be an affine triangle and let $\mathcal X,\mathcal Y$ be two finite families of normal arcs in $f$, each family embedded and pairwise disjoint, with disjoint endpoint sets on $\partial f$. There are PL representatives of the same individual arc types, fixing those endpoints, with these properties:

1. Every intersection is a transverse double point between the two families. Each original pair of arcs intersects at most once.
2. At every double point there is a chosen regular reconnection. For every subset of the double points, perform just those reconnections and otherwise retain the original transverse crossings. The resulting parametrizing components are embedded normal arcs, never circles, and their total counts of the three normal arc types are unchanged. Every remaining double point lies on two distinct parametrizing arcs.
3. The chosen reconnection at a crossing is the unique one of the two uncrossings that preserves the unordered pair of the two normal arc types there. Its alternative creates an edge-return arc in that local two-arc endpoint pairing. The same characterization holds at each remaining crossing after any partial reconnection.

Here parametrizing components follow the strands through unswitched crossings without joining them. The construction uses a small central triangle and three quadrilateral strips inside this original face. It changes no triangulation and uses only finite choices.

Let $P,Q$ be two normal disk types in one tetrahedron, subject to quadrilateral compatibility. Thus if both are quadrilaterals they have the same type. Choose two distinct faces $f,g$ met by both types, and cut each normal boundary word at one point of its arc in $f$ and one point of its arc in $g$. Each boundary is divided into two paths from $f$ to $g$.

There are two pairings that join one path from $P$ to one from $Q$ at both ends, producing two new closed boundary words. Exactly one pairing gives the original two normal disk boundary types, as an unordered pair, up to cyclic rotation and reversal of the words. The other pairing has a word crossing some tetrahedral edge at least twice and therefore cannot give those two normal types.

The conclusion concerns the finite boundary words and type counts in the original tetrahedron. It does not assert that arbitrary surface intersections already have the geometric regular-position or partial-switching properties.

We obtain normal surfaces $X,Y$ with their original vectors and with only proper transverse tetrahedral intersection arcs. Each such arc joins distinct faces, since two endpoints in one face would be two crossings of the same pair of face arcs, excluded by [F2]. Globally these arcs form finitely many double circles and proper double arcs, missing the edges.

Let $F_1,F_2$ be any two embedded normal realizations of the same vector. On each global edge their numbers of points agree: the local edge count is a sum of the prescribed disk coordinates, and face matching identifies this count around the edge star. Match the points in their linear order, after fixing an orientation of that edge. On a face, arcs cutting off a fixed vertex form the endpoint blocks nearest that vertex on its two sides, with the same nested ordering. Thus the ordered point matching determines the arc matching. It determines the same entire boundary circles on each tetrahedral sphere, and therefore a bijection of the normal disk pieces attached to those circles. Map each disk to its counterpart with these boundary maps; a boundary map of a PL disk extends over it by coning a finite subdivision of its polygonal parametrization. These maps agree on all glued sides and points. Their finite gluing and its inverse give a PL homeomorphism $F_1\to F_2$. Its boundary maps are homotopies in $\partial M$: move the matched edge points monotonically along their edges and join the corresponding arc maps by homotopies inside each convex boundary face. These homotopies agree at their endpoints and concatenate around each boundary circle.

Along a tetrahedral intersection arc choose the local switch prescribed by [F3]. At each endpoint on a face it induces the type-preserving uncrossing of its two face arcs: the two resulting disk boundary words have the same normal disk types, so their face arcs have the original two arc types and no edge return. By uniqueness in [F2], this is exactly that face's chosen monotone-strip reconnection. The adjacent tetrahedron prescribes the same reconnection, because its two face arc types are the same matched types. The local switches therefore continue consistently across faces and around each full double curve. We prove that any partial choice preserves normal disk pieces. It is enough first to work in one tetrahedron, allowing any subset of its intersection arcs; its face systems are then partial resolutions of the face braid. Order the chosen local arcs arbitrarily and use induction. Initially all pieces are embedded normal disks. Suppose this holds before processing the next remaining arc $\alpha$. Its two branches lie in distinct current disk pieces. Otherwise an endpoint of $\alpha$ on a face would be a transverse self-intersection of that disk's unique arc in the face. But every current face parametrizing arc is embedded by [F2]. This is impossible.

Cut the two distinct disks along $\alpha$. Each becomes two disks, since the arc is proper. Reconnecting them crosswise by either switch gives two abstract disks, each obtained by gluing one cut disk from each original disk along their cut boundary interval. Their current types are still compatible: the induction has preserved the original multiset of types. Apply [F3] to them. Its unique type-preserving choice agrees at both face endpoints with [F2], hence with the fixed switch in step 2.1. The two new disk boundary words consequently have their previous triangle or quadrilateral types, each with a single arc on every face it meets.

These new disk pieces are embedded. Local strip reconnection creates no new double points and removes just $\alpha$; all remaining double arcs are among the previous ones, still joining faces. If both branches of one belonged to the same new disk, its face endpoint would self-intersect that disk's unique face arc, again forbidden by [F2]. Thus no new disk has a self-intersection. There are no other singularities, since the original diagram was transverse and every switching neighborhood replaces two crossing sheets by two disjoint strips. It has used only finite original-tetrahedron disk words, face braids, cap replacements and ordered gluings; no transfer from a different normal-coordinate system was made.

If $K$ is a finite simplicial complex and $f_n(K)$ denotes the number of
$n$-simplices of $K$, the **simplicial Euler characteristic** of $K$ is
$$\chi(K):=\sum_{n \geq 0} (-1)^n f_n(K).$$
The sum is finite because a finite simplicial complex has only finitely many
simplices.

Let $S=|K|$ be a connected compact surface with nonempty boundary, where $K$ is a finite two-dimensional simplicial complex, each edge lies in one or two triangles, and each vertex link is a circle or interval. If its simplicial Euler characteristic is $\chi(K)=1$, then $S$ is homeomorphic to a closed disk.

Let $S := [0,1] \times [0,1]$ be the unit square, which carries one topology by
claim 1 of [[thm-product-of-subspaces-and-closures]]
([[lem-product-topology-on-rn]], [[def-subspace-topology-top]],
[[def-interval]]). Define two relations on $S$, in each case leaving every point
not on the two vertical edges alone:

$$\text{cylinder:}\quad (0,y) \sim_{\mathrm{c}} (1,y); \qquad\qquad \text{Mobius band:}\quad (0,y) \sim_{\mathrm{m}} (1, 1-y) \qquad (y \in [0,1]).$$

Precisely, $\sim_{\mathrm{c}}$ has as classes the pairs $\{(0,y),(1,y)\}$ and the
singletons $\{(s,t)\}$ with $0 < s < 1$; $\sim_{\mathrm{m}}$ has as classes the
pairs $\{(0,y),(1,1-y)\}$ and the same singletons. Write
$M_{\mathrm{c}} := S/\!\sim_{\mathrm{c}}$ (the **cylinder**) and
$M_{\mathrm{m}} := S/\!\sim_{\mathrm{m}}$ (the **Mobius band**), each with the
quotient topology ([[def-quotient-topology]]) and canonical projection
$P_{\mathrm{c}}$, $P_{\mathrm{m}}$. Then:

1. **Both projections are closed quotient maps**: the saturation of a closed
   subset of $S$ is closed, so $P_{\mathrm{c}}$ and $P_{\mathrm{m}}$ carry closed
   sets to closed sets ([[lem-open-or-closed-surjection-is-quotient]]).
2. **The cylinder is $(\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}) \times [0,1]$.** With
   $T = \mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$ and its open quotient map $q$
   ([[ex-circle-as-r-mod-z]]), the map $Q_1 := q \times \mathrm{id}_{[0,1]}$ is an
   open quotient map $\mathbb{R} \times [0,1] \to T \times [0,1]$ and induces a
   homeomorphism $M_{\mathrm{c}} \cong T \times [0,1]$
   ([[def-homeomorphism-and-open-maps]]).

**Nothing here claims that the cylinder and the Mobius band are different
spaces.** Distinguishing them needs an invariant, and the standard ones are not
available at this point in the reading order
([[rem-constructions-this-page-stops-short-of]]). Both are recorded as
constructions, and only the cylinder is identified with a space built earlier.

The digon whose two sides are paired in the same boundary direction — the
one-polygon word $a\,a$ — realizes the real projective plane
$\mathbb{RP}^2$, taken here as the antipodal quotient $S^2/(x\sim -x)$,
equivalently as the closed upper hemisphere with antipodal boundary points
identified. It is nonorientable and has $V=1$, $E=1$, $F=1$, so
$\chi(\mathbb{RP}^2)=1-1+1=1$
([[def-euler-characteristic-of-a-finite-cw-complex]]). This direct finite
quotient uses no choice axiom.

derivations.claim: Suppose first that $P$ has boundary. Apply the finite dual-tree collapse [F2], choosing a lexicographically first spanning tree, to obtain a connected graph $G$. Take small polygonal vertex disks and narrow rectangular edge bands inside $P$ to form a regular neighborhood $N(G)$. One can choose them after a finite subdivision by taking sufficiently small rational distances in the finitely many triangle charts. Reversing a free triangle-edge collapse enlarges this neighborhood by a boundary finger across that triangle. To see that its homeomorphism type is unchanged, use a triangle chart in which the removed edge is the base: the two retained sides make the tip of the finger, and moving its polygonal boundary from a small parallel arc to the base expands a disk along one boundary interval. Triangulate the region between these two arcs and map corresponding triangles linearly. This gives a PL homeomorphism between the two neighborhoods, fixed off that triangle and its small vertex sectors. Reverse the finitely many collapses in order and finally expand the boundary collar. Thus $P$ is PL homeomorphic to $N(G)$. This construction uses a finite list of local maps, rather than a general regular-neighborhood uniqueness theorem.

A spanning tree of the connected graph $G$ has $V(G)-1$ edges. Write $h=E(G)-V(G)+1\ge0$ for the number of remaining edges. The collapses and [F1] give $\chi(P)=V(G)-E(G)=1-h\le1$. If equality holds, $h=0$, so $G$ is a tree and its neighborhood is a disk by [F2].

If $\chi(P)=0$, the graph $G$ has exactly one edge outside a spanning tree. Delete its leaf edges successively. A leaf vertex disk and its band merely form a finger on the neighboring disk; removing that finger changes no neighborhood homeomorphism type by the same finite polygonal expansion as in step 1.1. The graph remaining is one cycle: alternatively, the unique extra edge and the unique tree path joining its endpoints form that cycle, and every other tree edge belongs to a tree attached to it. Thus $N(G)$ is the union of the vertex disks and bands around a single cycle.

Now suppose $P$ is closed. Remove the interior of a small polygonal disk $B$ inside one triangle and triangulate the remaining surface $P_0$. It is connected: any path crossing the disk can have each crossing segment replaced by a path along its boundary, and a finite polygonal path has only finitely many such segments after a small general-position displacement. It has exactly one boundary circle. By [F1], $\chi(P_0)=\chi(P)-1$, and step 2.1 gives $\chi(P)\le2$. If $\chi(P)=2$, then $P_0$ is a disk by step 2.1. Capping a disk by a disk gives a sphere. Any PL boundary identification can be reduced to the identity by extending the boundary map over a disk: cone a finite subdivision of its circle to the center, and map the resulting triangles linearly. Thus this identification is PL.

Cut this cycle across one band. Its neighborhood becomes one rectangular strip: glue the remaining vertex disks and bands consecutively, each along one boundary interval, and use the polygonal disk expansions of step 1.1 to straighten the strip. At its two ends the transverse intervals are identified by a PL interval homeomorphism. If this map is increasing, change the transverse coordinate at one end and interpolate that change along the strip to make the gluing the identity. Explicitly, prescribe the required increasing map on one short side of the rectangle and the identity on its other three sides. This is a PL homeomorphism of its boundary. Subdivide at its finitely many breakpoints, cone both boundary subdivisions to interior points and map corresponding triangles linearly. This extends the boundary map to a PL homeomorphism of the rectangle. If the gluing is decreasing, first compose with $y\mapsto1-y$ and apply the same construction. The two resulting quotients are exactly the two models in [F3]. In the first, the two long sides of the strip give two boundary circles; in the second they join to one. Hence $P$ is respectively an annulus or a Mobius band.

If $\chi(P)=1$, then $P_0$ has Euler characteristic zero and exactly one boundary circle. Steps 3.1–4.1 make it a Mobius band, since the annulus has two boundary circles. Capping a Mobius band gives the antipodal-boundary disk of [F3]: in that disk model, a small collar of the identified outer circle is the twisted interval band, while the remaining inner disk is the cap. Conversely those two pieces recover the model. Changing the cap's boundary identification does not change the resulting PL surface, by the coning extension from step 3.2. Therefore $P$ is a projective plane. Every construction above used only finite trees, finite collapses and finite polygonal maps. The final embedded-surface consequence follows by composing these homeomorphisms with the given embedding.

Let $T$ be a finite simplicial triangulation of a compact PL three-manifold. Let $x,y\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^{7t}$ be admissible normal-coordinate vectors such that $x+y$ satisfies the quadrilateral condition. There are embedded proper normal surfaces $X,Y$ with vectors $x,y$, a finite transverse double-curve diagram $X\cup Y$ disjoint from $T^{(1)}$, and pairwise disjoint switching neighborhoods with these properties:

1. In each tetrahedron all double arcs join distinct faces. At every such arc the chosen regular switch preserves the unordered pair of normal disk types.
2. The choices agree through every crossed face and hence along each entire double circle or proper double arc.
3. Any partial selection of whole-curve regular switches gives a finite immersed normal-disk diagram with only the unswitched double curves and no branch points. Its total vector is $x+y$. Switches in disjoint neighborhoods commute.
4. Switching all curves gives an embedded proper normal surface $F$ with $v(F)=x+y$ and $w(F)=w(X)+w(Y)$.

The realization of an admissible vector determines its abstract surface and its boundary curves up to PL homeomorphism of the surface and homotopy of the corresponding boundary curves in $\partial M$. In particular, if $x+y=v(D)$ for a connected essential normal disk $D$, then $F$ is a connected essential normal disk. Thus every nontrivial coordinate decomposition of such a disk has an actual regular normal-sum diagram of this kind in the original triangulation.

No irreducibility, orientability, sphere-separation or choice hypothesis is required. The assertion concerns these explicitly constructed realizations, without claiming an ambient isotopy between arbitrary prior realizations.

Let $f$ be an affine triangle and let $\mathcal X,\mathcal Y$ be two finite families of normal arcs in $f$, each family embedded and pairwise disjoint, with disjoint endpoint sets on $\partial f$. There are PL representatives of the same individual arc types, fixing those endpoints, with these properties:

1. Every intersection is a transverse double point between the two families. Each original pair of arcs intersects at most once.
2. At every double point there is a chosen regular reconnection. For every subset of the double points, perform just those reconnections and otherwise retain the original transverse crossings. The resulting parametrizing components are embedded normal arcs, never circles, and their total counts of the three normal arc types are unchanged. Every remaining double point lies on two distinct parametrizing arcs.
3. The chosen reconnection at a crossing is the unique one of the two uncrossings that preserves the unordered pair of the two normal arc types there. Its alternative creates an edge-return arc in that local two-arc endpoint pairing. The same characterization holds at each remaining crossing after any partial reconnection.

Here parametrizing components follow the strands through unswitched crossings without joining them. The construction uses a small central triangle and three quadrilateral strips inside this original face. It changes no triangulation and uses only finite choices.

Let $M$ be a compact PL three-manifold with a finite simplicial triangulation. If $M$ contains a properly embedded PL disk whose boundary is not null-homotopic in $\partial M$, then it contains a normal disk with that property. No orientability, irreducibility or projective-plane hypothesis is required. The construction is allowed to replace disk pieces and to change the isotopy class of the original disk; it asserts existence of a normal replacement.

derivations.claim: All switching neighborhoods miss $T^{(1)}$. Hence every original edge-intersection point belongs to exactly one parametrizing component, and the sum of their edge weights is $W$. In particular $w(P)\le W$. If $w(P)<W$, apply [F2] to obtain an essential normal disk of weight at most $w(P)$, which proves the result. It remains to consider $w(P)=W$. In this case every original edge-intersection point belongs to $P$, and every other parametrizing component has weight zero.

An irregularly switched global curve crosses some face by [F1]. Choose one of that face's rectangular strips containing an irregular reconnection. Parametrize it so the horizontal coordinate runs from the original edge $e$ to its central gate. Order its finitely many crossing neighborhoods from the outer edge toward the gate. If distinct neighborhoods have the same horizontal coordinate, shrink them and perturb their positions slightly along their monotone wires to order them; this keeps the wires monotone, preserves their crossings and changes none of their endpoint orders. Thus we may speak of the first irregular reconnection in this strip. To its outer side, all selected switches are regular, and any unswitched crossing just follows its original monotone wire.

Before that first irregular reconnection, every incoming parametrizing strand is horizontally monotone and joins its crossing neighborhood to an original endpoint on $e$. The two incoming branches come from distinct such strands and distinct endpoints: all preceding crossings either keep two monotone strands separate in the normalization or regularly reconnect them from outer side to gate side. The irregular reconnection joins precisely these two incoming branches. It consequently creates a parametrizing arc with its two distinct endpoints on $e$, lying entirely on the outer side of this reconnection except for its small turning cap. Later reconnections farther toward the gate cannot change this arc, since their neighborhoods lie beyond its maximal horizontal coordinate. This gives an edge-return parametrizing arc in the completed face diagram.

In the equality case of step 1.1, both endpoints of that return arc belong to $P$. A face parametrizing arc lies in one global parametrizing component, so this entire arc belongs to $P$. Its image is an embedded proper arc in the face, because $P$ is embedded. Its ends are two distinct intersections with the same original edge $e$. Possible intersections with other parametrizing components do not affect this assertion about the arc within $P$.

Normalize $P$ using [F2]. If a preliminary sphere discard or other move removes any edge intersection before all tetrahedral pieces are disks, its weight has already decreased and the final normal essential disk has weight less than $w(P)$. Otherwise no edge intersection has been removed. The cap preparations and tetrahedral compressions fix the face curves. A sphere discard could not have removed the return arc of step 3.1 without removing its two edge endpoints. Thus that arc remains on the retained essential disk when its tetrahedral pieces become disks. On either incident tetrahedron, its boundary circle then meets $e$ at least twice. The explicit bigon construction in [F2] gives a strictly weight-decreasing edge move; if $e$ is a boundary edge its two disk outputs have total weight smaller by two, and at least one has essential boundary. Keeping that disk again decreases weight strictly.

Finish the finite normalization [F2]. No subsequent move increases weight, so its essential normal disk satisfies $w(D')<w(P)=W$. Together with step 1.1 this proves the Statement. The strict decrease comes from a return to an original edge, and has not used an auxiliary normal-coordinate objective or an ambient sphere theorem.

Let $T$ be a finite simplicial triangulation of a compact PL three-manifold. Suppose a **regular normal-sum diagram** is supplied with the following data:

- Two nonempty embedded normal surfaces $X,Y$ in transverse PL position, with no triple points and finitely many disjoint double circles and proper double arcs.
- Pairwise disjoint switching neighborhoods of those double curves, disjoint from $T^{(1)}$, with compatible chosen regular switches. In each tetrahedron the local switch reconnects two crossing normal disks to normal disks of the same two types. A partial switch therefore leaves a finite immersed normal-disk diagram, with only the unswitched double curves and without branch points. Switches in disjoint neighborhoods commute.
- Performing all the switches gives a connected embedded normal surface $F$.

Then some partial switching gives a diagram whose normalization has exactly two components $G,H$. Here normalization means separating the two branches at every remaining double point; its components are the parametrizing surfaces, regardless of intersections between their images. Both $G$ and $H$ are connected embedded normal surfaces. They have

$$v(G)+v(H)=v(F),\qquad w(G)+w(H)=w(F),\qquad 0<w(G),w(H)<w(F).$$

Their remaining switching system is reduced in the following precise sense: switching any nonempty subset of its curves gives a diagram with connected normalization. In particular no remaining intersection circle or proper intersection arc separates both $G$ and $H$ when each is cut along its corresponding preimage.

All surfaces and vectors remain in the original triangulation $T$. No orientability, irreducibility or choice hypothesis is needed. The existence of a regular normal-sum diagram from an arbitrary coordinate decomposition is an input to this lemma, not a conclusion.
