The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $D$ be a finite regular oriented diagram of a nonempty labeled link, with
$n\geq1$ crossings and at least one underpassing point on each component. Fix a
smooth height realization $L_D=\{(\gamma(s),\eta(s))\}\subset\mathbb R^2\times[-1,0]$
such that $\eta(s)=-1$ exactly at the $n$ underpassing points and
$\eta(s)>-1$ elsewhere; at each crossing the overpassing point has height
strictly greater than $-1$. Put
$$A=(\mathbb R^2\times[-1,\infty))\cup\{\infty\},\quad B=(\mathbb R^2\times(-\infty,-1])\cup\{\infty\},\quad \Sigma=(\mathbb R^2\times\{-1\})\cup\{\infty\},$$
and write $X=S^3\setminus L_D$, $A_L=A\cap X$, $B_L=B\cap X$,
and $\Sigma_L=\Sigma\cap X$. Also put
$A_L^\circ=((\mathbb R^2\times(-1,\infty))\cup\{\infty\})\cap X$.
Then $\Sigma_L$ is a path-connected sphere
with $n$ punctures, $A_L\cup B_L=X$, and $A_L\cap B_L=\Sigma_L$. There are
path-connected open sets $U,V\subset X$ such that $X=U\cup V$, $U$ deformation
retracts onto $A_L$, $V$ deformation retracts onto $B_L$, and $U\cap V$
deformation retracts onto $\Sigma_L$. The set $B_L$ is contractible. The small
circles in $\Sigma_L$ around the $n$ punctures normally generate
$\pi_1(\Sigma_L)$, and they still normally generate after any one circle is
omitted. The inclusion $A_L^\circ\hookrightarrow A_L$ is a homotopy
equivalence. Radial retraction in each chosen product tube identifies
$\pi_1(X)$ with the fundamental group of the chosen link exterior.

Assume countable choice.

Let $D$ be a finite regular oriented diagram of a nonempty labeled link with
$n\geq1$ crossings. Fix a smooth height realization
$L_D=\{(\gamma(s),\eta(s))\}\subset\mathbb R^2\times[-1,0]$ such that
$\eta(s)=-1$ exactly at the $n$ underpassing points and $\eta(s)>-1$
elsewhere, and assume each component has at least one underpassing point. Put
$$M=(\mathbb R^2\times(-1,\infty))\setminus L_D.$$
Cut every component parameter circle at its underpassing points; the resulting
$n$ open intervals are the strands. For each strand interval $I_j$, its
vertical sheet is
$$D_j=\{(\gamma(s),z):s\in I_j,\ -1<z<\eta(s)\}\subset M.$$
Set $Z=M\setminus\bigcup_{j=1}^nD_j$. Choose a common basepoint in $Z$, and
for each strand choose a positive meridian circle meeting only its own sheet
once, with its access path in $Z$. Then $\pi_1(M)$ is free on these based
positive meridians $x_1,\ldots,x_n$. The inclusion $M\hookrightarrow A_L$
also induces an isomorphism on fundamental groups.

Let $X=U\cup V$, where $U$ and $V$ are open path-connected subsets of $X$, let $U\cap V$ be path-connected, and fix $x_0\in U\cap V$. For the inclusion-induced maps in the diagram

$$\pi_1(U,x_0)\longleftarrow\pi_1(U\cap V,x_0)\longrightarrow\pi_1(V,x_0),$$

the group $\pi_1(X,x_0)$, together with the two inclusion-induced homomorphisms, is a pushout ([[def-pushout-of-group-homomorphisms]]). Equivalently, the canonical homomorphism from any pushout $P$ of the displayed diagram to $\pi_1(X,x_0)$ is an isomorphism. No injectivity of either map from the overlap group is assumed.

For homomorphisms $f:K\to G$ and $h:K\to H$, let $N$ be the normal closure in $G\ast H$ of $$\{j_G(f(k))j_H(h(k))^{-1}:k\in K\}.$$ Then $(G\ast H)/N$, with the induced factor maps $j_G$ and $j_H$, is a pushout of $f$ and $h$.

At an oriented crossing let $o$ be the over-strand. Orient the projection plane
by the rule that $(v_1,v_2)$ is a positive basis exactly when the ordered triple
$(n,v_1,v_2)$ is positive in the ambient three-space, where $n$ is the viewing
normal. Let $n_o$ be the positive in-plane normal characterized by the condition
that $(v_o,n_o)$ is positive in this plane. Call the under-side from
which $n_o$ points the source $s$, and the side toward which it points the
target $t$. Use a common basepoint above the diagram and paths in the upper
collar to the positive meridians $m_o,m_s,m_t$. Then
$$m_t=m_o^{-1}m_sm_o.$$
Equivalently, the crossing relator is
$m_o^{-1}m_sm_om_t^{-1}=1$. Reversing the direction of the under-strand
does not change the side-based equation.

Let $F(X)$ be a free group and let $R\subseteq F(X)$ be a set of words, called
**relations**. The group with presentation

$$\langle X\mid R\rangle:=F(X)/\langle\!\langle R\rangle\!\rangle_{F(X)}$$

is the quotient by the normal closure of $R$. The members of $X$ are its
**generators**. In this quotient, every relation in $R$ becomes the identity,
as do all consequences forced by normality.

A **free group on a set $X$** is a group $F(X)$ together with a map
$i:X\to F(X)$ such that, for every group $G$ and every function $u:X\to G$,
there is a unique group homomorphism $\widehat u:F(X)\to G$ satisfying

$$\widehat u\circ i=u.$$

The reduced-word construction supplies such a group; the construction and its
universal property are established in [[thm-reduced-words-form-the-free-group]].
When no ambiguity arises, $x\in X$ is identified with its image $i(x)$.

$$

\subset\mathbb R^2\times[-1,0]

component $i$ and $\widehat\eta_i(s)>-1$ at every other parameter.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. For a discrete group $G$, Milnor's $BG$ is connected and

$$ \pi_1(BG)\cong G,\qquad \pi_n(BG)=0\quad(n>1). $$

Consequently any connected CW model of $BG$ is an Eilenberg--Mac Lane space $K(G,1)$.

Assume AC. Every group $G$ has a connected CW model $K(G,1)$. For every abelian group $A$ and every $n\geq2$, there is a connected CW model $K(A,n)$. If two models carry identifications with the same group, they are homotopy equivalent by maps inducing the prescribed identification (with the usual basepoint transport in degree one).

If $f,g:X\to Y$ are homotopic continuous maps, then for every $n\geq 0$ and
every abelian group $G$ the induced homomorphisms on singular homology agree:
$$H_n(f_\#)=H_n(g_\#):H_n^{\mathrm{sing}}(X;G)\to H_n^{\mathrm{sing}}(Y;G).$$

Every two-cell attaching loop represents the identity in $G$, so its image represents the identity in $H$ and extends over the two-cell. For a cell of dimension $k\geq3$, the attaching map is a sphere map into $BH$ and extends over the disk because $\pi_{k-1}(BH)=0$ by [F1]. AC chooses the extensions over the set of cells. This gives a based map inducing $\phi$.

The maps $B\phi\circ c_X$ and $c_Y\circ f$ induce the same homomorphism $\phi$ on fundamental groups. On the vertices choose based paths joining their values, and on each one-cell fill the resulting boundary loop; that loop is null because the two induced fundamental-group maps agree. Inductively, the obstruction to extending the homotopy across each $k$-cell is a map $S^k\to BH$, and it is null for $k\geq2$ by [F1]. AC supplies the cell extensions. Hence the maps are based homotopic.
By [F3], the homotopy of step 1.2 gives $(B\phi)_*\circ(c_X)_*=(c_Y)_*\circ f_*$. This is the asserted naturality, including degree two.

Then $H_1(E_L;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z^r$, with the positive meridians as its ordered basis. Each boundary torus $T_i$ has a product basis consisting of its positive meridian and a degree-one section. There is a unique degree-one class on $T_i$ whose image has zero $i$th meridian coordinate; this class is primitive and has a simple closed representative.

Let $\tau$ be an $r$-component string link with chosen disjoint product tubes in $D^2\times[0,1]$, exterior $X_\tau$, and bottom and top punctured disks $P_-$ and $P_+$. Then each $\pi_1(P_\pm)$ is free of rank $r$. Positive endpoint meridians with the compatible accesses transported from a point-punctured-disk spine form an ordered free basis. For arbitrary independently chosen access paths, the corresponding meridian is $c_i m_i c_i^{-1}$, where $m_i$ is the compatible-stem meridian and $c_i$ is the recorded access-path difference; these conjugates need not be a free basis. Each end inclusion sends its ordered positive meridian basis to the ordered positive meridian basis of $H_1(X_\tau;\mathbb Z)$. Consequently both induced homomorphisms on $H_1$ are isomorphisms and both induced homomorphisms on $H_2$ are surjective.

$$h:\pi_1(X,x_0)\longrightarrow H_1(X;\mathbb Z)$$
is surjective and has kernel $[\pi_1(X,x_0),\pi_1(X,x_0)]$. Hence it induces a natural isomorphism
$$\pi_1(X,x_0)^{\mathrm{ab}}\cong H_1(X;\mathbb Z).$$

$$
c_*:H_2(X;\mathbb Z)\longrightarrow H_2(BG;\mathbb Z)=H_2(G;\mathbb Z)
$$
is surjective.

the ODE interfaces below use no additional choice, so this hypothesis is
dispensable. A smooth manifold with corners here is Hausdorff and second
countable, with charts in relatively open subsets of $[0,\infty)^c\times\mathbb R^{n-c}$
and transition maps smoothly extendible with invertible derivative at corner
points; transitions preserve the local depth and its face germs. Let $M$ be
compact. Then $M$ has a finite corner-adapted whole-star smooth triangulation.

performed away from that protected subcomplex. No extension of arbitrary
incompatible boundary data is asserted.

in the letters $X_i$, with multiplication given by concatenation of words.
This is the degree-complete ring for the word-length filtration; a series with
invertible constant coefficient is a unit, with inverse determined recursively
degree by degree.
Filter it by total degree (word length), and let $\mathfrak m$ be the ideal of
series with zero constant term.
The Magnus expansion is the group homomorphism
$$
E:F_r\longrightarrow
\mathbb Z\langle\!\langle X_1,\ldots,X_r\rangle\!\rangle^\times,
\qquad E(x_i)=1+X_i.
$$
It sends $x_i^{-1}$ to $(1+X_i)^{-1}=\sum_{k\ge0}(-1)^kX_i^k$. For an
integer $d\ge0$, calculations through degree $d$ use the truncated ring
$R_d=\mathbb Z\langle X_1,\ldots,X_r\rangle/\mathfrak m^{d+1}$. As a
$\mathbb Z$-module it has the finite monomial basis of words of length at most
$d$. In $R_d$, the inverse of $1+A$ for $A\in\mathfrak m$ is the finite sum
$1-A+A^2-\cdots+(-A)^d$.

For a based string link, $x_1,\ldots,x_r$ may be used as formal symbols
corresponding to the positive bottom-end meridians. No freeness or
lower-central quotient isomorphism is asserted here; those properties require
separate proofs.

derivations.claim:
Write $E(u)=1+U$ and $E(\lambda)=1+V$ with $U,V\in\mathfrak m$. Then
$$
E(u^{-1}\lambda u)-E(\lambda)
=(1+U)^{-1}V(1+U)-V.
$$
Expand $(1+U)^{-1}=\sum_{a\geq0}(-U)^a$. The term with no $U$ on either side is $V$ and cancels the subtracted $V$. Every remaining term is a product $(-U)^a VU^b$ with $a+b\geq1$.

A coefficient of degree $m$ in such a product uses a degree-$p$ monomial of $U^a$, a degree-$s$ monomial of $V$, and a degree-$q$ monomial of $U^b$ with $p+s+q=m$ and $p+q\geq1$. The $V$ monomial therefore has degree $s<m$ and occupies a contiguous middle block of the target word $w$, while the nonempty left or right block comes from $U$. Summing the finitely many decompositions of $w$ expresses its coefficient as an integer linear combination of coefficients of $E(\lambda)$ on proper contiguous subwords. Appending the longitude index $j$ makes each such index a proper subsequence of $(w,j)$.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC for the string-link quotient branch. Use the closed-link residue
definition one finite maximum index length at a time, so its based word-lift
data are finite.

Let $\tau$ be a based $r$-component string link with bottom meridian symbol group
$F_r=\langle x_1,\ldots,x_r\rangle$, exterior group $G=\pi_1(X_\tau)$, and
based string-link longitudes $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_r$. With compatible stem accesses this free group identifies the full endpoint fundamental group. For arbitrary independently based meridians, use instead its meridian map on each finite nilpotent quotient, which is still an isomorphism by the end-identification theorem; no full-group free-basis assertion is made. Longitudes retain their specified parallel and access data. For a multi-index
$I=(i_1,\ldots,i_k,j)$ with $k\geq1$ and each index in $\{1,\ldots,r\}$,
let $w_{j,k}\in F_r/\Gamma_{k+1}F_r$ be the unique class whose image under
the bottom-end nilpotent isomorphism is the class of $\lambda_j$ in
$G/\Gamma_{k+1}G$. Define the integer coefficient
$$\mu_\tau(I)=[X_{i_1}\cdots X_{i_k}]\,E(w_{j,k})\in\mathbb Z,$$
where the bracket means the coefficient of that word in the finite Magnus
expansion through degree $k$. The commutator-degree lemma makes this coefficient
independent of the representative of $w_{j,k}$.

For a closed labeled link $L$, choose a common basing and its preferred
zero-self-meridian longitudes. For every component $j$ and every finite
$q\geq2$, choose a lift $w_{j,q}\in F_r/\Gamma_qF_r$ of the class of its
longitude in $G/\Gamma_qG$, where $G=\pi_1(E_L)$ and $F_r$ is free on the
component meridian symbols. Such lifts exist because those meridians generate
every finite nilpotent quotient. For $I=(i_1,\ldots,i_k,j)$, define the based
coefficient $\mu_L^b(I)$ by taking the coefficient of
$X_{i_1}\cdots X_{i_k}$ in $E(w_{j,k+1})$ through degree $k$. Let
$\Delta_I^b$ be the nonnegative greatest common divisor of the finite set of
all $\mu_L^b(J)$ for sequences $J$ of lengths from $2$ to $|I|-1$ that occur
as subsequences of cyclic permutations of $I$. The gcd of an empty set is $0$.
Define the based residue candidate
$$\bar\mu_L^b(I):=\mu_L^b(I)\pmod{\Delta_I^b}\in \mathbb Z/\Delta_I^b\mathbb Z,$$
with $\mathbb Z/0\mathbb Z=\mathbb Z$. Independence of the basing and word
lifts is not part of this definition; it is a separate theorem. A based
Borromean example with $I=(1,2,3)$ uses this convention.

Let $F_r$ be the free group with Magnus expansion $E$, let $u,\lambda\in F_r$,
and let $w$ be a nonempty word of length $m$. The coefficient of $X_w$ in
$E(u^{-1}\lambda u)-E(\lambda)$ is an integer linear combination of
coefficients of $E(\lambda)$ on proper contiguous subwords of $w$. Thus, when
$w$ is the prefix of a Milnor index $I=(w,j)$, conjugating the longitude can
change its degree-$m$ coefficient only by an integer combination of
coefficients indexed by proper subsequences of $I$.

At an oriented crossing let $o$ be the over-strand. Orient the projection plane
by the rule that $(v_1,v_2)$ is a positive basis exactly when the ordered triple
$(n,v_1,v_2)$ is positive in the ambient three-space, where $n$ is the viewing
normal. Let $n_o$ be the positive in-plane normal characterized by the condition
that $(v_o,n_o)$ is positive in this plane. Call the under-side from
which $n_o$ points the source $s$, and the side toward which it points the
target $t$. Use a common basepoint above the diagram and paths in the upper
collar to the positive meridians $m_o,m_s,m_t$. Then
$$m_t=m_o^{-1}m_sm_o.$$
Equivalently, the crossing relator is
$m_o^{-1}m_sm_om_t^{-1}=1$. Reversing the direction of the under-strand
does not change the side-based equation.

Let $L=K_1\cup\cdots\cup K_r$ be a nonempty labeled oriented link in $S^3$,
let $G=\pi_1(E_L)$, and choose one based positive meridian $m_i\in G$ for each
component. For every integer $q\geq1$, the homomorphism from the free group
$F_r=\langle x_1,\ldots,x_r\rangle$ defined by $x_i\mapsto m_i$ induces a
surjection
$$F_r\longrightarrow G/\Gamma_qG.$$

Assume countable choice.

Let $D$ be a finite regular oriented diagram of a nonempty labeled link, after
inserting a small type-I curl on any component that has no underpassing point.
Let $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ be the positive meridians of the strands between
successive underpassing points, with the compatible common-upper-collar accesses of the local crossing rule. At a crossing $c$, write $o(c)$ for the
over-strand and $s(c),t(c)$ for the source and target under-sides defined using
the positive in-plane normal to the over-strand. Set
$$r_c=x_{o(c)}^{-1}x_{s(c)}x_{o(c)}x_{t(c)}^{-1}.$$
Then the assignment of each generator to its based positive meridian induces
an isomorphism
$$\langle x_1,\ldots,x_n\mid r_c\ (c\text{ a crossing})\rangle \cong \pi_1(E_L).$$
Any one crossing relator may be omitted without changing the represented
group. The theorem makes no claim that all relators are independent.

Arbitrary independently based positive strand meridians remain recorded: if $g_e$ is the access difference for strand $e$, its actual class is $y_e=g_ex_eg_e^{-1}$ in this reference presentation. This gives their exact group elements without claiming that the independently conjugated $y_e$ themselves freely generate the upper region or give the displayed uncorrected presentation. A common access change conjugates every generator and preserves the displayed presentation map.

Assume AC. Let a nonempty labeled oriented closed link have a based regular diagram with an underpass on every component. Choose an initial arc on each component, its positive meridian $x_i$, and the common upper basing. Put $F=\langle x_1,\ldots,x_r\rangle$ and $G=\pi_1(E_L)$. For every $q\ge2$ there are explicit words $l_{i,q}\in F$ representing the preferred longitudes in $G/\Gamma_qG$ such that the meridian map identifies
$$G/\Gamma_qG\cong F/\langle\!\langle\Gamma_qF,[x_i,l_{i,q}]\ (1\le i\le r)\rangle\!\rangle.$$
The words can be chosen coherently through each finite degree. They are obtained through the $(q-1)$st approximation of the crossing-conjugation recursion, initialized by component meridians and using the preceding approximation for every over-arc. In particular this describes the kernel, rather than merely the surjectivity, of the component-meridian map. Quotienting further by commutators of arbitrary conjugates of each component meridian adds exactly those commutators to this presentation.

Let $F_r$ be the free group and $E$ the Magnus expansion from the preceding
definition, with augmentation ideal $\mathfrak m$. If
$u\in\Gamma_pF_r$ and $v\in\Gamma_qF_r$ for $p,q\ge1$, then
$$
E([u,v])\in 1+\mathfrak m^{p+q}.
$$
Consequently $E(\Gamma_qF_r)\subseteq1+\mathfrak m^q$ for every $q\ge1$.
In particular, reduction of $E$ modulo $\mathfrak m^{d+1}$ factors through
$F_r/\Gamma_{d+1}F_r$ and its coefficients through degree $d$ are independent
of the representative word.

For every group $G$ and $i,j\ge1$, $[\gamma_i(G),\gamma_j(G)]\le\gamma_{i+j}(G)$. The rule $(x\gamma_{i+1},y\gamma_{j+1})\mapsto[x,y]\gamma_{i+j+1}$ is a well-defined biadditive map between the abelian lower-central factors.

derivations.claim: Choose a finite regular diagram of the link. If a component has no underpass, insert a small type-I curl on a short arc in a ball meeting no other component, as in the local disk-push construction of the link-presentation theorem in [F4]. There are finitely many components, so the balls may be chosen disjoint and away from the common basepoint; the supported ambient isotopies carry the original chosen tubes, positive meridians, preferred longitudes and all access paths to their images. On each peripheral torus this transport preserves degree one and zero self-meridian coordinate. The induced based group isomorphism carries every original meridian to its transported meridian, so each original finite free word remains literally the same word and is still a lift of the corresponding transported longitude in every finite nilpotent quotient. This reduction imposes no upper-basing or coherence condition on the original word systems. The augmented diagram now has an underpass on every component, including originally crossingless components; its canonical upper basing will be compared with arbitrary transported basings and lifts by the subsequent variable-substitution and coefficient-ideal argument. First use the geometric root meridians and coherent longitude words $l_a$ from [F5], through degree $k$. For any index sequence $J$, write $c(J)$ for the corresponding coefficient of these words. Let $D_I$ be the ideal of $\mathbb Z$ generated by $c(J)$ for all proper subsequences of cyclic permutations of $I$ of length at least two. Its nonnegative generator is the gcd in [F1]. Work in the ring $R_I$ with finitely many surviving monomials, obtained from $(\mathbb Z/D_I)\langle X_1,\ldots,X_r\rangle$ by setting to zero every monomial whose index word is not a subsequence of $w$. The discarded words span a two-sided ideal: adjoining letters cannot turn a word that is not a subsequence into one that is. Thus multiplication and inversion of series with constant term $1$ are well-defined finite operations. Occurrences, including repeated indices, are retained in their original order; no assumption of distinct indices is used here.

For a self-crossing change on component $a$, quotient the diagram group by the normal closure of all commutators of two conjugates of its meridian, doing this for every component. These quotients on the two sides of the crossing change have identical based presentations. To see this locally, cut both branches into incoming and outgoing arc symbols. The branch that is over has equal incoming and outgoing symbols. On the under-branch the Wirtinger equation conjugates its incoming meridian by the over-meridian; both are conjugates of the same component meridian and commute in this quotient, so its outgoing symbol also equals its incoming symbol. Switching the crossing interchanges which branch uses which argument and leaves precisely the same two equalities. All other crossing relations, and root paths chosen outside this small ball, are unchanged. Thus the identification preserves the component meridians, with no assertion of an isomorphism of the original unreduced groups.

The coefficient of any surviving word in $E([x_a,l_a])-1$ is zero in $R_I$. Indeed put $E(l_a)=1+L_a$. The exact identity is $$E([x_a,l_a])-1=(X_aL_a-L_aX_a)(1+X_a)^{-1}(1+L_a)^{-1}.$$ Every summand contributing to a surviving word therefore contains one distinguished occurrence of $a$ and a nonempty block from $L_a$, as well as possibly other blocks. If that block has index word $B$, its coefficient is $c(Ba)$. The selected block and the distinguished $a$ occupy disjoint positions in a subsequence of $w$; starting just after that occurrence of $a$ and reading cyclically shows that $Ba$ is a subsequence of a cyclic permutation of $I$. It is proper, since its length is at most $k<|I|$. Hence $c(Ba)\in D_I$, and the whole summand vanishes. The same argument applies if $(1+L_a)^{-1}$ is expanded elsewhere in the expression; the distinguished block can always be taken from the displayed first factor. This proves the assertion for each relator, its inverse, conjugates and finite products. Also $E(\Gamma_{k+1}F)=1$ through degree $k$ by [F6]. Therefore [F5] makes the coefficient of $X_w$ independent modulo $D_I$ of every lift of a fixed longitude in $G/\Gamma_{k+1}G$.

Under that reduced-group identification, the longitude of a component different from $a$ is unchanged: its traversal has no undercrossing factor in the altered ball, and its other arc meridians have the common images in step 1.2. For component $a$, the local factor lost or gained is a conjugate of its own meridian. It disappears on further quotienting by the normal subgroup generated by that meridian. The self-writhe normalization also differs by a power of this same meridian, so the preferred longitudes agree in this further quotient. These statements follow from the actual ordered undercrossing product, not solely from the meridian crossing relation.

Consider a different basing. Each new meridian is a conjugate of the old one, and each new longitude is also a conjugate of the old degree-one zero-self-meridian curve. The conjugating loops may be different if the two accesses were chosen independently; retain both recorded loops. Lift the finitely many conjugating loops to $F/\Gamma_{k+1}F$ by [F4]. The resulting change of root variables is $\phi(x_a)=u_a^{-1}x_au_a$. This is an automorphism of the finite nilpotent free quotient. It is the identity on degree one, hence on every lower-central graded layer, whose commutators are generated by the degree-one generators by [F7]. To construct a preimage, correct a word successively in $\Gamma_s/\Gamma_{s+1}$ for $s=1,\ldots,k$; each correction has the prescribed image because the graded map is the identity. For injectivity, an element in the kernel is successively in $\Gamma_2,\ldots,\Gamma_{k+1}=1$. Its inverse is again a substitution by conjugates of the same respective generators. Thus the new longitude words are obtained by inverse variable substitution, their own independently recorded longitude conjugations, and elements of the transformed canonical kernel described in [F5]. No assertion that an independently based new meridian and longitude commute is needed; [F5] describes the reference presentation before these separate output conjugations.

Now suppose the entries of $I$ are distinct. In the ring $R_I$ of step 1.1 every monomial containing an index twice is zero. For any word $u$, every term of $E(u^{-1}x_bu)-1$ contains $b$. Products of two such positive-degree expressions are therefore zero when both refer to $b$, and their units commute. The additional reduced-group relators $[u^{-1}x_bu,v^{-1}x_bv]$ are consequently annihilated. By [F5], the kernel of the map to the reduced nilpotent group consists exactly of these additional relators, the peripheral commutators already annihilated in step 2.1, and $\Gamma_{k+1}F$. If the changed component is $j$, the further normal-meridian subgroup in step 2.2 is annihilated too, since $j$ does not occur in $w$. Thus the two longitude coefficients agree modulo $D_I$. If the changed component is not $j$, their equality in the reduced group from step 2.2 already gives this conclusion.

In a variable substitution of this kind, $X_a$ is replaced by $X_a$ plus terms of degree at least two, every one of which contains an occurrence of $a$: this follows by expanding $E(u_a)^{-1}(1+X_a)E(u_a)-1$. A coefficient of $X_w$ in the substituted longitude therefore differs from its old coefficient only by integer multiples of $c(Bj)$ for proper subsequences $B$ of $w$. These are generators of $D_I$. A longitude conjugation has the same property by direct multiplication, or by [F2]: its constant term cancels and every correction uses a shorter longitude coefficient. The transformed kernel is also annihilated. In the argument of step 2.1, substituting conjugates preserves the distinguished occurrence of each original variable, so the selected $B$ and the distinguished $a$ still form a proper cyclic subsequence of $I$. Hence every permitted basing and lift change preserves the target coefficient modulo the ideal of the old proper coefficients.

These assertions also identify the modulus exactly, including when it is zero. Induct on index length. At length two there are no lower coefficients; commutator kernels and all conjugation corrections start in degree two, so the degree-one coefficients agree as integers. For a longer $I$, apply the induction hypothesis to every proper cyclic subsequence $J$ of $I$. It says that its coefficient changes by an integer combination of coefficients on proper cyclic subsequences of $J$, all of which are proper cyclic subsequences of $I$. Order these finitely many sequences by length. The new coefficients thus lie in the ideal of the old proper coefficients. Conversely solve the same triangular relations in increasing length to express each old coefficient in the ideal of the new proper coefficients. The two ideals, their nonnegative gcd generators, and hence their residue groups are equal. Step 3.1 then proves equality of the target residues. Independent choices of word lifts at the separate finite degrees in [F1] are covered by step 2.1 and this same triangular argument; no unmentioned coherence hypothesis is imposed on those inputs.

Induct again on the distinct index length. Length-two coefficients are preserved by step 3.2 with zero lower ideal. For larger $I$, apply the lower-length conclusions to its proper cyclic subsequences. The triangular ideal argument of step 5.1 shows that the old and new proper-coefficient ideals are equal; step 3.2 therefore gives equality in the canonically identical residue group. Step 4.1 permits arbitrary basings and finite word lifts at either endpoint. Composing along the stipulated finite sequence proves the self-crossing assertion. For repeated indices the square-zero argument in step 3.2 is unavailable, and no such assertion has been made. This proves both claims with the inherited AC and no extra choice principle.

Use integral homology. Let $L=K_1\cup\cdots\cup K_r$ be a nonempty labeled oriented smooth link in $S^3$ with chosen pairwise disjoint product tubes and exterior $E_L$. Then $H_1(E_L;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z^r$, with the positive meridians as its ordered basis. Each boundary torus $T_i$ has a product basis consisting of its positive meridian and a degree-one section. There is a unique degree-one class on $T_i$ whose image has zero $i$th meridian coordinate; this class is primitive and has a simple closed representative.

Let $\tau$ be an $r$-component string link with chosen disjoint product tubes in $D^2\times[0,1]$, exterior $X_\tau$, and bottom and top punctured disks $P_-$ and $P_+$. Then each $\pi_1(P_\pm)$ is free on the positive endpoint meridians, $H_1(P_\pm;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z^r$, and $H_2(P_\pm;\mathbb Z)=0$. The exterior satisfies $H_1(X_\tau;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z^r$ and $H_2(X_\tau;\mathbb Z)=0$. Each end inclusion sends its ordered positive meridian basis to the ordered positive meridian basis of $H_1(X_\tau;\mathbb Z)$. Consequently both induced homomorphisms on $H_1$ are isomorphisms and both induced homomorphisms on $H_2$ are surjective.

For every path-connected topological space $X$ and $x_0\in X$, the Hurewicz map
$$h:\pi_1(X,x_0)\longrightarrow H_1(X;\mathbb Z)$$
is surjective and has kernel $[\pi_1(X,x_0),\pi_1(X,x_0)]$. Hence it induces a natural isomorphism
$$\pi_1(X,x_0)^{\mathrm{ab}}\cong H_1(X;\mathbb Z).$$
The proof is choice-free and requires no CW, separation, local path-connectivity or local simple-connectivity assumption.

symbols $x_i$, with the free-group convention of its stated generators.

\qquad E(x_i)=1+X_i.
$$

corresponding to the positive bottom-end meridians. No freeness or

For every group $G$ and $i,j\ge1$, $[\gamma_i(G),\gamma_j(G)]\le\gamma_{i+j}(G)$. The rule $(x\gamma_{i+1},y\gamma_{j+1})\mapsto[x,y]\gamma_{i+j+1}$ is a well-defined biadditive map between the abelian lower-central factors.

derivations.claim: Let $H=\langle m_1,\ldots,m_r\rangle$. By [F1] and [F2], the images of these meridians generate $G/\Gamma_2G$, so $G=H\Gamma_2G$.

For every $k\geq2$, the quotient $\Gamma_kG/\Gamma_{k+1}G$ is generated by iterated commutators of weight $k$ in the selected meridians. For $k=2$, [F4] makes the pairing $G/\Gamma_2\times G/\Gamma_2\to\Gamma_2/\Gamma_3$ biadditive, so [F1] implies this layer is generated by brackets of the $m_i$. If the claim holds at weight $k$, then [F3] writes the next layer as generated by brackets of a degree-one class with a weight-$k$ class; [F4] makes that pairing biadditive, so [F1] again reduces the degree-one entries to the $m_i$, and the induction hypothesis reduces the other entries to brackets of those meridians. Each such iterated commutator is a word in $H$ lying in $\Gamma_{k+1}G$, so its class is in the image of $H\cap\Gamma_{k+1}G$ in the graded layer.

The conclusion of step 1.2 implies $\Gamma_kG\subseteq H\Gamma_{k+1}G$ for every $k\geq2$, because each generator of the graded layer is represented by a word in the $m_i$ that lies in $H$. Starting from $G=H\Gamma_2G$ in step 1.1 and applying these inclusions successively gives $G=H\Gamma_qG$ for every finite $q$. Therefore the image of $H$, and hence of the free group map in the statement, is all of $G/\Gamma_qG$. For $q=1$ the quotient is trivial.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC for the string-link quotient branch. Use the closed-link residue
definition one finite maximum index length at a time, so its based word-lift
data are finite.

Let $\tau$ be a based $r$-component string link with bottom meridian free group
$F_r=\langle x_1,\ldots,x_r\rangle$, exterior group $G=\pi_1(X_\tau)$, and
based string-link longitudes $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_r$. For a multi-index
$I=(i_1,\ldots,i_k,j)$ with $k\geq1$ and each index in $\{1,\ldots,r\}$,
let $w_{j,k}\in F_r/\Gamma_{k+1}F_r$ be the unique class whose image under
the bottom-end nilpotent isomorphism is the class of $\lambda_j$ in
$G/\Gamma_{k+1}G$. Define the integer coefficient
$$
\mu_\tau(I)=[X_{i_1}\cdots X_{i_k}]\,E(w_{j,k})\in\mathbb Z,
$$
where the bracket means the coefficient of that word in the finite Magnus
expansion through degree $k$. The commutator-degree lemma makes this coefficient
independent of the representative of $w_{j,k}$.

For a closed labeled link $L$, choose a common basing and its preferred
zero-self-meridian longitudes. For every component $j$ and every finite
$q\geq2$, choose a lift $w_{j,q}\in F_r/\Gamma_qF_r$ of the class of its
longitude in $G/\Gamma_qG$, where $G=\pi_1(E_L)$ and $F_r$ is free on the
component meridian symbols. Such lifts exist because those meridians generate
every finite nilpotent quotient. For $I=(i_1,\ldots,i_k,j)$, define the based
coefficient $\mu_L^b(I)$ by taking the coefficient of
$X_{i_1}\cdots X_{i_k}$ in $E(w_{j,k+1})$ through degree $k$. Let
$\Delta_I^b$ be the nonnegative greatest common divisor of the finite set of
all $\mu_L^b(J)$ for sequences $J$ of lengths from $2$ to $|I|-1$ that occur
as subsequences of cyclic permutations of $I$. The gcd of an empty set is $0$.
Define the based residue candidate
$$
\bar\mu_L^b(I):=\mu_L^b(I)\pmod{\Delta_I^b}\in
\mathbb Z/\Delta_I^b\mathbb Z,
$$
with $\mathbb Z/0\mathbb Z=\mathbb Z$. Independence of the basing and word
lifts is not part of this definition; it is a separate theorem. A based
Borromean example with $I=(1,2,3)$ uses this convention.

Assume AC. Let $\tau$ be an $r$-component based string link with $r\geq1$,
exterior $X_\tau$, and endpoint punctured disks $P_-,P_+$. Use the positive
endpoint meridians to identify $\pi_1(P_-)$ and $\pi_1(P_+)$ with the free
group $F_r=\langle x_1,\ldots,x_r\rangle$, and let
$\iota_\pm:\pi_1(P_\pm)\to\pi_1(X_\tau)$ be the based end homomorphisms,
including the chosen top connecting path. For every integer $q\geq1$, each
induced map
$$
\iota_{\pm,q}:F_r/\Gamma_qF_r\longrightarrow
\pi_1(X_\tau)/\Gamma_q\pi_1(X_\tau)
$$
is an isomorphism. Their composite
$\iota_{-,q}^{-1}\iota_{+,q}$ is the based nilpotent comparison of the labeled
top and bottom peripheral systems.

Assume AC. Let $L$ be a nonempty labeled oriented link in $S^3$, let
$I=(i_1,\ldots,i_k,j)$ have length at least two, and let $b,b'$ be any two
based meridian-longitude word systems used in the preceding definition. Then
the based residue candidates $\bar\mu_L^b(I)$ and $\bar\mu_L^{b'}(I)$ agree
under the canonical identification of their residue groups. If $L$ and $L'$ are
related by a finite sequence of self-crossing changes, the same residue is
preserved whenever the entries of $I$ are pairwise distinct. No invariance for
repeated-index sequences under self-crossing changes is asserted.

Work in the smooth category ([[def-smooth-manifold]]). Fix once and for all the
three-sphere as the one-point compactification

$$S^3:=\mathbb R^3\cup\{\infty\}$$

of Euclidean three-space, carrying its standard smooth structure, and fix the
standard orientation of $S^3$: the orientation induced by the standard
orientation of $\mathbb R^3$ under the one-point compactification, so that the
charts of the standard atlas away from $\infty$ are orientation-preserving and
the orientation is that of a connected oriented $3$-manifold in the sense of
[[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]]. For $r>0$ write
$\overline B_r:=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:\lVert x\rVert_2\le r\}$, the closed ball of
[[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]] with the following restriction convention. Smoothness on a closed ball means
local extension to a smooth map on an open neighborhood in Euclidean space;
smoothness on $M\times I$, for a smooth manifold $M$ without boundary, means
local extension across $t=0,1$ in $M\times\mathbb R$. Thus these closed domains
are not asserted to be manifolds without boundary in the cited definition.

**Links.** The **standard oriented circle** is the circle
$S^1=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ with its standard counterclockwise orientation,
regarded as a smooth $1$-manifold; a
**finite disjoint union of oriented circles** is a smooth manifold
$C=S^1\sqcup\dots\sqcup S^1$ ($k$ summands, $k\in\mathbb N$)
diffeomorphic to the disjoint union of $k$ standard oriented circles. An
**oriented link** (with $k$ components) is a smooth embedding

$$L\colon C\longrightarrow S^3$$

of such a disjoint union in the sense of [[def-smooth-embedding]]. So $L$ is
injective, is an immersion, and is a homeomorphism onto its image with the
subspace topology, and its image $L(C)$ is a finite disjoint union of smoothly
embedded circles. Thus every link considered here is finite and tame: the
smoothness of $L$ is exactly the standing convention, and no polygonal or other
tame model is used. The **components** of $L$ are the images of the individual
summands, and the number of components is $k$.

**Ambient isotopy.** Let $I=[0,1]$. An **ambient isotopy** of $S^3$ is a smooth
map

$$H\colon S^3\times I\longrightarrow S^3$$

such that $H_0=\mathrm{id}_{S^3}$, each $H_t\colon S^3\to S^3$,
$H_t(x):=H(x,t)$, is a diffeomorphism ([[def-diffeomorphism-and-local-diffeomorphism-of-manifolds]]),
and each $H_t$ is orientation-preserving with respect to the fixed orientation.
The last clause is in fact automatic: $t\mapsto H_t$ is continuous in the
$C^\infty$ topology of the diffeomorphism group, the orientation sign is locally
constant in $t$, and $H_0=\mathrm{id}$ is orientation-preserving, so it is kept
only for emphasis.

**Equivalence of links.** Two oriented links $L_0\colon C_0\to S^3$ and
$L_1\colon C_1\to S^3$ are **equivalent** (written $L_0\sim L_1$), or
**ambient isotopic**, when there are an ambient isotopy $H$ and an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism $f:C_0\to C_1$ with
$H_1\circ L_0=L_1\circ f$. Thus parametrizations and component labels are
irrelevant, while the induced orientation of each image component is preserved. The relation is an equivalence relation on links:
it is reflexive with $H=\mathrm{id}$, transitive by composing isotopies, and
symmetric because a smooth family of diffeomorphisms has a smooth family of
inverses. An equivalence class is an **(oriented) link type**.

**Moving off $\infty$.** Because the definition of equivalence allows the
isotopy to move a link through $\infty$, the standard practice of this page is
to first apply an ambient isotopy that carries a given link into the open ball,
and only then to project; every projection and every Reidemeister move below is
read after moving the link off $\infty$ into $\mathbb R^3$ in this way. The
orientation-preserving clause in the definition of ambient isotopy is exactly
what the oriented Reidemeister moves and the oriented closure construction must
respect. The unoriented theory uses the same ambient isotopies but forgets
the orientations of the link components.

**Links in the three-sphere versus links in $\mathbb R^3$.** A link contained in
$\mathbb R^3\subset S^3$ is a link in $S^3$; conversely every link may be
assumed after isotopy to lie in $\mathbb R^3$, by choosing a point outside the compact one-dimensional image and moving that
point to $\infty$ by a smooth rotation of the standard sphere. When comparing
links already in $\mathbb R^3$, an isotopy can also be arranged to avoid
$\infty$ throughout; the track-avoidance argument is given in
[[thm-oriented-reidemeister-equivalence-theorem]].

Let $D^2$ be the oriented closed disk and give $C=D^2\times[0,1]$ the product orientation. An $r$-component string link is an ordered family of pairwise disjoint smooth proper embeddings $\tau_i:[0,1]\to C$, for $1\le i\le r$, with fixed distinct endpoints $\tau_i(0)=(p_i,0)$ and $\tau_i(1)=(p_i,1)$ and fixed product collars at the endpoints. Orient each interval from bottom to top. The exterior $X_\tau$ is obtained by removing the relative interiors of chosen pairwise disjoint product tubes around the intervals. The bottom and top punctured disks $P_-$ and $P_+$ are the copies of $D^2$ with the interiors of the endpoint tube disks removed.

Choose a basepoint on the outer boundary of $P_-$, a path in the side boundary of $C$ to the corresponding top basepoint, and basing paths from these points to the component meridians. Each end inclusion, with the chosen connecting path for the top end, induces a based homomorphism $\iota_\pm:\pi_1(P_\pm)\to\pi_1(X_\tau)$. For each string component choose a parallel path on its tube boundary from the bottom endpoint to the top endpoint, and choose access paths that close it to a based loop using the fixed side connector. The resulting element of $\pi_1(X_\tau)$ is its based string-link longitude; the parallel and access paths are part of the peripheral datum. The positively oriented boundaries of the endpoint tube disks are the designated meridian loops. Stacking two string links means rescaling them into the lower and upper halves of $C$ and identifying their matching endpoint collars; closure joins each top endpoint to the matching bottom endpoint outside $C$ and retains the component labels.

For a nonempty labeled oriented link $L=K_1\cup\cdots\cup K_r$ in the oriented three-sphere, choose pairwise disjoint closed product tubes $N(K_i)$, put $E_L=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}\bigl(\bigcup_iN(K_i)\bigr)$, and write $T_i=\partial N(K_i)$. A positive meridian $\mu_i$ is the oriented boundary of a normal disk, with the disk orientation fixed by the rule that the oriented tangent of $K_i$ followed by the disk orientation gives the ambient orientation. A degree-one parallel is a simple closed curve on $T_i$ whose projection to $K_i$ has degree $+1$. A based longitude is the class of such a parallel transported to the common basepoint by a specified path. When the positive meridians form a basis of $H_1(E_L;\mathbb Z)$, the self-meridian coordinate of a longitude is its coefficient on $[\mu_i]$. A preferred zero-self-meridian longitude is a chosen degree-one parallel whose self-meridian coordinate is zero. The choice, when it exists, is part of the peripheral datum; this definition asserts neither existence nor uniqueness. Changing a common basing path conjugates the peripheral group elements simultaneously.

derivations.claim: Under the stated axiom branch [A1], a string-link isotopy induces a homeomorphism of exteriors carrying each bottom meridian and based longitude to its corresponding class. By naturality of the end inclusion, it carries the unique preimage of the longitude in $F_r/\Gamma_{k+1}$ to the corresponding preimage for the isotopic string link. The finite Magnus expansion is a group homomorphism on that quotient, so every coefficient of degree at most $k$ agrees. This proves the string-link assertion.

Under [A1], an ambient isotopy of closed links induces the peripheral correspondence in [F3]. Applying that correspondence to the based word-lift data gives the transported based residue candidate. The first assertion of [F2] proves independence of every meridian basing and finite longitude-word lift, with exactly equal lower-coefficient ideals. Applying it to the transported word data proves that the two closed-link residues agree in the same residue group.

Under [A1], a link-homotopy is generated by ambient isotopies and self-crossing changes. For pairwise-distinct indices, ambient isotopy is handled by step 2.1 and each self-crossing change is the second assertion of [F2]. Each move identifies the lower-coefficient ideals by [F2]; composing these finitely many equalities proves the asserted residue equality. No repeated-index conclusion is drawn.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Let $\tau$ be an $r$-component based string link with $r\geq1$,
exterior $X_\tau$, and endpoint punctured disks $P_-,P_+$. Use compatible jointly transported stem accesses for the positive
endpoint meridians to identify $\pi_1(P_-)$ and $\pi_1(P_+)$ with the free
group $F_r=\langle x_1,\ldots,x_r\rangle$, and let
$\iota_\pm:\pi_1(P_\pm)\to\pi_1(X_\tau)$ be the based end homomorphisms,
including the chosen top connecting path. For every integer $q\geq1$, each
induced map
$$\iota_{\pm,q}:F_r/\Gamma_qF_r\longrightarrow \pi_1(X_\tau)/\Gamma_q\pi_1(X_\tau)$$
is an isomorphism. Their composite
$\iota_{-,q}^{-1}\iota_{+,q}$ is the based nilpotent comparison of the labeled
top and bottom peripheral systems.

Arbitrary independently based positive endpoint meridians are retained as well: the map from the free symbol group $F_r$ sending $x_i$ to that chosen meridian need not identify the full fundamental group, but its composites with the end maps still induce the displayed isomorphisms on every finite lower-central quotient. Their inverse/composite is the comparison for those exact choices, and the conjugating access differences are part of the data.

Assume AC. The input is either (a) a based $r$-component string-link diagram
with its endpoint collars and product-tube parallels equal to the diagram's
blackboard push-offs, or (b) a based finite regular
diagram of a closed $r$-component labeled oriented link with chosen product
tubes, one initial strand on each component, and a common basepoint and access
paths. The finite input records its compatible common-upper-collar reference accesses. In the compatible branch the actual accesses are these, up to a common base-path change, and the parallels are the blackboard parallels already specified. In the arbitrary-choice branch it additionally records finite words in the compatible strand meridians for each access difference $g_e$, the parallel endpoint differences $h_{0,j},h_{1,j}$, and its relative meridian winding $k_j$. These are word certificates for the chosen paths, part of the supplied based-word data; no evaluation of an unencoded smooth path is claimed. In closed-link mode the preferred longitude uses its own recorded access $h_j$, which may differ from the initial-meridian access $g_j$. Arbitrary parallels are allowed in this branch, with the recorded $k_j$. The input also includes a maximum index length $N\geq2$. The output is
the integer coefficients $\mu_\tau(I)$ in string-link mode, or the based
coefficients $\mu_L^b(I)$, their lower indeterminacy data $\Delta_I^b$, and
residues $\bar\mu_L^b(I)$ in closed-link mode, for every index sequence $I$
with $2\leq |I|\leq N$.

Set $d=N-1$ and work in the truncated noncommutative ring
$$R_d=\mathbb Z\langle X_1,\ldots,X_r\rangle/\mathfrak m^{d+1},$$
where $\mathfrak m$ is the ideal generated by the letters. Carry out the
following finite procedure.

1. Verify the finite crossing, orientation, over/under, and component data. If
   a closed-link component has no underpassing point, insert a small type-I
   curl on that component in a disk meeting no other component and record the
   resulting based diagram. Give every strand $a$ the component label $j(a)$.

2. First compute in the compatible reference root symbols $x_j$, irrespective of the actual access choices. For every strand $a$, initialize its meridian series by
   $Y_a^{(1)}=1+X_{j(a)}$. For each degree $\ell=2,\ldots,d$, copy every
   $Y_a^{(\ell-1)}$ into the constant and lower-degree part of
   $Y_a^{(\ell)}$, with new degree-$\ell$ terms initially zero, and reset each
   chosen root strand to $1+X_j$. Then do one pass over each component in its
   oriented order. In closed-link mode start at the chosen initial strand and
   omit the final undercrossing back to that strand; in string-link mode start
   at the bottom endpoint and use every undercrossing through to the top
   endpoint. At an undercrossing with over-strand $o$ and source and target
   under-arcs $s,t$, use the already available $Y_o^{(\ell-1)}$ and the
   current $Y_s^{(\ell)}$ to set
   $$Y_t^{(\ell)}=\operatorname{trunc}_{\ell}\bigl((Y_o^{(\ell-1)})^{-1} Y_s^{(\ell)}Y_o^{(\ell-1)}\bigr)$$
   when the traversal is source-to-target, and set
   $$Y_s^{(\ell)}=\operatorname{trunc}_{\ell}\bigl(Y_o^{(\ell-1)} Y_t^{(\ell)}(Y_o^{(\ell-1)})^{-1}\bigr)$$
   when it is target-to-source. Here $\operatorname{trunc}_{\ell}$ discards
   monomials of degree greater than $\ell$, and every inverse is the finite
   geometric series in the nilpotent ideal of $R_d$.

3. For each component $j$, traverse its undercrossings in order and form
   $W_j=\prod_c (Y_{o(c)}^{(d)})^{\epsilon_c}$, where the factors are in
   traversal order and $\epsilon_c=+1$ for source-to-target and $-1$ for
   target-to-source. In string-link mode set $\Lambda_j=W_j$. In closed-link
   mode set
   $$\Lambda_j=(1+X_j)^{-\operatorname{wr}_j(D)}W_j,$$
   where $\operatorname{wr}_j(D)$ is the sum of the determinant signs at
   self-crossings of component $j$.

4. In the arbitrary-choice branch evaluate each supplied transport word by the strand series from step 2. Write $G_e$ for the resulting unit series, and $H_{0,j},H_{1,j}$ for the endpoint transport series. In string-link mode replace the compatible $\Lambda_j=W_j$ by
   $$H_{0,j}(1+X_j)^{k_j}W_jH_{1,j}^{-1}.$$
   In closed-link mode replace the compatible preferred series by
   $$H_j(1+X_j)^{-\operatorname{wr}_j(D)}W_jH_j^{-1},$$
   where $H_j=H_{0,j}=H_{1,j}$ is the actual longitude access difference, independently of the initial-meridian difference $G_j$. The arbitrary parallel winding cancels in the preferred correction. All powers and inverses are finite truncated operations. To express this result in the actual component-meridian symbols, form
   $$G_j(1+X_j)G_j^{-1}=1+X_j+R_j(X),\qquad \deg R_j\ge2.$$
   With new letters $V_j$, initialize $Z_j^{(1)}=V_j$ and iterate
   $$Z_j^{(s+1)}=\operatorname{trunc}_d\bigl(V_j-R_j(Z^{(s)})\bigr),\qquad 1\le s<d.$$
   Substitute $X_j=Z_j^{(d)}(V)$ in the corrected longitude series. This is its expansion in the chosen actual meridians. For the compatible branch this step is the identity. Rename the final letters $V_j$ as $X_j$.

5. For every $I=(i_1,\ldots,i_k,j)$ with $1\leq k\leq d$, read the coefficient
   of $X_{i_1}\cdots X_{i_k}$ in $\Lambda_j$. In string-link mode return this
   integer. In closed-link mode, also compute the gcd of the coefficients for
   all proper subsequences of cyclic permutations of $I$ of lengths at least
   two, with empty gcd equal to zero, and return the corresponding residue
   class.

All scans, including the supplied transport words and the $d-1$ inverse-substitution iterations, are over finite crossing, strand, degree, and index sets. The
procedure makes no polynomial-time claim. If a finite-input validation fails,
return `invalid-input`.

At an oriented crossing let $o$ be the over-strand. Orient the projection plane
by the rule that $(v_1,v_2)$ is a positive basis exactly when the ordered triple
$(n,v_1,v_2)$ is positive in the ambient three-space, where $n$ is the viewing
normal. Let $n_o$ be the positive in-plane normal characterized by the condition
that $(v_o,n_o)$ is positive in this plane. Call the under-side from
which $n_o$ points the source $s$, and the side toward which it points the
target $t$. Use a common basepoint above the diagram and paths in the upper
collar to the positive meridians $m_o,m_s,m_t$. Then
$$m_t=m_o^{-1}m_sm_o.$$
Equivalently, the crossing relator is
$m_o^{-1}m_sm_om_t^{-1}=1$. Reversing the direction of the under-strand
does not change the side-based equation.

Assume countable choice.

Let $D$ be a finite regular oriented diagram of a nonempty labeled link, after
inserting a small type-I curl on any component that has no underpassing point.
Let $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ be the positive meridians of the strands between
successive underpassing points, with the compatible common-upper-collar accesses of the local crossing rule. At a crossing $c$, write $o(c)$ for the
over-strand and $s(c),t(c)$ for the source and target under-sides defined using
the positive in-plane normal to the over-strand. Set
$$r_c=x_{o(c)}^{-1}x_{s(c)}x_{o(c)}x_{t(c)}^{-1}.$$
Then the assignment of each generator to its based positive meridian induces
an isomorphism
$$\langle x_1,\ldots,x_n\mid r_c\ (c\text{ a crossing})\rangle \cong \pi_1(E_L).$$
Any one crossing relator may be omitted without changing the represented
group. The theorem makes no claim that all relators are independent.

Arbitrary independently based positive strand meridians remain recorded: if $g_e$ is the access difference for strand $e$, its actual class is $y_e=g_ex_eg_e^{-1}$ in this reference presentation. This gives their exact group elements without claiming that the independently conjugated $y_e$ themselves freely generate the upper region or give the displayed uncorrected presentation. A common access change conjugates every generator and preserves the displayed presentation map.

Let the diagram be either a based regular string-link
diagram in $D^2\times[0,1]$ or a finite regular oriented diagram of a nonempty
labeled closed link. In string-link mode, choose the product-tube parallel to
be the blackboard push-off determined by the projected tangent, carried
through the fixed endpoint collars. Choose one initial strand on each
component. For the literal diagram word below first use compatible common-upper-collar accesses to all positive strand meridians and the induced endpoint accesses for the parallel; a common change of the complement base path is allowed. Arbitrary independent access paths and other degree-one parallels remain allowed, with their exact correction formula specified below. Traverse component $K_j$ in its orientation
(from bottom to top for a string link and once around for a closed link). At
each undercrossing $c$ of $K_j$, let $o(c)$ be the over-strand, and set
$\epsilon_c=+1$ if the traversal goes from the source side to the target side
of the over-strand's positive in-plane normal, and $\epsilon_c=-1$ if it goes
from target to source. If the undercrossings in traversal order are
$c_1,\ldots,c_s$, define
$$W_j(D)=x_{o(c_1)}^{\epsilon_{c_1}}\cdots x_{o(c_s)}^{\epsilon_{c_s}}.$$
For a string link, this word represents its based longitude. For a closed
link, it represents the blackboard parallel in $\pi_1(E_L)$. The preferred
zero-self-meridian longitude in the closed-link case is represented by
$$\lambda_j(D)=x_j^{-\operatorname{wr}_j(D)}W_j(D),$$
where $x_j$ is the initial meridian on $K_j$ and $\operatorname{wr}_j(D)$ is
the sum of crossing signs at self-crossings of $K_j$.

For the arbitrary-choice branch, write $a_e$ for the compatible access to the chosen meridian circle of strand $e$ and $a_e'$ for the actual access, after recording any endpoint-on-the-circle connectors. Put $g_e=a_e'a_e^{-1}$ and $y_e=g_e x_e g_e^{-1}$. The compatible word expressed in these actual meridians is
$$\widehat W_j=\prod_{c\text{ in traversal order}}g_{o(c)}^{-1}y_{o(c)}^{\epsilon_c}g_{o(c)}=W_j.$$
Let $a_0,a_1$ be the compatible accesses to the initial and terminal points of the blackboard parallel, with the fixed side connector included in $a_1$ for a string link. For a closed component these are the same access. Record actual accesses $a_0',a_1'$ and put $h_0=a_0'a_0^{-1}$, $h_1=a_1'a_1^{-1}$. For a chosen parallel $\beta'$ with the same endpoint coordinates as the blackboard parallel $\beta$, let $k\in\mathbb Z$ be its relative meridian winding, so $\beta'\simeq\mu_0^k\beta$ on the tube. A closed degree-one parallel is included; then $h_0=h_1=h$. Its actual based class is exactly
$$h_0x_j^k\widehat W_jh_1^{-1}.$$
For a closed component its self-meridian coordinate is $k+\operatorname{wr}_j(D)$, and its preferred zero-self-meridian correction is
$$h\,x_j^{-\operatorname{wr}_j(D)}\widehat W_j\,h^{-1}.$$
Thus arbitrary changes are retained as explicit transport and winding factors; independent access choices are not silently assumed to give the literal uncorrected product in the $y_e$.

Let $L=K_1\cup\cdots\cup K_r$ be a nonempty labeled oriented link in $S^3$,
let $G=\pi_1(E_L)$, and choose one based positive meridian $m_i\in G$ for each
component. For every integer $q\geq1$, the homomorphism from the free group
$F_r=\langle x_1,\ldots,x_r\rangle$ defined by $x_i\mapsto m_i$ induces a
surjection
$$F_r\longrightarrow G/\Gamma_qG.$$

Assume AC. Let $\tau$ be an $r$-component based string link with $r\geq1$,
exterior $X_\tau$, and endpoint punctured disks $P_-,P_+$. Use compatible jointly transported stem accesses for the positive
endpoint meridians to identify $\pi_1(P_-)$ and $\pi_1(P_+)$ with the free
group $F_r=\langle x_1,\ldots,x_r\rangle$, and let
$\iota_\pm:\pi_1(P_\pm)\to\pi_1(X_\tau)$ be the based end homomorphisms,
including the chosen top connecting path. For every integer $q\geq1$, each
induced map
$$\iota_{\pm,q}:F_r/\Gamma_qF_r\longrightarrow \pi_1(X_\tau)/\Gamma_q\pi_1(X_\tau)$$
is an isomorphism. Their composite
$\iota_{-,q}^{-1}\iota_{+,q}$ is the based nilpotent comparison of the labeled
top and bottom peripheral systems.

Arbitrary independently based positive endpoint meridians are retained as well: the map from the free symbol group $F_r$ sending $x_i$ to that chosen meridian need not identify the full fundamental group, but its composites with the end maps still induce the displayed isomorphisms on every finite lower-central quotient. Their inverse/composite is the comparison for those exact choices, and the conjugating access differences are part of the data.

Let $F_r$ be the free group and $E$ the Magnus expansion from the preceding
definition, with augmentation ideal $\mathfrak m$. If
$u\in\Gamma_pF_r$ and $v\in\Gamma_qF_r$ for $p,q\ge1$, then
$$
E([u,v])\in 1+\mathfrak m^{p+q}.
$$
Consequently $E(\Gamma_qF_r)\subseteq1+\mathfrak m^q$ for every $q\ge1$.
In particular, reduction of $E$ modulo $\mathfrak m^{d+1}$ factors through
$F_r/\Gamma_{d+1}F_r$ and its coefficients through degree $d$ are independent
of the representative word.

Assume AC for the string-link quotient branch. Use the closed-link residue
definition one finite maximum index length at a time, so its based word-lift
data are finite.

Let $\tau$ be a based $r$-component string link with bottom meridian symbol group
$F_r=\langle x_1,\ldots,x_r\rangle$, exterior group $G=\pi_1(X_\tau)$, and
based string-link longitudes $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_r$. With compatible stem accesses this free group identifies the full endpoint fundamental group. For arbitrary independently based meridians, use instead its meridian map on each finite nilpotent quotient, which is still an isomorphism by the end-identification theorem; no full-group free-basis assertion is made. Longitudes retain their specified parallel and access data. For a multi-index
$I=(i_1,\ldots,i_k,j)$ with $k\geq1$ and each index in $\{1,\ldots,r\}$,
let $w_{j,k}\in F_r/\Gamma_{k+1}F_r$ be the unique class whose image under
the bottom-end nilpotent isomorphism is the class of $\lambda_j$ in
$G/\Gamma_{k+1}G$. Define the integer coefficient
$$\mu_\tau(I)=[X_{i_1}\cdots X_{i_k}]\,E(w_{j,k})\in\mathbb Z,$$
where the bracket means the coefficient of that word in the finite Magnus
expansion through degree $k$. The commutator-degree lemma makes this coefficient
independent of the representative of $w_{j,k}$.

For a closed labeled link $L$, choose a common basing and its preferred
zero-self-meridian longitudes. For every component $j$ and every finite
$q\geq2$, choose a lift $w_{j,q}\in F_r/\Gamma_qF_r$ of the class of its
longitude in $G/\Gamma_qG$, where $G=\pi_1(E_L)$ and $F_r$ is free on the
component meridian symbols. Such lifts exist because those meridians generate
every finite nilpotent quotient. For $I=(i_1,\ldots,i_k,j)$, define the based
coefficient $\mu_L^b(I)$ by taking the coefficient of
$X_{i_1}\cdots X_{i_k}$ in $E(w_{j,k+1})$ through degree $k$. Let
$\Delta_I^b$ be the nonnegative greatest common divisor of the finite set of
all $\mu_L^b(J)$ for sequences $J$ of lengths from $2$ to $|I|-1$ that occur
as subsequences of cyclic permutations of $I$. The gcd of an empty set is $0$.
Define the based residue candidate
$$\bar\mu_L^b(I):=\mu_L^b(I)\pmod{\Delta_I^b}\in \mathbb Z/\Delta_I^b\mathbb Z,$$
with $\mathbb Z/0\mathbb Z=\mathbb Z$. Independence of the basing and word
lifts is not part of this definition; it is a separate theorem. A based
Borromean example with $I=(1,2,3)$ uses this convention.

derivations.claim: Under [A1], the validation stage scans a finite diagram. The degree loop runs from $2$ to $d$, each component traversal visits finitely many undercrossings, and each multiplication, inverse, and truncation in $R_d$ involves only finitely many monomials of degree at most $d$. The output stage scans finitely many index sequences and their finitely many proper subsequences and cyclic permutations. Thus every loop is finite and the procedure terminates.

At degree one, every arc meridian on component $j$ maps to $1+X_j$: conjugate meridians have the same abelianization, and the component meridians are the chosen basis in the free source. This is exactly the initialization $Y_a^{(1)}$.

Assume the series $Y_a^{(\ell-1)}$ correctly represent every strand meridian through degree $\ell-1$, and that $Y_s^{(\ell)}$ represents the source meridian through degree $\ell$. At a source-to-target crossing the group relation is $m_t=m_o^{-1}m_sm_o$; at a target-to-source crossing it is $m_s=m_om_tm_o^{-1}$ by [F2]. In a conjugation $Y_o^{-1}Y_sY_o$, replacing the over-series by another series with the same terms through degree $\ell-1$ changes the product only in degree at least $\ell+1$: the degree-$\ell$ discrepancy in $Y_o$ commutes with the constant term $1$ and first meets a positive-degree term of $Y_s$ in degree $\ell+1$. The two update formulas therefore give the correct target meridian through degree $\ell$. Induction over the finite spanning paths and then over $\ell=2,\ldots,d$ proves every assigned strand series is correct through degree $d$.

By [F3], multiplying the ordered over-meridian factors gives the based string-link longitude or the closed-link blackboard parallel with its self-writhe correction. The arc-series just established make $\Lambda_j$ its Magnus expansion through degree $d$.

In the arbitrary-choice branch, evaluating the finite transport words gives their actual compatible-coordinate expansions by step 2.1 and [F5]. The formulas of [F3] therefore give the actual selected longitude expansion before changing root variables. The actual root meridian is $g_jx_jg_j^{-1}$, so its series is $1+X_j+R_j$ with $R_j$ of degree at least two. Substitution of two letter systems agreeing through degree $s$ into $R_j$ gives results agreeing through degree $s+1$, since each monomial has at least two letters. Hence the displayed iteration improves the inverse equation by one degree at each pass, starting correctly at degree one. At pass $d$ it solves $Z_j+R_j(Z)=V_j$ exactly in the truncated ring. The same degree argument proves uniqueness, and consequently also the other composition identity. Thus it is the inverse formal change from compatible to actual meridian coordinates. This also agrees with the group-theoretic change on the finite nilpotent quotient: substitution by the conjugates has identity degree-one map and induces an isomorphism on each finite free nilpotent quotient: apply the arbitrary-basing branch of [F4] to the trivial string link, whose compatible endpoint group is $F_r$, with these exact independently conjugated meridians. Its Magnus series satisfies the same unique inverse equations. The corrected-and-substituted series is therefore exactly the longitude expansion in the chosen actual symbols, including independently based endpoints and all supplied relative winding. No full-group free-basis assertion or unrecorded access cancellation is used.

Under the stated axiom branch [A1], for $I=(i_1,\ldots,i_k,j)$ with $k\leq d$, [F5] says the coefficient of $X_{i_1}\cdots X_{i_k}$ depends only on the longitude class in $F_r/\Gamma_{k+1}$ and is independent of the chosen representative. In string-link mode, [F4] identifies that class uniquely via the bottom-end isomorphism. In closed-link mode, [F4] supplies the required component-meridian lift; the procedure uses the based lift determined by its root arcs and traversal. Thus the coefficient read from $\Lambda_j$ is exactly the based coefficient in [F6].

In closed-link mode, each lower coefficient used for $\Delta_I^b$ is computed by the same procedure at its own finite degree; the finite gcd and quotient operation are exactly those in [F6]. Hence the returned indeterminacy and residue candidate are correct for the selected based word-lift data. The theorem asserts no independence of those choices; that is the separate basing theorem.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $D$ be a finite regular oriented diagram of a nonempty labeled link, with
$n\geq1$ crossings and at least one underpassing point on each component. Fix a
smooth height realization $L_D=\{(\gamma(s),\eta(s))\}\subset\mathbb R^2\times[-1,0]$
such that $\eta(s)=-1$ exactly at the $n$ underpassing points and
$\eta(s)>-1$ elsewhere; at each crossing the overpassing point has height
strictly greater than $-1$. Put
$$A=(\mathbb R^2\times[-1,\infty))\cup\{\infty\},\quad B=(\mathbb R^2\times(-\infty,-1])\cup\{\infty\},\quad \Sigma=(\mathbb R^2\times\{-1\})\cup\{\infty\},$$
and write $X=S^3\setminus L_D$, $A_L=A\cap X$, $B_L=B\cap X$,
and $\Sigma_L=\Sigma\cap X$. Also put
$A_L^\circ=((\mathbb R^2\times(-1,\infty))\cup\{\infty\})\cap X$.
Then $\Sigma_L$ is a path-connected sphere
with $n$ punctures, $A_L\cup B_L=X$, and $A_L\cap B_L=\Sigma_L$. There are
path-connected open sets $U,V\subset X$ such that $X=U\cup V$, $U$ deformation
retracts onto $A_L$, $V$ deformation retracts onto $B_L$, and $U\cap V$
deformation retracts onto $\Sigma_L$. The set $B_L$ is contractible. The small
circles in $\Sigma_L$ around the $n$ punctures normally generate
$\pi_1(\Sigma_L)$, and they still normally generate after any one circle is
omitted. The inclusion $A_L^\circ\hookrightarrow A_L$ is a homotopy
equivalence. Radial retraction in each chosen product tube identifies
$\pi_1(X)$ with the fundamental group of the chosen link exterior.

Let $X=U\cup V$, where $U$ and $V$ are open path-connected subsets of $X$, let $U\cap V$ be path-connected, and fix $x_0\in U\cap V$. For the inclusion-induced maps in the diagram

$$\pi_1(U,x_0)\longleftarrow\pi_1(U\cap V,x_0)\longrightarrow\pi_1(V,x_0),$$

the group $\pi_1(X,x_0)$, together with the two inclusion-induced homomorphisms, is a pushout ([[def-pushout-of-group-homomorphisms]]). Equivalently, the canonical homomorphism from any pushout $P$ of the displayed diagram to $\pi_1(X,x_0)$ is an isomorphism. No injectivity of either map from the overlap group is assumed.

Assume countable choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $i:S\hookrightarrow M$ be a closed smooth embedded submanifold. Then there are an open neighbourhood $\Omega\subseteq\nu(S)$ of the zero section in the quotient normal bundle and a diffeomorphism $\Phi:\Omega\to U$ onto an open neighbourhood $U$ of $i(S)$ in $M$, with $\Phi(0_p)=i(p)$ for every $p\in S$. Thus $S$ has a tubular neighbourhood in $M$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $M$ be a connected smooth $3$-manifold without boundary, and let $S\subset M$
be a nonempty closed connected smooth embedded surface with
$\pi_1(S)=1$. Suppose there is an open neighborhood $N$ of $S$ such that
$N$ is path-connected and simply connected, and $N\setminus S$ has exactly two
path-connected simply connected components $N_-$ and $N_+$. Suppose also that
$M\setminus S$ is path-connected and contains an embedded compact arc
$\nu$ joining $N_-$ to $N_+$, with an open tubular neighborhood $T$ such that
$T\cap N$ consists of exactly two disjoint open $3$-balls, one in each side
component. Then
$$
\pi_1(M)\cong \pi_1(M\setminus S)*\mathbb Z.
$$
The cyclic factor is represented by a loop that joins the two sides of $N$ and
returns between them through $M\setminus S$.

Let $D^2$ be the oriented closed disk and give $C=D^2\times[0,1]$ the product orientation. An $r$-component string link is an ordered family of pairwise disjoint smooth proper embeddings $\tau_i:[0,1]\to C$, for $1\le i\le r$, with fixed distinct endpoints $\tau_i(0)=(p_i,0)$ and $\tau_i(1)=(p_i,1)$ and fixed product collars at the endpoints. Orient each interval from bottom to top. The exterior $X_\tau$ is obtained by removing the relative interiors of chosen pairwise disjoint product tubes around the intervals. The bottom and top punctured disks $P_-$ and $P_+$ are the copies of $D^2$ with the interiors of the endpoint tube disks removed.

Choose a basepoint on the outer boundary of $P_-$, a path in the side boundary of $C$ to the corresponding top basepoint, and basing paths from these points to the component meridians. Each end inclusion, with the chosen connecting path for the top end, induces a based homomorphism $\iota_\pm:\pi_1(P_\pm)\to\pi_1(X_\tau)$. For each string component choose a parallel path on its tube boundary from the bottom endpoint to the top endpoint, and choose access paths that close it to a based loop using the fixed side connector. The resulting element of $\pi_1(X_\tau)$ is its based string-link longitude; the parallel and access paths are part of the peripheral datum. The positively oriented boundaries of the endpoint tube disks are the designated meridian loops. Stacking two string links means rescaling them into the lower and upper halves of $C$ and identifying their matching endpoint collars; closure joins each top endpoint to the matching bottom endpoint outside $C$ and retains the component labels.

For a nonempty labeled oriented link $L=K_1\cup\cdots\cup K_r$ in the oriented three-sphere, choose pairwise disjoint closed product tubes $N(K_i)$, put $E_L=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}\bigl(\bigcup_iN(K_i)\bigr)$, and write $T_i=\partial N(K_i)$. A positive meridian $\mu_i$ is the oriented boundary of a normal disk, with the disk orientation fixed by the rule that the oriented tangent of $K_i$ followed by the disk orientation gives the ambient orientation. A degree-one parallel is a simple closed curve on $T_i$ whose projection to $K_i$ has degree $+1$. A based longitude is the class of such a parallel transported to the common basepoint by a specified path. When the positive meridians form a basis of $H_1(E_L;\mathbb Z)$, the self-meridian coordinate of a longitude is its coefficient on $[\mu_i]$. A preferred zero-self-meridian longitude is a chosen degree-one parallel whose self-meridian coordinate is zero. The choice, when it exists, is part of the peripheral datum; this definition asserts neither existence nor uniqueness. Changing a common basing path conjugates the peripheral group elements simultaneously.

derivations.claim: Let $A_L^\circ=((\mathbb R^2\times(-1,\infty))\cup\{\infty\})\setminus L_D$. By [F1], $\pi_1(A_L^\circ)\cong\pi_1(A_L)$. A small neighborhood $H$ of $\infty$ in $A_L^\circ$ is the open upper half-ball together with its cone vertex $\infty$, disjoint from $L_D$; other points of the level-sphere boundary have been deleted. The open cover $A_L^\circ=M\cup H$ has intersection $H\setminus\{\infty\}$, which is homeomorphic to $(0,1)\times\operatorname{int}(S^2_+)$ and is contractible because the open hemisphere $\operatorname{int}(S^2_+)$ is an open disk. Since $H$ is also contractible, [F2] gives $\pi_1(M)\cong\pi_1(A_L^\circ)$.

Each $D_j$ is the image of the open region $(s,t)\mapsto(\gamma(s),-1+t(\eta(s)+1))$ with $s\in I_j$ and $0<t<1$; this is an embedded open disk. At a projected double point, the underpassing branch has height $-1$ and is absent from $M$, while the overpassing branch has height greater than $-1$. Thus sheets over distinct intervals are disjoint. Each sheet is closed in $M$: its only limit points outside itself lie on the excluded plane $z=-1$ or on the excluded link. Hence it is a proper smooth embedded simply connected surface.

At a fixed vertical line, every point of $Z$ lies above all link points on that line. Since every link height is at most $0$, the straight homotopy $(x,y,z)\mapsto(x,y,(1-t)z+t)$ ($0\le t\le1$) stays above those link points and contracts $Z$ onto the plane $z=1$. This plane is contained in $Z$, so $Z$ is contractible.

For $j=1,\ldots,n$, put $M_j=M\setminus\bigcup_{k>j}D_k$. Then $M_0=Z$ and $M_j=M_{j-1}\cup D_j$. At each stage $M_{j-1}$ is path-connected: it contains path-connected $Z$, and every point of an earlier sheet joins to $Z$ along a short normal segment. Orient $D_j$ by its interval and height coordinates. The ambient orientation orients its normal line, so that line bundle is trivial; a bundle metric gives the unique positive unit vector in each fibre. By [A1, F3], choose a tubular neighborhood disjoint from the other sheets. Radial contraction shows the whole neighborhood and each of its two side components are simply connected. Choose a small positive meridian circle around an interior point of the $j$th strand in a ball disjoint from all other sheets. It meets $D_j$ transversely once. Remove a short open arc about that intersection; the remaining compact arc lies in $M_{j-1}$ and joins the two sides of $D_j$. Shrink the tubular neighborhood so that it meets this arc only in two end balls. This gives the corridor required by [F4], and its complement hypothesis holds because $M_j\setminus D_j=M_{j-1}$ is path-connected.

The cut lemma [F4] gives $\pi_1(M_j)\cong\pi_1(M_{j-1})*\mathbb Z$. Its cyclic generator is represented by the short meridian arc crossing $D_j$ followed by the complementary arc from step 3.1. Joining this loop to the basepoint by its access path in $Z$ gives exactly $x_j$, with positive orientation fixed by [F5]. Since $\pi_1(M_0)=\pi_1(Z)=1$, induction yields that $\pi_1(M)$ is free on $x_1,\ldots,x_n$. Step 1.1 identifies this with $\pi_1(A_L)$.
