> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a specified real separable Banach or Hilbert parameter space with metric $d_X(x,x')=\|x-x'\|_X$ and its norm topology. Let $(Y,d_Y)$ be a metric data space equipped with a sigma-algebra $\Sigma_Y$, let $U\subseteq X$ be a nonempty admissible truth set, and let $F:U\to Y$ be a forward map. Choose a Borel set $D\in\mathcal B(X)$ with $D\subseteq U$ such that the restriction $G:=F|_D:D\to Y$ is measurable for the trace Borel sigma-algebra $\mathcal B(D):=\{D\cap A:A\in\mathcal B(X)\}$. A prior on this forward domain is a Borel probability measure $\mu$ on $X$ such that $\mu(D)=1$. Its restriction $\mu|_D$, defined by $\mu|_D(A)=\mu(A)$ for $A\in\mathcal B(D)$, is then a probability measure on $D$, and the induced data law is $G_\#(\mu|_D)$, defined by $G_\#(\mu|_D)(E)=(\mu|_D)(G^{-1}(E))$ for $E\in\Sigma_Y$. A Borel probability on $X$ with $\mu(D)<1$ is not a prior on this declared forward domain.

Let $X$ be a separable real Banach space with its norm topology, $D\subseteq X$ a Borel forward-map domain, and $\mu_0$ a Borel probability measure on $X$ with $\mu_0(D)=1$. Write $\mu_{0,D}$ for its restriction to $D$, so $\mu_{0,D}(A)=\mu_0(A)$ for $A\in\mathcal B(D):=\{D\cap B:B\in\mathcal B(X)\}$. Let $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ be a measurable data space. A likelihood potential is a function $\Phi:D\times\mathsf Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ that is measurable from $\bigl(D\times\mathsf Y,\mathcal B(D)\otimes\mathcal Y\bigr)$ to $\bigl((-\infty,+\infty],\mathcal B((-\infty,+\infty])\bigr)$, where $\mathcal B((-\infty,+\infty])$ is the trace of $\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R})$ on $(-\infty,+\infty]$. Viewing $\Phi$ via the inclusion $(-\infty,+\infty]\hookrightarrow\overline{\mathbb R}$, it is also product-measurable as an extended-real-valued map because for every Borel set $B\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$, $\Phi^{-1}(B)=\Phi^{-1}(B\cap(-\infty,+\infty])$ is measurable by the definition of the trace sigma-algebra. Here $+\infty$ is allowed and $-\infty$ is excluded; set $e^{-\infty}=0$. The scalar map $t\mapsto e^{-t}$ on this range is continuous at finite $t$, and is continuous at $+\infty$: given $\varepsilon>0$, the limit supplies $a\in\mathbb R$ such that $t>a$ implies $e^{-t}<\varepsilon$, and the order-topology neighborhood $(a,+\infty]$ maps into $[0,\varepsilon)$. Hence it is Borel, so $L_\Phi:D\times\mathsf Y\to[0,+\infty)$, $L_\Phi(u;y):=e^{-\Phi(u;y)}$, is product-measurable by composition, and each section $u\mapsto L_\Phi(u;y)$ is nonnegative and measurable. Define its evidence by
$$
Z_\Phi(y):=\int_D L_\Phi(u;y)\,\mu_{0,D}(du)\in[0,+\infty].
$$
For each fixed $y$ with $0<Z_\Phi(y)<+\infty$, define the normalized fiberwise update on $A\in\mathcal B(D)$ by
$$\Pi^y(A):=\frac{\int_A L_\Phi(u;y)\,\mu_{0,D}(du)}{Z_\Phi(y)}.$$
No normalized fiberwise update is defined by this formula when $Z_\Phi(y)=0$ or $Z_\Phi(y)=+\infty$.

For a data-indexed claim, an observation model and its version convention must also be specified. In the dominated case, let $Q$ be a proper probability kernel from $(D,\mathcal B(D))$ to $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$, let $\nu$ be a sigma-finite measure on $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$, and suppose $Q(u,B)=\int_B L_\Phi(u;y)\,\nu(dy)$ for every $u\in D$ and $B\in\mathcal Y$. Then $Z_\Phi$ is the density of the prior-predictive data law with respect to $\nu$; a data-indexed conditional-law version uses $\Pi^y$ when $0<Z_\Phi(y)<\infty$ and the prior $\mu_{0,D}$ when $Z_\Phi(y)$ is zero or infinite. These filled fibers have zero prior-predictive mass, and their chosen values are not normalized fiberwise updates. More generally, for a proper Bayesian model with standard-Borel parameter space $(D,\mathcal B(D))$ and data space $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ (each measurably isomorphic to the Borel space of a Polish space), the Axiom of Choice guarantees a data-indexed posterior kernel; its values are unique as probability measures outside one data-marginal-null set, and values on that null set remain version choices. The dominated construction is choice-free; the separate standard-Borel existence branch assumes the Axiom of Choice.

Let $X$ be a separable real Banach space with norm $\|\cdot\|_X$, let $D\subseteq X$ be Borel, and let $\mu_0$ be a Borel probability on $X$ with $\mu_0(D)=1$. Here $\mathcal B(X)$ is generated by the norm-open sets. Give $D$ the relative topology and Borel sigma-algebra $\mathcal B(D)=\{D\cap B:B\in\mathcal B(X)\}$, and let $\mu_{0,D}$ be the restriction of $\mu_0$ to $D$, so $\mu_{0,D}(A)=\mu_0(A)$ for $A\in\mathcal B(D)$. Let $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ be a measurable data space. Assume $\Phi:D\times\mathsf Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ is measurable from $\bigl(D\times\mathsf Y,\mathcal B(D)\otimes\mathcal Y\bigr)$ to $\bigl((-infty,+\infty],\mathcal B((-infty,+\infty])\bigr)$, where $\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R})$ is generated by the order topology on the extended real line and $\mathcal B((-infty,+\infty])$ is its trace on $(-\infty,+\infty]$; thus $+\infty$ is allowed and $-\infty$ is excluded. Let $\mathsf Y_0\subseteq\mathsf Y$. Suppose that for every $y\in\mathsf Y_0$, the section $u\mapsto\Phi(u;y)$ is finite and continuous as a real-valued function on $D$ with its relative topology inherited from the norm topology. Suppose there is one Borel function $M_1:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$, independent of $y\in\mathsf Y_0$, such that
$$
\Phi(u;y)\ge -M_1(\|u\|_X)\quad(u\in D,\ y\in\mathsf Y_0),\qquad
\int_D e^{M_1(\|u\|_X)}\,\mu_{0,D}(du)<\infty.
$$
Define $\operatorname{supp}\mu_0:=\{x\in X:\mu_0(U)>0\text{ for every open neighborhood }U\text{ of }x\}$. Then for every $y\in\mathsf Y_0$, the evidence $Z_\Phi(y)$ is finite and strictly positive, and the normalized fiberwise update $\Pi^y$ is a probability measure on $D$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $W$ be a centered Borel Gaussian random
element in a real separable Banach space $B$. There is a constant $a>0$ such
that
$$E\exp(a\|W\|^2)<\infty.$$
In particular, $E\|W\|^2<\infty$.

A topological space is **Polish** when it is separable ([[def-separable-space]]) and completely metrizable: its topology is induced by some complete metric ([[lem-complete-remetrisation]]). No particular compatible complete metric or countable dense subset is part of the structure.
Assume AC. Every Borel probability on a Polish space S is tight.

Assume AC and countable choice. Let $\mu$ be a centered tight Borel Gaussian
law on a real separable Banach
space $B$, and let $H\subseteq B$ be its covariance RKHS. Define
$\operatorname{supp}\mu$ to be the set of $x\in B$ for which every open
neighborhood has positive $\mu$-measure. Then
$$\operatorname{supp}\mu=\overline H^{\,B}.$$

Assume AC. Let $W$ be a centered Borel Gaussian random element in a real separable
Banach space $B$, with law $\mu$. For $\ell\in B^*$ define
$$C\ell=E[\ell(W)W]\in B,\qquad Q(\ell,m)=E[\ell(W)m(W)]\quad(\ell,m\in B^*).$$
The **Cameron–Martin reproducing-kernel Hilbert space** $H$ is the completion
of $B^*/N$ in the inner product induced by $Q$, where
$N=\{\ell\in B^*:Q(\ell,\ell)=0\}$. The canonical map sends the class of
$\ell$ to $C\ell$ and extends continuously to an injective map $i:H\to B$;
we identify $H$ with its image in $B$ and use the completed Hilbert norm
$\|\cdot\|_H$. The preceding construction is well-defined by
[[thm-banach-gaussian-covariance-rkhs-is-well-defined]].

The term *RKHS* here denotes this covariance-induced Hilbert space of shifts
inside $B$; it is not the space of all continuous functions on an arbitrary
index set.

Assume AC. Under the hypotheses and notation of
[[def-banach-gaussian-covariance-operator-and-rkhs]], each $C\ell$ exists as a
Bochner integral; $Q$ is a finite positive-semidefinite bilinear form;
$N=\{\ell:Q(\ell,\ell)=0\}$ is its nullspace; and the induced map from the
completion of $B^*/N$ to $B$ is continuous and injective. Thus the definition
identifies a Hilbert space of shifts in $B$.

Assume AC. Let $\mu$ be a centered tight Borel Gaussian law on a real separable Banach
space $B$, and let $H\subset B$ be its covariance RKHS. The closed Hilbert
unit ball
$$H_1=\{h\in H:\|h\|_H\le1\}$$
is compact in the Banach norm.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, the Hahn–Banach theorem, and countable choice. Let $B$ be a real separable Banach space, and let $W$ be a centered Borel Gaussian random element with law $\mu$. Define its covariance by $C\ell=\mathbb E[\ell(W)W]$ for $\ell\in B^*$, let $N=\{\ell:\mathbb E[\ell(W)^2]=0\}$, and let $E$ be the completion of $B^*/N$ with inner product $\langle[\ell],[m]\rangle_E=\mathbb E[\ell(W)m(W)]$. Let $i:E\to B$ be the canonical injection extending $[\ell]\mapsto C\ell$. For $z\in B$ and $r>0$, write $\overline B_B(z,r)=\{x\in B:\|x-z\|_B\le r\}$. Then for any $h_1,h_2\in E$,
$$ \frac{\mu(\overline B_B(ih_1,r))}{\mu(\overline B_B(ih_2,r))} \longrightarrow \exp\!\left(\frac{\|h_2\|_E^2-\|h_1\|_E^2}{2}\right) \qquad(r\downarrow0). $$
The denominator is positive for every $r>0$.

Let $B$ be a separable Banach space with norm $\|\cdot\|_B$, and let $\Pi$ be a Borel probability measure on $B$. For $z\in B$ and $r>0$, write $\overline B_B(z,r)=\{u\in B:\|u-z\|_B\le r\}$ and $m_r(z)=\Pi(\overline B_B(z,r))$. A **strong small-ball MAP** is a point $z\in B$ for which
$$ \frac{m_r(z)}{\sup_{x\in B}m_r(x)}\longrightarrow1\qquad(r\downarrow0). $$
Assume AC for the covariance-induced Cameron–Martin notation. If $\Pi$ is a posterior law formed by weighting a centered Gaussian prior $\Pi_0$ on $B$, let $C\ell=\int_B\ell(u)u\,\Pi_0(du)$ be its covariance operator and let $E$ be the completion of $B^*/\ker C$ with inner product $\langle[\ell],[m]\rangle_E=m(C\ell)$; the canonical injection $i:E\to B$ extends $[\ell]\mapsto C\ell$. A **Cameron–Martin ratio mode** is a point $ih\in iE$ such that, for every $k\in E$, the denominator is positive for all sufficiently small $r$ and
$$ \lim_{r\downarrow0}\frac{m_r(ih)}{m_r(ik)} $$
exists and is at least $1$. This pairwise comparison over fixed Cameron–Martin centers does not assert the global strong small-ball MAP condition.

For every $r>0$, $\sup_{x\in B}m_r(x)>0$: a countable dense subset gives a countable cover of $B$ by radius-$r$ open balls, each contained in its corresponding closed ball, and countable subadditivity rules out all such closed balls having zero probability.

Every bounded sequence of reals has a convergent subsequence: if $(x_k)$ is a
sequence of reals and there is $M \in \mathbb{R}$ with $|x_k| \le M$ for every
$k \in \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-sequence]]), then there is a strictly increasing
$n : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and a real $L$ with $x_{n_j} \to L$.

Equivalently: the subsequential limit set of a bounded sequence is nonempty
([[def-subsequential-limit]]).

The theorem is the exact repair of the false claim that a bounded sequence
converges. A bounded
sequence need not converge, and the alternating sequence is the standing witness;
what boundedness does force is that *some* subsequence converges. The converse of
the theorem is false, and badly so: a sequence with a convergent subsequence need
not be bounded.

derivations.claim:
Choose $0<\varepsilon<a$ with $a$ from [F3]. The lower bound gives $\Phi(u)\ge M_\varepsilon-\varepsilon\|u\|_B^2$. Define the nonnegative Borel function $M_1(t)=\max\{0,\varepsilon t^2-M_\varepsilon\}$. Then $\Phi(u)\ge-M_1(\|u\|_B)$ and
$$ e^{M_1(\|u\|_B)} \le 1+e^{-M_\varepsilon}e^{\varepsilon\|u\|_B^2}. $$
The right side is $\mu$-integrable by [F3]. Since $\Phi$ is locally Lipschitz it is finite and continuous on $B$. Apply [F2] with the single datum and $D=B$; the prior definition in [F1] makes $\mu$ a prior on $B$. Thus $0<Z<\infty$ and $\Pi$ is a probability.

Fix $h\in E$. Local Lipschitz continuity at $ih$ supplies constants $L_h<\infty$ and $\rho_h>0$ such that $|\Phi(u)-\Phi(ih)|\le L_h r$ whenever $\|u-ih\|_B\le r<\rho_h$. Therefore
$$ e^{-\Phi(ih)-L_hr}\mu(\overline B_B(ih,r)) \le \int_{\overline B_B(ih,r)}e^{-\Phi(u)}\,\mu(du) \le e^{-\Phi(ih)+L_hr}\mu(\overline B_B(ih,r)). $$
For fixed $h_1,h_2\in E$, divide the two integral bounds and cancel the common normalizer $Z$ in [F1]. The factors from the Lipschitz errors tend to $1$, and [F7] gives
$$ \frac{\Pi(\overline B_B(ih_1,r))}{\Pi(\overline B_B(ih_2,r))} \longrightarrow e^{\Phi(ih_2)-\Phi(ih_1)} e^{(\|h_2\|_E^2-\|h_1\|_E^2)/2} =e^{I(ih_2)-I(ih_1)}. $$
The denominator is positive for small $r$: [F4] gives positive prior mass to every open ball about $ih_2$ (since $ih_2\in iE$), and the likelihood is strictly positive and continuous there.

Let $C_i=\|i:E\to B\|$. If $E=\{0\}$, $I$ has the sole candidate $0$ and is minimized there. Otherwise $C_i>0$. Choose $\varepsilon<1/(4C_i^2)$ and use the potential lower bound to obtain, for every $h\in E$,
$$ I(ih)\ge M_\varepsilon+\frac12\|h\|_E^2-\varepsilon\|ih\|_B^2 \ge M_\varepsilon+\frac14\|h\|_E^2. $$
Since $I(0)=\Phi(0)$ is finite, $\inf_E I$ is finite and any minimizing sequence is bounded in $E$.

Choose a minimizing sequence $(h_n)$ in $E$ and, by [F9], pass to a subsequence for which $\|h_n\|_E\to L$. Its images lie in a fixed multiple of the closed $E$-unit ball, whose image is compact in $B$ by [F6]. Pass to a further subsequence with $ih_n\to v$ in $B$; compactness means $v=ih$ for some $h\in E$. For each $\ell\in B^*$, [F5] gives
$$ |\ell(ih)|=\lim_n|\ell(ih_n)| =\lim_n|\langle h_n,[\ell]\rangle_E| \le L\|[\ell]\|_E. $$
The classes $[\ell]$ are dense in $E$ by [F5]. For every unit $g\in E$, choose nonzero classes $[\ell_n]\to g$ and normalize them; then $[\ell_n]/\|[\ell_n]\|_E\to g$. Thus the normalized covariance classes are dense in the unit sphere, and the supremum of $|\langle h,[\ell]\rangle_E|$ over them is $\|h\|_E$. The displayed bound gives $\|h\|_E\le L$. Local Lipschitz continuity gives $\Phi(ih_n)\to\Phi(ih)$, and therefore
$$ I(ih)\le\lim_n\left(\Phi(ih_n)+\frac12\|h_n\|_E^2\right)=\inf_E I. $$
Thus $I$ attains its finite minimum.

By [F7], the posterior ball ratio for fixed $ih,ik\in iE$ is $e^{I(ik)-I(ih)}$. This limit is at least $1$ for every $k\in E$ exactly when $I(ih)\le I(ik)$ for every $k\in E$. By [F8], those points are precisely the Cameron–Martin ratio modes. The comparison is only over fixed centers in $iE$; no supremum over all $B$ centers has been controlled, so it does not establish a global strong small-ball MAP.

Statement: AC, HB and countable choice are explicit; the minimizer argument uses compact embedding and a real bounded-sequence subsequence.
Step 4.1 proves every minimizer is a Cameron-Martin ratio mode.
Step 4.1 proves every Cameron-Martin ratio mode minimizes I.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Assume AC. Let $d\ge1$, $m\in\mathbb R^d$, and let $\Sigma$ be a real symmetric positive-definite $d\times d$ matrix. If $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$, then its law has Lebesgue density
$$f_{m,\Sigma}(x)=(2\pi)^{-d/2}\det(\Sigma)^{-1/2} \exp\!\left(-\tfrac12(x-m)^T\Sigma^{-1}(x-m)\right), \qquad x\in\mathbb R^d.$$

Let $X$ be a separable real Banach space with its norm topology, $D\subseteq X$ a Borel forward-map domain, and $\mu_0$ a Borel probability measure on $X$ with $\mu_0(D)=1$. Write $\mu_{0,D}$ for its restriction to $D$, so $\mu_{0,D}(A)=\mu_0(A)$ for $A\in\mathcal B(D):=\{D\cap B:B\in\mathcal B(X)\}$. Let $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ be a measurable data space. A likelihood potential is a function $\Phi:D\times\mathsf Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ that is measurable from $\bigl(D\times\mathsf Y,\mathcal B(D)\otimes\mathcal Y\bigr)$ to $\bigl((-\infty,+\infty],\mathcal B((-\infty,+\infty])\bigr)$, where $\mathcal B((-\infty,+\infty])$ is the trace of $\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R})$ on $(-\infty,+\infty]$. Viewing $\Phi$ via the inclusion $(-\infty,+\infty]\hookrightarrow\overline{\mathbb R}$, it is also product-measurable as an extended-real-valued map because for every Borel set $B\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$, $\Phi^{-1}(B)=\Phi^{-1}(B\cap(-\infty,+\infty])$ is measurable by the definition of the trace sigma-algebra. Here $+\infty$ is allowed and $-\infty$ is excluded; set $e^{-\infty}=0$. The scalar map $t\mapsto e^{-t}$ on this range is continuous at finite $t$, and is continuous at $+\infty$: given $\varepsilon>0$, the limit supplies $a\in\mathbb R$ such that $t>a$ implies $e^{-t}<\varepsilon$, and the order-topology neighborhood $(a,+\infty]$ maps into $[0,\varepsilon)$. Hence it is Borel, so $L_\Phi:D\times\mathsf Y\to[0,+\infty)$, $L_\Phi(u;y):=e^{-\Phi(u;y)}$, is product-measurable by composition, and each section $u\mapsto L_\Phi(u;y)$ is nonnegative and measurable. Define its evidence by
$$
Z_\Phi(y):=\int_D L_\Phi(u;y)\,\mu_{0,D}(du)\in[0,+\infty].
$$
For each fixed $y$ with $0<Z_\Phi(y)<+\infty$, define the normalized fiberwise update on $A\in\mathcal B(D)$ by
$$\Pi^y(A):=\frac{\int_A L_\Phi(u;y)\,\mu_{0,D}(du)}{Z_\Phi(y)}.$$
No normalized fiberwise update is defined by this formula when $Z_\Phi(y)=0$ or $Z_\Phi(y)=+\infty$.

For a data-indexed claim, an observation model and its version convention must also be specified. In the dominated case, let $Q$ be a proper probability kernel from $(D,\mathcal B(D))$ to $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$, let $\nu$ be a sigma-finite measure on $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$, and suppose $Q(u,B)=\int_B L_\Phi(u;y)\,\nu(dy)$ for every $u\in D$ and $B\in\mathcal Y$. Then $Z_\Phi$ is the density of the prior-predictive data law with respect to $\nu$; a data-indexed conditional-law version uses $\Pi^y$ when $0<Z_\Phi(y)<\infty$ and the prior $\mu_{0,D}$ when $Z_\Phi(y)$ is zero or infinite. These filled fibers have zero prior-predictive mass, and their chosen values are not normalized fiberwise updates. More generally, for a proper Bayesian model with standard-Borel parameter space $(D,\mathcal B(D))$ and data space $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ (each measurably isomorphic to the Borel space of a Polish space), the Axiom of Choice guarantees a data-indexed posterior kernel; its values are unique as probability measures outside one data-marginal-null set, and values on that null set remain version choices. The dominated construction is choice-free; the separate standard-Borel existence branch assumes the Axiom of Choice.

Assume AC. Let $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$ with positive-definite covariance
$\Sigma$. Let $L:\mathbb R^d\to[0,M]$ be Borel measurable and symmetric,
$L(-x)=L(x)$, and quasi-convex, meaning each sublevel set
$\{x:L(x)\le t\}$ is convex. Then for every $a\in\mathbb R^d$,
$$E L(X-a)\ge E L(X-m).$$
Thus the Gaussian center $m$ minimizes expected loss. The result includes
quasi-convex losses whose sublevel sets are not closed.

Let $B$ be a separable Banach space with norm $\|\cdot\|_B$, and let $\Pi$ be a Borel probability measure on $B$. For $z\in B$ and $r>0$, write $\overline B_B(z,r)=\{u\in B:\|u-z\|_B\le r\}$ and $m_r(z)=\Pi(\overline B_B(z,r))$. A **strong small-ball MAP** is a point $z\in B$ for which
$$ \frac{m_r(z)}{\sup_{x\in B}m_r(x)}\longrightarrow1\qquad(r\downarrow0). $$
Assume AC for the covariance-induced Cameron–Martin notation. If $\Pi$ is a posterior law formed by weighting a centered Gaussian prior $\Pi_0$ on $B$, let $C\ell=\int_B\ell(u)u\,\Pi_0(du)$ be its covariance operator and let $E$ be the completion of $B^*/\ker C$ with inner product $\langle[\ell],[m]\rangle_E=m(C\ell)$; the canonical injection $i:E\to B$ extends $[\ell]\mapsto C\ell$. A **Cameron–Martin ratio mode** is a point $ih\in iE$ such that, for every $k\in E$, the denominator is positive for all sufficiently small $r$ and
$$ \lim_{r\downarrow0}\frac{m_r(ih)}{m_r(ik)} $$
exists and is at least $1$. This pairwise comparison over fixed Cameron–Martin centers does not assert the global strong small-ball MAP condition.

For every $r>0$, $\sup_{x\in B}m_r(x)>0$: a countable dense subset gives a countable cover of $B$ by radius-$r$ open balls, each contained in its corresponding closed ball, and countable subadditivity rules out all such closed balls having zero probability.

Let $n \ge 1$, let $h \in \mathbb{R}^n$, and let $E + h$ be the translate of
$E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-translation-of-a-set-in-rn]]). Then:

1. $\lambda_n^*(E+h) = \lambda_n^*(E)$ for **every** subset $E$;
2. $E$ is Lebesgue measurable if and only if $E+h$ is;
3. $\lambda_n(E+h) = \lambda_n(E)$ for every Lebesgue measurable $E$.

**No choice principle is used.** Lebesgue outer measure is defined as an infimum
and the Carathéodory condition is a family of equations between its values, so
all three clauses are statements about objects that exist in ZF; countable
choice is needed to know that $\lambda_n$ is a measure, not to know that it is
translation invariant.

derivations.claim: By [F1], the prior and noise have positive Gaussian densities proportional to $\exp(-\tfrac12u^TC^{-1}u)$ and $\exp(-\tfrac12(y-Au)^T\Gamma^{-1}(y-Au))$, respectively. For any $w$, $w^T\Gamma^{-1}w\ge0$: write $w=\Gamma v$, so $w^T\Gamma^{-1}w=v^T\Gamma v\ge0$. Thus $\Phi_y\ge0$ and $e^{-\Phi_y}\le1$, so the evidence is finite. It is positive because $\Phi_y$ is continuous and finite at $0$, hence $e^{-\Phi_y}$ is bounded below by a positive constant on a sufficiently small ball about $0$, and the prior density in [F1] gives that ball positive mass. The posterior update [F1] is therefore defined. Its Lebesgue density is proportional to the product of the prior density and likelihood, hence to $e^{-I_y(u)}$. Put $Q=C^{-1}+A^T\Gamma^{-1}A$. For $v\ne0$, $v^TQv=v^TC^{-1}v+(Av)^T\Gamma^{-1}(Av)>0$: if $z=C^{-1}v$, then $v^TC^{-1}v=z^TCz>0$, and the second term is nonnegative by the preceding argument. Thus $Q$ is positive definite. Completing the square gives the unique minimizer $m=Q^{-1}A^T\Gamma^{-1}y$, and the posterior is the nondegenerate Gaussian $N(m,Q^{-1})$.

For every $r>0$, apply [F2] to this posterior and the loss $L_r(x)=\mathbf1_{\{\|x\|_2>r\}}$. Its sublevel sets are the closed radius-$r$ ball and the whole space, so it is bounded, symmetric and quasi-convex. Thus every ball of radius $r$ has posterior mass at most the ball centered at $m$, and the supremum in [F3] is attained at $m$. Consequently $m$ is a strong small-ball MAP.

Let $q$ be the positive continuous posterior density. For any fixed $z\in\mathbb R^d$, the absolute difference between $|B_r|^{-1}\Pi(B_r(z))$ and $q(z)$ is at most $\sup_{\|x-z\|_2\le r}|q(x)-q(z)|$, which tends to zero by continuity. The same holds at any $v$, and [F4] makes the ball volumes equal; hence $\Pi(B_r(z))/\Pi(B_r(v))\to q(z)/q(v)$. Since $q$ is proportional to $e^{-I_y}$, the finite-dimensional small-ball ratio agrees with the density and Onsager–Machlup comparison.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $H_0$ and $H_1$ be separable real Hilbert spaces with a continuous inclusion $H_1\hookrightarrow H_0$. Let $(e_j)_{j\ge1}$ be an orthonormal basis of $H_0$ that is a complete orthogonal basis of $H_1$, write $w_j=\|e_j\|_{H_1}^2>0$, and set $f_j=e_j/\sqrt{w_j}$, so $(f_j)_{j\ge1}$ is an orthonormal basis of $H_1$. Let $(\xi_j)_{j\ge1}$ be independent real random variables on one probability space with $\mathbb E\xi_j=0$ and $\mathbb E\xi_j^2=1$, and let $\lambda_j\ge0$ satisfy $\sum_{j\ge1}\lambda_jw_j<\infty$. Then
$$S_N=\sum_{j=1}^N\sqrt{\lambda_j}\,\xi_j e_j$$
converges almost surely in $H_1$ and in $L^2(\Omega;H_1)$ to an $H_1$-valued Borel-measurable random element $S$, with
$$\mathbb E\|S\|_{H_1}^2=\sum_{j\ge1}\lambda_jw_j.$$
These norm-convergence conclusions use no choice axiom beyond the supplied probability space and variables. For the following Gaussian conclusions, assume in addition that each $\xi_j$ has the standard normal law $N(0,1)$. Under the Axiom of Choice and countable choice, $S$ is a centered Borel Gaussian random element in $H_1$. Its covariance map $C:H_1^*\to H_1$, transported to $H_1$ by the Hilbert-space Riesz identification, is diagonal in the basis $(f_j)_{j\ge1}$ with eigenvalues $\lambda_jw_j$, and these eigenvalues are summable. If $D$ is a Borel forward-map domain in $H_1$ and $\mathbb P(S\in D)=1$, then the law of $S$ is a prior on $D$. Under the Axiom of Choice there is $a>0$ such that
$$\mathbb E\exp\!\bigl(a\|S\|_{H_1}^2\bigr)<\infty.$$

Let $X$ be a set and let $\mathcal A$ be a sigma-algebra on $X$ ([[def-sigma-algebra]]). A **measure** on $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a function

$$\mu:\mathcal A\longrightarrow[0,+\infty]\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$$

such that:

1. $\mu(\varnothing)=0$;
2. for every pairwise disjoint sequence $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ in $\mathcal A$,
   $$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k),$$
   where the right side is the nonnegative extended sum of [[def-nonnegative-extended-series]].

The second condition is **countable additivity**. It begins at index $0$ and includes the case in which some term or the total sum is $+\infty$.

Let $\mu$ be a measure and let $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ be measurable. Then

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)\le\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k).$$

For every $m\in\mathbb N$ one also has

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k<m}E_k\right)\le\sum_{k<m}\mu(E_k),$$

including $m=0$, where both sides are $0$.

$\mathbb{Q} \approx \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]): the rationals are
countably infinite ([[def-countable]]).

**No choice principle is used.** The one place where a reader expects a choice,
"pick a representative $a/b$ of each rational", is exactly where
[[lem-rat-positive-denominator]] applies: every rational *has* a representative
with positive denominator, so the map $(a,b) \mapsto [(a,b)]$ defined on
$\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ is already **surjective** onto $\mathbb{Q}$,
and countability follows from a surjection without ever selecting a
representative. The same device handles $\mathbb{Z}$, which is a surjective image
of $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ by construction ([[def-integers]]).

The map $q \mapsto \hat q$ ([[def-real-numbers]]) is an embedding of ordered
fields. Every real is approximated by rationals: for $x \in \mathbb{R}$ and
rational $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $q \in \mathbb{Q}$ with
$|x - \hat q| < \hat\varepsilon$. Consequently, strictly between any two
reals lies a rational.

If $A$ and $B$ are at most countable ([[def-countable]]) then so is
$A \times B$.

**No choice principle is used**: the two enumerations are given, and the
enumeration of the product is written down from them.

**Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice** ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(A_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a family of at most countable sets
([[def-countable]]) indexed by $\mathbb{N}$. Then

$$U = \bigcup_{n \in \mathbb{N}} A_n$$

is at most countable.

**The role of $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$.** It is spent at exactly one step, step 3.1 below, where a surjection $\mathbb N\to A_n$ is selected simultaneously for each nonempty $A_n$. The individual countability hypotheses assert that these sets of surjections are nonempty; they specify no simultaneous selection.
Let $\mu$ be a measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$. If $A,B\in\mathcal A$ and $A\subseteq B$, then $\mu(A)\le\mu(B)$.

derivations.claim: In [F1], take $H_0=H_1=\ell^2$, $w_j=1$, and $\lambda_j=1/(j(j+1))$. The finite sums telescope as $\sum_{j=1}^N\lambda_j=\sum_{j=1}^N(1/j-1/(j+1))=1-1/(N+1)\le1$, so the required infinite sum is finite. Thus [F1] applies to the stated independent standard normals and proves that $W$ is a centered Borel Gaussian random element.

Suppose that $\lambda$ is a translation-invariant Borel measure finite on every bounded Borel set. Put $U_j=\{x:\|x-e_j\|_2<1/3\}$. For $j\ne k$, $\|e_j-e_k\|_2=\sqrt2>2/3$, so the $U_j$ are pairwise disjoint. Each lies in the bounded ball $\{x:\|x\|_2<2\}$ by the triangle inequality. Translation invariance gives $\lambda(U_j)=m$ independent of $j$. If $m>0$, the first $N$ disjoint balls have total measure $Nm$ for every $N$, contradicting finiteness of the radius-two ball. Hence $m=0$.

Translation invariance and step 2.1 make every radius-$1/3$ ball have measure zero. Let $D$ be the set of finitely supported rational sequences. [F3] makes $D$ countable: it is the countable union, over support lengths $N$, of the countable set $\mathbb Q^N$ padded with zeros. It is dense in $\ell^2$: for any $x\in\ell^2$ and $\epsilon>0$, choose $N$ so that the squared tail sum is less than $\epsilon^2/4$, then approximate the first $N$ coordinates by rationals with squared total error less than $\epsilon^2/4$; the resulting padded vector is within $\epsilon$ of $x$. The radius-$1/3$ balls centered at $D$ therefore form a countable cover of $\ell^2$. By [F2], $\lambda(\ell^2)=0$, and [F4] makes every Borel subset null. This contradicts that $\lambda$ is nonzero. Hence no such reference measure exists, refuting the statement; in particular, the displayed Gaussian has no density relative to one.

Let $X$ be a separable real Banach space with its norm topology, $D\subseteq X$ a Borel forward-map domain, and $\mu_0$ a Borel probability measure on $X$ with $\mu_0(D)=1$. Write $\mu_{0,D}$ for its restriction to $D$, so $\mu_{0,D}(A)=\mu_0(A)$ for $A\in\mathcal B(D):=\{D\cap B:B\in\mathcal B(X)\}$. Let $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ be a measurable data space. A likelihood potential is a function $\Phi:D\times\mathsf Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ that is measurable from $\bigl(D\times\mathsf Y,\mathcal B(D)\otimes\mathcal Y\bigr)$ to $\bigl((-\infty,+\infty],\mathcal B((-\infty,+\infty])\bigr)$, where $\mathcal B((-\infty,+\infty])$ is the trace of $\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R})$ on $(-\infty,+\infty]$. Viewing $\Phi$ via the inclusion $(-\infty,+\infty]\hookrightarrow\overline{\mathbb R}$, it is also product-measurable as an extended-real-valued map because for every Borel set $B\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$, $\Phi^{-1}(B)=\Phi^{-1}(B\cap(-\infty,+\infty])$ is measurable by the definition of the trace sigma-algebra. Here $+\infty$ is allowed and $-\infty$ is excluded; set $e^{-\infty}=0$. The scalar map $t\mapsto e^{-t}$ on this range is continuous at finite $t$, and is continuous at $+\infty$: given $\varepsilon>0$, the limit supplies $a\in\mathbb R$ such that $t>a$ implies $e^{-t}<\varepsilon$, and the order-topology neighborhood $(a,+\infty]$ maps into $[0,\varepsilon)$. Hence it is Borel, so $L_\Phi:D\times\mathsf Y\to[0,+\infty)$, $L_\Phi(u;y):=e^{-\Phi(u;y)}$, is product-measurable by composition, and each section $u\mapsto L_\Phi(u;y)$ is nonnegative and measurable. Define its evidence by
$$
Z_\Phi(y):=\int_D L_\Phi(u;y)\,\mu_{0,D}(du)\in[0,+\infty].
$$
For each fixed $y$ with $0<Z_\Phi(y)<+\infty$, define the normalized fiberwise update on $A\in\mathcal B(D)$ by
$$\Pi^y(A):=\frac{\int_A L_\Phi(u;y)\,\mu_{0,D}(du)}{Z_\Phi(y)}.$$
No normalized fiberwise update is defined by this formula when $Z_\Phi(y)=0$ or $Z_\Phi(y)=+\infty$.

For a data-indexed claim, an observation model and its version convention must also be specified. In the dominated case, let $Q$ be a proper probability kernel from $(D,\mathcal B(D))$ to $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$, let $\nu$ be a sigma-finite measure on $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$, and suppose $Q(u,B)=\int_B L_\Phi(u;y)\,\nu(dy)$ for every $u\in D$ and $B\in\mathcal Y$. Then $Z_\Phi$ is the density of the prior-predictive data law with respect to $\nu$; a data-indexed conditional-law version uses $\Pi^y$ when $0<Z_\Phi(y)<\infty$ and the prior $\mu_{0,D}$ when $Z_\Phi(y)$ is zero or infinite. These filled fibers have zero prior-predictive mass, and their chosen values are not normalized fiberwise updates. More generally, for a proper Bayesian model with standard-Borel parameter space $(D,\mathcal B(D))$ and data space $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ (each measurably isomorphic to the Borel space of a Polish space), the Axiom of Choice guarantees a data-indexed posterior kernel; its values are unique as probability measures outside one data-marginal-null set, and values on that null set remain version choices. The dominated construction is choice-free; the separate standard-Borel existence branch assumes the Axiom of Choice.

Let $B$ be a separable Banach space with norm $\|\cdot\|_B$, and let $\Pi$ be a Borel probability measure on $B$. For $z\in B$ and $r>0$, write $\overline B_B(z,r)=\{u\in B:\|u-z\|_B\le r\}$ and $m_r(z)=\Pi(\overline B_B(z,r))$. A **strong small-ball MAP** is a point $z\in B$ for which
$$ \frac{m_r(z)}{\sup_{x\in B}m_r(x)}\longrightarrow1\qquad(r\downarrow0). $$
Assume AC for the covariance-induced Cameron–Martin notation. If $\Pi$ is a posterior law formed by weighting a centered Gaussian prior $\Pi_0$ on $B$, let $C\ell=\int_B\ell(u)u\,\Pi_0(du)$ be its covariance operator and let $E$ be the completion of $B^*/\ker C$ with inner product $\langle[\ell],[m]\rangle_E=m(C\ell)$; the canonical injection $i:E\to B$ extends $[\ell]\mapsto C\ell$. A **Cameron–Martin ratio mode** is a point $ih\in iE$ such that, for every $k\in E$, the denominator is positive for all sufficiently small $r$ and
$$ \lim_{r\downarrow0}\frac{m_r(ih)}{m_r(ik)} $$
exists and is at least $1$. This pairwise comparison over fixed Cameron–Martin centers does not assert the global strong small-ball MAP condition.

For every $r>0$, $\sup_{x\in B}m_r(x)>0$: a countable dense subset gives a countable cover of $B$ by radius-$r$ open balls, each contained in its corresponding closed ball, and countable subadditivity rules out all such closed balls having zero probability.

Fix $n \ge 1$ and let $\lambda_n^*$ be the Lebesgue outer set function on $\mathbb{R}^n$
([[def-lebesgue-outer-measure]]). A set $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is
**Lebesgue measurable** when

$$\lambda_n^*(A) \;=\; \lambda_n^*(A \cap E) \;+\; \lambda_n^*(A \setminus E) \qquad \text{for every } A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n .$$

This formula makes sense before any outer-measure theorem is invoked. Under
countable choice, [[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-is-an-outer-measure-agreeing-with-volume]]
makes $\lambda_n^*$ an outer measure, and the displayed condition is then exactly
Carathéodory measurability in the sense of [[def-caratheodory-measurable-set]].

The family of Lebesgue measurable sets is written $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$,
and **Lebesgue measure** is the restriction

$$\lambda_n \;:=\; \lambda_n^*\!\restriction_{\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)} .$$

On the real line the subscript is dropped and $\lambda := \lambda_1$.

The quantifier over every test set $A$ is part of the condition, and no
hypothesis on $E$ is imposed before it is tested. That
$\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra and that $\lambda_n$ is a complete
measure on it are not part of this definition: they are proved, under the Axiom
of Countable Choice, in [[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]], which is
recorded in this item's `justified_by` because it is a statement about the
objects introduced here. Until that theorem the symbols $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$
and $\lambda_n$ name a family of sets and a restricted set function, nothing more.

derivations.claim:
On $[0,1]$, $p(\theta)=\theta^2(1-\theta)\ge0$. Its derivative is $p'(\theta)=\theta(2-3\theta)$, so its maximum is $p(2/3)=4/27<1$. Therefore $p$ and $1-p$ define valid conditional probabilities for $Y=1$ and $Y=0$. By [F3], the evidence for $Y=1$ is
$$ Z=\int_0^1\theta^2(1-\theta)\,d\theta=\frac13-\frac14=\frac1{12}>0. $$
The posterior formula [F1] gives density $q(\theta)=12\theta^2(1-\theta)$ on $[0,1]$, extended by zero on $\mathbb R\setminus[0,1]$.

On $(0,1)$, $q'(\theta)=12\theta(2-3\theta)$, so $q$ increases up to $2/3$ and decreases after it; $q(0)=q(1)=0$. Thus $q_{\max}=q(2/3)>0$ is the unique density maximum. For any center $x\in\mathbb R$ and $r>0$, [F3] gives $m_r(x)\le2r q_{\max}$. For $0<r<1/3$, the interval $[2/3-r,2/3+r]$ lies inside $[0,1]$, and continuity of $q$ gives $m_r(2/3)/(2r)\to q_{\max}$. Hence
$$ 1\ge\frac{m_r(2/3)}{\sup_{x\in\mathbb R}m_r(x)} \ge\frac{m_r(2/3)}{2r q_{\max}}\longrightarrow1. $$
By [F2], $2/3$ is a strong small-ball MAP.

The posterior mean is
$$ \int_0^1\theta q(\theta)\,d\theta =12\int_0^1(\theta^3-\theta^4)\,d\theta =12\left(\frac14-\frac15\right)=\frac35. $$
Since $3/5\ne2/3$, the posterior mean differs from the strong small-ball MAP.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, read in
the real case from [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and in the complex case from
[[def-complex-norm-and-complex-normed-space]]. A $\mathbb K$-linear map
$T:X\to Y$ ([[def-linear-map]]) is a **bounded linear operator** when there is a
real constant $C \ge 0$ such that

$$\|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \qquad \text{for all } x \in X.$$

Any such $C$ is called a **bound** for $T$.

Let $V$ be a real or complex inner-product space. Vectors $x,y\in V$ are
**orthogonal**, written $x\perp y$, when

$$\langle x,y\rangle=0 .$$

For a subset $S\subseteq V$ the **orthogonal complement** of $S$ is

$$S^\perp:=\{\,v\in V : \langle v,s\rangle=0 \text{ for every } s\in S\,\}.$$

**Orthogonality is symmetric.** If $\langle x,y\rangle=0$, then
$\langle y,x\rangle=\overline{\langle x,y\rangle}=0$, so $x\perp y$ exactly
when $y\perp x$; in particular the condition defining $S^\perp$ is symmetric in
its two arguments.

**$S^\perp$ is a linear subspace.** Let $s\in S$ and scalars $a,b$; then
$\langle 0,s\rangle=0$, and if $u,v\in S^\perp$ then
$\langle au+bv,s\rangle=a\langle u,s\rangle+b\langle v,s\rangle=0$ by linearity
in the first argument, so $au+bv\in S^\perp$. Thus $S^\perp$ is a linear
subspace of $V$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]) for every subset $S$, whether or not
$S$ is a subspace. Moreover $0\in S^\perp$ always, and $v\in V$ lies in
$\{0\}^\perp$ for every $v$, so $\{0\}^\perp=V$.

**Monotonicity.** If $S\subseteq T\subseteq V$, then every vector orthogonal to
all of $T$ is orthogonal to all of $S$, so $T^\perp\subseteq S^\perp$.

**Nontriviality of orthogonality.** By positive definiteness
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2=0$ exactly for $v=0$ ([[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]),
so a vector orthogonal to itself is zero, and $\{0\}^\perp=V$, $V^\perp=\{0\}$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $M$ be a closed linear subspace of a real or complex Hilbert space $H$. Then every $x\in H$ has a unique decomposition

$$x=m+n,\qquad m\in M,\quad n\in M^\perp ,$$

so that $H=M\oplus M^\perp$ as a direct sum of the subspace $M$ and its orthogonal complement.

Let $x_1,\dots,x_n$ be pairwise orthogonal vectors in a real or complex inner-product space, that is $\langle x_i,x_j\rangle=0$ whenever $i\ne j$ ([[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]). Then

$$\Bigl\|\sum_{j=1}^{n}x_j\Bigr\|^2=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\|x_j\|^2 ,$$

the empty sum on the right being $0$ at $n=0$.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $A \subseteq X$,
with closure, derived set and limit points as in
[[def-metric-interior-closure-boundary]]. Then:

1. If $A \ne \emptyset$, then $\overline{A} = \{\, x \in X : d(x,A) = 0 \,\}$,
   where $d(x,A)$ is the distance from a point to a nonempty set
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
2. $\overline{A} = A \cup A'$.
3. $\overline{A}$ is closed, contains $A$, and is contained in every closed
   $F \subseteq X$ with $A \subseteq F$. So $\overline{A}$ is the smallest closed
   superset of $A$, and $A$ is closed if and only if $A = \overline{A}$.

Claims 2 and 3 hold for every $A$, the empty set included: $\overline{\emptyset}$
is empty because no ball meets $\emptyset$, and $\emptyset$ is closed because $X$
is open ([[def-metric-topology]]). Claim 1 carries the hypothesis $A \ne \emptyset$
because $d(x,A)$ is defined only for nonempty $A$
([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with **conjugation** $z\mapsto\overline z$
the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of [[def-inner-product-space]]: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

**Induced length.** The **induced length**, or inner-product norm, of $v$ is

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

which is exactly the published [[def-inner-product-norm]]: positive definiteness
makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square
root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$.

**The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or
complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.
In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of
$\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex
modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either
scalar field.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: If $K=0$, then $N(K)=X$ is closed. Otherwise choose a bound $C>0$ from [F1]. For any $x\in\overline{N(K)}$, [F5] lets us choose, for every $\varepsilon>0$, an $n_\varepsilon\in N(K)$ with $\|x-n_\varepsilon\|<\varepsilon$. Hence $\|Kx\|=\|K(x-n_\varepsilon)\|\le C\varepsilon$ for every $\varepsilon>0$, so $\|Kx\|=0$ and $Kx=0$ by [F6]. Thus $\overline{N(K)}\subseteq N(K)$, and [F5] implies that $N(K)$ is closed.

Fix $r_0\in R(K)$ and choose $x_0\in X$ with $Kx_0=r_0$. By [F3] and step 1.1, write $x_0=p+n$ with $p\in N(K)^\perp$ and $n\in N(K)$; then $Kp=Kx_0-Kn=r_0$. The restriction $\widetilde K$ is therefore surjective. If $p,q\in N(K)^\perp$ and $Kp=Kq$, then $p-q\in N(K)\cap N(K)^\perp$, so $p=q$ by [F2]. Thus $\widetilde K$ is bijective.

If $x$ is any solution of $Kx=r_0$, then $x-p\in N(K)$. Since $p\perp(x-p)$, [F4] gives $\|x\|^2=\|p\|^2+\|x-p\|^2\ge\|p\|^2$, with equality only when $x=p$. So $p=\widetilde K^{-1}r_0$ is the unique minimum-norm solution.

For $y=r+z\in R(K)\oplus R(K)^\perp$, the decomposition is unique because $R(K)\cap R(K)^\perp=\{0\}$ by [F2], so the definition is single-valued. If $z\in R(K)^\perp$, then $r=0$ and the unique minimum-norm preimage of $0$ is $0$ by step 3.1; hence $K^\dagger z=0$. For $y_i=r_i+z_i$ and scalars $a,b$, the vector $aK^\dagger y_1+bK^\dagger y_2$ lies in $N(K)^\perp$ and maps under $K$ to $ar_1+br_2$, so uniqueness in step 2.1 gives $K^\dagger(ay_1+by_2)=aK^\dagger y_1+bK^\dagger y_2$. The definition is therefore a well-defined linear operator on the stated domain.

Let $X,Y$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces over the same scalar field, and let
$K:X\to Y$ be a compact linear operator. The associated compact linear inverse
model has parameter space $X$, data space $Y$, forward map $K$, and admissible
truth class $X$: for a true parameter $x^\dagger\in X$, the exact datum is
$y=Kx^\dagger\in Y$. Given an exact datum $y\in Y$, solving this inverse
problem means finding a parameter $x\in X$ such that $Kx=y$. No injectivity,
surjectivity, or closed-range assumption is included in the model.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $X$ and $Y$ be real or complex Hilbert
spaces over the same scalar field, and let $K:X\to Y$ be a bounded linear
operator. Write $R(K):=\{Kx:x\in X\}$ for its range,
$N(K):=\{x\in X:Kx=0\}$ for its kernel, and
$M^\perp:=\{z:\langle z,m\rangle=0\text{ for every }m\in M\}$ for the
orthogonal complement of a subspace $M$. The kernel $N(K)$ is closed, so the
restriction
$$\widetilde K:=K|_{N(K)^\perp}:N(K)^\perp\to R(K)$$
is a linear bijection. Define the Hilbert-space Moore–Penrose inverse $K^\dagger$
to have domain
$$D(K^\dagger):=R(K)\oplus R(K)^\perp$$
and, for the unique decomposition $y=r+z$ with $r\in R(K)$ and
$z\in R(K)^\perp$, set
$$K^\dagger y:=\widetilde K^{-1}r.$$
Thus $K^\dagger y$ is the unique minimum-norm solution of $Kx=r$, and the
orthogonal-range component is mapped to zero. Boundedness of $K^\dagger$ on
this domain is not part of the definition.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ and
$K$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces ([[def-hilbert-space]]), let
$T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ be a compact operator
([[def-compact-linear-operator]]), let $|T|$ and the singular values $s_n(T)$ be
as in the absolute-value definition
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]). Let
$J=\{1,2,3,\ldots\}$ when $\operatorname{ran}T$ is infinite-dimensional. When
$\operatorname{ran}T$ is finite-dimensional, put
$r:=\dim\operatorname{ran}T\in\mathbb N$ ([[def-dimension]]) and let
$J=\{1,\dots,r\}$, interpreted as $\varnothing$ when $r=0$. Thus $J$ indexes
exactly the positive singular values counted with multiplicity, which we write
as $(s_j)_{j\in J}$ in nonincreasing order. Then:

1. there are orthonormal families $(e_j)_{j\in J}$ in $(\ker T)^\perp$ and
   $(f_j)_{j\in J}$ in $\overline{\operatorname{ran}T}$, indexed by exactly $J$,
   with $|T|e_j=s_je_j$ and $f_j=s_j^{-1}Te_j$ for every $j\in J$;
2. for every $x\in H$ the series converges in norm and
   $$Tx=\sum_{j\in J}s_j\langle x,e_j\rangle f_j,$$
   and its finite partial sums
   $T_n:=\sum_{j\le n}s_j\langle\cdot,e_j\rangle f_j$ satisfy
   $\|T-T_n\|\le s_{n+1}$ for every $n$ with $n+1\in J$ (and $T_n=T$ for
   $n\ge r$ when $r<+\infty$);
3. the linear map $U$ defined on the span of $\{e_j:j\in J\}$ by $Ue_j:=f_j$,
   extended by continuity to $(\ker T)^\perp$ and by zero on $\ker T$, is a
   **partial isometry** with
   $$T=U|T|,\qquad U^*U=P_{(\ker T)^\perp},\qquad U^*U\text{ is the orthogonal projection onto }(\ker T)^\perp,$$
   and $UU^*$ the orthogonal projection onto $\overline{\operatorname{ran}T}$;
4. the zero-padded sequence $(s_n(T))_{n\ge1}$ is *not* used to index the
   orthonormal systems: the systems carry exactly the index set $J$ of the
   positive singular values, and the terms $s_n(T)=0$ beyond the rank in the
   finite-rank case are numerical padding only.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ and $K$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces and let $T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ be a bounded linear operator ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]], [[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]]). For fixed $y\in K$ the map

$$x\longmapsto\langle Tx,y\rangle_K$$

is a bounded linear functional on $H$: it is linear in $x$ because $T$ is linear and the pairing is linear in its first argument, and $|\langle Tx,y\rangle_K|\le\|Tx\|\,\|y\|\le\|T\|\,\|x\|\,\|y\|$ by Cauchy–Schwarz and the operator-norm inequality ([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]], [[def-operator-norm]]). By Riesz representation ([[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]) there is therefore a unique vector $T^*y\in H$ with

$$\langle Tx,y\rangle_K=\langle x,T^*y\rangle_H\qquad\text{for every }x\in H .$$

The **Hilbert adjoint** of $T$ is the map

$$T^*:K\longrightarrow H,\qquad y\longmapsto T^*y .$$

It is the unique map $K\to H$ satisfying the displayed identity, since two such maps have $\langle x,(T^*_1-T^*_2)y\rangle=0$ for all $x$ and hence $(T^*_1-T^*_2)y=0$ by positive definiteness.

**The dictionary with the Banach transpose.** Write $R_H:H\to H^*$ and $R_K:K\to K^*$ for the Riesz maps $R_H(x)=\langle\,\cdot\,,x\rangle_H$ and $R_K(y)=\langle\,\cdot\,,y\rangle_K$, and let $T'\in\mathcal B(K^*,H^*)$ be the transpose of $T$, $(T'g)(x)=g(Tx)$ ([[def-transpose-of-a-bounded-operator]]). Then for all $y\in K$ and $x\in H$,

$$\bigl(R_H(T^*y)\bigr)(x)=\langle x,T^*y\rangle_H=\langle Tx,y\rangle_K=(R_Ky)(Tx)=\bigl(T'(R_Ky)\bigr)(x),$$

so $R_H\,T^*=T'\,R_K$. The Hilbert adjoint is thus the Banach transpose conjugated by the Riesz identifications of $H$ and $K$ with their duals; it is a different operator from $T'$ whenever the Riesz maps are conjugate-linear.

Let $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ be an orthonormal family in a real or complex inner-product
space $H$ ([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]),
let $F\subseteq I$ be finite, and for $x\in H$ put

$$P_Fx:=\sum_{i\in F}\langle x,e_i\rangle e_i .$$Then: 1. $P_Fx$ lies in the span of $\{e_i : i\in F\}$, and $\|P_Fx\|^2=\sum_{i\in F}|\langle x,e_i\rangle|^2$; 2. the residual $x-P_Fx$ is orthogonal to every $e_j$ with $j\in F$, hence to every vector of the span of $\{e_i : i\in F\}$; 3. $\|x-P_Fx\|^2=\|x\|^2-\sum_{i\in F}|\langle x,e_i\rangle|^2$, and therefore the **finite Bessel inequality** holds:$$\sum_{i\in F}|\langle x,e_i\rangle|^2\le\|x\|^2 ;$$4. $P_Fx$ is the unique best approximation to $x$ from the span of $\{e_i : i\in F\}$: for every $y$ in that span,$$\|x-y\|^2=\|x-P_Fx\|^2+\|P_Fx-y\|^2\ge\|x-P_Fx\|^2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if $y=P_Fx$.

At $F=\varnothing$ the sum defining $P_Fx$ is empty, so $P_Fx=0$ and the
identities read $\|x\|^2=\|x\|^2$.

Let $x_1,\dots,x_n$ be pairwise orthogonal vectors in a real or complex inner-product space, that is $\langle x_i,x_j\rangle=0$ whenever $i\ne j$ ([[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]). Then

$$\Bigl\|\sum_{j=1}^{n}x_j\Bigr\|^2=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\|x_j\|^2 ,$$

the empty sum on the right being $0$ at $n=0$.

Let $V$ be a normed space over $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and let
$W\subseteq V$ be a normed subspace over that same field: use [[def-normed-subspace]] for $\mathbb R$ and [[def-complex-normed-subspace]] for $\mathbb C$. If $W$ admits an ordered basis of finite
length, including length zero, then $W$ is closed in $V$. This holds in ZF,
without a choice axiom; the ambient space need not be complete.

A **real Hilbert space** is a real inner-product space $H$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]) whose induced-length metric is complete in the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]]: every Cauchy sequence in $H$ for the norm $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ ([[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]) converges to a point of $H$. A **complex Hilbert space** is a complex inner-product space with the same completeness property, so that a Hilbert space is exactly a real or complex inner-product space that is a Banach space for its induced norm ([[def-banach-space]]).

**The completion convention is the Cauchy-sequence one.**
[[def-banach-space]] defines completeness by convergence of Cauchy sequences, and this page keeps that convention throughout. It is weaker than $\sigma$-completeness — the assertion that every decreasing sequence of nonempty closed subsets with diameters tending to zero has a nonempty intersection. The two agree in ZFC, but Blackadar, Farah and Karagila note that the closest-point theorem on a $\sigma$-complete inner-product space is provable in ZF, whereas the Cauchy-complete form used below consumes the Axiom of Countable Choice; nothing here silently imports the stronger notion.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) and let
$\varepsilon \in F$ with $\varepsilon > 0$. Then there is a natural number
$n \ge 1$ such that

$$\frac{1}{n \cdot 1_F} < \varepsilon ,$$

where $n \cdot 1_F$ is the canonical natural of $F$ ([[thm-of-archimedean]]) and
$1/(n \cdot 1_F)$ is its multiplicative inverse ([[def-field]]). As is standard
we abbreviate $n \cdot 1_F$ to $n$ and write the conclusion $1/n < \varepsilon$.

This is the **reciprocal form** of the Archimedean property.
[[thm-of-archimedean]] on its own delivers only the assertion that the canonical
naturals are cofinal, $x < n \cdot 1_F$; the form actually used in analysis, that
the reciprocals of the naturals get below every positive bound, is the statement
above, and it is recorded separately so that no proof has to reconstruct the
inversion step in passing.

Let $(N,0,\sigma)$ be a Peano system ([[def-peano-system]]), in particular the natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]). For any set $A$, any element $a \in A$, and any function $f : A \to A$, there is a unique function $g : N \to A$ such that $g(0) = a$ and $g(\sigma(n)) = f(g(n))$ for all $n \in N$.
Every nonempty subset $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ has a least element: there is $\ell \in S$ with $\ell \le s$ for all $s \in S$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Suppose the positive singular system is finite, with index set $J=\{1,\ldots,r\}$. If $r=0$, the SVD expansion gives $K=0$, so $R(K)=\{0\}$ is closed by [F7] and $K^\dagger=0$ is bounded on its domain. If $r>0$, each $u_j=s_j^{-1}Kv_j$ lies in $R(K)$, while the SVD expansion places every $Kx$ in $\operatorname{span}\{u_1,\ldots,u_r\}$; hence the range equals this finite-dimensional span and is closed by [F7]. For $y=q+z\in D(K^\dagger)$, $q\in R(K)$ and $z\in R(K)^\perp$, so $K^\dagger y=\sum_{j=1}^{r}s_j^{-1}\langle q,u_j\rangle v_j$ by [F2] and [F3]. Pythagoras and Bessel give $\|K^\dagger y\|^2=\sum_{j=1}^{r}s_j^{-2}|\langle q,u_j\rangle|^2 \le s_r^{-2}\|q\|^2\le s_r^{-2}\|y\|^2$; here $s_r$ is the smallest positive singular value, and the last inequality follows from $q\perp z$. Thus finite rank implies closed range and bounded $K^\dagger$.

Suppose instead that the positive singular index set is $J=\{1,2,3,\ldots\}$. Since $s_j\to0$, for each pair $(k,n)$ the set of integers $m>n$ with $s_m<2^{-(k+1)}$ is nonempty; [F12] gives its least element, so [F11] defines recursively $n_0=0$ and the strictly increasing sequence $n_k$ with $s_{n_k}<2^{-k}$. Set $y_N=\sum_{k=1}^{N}s_{n_k}u_{n_k}$. For $M>N$, [F6] gives $\|y_M-y_N\|^2=\sum_{k=N+1}^{M}s_{n_k}^2\le\sum_{k=N+1}^{M}4^{-k} \le 4^{-N}/3$, so $(y_N)$ is Cauchy and converges to some $y\in Y$ by [F8]. Each $y_N$ belongs to $R(K)$ because $s_{n_k}u_{n_k}=Kv_{n_k}$, hence $y\in\overline{R(K)}$. If $y=Kx$, then for every $k$ and every $N\ge k$, orthonormality gives $\langle y_N,u_{n_k}\rangle=s_{n_k}$; by [F9] we may pass to the limit to get $\langle y,u_{n_k}\rangle=s_{n_k}$. The SVD and adjoint identity [F3]–[F4] then give $s_{n_k}=\langle Kx,u_{n_k}\rangle=s_{n_k}\langle x,v_{n_k}\rangle$, so $\langle x,v_{n_k}\rangle=1$ for every $k$. Applying [F5] to any first $N$ of these orthonormal vectors gives $N\le\|x\|^2$ for every $N$. Taking $\varepsilon=1/(\|x\|^2+1)$ in [F10] yields an integer $N$ with $1/N<1/(\|x\|^2+1)$, hence $N>\|x\|^2$, a contradiction. Thus $y\notin R(K)$ and the range is not closed.

For each $k$, $Kv_{n_k}=s_{n_k}u_{n_k}\in D(K^\dagger)$ and $K^\dagger Kv_{n_k}=v_{n_k}$ by [F2], since $v_{n_k}\in N(K)^\perp$. Therefore $\|K^\dagger Kv_{n_k}\|/\|Kv_{n_k}\|=1/s_{n_k}>2^k$, so $K^\dagger$ is unbounded when the positive singular system is infinite.

By [F3], every compact $K$ has either finite range dimension, covered by step 1.1, or an infinite positive singular system, covered by steps 1.2 and 2.1. Thus $R(K)$ is closed exactly in the finite-dimensional case, and in exactly that case $K^\dagger$ is bounded. This proves both stated equivalences.

$P_Fx=\sum_{i\in F}\langle x,e_i\rangle e_i$ over finite $F\subseteq I$. Then:

1. $x$ is the norm limit of the finite-subset net $(P_Fx)$, that is
   $$x=\sum_{i\in I}\langle x,e_i\rangle e_i$$
   in the sense of convergence of the net of finite subsums;
2. **the coefficients are unique**: if $(a_i)_{i\in I}$ is a family in
   $\mathbb F$ whose finite-subset net $\sum_{i\in F}a_ie_i$ converges to $x$,
   then $a_i=\langle x,e_i\rangle$ for every $i\in I$;
3. the support $\{i : \langle x,e_i\rangle\ne0\}$ is at most countable, and the
   expansion does not depend on an ordering: if $(i_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ is a
   sequence of pairwise distinct elements of $I$ whose image contains the
   support, then the sequence of partial sums
   $\sum_{k<n}\langle x,e_{i_k}\rangle e_{i_k}$ also converges to $x$.

Claim 3 is the sense in which the expansion is **unconditional**: the sum is
independent of any ordering, because the finite-subset net converges and any
enumeration of a set containing the support by pairwise distinct indices is
cofinal in the squared mass.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $M$ be a closed linear subspace of a real or complex Hilbert space $H$. Then every $x\in H$ has a unique decomposition

$$x=m+n,\qquad m\in M,\quad n\in M^\perp ,$$

so that $H=M\oplus M^\perp$ as a direct sum of the subspace $M$ and its orthogonal complement.

A **real Hilbert space** is a real inner-product space $H$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]) whose induced-length metric is complete in the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]]: every Cauchy sequence in $H$ for the norm $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ ([[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]) converges to a point of $H$. A **complex Hilbert space** is a complex inner-product space with the same completeness property, so that a Hilbert space is exactly a real or complex inner-product space that is a Banach space for its induced norm ([[def-banach-space]]).

**The completion convention is the Cauchy-sequence one.**
[[def-banach-space]] defines completeness by convergence of Cauchy sequences, and this page keeps that convention throughout. It is weaker than $\sigma$-completeness — the assertion that every decreasing sequence of nonempty closed subsets with diameters tending to zero has a nonempty intersection. The two agree in ZFC, but Blackadar, Farah and Karagila note that the closest-point theorem on a $\sigma$-complete inner-product space is provable in ZF, whereas the Cauchy-complete form used below consumes the Axiom of Countable Choice; nothing here silently imports the stronger notion.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $X$ and $Y$ be real or complex Hilbert
spaces over the same scalar field, and let $K:X\to Y$ be a bounded linear
operator. Write $R(K):=\{Kx:x\in X\}$ for its range,
$N(K):=\{x\in X:Kx=0\}$ for its kernel, and
$M^\perp:=\{z:\langle z,m\rangle=0\text{ for every }m\in M\}$ for the
orthogonal complement of a subspace $M$. The kernel $N(K)$ is closed, so the
restriction
$$\widetilde K:=K|_{N(K)^\perp}:N(K)^\perp\to R(K)$$
is a linear bijection. Define the Hilbert-space Moore–Penrose inverse $K^\dagger$
to have domain
$$D(K^\dagger):=R(K)\oplus R(K)^\perp$$
and, for the unique decomposition $y=r+z$ with $r\in R(K)$ and
$z\in R(K)^\perp$, set
$$K^\dagger y:=\widetilde K^{-1}r.$$
Thus $K^\dagger y$ is the unique minimum-norm solution of $Kx=r$, and the
orthogonal-range component is mapped to zero. Boundedness of $K^\dagger$ on
this domain is not part of the definition.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field $\mathbb K$, read in
the real case from [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and in the complex case from
[[def-complex-norm-and-complex-normed-space]]. A linear map $T:X\to Y$
([[def-linear-map]]) is a **compact operator** when the image of every bounded
subset of $X$ ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]) has compact closure in $Y$
([[def-metric-compactness]]); explicitly, for every bounded $A\subseteq X$ the
closure $\overline{T(A)}$ in $Y$ is a compact subset of $Y$. The set of compact
operators $X\to Y$ is written $\mathcal K(X,Y)$. The metric used here is $d(x,y)=\|x-y\|$, supplied over $\mathbb R$ by [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and over $\mathbb C$ by [[lem-complex-norm-realification-is-a-real-norm]].

**The closed unit ball suffices.** Put
$\overline B_X:=\{x\in X:\|x\|\le 1\}$
([[def-metric-ball]]). Then $T$ is compact if and only if
$\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ is a compact subset of $Y$.

Indeed, if $T$ is compact then $\overline B_X$ is bounded, because
$\overline B_X\subseteq B(0,2)$ while $B(0,2)$ is bounded and a subset of a
bounded set is bounded, so $T(\overline B_X)$ has compact closure. Conversely
assume $\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ compact and let $A\subseteq X$ be bounded.
If $A=\varnothing$ then $T(A)=\varnothing$, whose closure is empty and hence
compact. Otherwise $A\subseteq B(x_0,r)$ for some $x_0\in X$ and real $r>0$, so
every $x\in A$ satisfies $\|x\|\le\|x_0\|+r=:R$; if $R>0$ then
$A\subseteq R\,\overline B_X$ and if $R=0$ then $A\subseteq\{0\}$, so in either
case $T(A)\subseteq R\,\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$. Scalar multiplication by
$R$ is continuous ([[lem-vector-operations-are-continuous-in-a-normed-space]]),
so $R\,\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ is a compact subset of $Y$
([[thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps]]), hence closed
([[thm-compact-subset-is-closed-and-bounded]]); therefore
$\overline{T(A)}\subseteq R\,\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ is a closed subset of a
compact set, hence compact, and $T$ is compact.

**A compact operator is bounded.** If $T$ is compact then the compact set
$\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ is bounded
([[thm-compact-subset-is-closed-and-bounded]]), so there is a real $C\ge0$ with
$\|Tx\|\le C$ for every $x\in\overline B_X$ and hence $\|Tx\|\le C\|x\|$ for
every $x\in X$; thus $T$ is a bounded linear operator
([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). This is a consequence of compactness, not a
hypothesis of the definition.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Suppose $y=Kx$. Then $y\perp N(K^*)$ by [F3]. For each $j\in J$, the adjoint identity and singular relation give $\langle y,u_j\rangle_Y=\langle Kx,u_j\rangle_Y =\langle x,K^*u_j\rangle_X=s_j\langle x,v_j\rangle_X$. Applying [F5] to finite subsets of the orthonormal family $(v_j)$ shows $P_K(y)=\sum_{j\in J}|\langle x,v_j\rangle_X|^2\le\|x\|_X^2<\infty$. This proves necessity in claim 1.

Now let $y\perp N(K^*)$ and $P_K(y)<\infty$. By [F3], $y\in\overline{R(K)}$. For finite $J$ take the finite sum; for infinite $J$ let $x_N=\sum_{j=1}^{N}s_j^{-1}\langle y,u_j\rangle_Yv_j$. For $M>N$, [F6] gives $\|x_M-x_N\|_X^2=\sum_{j=N+1}^{M}s_j^{-2}|\langle y,u_j\rangle_Y|^2$, whose tails tend to zero because $P_K(y)<\infty$. Thus $(x_N)$ is Cauchy and converges to $x\in X$ by [F9]. The complete right singular family places $x$ in $N(K)^\perp$.

By [F11], applying $K$ to the finite sums and passing to the limit gives $Kx=\lim_{N\to\infty}Kx_N=\lim_{N\to\infty}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\langle y,u_j\rangle_Yu_j=y$, where the last equality is [F7] on $\overline{R(K)}$. The finite-$J$ case is the same equality with a finite sum. Since $x\in N(K)^\perp$ and $Kx=y$, [F10] identifies $x=K^\dagger y$. This proves sufficiency in claim 1 and the formula there.

For arbitrary $y\in Y$, apply [F8] to the closed subspace $M=\overline{R(K)}$ and write $y=p+q$ with $p\in M$ and $q\in M^\perp$. Since $R(K)\subseteq M$, $q\in R(K)^\perp$. The Fourier coefficients of $p$ are $\langle p,u_j\rangle_Y=\langle y,u_j\rangle_Y$, and [F7] expands $p$ in the complete left singular family. If $P_K(y)<\infty$, the construction in steps 1.2–2.1 applied to $p\in M=(N(K^*))^\perp$ gives $p\in R(K)$ and $K^\dagger p=\sum_j s_j^{-1}\langle y,u_j\rangle_Yv_j$; hence $y=p+q\in R(K)\oplus R(K)^\perp=D(K^\dagger)$ and [F10] gives the displayed formula.

Conversely, let $y=r+q\in D(K^\dagger)$ with $r\in R(K)$ and $q\in R(K)^\perp$. By [F3], $q\in N(K^*)$ and each $u_j\in N(K^*)^\perp$, so $\langle q,u_j\rangle_Y=0$. Step 1.1 applied to $r$ shows $P_K(y)=P_K(r)<\infty$; [F10] gives $K^\dagger y=K^\dagger r$ and the same series formula. Thus the domain is exactly the set where the Picard sum is finite, completing claim 2.

citations.quote:
Let $X,Y$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces over the same scalar field, and let
$K:X\to Y$ be a compact linear operator. The associated compact linear inverse
model has parameter space $X$, data space $Y$, forward map $K$, and admissible
truth class $X$: for a true parameter $x^\dagger\in X$, the exact datum is
$y=Kx^\dagger\in Y$. Given an exact datum $y\in Y$, solving this inverse
problem means finding a parameter $x\in X$ such that $Kx=y$. No injectivity,
surjectivity, or closed-range assumption is included in the model.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field and let
$T:X\to Y$ be a bounded linear operator
([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]) whose range $T(X)$ admits an ordered basis of
finite length ([[def-linear-basis]]). Then $T$ is compact
([[def-compact-linear-operator]]).

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with **conjugation** $z\mapsto\overline z$
the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of [[def-inner-product-space]]: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

**Induced length.** The **induced length**, or inner-product norm, of $v$ is

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

which is exactly the published [[def-inner-product-norm]]: positive definiteness
makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square
root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$.

**The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or
complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.
In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of
$\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex
modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either
scalar field.

Every Cauchy sequence of real numbers ([[def-real-limit]]) converges to a real
number. Together with [[thm-reals-ordered-field]], this completes the
construction: $\mathbb{R}$ is a complete totally ordered field.
The proof uses no form of the axiom of choice.

A **real Hilbert space** is a real inner-product space $H$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]) whose induced-length metric is complete in the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]]: every Cauchy sequence in $H$ for the norm $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ ([[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]) converges to a point of $H$. A **complex Hilbert space** is a complex inner-product space with the same completeness property, so that a Hilbert space is exactly a real or complex inner-product space that is a Banach space for its induced norm ([[def-banach-space]]).

**The completion convention is the Cauchy-sequence one.**
[[def-banach-space]] defines completeness by convergence of Cauchy sequences, and this page keeps that convention throughout. It is weaker than $\sigma$-completeness — the assertion that every decreasing sequence of nonempty closed subsets with diameters tending to zero has a nonempty intersection. The two agree in ZFC, but Blackadar, Farah and Karagila note that the closest-point theorem on a $\sigma$-complete inner-product space is provable in ZF, whereas the Cauchy-complete form used below consumes the Axiom of Countable Choice; nothing here silently imports the stronger notion.

derivations.claim: The standard dot products on $\mathbb R$ and $\mathbb R^2$ satisfy the inner-product axioms [F3] by coordinatewise addition, multiplication and $\sum_i x_i^2=0\Rightarrow x_i=0$ for each coordinate. The standard Euclidean spaces $\mathbb R$ and $\mathbb R^2$ are complete: if a sequence is Cauchy in Euclidean norm, each coordinate is Cauchy because its absolute difference is bounded by the Euclidean distance; each coordinate converges by [F4], and the finite sum of squared coordinate errors tends to zero. Thus they are real Hilbert spaces by [F3] and [F5]. The map $K$ is linear and $\|Kx\|=|x|$, so it is bounded; its range is the one-dimensional span of $(1,0)$, and [F2] makes it compact. It therefore gives the stated compact linear inverse model by [F1].

For $a\in\mathbb R$ and $(b,c)\in\mathbb R^2$, $\langle Ka,(b,c)\rangle=ab=\langle a,K^*(b,c)\rangle$. Hence $N(K^*)=\{(0,c):c\in\mathbb R\}$, while $R(K)=\{(a,0):a\in\mathbb R\}$. In particular $y$ is a nonzero element of $N(K^*)$, and no scalar $x$ satisfies $Kx=y$.

The vector $v_1=1$ spans the input and $u_1=(1,0)$ spans $\overline{R(K)}$; they satisfy $Kv_1=u_1$ and $K^*u_1=v_1$. Thus the positive singular pair has $s_1=1$. The Picard sum defined in the statement has sole term $|\langle (0,1),(1,0)\rangle|^2/1^2=0$. Step 1.2 shows that $y\in N(K^*)\setminus\{0\}$, so the missing orthogonality condition allows finite Picard sum without exact solvability.
