citations.quote:
Throughout, $\mathbb F$ is $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$ and families are indexed by
an arbitrary set $I$, with no enumeration or countability assumed. Finite real lists use [[def-finite-sum]], and sums over finite subsets use [[def-finite-sum-in-a-commutative-monoid]] in the additive monoid of the scalar field. Disjoint splitting is [[lem-finite-sum-reindexing-and-fubini]], and scalar modulus estimates use [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]; all suprema and infima of real sets below are
taken in the complete ordered field $\mathbb R$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) or in $[0,+\infty]\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$
([[def-extended-reals]], [[lem-extended-reals-complete]]).

**Sums of nonnegative families.** Let $(c_i)_{i\in I}$ be a family of
nonnegative reals and let $\operatorname{Fin}(I)$ be the set of finite subsets of
$I$, ordered by inclusion. Define

$$\sum_{i\in I}c_i:=\sup\Bigl\{\sum_{i\in F}c_i \;:\; F\in\operatorname{Fin}(I)\Bigr\}\in[0,+\infty] .$$

The set of finite subsums is nonempty, since $\varnothing$ contributes the empty
sum $0$, so the supremum exists in $[0,+\infty]$; it is a real number exactly
when the finite subsums are bounded above in $\mathbb R$, and $+\infty$
otherwise. For finite $I$ the finite subsum at $I$ is the largest of all finite
subsums, because all terms are nonnegative, so the definition agrees with the
finite sum; in particular $\sum_{i\in I}c_i=0$ when every $c_i$ is $0$, and
$I=\varnothing$ gives the empty sum $0$.

**Splitting identity and small tails.** Fix a finite $F\subseteq I$. Every
finite $G\subseteq I$ splits as the disjoint union $(G\cap F)\cup(G\setminus F)$,
so $\sum_{i\in G}c_i=\sum_{i\in G\cap F}c_i+\sum_{i\in G\setminus F}c_i\le\sum_{i\in F}c_i+\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i$;
conversely the finite $G$ with $F\subseteq G$ satisfy
$\sum_{i\in G}c_i=\sum_{i\in F}c_i+\sum_{i\in G\setminus F}c_i$. Taking suprema,
with the constant $\sum_{i\in F}c_i$ passing through the supremum,

$$\sum_{i\in I}c_i=\sum_{i\in F}c_i+\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i . \qquad (1)$$

Consequently, if $S:=\sum_{i\in I}c_i$ is finite, then for every real
$\varepsilon>0$ there is a finite $F\subseteq I$ with
$\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i<\varepsilon$: the finite subsums form a nonempty
bounded-above set with supremum $S$, so by the epsilon characterisation of the
supremum ([[lem-sup-epsilon]]) some finite $F$ has
$S-\varepsilon<\sum_{i\in F}c_i$, and (1) gives
$\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i=S-\sum_{i\in F}c_i<\varepsilon$. Such an $F$ is
called a **tail-control set** for $\varepsilon$.

**Sums of scalar families.** Now let $(a_i)_{i\in I}$ be a family in $\mathbb F$
and put $s_F:=\sum_{i\in F}a_i$ for finite $F\subseteq I$. The set
$\operatorname{Fin}(I)$ with inclusion is a directed preorder: it is nonempty and
$F\cup G$ is a common upper bound of $F$ and $G$
([[def-directed-set-and-net]]). Hence $(s_F)_{F\in\operatorname{Fin}(I)}$ is a
net in $\mathbb F$, the **finite-subset net** of the family, and the family is
**summable** when this net converges
([[def-net-convergence-and-cluster-point]]). The scalar metric is the usual real metric or [[def-complex-metric-convergence-and-continuity]]. These metric spaces are Hausdorff by [[thm-metric-hausdorff-separation]]. A net in $\mathbb F$ has at most one limit
([[thm-hausdorff-iff-net-limits-are-unique]]), so for a summable family the
limit is unique and we write $\sum_{i\in I}a_i:=\lim_F s_F$ for it. The family is
**absolutely summable** when $\sum_{i\in I}|a_i|<+\infty$ in the sense above.

**Every absolutely summable family is summable, in ZF.** Assume
$S:=\sum_{i\in I}|a_i|$ is finite and put $S_F:=\sum_{i\in F}|a_i|$ for finite
$F$. For finite $F,G\subseteq I$ the triangle inequality for finite sums and the
fact that a finite subsum is at most the whole nonnegative sum give

$$|s_F-s_G|\le\sum_{i\in F\triangle G}|a_i|\le S-S_{F\cap G} . \qquad (2)$$

Now fix a real $\varepsilon>0$, let $F_0$ be a tail-control set for
$\varepsilon$, and let $F,G\supseteq F_0$ be finite. Then $F\cap G\supseteq F_0$,
so $S-S_{F\cap G}\le S-S_{F_0}<\varepsilon$ and (2) gives
$|s_F-s_G|<\varepsilon$.

First suppose $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$. For each finite $F$ define
$A_F:=\inf\{s_G : G\supseteq F\}$ and $B_F:=\sup\{s_G : G\supseteq F\}$ over
finite $G$. Both are real numbers, because $|s_G|\le S_G\le S$, so the two sets
are nonempty and bounded, and $A_F\le B_F$. If $H\supseteq F$ then
$A_H\ge A_F$ and $B_H\le B_F$. Let $L:=\sup_FA_F$ and $U:=\inf_FB_F$.
Since $A_F\le s_{F\cup H}\le B_H$ for all finite $F,H$, we get $L\le U$.
Moreover, the preceding estimate holds for every pair $F,G\supseteq F_0$;
taking the supremum over $F$ and the infimum over $G$ gives
$B_{F_0}-A_{F_0}\le\varepsilon$. Hence
$0\le U-L\le B_{F_0}-A_{F_0}\le\varepsilon$ for every $\varepsilon>0$, so
$L=U=:s$. If $F\supseteq F_0$, then both $s_F$ and $s$ lie in
$[A_{F_0},B_{F_0}]$, and therefore $|s_F-s|\le\varepsilon$.

If $\mathbb F=\mathbb C$, apply the real argument just proved to the families
$(\operatorname{Re}a_i)$ and $(\operatorname{Im}a_i)$. They are absolutely
summable because $|\operatorname{Re}a_i|,|\operatorname{Im}a_i|\le|a_i|$.
Their finite-subset nets converge to real numbers $r$ and $t$, respectively,
so $s_F\to r+it$ in $\mathbb C$. Thus every absolutely summable real or complex
family is summable. **No choice principle is used**: the construction uses only
two-sided suprema in $\mathbb R$.

**Linearity and absolute value.** If $(a_i)$ and $(b_i)$ are absolutely
summable and $\lambda\in\mathbb F$, then so are $(a_i+b_i)$ and
$(\lambda a_i)$, and

$$\sum_{i\in I}(a_i+b_i)=\sum_{i\in I}a_i+\sum_{i\in I}b_i,\qquad \sum_{i\in I}\lambda a_i=\lambda\sum_{i\in I}a_i,\qquad \Bigl|\sum_{i\in I}a_i\Bigr|\le\sum_{i\in I}|a_i| ,$$

because the corresponding identities hold for every finite subsum, both sides
are limits of the corresponding finite-subset nets, and addition, scalar
multiplication and the modulus are continuous. The splitting identity (1)
likewise passes to absolutely summable scalar families:
$\sum_{i\in I}a_i=\sum_{i\in F}a_i+\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}a_i$ for every finite
$F$, because finite subsums over sets containing $F$ converge to the left-hand
side and equal the finite sum over $F$ plus the finite subsum of the tail, whose
net converges to the tail sum.

**The finite-dimensional Cauchy-Schwarz inequality.** Let $(u_k)_{0\le k<m}$ and $(v_k)_{0\le k<m}$ be scalar lists, for $m\in\mathbb N$ and let $t\in\mathbb R$. Every term of
$\sum_{k<m}(|u_k|-t|v_k|)^2$ is nonnegative, so for all real $t$

$$0\le\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2-2t\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|+t^2\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2 .$$

If $\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2>0$, substituting
$t=\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|\bigr)/\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\bigr)$ gives
$\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|\bigr)^2\le\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2\bigr)\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\bigr)$;
if $\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2=0$ then every $v_k=0$ and both sides are $0$. In either case
$\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|\le\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2\bigr)^{1/2}\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\bigr)^{1/2}$
after taking square roots, and applying the modulus inequality for finite sums
to $u_k\overline{v_k}$ also gives

$$\Bigl|\sum_{k<m}u_k\overline{v_k}\Bigr|\le\Bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2\Bigr)^{1/2}\Bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\Bigr)^{1/2} . \qquad (3)$$

**The space $\ell^2(I)$.** For a family $a=(a_i)_{i\in I}$ in $\mathbb F$ define
$Q(a):=\sum_{i\in I}|a_i|^2$. If $Q(a)$ is finite, set $\|a\|_2:=\sqrt{Q(a)}$, using the nonnegative real square root of [[thm-of-square-roots]]; if $Q(a)=+\infty$, set $\|a\|_2:=+\infty$. This is a case definition, not exponentiation of an extended real. Let

$$\ell^2(I,\mathbb F):=\{\,a=(a_i)_{i\in I} : \|a\|_2<+\infty\,\}.$$

The set $\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ is a vector space over $\mathbb F$: it contains the
zero family, is closed under scalar multiplication because
$\|\lambda a\|_2=|\lambda|\,\|a\|_2$, and is closed under addition because (3)
applied to finite subsums gives $\|a+b\|_2\le\|a\|_2+\|b\|_2<+\infty$. The same
inequality is the triangle inequality for $\|\cdot\|_2$, which is moreover
nonnegative, vanishes only for the zero family (an arbitrary sum of nonnegative
terms with supremum $0$ has every term $0$) and satisfies
$\|\lambda a\|_2=|\lambda|\,\|a\|_2$; thus $\|\cdot\|_2$ is a norm on
$\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$. Finally the **pairing**
$\langle a,b\rangle:=\sum_{i\in I}a_i\overline{b_i}$ is well defined on
$\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)\times\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$, because
$|a_i\overline{b_i}|=|a_i||b_i|$ has finite nonnegative sum by (3); it is linear
in the first variable, conjugate symmetric, positive definite, and satisfies
$\langle a,a\rangle=\|a\|_2^2$, all by the corresponding finite identities and
the linearity of the sum. Consequently $\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ is an inner-product
space, and $e_i\in\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ denotes the family that is $1$ at $i$ and
$0$ elsewhere. **Nothing here asserts that $\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ is complete**;
that follows later, from an orthonormal basis of a Hilbert space.

reviewed.reason: The supplier defines the inner product on two vectors, defines each coordinate vector, and proves small tails for any finite-total nonnegative indexed family. F1 applies those clauses with the fixed index set N; its finite set F is the tail-control set, not a list of inner-product arguments.

citations.quote:
The real sequence space
$$\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)=\left\{x=(x_n):\sum_{n\in\mathbb N}|x_n|^2<\infty\right\},$$
with its canonical inner product and norm from
[[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]], is complete and
therefore is a real Hilbert space.

A **real Hilbert space** is a real inner-product space $H$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]) whose induced-length metric is complete in the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]]: every Cauchy sequence in $H$ for the norm $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ ([[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]) converges to a point of $H$. A **complex Hilbert space** is a complex inner-product space with the same completeness property, so that a Hilbert space is exactly a real or complex inner-product space that is a Banach space for its induced norm ([[def-banach-space]]).

**The completion convention is the Cauchy-sequence one.**
[[def-banach-space]] defines completeness by convergence of Cauchy sequences, and this page keeps that convention throughout. It is weaker than $\sigma$-completeness — the assertion that every decreasing sequence of nonempty closed subsets with diameters tending to zero has a nonempty intersection. The two agree in ZFC, but Blackadar, Farah and Karagila note that the closest-point theorem on a $\sigma$-complete inner-product space is provable in ZF, whereas the Cauchy-complete form used below consumes the Axiom of Countable Choice; nothing here silently imports the stronger notion.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field and let
$T:X\to Y$ be a bounded linear operator
([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]) whose range $T(X)$ admits an ordered basis of
finite length ([[def-linear-basis]]). Then $T$ is compact
([[def-compact-linear-operator]]).

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $X$ be a
normed space, let $Y$ be a Banach space ([[def-banach-space]]), and let
$T_n:X\to Y$, $n\in\mathbb N$, be compact operators
([[def-compact-linear-operator]]) with $\|T_n-T\|\to0$ for a bounded linear
operator $T:X\to Y$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]],
[[def-operator-norm]], [[def-metric-convergence]]). Then $T$ is compact.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $K:X\to Y$ be a compact linear map
between real or complex Hilbert spaces, with Hilbert adjoint $K^*:Y\to X$.
Write $\mathbb N_{>0}:=\{1,2,3,\ldots\}$. If $R(K)$ has finite dimension
$r\in\mathbb N$, put $J=\{1,\ldots,r\}$, interpreted as empty when $r=0$;
if $R(K)$ is infinite-dimensional, put $J=\mathbb N_{>0}$. Thus $J$ indexes
exactly the positive singular values $s_j>0$ in nonincreasing order. Let
$(v_j)_{j\in J}$ and $(u_j)_{j\in J}$ be complete
orthonormal families in $N(K)^\perp$ and $\overline{R(K)}$, respectively,
with $Kv_j=s_ju_j$ and $K^*u_j=s_jv_j$. The empty sum is zero, finite $J$
uses a finite sum, and infinite $J$ uses the norm-convergent series whenever
the stated square-summability condition holds. Use inner products linear in the
first argument. Define the Picard sum
$$P_K(y):=\sum_{j\in J}\frac{|\langle y,u_j\rangle_Y|^2}{s_j^2},\qquad y\in Y.$$
Then:

1. The exact equation $Kx=y$ is solvable if and only if
   $y\perp N(K^*)$ and $P_K(y)<\infty$.

2. The domain of the Hilbert-space Moore–Penrose inverse is
   $$D(K^\dagger)=R(K)\oplus R(K)^\perp=\{y\in Y:P_K(y)<\infty\},$$
   and for every $y\in D(K^\dagger)$,
   $$K^\dagger y=\sum_{j\in J}\frac{\langle y,u_j\rangle_Y}{s_j}v_j.$$
   Thus the orthogonal component in $R(K)^\perp=N(K^*)$ is discarded by
   $K^\dagger$; exact range membership additionally requires that component
   to be zero.

For every real $p$,
$$\sum_{k\ge1}\frac1{k^p}\text{ converges}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad p>1.$$

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) and let
$\varepsilon \in F$ with $\varepsilon > 0$. Then there is a natural number
$n \ge 1$ such that

$$\frac{1}{n \cdot 1_F} < \varepsilon ,$$

where $n \cdot 1_F$ is the canonical natural of $F$ ([[thm-of-archimedean]]) and
$1/(n \cdot 1_F)$ is its multiplicative inverse ([[def-field]]). As is standard
we abbreviate $n \cdot 1_F$ to $n$ and write the conclusion $1/n < \varepsilon$.

This is the **reciprocal form** of the Archimedean property.
[[thm-of-archimedean]] on its own delivers only the assertion that the canonical
naturals are cofinal, $x < n \cdot 1_F$; the form actually used in analysis, that
the reciprocals of the naturals get below every positive bound, is the statement
above, and it is recorded separately so that no proof has to reconstruct the
inversion step in passing.

Let $X,Y$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces over the same scalar field, and let
$K:X\to Y$ be a compact linear operator. The associated compact linear inverse
model has parameter space $X$, data space $Y$, forward map $K$, and admissible
truth class $X$: for a true parameter $x^\dagger\in X$, the exact datum is
$y=Kx^\dagger\in Y$. Given an exact datum $y\in Y$, solving this inverse
problem means finding a parameter $x\in X$ such that $Kx=y$. No injectivity,
surjectivity, or closed-range assumption is included in the model.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ and $K$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces and let $T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ be a bounded linear operator ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]], [[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]]). For fixed $y\in K$ the map

$$x\longmapsto\langle Tx,y\rangle_K$$

is a bounded linear functional on $H$: it is linear in $x$ because $T$ is linear and the pairing is linear in its first argument, and $|\langle Tx,y\rangle_K|\le\|Tx\|\,\|y\|\le\|T\|\,\|x\|\,\|y\|$ by Cauchy–Schwarz and the operator-norm inequality ([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]], [[def-operator-norm]]). By Riesz representation ([[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]) there is therefore a unique vector $T^*y\in H$ with

$$\langle Tx,y\rangle_K=\langle x,T^*y\rangle_H\qquad\text{for every }x\in H .$$

The **Hilbert adjoint** of $T$ is the map

$$T^*:K\longrightarrow H,\qquad y\longmapsto T^*y .$$

It is the unique map $K\to H$ satisfying the displayed identity, since two such maps have $\langle x,(T^*_1-T^*_2)y\rangle=0$ for all $x$ and hence $(T^*_1-T^*_2)y=0$ by positive definiteness.

**The dictionary with the Banach transpose.** Write $R_H:H\to H^*$ and $R_K:K\to K^*$ for the Riesz maps $R_H(x)=\langle\,\cdot\,,x\rangle_H$ and $R_K(y)=\langle\,\cdot\,,y\rangle_K$, and let $T'\in\mathcal B(K^*,H^*)$ be the transpose of $T$, $(T'g)(x)=g(Tx)$ ([[def-transpose-of-a-bounded-operator]]). Then for all $y\in K$ and $x\in H$,

$$\bigl(R_H(T^*y)\bigr)(x)=\langle x,T^*y\rangle_H=\langle Tx,y\rangle_K=(R_Ky)(Tx)=\bigl(T'(R_Ky)\bigr)(x),$$

so $R_H\,T^*=T'\,R_K$. The Hilbert adjoint is thus the Banach transpose conjugated by the Riesz identifications of $H$ and $K$ with their duals; it is a different operator from $T'$ whenever the Riesz maps are conjugate-linear.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: The map $K$ is linear and satisfies $\|Kx\|_2^2=\sum_n|x_n|^2/(n+1)^2\le\|x\|_2^2$, so it is bounded. For $N\in\mathbb N$, let $(K_Nx)_n=x_n/(n+1)$ when $n\le N$ and $0$ otherwise. The estimate $\|K_Nx\|_2^2\le\|x\|_2^2$ makes $K_N$ bounded, and its range is spanned by the finite ordered family $(e_0,\ldots,e_N)$: every output has no coordinates beyond $N$, and $K_N((n+1)e_n)=e_n$ for each $n\le N$, while these coordinate vectors are linearly independent. Thus they form an ordered basis of the range, and $K_N$ is compact by [F3]. For every $x$, $\|(K-K_N)x\|_2^2=\sum_{n>N}|x_n|^2/(n+1)^2\le\|x\|_2^2/(N+2)^2$, with equality in the operator norm at $x=e_{N+1}$. Hence $\|K-K_N\|=1/(N+2)\to0$. By [F2] the codomain is Banach, so [F4] gives compactness of $K$. It is a compact inverse model by [F8].

Every finitely supported $z\in H$ belongs to $R(K)$: set $x_n=(n+1)z_n$, which is finitely supported and satisfies $Kx=z$. For any $z\in H$ and $\varepsilon>0$, [F1] gives a finite set $F\subseteq\mathbb N$ with $\sum_{n\notin F}|z_n|^2<\varepsilon^2$; choose $N$ containing $F$. Then the truncation $z^{(N)}$ supported on indices $n\le N$ obeys $\|z-z^{(N)}\|_2^2=\sum_{n>N}|z_n|^2<\varepsilon^2$. Thus finitely supported vectors are dense, and since all lie in $R(K)$, $R(K)$ is dense in $H$.

For $y_n=1/(n+1)$, [F6] gives $y\in H$. Its finite truncations are in $R(K)$ by step 1.2 and converge to $y$ because the tails of its square-sum tend to zero; hence $y\in\overline{R(K)}$. If $Kx=y$, then every coordinate equation gives $x_n=1$, contradicting $x\in H$. Indeed, if the finite sums $\sum_{n=0}^{N}|x_n|^2=N+1$ had an upper bound $B\ge0$, [F7] with $\varepsilon=1/(B+1)$ would give $m>B+1$, and the partial sum at $N=m$ would exceed $B$. Therefore $y\notin R(K)$ and the dense range is not closed.

The coordinate vectors are orthonormal because [F1] gives $\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=1$ when $i=j$ and $0$ otherwise. They are complete: for any $x\in H$ and $\varepsilon>0$, [F1] gives a finite set $F$ with $\sum_{n\notin F}|x_n|^2<\varepsilon^2$; choose $N$ containing $F$, so the truncation's squared error is at most this tail. Direct calculation gives $N(K)=\{0\}$ and $\overline{R(K)}=H$ by step 1.2. For $x,z\in H$, the canonical inner product gives $\langle Kx,z\rangle=\sum_n x_nz_n/(n+1)=\langle x,Kz\rangle$; hence [F9] identifies $K^*=K$. Since all diagonal coefficients are positive, $N(K^*)=\{0\}$. Therefore $Ke_n=(n+1)^{-1}e_n$ and $K^*e_n=(n+1)^{-1}e_n$, and the family is complete on both $N(K)^\perp$ and $\overline{R(K)}$. Reindexing by $j=n+1$ gives the positive singular system $s_j=1/j$, $v_j=u_j=e_{j-1}$ for $j\ge1$. The datum has $\langle y,e_{j-1}\rangle=1/j$, so every Picard summand equals $1$. For any real bound $B\ge0$, [F7] applied with $\varepsilon=1/(B+1)$ gives an index $m>B+1$, so the corresponding finite subsums are unbounded and the Picard sum diverges, as [F5] predicts for a datum outside the range.

derivations.claim: For each fixed coordinate $j$, apply [F2] with one-dimensional prior variance $C_0=\tau_j^2$, observation map $A=s_j$, and noise variance $\Gamma=\epsilon^2$. Then $AC_0A^T+\Gamma=s_j^2\tau_j^2+\epsilon^2>0$, and [F2] gives posterior mean $\tau_j^2s_jY_j/(\epsilon^2+\tau_j^2s_j^2)=\lambda_jY_j/s_j$ and variance $\tau_j^2-\tau_j^4s_j^2/(\epsilon^2+\tau_j^2s_j^2)=v_j$.

For every finite coordinate set $J$, the prior/noise pairs indexed by $J$ are independent of the pairs outside $J$. Applying [F2] to the diagonal finite block gives the product of the scalar laws from step 1.1 as the conditional law of $\theta_J$ given $Y_J$; independence makes it the same conditional law given the full data. The product Gaussian law $Q_y=\bigotimes_{j\ge1}N(\lambda_jy_j/s_j,v_j)$ exists on $\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}$ by [F3]. On finite-coordinate cylinders its evaluations are Borel functions of $y$; the class of Borel sets $B$ for which $y\mapsto Q_y(B)$ is measurable is a Dynkin system containing the generating cylinder $\pi$-system, so [F6] makes $Q$ a probability kernel. The same finite-block conditional identity holds on data cylinders, and [F5] applied successively in the data and parameter coordinates extends it to all product-Borel events. Thus $Q_y$ is the prior-predictive conditional law on the product coordinate space.

Put $m_j(y)=\lambda_jy_j/s_j$ and $Y_0=\{y:\sum_jm_j(y)^2<\infty\}$. This is Borel because each $m_j$ is coordinate-measurable and $\ell^2=\bigcup_{k\ge1}\bigcap_{N\ge1}\{x:\sum_{j=1}^Nx_j^2\le k\}$. Since $v_j\le\tau_j^2$, [F7] gives $\int\sum_jx_j^2\,Q_y(dx)=\sum_j(m_j(y)^2+v_j)<\infty$ on $Y_0$, so $Q_y(\ell^2)=1$ there. Under the prior-predictive law, $\mathbb E m_j(Y)^2=\lambda_j^2\tau_j^2+\lambda_j^2\epsilon^2/s_j^2=\lambda_j\tau_j^2\le\tau_j^2$; under the fixed truth, $m_j(Y)=\lambda_j\theta_j^\dagger+\lambda_j\epsilon\xi_j/s_j$ and $\mathbb E_{\theta^\dagger}m_j(Y)^2=\lambda_j^2(\theta_j^\dagger)^2+\lambda_j^2\epsilon^2/s_j^2\le(\theta_j^\dagger)^2+\tau_j^2$. Applying [F7] to the partial sums shows $Y_0$ has full measure under both laws. Restrict $Q_y$ to $\ell^2$ on $Y_0$ and set it equal to $\delta_0$ outside $Y_0$; this is a posterior version on $\ell^2$ and is defined for fixed-truth-almost every observation.

For $y\in Y_0$, the product posterior has coordinate mean $m_j(y)$ and variance $v_j$, so its expected squared coordinate error is $(m_j(y)-\theta_j^\dagger)^2+v_j$. The partial sums of these nonnegative errors increase to $\|\theta-\theta^\dagger\|_2^2$; [F7] therefore gives $\int\|\theta-\theta^\dagger\|_2^2\,\Pi_\epsilon(d\theta\mid y)=\sum_j((m_j(y)-\theta_j^\dagger)^2+v_j)$, with the value $+\infty$ allowed.

Under the fixed truth, $m_j(Y)-\theta_j^\dagger=-(1-\lambda_j)\theta_j^\dagger+\lambda_j\epsilon\xi_j/s_j$. The noise has mean zero and variance one, so its cross term has expectation zero and $\mathbb E_{\theta^\dagger}(m_j(Y)-\theta_j^\dagger)^2=(1-\lambda_j)^2(\theta_j^\dagger)^2+\lambda_j^2\epsilon^2/s_j^2$. The identity $v_js_j^2/\epsilon^2=\lambda_j$ gives $\lambda_j^2\epsilon^2/s_j^2=v_j^2s_j^2/\epsilon^2$. Taking expectations in step 4.1 and applying [F7] to the nonnegative partial sums proves the displayed exact series identity.

For each fixed data sequence, apply [F8] to the posterior probability measure with $f(\theta)=\|\theta-\theta^\dagger\|_2^2$ and threshold $R^2>0$. This gives posterior tail mass at most $R^{-2}$ times the posterior second moment. Taking fixed-truth expectation and using step 5.1 yields the stated bound. If $S_\epsilon(\theta^\dagger)\le C r_\epsilon^2$, substitute $R=M_\epsilon r_\epsilon$ to obtain expected tail mass at most $C/M_\epsilon^2\to0$ for every $M_\epsilon\to\infty$; [F9] identifies $r_\epsilon$ as a posterior contraction rate.

derivations.claim: Let $H=\ell^2$ with standard basis $(e_j)$ and set $\tau_j^2=j^{-1-2\alpha}$. Each dyadic block $2^k\le j<2^{k+1}$ has at most $2^k$ terms, each at most $2^{-k(1+2\alpha)}$, so [F5] gives $\sum_j\tau_j^2\le\sum_{k\ge0}2^{-2\alpha k}<\infty$. Define $\Gamma e_j=\tau_j^2e_j$. It is positive and self-adjoint; its truncations $\Gamma_N$ have finite rank, and $\|\Gamma-\Gamma_N\|\le\sup_{j>N}\tau_j^2\le\sum_{j>N}\tau_j^2\to0$, so [F6] makes $\Gamma$ compact. The expansion $\Gamma x=\sum_j\langle x,\tau_j^2e_j\rangle e_j$ has nuclear sum $\sum_j\tau_j^2<\infty$, so [F6] also makes it trace class. By [F7] there is a Borel centered Gaussian random element $G$ in $H$ with covariance $\Gamma$. For each finite coordinate vector, every linear projection is centered normal by [F7], hence it is jointly Gaussian by [F8]; its covariance matrix is diagonal with entries $\tau_j^2$. Repeatedly applying [F9] to the first coordinate and the remaining block proves that the coordinates are independent, and [F10] identifies their laws as $N(0,\tau_j^2)$. Thus the law of $G$ is the stated prior on $\ell^2$.

Put $d=1+2\alpha+2p$ and $J=\lceil\epsilon^{-2/d}\rceil$. Since $\epsilon^{-2/d}\ge1$, one has $\epsilon^{-2/d}\le J\le2\epsilon^{-2/d}$. The posterior variance satisfies $v_j\le\min\{j^{-1-2\alpha},\epsilon^2j^{2p}\}$. Therefore $\sum_{j\ge1}v_j\le\epsilon^2\sum_{j\le J}j^{2p}+\sum_{j>J}j^{-1-2\alpha}\le\epsilon^2J^{2p+1}+2J^{-2\alpha}\sum_{k\ge0}2^{-2\alpha k}\le C_{\alpha,p}\epsilon^{4\alpha/d}$. The finite sum has at most $J$ terms each at most $J^{2p}$; for the tail, the block $2^kJ<j\le2^{k+1}J$ has at most $2^{k+1}J$ terms, each at most $(2^kJ)^{-1-2\alpha}$.

Write $b_j=1-\lambda_j=\epsilon^2/(\epsilon^2+j^{-d})\le\min\{1,\epsilon^2j^d\}$. The ellipsoid condition gives $\sum_jb_j^2(\theta_j^\dagger)^2\le L^2\sup_j b_j^2j^{-2\beta}$. For $j\le J$, this supremum is bounded by $\epsilon^4J^{2d-2\beta}$ when $\beta\le d$, and by $\epsilon^4$ when $\beta>d$. For $j>J$, it is at most $J^{-2\beta}$. The bounds on $J$ in step 1.2 give $\sum_jb_j^2(\theta_j^\dagger)^2\le C_{\alpha,\beta,p,L}\epsilon^{\min\{4\beta/d,4\}}$. This treats the equality case $\beta=d$ in the first branch.

Since $v_js_j^2/\epsilon^2=\lambda_j\le1$, one has $v_j^2s_j^2/\epsilon^2=v_j\lambda_j\le v_j$. The exact sum [F1] and steps 1.2–2.1 therefore give $S_\epsilon(\theta^\dagger)\le C_{\alpha,\beta,p,L}\epsilon^{4\min\{\alpha,\beta\}/d}$; here $4\alpha/d<4$. Setting $r_\epsilon=\epsilon^{2\min\{\alpha,\beta\}/d}$ makes the expected posterior tail outside $M_\epsilon r_\epsilon$ at most $C/M_\epsilon^2$, which tends to zero for every $M_\epsilon\to\infty$. By [F2], this is the stated contraction rate.

Since $e=\exp(1)$, real-power definition and logarithm inversion give $e^{-2\alpha}=\exp(-2\alpha)$; strict increase, positivity and $\exp(0)=1$ imply $0<e^{-2\alpha}<1$. By the exponent laws, $\tau_j^2=(e^{-2\alpha})^j$, so [F6] gives $\sum_j\tau_j^2<\infty$. Define $\Gamma e_j=\tau_j^2e_j$. It is positive and self-adjoint; its truncations $\Gamma_N$ have finite rank, and $\|\Gamma-\Gamma_N\|\le\sup_{j>N}\tau_j^2\le\sum_{j>N}\tau_j^2\to0$, so [F7] makes $\Gamma$ compact. The expansion $\Gamma x=\sum_j\langle x,\tau_j^2e_j\rangle e_j$ has nuclear sum $\sum_j\tau_j^2<\infty$, so [F7] also makes it trace class. By [F8] there is a Borel centered Gaussian random element $G$ in $H$ with covariance $\Gamma$. For each finite coordinate vector, every linear projection is centered normal by [F8], hence it is jointly Gaussian by [F9]; its covariance matrix is diagonal with entries $\tau_j^2$. Repeatedly applying [F10] to the first coordinate and the remaining block proves that the coordinates are independent, and [F11] identifies their laws as $N(0,\tau_j^2)$. Thus the law of $G$ is the stated prior on $\ell^2$.

Put $q=\alpha+p$. For sufficiently small $\epsilon$, let $J$ be the largest positive integer with $e^{qJ}\le1/\epsilon$. Since $q>0$, the exponential is increasing and unbounded, so $J$ exists and $J\to\infty$ as $\epsilon\downarrow0$. Maximality gives $e^{qJ}\le1/\epsilon<e^q e^{qJ}$, hence $e^{-q}/\epsilon<e^{qJ}\le1/\epsilon$. The posterior variance satisfies $v_j\le\min\{e^{-2\alpha j},\epsilon^2e^{2pj}\}$. Reversing the finite geometric sum for $j\le J$ and summing the tail gives $\sum_{j\ge1}v_j\le C_{\alpha,p}(\epsilon^2e^{2pJ}+e^{-2\alpha J})\le C'_{\alpha,p}\epsilon^{2\alpha/q}$. For the first term, $e^{2pJ}=(e^{qJ})^{2p/q}\le\epsilon^{-2p/q}$. For the second, $e^{qJ}>e^{-q}/\epsilon$ gives $e^{-2\alpha J}<e^{2\alpha}\epsilon^{2\alpha/q}$.

Write $b_j=1-\lambda_j=\epsilon^2/(\epsilon^2+e^{-2qj})\le\min\{1,\epsilon^2e^{2qj}\}$. The truth ellipsoid implies $\sum_jb_j^2(\theta_j^\dagger)^2\le L^2\sup_j b_j^2e^{-2\beta j}$. For $j\le J$, this is bounded coordinatewise by $\epsilon^4e^{(4q-2\beta)j}$; its maximum is at $J$ if $\beta\le2q$, and then is at most $\epsilon^4(e^{qJ})^{4-2\beta/q}\le\epsilon^{2\beta/q}$. If $\beta>2q$, the exponent is negative and the maximum is at $j=1$, bounded by a constant times $\epsilon^4$. For $j>J$, the source weight gives $b_j^2e^{-2\beta j}\le e^{-2\beta J}=(e^{qJ})^{-2\beta/q}\le e^{2\beta}\epsilon^{2\beta/q}$. Thus the squared-bias term is at most $C_{\alpha,\beta,p,L}\epsilon^{\min\{2\beta/q,4\}}$.

Since $v_js_j^2/\epsilon^2=\lambda_j\le1$, one has $v_j^2s_j^2/\epsilon^2=v_j\lambda_j\le v_j$. Combining [F1] with steps 1.2–2.1 gives $S_\epsilon(\theta^\dagger)\le C_{\alpha,\beta,p,L}\epsilon^{2\min\{\alpha,\beta\}/q}$: when $\beta\le\alpha$, the bias exponent is $2\beta/q$; when $\beta>\alpha$, the variance exponent $2\alpha/q<2$ dominates the bias bound, including the branch $\beta>2q$. Taking $r_\epsilon=\epsilon^{\min\{\alpha,\beta\}/q}$, [F1] bounds the expected tail outside $M_\epsilon r_\epsilon$ by $C/M_\epsilon^2\to0$. By [F2], this is the claimed posterior contraction rate.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

A **real Hilbert space** is a real inner-product space $H$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]) whose induced-length metric is complete in the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]]: every Cauchy sequence in $H$ for the norm $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ ([[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]) converges to a point of $H$. A **complex Hilbert space** is a complex inner-product space with the same completeness property, so that a Hilbert space is exactly a real or complex inner-product space that is a Banach space for its induced norm ([[def-banach-space]]).

**The completion convention is the Cauchy-sequence one.**
[[def-banach-space]] defines completeness by convergence of Cauchy sequences, and this page keeps that convention throughout. It is weaker than $\sigma$-completeness — the assertion that every decreasing sequence of nonempty closed subsets with diameters tending to zero has a nonempty intersection. The two agree in ZFC, but Blackadar, Farah and Karagila note that the closest-point theorem on a $\sigma$-complete inner-product space is provable in ZF, whereas the Cauchy-complete form used below consumes the Axiom of Countable Choice; nothing here silently imports the stronger notion.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

Let $V$ be a real or complex inner-product space with induced length $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$. Then $\|v\|\ge0$ with $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, $\|\lambda v\|=|\lambda|\,\|v\|$ for every scalar $\lambda$, and $\|u+v\|\le\|u\|+\|v\|$; hence $\|\cdot\|$ is a norm on $V$, read over $\mathbb R$ by [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and over $\mathbb C$ by [[def-complex-norm-and-complex-normed-space]].

Throughout this page $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) constructed in this library, in particular a
field, so that "vector space" below always means vector space over $\mathbb{R}$
([[def-vector-space]]).

Let $V$ be a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$, with zero vector $0_V$. A **norm on
$V$** is a function $N : V \to \mathbb{R}$ such that for all $u, v \in V$ and all
$\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

- **(N1) Separation.** $N(v) = 0$ if and only if $v = 0_V$.
- **(N2) Absolute homogeneity.** $N(\lambda v) = |\lambda|\,N(v)$, the absolute
  value being that of [[def-abs-value]].
- **(N3) Triangle inequality.** $N(u + v) \le N(u) + N(v)$.

A **normed space** is a pair $(V, N)$ consisting of a vector space $V$ over
$\mathbb{R}$ and a norm $N$ on it. When only one norm is in play we write
$\lVert v\rVert$ for $N(v)$; when several are, the norm is always named.

**The values of a norm are real numbers.** The codomain is $\mathbb{R}$, so
$N(v)$ is an honest element of the complete ordered field and no infinite value
is permitted. The same real-valued codomain is required of a metric by
[[def-metric-space]].

### Nonnegativity is a theorem, not an axiom

Many texts add a fourth condition $N(v) \ge 0$. It is redundant. Applying (N2)
with $\lambda = -1$ gives $N(-v) = |-1|\,N(v) = N(v)$ ([[lem-of-abs-value]],
[[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]] for $(-1)v = -v$), and then (N3)
with $u = v$ and $-v$ gives

$$0 \;=\; N(0_V) \;=\; N\bigl(v + (-v)\bigr) \;\le\; N(v) + N(-v) \;=\; N(v) + N(v),$$

where $N(0_V) = 0$ is (N1). So $N(v) + N(v) \ge 0$, and if $N(v) < 0$ then
$N(v) + N(v) < 0$ by addition of inequalities, which trichotomy forbids
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Hence $N(v) \ge 0$ for every $v \in V$.

**Consequently the verification of a candidate norm has three things to check and
not four**, exactly as the verification of a candidate metric has three and not
four ([[def-metric-space]], [[lem-metric-nonnegativity]]). No item in this
library assumes nonnegativity of a norm before the argument above.

### The induced metric

Let $N$ be a norm on $V$ and define

$$d_N(u,v) \;:=\; N(u - v) \qquad (u, v \in V),$$

where $u - v = u + (-v)$ ([[def-vector-space]]). **Then $d_N$ is a metric on
$V$** ([[def-metric-space]]), and the three axioms are the three conditions
above, in order:

- **(M1)** $d_N(u,v) = 0$ means $N(u-v) = 0$, which by (N1) says $u - v = 0_V$,
  that is $u = v$; and conversely $d_N(v,v) = N(0_V) = 0$.
- **(M2)** $d_N(v,u) = N(v-u) = N\bigl((-1)(u-v)\bigr) = |-1|\,N(u-v) = d_N(u,v)$,
  by (N2), [[lem-of-abs-value]] and $(-1)w = -w$
  ([[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]]).
- **(M3)** $d_N(u,w) = N\bigl((u-v) + (v-w)\bigr) \le N(u-v) + N(v-w) = d_N(u,v) + d_N(v,w)$,
  by (N3).

A normed space is therefore a metric space, and every notion defined for metric
spaces — open set ([[def-metric-topology]]), convergence, Cauchyness,
continuity, compactness — is available in it with no further definition. **This
library never introduces a second notion of any of them for normed spaces.**

### Two properties an arbitrary metric need not have

The metric $d_N$ satisfies, for all $u, v, w \in V$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

- **translation invariance**, $d_N(u + w, v + w) = N\bigl((u+w)-(v+w)\bigr) = N(u-v) = d_N(u,v)$;
- **absolute homogeneity**, $d_N(\lambda u, \lambda v) = N\bigl(\lambda(u-v)\bigr) = |\lambda|\,d_N(u,v)$, by (N2).

**Not every metric on a vector space arises from a norm**, and homogeneity is
what fails. The published bounded remetrisation [[lem-bounded-remetrisation]]
replaces a metric $d$ by $d' = \min\{d, 1\}$, a metric with the same topology
whose values never exceed $1$; on a vector space $V$ containing a vector $v$ with
$d(v, 0_V) > 0$ this $d'$ cannot be $d_M$ for any norm $M$, since absolute
homogeneity would force $d'(\lambda v, 0_V) = |\lambda|\,d'(v, 0_V)$, which is
unbounded in $\lambda$, while $d'$ is bounded by $1$. So the passage from norms
to metrics is not reversible, and a statement about a metric on a vector space is
strictly weaker than the corresponding statement about a norm.

Let $(X,\mathcal T)$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]). The
**Borel sigma-algebra of $X$** is the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets:

$$\mathcal B(X):=\sigma_X(\mathcal T).$$

Its members are the **Borel subsets** of $X$. The generated sigma-algebra exists
and is minimal by [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]].

Let S be Polish in the sense of [[def-polish-space]]. A **Borel probability law on S** is a countably additive measure on $\mathcal B(S)$ with total mass one. Here $\mathcal B(S)$ is [[def-borel-sigma-algebra]] and probability measure means [[def-probability-measure]]. A compatible complete metric may be fixed for a construction; it is not additional data in the law. The empty space admits no such law, since its measure must be both zero and one.

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(e_i)_{i\in I}$ be an orthonormal family in a real or complex Hilbert space $H$
([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]), and
for $x\in H$ and finite $F\subseteq I$ put

$$P_Fx:=\sum_{i\in F}\langle x,e_i\rangle e_i .$$

Then the following four assertions are equivalent:

1. **(completeness)** the closed linear span of $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ is $H$;
2. **(zero complement)** the only vector orthogonal to every $e_i$ is $0$;
3. **(Parseval)** $\displaystyle\sum_{i\in I}|\langle x,e_i\rangle|^2=\|x\|^2$
   for every $x\in H$, the sum being the supremum of the finite subsums
   ([[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]]);
4. **(net convergence)** the finite-subset net $(P_Fx)_{F\in\operatorname{Fin}(I)}$
   converges to $x$ for every $x\in H$.

Assertion 2 is the statement
$\operatorname{span}\{e_i : i\in I\}^\perp=\{0\}$
([[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]).

A topological space $X$ is **separable** if some at most countable subset $D\subseteq X$ is dense in $X$ ([[def-dense-top]], [[def-countable]]). Equivalently, every nonempty open subset of $X$ meets $D$.

$\mathbb{Q} \approx \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]): the rationals are
countably infinite ([[def-countable]]).

**No choice principle is used.** The one place where a reader expects a choice,
"pick a representative $a/b$ of each rational", is exactly where
[[lem-rat-positive-denominator]] applies: every rational *has* a representative
with positive denominator, so the map $(a,b) \mapsto [(a,b)]$ defined on
$\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ is already **surjective** onto $\mathbb{Q}$,
and countability follows from a surjection without ever selecting a
representative. The same device handles $\mathbb{Z}$, which is a surjective image
of $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ by construction ([[def-integers]]).

Write $\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ for the image of $\mathbb{Q}$ in $\mathbb{R}$
under the canonical embedding $q \mapsto \hat q$ ([[lem-rat-embeds-dense]]), the
set usually written $\mathbb{Q}$ once the identification is made, and put
$X := \mathbb{R} \setminus \mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ for the irrationals. Then:

1. $\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ is dense in $\mathbb{R}$, that is,
   $\overline{\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}} = \mathbb{R}$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]);
2. $X$ is dense in $\mathbb{R}$;
3. every nonempty open subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is uncountable
   ([[def-countable]]).

Claim 2 is not a symmetry of claim 1: the rationals are dense because they are
*constructed* to approximate, whereas the irrationals are dense because there are
too many points in any interval for a countable set to exhaust it, which is why
claim 3 is proved alongside and used for it.

If $A$ and $B$ are at most countable ([[def-countable]]) then so is
$A \times B$.

**No choice principle is used**: the two enumerations are given, and the
enumeration of the product is written down from them.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$ and let $\mathcal A=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. If finite measures $\mu$ and $
u$ on $(X,\mathcal A)$ agree on $\mathcal P$ and satisfy $\mu(X)=
u(X)$, then $\mu=
u$ on $\mathcal A$.

The total-mass equality is separate because this library's pi-system convention does not require $X\in\mathcal P$.

derivations.claim:
If $H=\{0\}$, then it has only one Borel probability measure and the
conclusion holds. Otherwise, let $\mathcal C$ be the family of all finite
coordinate cylinder sets $\pi_F^{-1}(B)$, where $F\subseteq J$ is finite and
$B\subseteq\mathbb R^F$ is Borel. Each cylinder is Borel by continuity in [F1].
The family contains $H$, and the intersection of two cylinders is the
finite-coordinate cylinder obtained on the union of their index sets. Hence
$\mathcal C$ is a pi-system.

Enumerate the basis if it is infinite, and in the finite case repeat the
last partial sum after all basis vectors have appeared. For $x_0\in H$ and
$r>0$, put $S_N(x)=\sum_{j\le N}|\langle x-x_0,e_j\rangle|^2$. By [F2],
$\|x-x_0\|^2=\sup_N S_N(x)$, so
$$B(x_0,r)=\bigcup_{\substack{q\in\mathbb Q\\0\le q<r^2}}\ \bigcap_{N\ge1}\{x:S_N(x)\le q\}.$$
Indeed, if $\|x-x_0\|^2<r^2$, choose a rational strictly between these two
numbers; conversely, membership in one intersection gives
$\|x-x_0\|^2\le q<r^2$. Each set $\{S_N\le q\}$ is a cylinder, so every open
ball belongs to $\sigma(\mathcal C)$.

Fix an at most countable dense set $D\subseteq H$ from separability. The
balls $B(d,s)$ with $d\in D$ and positive rational $s$ form an at most
countable family by [F3]. They are a base: given $x\in U$ with $U$ open, choose
$r>0$ with $B(x,r)\subseteq U$, then $d\in D$ with $\|d-x\|<r/3$, and a
rational $s$ with $\|d-x\|<s<r-\|d-x\|$. The triangle inequality gives
$x\in B(d,s)\subseteq B(x,r)\subseteq U$. By step 1.2 every such ball lies in
$\sigma(\mathcal C)$, so every open set, as a union of a subfamily of this
countable base, lies in $\sigma(\mathcal C)$.

Every coordinate map is continuous by [F1], so
$\sigma(\mathcal C)\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$. Step 2.1 and the definition of
the Borel sigma-algebra give the reverse inclusion. Thus
$\sigma(\mathcal C)=\mathcal B(H)$.

The assumed equality of finite-coordinate measures makes $
u$ and
$
u'$ agree on every cylinder in $\mathcal C$. They are probability measures,
so they agree on $H$ as well. The pi-system $\mathcal C$ generates
$\mathcal B(H)$ by step 2.2; [F4] therefore gives $
u=
u'$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H$ be a separable real Hilbert space, let
$\mu_0$ be a centered Borel Gaussian probability measure on $H$, let
$D\subseteq H$ be Borel with $\mu_0(D)=1$, and let
$\Phi_D:D\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be Borel. Assume the evidence
$$
Z:=\int_D e^{-\Phi_D(u)}\,\mu_0(du)
$$
satisfies $0<Z<\infty$. Extend the potential to all of $H$ by setting
$\bar\Phi(u)=\Phi_D(u)$ for $u\in D$ and $\bar\Phi(u)=+\infty$ for
$u\notin D$, and define the target probability
$\mu(du)=Z^{-1}e^{-\bar\Phi(u)}\mu_0(du)$. For a scale $\beta\in[0,1]$,
write $\rho=\sqrt{1-\beta^2}$. At state $u\in H$, draw $\xi\sim\mu_0$
independently and propose $v=\rho u+\beta\xi$. Set the acceptance probability
to $0$ if either $\bar\Phi(u)$ or $\bar\Phi(v)$ is $+\infty$, and otherwise set
$$
\alpha(u,v)=\min\{1,\exp(\bar\Phi(u)-\bar\Phi(v))\}.
$$
Draw an independent uniform random variable on $[0,1]$ and move to $v$ if it
is at most $\alpha(u,v)$; otherwise remain at $u$. The resulting one-step
transition rule is the prior-preserving Crank–Nicolson, or pCN, rule
$P_\beta$. States with infinite potential are absorbing under this total
definition; they have $\mu$-measure zero.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

Let K be a finite kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$, in particular a probability kernel, or a uniformly sigma-finite kernel with the specified exhaustion of the kernel definition. For every nonnegative $\Sigma\otimes\Tau$-measurable function $f:S\times T\to[0,\infty]$, the function
$$I_f(s)=\int_T f(s,t)\,K(s,dt)$$
is $\Sigma$-measurable, with infinity allowed. For a real product-measurable f, the set $D=\{s:I_{|f|}(s)<\infty\}$ is measurable, and its signed integral on D, extended by zero on $S\setminus D$, is a measurable real function. No assertion here is made for a general kernel lacking a common measurable finite-mass exhaustion.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and define
$$\nu_f(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu \qquad (A\in\mathcal A).$$
Then $\nu_f$ is a measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$.

If $f:X\to Y$ is continuous between topological spaces, then
$f^{-1}[B]\in\mathcal B(X)$ for every $B\in\mathcal B(Y)$.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$, $(Y,\mathcal{B})$, and $(Z,\mathcal{C})$ be measurable
spaces. If $f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Y,\mathcal{B})$ is measurable and
$g : (Y,\mathcal{B}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable, then
$g \circ f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable.

In particular, if $f$ is measurable and $g$ is a Borel measurable function on
its codomain, then $g \circ f$ is measurable.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ be a measurable space and let
$f,g:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ be measurable for the Borel sigma-algebra on
the extended real line. Products of functions use
$\odot_X$ from [[def-measurable-pointwise-extended-real-product]], and $cf$
abbreviates $\underline c\odot_X f$ for the constant function $\underline c$.
The magnitude function is $|f|=\max(f,-f)$ as in
[[def-positive-and-negative-parts-of-a-function]]. Then:

1. $cf$ is measurable for every real scalar $c$;
2. $\max(f,g)$, $\min(f,g)$, $|f|$, $f^+$, and $f^-$ are measurable;
3. if the partial pointwise sum $f+g$ is defined at every point, then it is measurable;
4. the pointwise product $fg:=f\odot_X g$ is measurable.

For each Borel set $B$ in the extended potential range, the preimage
$\bar\Phi^{-1}(B)$ is the union of $D\cap\Phi_D^{-1}(B)$ and $H\setminus D$
when $+\infty\in B$, and is just $D\cap\Phi_D^{-1}(B)$ otherwise. Since $D$ is
Borel and $\Phi_D$ is Borel on the trace Borel structure of $D$, every such
preimage is Borel in $H$. Thus the extended potential used by the algorithm is
Borel.

Write $\rho=\sqrt{1-\beta^2}$ and define
$Q_\beta(u,B)=\int_H\mathbf1_B(\rho u+\beta z)\,\mu_0(dz)$ for Borel
$B\subseteq H$. For fixed $u$, this is the pushforward of the probability
$\mu_0$ under the continuous map $z\mapsto\rho u+\beta z$, so it is a
probability measure in $B$. The joint map $(u,z)\mapsto\rho u+\beta z$ is
continuous; hence $(u,z)\mapsto\mathbf1_B(\rho u+\beta z)$ is product-Borel by
[F5]. The constant kernel $u\mapsto\mu_0$ is a probability kernel, so [F3]
makes $u\mapsto Q_\beta(u,B)$ measurable. Therefore $Q_\beta$ is a probability
kernel by [F2].

The finite-potential set $E=\{u:\bar\Phi(u)<+\infty\}$ is Borel by step
1.1. On $E\times E$ the difference
$(u,v)\mapsto\bar\Phi(u)-\bar\Phi(v)$ is Borel, and [F6] makes its exponential
Borel. Extending $\min\{1,\exp(\bar\Phi(u)-\bar\Phi(v))\}$ by $0$ off
$E\times E$ therefore makes the algorithm's $\alpha$ a Borel function with
values in $[0,1]$. Put $a(u)=\int_H\alpha(u,v)Q_\beta(u,dv)$. By [F3],
$a$ is measurable; the probability rows of $Q_\beta$ give
$0\le a(u)\le1$.

For each $u$ and Borel $A\subseteq H$, define
$$P_\beta(u,A)=\int_A\alpha(u,v)Q_\beta(u,dv)+\mathbf1_A(u)(1-a(u)).$$
The first term is a measure in $A$ by [F4] and step 3.1. The second term is
also a measure: among any pairwise-disjoint sequence of sets, at most one
contains $u$, so the indicator of their union is the sum of their indicators
at $u$. Their sum has total mass $a(u)+1-a(u)=1$. For fixed $A$, the first
term is measurable in $u$ by [F3], and the second is measurable because both
$\mathbf1_A(u)$ and $a(u)$ are measurable. Thus $P_\beta$ is a probability
kernel by [F2].

Steps 1.1, 2.1, 3.1, and 4.1 establish that the potential extension, the
proposal, the acceptance function, and the accept-reject transition have the
claimed Borel and probability properties.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H$ be a separable real Hilbert space, let
$\mu_0$ be a centered Borel Gaussian probability measure on $H$, let
$D\subseteq H$ be Borel with $\mu_0(D)=1$, and let
$\Phi_D:D\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be Borel. Assume the evidence
$$
Z:=\int_D e^{-\Phi_D(u)}\,\mu_0(du)
$$
satisfies $0<Z<\infty$. Extend the potential to all of $H$ by setting
$\bar\Phi(u)=\Phi_D(u)$ for $u\in D$ and $\bar\Phi(u)=+\infty$ for
$u\notin D$, and define the target probability
$\mu(du)=Z^{-1}e^{-\bar\Phi(u)}\mu_0(du)$. For a scale $\beta\in[0,1]$,
write $\rho=\sqrt{1-\beta^2}$. At state $u\in H$, draw $\xi\sim\mu_0$
independently and propose $v=\rho u+\beta\xi$. Set the acceptance probability
to $0$ if either $\bar\Phi(u)$ or $\bar\Phi(v)$ is $+\infty$, and otherwise set
$$
\alpha(u,v)=\min\{1,\exp(\bar\Phi(u)-\bar\Phi(v))\}.
$$
Draw an independent uniform random variable on $[0,1]$ and move to $v$ if it
is at most $\alpha(u,v)$; otherwise remain at $u$. The resulting one-step
transition rule is the prior-preserving Crank–Nicolson, or pCN, rule
$P_\beta$. States with infinite potential are absorbing under this total
definition; they have $\mu$-measure zero.

A topological space $X$ is **separable** if some at most countable subset $D\subseteq X$ is dense in $X$ ([[def-dense-top]], [[def-countable]]). Equivalently, every nonempty open subset of $X$ meets $D$.

Let $A$ be a nonempty set. Then $A$ is at most countable ([[def-countable]]) if
and only if there is a surjection $s : \mathbb{N} \to A$
([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]).

Moreover, from any such surjection an injection $A \to \mathbb{N}$ is obtained
explicitly, without any choice, by

$$j(a) := \min\{\, k \in \mathbb{N} : s(k) = a \,\}.$$

This is the working form of countability used everywhere below: to prove a
nonempty set countable it suffices to list its elements, repetitions and all.

**No choice principle is used.** The backward direction is where an appeal to
choice would be natural ("for each $a$ pick some $k$ with $s(k) = a$") and it is
avoided outright, because $\min$ is canonical: every nonempty set of naturals has
a *least* element ([[thm-well-ordering-principle]]), so $j(a)$ is determined by
$a$ and $s$ alone.

Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space, let $(x_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be a
sequence in $H$ whose range $\{x_n : n\in\mathbb N\}$ is dense in $H$
([[def-dense-top]]), and let

$$L_0:=\varnothing,\qquad L_{n+1}:=L_n\cup\Bigl\{\tfrac{v_n}{\|v_n\|}\Bigr\}\ \text{ if }\ v_n:=x_n-\sum_{e\in L_n}\langle x_n,e\rangle e\ne0, \qquad L_{n+1}:=L_n\ \text{ otherwise}.$$

Then $L:=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}L_n$ is a finite or countably infinite orthonormal
set whose closed linear span is $H$; that is, $L$ is an orthonormal basis of $H$
([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]), and
it is obtained from the given sequence by Gram–Schmidt elimination. The
enumeration of $L$ is the canonical one by the stage at which an element
appears, and no choice principle is used.

If $A$ and $B$ are at most countable ([[def-countable]]) then so is
$A \times B$.

**No choice principle is used**: the two enumerations are given, and the
enumeration of the product is written down from them.

Let $X$ be a normed space over the scalar field $\mathbb{K}$, where
$\mathbb{K}\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, using [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] over $\mathbb R$ and [[def-complex-norm-and-complex-normed-space]] over $\mathbb C$. The
**dual space** of $X$ is

$$X^*:=\mathcal{B}(X,\mathbb{K}),$$

the space of bounded linear functionals on $X$
([[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]]).

Each $f \in X^*$ is in particular a linear functional in the algebraic sense,
so $X^*$ is a subspace of the algebraic dual from
[[def-algebraic-dual-and-linear-functional]].

The **dual norm** on $X^*$ is the operator norm:

$$\|f\|_{X^*}:=\|f\| =\sup\{|f(x)|:\|x\| \le 1\}.$$

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space and let $B$ be a real
separable Banach space with its norm Borel sigma-algebra. A map
$W:\Omega\to B$ is a **centered Borel Gaussian random element** if it is
Borel-measurable and, for every $\ell\in B^*$, the real random variable
$\ell(W)$ has a centered (possibly zero-variance) normal law. Its law is the
Borel probability $\mu=P\circ W^{-1}$. When the word *tight* is used, it means
that for every $\delta>0$ there is a norm-compact $K\subseteq B$ with
$\mu(K)>1-\delta$.

This definition concerns a random element in $B$. A Gaussian process on an
arbitrary index set with only a cylinder-space law does not satisfy it unless
a Borel $B$-valued realization is separately constructed.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $W$ be a centered Borel Gaussian random
element in a real separable Banach space $B$. There is a constant $a>0$ such
that
$$E\exp(a\|W\|^2)<\infty.$$
In particular, $E\|W\|^2<\infty$.

Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]].

When $\Sigma_i$ is a Borel sigma-algebra, this agrees with the notation
$\sigma(X_i)$ from [[def-sigma-algebra-generated-by-a-function]].

Let $n\ge1$, and let
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ for $i<n$ be independent
random elements. Define

$$X=(X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}):\Omega\to\prod_{i<n}S_i.$$

Then $X$ is a random element of
$\left(\prod_{i<n}S_i,\bigotimes_{i<n}\Sigma_i\right)$, and its law is the
finite product of the marginal laws:

$$\mathbb P_X=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathbb P_{X_i}.$$

For real $a,b,t$, $\varphi_{aX+b}(t)=e^{itb}\varphi_X(at)$. For a finite mutually independent family $(X_j)_{j=1}^n$ of real random variables, $\varphi_{\sum_jX_j}(t)=\prod_j\varphi_{X_j}(t)$. The empty sum has characteristic function one.

Assume AC. If $X$ has law $N(m,\sigma^2)$ with $\sigma\ge0$, then $\varphi_X(t)=\exp(imt-\sigma^2t^2/2)$ for every real $t$. Moreover $\mathbb EX=m$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X)=\sigma^2$, including $\sigma=0$.

Assume AC. Two Borel probability laws on $\mathbb R$ with equal characteristic functions are equal. In particular a real random variable has a real-valued characteristic function if and only if its law is symmetric under $x\mapsto-x$.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Assume AC. If $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$, then $$\Phi_X(t):=\mathbb E e^{it\cdot X}=\exp(it\cdot m-t^T\Sigma t/2)\qquad(t\in\mathbb R^d).$$ This transform uniquely determines the law, including singular Sigma.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ be a real Hilbert space with a
finite or countable complete orthonormal basis $(e_j)_{j\in J}$. For each finite
$F\subseteq J$, define the coordinate map
$\pi_F:H\to\mathbb R^F$ by
$\pi_F(x)=(\langle x,e_j\rangle)_{j\in F}$. If $\nu$ and $\nu'$ are Borel
probability measures on $H$ and
$\nu(\pi_F^{-1}(B))=\nu'(\pi_F^{-1}(B))$ for every finite $F\subseteq J$ and
every Borel $B\subseteq\mathbb R^F$, then $\nu=\nu'$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}$ be independent real random variables on a
common probability space, and let $g_i:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be Borel
measurable for each $i<n$.

1. If every $g_i$ is nonnegative, then
   $$\mathbb E\left[\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)\right]=\prod_{i<n}\mathbb E[g_i(X_i)]$$
   in $[0,+\infty]$. In this finite product of expectations, a zero factor
   makes the product zero even when another factor is $+\infty$; otherwise
   multiplication has its usual extended nonnegative meaning.
2. If every $g_i(X_i)$ is integrable, then $\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)$ is integrable
   and the same factorization holds in $\mathbb R$.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

A topological space $X$ is **second countable** when its topology has a basis $\mathcal B$ that is at most countable ([[def-topology-basis-subbasis]], [[def-countable]]). Thus every open set is a union of members of one at most countable family $\mathcal B$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
[[def-measurable-rectangle]].

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

Let $X,Y$ be second-countable topological spaces and give $X\times Y$ the
product topology. Then
$$\mathcal B(X\times Y)=\mathcal B(X)\otimes\mathcal B(Y).$$

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element. Its
**law** or **distribution** is the set function
$$\mathbb P_X:\Sigma\to[0,+\infty],\qquad \mathbb P_X(B):=\mathbb P(X^{-1}(B)).$$

Thus the law of $X$ records the probability of each measurable target set by
pulling it back to an event in the original probability space.

derivations.claim:
By [F2], take a finite or countable complete orthonormal basis $(e_j)$ of
$H$. Give $H\times H$ the inner product
$\langle(u,v),(x,y)\rangle_\times=\langle u,x\rangle+\langle v,y\rangle$.
Its induced norm is $\sqrt{\|u\|^2+\|v\|^2}$. It is complete because a
Cauchy sequence has Cauchy coordinate sequences in $H$, whose limits in $H$
give its product limit. Thus this is a Hilbert space. The family
$(e_j,0),(0,e_j)$ is orthonormal, and any vector orthogonal to every listed
vector has both components orthogonal to every $e_j$, hence both components
are zero by completeness; it is a complete orthonormal basis. Let
$D\subseteq H$ be countable and dense. Then $D\times D$ is countable by [F2]
and dense, since each coordinate of a pair can be approximated within
$\varepsilon/2$ to make the product norm error less than $\varepsilon$.
Balls with centers in $D\times D$ and positive rational radii form a
countable base: for $z$ in an open set choose $r>0$ with $B(z,r)$ contained
there, then a center $d$ with $\|d-z\|<r/3$ and rational $s$ with
$\|d-z\|<s<r-\|d-z\|$ give $z\in B(d,s)\subseteq B(z,r)$. Thus $H\times H$
is second-countable, and [F10] identifies its Borel sigma-algebra with the
product Borel sigma-algebra. Since $U$ and $\xi$ are Borel random elements,
the pair $(U,\xi)$ is measurable into this product sigma-algebra, and
continuous addition and scalar multiplication make $(U,V)$ and $(V,U)$ Borel
random elements of $H\times H$. Their Borel laws are therefore defined.

Fix a finite list of continuous linear functionals on $H\times H$. Each
has the form $(u,v)\mapsto\ell(u)+m(v)$, because its restrictions to the two
coordinate subspaces sum to the functional. Any real linear combination of
the listed projections is another such functional. Under $(U,V)$ that
combination is $(\ell+\rho m)(U)+\beta m(\xi)$; under $(V,U)$ it is
$(\rho\ell+m)(U)+\beta\ell(\xi)$. By [F3], the two summands in each display
are centered normal, and [F5] makes them independent; [F6] makes their sum
normal, including a zero coefficient. Hence every finite projection vector
under either pair is multivariate normal by the projection definition in
[F7], with zero mean.

Define the symmetric covariance form
$\Gamma(\ell,m)=\mathbb E[\ell(U)m(U)]$. These products are integrable:
[F4] gives finite second moments of $\|U\|$, boundedness of $\ell,m$ gives
finite second moments of their evaluations, and $|ab|\le(a^2+b^2)/2$. The
same argument applies to evaluations of $\xi$. For functionals $(\ell,m)$ and
$(\ell',m')$, the projection under $(U,V)$ is
$(\ell+\rho m)(U)+\beta m(\xi)$. Independence and centering make its mixed
covariance terms zero by [F9], so its covariance with the corresponding
projection for $(\ell',m')$ is
$$\Gamma(\ell,\ell')+\rho\Gamma(\ell,m')+\rho\Gamma(m,\ell')+\Gamma(m,m'),$$
using $\rho^2+\beta^2=1$. Under $(V,U)$ the projections are
$(\rho\ell+m)(U)+\beta\ell(\xi)$ and
$(\rho\ell'+m')(U)+\beta\ell'(\xi)$; expansion gives the same expression
because $\Gamma$ is symmetric. Therefore the finite projection vectors from
step 1.2 have equal covariance matrices and zero means.

By [F7], the finite projection laws in step 2.1 are equal, in particular
the finite coordinate laws for the product basis from step 1.1. That step also
shows that $H\times H$ is a separable Hilbert space. By [A1], Countable Choice
follows from AC; the coordinate-law result [F8] therefore identifies the two
Borel probability laws. Hence
$\operatorname{Law}(U,V)=\operatorname{Law}(V,U)$.

Step 2.2 is the claimed invariance of the joint law under coordinate
swap, for every $\beta\in[0,1]$, including the identity proposal at $\beta=0$
and the independent-reference proposal at $\beta=1$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H$ be a separable real Hilbert space, let
$\mu_0$ be a centered Borel Gaussian probability measure on $H$, let
$D\subseteq H$ be Borel with $\mu_0(D)=1$, and let
$\Phi_D:D\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be Borel. Assume the evidence
$$
Z:=\int_D e^{-\Phi_D(u)}\,\mu_0(du)
$$
satisfies $0<Z<\infty$. Extend the potential to all of $H$ by setting
$\bar\Phi(u)=\Phi_D(u)$ for $u\in D$ and $\bar\Phi(u)=+\infty$ for
$u\notin D$, and define the target probability
$\mu(du)=Z^{-1}e^{-\bar\Phi(u)}\mu_0(du)$. For a scale $\beta\in[0,1]$,
write $\rho=\sqrt{1-\beta^2}$. At state $u\in H$, draw $\xi\sim\mu_0$
independently and propose $v=\rho u+\beta\xi$. Set the acceptance probability
to $0$ if either $\bar\Phi(u)$ or $\bar\Phi(v)$ is $+\infty$, and otherwise set
$$
\alpha(u,v)=\min\{1,\exp(\bar\Phi(u)-\bar\Phi(v))\}.
$$
Draw an independent uniform random variable on $[0,1]$ and move to $v$ if it
is at most $\alpha(u,v)$; otherwise remain at $u$. The resulting one-step
transition rule is the prior-preserving Crank–Nicolson, or pCN, rule
$P_\beta$. States with infinite potential are absorbing under this total
definition; they have $\mu$-measure zero.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H$ be a separable real Hilbert space, let
$\mu_0$ be a centered Borel Gaussian probability measure on $H$, let
$D\subseteq H$ be Borel with $\mu_0(D)=1$, and let
$\Phi_D:D\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be Borel. Assume the evidence
$$

satisfies $0<Z<\infty$. Extend the potential to all of $H$ by setting
$\bar\Phi(u)=\Phi_D(u)$ for $u\in D$ and $\bar\Phi(u)=+\infty$ for
$u\notin D$, and define the target probability
$\mu(du)=Z^{-1}e^{-\bar\Phi(u)}\mu_0(du)$. For a scale $\beta\in[0,1]$,
write $\rho=\sqrt{1-\beta^2}$. At state $u\in H$, draw $\xi\sim\mu_0$
independently and propose $v=\rho u+\beta\xi$. Set the acceptance probability
to $0$ if either $\bar\Phi(u)$ or $\bar\Phi(v)$ is $+\infty$, and otherwise set
$$

$$
Draw an independent uniform random variable on $[0,1]$ and move to $v$ if it
is at most $\alpha(u,v)$; otherwise remain at $u$. The resulting one-step
transition rule is the prior-preserving Crank–Nicolson, or pCN, rule
$P_\beta$. States with infinite potential are absorbing under this total
definition; they have $\mu$-measure zero.

Let $X$ be a specified real separable Banach or Hilbert parameter space with metric $d_X(x,x')=\|x-x'\|_X$ and its norm topology. Let $(Y,d_Y)$ be a metric data space equipped with a sigma-algebra $\Sigma_Y$, let $U\subseteq X$ be a nonempty admissible truth set, and let $F:U\to Y$ be a forward map. Choose a Borel set $D\in\mathcal B(X)$ with $D\subseteq U$ such that the restriction $G:=F|_D:D\to Y$ is measurable for the trace Borel sigma-algebra $\mathcal B(D):=\{D\cap A:A\in\mathcal B(X)\}$. A prior on this forward domain is a Borel probability measure $\mu$ on $X$ such that $\mu(D)=1$. Its restriction $\mu|_D$, defined by $\mu|_D(A)=\mu(A)$ for $A\in\mathcal B(D)$, is then a probability measure on $D$, and the induced data law is $G_\#(\mu|_D)$, defined by $G_\#(\mu|_D)(E)=(\mu|_D)(G^{-1}(E))$ for $E\in\Sigma_Y$. A Borel probability on $X$ with $\mu(D)<1$ is not a prior on this declared forward domain.

Let $X$ be a separable real Banach space with its norm topology, $D\subseteq X$ a Borel forward-map domain, and $\mu_0$ a Borel probability measure on $X$ with $\mu_0(D)=1$. Write $\mu_{0,D}$ for its restriction to $D$, so $\mu_{0,D}(A)=\mu_0(A)$ for $A\in\mathcal B(D):=\{D\cap B:B\in\mathcal B(X)\}$. Let $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ be a measurable data space. A likelihood potential is a function $\Phi:D\times\mathsf Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ that is measurable from $\bigl(D\times\mathsf Y,\mathcal B(D)\otimes\mathcal Y\bigr)$ to $\bigl((-\infty,+\infty],\mathcal B((-\infty,+\infty])\bigr)$, where $\mathcal B((-\infty,+\infty])$ is the trace of $\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R})$ on $(-\infty,+\infty]$. Viewing $\Phi$ via the inclusion $(-\infty,+\infty]\hookrightarrow\overline{\mathbb R}$, it is also product-measurable as an extended-real-valued map because for every Borel set $B\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$, $\Phi^{-1}(B)=\Phi^{-1}(B\cap(-\infty,+\infty])$ is measurable by the definition of the trace sigma-algebra. Here $+\infty$ is allowed and $-\infty$ is excluded; set $e^{-\infty}=0$. The scalar map $t\mapsto e^{-t}$ on this range is continuous at finite $t$, and is continuous at $+\infty$: given $\varepsilon>0$, the limit supplies $a\in\mathbb R$ such that $t>a$ implies $e^{-t}<\varepsilon$, and the order-topology neighborhood $(a,+\infty]$ maps into $[0,\varepsilon)$. Hence it is Borel, so $L_\Phi:D\times\mathsf Y\to[0,+\infty)$, $L_\Phi(u;y):=e^{-\Phi(u;y)}$, is product-measurable by composition, and each section $u\mapsto L_\Phi(u;y)$ is nonnegative and measurable. Define its evidence by
$$
Z_\Phi(y):=\int_D L_\Phi(u;y)\,\mu_{0,D}(du)\in[0,+\infty].
$$
For each fixed $y$ with $0<Z_\Phi(y)<+\infty$, define the normalized fiberwise update on $A\in\mathcal B(D)$ by
$$\Pi^y(A):=\frac{\int_A L_\Phi(u;y)\,\mu_{0,D}(du)}{Z_\Phi(y)}.$$
No normalized fiberwise update is defined by this formula when $Z_\Phi(y)=0$ or $Z_\Phi(y)=+\infty$.

For a data-indexed claim, an observation model and its version convention must also be specified. In the dominated case, let $Q$ be a proper probability kernel from $(D,\mathcal B(D))$ to $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$, let $\nu$ be a sigma-finite measure on $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$, and suppose $Q(u,B)=\int_B L_\Phi(u;y)\,\nu(dy)$ for every $u\in D$ and $B\in\mathcal Y$. Then $Z_\Phi$ is the density of the prior-predictive data law with respect to $\nu$; a data-indexed conditional-law version uses $\Pi^y$ when $0<Z_\Phi(y)<\infty$ and the prior $\mu_{0,D}$ when $Z_\Phi(y)$ is zero or infinite. These filled fibers have zero prior-predictive mass, and their chosen values are not normalized fiberwise updates. More generally, for a proper Bayesian model with standard-Borel parameter space $(D,\mathcal B(D))$ and data space $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ (each measurably isomorphic to the Borel space of a Polish space), the Axiom of Choice guarantees a data-indexed posterior kernel; its values are unique as probability measures outside one data-marginal-null set, and values on that null set remain version choices. The dominated construction is choice-free; the separate standard-Borel existence branch assumes the Axiom of Choice.

Let $X$ be a separable real Banach space with norm $\|\cdot\|_X$, let $D\subseteq X$ be Borel, and let $\mu_0$ be a Borel probability on $X$ with $\mu_0(D)=1$. Here $\mathcal B(X)$ is generated by the norm-open sets. Give $D$ the relative topology and Borel sigma-algebra $\mathcal B(D)=\{D\cap B:B\in\mathcal B(X)\}$, and let $\mu_{0,D}$ be the restriction of $\mu_0$ to $D$, so $\mu_{0,D}(A)=\mu_0(A)$ for $A\in\mathcal B(D)$. Let $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ be a measurable data space. Assume $\Phi:D\times\mathsf Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ is measurable from $\bigl(D\times\mathsf Y,\mathcal B(D)\otimes\mathcal Y\bigr)$ to $\bigl((-infty,+\infty],\mathcal B((-infty,+\infty])\bigr)$, where $\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R})$ is generated by the order topology on the extended real line and $\mathcal B((-infty,+\infty])$ is its trace on $(-\infty,+\infty]$; thus $+\infty$ is allowed and $-\infty$ is excluded. Let $\mathsf Y_0\subseteq\mathsf Y$. Suppose that for every $y\in\mathsf Y_0$, the section $u\mapsto\Phi(u;y)$ is finite and continuous as a real-valued function on $D$ with its relative topology inherited from the norm topology. Suppose there is one Borel function $M_1:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$, independent of $y\in\mathsf Y_0$, such that
$$
\Phi(u;y)\ge -M_1(\|u\|_X)\quad(u\in D,\ y\in\mathsf Y_0),\qquad
\int_D e^{M_1(\|u\|_X)}\,\mu_{0,D}(du)<\infty.
$$
Define $\operatorname{supp}\mu_0:=\{x\in X:\mu_0(U)>0\text{ for every open neighborhood }U\text{ of }x\}$. Then for every $y\in\mathsf Y_0$, the evidence $Z_\Phi(y)$ is finite and strictly positive, and the normalized fiberwise update $\Pi^y$ is a probability measure on $D$.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space and let $B$ be a real
separable Banach space with its norm Borel sigma-algebra. A map
$W:\Omega\to B$ is a **centered Borel Gaussian random element** if it is
Borel-measurable and, for every $\ell\in B^*$, the real random variable
$\ell(W)$ has a centered (possibly zero-variance) normal law. Its law is the
Borel probability $\mu=P\circ W^{-1}$. When the word *tight* is used, it means
that for every $\delta>0$ there is a norm-compact $K\subseteq B$ with
$\mu(K)>1-\delta$.

This definition concerns a random element in $B$. A Gaussian process on an
arbitrary index set with only a cylinder-space law does not satisfy it unless
a Borel $B$-valued realization is separately constructed.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $W$ be a centered Borel Gaussian random
element in a real separable Banach space $B$. There is a constant $a>0$ such
that
$$E\exp(a\|W\|^2)<\infty.$$
In particular, $E\|W\|^2<\infty$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space and let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then
$$\int f\,d\mu=0 \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad f=0 \text{ almost everywhere.}$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let
$f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable, and let $E\in\mathcal A$. Since
[[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]]
implies that $f\chi_E$ is measurable, define the **integral of $f$ over $E$**
by
$$\int_E f\,d\mu:=\int f\chi_E\,d\mu,$$
where the integral on the right is the nonnegative Lebesgue integral of
[[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]].

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Apply [F2] with parameter space $H$, domain $D=H$, one-point data space
$\{*\}$, potential $\widetilde\Phi(u,*)=\Phi(u)$, and envelope $M_1=0$.
The domain has full $\mu_0$-mass. For any $u\in H$, choose $R>\|u\|$;
all sufficiently close $v$ satisfy $\max\{\|u\|,\|v\|\}<R$, so the
stated Lipschitz bound proves continuity at $u$. Also
$\int_H e^{M_1(\|u\|)}\,\mu_0(du)=1$. Hence $0<Z<\infty$ and $\mu$ is a
probability. The density $e^{-\Phi}$ is strictly positive everywhere. If
$\mu(A)=0$, then $\int_H e^{-\Phi}\mathbf1_A\,d\mu_0=0$, so [F4] gives
$e^{-\Phi}\mathbf1_A=0$ $\mu_0$-almost everywhere; strict positivity yields
$\mu_0(A)=0$. Conversely, $\mu_0(A)=0$ implies $\mu(A)=0$ directly from the
integral formula. Thus $\mu$ and $\mu_0$ are equivalent.

View the identity map $x\mapsto x$ on $(H,\mathcal B(H),\mu_0)$ as a
centered Borel Gaussian random element. By [F3], there is $a>0$ such that
$\int_H e^{a\|x\|^2}\,\mu_0(dx)<\infty$. For every $q>0$, the function
$r\mapsto r^q e^{-ar^2}$ is bounded on $[0,\infty)$, so
$\int_H\|x\|^q\,\mu_0(dx)<\infty$. Since $e^{-\Phi}\le1$ and $Z>0$,
$$\mathbb E\|U\|^q=Z^{-1}\int_H\|x\|^q e^{-\Phi(x)}\,\mu_0(dx)
\le Z^{-1}\int_H\|x\|^q\,\mu_0(dx)<\infty.$$
The same Gaussian moment bound gives $\mathbb E\|\xi\|^q<\infty$ for every
$q>0$.

Fix any sequence $\beta_n\in[0,1]$ with $\beta_n\to0$. For every
realization with $U,\xi\in H$, $\rho_n:=\sqrt{1-\beta_n^2}\to1$ and
$$\|V_{\beta_n}-U\|\le |1-\rho_n|\|U\|+\beta_n\|\xi\|\longrightarrow0.$$
Choose $R>\|U\|+1$ for that realization. Eventually
$\max\{\|U\|,\|V_{\beta_n}\|\}<R$, and the assumed ball-wise Lipschitz
bound gives
$$|\Phi(V_{\beta_n})-\Phi(U)|\le L_R\|V_{\beta_n}-U\|\longrightarrow0.$$
Therefore $\Delta_n:=\Phi(V_{\beta_n})-\Phi(U)\to0$ almost surely.

The growth bound and $\|V_{\beta_n}\|\le\|U\|+\|\xi\|$ imply
$$|\Delta_n|\le 2K+K\|U\|^p+K(\|U\|+\|\xi\|)^p
\le C_{p,K}(1+\|U\|^p+\|\xi\|^p),$$
where the last inequality follows from
$(a+b)^p\le2^p(a^p+b^p)$ for $a,b\ge0$ (use
$a+b\le2\max(a,b)$ and $\max(a,b)^p\le a^p+b^p$), with
$C_{p,K}:=\max\{2K,K(1+2^p),K2^p\}$. By step 1.2 the right
side is integrable and does not depend on $n$. Applying [F5] to the sequence
$|\Delta_n|$ and step 2.1 gives $\mathbb E|\Delta_n|\to0$.

The scalar function $g(t)=\min\{1,e^{-t}\}$ is continuous and
$g(0)=1$. Step 2.1 therefore implies
$\alpha_{\beta_n}=g(\Delta_n)\to1$ almost surely. Since
$0\le\alpha_{\beta_n}\le1$, [F5] with the integrable dominating constant
$1$ yields $\mathbb E\alpha_{\beta_n}\to1$. The sequence $\beta_n\to0$ was
arbitrary, so the sequential criterion for real limits proves
$\lim_{\beta\downarrow0}\mathbb E[\alpha_\beta]=1$. This is the stationary
mean acceptance limit; it asserts no convergence or mixing rate for the
resulting chain.
