Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H$ be a separable real Hilbert space and let
$\mu_0$ be a centered Borel Gaussian probability measure on $H$. Let $U$ and
$\xi$ be independent random elements with law $\mu_0$. For
$\beta\in[0,1]$, set $\rho=\sqrt{1-\beta^2}$ and
$V=\rho U+\beta\xi$. The joint Borel law of $(U,V)$ on $H\times H$ is
unchanged by the coordinate swap $(u,v)\mapsto(v,u)$.

Let $X,Y$ be second-countable topological spaces and give $X\times Y$ the
product topology. Then
$$\mathcal B(X\times Y)=\mathcal B(X)\otimes\mathcal B(Y).$$

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ and $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be measurable spaces,
let $\pi$ be a probability measure on $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$, and let
$K:\Theta\times\mathcal A\to[0,1]$ be a probability kernel. For
$C\in\mathcal T\otimes\mathcal A$, write
$C_\theta=\{x\in\mathcal X:(\theta,x)\in C\}$ and set
$$J(C)=\int_\Theta K(\theta,C_\theta)\,\pi(d\theta).$$
Then $J$ is a probability measure on the product sigma-algebra, and for every
nonnegative product-measurable $h$,
$$\int_{\Theta\times\mathcal X}h(\theta,x)\,J(d\theta,dx)=\int_\Theta\left(\int_\mathcal Xh(\theta,x)\,K(\theta,dx)\right)\pi(d\theta).$$
In particular, $J(A\times B)=\int_AK(\theta,B)\,\pi(d\theta)$ for
$A\in\mathcal T$ and $B\in\mathcal A$.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element. Its
**law** or **distribution** is the set function
$$\mathbb P_X:\Sigma\to[0,+\infty],\qquad \mathbb P_X(B):=\mathbb P(X^{-1}(B)).$$

Thus the law of $X$ records the probability of each measurable target set by
pulling it back to an event in the original probability space.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element, let
$\mathbb P_X$ be its law, and let $g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb R$ or
$g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb C$ be measurable.

1. If $g\ge0$, then
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$
2. If $g(X)$ is integrable, then $g$ is integrable with respect to
   $\mathbb P_X$ and the same formula holds:
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of
   [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] is a measure on
   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B),$$
   with the nonnegative extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=\infty\cdot0=0$;
3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the
   rectangle formula.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$. Then the following are
equivalent:

1. the family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is independent;
2. for every natural number $n\ge1$, every choice of distinct indices
   $i_0,\dots,i_{n-1}\in I$, and every choice of measurable sets
   $B_k\in\Sigma_{i_k}$,
   $$\mathbb P\bigl(X_{i_0}\in B_0,\dots,X_{i_{n-1}}\in B_{n-1}\bigr)=\prod_{k<n}\mathbb P(X_{i_k}\in B_k).$$

Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]].

When $\Sigma_i$ is a Borel sigma-algebra, this agrees with the notation
$\sigma(X_i)$ from [[def-sigma-algebra-generated-by-a-function]].

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
[[def-measurable-rectangle]].

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$ be a measurable space, let $P$ be a probability
kernel on it, meaning that $P(x,\cdot)$ is a probability measure for each $x$
and $x\mapsto P(x,A)$ is measurable for each $A\in\mathcal X$
([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]), and let $\pi$ be a
probability measure, that is a countably additive measure of total mass one
([[def-probability-measure]]). The product sigma-algebra
$\mathcal X\otimes\mathcal X$ is generated by measurable rectangles
([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]). The joint
flow measure of $(\pi,P)$ is the probability measure $\Lambda_{\pi,P}$ on
$(\mathsf X\times\mathsf X,\mathcal X\otimes\mathcal X)$ given, for each
$C\in\mathcal X\otimes\mathcal X$, by

$$\Lambda_{\pi,P}(C):=\int_{\mathsf X}P(x,C_x)\,\pi(dx),\qquad C_x:=\{y\in\mathsf X:(x,y)\in C\}.$$

Existence, countable additivity, and the nonnegative iterated-integral identity
for this measure follow from
[[lem-prior-and-model-kernel-define-joint-law]]. Let $\tau(x,y):=(y,x)$ be
the coordinate-swap map. It is measurable because the preimage of a measurable
rectangle $A\times B$ is $B\times A$ and such rectangles generate the product
sigma-algebra. Define the transpose measure by
$\Lambda_{\pi,P}^{\top}(C):=\Lambda_{\pi,P}(\tau^{-1}(C))$.

The kernel $P$ is **reversible with respect to $\pi$** when
$$\Lambda_{\pi,P}=\Lambda_{\pi,P}^{\top}.$$
This definition uses equality of measures and requires no density, standard
Borel assumption, or prior assumption that $\pi$ is invariant.

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$ be a measurable space, $P$ a probability kernel
([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]) on it, and $\pi$ a probability
measure ([[def-probability-measure]]) on it. If $P$ is reversible with
respect to $\pi$ in the sense of
[[def-general-state-reversibility-by-symmetric-flow-measure]], then $\pi$ is
invariant for $P$: for every $A\in\mathcal X$,

$$\int_{\mathsf X}P(x,A)\,\pi(dx)=\pi(A).$$

derivations.claim:
AC is assumed as recorded in [A1]. Put $\rho=\sqrt{1-\beta^2}$ and let
$\Lambda_0(du,dv)=\mu_0(du)Q_\beta(u,dv)$ be the joint flow of the reference
probability and proposal kernel. It exists by [F4]. Take the product
probability space $(H\times H,\mu_0\otimes\mu_0)$ and its coordinate random
elements $U_0,\xi$; [F6] gives their independence and common law $\mu_0$.
For every nonnegative
product-Borel $h$, the iterated-integral identity in [F4] and [F1] give
$$\int h\,d\Lambda_0
=\int_H\int_H h(u,\rho u+\beta z)\,\mu_0(dz)\,\mu_0(du)
=\mathbb E[h(U_0,\rho U_0+\beta\xi)],$$
where the proposal-row pushforward and change of variables [F5] give the first
identity, and the product joint law [F5] gives the second. Thus
$\Lambda_0$ is the law in [F3], so $\Lambda_0$ is symmetric.

Define $w(u)=e^{-\bar\Phi(u)}$ and
$m(u,v)=\min\{w(u),w(v)\}$. For every $(u,v)$, if both potential values are
finite, then
$$w(u)\alpha(u,v)=e^{-\bar\Phi(u)}\min\{1,e^{\bar\Phi(u)-\bar\Phi(v)}\}
=\min\{e^{-\bar\Phi(u)},e^{-\bar\Phi(v)}\}=m(u,v).$$
If either value is $+\infty$, the algorithm sets $\alpha(u,v)=0$ and
$m(u,v)=0$, so the identity still holds. In particular, $m$ is a symmetric
nonnegative Borel function.

For Borel $C\subseteq H\times H$, the accepted part of the target joint
flow is
$$\Lambda_{\rm acc}(C):=\int_H\int_H
\mathbf1_C(u,v)\alpha(u,v)Q_\beta(u,dv)\,\mu(du)
=Z^{-1}\int_{H\times H}\mathbf1_C(u,v)m(u,v)\,\Lambda_0(du,dv).$$
The equality follows from the target density in [F2], identity 1.2, and the
iterated-integral formula [F4]. Since $\Lambda_0$ is symmetric by step 1.1
and $m(u,v)=m(v,u)$, this accepted measure is symmetric. Indeed, for
$\tau(u,v)=(v,u)$, the change-of-variables identity [F5] gives
$$\int\mathbf1_C(u,v)m(u,v)\,d\Lambda_0
=\int\mathbf1_C(v,u)m(v,u)\,d\Lambda_0
=\int\mathbf1_{\tau^{-1}C}(u,v)m(u,v)\,d\Lambda_0.$$
Equality for every Borel $C$ is symmetry under $\tau$.

Set $r(u)=1-a(u)\in[0,1]$. By the diagonal term in [F1] and the joint-flow
formula [F4], the rejection part of the target joint flow has mass on $C$
$$\Lambda_{\rm rej}(C)=\int_H\mathbf1_C(u,u)r(u)\,\mu(du).$$
It is symmetric because $\tau(d(u))=d(u)$ for every $u$: for every Borel
$C$, $\mathbf1_{\tau^{-1}C}(u,u)=\mathbf1_C(u,u)$.

By the decomposition of $P_\beta$ in [F1] and the joint-flow identity
[F4], $\Lambda_\beta=\Lambda_{\rm acc}+\Lambda_{\rm rej}$. The accepted
and rejection pieces are symmetric by steps 2.1 and 2.2, hence $\Lambda_\beta$
is symmetric.
By [F7], $P_\beta$ is reversible with respect to $\mu$.

The hypotheses of [F8] hold: [F1] gives a probability kernel and the
algorithm gives the probability measure $\mu$. Therefore [F8] yields
$\int_H P_\beta(u,A)\,\mu(du)=\mu(A)$ for every Borel $A$. The proof uses
only the symmetric-flow identity; it establishes no uniqueness or convergence
claim.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]],
> [[def-natural-numbers]]) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** [[def-choice-function]] and
[[def-axiom-of-choice]] select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and [[def-countable-choice]] does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ ([[def-power-set]], [[def-cartesian-product]], [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]]); a natural is the set of its predecessors ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense ([[def-chain]]). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

Assume countable choice and dependent choice. Every probability measure $\nu$
on $(S,\Sigma)$ is the common law of a countable independent family of
$S$-valued random elements.

Let $H=\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$ with its canonical real inner product, and for each $j\in\mathbb N$ let $e_j$ be the sequence whose $j$th coordinate is $1$ and whose other coordinates are $0$. Then $(e_j)_{j\in\mathbb N}$ is a complete orthonormal basis of $H$. For every $x=(x_j)\in H$, the truncations $\sum_{j=1}^N x_je_j$ converge in $H$ to $x$, and $\|x\|_2^2=\sum_{j\in\mathbb N}|x_j|^2$.

Let $H_0$ and $H_1$ be separable real Hilbert spaces with a continuous inclusion $H_1\hookrightarrow H_0$. Let $(e_j)_{j\ge1}$ be an orthonormal basis of $H_0$ that is a complete orthogonal basis of $H_1$, write $w_j=\|e_j\|_{H_1}^2>0$, and set $f_j=e_j/\sqrt{w_j}$, so $(f_j)_{j\ge1}$ is an orthonormal basis of $H_1$. Let $(\xi_j)_{j\ge1}$ be independent real random variables on one probability space with $\mathbb E\xi_j=0$ and $\mathbb E\xi_j^2=1$, and let $\lambda_j\ge0$ satisfy $\sum_{j\ge1}\lambda_jw_j<\infty$. Then
$$S_N=\sum_{j=1}^N\sqrt{\lambda_j}\,\xi_j e_j$$
converges almost surely in $H_1$ and in $L^2(\Omega;H_1)$ to an $H_1$-valued Borel-measurable random element $S$, with
$$\mathbb E\|S\|_{H_1}^2=\sum_{j\ge1}\lambda_jw_j.$$
These norm-convergence conclusions use no choice axiom beyond the supplied probability space and variables. For the following Gaussian conclusions, assume in addition that each $\xi_j$ has the standard normal law $N(0,1)$. Under the Axiom of Choice and countable choice, $S$ is a centered Borel Gaussian random element in $H_1$. Its covariance map $C:H_1^*\to H_1$, transported to $H_1$ by the Hilbert-space Riesz identification, is diagonal in the basis $(f_j)_{j\ge1}$ with eigenvalues $\lambda_jw_j$, and these eigenvalues are summable. If $D$ is a Borel forward-map domain in $H_1$ and $\mathbb P(S\in D)=1$, then the law of $S$ is a prior on $D$. Under the Axiom of Choice there is $a>0$ such that
$$\mathbb E\exp\!\bigl(a\|S\|_{H_1}^2\bigr)<\infty.$$

Let $H=\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$ with its canonical real inner product, and for each $j\in\mathbb N$ let $e_j$ be the sequence whose $j$th coordinate is $1$ and whose other coordinates are $0$. Then $(e_j)_{j\in\mathbb N}$ is a complete orthonormal basis of $H$. For every $x=(x_j)\in H$, the truncations $\sum_{j=1}^N x_je_j$ converge in $H$ to $x$, and $\|x\|_2^2=\sum_{j\in\mathbb N}|x_j|^2$.

Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]].

When $\Sigma_i$ is a Borel sigma-algebra, this agrees with the notation
$\sigma(X_i)$ from [[def-sigma-algebra-generated-by-a-function]].

Let $(\mathcal F_i)_{i\in I}$ be an independent family of sigma-algebras on a
probability space, and let $J_0,\dots,J_{m-1}\subseteq I$ be pairwise disjoint
index sets. For each $r<m$, define

$$\mathcal G_r:=\sigma\left(\bigcup_{i\in J_r}\mathcal F_i\right).$$

Then the sigma-algebras $\mathcal G_0,\dots,\mathcal G_{m-1}$ are independent.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be an independent family of random elements
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$. For each $i$, let
$g_i:(S_i,\Sigma_i)\to(T_i,\mathcal T_i)$ be measurable. Then the family
$(g_i\circ X_i)_{i\in I}$ is independent.

Assume AC. For $m\in\mathbb R$, $\sigma\ge0$, and a real random variable
$X$ with law $N(m,\sigma^2)$,
$$E[X]=m,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(X)=\sigma^2.$$

Assume AC and let $G\sim N(0,\sigma^2)$ for $\sigma\ge0$. Then $\mathbb E[G^2]=\sigma^2$ and $\mathbb E[G^4]=3\sigma^4$; in particular the fourth moment is finite. For independent centered normal coordinates $G_j\sim N(0,\sigma_j^2)$, every finite linear combination of the variables $G_j^2$ has finite second moment.

Let $n\ge1$, let $X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}$ be independent real random variables on a
common probability space, and let $g_i:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be Borel
measurable for each $i<n$.

1. If every $g_i$ is nonnegative, then
   $$\mathbb E\left[\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)\right]=\prod_{i<n}\mathbb E[g_i(X_i)]$$
   in $[0,+\infty]$. In this finite product of expectations, a zero factor
   makes the product zero even when another factor is $+\infty$; otherwise
   multiplication has its usual extended nonnegative meaning.
2. If every $g_i(X_i)$ is integrable, then $\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)$ is integrable
   and the same factorization holds in $\mathbb R$.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.
IID square-integrable real variables satisfy $S_n/n\to\mathbb EX_1$ almost surely.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ and $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be measurable spaces,
let $\pi$ be a probability measure on $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$, and let
$K:\Theta\times\mathcal A\to[0,1]$ be a probability kernel. For
$C\in\mathcal T\otimes\mathcal A$, write
$C_\theta=\{x\in\mathcal X:(\theta,x)\in C\}$ and set
$$J(C)=\int_\Theta K(\theta,C_\theta)\,\pi(d\theta).$$
Then $J$ is a probability measure on the product sigma-algebra, and for every
nonnegative product-measurable $h$,

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element, let

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by

By [A1] and [F1], take a countable independent sequence
$(Z_n)_{n\ge1}$ with law $N(0,1)$ and put
$X_j=Z_{2j-1}$, $Y_j=Z_{2j}$. Each subsequence is again IID standard normal.
The odd and even coordinate sigma-algebras are independent by [F4]. Apply
[F3] with $H_0=H_1=H$, $w_j=1$, and $\lambda_j=2^{-j}$ to each subsequence.
Since $\sum_j2^{-j}=1$, both series converge almost surely in $H$ and define
centered Borel Gaussian random elements. Their finite coordinate laws agree:
by [F3], each finite coordinate vector is obtained by multiplying independent
standard normals by the same coefficients $2^{-j/2}$, so each vector has the
same product normal law by [F5] and [F9]. AC implies Countable Choice by
[A1], so [F13] identifies their Borel laws. Each limit is measurable with
respect to its own coordinate sigma-algebra: its partial sums are
block-measurable, the event that they are Cauchy is a countable combination
of measurable norm inequalities, and the limit, set to zero on the null
complement, is therefore block-measurable. In detail, for a proper open
$O\subset H$ with closed complement $C$, on the convergence event the
preimage of $O$ is the condition
$\liminf_N\operatorname{dist}(S_N,C)>0$; the distance function is
1-Lipschitz, and the zero value assigned off that event is included exactly
when $0\in O$. This is a measurable condition on the block. The odd and even
coordinate sigma-algebras are independent by [F4], hence $U$ and $\xi$ are
independent.
Denote their common law by $\mu_0$.

For each $u\in H$, $Q_\beta(u,\cdot)$ is the pushforward of $\mu_0$
under the continuous map $z\mapsto u+\beta z$, hence is a probability
measure. For Borel $B\subseteq H$, the map
$(u,z)\mapsto\mathbf1_B(u+\beta z)$ is product-Borel because addition and
scalar multiplication are continuous. Integrating it against the constant
kernel $u\mapsto\mu_0$ is measurable by [F11], so $Q_\beta$ is a probability
kernel. Its joint flow $\eta$ exists by [F8]. By the product joint law [F9]
and the proposal pushforward, $\eta$ is the law of $(U,U+\beta\xi)$.

For each $j$, define
$$D_j:=2^j\bigl((U+\beta\xi)_j^2-U_j^2\bigr)
=(X_j+\beta Y_j)^2-X_j^2=2\beta X_jY_j+\beta^2Y_j^2.$$
The pairs $(X_j,Y_j)$ are independent by grouping the independent
coordinates, and have the same product standard-normal law by [F9]. Applying
the same polynomial map to each pair therefore makes $(D_j)$ IID by [F4]
and [F9]. By [F5]–[F6],
$\mathbb E[X_jY_j]=\mathbb E[X_j]\mathbb E[Y_j]=0$,
$\mathbb E[Y_j^2]=1$, and
$$\mathbb E[D_j]=\beta^2.$$
They are square-integrable: using $(a+b)^2\le2a^2+2b^2$,
$$\mathbb E[D_j^2]\le8\beta^2\mathbb E[X_j^2Y_j^2]
+2\beta^4\mathbb E[Y_j^4]
=8\beta^2+6\beta^4<\infty,$$
where independence gives $\mathbb E[X_j^2Y_j^2]=1$ and [F5] gives
$\mathbb E[Y_j^4]=3$. By [F7],
$$\frac1n\sum_{j=1}^nD_j\longrightarrow\beta^2\quad\text{almost surely}.$$

For $(u,v)\in H\times H$, set
$$f_n(u,v):=\frac1n\sum_{j=1}^n2^j(v_j^2-u_j^2),\qquad
A_\beta:=\left\{(u,v):f_n(u,v)\to\beta^2\right\}.$$
Each coordinate map is continuous since $|u_j-v_j|\le\|u-v\|_2$ by
[F2]; finite arithmetic operations make $f_n$ Borel by [F10]. Explicitly,
$$A_\beta=\bigcap_{k=1}^\infty\bigcup_{N=1}^\infty
\bigcap_{n=N}^\infty\{|f_n-\beta^2|<1/k\},$$
so $A_\beta$ is Borel by [F10]. The limit criterion follows because for
every $\varepsilon>0$ one can choose $k$ with $1/k<\varepsilon$.

Under the forward flow $\eta$, the pair has the law of $(U,V)$ from
step 1.2, and $f_n(U,V)=n^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^nD_j$. Step 2.1 therefore gives
$\eta(A_\beta)=1$. Under the transpose $\eta^\top$, the pair has the law of
$(V,U)$, and $f_n(V,U)=-f_n(U,V)\to-\beta^2$. Since $\beta>0$,
$-\beta^2\ne\beta^2$, hence $\eta^\top(A_\beta)=0$.

Thus $A_\beta$ and its complement are disjoint Borel sets with
$\eta(A_\beta)=1$ and $\eta^\top(A_\beta^c)=1$. This is mutual singularity
of the two probability measures, and in particular neither is absolutely
continuous with respect to the other. By [F12], the pCN reference proposal
flow at this same scale equals its transpose.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H$ be a separable real Hilbert space, let
$\mu_0$ be a centered Borel Gaussian probability measure on $H$, let
$D\subseteq H$ be Borel with $\mu_0(D)=1$, and let
$\Phi_D:D\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be Borel. Assume the evidence
$$
Z:=\int_D e^{-\Phi_D(u)}\,\mu_0(du)
$$
satisfies $0<Z<\infty$. Extend the potential to all of $H$ by setting
$\bar\Phi(u)=\Phi_D(u)$ for $u\in D$ and $\bar\Phi(u)=+\infty$ for
$u\notin D$, and define the target probability
$\mu(du)=Z^{-1}e^{-\bar\Phi(u)}\mu_0(du)$. For a scale $\beta\in[0,1]$,
write $\rho=\sqrt{1-\beta^2}$. At state $u\in H$, draw $\xi\sim\mu_0$
independently and propose $v=\rho u+\beta\xi$. Set the acceptance probability
to $0$ if either $\bar\Phi(u)$ or $\bar\Phi(v)$ is $+\infty$, and otherwise set
$$
\alpha(u,v)=\min\{1,\exp(\bar\Phi(u)-\bar\Phi(v))\}.
$$
Draw an independent uniform random variable on $[0,1]$ and move to $v$ if it
is at most $\alpha(u,v)$; otherwise remain at $u$. The resulting one-step
transition rule is the prior-preserving Crank–Nicolson, or pCN, rule
$P_\beta$. States with infinite potential are absorbing under this total
definition; they have $\mu$-measure zero.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the inputs of the prior-preserving
Crank–Nicolson algorithm: a separable real Hilbert space $H$, centered Borel
Gaussian reference probability $\mu_0$, full-mass Borel domain $D$, Borel
potential $\Phi_D:D\to(-\infty,+\infty]$, positive finite evidence $Z$, and
scale $\beta\in[0,1]$. Let $\mu$ be the normalized target on $H$ obtained by
extending $\Phi_D$ by $+\infty$ off $D$, and let $P_\beta$ be the algorithm's
accept-reject transition. Then $P_\beta$ is reversible with respect to $\mu$:
its joint flow
$$\Lambda_\beta(C):=\int_H P_\beta(u,C_u)\,\mu(du),\qquad
C_u:=\{v\in H:(u,v)\in C\},$$
is unchanged by $(u,v)\mapsto(v,u)$ for every Borel
$C\subseteq H\times H$. Consequently, $\mu$ is invariant:
$$\int_H P_\beta(u,A)\,\mu(du)=\mu(A)\qquad(A\in\mathcal B(H)).$$
This conclusion gives invariance only; it does not assert uniqueness,
convergence, mixing, an effective-sample-size bound, mesh-independent cost,
or correctness of an approximate forward solver.

citations.quote: A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. Assume the axiom of choice. Let $K$ be a probability kernel on $(E,\mathcal E)$,
let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P,(\mathcal F_n)_{n\ge0})$ be a filtered
probability space, and let $X=(X_n)_{n\ge0}$ be an adapted $E$-valued process.
We call $X$ a **time-homogeneous Markov chain with transition kernel $K$ relative
to $(\mathcal F_n)$** if, for every $n\ge0$ and $A\in\mathcal E$,
$$ \mathbb P(X_{n+1}\in A\mid\mathcal F_n)=K(X_n,A)\qquad\text{a.s.} $$

If $\sum_{k\ge1}|\rho_h(k)|<\infty$ and
$\tau_h:=1+2\sum_{k\ge1}\rho_h(k)>0$, define the theoretical
**functional-specific effective sample size** for an integer $n\ge1$ draws by
$\operatorname{ESS}_h(n):=n/\tau_h$. Here $Y_n$ is the scalar
functional whose Monte Carlo average is being assessed. When a central limit
theorem for that average has asymptotic variance
$\sigma_h^2\tau_h$, this definition is the iid sample size with the same
asymptotic variance. It does not assert that such a central limit theorem holds.
If the covariance series is not absolutely summable or $\tau_h\le0$, this
definition does not assign a finite positive effective sample size.

Let $(E,\mathcal E)$ be a measurable space, let $\mu,\nu$ be probability
measures on it, and let $f:E\to\mathbb R$ be measurable with
$|f|\le M$ for some $0\le M<\infty$. Use the library convention
$$\|\mu-\nu\|_{\rm TV}:=\sup_{A\in\mathcal E}|\mu(A)-\nu(A)|.$$
Then
$$|\mu(f)-\nu(f)|\le2M\|\mu-\nu\|_{\rm TV}.$$

For the complete posterior computation error budget defined above, the
pathwise total error satisfies
$$|\mu_\star(f)-\bar f_{b,N}|\le\mathcal B_f.$$
This is a telescoping bound; it does not estimate any component.

Separately, let $(X_n)_{n\ge0}$ be a stationary time-homogeneous Markov chain
with transition kernel $K$, invariant law $\pi_K$, and initial law
$X_0\sim\pi_K$, and use the same bounded functional $f$. Put
$$\gamma_k:=\operatorname{Cov}(f(X_0),f(X_k))\qquad(k\ge0).$$
If $\sum_{k=1}^\infty|\gamma_k|<\infty$, then for every burn-in $b\ge0$ and
sample size $N\ge1$,
$$\mathbb E\left[|\bar f_{b,N}-\pi_K(f)|^2\right]=\frac{1}{N^2}\left[N\gamma_0+2\sum_{k=1}^{N-1}(N-k)\gamma_k\right]\le\frac{\gamma_0+2\sum_{k=1}^\infty|\gamma_k|}{N}.$$
The sample bound assumes stationarity; for a nonstationary start, the budget
keeps $|\pi_K(f)-\mathbb E_\lambda\bar f_{b,N}|$ as a separate burn-in term.
This finite-$N$ variance bound is not a central limit theorem or a confidence
interval.

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

When all stages are present, define the component errors
$$\begin{aligned}\delta_{\rm model}&:=|\mu_\star(f)-\mu_{\rm model}(f)|,\\ \delta_{\rm solver}&:=|\mu_{\rm model}(f)-\mu_{\rm solver}(f)|,\\ \delta_{\rm disc}&:=|\mu_{\rm solver}(f)-\mu_{\rm disc}(f)|,\\ \delta_K&:=|\mu_{\rm disc}(f)-\pi_K(f)|,\\ \delta_{\rm burn}&:=|\pi_K(f)-\mathbb E_\lambda\bar f_{b,N}|,\\ \delta_{\rm MC}&:=|\mathbb E_\lambda\bar f_{b,N}-\bar f_{b,N}|.\end{aligned}$$
The last component is random and the earlier components are fixed for the
declared data and computation. The **posterior computation error budget** is
$$\mathcal B_f:=\delta_{\rm model}+\delta_{\rm solver}+\delta_{\rm disc}+\delta_K+\delta_{\rm burn}+\delta_{\rm MC}.$$
If a computation stops before one of these stages, report the shorter reference
chain and its component terms. The term $\delta_K$ measures the invariant-law
discrepancy induced by the implemented transition rule; it is not a one-step
distance between kernels. A one-step kernel error cannot replace it without a
separate perturbation theorem with its own hypotheses.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]],
> [[def-natural-numbers]]) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** [[def-choice-function]] and
[[def-axiom-of-choice]] select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and [[def-countable-choice]] does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ ([[def-power-set]], [[def-cartesian-product]], [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]]); a natural is the set of its predecessors ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense ([[def-chain]]). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

For a measure $\mu$, write
$$L^1(\mu):=\{f:X\to\mathbb C:\ f \text{ is integrable}\}.$$
Here **integrable** is the notion introduced in
[[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]].

On this page $L^1(\mu)$ is the class of integrable representatives. The later
Banach-space page will pass to almost-everywhere equivalence classes.
For $f\in L^1[a,b]$, the function $I_f(x)=\int_a^x f$ is absolutely continuous.

Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. For $F:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$, the following are equivalent:

1. $F$ is absolutely continuous.
2. $F'$ exists almost everywhere, $F'\in L^1[a,b]$, and
$$F(x)-F(a)=\int_a^xF'(t)\,dt\quad\text{for every }x\in[a,b].$$
If $F\in AC[a,b]$ and $h$ is Lipschitz on $F([a,b])$, then $h\circ F\in AC[a,b]$.
If $F,G\in AC[a,b]$, then $FG\in AC[a,b]$.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

Let $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on
$(a,b)$, with $a<b$. Then there is $c\in(a,b)$ such that
$$
f(b)-f(a)=f'(c)(b-a).
$$

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Every function differentiable at $c$ is continuous at $c$.
If $f,g$ are real functions differentiable at $c$, then $f+g$ and $fg$ are
differentiable there and
$$
(f+g)'(c)=f'(c)+g'(c),\qquad (fg)'(c)=f'(c)g(c)+f(c)g'(c).
$$
If $g(c)\ne0$, then $f/g$ is differentiable at $c$ and
$$
(f/g)'(c)=\frac{f'(c)g(c)-f(c)g'(c)}{g(c)^2}.
$$
If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, $g$ is differentiable at $f(c)$, and the
composition is defined near $c$, then $g\circ f$ is differentiable at $c$ and
$(g\circ f)'(c)=g'(f(c))f'(c)$. For every integer $m\ge1$,
$(x^m)'=mx^{m-1}$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. If $f : V \to \mathbb C$ belongs to $L^1(\lambda_n)$,
then
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

derivations.claim: If $a=b$, both hypotheses reduce to $u(a)\le A$, which is the claimed bound. Hence assume $a<b$ and first consider the forward inequality. Define $C(t)=\int_a^t\ell(s)\,ds$ and $V(t)=A+\int_a^t\ell(s)u(s)\,ds$. Continuity of $u$ on the compact interval makes it bounded, so $\ell u\in L^1$. By [F2], both $C$ and $V$ are absolutely continuous, and the hypothesis says $0\le u(t)\le V(t)$. The range of $C$ is contained in the compact interval $[0,C(b)]$; [F6] makes $r\mapsto e^{-r}$ Lipschitz there. Thus $e^{-C}$ is absolutely continuous by [F4], and $W(t):=e^{-C(t)}V(t)$ is absolutely continuous by [F5].

By [F3] and [F4], there is a full-measure set where $C,V,W$ are all differentiable and $C'=\ell$, $V'=\ell u$. At every such point, [F7] gives $W'=e^{-C}(V'-C'V)=e^{-C}\ell(u-V)\le0,$ since $u\le V$ and $\ell\ge0$. Applying [F4] to $W$ yields $W(t)-W(a)=\int_a^tW'(s)\,ds\le0$. As $W(a)=A$ and $u(t)\le V(t)$, we obtain $u(t)\le V(t)\le A e^{C(t)}$, the claimed forward estimate.

By step 1.1, assume $a<b$. Set $\widetilde u(r)=u(a+b-r)$ and $\widetilde\ell(r)=\ell(a+b-r)$. By [F8], reflection preserves measurability and integrability and gives $\int_a^r\widetilde\ell(q)\widetilde u(q)\,dq=\int_{a+b-r}^b\ell(s)u(s)\,ds$. Thus $\widetilde u(r)\le A+\int_a^r\widetilde\ell(q)\widetilde u(q)\,dq$. The forward result in steps 1.1–2.1 applies to these continuous and integrable functions. Substituting $r=a+b-t$ into its bound gives $u(t)\le A\exp(\int_t^b\ell(s)\,ds)$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense ([[def-chain]]). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

Let $a\le b$, let $A\ge0$, let $u:[a,b]\to[0,\infty)$ be continuous, and let $\ell:[a,b]\to[0,\infty)$ be Lebesgue measurable with $\int_a^b\ell(s)\,ds<\infty$. If
$$u(t)\le A+\int_a^t\ell(s)u(s)\,ds\qquad(a\le t\le b),$$
then
$$u(t)\le A\exp\!\left(\int_a^t\ell(s)\,ds\right)\qquad(a\le t\le b).$$
If instead $u(t)\le A+\int_t^b\ell(s)u(s)\,ds$ for every $t\in[a,b]$, then
$$u(t)\le A\exp\!\left(\int_t^b\ell(s)\,ds\right)\qquad(a\le t\le b).$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable
$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

Let $J$ be a nonempty compact interval and $n\ge1$. Continuous $\mathbb R^n$-valued curves on $J$ are complete in the supremum metric

$$d_\infty(x,y):=\sup_{t\in J}\|x(t)-y(t)\|_2.$$

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty complete metric space ([[def-complete-metric-space]])
and let $f : X \to X$ be a contraction with constant $q$, so
$d(f(u),f(v)) \le q\,d(u,v)$ for all $u,v \in X$ and $0 \le q < 1$
([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]]). Then:

1. There is exactly one $x^{*} \in X$ with $f(x^{*}) = x^{*}$.
2. For every $x_0 \in X$ the sequence of **iterates**, defined by recursion
   ([[thm-recursion]]) by $x_{n+1} := f(x_n)$, converges to $x^{*}$ in $(X,d)$
   ([[def-metric-convergence]]). In particular the limit does not depend on
   $x_0$.
3. For all $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge n$,
   $$d(x_m, x_n) \;\le\; \frac{q^{\,n}\, d(x_1,x_0)}{1-q},$$
   with the integer power of [[def-integer-power]].

Claim 3 is the quantitative form of the argument that proves claims 1 and 2, and
it is recorded in the statement because the error estimates
([[cor-banach-error-estimates]]) are read off from it.

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$, let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$
and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$. If $a<b$, assume that $f$ is integrable
([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]). Then:

1. if $a < b$, the real-valued function $t \mapsto \lVert f(t)\rVert_2$ is
   integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]], [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]);
2. $$\Bigl\lVert \int_a^b f \Bigr\rVert_2 \;\le\; \int_a^b \lVert f\rVert_2 .$$

**The hypothesis $a \le b$ is not decoration.** With the orientation convention
of [[def-oriented-integral]] and
[[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], interchanging the limits changes
the sign of the right-hand side but not of the left, so for $b < a$ the correct
statement is $\bigl\lVert\int_a^b f\bigr\rVert_2 \le \bigl|\int_a^b \lVert f\rVert_2\bigr|$;
the displayed inequality as written is false in that case. This is the same trap
the scalar inequality of
[[cor-integrability-of-absolute-values-products-and-lattice-operations]] carries.

**Clause 1 is a genuine obligation and is discharged before the estimate.** That
each $f_i$ is integrable does not by itself say that
$\sqrt{\sum_{i<m} f_i^{2}}$ is; the square root has to be brought in through
[[thm-composition-with-a-continuous-function]].
For $f\in L^1[a,b]$, the function $I_f(x)=\int_a^x f$ is absolutely continuous.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the
   undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) for the Lebesgue-measure interfaces. Let $X$ be a real or complex Banach space, let $a<b$, and let $f:[a,b]\to X$ be continuous. Differentiation uses the underlying real structure. Then $G(t):=\int_a^t f(s)\,ds$ is differentiable on $(a,b)$ and has the corresponding one-sided derivatives at $a,b$, with $G'(t)=f(t)$, and this derivative extends continuously to $[a,b]$. Consequently, if $\varphi:[a,b]\to X$ is continuous, differentiable on $(a,b)$ with $\varphi'$ continuous on $(a,b)$ and extendable to a continuous $X$-valued function on $[a,b]$, then $\int_a^b\varphi'(s)\,ds=\varphi(b)-\varphi(a)$. The Bochner integral here is the one of [[def-bochner-integrable-function]]; the identities also hold for continuous curves on $[0,\infty)$ restricted to compact subintervals.

Let $(X,d_X)$ be a compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]]), let
$(Y,d_Y)$ be any metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to Y$ be
continuous ([[def-metric-continuity]]). Then $f$ is uniformly continuous
([[def-metric-uniform-continuity]]).

No choice principle is used: the cover built below is cut out by a property, and
the Lebesgue number lemma it is fed to is itself choice free
([[thm-lebesgue-number-lemma]]).

Let $F:D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous and
$C^1$ in the state variable. Fix data $(t_0,x_0)\in D$ and a compact time
interval $I=[t_0-h,t_0+h]$ on which the corresponding solutions through nearby
initial states all exist. Then the solution map

$$\Phi:I\times U_0\to\mathbb R^n,\qquad \Phi(t,y)=x(t;y),$$

is $C^1$ in the initial-state variable $y$ on some neighbourhood $U_0$ of
$x_0$. For each $y\in U_0$, the derivative matrix
$D_y\Phi(t,y)$ is the solution of the variational equation along $t\mapsto x(t;y)$.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $A$ be an $n\times n$ matrix and let $H$ be a direction matrix. Then

$$D\det(A)[H]=\operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{adj}(A)H).$$

If $A$ is invertible, then

$$D\det(A)[H]=\det(A)\operatorname{tr}(A^{-1}H).$$

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $n\ge1$, and let $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(R)$. Its **determinant** is
$$\det(A):=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\prod_{i<n}a_{\sigma(i),i}.$$
The sum is finite because $S_n$ has $n!$ elements. The product is taken in $R$, so the signs $1$ and $-1$ act through the ring identities. The formula uses columns indexed by $i<n$ and rows indexed by $\sigma(i)$.

When $A$ is real, $|\det A|$ means the ordinary real absolute value of its real determinant. It is not alternate notation for the determinant itself.

For a square matrix $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(F)$, its **trace** is the sum of its
diagonal entries,

$$\operatorname{tr}(A):=\sum_{i\in n}a_{ii}.$$

For $n=0$, this is the empty sum, so the unique empty matrix has trace $0$.

For $A\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and $B\in M_{n\times m}(F)$,

$$\operatorname{tr}(AB)=\operatorname{tr}(BA).$$

The two products may have different sizes, and the equality includes $m=0$ or
$n=0$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable
$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Every function differentiable at $c$ is continuous at $c$.
If $f,g$ are real functions differentiable at $c$, then $f+g$ and $fg$ are
differentiable there and
$$
(f+g)'(c)=f'(c)+g'(c),\qquad (fg)'(c)=f'(c)g(c)+f(c)g'(c).
$$
If $g(c)\ne0$, then $f/g$ is differentiable at $c$ and
$$
(f/g)'(c)=\frac{f'(c)g(c)-f(c)g'(c)}{g(c)^2}.
$$
If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, $g$ is differentiable at $f(c)$, and the
composition is defined near $c$, then $g\circ f$ is differentiable at $c$ and
$(g\circ f)'(c)=g'(f(c))f'(c)$. For every integer $m\ge1$,
$(x^m)'=mx^{m-1}$.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

Let $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on
$(a,b)$, with $a<b$. Then there is $c\in(a,b)$ such that
$$
f(b)-f(a)=f'(c)(b-a).
$$

For a measure $\mu$, write
$$L^1(\mu):=\{f:X\to\mathbb C:\ f \text{ is integrable}\}.$$
Here **integrable** is the notion introduced in
[[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]].

On this page $L^1(\mu)$ is the class of integrable representatives. The later
Banach-space page will pass to almost-everywhere equivalence classes.

Let $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ and $(Y, \mathcal{T}_Y)$ be topological spaces
([[def-topological-space]]), let $f : X \to Y$ be a function and let $x \in X$.
Neighbourhoods are as in [[def-neighbourhood-top]].

$f$ is **continuous at $x$** if for every neighbourhood $V$ of $f(x)$ in $Y$ the
preimage $f^{-1}[V]$ is a neighbourhood of $x$ in $X$.

$f$ is **continuous** if it is continuous at every point of $X$.

**The same condition with open sets only.** $f$ is continuous at $x$ if and only
if for every open $V \subseteq Y$ with $f(x) \in V$ there is an open
$U \subseteq X$ with $x \in U$ and $f[U] \subseteq V$. Indeed, if $f$ is
continuous at $x$ and $V$ is such an open set, then $V$ is a neighbourhood of
$f(x)$, so $f^{-1}[V]$ is a neighbourhood of $x$ and contains an open $U \ni x$,
which satisfies $f[U] \subseteq V$. Conversely, given the displayed condition and
a neighbourhood $V$ of $f(x)$, fix open $V_0$ with $f(x) \in V_0 \subseteq V$ and
then open $U \ni x$ with $f[U] \subseteq V_0$; then $x \in U \subseteq f^{-1}[V_0] \subseteq f^{-1}[V]$,
so $f^{-1}[V]$ is a neighbourhood of $x$. Both forms are used below and are the
same statement written twice.

**Preimage, not image.** $f^{-1}[V] = \{\, x \in X : f(x) \in V \,\}$
is the preimage in the sense of [[def-injection-surjection-bijection]] and is
defined for every function, invertible or not; no inverse function is being
asserted to exist. Continuity is a condition on preimages throughout, and the
corresponding conditions on images define the *open* and *closed* maps of a later
item, which are different notions.

derivations.claim: Fix a compact parameter set $K$. Let $C(t)=\int_0^tL_K(s)ds$. By [F4] and [F12], $C$ is continuous and nondecreasing on $[0,T]$, and [F6] makes it uniformly continuous. Choose a finite partition $0=t_0<\cdots<t_N=T$ with mesh small enough that $C(t_{i+1})-C(t_i)=\int_{t_i}^{t_{i+1}}L_K(s)ds\le1/2$ on each cell. On a cell $J=[t_i,t_{i+1}]$, with initial value $z_i$, consider the closed supremum-norm ball of radius $R=2(1+|z_i|+\int_Ja_K)$ about the constant curve $z_i$. For $z$ in that ball define $\mathcal Tz(t)=z_i+\int_{t_i}^t b(s,z(s),y)\,ds.$ The integrand is continuous by [F13], so $\mathcal Tz$ is continuous.

Put $q_J=\int_JL_K\le1/2$. The triangle inequality and spatial Lipschitz bound with $x'=0$ give $|b(s,z(s),y)|\le a_K(s)+L_K(s)|z(s)|$ almost everywhere. Hence $\|\mathcal Tz-z_i\|_\infty\le\int_Ja_K+q_J(|z_i|+R)\le R,$ so the ball maps into itself. For two curves, [F3] and the Lipschitz bound give $\|\mathcal Tz-\mathcal Tw\|_\infty\le q_J\|z-w\|_\infty$. The ball is nonempty and complete by [F1], so [F2] gives a unique fixed point, which solves the integral equation and hence the ODE on $J$ by [F5]. Applying this construction on the finite partition and using uniqueness at each shared endpoint gives a unique solution on all of $[0,T]$.

For solutions $x(t),x'(t)$ with the same $y$ and initial values $x_0,x'_0$, subtract their integral equations and use [F3] to obtain $|x(t)-x'(t)|\le|x_0-x'_0|+\int_0^t L_K(s)|x(s)-x'(s)|\,ds.$ The forward clause of the integrable-coefficient Grönwall lemma gives the factor $\exp(\int_0^tL_K)$, proving uniqueness and the forward Lipschitz bound. Applying the same existence and uniqueness construction to the reversed drift $\bar b(s,z,y)=-b(T-s,z,y)$ gives a backward solution from any terminal value; uniqueness shows that its time-zero map is the inverse of $T_y$ and the same estimate gives the inverse Lipschitz bound.

From the integral equation and [F3], $|x_y(t;x_0)|\le |x_0|+\int_0^T a_K+\int_0^tL_K(s)|x_y(s;x_0)|ds$. The integrable Grönwall estimate therefore gives $|x_y(t;x_0)|\le(|x_0|+\int_0^Ta_K)\exp(\int_0^TL_K)$, uniformly in $t$ and for $x_0,y$ in compact sets. Thus all such trajectories lie in a common compact state ball. The drift is uniformly continuous on the product of this ball, $[0,T]$, and $K$ by [F6]. Choose a compact $K$ containing a convergent sequence $y_n$ and its limit. For $(x_n,y_n)\to(x,y)$, subtract the integral equations along $x_{y_n}(\cdot;x_n)$ and $x_y(\cdot;x)$; the result is bounded by $|x_n-x|+T\omega(|y_n-y|)+\int_0^tL_K(s)|x_{y_n}(s;x_n)-x_y(s;x)|ds$, where $\omega(r)\to0$ is a modulus from [F6]. Grönwall proves uniform convergence of the paths. Repeating for the reversed drift proves continuity of the inverse map in initial value and parameter.

In the C$^1$ clause, fix $y$ and any initial state. The global existence just proved gives solutions through every nearby initial state on the same compact interval, so [F7] applies and gives the variational equation. Apply the same argument to the reversed flow; the identity of the two compositions with the identity map and [F8] show that $T_y$ has a C$^1$ inverse, hence is a C$^1$ diffeomorphism.

Write $B(t)=D_xb(t,x_y(t;x_0),y)$ and $A(t)=A_y(t,x_0)$. Since $A$ is invertible by step 4.2, [F9] and the variational equation give $\frac{d}{dt}\det A(t)=\det A(t)\operatorname{tr}(A(t)^{-1}B(t)A(t))=\det A(t)\operatorname{tr}B(t).$ The scalar product rule, chain rule and mean-value theorem in [F11] show that $e^{-\int_0^t\operatorname{tr}B(s)ds}\det A(t)$ is constant and equals $1$ at $t=0$. Rearranging gives the asserted Liouville formula.

If $\eta(dx)=q(x)dx$, then for every Borel $E\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, $T_y{}_{\#}\eta(E)=\int_{T_y^{-1}(E)}q(x)dx.$ Apply [F10] to the diffeomorphism $T_y^{-1}$ and the nonnegative measurable integrand $x\mapsto\mathbf1_{T_y^{-1}(E)}(x)q(x)$. This rewrites the last integral as $\int_Eq(T_y^{-1}(z))|\det DT_y^{-1}(z)|dz$, which proves the stated density formula. The first part of the Statement used no C$^1$ assumption; therefore global Lipschitzness alone yields only the bi-Lipschitz flow conclusion.

boundaries.reason: The state and parameter dimensions are explicitly positive and the time horizon T is positive.

boundaries.evidence: steps 3.1 and 3.2 cover b≡0: the flow is the identity, L=0, and the determinant formula gives 1.
The Statement permits d=m=1; all finite-dimensional flow and determinant formulas remain defined.

A1 declares Countable Choice and Dependent Choice; step 3.1 uses their Grönwall consequence and step 6.1 uses Countable Choice for change of variables.

The flow and density conclusions are implications, not if-and-only-if claims.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Let $\lambda$ be a probability on $(E\times T,\mathcal S\otimes\mathcal T)$, where E and T are standard-Borel spaces, and let $\beta(B)=\lambda(E\times B)$ be its second marginal. There is a probability kernel $K:(T,\mathcal T)\to(E,\mathcal S)$ such that

$$\lambda(A\times B)=\int_B K(y,A)\,\beta(dy)\quad(A\in\mathcal S,\ B\in\mathcal T).$$

It is unique as a kernel outside a single measurable $\beta$-null set. For every nonnegative product-measurable $f:E\times T\to[0,\infty]$,

$$\int f(x,y)\,\lambda(d(x,y))=\int_T\left(\int_E f(x,y)K(y,dx)\right)\beta(dy).$$

In particular this applies to the joint law of random elements $(X,Y)$, with $\beta=P_Y$; the direction is the law of X given Y.

For every natural $n\ge1$, let $\mathbb R^n$ be the set of functions
$x:n\to\mathbb R$ with its finite-product topology and Borel sigma-algebra
([[def-product-topology]], [[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]). Then
$(\mathbb R^n,\mathcal B(\mathbb R^n))$ is standard Borel.

Assume AC. Let $\lambda$ be a probability on $(E\times T,\mathcal S\otimes\mathcal T)$, where E and T are standard-Borel spaces, and let $\beta(B)=\lambda(E\times B)$ be its second marginal. There is a probability kernel $K:(T,\mathcal T)\to(E,\mathcal S)$ such that

$$\lambda(A\times B)=\int_B K(y,A)\,\beta(dy)\quad(A\in\mathcal S,\ B\in\mathcal T).$$

It is unique as a kernel outside a single measurable $\beta$-null set. For every nonnegative product-measurable $f:E\times T\to[0,\infty]$,

$$\int f(x,y)\,\lambda(d(x,y))=\int_T\left(\int_E f(x,y)K(y,dx)\right)\beta(dy).$$

In particular this applies to the joint law of random elements $(X,Y)$, with $\beta=P_Y$; the direction is the law of X given Y.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
[[def-measurable-rectangle]].

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ and $(Y,\mathcal{B})$ be measurable spaces
([[def-measurable-space]]). A function $f : X \to Y$ is **measurable** when

$$f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \qquad \text{for every } B \in \mathcal{B}.$$

Equivalently, the family

$$\mathcal{C}_f := \{\, B \subseteq Y : f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \,\}$$

is a sigma-algebra on $Y$ containing $\mathcal{B}$.

Let $(S_i,\Sigma_i)$, $1\le i\le n$, be finitely many measurable spaces, with
$n\ge1$, and equip $\prod_{i=1}^nS_i$ with its finite product sigma-algebra.
If $f_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ are measurable, then the tuple
$f=(f_1,\ldots,f_n)$ is measurable. If all factors equal one measurable space
$(S,\Sigma)$, every coordinate permutation $\tau_\pi:S^n\to S^n$ is
measurable, where $(\tau_\pi z)_i=z_{\pi(i)}$.

Let K be a finite kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$, in particular a probability kernel, or a uniformly sigma-finite kernel with the specified exhaustion of the kernel definition. For every nonnegative $\Sigma\otimes\Tau$-measurable function $f:S\times T\to[0,\infty]$, the function
$$I_f(s)=\int_T f(s,t)\,K(s,dt)$$
is $\Sigma$-measurable, with infinity allowed. For a real product-measurable f, the set $D=\{s:I_{|f|}(s)<\infty\}$ is measurable, and its signed integral on D, extended by zero on $S\setminus D$, is a measurable real function. No assertion here is made for a general kernel lacking a common measurable finite-mass exhaustion.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of
   [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] is a measure on
   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B),$$
   with the nonnegative extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=\infty\cdot0=0$;
3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the
   rectangle formula.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. Let $T>0$, let $d,m\ge1$, and let $b:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^d$ be jointly continuous on the product Euclidean domain. Suppose that for every compact $K\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ there are nonnegative Lebesgue-measurable $a_K,L_K\in L^1([0,T])$ such that for almost every $t$, simultaneously for all $y\in K$ and $x,x'\in\mathbb R^d$,
$$|b(t,0,y)|\le a_K(t),\qquad |b(t,x,y)-b(t,x',y)|\le L_K(t)|x-x'|.$$
Here $L^1([0,T])$ means the functions have finite Lebesgue integral of their absolute values. Then for every $x_0\in\mathbb R^d$ and $y\in\mathbb R^m$ there is a unique continuously differentiable solution $x_y(\cdot;x_0)$ of
$$\dot x(t)=b(t,x(t),y),\qquad x(0)=x_0,$$
on all of $[0,T]$. Its terminal map $T_y(x_0):=x_y(T;x_0)$ is a bijection with jointly continuous forward and inverse maps in $(x_0,y)$, and for all $x_0,x_1$ and $y\in K$,
$$|T_y(x_0)-T_y(x_1)|\le e^{\int_0^T L_K(t)dt}|x_0-x_1|,\qquad |T_y^{-1}(x_0)-T_y^{-1}(x_1)|\le e^{\int_0^T L_K(t)dt}|x_0-x_1|.$$

In the separate C$^1$ clause, suppose additionally that the state derivative $D_xb$ exists and is jointly continuous. Then for fixed $y$, $T_y$ is a bijection and both $T_y$ and its inverse are continuously differentiable. For a measurable map $S$ and a measure $\mu$, define its image measure by $S_{\#}\mu(E):=\mu(S^{-1}(E))$. The derivative $A_y(t,x_0):=D_{x_0}x_y(t;x_0)$ solves
$$\dot A_y(t,x_0)=D_xb(t,x_y(t;x_0),y)A_y(t,x_0),\qquad A_y(0,x_0)=I_d,$$
with Liouville formula
$$\det A_y(t,x_0)=\exp\!\left(\int_0^t\operatorname{tr}D_xb(s,x_y(s;x_0),y)\,ds\right).$$
Consequently, if a probability measure $\eta$ on $\mathbb R^d$ has Lebesgue density $q$, meaning $\eta(E)=\int_Eq(x)\,dx$ for Borel $E$, the image measure $T_y{}_{\#}\eta$ has density
$$z\longmapsto q(T_y^{-1}(z))\,|\det D T_y^{-1}(z)|.$$
The global Lipschitz clause alone gives a bi-Lipschitz flow and does not assert a Jacobian density formula.

Let $X$ be a separable real Banach space with its norm topology, $D\subseteq X$ a Borel forward-map domain, and $\mu_0$ a Borel probability measure on $X$ with $\mu_0(D)=1$. Write $\mu_{0,D}$ for its restriction to $D$, so $\mu_{0,D}(A)=\mu_0(A)$ for $A\in\mathcal B(D):=\{D\cap B:B\in\mathcal B(X)\}$. Let $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ be a measurable data space. A likelihood potential is a function $\Phi:D\times\mathsf Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ that is measurable from $\bigl(D\times\mathsf Y,\mathcal B(D)\otimes\mathcal Y\bigr)$ to $\bigl((-\infty,+\infty],\mathcal B((-\infty,+\infty])\bigr)$, where $\mathcal B((-\infty,+\infty])$ is the trace of $\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R})$ on $(-\infty,+\infty]$. Viewing $\Phi$ via the inclusion $(-\infty,+\infty]\hookrightarrow\overline{\mathbb R}$, it is also product-measurable as an extended-real-valued map because for every Borel set $B\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$, $\Phi^{-1}(B)=\Phi^{-1}(B\cap(-\infty,+\infty])$ is measurable by the definition of the trace sigma-algebra. Here $+\infty$ is allowed and $-\infty$ is excluded; set $e^{-\infty}=0$. The scalar map $t\mapsto e^{-t}$ on this range is continuous at finite $t$, and is continuous at $+\infty$: given $\varepsilon>0$, the limit supplies $a\in\mathbb R$ such that $t>a$ implies $e^{-t}<\varepsilon$, and the order-topology neighborhood $(a,+\infty]$ maps into $[0,\varepsilon)$. Hence it is Borel, so $L_\Phi:D\times\mathsf Y\to[0,+\infty)$, $L_\Phi(u;y):=e^{-\Phi(u;y)}$, is product-measurable by composition, and each section $u\mapsto L_\Phi(u;y)$ is nonnegative and measurable. Define its evidence by
$$
Z_\Phi(y):=\int_D L_\Phi(u;y)\,\mu_{0,D}(du)\in[0,+\infty].
$$
For each fixed $y$ with $0<Z_\Phi(y)<+\infty$, define the normalized fiberwise update on $A\in\mathcal B(D)$ by
$$\Pi^y(A):=\frac{\int_A L_\Phi(u;y)\,\mu_{0,D}(du)}{Z_\Phi(y)}.$$
No normalized fiberwise update is defined by this formula when $Z_\Phi(y)=0$ or $Z_\Phi(y)=+\infty$.

For a data-indexed claim, an observation model and its version convention must also be specified. In the dominated case, let $Q$ be a proper probability kernel from $(D,\mathcal B(D))$ to $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$, let $\nu$ be a sigma-finite measure on $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$, and suppose $Q(u,B)=\int_B L_\Phi(u;y)\,\nu(dy)$ for every $u\in D$ and $B\in\mathcal Y$. Then $Z_\Phi$ is the density of the prior-predictive data law with respect to $\nu$; a data-indexed conditional-law version uses $\Pi^y$ when $0<Z_\Phi(y)<\infty$ and the prior $\mu_{0,D}$ when $Z_\Phi(y)$ is zero or infinite. These filled fibers have zero prior-predictive mass, and their chosen values are not normalized fiberwise updates. More generally, for a proper Bayesian model with standard-Borel parameter space $(D,\mathcal B(D))$ and data space $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ (each measurably isomorphic to the Borel space of a Polish space), the Axiom of Choice guarantees a data-indexed posterior kernel; its values are unique as probability measures outside one data-marginal-null set, and values on that null set remain version choices. The dominated construction is choice-free; the separate standard-Borel existence branch assumes the Axiom of Choice.

derivations.claim: By [A1], [F1], and [F2], the supplied $\pi_y$ is a disintegration of $\pi$ given its second coordinate. For Borel $A\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, define $\kappa_y(A):=\eta(\{x:T_y(x)\in A\})=\int_{\mathbb R^d}\mathbf1_A(T_y(x))\,\eta(dx)$. Since $T_y$ is Borel, each $\kappa_y$ is the image probability measure $T_y{}_{\#}\eta$. For fixed $A$, [F4] makes $(y,x)\mapsto\mathbf1_A(T_y(x))$ product-measurable; applying [F5] to the constant probability kernel $y\mapsto\eta$ makes $y\mapsto\kappa_y(A)$ measurable. Thus [F3] shows that $\kappa$ is a probability kernel.

Fix Borel $A\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ and $B\subseteq\mathbb R^m$. By [F6] and the definition of $\kappa_y$, $\int_B\kappa_y(A)\,\pi_Y(dy)=(\eta\otimes\pi_Y)(\{(x,y):T_y(x)\in A,\ y\in B\})=(\eta\otimes\pi_Y)(T^{-1}(A\times B))$. The exact joint pushforward identity makes this $\pi(A\times B)$, and the disintegration identity in the Statement makes it $\int_B\pi_y(A)\,\pi_Y(dy)$. Hence $\kappa$ also disintegrates $\pi$.

Apply the simultaneous almost-everywhere uniqueness in [F2] to the disintegration kernels $\kappa$ and $\pi_y$. There is one Borel $\pi_Y$-null set $N$ such that for every $y\notin N$, $\kappa_y=\pi_y$ as measures on every Borel subset of $\mathbb R^d$. Since $\kappa_y=T_y{}_{\#}\eta$, this proves the asserted fiber identity.

For a terminal map satisfying the ODE flow hypotheses, [F7] gives joint continuity and bijectivity of every fiber, so the exact pushforward case is covered by steps 1.1–3.1. By [F8], when $\pi$ is the proper Bayesian parameter/data joint law, the conditional kernel is a posterior version. No step uses the separate C$^1$ clause or its density formula.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

Assume AC. Real $L^2(\Omega,\mathcal G,P|_{\mathcal G})$ embeds isometrically as a closed subspace of real $L^2(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$. For $X\in L^2(P)$, $U=E[X\mid\mathcal G]$ is its orthogonal projection onto this subspace. It uniquely minimizes $E[(X-Z)^2]$ over $Z\in L^2(\mathcal G)$ as an almost-sure class.

Let $X$ be a separable real Banach space with its norm topology, $D\subseteq X$ a Borel forward-map domain, and $\mu_0$ a Borel probability measure on $X$ with $\mu_0(D)=1$. Write $\mu_{0,D}$ for its restriction to $D$, so $\mu_{0,D}(A)=\mu_0(A)$ for $A\in\mathcal B(D):=\{D\cap B:B\in\mathcal B(X)\}$. Let $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ be a measurable data space. A likelihood potential is a function $\Phi:D\times\mathsf Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ that is measurable from $\bigl(D\times\mathsf Y,\mathcal B(D)\otimes\mathcal Y\bigr)$ to $\bigl((-\infty,+\infty],\mathcal B((-\infty,+\infty])\bigr)$, where $\mathcal B((-\infty,+\infty])$ is the trace of $\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R})$ on $(-\infty,+\infty]$. Viewing $\Phi$ via the inclusion $(-\infty,+\infty]\hookrightarrow\overline{\mathbb R}$, it is also product-measurable as an extended-real-valued map because for every Borel set $B\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$, $\Phi^{-1}(B)=\Phi^{-1}(B\cap(-\infty,+\infty])$ is measurable by the definition of the trace sigma-algebra. Here $+\infty$ is allowed and $-\infty$ is excluded; set $e^{-\infty}=0$. The scalar map $t\mapsto e^{-t}$ on this range is continuous at finite $t$, and is continuous at $+\infty$: given $\varepsilon>0$, the limit supplies $a\in\mathbb R$ such that $t>a$ implies $e^{-t}<\varepsilon$, and the order-topology neighborhood $(a,+\infty]$ maps into $[0,\varepsilon)$. Hence it is Borel, so $L_\Phi:D\times\mathsf Y\to[0,+\infty)$, $L_\Phi(u;y):=e^{-\Phi(u;y)}$, is product-measurable by composition, and each section $u\mapsto L_\Phi(u;y)$ is nonnegative and measurable. Define its evidence by
$$
Z_\Phi(y):=\int_D L_\Phi(u;y)\,\mu_{0,D}(du)\in[0,+\infty].
$$
For each fixed $y$ with $0<Z_\Phi(y)<+\infty$, define the normalized fiberwise update on $A\in\mathcal B(D)$ by
$$\Pi^y(A):=\frac{\int_A L_\Phi(u;y)\,\mu_{0,D}(du)}{Z_\Phi(y)}.$$
No normalized fiberwise update is defined by this formula when $Z_\Phi(y)=0$ or $Z_\Phi(y)=+\infty$.

For a data-indexed claim, an observation model and its version convention must also be specified. In the dominated case, let $Q$ be a proper probability kernel from $(D,\mathcal B(D))$ to $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$, let $\nu$ be a sigma-finite measure on $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$, and suppose $Q(u,B)=\int_B L_\Phi(u;y)\,\nu(dy)$ for every $u\in D$ and $B\in\mathcal Y$. Then $Z_\Phi$ is the density of the prior-predictive data law with respect to $\nu$; a data-indexed conditional-law version uses $\Pi^y$ when $0<Z_\Phi(y)<\infty$ and the prior $\mu_{0,D}$ when $Z_\Phi(y)$ is zero or infinite.
