Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\to(E,\mathcal S)$ and $Y:(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\to(T,\mathcal T)$ be measurable random elements. A **conditional law of X given Y** is a probability kernel $K:(T,\mathcal T)\to(E,\mathcal S)$ such that $\omega\mapsto K(Y(\omega),\cdot)$ is a regular conditional distribution of X given $\sigma(Y)$ in [[def-regular-conditional-distribution]]. Thus for every $A\in\mathcal S$ and $H\in\sigma(Y)$,
$$\int_H K(Y(\omega),A)\,dP=P(H\cap\{X\in A\}).$$

Composition with Y makes each evaluation $\sigma(Y)$-measurable, and every section remains a probability by [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]. The notation $P(X\in A\mid Y=y)=K(y,A)$ refers to a chosen kernel; it is not a ratio involving the possibly zero probability $P(Y=y)$.

Write $P_Y(B)=P(Y^{-1}(B))$ for the law in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]. If a specified countable family $\mathcal C\subseteq\mathcal S$ determines probability measures, two conditional laws K,L agree as measures outside a single $\mathcal T$-measurable $P_Y$-null set. Indeed for each $A\in\mathcal C$ the measurable discrepancy $D_A=\{y:K(y,A)\ne L(y,A)\}$ has null inverse image under Y by [[lem-conditional-expectation-is-unique-almost-surely]]. Hence $P_Y(D_A)=0$ by the law definition; the countable union $D$ is null by [[thm-finite-and-countable-subadditivity-of-measures]], and off D the determining property gives equality of measures. This uses a supplied determining family and makes no AC assertion about obtaining one.

Values on a measurable $P_Y$-null subset may be replaced by a specified fixed probability on E without changing these identities. The inverse image of that subset is measurable null, and all event evaluations are bounded, so the modified event integrals agree. Empty-event evaluations remain zero and whole-target evaluations remain one. Existence on standard-Borel spaces is proved separately; the definition alone does not assert a conditional kernel exists.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space, $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ a sub-sigma-algebra, and $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ integrable. A **conditional-expectation version of $X$ given $\mathcal G$** is a real, $\mathcal G$-measurable, integrable function $Y$ such that $\int_A Y\,dP=\int_A X\,dP$ for every $A\in\mathcal G$. No completeness of $\mathcal G$ is assumed.

Expectation means the integral of [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]. Integrable representatives use [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]; quotient notation is introduced after uniqueness.

Assume AC. Real $L^2(\Omega,\mathcal G,P|_{\mathcal G})$ embeds isometrically as a closed subspace of real $L^2(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$. For $X\in L^2(P)$, $U=E[X\mid\mathcal G]$ is its orthogonal projection onto this subspace. It uniquely minimizes $E[(X-Z)^2]$ over $Z\in L^2(\mathcal G)$ as an almost-sure class.

Assume AC. Let X,Y take values in standard-Borel E,T, and let K be a disintegration kernel giving the conditional law of X given Y. For measurable $f:E\to[0,\infty]$, put $h(y)=\int_E f(x)K(y,dx)$. Then h is measurable and
$$E[f(X)\mid\sigma(Y)]=h(Y)\quad\text{almost surely}.$$

For measurable real f with $E|f(X)|<\infty$, define $D=\{y:\int|f(x)|K(y,dx)<\infty\}$ and use the signed integral for h on D, zero off D. Then $P_Y(D)=1$, h is real measurable, and the same identity holds.

For every natural $n\ge1$, let $\mathbb R^n$ be the set of functions
$x:n\to\mathbb R$ with its finite-product topology and Borel sigma-algebra
([[def-product-topology]], [[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]). Then
$(\mathbb R^n,\mathcal B(\mathbb R^n))$ is standard Borel.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of
   [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] is a measure on
   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B),$$
   with the nonnegative extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=\infty\cdot0=0$;
3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the
   rectangle formula.

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. Let $T>0$, let $d,m\ge1$, and let $b:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^d$ be jointly continuous on the product Euclidean domain. Suppose that for every compact $K\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ there are nonnegative Lebesgue-measurable $a_K,L_K\in L^1([0,T])$ such that for almost every $t$, simultaneously for all $y\in K$ and $x,x'\in\mathbb R^d$,
$$|b(t,0,y)|\le a_K(t),\qquad |b(t,x,y)-b(t,x',y)|\le L_K(t)|x-x'|.$$
Here $L^1([0,T])$ means the functions have finite Lebesgue integral of their absolute values. Then for every $x_0\in\mathbb R^d$ and $y\in\mathbb R^m$ there is a unique continuously differentiable solution $x_y(\cdot;x_0)$ of
$$\dot x(t)=b(t,x(t),y),\qquad x(0)=x_0,$$
on all of $[0,T]$. Its terminal map $T_y(x_0):=x_y(T;x_0)$ is a bijection with jointly continuous forward and inverse maps in $(x_0,y)$, and for all $x_0,x_1$ and $y\in K$,
$$|T_y(x_0)-T_y(x_1)|\le e^{\int_0^T L_K(t)dt}|x_0-x_1|,\qquad |T_y^{-1}(x_0)-T_y^{-1}(x_1)|\le e^{\int_0^T L_K(t)dt}|x_0-x_1|.$$

$$\dot A_y(t,x_0)=D_xb(t,x_y(t;x_0),y)A_y(t,x_0),\qquad A_y(0,x_0)=I_d,$$
with Liouville formula
$$\det A_y(t,x_0)=\exp\!\left(\int_0^t\operatorname{tr}D_xb(s,x_y(s;x_0),y)\,ds\right).$$
Consequently, if a probability measure $\eta$ on $\mathbb R^d$ has Lebesgue density $q$, meaning $\eta(E)=\int_Eq(x)\,dx$ for Borel $E$, the image measure $T_y{}_{\#}\eta$ has density
$$z\longmapsto q(T_y^{-1}(z))\,|\det D T_y^{-1}(z)|.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\pi$ be a probability measure on $\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R^m$, where $d,m\ge1$, and let $\pi_Y(B):=\pi(\mathbb R^d\times B)$ be its second marginal. Let $\eta$ be a probability measure on $\mathbb R^d$, and let $y\mapsto\pi_y$ be a probability kernel satisfying
$$\pi(A\times B)=\int_B\pi_y(A)\,\pi_Y(dy)$$
for all Borel $A\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ and $B\subseteq\mathbb R^m$. Suppose $T:\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R^m$ is Borel and triangular, $T(x,y)=(T_y(x),y)$, with each $T_y$ a Borel bijection, and define the image measure by $T_{\#}\mu(E):=\mu(T^{-1}(E))$. If

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$ be standard Borel
([[def-standard-borel-space]]) and let $\lambda$ be a sigma-finite positive
measure ([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]) on it. Let the
target probability have a finite-valued nonnegative measurable density
$p:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$, and suppose the proposal kernel has a finite-valued
nonnegative jointly measurable density $q:\mathsf X\times\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$,
so $\pi(A)=\int_Ap\,d\lambda$ and
$Q(x,A)=\int_Aq(x,y)\,d\lambda(y)$ for every $x$ and $A$. Let
$\mu(dx,dy)=\pi(dx)Q(x,dy)$ be the forward proposal flow and let
$\mu^{\mathsf T}$ be its transpose. Put
$$m(x,y)=p(x)q(x,y),\qquad m^{\mathsf T}(x,y)=p(y)q(y,x).$$
There is a jointly measurable version $\alpha_{\rm cd}$ of
$d(\mu\wedge\mu^{\mathsf T})/d\mu$ given by
$$\alpha_{\rm cd}(x,y)=\begin{cases}\min\left\{1,\dfrac{p(y)q(y,x)}{p(x)q(x,y)}\right\},&m(x,y)>0,\\1,&m(x,y)=0.\end{cases}$$
The version chosen by [[alg-metropolis-hastings-kernel]] agrees with this
common-density version $\mu$-almost everywhere; values on a forward-flow null
set do not alter the accepted flow.

Let $X$ be a separable real Banach space with its norm topology, $D\subseteq X$ a Borel forward-map domain, and $\mu_0$ a Borel probability measure on $X$ with $\mu_0(D)=1$. Write $\mu_{0,D}$ for its restriction to $D$, so $\mu_{0,D}(A)=\mu_0(A)$ for $A\in\mathcal B(D):=\{D\cap B:B\in\mathcal B(X)\}$. Let $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ be a measurable data space. A likelihood potential is a function $\Phi:D\times\mathsf Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ that is measurable from $\bigl(D\times\mathsf Y,\mathcal B(D)\otimes\mathcal Y\bigr)$ to $\bigl((-\infty,+\infty],\mathcal B((-\infty,+\infty])\bigr)$, where $\mathcal B((-\infty,+\infty])$ is the trace of $\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R})$ on $(-\infty,+\infty]$. Viewing $\Phi$ via the inclusion $(-\infty,+\infty]\hookrightarrow\overline{\mathbb R}$, it is also product-measurable as an extended-real-valued map because for every Borel set $B\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$, $\Phi^{-1}(B)=\Phi^{-1}(B\cap(-\infty,+\infty])$ is measurable by the definition of the trace sigma-algebra. Here $+\infty$ is allowed and $-\infty$ is excluded; set $e^{-\infty}=0$. The scalar map $t\mapsto e^{-t}$ on this range is continuous at finite $t$, and is continuous at $+\infty$: given $\varepsilon>0$, the limit supplies $a\in\mathbb R$ such that $t>a$ implies $e^{-t}<\varepsilon$, and the order-topology neighborhood $(a,+\infty]$ maps into $[0,\varepsilon)$. Hence it is Borel, so $L_\Phi:D\times\mathsf Y\to[0,+\infty)$, $L_\Phi(u;y):=e^{-\Phi(u;y)}$, is product-measurable by composition, and each section $u\mapsto L_\Phi(u;y)$ is nonnegative and measurable. Define its evidence by
$$
Z_\Phi(y):=\int_D L_\Phi(u;y)\,\mu_{0,D}(du)\in[0,+\infty].
$$
For each fixed $y$ with $0<Z_\Phi(y)<+\infty$, define the normalized fiberwise update on $A\in\mathcal B(D)$ by
$$\Pi^y(A):=\frac{\int_A L_\Phi(u;y)\,\mu_{0,D}(du)}{Z_\Phi(y)}.$$
No normalized fiberwise update is defined by this formula when $Z_\Phi(y)=0$ or $Z_\Phi(y)=+\infty$.

For a data-indexed claim, an observation model and its version convention must also be specified. In the dominated case, let $Q$ be a proper probability kernel from $(D,\mathcal B(D))$ to $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$, let $\nu$ be a sigma-finite measure on $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$, and suppose $Q(u,B)=\int_B L_\Phi(u;y)\,\nu(dy)$ for every $u\in D$ and $B\in\mathcal Y$. Then $Z_\Phi$ is the density of the prior-predictive data law with respect to $\nu$; a data-indexed conditional-law version uses $\Pi^y$ when $0<Z_\Phi(y)<\infty$ and the prior $\mu_{0,D}$ when $Z_\Phi(y)$ is zero or infinite. These filled fibers have zero prior-predictive mass, and their chosen values are not normalized fiberwise updates. More generally, for a proper Bayesian model with standard-Borel parameter space $(D,\mathcal B(D))$ and data space $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ (each measurably isomorphic to the Borel space of a Polish space), the Axiom of Choice guarantees a data-indexed posterior kernel; its values are unique as probability measures outside one data-marginal-null set, and values on that null set remain version choices. The dominated construction is choice-free; the separate standard-Borel existence branch assumes the Axiom of Choice.

Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. Let $T>0$, let $d,m\ge1$, and let $b:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^d$ be jointly continuous on the product Euclidean domain. Suppose that for every compact $K\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ there are nonnegative Lebesgue-measurable $a_K,L_K\in L^1([0,T])$ such that for almost every $t$, simultaneously for all $y\in K$ and $x,x'\in\mathbb R^d$,
$$|b(t,0,y)|\le a_K(t),\qquad |b(t,x,y)-b(t,x',y)|\le L_K(t)|x-x'|.$$
Here $L^1([0,T])$ means the functions have finite Lebesgue integral of their absolute values. Then for every $x_0\in\mathbb R^d$ and $y\in\mathbb R^m$ there is a unique continuously differentiable solution $x_y(\cdot;x_0)$ of
$$\dot x(t)=b(t,x(t),y),\qquad x(0)=x_0,$$
on all of $[0,T]$. Its terminal map $T_y(x_0):=x_y(T;x_0)$ is a bijection with jointly continuous forward and inverse maps in $(x_0,y)$, and for all $x_0,x_1$ and $y\in K$,
$$|T_y(x_0)-T_y(x_1)|\le e^{\int_0^T L_K(t)dt}|x_0-x_1|,\qquad |T_y^{-1}(x_0)-T_y^{-1}(x_1)|\le e^{\int_0^T L_K(t)dt}|x_0-x_1|.$$

In the separate C$^1$ clause, suppose additionally that the state derivative $D_xb$ exists and is jointly continuous. Then for fixed $y$, $T_y$ is a bijection and both $T_y$ and its inverse are continuously differentiable. For a measurable map $S$ and a measure $\mu$, define its image measure by $S_{\#}\mu(E):=\mu(S^{-1}(E))$. The derivative $A_y(t,x_0):=D_{x_0}x_y(t;x_0)$ solves
$$\dot A_y(t,x_0)=D_xb(t,x_y(t;x_0),y)A_y(t,x_0),\qquad A_y(0,x_0)=I_d,$$
with Liouville formula
$$\det A_y(t,x_0)=\exp\!\left(\int_0^t\operatorname{tr}D_xb(s,x_y(s;x_0),y)\,ds\right).$$
Consequently, if a probability measure $\eta$ on $\mathbb R^d$ has Lebesgue density $q$, meaning $\eta(E)=\int_Eq(x)\,dx$ for Borel $E$, the image measure $T_y{}_{\#}\eta$ has density
$$z\longmapsto q(T_y^{-1}(z))\,|\det D T_y^{-1}(z)|.$$
The global Lipschitz clause alone gives a bi-Lipschitz flow and does not assert a Jacobian density formula.

Here $I$ is the identity on $X$ and $P:X\to X$ is a bounded linear projection with $P^2=P$, $P|_{X_0}=0$, and $(I-P)(X)\subseteq X_0$. $$\mathcal R(\widehat r):=\check R\big((I-P)r^{-1}(\widehat r)\big)+R_P\big(Pr^{-1}(\widehat r)\big).$$

For $p\in[1,\infty)$, data $y^\delta\in Y$, and parameters $\alpha,\beta>0$, the **joint relaxed objective** is

$$\mathcal J_{\alpha,\beta}^\delta(\widehat r,x):=\|K\widehat r+F(x_0)-y^\delta\|_Y^p+\alpha\mathcal R(\widehat r)+\beta Q(r(x),\widehat r)^p+\|Px\|_X^p,\qquad (\widehat r,x)\in\widetilde U\times U.$$

Thus every data increment lies in the range of the fixed operator $K$. The factorization alone does not assert that $K$ is injective, that $r$ is unique, or that a tangential-cone inequality holds. If $U$ is open and $F$ and $r$ are Fréchet differentiable, differentiating this identity gives $F'(x)=Kr'(x)$ at every $x\in U$; no converse is asserted without further hypotheses.

Let $X,Y,Z$ be real Banach spaces, let $X_0$ be a closed linear subspace of $X$, and let $D\subseteq X$ contain $X_0$ and a nonempty set $U$. Fix $x_0\in X_0\cap U$, a map $F:D\to Y$, a bounded linear map $K:Z\to Y$, and a map $r:D\to Z$ such that $F(x)-F(x_0)=Kr(x)$ for every $x\in D$. Assume that $r|_U$ is a bijection from $U$ onto a set $\widetilde U\subseteq Z$, and that $(I-P)r^{-1}(\widehat r)\in X_0\cap D$ for every $\widehat r\in\widetilde U$ admitted below. Here $I$ is the identity on $X$ and $P:X\to X$ is a bounded linear projection with $P^2=P$, $P|_{X_0}=0$, and $(I-P)(X)\subseteq X_0$. Let $\check R:X_0\to[0,+\infty]$ be a proper convex regularizer, let $R_P:P(X)\to[0,+\infty]$ be a nonnegative penalty, and let $Q:Z\times Z\to[0,+\infty]$ satisfy $Q(a,b)=Q(b,a)$ and $Q(a,b)=0$ exactly when $a=b$. For $\widehat r\in\widetilde U$, set

$$\mathcal R(\widehat r):=\check R\big((I-P)r^{-1}(\widehat r)\big)+R_P\big(Pr^{-1}(\widehat r)\big).$$

For $p\in[1,\infty)$, data $y^\delta\in Y$, and parameters $\alpha,\beta>0$, the **joint relaxed objective** is

$$\mathcal J_{\alpha,\beta}^\delta(\widehat r,x):=\|K\widehat r+F(x_0)-y^\delta\|_Y^p+\alpha\mathcal R(\widehat r)+\beta Q(r(x),\widehat r)^p+\|Px\|_X^p,\qquad (\widehat r,x)\in\widetilde U\times U.$$

The joint source-condition objective takes $R_P=0$. The term $\beta Q(r(x),\widehat r)^p$ ties the relaxed range variable to the physical variable, while $\|Px\|_X^p$ penalizes the component outside $X_0$.

If $r$ is Gâteaux differentiable at a current iterate $x_n\in U$, the **frozen-Newton objective** with parameters $\alpha_n,\beta_n>0$ is

$$\mathcal J_n^\delta(\widehat r,x):=\|K\widehat r+F(x_0)-y^\delta\|_Y^p+\alpha_n\mathcal R(\widehat r)+\beta_n Q\big(r(x_n)+r'(x_n)(x-x_n),\widehat r\big)^p+\|Px\|_X^p.$$

Here $r'(x_n)$ is the bounded linear Gâteaux derivative used to form the affine range proxy; no minimizer existence or uniqueness is part of either definition.

Let $X$ be a real Banach space and let $X^*$ be its continuous real dual. The dual pairing is evaluation, written $\langle \xi,x\rangle_{X^*,X}:=\xi(x)$ for $\xi\in X^*$ and $x\in X$. Let $R:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be a proper convex functional: $R$ never takes the value $-\infty$, its effective domain $\operatorname{dom}R:=\{x\in X:R(x)<+\infty\}$ is nonempty, and $R((1-t)x+tz)\le (1-t)R(x)+tR(z)$ for $x,z\in X$ and $t\in[0,1]$, with $0\cdot(+\infty):=0$ for this convex-combination formula. For $x\in\operatorname{dom}R$, its subdifferential is

$$\partial R(x):=\{\xi\in X^*:R(z)\ge R(x)+\langle\xi,z-x\rangle_{X^*,X}\text{ for every }z\in X\}.$$

An element of $\partial R(x)$ is a subgradient of $R$ at $x$. Set $\partial R(x):=\varnothing$ when $x\notin\operatorname{dom}R$. The subdifferential may be empty at a point of $\operatorname{dom}R$; no nonemptiness assertion is part of this definition.

Let $X$ be a real Banach space, let $R:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper and convex, choose $x^\dagger\in\operatorname{dom}R$, and choose $\xi^\dagger\in\partial R(x^\dagger)$. For $x\in\operatorname{dom}R$, the **Bregman distance** generated by $\xi^\dagger$ from the reference point $x^\dagger$ to $x$ is

$$D_R^{\xi^\dagger}(x,x^\dagger):=R(x)-R(x^\dagger)-\langle\xi^\dagger,x-x^\dagger\rangle_{X^*,X}.$$

The subgradient inequality makes this quantity nonnegative, and $D_R^{\xi^\dagger}(x^\dagger,x^\dagger)=0$. The definition fixes the orientation: the first argument is the comparison point and the second is the reference point carrying the chosen subgradient.

Let $X,Y$ be real Banach spaces, let $F:D(F)\subseteq X\to Y$, let $x^\dagger\in D(F)$ with exact datum $y=F(x^\dagger)$, and let $R:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper and convex with $x^\dagger\in\operatorname{dom}R$. Fix $\xi^\dagger\in\partial R(x^\dagger)$, an exponent $1\le p<\infty$, a continuous nondecreasing concave function $\psi:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ with $\psi(0)=0$ and $\psi(t)>0$ for $t>0$, a coefficient $0\le\beta<1$, and a level $R_0\ge R(x^\dagger)$. The **variational source condition** with these data holds on the named regularizer sublevel $L_{R_0}:=\{x\in D(F):R(x)\le R_0\}$ when

$$-\langle\xi^\dagger,x-x^\dagger\rangle_{X^*,X}\le\beta D_R^{\xi^\dagger}(x,x^\dagger)+\psi\!\left(\|F(x)-F(x^\dagger)\|_Y^p\right)\qquad(x\in L_{R_0}).$$

The condition is an assumption on the selected subgradient and the stated sublevel; it makes no assertion that a subgradient exists at every point or that a regularized minimizer exists.

Let $\psi:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ be continuous, nondecreasing, concave, and satisfy $\psi(0)=0$. Extend $g=-\psi$ to $\mathbb R$ by $g(s)=+\infty$ for $s<0$, and define $H(q):=g^*(-q)=\sup_{s\ge0}(\psi(s)-qs)$ for $q>0$, assuming the displayed suprema below are finite. For $c_1,c_2,C_3,\alpha>0$ and $d,r,e\ge0$, if

$$c_1r+c_2\alpha e\le d+\alpha\psi(C_3r),$$

then

$$e\le\frac1{c_2}\left(\frac d\alpha+H\!\left(\frac{c_1}{C_3\alpha}\right)\right),\qquad r\le\frac2{c_1}\left(d+\alpha H\!\left(\frac{c_1}{2C_3\alpha}\right)\right).$$

derivations.claim: Write $r^\dagger:=r(x^\dagger)$, $u:=r^{-1}(\widehat r_{n+1})$, $\check x:=(I-P)u$, and $\ell_n(x):=r(x_n)+r'(x_n)(x-x_n)$. Compare the approximate-minimum inequality with $(\widehat r,x)=(r^\dagger,x^\dagger)$. The competitor has data residual at most $\delta^p$, penalty $R_P(0)=0$, and $Px^\dagger=0$. If $g:=K\widehat r_{n+1}+F(x_0)-y^\delta$, then $K(\widehat r_{n+1}-r^\dagger)=g+(y^\delta-y)$; convexity of $s\mapsto s^p$ gives $\|K(\widehat r_{n+1}-r^\dagger)\|^p\le2^{p-1}(\|g\|^p+\delta^p)$. Thus the comparison gives $2^{1-p}\|K(\widehat r_{n+1}-r^\dagger)\|^p+\alpha_n(\mathcal R(\widehat r_{n+1})-\check R(x^\dagger))+\beta_n\|\ell_n(x_{n+1})-\widehat r_{n+1}\|^p+\|Px_{n+1}\|^p\le2\delta^p+\eta_n+\beta_n\|\ell_n(x^\dagger)-r^\dagger\|^p$. The remainder hypothesis at $(x^\dagger,x_n)$ and $c_{\rm tcr}<1$ imply $\|\ell_n(x^\dagger)-r^\dagger\|^p\le c_{\rm tcr}^p\|r(x_n)-r^\dagger\|^p$.

Let $A:=\|r(x_{n+1})-\widehat r_{n+1}\|$, $B:=\|\ell_n(x_{n+1})-\widehat r_{n+1}\|$, and $D_n:=\|r(x_{n+1})-\ell_n(x_{n+1})\|$. The triangle inequality gives $A\le B+D_n$, hence $B^p\ge2^{1-p}A^p-D_n^p$. Applying the same power inequality to $\|r(x_{n+1})-r^\dagger\|\le A+\|\widehat r_{n+1}-r^\dagger\|$ gives $A^p\ge2^{1-p}\|r(x_{n+1})-r^\dagger\|^p-\|\widehat r_{n+1}-r^\dagger\|^p$. The Taylor hypothesis and another triangle-power estimate give $D_n^p\le2^{p-1}c_{\rm tcr}^p(\|r(x_{n+1})-r^\dagger\|^p+\|r(x_n)-r^\dagger\|^p)$. Therefore $\|\ell_n(x_{n+1})-\widehat r_{n+1}\|^p\ge t\|r(x_{n+1})-r^\dagger\|^p-\lambda\|\widehat r_{n+1}-r^\dagger\|^p-2^{p-1}c_{\rm tcr}^p\|r(x_n)-r^\dagger\|^p$, with $t=2^{2-2p}-2^{p-1}c_{\rm tcr}^p$ and $\lambda=2^{1-p}$.

Set $z:=Pu$. Since $\|r(\check x)-r(u)\|\le L_r\|z\|$, the factorization and power inequality give $\|F(\check x)-F(x^\dagger)\|^p\le2^{p-1}\|K(\widehat r_{n+1}-r^\dagger)\|^p+2^{p-1}\|K\|^pL_r^p\|z\|^p$. By the VSC [F5], the Bregman identity [F4], the penalty lower bound, and $\psi(a+b)\le C_\psi(\psi(a)+\psi(b))$, we obtain $\mathcal R(\widehat r_{n+1})-\check R(x^\dagger)\ge m(D_{\check R}^{\xi^\dagger}(\check x,x^\dagger)+\psi(C_P\|z\|^p))-C_\psi\psi(2^{p-1}\|K(\widehat r_{n+1}-r^\dagger)\|^p)$. Indeed, the VSC yields coefficient $1-b$ on the Bregman term, and the penalty leaves coefficient $\gamma-C_\psi$ on the penalty-index term; their minimum is $m$.

Substituting steps 1.1–1.3 into the objective comparison and applying the compatibility inequality gives $C_\psi S_{n+1}+\alpha_nmT+\beta_nt\|r(x_{n+1})-r^\dagger\|^p\le\beta_nv\|r(x_n)-r^\dagger\|^p+\beta_n\lambda\|\widehat r_{n+1}-r^\dagger\|^p+\alpha_nC_\psi\psi(2^{p-1}\|K(\widehat r_{n+1}-r^\dagger)\|^p)+2\delta^p+\eta_n$, where $T:=D_{\check R}^{\xi^\dagger}(\check x,x^\dagger)+\psi(C_P\|Pu\|^p)$. By [F3], $D_{\check R}^{\xi^\dagger}(\check x,x^\dagger)\ge0$, so $T\ge0$. Since $\|\widehat r_{n+1}-r^\dagger\|^p\le\widetilde C_QT$ and $\beta_n\lambda\widetilde C_Q\le\alpha_nm/4$, the left regularizer term absorbs the displayed compatibility term and a second copy of it, leaving $\alpha_nmT/2$; in particular it bounds another $\beta_n\lambda\|\widehat r_{n+1}-r^\dagger\|^p$. The resulting inequality is $C_\psi S_{n+1}+\beta_n\lambda\|\widehat r_{n+1}-r^\dagger\|^p+\beta_nt\|r(x_{n+1})-r^\dagger\|^p\le\beta_nv\|r(x_n)-r^\dagger\|^p+\alpha_nC_\psi\psi(2^{p-1}\|K(\widehat r_{n+1}-r^\dagger)\|^p)+2\delta^p+\eta_n$.

Divide step 2.1 by $C_\psi$ and use $\beta_n=c_{\beta\alpha}\alpha_n$. Since $C_\psi S_{n+1}\ge2^{1-p}\|K(\widehat r_{n+1}-r^\dagger)\|^p$, we have $2^{p-1}\|K(\widehat r_{n+1}-r^\dagger)\|^p\le C_\psi2^{2p-2}S_{n+1}=\overline C S_{n+1}$. Monotonicity of $\psi$ gives $S_{n+1}+\alpha_nE_{n+1}\le d_n+\alpha_n\psi(\overline C S_{n+1})$. Applying [F6] with $c_1=c_2=1$, $C_3=\overline C$, $r=S_{n+1}$, and $e=E_{n+1}$ proves both conjugate bounds.

Let $1\le p<\infty$. Let $X,Y,Z$ be real Banach spaces, $X_0\subseteq X$ a closed linear subspace, $D\subseteq X$ a domain containing $X_0$ and $U$, and $x_0\in U\cap X_0$. Let $F:D\to Y$, $K\in\mathcal L(Z,Y)$, and $r:D\to Z$ satisfy $F(x)-F(x_0)=Kr(x)$ on $D$, with $r|_U:U\to\widetilde U$ bijective and $r$ Lipschitz with constant $L_r$ on $D$. Let $P:X\to X$ be a bounded linear projection such that $P|_{X_0}=0$, $(I-P)(X)\subseteq X_0$, and $P(x_0)=P(x^\dagger)=0$ for an exact solution $x^\dagger\in U\cap X_0$; put $y:=F(x^\dagger)$. Assume the projected points $(I-P)r^{-1}(\widehat r)$ belong to $D\cap X_0$ for all admitted $\widehat r\in\widetilde U$.

Let $\check R:X_0\to[0,+\infty]$ be proper and convex, choose $\xi^\dagger\in\partial\check R(x^\dagger)\subseteq X_0^*$, and suppose that for some $R_0\ge\check R(x^\dagger)$, $b\in[0,1)$, and continuous nondecreasing concave $\psi:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ with $\psi(0)=0$, the variational source inequality

$$-\langle\xi^\dagger,\check x-x^\dagger\rangle\le bD_{\check R}^{\xi^\dagger}(\check x,x^\dagger)+\psi\big(\|F(\check x)-F(x^\dagger)\|_Y^p\big)$$

holds whenever $\check x\in D\cap X_0$ and $\check R(\check x)\le R_0$, where $D_{\check R}^{\xi^\dagger}(\check x,x^\dagger):=\check R(\check x)-\check R(x^\dagger)-\langle\xi^\dagger,\check x-x^\dagger\rangle$. Set $R_P=0$ in the joint objective. Let $Q:\widetilde U\times\widetilde U\to[0,\infty]$ satisfy $Q(a,b)=Q(b,a)$ and $Q(a,b)=0$ exactly when $a=b$, and assume there is a constant $C_Q\ge0$ such that

$$\|P(r^{-1}(a))-P(r^{-1}(b))\|_X\le C_Q Q(a,b)\qquad(a,b\in\widetilde U).$$

For $\delta>0$, let $y^\delta\in Y$ satisfy $\|y^\delta-y\|_Y\le\delta$. Let $\alpha,\beta>0$, $C_\eta\ge0$, and let $(\widehat r_\delta,x_\delta)\in\widetilde U\times U$ be an $\eta_\delta$-minimizer of the joint objective, meaning

$$\mathcal J_{\alpha,\beta}^\delta(\widehat r_\delta,x_\delta)\le\mathcal J_{\alpha,\beta}^\delta(\widehat r,x)+\eta_\delta\qquad((\widehat r,x)\in\widetilde U\times U),\qquad 0\le\eta_\delta\le C_\eta\delta^p.$$

Assume $\check x_\delta:=(I-P)r^{-1}(\widehat r_\delta)$ lies in the stated VSC sublevel. Define

$$s_\delta:=2^{1-p}\|K(\widehat r_\delta-r(x^\dagger))\|_Y^p+\beta Q(r(x_\delta),\widehat r_\delta)^p+\|Px_\delta\|_X^p,\qquad e_\delta:=D_{\check R}^{\xi^\dagger}(\check x_\delta,x^\dagger),$$

and

$$C_*:=2^{2p-2}\max\left\{1,\|K\|^pL_r^p,\frac{\|K\|^pL_r^pC_Q^p}{\beta}\right\},\qquad d_\delta:=(2+C_\eta)\delta^p.$$

Then

$$s_\delta+(1-b)\alpha e_\delta\le d_\delta+\alpha\psi(C_*s_\delta).$$

Let $\psi:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ be continuous, nondecreasing, concave, and satisfy $\psi(0)=0$. Extend $g=-\psi$ to $\mathbb R$ by $g(s)=+\infty$ for $s<0$, and define $H(q):=g^*(-q)=\sup_{s\ge0}(\psi(s)-qs)$ for $q>0$, assuming the displayed suprema below are finite. For $c_1,c_2,C_3,\alpha>0$ and $d,r,e\ge0$, if

$$c_1r+c_2\alpha e\le d+\alpha\psi(C_3r),$$

then

$$e\le\frac1{c_2}\left(\frac d\alpha+H\!\left(\frac{c_1}{C_3\alpha}\right)\right),\qquad r\le\frac2{c_1}\left(d+\alpha H\!\left(\frac{c_1}{2C_3\alpha}\right)\right).$$

Let $X$, $Y$, and $Z$ be real Banach spaces, let $U\subseteq X$ be nonempty, let $x_0\in U$, and let $F:U\to Y$ be a map. A **differential range-invariance factorization at $x_0$ on $U$** consists of a bounded linear map $K:Z\to Y$ and a map $r:U\to Z$ such that

$$F(x)-F(x_0)=Kr(x)\qquad(x\in U).$$

Thus every data increment lies in the range of the fixed operator $K$. The factorization alone does not assert that $K$ is injective, that $r$ is unique, or that a tangential-cone inequality holds. If $U$ is open and $F$ and $r$ are Fréchet differentiable, differentiating this identity gives $F'(x)=Kr'(x)$ at every $x\in U$; no converse is asserted without further hypotheses.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. Let $\Omega=B_1\subset\mathbb R^3$, $0<\rho<1$, $0<m<1<M$, and $5/2<s_1<7/2$. Use the exact intrinsic $H^{s_1}(\Omega)$ Hilbert norm from the collared source-functional lemma, and put
$$V=\{a\in H^{s_1}(\Omega;\mathbb R):a=0\text{ a.e. on }\Omega\setminus B_\rho\},\qquad \mathcal C=\{\sigma\in1+V:m\le\sigma\le M\}.$$
Let $\sigma_0,\sigma^\dagger\in\mathcal C$, and assume $\sigma^\dagger\in B^{s_2}_{2,\infty}(\Omega)$ for $s_1<s_2<2s_1-1$. Set $a^\dagger=\sigma^\dagger-\sigma_0$, and choose $R>\|a^\dagger\|_V$. Write $Y=\ell^2(L^2(S^2;\mathbb C))$ for the centered mean-zero Neumann voltage sequence space, regarded as a real Hilbert space, and give $X=Z=V\times Y$ the sum norm. Let $X_0=V\times\{0\}$, $D=X$, $x_0=(0,0)$ and $P(a,z)=(0,z)$.

There is a globally Lipschitz, continuously Fréchet differentiable map $\Gamma:V\to Y$ with globally Lipschitz derivative, agreeing for $\sigma_0+a\in\mathcal C$ with the centered physical observation $((\mathscr N_{\sigma_0+a}-\mathscr N_1)Y_{\ell k})_{\ell,k}$. Define
$$T(a)=\Gamma(a)-\Gamma(0)-\Gamma'(0)a,\quad r(a,z)=(a,z+T(a)),\quad K(a,b)=\Gamma'(0)a+b,\quad F(a,z)=\Gamma(a)+z.$$
Then $F(x)-F(x_0)=Kr(x)$ on $D$, $r$ and its inverse $r^{-1}(a,b)=(a,b-T(a))$ are globally Lipschitz, and these facts hold on the admitted set
$$U=\{(a,z):\sigma_0+a\in\mathcal C,\ \|a\|_V<R,\ \|z\|_Y<R\}.$$
The projected points $(I-P)r^{-1}(\widehat r)$ belong to $U\cap X_0$ for $\widehat r\in r(U)$.

On the ambient linear space $V$ define the proper convex regularizer
$$\check R(a)=\tfrac12\|\sigma_0+a\|_{s_1,\Omega}^2+I_{\mathcal C}(\sigma_0+a),$$
where the indicator is zero on $\mathcal C$ and $+\infty$ elsewhere. On every admitted physical coefficient this is exactly the original quadratic Sobolev penalty. The functional $\xi^\dagger(v)=(\sigma^\dagger,v)_{s_1,\Omega}$ is a subgradient at $a^\dagger$, and its Bregman distance on $\mathcal C-\sigma_0$ is exactly $\frac12\|a-a^\dagger\|_V^2$. On every fixed sublevel containing the truth, the VSC holds with $b=3/4$ and a continuous nondecreasing concave truncated logarithmic index
$$\psi(u)=C[\log(1/u)]^{-\nu}\quad(0<u\le u_0),\qquad \psi(0)=0,\qquad \nu=\frac{(s_2-s_1)(2s_1-3)}{s_2-1},$$
continued constantly above a sufficiently small $u_0>0$. Its subadditivity constant may be taken as $C_\psi=1$.

Put $L_T=\operatorname{Lip}(T)$ and let $L=\operatorname{Lip}(\Gamma')$. For $Q(\widehat r,\widehat r')=\|\widehat r-\widehat r'\|_Z$, the projection-coupling constant may be taken as $1+L_T$, and
$$\|r(x_1)-r(x_2)-r'(x_2)(x_1-x_2)\|_Z\le LR\|r(x_1)-r(x_2)\|_Z\qquad(x_1,x_2\in U).$$
For the frozen method choose $C_P\ge2\|K\|^2\operatorname{Lip}(r)^2$, $\gamma>1$ and $R_P(z)=\gamma\psi(C_P\|z\|_Y^2)$. Then the required compatibility bound holds with
$$\widetilde C_Q=\max\left\{4(1+L_T)^2,\frac{2R^2}{\psi(C_PR^2)}\right\}.$$
In particular, the structural hypotheses of the joint and frozen one-step estimates hold with $p=2$, the displayed exact regularizer, $R_P=0$ for the joint method, and the displayed $R_P$ for the frozen method. For frozen rates additionally require $LR<c_{\rm tcr}<1/\sqrt{20}$, choose $c_{\beta\alpha}\le\min\{1/4,\gamma-1\}/(4\widetilde C_Q)$, and use the remaining parameter, tolerance and stopping conditions of the frozen rate theorem. This small-neighborhood hypothesis is local around the chosen initial conductivity; it restricts neither the stated Besov truth class nor its logarithmic exponent.

u})$ and $S_\delta=O(\delta^kL_\delta^{-
u})$. The fixed positive coupling coefficient and nonnegative summands of $S_\delta$ give the claimed artificial-voltage and coupling bounds. Step 1.3 then gives the same physical conductivity norm rate because $\delta^{k/2}L_\delta^{-
u/2}=O(L_\delta^{-
u/2})$.

By [F5], for $\alpha\asymp\delta^2L_\delta^
u$ the values $H(1/(C_*\alpha))$ and $H(1/(2C_*\alpha))$ are both of order $L_\delta^{-
u}$, their ratio is bounded, and $\alpha H(1/(C_*\alpha))\asymp\delta^2$. Hence the generic theorem assumptions apply and steps 1.1–2.1 give $e_\delta=O(L_\delta^{-
u})$, $S_\delta=O(\delta^2)$, and the stated residual, coupling and projection bounds. Taking square roots in step 1.3 and using the coupling bound proves the physical conductivity norm rate.

At the endpoint use the actual noise $\varepsilon_\delta=\|y^\delta-y\|$ in the approximate-minimum comparison, so its scalar right-side constant is $d=2\varepsilon_\delta^2+\eta_\delta$. The explicit endpoint assumption and [F6] give $e_\delta=O(L_\delta^{-\nu})$ and $S_\delta=O(\delta^2L_\delta^{-\nu})$. Nonnegativity of the projection and coupling terms and step 1.3 give all displayed norm bounds. In each regime the relaxed data residual is at most $\|K(\widehat r_\delta-r(x^\dagger))\|+\varepsilon_\delta=O(\sqrt{S_\delta}+\varepsilon_\delta)$, exactly as in step 2.1. This completes every stated EIT regime with its explicit noise assumptions.

Let $1\le p<\infty$. Let $X,Y,Z$ be real Banach spaces, let $X_0$ be a closed linear subspace of $X$, and let $D,U\subseteq X$. Let $x_0,x^\dagger\in D\cap U\cap X_0$, let $F:D\to Y$, $K\in\mathcal L(Z,Y)$, and $r:D\to Z$ satisfy $F(x)-F(x_0)=Kr(x)$ for all $x\in D$. Assume $r|_U:U\to\widetilde U$ is a bijection, $r$ is Lipschitz on $D$ with constant $L_r$, and $r$ has bounded linear Gâteaux derivatives on $U$. Let $P:X\to X$ be a bounded linear projection with $P^2=P$, $P|_{X_0}=0$, and $(I-P)(X)\subseteq X_0$. Assume $P(x^\dagger)=0$ and $(I-P)r^{-1}(\widehat r)\in D\cap X_0$ for each admitted $\widehat r\in\widetilde U$.

Let $\check R:X_0\to[0,+\infty]$ be proper and convex, choose $\xi^\dagger\in\partial\check R(x^\dagger)$, and write

$$D_{\check R}^{\xi^\dagger}(z,x^\dagger):=\check R(z)-\check R(x^\dagger)-\langle\xi^\dagger,z-x^\dagger\rangle_{X_0^*,X_0}.$$

Suppose that, on the stated sublevel $\check R(z)\le R_0$, the variational source inequality

$$-\langle\xi^\dagger,z-x^\dagger\rangle_{X_0^*,X_0}\le bD_{\check R}^{\xi^\dagger}(z,x^\dagger)+\psi\!\left(\|F(z)-F(x^\dagger)\|_Y^p\right)$$

holds for some $R_0\ge\check R(x^\dagger)$ and $0\le b<1$. Assume that $\psi:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ is continuous, nondecreasing and concave, with $\psi(0)=0$, and that for a constant $C_\psi>0$,

$$\psi(a+b)\le C_\psi\bigl(\psi(a)+\psi(b)\bigr)\qquad(a,b\ge0).$$

Let $H(q):=\sup_{s\ge0}(\psi(s)-qs)$, and assume the values of $H$ used below are finite. Let $\gamma>C_\psi$, $C_P\ge2^{p-1}\|K\|^pL_r^p$, and $\widetilde C_Q>0$. Let $R_P:P(X)\to[0,+\infty]$ satisfy $R_P(0)=0$ and

$$R_P(z)\ge\gamma\psi(C_P\|z\|_X^p)\qquad(z\in P(X)).$$

For each admitted $\widehat r\in\widetilde U$, put $u(\widehat r):=r^{-1}(\widehat r)$ and $\check x(\widehat r):=(I-P)u(\widehat r)$. Assume the compatibility bound

$$\|\widehat r-r(x^\dagger)\|_Z^p\le\widetilde C_Q\left(D_{\check R}^{\xi^\dagger}(\check x(\widehat r),x^\dagger)+\psi(C_P\|Pu(\widehat r)\|_X^p)\right).$$

Choose $c_{\beta\alpha}>0$ with $c_{\beta\alpha}\le\min\{1-b,\gamma-C_\psi\}/(4\widetilde C_Q)$, and set

$$m:=\min\{1-b,\gamma-C_\psi\},\quad a:=2^{1-p},\quad \lambda:=2^{1-p},\quad t:=2^{2-2p}-2^{p-1}c_{\rm tcr}^p,\quad v:=(1+2^{p-1})c_{\rm tcr}^p,\quad \overline C:=C_\psi 2^{2p-2}.$$

Assume $0<c_{\rm tcr}<1$ and $t>0$, and for all $x_1,x_2\in U$ assume

$$\|r(x_1)-r(x_2)-r'(x_2)(x_1-x_2)\|_Z\le c_{\rm tcr}\|r(x_1)-r(x_2)\|_Z.$$

Assume the candidate projected point satisfies $\check R(\check x(\widehat r_{n+1}))\le R_0$.

Let $Q(a,b):=\|a-b\|_Z$. Fix $\delta>0$, $y^\delta\in Y$ with $\|y^\delta-F(x^\dagger)\|_Y\le\delta$, and $\alpha_n>0$, with $\beta_n:=c_{\beta\alpha}\alpha_n$. Suppose $(\widehat r_{n+1},x_{n+1})\in\widetilde U\times U$ satisfies, for some $\eta_n\ge0$,

$$\mathcal J_n^\delta(\widehat r_{n+1},x_{n+1})\le\mathcal J_n^\delta(\widehat r,x)+\eta_n\qquad((\widehat r,x)\in\widetilde U\times U),$$

where $\mathcal J_n^\delta$ is the frozen objective in the Joint and frozen-Newton objectives definition, with regularizer $\mathcal R(\widehat r)=\check R(\check x(\widehat r))+R_P(Pu(\widehat r))$ and distance $Q$.

Define

$$E_{n+1}:=\frac{c_{\beta\alpha}}{C_\psi}\left(\lambda\|\widehat r_{n+1}-r(x^\dagger)\|_Z^p+t\|r(x_{n+1})-r(x^\dagger)\|_Z^p\right),$$

$$S_{n+1}:=\frac{1}{C_\psi}\left(2^{1-p}\|K(\widehat r_{n+1}-r(x^\dagger))\|_Y^p+\|Px_{n+1}\|_X^p\right),$$

and

$$d_n:=\frac{c_{\beta\alpha}}{C_\psi}\alpha_n v\|r(x_n)-r(x^\dagger)\|_Z^p+\frac{2\delta^p+\eta_n}{C_\psi}.$$

Then

$$S_{n+1}+\alpha_nE_{n+1}\le d_n+\alpha_n\psi(\overline C S_{n+1}).$$

Consequently,

$$E_{n+1}\le\frac{d_n}{\alpha_n}+H\!\left(\frac{1}{\overline C\alpha_n}\right),\qquad S_{n+1}\le2\left(d_n+\alpha_nH\!\left(\frac{1}{2\overline C\alpha_n}\right)\right).$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice, Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. Let $\Omega=B_1\subset\mathbb R^3$, $0<\rho<1$, $0<m<1<M$, and $5/2<s_1<7/2$. Use the exact intrinsic $H^{s_1}(\Omega)$ Hilbert norm from the collared source-functional lemma, and put
$$V=\{a\in H^{s_1}(\Omega;\mathbb R):a=0\text{ a.e. on }\Omega\setminus B_\rho\},\qquad \mathcal C=\{\sigma\in1+V:m\le\sigma\le M\}.$$
Let $\sigma_0,\sigma^\dagger\in\mathcal C$, and assume $\sigma^\dagger\in B^{s_2}_{2,\infty}(\Omega)$ for $s_1<s_2<2s_1-1$. Set $a^\dagger=\sigma^\dagger-\sigma_0$, and choose $R>\|a^\dagger\|_V$. Write $Y=\ell^2(L^2(S^2;\mathbb C))$ for the centered mean-zero Neumann voltage sequence space, regarded as a real Hilbert space, and give $X=Z=V\times Y$ the sum norm. Let $X_0=V\times\{0\}$, $D=X$, $x_0=(0,0)$ and $P(a,z)=(0,z)$.

There is a globally Lipschitz, continuously Fréchet differentiable map $\Gamma:V\to Y$ with globally Lipschitz derivative, agreeing for $\sigma_0+a\in\mathcal C$ with the centered physical observation $((\mathscr N_{\sigma_0+a}-\mathscr N_1)Y_{\ell k})_{\ell,k}$. Define
$$T(a)=\Gamma(a)-\Gamma(0)-\Gamma'(0)a,\quad r(a,z)=(a,z+T(a)),\quad K(a,b)=\Gamma'(0)a+b,\quad F(a,z)=\Gamma(a)+z.$$
Then $F(x)-F(x_0)=Kr(x)$ on $D$, $r$ and its inverse $r^{-1}(a,b)=(a,b-T(a))$ are globally Lipschitz, and these facts hold on the admitted set
$$U=\{(a,z):\sigma_0+a\in\mathcal C,\ \|a\|_V<R,\ \|z\|_Y<R\}.$$
The projected points $(I-P)r^{-1}(\widehat r)$ belong to $U\cap X_0$ for $\widehat r\in r(U)$.

On the ambient linear space $V$ define the proper convex regularizer
$$\check R(a)=\tfrac12\|\sigma_0+a\|_{s_1,\Omega}^2+I_{\mathcal C}(\sigma_0+a),$$
where the indicator is zero on $\mathcal C$ and $+\infty$ elsewhere. On every admitted physical coefficient this is exactly the original quadratic Sobolev penalty. The functional $\xi^\dagger(v)=(\sigma^\dagger,v)_{s_1,\Omega}$ is a subgradient at $a^\dagger$, and its Bregman distance on $\mathcal C-\sigma_0$ is exactly $\frac12\|a-a^\dagger\|_V^2$. On every fixed sublevel containing the truth, the VSC holds with $b=3/4$ and a continuous nondecreasing concave truncated logarithmic index
$$\psi(u)=C[\log(1/u)]^{-\nu}\quad(0<u\le u_0),\qquad \psi(0)=0,\qquad \nu=\frac{(s_2-s_1)(2s_1-3)}{s_2-1},$$
continued constantly above a sufficiently small $u_0>0$. Its subadditivity constant may be taken as $C_\psi=1$.

Put $L_T=\operatorname{Lip}(T)$ and let $L=\operatorname{Lip}(\Gamma')$. For $Q(\widehat r,\widehat r')=\|\widehat r-\widehat r'\|_Z$, the projection-coupling constant may be taken as $1+L_T$, and
$$\|r(x_1)-r(x_2)-r'(x_2)(x_1-x_2)\|_Z\le LR\|r(x_1)-r(x_2)\|_Z\qquad(x_1,x_2\in U).$$
For the frozen method choose $C_P\ge2\|K\|^2\operatorname{Lip}(r)^2$, $\gamma>1$ and $R_P(z)=\gamma\psi(C_P\|z\|_Y^2)$. Then the required compatibility bound holds with
$$\widetilde C_Q=\max\left\{4(1+L_T)^2,\frac{2R^2}{\psi(C_PR^2)}\right\}.$$
In particular, the structural hypotheses of the joint and frozen one-step estimates hold with $p=2$, the displayed exact regularizer, $R_P=0$ for the joint method, and the displayed $R_P$ for the frozen method. For frozen rates additionally require $LR<c_{\rm tcr}<1/\sqrt{20}$, choose $c_{\beta\alpha}\le\min\{1/4,\gamma-1\}/(4\widetilde C_Q)$, and use the remaining parameter, tolerance and stopping conditions of the frozen rate theorem. This small-neighborhood hypothesis is local around the chosen initial conductivity; it restricts neither the stated Besov truth class nor its logarithmic exponent.

Let $X$ be a real Banach space, let $R:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper and convex, choose $x^\dagger\in\operatorname{dom}R$, and choose $\xi^\dagger\in\partial R(x^\dagger)$. For $x\in\operatorname{dom}R$, the **Bregman distance** generated by $\xi^\dagger$ from the reference point $x^\dagger$ to $x$ is

$$D_R^{\xi^\dagger}(x,x^\dagger):=R(x)-R(x^\dagger)-\langle\xi^\dagger,x-x^\dagger\rangle_{X^*,X}.$$

The subgradient inequality makes this quantity nonnegative, and $D_R^{\xi^\dagger}(x^\dagger,x^\dagger)=0$. The definition fixes the orientation: the first argument is the comparison point and the second is the reference point carrying the chosen subgradient.

Assume the hypotheses of the joint range-invariance VSC estimate lemma, with the same notation, with fixed $\beta>0$, and with $R_P=0$ in the joint objective. Define

$$H(q):=\sup_{s\ge0}\bigl(\psi(s)-qs\bigr)\qquad(q>0),\quad \rho_\delta:=H\!\left(\frac{1}{C_*\alpha(\delta)}\right).$$

Assume $H(1/(C_*\alpha(\delta)))$ and $H(1/(2C_*\alpha(\delta)))$ are finite, $\alpha(\delta)\to0$, $\rho_\delta\to0$, $\eta_\delta\le C_\eta\delta^p$, and there are constants $c_-,c_+,C_H>0$ independent of $\delta$ such that

$$c_-\delta^p\le\alpha(\delta)\rho_\delta\le c_+\delta^p,\qquad H\!\left(\frac{1}{2C_*\alpha(\delta)}\right)\le C_H\rho_\delta.$$

Then the approximate joint reconstructions satisfy, as $\delta\downarrow0$,

$$D_{\check R}^{\xi^\dagger}(\check x_\delta,x^\dagger)=O(\rho_\delta),\qquad S_\delta=O(\delta^p),$$

where $S_\delta$ is the scalar residual, coupling, and projection error defined in the joint range-invariance VSC estimate lemma. In particular,

$$\|K(\widehat r_\delta-r(x^\dagger))\|_Y=O(\delta),\quad \|Px_\delta\|_X=O(\delta),\quad Q(r(x_\delta),\widehat r_\delta)=O(\delta),$$

and the data residual $\|K\widehat r_\delta+F(x_0)-y^\delta\|_Y$ is $O(\delta)$.

For the following three-dimensional EIT specialization, assume the Axiom of Choice, Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. Let $\Omega=B_1\subset\mathbb R^3$, let the known background be $1$ outside $B_\rho\Subset B_1$, and impose fixed bounds $0<m<1<M$ and $m\le\sigma\le M$. Let $s_1\in(5/2,7/2)$, use the intrinsic quadratic penalty $\frac12\|\sigma\|_{H^{s_1}(\Omega)}^2$ on this admissible class, and let $\sigma^\dagger\in B^{s_2}_{2,\infty}(\Omega)$ with $s_2\in(s_1,2s_1-1)$. The Sobolev norm is the exact intrinsic Hilbert norm in the EIT compatibility lemma. Use centered mean-zero Neumann voltage data $(\mathscr N_\sigma-\mathscr N_1)Y_{\ell k}$ in $Y=\ell^2(L^2(S^2))$, its observation-augmentation range coordinates, and admitted approximate joint minimizers in the set $U$ specified by that lemma. The artificial voltage is $z\in Y$ and the projection is $P(\sigma-\sigma_0,z)=(0,z)$. Put

$$\nu=\frac{(s_2-s_1)(2s_1-3)}{s_2-1},\qquad L_\delta=\log(1/\delta).$$

For fixed $\beta>0$, noise bounded by $\delta$, and $\eta_\delta=O(\delta^2)$, the balanced choice $\alpha\asymp\delta^2L_\delta^\nu$ gives

$$\|\sigma_\delta-\sigma^\dagger\|_{H^{s_1}(\Omega)}=O(L_\delta^{-\nu/2}),\qquad \|z_\delta\|_Y=O(\delta),\qquad S_\delta=O(\delta^2).$$

Every pure power $\alpha\asymp\delta^k$ with $0<k<2$ gives the same conductivity norm rate and $S_\delta=O(\delta^kL_\delta^{-\nu})$, hence $\|z_\delta\|_Y=O(\delta^{k/2}L_\delta^{-\nu/2})$. At the nominal endpoint $\alpha\asymp\delta^2$, the same conductivity norm rate holds under the explicit actual-noise and tolerance condition

$$2\|y^\delta-y\|_Y^2+\eta_\delta=O(\delta^2L_\delta^{-\nu});$$

then $S_\delta=O(\delta^2L_\delta^{-\nu})$ and $\|z_\delta\|_Y=O(\delta L_\delta^{-\nu/2})$. In each case the coupling distance and relaxed data residual have order $O(\sqrt{S_\delta}+\|y^\delta-y\|_Y)$. In particular the sum of the conductivity norm error and the artificial-voltage norm is $O(L_\delta^{-\nu/2})$ in all three stated regimes.

Let $X_0=V\times\{0\}$, $D=X$, $x_0=(0,0)$ and $P(a,z)=(0,z)$.

$$T(a)=\Gamma(a)-\Gamma(0)-\Gamma'(0)a,\quad r(a,z)=(a,z+T(a)),\quad K(a,b)=\Gamma'(0)a+b,\quad F(a,z)=\Gamma(a)+z.$$
Then $F(x)-F(x_0)=Kr(x)$ on $D$, $r$ and its inverse $r^{-1}(a,b)=(a,b-T(a))$ are globally Lipschitz, and these facts hold on the admitted set
$$U=\{(a,z):\sigma_0+a\in\mathcal C,\ \|a\|_V<R,\ \|z\|_Y<R\}.$$
The projected points $(I-P)r^{-1}(\widehat r)$ belong to $U\cap X_0$ for $\widehat r\in r(U)$.

On the ambient linear space $V$ define the proper convex regularizer
$$\check R(a)=\tfrac12\|\sigma_0+a\|_{s_1,\Omega}^2+I_{\mathcal C}(\sigma_0+a),$$
where the indicator is zero on $\mathcal C$ and $+\infty$ elsewhere. On every admitted physical coefficient this is exactly the original quadratic Sobolev penalty. The functional $\xi^\dagger(v)=(\sigma^\dagger,v)_{s_1,\Omega}$ is a subgradient at $a^\dagger$, and its Bregman distance on $\mathcal C-\sigma_0$ is exactly $\frac12\|a-a^\dagger\|_V^2$. On every fixed sublevel containing the truth, the VSC holds with $b=3/4$ and a continuous nondecreasing concave truncated logarithmic index
$$\psi(u)=C[\log(1/u)]^{-\nu}\quad(0<u\le u_0),\qquad \psi(0)=0,\qquad \nu=\frac{(s_2-s_1)(2s_1-3)}{s_2-1},$$
continued constantly above a sufficiently small $u_0>0$. Its subadditivity constant may be taken as $C_\psi=1$.

Put $L_T=\operatorname{Lip}(T)$ and let $L=\operatorname{Lip}(\Gamma')$. For $Q(\widehat r,\widehat r')=\|\widehat r-\widehat r'\|_Z$, the projection-coupling constant may be taken as $1+L_T$, and
$$\|r(x_1)-r(x_2)-r'(x_2)(x_1-x_2)\|_Z\le LR\|r(x_1)-r(x_2)\|_Z\qquad(x_1,x_2\in U).$$
For the frozen method choose $C_P\ge2\|K\|^2\operatorname{Lip}(r)^2$, $\gamma>1$ and $R_P(z)=\gamma\psi(C_P\|z\|_Y^2)$. Then the required compatibility bound holds with
$$\widetilde C_Q=\max\left\{4(1+L_T)^2,\frac{2R^2}{\psi(C_PR^2)}\right\}.$$
In particular, the structural hypotheses of the joint and frozen one-step estimates hold with $p=2$, the displayed exact regularizer, $R_P=0$ for the joint method, and the displayed $R_P$ for the frozen method. For frozen rates additionally require $LR<c_{\rm tcr}<1/\sqrt{20}$, choose $c_{\beta\alpha}\le\min\{1/4,\gamma-1\}/(4\widetilde C_Q)$, and use the remaining parameter, tolerance and stopping conditions of the frozen rate theorem. This small-neighborhood hypothesis is local around the chosen initial conductivity; it restricts neither the stated Besov truth class nor its logarithmic exponent.

Fix $p,
u,a,C_*,C>0$ and let $\psi$ be a continuous nondecreasing concave source index with $\psi(0)=0$. Suppose its conjugate $H(q)=\sup_{t\ge0}(\psi(t)-qt)$ satisfies $H(q)\le C(\log q)^{-
u}$ for all sufficiently large $q$. Let $\delta\downarrow0$ be a nominal parameter, and put $L_\delta=\log(1/\delta)$. Suppose nonnegative errors satisfy
$$S_\delta+a\alpha_\delta e_\delta\le d_\delta+\alpha_\delta\psi(C_*S_\delta),\qquad \alpha_\delta\asymp\delta^p,\qquad d_\delta=O(\delta^pL_\delta^{-
u}).$$
Then
$$e_\delta=O(L_\delta^{-
u}),\qquad S_\delta=O(\delta^pL_\delta^{-
u}).$$
For the joint objective estimate with actual data noise $\varepsilon_\delta=\|y^\delta-y\|$, the hypothesis on $d_\delta$ is supplied by $2\varepsilon_\delta^p+\eta_\delta=O(\delta^pL_\delta^{-
u})$. This condition explicitly strengthens the usual nominal bound $\varepsilon_\delta\le\delta$, $\eta_\delta=O(\delta^p)$ at the endpoint. If $e_\delta= rac12\|u_\delta-u^\dagger\|^2$, the norm rate is $O(L_\delta^{-
u/2})$.

The universal assertion that $\alpha\asymp\delta^2$ yields a vanishing norm error for every deterministic noise family bounded by $\delta$ is false, even for an exact quadratic Tikhonov minimizer and a truth satisfying every nonnegative variational source inequality: on real $\ell^2$, take $Ke_j=j^{-1}e_j$, $x^\dagger=0$, $y^{\delta_j}=\delta_j e_j$, $\delta_j=1/j$, $\alpha_j=\delta_j^2$, and objective $\|Kx-y^{\delta_j}\|^2+ rac{\alpha_j}{2}\|x\|^2$. Its unique minimizer is $2e_j/3$. This counterexample refutes the universal abstract endpoint assertion; it makes no assertion that these data arise from an EIT conductivity map.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. Let $\Omega=B_1(0)\subset\mathbb R^3$, fix $0<\rho<1$ and $0<m<1<M$, and let $E$ be the closed real subspace of $L^\infty(\Omega)$ consisting of functions vanishing almost everywhere outside $B_\rho(0)$. Set $\mathcal A=\{a\in E:\operatorname*{ess\,inf}(1+a)>m,\ \operatorname*{ess\,sup}(1+a)<M\}$ and $\sigma=1+a$. Choose an orthonormal spherical-harmonic basis $Y_{\ell k}$ of mean-zero $L^2(S^2)$, with $\ell\ge1$ and $1\le k\le2\ell+1$. For each basis current there is a unique weak solution $u_{\sigma,\ell k}\in H^1(\Omega)$ with boundary mean zero such that
$$\int_\Omega\sigma\nabla u_{\sigma,\ell k}\cdot\overline{\nabla v}=\int_{S^2}Y_{\ell k}\overline{\operatorname{Tr}v}\qquad(v\in H^1(\Omega)).$$
The centered sequence
$$G(a):=\big(\operatorname{Tr}(u_{\sigma,\ell k}-u_{1,\ell k})\big)_{\ell,k}$$
belongs to $Y=\ell^2(L^2(S^2))$. The map $G:\mathcal A\to Y$ is Fréchet differentiable, and both $G$ and $G'$ are Lipschitz on $\mathcal A$, with constants depending only on $m,M,\rho$ and the ball. Its derivative in direction $h\in E$ is the trace sequence of the unique boundary-mean-zero solutions
$$\int_\Omega\sigma\nabla v_{h,\ell k}\cdot\overline{\nabla w}=-\int_\Omega h\nabla u_{\sigma,\ell k}\cdot\overline{\nabla w}.$$
The uncentered sequence $(\operatorname{Tr}u_{1,\ell k})_{\ell,k}$ does not belong to $Y$. Thus absolute voltage data in this convention lie in an affine translate of $Y$, whereas data differences belong to $Y$. All complex spaces here may be regarded as real Banach spaces when taking derivatives with respect to real conductivities.

derivations.claim: Substituting $p=2$ into [F2] gives $s_1=5/2+\tau$ and $\mu=2(s_2-s_1)/(s_2-1)$. The logarithmic VSC exponent contributed by the source Sobolev gap is therefore $(s_2-s_1)(2s_1-3)/(s_2-1)$. This differs from [F1]'s denominator $s_1-1$ because the allowed range has $s_2>s_1$; the cited theorem does not directly yield the exponent printed in Kaltenbacher's Theorem 10.

For $R(\sigma)= rac12\|\sigma\|_{H^{s_1}}^2$, the Hilbert-space subgradient is $\xi^\dagger=\sigma^\dagger$ under the $H^{s_1}$ inner product. Expanding the square gives $D_R^{\xi^\dagger}(\sigma,\sigma^\dagger)= rac12\|\sigma-\sigma^\dagger\|_{H^{s_1}}^2$. Therefore $D_R^{\xi^\dagger}=O((\log(1/\delta))^{-
u})$ implies only $\|\sigma-\sigma^\dagger\|_{H^{s_1}}=O((\log(1/\delta))^{-
u/2})$ by taking square roots; it does not imply exponent $
u$.

By [F6], $\psi(t)\asymp(\log(1/t))^{-
u_{m paper}}$ for sufficiently small positive $t$, and $\psi$ is bounded because of the truncation at $t_0$. For $q$ large, if $0<t<q^{-1/2}$ then $\psi(t)\le C2^{
u_{m paper}}(\log q)^{-
u_{m paper}}$; if $t\ge q^{-1/2}$ then $\psi(t)-qt\le\psi(t)-\sqrt q<0$. Thus $H(q)\le C'(\log q)^{-
u_{m paper}}$. Conversely, choosing $t_q=q^{-1}(\log q)^{-
u_{m paper}-1}$ gives $\log(1/t_q)\sim\log q$, $\psi(t_q)\ge c'(\log q)^{-
u_{m paper}}$, and $qt_q=(\log q)^{-
u_{m paper}-1}$, hence $H(q)\ge c''(\log q)^{-
u_{m paper}}$ for large $q$. Therefore $H(q)\asymp(\log q)^{-
u_{m paper}}$. For $\alpha\asymp\delta^{\widetilde p}$, $0<\widetilde p\le2$, this gives $\alpha H(c/\alpha)\asymp\delta^{\widetilde p}(\log(1/\delta))^{-
u_{m paper}}$. If $\widetilde p=2$, the ratio to $\delta^2$ tends to zero; if $\widetilde p<2$, that ratio tends to infinity. Hence no such pure-power choice satisfies the two-sided sufficient coupling in Theorem 3; this does not decide the separate assertion in Remark 1.

The local interface [F7] verifies the full admitted EIT hypotheses, with the corrected VSC exponent from step 1.1 and the exact quadratic norm conversion from step 1.2. The two local rate theorems therefore give their explicit EIT conclusions from proved suppliers. Finally [F9] establishes the centered observation space and its necessary affine-data interpretation. These are proved source corrections preserving the full truth regularity classes, rather than unsupported imports of the printed formulas.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$, be a
bounded $C^1$ domain, $1<p<\infty$ and $\theta=1-1/p$, with
$W^{\theta,p}(\partial\Omega)$ as in
[[def-fractional-sobolev-space-on-a-compact-c-one-boundary]]. Then the trace
operator $T$ of [[thm-lp-trace-operator-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]] satisfies
$$\|Tu\|_{W^{\theta,p}(\partial\Omega)}\le C(\Omega,p)\|u\|_{W^{1,p}(\Omega)} \qquad(u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)),$$
and it is onto: $T(W^{1,p}(\Omega))=W^{\theta,p}(\partial\Omega)$. For $p>1$
the range is a strict subset of $L^p(\partial\Omega)$, and the trace is not a
compact operator into $W^{\theta,p}(\partial\Omega)$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$, be a
bounded $C^1$ domain and $1\le p<\infty$. Then the kernel of the trace
operator of [[thm-lp-trace-operator-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]] equals the
zero-boundary Sobolev space:
$$\{u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K):Tu=0\}=W_0^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K),$$
the $W^{1,p}$-closure of $C_c^\infty(\Omega)$
([[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]]).

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, let $1\le p\le\infty$, and let
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.

Every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ belongs to
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Indeed $\varphi$ is bounded with compact support,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ for every exponent in range, and each of
its classical partial derivatives is again smooth and compactly supported,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and is the corresponding weak derivative
by [[lem-classical-derivatives-are-weak-derivatives]].

Define the **zero-boundary Sobolev space**
$$W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K):=\overline{C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)},$$
the closure taken in the normed space
$(W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K),\|\cdot\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)})$ of
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]. The norm is a genuine norm on classes
by [[lem-sobolev-norm-is-well-defined-and-definite]], so this is the usual
metric closure of a subset of a normed space: $u\in W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$
if and only if for every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with
$\|u-\varphi\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}<\delta$. Write
$H_0^k(\Omega):=W_0^{k,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ when the scalar field is fixed by
context.

Three warnings are part of the definition. First, this is a closure of
almost-everywhere classes, and all its equalities are equalities of Sobolev
classes. Second, no pointwise boundary values and no trace characterization
are asserted: a description of $W_0^{k,p}$ by vanishing boundary data belongs
to the later trace theory and is not used here. Third, the closure is defined
for every $1\le p\le\infty$, but for $p=\infty$ it is not claimed that every
compactly supported $W^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$ function lies in $W_0^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$;
the definition merely names the closure of the test functions.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$, be a
bounded $C^1$ domain, $1<p<\infty$, $\theta=1-1/p$, and let $T$ be the trace
operator of [[thm-lp-trace-operator-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]]. Then there is
a bounded linear operator
$$R:W^{\theta,p}(\partial\Omega;\mathbb K)\longrightarrow W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$$
with $T\circ R=\mathrm{id}_{W^{\theta,p}(\partial\Omega)}$ and
$\|Rg\|_{W^{1,p}(\Omega)}\le C(\Omega,p)\|g\|_{W^{\theta,p}(\partial\Omega)}$.
Moreover, for every open neighbourhood $U$ of $\partial\Omega$ in
$\mathbb R^n$ there is such an operator $R_U$ whose image is contained in the
classes vanishing a.e. outside $U$, with
$\|R_Ug\|_{W^{1,p}(\Omega)}\le C(\Omega,p,U)\|g\|_{W^{\theta,p}(\partial\Omega)}$.
The right inverse is not unique and no canonical choice is claimed.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) and the boundary
conventions of
[[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]]. Let
$\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$, be a bounded $C^1$ domain, let
$0<s<1$, $1\le p<\infty$ and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Fix a
finite family of boundary charts: for each $j$ let $W_j\subseteq\mathbb R^n$
be open and $\Phi_j:W_j\to\Phi_j(W_j)\subseteq B_j\times\mathbb R$ a
flattening chart as in
[[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]], so that
$\Phi_j(\Omega\cap W_j)=\Phi_j(W_j)\cap\{t<0\}$ and the boundary corresponds
to the graph $\{t=0\}$; write $\Psi_j:=\pi\circ\Phi_j|_{\partial\Omega\cap W_j}$
for the induced parametrisation of $\partial\Omega\cap W_j$ by an open subset
$V_j:=\Psi_j(\partial\Omega\cap W_j)\subseteq\mathbb R^{n-1}$, and assume the
$\partial\Omega\cap W_j$ cover $\partial\Omega$. Fix a subordinate finite
ambient partition: nonnegative $\chi_j\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n)$ with
$\operatorname{supp}\chi_j\subseteq W_j$ and $\sum_j\chi_j=1$ on a
neighbourhood of $\partial\Omega$
([[lem-finite-ambient-partitions-for-euclidean-boundary-integration]]).
Finally let $\partial\Omega$ carry the chart-independent surface measure of
[[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]], which fixes the
meaning of almost-everywhere equality and of $L^p(\partial\Omega;\mathbb K)$
([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]).

For a Borel function $g:\partial\Omega\to\mathbb K$ put
$$\|g\|_{W^{s,p}(\partial\Omega)}:=\sum_j\bigl\|(\chi_jg)\circ\Psi_j^{-1}\bigr\|_{W^{s,p}(\mathbb R^{n-1})},$$
where the chart representation $(\chi_jg)\circ\Psi_j^{-1}$ is read in graph
coordinates and extended by zero off $V_j$, and the norm on the right is that
of [[def-fractional-slobodeckij-space-on-euclidean-space]]. The **fractional
Sobolev space of the boundary** is
$$W^{s,p}(\partial\Omega;\mathbb K):=\{g\in L^p(\partial\Omega;\mathbb K):\|g\|_{W^{s,p}(\partial\Omega)}<\infty\}.$$
The right-hand side is a finite sum of finite norms of compactly supported
chart representations, so $W^{s,p}(\partial\Omega;\mathbb K)$ is exactly the
set of $L^p(\partial\Omega)$ classes whose chart representations all lie in
the Euclidean space of
[[def-fractional-slobodeckij-space-on-euclidean-space]]; that the resulting
space and the topology of the norm do not depend on the choices of atlas and
partition, up to equivalence of norms, is proved in
[[lem-fractional-boundary-norm-is-independent-of-atlas]] and is not assumed
here.

Three conventions belong to the definition. First, membership is a property of
the $L^p(\partial\Omega)$ class: $g$ is an almost-everywhere class with respect
to the surface measure, and the chart representations are classes in
$W^{s,p}(\mathbb R^{n-1})$; representative independence for the Euclidean
factor is established together with the well-definedness lemma on this page
and is not presupposed here. Second, the norm is a finite sum
over a finite atlas, and each $\chi_jg$ is supported in the interior of the
chart, so the localisations are compactly supported and no boundary behaviour
of $\Psi_j^{-1}$ outside $V_j$ enters. Third, on this page the exponent used
is the trace exponent $s=\theta=1-1/p$ for $1<p<\infty$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: If $u-v\in H_0^1(\Omega)$, then [F2] gives $Tu=Tv$, so $\overline T[u]:=Tu$ is well-defined on $\mathcal D(\Omega)$. By [F1], $\|\overline T[u]\|_{W^{1/2,2}(\partial\Omega)}\le C\|u\|_{H^1(\Omega)}$ for every representative $u$; taking the infimum over its coset gives $\|\overline T[u]\|\le C\|[u]\|_{\mathcal D}$. If $\overline T[u]=0$, [F2] gives $u\in H_0^1$, hence $[u]=0$; thus the induced map is injective.

By [F1], every $f\in W^{1/2,2}(\partial\Omega)$ is $Tu$ for some $u\in H^1(\Omega)$, so $\overline T$ is onto. More quantitatively, choose the lift $Rf$ from [F3]. Then $\overline T[Rf]=f$ and $\|[Rf]\|_{\mathcal D}\le\|Rf\|_{H^1}\le C\|f\|_{W^{1/2,2}}$, proving that the inverse is bounded.

The trace of a constant function is that same constant, so $\overline T$ maps the closed constant subspace $\mathbb K\mathbf1\subset\mathcal D(\Omega)$ onto the constant subspace of $W^{1/2,2}(\partial\Omega)$. The bounded isomorphism and its bounded inverse from steps 1.1–1.2 therefore induce a bounded isomorphism on the two quotient spaces, with equivalent quotient norms.

If $\ell$ is a continuous linear functional on $W^{1/2,2}(\partial\Omega)$ that annihilates constants, then $\dot\ell([f]):=\ell(f)$ is independent of the representative because $\ell(f+c)=\ell(f)$ for every constant $c$. By the quotient-norm definition, $|\dot\ell([f])|\le\|\ell\|\inf_c\|f+c\|_{W^{1/2,2}}$, so $\dot\ell$ is continuous with quotient dual norm at most $\|\ell\|$. Conversely, any functional that factors as $\ell=\varphi\circ q$ vanishes on constants because $q(c)=0$; and $|\varphi(qf)|\le\|\varphi\|\|qf\|\le\|\varphi\|\|f\|$ because the quotient map $q$ has norm at most one. Hence $\|\ell\|\le\|\varphi\|$, while the first inequality gives $\|\varphi\|\le\|\ell\|$ for the induced functional. This proves the equivalence and equality of dual norms.

Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. Use $\mathcal H_\ell$ from [[def-spherical-harmonic-partial-wave-conventions]]. For every $\ell\ge0$, $\dim_\mathbb C\mathcal H_\ell=2\ell+1$; the spaces $\mathcal H_\ell$ are pairwise orthogonal in $L^2(S^2,d\sigma;\mathbb C)$ and their algebraic sum is dense there. Thus they give a complete orthogonal spherical-harmonic expansion. For any orthonormal basis $Y_{\ell 1},\ldots,Y_{\ell,2\ell+1}$ of $\mathcal H_\ell$, the basis-independent reproducing kernel
$$Z_\ell(\omega,\eta):=\sum_{m=1}^{2\ell+1}Y_{\ell m}(\omega)\overline{Y_{\ell m}(\eta)}$$
satisfies $Z_\ell(\omega,\omega)=(2\ell+1)/(4\pi)$. In particular,
$$|g(\omega)|\le\sqrt{\frac{2\ell+1}{4\pi}}\,\|g\|_{L^2(S^2)}\qquad(g\in\mathcal H_\ell).$$
For fixed $\eta$, rotational invariance makes $Z_\ell(\omega,\eta)$ a degree-$\ell$ zonal polynomial of $\omega\cdot\eta$; normalizing $P_\ell(1)=1$ gives the usual addition identity $Z_\ell(\omega,\eta)=\frac{2\ell+1}{4\pi}P_\ell(\omega\cdot\eta)$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $k\ge1$, $1\le p\le\infty$,
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a
bounded $C^k$ domain in the graph sense of
[[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]]. Then for every open set
$V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $\overline\Omega\subseteq V$ there is a bounded
linear extension operator
$$E:W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)\longrightarrow W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K),\qquad (Eu)|_\Omega=u\ \text{a.e. on }\Omega,$$
such that $\operatorname{supp}(Eu)$ is a compact subset of $V$ for every
$u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. In particular each bounded $C^k$ domain is a
$W^{k,p}$-extension domain, with an operator whose output is supported in any
prescribed neighbourhood of $\overline\Omega$. For $k=0$, extension by zero
is an isometric $L^p$ extension on any open $\Omega$; its output is supported
in the compact set $\overline\Omega\subseteq V$ when $\Omega$ is bounded.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $n\ge1$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be a
nonempty bounded connected extension domain, and let $1\le p<\infty$. Then there is
$C=C(\Omega,p)$ such that every $u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ satisfies
$$\|u-u_\Omega\|_{L^p(\Omega)}\le C\|Du\|_{L^p(\Omega)},\qquad u_\Omega:=|\Omega|^{-1}\int_\Omega u(x)\,dx.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $n\ge2$ and let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a nonempty bounded connected open set whose boundary is covered by finitely many $C^1$ graph charts. Give $H^1(\Omega;\mathbb K)=W^{1,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ its Sobolev norm, let $H_0^1(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ be the $H^1$-closure of $C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$, and let $W^{1/2,2}(\partial\Omega;\mathbb K)$ have the finite-chart Slobodeckij norm. Define $\mathcal D(\Omega):=H^1(\Omega;\mathbb K)/H_0^1(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with its quotient norm. The trace induces a bounded linear bijection $\overline T:\mathcal D(\Omega)\to W^{1/2,2}(\partial\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with bounded inverse, so these two norms are equivalent under the induced identification. The induced map after quotienting by constants is also a bounded linear bijection $\mathcal D(\Omega)/\mathbb K\mathbf1\to W^{1/2,2}(\partial\Omega;\mathbb K)/\mathbb K$, with equivalent quotient norms. A continuous linear functional on $W^{1/2,2}(\partial\Omega;\mathbb K)$ descends to the constant quotient exactly when it annihilates constants, and its descended functional has the quotient dual norm.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space, let $a$ be a bounded coercive sesquilinear form on $H$ with constants $M,\alpha$ ([[def-bounded-coercive-and-symmetric-sesquilinear-forms]]), and let $F:H\to\mathbb K$ be a bounded conjugate-linear functional with norm $\|F\|=\sup_{\|v\|\le1}|F(v)|$. Then there is a unique $u\in H$ with $$a(u,v)=F(v)\qquad\text{for every }v\in H,$$ and it satisfies $\alpha\|u\|\le\|F\|$, that is $\|u\|\le\|F\|/\alpha$. The real bilinear case is the same statement with $a$ symmetric or not, $F$ a bounded linear functional, and the conjugation read as the identity.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.

statement.

countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]],
> [[def-natural-numbers]]) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** [[def-choice-function]] and
[[def-axiom-of-choice]] select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and [[def-countable-choice]] does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ ([[def-power-set]], [[def-cartesian-product]], [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]]); a natural is the set of its predecessors ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense ([[def-chain]]). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. Let $\Omega=B_1(0)\subset\mathbb R^3$, fix $0<\rho<1$ and $0<m<1<M$, and let $E$ be the closed real subspace of $L^\infty(\Omega)$ consisting of functions vanishing almost everywhere outside $B_\rho(0)$. Set $\mathcal A=\{a\in E:\operatorname*{ess\,inf}(1+a)>m,\ \operatorname*{ess\,sup}(1+a)<M\}$ and $\sigma=1+a$. Choose an orthonormal spherical-harmonic basis $Y_{\ell k}$ of mean-zero $L^2(S^2)$, with $\ell\ge1$ and $1\le k\le2\ell+1$. For each basis current there is a unique weak solution $u_{\sigma,\ell k}\in H^1(\Omega)$ with boundary mean zero such that
$$\int_\Omega\sigma\nabla u_{\sigma,\ell k}\cdot\overline{\nabla v}=\int_{S^2}Y_{\ell k}\overline{\operatorname{Tr}v}\qquad(v\in H^1(\Omega)).$$
The centered sequence
$$G(a):=\big(\operatorname{Tr}(u_{\sigma,\ell k}-u_{1,\ell k})\big)_{\ell,k}$$
belongs to $Y=\ell^2(L^2(S^2))$. The map $G:\mathcal A\to Y$ is Fréchet differentiable, and both $G$ and $G'$ are Lipschitz on $\mathcal A$, with constants depending only on $m,M,\rho$ and the ball. Its derivative in direction $h\in E$ is the trace sequence of the unique boundary-mean-zero solutions
$$\int_\Omega\sigma\nabla v_{h,\ell k}\cdot\overline{\nabla w}=-\int_\Omega h\nabla u_{\sigma,\ell k}\cdot\overline{\nabla w}.$$
The uncentered sequence $(\operatorname{Tr}u_{1,\ell k})_{\ell,k}$ does not belong to $Y$. Thus absolute voltage data in this convention lie in an affine translate of $Y$, whereas data differences belong to $Y$. All complex spaces here may be regarded as real Banach spaces when taking derivatives with respect to real conductivities.

Assume Countable Choice. Fix $5/2<s<7/2$, $0<\rho<1$, $0<m<1<M$ and $A>0$. Suppose $\sigma_j=1+a_j$ on $\mathbb R^3$, where $a_j$ is real, supported in $\overline{B_\rho}$, $\|a_j\|_{H^s(\mathbb R^3)}\le A$, and $m\le\sigma_j\le M$, for $j=1,2$. Then $g_j=\sqrt{\sigma_j}$ and $\log g_j$ belong to $C^1$, with $g_j-1,\log g_j\in H^s(\mathbb R^3)$ supported in $\overline{B_\rho}$ and uniformly bounded in $H^s$ and $C^1$. The real Liouville potentials
$$q_j=g_j^{-1}\Delta g_j$$
belong to $H^{s-2}(\mathbb R^3)$, have support in $\overline{B_\rho}$, and have norms bounded in terms of $s,\rho,m,M,A$. Moreover,
$$\|\sigma_1-\sigma_2\|_{H^1(\mathbb R^3)}\le C\|q_1-q_2\|_{H^{-1}(\mathbb R^3)},$$
with the same dependence. In particular the right side may be replaced by $C\|q_1-q_2\|_{H^{-1/2}}$ when that stronger norm is used. The Fourier and intrinsic norms for collared variations are those of the collared Sobolev source-functional lemma.

Assume Countable Choice. Fix $0<\tau<1$, $0<\rho<1$ and $M>0$. If $q\in H^{1/2+\tau}(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$ has support in $\overline{B_\rho}$ and norm at most $M$, there are constants $T,C>0$, depending only on $\tau,\rho,M$, such that for every $\zeta\in\mathbb C^3$ with $\zeta\cdot\zeta=0$ and $|\zeta|\ge T$, there is $r_\zeta\in H^2(B_2)$ for which
$$(-\Delta+q)\big(e^{i\zeta\cdot x}(1+r_\zeta)\big)=0\quad\hbox{in }B_2,$$
$$\|r_\zeta\|_{H^{1/2}(B_2)}\le C|\zeta|^{-1}M,\qquad \|r_\zeta\|_{L^\infty(B_2)}\le C|\zeta|^{-\tau/2}M,\qquad \|r_\zeta\|_{H^2(B_2)}\le C|\zeta|M(1+M).$$
Here fractional Sobolev norms on the ball are restriction norms from the whole-space Fourier Sobolev spaces. No boundary condition is imposed. The construction is on a larger cube, so the stated regularity holds on a neighborhood of the closed unit ball.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $n\ge2$ and let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a nonempty bounded connected open set whose boundary is covered by finitely many $C^1$ graph charts. Give $H^1(\Omega;\mathbb K)=W^{1,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ its Sobolev norm, let $H_0^1(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ be the $H^1$-closure of $C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$, and let $W^{1/2,2}(\partial\Omega;\mathbb K)$ have the finite-chart Slobodeckij norm. Define $\mathcal D(\Omega):=H^1(\Omega;\mathbb K)/H_0^1(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with its quotient norm. The trace induces a bounded linear bijection $\overline T:\mathcal D(\Omega)\to W^{1/2,2}(\partial\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with bounded inverse, so these two norms are equivalent under the induced identification. The induced map after quotienting by constants is also a bounded linear bijection $\mathcal D(\Omega)/\mathbb K\mathbf1\to W^{1/2,2}(\partial\Omega;\mathbb K)/\mathbb K$, with equivalent quotient norms. A continuous linear functional on $W^{1/2,2}(\partial\Omega;\mathbb K)$ descends to the constant quotient exactly when it annihilates constants, and its descended functional has the quotient dual norm.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above.
