derivations.claim: The energy argument in [F1] applies to every mean-zero $f\in L^2(S^2)$: the functional $v\mapsto\int f\overline{\operatorname{Tr}v}$ is bounded on the boundary-mean-zero $H^1$ subspace by [F4], and its uniformly coercive conductivity form has a unique solution with norm at most $C\|f\|_2$. This defines a bounded map $\mathscr N_j:L^2_0\to L^2_0$. Its centered sequence columns are those in [F1], so their difference has finite squared sum. For a finite current expansion $f=\sum c_{\ell k}Y_{\ell k}$, Cauchy–Schwarz gives $\|(\mathscr N_1-\mathscr N_2)f\|_2\le\delta(\sum|c_{\ell k}|^2)^{1/2}$. Density and boundedness extend this to every $f\in L^2_0$. Finally the bilinear symmetry $\int f\mathscr N_jh=\int h\mathscr N_jf$ follows by testing the two weak equations against one another, using real coefficients and complex bilinear extension.

Put $u_j=U_j/g_j$. The weak Liouville identity gives $\operatorname{div}(\sigma_j
abla u_j)=0$: expand $\sigma_j
abla(U_j/g_j)=g_j
abla U_j-U_j
abla g_j$, whose divergence is $g_j\Delta U_j-U_j\Delta g_j=0$. Products are legitimate by [F2]–[F3]; one may also verify the equality first on smooth approximations and pass in distributions. Since $g_j=1$ on a full collar of $S^2$, the boundary normal flux of $u_j$ is exactly $f_j=\partial_
u U_j$. It belongs to $L^2$ because $U_j\in H^2(B_2)$ and [F4] applies to each first derivative. Integration by parts gives the weak Neumann equation with this flux. For completeness this Green identity follows first for smooth functions by the divergence theorem and then by smooth $H^2$ approximation of $U_j$ on the larger ball and the trace bound [F4]; on the collar $U_j$ is harmonic and the coefficient is identically one. Taking the test function one shows $\int f_j=0$. Thus $\operatorname{Tr}u_j=\mathscr N_j f_j+c_j$ for a constant $c_j$.

Subtract the two bilinear Schrödinger Green identities, testing the $j=1$ equation against $U_2$ and the $j=2$ equation against $U_1$. Their gradient terms cancel, giving $\int Q U_1U_2=\int_{S^2}(f_1\operatorname{Tr}U_2-f_2\operatorname{Tr}U_1)$. Since $U_j=u_j$ on the boundary, step 2.1 identifies these traces with $\mathscr N_jf_j+c_j$. The constant terms disappear because the fluxes have mean zero; the symmetry from step 1.1 gives exactly the displayed centered NtD identity. All volume terms are integrable since $Q\in L^2$ and $U_j\in H^2(B_2)\subset L^\infty(B_1)$; boundedness follows, for example, by weighted Fourier Cauchy–Schwarz after multiplication by an interior cutoff.

If $|\zeta_j|=\sqrt2t$, [F3] and differentiation of the exponential give $\|U_j\|_{H^2(B_1)}\le Ce^{Ct}t^3$ for $t\ge T$. The trace bound on first derivatives then gives $\|f_j\|_2\le Ce^{Ct}$, increasing $C$ to absorb the polynomial. The operator-norm bound in step 1.1 and Cauchy–Schwarz in the bilinear boundary pairing yield $|\int Q U_1U_2|\le C\delta e^{Ct}$.

For $\xi\ne0$, choose real orthonormal $d_1,d_2$ perpendicular to $\xi$ and set $\zeta_1=-\xi/2+\sqrt{t^2-|\xi|^2/4}\,d_2+itd_1$, $\zeta_2=-\xi/2-\sqrt{t^2-|\xi|^2/4}\,d_2-itd_1$; for $\xi=0$ choose any orthonormal pair. Direct expansion gives $\zeta_j\cdot\zeta_j=0$, $\zeta_1+\zeta_2=-\xi$ and $|\zeta_j|=\sqrt2t$. Hence $U_1U_2=e^{-i\xi\cdot x}(1+r_1+r_2+r_1r_2)$. Take a fixed smooth cutoff $\chi=1$ on $B_\rho$, supported in $B_1$. By the fractional difference norm, $\|fg\|_{H^{1/2}}\le C(\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_{H^{1/2}}+\|g\|_\infty\|f\|_{H^{1/2}})$ for bounded compactly supported factors, since the difference of a product splits into two terms. Applying this to cutoff remainders and [F3] gives $\|\chi(r_1+r_2+r_1r_2)\|_{H^{1/2}(\mathbb R^3)}\le C/t$. Fourier translation and $\langle\eta+\xi\rangle\le\sqrt2\langle\eta\rangle\langle\xi\rangle$ then give $\|e^{-i\xi\cdot x}\chi(r_1+r_2+r_1r_2)\|_{H^{1/2}}\le C\langle\xi\rangle^{1/2}/t$.

Extract the Fourier coefficient of $Q$ from the exact product identity in step 5.1. Its remainder is precisely the signed pairing of $Q$ with $e^{-i\xi\cdot x}\chi(r_1+r_2+r_1r_2)$, not with the unmodulated remainder. Weighted Fourier Cauchy–Schwarz bounds its absolute value by $CN\langle\xi\rangle^{1/2}/t$. Combine this with step 4.1 and absorb the fixed unitary Fourier factor $(2\pi)^{-3/2}$ into $C$. This proves the stated estimate with its modulation factor retained.

citations.quote: Assume countable choice and let $n\ge1$. Fourier transformation on Schwartz space extends uniquely to a surjective complex-linear isometry $\mathcal F_2:L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)\to L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$. It preserves the first-variable-linear inner product, and hence is unitary.

Assume Countable Choice. Put $\Omega=B_1(0)\subset\mathbb R^3$, fix $0<\rho<1$, and let $5/2<s<7/2$ and $s<t<2s-1$. Use the following precise intrinsic Hilbert norm on $H^s(\Omega)$. If $s=m+\theta$ with integer $m\ge0$ and $0<\theta<1$, set
$$\|v\|_{s,\Omega}^2=\sum_{|\alpha|\le m}\|D^\alpha v\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2+\sum_{|\alpha|=m}\int_{\Omega\times\Omega}\frac{|D^\alpha v(x)-D^\alpha v(y)|^2}{|x-y|^{3+2\theta}}\,dx\,dy.$$
For integer $s=3$ use just the derivative sum with $m=3$. Denote the corresponding real inner product by $(\cdot,\cdot)_{s,\Omega}$. On $\mathbb R^3$ use the unitary Fourier transform and $\|f\|_{H^r}^2=\int\langle\xi\rangle^{2r}|\widehat f(\xi)|^2d\xi$. Let $B^r_{2,\infty}(\mathbb R^3)$ have norm $\sup_{j\ge0}2^{jr}\|\mathbf1_{A_j}\widehat f\|_2$, where $A_0=\{|\xi|<2\}$ and $A_j=\{2^j\le|\xi|<2^{j+1}\}$ for $j\ge1$; the restriction space on $\Omega$ consists of restrictions of members of this whole-space Besov space.

Let $\sigma^\dagger\in H^s(\Omega)\cap B^t_{2,\infty}(\Omega)$ be real and equal to $1$ almost everywhere on $\Omega\setminus B_\rho$. Then there is $C>0$, depending on $\sigma^\dagger,s,t,\rho$, such that for every real $\sigma\in H^s(\Omega)$ also equal to $1$ there and every integer $J\ge0$,
$$-(\sigma^\dagger,\sigma-\sigma^\dagger)_{s,\Omega}\le C2^{J(2s-t-1)}\|\sigma-\sigma^\dagger\|_{H^1(\Omega)}+C2^{-J(t-s)}\|\sigma-\sigma^\dagger\|_{s,\Omega}.$$
Consequently, suppose on a specified admissible sublevel a forward map $G$ satisfies $\|\sigma-\sigma^\dagger\|_{H^1(\Omega)}\le C_0\omega(\|G(\sigma)-G(\sigma^\dagger)\|)$ with $\omega(0)=0$ and $0\le\omega\le1$. For the exact regularizer $R(\sigma)=\frac12\|\sigma\|_{s,\Omega}^2$, its exact Bregman distance is $D_R(\sigma,\sigma^\dagger)=\frac12\|\sigma-\sigma^\dagger\|_{s,\Omega}^2$, and
$$-(\sigma^\dagger,\sigma-\sigma^\dagger)_{s,\Omega}\le\frac34D_R(\sigma,\sigma^\dagger)+C_1\omega(\|G(\sigma)-G(\sigma^\dagger)\|)^{2(t-s)/(t-1)}.$$
In particular, an $H^1$ stability modulus of order $[\log(1/u)]^{-(s-3/2)}$ yields a VSC source term of order $[\log(1/u)]^{-\nu}$ with $\nu=(t-s)(2s-3)/(t-1)$. The conditional stability estimate is a hypothesis here, not a conclusion.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Weighted Fourier Cauchy–Schwarz gives $\|a\|_\infty+\|\nabla a\|_\infty\le C_s\|a\|_{H^s}$ because $\int(1+|\xi|^2)^{-s}(1+|\xi|)^2d\xi<\infty$ for $s>5/2$. The Fourier integrals for $a$ and its first derivatives converge absolutely and are continuous by dominated convergence, so these bounds hold for a $C^1$ representative. We shall also use $\|fg\|_{H^b}\le C\|f\|_{H^r}\|g\|_{H^b}$ when $r>3/2$ and $0\le b\le r$. Here is a direct justification: split Fourier space into dyadic annuli, use $\|f_j\|_\infty\le C2^{3j/2}\|f_j\|_2$ for low-high products, and $\|Q_j(f_kg_k)\|_2\le C2^{3j/2}\|f_k\|_2\|g_k\|_2$ when comparable high shells $k$ produce a shell $j\le k+C$. The low-high sum is bounded by $\|f\|_{H^r}\|g\|_{H^b}$ since $r>3/2$. For high-low products, sum the low $g$ blocks with bound $C2^{j(3/2-b)}\|g\|_{H^b}$ if $b<3/2$, a square-root logarithmic factor if $b=3/2$, or $C\|g\|_{H^b}$ if $b>3/2$; the excess $r-3/2>0$ makes the resulting geometric sum converge. For high-high products, weighted summation over $k\ge j-C$ has geometric kernel $2^{-(k-j)(r+b)}$ and excess factor $2^{j(3/2-r)}$; Cauchy–Schwarz for the input shell sequences completes the bound. The estimates are first proved for Fourier truncations and then passed to their norm limits.

For $0<\theta<1$, multiplication by a bounded $C^1$ function $h$ is bounded on $H^\theta$. Indeed $|h(x)f(x)-h(y)f(y)|^2\le2\|h\|_\infty^2|f(x)-f(y)|^2+2|f(y)|^2|h(x)-h(y)|^2$. In the last term use $|h(x)-h(y)|\le\min\{2\|h\|_\infty,\|\nabla h\|_\infty|x-y|\}$; integrating the kernel $|x-y|^{-3-2\theta}$ near and far from the diagonal gives a finite constant times $\|f\|_2^2$. Apply [F2] to get the Fourier Sobolev bound. For $\theta=0$ this is just the $L^2$ multiplier bound.

If $F$ is any smooth scalar function on a neighborhood of $[m,M]$, then $F(1+a)-F(1)$ belongs to $H^s$ with a uniform bound over this class. To verify the fractional highest derivative directly, write $s=k+\theta$ with $k=2$ or $3$ and $0\le\theta<1$. For $k=2$, the chain rule gives terms $F'(\sigma)D^2a$ and $F''(\sigma)Da\,Da$. The first term is in $H^\theta$ by step 2.1, since $F'(\sigma)$ is bounded $C^1$ uniformly; for the second, $Da\in H^{s-1}$ with $s-1>3/2$, so the algebra bound in step 1.1 and then step 2.1 apply. For $k=3$, the terms are $F'(\sigma)D^3a$, $F''(\sigma)D^2a\,Da$, and $F'''(\sigma)(Da)^3$. Here $Da\in H^{s-1}$ is a multiplier on $H^{s-2}$ by step 1.1, so $D^2a\,Da\in H^{s-2}\subset H^\theta$; the remaining products follow from the same algebra and step 2.1. Lower derivatives have the corresponding easier estimates; the function itself has an $L^2$ bound by the mean value theorem and vanishes wherever $a=0$. These calculations may first be made for smooth approximations: convolve $a$ with a nonnegative mollifier, which preserves $m\le1+a\le M$ and uniform $H^s$ and $C^1$ bounds, and then use convergence in lower Sobolev orders and weak compactness in the Hilbert $H^s$ space to identify the asserted weak derivatives and bound. A bounded sequence in this separable Fourier Hilbert space has a weakly convergent subsequence by diagonal convergence of its countable Fourier coordinates and the norm bound; hence only Countable Choice is used.

Apply step 3.1 to $F(t)=\sqrt t$, $\frac12\log t$, and $t^{-1/2}$ to obtain the stated regularity and support of $g_j-1$, $\log g_j$, and $g_j^{-1}-1$. To bound $q_j=g_j^{-1}\Delta g_j$ in $H^{s-2}$, for $s<3$ use step 2.1 with $\theta=s-2\in(1/2,1)$ and the uniform $C^1$ norm of $g_j^{-1}$; for $s\ge3$ use the multiplier bound in step 1.1 with $r=s$ and $b=s-2$. Split $g_j^{-1}=1+(g_j^{-1}-1)$ for that whole-space bound. The support statement follows from $g_j=1$ outside the collar ball and from the local definition of weak derivatives.

Put $w=\log g_1-\log g_2$, $H=g_1g_2$ and $Q=q_1-q_2$. Since $H
abla w=g_2
abla g_1-g_1
abla g_2$, distributional differentiation gives $\operatorname{div}(H
abla w)=g_2\Delta g_1-g_1\Delta g_2=HQ$. The equality follows first for smooth positive approximations and then in distributions using step 4.1 and the Sobolev products from steps 1.1–2.1; all terms also have their ordinary weak-product interpretation because $g_j$ are $C^1$ and $\Delta g_j\in L^2$. The functions $w$ and its gradient vanish outside $\overline{B_ho}$. Testing the identity with $w$ is legitimate by smooth $H^1$ approximation on a larger fixed ball, since $Q\in H^{-1}$ and multiplication by the bounded $C^1$ function $H$ is bounded on $H^1$. It gives $\int H|

A compactly supported $H^1$ function in $B_\rho\subset(-2,2)^3$ obeys $\|w\|_2\le4\|\partial_1w\|_2$: for a smooth approximation supported in the same larger cube, write $w(x_1,x')=\int_{-2}^{x_1}\partial_1w(t,x')dt$, apply Cauchy–Schwarz, and integrate in $x_1,x'$; passing to $H^1$ limits gives the inequality. Since $H\ge m$, step 5.1 and the Fourier dual bound yield $m\|\nabla w\|_2^2\le\|Q\|_{H^{-1}}\|Hw\|_{H^1}\le C\|Q\|_{H^{-1}}\|w\|_{H^1}$. Poincaré in the first sentence then implies $\|w\|_{H^1}\le C\|Q\|_{H^{-1}}$, dividing by its norm if nonzero. Finally $\sigma_1-\sigma_2=\sigma_2(e^{2w}-1)$; the uniform bounds for $w$, $\sigma_2$ and $\nabla\sigma_2$, the mean value theorem, and the ordinary weak product rule give $\|\sigma_1-\sigma_2\|_{H^1}\le C\|w\|_{H^1}$. Also $\|Q\|_{H^{-1}}\le\|Q\|_{H^{-1/2}}$ by the Fourier weights. This proves all recovery claims.

Fourier transformation on Schwartz space extends uniquely to a surjective complex-linear isometry $\mathcal F_2:L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)\to L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$. Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n\ge1$ and
$s\in\mathbb R$, and let $H^s(\mathbb R^n)$ be the real-order Bessel-potential
space with the exact norm
$$\|U\|_{H^s}=\bigl\|\langle\xi\rangle^s\mathcal F(E_sU)\bigr\|_2$$
of [[thm-fourier-characterisation-of-fractional-hilbert-sobolev-spaces]],
where $\langle\xi\rangle=(1+|\xi|^2)^{1/2}$. Fix the partition of
[[def-inhomogeneous-dyadic-frequency-partition]] and let $\Delta_jU$ be the
tempered distributions obtained by the multipliers $\varphi_j$. Then for every
$U\in\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$, $U$ lies in the image of the canonical
embedding $E_s$ (and is identified with its preimage in $H^s$) if and only if
$$\sum_{j\ge0}2^{2js}\|\Delta_jU\|_{L^2}^2<\infty,$$
where $\|\Delta_jU\|_{L^2}$ denotes the $L^2$ norm of the unique $L^2$ function
representing the tempered distribution $\Delta_jU$ when such a function exists
and is set equal to $+\infty$ otherwise (the convention is needed only for the
converse direction; for $U$ in the image of $E_s$ every $\Delta_jU$ is a
regular $L^2$ distribution, as the proof records), and in that case
$$c_{n,s,\psi}\|U\|_{H^s}^2\le\sum_{j\ge0}2^{2js}\|\Delta_jU\|_{L^2}^2\le C_{n,s,\psi}\|U\|_{H^s}^2$$
with constants depending only on $n,s$ and the partition. The low-frequency
block carries the weight $2^{0}=1$, and the series converges absolutely.

statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by

derivations.claim: We record explicitly the smooth-multiplication bound for the stated Besov convention. Write $Q_j=\mathbf1_{A_j}(D)$. For $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$, $Q_j\chi Q_k$ has Fourier kernel $(2\pi)^{-3/2}\mathbf1_{A_j}(\xi)\widehat\chi(\xi-\eta)\mathbf1_{A_k}(\eta)$. If $|j-k|\le2$, Young's integral inequality bounds its $L^2$ operator norm by a constant times $\|\widehat\chi\|_1$. If $|j-k|>2$, then $|\xi-\eta|\ge c2^{\max(j,k)}$ on these supports. Repeated integration by parts in the Fourier integral of $\chi$ gives $|\widehat\chi(\zeta)|\le C_N(1+|\zeta|)^{-N}$. Cauchy–Schwarz in the two frequency variables therefore bounds the operator norm by $C_N2^{-N\max(j,k)}2^{3(j+k)/2}$. For any real $r$, multiply these bounds by $2^{jr-kr}$ and sum over $k$. Choosing $N>2|r|+8$ makes both off-diagonal geometric sums uniformly bounded in $j$, while the near-diagonal sum has at most five terms. Hence $\|\chi f\|_{B^r_{2,\infty}}\le C_{r,\chi}\|f\|_{B^r_{2,\infty}}$. These calculations first apply to finite block sums; the same estimates give their convergence in distributions, since a Schwartz test has faster-than-polynomial Fourier decay.

The sharp annular definition agrees, up to constants, with any usual smooth inhomogeneous dyadic definition at $p=2$. Indeed a sharp annulus meets at most a fixed number of the smooth supports at neighboring scales. On that annulus, the identity $\sum\varphi_j=1$ and Cauchy–Schwarz give its $L^2$ norm at most the sum of those finitely many smooth-block $L^2$ norms; conversely each smooth symbol has magnitude at most one and support in finitely many sharp annuli. The weights $2^{jr}$ differ by only a constant at neighboring scales. The low blocks also meet only finitely many supports. This proves both Besov norm comparisons. For Hilbert Sobolev norms, [F1] gives directly $\|f\|_{H^r}^2\asymp\sum_j2^{2jr}\|Q_jf\|_2^2$, consistently with [F2].

Choose $\chi_0\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ equal to one near $\overline{B_\rho}$, and choose $\eta\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$ equal to one near $\overline\Omega$. Let $\widetilde\sigma^\dagger$ be one whole-space $B^t_{2,\infty}$ extension, whose existence is part of the restriction-space hypothesis. The compactly supported distribution $f^\dagger:=\chi_0(\widetilde\sigma^\dagger-1)$ is in $B^t_{2,\infty}(\mathbb R^3)$ by step 1.1 (the constant term multiplied by $\chi_0$ is smooth). It equals $\sigma^\dagger-1$ on $\Omega$ and vanishes outside $\overline{B_\rho}$, since the conductivity equals one in the collar. Thus $v^\dagger=\eta+f^\dagger$ is a compactly supported $B^t_{2,\infty}$ extension of $\sigma^\dagger$. In particular $v^\dagger\in H^s(\mathbb R^3)$: the squared block sum is bounded by a constant times $\sum_j2^{-2j(t-s)}<\infty$.

For $e=\sigma-\sigma^\dagger$, let $e_0$ be its zero extension. Its support lies in $\overline{B_\rho}$. Zero extension creates no boundary derivatives because $e$ vanishes on an open collar: local distributional tests near $\partial\Omega$ see zero, and interior tests give exactly the zero extensions of the weak derivatives. For $s=m+\theta$ noninteger, the whole-space top-order difference integral equals the integral over $\Omega^2$ plus $2\int_\Omega|D^\alpha e(x)|^2\int_{\mathbb R^3\setminus\Omega}|x-y|^{-3-2\theta}dy\,dx$. Where $D^\alpha e$ can be nonzero, the inner integral is bounded by $\int_{|z|\ge1-\rho}|z|^{-3-2\theta}dz<\infty$. The whole-space difference norm is therefore bounded by $C\|e\|_{s,\Omega}$, and the integer case is immediate. For $g\in L^2$, [F1] and nonnegative integration give $\int\int|g(x+h)-g(x)|^2|h|^{-3-2\theta}dx\,dh=\int|\widehat g(\xi)|^2\int|e^{i\xi\cdot h}-1|^2|h|^{-3-2\theta}dh\,d\xi$. The inner integral equals $c_\theta|\xi|^{2\theta}$ by rotation and dilation; $0<c_\theta<\infty$ follows by the bounds $|e^{iu}-1|\le\min\{2,|u|\}$. Summing derivative multipliers shows that this whole-space difference norm is equivalent to $\|e_0\|_{H^s}$. Thus $\|e_0\|_{H^s}\le C\|e\|_{s,\Omega}$, while exactly $\|e_0\|_{H^1}=\|e\|_{H^1(\Omega)}$.

Let $B_s(v,w)$ be the whole-space intrinsic bilinear form associated with the derivative and difference norm in step 3.2. Its Fourier multiplier $p_s(\xi)$ equals $\sum_{|\alpha|\le m}\xi^{2\alpha}+c_\theta\sum_{|\alpha|=m}\xi^{2\alpha}|\xi|^{2\theta}$ in the noninteger case, and just the first polynomial in the integer case. Thus $|p_s(\xi)|\le C\langle\xi\rangle^{2s}$, and $P_0:=p_s(D)v^\dagger$ belongs to $B^{t-2s}_{2,\infty}$ by the annular multiplier bound and step 3.1. Its distributional pairing with $e_0$ is $B_s(v^\dagger,e_0)$. The pairing is defined by convergent Fourier blocks: high blocks have the product bound $C2^{-j(t-s)}\|e_0\|_{H^s}$, a summable sequence. This also justifies the bilinear identity by truncation and limits, without assuming classical derivatives of order $2s$.

In the integer case the whole-space and domain pairings are identical, since every derivative of $e_0$ is supported in $\overline{B_\rho}$; take $P=P_0$. For noninteger $s=m+\theta$, their difference is $$B_s(v^\dagger,e_0)-(\sigma^\dagger,e)_{s,\Omega}=2\sum_{|\alpha|=m}\int_\Omega D^\alpha e(x)\big(A(x)D^\alpha v^\dagger(x)-b_\alpha(x)\big)dx,$$ where $A(x)=\int_{\Omega^c}|x-y|^{-3-2\theta}dy$ and $b_\alpha(x)=\int_{\Omega^c}D^\alpha\eta(y)|x-y|^{-3-2\theta}dy$. To obtain the formula, split each whole-space double integral into $\Omega^2$, $\Omega\times\Omega^c$ and its transpose; $D^\alpha e_0$ is zero outside and $v^\dagger=\eta$ there. On any fixed neighborhood of $\overline{B_\rho}$ compact in $\Omega$, every derivative of $A,b_\alpha$ is bounded, by differentiating the separated kernel and using its integrable tail. Choose $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ equal to one on that neighborhood. The domain pairing is therefore the pairing of $e_0$ with $$P=P_0-2\sum_{|\alpha|=m}(-1)^mD^\alpha\big(\chi A D^\alpha v^\dagger-\chi b_\alpha\big).$$ By step 1.1, its correction terms lie in $B^{t-2m}_{2,\infty}$: differentiation lowers the block regularity by the derivative order, multiplication by the smooth compact coefficient preserves it, and $\chi b_\alpha$ is smooth and compactly supported. Since $2m\le2s$, they also lie in $B^{t-2s}_{2,\infty}$. Hence $P\in B^{t-2s}_{2,\infty}$ in every case, and $\langle P,e_0\rangle=(\sigma^\dagger,e)_{s,\Omega}$. This treats the exact domain penalty pairing rather than replacing its norm by an equivalent one.

Put $d=t-s>0$ and $a=2s-t-1>0$. Let $P_{\le J}=\sum_{j\le J}Q_jP$. By step 5.1 and the Hilbert block norm formula, $\|P_{\le J}\|_{H^{-1}}^2\le C\sum_{j\le J}2^{2j(2s-t-1)}\le C2^{2Ja}$. Similarly $\|P-P_{\le J}\|_{H^{-s}}^2\le C\sum_{j>J}2^{2j(s-t)}\le C2^{-2Jd}$. Weighted Fourier Cauchy–Schwarz and step 3.2 now give $|\langle P,e_0\rangle|\le C2^{Ja}\|e\|_{H^1(\Omega)}+C2^{-Jd}\|e\|_{s,\Omega}$, the first claimed estimate.

Expansion of the quadratic form gives exactly $D_R(\sigma,\sigma^\dagger)=\|e\|_{s,\Omega}^2/2$. Set $W=\omega(\|G(\sigma)-G(\sigma^\dagger)\|)$. The conditional stability hypothesis and $uv\le3u^2/8+2v^2/3$ applied to the high-frequency term in step 6.1 yield $-(\sigma^\dagger,e)_{s,\Omega}\le3\|e\|_{s,\Omega}^2/8+C(2^{Ja}W+2^{-2Jd})$. If $W=0$, stability gives $e=0$. For $0<W\le1$, take the integer $J\ge0$ with $2^{-J(a+2d)}\ge W>2^{-(J+1)(a+2d)}$. Then $2^{-2Jd}\le2^{2d}W^{2d/(a+2d)}$ and $2^{Ja}W\le W^{2d/(a+2d)}$. Since $a+2d=t-1$, this proves the asserted source inequality with coefficient $3/4$ on the exact Bregman distance. Substitution of the stated logarithmic stability exponent gives $\nu=2(s-3/2)(t-s)/(t-1)$ by multiplying exponents.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. Let $\Omega=B_1(0)\subset\mathbb R^3$, fix $0<\rho<1$ and $0<m<1<M$, and let $E$ be the closed real subspace of $L^\infty(\Omega)$ consisting of functions vanishing almost everywhere outside $B_\rho(0)$. Set $\mathcal A=\{a\in E:\operatorname*{ess\,inf}(1+a)>m,\ \operatorname*{ess\,sup}(1+a)<M\}$ and $\sigma=1+a$. Choose an orthonormal spherical-harmonic basis $Y_{\ell k}$ of mean-zero $L^2(S^2)$, with $\ell\ge1$ and $1\le k\le2\ell+1$. For each basis current there is a unique weak solution $u_{\sigma,\ell k}\in H^1(\Omega)$ with boundary mean zero such that
$$\int_\Omega\sigma\nabla u_{\sigma,\ell k}\cdot\overline{\nabla v}=\int_{S^2}Y_{\ell k}\overline{\operatorname{Tr}v}\qquad(v\in H^1(\Omega)).$$
The centered sequence
$$G(a):=\big(\operatorname{Tr}(u_{\sigma,\ell k}-u_{1,\ell k})\big)_{\ell,k}$$
belongs to $Y=\ell^2(L^2(S^2))$. The map $G:\mathcal A\to Y$ is Fréchet differentiable, and both $G$ and $G'$ are Lipschitz on $\mathcal A$, with constants depending only on $m,M,\rho$ and the ball. Its derivative in direction $h\in E$ is the trace sequence of the unique boundary-mean-zero solutions
$$\int_\Omega\sigma\nabla v_{h,\ell k}\cdot\overline{\nabla w}=-\int_\Omega h\nabla u_{\sigma,\ell k}\cdot\overline{\nabla w}.$$
The uncentered sequence $(\operatorname{Tr}u_{1,\ell k})_{\ell,k}$ does not belong to $Y$. Thus absolute voltage data in this convention lie in an affine translate of $Y$, whereas data differences belong to $Y$. All complex spaces here may be regarded as real Banach spaces when taking derivatives with respect to real conductivities.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. Fix $5/2<s<7/2$, $0<\rho<1$, $0<m<1<M$ and $A>0$. Let $\sigma_j=1+a_j$ be real conductivities on $\mathbb R^3$, with $a_j$ supported in $\overline{B_\rho}$, $\|a_j\|_{H^s}\le A$, and $m\le\sigma_j\le M$, for $j=1,2$. Let $\mathscr N_j$ be their boundary-mean-zero NtD maps on $S^2=\partial B_1$, and let
$$\delta=\left(\sum_{\ell\ge1}\sum_{k=1}^{2\ell+1}\|(\mathscr N_1-\mathscr N_2)Y_{\ell k}\|_{L^2(S^2)}^2\right)^{1/2}.$$
Then there is $C>0$ depending only on $s,\rho,m,M,A$ such that
$$\|\sigma_1-\sigma_2\|_{H^1(\mathbb R^3)}\le C\left[\log(3+\delta^{-1})\right]^{-(s-3/2)}\qquad(\delta>0).$$
If $\delta=0$, the conductivities are equal. The zero-noise modulus is therefore defined to be zero. Restricting the left side to $B_1$ gives the same $H^1$ norm because the difference is supported in $\overline{B_\rho}$.

Assume Countable Choice. Put $\Omega=B_1(0)\subset\mathbb R^3$, fix $0<\rho<1$, and let $5/2<s<7/2$ and $s<t<2s-1$. Use the following precise intrinsic Hilbert norm on $H^s(\Omega)$. If $s=m+\theta$ with integer $m\ge0$ and $0<\theta<1$, set
$$\|v\|_{s,\Omega}^2=\sum_{|\alpha|\le m}\|D^\alpha v\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2+\sum_{|\alpha|=m}\int_{\Omega\times\Omega}\frac{|D^\alpha v(x)-D^\alpha v(y)|^2}{|x-y|^{3+2\theta}}\,dx\,dy.$$
For integer $s=3$ use just the derivative sum with $m=3$. Denote the corresponding real inner product by $(\cdot,\cdot)_{s,\Omega}$. On $\mathbb R^3$ use the unitary Fourier transform and $\|f\|_{H^r}^2=\int\langle\xi\rangle^{2r}|\widehat f(\xi)|^2d\xi$. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]],
> [[def-natural-numbers]]) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** [[def-choice-function]] and
[[def-axiom-of-choice]] select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and [[def-countable-choice]] does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ ([[def-power-set]], [[def-cartesian-product]], [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]]); a natural is the set of its predecessors ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense ([[def-chain]]). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

For $A_\zeta=D^2+2\zeta\cdot D$, $D=-i\nabla$, its symbol is $p_k=|\eta_k|^2+2\zeta\cdot\eta_k$, with $|\operatorname{Im}p_k|\ge s/L$. For $|\eta_k|\le4s$, this gives $|p_k|\ge s/L$; for $|\eta_k|>4s$, its real part has magnitude at least $|\eta_k|^2/2$. Hence for every real $\mu$ and $0\le v\le2$ the coefficient multiplier $G_\zeta:p_k^{-1}$ satisfies $\|G_\zeta f\|_{H^{\mu+v}(Q)}\le C_v s^{v-1}\|f\|_{H^\mu(Q)}$ for $s\ge1$. The Sobolev spaces here are defined by the shifted weighted coefficient norms. Parseval proves these bounds and $A_\zeta G_\zeta f=f$ in distributions inside $Q$, first on finite sums and then by convergence.

A second bound is $\|fg\|_{H^{-1/2}}\le C_\varepsilon\|f\|_{H^{1/2+\varepsilon}}\|g\|_{H^{1/2}}$ for every $0<\varepsilon<1$. Here the low-high and high-low estimates from step 1.1, with output weight $2^{-j/2}$, have the additional decay $2^{-\varepsilon j}$. For comparable high shells, the output estimate becomes $2^j\sum_{k\ge j-C}\|f_k\|_2\|g_k\|_2=2^{-\varepsilon j}\sum_{k\ge j-C}2^{-(k-j)(1+\varepsilon)}F_kG_k$, with $F_k=2^{k(1/2+\varepsilon)}\|f_k\|_2$ and $G_k=2^{k/2}\|g_k\|_2$. The geometric kernel has finite sum, and Cauchy–Schwarz bounds the product sequence in $\ell^1$ by $\|F\|_2\|G\|_2$. This proves the claimed bound. All product calculations first hold for finite Fourier sums; the bounds give convergence in the target Sobolev space and identify the product as the distributional limit. Whenever one factor belongs to $H^r$, $r>3/2$, its Fourier coefficients are absolutely summable by weighted Cauchy–Schwarz, so it is a bounded continuous multiplier and this distributional product agrees with the ordinary product.

The periodic and shifted Sobolev norms of the compactly supported potential are bounded by $C\|q\|_{H^{1/2+\tau}(\mathbb R^3)}\le CM$. For completeness, choose a fixed smooth cutoff equal to one on $B_1$ and supported in $B_2$. Since it multiplies $q$ without changing it, each Fourier coefficient of $q$ is the convolution of its whole-space Fourier transform with a translate of the rapidly decreasing transform of this cutoff, sampled at an integer or shifted lattice point. Weighted Cauchy–Schwarz, followed by summation over the lattice, bounds the coefficient norm by the whole-space norm: the sums $\sup_\xi\sum_k(1+|\eta_k-\xi|)^{-N}$ and the corresponding integrals are finite for $N>3$, and polynomial Sobolev weights are absorbed by increasing $N$. The reverse local bound needed later follows in the same way by multiplying the Fourier series by a smooth cutoff supported inside $Q$ and equal to one on $B_2$, then estimating the resulting convolution sum in whole-space weighted $L^2$. The cutoffs can be chosen radial before rotation, so all constants are independent of the phase direction.

Put $r_0=3/2+\tau/2$ and $h_0=r_0-1=1/2+\tau/2$. Split the periodic potential into $q=q_\sharp+q_\flat$ by retaining frequencies of size at most $2^J$ in $q_\sharp$. Then $\|q_\flat\|_{H^{h_0}}\le C2^{-J\tau/2}M$, whereas $q_\sharp$ has bounded Sobolev norms of every order with bounds depending only on $J,M$. Choose $J$, depending only on $\tau,M$, so that $G_\zeta q_\flat$ as a multiplication-composition operator has norm at most $1/4$ both on shifted $H^{r_0}$ and on shifted $H^{1/2}$. On $H^{r_0}$ this follows from the product bound in step 1.1, with multiplier $r\in H^{r_0}$ and $q_\flat\in H^{h_0}$, and the $v=1$ bound of step 1.2. On $H^{1/2}$ it follows from step 2.1 with $\varepsilon=\tau/2$ and the same $v=1$ bound. Next choose $s$ large enough, depending only on $J,M,\tau$, that $G_\zeta q_\sharp$ has norm at most $1/4$ on both spaces, using the smooth multiplier bound from step 1.1 and the $v=0$ bound $C/s$ from step 1.2. Thus $I+G_\zeta q$ has inverse given by a convergent geometric series, of norm at most two, on both spaces.

Define $r_\zeta=-(I+G_\zeta q)^{-1}G_\zeta q$ in shifted $H^{r_0}$. The forcing $q$ in the last position is the actual compactly supported function on $Q$, represented in the shifted basis; the multiplication operators use the periodic representation of the same function. These agree pointwise inside $Q$. Step 1.2 with $\mu=1/2+\tau$ and $v=1-\tau/2$ gives $\|r_\zeta\|_{H^{r_0}(Q)}\le Cs^{-\tau/2}M$. Since $r_0>3/2$, weighted Cauchy–Schwarz for its coefficients gives $\|r_\zeta\|_\infty\le C\|r_\zeta\|_{H^{r_0}(Q)}$. This solution is also the unique shifted $H^{1/2}$ solution, by the second invertibility statement in step 3.1; using step 1.2 with $\mu=1/2,v=0$ gives $\|r_\zeta\|_{H^{1/2}(Q)}\le Cs^{-1}M$. Finally, its equation is $r_\zeta=-G_\zeta(q+qr_\zeta)$; since $q\in L^2$ and $r_\zeta\in L^\infty$, the $v=2$ bound from $L^2$ gives $\|r_\zeta\|_{H^2(Q)}\le CsM(1+M)$, enlarging the threshold to keep $s\ge1$.

Applying $A_\zeta$ to the equation in step 4.1 gives $A_\zeta r_\zeta+q(1+r_\zeta)=0$ in the interior of $Q$. Direct conjugation and $\zeta\cdot\zeta=0$ show this is exactly $(-\Delta+q)(e^{i\zeta\cdot x}(1+r_\zeta))=0$. The local comparison in step 2.2 transfers the fractional bounds to restriction norms on $B_2$, and restriction gives the integer $H^2$ bound there. Pulling back the initial rotation preserves the whole-space potential norm, the support ball, and the Euclidean PDE. Since $s=|\zeta|/\sqrt2$, step 4.1 yields all displayed estimates. The construction was on a fixed larger cube, so it imposes no boundary condition on the unit ball and supplies regularity on its full neighborhood.

Assume Countable Choice. Fix $5/2<s<7/2$, $0<\rho<1$, $0<m<1<M$ and $A>0$. Suppose $\sigma_j=1+a_j$ on $\mathbb R^3$, where $a_j$ is real, supported in $\overline{B_\rho}$, $\|a_j\|_{H^s(\mathbb R^3)}\le A$, and $m\le\sigma_j\le M$, for $j=1,2$. Then $g_j=\sqrt{\sigma_j}$ and $\log g_j$ belong to $C^1$, with $g_j-1,\log g_j\in H^s(\mathbb R^3)$ supported in $\overline{B_\rho}$ and uniformly bounded in $H^s$ and $C^1$. The real Liouville potentials
$$q_j=g_j^{-1}\Delta g_j$$
belong to $H^{s-2}(\mathbb R^3)$, have support in $\overline{B_\rho}$, and have norms bounded in terms of $s,\rho,m,M,A$. Moreover,
$$\|\sigma_1-\sigma_2\|_{H^1(\mathbb R^3)}\le C\|q_1-q_2\|_{H^{-1}(\mathbb R^3)},$$
with the same dependence. In particular the right side may be replaced by $C\|q_1-q_2\|_{H^{-1/2}}$ when that stronger norm is used. The Fourier and intrinsic norms for collared variations are those of the collared Sobolev source-functional lemma.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. Let $\Omega=B_1\subset\mathbb R^3$, and let $\sigma_j=1+a_j$ be positive real conductivities with $a_j$ supported in $\overline{B_\rho}$, $\|a_j\|_{H^s}\le A$, $5/2<s<7/2$, $0<\rho<1$, and $m\le\sigma_j\le M$, for fixed positive bounds. Put $g_j=\sqrt{\sigma_j}$, $q_j=g_j^{-1}\Delta g_j$, $Q=q_1-q_2$, and $N=\|Q\|_{H^{-1/2}(\mathbb R^3)}$. Let $\mathscr N_j$ be the boundary-mean-zero Neumann-to-Dirichlet map for $\sigma_j$ on $L^2_0(S^2)$, and define the actual data difference by the centered voltage sequences
$$\delta=\left(\sum_{\ell\ge1}\sum_{k=1}^{2\ell+1}\|(\mathscr N_1-\mathscr N_2)Y_{\ell k}\|_{L^2(S^2)}^2\right)^{1/2}.$$
This quantity is finite. If $U_j=e^{i\zeta_j\cdot x}(1+r_j)$ are the solutions from the positive-Sobolev CGO lemma, then
$$\int_\Omega Q U_1U_2\,dx=\int_{S^2}f_1(\mathscr N_2-\mathscr N_1)f_2\,dS,\qquad f_j=\partial_\nu U_j\big|_{S^2},$$
and the fluxes $f_j$ have mean zero. The boundary pairing is bilinear, without complex conjugation. In particular, there are $C,T>0$ depending only on the fixed class such that for $t\ge T$ and $|\xi|\le t$ one can choose null phases with $\zeta_1+\zeta_2=-\xi$, $|\zeta_j|=\sqrt2t$, and obtain the rigorous estimate
$$|\widehat Q(\xi)|\le C\delta e^{Ct}+C\langle\xi\rangle^{1/2}t^{-1}N.$$
The factor $\langle\xi\rangle^{1/2}$ is part of this conclusion; this lemma does not assert the sharper stability estimate that would follow from dropping it.

Assume Countable Choice. Write $\langle\xi\rangle=(1+|\xi|^2)^{1/2}$ and use unitary Fourier transformation on $\mathbb R^3$. There is an absolute constant $C$ such that for every $b\ge1$ and $Q\in H^{-1/2}(\mathbb R^3)$,
$$\int_{|\xi|\le b}\langle\xi\rangle^{-1}\|e^{-i\xi\cdot x}Q\|_{H^{-1/2}}^2\,d\xi\le Cb^2\|Q\|_{H^{-1/2}}^2.$$
Consequently, if $t>0$, $L\ge0$ and $a_\xi\in H^{1/2}(\mathbb R^3)$ is any family with $\|a_\xi\|_{H^{1/2}}\le L/t$ for $|\xi|\le b$, its modulated bilinear distributional remainders
$$R(\xi)=\langle e^{-i\xi\cdot x}Q,a_\xi\rangle$$
satisfy
$$\left(\int_{|\xi|\le b}\langle\xi\rangle^{-1}|R(\xi)|^2\,d\xi\right)^{1/2}\le C\frac{Lb}{t}\|Q\|_{H^{-1/2}},$$
whenever the scalar family $R$ is measurable. No continuity or derivative bound in $\xi$ is required.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]],
> [[def-natural-numbers]]) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** [[def-choice-function]] and
[[def-axiom-of-choice]] select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and [[def-countable-choice]] does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ ([[def-power-set]], [[def-cartesian-product]], [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]]); a natural is the set of its predecessors ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense ([[def-chain]]). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

derivations.claim: Put $N=\|Q\|_{H^{-1/2}}$ and $\kappa=s-3/2>0$. For $b\ge1$, the high-frequency contribution satisfies $\int_{|\xi|>b}\langle\xi\rangle^{-1}|\widehat Q(\xi)|^2d\xi\le Cb^{-2\kappa}\|Q\|_{H^{s-2}}^2\le Cb^{-2\kappa}$. Indeed the ratio of the two Fourier weights is $\langle\xi\rangle^{-1-2(s-2)}=\langle\xi\rangle^{-2\kappa}$.

For $t\ge\max\{T,b\}$, [F2] gives the pointwise inequality $|\widehat Q(\xi)|\le C\delta e^{Ct}+(C/t)\|e^{-i\xi\cdot x}Q\|_{H^{-1/2}}$ for $|\xi|\le b$. The right side is measurable by the nonnegative Fourier integral in [F3]; thus this inequality can be integrated without selecting a measurable family of CGO phases. Square it using $(u+v)^2\le2u^2+2v^2$, multiply by $\langle\xi\rangle^{-1}$ and integrate. Since $\int_{|\xi|\le b}\langle\xi\rangle^{-1}d\xi\le Cb^2$, [F3] yields a low-frequency bound $Cb^2\delta^2 e^{Ct}+Cb^2t^{-2}N^2$, after increasing the exponential constant. Combining with step 1.1 gives $N^2\le Cb^{-2\kappa}+Cb^2\delta^2e^{Ct}+Cb^2t^{-2}N^2$. This uses the integrated modulated estimate, not an unmodulated pointwise Sobolev pairing.

Choose a fixed $K\ge\max\{T,1\}$ large enough that $C/K^2\le1/2$ for the last constant in step 2.1, and set $t=Kb$. Absorb that term into the left side and take square roots. Increasing fixed constants and using $b\le e^b$ for $b\ge1$ gives $N\le Cb^{-\kappa}+C\delta e^{Db}$ for some $D>0$ depending only on the fixed class. If $\delta=0$, let $b\to\infty$ to obtain $N=0$. If $0<\delta<e^{-2D}$, take $b=\log(1/\delta)/(2D)\ge1$. Then $\delta e^{Db}=\sqrt\delta$, which is bounded by a constant times $[\log(1/\delta)]^{-\kappa}$ because $e^{-x/2}x^\kappa$ is bounded for $x\ge1$. Hence $N\le C[\log(1/\delta)]^{-\kappa}$ for all sufficiently small positive $\delta$.

By [F1] and the Fourier weight inequality, $\|\sigma_1-\sigma_2\|_{H^1}\le C\|Q\|_{H^{-1}}\le CN$. This proves the claimed small-noise rate and, if $\delta=0$, equality of the conductivities. For larger positive $\delta$, the uniform bound $\|a_1-a_2\|_{H^1}\le2A$ and the positive lower bound for $[\log(3+\delta^{-1})]^{-\kappa}$ on that region prove the same displayed estimate after increasing $C$. On a sufficiently small noise interval, $\log(3+\delta^{-1})$ is comparable to $\log(1/\delta)$, so the two small-noise formulations agree. All constants came from the fixed class.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume countable choice and let $n\ge1$. Fourier transformation on Schwartz space extends uniquely to a surjective complex-linear isometry $\mathcal F_2:L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)\to L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$. It preserves the first-variable-linear inner product, and hence is unitary.

derivations.claim: Define $J_b(\eta)=\int_{|\xi|\le b}\langle\xi\rangle^{-1}\langle\eta-\xi\rangle^{-1}\,d\xi$. For $|\eta|\ge2b$, $|\eta-\xi|\ge|\eta|/2$ throughout the integration ball, so $\langle\eta-\xi\rangle^{-1}\le2\langle\eta\rangle^{-1}$. Polar integration gives $\int_{|\xi|\le b}\langle\xi\rangle^{-1}\,d\xi\le Cb^2$ for $b\ge1$. Hence $J_b(\eta)\le Cb^2\langle\eta\rangle^{-1}$ in this region.

If $|\eta|<2b$, Cauchy–Schwarz gives $J_b(\eta)\le(\int_{|\xi|\le b}\langle\xi\rangle^{-2}\,d\xi)^{1/2}(\int_{|\xi|\le b}\langle\eta-\xi\rangle^{-2}\,d\xi)^{1/2}$. The first integral is at most $Cb$ by polar integration. In the second, the substitution $z=\eta-\xi$ places its domain inside $B_{3b}$, so it is also at most $Cb$. Thus $J_b(\eta)\le Cb$. Since $\langle\eta\rangle\le\sqrt{1+4b^2}\le\sqrt5b$, this is at most $C' b^2\langle\eta\rangle^{-1}$. Together with step 1.1 this proves $J_b(\eta)\le Cb^2\langle\eta\rangle^{-1}$ for every $\eta$.

Fourier translation gives $\|e^{-i\xi\cdot x}Q\|_{H^{-1/2}}^2=\int\langle\eta-\xi\rangle^{-1}|\widehat Q(\eta)|^2\,d\eta$. This identity holds for Sobolev distributions as well as smooth functions, because the Fourier transform is represented by a locally square integrable function with the indicated weight, and translation preserves weighted square integrability for every fixed $\xi$. Tonelli's theorem for the nonnegative integrand and step 2.1 now give $\int_{|\xi|\le b}\langle\xi\rangle^{-1}\|e^{-i\xi\cdot x}Q\|_{H^{-1/2}}^2\,d\xi=\int|\widehat Q(\eta)|^2J_b(\eta)\,d\eta\le Cb^2\|Q\|_{H^{-1/2}}^2$.

For the bilinear duality pairing, weighted Fourier Cauchy–Schwarz gives $|\langle e^{-i\xi\cdot x}Q,a_\xi\rangle|\le\|e^{-i\xi\cdot x}Q\|_{H^{-1/2}}\|a_\xi\|_{H^{1/2}}$. The absence of complex conjugation changes the second Fourier factor to its reflection and does not change its Sobolev norm. Squaring, integrating with weight $\langle\xi\rangle^{-1}$, using the bound $L/t$, and applying step 3.1 prove the remainder estimate.

Let $X$ be a locally compact Hausdorff space. A complex Borel measure $\mu$
on $X$ is **regular** if its total variation
$|\mu|$ is a regular Borel measure in the preceding, all-Borel sense. This
total-variation convention is the one that controls $|\int f\,d\mu|$ and the
norm in the $C_0$ representation theorem.

The map $q \mapsto \hat q$ ([[def-real-numbers]]) is an embedding of ordered
fields. Every real is approximated by rationals: for $x \in \mathbb{R}$ and
rational $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $q \in \mathbb{Q}$ with
$|x - \hat q| < \hat\varepsilon$. Consequently, strictly between any two
reals lies a rational.

$\mathbb{Q} \approx \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]): the rationals are
countably infinite ([[def-countable]]).

**No choice principle is used.** The one place where a reader expects a choice,
"pick a representative $a/b$ of each rational", is exactly where
[[lem-rat-positive-denominator]] applies: every rational *has* a representative
with positive denominator, so the map $(a,b) \mapsto [(a,b)]$ defined on
$\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ is already **surjective** onto $\mathbb{Q}$,
and countability follows from a surjection without ever selecting a
representative. The same device handles $\mathbb{Z}$, which is a surjective image
of $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ by construction ([[def-integers]]).

If $A$ and $B$ are at most countable ([[def-countable]]) then so is
$A \times B$.

**No choice principle is used**: the two enumerations are given, and the
enumeration of the product is written down from them.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.
Let $0<r<R$ and $n\ge 1$. Then there exists a smooth function $\rho:\mathbb R^n\to [0,1]$ such that $\rho=1$ on $\overline B_r(0)$ and $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)\subseteq B_R(0)$.

derivations.claim: Set $\lambda:=\mu-\nu$. Let $X$ be a locally compact Hausdorff space. A complex Borel measure $\mu$
on $X$ is **regular** if its total variation
$|\mu|$ is a regular Borel measure in the preceding, all-Borel sense. This
total-variation convention is the one that controls $|\int f\,d\mu|$ and the
norm in the $C_0$ representation theorem.

Let $\nu$ be a signed measure or a complex measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$. Then
$|\nu|$ is a measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$.

derivations.claim: For every Borel $A$ and every countable Borel partition $(A_j)$ of $A$, the Euclidean norm satisfies $|\mu(A_j)|\le\sum_{i=1}^m|\mu_i(A_j)|$. Summing over $j$ gives $V(A)\le\lambda(A)$ for $\lambda:=\sum_{i=1}^m|\mu_i|$, so $V$ is finite and $V(\Omega)<\infty$.

If $A=\bigsqcup_{k\ge1}E_k$ is a disjoint Borel union, then intersecting any partition of $A$ with each $E_k$ and using countable additivity of each coordinate shows $V(A)\le\sum_kV(E_k)$. Conversely, for fixed $N$ and $\varepsilon>0$, choose for each of the finitely many $k\le N$ a partition of $E_k$ whose sum exceeds $V(E_k)-\varepsilon/N$. Their union, together with $A\setminus\bigcup_{k\le N}E_k$, is a partition of $A$, so $V(A)\ge\sum_{k\le N}V(E_k)-\varepsilon$. Letting $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ and then $N\to\infty$ proves countable additivity. Thus $V$ is a finite positive Borel measure.

For every $f\in C_c(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)$ with $|f|\le1$, approximate $f$ uniformly by finite-valued Borel simple functions whose values have norm at most one. The partition definition bounds each simple integral by $V(\Omega)$, and finiteness of the coordinate measures lets the uniform errors tend to zero. Hence the displayed supremum is at most $V(\Omega)$.

Since $V\le\lambda$ and $\lambda$ is a finite Radon measure, for every Borel $A$ and $\varepsilon>0$ there is compact $K\subseteq A$ with $\lambda(A\setminus K)<\varepsilon$, whence $V(A\setminus K)<\varepsilon$. There is also an open $G\supseteq A$ with $\lambda(G\setminus A)<\varepsilon$, whence $V(G\setminus A)<\varepsilon$. These are inner and outer regularity of $V$; therefore $V$ is Radon.

If $V(\Omega)=0$, the zero field proves the reverse inequality. Otherwise fix $0<\varepsilon<V(\Omega)/4$ and choose a countable Borel partition $(A_j)$ with sum greater than $V(\Omega)-\varepsilon$; truncate after $N\ge1$ so the tail is below $\varepsilon$. Omit indices with $\mu(A_j)=0$ or $V(A_j)\le\varepsilon/(4N)$; the sum of the omitted partition values is at most $\varepsilon/4$. For every retained index, inner regularity [F1] gives a nonempty compact $K_j\subset A_j$ with $V(A_j\setminus K_j)<\varepsilon/(8N)$. The finitely many disjoint compact sets have disjoint relatively compact open neighborhoods; outer regularity [F1] lets us choose such neighborhoods $U_j$ with $V(U_j\setminus K_j)<\varepsilon/(8N)$. Define $$\psi_j(x):=\frac{\operatorname{dist}(x,\Omega\setminus U_j)}{\operatorname{dist}(x,\Omega\setminus U_j)+\operatorname{dist}(x,K_j)}.$$ This is continuous and compactly supported, equals one on $K_j$, and vanishes outside $U_j$. Set $e_j=\mu(A_j)/|\mu(A_j)|$ and $f=\sum_j e_j\psi_j$. The disjoint supports imply $|f|\le1$. For bounded Borel vector fields, the partition definition and uniform simple-function approximation give $|\int g\cdot d\mu|\le\int|g|\,dV$. Thus replacing $e_j\mathbf1_{A_j}$ by $e_j\psi_j$ loses at most $V(A_j\setminus K_j)+V(U_j\setminus K_j)$ for each retained $j$. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

The map $q \mapsto \hat q$ ([[def-real-numbers]]) is an embedding of ordered
fields. Every real is approximated by rationals: for $x \in \mathbb{R}$ and
rational $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $q \in \mathbb{Q}$ with
$|x - \hat q| < \hat\varepsilon$. Consequently, strictly between any two
reals lies a rational.

$\mathbb{Q} \approx \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]): the rationals are
countably infinite ([[def-countable]]).

**No choice principle is used.** The one place where a reader expects a choice,
"pick a representative $a/b$ of each rational", is exactly where
[[lem-rat-positive-denominator]] applies: every rational *has* a representative
with positive denominator, so the map $(a,b) \mapsto [(a,b)]$ defined on
$\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ is already **surjective** onto $\mathbb{Q}$,
and countability follows from a surjection without ever selecting a
representative. The same device handles $\mathbb{Z}$, which is a surjective image
of $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ by construction ([[def-integers]]).

If $A$ and $B$ are at most countable ([[def-countable]]) then so is
$A \times B$.

**No choice principle is used**: the two enumerations are given, and the
enumeration of the product is written down from them.
Let $0<r<R$ and $n\ge 1$. Then there exists a smooth function $\rho:\mathbb R^n\to [0,1]$ such that $\rho=1$ on $\overline B_r(0)$ and $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)\subseteq B_R(0)$.

derivations.claim: If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the empty family proves the claim. Otherwise, for $m\ge1$ set $K_m=\{x:|x|\le m,\ \operatorname{dist}(x,\Omega^c)\ge1/m\}$ when $\Omega\ne\mathbb R^n$, and set $K_m=\overline B(0,m)$ when $\Omega=\mathbb R^n$; put $K_m=\varnothing$ for $m\le0$. Each $K_m$ is compact by [F1], the sets are nested, $K_m\subset\operatorname{int}K_{m+1}$, and their interiors cover $\Omega$. The compact shells $S_m:=K_m\setminus\operatorname{int}K_{m-1}$ cover $\Omega$ and lie in the open sets $U_m:=\operatorname{int}K_{m+1}\setminus K_{m-2}$. The family $(U_m)$ is locally finite: any compact subset of $\Omega$ lies in some $\operatorname{int}K_N$ and hence in $K_{m-2}$ for all sufficiently large $m$.

Fix once a smooth nonnegative cutoff $\theta$ equal to one on $\overline B(0,1)$ and supported in $B(0,2)$, whose existence is [F3]. In each $U_m$, consider the rational inner balls $B(q,r)$ for which $\overline B(q,2r)\subset U_m\cap V_\ell$ for some cover index $\ell$. Indexed by $(\ell,q,r)$, these balls form a countable cover of $S_m$: for each point choose a cover member containing it, then density [F2] gives a rational center and radius with the required doubled closure. Compactness of $S_m$ gives a finite subcover. Order all finite lists of eligible indexed balls by natural-number codes and take the first list covering $S_m$; thus no choice principle is needed. For each selected ball use the fixed rescaled cutoff $\psi_{m,j}(x):=\theta((x-q)/r)$. The family is locally finite because each shell contributes finitely many cutoffs supported in $U_m$, and each support also lies in its assigned cover member. Its sum $s:=\sum_{m,j}\psi_{m,j}$ is smooth and positive on $\Omega$ because the shells cover $\Omega$.

Define $\eta_{m,j}:=\psi_{m,j}/s$. Then each function is smooth, nonnegative and compactly supported in $\Omega$, the family is locally finite, and $\sum_{m,j}\eta_{m,j}=1$. Each support remains in its assigned cover member, and enumeration gives the required countable family.

If $K=\varnothing$, the zero function approximates $f$ within $\varepsilon/3$. Otherwise cover $K$ by finitely many inner balls whose doubled closed balls lie in $\Omega$, using compactness [F1]. Choose the corresponding bumps from [F2] and combine them as $\chi:=1-\prod_j(1-\chi_j)$. Then $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ and $\chi=1$ on $K$, so $\|f-\chi f\|_\infty\le\varepsilon/3$.

Extend $g:=\chi f$ by zero to $\mathbb R^n$. It is continuous and compactly supported, hence uniformly continuous. Fix a nonnegative smooth bump from [F2], normalize its integral to one, and rescale it as $\rho_\delta(x)=\delta^{-n}\rho(x/\delta)$. Then $g*\rho_\delta\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n)$ and $$\|g*\rho_\delta-g\|_\infty\le\sup_{|h|\le\delta,\ x\in\mathbb R^n}|g(x-h)-g(x)|\to0.$$ For sufficiently small $\delta$, its support remains in $\Omega$ because $\operatorname{supp}g$ is compactly contained there. Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

For $n\ge3$, assume [A1]. For $i<n$ define $h_i(x_1,\ldots,\widehat{x_i},\ldots,x_{n-1}):=\int_\mathbb R g_i(x_1,\ldots,\widehat{x_i},\ldots,x_{n-1},x_n)\,dx_n$. Tonelli [F1] makes each $h_i$ integrable. Applying Hölder [F2] in $x_n$ to the first $n-1$ factors and then Tonelli gives an upper bound for the left side of $\int_{\mathbb R^{n-1}}g_n(x')^{1/(n-1)}\prod_{i<n}h_i(\widehat{x_i}')^{1/(n-1)}\,dx'$. Set $H(x'):=\prod_{i<n}h_i(\widehat{x_i}')^{1/(n-2)}$. Hölder in $x'$ with exponents $(n-1)/(n-2)$ and $n-1$ bounds this by $(\int H)^{(n-2)/(n-1)}(\int g_n)^{1/(n-1)}$. The induction hypothesis [A1] bounds $\int H\le\prod_{i<n}(\int h_i)^{1/(n-2)}$, while Tonelli gives $\int h_i=\int g_i$. Substitution yields the claimed product bound in dimension $n$.
Induction from the base case [step 1.1] through step 1.2 proves the inequality for every integer $n\ge2$.

approximation for arbitrary Borel $E$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.
Let $0<r<R$ and $n\ge 1$. Then there exists a smooth function $\rho:\mathbb R^n\to [0,1]$ such that $\rho=1$ on $\overline B_r(0)$ and $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)\subseteq B_R(0)$.

For a distribution $u\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ in the convention of [[def-distribution]] and a multi-index $\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$, its **distributional derivative** is
$$\langle\partial^\alpha u,\varphi\rangle=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\langle u,\partial^\alpha\varphi\rangle\qquad(\varphi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)).$$
The test derivative is a continuous linear endomorphism by [[thm-test-function-operations-are-continuous]]. Its composition with $u$, multiplied by the indicated sign, is therefore a continuous complex-linear functional, so this definition produces a distribution. The pairing is bilinear, with no complex conjugation. For $\alpha=0$ the operation is the identity; for one coordinate derivative its sign is minus. Every derivative of the zero distribution is zero, including on the empty domain. No choice axiom enters this construction. Compatibility with classical derivatives requires an integration-by-parts argument where it is used; it is not part of the definition.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

Let $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{C}$ be locally integrable, let
$\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ have mass $1$, and let
$\varphi_\varepsilon$ be the associated mollifier. Then for every
$\varepsilon > 0$, the convolution

$$ (f*\varphi_\varepsilon)(x) := \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f(y)\varphi_\varepsilon(x-y)\,dy $$

is smooth, and for every multi-index $\alpha$,

$$ \partial^\alpha(f*\varphi_\varepsilon) = f*(\partial^\alpha \varphi_\varepsilon). $$

An **$L^1$ approximate identity** on $\mathbb{R}^n$ is a family
$(K_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ of functions in $L^1(\mathbb{R}^n)$, where

$$\|K_\varepsilon\|_1:=\int_{\mathbb{R}^n}|K_\varepsilon(x)|\,dx,$$

such that:

1. $\int_{\mathbb{R}^n} K_\varepsilon(x)\,dx = 1$ for every $\varepsilon > 0$;
2. there is $M < \infty$ with $\|K_\varepsilon\|_1 \le M$ for every
   $\varepsilon > 0$;
3. for every $\delta > 0$,
   $$ \int_{|x|>\delta} |K_\varepsilon(x)|\,dx \longrightarrow 0 \qquad(\varepsilon \to 0^+). $$

This is the general notion used later for both compactly supported mollifiers
and the Gaussian family.

Let $\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ satisfy

$$ \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} \varphi(x)\,dx = 1. $$

For $\varepsilon > 0$, define

$$ \varphi_\varepsilon(x) := \varepsilon^{-n}\varphi(x/\varepsilon) \qquad(x \in \mathbb{R}^n). $$

The family $(\varphi_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ is the **mollifier family
generated by $\varphi$**.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice.

Let $\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ satisfy
$\int \varphi = 1$, and let
$\varphi_\varepsilon(x) = \varepsilon^{-n}\varphi(x/\varepsilon)$. Then
$(\varphi_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ is an $L^1$ approximate identity.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice.

Let $(K_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ be an $L^1$ approximate identity on
$\mathbb{R}^n$. If $1 \le p < \infty$ and $f \in L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$, then

$$\|f*K_\varepsilon - f\|_p \longrightarrow 0 \qquad(\varepsilon \to 0^+).$$

Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]).

- A **separation** of $X$ is an ordered pair $(U, V)$ of **open**, **nonempty**,
  **disjoint** subsets of $X$ with $U \cup V = X$.
- $X$ is **disconnected** when a separation of $X$ exists, and **connected** when
  none does.
- A subset $A \subseteq X$ is a **connected subset** of $X$ when the space
  $(A, \mathcal{T}_A)$ is connected, $\mathcal{T}_A$ being the subspace topology
  ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]). "Disconnected subset" is read the same way.

Since $U$ and $V$ are complementary in $X$, each of them is closed as well as
open; so a separation is the same thing as a partition of $X$ into two nonempty
clopen pieces ([[def-topological-space]]). The **clopen** subsets of $X$ are
those that are both open and closed, and $\varnothing$ and $X$ are always among
them.

**The empty space and the one-point space are connected in this library.**
Neither admits a separation: a separation requires two nonempty disjoint sets
whose union is the whole space, and neither $\varnothing$ nor a singleton can be
written as such a union. So both are connected under the definition above,
without any special clause. **This is a live convention fork** and the competing
choice is recorded in [[rem-connectedness-conventions]]; nothing on this page
depends on which is taken except the reading of the word "connected" applied to
those two spaces.

**Connectedness is a property of a space, not of an ambient pair.** The condition
above mentions only $(X,\mathcal{T})$. When it is applied to $A \subseteq X$ it
is applied to the space $(A, \mathcal{T}_A)$, so it does not change if $A$ is
regarded as a subspace of some other space inducing the same topology on $A$; in
particular a subset of $A$ is connected as a subset of $A$ exactly when it is
connected as a subset of $X$, by transitivity of the subspace topology
([[def-subspace-topology-top]]). This is why "connected" may be used of a subset
with no ambient space named.

**Spelled out for a subset.** $A \subseteq X$ is disconnected exactly when there
are open $U, V \subseteq X$ with

$$A \subseteq U \cup V, \qquad U \cap A \ne \varnothing, \qquad V \cap A \ne \varnothing, \qquad U \cap V \cap A = \varnothing,$$

because the open sets of $(A,\mathcal{T}_A)$ are precisely the traces $U \cap A$.
Note the last condition: it asks $U$ and $V$ to be disjoint **on $A$**, not in
$X$. Requiring $U \cap V = \varnothing$ outright is a strictly stronger demand
and is a different notion.

**The two-point discrete space.** Write $\mathbf{2} := \{0,1\}$ with the discrete
topology ([[def-standard-topologies]]), in which every subset is open. A
separation of $X$ is the same datum as a surjective continuous map
$X \to \mathbf{2}$ ([[def-continuous-map-top]]): given $(U,V)$, the map sending
$U$ to $0$ and $V$ to $1$ is continuous because the preimage of each of the four
open subsets of $\mathbf{2}$ is one of $\varnothing$, $U$, $V$, $X$; given a
surjective continuous $\chi : X \to \mathbf{2}$, the pair
$(\chi^{-1}[\{0\}], \chi^{-1}[\{1\}])$ is a separation. This reformulation is
proved as a theorem on this page and is recorded here only to name $\mathbf{2}$.

**Separated sets.** Two subsets $A_1, A_2 \subseteq X$ are **separated in $X$**
when

$$\overline{A_1} \cap A_2 = \varnothing \qquad \text{and} \qquad A_1 \cap \overline{A_2} = \varnothing,$$

closures taken in $X$ ([[def-interior-closure-boundary-top]],
[[thm-closure-characterisation-top]]). Separated sets are disjoint, since
$A_1 \subseteq \overline{A_1}$; the converse fails. This is verbatim the
condition [[def-connected-r]] uses on the real line, transported to an arbitrary
space, and the theorem relating it to the definition above is the next lemma on
this page.

**Totally disconnected spaces, and the empty case.** The vocabulary for a space
all of whose connected subsets are single points is fixed later on this page,
together with the components; it is not defined here because it is stated in
terms of components.

The map $q \mapsto \hat q$ ([[def-real-numbers]]) is an embedding of ordered
fields. Every real is approximated by rationals: for $x \in \mathbb{R}$ and
rational $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $q \in \mathbb{Q}$ with
$|x - \hat q| < \hat\varepsilon$. Consequently, strictly between any two
reals lies a rational.

$\mathbb{Q} \approx \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]): the rationals are
countably infinite ([[def-countable]]).

**No choice principle is used.** The one place where a reader expects a choice,
"pick a representative $a/b$ of each rational", is exactly where
[[lem-rat-positive-denominator]] applies: every rational *has* a representative
with positive denominator, so the map $(a,b) \mapsto [(a,b)]$ defined on
$\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ is already **surjective** onto $\mathbb{Q}$,
and countability follows from a surjection without ever selecting a
representative. The same device handles $\mathbb{Z}$, which is a surjective image
of $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ by construction ([[def-integers]]).

If $A$ and $B$ are at most countable ([[def-countable]]) then so is
$A \times B$.

**No choice principle is used**: the two enumerations are given, and the
enumeration of the product is written down from them.

derivations.claim: Let $B\Subset\Omega$ be any open ball and choose concentric balls $B\Subset B'\Subset B''\Subset\Omega$. By [F1] take $\chi\in C_c^\infty(B'')$ equal to one on $B'$, and extend $w:=\chi u$ by zero to $\mathbb R^n$. For sufficiently small $\varepsilon$, every mollifier centered at a point of $B$ is supported in $B'$. For such a point $x$, differentiating the convolution gives $\partial_i(w*\rho_\varepsilon)(x)=-\int_{B'}u(y)\partial_{y_i}\rho_\varepsilon(x-y)\,dy=0$ by the distributional identity [F2]. Thus $w*\rho_\varepsilon$ is constant on the convex ball $B$ by the one-dimensional fundamental theorem along each segment.

Since $w=u$ on $B'$, the approximate-identity property [F4] gives $w*\rho_{\varepsilon_j}\to u$ in $L^1(B)$ for a sequence $\varepsilon_j\downarrow0$. Write each constant from step 1.1 as $c_j$. The $L^1(B)$ convergence makes $(c_j)$ Cauchy because $|B||c_j-c_k|\le\|c_j-u\|_{L^1(B)}+\|c_k-u\|_{L^1(B)}$. Its limit $c_B$ satisfies $u=c_B$ almost everywhere on $B$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, any constant satisfies the conclusion. Otherwise fix one ball and let $c$ be its almost-everywhere value. Let $S$ be the set of points of $\Omega$ having a neighborhood on which $u=c$ almost everywhere. It is nonempty and open. If $x\in\overline S\cap\Omega$, choose a ball $B\Subset\Omega$ containing $x$ and a point of $S$; step 2.1 makes $u$ almost everywhere constant on $B$, and its positive-measure intersection with a neighborhood from $S$ forces that constant to be $c$. Thus $x\in S$, so $S$ is relatively closed. Connectedness [F5] gives $S=\Omega$. By the countable rational base [F6], choose a countable cover of $\Omega$ by rational balls contained in these neighborhoods; the union of their exceptional null sets is null, hence $u=c$ almost everywhere on all of $\Omega$.
