citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $u\in L^1(\Omega;\mathbb R)$, where elements of $L^1$ are almost-everywhere equivalence classes. For each $i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}$, its distributional derivative $D_i u$ acts on $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ by
$$\langle D_i u,\varphi\rangle:=-\int_\Omega u\,\partial_i\varphi\,dx.$$
The function $u$ is in $BV(\Omega)$ when each $D_i u$ is represented by a finite signed Radon measure and the resulting vector-valued measure $Du=(D_1u,\ldots,D_nu)$ has finite total variation. Here a finite vector-valued Radon measure means that its partition variation is a finite Radon measure. For a Borel set $A\subseteq\Omega$, define
$$|Du|(A):=\sup\left\{\sum_{j=1}^\infty |Du(A_j)|:\ (A_j)_{j\ge1}\text{ is a Borel partition of }A\right\},$$
using the Euclidean norm on each vector value. Define the spatial total variation by $TV(u;\Omega):=|Du|(\Omega)$. A Lebesgue-measurable set $E\subseteq\Omega$ of finite measure has finite perimeter relative to $\Omega$ when $\chi_E\in BV(\Omega)$; its relative perimeter is $P(E;\Omega):=TV(\chi_E;\Omega)$.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $\mu=(\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_m)$ have finite signed Radon coordinate measures. For Borel $A\subseteq\Omega$ define $$V(A):=\sup\left\{\sum_{j=1}^\infty |\mu(A_j)|:(A_j)_{j\ge1}\text{ is a Borel partition of }A\right\},$$ where the norm is Euclidean. Then $V$ is a finite positive Radon measure and $$V(\Omega)=\sup\left\{\int_\Omega f\cdot d\mu:f\in C_c(\Omega;\mathbb R^m),\ |f(x)|\le1\right\}.$$

Let $X$ be locally compact Hausdorff and let $f:X\to\mathbb F$ be continuous,
where $\mathbb F$ is $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$. Its support is
$\operatorname{supp}f:=\overline{\{x:f(x)\ne0\}}$. Put
$C_c(X;\mathbb F)=\{f\in C(X;\mathbb F):\operatorname{supp}f\text{ is compact}\}$.
Also $C_0(X;\mathbb F)$ consists of those $f$ for which, for every $\epsilon>0$,
$\{x:|f(x)|\ge\epsilon\}$ is compact. We write $C_c(X)$ for the real space
until the bounded complex $C_0$ theorem is invoked; $C_0(X)$ later means the
complex space when its scalar field matters.
For every open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, the space $C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ is dense in $C_0(\Omega)$ in the uniform norm.

Assume Countable Choice. For every open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, every bounded real linear functional on $C_0(U;\mathbb R)$ is integration against a unique finite signed Radon measure. No Dependent Choice assumption is required.

derivations.claim: Suppose $u\in BV(\Omega)$ and write $\mu=Du$. The distributional derivative identity gives $\int_\Omega u\,\operatorname{div}\varphi\,dx=-\int_\Omega\varphi\cdot d\mu$. The continuous-field dual formula [F2] bounds the supremum over smooth fields by $|\mu|(\Omega)$. Conversely, for any $f\in C_c(\Omega;\mathbb R^n)$ with $|f|\le1$, for every $\varepsilon>0$, density [F3] gives one smooth compactly supported $g$ with $\|g-f\|_\infty<\varepsilon$; replacing $g$ by $g/\max(1,\|g\|_\infty)$ keeps the unit bound and changes this error by at most another $\varepsilon$. Finiteness of the coordinate measures bounds the integral error by a fixed constant times $\varepsilon$. Letting $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ (without selecting a sequence of approximants) shows that the smooth supremum is at least the continuous-field supremum $|\mu|(\Omega)$. Thus $V(u)=TV(u;\Omega)$.

Assume [A1], let real-valued $u\in L^1(\Omega)$, and suppose $M:=V(u)<\infty$. For each coordinate $i$, define $L_i(\psi):=-\int_\Omega u\,\partial_i\psi\,dx$ on real $C_c^\infty(\Omega)$. Taking the test vector with only its $i$th component equal to $\psi$ and also its negative shows $|L_i(\psi)|\le M\|\psi\|_\infty$. By density [F3], $L_i$ extends uniquely to a bounded real linear functional on real $C_0(\Omega)$. Apply [F4] directly to this real functional to obtain a finite signed Radon measure $\mu_i$ representing $D_i u$. Applying [F2] to $\mu=(\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_n)$ and using [F3] to pass between continuous and smooth unit fields gives $|\mu|(\Omega)=M$. Hence $u\in BV(\Omega)$ and $TV(u;\Omega)=M$.

If the $L^1$ limit $u$ is already in $BV(\Omega)$, boundedness of $\operatorname{div}\varphi$ gives $\int u\,\operatorname{div}\varphi=\lim_k\int u_k\,\operatorname{div}\varphi$ for each admissible $\varphi$. Each approximating integral is at most $TV(u_k;\Omega)$ by step 1.1, so taking the supremum gives $TV(u;\Omega)\le\liminf_kTV(u_k;\Omega)$; this branch uses no choice axiom.

If only $L:=\liminf_kTV(u_k;\Omega)<\infty$ is known, choose a subsequence whose variations converge to $L$. The same test-integral limit gives $V(u)\le L$. Under [A1], step 1.2 implies $u\in BV(\Omega)$ and $TV(u;\Omega)=V(u)\le L$. If $L=+\infty$, the extended inequality is automatic.

boundaries.evidence: For Omega=empty, test integrals, derivative measures and both variation values are zero. Steps 1.1–1.2 and2.1–3.1 remain valid in the zero L1/C0 spaces.

If the test supremum M=0, every coordinate functional L_i in step 1.2 is zero, so its representing measure is zero. The already-BV formula in step 1.1 also includes Du=0 without normalization by its mass.

For n=1 the vector test has a single scalar component. The coordinate extension and real Radon representation in step 1.2 then require only one finite signed measure; all later inequalities are unchanged.

Step 3.1 distinguishes finite liminf L, which implies BV membership under CC, from L=+infinity, which gives only the automatic extended inequality. It does not incorrectly infer finite variation of an arbitrary infinite-liminf limit.

boundaries.reason: All distributional tests have compact support inside open Omega; no trace or domain-boundary endpoint value is asserted. Lower-semicontinuity concerns L1 limits, not pointwise endpoint limits.

boundaries.evidence: Step 1.1 takes one smooth approximant for each fixed epsilon and then lets epsilon tend to0, preserving the choice-free already-BV formula. Step 1.2 invokes the explicitly CC real Euclidean Radon supplier; no general DC Riesz theorem is used. Subsequence indices in step 3.1 exist by the finite-liminf condition.
For the finite-test characterization V(u)<infinity iff u in BV, the direction BV implies finite V and equality is proved in step 1.1, using the finite vector measure dual formula.

For the same characterization, finite V on arbitrary L1 yields bounded coordinate functionals and finite signed Radon derivatives by the CC real representation theorem in step 1.2; equality to vector variation is then established there.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $n\ge1$ and assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Lebesgue measure on
$\mathbb R^n$ is a Radon measure, and it is regular in the stronger
compact-inner-regular-on-all-Borel-sets convention.

An **$L^1$ approximate identity** on $\mathbb{R}^n$ is a family
$(K_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ of functions in $L^1(\mathbb{R}^n)$, where

$$\|K_\varepsilon\|_1:=\int_{\mathbb{R}^n}|K_\varepsilon(x)|\,dx,$$

such that:

1. $\int_{\mathbb{R}^n} K_\varepsilon(x)\,dx = 1$ for every $\varepsilon > 0$;
2. there is $M < \infty$ with $\|K_\varepsilon\|_1 \le M$ for every
   $\varepsilon > 0$;
3. for every $\delta > 0$,
   $$ \int_{|x|>\delta} |K_\varepsilon(x)|\,dx \longrightarrow 0 \qquad(\varepsilon \to 0^+). $$

This is the general notion used later for both compactly supported mollifiers
and the Gaussian family.

Let $\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ satisfy

$$ \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} \varphi(x)\,dx = 1. $$

For $\varepsilon > 0$, define

$$ \varphi_\varepsilon(x) := \varepsilon^{-n}\varphi(x/\varepsilon) \qquad(x \in \mathbb{R}^n). $$

The family $(\varphi_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ is the **mollifier family
generated by $\varphi$**.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice.

Let $\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ satisfy
$\int \varphi = 1$, and let
$\varphi_\varepsilon(x) = \varepsilon^{-n}\varphi(x/\varepsilon)$. Then
$(\varphi_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ is an $L^1$ approximate identity.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice.

Let $(K_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ be an $L^1$ approximate identity on
$\mathbb{R}^n$. If $1 \le p < \infty$ and $f \in L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$, then

$$\|f*K_\varepsilon - f\|_p \longrightarrow 0 \qquad(\varepsilon \to 0^+).$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

Let $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{C}$ be locally integrable, let
$\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ have mass $1$, and let
$\varphi_\varepsilon$ be the associated mollifier. Then for every
$\varepsilon > 0$, the convolution

$$ (f*\varphi_\varepsilon)(x) := \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f(y)\varphi_\varepsilon(x-y)\,dy $$

is smooth, and for every multi-index $\alpha$,

$$ \partial^\alpha(f*\varphi_\varepsilon) = f*(\partial^\alpha \varphi_\varepsilon). $$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

For every open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and real-valued $u\in BV(\Omega)$, $$TV(u;\Omega)=\sup\left\{\int_\Omega u\,\operatorname{div}\varphi\,dx:\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^n),\ |\varphi(x)|\le1\right\}.$$ If $u_k,u\in BV(\Omega)$ are real-valued and $u_k\to u$ in $L^1(\Omega)$, then $TV(u;\Omega)\le\liminf_kTV(u_k;\Omega)$. In addition, assuming Countable Choice, for any real-valued $u\in L^1(\Omega)$ the displayed supremum is finite if and only if $u\in BV(\Omega)$, with equality to $TV(u;\Omega)$; under the same assumption, an $L^1$ limit of real-valued BV functions with bounded liminf total variation belongs to $BV(\Omega)$ and satisfies the same lower-semicontinuity inequality.

If an open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ is covered by a countable family of open sets $(V_\ell)_{\ell\in I}$, then there is a countable locally finite family of nonnegative functions $(\eta_j)\subset C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ summing to one, with each $\operatorname{supp}\eta_j$ contained in one member $V_\ell$ of the cover. Locally finite means that each point has a neighborhood meeting only finitely many supports.
Let $0<r<R$ and $n\ge 1$. Then there exists a smooth function $\rho:\mathbb R^n\to [0,1]$ such that $\rho=1$ on $\overline B_r(0)$ and $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)\subseteq B_R(0)$.

abla\eta_j)*ho_\varepsilon	o u

abla\eta_j)*ho_{\varepsilon_j}-u

This sum is locally finite: for a compact $C\Subset\Omega$, choose $r>0$ so its closed $r$-neighborhood $C_r$ is compactly contained in $\Omega$. For all sufficiently large $j$, $\varepsilon_j<r$; if the thickened support of $w_j$ meets $C$, then $\operatorname{supp}\eta_j$ meets $C_r$, and local finiteness of $(\eta_j)$ leaves only finitely many such indices. Thus $u_\delta$ is smooth by [F3]. Summing the first error terms and using $\sum_j\eta_j=1$ gives $\|u_\delta-u\|_{L^1(\Omega)}<\delta$.

The product rule follows by testing against $C_c^\infty$: $D(\eta_j u)=\eta_jDu+u
abla\eta_j\,dx$. Convolution commutes with distributional derivatives by the defining test pairing and Fubini [F4]. Since $\sum_j\eta_j=1$, local finiteness gives $\sum_j u
abla\eta_j=0$. Therefore $
abla u_\delta=\sum_j (\eta_jDu)*ho_{\varepsilon_j}+\sum_j ig((u
abla\eta_j)*ho_{\varepsilon_j}-u

Take $\delta_k=1/k$ and set $u_k=u_{\delta_k}$. Step 2.1 gives $u_k\to u$ in $L^1$, while step 3.1 gives $\limsup_k\int_\Omega|\nabla u_k|\,dx\le TV(u;\Omega)$. Since each $u_{1/(2k)}$ and its gradient are integrable, choose $R_k$ so its $L^1$ tail, gradient tail, and $C\|u_{1/(2k)}\|_1/R_k$ are all below $1/k$. The products $\chi_{R_k}u_{1/(2k)}$ are compactly supported and smooth, converge to $u$ in $L^1$, and have gradient integrals bounded above by $TV(u;\mathbb R^n)+O(1/k)$; lower semicontinuity gives convergence of their variations as well.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice. For every open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and $u\in BV(\Omega)$ there is a sequence $u_k\in C^\infty(\Omega)$ such that $u_k\to u$ in $L^1(\Omega)$ and $\int_\Omega |\nabla u_k|\,dx\to TV(u;\Omega)$. When $\Omega=\mathbb R^n$, the approximating functions may be chosen compactly supported.

Let $n\ge2$. For each $i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}$ let $g_i:\mathbb R^{n-1}\to[0,\infty)$ be Lebesgue-measurable and integrable, with its arguments identified with all coordinates except $x_i$. Then $$\int_{\mathbb R^n}\prod_{i=1}^n g_i(x_1,\ldots,\widehat{x_i},\ldots,x_n)^{1/(n-1)}\,dx\le\prod_{i=1}^n\left(\int_{\mathbb R^{n-1}}g_i\right)^{1/(n-1)}.$$

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) for the Lebesgue-measure interfaces. Let $X$ be a real or complex Banach space, let $a<b$, and let $f:[a,b]\to X$ be continuous. Differentiation uses the underlying real structure. Then $G(t):=\int_a^t f(s)\,ds$ is differentiable on $(a,b)$ and has the corresponding one-sided derivatives at $a,b$, with $G'(t)=f(t)$, and this derivative extends continuously to $[a,b]$. Consequently, if $\varphi:[a,b]\to X$ is continuous, differentiable on $(a,b)$ with $\varphi'$ continuous on $(a,b)$ and extendable to a continuous $X$-valued function on $[a,b]$, then $\int_a^b\varphi'(s)\,ds=\varphi(b)-\varphi(a)$. The Bochner integral here is the one of [[def-bochner-integrable-function]]; the identities also hold for continuous curves on $[0,\infty)$ restricted to compact subintervals.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

For each $i$, put $$g_i(x_{\widehat i}):=\int_\mathbb R|\partial_i f(x_1,\ldots,x_{i-1},s,x_{i+1},\ldots,x_n)|\,ds.$$ Tonelli [F4] shows $g_i$ is nonnegative measurable and integrable. By [F3], integrating from a point to the left of the compact support up to $x_i$ gives $|f(x)|\le g_i(x_{\widehat i})$ for every coordinate $i$. Multiplication and raising to the power $1/(n-1)$ yield $$|f(x)|^{n/(n-1)}\le\prod_{i=1}^n g_i(x_{\widehat i})^{1/(n-1)}.$$

Integrating this inequality and applying [F2] gives $$\|f\|_{L^{n/(n-1)}}\le\prod_{i=1}^n\|\partial_i f\|_1^{1/n}\le\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\|\partial_i f\|_1\le\frac1{\sqrt n}\int_{\mathbb R^n}|\nabla f|\,dx.$$ The middle inequality is arithmetic-geometric mean; the last follows pointwise from $\sum_i|\partial_i f|\le\sqrt n|\nabla f|$. Thus the desired inequality holds for smooth compactly supported $f$, with the stronger constant $1/\sqrt n$.

By [A1] and [F1], choose $f_k\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n)$ with $f_k\to u$ in $L^1$ and $\int|\nabla f_k|\to TV(u;\mathbb R^n)$. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $u\in L^1(\Omega;\mathbb R)$, where elements of $L^1$ are almost-everywhere equivalence classes. For each $i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}$, its distributional derivative $D_i u$ acts on $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ by
$$\langle D_i u,\varphi\rangle:=-\int_\Omega u\,\partial_i\varphi\,dx.$$
The function $u$ is in $BV(\Omega)$ when each $D_i u$ is represented by a finite signed Radon measure and the resulting vector-valued measure $Du=(D_1u,\ldots,D_nu)$ has finite total variation. Here a finite vector-valued Radon measure means that its partition variation is a finite Radon measure. For a Borel set $A\subseteq\Omega$, define
$$|Du|(A):=\sup\left\{\sum_{j=1}^\infty |Du(A_j)|:\ (A_j)_{j\ge1}\text{ is a Borel partition of }A\right\},$$
using the Euclidean norm on each vector value. Define the spatial total variation by $TV(u;\Omega):=|Du|(\Omega)$. A Lebesgue-measurable set $E\subseteq\Omega$ of finite measure has finite perimeter relative to $\Omega$ when $\chi_E\in BV(\Omega)$; its relative perimeter is $P(E;\Omega):=TV(\chi_E;\Omega)$.

For every open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and real-valued $u\in BV(\Omega)$, $$TV(u;\Omega)=\sup\left\{\int_\Omega u\,\operatorname{div}\varphi\,dx:\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^n),\ |\varphi(x)|\le1\right\}.$$ If $u_k,u\in BV(\Omega)$ are real-valued and $u_k\to u$ in $L^1(\Omega)$, then $TV(u;\Omega)\le\liminf_kTV(u_k;\Omega)$. Every Borel subset of a metric space is Carathéodory measurable for every metric outer measure.
For an outer measure $\mu^*$ on $X$, the Carathéodory measurable subsets form a sigma-algebra, and the restriction of the outer measure to it is a complete measure.

Then $0\le p(G)\le\|P\|$, $p(\varnothing)=0$, and $p$ is monotone. If a compact $K$ is covered by open sets $G_j$, finitely many suffice, and there are continuous nonnegative compactly supported functions $b_1,\ldots,b_N$, each supported in one of these sets, whose sum is positive on $K$. Indeed cover $K$ by finitely many balls with doubled closures compactly contained in the relevant $G_j$ and use distance cutoffs on these balls. On a neighborhood of $K$ normalize the $b_i$ by their sum. Thus any $f$ supported on $K$ with $0\le f\le1$ decomposes into finitely many $f_i\ge0$ with $\sum f_i=f$ and each $f_i\le1$ compactly supported in its assigned $G_j$; combine terms assigned to the same $j$. Consequently $p(\bigcup_jG_j)\le\sum_jp(G_j)$. For pairwise disjoint opens, adding finitely many admissible functions gives the reverse inequality for every finite partial sum, so $p$ is countably additive on disjoint open unions. These compact partitions use only finite choices.

Every open $G\supseteq A\cup B$ satisfies $p(G)\ge p(G\cap V)+p(G\cap W)\ge\mu^*(A)+\mu^*(B)$, by step 1.1. Taking the infimum and using subadditivity proves the metric condition. By [F2], restriction to Borel sets is a finite measure $\mu$ with $\mu(U)\le\|P\|$.

For an admissible $f$ in the definition of $p(G)$, let $K=\operatorname{supp}f$. Every open $V\supseteq K$ admits $f$, hence $\mu(K)=\inf_{V\supseteq K}p(V)\ge P(f)$. Taking the supremum over $f$ proves $\mu(G)=\sup_{K\subseteq G\text{ compact}}\mu(K)$. Outer regularity on every Borel set is the definition of $\mu^*$. Finiteness gives compact inner regularity on every Borel set as well: given Borel $A$ and $\varepsilon>0$, choose compact $H\subseteq U$ with $\mu(U\setminus H)<\varepsilon$ and open $V\supseteq U\setminus A$ with $\mu(V\setminus(U\setminus A))<\varepsilon$. Then $H\setminus V\subseteq A$ is compact and misses at most $2\varepsilon$ of $\mu(A)$. Thus $\mu$ is finite Radon, including regularity on all Borel sets.

If $0\le g\in C_c(U)$ and $g\le\mathbf1_K$ for compact $K$, the argument in step 3.1 gives $P(g)\le\mu(K)$. If instead $g\ge\mathbf1_K$, then for $0<\eta<1$, the open set $G_\eta=\{g>1-\eta\}$ contains $K$ and every admissible $f$ for $p(G_\eta)$ satisfies $f\le g/(1-\eta)$ on all of $U$. Positivity yields $\mu(K)\le p(G_\eta)\le P(g)/(1-\eta)$. Letting $\eta\downarrow0$ gives $\mu(K)\le P(g)$.

Fix $0\le f\in C_c(U)$ and $\varepsilon>0$, take $N$ with $N\varepsilon\ge\|f\|_\infty$, and put $f_j=\min(\varepsilon,(f-(j-1)\varepsilon)_+)$, $K_0=\operatorname{supp}f$, $K_j=\{f\ge j\varepsilon\}$ for $1\le j\le N$. The sum of the $f_j$ is $f$, and $\varepsilon\mathbf1_{K_j}\le f_j\le\varepsilon\mathbf1_{K_{j-1}}$. Step 4.1 gives the same lower and upper bounds $\varepsilon\mu(K_j)$ and $\varepsilon\mu(K_{j-1})$ for $P(f_j)$ as for $\int f_j\,d\mu$. Apply [F1] to $L=P-Q$ and the preceding construction to $P,Q$, obtaining finite positive Radon measures $\alpha,\beta$. Their difference $\sigma=\alpha-\beta$ represents $L$. The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), and let
$\overline{\mu 	imes 
u}$ be the completed product of two sigma-finite
measure spaces.

1. If $f : X 	imes Y 	o [0,\infty]$ is $\overline{\mu 	imes 
u}$-measurable, there are measurable null sets $A\subseteq X$ and $B\subseteq Y$ such that $f_x$ is $\overline{\mathcal B}$-measurable for $x
otin A$ and $f^y$ is $\overline{\mathcal A}$-measurable for $y
otin B$. Define $I_f(x)=\int_Y f_x\,d\overline
u$ for $x
otin A$ and $I_f(x)=0$ on $A$; define $J_f(y)=\int_X f^y\,d\overline\mu$ for $y
otin B$ and $J_f(y)=0$ on $B$. Then $I_f,J_f$ are measurable and
$$\int f\,d\overline{\mu 	imes 
u}=\int_X I_f\,d\mu=\int_Y J_f\,d
u.$$
2. If $f \in L^1(\overline{\mu 	imes 
u})$, there are measurable null sets $A\subseteq X$ and $B\subseteq Y$ such that the sections are measurable and integrable outside them. Define $I_f,J_f$ by the same section integrals outside $A,B$ and by zero on $A,B$. They are measurable and integrable, and the same equality holds.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$m,n \ge 1$. Under the identification
$$\mathbb R^{m+n}=\mathbb R^m \times \mathbb R^n,$$
the Lebesgue measure $\lambda_{m+n}$ is the completion of the product measure
$\lambda_m \times \lambda_n$.

Let $n \ge 1$, let $h \in \mathbb{R}^n$, and let $E + h$ be the translate of
$E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-translation-of-a-set-in-rn]]). Then:

1. $\lambda_n^*(E+h) = \lambda_n^*(E)$ for **every** subset $E$;
2. $E$ is Lebesgue measurable if and only if $E+h$ is;
3. $\lambda_n(E+h) = \lambda_n(E)$ for every Lebesgue measurable $E$.

**No choice principle is used.** Lebesgue outer measure is defined as an infimum
and the Carathéodory condition is a family of equations between its values, so
all three clauses are statements about objects that exist in ZF; countable
choice is needed to know that $\lambda_n$ is a measure, not to know that it is
translation invariant.

derivations.claim: For $\delta>0$, tile $\mathbb R^n$ by the half-open cubes $Q=\delta(z+[0,1)^n)$, $z\in\mathbb Z^n$, and let $A_\delta v$ equal $\delta^{-n}\int_Qv$ on $Q$. The triangle inequality, followed by [F1] and the substitution $y=x+h$ using [F2], gives $\|v-A_\delta v\|_1\le\delta^{-n}\sum_Q\int_Q\int_Q|v(x)-v(y)|\,dy\,dx\le\delta^{-n}\int_{[-\delta,\delta]^n}\|v(\cdot+h)-v\|_1\,dh$. Thus, writing $\omega(r)=\sup_{k,|h|\le r}\|v_k(\cdot+h)-v_k\|_1$, one has $\sup_k\|v_k-A_\delta v_k\|_1\le2^n\omega(\sqrt n\delta)\to0$ as $\delta\downarrow0$.

For each $m\ge1$, only finitely many cubes of side $2^{-m}$ meet a fixed ball containing the common supports; all other cell averages vanish. Enumerate all these cells at all levels by first increasing $m$ and then lexicographic order of their integer coordinates. Each cell-average coefficient $a_j(k)$ is a bounded real sequence, with bound $M$ divided by that cell's volume. There is a deterministically defined nested sequence of infinite subsets $S_m\subseteq\mathbb N$. Set $S_0=\mathbb N$. At stage $m$, partition the bounded ranges of the first $m$ coefficients into finitely many half-open dyadic bins of width $2^{-m}$, adding an endpoint bin if necessary. Among the finitely many vector bins containing infinitely many indices in $S_{m-1}$, take the lexicographically first; let $S_m$ be exactly that infinite set of indices. The finite pigeonhole principle guarantees existence and the specified order gives uniqueness. Ordinary recursion therefore defines $(S_m)$ without an instance of dependent choice. Take $k_m$ to be the least member of $S_m$ larger than $k_{m-1}$. For fixed $j$ and $m\ge j$, all later indices lie in $S_m$, so their $j$th coefficients differ by at most $2^{-m}$. Consequently every coefficient converges and, at each fixed cell level $\ell$, $(A_{2^{-\ell}}v_{k_m})_m$ is Cauchy in $L^1$, being a finite weighted sum of these coefficients.

Given $\varepsilon>0$, choose a cell level $\ell$ for which $2^n\omega(\sqrt n2^{-\ell})<\varepsilon/3$, using step 1.1. For sufficiently large $a,b$, step 1.2 gives $\|A_{2^{-\ell}}v_{k_a}-A_{2^{-\ell}}v_{k_b}\|_1<\varepsilon/3$. The two approximation errors from step 1.1 then show $\|v_{k_a}-v_{k_b}\|_1<\varepsilon$. Thus the subsequence is Cauchy.

For completeness at exactly the stated axiom strength, choose representatives of this countable sequence by [A1]. Select a further subsequence $g_j$ with $\|g_{j+1}-g_j\|_1<2^{-j}$, always choosing the least sufficiently late index, which exists by the Cauchy property. By [F1], $\sum_j|g_{j+1}-g_j|$ is integrable and finite almost everywhere. Hence $g_j$ has a measurable almost-everywhere limit $g$; moreover $|g|\le|g_1|+\sum_j|g_{j+1}-g_j|$, so $g\in L^1$, and $\|g-g_j\|_1\le\sum_{i\ge j}2^{-i}\to0$. The original Cauchy subsequence also converges to this $L^1$ class by the triangle inequality. This proves the assertion using only [A1].

interval.

for Lebesgue-almost every $x\in\mathbb{R}^n$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. For each integer $n\ge1$ there is a finite $c_n\in[1,n^{n/2}]$ such that

$$\mathcal H^n(B)=c_n\lambda_n(B)\quad(B\text{ Borel}),\qquad \mathcal H^n(A)=c_n\lambda_n^*(A)\quad(A\subseteq\mathbb R^n).$$

Here $c_n=\mathcal H^n((0,1]^n)$ and $c_1=1$. For $n\ge2$ no exact identification of $c_n$ is proved here.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. If $f:D\subseteq X\to Y$ satisfies $d_Y(f(x),f(y))=c\,d_X(x,y)$ for a finite constant $c>0$, then for every $A\subseteq D$ and finite $s\ge0$,

$$\mathcal H^s(f(A))=c^s\mathcal H^s(A).$$

This includes isometries and Euclidean translations and dilations. The Hausdorff outer value of a subset of a metric subspace equals its value computed in the ambient metric space.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $f:D\subseteq X\to Y$ be an $L$-Lipschitz map between metric spaces and $A\subseteq D$. For finite $s\ge0$ and $L>0$,

$$\mathcal H^s(f(A))\le L^s\mathcal H^s(A).$$

If $L=0$, the image is empty or a singleton: $\mathcal H^s(f(A))=0$ for $s>0$ and $\mathcal H^0(f(A))\le\mathcal H^0(A)$. No product $0\cdot\infty$ is used.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]) and let $T : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ be linear
with matrix $A$ ([[def-linear-map]],
[[lem-euclidean-linear-maps-have-matrices-and-are-bounded]]).

1. **Invertible case.** If $\det A \ne 0$, then $T[E]$ is Lebesgue measurable for
   every Lebesgue measurable $E$ and
   $$\lambda_n\big(T[E]\big) \;=\; |\det A|\;\lambda_n(E),$$
   both sides possibly $+\infty$; the product is defined in
   $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$ because $|\det A| > 0$.
2. **Singular case.** If $\det A = 0$, then $T[E]$ is Lebesgue measurable with
   $\lambda_n(T[E]) = 0$ for **every** $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$.

**The singular clause is stated as nullity and not as a product.** When
$\det A = 0$ and $\lambda_n(E) = +\infty$ the expression
$|\det A|\,\lambda_n(E)$ is $0\cdot(+\infty)$, which [[def-extended-reals]]
leaves undefined; writing the conclusion as $\lambda_n(T[E]) = 0$ says the same
thing wherever the product is defined and remains a statement where it is not.

derivations.claim: We first need the integral identity for Lipschitz interval functions without invoking the stronger published general absolutely continuous FTC. If $b$ is $L$-Lipschitz on $[a,d]$, extend it constantly past the endpoints. Its difference quotients are bounded by $L$ and converge to $b'$ almost everywhere by [F1]. For any $a\le s<t\le d$, dominated convergence gives $$\int_s^t b'(r)\,dr=\lim_{\epsilon\downarrow0}\frac1\epsilon\left(\int_t^{t+\epsilon}b(r)\,dr-\int_s^{s+\epsilon}b(r)\,dr\right)=b(t)-b(s).$$ Coordinate difference quotients of $h$ are measurable; [F1] and [F2] show their limits $g_i$ exist almost everywhere, with $|g_i|\le L$. Define them to be zero on the exceptional sets. Applying the preceding identity and one-dimensional integration by parts on each line, then [F2], gives $\int h\partial_i\eta=-\int g_i\eta$ for smooth compactly supported $\eta$. The same line identities hold for every coordinate line of $h$, outside the appropriate line-null exceptional set of derivatives.

For a cube $C$ of side $2r$ and a Lipschitz $w$, join $x$ to $y$ by the $m$ coordinate segments replacing their coordinates in order. Step 1.1 bounds $|w(x)-w(y)|$ by the sum of the line integrals of $|\partial_iw|$. Integrate in $x,y\in C$. For coordinate $i$, the unused coordinates contribute $(2r)^{m-1}$, while the measure of endpoint pairs whose interval contains a fixed coordinate value is at most $(2r)^2$. Thus, after division by $|C|$, the triangle inequality yields $$\int_C|w-w_C|\le 2r\sum_{i=1}^m\int_C|\partial_iw|,$$ where $w_C$ is its mean. Outside a null set, $g=(g_i)$ has strong Lebesgue points: apply [F3] to its coordinates and to $|g-q|$ for every rational vector $q$, then approximate $g(x)$ by such $q$. The countable union of the exceptional null sets is null under Countable Choice. Ball differentiation also gives cube differentiation by the fixed volume comparison. At such a point $x$, set $p=g(x)$ and $w(y)=h(y)-h(x)-p\cdot(y-x)$. The displayed inequality gives $\int_{C(x,r)}|w-w_C|=o(r^{m+1})$. As $w(x)=0$ and $w$ has a fixed Lipschitz bound, a mean with $|w_C|\ge\epsilon r$ would give $|w-w_C|\ge\epsilon r/2$ on a cube of side proportional to $r$ centered at $x$, contradicting this estimate. Thus $w_C=o(r)$. If $|w(y)|\ge\epsilon r$ at some $y$ in the half cube, the Lipschitz bound gives the same contradiction on a cube of side proportional to $r$ centered at $y$. Hence $\sup_{C(x,r/2)}|w|=o(r)$, proving differentiability with derivative $p$. Difference quotients then give $|p|\le L$. Countably many rational boxes cover $Q$, so the assertion is global.

We prove the area identity first for bounded Borel base sets within one $L$-Lipschitz box. On the differentiability set, for any $0<\epsilon<1/4$, form countably many Borel pieces on each of which $Dh$ lies within $\epsilon$ of a fixed rational vector $p$, the differentiability remainder is at most $\epsilon|z-y|$ whenever $|z-y|<1/k$, and the points lie in one cube of diameter less than $1/k$. Such pieces cover the differentiability set: the remainder condition follows from differentiability, can be tested on countably many rational $z$ by continuity, and is measurable; use increasing integers $k$ and a rational-vector enumeration. Subtract earlier pieces to make them disjoint. For two points $y,z$ of a single piece $E$, set $A_pv=(v,p\cdot v)$. Then $|F(z)-F(y)-A_p(z-y)|\le2\epsilon|z-y|\le2\epsilon|A_p(z-y)|$. Consequently $F\circ A_p^{-1}:A_p(E)\to F(E)$ is at most $(1+2\epsilon)$-Lipschitz, and its inverse is at most $(1-2\epsilon)^{-1}$-Lipschitz. The sets $F(E)$ are Borel because $F$ is a homeomorphism from $Q$ onto its graph.

Choose an orthonormal coordinate system on the range plane of $A_p$. Its square coordinate matrix has determinant of absolute value $J_p=\sqrt{\det(A_p^TA_p)}=\sqrt{1+|p|^2}$. Thus [F4] gives $\sigma_m(A_p(E))=J_p|E|$. Apply [F4] to the two maps in step 3.1 to obtain $$(1-2\epsilon)^mJ_p|E|\le\sigma_m(F(E))\le(1+2\epsilon)^mJ_p|E|.$$ The function $p\mapsto\sqrt{1+|p|^2}$ is $1$-Lipschitz, so $|J_p-\sqrt{1+|Dh(y)|^2}|\le\epsilon$ on $E$. The excluded base-null set has graph image of zero $\sigma_m$ by [F4], since $F$ is Lipschitz. Sum the displayed inequalities over the disjoint pieces, using $|p|\le L+\epsilon$. The difference between $\sigma_m(F(B))$ and $\int_B\sqrt{1+|Dh|^2}$ is bounded by $C_{m,L}\epsilon|B|$. Letting $\epsilon\downarrow0$ proves equality. Exhaustion and countable localization extend it to arbitrary Borel $B\subseteq Q$; indicator functions, simple functions and monotone convergence prove the asserted integral formula.

For a compactly supported smooth scalar $b$ in the chart, vertical integration gives $\int_G\partial_zb=-\int_Qb(y,h(y))\,dy$. For a horizontal coordinate put $B_i(y)=\int_{h(y)}^\infty b(y,z)\,dz$. This is Lipschitz and compactly supported in $Q$; step 2.1 and ordinary differentiation of the smooth integral give $\partial_iB_i=\int_{h(y)}^\infty\partial_i b\,dz-b(y,h(y))g_i$ almost everywhere. Its weak derivative integrates to zero by step 1.1 and [F2]. Apply these identities to the components of $\phi$ and sum. Step 4.1 converts the resulting flux into the unit-normal formula. The graph measure is a graph pushforward of the locally bounded measurable density $\sqrt{1+|Dh|^2}\,dy$; compact and open approximation in the base show it is locally Radon on the graph with its relative topology. The density is between $1$ and $\sqrt{1+L^2}$ on every local box, which also proves the null-set assertion.

On every compact subset of $G$, mollify $u$ using a nonnegative unit-mass bump, writing $u_\epsilon=u*\rho_\epsilon$ where the convolution ball stays in $G$. The distributional derivative identity and [F2] give $\partial_z u_\epsilon=(D_zu)*\rho_\epsilon$ there. For $0<s<t<a$, ordinary line integration gives $$\int_B|u_\epsilon(y,h(y)+t)-u_\epsilon(y,h(y)+s)|\,dy\le\int_{\{y\in B,\ s<z-h(y)<t\}}|\partial_z u_\epsilon|\,dx.$$ For sufficiently small $\epsilon$, the $\epsilon$-neighborhood of this last strip lies in $C_{2a}$: its lower height is positive since $s>0$, its upper height is below $2a$, and its lateral projection lies in $B'$. The convolution bound and [F2] make the right side at most $|D_zu|(C_{2a})$, since each kernel integrates to at most one.

On each compact-height collar $y\in B$, $1/j<z-h(y)<a-1/j$, [F1] gives $L^1$ convergence of $u_\epsilon$ to $u$. Choose a sequence $\epsilon_\ell\downarrow0$ whose $L^1$ errors on the first $\ell$ such collars are below $2^{-\ell}$, always using the least sufficiently large dyadic exponent. By [F2], for a full-measure set of heights the slice functions converge in $L^1(B)$. Applying step 1.1 at two such heights proves $$\|u_t-u_s\|_{L^1(B)}\le |D_zu|(C_{2a}),\qquad u_t(y)=u(y,h(y)+t),\quad 0<s,t<a.$$ Repeat this construction for a countable sequence of smaller $a$ tending to zero and intersect the full-measure height sets. The collars $C_{2a}$ decrease to the empty set inside $G$, so finiteness of $|D_zu|$ implies their measures tend to zero. Thus $u_t$ is Cauchy in $L^1(B)$ as $t\downarrow0$ outside one null set.

Choose one height from each interval $(2^{-j-1}a,2^{-j}a)$ outside that null set by Countable Choice. The corresponding Cauchy sequence has an $L^1$ limit: choose measurable representatives, then a subsequence whose successive $L^1$ differences are below $2^{-j}$; [F2] makes the sum of the absolute differences integrable and gives its almost-everywhere and $L^1$ limit. The Cauchy estimate in step 2.1 makes this limit independent of heights and gives the asserted convergence along all good heights. This also proves uniqueness and linearity. Averaging the bound $\|\tau u\|_1\le\|u_t\|_1+|D_zu|(C_{2a})$ over $0<t<a$ using [F2] gives $\|\tau u\|_1\le a^{-1}\|u\|_{L^1(C_a)}+|D_zu|(C_{2a})$. Since $|D_zu|\le|Du|$, this is the stated bound. The distributional identity extends from smooth to compactly supported Lipschitz vector fields $\psi$ inside $G$. For fixed $\epsilon>0$ use $\psi=\phi\theta((r-\epsilon)/\epsilon)$, whose support is a compact subset of $G$. Its almost-everywhere gradient uses the ordinary chain rule from [F3], and its transition term is $$\epsilon^{-1}\int_\epsilon^{2\epsilon}\int u_t(y)\phi(y,h(y)+t)\cdot(-Dh(y),1)\,dy\,dt.$$ By step 3.1, the uniform bound on $Dh$, and uniform continuity of $\phi$, this converges to $\int\tau u\,\phi(y,h(y))\cdot(-Dh,1)\,dy$. Subtract the two Green formulas for general $u$; [F4] makes $(\tau_1u-\tau_2u)n\mu$ zero, and the same variation argument gives $\tau_1u=\tau_2u$ almost everywhere. Reflection gives the subgraph formulas. In dimension one, omit the base integral: the convolution and line estimate in steps 1.1–2.1 make $u(t)$ Cauchy through almost every $t$ approaching an endpoint, and step 4.1 gives the endpoint boundary term. All arguments and bounds remain valid, with scalar absolute value and counting measure.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice. For every open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and $u\in BV(\Omega)$ there is a sequence $u_k\in C^\infty(\Omega)$ such that $u_k\to u$ in $L^1(\Omega)$ and $\int_\Omega |\nabla u_k|\,dx\to TV(u;\Omega)$. When $\Omega=\mathbb R^n$, the approximating functions may be chosen compactly supported.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $u\in C^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R)\cap L^1(\Omega)$ satisfy $\int_\Omega|\nabla u|\,dx<\infty$. For $t>0$ set $E_t^+:=\{x\in\Omega:u(x)>t\}$ and for $t<0$ set $E_t^-:=\{x\in\Omega:u(x)<t\}$. Then the level sets have finite perimeter relative to $\Omega$ for almost every applicable $t$, and
$$\int_\Omega|\nabla u|\,dx=\int_0^\infty P(E_t^+;\Omega)\,dt+\int_{-\infty}^0P(E_t^-;\Omega)\,dt.$$

For every open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and real-valued $u\in BV(\Omega)$, $$TV(u;\Omega)=\sup\left\{\int_\Omega u\,\operatorname{div}\varphi\,dx:\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^n),\ |\varphi(x)|\le1\right\}.$$ If $u_k,u\in BV(\Omega)$ are real-valued and $u_k\to u$ in $L^1(\Omega)$, then $TV(u;\Omega)\le\liminf_kTV(u_k;\Omega)$. In addition, assuming Countable Choice, for any real-valued $u\in L^1(\Omega)$ the displayed supremum is finite if and only if $u\in BV(\Omega)$, with equality to $TV(u;\Omega)$; under the same assumption, an $L^1$ limit of real-valued BV functions with bounded liminf total variation belongs to $BV(\Omega)$ and satisfies the same lower-semicontinuity inequality.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$m,n \ge 1$. Under the identification
$$\mathbb R^{m+n}=\mathbb R^m \times \mathbb R^n,$$
the Lebesgue measure $\lambda_{m+n}$ is the completion of the product measure

Let $(f_n)$ be nonnegative measurable functions. Then
$$\int \liminf_{n\to\infty}f_n\,d\mu\le\liminf_{n\to\infty}\int f_n\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then

derivations.claim: For any real $f\in L^1(\Omega)$, define its extended test variation $V(f)$ as the supremum of $\int f\operatorname{div}\varphi$ over smooth compactly supported vector fields with $|\varphi|\le1$. It is a lower semicontinuous extended nonnegative function on $L^1$: each test integral is a continuous linear functional and $\{f:V(f)>a\}$ is the union of its open superlevel sets. By [F2], $V(f)<\infty$ is equivalent to $f\in BV$, in which case $V(f)=TV(f;\Omega)$. For $t>0$ the indicator $\chi_{\{f>t\}}$ lies in $L^1$, since its norm is at most $\|f\|_1/t$, and it is right continuous as an $L^1$-valued function of $t$: if $t_j\downarrow t>0$, its indicators increase to $\chi_{\{f>t\}}$ and their errors tend to zero by monotone convergence. Dyadic right-step approximations therefore make this map Borel measurable. For $t<0$, $t\mapsto\chi_{\{f<t\}}$ is similarly left continuous and Borel. Composition with the lower semicontinuous $V$ shows that both extended level-variation functions are measurable.

By [F1], take smooth strict approximants $u_j$ with $\|u_j-u\|_1<2^{-j}$ and $\int|\nabla u_j|\to TV(u;\Omega)$, passing to a subsequence by least indices if needed. For real numbers $a,b$, the total length of the positive and negative levels at which their signed superlevel or sublevel indicators differ is $|a-b|$. Hence [F3] gives $$\int_0^\infty\|\chi_{\{u_j>t\}}-\chi_{\{u>t\}}\|_1\,dt+\int_{-\infty}^0\|\chi_{\{u_j<t\}}-\chi_{\{u<t\}}\|_1\,dt=\|u_j-u\|_1.$$ Sum over $j$ and apply [F3]: for almost every applicable nonzero level, the indicator errors are summable, and in particular the level indicators converge in $L^1$. The lower semicontinuity from step 1.1 gives $V(\chi_{E_t^\pm})\le\liminf_jV(\chi_{\{u_j\gtrless t\}})$ at those levels. Fatou and the smooth coarea identity [F1] consequently give $$\int_0^\infty V(\chi_{E_t^+})\,dt+\int_{-\infty}^0V(\chi_{E_t^-})\,dt\le\liminf_j\int_\Omega|\nabla u_j|\,dx=TV(u;\Omega).$$ The integral is finite, so its integrands are finite almost everywhere; [F2] then proves the stated almost-everywhere finite-perimeter assertion.

For any admissible smooth test field $\varphi$, signed layer cake gives $u(x)=\int_0^\infty\chi_{E_t^+}(x)\,dt-\int_{-\infty}^0\chi_{E_t^-}(x)\,dt$ almost everywhere. The absolute integral against $\operatorname{div}\varphi$ is bounded by $\|\operatorname{div}\varphi\|_\infty\|u\|_1$, so iterated integration is valid. Each level test integral in absolute value is at most its extended variation, using also $-\varphi$ in step 1.1. Therefore $\int u\operatorname{div}\varphi$ is at most the sum of the two perimeter integrals. Take the supremum over $\varphi$ and apply [F2] to $u$ to obtain the reverse of the inequality in step 2.1. Equality follows. Changing the representative of $u$ changes each level set only by a spatial null set, so all conclusions concern the given $L^1$ class.

$$u(y,h(y)+t)\longrightarrow\tau u(y)\quad\text{in }L^1(B)\text{ as }t\downarrow0\text{ through almost every }t.$$
The trace is linear and satisfies a bound $\|\tau u\|_{L^1(B)}\le C(a^{-1}\|u\|_{L^1(C_{2a})}+|Du|(C_{2a}))$, where $C_{2a}$ is a fixed larger graph collar with positive margins at the chart sides and $a>0$ is sufficiently small. $$\int_Gu\operatorname{div}\phi=-\int_G\phi\cdot dDu+\int \tau u(y)\phi(y,h(y))\cdot(Dh(y),-1)\,dy.$$
The corresponding assertions hold for the subgraph with the normal reversed. For an interval endpoint in dimension one, the same assertions mean the one-sided scalar limit, the usual endpoint sign, and counting measure on the boundary.

derivations.claim: If $\Omega=\varnothing$, its BV space and boundary $L^1$ space are both the zero space, the zero trace is unique, and every formula and estimate holds with both sides zero. Assume henceforth $\Omega\ne\varnothing$. Shrink the finitely many boundary graph neighborhoods to smaller charts still covering the compact boundary and with positive margins inside the original charts. Each smaller graph base is bounded and its Lipschitz constant finite, so [F2] gives finite surface measure. In each chart [F1] defines a local trace and bounds its surface $L^1$ norm, using [F2], by a chart constant times $\|u\|_1+|Du|(\Omega)$. On overlaps these local traces agree by [F1]. Consequently they define one class $Tu\in L^1(\partial\Omega,\mathcal H^{n-1})$ with $\|Tu\|_1\le C(\|u\|_1+TV(u;\Omega))$. Linearity follows locally from [F1], hence globally.

Construct a finite smooth partition equal to one on a neighborhood of $\overline\Omega$, subordinate to the boundary charts and the interior open set $\Omega$: cover this compact set by finitely many balls with doubled closures in those open sets, take the bumps in [F3], and divide them by their positive sum near $\overline\Omega$. Multiply by one further smooth cutoff supported where the sum is positive and equal to one near $\overline\Omega$. Apply the local Green identity [F1] to each chart-supported field $\eta_j\phi$. For the interior-supported field the defining distributional identity applies. Sum the identities. Since $\sum_j\eta_j=1$ and $\sum_j\nabla\eta_j=0$ near $\overline\Omega$, the interior and boundary sums are exactly $$\int_\Omega u\operatorname{div}\phi=-\int_\Omega\phi\cdot dDu+\int_{\partial\Omega}Tu\,\phi\cdot\nu\,d\mathcal H^{n-1}.$$ The argument first applies to smooth fields. Compactly supported $C^1$ fields and their first derivatives are uniformly approximated by mollification, which passes every term by finite variation and $L^1$ integrability.

Extend each coordinate of $Du$ by zero from $\Omega$ to $\mathbb R^n$. It is a finite signed Radon measure: compact inner approximation can be performed inside $\Omega$, and outer approximation in the ambient space follows by applying that inner approximation to the complement and using finiteness. The boundary term $Tu\,\nu\mathcal H^{n-1}|_{\partial\Omega}$ is also finite signed Radon coordinatewise, by [F2], compactness and the $L^1$ bound in step 1.1. Thus their difference $\mu=i_\#Du-Tu\,\nu\mathcal H^{n-1}|_{\partial\Omega}$ is a finite Radon vector measure by [F4]. The formula in step 2.1 says exactly that $D\widetilde u=\mu$, so $\widetilde u\in BV(\mathbb R^n)$.

The two summands defining $\mu$ in step 3.1 are supported on the disjoint Borel sets $\Omega$ and $\partial\Omega$. The partition definition of variation therefore gives the sum of their variations. For a unit measurable vector density $
u$ and scalar density $Tu$, the boundary variation is $|Tu|\mathcal H^{n-1}$: the triangle inequality gives the upper bound, and a finite partition of the unit sphere into pieces of diameter below $\epsilon$, applied to the direction $\operatorname{sgn}(Tu)
u$, gives the lower bound $(1-\epsilon)|Tu|\mathcal H^{n-1}$ by projection; let $\epsilon\downarrow0$. Hence $TV(\widetilde u)=TV(u;\Omega)+\|Tu\|_1$. Step 1.1 gives the asserted bound. If another trace satisfied the Green identity, their difference times $
u\mathcal H^{n-1}$ would integrate to zero on all smooth tests, hence be zero by [F3]; the same variation calculation gives equality of the trace classes.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ be open and let $X=L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R)$. Every $u\in X$ is integrable on compact subsets by Cauchy–Schwarz. Define its extended distributional total variation by
$$TV_2(u;\Omega):=\sup\left\{\int_\Omega u\,\operatorname{div}\varphi\,dx:\ \varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^2),\ \sup_{x\in\Omega}|\varphi(x)|\le1\right\}\in[0,+\infty],$$
where $C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^2)$ denotes smooth compactly supported vector fields, $|\cdot|$ is the Euclidean norm, and $\operatorname{div}\varphi=\partial_1\varphi_1+\partial_2\varphi_2$. This definition treats $L^2$ functions as almost-everywhere classes and does not require $u\in L^1(\Omega)$.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $u\in L^1(\Omega;\mathbb R)$, where elements of $L^1$ are almost-everywhere equivalence classes. For each $i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}$, its distributional derivative $D_i u$ acts on $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ by
$$\langle D_i u,\varphi\rangle:=-\int_\Omega u\,\partial_i\varphi\,dx.$$
The function $u$ is in $BV(\Omega)$ when each $D_i u$ is represented by a finite signed Radon measure and the resulting vector-valued measure $Du=(D_1u,\ldots,D_nu)$ has finite total variation. Here a finite vector-valued Radon measure means that its partition variation is a finite Radon measure. For a Borel set $A\subseteq\Omega$, define
$$|Du|(A):=\sup\left\{\sum_{j=1}^\infty |Du(A_j)|:\ (A_j)_{j\ge1}\text{ is a Borel partition of }A\right\},$$
using the Euclidean norm on each vector value. Define the spatial total variation by $TV(u;\Omega):=|Du|(\Omega)$. A Lebesgue-measurable set $E\subseteq\Omega$ of finite measure has finite perimeter relative to $\Omega$ when $\chi_E\in BV(\Omega)$; its relative perimeter is $P(E;\Omega):=TV(\chi_E;\Omega)$.
For every open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, the space $C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ is dense in $C_0(\Omega)$ in the uniform norm.

Assume Countable Choice. For every open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, every bounded real linear functional on $C_0(U;\mathbb R)$ is integration against a unique finite signed Radon measure. No Dependent Choice assumption is required.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $\mu=(\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_m)$ have finite signed Radon coordinate measures. For Borel $A\subseteq\Omega$ define $$V(A):=\sup\left\{\sum_{j=1}^\infty |\mu(A_j)|:(A_j)_{j\ge1}\text{ is a Borel partition of }A\right\},$$ where the norm is Euclidean. Then $V$ is a finite positive Radon measure and $$V(\Omega)=\sup\left\{\int_\Omega f\cdot d\mu:f\in C_c(\Omega;\mathbb R^m),\ |f(x)|\le1\right\}.$$

For $i=1,2$, set $L_i(\psi):=-\int_\Omega u\,\partial_i\psi\,dx$ on $C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R)$. If $\psi\ne0$, the vector field $\varphi=\psi e_i/\|\psi\|_\infty$ and its negative are admissible in [F1]; hence $|L_i(\psi)|\le M\|\psi\|_\infty$. The same bound is immediate for $\psi=0$. By [F3], $L_i$ extends uniquely to a bounded real linear functional on $C_0(\Omega)$.

Countable Choice and [F4] represent each extension by a finite signed Radon measure $\mu_i$. Formula [F2] identifies $\mu_i$ with $D_i u$, so $\mu=(\mu_1,\mu_2)$ has finite vector Radon variation by [F5]. For every continuous compactly supported $g$ with $\|g\|_\infty\le1$, approximate uniformly by a smooth compactly supported $h$ with $\|h-g\|_\infty<\varepsilon$, and replace $h$ by $h/\max\{1,\|h\|_\infty\}$. The replacement has norm at most one and differs from $g$ by at most $2\varepsilon$. Since $\sum_i|\mu_i|(\Omega)<\infty$, its integral against $\mu$ approaches that of $g$ as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$. Thus the supremum over smooth unit fields equals the continuous-field supremum in [F5]. By [F2], $\int u\,\operatorname{div}\varphi=-\int\varphi\cdot d\mu$; symmetry of the unit test class removes this minus sign. Consequently $|Du|(\Omega)=M=TV_2(u;\Omega)$, proving the assertion.

$$\int_{\partial D}(P\,dx+Q\,dy)=\int_D(Q_x-P_y)\,dx\,dy,$$
$$\int_{\partial D}(P\,dy-Q\,dx)=\int_D(P_x+Q_y)\,dx\,dy.$$
When $D$ also has the supplied finite elementary Green decomposition required by the classical results, these are exactly their circulation and outward-flux formulas. Outer boundary curves run counterclockwise and holes clockwise.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $\mu=(\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_m)$ have finite signed Radon coordinate measures. For Borel $A\subseteq\Omega$ define $$V(A):=\sup\left\{\sum_{j=1}^\infty |\mu(A_j)|:(A_j)_{j\ge1}\text{ is a Borel partition of }A\right\},$$ where the norm is Euclidean. Then $V$ is a finite positive Radon measure and $$V(\Omega)=\sup\left\{\int_\Omega f\cdot d\mu:f\in C_c(\Omega;\mathbb R^m),\ |f(x)|\le1\right\}.$$

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice-principle-for-foliation-pair]]). Let $X$ be a nonempty
compact connected one-dimensional topological manifold without boundary
([[def-compact-space]], [[def-connected-space]],
[[def-hausdorff-space]]). Then $X$ is homeomorphic to the circle
$S^1=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:x^2+y^2=1\}$
([[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]]). If in addition $X$ carries a
smooth structure making it a smooth one-manifold without boundary, then $X$ is
diffeomorphic to this circle
([[def-diffeomorphism-and-local-diffeomorphism-of-manifolds]]).

The empty manifold is excluded by the hypothesis: it is compact and connected
under the conventions of this library, but it is not homeomorphic to a circle.
The hypothesis "without boundary" is likewise essential: the closed interval
$[0,1]$ is compact and connected but has boundary points and is not a circle.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). For all
$f,g\in L^2(\mathbb T;\mathbb C)$,

$$\|f\|_2^2=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}|\widehat f(k)|^2,\qquad \langle f,g\rangle=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}\widehat f(k)\overline{\widehat g(k)} ,$$where both sums are taken in the finite-subset-supremum/finite-subset-net sense of [[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]]. The bilinear series is absolutely convergent,$$\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}\bigl|\widehat f(k)\overline{\widehat g(k)}\bigr|\le \Bigl(\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}|\widehat f(k)|^2\Bigr)^{1/2} \Bigl(\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}|\widehat g(k)|^2\Bigr)^{1/2},$$

and the value is also the limit of the canonical symmetric partial sums
$\sum_{|k|\le N}\widehat f(k)\overline{\widehat g(k)}$.

derivations.claim:
First suppose $G\subset\mathbb R^2$ is a bounded open set with compact smooth boundary $\Gamma$. The boundary is a compact smooth one-dimensional manifold without boundary. Connected coordinate arcs cover $\Gamma$; compactness gives a finite subcover, so $\Gamma$ has finitely many connected components. By [F5] each component is a smooth embedded circle. Parametrize component $i$ by an orientation-compatible unit-speed smooth periodic curve $\gamma_i:[0,L_i]\to\mathbb R^2$, where $L_i$ is its length. The divergence formula in [F3] gives $D\chi_G=-\nu\,\mathcal H^1|_\Gamma$ with $\nu$ the outward normal, and [F4] therefore gives $P(G;\mathbb R^2)=\mathcal H^1(\Gamma)=\sum_iL_i$. Applying Stokes in [F3] to $\omega=(x\,dy-y\,dx)/2$, whose exterior derivative is $dx\wedge dy$, gives
$$|G|=\frac12\sum_i\int_0^{L_i}(\gamma_{i,1}\gamma'_{i,2}-\gamma_{i,2}\gamma'_{i,1})\,ds.$$
For each $i$, translating $\gamma_i$ by its arclength mean $\bar\gamma_i=L_i^{-1}\int_0^{L_i}\gamma_i(s)\,ds$ does not change this integral, since each coordinate derivative integrates to zero over a period. Write $z_i=\gamma_i-\bar\gamma_i$.

For a smooth $L$-periodic scalar function $z$ of mean zero, set $v(\theta)=z(L\theta/(2\pi))$. Its zeroth Fourier coefficient vanishes. Integration by parts gives $\widehat{v'}(k)=ik\widehat v(k)$ for every integer $k$. Parseval [F6] and $k^2\ge1$ for $k\ne0$ imply $\int_0^{2\pi}|v|^2\,d\theta\le\int_0^{2\pi}|v'|^2\,d\theta$. Changing variables yields
$$\int_0^L|z(s)|^2\,ds\le\left(\frac L{2\pi}\right)^2\int_0^L|z'(s)|^2\,ds.$$
Apply this to both coordinates of $z_i$ and add. Since $|z'_i|=|\gamma'_i|=1$, the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality gives
$$\left|\frac12\int_0^{L_i}(z_{i,1}z'_{i,2}-z_{i,2}z'_{i,1})\,ds\right|\le\frac12\|z_i\|_{L^2}\|z'_i\|_{L^2}\le\frac{L_i^2}{4\pi}.$$
Summing over the finitely many boundary components and using $\sum_iL_i^2\le(\sum_iL_i)^2$ proves $4\pi|G|\le P(G;\mathbb R^2)^2$.

Now let $E$ be as in the Statement and put $u=\chi_E$. By [F1], choose $u_j\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2)$ with $e_j:=\|u_j-\chi_E\|_1\to0$ and $a_j:=\int|\nabla u_j|\to P(E;\mathbb R^2)$. If $|E|=0$, the result is immediate. If some $e_j=0$, continuity forces $u_j$ to take only the values $0$ and $1$ everywhere; connectedness of $\mathbb R^2$ and compact support then force $u_j=0$, contradicting $|E|>0$. Thus $e_j>0$. Let $\tau_j=\sqrt{e_j}$ and discard finitely many terms so $0<\tau_j<\min\{1/2,|E|/2\}$. For every $t\in I_j:=[\tau_j,1-\tau_j]$, a point where $\chi_E$ and $\chi_{\{u_j>t\}}$ differ contributes at least $\tau_j$ to $|u_j-\chi_E|$; hence $|\{u_j>t\}\mathbin\triangle E|\le e_j/\tau_j=\tau_j$.

By [F2], the measurable level-perimeter function has integral at most $a_j$ on $I_j$, whose length is $1-2\tau_j$. For any $\varepsilon>0$, the set of $t\in I_j$ with $P(\{u_j>t\};\mathbb R^2)\le a_j/(1-2\tau_j)+\varepsilon$ has positive measure; otherwise its integral over $I_j$ would exceed $a_j$. The critical values of $u_j$ form a null set by [F2], so choose such a regular value $t_j$ and take $\varepsilon=1/j$. Since $t_j>0$ and $u_j$ is compactly supported, $G_j:=\{u_j>t_j\}$ is bounded and its closure is a compact smooth domain with boundary $\{u_j=t_j\}$. Thus step 1.2 applies to $G_j$, and
$$|G_j\mathbin\triangle E|\le\tau_j,\qquad P(G_j;\mathbb R^2)\le\frac{a_j}{1-2\tau_j}+\frac1j.$$
The right side has limit $P(E;\mathbb R^2)$, while $|G_j|\to|E|$.

Step 1.2 gives $4\pi|G_j|\le P(G_j;\mathbb R^2)^2$ for every selected $j$. Taking upper limits, the convergence $|G_j|\to|E|$ and the perimeter upper bound from step 2.2 give $4\pi|E|\le P(E;\mathbb R^2)^2$. This proves the claimed inequality for every finite-measure finite-perimeter set.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ be open and let $X=L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R)$. Every $u\in X$ is integrable on compact subsets by Cauchy–Schwarz. Define its extended distributional total variation by
$$TV_2(u;\Omega):=\sup\left\{\int_\Omega u\,\operatorname{div}\varphi\,dx:\ \varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^2),\ \sup_{x\in\Omega}|\varphi(x)|\le1\right\}\in[0,+\infty],$$
where $C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^2)$ denotes smooth compactly supported vector fields, $|\cdot|$ is the Euclidean norm, and $\operatorname{div}\varphi=\partial_1\varphi_1+\partial_2\varphi_2$. This definition treats $L^2$ functions as almost-everywhere classes and does not require $u\in L^1(\Omega)$.

Assume Countable Choice. If $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ is open, $u\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R)$, and $TV_2(u;\Omega)<\infty$, then each distributional derivative of $u$ is represented by a finite signed Radon measure. Their vector measure $Du$ has finite Radon variation and $|Du|(\Omega)=TV_2(u;\Omega)$.
Let $0<r<R$ and $n\ge 1$. Then there exists a smooth function $\rho:\mathbb R^n\to [0,1]$ such that $\rho=1$ on $\overline B_r(0)$ and $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)\subseteq B_R(0)$.

derivations.claim: By [F2], choose $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2)$ with $0\le\chi\le1$, $\chi=1$ on $B(0,1)$, $\operatorname{supp}\chi\subset B(0,2)$, and let $\chi_R(x)=\chi(x/R)$ for integers $R\ge1$. Put $v_R=\chi_Ru$. Then $v_R\in L^2$ has compact support, hence is in $L^1$, and $v_R\to u$ in $L^2$ because $\chi_R=1$ on $B(0,R)$ and $u\in L^2$.

For every scalar $\psi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2)$, local integrability of $u$ and the definition of distributional derivative give
$$-\int \chi_Ru\,\partial_i\psi=-\int u\,\partial_i(\chi_R\psi)+\int u\psi\,\partial_i\chi_R=\int\chi_R\psi\,dD_i u+\int u\psi\,\partial_i\chi_R.$$
Thus $D v_R=\chi_RDu+u\nabla\chi_R\,dx$. The variation of the first term is at most $|Du|(\mathbb R^2)$, and the second has variation at most
$$\frac CR\int_{B(0,2R)\setminus B(0,R)}|u|\,dx\le C'\|u\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^2\setminus B(0,R))},$$
by Cauchy–Schwarz and the annulus area bound $|B(0,2R)\setminus B(0,R)|^{1/2}\le C''R$. This error tends to zero. Since $v_R\in L^1$ and its derivative is a finite vector Radon measure, $v_R\in BV(\mathbb R^2)$, and [F1] yields $\limsup_R TV(v_R;\mathbb R^2)\le |Du|(\mathbb R^2)=TV_2(u;\mathbb R^2)$. Taking $v_k=v_R$ proves the statement.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $\Omega=\mathbb R^2$, or let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ be a bounded Lipschitz domain. Set $X=L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ and let $Y=L^2(\Sigma,\mu;\mathbb R)$ for a measure space $(\Sigma,\mu)$, using the real integral inner products. Let $A:X\to Y$ be bounded and real-linear, and let $A^*:Y\to X$ be its Hilbert adjoint, characterized by $\langle Au,p\rangle_Y=\langle u,A^*p\rangle_X$. Define $R:X\to[0,+\infty]$ as follows. If $\Omega=\mathbb R^2$, take $R(u)=TV_2(u;\mathbb R^2)$, the supremum of $\int u\,\operatorname{div}\varphi$ over smooth compactly supported vector fields of Euclidean norm at most one. For bounded $\Omega$, either take Neumann TV, $R(u)=TV(u;\Omega)$ when $u\in BV(\Omega)$ and $+\infty$ otherwise, or Dirichlet TV, $R(u)=TV(\widetilde u;\mathbb R^2)$ when the zero extension $\widetilde u$ belongs to $BV(\mathbb R^2)$ and $+\infty$ otherwise. Thus the bounded-domain choices count, respectively, only the interior derivative or also the jump of the zero extension across the boundary. In the full-space case finite $R$ does not require global $L^1$ integrability.

Identify each $q\in X$ with the continuous linear functional $h\mapsto\langle q,h\rangle_X$ by the real Hilbert-space Riesz representation. For exact data $f=Au^\dagger$, a **minimum-TV exact solution** is a point $u^\dagger\in X$ satisfying $Au^\dagger=f$ and $R(u^\dagger)\le R(u)$ for every $u\in X$ with $Au=f$. A vector $p^\dagger\in Y$ is a **dual source certificate** for $u^\dagger$ if $A^*p^\dagger\in\partial R(u^\dagger)$, where $\partial R$ is the convex subdifferential on the real Banach space $X$. The **TV source condition** at $u^\dagger$ is that such a certificate exists; it does not assert uniqueness of the truth or of the certificate. For a chosen certificate, the associated Bregman distance is

$$D_R^{A^*p^\dagger}(u,u^\dagger):=R(u)-R(u^\dagger)-\langle A^*p^\dagger,u-u^\dagger\rangle_X,$$

for $u\in\operatorname{dom}R$.

Let $X$ be a real Banach space and let $X^*$ be its continuous real dual. The dual pairing is evaluation, written $\langle \xi,x\rangle_{X^*,X}:=\xi(x)$ for $\xi\in X^*$ and $x\in X$. Let $R:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be a proper convex functional: $R$ never takes the value $-\infty$, its effective domain $\operatorname{dom}R:=\{x\in X:R(x)<+\infty\}$ is nonempty, and $R((1-t)x+tz)\le (1-t)R(x)+tR(z)$ for $x,z\in X$ and $t\in[0,1]$, with $0\cdot(+\infty):=0$ for this convex-combination formula. For $x\in\operatorname{dom}R$, its subdifferential is

$$\partial R(x):=\{\xi\in X^*:R(z)\ge R(x)+\langle\xi,z-x\rangle_{X^*,X}\text{ for every }z\in X\}.$$

An element of $\partial R(x)$ is a subgradient of $R$ at $x$. Set $\partial R(x):=\varnothing$ when $x\notin\operatorname{dom}R$. The subdifferential may be empty at a point of $\operatorname{dom}R$; no nonemptiness assertion is part of this definition.

Let $X$ be a real Banach space, let $R:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper and convex, choose $x^\dagger\in\operatorname{dom}R$, and choose $\xi^\dagger\in\partial R(x^\dagger)$. For $x\in\operatorname{dom}R$, the **Bregman distance** generated by $\xi^\dagger$ from the reference point $x^\dagger$ to $x$ is

$$D_R^{\xi^\dagger}(x,x^\dagger):=R(x)-R(x^\dagger)-\langle\xi^\dagger,x-x^\dagger\rangle_{X^*,X}.$$

The subgradient inequality makes this quantity nonnegative, and $D_R^{\xi^\dagger}(x^\dagger,x^\dagger)=0$. The definition fixes the orientation: the first argument is the comparison point and the second is the reference point carrying the chosen subgradient.

Let $X$ be a real Banach space, let $R:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper and convex, and define its Fenchel conjugate $R^*:X^*\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ by $R^*(\xi):=\sup_{z\in X}(\langle\xi,z\rangle_{X^*,X}-R(z))$. For every $x\in\operatorname{dom}R$ and $\xi\in X^*$, the Fenchel–Young inequality and its equality characterization are

$$R(x)+R^*(\xi)\ge\langle\xi,x\rangle_{X^*,X},\qquad R(x)+R^*(\xi)=\langle\xi,x\rangle_{X^*,X}\ \Longleftrightarrow\ \xi\in\partial R(x).$$

Let $X,Y$ be real Banach spaces, let $F:D(F)\subseteq X\to Y$, let $x^\dagger\in D(F)$ with exact datum $y=F(x^\dagger)$, and let $R:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper and convex with $x^\dagger\in\operatorname{dom}R$. Fix $\xi^\dagger\in\partial R(x^\dagger)$, an exponent $1\le p<\infty$, a continuous nondecreasing concave function $\psi:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ with $\psi(0)=0$ and $\psi(t)>0$ for $t>0$, a coefficient $0\le\beta<1$, and a level $R_0\ge R(x^\dagger)$. The **variational source condition** with these data holds on the named regularizer sublevel $L_{R_0}:=\{x\in D(F):R(x)\le R_0\}$ when

$$-\langle\xi^\dagger,x-x^\dagger\rangle_{X^*,X}\le\beta D_R^{\xi^\dagger}(x,x^\dagger)+\psi\!\left(\|F(x)-F(x^\dagger)\|_Y^p\right)\qquad(x\in L_{R_0}).$$

The condition is an assumption on the selected subgradient and the stated sublevel; it makes no assertion that a subgradient exists at every point or that a regularized minimizer exists.

Let $X,Y$ be real Banach spaces, $D(F)\subseteq X$, and $F:D(F)\to Y$. Let $R:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper and convex, let $x^\dagger\in D(F)\cap\operatorname{dom}R$, set $y=F(x^\dagger)$, and choose $\xi^\dagger\in\partial R(x^\dagger)$. Fix $1\le p<\infty$, $0\le\beta<1$, and a level $R_0>R(x^\dagger)$. Let $\psi:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ be continuous, nondecreasing and concave, with $\psi(0)=0$ and $\psi(t)>0$ for $t>0$, and assume the variational source inequality

$$-\langle\xi^\dagger,x-x^\dagger\rangle_{X^*,X}\le\beta D_R^{\xi^\dagger}(x,x^\dagger)+\psi\!\left(\|F(x)-F(x^\dagger)\|_Y^p\right)\qquad\left(x\in L_{R_0}:=\{x\in D(F):R(x)\le R_0\}\right),$$

where $D_R^{\xi^\dagger}(x,x^\dagger):=R(x)-R(x^\dagger)-\langle\xi^\dagger,x-x^\dagger\rangle_{X^*,X}$. Extend $-\psi$ by $+\infty$ on negative arguments and write $H(q):=(-\psi)^*(-q)=\sup_{s\ge0}(\psi(s)-qs)$; assume $H(q)$ is finite for sufficiently large $q$ and $H(q)\to0$ as $q\to\infty$. For sufficiently small noise levels $\delta>0$ and data $y^\delta\in Y$ with $\|y^\delta-y\|_Y\le\delta$, define $J_\alpha^\delta(x):=p^{-1}\|F(x)-y^\delta\|_Y^p+\alpha R(x)$. Suppose $\alpha=\alpha(\delta)>0$ tends to zero, $0\le\varepsilon_\delta\le C_\varepsilon\delta^p$, and $x_\alpha^{\delta,\varepsilon}\in D(F)$ is an $\varepsilon_\delta$-minimizer, meaning $J_\alpha^\delta(x_\alpha^{\delta,\varepsilon})\le\inf_{z\in D(F)}J_\alpha^\delta(z)+\varepsilon_\delta$. Set $c_p:=2^{1-p}/p$ and $\rho_\delta:=H(c_p/\alpha(\delta))$. Assume that for constants $c_-,c_+,C_H>0$ independent of $\delta$,

$$c_-\delta^p\le\alpha(\delta)\rho_\delta\le c_+\delta^p,\qquad H(c_p/(2\alpha(\delta)))\le C_H\rho_\delta$$

for all sufficiently small $\delta$. Then for all sufficiently small $\delta$, $x_\alpha^{\delta,\varepsilon}\in L_{R_0}$ and

$$D_R^{\xi^\dagger}(x_\alpha^{\delta,\varepsilon},x^\dagger)=O(\rho_\delta),\qquad \|F(x_\alpha^{\delta,\varepsilon})-y^\delta\|_Y=O(\delta).$$

If, in addition, $\psi(C_0\delta^p)=O(\rho_\delta)$ for a fixed $C_0$ such that $T_\delta:=\|F(x_\alpha^{\delta,\varepsilon})-F(x^\dagger)\|_Y^p\le C_0\delta^p$ for all sufficiently small $\delta$, then $|R(x_\alpha^{\delta,\varepsilon})-R(x^\dagger)|=O(\rho_\delta)$. If also $D_R^{\xi^\dagger}(x,x^\dagger)\ge c_R\|x-x^\dagger\|_X^s$ on $L_{R_0}$ for constants $c_R,s>0$, then $\|x_\alpha^{\delta,\varepsilon}-x^\dagger\|_X^s=O(\rho_\delta)$.

In the Hilbert special case, set $p=2$ and suppose $X,Y$ are real Hilbert spaces, $F:U\to Y$ has the real open-domain interface of a nonlinear forward map, $x^\dagger$ is an $x_0$-minimum-norm exact solution, $R(x)=\frac12\|x-x_0\|_X^2$, and the source inequality on a regularizer sublevel contained in $U$ is

$$\langle x^\dagger-x_0,x^\dagger-x\rangle_X\le\beta_1\frac12\|x-x^\dagger\|_X^2+\beta_2\|F(x)-F(x^\dagger)\|_Y$$

with $0\le\beta_1<1$ and $\beta_2\ge0$. For exact global minimizers of the nonlinear Tikhonov functional with $\alpha(\delta)\asymp\delta$, the theorem gives $\|x_{\alpha(\delta)}^\delta-x^\dagger\|_X=O(\sqrt\delta)$ and $\|F(x_{\alpha(\delta)}^\delta)-y^\delta\|_Y=O(\delta)$. The assertion is conditional on such a global minimizer being supplied; it does not assert existence or cover local numerical minima.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

Every bounded sequence of reals has a convergent subsequence: if $(x_k)$ is a
sequence of reals and there is $M \in \mathbb{R}$ with $|x_k| \le M$ for every
$k \in \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-sequence]]), then there is a strictly increasing
$n : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and a real $L$ with $x_{n_j} \to L$.

Equivalently: the subsequential limit set of a bounded sequence is nonempty
([[def-subsequential-limit]]).

The theorem is the exact repair of the false claim that a bounded sequence
converges. A bounded
sequence need not converge, and the alternating sequence is the standing witness;
what boundedness does force is that *some* subsequence converges. The converse of
the theorem is false, and badly so: a sequence with a convergent subsequence need
not be bounded.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space and let $f$ be a bounded linear functional on $H$ ([[def-dual-space-of-a-normed-space]]). Then there is a unique $y\in H$ with

$$f(x)=\langle x,y\rangle\qquad\text{for every }x\in H,$$

and $\|f\|=\|y\|$, where $\|f\|$ is the dual norm ([[def-operator-norm]]). Under the first-variable-linear convention the representing vector depends conjugate-linearly and isometrically on $f$: if $f_i$ is represented by $y_i$ and $a,b$ are scalars, then $af_1+bf_2$ is represented by $\overline a\,y_1+\overline b\,y_2$.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with **conjugation** $z\mapsto\overline z$
the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of [[def-inner-product-space]]: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

**Induced length.** The **induced length**, or inner-product norm, of $v$ is

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

which is exactly the published [[def-inner-product-norm]]: positive definiteness
makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square
root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$.

**The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or
complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.
In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of
$\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex
modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either
scalar field.

derivations.claim: Put $q^\dagger=A^*p^\dagger$. Applying [F2] at $u^\dagger$ with $z=0$ and $z=2u^\dagger$, and using $R(0)=0$ and $R(2u^\dagger)=2R(u^\dagger)$, gives $\langle q^\dagger,u^\dagger\rangle_X=R(u^\dagger)$. For arbitrary $z\in X$, [F2] then yields $R(z)\ge\langle q^\dagger,z\rangle_X$, so $q^\dagger\in\partial R(0)$ and $p^\dagger\in K$. Every $p\in K$ satisfies $\langle f,p\rangle_Y=\langle u^\dagger,A^*p\rangle_X\le R(u^\dagger)$; equality holds for $p^\dagger$. Thus $P_0$ is nonempty, closed, and convex.

The set $K$ is nonempty because $0\in\partial R(0)$, convex by the subgradient inequality, and closed because $\partial R(0)=\{q:R(z)\ge\langle q,z\rangle_X\text{ for all }z\}$ is an intersection of closed half-spaces and $A^*$ is continuous. For any nonempty closed convex subset $C$ of a Hilbert space, let $d=\inf_{c\in C}\|x-c\|$ and use Countable Choice to select $c_n\in C$ with $\|x-c_n\|^2\le d^2+1/n$. The midpoint belongs to $C$, so the parallelogram identity gives $\|c_n-c_m\|^2\le2/n+2/m$; thus $(c_n)$ is Cauchy. Completeness and closedness yield a nearest point, and strict convexity of squared norm makes it unique. Applying this to $K$ and $P_0$ defines their projections.

As $t\downarrow0$, the lower limit of these secants is at least $\langle A^*p,h\rangle_X$; convexity makes the unit secant at least every smaller positive secant, so $R(u_{\alpha,w}+h)-R(u_{\alpha,w})\ge\langle A^*p,h\rangle_X$. This for every $h$ proves $A^*p\in\partial R(u_{\alpha,w})$. For each finite initial segment, expanding the nonnegative squared norm after orthogonal projection shows that the sum of squared limiting coordinates is at most $\|p_0\|_Y^2$; hence the coordinates define a vector $p$ in that closed span. > For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by

> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice. If $u\in L^2(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb R)$ and $TV_2(u;\mathbb R^2)<\infty$, choose smooth cutoffs $\chi_k$ with $0\le\chi_k\le1$, $\chi_k=1$ on $B(0,k)$, and support in $B(0,2k)$. Then $v_k:=\chi_ku$ belongs to $BV(\mathbb R^2)\cap L^1(\mathbb R^2)$, has support in $B(0,2k)$, converges to $u$ in $L^2(\mathbb R^2)$, and
$$\limsup_{k\to\infty}TV(v_k;\mathbb R^2)\le TV_2(u;\mathbb R^2).$$

Then for almost every applicable $t$ these sets have finite perimeter relative to $\Omega$, and $$TV(u;\Omega)=\int_0^\infty P(E_t^+;\Omega)\,dt+\int_{-\infty}^0P(E_t^-;\Omega)\,dt.$$

For every open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and real-valued $u\in BV(\Omega)$, $$TV(u;\Omega)=\sup\left\{\int_\Omega u\,\operatorname{div}\varphi\,dx:\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^n),\ |\varphi(x)|\le1\right\}.$$ If $u_k,u\in BV(\Omega)$ are real-valued and $u_k\to u$ in $L^1(\Omega)$, then $TV(u;\Omega)\le\liminf_kTV(u_k;\Omega)$. For each fixed $t\ne0$, $\chi_{E_{R,t}}\to\chi_{E_t}$ in $L^1$: the symmetric difference is outside $B(0,R)$ for the cutoffs constructed in [F1] and contained in $\{|u|>|t|\}$, whose tail measure is at most $|t|^{-2}\int_{\mathbb R^2\setminus B(0,R)}|u|^2$. Here $E_{R,t}$ and $E_t$ are the corresponding signed superlevel or sublevel sets.

For $t>0$, $|E_t^+|\le t^{-2}\|u\|_2^2$, and for $t<0$, $|E_t^-|\le |t|^{-2}\|u\|_2^2$. The indicator-valued maps are Borel on each half-line: on positive levels they are right-continuous in $L^1$ when $t_j\downarrow t>0$, by continuity from below of measure; on negative levels they are left-continuous when $t_j\uparrow t<0$. $$\int_\varepsilon^\infty P(E_t^+;\mathbb R^2)\,dt+\int_{-\infty}^{-\varepsilon}P(E_t^-;\mathbb R^2)\,dt\le TV_2(u;\mathbb R^2).$$
Letting $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ and using monotone convergence [F5] proves that the full perimeter sum is at most $TV_2(u;\mathbb R^2)$; its finiteness and [F3] give finite perimeter for almost every applicable level.

Let $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb R^2)$ with $\|\varphi\|_\infty\le1$. The signed layer-cake identity is $u(x)=\int_0^\infty\chi_{E_t^+}(x)\,dt-\int_{-\infty}^0\chi_{E_t^-}(x)\,dt$. On the compact support of $\operatorname{div}\varphi$, $\int |u|\,|\operatorname{div}\varphi|<\infty$, so Tonelli and Fubini [F4] permit integration of this identity against $\operatorname{div}\varphi$. At almost every level the absolute value of the resulting indicator test integral is at most its perimeter by [F3]. Therefore $\int u\operatorname{div}\varphi$ is at most the perimeter sum in step 2.1. Taking the supremum over admissible $\varphi$ gives $TV_2(u;\mathbb R^2)$ at most that sum, which together with step 2.1 proves equality.

If $\Omega=\mathbb R^2$, take $R(u)=TV_2(u;\mathbb R^2)$, the supremum of $\int u\,\operatorname{div}\varphi$ over smooth compactly supported vector fields of Euclidean norm at most one. For bounded $\Omega$, either take Neumann TV, $R(u)=TV(u;\Omega)$ when $u\in BV(\Omega)$ and $+\infty$ otherwise, or Dirichlet TV, $R(u)=TV(\widetilde u;\mathbb R^2)$ when the zero extension $\widetilde u$ belongs to $BV(\mathbb R^2)$ and $+\infty$ otherwise. Thus the bounded-domain choices count, respectively, only the interior derivative or also the jump of the zero extension across the boundary. In the full-space case finite $R$ does not require global $L^1$ integrability.

A vector $p^\dagger\in Y$ is a **dual source certificate** for $u^\dagger$ if $A^*p^\dagger\in\partial R(u^\dagger)$, where $\partial R$ is the convex subdifferential on the real Banach space $X$. The **TV source condition** at $u^\dagger$ is that such a certificate exists; it does not assert uniqueness of the truth or of the certificate. For a chosen certificate, the associated Bregman distance is

$$D_R^{A^*p^\dagger}(u,u^\dagger):=R(u)-R(u^\dagger)-\langle A^*p^\dagger,u-u^\dagger\rangle_X,$$

for $u\in\operatorname{dom}R$.
