Let $P_0:=\{p\in K:\langle f,p\rangle_Y=R(u^\dagger)\}$ and let $p_0$ be its unique minimum-norm element. For every sequence $\alpha_n>0$ with $\alpha_n\to0$, $p_{\alpha_n,0}\to p_0$ strongly in $Y$ and $A^*p_{\alpha_n,0}\to A^*p_0$ strongly in $X$. For every $\alpha>0$ and $w\in Y$,

$$\|p_{\alpha,w}-p_{\alpha,0}\|_Y\le\frac{\|w\|_Y}{\alpha},\qquad \|A^*p_{\alpha,w}-A^*p_{\alpha,0}\|_X\le\frac{\|A^*\|\,\|w\|_Y}{\alpha}.$$

Moreover, for any $R_0>R(u^\dagger)$ the certificate yields a variational source condition on $\{u:R(u)\le R_0\}$ with exponent $2$, coefficient $\beta=0$, and index function $\psi(s)=(1+\|p^\dagger\|_Y)\sqrt{s}$. Consequently, if $\delta_n\downarrow0$, $\|w_n\|_Y\le\delta_n$, $\alpha_n\asymp\delta_n$, and exact global minimizers $u_n$ are supplied, then the variational-source rate theorem gives

$$D_R^{A^*p^\dagger}(u_n,u^\dagger)=O(\delta_n),\qquad \|Au_n-(f+w_n)\|_Y=O(\delta_n).$$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be a bounded Lipschitz domain, meaning a bounded open set whose boundary has a finite cover by Lipschitz graph neighborhoods with $\Omega$ on one side of each graph. Total variation is lower semicontinuous under $L^1(\Omega)$ convergence of BV functions. Every sequence $(u_k)\subset BV(\Omega)$ satisfying $$\sup_k\bigl(\|u_k\|_{L^1(\Omega)}+TV(u_k;\Omega)\bigr)<\infty$$ has a subsequence converging in $L^1(\Omega)$ to a function in $BV(\Omega)$.
Assume Countable Choice and let $n\ge2$. Every $u\in BV(\mathbb R^n)$ satisfies $$\|u\|_{L^{n/(n-1)}(\mathbb R^n)}\le TV(u;\mathbb R^n).$$

Assume Countable Choice. Every $u\in L^2(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb R)$ with $TV_2(u;\mathbb R^2)<\infty$ satisfies
$$\|u\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^2)}\le TV_2(u;\mathbb R^2).$$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and connected. If $u\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ satisfies $\partial_i u=0$ as a distribution for every coordinate $i$, then there is a constant $c\in\mathbb R$ such that $u=c$ almost everywhere on $\Omega$.

Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a bounded Lipschitz domain, meaning a bounded open set whose boundary has a finite cover by coordinate neighborhoods in which it is the graph of a Lipschitz function and $\Omega$ lies on one side of that graph. For $u\in BV(\Omega)$ define the Neumann total variation by $TV_N(u;\Omega):=|Du|(\Omega)$. Define its zero extension $\widetilde u\in L^1(\mathbb R^n)$ by $\widetilde u=u$ almost everywhere on $\Omega$ and $\widetilde u=0$ almost everywhere on $\mathbb R^n\setminus\Omega$. Define the Dirichlet total variation by $TV_D(u;\Omega):=TV(\widetilde u;\mathbb R^n)$ when $\widetilde u\in BV(\mathbb R^n)$ and by $TV_D(u;\Omega):=+\infty$ otherwise. For $v\in BV(\mathbb R^n)$ define the full-space total variation by $TV_F(v):=TV(v;\mathbb R^n)$. Thus Neumann variation counts only the distributional derivative inside $\Omega$, while Dirichlet variation also counts any jump created by zero extension across $\partial\Omega$.

For every open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and real-valued $u\in BV(\Omega)$, $$TV(u;\Omega)=\sup\left\{\int_\Omega u\,\operatorname{div}\varphi\,dx:\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^n),\ |\varphi(x)|\le1\right\}.$$ If $u_k,u\in BV(\Omega)$ are real-valued and $u_k\to u$ in $L^1(\Omega)$, then $TV(u;\Omega)\le\liminf_kTV(u_k;\Omega)$. In addition, assuming Countable Choice, for any real-valued $u\in L^1(\Omega)$ the displayed supremum is finite if and only if $u\in BV(\Omega)$, with equality to $TV(u;\Omega)$; under the same assumption, an $L^1$ limit of real-valued BV functions with bounded liminf total variation belongs to $BV(\Omega)$ and satisfies the same lower-semicontinuity inequality.

Assume Countable Choice. If $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ is open, $u\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R)$, and $TV_2(u;\Omega)<\infty$, then each distributional derivative of $u$ is represented by a finite signed Radon measure. Their vector measure $Du$ has finite Radon variation and $|Du|(\Omega)=TV_2(u;\Omega)$.

Every bounded sequence of reals has a convergent subsequence: if $(x_k)$ is a
sequence of reals and there is $M \in \mathbb{R}$ with $|x_k| \le M$ for every
$k \in \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-sequence]]), then there is a strictly increasing
$n : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and a real $L$ with $x_{n_j} \to L$.

Equivalently: the subsequential limit set of a bounded sequence is nonempty
([[def-subsequential-limit]]).

The theorem is the exact repair of the false claim that a bounded sequence
converges. A bounded
sequence need not converge, and the alternating sequence is the standing witness;
what boundedness does force is that *some* subsequence converges. The converse of
the theorem is false, and badly so: a sequence with a convergent subsequence need
not be bounded.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space and let $f$ be a bounded linear functional on $H$ ([[def-dual-space-of-a-normed-space]]). Then there is a unique $y\in H$ with

$$f(x)=\langle x,y\rangle\qquad\text{for every }x\in H,$$

and $\|f\|=\|y\|$, where $\|f\|$ is the dual norm ([[def-operator-norm]]). Under the first-variable-linear convention the representing vector depends conjugate-linearly and isometrically on $f$: if $f_i$ is represented by $y_i$ and $a,b$ are scalars, then $af_1+bf_2$ is represented by $\overline a\,y_1+\overline b\,y_2$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. The map $f\mapsto u_f$, $u_f(\varphi)=\int_\Omega f\varphi$, is a complex-linear injection from $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ modulo almost-everywhere equality into $\mathcal D'(\Omega)$. It is continuous from the local $L^1$ topology, generated by $f\mapsto\int_K|f|$ for compact $K\subseteq\Omega$, to the strong distribution topology. In particular local $L^1$ convergence implies strong distribution convergence. The continuity estimate itself is choice-free; Countable Choice is used in the cited $L^1$ approximate-identity theorem proving injectivity.

Assume Countable Choice. For every nonempty bounded connected Lipschitz domain $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^2$, there is a finite constant $C_\Omega>0$ such that every $u\in BV(\Omega)$ satisfies
$$\|u-u_\Omega\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\le C_\Omega TV(u;\Omega),\qquad u_\Omega:=|\Omega|^{-1}\int_\Omega u\,dx.$$

derivations.claim: If $\|A^*\|=0$, the adjoint identity implies $A=0$ and $f=0$. Since $0$ is exact, minimality gives $R(u^\dagger)=0$. The data term of $J_n$ is then constant, so every global minimizer has $R(u_n)=0$. In the full-space case [F6] makes $u_n$ constant and $L^2(\mathbb R^2)$ forces it to be zero; in the Dirichlet case apply [F6] to its zero extension, which vanishes outside bounded $\Omega$, and again obtain zero; in the Neumann case [F6] makes it constant and the prescribed zero-mean choice makes it zero. Thus $u_0=0$ is an exact minimum-TV solution. Since $R\ge0$ and $R(0)=0$, $0\in\partial R(0)=\partial R(u_0)$, so $A^*p^\dagger=0\in\partial R(u_0)$ and the assertion holds. For the remainder assume $\|A^*\|>0$.

Put $p_n=(f+w_n-Au_n)/\alpha_n$. By [F2], $p_n=p_{\alpha_n,w_n}$ and $p_{\alpha_n,0}$ is bounded. The noise hypothesis gives $\|w_n\|_Y/\alpha_n\le\eta/\|A^*\|$, hence [F2] makes $(p_n)$ bounded and $\|w_n\|_Y\to0$. The identity $Au_n=f+w_n-\alpha_np_n$ therefore gives $Au_n\to f$ strongly in $Y$. Comparing the objective at $u_n$ and $u^\dagger$ gives
$$\tfrac12\|Au_n-(f+w_n)\|_Y^2+\alpha_nR(u_n)\le\tfrac12\|w_n\|_Y^2+\alpha_nR(u^\dagger),$$
so $R(u_n)\le R(u^\dagger)+\|w_n\|_Y^2/(2\alpha_n)\le R(u^\dagger)+\eta^2\alpha_n/(2\|A^*\|^2)$. In particular the variations are bounded and $\limsup_nR(u_n)\le R(u^\dagger)$.

In the Neumann branch on bounded connected $\Omega$, write $m_n=|\Omega|^{-1}\int_\Omega u_n$ and $v_n=u_n-m_n$. The Poincaré inequality [F14] gives $\|v_n\|_2\le C_\Omega TV(v_n;\Omega)=C_\Omega R(u_n)$, which is uniformly bounded by step 2.1.

If $A\mathbf1_\Omega=0$, subtracting $m_n$ leaves both $Au_n$ and Neumann TV unchanged, so we use the zero-mean minimizer specified in the Statement, which is uniformly bounded in $L^2$ by step 3.1. If $A\mathbf1_\Omega\ne0$, then [F1] and step 2.1 give bounded $\|Au_n\|_Y$ and
$$|m_n|\,\|A\mathbf1_\Omega\|_Y=\|Au_n-Av_n\|_Y\le\|Au_n\|_Y+\|A\|\|v_n\|_2,$$
so the means, and therefore $\|u_n\|_2$, are bounded. In the full-space case [F5] gives $\|u_n\|_2\le R(u_n)$. In the Dirichlet case [F4] applied to $\widetilde u_n$ gives $\|u_n\|_2\le R(u_n)$. Thus in every branch the selected sequence is bounded in $L^2$.

If $\Omega$ is bounded, the $L^2$ bound gives an $L^1$ bound by [F11]; the interior variation is bounded by $R(u_n)$ in both boundary conventions [F7]. [F3] therefore supplies a subsequence converging strongly in $L^1(\Omega)$. If $\Omega=\mathbb R^2$, restrict to each ball $B(0,m)$: the $L^1$ norms are bounded by $|B(0,m)|^{1/2}\sup_n\|u_n\|_2$, and [F9] bounds the variation there. Applying [F3] on each ball and taking a countable diagonal subsequence using [A1] gives convergence in $L^1$ on every bounded ball.

The resulting sequence is still bounded in the Hilbert space $L^2(\Omega)$. Its closed linear span is separable, since rational finite linear combinations of its terms are dense. Gram–Schmidt gives a finite or countable orthonormal family with dense span. Each coordinate sequence is bounded by [F11]; repeated use of [F10] and [A1] yields a subsubsequence on which every coordinate converges. Pythagoras applied to each finite orthogonal projection bounds the sums of squared limiting coordinates by the common squared norm bound, so these coordinates define a vector $u_0$ in the closed span. Approximation by finite linear combinations proves convergence of inner products against every vector in the span. For any $z\in L^2(\Omega)$, [F12] represents $x\mapsto\langle x,z\rangle$ restricted to that span by a vector in the span, so the convergence is weak in all of $L^2$. Testing against compactly supported smooth functions shows that this weak limit and the strong $L^1$ or local-$L^1$ limit from step 4.1 define the same distribution; injectivity [F13] makes them equal almost everywhere.

Weak convergence and boundedness of $A$ imply $Au_n\rightharpoonup Au_0$, while step 2.1 gives $Au_n\to f$ strongly; hence $Au_0=f$. In the full-space case, for every admissible test field $\varphi$, local $L^1$ convergence gives $\int u_0\operatorname{div}\varphi=\lim_n\int u_n\operatorname{div}\varphi\le\liminf_nR(u_n)$; taking the supremum gives $R(u_0)\le\liminf_nR(u_n)$. In the Neumann case the same lower semicontinuity follows from [F8] and strong $L^1(\Omega)$ convergence. In the Dirichlet case the zero extensions converge strongly in $L^1(\mathbb R^2)$, so [F8] gives the same inequality for their full-space TV. Thus $R(u_0)\le\liminf_nR(u_n)\le\limsup_nR(u_n)\le R(u^\dagger)$. Exactness and the minimum property of $u^\dagger$ force equality, so $u_0$ is a minimum-TV exact solution.

Let $\xi=A^*p^\dagger$. Since $Au_0=Au^\dagger=f$, the adjoint identity in [F1] gives $\langle\xi,u_0-u^\dagger\rangle_X=\langle p^\dagger,A(u_0-u^\dagger)\rangle_Y=0$. For every $v\in X$, the subgradient inequality at $u^\dagger$ therefore gives
$$R(v)\ge R(u^\dagger)+\langle\xi,v-u^\dagger\rangle_X=R(u_0)+\langle\xi,v-u_0\rangle_X.$$
This is exactly $A^*p^\dagger\in\partial R(u_0)$, as required.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $X=L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ and $Y=L^2(\Sigma,\mu;\mathbb R)$ be real Hilbert spaces, let $A:X\to Y$ be bounded and real-linear, and let $R:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be one of the full-space, Dirichlet, or Neumann TV functionals. Assume that $R$ is proper, convex, lower semicontinuous, and positively one-homogeneous, and that $u^\dagger$ is a minimum-$R$ exact solution of $Au=f$ with a dual source certificate $p^\dagger\in Y$, so $A^*p^\dagger\in\partial R(u^\dagger)$. Define $K:=\{p\in Y:A^*p\in\partial R(0)\}$ and $D_{\alpha,w}(p):=\langle f+w,p\rangle_Y-\frac{\alpha}{2}\|p\|_Y^2$ for $\alpha>0$ and $w\in Y$.

For each $\alpha>0$ and $w\in Y$, $D_{\alpha,w}$ has a unique maximizer $p_{\alpha,w}=\operatorname{Proj}_K((f+w)/\alpha)$. If $u_{\alpha,w}$ is any supplied global minimizer of $u\mapsto\frac12\|Au-(f+w)\|_Y^2+\alpha R(u)$, then $p_{\alpha,w}=(f+w-Au_{\alpha,w})/\alpha$, $A^*p_{\alpha,w}\in\partial R(u_{\alpha,w})$, and $A^*p_{\alpha,w}\in\partial R(0)$. For every such supplied minimizer, the correctly normalized primal-dual value identity is

$$\min_u\{\tfrac12\|Au-(f+w)\|_Y^2+\alpha R(u)\}=\alpha D_{\alpha,w}(p_{\alpha,w}).$$

Let $P_0:=\{p\in K:\langle f,p\rangle_Y=R(u^\dagger)\}$ and let $p_0$ be its unique minimum-norm element. For every sequence $\alpha_n>0$ with $\alpha_n\to0$, $p_{\alpha_n,0}\to p_0$ strongly in $Y$ and $A^*p_{\alpha_n,0}\to A^*p_0$ strongly in $X$. For every $\alpha>0$ and $w\in Y$,

$$\|p_{\alpha,w}-p_{\alpha,0}\|_Y\le\frac{\|w\|_Y}{\alpha},\qquad \|A^*p_{\alpha,w}-A^*p_{\alpha,0}\|_X\le\frac{\|A^*\|\,\|w\|_Y}{\alpha}.$$

Moreover, for any $R_0>R(u^\dagger)$ the certificate yields a variational source condition on $\{u:R(u)\le R_0\}$ with exponent $2$, coefficient $\beta=0$, and index function $\psi(s)=(1+\|p^\dagger\|_Y)\sqrt{s}$. Consequently, if $\delta_n\downarrow0$, $\|w_n\|_Y\le\delta_n$, $\alpha_n\asymp\delta_n$, and exact global minimizers $u_n$ are supplied, then the variational-source rate theorem gives

$$D_R^{A^*p^\dagger}(u_n,u^\dagger)=O(\delta_n),\qquad \|Au_n-(f+w_n)\|_Y=O(\delta_n).$$

Let $\Omega=\mathbb R^2$, or let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ be a bounded Lipschitz domain. Set $X=L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ and let $Y=L^2(\Sigma,\mu;\mathbb R)$ for a measure space $(\Sigma,\mu)$, using the real integral inner products. Let $A:X\to Y$ be bounded and real-linear, and let $A^*:Y\to X$ be its Hilbert adjoint, characterized by $\langle Au,p\rangle_Y=\langle u,A^*p\rangle_X$. Define $R:X\to[0,+\infty]$ as follows. If $\Omega=\mathbb R^2$, take $R(u)=TV_2(u;\mathbb R^2)$, the supremum of $\int u\,\operatorname{div}\varphi$ over smooth compactly supported vector fields of Euclidean norm at most one. For bounded $\Omega$, either take Neumann TV, $R(u)=TV(u;\Omega)$ when $u\in BV(\Omega)$ and $+\infty$ otherwise, or Dirichlet TV, $R(u)=TV(\widetilde u;\mathbb R^2)$ when the zero extension $\widetilde u$ belongs to $BV(\mathbb R^2)$ and $+\infty$ otherwise. Thus the bounded-domain choices count, respectively, only the interior derivative or also the jump of the zero extension across the boundary. In the full-space case finite $R$ does not require global $L^1$ integrability.

Identify each $q\in X$ with the continuous linear functional $h\mapsto\langle q,h\rangle_X$ by the real Hilbert-space Riesz representation. For exact data $f=Au^\dagger$, a **minimum-TV exact solution** is a point $u^\dagger\in X$ satisfying $Au^\dagger=f$ and $R(u^\dagger)\le R(u)$ for every $u\in X$ with $Au=f$. A vector $p^\dagger\in Y$ is a **dual source certificate** for $u^\dagger$ if $A^*p^\dagger\in\partial R(u^\dagger)$, where $\partial R$ is the convex subdifferential on the real Banach space $X$. The **TV source condition** at $u^\dagger$ is that such a certificate exists; it does not assert uniqueness of the truth or of the certificate. For a chosen certificate, the associated Bregman distance is

$$D_R^{A^*p^\dagger}(u,u^\dagger):=R(u)-R(u^\dagger)-\langle A^*p^\dagger,u-u^\dagger\rangle_X,$$

for $u\in\operatorname{dom}R$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $u\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^2)$, with functions identified when they agree almost everywhere. For full-space TV, use $u$ itself. For a bounded-domain Dirichlet or Neumann problem, use the zero extension $\widetilde u$ only to define the geometric level sets; this does not change the selected regularizer, and for each nonzero level the resulting set lies inside $\Omega$. For $t>0$, the positive $t$-level class is the measurable-set class of $E_t^+(u):=\{x\in\mathbb R^2:u(x)>t\}$; for $t<0$, the negative $t$-level class is the class of $E_t^-(u):=\{x\in\mathbb R^2:u(x)<t\}$. These classes do not depend on the representative of $u$. For any measurable set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^2$, its density-one representative is

$$E^{(1)}:=\left\{x\in\mathbb R^2:\lim_{r\downarrow0}\frac{|E\cap B(x,r)|}{|B(x,r)|}=1\right\}.$$

This representative depends only on the almost-everywhere class of $E$. The canonical level set $U_u^{(t)}$ is $(E_t^+(u))^{(1)}$ when $t>0$ and $(E_t^-(u))^{(1)}$ when $t<0$. Its canonical boundary is the ordinary topological boundary $\partial U_u^{(t)}$ in $\mathbb R^2$. For two nonempty boundary sets, use the usual extended Hausdorff distance induced by Euclidean distance; set $d_H(\varnothing,\varnothing)=0$ and $d_H(E,F)=+\infty$ if exactly one set is empty. Hausdorff convergence uses this convention and is invariant under changes to a function on a null set.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $u\in L^2(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb R)$ satisfy $TV_2(u;\mathbb R^2)<\infty$. For $t>0$ set $E_t^+=\{x:u(x)>t\}$, and for $t<0$ set $E_t^-=\{x:u(x)<t\}$. Each set has finite area, almost every applicable level set has finite perimeter, and
$$TV_2(u;\mathbb R^2)=\int_0^\infty P(E_t^+;\mathbb R^2)\,dt+\int_{-\infty}^0P(E_t^-;\mathbb R^2)\,dt.$$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $u\in BV(\Omega)$, and for $t>0$ set $E_t^+:=\{x\in\Omega:u(x)>t\}$ while for $t<0$ set $E_t^-:=\{x\in\Omega:u(x)<t\}$. Then for almost every applicable $t$ these sets have finite perimeter relative to $\Omega$, and $$TV(u;\Omega)=\int_0^\infty P(E_t^+;\Omega)\,dt+\int_{-\infty}^0P(E_t^-;\Omega)\,dt.$$

Let $\Omega=\mathbb R^2$ or let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ be a bounded Lipschitz domain. Choose one of three perimeter functionals for measurable $E\subseteq\Omega$: full-space perimeter $P_R(E)=P(E;\mathbb R^2)$ when $\Omega=\mathbb R^2$; Neumann relative perimeter $P_N(E)=P(E;\Omega)$ on a bounded domain; or Dirichlet perimeter $P_D(E)=P(\widetilde E;\mathbb R^2)$, where $\widetilde E$ is $E$ extended by the empty set outside $\Omega$. Require finite measure and finite selected perimeter, and let $\kappa$ be measurable with $\int_F|\kappa|<\infty$ for every set considered. The set $E$ has **variational curvature** $\kappa$ for the selected model if its selected perimeter minus $\int_E\kappa\,dx$ is no greater than the same quantity for every finite-measure finite-selected-perimeter competitor $F\subseteq\Omega$ whose symmetric difference $F\mathbin\triangle E$ has compact closure in $\Omega$. In the full-space model, this means compact closure in $\mathbb R^2$.

For bounded Dirichlet TV, a separate **obstacle curvature** condition on $\Omega$ means that $\Omega$, viewed as a finite-perimeter set in $\mathbb R^2$, minimizes $F\mapsto P(F;\mathbb R^2)-\int_F\kappa_\Omega\,dx$ over all finite-measure finite-perimeter $F\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ whose symmetric difference with $\Omega$ has compact closure in $\mathbb R^2$.

Assume Countable Choice. Every Lebesgue-measurable set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ with finite area and finite perimeter satisfies
$$4\pi |E|\le P(E;\mathbb R^2)^2.$$

Assume Countable Choice. For every nonempty bounded connected Lipschitz domain $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^2$, there is a finite constant $C_\Omega>0$ such that every $u\in BV(\Omega)$ satisfies
$$\|u-u_\Omega\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\le C_\Omega TV(u;\Omega),\qquad u_\Omega:=|\Omega|^{-1}\int_\Omega u\,dx.$$

For every open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and real-valued $u\in BV(\Omega)$, $$TV(u;\Omega)=\sup\left\{\int_\Omega u\,\operatorname{div}\varphi\,dx:\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^n),\ |\varphi(x)|\le1\right\}.$$ If $u_k,u\in BV(\Omega)$ are real-valued and $u_k\to u$ in $L^1(\Omega)$, then $TV(u;\Omega)\le\liminf_kTV(u_k;\Omega)$. In addition, assuming Countable Choice, for any real-valued $u\in L^1(\Omega)$ the displayed supremum is finite if and only if $u\in BV(\Omega)$, with equality to $TV(u;\Omega)$; under the same assumption, an $L^1$ limit of real-valued BV functions with bounded liminf total variation belongs to $BV(\Omega)$ and satisfies the same lower-semicontinuity inequality.

Every bounded sequence of reals has a convergent subsequence: if $(x_k)$ is a
sequence of reals and there is $M \in \mathbb{R}$ with $|x_k| \le M$ for every
$k \in \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-sequence]]), then there is a strictly increasing
$n : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and a real $L$ with $x_{n_j} \to L$.

Equivalently: the subsequential limit set of a bounded sequence is nonempty
([[def-subsequential-limit]]).

The theorem is the exact repair of the false claim that a bounded sequence
converges. A bounded
sequence need not converge, and the alternating sequence is the standing witness;
what boundedness does force is that *some* subsequence converges. The converse of
the theorem is false, and badly so: a sequence with a convergent subsequence need
not be bounded.

Assume Countable Choice. In this lemma $\mathcal H^1$ means arclength, equivalently normalized one-dimensional Hausdorff measure. Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ be open, let $E\subseteq U$ have finite measure and finite relative perimeter, and fix $x\in\mathbb R^2$. Put $\mu=|D\chi_E|$ on $U$. For almost every $r>0$, $\mu(\partial B(x,r))=0$ and, with $s_E(r)=\mathcal H^1(E^{(1)}\cap U\cap\partial B(x,r))$,
$$P(E\cap B(x,r);U)=\mu(U\cap B(x,r))+s_E(r),\qquad P(E\setminus B(x,r);U)=\mu(U\setminus\overline B(x,r))+s_E(r).$$
The volume $a(r)=|E\cap B(x,r)|$ is locally absolutely continuous with $a'(r)=s_E(r)$ almost everywhere. The analogous inside-cut formula holds for $(U\setminus E)\cap B(x,r)$, with the complementary sphere slice. When $U=\mathbb R^2$ this clause requires no finite area for the uncut complement. For finite-area $E$, the outside volume $|E\setminus B(x,r)|$ has derivative $-s_E(r)$ almost everywhere.

If $E$ globally minimizes $P(F;U)-\int_F k$ among the finite-measure finite-relative-perimeter sets in $U$, with all displayed integrals finite, then for almost every $r$,
$$P(E\cap B;U)\le2s_E(r)+\int_{E\cap B}k,\qquad P((U\setminus E)\cap B;U)\le2s_{U\setminus E}(r)-\int_{(U\setminus E)\cap B}k.$$
For $U=\mathbb R^2$ one also has $P(E\setminus B)\le2s_E(r)+\int_{E\setminus B}k$. Here $B=B(x,r)$; the competitors may touch the boundary of $U$.

Full-space finite-measure finite-perimeter sets satisfy $P(F\cap G)+P(F\cup G)\le P(F)+P(G)$. Consequently, suppose bounded $\Omega$ has the global obstacle curvature $\kappa_\Omega$ and $\kappa_\Omega\ge g$ outside $\Omega$, with $g\in L^2(\mathbb R^2\setminus\Omega)$. If $E\subseteq\Omega$ globally minimizes $P(F)-\int_F k$ among $F\subseteq\Omega$, then it minimizes against all full-space competitors with bounded symmetric difference for the extended field $k\chi_\Omega+g\chi_{\Omega^c}$. In particular all bounded-ball removal and filling comparisons above apply to this extended field.

Assume Countable Choice. Suppose $z_n\to z_\infty$ in $L^2(U)$ and $v_n=z_n+e_n$ with $\|e_n\|_2\le\eta$. Include $v_\infty=z_\infty$ with zero perturbation if desired. For each index, either sign $\sigma\in\{-1,1\}$, and any finite-measure finite-selected-perimeter set $E\subseteq U$ globally minimizing the selected perimeter minus $\int_E\sigma v_n$, use its ambient density-one representative $E^{(1)}$ and ambient boundary. The selected branch is full-space perimeter on $U=\mathbb R^2$; zero-extension Dirichlet perimeter on bounded Lipschitz $U=\Omega$ with the obstacle curvature and exterior lower bound $g\in L^2(\Omega^c)$; or relative Neumann perimeter on bounded connected Lipschitz $U=\Omega$ with specified $C_\Omega$ satisfying $\|u-u_\Omega\|_2\le C_\Omega TV(u;\Omega)$.

If $\eta<2\sqrt\pi$ in the full-space and Dirichlet branches, or $\eta<1/C_\Omega$ in the Neumann branch, there exist $c,r_0>0$, independent of the index, sign and minimizing set, such that
$$|E\cap B(x,r)|\ge c\pi r^2,\qquad |B(x,r)\setminus E|\ge c\pi r^2\quad(x\in\partial E^{(1)},\ 0<r<r_0).$$
All the full-space representatives and their boundaries lie in one common closed ball; in bounded branches they lie in $\overline\Omega$. The full-space sets also have uniform area and perimeter bounds. These conclusions include the limiting field and the empty set. They require no connected-component or Jordan decomposition of finite-perimeter sets.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ be open and let $TV_2(\cdot;\Omega)$ be the extended distributional total variation on $L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R)$. It is proper, convex, lower semicontinuous in the $L^2$ norm, and positively one-homogeneous for nonnegative scalars. For every $u\in BV(\Omega)\cap L^2(\Omega)$, it agrees with spatial TV: $TV_2(u;\Omega)=TV(u;\Omega)$.

Assume Countable Choice. Here $\mathcal H^m$ on a boundary denotes normalized Hausdorff measure: the repository's unnormalised $m$-dimensional Hausdorff measure divided by $c_m=H^m((0,1]^m)$ for $m\ge1$, and counting measure for $m=0$. Let $n\ge2$ and let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a bounded Lipschitz domain, meaning a bounded open set whose boundary has a finite cover by coordinate neighborhoods in which it is the graph of a Lipschitz function and $\Omega$ lies on one side of the graph. There is a unique bounded linear trace operator $T:BV(\Omega)\to L^1(\partial\Omega,\mathcal H^{n-1})$ such that for every $u\in BV(\Omega)$ and $\phi\in C_c^1(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb R^n)$, $$\int_\Omega u\,\operatorname{div}\phi\,dx=-\int_\Omega\phi\cdot dDu+\int_{\partial\Omega}Tu\,\phi\cdot\nu\,d\mathcal H^{n-1},$$ where $\nu$ is the outward unit normal defined almost everywhere on $\partial\Omega$. The zero extension $\widetilde u$ belongs to $BV(\mathbb R^n)$ and satisfies $$TV(\widetilde u;\mathbb R^n)=TV(u;\Omega)+\|Tu\|_{L^1(\partial\Omega)}\le C_\Omega\bigl(\|u\|_{L^1(\Omega)}+TV(u;\Omega)\bigr)$$ for a finite constant $C_\Omega$ depending only on the domain. The same conclusions hold in dimension one for a bounded open set with a finite one-sided graph cover, with the two one-sided endpoint traces and counting measure on its finite boundary.

$\overline{\mu 	imes 
u}$ be the completed product of two sigma-finite
measure spaces.

1. If $f : X 	imes Y 	o [0,\infty]$ is $\overline{\mu 	imes 
u}$-measurable, there are measurable null sets $A\subseteq X$ and $B\subseteq Y$ such that $f_x$ is $\overline{\mathcal B}$-measurable for $x
otin A$ and $f^y$ is $\overline{\mathcal A}$-measurable for $y
otin B$. Define $I_f(x)=\int_Y f_x\,d\overline
u$ for $x
otin A$ and $I_f(x)=0$ on $A$; define $J_f(y)=\int_X f^y\,d\overline\mu$ for $y
otin B$ and $J_f(y)=0$ on $B$. Then $I_f,J_f$ are measurable and
$$\int f\,d\overline{\mu 	imes 
u}=\int_X I_f\,d\mu=\int_Y J_f\,d
u.$$
2. If $f \in L^1(\overline{\mu 	imes 
u})$, there are measurable null sets $A\subseteq X$ and $B\subseteq Y$ such that the sections are measurable and integrable outside them. Define $I_f,J_f$ by the same section integrals outside $A,B$ and by zero on $A,B$. They are measurable and integrable, and the same equality holds.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

derivations.claim: The TV functional is proper, convex, lower semicontinuous and positively one-homogeneous by [F12]. On a bounded domain $L^2\subset L^1$, so the relative functional agrees with that test-field functional by [F8]; the Dirichlet version is its composition with the linear isometric zero-extension map into full-space L2. Thus the hypotheses of [F1] hold. Comparison of each objective with its finite value at zero also gives finite TV at a supplied minimizer. Put $z_n=v_{\alpha_n,0}=A^*p_{\alpha_n,0}$. By [F1], $z_n\to v_0=A^*p_0$ strongly in $L^2(\Omega)$ and $v_n=z_n+e_n$ with $\|e_n\|_2\le\eta$. Thus the exact-field sequence, its limit and the noisy fields have precisely the coefficient decomposition required by [F10]. In particular their uniform small-measure moduli and, in full space, exact-field tail moduli follow from strong convergence, as proved there, without an assumed uniform integrability of the noisy perturbations.

For each supplied minimizer, [F1] and positive one-homogeneity imply $R(u_n)=\langle v_n,u_n\rangle$ and $v_n\in\partial R(0)$. The selected TV is even, since its test-field class is symmetric and zero extension is linear. Applying its inequality to both $\chi_F$ and $-\chi_F$ gives $P_*(F)\ge\sigma\int_Fv_n$ for either sign $\sigma$, for every finite-area finite-selected-perimeter competitor; $P_*$ denotes the selected branch perimeter throughout this proof. Indeed these indicators belong to $L^2$ and their selected TV is exactly $P_*$ by [F8] and the boundary conventions. In full space every nonzero level has finite area by $|\{|u_n|>|t|\}|\le\|u_n\|_2^2/t^2$. Bounded-domain levels have finite area automatically. Coarea [F4] gives finite selected perimeter for almost every nonzero level. Relative-perimeter Neumann levels also have finite ambient perimeter by [F11]. Signed layer cake and Cauchy–Schwarz give an absolutely integrable level pairing: the integral over levels of $\int_{E_n(t)}|v_n|$ is $\int|u_n||v_n|\le\|u_n\|_2\|v_n\|_2$. Hence [F11] and coarea show that the integral of the nonnegative gaps $P_*(E_n(t))-\operatorname{sgn}(t)\int_{E_n(t)}v_n$ equals $R(u_n)-\langle v_n,u_n\rangle=0$. Each gap therefore vanishes almost everywhere. Their value zero is the global minimum of $P_*(F)-\operatorname{sgn}(t)\int_Fv_n$, since every competitor has nonnegative value. This proves the stated equality and even global branch minimization, which in particular implies compact-perturbation variational curvature [F5]. Taking the countable union of exceptional level sets makes this true simultaneously for all $n$.

The threshold and actual obstacle assumptions are exactly those of [F10]. Apply it to every calibrated set from step 1.2, with either level sign. It supplies one $c,r_0>0$ for both ambient density inequalities at every point of each canonical boundary, independently of the index and the nonexceptional level. In the Dirichlet branch the actual obstacle extension uses perimeter submodularity from [F10]; in the Neumann branch its proof uses relative cuts and the specified $C_\Omega$, and at points on $\partial\Omega$ it uses the uniform Lipschitz exterior area for the ambient complement. Thus no false relative-complement estimate is imposed on the valid case $E=\Omega$. In full space [F10] compares $E$ with actual radial cuts and proves finite-radius extinction of $|E\setminus B(0,r)|$, giving one common ball containing the density-one sets and their topological boundaries. Bounded-domain representatives and boundaries lie in $\overline\Omega$. These are the full density and support conclusions, rather than assumptions for the transfer below.

The limiting field calibrates every minimum-TV exact solution $u_0$ under consideration. More explicitly, the dual supplier [F1] defines $p_0\in\{p:A^*p\in\partial R(0),\ \langle f,p\rangle=R(u^\dagger)\}$. For any such exact minimum $Au_0=f$ and $R(u_0)=R(u^\dagger)$, one has $\langle v_0,u_0\rangle=\langle p_0,f\rangle=R(u_0)$, while $v_0\in\partial R(0)$. Its subgradient inequality is therefore also the inequality at $u_0$. Repeat step 1.2 with $u_0,v_0$; its almost-everywhere level sets are calibrated global minimizers. Adjoin the limiting exact field with perturbation zero in [F10]. The very same coefficient moduli and noise threshold used in step 2.1 then give the same uniform density and support conclusions for this limit. This includes any selected minimum-TV exact limit carrying the inherited certificate; it does not identify that solution with $u^\dagger$ without uniqueness.

Fix a nonzero nonexceptional level for which the corresponding sets converge in measure to such a canonical limit $E_0$. If $E_0=\varnothing$ and infinitely many $E_n$ are nonempty, their bounded common support makes each boundary nonempty: a boundaryless subset of connected $\mathbb R^2$ is clopen, and the only bounded clopen set is empty. Choose a boundary point and one fixed $0<r<r_0$; the density estimate gives $|E_n\triangle E_0|\ge c\pi r^2$, a contradiction. If $E_0$ is nonempty, it has positive measure by its density-one definition, so convergence rules out infinitely many empty $E_n$. The empty status therefore agrees eventually; two empty boundaries have Hausdorff distance zero. In the nonempty case, if $x_n\in\partial E_n$ stays at distance at least $\delta>0$ from $\partial E_0$, common compact support and [F9] give a subsequence $x_n\to x$. For $r<\min(r_0,\delta/4)$ the connected ball $B(x_n,r)$ misses $\partial E_0$ and is entirely in $E_0$ or entirely outside it. The two-sided density of $E_n$ forces symmetric difference at least $c\pi r^2$, again a contradiction. Conversely, if $y_n\in\partial E_0$ stays at distance at least $\delta$ from $\partial E_n$, take a convergent subsequence with limit $y\in\partial E_0$. A fixed smaller connected ball about $y$ misses every corresponding $\partial E_n$, so along a further subsequence its status is always full or always empty. Measure convergence makes $E_0$ full or empty almost everywhere on that ball. By the density-one definition it is then actually full or empty in a smaller ball, contradicting $y\in\partial E_0$. Both directed Hausdorff distances tend to zero, with all point and subsequence selections allowed by [A1].

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $X=L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ and let $Y=L^2(\Sigma,\mu;\mathbb R)$ be real Hilbert spaces. Let $A:X\to Y$ be bounded and real-linear, let $f=Au^\dagger$, and assume $u^\dagger$ is an exact solution minimizing a proper, convex, lower semicontinuous, positively one-homogeneous TV functional $R:X\to[0,+\infty]$ with a source certificate $p^\dagger\in Y$, so $A^*p^\dagger\in\partial R(u^\dagger)$. Use full-space $R=TV_2(\cdot;\mathbb R^2)$ if $\Omega=\mathbb R^2$; for a bounded connected Lipschitz $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^2$, use either Neumann $R(u)=TV(u;\Omega)$ or Dirichlet $R(u)=TV(\widetilde u;\mathbb R^2)$ for the zero extension $\widetilde u$, assigning $+\infty$ outside the respective finite-variation domain. A bounded connected Lipschitz domain here is a bounded open set with a finite Lipschitz graph cover of its boundary, with the domain on one side of each graph, and it has no separation into two disjoint nonempty relatively open sets.

Let $\alpha_n>0$ tend to zero, let $w_n\in Y$, and suppose $\|A^*\|\,\|w_n\|_Y/\alpha_n\le\eta$ for some finite $\eta$. For each $n$, suppose a supplied global minimizer $u_n\in X$ minimizes
$$J_n(u)=\tfrac12\|Au-(f+w_n)\|_Y^2+\alpha_nR(u).$$
In the Neumann case, if $A\mathbf1_\Omega=0$, take $u_n$ after subtracting its mean $|\Omega|^{-1}\int_\Omega u_n$; this leaves $J_n$ unchanged. Then a subsequence converges weakly in $L^2(\Omega)$ and, in addition, strongly in $L^1(\Omega)$ when $\Omega$ is bounded or strongly in $L^1$ on every bounded ball when $\Omega=\mathbb R^2$. Its limit $u_0$ is an exact solution $Au_0=f$ minimizing $R$ among exact solutions, and $A^*p^\dagger\in\partial R(u_0)$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $u\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^2)$, with functions identified when they agree almost everywhere. For full-space TV, use $u$ itself. For a bounded-domain Dirichlet or Neumann problem, use the zero extension $\widetilde u$ only to define the geometric level sets; this does not change the selected regularizer, and for each nonzero level the resulting set lies inside $\Omega$. For $t>0$, the positive $t$-level class is the measurable-set class of $E_t^+(u):=\{x\in\mathbb R^2:u(x)>t\}$; for $t<0$, the negative $t$-level class is the class of $E_t^-(u):=\{x\in\mathbb R^2:u(x)<t\}$. These classes do not depend on the representative of $u$. For any measurable set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^2$, its density-one representative is

$$E^{(1)}:=\left\{x\in\mathbb R^2:\lim_{r\downarrow0}\frac{|E\cap B(x,r)|}{|B(x,r)|}=1\right\}.$$

This representative depends only on the almost-everywhere class of $E$. The canonical level set $U_u^{(t)}$ is $(E_t^+(u))^{(1)}$ when $t>0$ and $(E_t^-(u))^{(1)}$ when $t<0$. Its canonical boundary is the ordinary topological boundary $\partial U_u^{(t)}$ in $\mathbb R^2$. For two nonempty boundary sets, use the usual extended Hausdorff distance induced by Euclidean distance; set $d_H(\varnothing,\varnothing)=0$ and $d_H(E,F)=+\infty$ if exactly one set is empty. Hausdorff convergence uses this convention and is invariant under changes to a function on a null set.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), and let
$\overline{\mu 	imes 
u}$ be the completed product of two sigma-finite
measure spaces.

1. If $f : X 	imes Y 	o [0,\infty]$ is $\overline{\mu 	imes 
u}$-measurable, there are measurable null sets $A\subseteq X$ and $B\subseteq Y$ such that $f_x$ is $\overline{\mathcal B}$-measurable for $x
otin A$ and $f^y$ is $\overline{\mathcal A}$-measurable for $y
otin B$. Define $I_f(x)=\int_Y f_x\,d\overline
u$ for $x
otin A$ and $I_f(x)=0$ on $A$; define $J_f(y)=\int_X f^y\,d\overline\mu$ for $y
otin B$ and $J_f(y)=0$ on $B$. Then $I_f,J_f$ are measurable and
$$\int f\,d\overline{\mu 	imes 
u}=\int_X I_f\,d\mu=\int_Y J_f\,d
u.$$
2. If $f \in L^1(\overline{\mu 	imes 
u})$, there are measurable null sets $A\subseteq X$ and $B\subseteq Y$ such that the sections are measurable and integrable outside them. Define $I_f,J_f$ by the same section integrals outside $A,B$ and by zero on $A,B$. They are measurable and integrable, and the same equality holds.

Every bounded sequence of reals has a convergent subsequence: if $(x_k)$ is a
sequence of reals and there is $M \in \mathbb{R}$ with $|x_k| \le M$ for every
$k \in \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-sequence]]), then there is a strictly increasing
$n : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and a real $L$ with $x_{n_j} \to L$.

Equivalently: the subsequential limit set of a bounded sequence is nonempty
([[def-subsequential-limit]]).

The theorem is the exact repair of the false claim that a bounded sequence
converges. A bounded
sequence need not converge, and the alternating sequence is the standing witness;
what boundedness does force is that *some* subsequence converges. The converse of
the theorem is false, and badly so: a sequence with a convergent subsequence need
not be bounded.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $A:L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R)\to L^2(\Sigma,\mu;\mathbb R)$ be bounded and real-linear, let $f=Au^\dagger$, and suppose $u^\dagger$ is a minimum-TV exact solution with a source certificate $p^\dagger$. For $\alpha_n>0$ tending to zero and noises $w_n\in L^2(\Sigma,\mu;\mathbb R)$, assume $\|A^*\|\|w_n\|_2/\alpha_n\le\eta$ and let $u_n$ be supplied global minimizers of $\frac12\|Au-(f+w_n)\|_2^2+\alpha_n TV(u)$. Define $p_n=(f+w_n-Au_n)/\alpha_n$ and $v_n=A^*p_n$. Use $TV_2$ on $L^2(\mathbb R^2)$ for full-space TV, zero-extension Dirichlet TV on a bounded Lipschitz domain, and relative Neumann TV on a bounded connected Lipschitz domain; for bounded-domain geometry use the ambient zero-extended level sets and their topological boundaries in $\mathbb R^2$.

For full-space or Dirichlet TV, assume $\eta<2\sqrt\pi$; in the bounded Dirichlet case also assume $\Omega$ has global obstacle curvature $\kappa_\Omega\in L^1(\mathbb R^2)$ with $\kappa_\Omega\ge g$ almost everywhere outside $\Omega$ for some $g\in L^2(\mathbb R^2\setminus\Omega)$. For Neumann TV, let $C_\Omega$ be a constant from the BV Sobolev–Poincaré inequality $\|u-u_\Omega\|_2\le C_\Omega TV(u;\Omega)$ and assume $\eta<1/C_\Omega$.

For almost every nonzero $t$, the level set $E_n(t)$ has finite measure and perimeter, minimizes the branch-specific perimeter minus $\int_{E}\operatorname{sgn}(t)v_n$ under compactly supported perturbations, and satisfies $P(E_n(t))=\operatorname{sgn}(t)\int_{E_n(t)}v_n$. There are constants $c>0$ and $r_0>0$, independent of $n$ and almost every such $t$, such that for every $x\in\partial E_n(t)$ and $0<r<r_0$,
$$|B(x,r)\cap E_n(t)|\ge c|B(x,r)|,\qquad |B(x,r)\setminus E_n(t)|\ge c|B(x,r)|.$$
In the full-space branch all these level sets are contained in one common ball; in the bounded branches they lie in $\overline\Omega$. The same density and support conclusions are asserted for any selected minimum-TV exact limit that carries the inherited source certificate, using zero noise. Whenever the corresponding level sets converge in measure, their canonical boundaries converge in Hausdorff distance.

derivations.claim: Apply [F1] to the supplied minimizers, retaining its subsequence, and call its limit $u_0$. Then $Au_0=f$, $R(u_0)$ is minimal among exact solutions, and $A^*p^\dagger\in\partial R(u_0)$. In bounded domains the subsequence already converges strongly in $L^1(\Omega)$. In full space, [F5] supplies a common ball containing the regularized and limit level sets for almost every nonzero level. By [F2] and the positive and negative layer-cake identities, for each fixed $n$ the integral of $|u_n|$ outside that ball is the integral over levels of the measures of those level sets outside it; Tonelli [F3] makes this integral zero. The same argument applies to $u_0$, so local $L^1$ convergence from [F1] is global $L^1$ convergence.

By [F2], for each real-valued $u$ the positive and negative level sets use $\{u>t\}$ for $t>0$ and $\{u<t\}$ for $t<0$. They satisfy the pointwise layer-cake identity $$|u(x)-u_0(x)|=\int_0^\infty|\mathbf1_{\{u>t\}}-\mathbf1_{\{u_0>t\}}|\,dt+\int_{-\infty}^0|\mathbf1_{\{u<t\}}-\mathbf1_{\{u_0<t\}}|\,dt.$$ Integrating and applying [F3] gives $$\|u_n-u_0\|_1=\int_0^\infty|E_n^+(t)\mathbin\triangle E_0^+(t)|\,dt+\int_{-\infty}^0|E_n^-(t)\mathbin\triangle E_0^-(t)|\,dt.$$ The right side tends to zero by step 1.1.

Let $g_n(t)$ denote the symmetric-difference measure of the positive level sets for $t>0$ and of the negative level sets for $t<0$. Step 2.1 says $g_n\to0$ in $L^1(\mathbb R\setminus\{0\})$. Choose a further subsequence with $\sum_k\|g_{n_k}\|_1<\infty$; Tonelli implies $\sum_k g_{n_k}(t)<\infty$ for almost every nonzero $t$, hence the level sets converge in measure there.

Fix a nonzero level for which step 3.1 gives measure convergence. If the limit level set is empty and infinitely many regularized level sets are nonempty, [F5] gives compact common support, so each such set has a boundary point; choose one for each index using [A1]. Its two-sided density estimate at a fixed radius $r<r_0$ forces symmetric-difference measure at least $c\pi r^2$, contradicting convergence to the empty limit. If the limit set is nonempty, it has positive measure because it is a nonempty density-one representative; measure convergence therefore rules out infinitely many empty regularized sets. Hence empty status agrees eventually, and the empty boundaries have Hausdorff distance zero by [F2]. For the remaining nonempty sets, [F5] supplies the two-sided density and support bounds. If boundary points of $E_{n_k}(t)$ stayed a fixed distance from $\partial E_0(t)$, choose them using [A1]; bounded support and [F4] give a convergent subsequence. A ball around its limit lies on one side of $E_0(t)$, while the two-sided density bound forces a fixed positive symmetric-difference measure, contradicting step 3.1. Conversely, if a boundary point of $E_0(t)$ stayed a fixed distance from every $\partial E_{n_k}(t)$, choose these points using [A1]; compact support and [F4] give a subsequence converging to $y\in\partial E_0(t)$. A connected ball around $y$ misses those boundaries for all large $k$, so each $E_{n_k}(t)$ is either full or empty there. A subsequence with one fixed status and measure convergence would make $E_0(t)$ full or empty almost everywhere on a smaller ball, contradicting that $y$ lies on the boundary of its canonical density-one representative. Thus the canonical boundaries converge in Hausdorff distance. The limit is the selected solution from [F1]; if the exact minimum-TV solution is unique it equals $u^\dagger$, and otherwise no such identification is asserted.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $u\in L^1(\Omega;\mathbb R)$, where elements of $L^1$ are almost-everywhere equivalence classes. For each $i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}$, its distributional derivative $D_i u$ acts on $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ by
$$\langle D_i u,\varphi\rangle:=-\int_\Omega u\,\partial_i\varphi\,dx.$$
The function $u$ is in $BV(\Omega)$ when each $D_i u$ is represented by a finite signed Radon measure and the resulting vector-valued measure $Du=(D_1u,\ldots,D_nu)$ has finite total variation. Here a finite vector-valued Radon measure means that its partition variation is a finite Radon measure. For a Borel set $A\subseteq\Omega$, define
$$|Du|(A):=\sup\left\{\sum_{j=1}^\infty |Du(A_j)|:\ (A_j)_{j\ge1}\text{ is a Borel partition of }A\right\},$$
using the Euclidean norm on each vector value. Define the spatial total variation by $TV(u;\Omega):=|Du|(\Omega)$. A Lebesgue-measurable set $E\subseteq\Omega$ of finite measure has finite perimeter relative to $\Omega$ when $\chi_E\in BV(\Omega)$; its relative perimeter is $P(E;\Omega):=TV(\chi_E;\Omega)$.

Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a bounded Lipschitz domain, meaning a bounded open set whose boundary has a finite cover by coordinate neighborhoods in which it is the graph of a Lipschitz function and $\Omega$ lies on one side of that graph. For $u\in BV(\Omega)$ define the Neumann total variation by $TV_N(u;\Omega):=|Du|(\Omega)$. Define its zero extension $\widetilde u\in L^1(\mathbb R^n)$ by $\widetilde u=u$ almost everywhere on $\Omega$ and $\widetilde u=0$ almost everywhere on $\mathbb R^n\setminus\Omega$. Define the Dirichlet total variation by $TV_D(u;\Omega):=TV(\widetilde u;\mathbb R^n)$ when $\widetilde u\in BV(\mathbb R^n)$ and by $TV_D(u;\Omega):=+\infty$ otherwise. For $v\in BV(\mathbb R^n)$ define the full-space total variation by $TV_F(v):=TV(v;\mathbb R^n)$. Thus Neumann variation counts only the distributional derivative inside $\Omega$, while Dirichlet variation also counts any jump created by zero extension across $\partial\Omega$.

Let $X$ be a real Banach space and let $X^*$ be its continuous real dual. The dual pairing is evaluation, written $\langle \xi,x\rangle_{X^*,X}:=\xi(x)$ for $\xi\in X^*$ and $x\in X$. Let $R:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be a proper convex functional: $R$ never takes the value $-\infty$, its effective domain $\operatorname{dom}R:=\{x\in X:R(x)<+\infty\}$ is nonempty, and $R((1-t)x+tz)\le (1-t)R(x)+tR(z)$ for $x,z\in X$ and $t\in[0,1]$, with $0\cdot(+\infty):=0$ for this convex-combination formula. For $x\in\operatorname{dom}R$, its subdifferential is

$$\partial R(x):=\{\xi\in X^*:R(z)\ge R(x)+\langle\xi,z-x\rangle_{X^*,X}\text{ for every }z\in X\}.$$

the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of [[def-inner-product-space]]: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$.

complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.

$\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex
modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either
scalar field.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

For Borel $A\subseteq\Omega$ define $$V(A):=\sup\left\{\sum_{j=1}^\infty |\mu(A_j)|:(A_j)_{j\ge1}\text{ is a Borel partition of }A\right\},$$ where the norm is Euclidean. derivations.claim: The function $u^\dagger=|x_1|$ is bounded on the bounded Lipschitz domain $\Omega$, hence belongs to $L^2(\Omega)$. Fubini and one-dimensional integration by parts show that its distributional gradient is $Du^\dagger=\operatorname{sgn}(x_1)e_1\,dx$: for every compactly supported smooth vector field $\varphi$, the $x_1$ derivative pairing is $-\int |x_1|\partial_1\varphi=\int\operatorname{sgn}(x_1)\varphi_1$, and the $x_2$ derivative pairing vanishes. This bounded density defines a finite vector Radon measure by [F6], so $u^\dagger\in BV(\Omega)$. Since $A=I$, its Hilbert adjoint is also $I$. The equation $Au=f$ forces $u=f=u^\dagger$, so $u^\dagger$ is the unique exact solution and therefore minimizes $R$ among exact solutions.

For $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ and $t\in\mathbb R$, the distributional gradient of $u^\dagger+t\varphi$ has density $g_t=\operatorname{sgn}(x_1)e_1+t\nabla\varphi$. For any integrable vector density $g$, its partition variation mass is $\int|g|$: every partition gives $\sum_j|\int_{B_j}g|\le\int|g|$; conversely, for $\varepsilon>0$ choose a finite-valued measurable simple function $s=\sum_{k=1}^N c_k\mathbf1_{B_k}$ with $\|g-s\|_1<\varepsilon$, where the disjoint $B_k$ partition the set and $s=0$ off their union. $$R(u^\dagger+t\varphi)=\int_\Omega|\operatorname{sgn}(x_1)e_1+t\nabla\varphi|\,dx.$$
For almost every $x$, the vector $q=\operatorname{sgn}(x_1)e_1$ has norm one and $\lim_{t\downarrow0}(|q+t h|-|q|)/t=q\cdot h$. The quotient is bounded in absolute value by $|h|$, by the reverse triangle inequality. Dominated convergence with $h=\nabla\varphi$ therefore yields the one-sided derivative
$$L(\varphi):=\lim_{t\downarrow0}\frac{R(u^\dagger+t\varphi)-R(u^\dagger)}{t}=\int_\Omega\operatorname{sgn}(x_1)\partial_1\varphi\,dx=-2\int_{-1}^1\varphi(0,x_2)\,dx_2,$$
where the last equality is integration by parts on $(-1,0)$ and $(0,1)$; compact support removes the endpoint terms. Replacing $\varphi$ by $-\varphi$ gives directional derivative $-L(\varphi)$.

The subgradient inequality [F3] applied to $u^\dagger+t\varphi$ for $t>0$, divided by $t$ and passed to the limit in step 2.1, gives $\int_\Omega p\varphi\le L(\varphi)$. Applying the same inequality to $u^\dagger-t\varphi$ gives $-\int_\Omega p\varphi\le-L(\varphi)$. Thus $\int_\Omega p\varphi=L(\varphi)$ for every compactly supported smooth $\varphi$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ be open and let $X=L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R)$. Every $u\in X$ is integrable on compact subsets by Cauchy–Schwarz. Define its extended distributional total variation by
$$TV_2(u;\Omega):=\sup\left\{\int_\Omega u\,\operatorname{div}\varphi\,dx:\ \varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^2),\ \sup_{x\in\Omega}|\varphi(x)|\le1\right\}\in[0,+\infty],$$
where $C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^2)$ denotes smooth compactly supported vector fields, $|\cdot|$ is the Euclidean norm, and $\operatorname{div}\varphi=\partial_1\varphi_1+\partial_2\varphi_2$. This definition treats $L^2$ functions as almost-everywhere classes and does not require $u\in L^1(\Omega)$.

Let $\Omega=\mathbb R^2$, or let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ be a bounded Lipschitz domain. Set $X=L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ and let $Y=L^2(\Sigma,\mu;\mathbb R)$ for a measure space $(\Sigma,\mu)$, using the real integral inner products. Let $A:X\to Y$ be bounded and real-linear, and let $A^*:Y\to X$ be its Hilbert adjoint, characterized by $\langle Au,p\rangle_Y=\langle u,A^*p\rangle_X$. Define $R:X\to[0,+\infty]$ as follows. If $\Omega=\mathbb R^2$, take $R(u)=TV_2(u;\mathbb R^2)$, the supremum of $\int u\,\operatorname{div}\varphi$ over smooth compactly supported vector fields of Euclidean norm at most one. For bounded $\Omega$, either take Neumann TV, $R(u)=TV(u;\Omega)$ when $u\in BV(\Omega)$ and $+\infty$ otherwise, or Dirichlet TV, $R(u)=TV(\widetilde u;\mathbb R^2)$ when the zero extension $\widetilde u$ belongs to $BV(\mathbb R^2)$ and $+\infty$ otherwise. Thus the bounded-domain choices count, respectively, only the interior derivative or also the jump of the zero extension across the boundary. In the full-space case finite $R$ does not require global $L^1$ integrability.

Identify each $q\in X$ with the continuous linear functional $h\mapsto\langle q,h\rangle_X$ by the real Hilbert-space Riesz representation. For exact data $f=Au^\dagger$, a **minimum-TV exact solution** is a point $u^\dagger\in X$ satisfying $Au^\dagger=f$ and $R(u^\dagger)\le R(u)$ for every $u\in X$ with $Au=f$. A vector $p^\dagger\in Y$ is a **dual source certificate** for $u^\dagger$ if $A^*p^\dagger\in\partial R(u^\dagger)$, where $\partial R$ is the convex subdifferential on the real Banach space $X$. The **TV source condition** at $u^\dagger$ is that such a certificate exists; it does not assert uniqueness of the truth or of the certificate. For a chosen certificate, the associated Bregman distance is

$$D_R^{A^*p^\dagger}(u,u^\dagger):=R(u)-R(u^\dagger)-\langle A^*p^\dagger,u-u^\dagger\rangle_X,$$

for $u\in\operatorname{dom}R$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $u\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^2)$, with functions identified when they agree almost everywhere. For full-space TV, use $u$ itself. For a bounded-domain Dirichlet or Neumann problem, use the zero extension $\widetilde u$ only to define the geometric level sets; this does not change the selected regularizer, and for each nonzero level the resulting set lies inside $\Omega$. For $t>0$, the positive $t$-level class is the measurable-set class of $E_t^+(u):=\{x\in\mathbb R^2:u(x)>t\}$; for $t<0$, the negative $t$-level class is the class of $E_t^-(u):=\{x\in\mathbb R^2:u(x)<t\}$. These classes do not depend on the representative of $u$. For any measurable set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^2$, its density-one representative is

$$E^{(1)}:=\left\{x\in\mathbb R^2:\lim_{r\downarrow0}\frac{|E\cap B(x,r)|}{|B(x,r)|}=1\right\}.$$

This representative depends only on the almost-everywhere class of $E$. The canonical level set $U_u^{(t)}$ is $(E_t^+(u))^{(1)}$ when $t>0$ and $(E_t^-(u))^{(1)}$ when $t<0$. Its canonical boundary is the ordinary topological boundary $\partial U_u^{(t)}$ in $\mathbb R^2$. For two nonempty boundary sets, use the usual extended Hausdorff distance induced by Euclidean distance; set $d_H(\varnothing,\varnothing)=0$ and $d_H(E,F)=+\infty$ if exactly one set is empty. Hausdorff convergence uses this convention and is invariant under changes to a function on a null set.

let $S^{n-1} \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be the unit sphere, and let $\sigma$ be the

Moreover, $\sigma$ is the unique Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$ with this
property.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

Assume countable choice. On every measure space, complex $L^p$ is complete for $1\le p\le\infty$, and every norm-convergent sequence has a subsequence of measurable representatives converging a.e. to its limit. For finite $p$, finite simple functions with finite-measure support are dense, and on $\mathbb R^n$ with Lebesgue measure, $n\ge1$, complex $C_c^\infty$ is dense. Complex $L^2$ has the first-variable-linear inner product $\int f\overline g$, its norm is $\|\cdot\|_2$, and Cauchy–Schwarz has the following equality criterion: if $g\ne0$, equality iff $f=cg$ a.e.; if $g=0$, equality for all $f$. The finite-tuple version uses a common scalar across components.

Put $S=\sigma(S^1)<\infty$. For each fixed $z\in S^1$, polar coordinates [F5] give
$$\int_0^2\int_{S^1}|u(z+t\omega)|^2t\,d\sigma(\omega)\,dt=\int_{B(z,2)}|u(x)|^2\,dx<\infty,$$
so for almost every $t>0$ the circle section is square-integrable. Cauchy–Schwarz [F4] then gives
$$|(A_0u)(z,t)|^2\le S t^2\int_{S^1}|u(z+t\omega)|^2\,d\sigma(\omega).$$
Integrating in $z,t$, using polar coordinates [F5] around each center and Tonelli [F6], yields
$$\|A_0u\|_{L^2(\Sigma)}^2\le S\int_{S^1}\int_{|x-z|<2}|x-z||u(x)|^2\,dx\,d\sigma(z)\le2S^2\|u\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^2)}^2,$$
where $|x-z|<2$ and $\sigma(S^1)=S$. Thus $A_0$ is real-linear and bounded on real Schwartz functions with norm at most $\sqrt2S$.

By [F7], real Schwartz functions are dense in real $L^2$: approximate a real function by complex Schwartz classes and take real parts, which cannot increase the $L^2$ error. By [F8], the target real $L^2(\Sigma)$ is complete. For any real $u\in L^2$, choose real Schwartz $u_k\to u$; step 1.1 makes $(A_0u_k)$ Cauchy, and its limit is independent of the approximating sequence by the same bound. This defines a bounded real-linear extension $A$ with $\|A\|\le\sqrt2S$. If another bounded extension agrees with $A_0$ on the dense Schwartz subspace, continuity forces equality on all of $L^2$.

The zero vector $u^\dagger=0$ satisfies $Au^\dagger=f=0$ and $TV_2(u^\dagger)=0$. Since $TV_2\ge0$, it minimizes TV over the exact solution set, regardless of the kernel of $A$. Its adjoint certificate $p^\dagger=0$ satisfies $A^*p^\dagger=0\in\partial TV_2(0)$ because $TV_2(v)\ge0=TV_2(0)+\langle0,v\rangle$ for every $v\in L^2$.

For $w_n=0$, the regularized objective is $J_n(u)=\tfrac12\|Au\|_2^2+\alpha_nTV_2(u)\ge0$, and $J_n(0)=0$. Hence $u_n=0$ is a global minimizer for every $n$. If $t>0$, $\{u_n>t\}=\varnothing$; if $t<0$, $\{u_n<t\}=\varnothing$. The same holds for $u^\dagger$, so all canonical density-one sets and ambient boundaries agree as empty sets; symmetric-difference measures and the extended Hausdorff distances are zero. The noise ratio is $\|A^*\|\|w_n\|_2/\alpha_n=0<2\sqrt\pi$, so the full-space threshold is met.

**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of [[def-inner-product-space]]: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

**Induced length.** The **induced length**, or inner-product norm, of $v$ is

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

which is exactly the published [[def-inner-product-norm]]: positive definiteness
makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square
root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$.

**The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or
complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.
In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of
$\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex
modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either
scalar field.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ be the function space of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]], with $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$.

### The $p$-norm, for a rational exponent $p \ge 1$

Let $p \in \mathbb{Q}$ with $p \ge 1$. For $x \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ put

$$\lVert x\rVert_p \;:=\; \Bigl(\sum_{k<n} |x_k|^{p}\Bigr)^{1/p},$$

where $|\cdot|$ is the absolute value ([[def-abs-value]]), the sum is the finite
sum of [[def-finite-sum]], and both powers are the **rational** powers of
[[def-rational-power]].

**Every power written here is defined.** Each base $|x_k|$ is a nonnegative real
and $p > 0$, so $|x_k|^{p}$ is given by [[def-rational-power]] for $|x_k| > 0$
and by its supplementary clause $0^{p} = 0$ for $|x_k| = 0$; the sum of these
nonnegative terms is nonnegative ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), and
$1/p$ is a positive rational, so the outer power is defined for the same two
reasons. The value does not depend on which representative of $p$ or of $1/p$ is
used ([[lem-rational-power-well-defined]]).

**The exponent is rational in this definition.**
[[def-rational-power]] supplies the nonnegative-base powers used here, and
[[thm-minkowski-finite]] supplies the corresponding triangle inequality for
rational $p \ge 1$. This item makes no claim with $p$ ranging over a real
interval; its rational domain is unchanged.

### The maximum norm

For $n \ge 1$ and $x \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ put

$$\lVert x\rVert_\infty \;:=\; \max\{\, |x_k| \;:\; k < n \,\},$$

the maximum of a nonempty finite set of reals, which exists and is one of its
elements ([[lem-finite-set-has-max]], [[def-max-min]]).

**The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is required and propagates.** At $n = 0$ the set
$\{|x_k| : k<n\}$ is empty and has no maximum ([[def-max-min]]). This is the same
restriction the published [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] carries, for the same reason, and
**every statement on this page that mentions $\lVert\cdot\rVert_\infty$ inherits
it**. The $p$-norms for rational $p \ge 1$ carry no such restriction: at $n = 0$
each is the empty sum raised to a positive rational power, hence $0$.

### The three cases the rest of the page uses

- $\lVert x\rVert_1 = \sum_{k<n}|x_k|$, since $t^{1} = t$ for $t \ge 0$
  ([[lem-rational-power-laws]], and $0^{1} = 0$ by the supplementary clause).
- $\lVert x\rVert_2 = \bigl(\sum_{k<n}|x_k|^{2}\bigr)^{1/2} = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}x_k^{2}}$,
  which is exactly the Euclidean norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]: the
  exponent $2$ agrees with the integer power, so $|x_k|^{2} = x_k^{2}$
  ([[lem-of-abs-value]]), and $t^{1/2}$ is the unique nonnegative square root of
  $t$, which is $\sqrt{t}$ ([[def-rational-power]], [[thm-of-square-roots]]).
  **The two notations denote the same function and no second Euclidean norm is
  introduced.**
- $\lVert x\rVert_\infty$ as above, for $n \ge 1$.

That each of these is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]], and
that the metrics they induce are exactly the published $d_1$, $d_2$ and
$d_\infty$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], is
[[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]]; it is proved there
and is not assumed here.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $p \in \mathbb{Q}$ with $p \ge 1$, with the norms
of [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]. Then:

1. $\lVert\cdot\rVert_p$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]).
2. For $n \ge 1$, $\lVert\cdot\rVert_\infty$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.
3. **The dictionary.** For $n \ge 1$ and all $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $$\lVert x-y\rVert_1 = d_1(x,y), \qquad \lVert x-y\rVert_2 = d_2(x,y), \qquad \lVert x-y\rVert_\infty = d_\infty(x,y),$$
   where $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are the metrics of the published
   [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]. So the metric induced by each of these three norms
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]) **is** the correspondingly named published
   metric, not merely one equivalent to it.

**Consequence, used repeatedly below and stated once here.** By clause 3 at
$p = 2$, the metric space $(\mathbb{R}^{n}, d_2)$ of the published metric-spaces
page and the metric space underlying the normed space
$(\mathbb{R}^{n}, \lVert\cdot\rVert_2)$ of this page are the same object. Hence
completeness ([[thm-euclidean-space-complete]] clause 2), Heine-Borel
([[thm-heine-borel-rn]] clause 2) and the compactness equivalences
([[thm-metric-compactness-equivalences]]) are statements about this page's normed
space, **with their hypothesis $n \ge 1$ inherited unchanged and not weakened**.
Nothing below cites any of those three theorems for $n = 0$.

**Why this lemma exists.** Without it the library would hold a norm-induced
metric on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ and a separately published metric on the same set with
no recorded relation, and every later citation would have to guess which was
meant. The proof of clause 3 is a comparison of two written expressions; the
value is that the comparison is made and recorded.

**Clause 1 is about an arbitrary norm; clauses 2 to 4 are about
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ with $n \ge 1$.**

1. **Finite and reverse triangle inequalities.** Let $V$ be a vector space over
   $\mathbb{R}$ and $N$ a norm on it ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]). For every
   $p \in \mathbb{N}$ and every list $u : p \to V$
   ([[def-linear-combination-and-span]]),
   $$N\Bigl(\sum_{j<p} u_j\Bigr) \;\le\; \sum_{j<p} N(u_j),$$
   and for all $u, w \in V$,
   $$\bigl|N(u) - N(w)\bigr| \;\le\; N(u - w).$$

Now let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ carry the norms of
[[def-p-norms-on-rn]] and write $\iota$ for the canonical natural
([[def-canonical-natural]]).

2. **Every norm is dominated by the $1$-norm.** Let $N$ be a norm on
   $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ and put $C := \max\{\, N(e_k) : k<n \,\}$, a maximum over a
   nonempty finite set of reals ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]],
   [[lem-finite-set-has-max]]). Then $C \ge 0$ and
   $$N(x) \;\le\; C\,\lVert x\rVert_1 \qquad \text{for every } x \in \mathbb{R}^{n}.$$
3. **The comparison chain.** For every $x \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $$\lVert x\rVert_\infty \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2 \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_1 \;\le\; \iota(n)\,\lVert x\rVert_\infty , \qquad \lVert x\rVert_1 \;\le\; \sqrt{\iota(n)}\;\lVert x\rVert_2 .$$
   In particular $\lVert\cdot\rVert_1$, $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ and
   $\lVert\cdot\rVert_\infty$ are pairwise equivalent norms on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   with the constants displayed ([[def-equivalent-norms]]).
4. **Every norm is Lipschitz for the Euclidean metric.** With $N$ and $C$ as in
   clause 2, $N : (\mathbb{R}^{n}, d_2) \to (\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$ is
   Lipschitz with constant $C\sqrt{\iota(n)}$
   ([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]], [[lem-metrics-on-rn]],
   [[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), hence uniformly continuous and
   continuous ([[thm-metric-regularity-hierarchy]], [[def-metric-continuity]]).

**Where $n \ge 1$ enters.** Clauses 2 and 4 need the maximum defining $C$ to
exist, and clause 3 mentions $\lVert\cdot\rVert_\infty$; at $n = 0$ each is a
maximum over the empty index set and does not exist, exactly as in
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] and [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]. Clause 1 carries no hypothesis
on the dimension and no hypothesis on the space.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$ and let $g:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$. Its effective domain is $\operatorname{dom}g=\{x:g(x)<+\infty\}$. The function is **proper** if $\operatorname{dom}g\ne\varnothing$; it is **convex** if
$$g((1-\theta)x+\theta y)\le(1-\theta)g(x)+\theta g(y)\qquad(x,y\in\mathbb R^n,\ 0\le\theta\le1),$$
using the endpoint convention $0\cdot(+\infty)=0$ of [[def-convex-and-strictly-convex-functionals-on-a-banach-space]]. It is **closed** (equivalently, lower semicontinuous in the extended-real convex-analysis convention used here) if its epigraph
$$\operatorname{epi}g=\{(x,s)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R:g(x)\le s\}$$
is closed in $\mathbb R^{n+1}$. The proximal-gradient items on this page assume $g$ is proper, closed and convex.

This page's closed-epigraph convention is explicit: it does not silently use an equivalence between sequential lower semicontinuity and topological closedness that would require an additional choice principle in the library's generic sequential convention. In finite dimensions this is the standard closed proper convex input to proximal algorithms.

Let $X$ be a real vector space and $K\subseteq X$. The set $K$ is **convex** if $\lambda u+(1-\lambda)v\in K$ for all $u,v\in K$ and $\lambda\in[0,1]$. Fix a nonempty convex $K$ and an extended-real functional $I:K\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ ([[def-proper-coercive-and-weakly-lower-semicontinuous-functional]]), with the sums and positive-weight products of [[def-extended-reals]]. For convex combinations only, additionally define $0\cdot(+\infty)=0$; this is a local convention, since that product is left undefined in the general extended-real arithmetic. Then $I$ is **convex** if
$$I\big(\lambda u+(1-\lambda)v\big)\le\lambda I(u)+(1-\lambda)I(v),\qquad u,v\in K,\ \lambda\in[0,1],$$
and **strictly convex** if the inequality is strict whenever $u\ne v$, $I(u),I(v)<+\infty$ and $\lambda\in(0,1)$. A convex functional has convex sublevel sets: for every $t\in\mathbb R$ the set $\{u\in K:I(u)\le t\}$ is convex. Only real coefficients are used: on a complex vector space these notions are read on the underlying real structure.

A subset $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is **convex** when, for all $x,y\in U$ and $t\in[0,1]$ ([[def-interval]]), the point $(1-t)x+ty$ lies in $U$. Thus the full line segment from $x$ to $y$ remains in $U$.

For any set $C\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, its extended-real indicator is
$$\iota_C(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x\in C,\\+\infty,&x\notin C.\end{cases}$$

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $F$ be a field ([[def-field]]) with additive identity $0_F$ and
multiplicative identity $1_F$. Define
$\iota : \mathbb{N} \to F$ by recursion on $\mathbb{N}$
([[def-natural-numbers]], [[thm-recursion]]):

$$\iota(0) \;:=\; 0_F, \qquad \iota(n+1) \;:=\; \iota(n) + 1_F .$$

$\iota(n)$ is the **canonical natural** of $n$ in $F$. It is also written
$n \cdot 1_F$, and for $n \ge 1$ it is $1_F$ added to itself $n$ times.

**Why the notation is needed at all.** A natural number in this library is a von
Neumann natural, that is a set ([[def-natural-numbers]]), and a set is not an
element of $F$. So $1/n$, $n^{\alpha}$ and $x/n$ are not expressions of $F$ when
$n$ is a natural: what they mean is $1/\iota(n)$, $\iota(n)^{\alpha}$ and
$x/\iota(n)$. The map $\iota$ is what carries a counting number into the field,
and writing it is the whole reason a reader meets $1/\iota(k+1)$ where an
informal text would write $1/(k+1)$.

Let $F$ be an ordered field, with field structure as in [[def-field]], and for
$n \ge 1$ let $n \cdot 1_F$ denote the canonical natural number
$\underbrace{1_F + \cdots + 1_F}_{n}$, defined recursively by $1 \cdot 1_F = 1_F$
and $(n+1) \cdot 1_F = n \cdot 1_F + 1_F$. Then for every $n \ge 1$:

- $n \cdot 1_F > 0$ and $(n+1) \cdot 1_F > n \cdot 1_F$;
- the map $n \mapsto n \cdot 1_F$ is strictly increasing, hence injective, on $\{1, 2, 3, \dots\}$;
- $(m+n) \cdot 1_F = m \cdot 1_F + n \cdot 1_F$ and $(mn) \cdot 1_F = (m \cdot 1_F)(n \cdot 1_F)$ for all $m, n \ge 1$.

Let $a, b, c : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be sequences of reals, let
$\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, and let $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$, with finite sums and
finite products as in [[def-finite-sum]]. Then:

1. **Additivity.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}(a_k + b_k) = \sum_{k<n} a_k + \sum_{k<n} b_k$.
2. **Scaling.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda a_k = \lambda \sum_{k<n} a_k$; in particular $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda = n\lambda$, where $n$ denotes the canonical field image $n\cdot1_{\mathbb{R}}$ of the natural n ([[lem-of-q-embeds]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]).
3. **Splitting.** If $m \le n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k = \sum_{k<m} a_k + \sum_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k$, and $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n} a_k = \Big(\prod_{k<m} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k\Big)$.
4. **Monotonicity.** If $a_k \le b_k$ for all $k < n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k \le \sum_{k<n} b_k$. In particular, if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\sum_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, every single term satisfies $a_j \le \sum_{k<n} a_k$ for $j < n$, and $\sum_{k<n} a_k = 0$ forces $a_k = 0$ for every $k < n$.
5. **Telescoping.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}\big(c_{k+1} - c_k\big) = c_n - c_0$.
6. **Products.** $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n}(a_k b_k) = \Big(\prod_{k<n} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k<n} b_k\Big)$; if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, and if $a_k > 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k > 0$.

Let $F$ be an ordered field. For $a, b \ge 0$:

$$a < b \iff a^2 < b^2, \qquad a \le b \iff a^2 \le b^2.$$

More generally, for arbitrary $a, b \in F$, $a^2 < b^2 \iff |a| < |b|$.

derivations.claim: The function $f$ is finite everywhere because it is a finite sum of absolute values, and $f(0)=0$, so its effective domain is nonempty. For $0\le\theta\le1$, the triangle inequality and homogeneity in [F1] give $f((1-\theta)x+\theta z)\le f((1-\theta)x)+f(\theta z)=(1-\theta)f(x)+\theta f(z).$ Thus $f$ is proper and convex by [F2,F3].

For $(x,t)\in\mathbb R^{n+1}$ outside $\operatorname{epi}f$, the gap $d=f(x)-t$ is positive. Put $L=\sqrt{\iota(n)}+1>0$. If $(x',t')$ has product Euclidean distance $D<d/(2L)$ from $(x,t)$, then coordinate-square domination gives $\|x'-x\|_2\le D$ and $|t'-t|\le D$. By [F1], $f(x')-t'\ge f(x)-t-|f(x')-f(x)|-|t'-t|\ge d-(\sqrt{\iota(n)}+1)D>d/2>0.$ So the complement of $\operatorname{epi}f$ is open and its epigraph is closed. The scalar $L$ is positive by [F8]; the coordinate-square domination follows by comparing a partial sum with the full nonnegative sum and using [F9].

The residual ball $C$ contains $y$ because $\epsilon\ge0$. If $u,v\in C$ and $0\le\theta\le1$, homogeneity and the triangle inequality in [F1] give $\|(1-\theta)u+\theta v-y\|_2\le(1-\theta)\|u-y\|_2+\theta\|v-y\|_2\le\epsilon,$ so $C$ is convex. If $u\notin C$, the gap $d=\|u-y\|_2-\epsilon>0$ and the reverse triangle inequality show that every $v$ with $\|v-u\|_2<d/2$ also lies outside $C$. Thus $C$ is closed.

By [F5], $\operatorname{epi}g=C\times[0,\infty)$. If $(u,t)$ is outside this epigraph, either $u\notin C$ or $t<0$. In the first case step 1.3 supplies an open ball about $u$ disjoint from $C$, hence a product neighborhood disjoint from the epigraph; in the second case an interval about $t$ contained in $(-\infty,0)$ supplies such a product neighborhood. Therefore $\operatorname{epi}g$ is closed. Since $C$ is nonempty by step 1.3, $g$ is proper. If both endpoints lie in $C$, their convex combination lies in $C$ by step 1.3 and $g$ is zero there; if either endpoint has value $+\infty$ with positive coefficient, the convexity inequality has right side $+\infty$. Endpoint coefficients reduce to equality at the endpoint with coefficient one. Thus $g$ is convex, and [F2] proves that both functions have the asserted proper, closed, convex properties.
