A smooth density $\mu$ times a distribution $u$ in the test-density convention is the distributional density $\mu u$ defined by $\langle\mu u,\varphi\rangle=\langle u,\varphi\mu\rangle$.

Let $Z\subseteq G\times X$ be an embedded submanifold whose two projections are submersions. For a smooth density $\omega_Z$ on $Z$, its incidence delta kernel is the distributional density
$$

$$
In coordinates $(g,x)=(u,t)$ with $Z=\{t=0\}$, this is the delta distribution in the $t$ variables paired with the chosen density on $Z$. The conormal bundle and associated cotangent relation are
$$
N^*Z=\{(z,\zeta)\in T^*(G\times X):z\in Z,\ \zeta|_{T_zZ}=0\}, \qquad C_Z=\{(g,\eta;x,\xi):(g,x;\eta,-\xi)\in N^*Z\setminus0\}.
$$

Since both projections are submersions, every nonzero conormal in this relation has both $\eta\ne0$ and $\xi\ne0$. An analytic incidence kernel means that $Z$, its local defining maps, and the coefficients of $\omega_Z$ are real analytic. Every compactly supported distribution $v\in\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^n)$ has a
unique extension $\widetilde v\in\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$.  Restricting
$\widetilde v$ to $\mathcal D$ recovers $v$.  No choice axiom is required.

Give $C^\infty(\Omega)$ the topology generated by $q_{K,m}(f)=\max_{|\alpha|\le m}\sup_K|\partial^\alpha f|$ for compact $K\subseteq\Omega$ and $m\ge0$. A compactly supported distribution $u$ has a unique continuous complex-linear extension to this space, given by
$$\widetilde u(f)=u(\chi f),$$
where $\chi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$ is any cutoff equal to one near $\operatorname{supp}u$. The result is independent of $\chi$. The extension vanishes on every smooth function zero near the support. No Hahn–Banach or choice axiom is needed.

$$

$$

derivations.claim: Fix one real-analytic chart and two smooth cutoffs $\chi,\widetilde\chi$ that both equal one on a neighborhood of the base point. Choose a smaller center neighborhood $U_0$ and a compact support neighborhood so that $|x-y|\ge d>0$ whenever $x\in U_0$ and $y\in\operatorname{supp}(\chi-\widetilde\chi)$. By continuity in the fixed-support topology [F3], in either distributional type the pairing is bounded by $C_0$ times the maximum of finitely many derivatives of its test object; a coordinate density factor, when present, has bounded derivatives on the compact chart support. Those derivatives of $(\chi-\widetilde\chi)e^{i\lambda(x-y)\cdot\omega-\lambda|x-y|^2/2}$ are bounded by $C_1(1+\lambda)^m e^{-\lambda d^2/2}$ uniformly for $x\in U_0$, directions near $\omega_0$, and $\lambda\ge1$. Since a polynomial times $e^{-\lambda d^2/2}$ is bounded by $C_2e^{-c\lambda}$ for any fixed $0<c<d^2/2$, replacing one fixed-chart cutoff by the other changes the FBI packet by an exponentially small term.

Let $\kappa$ be an analytic chart change. After shrinking to nested compact neighborhoods, $|\kappa(q)-\kappa(y)|\ge c|q-y|$ and $D\kappa(q)$ is invertible uniformly. The pulled-back packet has phase $ \phi(y,q,\omega)=\omega\cdot(\kappa(q)-\kappa(y))+\frac{i}{2}|\kappa(q)-\kappa(y)|^2. $ It is holomorphic after complexification, vanishes at $y=q$, and has derivative $-D\kappa(q)^T\omega$ there. Apply the same reference criterion in the new chart before pulling its packets back. We may therefore reparameterize the open frequency ball by $p=D\kappa(q)^T\omega$; this is an analytic local diffeomorphism of open frequency parameters and is precisely the cotangent rule. The phase is now normalized and positive in the sense of [F6]. The Jacobian amplitude for scalar distributions is analytic and nonzero: the sign of the real determinant is constant on the smaller connected chart, so its absolute value has an analytic continuation. For distributional densities the amplitude is $1$.

Thus the exponential-decay criterion is independent of the fixed-chart cutoff. The finite-order sequence [F2] supplies the uniform localizers required when a distribution is restricted to a smaller chart; it avoids any use of compactly supported analytic bumps. For a distributional density $V$ in the fixed chart, define the scalar distribution $u_V$ by $\langle u_V,\varphi|dy|\rangle=\langle V,\varphi\rangle$. Continuity follows from [F3], and the vanishing-open sets of $u_V$ and $V$ agree because $|dy|$ is nowhere zero, so their supports agree. The packet pairings agree by definition. Hence [F4]–[F5] give the local Euclidean tempered and smooth-function realizations for either distributional type. This proves the cutoff and localization clauses without a choice axiom.

Apply [F6] to the standard and pulled-back packets on the smaller neighborhoods. It supplies actual transition representations in both directions, with polynomially bounded transition kernels and errors exponentially small in every fixed derivative; the finite distributional order from [F3] therefore preserves their exponential size after pairing. The known exponential estimate on the source parameter neighborhood transfers to the target one. Swapping the two families gives the converse. Step 1.1 removes all fixed cutoff choices, and step 2.1 covers both distributional conventions. An analytic double fibration is a diagram of real-analytic manifolds and real-analytic submersions
$$
G\xleftarrow{\ \pi_G\ }Z\xrightarrow{\ \pi_X\ }X
$$
such that $Z$ is embedded in $G\times X$, both projections are submersions, and
$$
\dim G+\dim X>\dim Z>\dim G\ge\dim X.
$$
Write $C_Z=\{(g,\eta;x,\xi):(g,x;\eta,-\xi)\in N^*Z\setminus0\}$ for the incidence cotangent relation. Assume $\pi_G$ is proper on $\pi_X^{-1}(K)$ for every compact $K\subset X$. Let $\omega_Z$ be a nowhere vanishing real-analytic smooth density on $Z$ and let $\kappa\colon Z\to\mathbb C$ be real analytic and nowhere zero. For a compactly supported distribution $u$ on $X$, the weighted transform is the distributional density
$$
Ru=(\pi_G)_*\bigl(\kappa\,\omega_Z\,\pi_X^*u\bigr),
$$
where pullback, multiplication by a density, proper pushforward, and $C_Z$ use the conventions of the preceding definition. In local fiber coordinates this is integration of $u$ over the incidence fibers with weight $\kappa$ and density $\omega_Z$. The hypotheses on proper support ensure this transform is defined for every compactly supported input. This is the class treated on this page; no noisy-data or stability assertion is included.

For an analytic double fibration with incidence cotangent relation $C_Z\subset(T^*G\setminus0)\times(T^*X\setminus0)$, let
$$
\pi_L:C_Z\longrightarrow T^*G\setminus0,\qquad \pi_L(g,\eta;x,\xi)=(g,\eta).
$$
The double fibration satisfies the global Bolker condition if $\pi_L$ is an injective immersion. The Bolker condition holds at a specified point $c=(g,\eta;x,\xi)\in C_Z$ if the full fiber over its data covector is the singleton $\pi_L^{-1}(g,\eta)=\{c\}$ and $d\pi_L|_c$ is injective. Thus the pointwise condition has both a fiber-uniqueness clause, which excludes every other relation point over the same data covector even outside a chosen chart, and a local differential-rank clause.

Let $Z\subseteq G\times X$ be an embedded incidence submanifold of codimension $k>0$, and let $(g_0,x_0)\in Z$. Choose coordinates near this point and a submersion $F:G\times X\to\mathbb R^k$ with $Z=\{F=0\}$. Write $F=(F_1,\ldots,F_k)$. For every $\tau\in\mathbb R^k\setminus\{0\}$, the conormal covector at $(g,x)\in Z$ is
$$
(g,x;D_gF(g,x)^T\tau,\ D_xF(g,x)^T\tau).
$$
Consequently the incidence kernel has local delta representation $b(g,x)\delta(F(g,x))|dg\,dx|$, with a smooth density coefficient $b$, and its cotangent relation consists exactly of
$$
(g,D_gF^T\tau;\ x,-D_xF^T\tau),\qquad (g,x)\in Z,\quad \tau\ne0.
$$
No general Fourier-integral-operator composition calculus is used.

derivations.claim: A tangent vector to $Z$ at $(g,x(g,s))$ has the form $ (\dot g,D_gx\,\dot g+D_sx\,\dot s). $ A pair $(\eta,-\xi)$ annihilates every such tangent vector exactly when $(D_sx)^T\xi=0$ and $\eta=(D_gx)^T\xi$. This follows by setting $\dot g=0$ and then varying $\dot g$ arbitrarily. Thus all conormal pairs, except the zero pair, are parameterized by $(g,s,\xi)\in E_g$. The rank condition on $D_sx$ makes this conormal parameterization smooth.

Under this parameterization, the left projection sends $(g,s,\xi)$ to $(g,(D_gx)^T\xi)$, as stated. Because the first component is retained, two points in this chart portion have the same left image exactly when their $g$ coordinates agree and their values under $L_g$ agree. This proves the chart-portion injectivity criterion; it says nothing about a second preimage outside this chart.

A tangent vector in the kernel of the differential of the left projection has $\dot g=0$. Differentiating the defining equation $(D_sx)^T\xi=0$ along $(\dot s,\dot\xi)$ gives $ (D_sx)^T\dot\xi+(D_s^2x[\dot s, \cdot])^T\xi=0. $ Differentiating its output $(D_gx)^T\xi$ gives the second displayed equation in the statement. Therefore the differential is injective exactly when the simultaneous system has only the zero solution. This is the asserted rank test, and by [F2] it is precisely the local immersion clause of Bolker.

If $\Omega$ is a bounded complex domain and $f$ is continuous on $\overline\Omega$ and holomorphic on $\Omega$, then $|f|$ attains its maximum on $\partial\Omega$.

Equivalently, there is $\zeta\in\partial\Omega$ such that
$$|f(z)|\le|f(\zeta)|\qquad(z\in\overline\Omega).$$

Give $C^\infty(\Omega)$ the topology generated by $q_{K,m}(f)=\max_{|\alpha|\le m}\sup_K|\partial^\alpha f|$ for compact $K\subseteq\Omega$ and $m\ge0$. A compactly supported distribution $u$ has a unique continuous complex-linear extension to this space, given by
$$\widetilde u(f)=u(\chi f),$$
where $\chi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$ is any cutoff equal to one near $\operatorname{supp}u$. The result is independent of $\chi$. The extension vanishes on every smooth function zero near the support. No Hahn–Banach or choice axiom is needed.

For $u\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$, say $u$ **vanishes on** an open $V\subseteq\Omega$ if its restriction to $V$ is zero. Let $Z$ be the union of all such open sets. Locality in [[thm-distributions-form-a-sheaf]] shows that $u|_Z=0$, since these sets cover $Z$ and all its restrictions are zero. Thus $Z$ is the largest vanishing open set. The **support** is the relatively closed set $\operatorname{supp}u=\Omega\setminus Z$.

In particular $\operatorname{supp}u=\varnothing$ if and only if $u=0$: emptiness gives $Z=\Omega$ and vanishing there, while the zero distribution vanishes everywhere. If a test $\varphi$ vanishes on a neighborhood of $\operatorname{supp}u$, its compact support is contained in $Z$, so $u(\varphi)=0$ by restriction. Consequently two tests agreeing on a neighborhood of $\operatorname{supp}u$ have equal pairings with $u$, by applying this fact to their difference.

**Compactly supported** means that $\operatorname{supp}u$ is a compact subset of $\Omega$. Relative closedness in an arbitrary open domain is not by itself compactness or closedness in the ambient Euclidean space. On the empty domain support is empty. The union and locality argument require no selection of vanishing neighborhoods and no choice axiom.

derivations.claim: Multiply $u$ by a compact smooth cutoff equal to one near $0$ and supported where the one-sided hypothesis holds. It remains supported in $y_n\ge0$, and the wavefront hypothesis is unchanged by exponential Gaussian tail estimates. Denote this compact distribution again by $u$ and put $ U(z,\lambda)=\langle u(y),e^{-\lambda(z-y)^2/2}\rangle,\qquad z\in\mathbb C^n. $ This is entire by [F3]. A finite distributional derivative order gives the following bound on every fixed bounded complex set: $ |U(z,\lambda)|\le C\lambda^M e^{\lambda\Phi(z)},\qquad \Phi(z)=\frac{|\operatorname{Im}z|^2-(\operatorname{Re}z_n)_-^2}{2}, $ where $s_-:=\max(-s,0)$. To justify the sharp half-space bound for a distribution, insert a smooth factor $\vartheta(\lambda y_n)$ that is one for $\lambda y_n>-1/2$ and zero for $\lambda y_n<-1$. It equals one on a neighborhood of the support, so does not change the pairing. Its derivatives of each fixed order cost only a power of $\lambda$. On its support, $y_n\ge-1/\lambda$, and $\operatorname{Re}(z-y)^2=|\operatorname{Re}z-y|^2-|\operatorname{Im}z|^2$ gives the bound with $(s+1/\lambda)_-^2$ in place of $s_-^2$. Their difference is $O(1/\lambda)$ uniformly for bounded $s$, so it changes the exponential by a bounded factor. Gaussian derivatives contribute another fixed power of $\lambda$. This proves the displayed bound using the ordinary fixed-support distributional seminorm, without assuming an estimate on the exact support set.

We record the elementary quantitative continuation used in the left half-plane. If a holomorphic $g$ is bounded by $1$ on a disk of radius $R$ and by $e^{-d\lambda}$ on the concentric disk of radius $r<R$, then on the disk of radius $r<\rho<R$, $ |g|\le \exp\!\left(-d\lambda\frac{\log(R/\rho)}{\log(R/r)}\right). $ For the annulus compare $\log|g|$ with the harmonic function that is $-d\lambda$ on the inner circle and $0$ on the outer circle. This comparison follows from [F2]: near any hypothetical positive interior maximum of their difference, subtract a local harmonic conjugate and apply the maximum modulus principle; a small strict harmonic perturbation excludes a non-strict maximum, then let that perturbation decrease to zero. Zeros of $g$ cannot be positive maxima. Chaining finitely many overlapping disks contained in the connected left half-plane propagates a strictly positive exponent from the initial disk to any chosen compact subset there. To make the finite chain explicit, cover a polygonal path from the initial disk to the compact set by equal small disks whose doubled disks lie in the half-plane, take successive center distances less than one quarter of the radius, and iterate the displayed estimate. The exponent is multiplied by finitely many positive radius ratios.

Write $z=(z',s+it)$. The identity $ e^{-\lambda|p|^2/2}U(x-ip,\lambda) =\langle u,e^{i\lambda(x-y)\cdot p-\lambda|x-y|^2/2}\rangle $ and [F1] imply that absence of either normal gives $ |U(z,\lambda)|\le C e^{\lambda(|\operatorname{Im}z|^2/2-c)} $ in a fixed complex neighborhood of $(0,\mp i)$ for some $c>0$. The use of [F1] here is only to let $p$ range over an open ball about $\pm e_n$, rather than the unit sphere. Fix a small neighborhood of $z'=0$ and treat $z'$ as a parameter. For each such $z'$ the holomorphic function of one variable $ G(z_n,\lambda)=e^{-\lambda|\operatorname{Im}z'|^2/2}e^{\lambda z_n^2/2}U(z',z_n,\lambda) $ satisfies $|G|\le C\lambda^M e^{\lambda s_+^2/2}$ on bounded rectangles. Constants are uniform in $z'$.

Divide $G$ by its uniform polynomial bound $C\lambda^M$. In the left half-plane this quotient has modulus at most $1$. Step 1.2 gives $r,b,d>0$ such that on the segment $s=-r$, $|t|\le b$, it is at most $e^{-d\lambda}$, after decreasing $d$ and taking $\lambda$ large. The same construction works whether the initial disk is near $i$ or $-i$; both lie in the same connected left half-plane neighborhood joined by a bounded path to this segment. All paths, rectangles and constants can be fixed uniformly for the chosen $z'$ parameters.

Extend to the rectangle $-r\le s\le a$, $|t|\le b$, where $a>0$ will be small. Let $M$ be a smooth $n$-manifold. A distribution on $M$ is a continuous complex-linear functional on compactly supported smooth densities on $M$. Its topology is generated locally by the fixed-support seminorms $\max_{|\alpha|\le m}\sup_K|\partial^\alpha\varphi|$, followed by the locally convex test-function topology. In a chart $x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$ a test density is $\varphi(x)|dx|$; under a coordinate change it transforms by the absolute Jacobian. A distribution is compactly supported when its support, the complement of its largest vanishing open set, is compact.

For a smooth submersion $p:Y\to M$, define the pullback $p^*u$ by transposing fiber integration: in submersion coordinates $p(x,v)=x$,
$$
\langle p^*u,\psi(x,v)|dx\,dv|\rangle =\left\langle u,\left(\int\psi(x,v)|dv|\right)|dx|\right\rangle.
$$
The absolute density quotient gives the fiber density in other submersion coordinates. For a distributional density $V$ on $Y$, meaning a continuous functional on compactly supported smooth scalar functions, define its support by the same largest-vanishing-open-set rule. If $q:Y\to M$ is proper on $\operatorname{supp}V$, then for a test function $\varphi$ on $M$ the set $q^{-1}(\operatorname{supp}\varphi)\cap\operatorname{supp}V$ is compact. Choose a smooth compact cutoff $\beta$ equal to one near this set and define the pushforward by
$$
\langle q_*V,\varphi\rangle=\langle V,\beta(\varphi\circ q)\rangle.
$$
The support property makes this independent of $\beta$; the cutoff is needed because $\varphi\circ q$ need not be compactly supported on all of $Y$.
A smooth density $\mu$ times a distribution $u$ in the test-density convention is the distributional density $\mu u$ defined by $\langle\mu u,\varphi\rangle=\langle u,\varphi\mu\rangle$.

Let $Z\subseteq G\times X$ be an embedded submanifold whose two projections are submersions. For a smooth density $\omega_Z$ on $Z$, its incidence delta kernel is the distributional density
$$
\langle K_Z,\Phi\rangle=\int_Z\Phi|_Z\,\omega_Z.
$$
In coordinates $(g,x)=(u,t)$ with $Z=\{t=0\}$, this is the delta distribution in the $t$ variables paired with the chosen density on $Z$. The conormal bundle and associated cotangent relation are
$$
N^*Z=\{(z,\zeta)\in T^*(G\times X):z\in Z,\ \zeta|_{T_zZ}=0\}, \qquad C_Z=\{(g,\eta;x,\xi):(g,x;\eta,-\xi)\in N^*Z\setminus0\}.
$$
Here $N^*Z\setminus0$ removes the zero covector, and the minus sign is the distribution-kernel convention for an operator from $X$ to $G$. Since both projections are submersions, every nonzero conormal in this relation has both $\eta\ne0$ and $\xi\ne0$. An analytic incidence kernel means that $Z$, its local defining maps, and the coefficients of $\omega_Z$ are real analytic. This definition covers the incidence kernels used below; it does not assert a general Fourier-integral-operator calculus.

An analytic double fibration is a diagram of real-analytic manifolds and real-analytic submersions
$$
G\xleftarrow{\ \pi_G\ }Z\xrightarrow{\ \pi_X\ }X
$$
such that $Z$ is embedded in $G\times X$, both projections are submersions, and
$$
\dim G+\dim X>\dim Z>\dim G\ge\dim X.
$$
Write $C_Z=\{(g,\eta;x,\xi):(g,x;\eta,-\xi)\in N^*Z\setminus0\}$ for the incidence cotangent relation. Assume $\pi_G$ is proper on $\pi_X^{-1}(K)$ for every compact $K\subset X$. Let $\omega_Z$ be a nowhere vanishing real-analytic smooth density on $Z$ and let $\kappa\colon Z\to\mathbb C$ be real analytic and nowhere zero. For a compactly supported distribution $u$ on $X$, the weighted transform is the distributional density
$$
Ru=(\pi_G)_*\bigl(\kappa\,\omega_Z\,\pi_X^*u\bigr),
$$
where pullback, multiplication by a density, proper pushforward, and $C_Z$ use the conventions of the preceding definition. In local fiber coordinates this is integration of $u$ over the incidence fibers with weight $\kappa$ and density $\omega_Z$. The hypotheses on proper support ensure this transform is defined for every compactly supported input. This is the class treated on this page; no noisy-data or stability assertion is included.

Let $f$ be a real analytic map between open subsets of $\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge1$. If $Df(a)$ is invertible, $f$ has a real analytic local inverse near $f(a)$. Let $P(x,y)$ be real analytic near $(a,b)\in\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R^k$, $k\ge1$, with $P(a,b)=0$ and $D_yP(a,b)$ invertible. On sufficiently small neighborhoods its zero set is exactly the graph of a unique real analytic $y=g(x)$ with $g(a)=b$.

Let $\phi$ be holomorphic on a neighborhood of $0\in\mathbb C^n$, with $d\phi(0)=0$ and complex Hessian $H=\phi''(0)$ invertible. There is a local biholomorphic coordinate map $w=\Psi(z)$ with $\Psi(0)=0$ such that
$$
\phi(z)=\phi(0)+\tfrac12\sum_{j=1}^n w_j^2.
$$
Its linear part satisfies $(\det D\Psi(0))^2=\det H$. For a continuous parameter family of invertible Hessians $H(p)$, near any fixed parameter $p_0$ the determinant remains in a disc avoiding $0$; choosing one square root at $p_0$ therefore fixes a continuous branch on that neighborhood. If $\operatorname{Re}H$ is positive definite, then
$$
\int_{\mathbb R^n}e^{-\lambda x^THx/2}\,dx =(2\pi/\lambda)^{n/2}(\det H)^{-1/2},\qquad \lambda>0,
$$
with the integral interpreted as an absolutely convergent improper integral and the branch analytically continued from real positive-definite matrices. Finally, deforming a holomorphic contour preserves the integral of a holomorphic top-degree form when the contours are homologous through a region of holomorphy and the swept boundary integrals tend to zero.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a bounded open set, let $\Phi$ be holomorphic on a complex neighborhood of $\overline U$, and let $a\in C_c^\infty(U)$ have a holomorphic extension near $0$. Assume $0\in\operatorname{supp}a$, $\Phi(0)=\Phi_0$, $d\Phi(0)=0$, and $d\Phi(x)\ne0$ at every $x\in\operatorname{supp}a\setminus\{0\}$. Let $H=-i\Phi''(0)$ be complex symmetric with positive-definite real part. Assume there are $r,c_0,d_0>0$ such that
$$
\operatorname{Im}(\Phi(x)-\Phi_0)\ge c_0|x|^2 \quad(|x|\le r),\qquad \operatorname{Im}(\Phi(x)-\Phi_0)\ge d_0 \quad(x\in\operatorname{supp}a,\ |x|\ge r).
$$
Let $\chi_N$ be the finite-order cutoff sequence equal to one on a fixed neighborhood of $0$, with $0\le\chi_N\le1$, and supported where these phase hypotheses hold. For every integer $N\ge1$ and every $\lambda\ge1$, put $I_N(\lambda)=\int e^{i\lambda\Phi(x)}a(x)\chi_N(x)\,dx$. There are coefficients $c_j$ determined by the full Taylor series of the phase and amplitude at $0$ and constants $C,\delta>0$, independent of $N,\lambda$, such that
$$
I_N(\lambda)=e^{i\lambda\Phi_0}(2\pi/\lambda)^{n/2}(\det H)^{-1/2} \left(\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}c_j\lambda^{-j}\right)+E_N(\lambda),
$$
$$
|c_j|\le C^{j+1}j!,\qquad |e^{-i\lambda\Phi_0}E_N(\lambda)|\le C^{N+1}N!\lambda^{-N-n/2}+Ce^{-\delta\lambda}.
$$
The square-root branch is fixed by the preceding holomorphic Morse/Gaussian-contour lemma, and $c_0=a(0)$. Taking $N=\lfloor\epsilon\lambda\rfloor$ for sufficiently small fixed $\epsilon>0$ and sufficiently large $\lambda$ makes the normalized remainder $e^{-i\lambda\Phi_0}E_N(\lambda)=O(e^{-\delta_2\lambda})$ for some $\delta_2>0$. The expansion includes every coefficient through the stated truncation order; it is not only a leading-term estimate.

Work near $(q_0,p_0)\in\mathbb R^n\times(\mathbb R^n\setminus0)$. A normalized positive analytic packet phase is a holomorphic function $\phi(y,q,p)$ on a fixed complex neighborhood of the indicated real variables, such that, for real arguments,
$$
\phi(q,q,p)=0,\qquad \partial_y\phi(q,q,p)=-p,\qquad \operatorname{Im}\phi(y,q,p)\ge c|y-q|^2
$$
for some $c>0$. A classical analytic amplitude is realized on each smaller complex neighborhood by
$$
a(y,q,p;\lambda)=\sum_{j<\epsilon\lambda}a_j(y,q,p)\lambda^{-j},\qquad \sup|a_j|\le C^{j+1}j!,
$$
with sufficiently small fixed $\epsilon>0$. Changing $\epsilon$ to a smaller positive number changes the realization by an exponentially small function on a smaller neighborhood. An elliptic amplitude has $a_0(q_0,q_0,p_0)\ne0$.

For a distribution $u$ localized to a sufficiently small fixed compact neighborhood of $q_0$, the uniform exponential decay of
$$
\langle u(y),a(y,q,p;\lambda)e^{i\lambda\phi(y,q,p)}\rangle
$$
for $(q,p)$ in a neighborhood of $(q_0,p_0)$ is independent of the normalized positive phase and elliptic classical analytic amplitude. Smooth fixed cutoffs equal to one near the packet centers are understood. This criterion agrees with the Gaussian criterion with unit directions and arbitrary $\lambda\ge1$.

More precisely, after shrinking the parameter neighborhood $W$, every other such packet $v_\beta$ with $\beta$ in a smaller $W_0\Subset W$ has a representation
$$
v_\beta(y;\lambda)=\int_W a(y,\alpha;\lambda)e^{i\lambda\phi(y,\alpha)}K(\beta,\alpha;\lambda)\,d\alpha+R_\beta(y;\lambda),
$$
where $|K|\le C\lambda^L$ and $\|R_\beta\|_{C^m}\le C_m e^{-c_m\lambda}$ on the fixed localization compact, for every fixed $m$. There is a representation in the reverse direction as well. All estimates are uniform on the stated smaller neighborhoods. Thus the inverse is an actual local operator modulo exponentially small errors, rather than just a formal inverse series.

Let $m\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb C^m$ be open, let $F:U\to\mathbb C^m$ be
holomorphic, and let $a\in U$. If $\det J_{\mathbb C}F(a)\ne0$, then there are
open neighbourhoods $U_0\subseteq U$ of $a$ and $V_0$ of $F(a)$ such that
$F|_{U_0}:U_0\to V_0$ is biholomorphic.

If $G:V_0\to U_0$ denotes the inverse, then

$$DG(w)=DF(G(w))^{-1}\qquad(w\in V_0).$$

derivations.claim: Choose analytic fiber coordinates for $\pi_X$, $ (t,x)\longmapsto (z(t,x),x)\in Z,\qquad t\in\mathbb R^d. $ The matrix $D_tz$ is injective because this map is an immersion with $x$ retained. The conormal equations from [F1] are $ (D_tz)^Tp=0,\qquad \xi=(D_xz)^Tp. $ The first equations define an analytic bundle of rank $\dim G-d$ in the $p$ variables, so $(t,x,p)$ with these equations parameterize $C_Z$ locally. The map to data cotangent space is $(t,x,p)\mapsto(z(t,x),p)$. Its derivative is injective by the hypothesis; selecting a full-rank coordinate minor and applying [F3] makes it an analytic embedding on a smaller neighborhood. Denote its image by $V$.

We make the exact packet resolution explicit, without importing a Fourier inversion theorem with an additional choice assumption. In $\mathbb R^n$, set $ m^\lambda_{a,b}(y)=2^{-n/2}\pi^{-3n/4}\lambda^{3n/4}e^{i\lambda y\cdot b-\lambda|y-a|^2/2}. $ Then, with the frequency integral interpreted by the indicated Gaussian regularization, $ u(y)=\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}\int e^{-\varepsilon|b|^2}\langle u,\overline{m^\lambda_{a,b}}\rangle m^\lambda_{a,b}(y)\,da\,db $ in distributions. Indeed the $b$ integral is $(\pi/\varepsilon)^{n/2}e^{-\lambda^2|y-y'|^2/(4\varepsilon)}$, by completing the square and the Gaussian contour formula [F4]. The $a$ integral is $(\pi/\lambda)^{n/2}e^{-\lambda|y-y'|^2/4}$. Including the squared normalization, their product is a Gaussian kernel in $y-y'$ with mass tending to $1$ as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ and width tending to $0$. Pairing against a compact test, each fixed derivative converges uniformly on the support of $u$: split into a small translation neighborhood controlled by uniform continuity and its Gaussian tail. Thus [F1] justifies the distributional limit. The limiting normalization is exactly one, as also follows by multiplying $(2\pi/\lambda)^n$ and $(\pi/\lambda)^{n/2}$ by the squared packet constant. Applying this identity on data space, or directly transposing the incidence integral, gives the same object kernel as direct transposition of the incidence integral.

The paired map $\chi:V\to T^*X$ is a submersion. Here is a local linear-algebra proof. On $C_Z$, the one-form $p\,dz-\xi\,dx$ vanishes by the conormal equations; hence its differential also vanishes. The tangent space $L$ of $C_Z$ therefore is isotropic for the nondegenerate bilinear alternating form $dp\wedge dz-d\xi\wedge dx$. Its dimension is $\dim G+\dim X$, half the ambient dimension, so $L$ equals its alternating orthogonal complement. If $d\pi_R(L)$ were a proper subspace, the nondegenerate form $d\xi\wedge dx$ would give a nonzero vector $w$ orthogonal to it. Then $(0,w)$ would be orthogonal to $L$, hence in $L$, and would lie in the kernel of $d\pi_L$. This contradicts injectivity. Thus $d\pi_R$ is onto. The argument uses only the matrix criterion for an alternating form to be nondegenerate and the dimension formula for its orthogonal complement. By [F3], $\chi$ has a local analytic section $v=v(Q,P)$ onto an open neighborhood of $(x_0,\xi_0)$.

Pair $Ru$ with the data Gaussian and use the typed transpose in [F1]. Up to the harmless unit factor $e^{i\lambda q\cdot p}$ its object kernel is $ K_\lambda(x,v)=\int e^{i\lambda\Psi(t,x,v)}b(t,x)\,dt,\qquad \Psi=-z(t,x)\cdot p+\frac i2|z(t,x)-q|^2. $ The analytic coefficient $b$ is nowhere zero by [F2] and the fiber-coordinate Jacobian. Data and fiber cutoffs are one near the base incidence point. Their transition pieces have $|z-q|\ge r>0$ after shrinking $x,v$; their integrals are $O(e^{-c\lambda})$ in every fixed object derivative by the finite-order distribution estimates and the Gaussian factor. Properness ensures the remaining relevant incidence portion is compact, so finitely many such estimates suffice. A fixed fiber cutoff can therefore be inserted without changing the formula except for these errors.

For $v\in V$ real there is a unique nearby real $t_0(v)$ with $z(t_0(v),X(v))=q$. At this point $\Psi_t=0$ by step 1.1. Put $D=D_xz$, $T=D_tz$, evaluated there. Its complex $t$ Hessian is $ H=B+iT^TT,\qquad B=-\partial_t^2(z\cdot p), $ where $B$ is real symmetric and $T$ is injective. This matrix is invertible: if $Hw=0$, the imaginary part of $w^*Hw$ is $|Tw|^2$, forcing $w=0$. Apply [F7] to the map retaining $(x,v)$ and replacing $t$ by $\Psi_t$; it gives a unique nearby complex critical point $t_c(x,v)$ for all nearby complex $x,v$. Shrink the original fiber neighborhood so it contains no other critical point: outside a small ball about $t_0$, continuity and the injectivity of the local coordinate chart preserve a positive lower bound for the phase gradient or for $|z-q|$. Define $\psi(x,v)=\Psi(t_c(x,v),x,v)$.

We prove its strict object positivity directly, rather than assume a positivity property of a formal stationary phase. At $(t_0,X(v),v)$ the full Hessian in $(t,x)$ is a complex symmetric matrix $ \mathcal H=\mathcal R+i\mathcal S,\qquad \mathcal S=[T\ D]^T[T\ D],\qquad \mathcal R=-\partial^2_{t,x}(z\cdot p). $ For a real object variation $h$, let $\tau$ be the complex solution of the stationary linearized equation $\mathcal H_{tt}\tau+\mathcal H_{tx}h=0$. Write $U=(\operatorname{Re}\tau,h)$ and $W=(\operatorname{Im}\tau,0)$. The real part of the stationary equation gives $(\mathcal R U)_t=(\mathcal S W)_t$. Therefore $ \operatorname{Im}\bigl((\tau,h)^T\mathcal H(\tau,h)\bigr) =U^T\mathcal S U-W^T\mathcal S W+2W^T\mathcal R U =|T\operatorname{Re}\tau+Dh|^2+|T\operatorname{Im}\tau|^2. $ This is precisely $\operatorname{Im}(h^T\psi_{xx}h)$ by differentiating the critical-point identity. If it is zero, injectivity of $T$ gives $\operatorname{Im}\tau=0$, and $T\tau+Dh=0$. The remaining stationary equation is $\mathcal R_{tt}\tau+\mathcal R_{tx}h=0$. These two equations say that $(\tau,h,\dot p=0)$ is a tangent variation of the conormal equations $(D_tz)^Tp=0$ and has $\dot z=\dot p=0$. By injectivity of $d\pi_L$ it is zero, so $h=0$. Compactness of the real unit sphere now gives a strictly positive lower bound for $\operatorname{Im}\psi_{xx}$, uniform for $v$ in a smaller compact neighborhood in $V$.

The critical-value and derivative identities are $ \psi(X(v),v)=-q\cdot p,\qquad \psi_x(X(v),v)=-D_xz(t_0,X(v))^Tp=-\Xi(v). $ The imaginary part and its first object derivative vanish there. Taylor's integral formula and the strict Hessian bound in step 3.1 therefore give $\operatorname{Im}\psi(x,v)\ge c|x-X(v)|^2$ for real $x,v$ nearby. This fixes the sign for the FBI pairing: the test function has derivative $-\Xi$, while the distributional covector detected is $+\Xi$.

Apply analytic stationary phase at the complex critical point in step 2.3. Its applicability here includes uniform contour and remainder estimates as follows. At the base real parameters the real $t$ contour has positive quadratic imaginary part $T^TT$; its outer boundary has a fixed positive imaginary margin by step 2.2. For nearby parameters move the interior contour through $t_c(x,v)$ using the holomorphic quadratic coordinates in [F4], keeping the boundary fixed. In those coordinates the contour remains a graph whose Gaussian real part is bounded below by a fixed positive quadratic form, by openness of positive definiteness. Interpolate to its linear tangent contour as in the Gaussian-contour proof; the cubic error is dominated after shrinking the fixed ball. Stokes deformation consequently has a fixed exponential boundary margin. Cauchy bounds for the amplitude and the inverse coordinate map are uniform on smaller complex parameter neighborhoods. Applying the normalized remainder in [F4] with $N=\lfloor\epsilon\lambda\rfloor$ gives $ K_\lambda=\lambda^{-d/2}e^{i\lambda\psi}A+E_\lambda. $ The leading coefficient of $A$ is $(2\pi)^{d/2}b(t_c(x,v),x)(\det(-i\Psi_{tt}(t_c(x,v),x,v)))^{-1/2}$ on the fixed analytic branch. At $x=X(v)$ the critical point is the real $t_0(v)$, where the density coefficient and Hessian determinant are nonzero; continuity and holomorphy therefore make this coefficient elliptic on a smaller neighborhood. Its coefficients have uniform factorial bounds. For real parameters $\operatorname{Im}\psi\ge0$, so normalized exponential errors also give absolute exponential errors. For fixed object derivatives take a smaller complex neighborhood where $|\operatorname{Im}\psi|$ is less than half the boundary/remainder margin and apply Cauchy; the cutoff transition pieces already have the corresponding finite-order real derivative bounds. Hence $E_\lambda=O(e^{-c_m\lambda})$ in every fixed object derivative as claimed.

Suppose the data Gaussian criterion holds. By [F5], its unit-direction formulation is equivalent to the Gaussian packet with $p$ in an open ball about the supplied nonzero data covector; positive radial frequency scaling only changes the exponential constant. Thus the data Gaussian pairings used in step 2.2 are uniformly exponentially small on an open parameter neighborhood. Pair the formula in step 5.1 with $u$; its finite order absorbs the errors. Multiply by $\lambda^{d/2}e^{i\lambda q\cdot p}$, whose modulus on real parameters is only polynomial. Pull back $v$ by the analytic section $v(Q,P)$ from step 2.1. The resulting object test phase $ \widetilde\psi(x,Q,P)=\psi(x,v(Q,P))+q(Q,P)\cdot p(Q,P) $ vanishes at $x=Q$, has derivative $-P$ there and imaginary part at least $c|x-Q|^2$. Its amplitude is elliptic by step 5.1. Thus [F5] converts this exponential estimate into the Gaussian criterion at $(x_0,\xi_0)$. All input support here is in the chosen local object neighborhood, and every tail and inverse error has been estimated before pairing with the distribution. This proves the local implication.

citations.quote:
Let $M$ be a smooth $n$-manifold. A distribution on $M$ is a continuous complex-linear functional on compactly supported smooth densities on $M$. Its topology is generated locally by the fixed-support seminorms $\max_{|\alpha|\le m}\sup_K|\partial^\alpha\varphi|$, followed by the locally convex test-function topology. In a chart $x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$ a test density is $\varphi(x)|dx|$; under a coordinate change it transforms by the absolute Jacobian. A distribution is compactly supported when its support, the complement of its largest vanishing open set, is compact.

For a smooth submersion $p:Y\to M$, define the pullback $p^*u$ by transposing fiber integration: in submersion coordinates $p(x,v)=x$,
$$
\langle p^*u,\psi(x,v)|dx\,dv|\rangle =\left\langle u,\left(\int\psi(x,v)|dv|\right)|dx|\right\rangle.
$$
The absolute density quotient gives the fiber density in other submersion coordinates. For a distributional density $V$ on $Y$, meaning a continuous functional on compactly supported smooth scalar functions, define its support by the same largest-vanishing-open-set rule. If $q:Y\to M$ is proper on $\operatorname{supp}V$, then for a test function $\varphi$ on $M$ the set $q^{-1}(\operatorname{supp}\varphi)\cap\operatorname{supp}V$ is compact. Choose a smooth compact cutoff $\beta$ equal to one near this set and define the pushforward by
$$
\langle q_*V,\varphi\rangle=\langle V,\beta(\varphi\circ q)\rangle.
$$
The support property makes this independent of $\beta$; the cutoff is needed because $\varphi\circ q$ need not be compactly supported on all of $Y$.
A smooth density $\mu$ times a distribution $u$ in the test-density convention is the distributional density $\mu u$ defined by $\langle\mu u,\varphi\rangle=\langle u,\varphi\mu\rangle$.

Let $Z\subseteq G\times X$ be an embedded submanifold whose two projections are submersions. For a smooth density $\omega_Z$ on $Z$, its incidence delta kernel is the distributional density
$$
\langle K_Z,\Phi\rangle=\int_Z\Phi|_Z\,\omega_Z.
$$
In coordinates $(g,x)=(u,t)$ with $Z=\{t=0\}$, this is the delta distribution in the $t$ variables paired with the chosen density on $Z$. The conormal bundle and associated cotangent relation are
$$
N^*Z=\{(z,\zeta)\in T^*(G\times X):z\in Z,\ \zeta|_{T_zZ}=0\}, \qquad C_Z=\{(g,\eta;x,\xi):(g,x;\eta,-\xi)\in N^*Z\setminus0\}.
$$
Here $N^*Z\setminus0$ removes the zero covector, and the minus sign is the distribution-kernel convention for an operator from $X$ to $G$. Since both projections are submersions, every nonzero conormal in this relation has both $\eta\ne0$ and $\xi\ne0$. An analytic incidence kernel means that $Z$, its local defining maps, and the coefficients of $\omega_Z$ are real analytic. This definition covers the incidence kernels used below; it does not assert a general Fourier-integral-operator calculus.

For $u\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$, say $u$ **vanishes on** an open $V\subseteq\Omega$ if its restriction to $V$ is zero. Let $Z$ be the union of all such open sets. Locality in [[thm-distributions-form-a-sheaf]] shows that $u|_Z=0$, since these sets cover $Z$ and all its restrictions are zero. Thus $Z$ is the largest vanishing open set. The **support** is the relatively closed set $\operatorname{supp}u=\Omega\setminus Z$.

In particular $\operatorname{supp}u=\varnothing$ if and only if $u=0$: emptiness gives $Z=\Omega$ and vanishing there, while the zero distribution vanishes everywhere. If a test $\varphi$ vanishes on a neighborhood of $\operatorname{supp}u$, its compact support is contained in $Z$, so $u(\varphi)=0$ by restriction. Consequently two tests agreeing on a neighborhood of $\operatorname{supp}u$ have equal pairings with $u$, by applying this fact to their difference.

**Compactly supported** means that $\operatorname{supp}u$ is a compact subset of $\Omega$. Relative closedness in an arbitrary open domain is not by itself compactness or closedness in the ambient Euclidean space. On the empty domain support is empty. The union and locality argument require no selection of vanishing neighborhoods and no choice axiom.

Let $u$ be a distribution near $0\in\mathbb R^n$, vanishing where $x_n<0$. If either $(0,dx_n)$ or $(0,-dx_n)$ is absent from its Gaussian analytic wavefront set, then $u=0$ on a neighborhood of $0$. Equivalently, if $0\in\operatorname{supp}u$, both normal orientations belong to that wavefront set. The assertion also holds with the two half-spaces interchanged.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be
$C^1$, and let $a\in U$.  If $Df(a)$ is invertible, then there are open sets
$V,W\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $a\in V\subseteq U$ and $f(a)\in W$ such that
$f|_V:V\to W$ is bijective.  Its inverse $g:W\to V$ is $C^1$, and

$$Dg(y)=Df(g(y))^{-1}\qquad(y\in W).$$

Thus $f$ is a local diffeomorphism at $a$.

Let $u$ be a compactly supported distribution or a compactly supported distributional density on a real-analytic manifold. In each analytic chart use the Gaussian FBI packets of the preceding definition, paired with test densities in the first case and test functions in the second. The exponential-decay criterion is independent of the compact cutoff that equals one near the base point. It is also equivalent after an analytic chart change, with covectors transformed by the cotangent differential, and after replacing the standard Gaussian packets by their analytic pullbacks under that chart change. The latter equivalence is asserted only for the local packet and chart changes used on this page; it is the analytic-wavefront invariance needed to interpret the set geometrically.

derivations.claim: Work in an analytic ambient chart centered at $x_0$. The hypersurface remains $C^2$ in that chart, since changing from its given smooth chart is a smooth diffeomorphism. A real linear coordinate change makes its tangent plane nonvertical. The $C^2$ implicit graph theorem then writes it as $x_n=\psi(x')$, with $\psi$ of class $C^2$: the inverse of a $C^2$ map with invertible derivative is $C^2$, by differentiating the identity for its inverse twice. Translate to have $\psi(0)=0$. Shrink to a convex $x'$ ball on which $\|D^2\psi\|\le 2C$. Taylor's integral formula gives $ q_-(x'):=D\psi(0)x'-C|x'|^2\le\psi(x')\le D\psi(0)x'+C|x'|^2=:q_+(x'). $ Both supporting quadratics are real analytic and have the same differential as $\psi$ at $0$.

Suppose first that $f$ vanishes on the strict subgraph of $\psi$. Its local support lies in $x_n\ge\psi(x')$, hence in $x_n\ge q_-(x')$. The analytic shear $(x',x_n)\mapsto(x',x_n-q_-(x'))$ has analytic inverse $(y',y_n)\mapsto(y',y_n+q_-(y'))$, determinant $1$, and sends this latter closed side into $y_n\ge0$. If instead $f$ vanishes on the strict epigraph, its support lies in $x_n\le\psi(x')\le q_+(x')$ and use the corresponding analytic shear with $q_+$. In either case the pulled-back normal $dy_n$ at $0$ is $dx_n-D\psi(0)dx'$, a nonzero scalar multiple of the supplied conormal $\nu_0$. This flattens an analytic supporting quadratic; it does not flatten the original $C^2$ graph analytically.

If $f$ already vanishes near $x_0$, there is nothing to prove. Otherwise $x_0\in\operatorname{supp}f$ by [F2]. Localize inside the chart. Under the appropriate shear, [F3] then puts both $dy_n$ and $-dy_n$ in the analytic wavefront set at the origin. By [F4] these are exactly both conormal orientations at $x_0$, up to positive frequency scaling. Either absence hypothesis in the statement contradicts this conclusion. Thus $f=0$ near $x_0$. Every construction used finite-dimensional coordinates and explicit quadratics; it introduces no choice assumption.

An analytic double fibration is a diagram of real-analytic manifolds and real-analytic submersions
$$
G\xleftarrow{\ \pi_G\ }Z\xrightarrow{\ \pi_X\ }X
$$
such that $Z$ is embedded in $G\times X$, both projections are submersions, and
$$
\dim G+\dim X>\dim Z>\dim G\ge\dim X.
$$
Write $C_Z=\{(g,\eta;x,\xi):(g,x;\eta,-\xi)\in N^*Z\setminus0\}$ for the incidence cotangent relation. Assume $\pi_G$ is proper on $\pi_X^{-1}(K)$ for every compact $K\subset X$. Let $\omega_Z$ be a nowhere vanishing real-analytic smooth density on $Z$ and let $\kappa\colon Z\to\mathbb C$ be real analytic and nowhere zero. For a compactly supported distribution $u$ on $X$, the weighted transform is the distributional density
$$
Ru=(\pi_G)_*\bigl(\kappa\,\omega_Z\,\pi_X^*u\bigr),
$$
where pullback, multiplication by a density, proper pushforward, and $C_Z$ use the conventions of the preceding definition. In local fiber coordinates this is integration of $u$ over the incidence fibers with weight $\kappa$ and density $\omega_Z$. The hypotheses on proper support ensure this transform is defined for every compactly supported input. This is the class treated on this page; no noisy-data or stability assertion is included.

For an analytic double fibration with incidence cotangent relation $C_Z\subset(T^*G\setminus0)\times(T^*X\setminus0)$, let
$$
\pi_L:C_Z\longrightarrow T^*G\setminus0,\qquad \pi_L(g,\eta;x,\xi)=(g,\eta).
$$
The double fibration satisfies the global Bolker condition if $\pi_L$ is an injective immersion. The Bolker condition holds at a specified point $c=(g,\eta;x,\xi)\in C_Z$ if the full fiber over its data covector is the singleton $\pi_L^{-1}(g,\eta)=\{c\}$ and $d\pi_L|_c$ is injective. Thus the pointwise condition has both a fiber-uniqueness clause, which excludes every other relation point over the same data covector even outside a chosen chart, and a local differential-rank clause.

Let $R$ be an analytic double-fibration transform and $u\in\mathcal E'(X)$ with support $K$. Fix a nonzero data covector $(z_0,\zeta_0)$. Suppose there is no relation point $(z_0,\zeta_0;x,\xi)\in C_Z$ with $x\in K$. Then $(z_0,\zeta_0)\notin\operatorname{WF}_A(Ru)$. More precisely, the transpose of a data Gaussian packet, localized near $z_0$, is exponentially small with every fixed number of object derivatives on a neighborhood of $K$, uniformly for data centers and directions near $(z_0,\zeta_0/|\zeta_0|)$.

Let $R$ be an analytic double-fibration transform, and fix a relation point $(z_0,\zeta_0;x_0,\xi_0)$ at which $d\pi_L$ is injective. For distributions $u$ supported in a sufficiently small neighborhood of $x_0$, data Gaussian exponential regularity at $(z_0,\zeta_0)$ implies object Gaussian exponential regularity at $(x_0,\xi_0)$.

More precisely, for data parameters $v=(q,p)$ near that point on the local embedded image $V$ of $\pi_L$, write $\chi(v)=(X(v),\Xi(v))$ for the paired object covector. The transpose localized data Gaussian has the form
$$
K_\lambda(x,v)=\lambda^{-d/2}e^{i\lambda\psi(x,v)}A(x,v;\lambda)+E_\lambda(x,v), \qquad d=\dim Z-\dim X,
$$
where $A$ is an elliptic classical analytic amplitude, $E_\lambda=O(e^{-c_m\lambda})$ in every fixed object derivative, and
$$
\psi(X(v),v)=-q\cdot p,\quad d_x\psi(X(v),v)=-\Xi(v),\quad \operatorname{Im}\psi(x,v)\ge c|x-X(v)|^2
$$
for real parameters. The map $\chi$ is an analytic submersion onto an open object cotangent neighborhood and has a local analytic section there. The constant factor in the kernel formula includes the nonzero Gaussian determinant on its continuous branch.

Let $u$ be a compactly supported distribution or a compactly supported distributional density on a real-analytic manifold. In each analytic chart use the Gaussian FBI packets of the preceding definition, paired with test densities in the first case and test functions in the second. The exponential-decay criterion is independent of the compact cutoff that equals one near the base point. It is also equivalent after an analytic chart change, with covectors transformed by the cotangent differential, and after replacing the standard Gaussian packets by their analytic pullbacks under that chart change. The latter equivalence is asserted only for the local packet and chart changes used on this page; it is the analytic-wavefront invariance needed to interpret the set geometrically.

derivations.claim: Choose a smooth compact object cutoff $\rho$ equal to one near $x_0$ and supported in the small object neighborhood supplied by [F4]. Write $f=\rho f+(1-\rho)f$. The second summand is compactly supported away from $x_0$. By [F2] its support has no relation point over $(z_0,\zeta_0)$, because that full fiber consists of the supplied point over $x_0$. Hence [F3] gives $(z_0,\zeta_0)\notin\operatorname{WF}_A(R((1-\rho)f))$. This includes all incidence points outside the local coordinate patch; it is not inferred merely from local injectivity.

By hypothesis the Gaussian data transform of $Rf$ is exponentially small on some data parameter neighborhood. Subtract the exponential estimate from step 1.1, using the same data chart and a common smaller cutoff neighborhood by [F5]. Linearity gives the same estimate for $R(\rho f)$ at the supplied data covector. The differential clause of [F2] supplies the local Bolker hypothesis in [F4]. Since $\rho f$ is supported in its chosen small object neighborhood, [F4] yields $(x_0,\xi_0)\notin\operatorname{WF}_A(\rho f)$.

The localized distributions $\rho f$ and $f$ agree on a neighborhood of $x_0$. Their Gaussian transforms with any common cutoff supported there agree exactly; all other cutoff choices differ only by the exponential Gaussian tails in [F5]. Thus step 2.1 gives $(x_0,\xi_0)\notin\operatorname{WF}_A(f)$, as asserted. The two suppliers account separately for global fiber uniqueness and local differential injectivity, and all errors are controlled in the finite number of derivatives needed by the compact distribution. No stability or choice assumption has been added.

Let $u$ be a distribution, not necessarily compactly supported, or a distributional density (a continuous functional on compactly supported smooth scalar functions), on a real-analytic $n$-manifold $X$. $$

$$

The covector $(x_0,\xi_0)$ is analytically regular for $u$ in this chart if there are such a cutoff $\chi$, a neighborhood $U$ of $x_0$, an open neighborhood $\Gamma$ of $\xi_0/|\xi_0|$ in the unit sphere, and constants $c,C>0$ such that

Write $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C)$ for the complex-valued smooth functions of compact support on the Euclidean plane. For $u\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$, $n=1$ or $2$, use the compact-support Riemann Fourier transform
$$\widehat u(\xi)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}u(x)e^{-2\pi i x\cdot\xi}\,dx.$$
For $\theta=(\theta_1,\theta_2)\in S^1:=\{x\in\mathbb R^2:|x|=1\}$ put $\theta^\perp=(-\theta_2,\theta_1)$. The line with normal $\theta$ and signed offset $s$ is $\{x\in\mathbb R^2:x\cdot\theta=s\}$. Its **Euclidean Radon transform** is
$$Rf(\theta,s):=\int_{\mathbb R}f(s\theta+t\theta^\perp)\,dt,\qquad f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C),\ (\theta,s)\in S^1\times\mathbb R.$$
The line integral is a compact-support Riemann integral.
The full data set uses every oriented normal $\theta\in S^1$ and every $s\in\mathbb R$; the same unoriented line is represented by $(\theta,s)$ and $(-\theta,-s)$.
For a one-dimensional function $h$ with integrable Fourier transform, define
$$|D_s|h(s):=\int_{\mathbb R}2\pi|\sigma|\,\widehat h(\sigma)e^{2\pi i s\sigma}\,d\sigma.$$
For $f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C)$ define the Riesz potential notation used here by
$$|D|^{-1}f(x):=\int_{\mathbb R^2}e^{2\pi i x\cdot\xi}\frac{\widehat f(\xi)}{2\pi|\xi|}\,d\xi.$$
The quotient in the last integral is assigned value $0$ at $\xi=0$. These integrals are absolutely convergent on the stated classes: compact-support integration by parts gives rapid decay of $\widehat f$ and $\widehat h$, while $\widehat f$ is bounded near $0$ and $|\xi|^{-1}$ is locally integrable in two dimensions. Here the multiplier for $|D_s|$ is $2\pi|\sigma|$, corresponding to the $e^{-2\pi i s\sigma}$ Fourier convention.

Let $\Theta\subset S^1$ be a nonempty proper open set of line normals, assume $\theta\in\Theta$ if and only if $-\theta\in\Theta$, and assume $S^1\setminus\overline{\Theta}$ contains a nonempty open arc. The measured line with normal $\theta$ and signed offset $s$ is $\ell_{\theta,s}=\{y\in\mathbb R^2:y\cdot\theta=s\}$. Identify the nonzero cotangent vectors of the Euclidean plane with pairs $(x,\xi)\in\mathbb R^2\times(\mathbb R^2\setminus\{0\})$. Such a covector is visible from $\Theta$ when $\xi/|\xi|\in\Theta$, and invisible when $\xi/|\xi|\notin\Theta$. The associated measured Fourier wedge is

$$W_\Theta=\{\sigma\theta:\theta\in\Theta,\ \sigma\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}\}.$$

Let $M$ be a smooth $n$-manifold. A distribution on $M$ is a continuous complex-linear functional on compactly supported smooth densities on $M$. Its topology is generated locally by the fixed-support seminorms $\max_{|\alpha|\le m}\sup_K|\partial^\alpha\varphi|$, followed by the locally convex test-function topology. In a chart $x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$ a test density is $\varphi(x)|dx|$; under a coordinate change it transforms by the absolute Jacobian. A distribution is compactly supported when its support, the complement of its largest vanishing open set, is compact.

For a smooth submersion $p:Y\to M$, define the pullback $p^*u$ by transposing fiber integration: in submersion coordinates $p(x,v)=x$,
$$
\langle p^*u,\psi(x,v)|dx\,dv|\rangle =\left\langle u,\left(\int\psi(x,v)|dv|\right)|dx|\right\rangle.
$$
The absolute density quotient gives the fiber density in other submersion coordinates. For a distributional density $V$ on $Y$, meaning a continuous functional on compactly supported smooth scalar functions, define its support by the same largest-vanishing-open-set rule. If $q:Y\to M$ is proper on $\operatorname{supp}V$, then for a test function $\varphi$ on $M$ the set $q^{-1}(\operatorname{supp}\varphi)\cap\operatorname{supp}V$ is compact. Choose a smooth compact cutoff $\beta$ equal to one near this set and define the pushforward by
$$
\langle q_*V,\varphi\rangle=\langle V,\beta(\varphi\circ q)\rangle.
$$
The support property makes this independent of $\beta$; the cutoff is needed because $\varphi\circ q$ need not be compactly supported on all of $Y$.
A smooth density $\mu$ times a distribution $u$ in the test-density convention is the distributional density $\mu u$ defined by $\langle\mu u,\varphi\rangle=\langle u,\varphi\mu\rangle$.

Let $Z\subseteq G\times X$ be an embedded submanifold whose two projections are submersions. For a smooth density $\omega_Z$ on $Z$, its incidence delta kernel is the distributional density
$$
\langle K_Z,\Phi\rangle=\int_Z\Phi|_Z\,\omega_Z.
$$
In coordinates $(g,x)=(u,t)$ with $Z=\{t=0\}$, this is the delta distribution in the $t$ variables paired with the chosen density on $Z$. The conormal bundle and associated cotangent relation are
$$
N^*Z=\{(z,\zeta)\in T^*(G\times X):z\in Z,\ \zeta|_{T_zZ}=0\}, \qquad C_Z=\{(g,\eta;x,\xi):(g,x;\eta,-\xi)\in N^*Z\setminus0\}.
$$
Here $N^*Z\setminus0$ removes the zero covector, and the minus sign is the distribution-kernel convention for an operator from $X$ to $G$. Since both projections are submersions, every nonzero conormal in this relation has both $\eta\ne0$ and $\xi\ne0$. An analytic incidence kernel means that $Z$, its local defining maps, and the coefficients of $\omega_Z$ are real analytic. This definition covers the incidence kernels used below; it does not assert a general Fourier-integral-operator calculus.

Let $Z\subseteq G\times X$ be an embedded incidence submanifold of codimension $k>0$, and let $(g_0,x_0)\in Z$. Choose coordinates near this point and a submersion $F:G\times X\to\mathbb R^k$ with $Z=\{F=0\}$. Write $F=(F_1,\ldots,F_k)$. For every $\tau\in\mathbb R^k\setminus\{0\}$, the conormal covector at $(g,x)\in Z$ is
$$
(g,x;D_gF(g,x)^T\tau,\ D_xF(g,x)^T\tau).
$$
Consequently the incidence kernel has local delta representation $b(g,x)\delta(F(g,x))|dg\,dx|$, with a smooth density coefficient $b$, and its cotangent relation consists exactly of
$$
(g,D_gF^T\tau;\ x,-D_xF^T\tau),\qquad (g,x)\in Z,\quad \tau\ne0.
$$
No general Fourier-integral-operator composition calculus is used.

Let $f$ be a real analytic map between open subsets of $\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge1$. If $Df(a)$ is invertible, $f$ has a real analytic local inverse near $f(a)$. Let $P(x,y)$ be real analytic near $(a,b)\in\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R^k$, $k\ge1$, with $P(a,b)=0$ and $D_yP(a,b)$ invertible. derivations.claim: The defining function $F(\theta,s,x)=s-x\cdot\theta$ is real analytic and has $\partial_sF=1$. Thus $dF$ is surjective at every point of $Z_\Theta$, and [F6] makes $Z_\Theta$ an analytic hypersurface of dimension $3$.

Use a local angular coordinate $\alpha$ on $S^1$, so $\partial_\alpha\theta=\theta^\perp$. The defining function $F(\theta,s,x)=s-x\cdot\theta$ has differential $ dF=ds-(x\cdot\theta^\perp)d\alpha-\theta\cdot dx. $ By [F4], a conormal covector is $\tau dF$ for a nonzero scalar $\tau$. Matching its data components and object component with the sign convention [F3] gives $ \eta_s=\tau,\qquad \eta_\alpha=-\tau x\cdot\theta^\perp,\qquad \xi=\tau\theta. $ Thus any object covector in the relation is parallel to the measured normal $\theta$.

A tangent vector satisfies $\dot s-\dot x\cdot\theta-x\cdot\dot\theta=0$. Given any data tangent pair $(\dot\theta,\dot s)$, choose $\dot x=(\dot s-x\cdot\dot\theta)\theta$; then $\pi_G$ has a tangent lift and is a submersion. Given any object tangent vector $\dot x$, choose $\dot\theta=0$, $\dot s=\dot x\cdot\theta$; hence $\pi_X$ is a submersion. Both maps are analytic restrictions of product projections and $4>3>2\ge2$. The displayed analytic total density is nowhere zero in these incidence coordinates. For compact $K\subset\mathbb R^2$ and compact $L\subset\Theta\times\mathbb R$, the preimage of $L$ under $\pi_G|_{\pi_X^{-1}(K)}$ is closed in $\operatorname{pr}_1(L)\times K$, which is compact because $\operatorname{pr}_1(L)\Subset\Theta$. Thus the restricted projection is proper and [F5] applies.

If $(\theta,s,\eta;x_0,\xi_0)\in C_{Z_\Theta}$, step 1.2 implies $\xi_0/|\xi_0|=\theta$ or $-\theta$. Since $\Theta=-\Theta$, this would place $\xi_0/|\xi_0|$ in $\Theta$, contradicting the hypothesis. No such data covector exists.

A **Riemannian metric** on a Hausdorff second-countable smooth manifold $M$ is a smooth symmetric covariant two-tensor $g$ such that $g_p(v,v)>0$ for every point $p$ and every nonzero $v\in T_pM$. A **Riemannian manifold** is the pair $(M,g)$.

This is a [[def-smooth-tensor-field]] giving a [[def-smooth-bundle-metric]] on $TM$. Dimension zero is allowed: its zero bilinear form is positive definite because there are no nonzero vectors. The empty manifold has its unique empty metric. Boundaries are allowed where stated, with smoothness understood up to the boundary.

For $R>0$, the sphere $S_R^{m-1}=\{x\in\mathbb R^m:\|x\|_2=R\}$ is the regular level $F^{-1}(R^2)$ of $F(x)=\|x\|_2^2$. At $x\in S_R^{m-1}$,

Let $a<b$, let $\varepsilon>0$, and let
$$F:(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)\times[a,b]\longrightarrow M$$
be a smooth map, smooth up to the two time endpoints. It is a **geodesic
variation** when for every $s\in(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)$ the longitudinal
curve $t\mapsto F(s,t)$ is an affinely parametrized geodesic; equivalently,
$$D_t\partial_tF(s,t)=0.$$
The central geodesic is $\gamma(t)=F(0,t)$, and its **variation field** is
$$V(t)=\left.\partial_sF(s,t)\right|_{s=0}\in T_{\gamma(t)}M.$$
This is the variation-field construction in
[[def-smooth-variation-and-variation-field-of-a-curve]], with the additional
condition that every longitudinal curve is geodesic. No fixed-endpoint
condition is imposed: $V(a)$ and $V(b)$ may be nonzero. Constant geodesics are
allowed, including on zero-dimensional manifolds; dimension one is covered by
the same definition. If $M$ is empty, there is no such map on the nonempty
parameter interval, so the definition assigns no variation object.

Let $(M,g)$ be a Riemannian manifold, let $I$ be a nondegenerate interval,
and let $\gamma:I\to M$ be an affinely parametrized geodesic. For a smooth
vector field $J$ along $\gamma$, write $D_tJ$ for its covariant derivative
along $\gamma$ and $D_t^2J=D_t(D_tJ)$, using
[[def-covariant-derivative-along-a-curve]]. The curvature operator $R$ has the
convention
$$R(X,Y)Z=\nabla_X\nabla_YZ-\nabla_Y\nabla_XZ-\nabla_{[X,Y]}Z,$$
as fixed by [[lem-covariant-derivatives-commute-up-to-curvature-in-a-two-parameter-variation]]
and used in [[def-riemann-curvature-four-tensor]]. A smooth field $J$ is a
**Jacobi field** along $\gamma$ when it satisfies the Jacobi equation
$$D_t^2J+R(J,\dot\gamma)\dot\gamma=0$$
throughout $I$. We write $\mathcal J(\gamma)$ for the set of these fields.

The interval is required to have nonempty interior so that the covariant
derivatives are defined; if an endpoint is included, the equation there uses
the one-sided derivatives of the smooth field. Constant geodesics are included:
when $\dot\gamma=0$, the curvature term vanishes and the equation is
$D_t^2J=0$. On a zero-dimensional manifold the only field is zero, so the
equation holds. In dimension one the same equation and curvature convention
apply without a separate restriction. The definition classifies a specified
field and geodesic and makes no existence choice.

Let $(M,g)$ be a finite-dimensional Riemannian manifold without boundary of dimension $n\ge0$,
let $a<b$, and let $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ be an affinely parametrized geodesic.
Define
$$\mathcal K_\gamma(a,b):=\{J\in\mathcal J(\gamma):J(a)=0,\ J(b)=0\}.$$
This is a finite-dimensional real vector space. The points $\gamma(a)$ and
$\gamma(b)$ are **conjugate along $\gamma$** exactly when
$\mathcal K_\gamma(a,b)$ contains a nonzero Jacobi field. For a conjugate pair,
its **multiplicity** is $\dim_\mathbb R\mathcal K_\gamma(a,b)$. If $\gamma$ is
constant, then $\mathcal K_\gamma(a,b)=\{0\}$ and the endpoints are not
conjugate. If $\gamma$ is nonconstant, then
$\dim_\mathbb R\mathcal K_\gamma(a,b)\le n-1$. Included endpoint derivatives
are one-sided. No completeness or choice axiom is assumed.

Let $n\geq1$, and give
$$S^n=\{x\in\mathbb R^{n+1}:\langle x,x\rangle=1\}$$
the round metric induced by the Euclidean inner product. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with nonempty interior. For any supplied $t_0\in I$, a nonconstant affinely parametrized geodesic $\gamma:I\to S^n$ has constant speed $c>0$ and can be written
$$\gamma(t)=\cos(c(t-t_0))p+\sin(c(t-t_0))u,$$
where $p=\gamma(t_0)$ and $u=\gamma'(t_0)/c$ are orthonormal. Its image is therefore an arc of the great circle $S^n\cap\operatorname{span}\{p,u\}$; the corresponding maximal geodesic has the whole great circle as its image. Conversely, every such constant-speed parametrization of a great circle is a geodesic. Constant geodesics are obtained separately by taking $\gamma(t)=p$.

on $[a,b]$, using one-sided derivatives at included endpoints. No fixed
endpoint condition is imposed; constant geodesics and dimension zero are
included. This implication uses no axiom of choice.

Thus $dF\ne0$; [F6] makes $Z=F^{-1}(0)$ an analytic hypersurface of dimension $3$ in the $4$-dimensional product.

A tangent vector to $Z$ satisfies $x\cdot\dot n+n\cdot\dot x=0$. Given any $\dot n\in T_nS^2$, set $\dot x=-(x\cdot\dot n)n$; then $\dot x\in T_xS^2$ by [F5], and the tangent equation holds. Hence $\pi_G$ is a submersion. Given any $\dot x\in T_xS^2$, set $\dot n=-(n\cdot\dot x)x$; the same calculation proves $\pi_X$ is a submersion. Both maps are analytic restrictions of product projections. Since $Z$ is compact, $\pi_G$ is proper on $\pi_X^{-1}(K)$ for every compact $K\subset X$. The density induced by the positive-definite analytic product round metric has strictly positive analytic coefficient in every local incidence chart. The dimensions satisfy $4>3>2\ge2$, so [F1] applies.

The defining differential on tangent vectors to the product is $dF=(x^\flat,n^\flat)$ by the metric identification [F4]. Therefore by [F3] the relation at $(n,x)$ consists of $ (n,\eta;x,\xi)=(n,\tau x^\flat;x,-\tau n^\flat),\qquad \tau\ne0. $ At the antipodal point $-x$, choose multiplier $-\tau$. Its data covector is $(-\tau)(-x)^\flat=\tau x^\flat$, the same as at $x$, while the object point changes from $x$ to $-x$. Both are nonzero relation points. Hence the left projection is not injective, and [F2] implies failure of global Bolker.

Let $v=n\times x$, a unit tangent vector at $x$. For $s$ near zero put $n_s=\cos(s)n+\sin(s)v$, $v_s=n_s\times x$, and $ \gamma_s(t)=\cos(t)x+\sin(t)v_s,\qquad 0\le t\le\pi. $ Each $n_s$ is a unit vector orthogonal to $x$, and $v_s$ is a unit vector orthogonal to $x$; hence $\gamma_s$ parametrizes a great circle at unit speed and is a geodesic by [F10]. Thus [F7] makes this a geodesic variation. Its endpoints are fixed: $\gamma_s(0)=x$ and $\gamma_s(\pi)=-x$. Differentiating in $s$ at zero gives $ J(t)=\left.\partial_s\gamma_s(t)\right|_{s=0} =\sin(t)(v\times x)=-\sin(t)n, $ because $(n\times x)\times x=-n$ when $n\cdot x=0$ and $|x|=1$. By [F11] this field is Jacobi and hence satisfies the Jacobi equation in [F8]. It is nonzero for $0<t<\pi$ and vanishes at both endpoints, so [F9] makes the endpoints conjugate. and, for each $a\in A$, let $P_a$ be a polynomial of degree at most $r$
with values in $\mathbb R^N$. Suppose that on each compact part of $A$,
for every multi-index $|\alpha|\le r$,
$$D^\alpha P_a(b)-D^\alpha P_b(b)=o(|a-b|^{r-|\alpha|})\quad(a,b\in A,\ |a-b|\to0)$$
uniformly in $a,b$. Then there is a $C^r$ map

These facts follow from the fixed maximal dyadic retention test and rescaled bump quotient in that proof, independently of the jet order. Put $\sigma(z)=\sum_Q\ell(Q)\psi_Q(z)$. This is smooth and positive off $A$, and for $t=\operatorname{dist}(z,A)$ it satisfies $c t\le\sigma(z)\le C t$ and $|D^\alpha\sigma(z)|\le C_\alpha t^{1-|\alpha|}$. Each derivative estimate follows by bounded overlap and the side-length comparison. Fix $\chi\in C^\infty(\mathbb R)$ with $\chi=1$ on $(-\infty,1]$ and $\chi=0$ on $[2,\infty)$. It is $C^k$ everywhere and smooth off $A$, since there it is a locally finite sum of smooth partition functions times polynomials. Taylor's formula at a nearest point of $A$, on a fixed compact neighborhood of $A$, gives for every $|\beta|\le k$ $$|D^\beta\Delta_k(z)|=o(t^{k-|\beta|})\qquad(t=\operatorname{dist}(z,A)\downarrow0),$$ uniformly near $A$. The product rule and step 1.1 show that, for $|\alpha|\le k$, $D^\alpha(\eta_\delta\Delta_k)$ is bounded by a constant $B_k$ times $\max_{|\beta|\le k}t^{|\beta|-|\alpha|}|D^\beta\Delta_k|$, wherever $\eta_\delta$ is nonzero. Enlarge $B_k$ to include the finitely many binomial constants. Then $$|D^\alpha(\eta_{\delta_k}\Delta_k)(z)|\le2^{-k}t^{k-|\alpha|}\qquad(|\alpha|\le k).$$ Uniform moduli in step 2.1 give the same scales for the parameter family.

Define off $A$ $$F=H_1+\sum_{k\ge1}\eta_{\delta_k}(H_{k+1}-H_k),$$ and set $F(a)=f_0(a)$ on $A$. At each point off $A$ the sum is locally finite because $\delta_k\to0$, so $F$ is smooth there. Fix $K\ge1$. Sufficiently near $A$, all factors $\eta_{\delta_k}$ with $k<K$ equal one, and telescoping gives $F-H_K=\sum_{k\ge K}\eta_{\delta_k}\Delta_k$. $u,v\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$, and let
$\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$ be the multi-index of
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. We say that $v$ is
the **weak derivative** $D^\alpha u$ if
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Both integrals are finite because the test and all its derivatives are bounded
and compactly supported. The test identity is choice-free. By
[[def-locally-integrable-function-as-a-regular-distribution]] and the signed
transpose convention in [[def-distributional-derivative]], it is equivalent
to $\partial^\alpha T_u=T_v$ as distributions. For $\alpha=0$, this identity
reduces to $T_u=T_v$, hence to $u=v$ almost everywhere by the published
embedding theorem under [[def-countable-choice]].

**Well-definedness.** Changing either representative on a null set leaves each
test integral unchanged. Weak derivatives are therefore statements about
almost-everywhere classes; existence and uniqueness of their locally
integrable value classes are audited separately.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, with
$n\ge1$, and let all functions below be real- or complex-valued classes in
$L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$. Weak differentiation is complex-linear wherever
the derivatives exist: if $v_j=D^\alpha u_j$ weakly for $j=1,2$ and
$a,b\in\mathbb C$, then
$$av_1+bv_2=D^\alpha(au_1+bu_2)\quad\text{weakly}.$$
If $v=D^\alpha u$ weakly on $\Omega$ and $V\subseteq\Omega$ is open, then
$$v|_V=D^\alpha(u|_V)\quad\text{weakly on }V.$$

For the commutation assertion, let $u\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ and
$\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb N_0^n$. Suppose that the weak derivatives
$$v=D^\alpha u,\qquad w=D^\beta u$$
exist in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$. Then the following three existence
conditions are equivalent: $D^\beta v$ exists in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$;
$D^\alpha w$ exists in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$; and
$D^{\alpha+\beta}u$ exists in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$. Whenever they
exist, their value classes are equal almost everywhere on $\Omega$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, every class is zero, so all these statements hold.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge1$,
$\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$, and $u,v,w\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$. If both
$v$ and $w$ are weak $\alpha$-derivatives of $u$, then
$$v=w\quad\text{almost everywhere on }\Omega.$$
Thus a weak derivative, when it exists, is unique as an almost-everywhere
class. No connectedness assumption is needed.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the assertion holds because there is only the zero
class and no nonzero tests.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]) and let $T : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ be linear
with matrix $A$ ([[def-linear-map]],
[[lem-euclidean-linear-maps-have-matrices-and-are-bounded]]).

1. **Invertible case.** If $\det A \ne 0$, then $T[E]$ is Lebesgue measurable for
   every Lebesgue measurable $E$ and
   $$\lambda_n\big(T[E]\big) \;=\; |\det A|\;\lambda_n(E),$$
   both sides possibly $+\infty$; the product is defined in
   $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$ because $|\det A| > 0$.
2. **Singular case.** If $\det A = 0$, then $T[E]$ is Lebesgue measurable with
   $\lambda_n(T[E]) = 0$ for **every** $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$.

**The singular clause is stated as nullity and not as a product.** When
$\det A = 0$ and $\lambda_n(E) = +\infty$ the expression
$|\det A|\,\lambda_n(E)$ is $0\cdot(+\infty)$, which [[def-extended-reals]]
leaves undefined; writing the conclusion as $\lambda_n(T[E]) = 0$ says the same
thing wherever the product is defined and remains a statement where it is not.

Choose a boundary-compatible coordinate cover and subordinate partition $(\chi_j)$ by [F7]. On a boundary half-chart, one-dimensional integration by parts in the normal half-line includes the endpoint value; [F6] identifies its coordinate density with $\eta\partial_tu\partial_{

The inequality $|\partial_tu|\,|
abla_gu|_g\le e$ and step 4.1 give $$(\partial_t\eta)e-\langle

Set $\delta=d_g(Q,\partial M)>T/2$. For every $t\in[0,T]$, either $t<\delta$ or $T-t<\delta$: if $t\le T/2$ the first holds, and if $t\ge T/2$ the second holds. citations.quote: Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space, let $a$ be a bounded coercive sesquilinear form on $H$ with constants $M,\alpha$ ([[def-bounded-coercive-and-symmetric-sesquilinear-forms]]), and let $F:H\to\mathbb K$ be a bounded conjugate-linear functional with norm $\|F\|=\sup_{\|v\|\le1}|F(v)|$. Then there is a unique $u\in H$ with $$a(u,v)=F(v)\qquad\text{for every }v\in H,$$ and it satisfies $\alpha\|u\|\le\|F\|$, that is $\|u\|\le\|F\|/\alpha$. The real bilinear case is the same statement with $a$ symmetric or not, $F$ a bounded linear functional, and the conjugation read as the identity.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be a compact self-adjoint operator
([[def-compact-linear-operator]],
[[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]],
[[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). Let

$$\Sigma:=\{\lambda:\lambda\ \text{is an eigenvalue of}\ T,\ \lambda\ne0\}$$

be its set of nonzero eigenvalues
([[def-eigenvalue-eigenvector-eigenspace-and-spectrum]]), with eigenspaces
$E_\lambda=\ker(T-\lambda I)$ for $\lambda\in\Sigma$. Then:

1. $\Sigma$ is a finite or countably infinite set of **real** numbers, each
   eigenvalue has finite multiplicity in the sense $\dim E_\lambda<+\infty$, and
   for every real $\varepsilon>0$ there are only finitely many
   $\lambda\in\Sigma$ with $|\lambda|\ge\varepsilon$; in particular every point
   of $\mathbb F\setminus\{0\}$ has a neighbourhood containing only finitely
   many elements of $\Sigma$, so the only possible accumulation point of
   $\Sigma$ is $0$;
2. the closed linear span $M$ of $\bigcup_{\lambda\in\Sigma}E_\lambda$ satisfies
   $$M=(\ker T)^\perp=\overline{\operatorname{ran}T}$$
   ([[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]), and $H=M\oplus M^\perp$
   with $M^\perp\subseteq\ker T$;
3. for every $x\in H$ the finite-subset net of $\sum_{\lambda\in\Sigma}\lambda P_\lambda x$
   over the orthogonal projections $P_\lambda$ onto $E_\lambda$ converges in
   norm and
   $$Tx=\sum_{\lambda\in\Sigma}\lambda P_\lambda x ;$$
4. if in addition $H$ is a complex Hilbert space, then the nonzero spectrum
   agrees with the nonzero eigenvalues,
   $$\sigma(T)\cap\{\mu\in\mathbb C:\mu\ne0\}=\Sigma .$$

No Hilbert basis of $\ker T$ is selected anywhere: only the orthonormal bases of
the finite-dimensional eigenspaces $E_\lambda$, $\lambda\ne0$, are used.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a bounded $C^2$
domain, $n\ge2$, $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, let $L,a$ be as in
[[def-uniformly-elliptic-divergence-form-operator]] with ellipticity
constant $\theta$, bounds $M_a,M_b,M_c$ and $a^{ij}\in W^{1,\infty}(\Omega)$,

$u\in H^1_0(\Omega)$ is a weak solution of $Lu=f$ with zero boundary values
([[def-weak-dirichlet-solution-for-a-divergence-form-operator]]), then
$u\in H^2(\Omega)$ and there is
$C=C(n,\Omega,\theta,M_a,M_b,M_c,\|Da^{ij}\|_\infty)$ with
$$\|u\|_{H^2(\Omega)}\le C\big(\|f\|_{L^2(\Omega)}+\|u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\big).$$
The $L^2$ norm of $u$ on the right cannot be deleted without a hypothesis
excluding the homogeneous kernel, as the companion counterexample shows; the
theorem is stated for zero Dirichlet data, and nonzero compatible boundary
data are handled by an $H^2$ lifting, with an $L^2$ residual forcing,
before the theorem is applied.

derivations.claim: On each of finitely many relatively compact coordinate charts, metric eigenvalues and the volume density have positive lower and finite upper bounds. Thus the intrinsic $H^1$ norm is equivalent to the sum of coordinate $H^1$ norms of a fixed smooth partition of unity. A Cauchy sequence has $L^2$ limits for the localized functions and their first derivatives; testing against a smooth function and passing to the limit identifies the derivative limits as the weak derivatives of the function limit. This proves completeness; $V$, being a closure, is closed. Moreover $1\le q+c\le1+2\|q\|_\infty$, so $b$ and the $H^1$ inner product have equivalent norms. Local mollification of compactly supported functions and a finite partition prove density of $V$ in $H$.

The inclusion $V\hookrightarrow H$ is compact without an arbitrary-index choice argument. Indeed, a localized $v\in V$ extends by zero across a flattened boundary: approximate in $H^1$ by localized interior smooth functions, extend those, and pass to the weak-derivative identities. All extensions have bounded support in a fixed coordinate box. On a cube $C$ of side $\delta$, successively average in its $n$ coordinate variables. The one-variable identity $f(s)-f(t)=\int_t^s f'(r)dr$ and Cauchy–Schwarz give $\|f-\operatorname{avg}_C f\|_{L^2(C)}\le n\delta\|Df\|_{L^2(C)}$ by telescoping those averages; density extends this to $H^1$. Replacement by the mean on each cube of a fixed finite grid is therefore a finite-rank approximation to each coordinate inclusion, with error $O(\delta)$ uniformly on the $H^1$ unit ball. Sum the finitely many coordinate reconstructions to approximate $V\hookrightarrow H$ in operator norm by finite-rank maps. A bounded finite-dimensional set has finite nets; choosing $\delta=2^{-k}$ makes the inclusion's image totally bounded, and completeness of $H$ makes its closure compact. Only countably many finite nets are involved.

In a coordinate chart $Av=f$ is $$-\partial_i(\rho g^{ij}\partial_jv)+\rho qv=\rho f,\qquad \rho=\sqrt{\det g}.$$ The principal matrix is smooth uniformly positive on each compact chart. Localize by a smooth cutoff; its commutator with $A$ has order one. In a boundary chart flatten to $x_n\ge0$ and localize away from the chart sides. The localization can be regarded as a zero-Dirichlet function on a bounded smooth domain agreeing with the half-space near its support and rounded elsewhere. Applying [F3] and the same interior estimate, then summing the finite cover, gives $\|v\|_{H^2}\le C(\|f\|_2+\|v\|_{H^1})$. Testing the equation with $v$ gives $\|v\|_{H^1}\le C(\|f\|_2+\|v\|_2)$ by absorbing the gradient term, so this is the stated $k=0$ estimate.

For $f\in H$, use [F1] to solve $b(Kf,v)=(f,v)_H$. The map $K:H\to V$ is bounded, and step 2.1 makes $K:H\to H$ compact. Symmetry gives $(Kf,h)_H=b(Kf,Kh)=(f,Kh)_H$, positivity gives $(Kf,f)_H=b(Kf,Kf)>0$ for $f\ne0$, and density of $V$ makes $K$ injective. Its range is dense since a vector orthogonal to the range lies in the kernel by self-adjointness. Apply [F2] to obtain positive eigenvalues $\kappa_j\to0$ and a complete $H$-orthonormal family; put $\mu_j=\kappa_j^{-1}$. Repeated finite multiplicities are included. The vectors $e_j/\sqrt{\mu_j}$ are $b$-orthonormal and complete in $V$: if $b(v,e_j)=0$ for every $j$, then $(v,e_j)_H=0$ for every $j$, hence $v=0$. Orthogonal projection and completeness therefore give the asserted $b$-Parseval identity and convergence of the spectral projections in $V$.

Here is the boundary induction for higher orders. Suppose $f\in H^k$ and $v\in H^{k+1}$ is already known. In a flattened boundary chart apply a tangential derivative $D_{x'}^\alpha$, $|\alpha|=k$, to the localized equation. Its commutator with the second-order operator contains derivatives of $v$ of order at most $k+1$ with bounded smooth coefficients. The localized $D_{x'}^\alpha v$ has zero trace and lies in $H^1$; this follows first for tangential difference quotients, which preserve zero trace, and then by their $H^1$ limit. The $k=0$ local estimate of step 2.2 gives its $H^2$ bound in terms of $\|f\|_{H^k}+\|v\|_{H^{k+1}}$. If a derivative has total order $k+2$ and at least three normal factors, differentiate the equation $k$ times, isolating the term $\rho g^{nn}D_n^2v$. Divide by the positive coefficient $\rho g^{nn}$. Each other highest-order derivative has fewer normal factors because its two principal derivatives include a tangential derivative; all commutators have order at most $k+1$. Induction on the number of normal factors therefore bounds every derivative of order $k+2$. Interior patches allow derivatives in all directions. Difference quotients justify each differentiation before regularity is established; the bounds are uniform in their increments, and testing their weak limits identifies the claimed derivatives. Nested cutoffs and the finite cover give $\|v\|_{H^{k+2}}\le C_k(\|f\|_{H^k}+\|v\|_{H^{k+1}})$, and the previous induction level absorbs the last term into $C_k(\|f\|_{H^k}+\|v\|_2)$. This proves all asserted elliptic estimates.

For completeness the needed high-order embedding also has a finite-chart proof with this axiom base. In a half-chart extend across $x_n=0$ by $\sum_{j=1}^{k+1}a_jv(x',-jx_n)$ for $x_n<0$, where the finite Vandermonde system $\sum_j a_j(-j)^\ell=1$ for $0\le\ell\le k$ matches the derivatives at the interface. After a cutoff this is a bounded $H^k$ extension; the assertion follows first on smooth functions and then by the weak derivative identities and approximation. On a bounded support box, iterated one-dimensional integration gives $\|D^\alpha w\|_\infty\le C\|D_1\cdots D_nD^\alpha w\|_2$ for smooth compactly supported $w$. Apply this also to first derivatives of $D^\alpha w$ and to differences of mollifications. For $k\ge n+a+1$ these mollifications and all derivatives through order $a$ are uniformly Cauchy and their limits are continuous, with the asserted norm bound; passing to the coordinate segment integral identifies them as classical derivatives. Sum the finite chart extensions. This proves the embedding and completes the lemma.
