Assume Countable Choice. Let $(M,g)$ be a nonempty compact smooth Riemannian manifold of positive dimension with smooth boundary and $q$ a smooth real function. Set $H=L^2(M,dV_g)$, $V=H^1_0(M)$ and $c=1+\|q\|_\infty$. Then
$$b(u,v)=\int_M(\langle\nabla u,\nabla\bar v\rangle+(q+c)u\bar v)\,dV_g$$
is an equivalent Hilbert inner product on $V$. There are an $H$-orthonormal sequence $(e_j)$ complete in $H$ and positive numbers $\mu_j\to\infty$ such that $b(e_j,v)=\mu_j(e_j,v)_H$ for every $v\in V$, and
$$b(u,u)=\sum_j\mu_j|(u,e_j)_H|^2\qquad(u\in V).$$
For $A=-\Delta_g+q$, weak solutions $v\in V$ of $Av=f\in H^k(M)$ satisfy
$$\|v\|_{H^{k+2}(M)}\le C_k(\|f\|_{H^k(M)}+\|v\|_{L^2(M)}),\qquad k=0,1,\ldots.$$
Here integer Sobolev norms use any finite smooth atlas. For every integer $a$, the inclusion $H^k(M)\to C^a(M)$ is bounded for all sufficiently large integers $k$.

Let $(M,g)$ be a compact, nonempty smooth Riemannian manifold with smooth boundary, let $T>0$, set $Q=(0,T)	imes M$ and $\Sigma=(0,T)	imes\partial M$, and let $
u_{\mathrm{out}}$ be the outward unit normal. Write $
abla_g u$ for the metric gradient, $\Delta_g u=\operatorname{div}_g
abla_g u$, $dV_g$ for Riemannian volume, and $dS_g$ for the induced boundary measure. The $C^1$ norms below are computed in any fixed finite smooth atlas of the indicated compact sets. For $u,v\in C^2([0,T]	imes M)$,
$$\int_Q ig((\partial_t^2-\Delta_g)u\,v-u(\partial_t^2-\Delta_g)v ig)\,dV_gdt =\int_\Sigma ig(u\,\partial_{
u_{\mathrm{out}}}v-v\,\partial_{
u_{\mathrm{out}}}u ig)\,dS_gdt +\int_M[\partial_tu\,v-u\,\partial_tv]_{t=0}^{t=T}\,dV_g.$$
For every $h\in C_c^\infty(\Sigma)$ there is a smooth lift $H$ on $[0,T]	imes M$ with $H|_\Sigma=h$, supported in a fixed boundary collar and zero near $t=0,T$, such that $\|H\|_{C^1([0,T]	imes M)}\le C\|h\|_{C^1(\Sigma)}$. For every $u\in C^1([0,T]	imes M)$ the classical normal trace obeys
$$\|\partial_{
u_{\mathrm{out}}}u\|_{L^2(\Sigma)}\le  ig(T\,\operatorname{area}_g(\partial M) ig)^{1/2}\|
abla_g u\|_{C^0([0,T]	imes M)}.$$

derivations.claim: Set $c=1+\|q\|_\infty$, $a(u,v)=b(u,v)-c(u,v)_{L^2}$, and let $P_J$ be projection on $e_1,\ldots,e_J$. Solve the scalar equations $d_j''+(\mu_j-c)d_j=(F,e_j)$ with the projected initial data, and put $u_J=\sum_{j\le J}d_je_j$. The scalar solutions exist for $L^1$ forcing by integration against the sine/hyperbolic-sine fundamental solution (at zero frequency use $t$); they have continuous first derivatives and absolutely continuous first derivatives on compact intervals. For $E_J=(\|u_J'\|_2^2+b(u_J,u_J))/2$, multiply each equation by $\bar d_j'$ and take real parts to obtain $$E_J'=\operatorname{Re}(P_JF+cu_J,u_J')\le C E_J+\sqrt{2E_J}\|F\|_2.$$ Apply this to $\sqrt{E_J+\eta}$ and let $\eta\downarrow0$ after integrating: multiplication by $e^{-Ct}$ gives $\sqrt{E_J(t)}\le C_T(\sqrt{E_J(0)}+\int_0^T\|F\|_2dt)$. This is exactly the asserted estimate, uniformly in $J$.

For $J>K$, the same estimate for $u_J-u_K$ has data $(P_J-P_K)u_0,(P_J-P_K)u_1$ and forcing $(P_J-P_K)F$. These data tend to zero in $V\times H$ by [F1]. The forcing tends to zero in $L^1_tH$ because the projections converge pointwise in $H$ and are contractive, so dominated convergence applies. Hence $u_J$ is Cauchy in $C([0,T];V)$ and $u_J'$ in $C([0,T];H)$. Their limits $u,w$ satisfy $u(t)-u(s)=\int_s^t w(r)dr$, so $u\in C^1([0,T];H)$ with derivative $w$ and the exact strong initial traces. Pass to the limit in the integrated finite-dimensional equation first for a finite spectral test and then for every $\phi\in V$, using boundedness of $a$ and the form-density in [F1]. This gives precisely the displayed weak equation and energy bound. No weak-in-time limiting trace is substituted for a strong trace.

If two energy solutions have the same data and forcing, test their difference against $e_j$. The scalar coefficient is a distributional solution of $d_j''+(\mu_j-c)d_j=0$ with zero strong data. Its integral equation, or the scalar fundamental solution, gives $d_j=0$. Completeness in [F1] makes the difference zero for every time. The estimate of step 1.1 passes to the strong limit, including its zero-data version. Replacing $t$ by $T-t$ proves terminal well-posedness with the same bound.

We also establish the classical regularity needed by the last assertion and the DN interfaces. Let $h$ be smooth and zero near the temporal endpoints, take the smooth lift $H$ from [F2], and solve for $w=u-H$ with zero Dirichlet and initial data and forcing $G=-L_qH$. This $G$ is smooth and zero near $t=0$. For every integer $\ell\ge0$, solve the same zero-data energy problem with forcing $\partial_t^\ell G$. Integration in time and uniqueness in step 3.1 identify these solutions successively with $\partial_t^\ell w$: for example integrating the solution with forcing $G_t$ gives a solution with forcing $G-G(0)=G$ and zero data. Thus all time derivatives of $w$ are continuous in $V$. At every time, $Aw=G-w_{tt}$; the right side is continuous in $L^2$, so [F1]'s elliptic estimate gives continuity of $w$ in $H^2$, by applying the estimate to time differences. Apply this argument to every time derivative. Inductively if all time derivatives are continuous in $H^k$, the identity $A\partial_t^\ell w=\partial_t^\ell G-\partial_t^{\ell+2}w$ and [F1] give continuity in $H^{k+2}$. Thus all mixed derivatives have arbitrarily high spatial Sobolev regularity, and [F1]'s embedding gives a smooth representative on the closed cylinder, in particular $C^2$. Adding $H$ proves the stated smooth boundary reduction and actual classical forward solvability; time reversal gives the terminal version.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $n\ge2$ and let $(M,g)$ be a compact, connected, nonempty smooth $n$-dimensional Riemannian manifold with smooth boundary. Let $\nu_{\mathrm{out}}$ be the outward unit normal and let $\nabla$ be the Levi–Civita connection of $g$. The boundary is **strictly convex** when
$$
g(\nabla_w\nu_{\mathrm{out}},w)>0
$$
for every boundary point and every nonzero boundary-tangent vector $w$. Use the curvature convention
$$
R(X,Y)Z=\nabla_X\nabla_YZ-\nabla_Y\nabla_XZ-\nabla_{[X,Y]}Z.
$$
A Jacobi field along a unit-speed geodesic $\gamma$ is a smooth vector field $J$ satisfying $D_t^2J+R(J,\dot\gamma)\dot\gamma=0$, where $D_tJ=\nabla_{\dot\gamma}J$. The manifold has **no conjugate points** if every positive-length unit-speed geodesic segment $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ has no nonzero Jacobi field with $J(a)=J(b)=0$. It is **nontrapping** if every maximal unit-speed geodesic starting in $M^\circ$ reaches $\partial M$ in finite forward and backward time. The pair $(M,g)$ is a **simple Riemannian background** if its boundary is strictly convex, it has no conjugate points, and it is nontrapping.

When $n=2$, this is the simple-surface convention used for the scalar geodesic X-ray transform on the required inverse-problems page.
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every smooth manifold with boundary has a smooth collar.
Every smooth function or tensor field on a manifold with boundary extends smoothly across each boundary point to some neighbourhood in its double; the extension is not canonical.
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every open cover of a smooth manifold with boundary admits a smooth partition of unity subordinate to it.

For a supplied Riemannian metric $g$, a **Levi–Civita connection** is an affine connection on $TM$ that is both metric compatible and torsion free, in the senses of [[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]], [[def-metric-compatible-connection-on-a-riemannian-vector-bundle]] and [[def-torsion-tensor-of-an-affine-connection]]. Thus for all local fields
$$Xg(Y,Z)=g(
abla_XY,Z)+g(Y,
abla_XZ),\qquad 
abla_XY-
abla_YX=[X,Y].$$
Existence and uniqueness are proved below from the supplied metric by the Koszul formula. This definition does not choose an arbitrary connection first and does not assume the general connection-existence theorem. In dimension zero the unique tangent-bundle connection satisfies both identities; in dimension one torsion freeness alone imposes no restriction, so metric compatibility remains essential.
Every supplied smooth Riemannian metric on a smooth manifold, including a manifold with boundary, has exactly one Levi–Civita connection. The construction adds no choice assumption.

Let $X$ be a smooth vector field on $M$ and let $p\in M$. Then there exist
$h>0$, an open neighbourhood $U$ of $p$, and a smooth map

$$ \Phi:(-h,h)\times U\to M $$

such that for every $q\in U$, the curve $t\mapsto \Phi(t,q)$ is the unique
integral curve of $X$ on $(-h,h)$ with initial value $\Phi(0,q)=q$.

On a connected Riemannian manifold define $d_g(p,q)=\inf\{L_g(\gamma):\gamma\text{ is piecewise }C^1\text{ from }p\text{ to }q\}$.

Lengths are those of [[def-riemannian-speed-and-length]]. For each pair $p,q$, [[lem-any-two-points-in-a-connected-smooth-manifold-can-be-joined-by-a-piecewise-c-one-curve]] supplies a curve, so the set of lengths is nonempty, contains a finite real number and is bounded below by zero. Applying the least-upper-bound property [[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]] to the negatives gives a finite nonnegative infimum. On the empty connected manifold this defines the empty distance function; there are no pairs to evaluate. No minimizing curve is part of this definition.

The **Riemannian speed** on a $C^1$ piece is $|\dot\gamma(t)|_g=\sqrt{g_{\gamma(t)}(\dot\gamma(t),\dot\gamma(t))}$. Its **length** is $L_g(\gamma)=\sum_j\int_{t_{j-1}}^{t_j}|\dot\gamma(t)|_g\,dt$.

The curve convention is [[def-piecewise-c-one-curve-on-a-manifold]] and the norm is [[def-pointwise-norm-and-angle-from-a-riemannian-metric]]. Each integrand is continuous on its closed piece with the one-sided endpoint derivative, hence Riemann integrable and nonnegative. Values chosen at the finitely many corners do not change its integral. For a singleton interval the empty sum is zero; a constant curve also has zero length. Partition independence is established by [[lem-riemannian-length-is-independent-of-piecewise-c-one-subdivision]].

The **pointwise norm** is $|v|_g=\sqrt{g(v,v)}$. For nonzero $v,w$ in the same tangent space, the **angle** is the unique $\theta\in[0,\pi]$ with $\cos\theta=g(v,w)/(|v|_g|w|_g)$.

Positive definiteness in [[def-riemannian-metric-and-riemannian-manifold]] makes both denominators positive. [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-for-real-and-complex-inner-product-spaces]] places the quotient in $[-1,1]$, on which the inverse of cosine restricted to $[0,\pi]$ is defined. Angles $0$ and $\pi$ are included. The norm of zero is zero; no angle is assigned when either vector is zero.

For a compact set $K$ contained in one coordinate chart of an $n$-dimensional Riemannian manifold, there are $0<c\le C<\infty$ such that $c|v|^2\le g_x(v,v)\le C|v|^2$ for $x\in K$. The dimension-zero assertion is vacuous.
$d_g$ is a finite metric on a connected Riemannian manifold.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $\mathcal{T}_d$ be
its metric topology ([[def-metric-topology]]), so that $(X, \mathcal{T}_d)$ is a
topological space ([[def-topological-space]]) and is metrizable
([[def-metrizable-space]]). Then:

1. $(X,d)$ is a compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]]) **if and only
   if** $(X, \mathcal{T}_d)$ is a compact topological space
   ([[def-compact-space]]).
2. For every $A \subseteq X$: $A$ is a compact subset of the metric space
   $(X,d)$ if and only if $A$ is a compact subset of the topological space
   $(X, \mathcal{T}_d)$, the two readings of "compact subset" being the metric
   subspace $(A, d_A)$ ([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]) and the topological
   subspace $(A, (\mathcal{T}_d)_A)$ ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]).

**Nothing here is a coincidence and nothing is transported.** The open-cover
condition of [[def-metric-compactness]] quantifies over families of subsets open
in $(X,d)$, and by [[def-metric-topology]] those are exactly the members of
$\mathcal{T}_d$; so the two conditions are not merely equivalent, they are the
same condition written twice. No choice principle is used.

Let $(X,d)$ be a compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]). Then $(X,d)$ is totally bounded
([[def-totally-bounded]]) and complete ([[def-complete-metric-space]]).

**Both implications are theorems of ZF.** Completeness is obtained here from the
finite intersection characterisation ([[thm-compact-iff-finite-intersection-property]])
applied to the closures of the tails of a Cauchy sequence, and not from the
extraction of a convergent subsequence, which would route the argument through
sequential compactness. What matters for the ledger is that the route taken below
selects nothing at all; the first remark below says why the other route was not
taken.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $(M,g)$ be a **nonempty**, connected,
boundaryless Riemannian manifold, and let $d=d_g$ be its Riemannian distance.
The following conditions are equivalent.

1. The metric space $(M,d)$ is complete.
2. The Riemannian manifold $(M,g)$ is geodesically complete.
3. For every $p\in M$, the fibre exponential domain is all of the tangent
   space: $\mathcal E_p=T_pM$.
4. There is a point $p_0\in M$ for which $\mathcal E_{p_0}=T_{p_0}M$.
5. Every closed bounded subset of the metric space $(M,d)$ is compact.

Whenever these conditions hold, every $x,y\in M$ are joined by a minimizing
geodesic. More exactly, there is $v\in T_xM$ with
$$
\exp_x(v)=y,\qquad |v|_{g_x}=d(x,y),
$$
and $t\mapsto\exp_x(tv)$ on $[0,1]$ has length $d(x,y)$.

The nonemptiness hypothesis is essential for this formulation: on the empty
manifold conditions 1--3 and 5 are vacuous, whereas condition 4 is false.

Let $a<b$. Suppose $G:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$. If $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is Riemann integrable and

$$f(x)=G'(x)\qquad(a<x<b),$$

then

$$\int_a^b f=G(b)-G(a).$$

No derivative of $G$ at either endpoint is assumed, and the two endpoint values assigned to the integrable extension $f$ do not enter the conclusion.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be
$C^1$, and let $a\in U$.  If $Df(a)$ is invertible, then there are open sets
$V,W\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $a\in V\subseteq U$ and $f(a)\in W$ such that
$f|_V:V\to W$ is bijective.  Its inverse $g:W\to V$ is $C^1$, and

$$Dg(y)=Df(g(y))^{-1}\qquad(y\in W).$$

Thus $f$ is a local diffeomorphism at $a$.

If $M$ has dimension $n\ge1$, the restrictions of boundary charts to their faces give $\partial M$ the structure of a closed embedded smooth boundaryless $(n-1)$-manifold. For $n=0$, $\partial M=\varnothing$.

For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]) and every family
$(X_k)_{k < n}$ of compact topological spaces ([[def-compact-space]],
[[def-topological-space]]), the product

$$\prod_{k < n} X_k$$

with the product topology ([[def-product-topology]]) is compact. In particular a
binary product $X \times Y$ of compact spaces is compact, and the empty product,
a one-point space, is compact.

**No choice principle is used beyond [[lem-finite-choice]]**, which is a theorem
of ZF. That is what separates the finite case from the arbitrary one, where the
Axiom of Choice is genuinely spent.

For vectors $u,v$ in a real or complex inner product space,

$$|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\lVert u\rVert\lVert v\rVert.$$

Equality holds if and only if $u$ and $v$ are linearly dependent, including the case in which either vector is zero.

derivations.claim: Use [F2] to attach the smooth cylinder $[0,\infty)\times\partial M$ to $M$ along its boundary. By [F3], the metric coefficients extend smoothly across each boundary point to the double. Compactness of $\partial M$ gives a finite such cover; [F4] patches these local extensions by a smooth partition of unity. After shrinking the collar, the patched tensor remains positive definite, since it agrees with $g$ on $M$ and positive definiteness is open. Solve the geodesic ODE for the extended metric from each boundary point in the outward unit-normal direction. At $(x,0)$ the derivative of $(x,s)\mapsto\exp_x(s\nu_{\mathrm{out}}(x))$ sends $(w,a)$ to $w+a\nu_{\mathrm{out}}(x)$, an isomorphism; [F15] therefore gives local inverse charts along the zero section. A finite subcover gives a common domain where this map is a local diffeomorphism. If no uniform collar width made it injective, there would be distinct pairs $(x_j,s_j)$ and $(y_j,t_j)$ with equal images and $0\le s_j,t_j\downarrow0$; compactness gives subsequences converging to $(x,0)$ and $(y,0)$, equality of the images forces $x=y$, and both pairs then lie in one local inverse chart at $(x,0)$, a contradiction. Thus a uniform outward normal collar exists.

In this normal collar, use $s$ for outward normal distance and write the extended metric as $ds^2+\widetilde h_s$, where $\widetilde h_s$ is a smooth family of metrics on $\partial M$. The Gauss-lemma orthogonality follows by differentiating $G(\partial_s,J)$ along a variation field $J$ of normal geodesics: $D_s\partial_s=0$, $[\partial_s,J]=0$, and metric compatibility give $\partial_sG(\partial_s,J)=\tfrac12J(G(\partial_s,\partial_s))=0$, while the initial value is zero. Also $G(\partial_s,\partial_s)=1$. For tangent fields $X,Y$ transported along this collar, metric compatibility and torsion freeness yield $\partial_s\widetilde h_s(X,Y)=G(\nabla_X\partial_s,Y)+G(X,\nabla_Y\partial_s)$; hence $\tfrac12\partial_s\widetilde h_s|_{s=0}$ is the second fundamental form for the outward normal. By [F1], $\partial_s\widetilde h_s$ is positive definite at $s=0$, and compactness makes it positive definite for $0\le s<2\varepsilon$ for some $\varepsilon>0$.

Choose smooth nonincreasing $\xi_1:[0,\infty)\to[0,1]$ with $\xi_1=1$ on $[0,\varepsilon]$ and $\xi_1=0$ on $[2\varepsilon,\infty)$, and set $\xi_2=1-\xi_1$. Since the family $\widetilde h_s/s$ is bounded relative to the positive metric $\widetilde h_0$ on the compact transition interval $[\varepsilon,2\varepsilon]\times\partial M$, choose $C>0$ large enough that $sk-\widetilde h_s$ is positive semidefinite there for $k=C\widetilde h_0$. Define $h_s=\xi_1(s)\widetilde h_s+s\xi_2(s)k$. This is positive definite: on $[0,\varepsilon]$ it equals $\widetilde h_s$, on $[2\varepsilon,\infty)$ it equals $sk$, and on the transition both terms are positive semidefinite with positive-definite sum.

Differentiate the definition to obtain $\partial_sh_s=\xi_1\partial_s\widetilde h_s+\xi_2k+\xi_2'(sk-\widetilde h_s)$. Each term is positive semidefinite on the transition interval, and at least one of the first two is positive definite at every point; outside the transition, $\partial_sh_s=\partial_s\widetilde h_s>0$ near $s=0$ and $\partial_sh_s=k>0$ for $s\ge2\varepsilon$. Thus $\partial_sh_s$ is positive definite for every $s\ge0$. Gluing $ds^2+h_s$ to $g$ gives a smooth Riemannian metric $G$ on the cylinder attachment, because $h_s=\widetilde h_s$ near $s=0$.

Let $p:N\to\mathbb R$ equal $s$ on the cylinder and be smooth and nonpositive on $M$, agreeing with the collar coordinate near $\partial M$; such an extension is obtained by a smooth one-variable cutoff on the compact interior side of the collar. The sublevel set $\{p\le R\}$ is closed by continuity of $p$ and contained in the union of compact $M$ and $[0,\max(R,0)]\times\partial M$, so it is compact by [F16, F17]. The differential of $p$ has bounded metric norm: it has norm $1$ on the cylinder and is bounded on compact $M$. If $C$ is such a bound, then on each $C^1$ piece of a path $\alpha$, [F18] and the chain rule give $|(p\circ\alpha)'|\le C|\dot\alpha|_G$; integrating by [F14] on each piece and summing gives $|p(\alpha(b))-p(\alpha(a))|\le C L_G(\alpha)$. Taking the infimum over paths in [F7] shows that $p$ is $C$-Lipschitz for $d_G$. Hence every $d_G$-Cauchy sequence has bounded $p$ and lies in one compact sublevel set. The metric topology agrees locally with the manifold topology by [F9]: the upper coordinate bound makes nearby coordinate points close in $d_G$, and the lower bound on a smaller chart ball makes any path leaving that ball have a fixed positive length. Thus the sublevel is compact as a metric subspace by [F11], and complete by [F12]. Every Cauchy sequence in $N$ therefore converges in $N$, so $(N,G)$ is complete.

The manifold $N$ is connected, nonempty, and boundaryless, so [F13] extends every geodesic from its initial data to all $t\in\mathbb R$. Let $\gamma$ start at $\partial M$ with unit outward or tangent velocity, and put $r(t)=s(\gamma(t))$ while it is in the exterior. From $G=ds^2+h_s$, the Levi–Civita formula gives $\operatorname{Hess}_G s(\dot\gamma,\dot\gamma)=\tfrac12(\partial_sh_s)(\dot\gamma_T,\dot\gamma_T)\ge0$, where $\dot\gamma_T$ is the component tangent to the level set $\{s=\mathrm{constant}\}$. Thus $r''(t)\ge0$. If $r'(0)>0$, then $r'(t)\ge r'(0)$ and $r(t)>0$ grows without bound. If $r'(0)=0$, then $\dot\gamma(0)$ is a nonzero boundary-tangent vector and strict convexity gives $r''(0)>0$; continuity makes $r'(t)>0$ for some sufficiently small $t>0$, after which the same convexity estimate keeps $r'$ positive and $r(t)\to\infty$. In either case the geodesic never returns to $M$ and eventually leaves every compact subset of $N$.

citations.quote: Let $X$ be a smooth manifold with an auxiliary smooth Riemannian metric, let $J=[a,b]$ be a compact interval, and let $\beta:J\to X$ be a smooth embedding with nonzero derivative. The normal fiber at $s$ is $N_s\beta=\{v\in T_{\beta(s)}X:g(v,\dot\beta(s))=0\}$. A **formal scalar jet along $\beta$** means a family of symmetric coordinate Taylor coefficients $T_{i,\alpha}(s)$ on a finite coordinate cover of a tubular neighborhood, smooth in $s\in J$, whose formal Taylor series transform on overlaps by the ordinary chain rule for a scalar function. Then there is an open neighborhood $U$ of $\beta(J)$ and, for either scalar field $\mathbb K=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, an $F\in C^\infty(U;\mathbb K)$ whose transverse derivatives along $\beta$ realize every prescribed transverse coefficient $T_{i,\alpha}(s)$. The construction is uniform for a compact parameter family of such jets when all coefficient seminorms are uniformly bounded. The same assertion holds on a finite union $A$ of embedded compact segments provided the induced full ambient jets satisfy full Whitney compatibility on that compact union: in each coordinate chart, for every $k$ and $|\alpha|\le k$, the degree-$k$ Taylor polynomials $P_x^k$ satisfy $D^\alpha P_x^k(y)-D^\alpha P_y^k(y)=o(|x-y|^{k-|\alpha|})$ uniformly for $x,y\in A$ as $|x-y|\to0$. Tangential components of a full jet are obtained by differentiating the transverse coefficients along each segment and applying the coordinate chain rule. For parameter families on the same finite union, require these Whitney remainder moduli as well as all coefficient bounds to be uniform. The single-segment construction requires no choice axiom.

Let $X$ be a smooth vector field on $M$ and let $p\in M$. Then there exist
$h>0$, an open neighbourhood $U$ of $p$, and a smooth map

$$ \Phi:(-h,h)\times U\to M $$

such that for every $q\in U$, the curve $t\mapsto \Phi(t,q)$ is the unique
integral curve of $X$ on $(-h,h)$ with initial value $\Phi(0,q)=q$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(M,g)$ be a compact, connected, nonempty smooth Riemannian manifold with nonempty smooth boundary, let $T>0$, and let $q\in C^\infty(M;\mathbb R)$ be independent of time. Let $dV_g$ be Riemannian volume and $L^2(M)=L^2(M,dV_g)$. A weak coordinate derivative $D_iw$ is defined by $\int w\,\partial_i\psi=-\int D_iw\,\psi$ for every smooth compactly supported coordinate test $\psi$. Let $H^1(M)$ be the space of $L^2$ functions whose weak coordinate first derivatives are locally $L^2$ in smooth charts and whose weak differential has finite metric $L^2$ norm; write $\nabla_gu$ for the metric dual of that weak differential. Give it norm
$$\|w\|_{H^1(M)}^2=\int_M(|w|^2+|\nabla_gw|_g^2)\,dV_g,$$
and let $H_0^1(M)$ be the closure of $C_c^\infty(M^\circ)$ in this norm. For $u_0\in H_0^1(M)$, $u_1\in L^2(M)$, and $F\in L^1((0,T);L^2(M))$, there is a unique energy solution of the homogeneous Dirichlet problem
$$u_{tt}-\Delta_gu+q(x)u=F,\qquad u|_{(0,T)\times\partial M}=0,\qquad (u(0),u_t(0))=(u_0,u_1),$$
where energy solution means
$$u\in C([0,T];H_0^1(M))\cap C^1([0,T];L^2(M)),$$

derivations.claim: Cover the parameter interval by finitely many small overlapping intervals on which the immersed base curve is embedded. In such an interval choose coordinates $(s,y)$ with the curve $y=0$ and with $s$ its prescribed parameter. The central covector satisfies $p=0$ and $p_{\xi_s}\ne0$, since the Hamilton velocity in these coordinates is a nonzero multiple of $\partial_s$. The formal implicit equation $p(s,y,\partial_s\phi,\partial_y\phi)=0$ can thus be solved recursively for the jets of $\partial_s\phi$. This is an evolution eikonal equation in $s$, with a smooth real reduced Hamiltonian in the real variables. Its zeroth and first jet equations are exactly the given Hamilton curve (after its parameter change). Initialize the transverse Hessian by $H(0)=iI$ in the chosen transverse coordinates.

The quadratic jet equation is the matrix Riccati equation $$H'+D+BH+HB^T+HCH=0,$$ where $C,D$ are real symmetric and $B$ real, the corresponding blocks of the reduced Hamiltonian Hessian. Solve instead $Y'=B^TY+CZ$, $Z'=-DY-BZ$, $Y(0)=I$, $Z(0)=iI$. Direct differentiation gives $Y^TZ-Z^TY=0$ and $Y^*Z-Z^*Y=2iI$. If $Yv=0$ the second identity gives $0=2i|v|^2$, so $Y$ is invertible on the whole interval. Consequently $H=ZY^{-1}$ is symmetric, solves the Riccati equation, and $$\operatorname{Im}H=(Y^{-1})^*Y^{-1}>0.$$ Compactness gives uniform positive lower and finite upper bounds. At an overlap transform all jets by the coordinate chain rule, carry these initial data to the next chart, and use ODE uniqueness. Positivity is unchanged by real coordinate change and persists on the finite cover.

For transverse degree $k\ge3$, differentiating the reduced eikonal equation $k$ times gives a finite linear ODE for the degree-$k$ phase jet: its highest jet enters linearly, with coefficients determined by the Hessian and the first derivatives of the reduced Hamiltonian; the inhomogeneous terms involve only lower jets and derivatives of the symbol. This follows by the product rule: terms containing a highest derivative of $\phi$ can have only one such factor, and the degree-$k+1$ derivative cancels against differentiation along the central Hamilton curve. Thus solve successively for every degree using [F2], matching all jets on overlaps. Apply [F1], or its explicit shrinking-cutoff series, to realize them. This yields a smooth phase with eikonal defect flat on each branch and $\operatorname{Im}\phi\ge c|y|^2$ after shrinking the transverse tube.

Define $T_\phi$ to be the coefficient of $h^{-1}$ in the exact conjugation identity $$P(e^{i\phi/h}a)=e^{i\phi/h}(h^{-2}p(x,d\phi)a+h^{-1}T_\phi a+Pa).$$ It is a first-order operator with derivative part $p_\xi(x,d\phi)\cdot D$, so its coefficient of $\partial_s$ on the ray is nonzero. Solve $T_\phi a_0=0$ and $T_\phi a_j=-Pa_{j-1}$ for $j\ge1$ to infinite transverse order. The central $a_0$ equation is a scalar homogeneous ODE with nonzero initial value, hence has nonvanishing exponential solution. For each successive transverse degree and amplitude index the differentiated equations are linear ODEs with already known right sides, by the same cancellation of derivatives along the curve as in step 3.1. Realize these jets by [F1]. The separate asymptotic series $a(x;h)\sim\sum_{j\ge0}h^ja_j(x)$ is realized by $\sum_jh^ja_j(x)\eta(h/\delta_j)$, with $\eta=1$ near zero and $\delta_j\downarrow0$ chosen so its $C^k$ tails are summable for every fixed $k$ and have the required $h$ asymptotic bounds. Explicitly, for each $j$ make $\delta_j<2^{-j}$ and $\delta_j^{j/2}(1+\|a_j\|_{C^j})<2^{-j}$; for fixed $k,J$, terms $j\ge\max(k,2J+2)$ are then $O(h^J)$ in $C^k$. Only finitely many earlier terms remain. This proves the full transport and Borel realization.

On an embedded branch take $u_h=h^{-d/4}e^{i\phi/h}a(x;h)$ and a fixed transverse cutoff. For a flat defect $r$, Taylor's formula gives $|D^\alpha r|\le C_{k,\alpha}|y|^k$ for every $k$. Scaling $y=\sqrt h z$ and using $\operatorname{Im}\phi\ge c|y|^2$ shows $$\|h^{-d/4}|y|^ke^{-c|y|^2/h}\|_{L^2}\le C_kh^{k/2}.$$ Every application of $P$ loses at most two powers of $h$. Choose $k$ and the amplitude order large enough to dominate that loss and any requested $N$. Derivatives of the transverse cutoff are supported at fixed positive distance from the ray and are $O(h^\infty)$ by Gaussian decay. Thus the residual is $O(h^N)$ away from longitudinal endpoint cutoffs; at endpoints the commutator with a longitudinal cutoff remains, and no vanishing assertion is made there. This also proves uniform $L^2$ boundedness on each branch.

To patch, use the compatible phase and amplitude jets constructed above and a finite partition in the curve parameter. On the overlap of adjacent descriptions, their phases and amplitudes differ by flat terms, so after multiplication by $h^{-d/4}e^{i\phi/h}$ their difference and any fixed number of derivatives are $O(h^N)$ for every $N$, by step 5.1. Derivatives of the partition cancel because its sum is one on each branch; their remaining flat differences have the same bound. Nonadjacent branches meeting at a projected crossing have distinct covectors: otherwise the phase-space curve would repeat a point. Compactness separates those covectors uniformly off a small neighborhood of the parameter diagonal. Mixed products therefore tend to zero: integrate by parts against the nonzero difference of the two real phase gradients, shrinking crossing neighborhoods so it remains bounded below. Each integration gains $h$, while each transverse Gaussian derivative loses at most $h^{-1/2}$ in its integral bounds; arbitrarily many integrations give arbitrary decay. Away from crossings ordinary Gaussian decay applies. Thus patching preserves the residual, positivity, and the sum of the branch mass limits, including at projected self-intersections.

Write the density in a branch as $\rho(s,y)|dsdy|$. Gaussian scaling and dominated convergence give $$|u_h|^2dV_X\ \longrightarrow\ w(s)ds,\qquad w(s)=\frac{\pi^{d/2}|a_0(s,0)|^2\rho(s,0)}{\sqrt{\det\operatorname{Im}H(s)}}.$$ This positive smooth function is fixed by the leading transport equation; choose the initial scalar amplitude to make $w(0)=1$. Coordinate changes preserve this expression as a density, and step 6.1 removes mixed terms. For a formally self-adjoint operator the leading transport equation and the Riccati determinant identity give $(p_{\xi_s}w)'=0$: this follows by multiplying $T_\phi a_0=0$ by $\bar a_0$, subtracting its conjugate, and using $\rho^{-1}\partial_j(\rho p_{\xi_j})$ for the real divergence term. For the real wave operator in physical-time coordinates the normalized central covector has $|\xi_t|=1$, hence $|p_{\xi_t}|=2$ is constant; its mass density is therefore constant and the chosen normalization gives $w=1$. Arbitrary complex lower-order terms instead enter the scalar amplitude ODE, giving precisely the transported weight above.

If the endpoint cutoff regions lie outside the measurement cylinder, step 5.1 gives $\|Pu_h\|_{L^2(Q)}=O(h^N)$ for every $N$. In the wave case assume also the approximate beam vanishes near the initial slice for a forward correction or terminal slice for a backward correction. Apply [F3] to $-Pu_h$ with zero boundary and the corresponding zero endpoint data. Its energy norm is $O(h^N)$, since $\|Pu_h\|_{L^1_tL^2_x}\le\sqrt T\|Pu_h\|_{L^2(Q)}$. Adding this correction gives an exact solution with the actual approximate boundary data and the same normalized wave ray limit; the product error is bounded by Cauchy–Schwarz and uniform $L^2$ bounds. This proves every claimed localization and correction assertion.

Let $n\ge2$ and let $(M,g)$ be a compact, connected, nonempty smooth $n$-dimensional Riemannian manifold with smooth boundary. Let $\nu_{\mathrm{out}}$ be the outward unit normal and let $\nabla$ be the Levi–Civita connection of $g$. The boundary is **strictly convex** when
$$
g(\nabla_w\nu_{\mathrm{out}},w)>0
$$
for every boundary point and every nonzero boundary-tangent vector $w$. Use the curvature convention
$$
R(X,Y)Z=\nabla_X\nabla_YZ-\nabla_Y\nabla_XZ-\nabla_{[X,Y]}Z.
$$
A Jacobi field along a unit-speed geodesic $\gamma$ is a smooth vector field $J$ satisfying $D_t^2J+R(J,\dot\gamma)\dot\gamma=0$, where $D_tJ=\nabla_{\dot\gamma}J$. The manifold has **no conjugate points** if every positive-length unit-speed geodesic segment $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ has no nonzero Jacobi field with $J(a)=J(b)=0$. It is **nontrapping** if every maximal unit-speed geodesic starting in $M^\circ$ reaches $\partial M$ in finite forward and backward time. The pair $(M,g)$ is a **simple Riemannian background** if its boundary is strictly convex, it has no conjugate points, and it is nontrapping.

When $n=2$, this is the simple-surface convention used for the scalar geodesic X-ray transform on the required inverse-problems page.

The following conditions are equivalent.

and let $\gamma:I\to M$ be an affinely parametrized geodesic. For a smooth
vector field $J$ along $\gamma$, write $D_tJ$ for its covariant derivative
along $\gamma$ and $D_t^2J=D_t(D_tJ)$, using
[[def-covariant-derivative-along-a-curve]]. The curvature operator $R$ has the
convention
$$R(X,Y)Z=\nabla_X\nabla_YZ-\nabla_Y\nabla_XZ-\nabla_{[X,Y]}Z,$$
as fixed by [[lem-covariant-derivatives-commute-up-to-curvature-in-a-two-parameter-variation]]
and used in [[def-riemann-curvature-four-tensor]]. A smooth field $J$ is a

$$D_t^2J+R(J,\dot\gamma)\dot\gamma=0$$
throughout $I$. We write $\mathcal J(\gamma)$ for the set of these fields.

The interval is required to have nonempty interior so that the covariant
derivatives are defined; if an endpoint is included, the equation there uses
the one-sided derivatives of the smooth field. Constant geodesics are included:
when $\dot\gamma=0$, the curvature term vanishes and the equation is

equation holds. In dimension one the same equation and curvature convention
apply without a separate restriction. The definition classifies a specified
field and geodesic and makes no existence choice.

derivations.claim: Choose a smooth boundary defining function $\rho$ positive inside. At a tangent unit vector $\omega$ at $x_0$, strict convexity says $(\rho\circ\gamma_\omega)''(0)<0$. Compactness of the tangent sphere makes this bound uniform near tangency. For a nearby inward direction, put $a=d\rho_{x_0}(\omega)>0$. Taylor's formula factors the boundary equation as $\rho(\gamma_\omega(s))=s(a+sB(\omega,s))$, with $B<0$ uniformly near tangency. The implicit function theorem gives the first positive exit $\tau(\omega)$ there, with $\tau/a$ extending continuously and positively to tangent directions. Every other exit is transverse: a first exit with zero normal derivative would have $\rho=0$, $\rho'=0$, $\rho''<0$, forcing $\rho<0$ immediately before the exit. Thus all inward exits vary smoothly, and $\tau\to0$ at the equator.

These exit times are uniformly bounded. Otherwise take inward unit directions $\omega_j$ and increasing lengths tending to infinity with no exit before those lengths. Compactness gives a limiting direction. Step 1.1 excludes a tangent limit. Smooth dependence then gives an inward geodesic remaining in $M$ for every positive time, contrary to nontrapping. Define $$B_{x_0}=\{s\omega:\omega\text{ inward unit},\ 0\le s\le\tau(\omega)\},$$ including $0$ and tangent endpoints only as $0$. It is compact. Identify the inward normal with the last Euclidean coordinate and compare this radial set with the closed ball of radius one centred at the inward normal, whose radial length is $2\omega_n$ on the inward hemisphere. The radial map multiplies by $\tau(\omega)/(2\omega_n)$. Step 1.1 makes this ratio extend positively and continuously to the equator, so the radial map and its inverse are continuous also at zero. Hence $B_{x_0}$ is homeomorphic to a closed $n$-ball.

In the complete exterior of [F2], the exponential map $E(v)=\exp_{x_0}(v)$ is smooth on a neighborhood of $B_{x_0}$. Its differential is nonsingular for $v\ne0$ in that set: a kernel vector produces a Jacobi field vanishing at the two endpoints, excluded by [F1]; its radial component cannot be in the kernel since the geodesic has unit speed. At $0$ the differential is the identity. On the radial boundary $s=\tau(\omega)>0$, transversality from step 1.1 identifies $B_{x_0}$ locally with the inverse image of $M$ under this inverse chart, so the restricted map is a local homeomorphism of manifolds with boundary. The same is true at $0$: in a small normal neighborhood the inverse image of $M$ is precisely the short inward radial segments; tangent and outward rays immediately leave by strict convexity, and inward directions with very small exit time have already left. The exterior no-return property excludes extra portions of a ray in this local description. Thus $E:B_{x_0}\to M$ is a local homeomorphism everywhere.

Apply [F3] to this compact radial ball. It is a finite covering of $M$, and its simply connected total space makes it regular. If a fibre had two points, transitivity would supply a nonidentity deck transformation of $B_{x_0}$. Conjugate it by the ball homeomorphism of step 2.1. By [F4] it has a fixed point, and by uniqueness of lifts in [F3] a deck transformation with a fixed point is the identity, a contradiction. Every fibre therefore has one point. Interior inverse charts show that $E$ restricted to $\mathcal D_{x_0}$ is a smooth diffeomorphism onto $M^\circ$. This proves global injectivity without a path-space Morse theorem.

A minimizing exterior geodesic from $x_0$ to $y\in M^\circ$ exists by [F5]. It cannot leave $M$ and return, by [F2]; it must start inward, since an outward or tangent launch never enters $M$. It is therefore one of the radial segments just shown unique. Its length equals exterior distance and, being contained in $M$, equals intrinsic distance as well. To compute the metric in polar coordinates, vary the unit initial direction. The resulting Jacobi field $J$ has $J(0)=0$ and $g(D_sJ(0),\dot\gamma(0))=0$. Metric compatibility and the Jacobi equation give $(g(D_sJ,\dot\gamma))'=0$, and hence $(g(J,\dot\gamma))'=0$ with zero initial value. Thus the radial vector has unit length and is orthogonal to every angular vector. Consequently $r_{x_0}=s$ is smooth in the interior and $|\nabla r_{x_0}|_g=1$. Completeness and no return are exactly [F2].

A Jacobi field along a unit-speed geodesic $\gamma$ is a smooth vector field $J$ satisfying $D_t^2J+R(J,\dot\gamma)\dot\gamma=0$, where $D_tJ=\nabla_{\dot\gamma}J$. The manifold has **no conjugate points** if every positive-length unit-speed geodesic segment $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ has no nonzero Jacobi field with $J(a)=J(b)=0$. It is **nontrapping** if every maximal unit-speed geodesic starting in $M^\circ$ reaches $\partial M$ in finite forward and backward time. The pair $(M,g)$ is a **simple Riemannian background** if its boundary is strictly convex, it has no conjugate points, and it is nontrapping.

When $n=2$, this is the simple-surface convention used for the scalar geodesic X-ray transform on the required inverse-problems page.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(M,g)$ be a compact, connected, nonempty smooth Riemannian manifold with nonempty smooth boundary, let $T>0$, and let $q\in C^\infty(M;\mathbb R)$ be independent of time. Let $dV_g$ be Riemannian volume and $L^2(M)=L^2(M,dV_g)$. A weak coordinate derivative $D_iw$ is defined by $\int w\,\partial_i\psi=-\int D_iw\,\psi$ for every smooth compactly supported coordinate test $\psi$. Let $H^1(M)$ be the space of $L^2$ functions whose weak coordinate first derivatives are locally $L^2$ in smooth charts and whose weak differential has finite metric $L^2$ norm; write $\nabla_gu$ for the metric dual of that weak differential. Give it norm
$$\|w\|_{H^1(M)}^2=\int_M(|w|^2+|\nabla_gw|_g^2)\,dV_g,$$
and let $H_0^1(M)$ be the closure of $C_c^\infty(M^\circ)$ in this norm. For $u_0\in H_0^1(M)$, $u_1\in L^2(M)$, and $F\in L^1((0,T);L^2(M))$, there is a unique energy solution of the homogeneous Dirichlet problem
$$u_{tt}-\Delta_gu+q(x)u=F,\qquad u|_{(0,T)\times\partial M}=0,\qquad (u(0),u_t(0))=(u_0,u_1),$$
where energy solution means
$$u\in C([0,T];H_0^1(M))\cap C^1([0,T];L^2(M)),$$
and, for every $\phi\in H_0^1(M)$ and every $\zeta\in C_c^\infty(0,T)$, the weak equation is
$$\int_0^T(u(t),\phi)_{L^2}\zeta''(t)\,dt+\int_0^T\!\int_M\big(\langle\nabla_gu(t),\nabla_g\phi\rangle_g+q\,u(t)\phi\big)\zeta(t)\,dV_gdt=\int_0^T(F(t),\phi)_{L^2}\zeta(t)\,dt.$$
There is a constant $C=C(M,g,q,T)<\infty$ such that
$$\sup_{0\le t\le T}\big(\|u(t)\|_{H^1(M)}+\|u_t(t)\|_{L^2(M)}\big)\le C\big(\|u_0\|_{H^1(M)}+\|u_1\|_{L^2(M)}+\|F\|_{L^1((0,T);L^2(M))}\big).$$
In particular, the solution $w$ with zero initial data satisfies the correction estimate
$$\sup_{0\le t\le T}\big(\|w(t)\|_{H^1(M)}+\|w_t(t)\|_{L^2(M)}\big)\le C\|F\|_{L^1((0,T);L^2(M))}.$$
The corresponding assertion for prescribed terminal data follows by time reversal. For smooth Dirichlet data compactly supported away from the time endpoints, the boundary lifting in the Riemannian Green-and-lifting lemma reduces the problem to this homogeneous-boundary assertion.

derivations.claim: Extend the central geodesic a distance $\delta>0$ through both boundary endpoints in the no-return extension used by [F1], and take the polar centre $p=\gamma(-\delta)$ outside $M$. Choose $\delta<t_0/4$ and $\delta<(T-t_0-L)/4$. The polar differential based at $p$ is nonsingular along this extended ray for sufficiently small $\delta$: on a short initial segment this follows from the identity differential at the origin, and on the remaining compact segment it follows by continuous dependence of the Jacobi matrix and the nonsingularity in [F1] as $\delta\downarrow0$. It is injective on a sufficiently narrow ray tube as well. Otherwise a sequence of collisions in shrinking tubes has limits on the central ray; that ray is embedded by [F1], so its two limiting parameters agree and one local inverse chart excludes the collision. Thus there is a nonsingular polar tube containing the whole ray, with its two radial ends outside $M$. In the tube write $x=(r,\theta)$, $r=\delta+s$ along the ray, and $dV_g=m(r,\theta)drd\theta$. The Gauss orthogonality proved in [F1] gives $g=dr^2+g_{\alpha\beta}d\theta^\alpha d\theta^\beta$ and $\Delta_gr=m^{-1}\partial_rm$.

Put $\phi=t-r$, $z=t-r-(t_0-\delta)$, and $D=\partial_t+\partial_r$. Then $\phi_t^2-|\nabla\phi|^2=0$ and, for $L_q=\partial_t^2-\Delta_g+q$, direct differentiation gives $$L_q(e^{i\lambda\phi}a)=e^{i\lambda\phi}(i\lambda\mathcal T a+L_qa),\qquad \mathcal T=2D+\partial_r\log m.$$ The variable $z$ and the angle $\theta$ are constant along $D$, and $D(m^{1/2}a)=m^{1/2}\mathcal T a/2$. Consequently $$a_0=m^{-1/2}\chi_\lambda(\theta,z),\qquad a_{1,q}=\frac{i}{2}m^{-1/2}\int_{r_*}^{r}m(\sigma,\theta)^{1/2}(L_qa_0)(\sigma,\theta,z)\,d\sigma$$ solve $\mathcal T a_0=0$, $\mathcal T a_{1,q}=iL_qa_0$, where all functions in the integral are expressed in $(r,\theta,z)$ and $r_*$ is a fixed exterior radial start. Extend the smooth metric coefficients and the interior potentials over this slightly longer tube. Integration in $r$ preserves support in $(\theta,z)$. The same recursion $\mathcal T a_{j,q}=iL_qa_{j-1,q}$ supplies every higher requested finite order; two amplitude terms already suffice for the stated bound.

Choose the angular and $z$ supports sufficiently small. Transversality of the entry and exit makes the tube's part in $M$ lie between smooth nearby entry and exit radii; all these packets are zero on $M$ near $t=0,T$. Put a radial cutoff equal to one near the entire tube intersection with $M$ and supported with its radial derivatives outside $M$. Then $$v_{+,q}=e^{i\lambda\phi}(a_0+\lambda^{-1}a_{1,q}),\qquad L_qv_{+,q}=\lambda^{-1}e^{i\lambda\phi}L_qa_{1,q}\quad\text{on }Q.$$ On the fixed compact nonsingular tube, coefficient derivatives, integration lengths, and coordinate Jacobians are bounded independently of $\lambda$. The formula in step 2.1 and the chain rule therefore give $\|a_{1,q}\|_{C^k}\le C_k\|\chi_\lambda\|_{W^{k+2,\infty}}$ and $$\|L_qv_{+,q}\|_{L^1_tL^2_x}\le C\lambda^{-1}\|\chi_\lambda\|_{W^{4,\infty}}.$$ For the opposite phase use $v_{-,q}=\overline{v_{+,q}}$ (real $q$), obtaining the identical estimate. In particular the cutoff creates no residual inside the measurement domain.

Apply [F2] to $-L_{q_1}v_{+,q_1}$ with zero initial and boundary data, and to $-L_{q_2}v_{-,q_2}$ with zero terminal and boundary data. The smooth right sides vanish near the relevant time endpoints, so the regularity part of [F2] makes the corrections smooth. The resulting $u_1=v_{+,q_1}+R_1$ and $u_2=v_{-,q_2}+R_2$ are actual forward and terminal classical solutions, with smooth boundary traces compactly supported in time. The energy estimate gives $$\|R_j\|_{L^\infty_tH^1_x}+\|\partial_tR_j\|_{L^\infty_tL^2_x}\le C\lambda^{-1}\|\chi_\lambda\|_{W^{4,\infty}}.$$ Thus the remainder here is the correction to the complete two-term approximate solution, including its $\lambda^{-1}$ transport amplitude.

In local coordinates about $(\theta_0,0)$ let $\zeta\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb R)$ satisfy $\int\zeta^2dy=1$, choosing a cutoff Gaussian and dividing by its $L^2$ norm. Set $$\varepsilon=\lambda^{-1/(n+8)},\qquad \chi_\lambda(\theta,z)=\varepsilon^{-n/2}\zeta((\theta-\theta_0,z)/\varepsilon).$$ For bounded small $\lambda$ enlarge the constants and keep the support inside the tube; all asymptotic assertions concern sufficiently large $\lambda$. Then $\|\chi_\lambda\|_2=1$ and $\|\chi_\lambda\|_{W^{k,\infty}}\le C_k\varepsilon^{-n/2-k}$. For $k=4$ the exponent is exactly $\lambda^{1/2}$, so step 4.1 proves $\|R_j\|_{L^2(Q)}=O(\lambda^{-1/2})$. Also $\|a_0\|_{L^2(Q)}\le C$ since its squared metric density cancels $m$, and $$\|\lambda^{-1}a_{1,q}\|_2\le C\lambda^{-1}\varepsilon^{-n/2-2}=o(1).$$ This verifies every normalization and derivative loss used in the correction estimate.

For a smooth test $A$, the leading product is $a_0^2=m^{-1}\chi_\lambda^2$. Since $dt=dz$ at fixed $r$, $$\int_Q A a_0^2\,dV_gdt=\int \chi_\lambda(\theta,z)^2\left[\int_{r_-(\theta)}^{r_+(\theta)} A(r+t_0-\delta+z,x(r,\theta))\,dr\right]d\theta dz.$$ The nearby entry and exit radii are smooth by transversality. The bracket converges uniformly as $(\theta,z)\to(\theta_0,0)$ to $\int_0^L A(t_0+s,\gamma(s))ds$. The change of variables $(\theta-\theta_0,z)=\varepsilon y$ and $\int\zeta^2=1$ prove the required ray limit with coefficient exactly one. The terms containing a $\lambda^{-1}a_{1,q}$ vanish by the $L^2$ bounds in step 5.1 and Cauchy–Schwarz; the terms containing $R_j$ vanish by the same inequality and step 4.1. These arguments also apply to any smooth function on the closed cylinder, not only a compactly supported interior test, because all approximate packets are supported away from the temporal endpoints and the global correction errors have vanishing $L^2$ norm. Thus the exact forward/terminal product has the asserted normalized limit.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(M,g)$ be a compact, connected, nonempty smooth Riemannian manifold with smooth boundary, let $T>0$, and write $Q=(0,T)\times M$ and $\Sigma=(0,T)\times\partial M$. where $\nu_{out}$ is the outward unit normal. Also assume that for every $k\in\mathcal H$ the terminal-data Dirichlet problem $L_qv=0$, $v|_\Sigma=k$, $(v(T),v_t(T))=(0,0)$ has a unique solution $v_{q,k}\in C^2([0,T]\times M)$, and define

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

Let $q\in C^\infty(M;\mathbb R)$ be independent of time, and set
$$L_q=\partial_t^2-\Delta_g+q(x),\qquad \Delta_g=\operatorname{div}_g\nabla_g.$$
For a smooth solution $u$ up to the boundary on $[0,T]\times M$, let $u_0=u(0,\cdot)$, $u_1=\partial_tu(0,\cdot)$, and let $h=u|_{[0,T]\times\partial M}$ be its Dirichlet boundary value. The support of a function is the closure of the set where it is nonzero.

(i) If $h=0$ and $\operatorname{supp}u_0\cup\operatorname{supp}u_1\subseteq K$ for a nonempty closed $K\subseteq M$, then
$$\operatorname{supp}u(t,\cdot)\subseteq\{x\in M:d_g(x,K)\le t\}\qquad(0\le t\le T).$$

(ii) If $u_0=u_1=0$ and $h(t,\cdot)=0$ for $0\le t\le s_0$ with $0\le s_0<T$, then
$$\operatorname{supp}u(t,\cdot)\subseteq\{x\in M:d_g(x,\partial M)\le t-s_0\}\qquad(s_0\le t\le T).$$
The same assertion holds backward in time for a smooth solution with zero terminal data and boundary value vanishing for $s_1\le t\le T$, with $0\le t\le s_1$ and $t-s_0$ replaced by $s_1-t$.

(iii) Let $q_1,q_2\in C^\infty(M;\mathbb R)$ be time independent, put $Q=\operatorname{supp}(q_1-q_2)$, and suppose $Q\ne\varnothing$ and $d_g(Q,\partial M)>T/2$. If $u$ solves $L_{q_1}u=0$ with zero initial data and smooth boundary value compactly supported in $(0,T)\times\partial M$, and $v$ solves $L_{q_2}v=0$ with zero terminal data and smooth boundary value compactly supported in $(0,T)\times\partial M$, then
$$\int_0^T\!\int_M(q_1-q_2)u(t,x)v(t,x)\,dV_g(x)\,dt=0.$$
This is the two-boundary-trip finite-time invisibility statement at the level of the interior pairing.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(M,g)$ be a compact, connected, nonempty smooth Riemannian manifold with smooth boundary, let $T>0$, and write $Q=(0,T)\times M$ and $\Sigma=(0,T)\times\partial M$. Let $q\in C^\infty(M;\mathbb R)$ be independent of time, and let $L_q=\partial_t^2-\Delta_g+q$. Write $\mathcal H=C_c^\infty(\Sigma)$ for smooth Dirichlet data compactly supported away from the temporal endpoints. Assume that for every $h\in\mathcal H$ the zero-initial-data Dirichlet problem $L_qu=0$, $u|_\Sigma=h$, $(u(0),u_t(0))=(0,0)$ has a unique solution $u_{q,h}\in C^2([0,T]\times M)$. Define the full time-dependent Dirichlet-to-Neumann map by
$$\Lambda_q^+ :\mathcal H\to L^2(\Sigma,dS_gdt),\qquad \Lambda_q^+h=\partial_{\nu_{out}}u_{q,h}|_\Sigma,$$
where $\nu_{out}$ is the outward unit normal. Also assume that for every $k\in\mathcal H$ the terminal-data Dirichlet problem $L_qv=0$, $v|_\Sigma=k$, $(v(T),v_t(T))=(0,0)$ has a unique solution $v_{q,k}\in C^2([0,T]\times M)$, and define
$$\Lambda_q^- :\mathcal H\to L^2(\Sigma,dS_gdt),\qquad \Lambda_q^-k=\partial_{\nu_{out}}v_{q,k}|_\Sigma.$$
The Green boundary pairing is the bilinear pairing $\int_\Sigma h\,\partial_{\nu_{out}}v\,dS_gdt$; the classical normal trace is in $L^2(\Sigma)$ for each stated $C^2$ solution class. Equality of two forward maps means equality on every $h\in\mathcal H$ over the whole time interval $(0,T)$, with the analogous convention for terminal maps.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(M,g)$ be a compact, connected, nonempty smooth Riemannian manifold with smooth boundary, let $T>0$, and let $q_1,q_2\in C^\infty(M;\mathbb R)$ be independent of time. Write $Q=(0,T)\times M$, $\Sigma=(0,T)\times\partial M$, and $P=\partial_t^2-\Delta_g$. For $h,k\in C_c^\infty(\Sigma)$, let $u$ be the zero-initial-data solution for $P+q_1$ with boundary value $h$, and let $v$ be the zero-terminal-data solution for $P+q_2$ with boundary value $k$, in the classical solution classes used to define the forward map $\Lambda_{q_1}^+$ and terminal map $\Lambda_{q_2}^-$; thus $u,v\in C^2([0,T]\times M)$. Then
$$\int_0^T\!\int_M(q_1-q_2)u(t,x)v(t,x)\,dV_g(x)\,dt=\int_0^T\!\int_{\partial M}\big(k\,\Lambda_{q_1}^+h-h\,\Lambda_{q_2}^-k\big)\,dS_g\,dt.$$
The boundary factors are paired bilinearly, without complex conjugation, and each normal derivative is the outward classical normal trace.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(M,g)$ be a compact smooth Riemannian manifold with smooth boundary, let $T>0$, and let $\Sigma=(0,T)\times\partial M$. Write $dS_g$ for the Riemannian volume density of the metric restricted to $T\partial M$, and give $\Sigma$ the product density $dt\,dS_g$. If a measurable function $f$ is locally integrable in every smooth product chart of $\Sigma$ and
$$\int_\Sigma f\psi\,dS_gdt=0\qquad\text{for every }\psi\in C_c^\infty(\Sigma),$$
then $f=0$ almost everywhere on $\Sigma$.

derivations.claim: Fix arbitrary $k\in C_c^\infty((0,T)\times\partial M)$. Let $u_1$ be the forward solution for $q_1$ with boundary input $h$, and let $v_2$ be the terminal solution for $q_2$ with boundary input $k$. By [F1], $$\int_Q(q_1-q_2)u_1v_2\,dV_gdt=0.$$ Using [F3] therefore gives $$\int_\Sigma(k\Lambda_{q_1}^+h-h\Lambda_{q_2}^-k)\,dS_gdt=0.$$
Apply [F3] again with both potentials equal to $q_2$. Its interior term is then zero, so $$\int_\Sigma(k\Lambda_{q_2}^+h-h\Lambda_{q_2}^-k)\,dS_gdt=0.$$

Subtract step 1.2 from step 1.1. The terminal terms cancel, yielding $$\int_\Sigma k(\Lambda_{q_1}^+h-\Lambda_{q_2}^+h)\,dS_gdt=0$$ for every smooth compactly supported $k$. The difference of the two traces belongs to $L^2(\Sigma)$ by [F2], hence is locally integrable. Its pairing with every $k$ is zero; [F4] implies that its $L^2$ class vanishes. This is the asserted equality of forward DN data.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n\ge1$
and let $e_k(x)=\exp(2\pi i\,k\cdot x)$, $k\in\mathbb Z^n$, be the coordinate
characters on $\mathbb T^n$
([[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]],
[[def-fourier-coefficients-and-trigonometric-polynomials]]). Then:

1. $(e_k)_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}$ is an orthonormal family in the complex Hilbert
   space $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$;
2. it is an orthonormal basis: its closed linear span is $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$;
3. consequently the Fourier expansion
   $f=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}\widehat f(k)e_k$ and Parseval's identity
   $$\|f\|_2^2=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}|\widehat f(k)|^2,\qquad \langle f,g\rangle=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}\widehat f(k)\overline{\widehat g(k)}$$
   hold for all $f,g\in L^2(\mathbb T^n)$, in the finite-subset-net sense; and
4. the Fourier coefficient map is a surjective linear isometry of
   $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$ onto $\ell^2(\mathbb Z^n,\mathbb C)$.

No Hilbert tensor-product identification is used anywhere.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and
[[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]
for real scalars and
[[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]] for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
[[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]. Under
[[def-countable-choice]], local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
[[lem-weak-derivative-is-independent-of-lp-representatives]], while
[[lem-weak-derivatives-are-unique-almost-everywhere]] gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

For a smooth real function $f$, its **Riemannian gradient** is $\operatorname{grad}_g f=(df)^\sharp$.

[[prop-exterior-derivative-of-a-function-is-its-differential]] identifies $df(X)=Xf$. The smooth bundle isomorphism in [[thm-the-musical-maps-are-smooth-inverse-bundle-isomorphisms]] therefore makes the gradient a smooth vector field. In coordinates $(\operatorname{grad}_g f)^i=\sum_jg^{ij}\partial_jf$. Constants, and all functions in dimension zero, have zero gradient.

Let $(M,g)$ be a Riemannian manifold, possibly with boundary, and let
$f:M\to\mathbb R$ be smooth. At each interior point, the
**Laplace–Beltrami operator** of $g$ is defined by the metric trace of the Hessian,
$$\Delta_gf(p):=\operatorname{tr}_g(\operatorname{Hess}f)_p:=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{Hess}f(e_i,e_i),$$
where $n=\dim M$ and $e_1,\dots,e_n$ is any $g_p$-orthonormal basis of $T_pM$; the
trace of a bilinear form with respect to a positive-definite inner product does not
depend on that choice, so $\Delta_gf$ is well-defined and smooth in the interior;
when $f$ is smooth up to the boundary, it has the usual one-sided extension there.
Here
$\operatorname{Hess}f(X,Y)=g(\nabla_X\operatorname{grad}f,Y)$ is the Levi-Civita
Hessian of
[[prop-gradient-hessian-and-divergence-connection-formulas]].

Equivalently, and with the **positive-divergence convention** of this library,
$$\Delta_gf=\operatorname{div}_g(\operatorname{grad}f),$$
where $\operatorname{div}_gX=\operatorname{tr}(v\mapsto\nabla_vX)$ is the Riemannian
divergence of [[def-riemannian-divergence]] as computed in
[[prop-gradient-hessian-and-divergence-connection-formulas]]. The equivalence is the
pointwise computation
$$\sum_i\operatorname{Hess}f(e_i,e_i)=\sum_i g(\nabla_{e_i}\operatorname{grad}f,e_i)=\operatorname{tr}(v\mapsto\nabla_v\operatorname{grad}f),$$
the middle sum being the endomorphism trace of $v\mapsto\nabla_v\operatorname{grad}f$
in the orthonormal basis $(e_i)$, which the same supplier identifies with
$\operatorname{div}_g(\operatorname{grad}f)$; no local coordinates are needed and no
analytic regularity beyond the smoothness of $f$ is used. On a zero-dimensional manifold
both sides are the empty sum $0$, and on a manifold with boundary the operator is defined
at interior points, with the usual one-sided extension at boundary points when $f$ is
smooth up to the boundary.

**This definition is the pointwise geometric operator only.** It records the trace
formula, the divergence form and the sign convention
$\Delta_g=\operatorname{div}_g\circ\operatorname{grad}$ fixed by
[[def-riemannian-divergence]]. It does not assert any analytic conclusion about
harmonic functions on manifolds — no maximum principle, no Harnack inequality, no
boundary-value solvability, no spectral theory, and no Liouville theorem. Those are
separate results with their own hypotheses, and their Euclidean forms are not licensed
on a general Riemannian manifold merely by writing down this definition.

derivations.claim: Write $\zeta=a+ib$. The null condition gives $|a|=|b|=:s=|\zeta|/\sqrt2$ and $a\cdot b=0$. Choose an orthogonal map $U$ with $Ua=se_1$ and $Ub=se_2$. Work temporarily with $U\Omega$, $q\circ U^{-1}$, and the phase $U\zeta$, relabeling them $\Omega$, $q$, and $\zeta$ for the construction; the Euclidean Laplacian, Lebesgue norms, and null phase are invariant under this change, and the constructed remainder is pulled back by $U$ at the end. As $\Omega\subset B(0,R)$, choose $L>\max\{1,(R+1)/\pi\}$; then $\Omega\subset Q_L=(-\pi L,\pi L)^n$. Put $\eta_k=(k+\tfrac12e_2)/L$ and $w_k(x)=(2\pi L)^{-n/2}e^{i\eta_k\cdot x}$ for $k\in\mathbb Z^n$. By [F1], these form an orthonormal basis on $Q_L$: they are the rescaled standard Fourier characters multiplied by the unitary factor $e^{ix_2/(2L)}$. For $A_\zeta=D^2+2\zeta\cdot D$, one has $A_\zeta w_k=p_kw_k$, where $p_k=|\eta_k|^2+2\zeta\cdot\eta_k$ and $|\operatorname{Im}p_k|=2s|k_2+\tfrac12|/L\geq s/L$. If $|\eta_k|\leq4s$, then $|p_k|\geq s/L$ and $|\eta_k/p_k|\leq4L$. If $|\eta_k|>4s$, then $|\operatorname{Re}p_k|\geq|\eta_k|^2-2s|\eta_k|\geq|\eta_k|^2/2$, so $|p_k|^{-1}<1/(8s^2)\leq L/s$ and $|\eta_k/p_k|<1/(2s)$. Thus $\sup_k|p_k|^{-1}\leq L/s$ and $\sup_k|\eta_k/p_k|\leq C_L$. Define $G_\zeta f=\sum_k p_k^{-1}(f,w_k)w_k$. Parseval [F1] gives $\|G_\zeta f\|_2\leq (L/s)\|f\|_2$ and $\|\nabla G_\zeta f\|_2\leq C_L\|f\|_2$. For finite Fourier sums $f_N$, the corresponding partial sums $G_\zeta f_N$ satisfy $A_\zeta G_\zeta f_N=f_N$ termwise. Parseval and the multiplier bounds give $f_N\to f$ in $L^2(Q_L)$ and $G_\zeta f_N\to G_\zeta f$ in $H^1(Q_L)$. Since $A_\zeta:H^1(Q_L)\to H^{-1}_{\rm loc}(Q_L)$ continuously, passage to distributions yields $A_\zeta G_\zeta f=f$.

$$\|qG_\zeta\|_{L^2\to L^2}\leq \|q\|_\infty L/s.$$
Choose $\tau_0$ large enough that $s\geq2L\|q\|_\infty$ and $s\geq1$ whenever $|\zeta|\geq\tau_0$. Then the series $\widetilde F=\sum_{m=0}^\infty(-qG_\zeta)^mF$ converges in $L^2(Q_L)$, satisfies $(I+qG_\zeta)\widetilde F=F$, and has norm at most $2\|q\|_{L^2(\Omega)}$. Set $r_\zeta=G_\zeta\widetilde F$ and restrict it to $\Omega$. Step 1.1 gives $A_\zeta r_\zeta+q r_\zeta=F=-q$ on $\Omega$, as well as $\|r_\zeta\|_2\leq (2L/s)\|q\|_2$ and $\|\nabla r_\zeta\|_2\leq2C_L\|q\|_2$.

Since $D=-i\nabla$, conjugation gives
$$e^{-i\zeta\cdot x}(-\Delta+q)e^{i\zeta\cdot x}(1+r_\zeta) =(D^2+2\zeta\cdot D+\zeta\cdot\zeta+q)(1+r_\zeta).$$
The null condition removes $\zeta\cdot\zeta$, the constant amplitude has zero derivatives, and step 2.1 makes the remaining expression $q+A_\zeta r_\zeta+q r_\zeta=0$. Multiplication by the smooth exponential preserves $H^1(\Omega)$ for this fixed $\zeta$, so $u_\zeta\in H^1(\Omega)$ and solves the equation distributionally. The estimates in step 2.1 have $s=|\zeta|/\sqrt2$, giving the asserted bounds after changing the constant.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice for the Sobolev interfaces used by consumers of this
definition. Let $k\ge1$ and $n\ge2$. A **bounded $C^k$ domain** in
$\mathbb R^n$ is a nonempty bounded open set $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ with
the following local graph property. For every boundary point
$x\in\partial\Omega$ there are an open neighbourhood
$W\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ of $x$, a rigid motion $R(p)=Qp+b$ with orthogonal
$Q$ and $b\in\mathbb R^n$, an open ball $B\subseteq\mathbb R^{n-1}$, and a
function $h\in C^k(B;\mathbb R)$ such that, after shrinking $W$ so that
$R(W)\subseteq B\times\mathbb R$,
$$R(\Omega\cap W)=R(W)\cap\{(y,s)\in B\times\mathbb R:s<h(y)\}.$$
In the coordinates $z=R(p)$ the domain therefore lies locally strictly below
the graph $s=h(y)$, and the boundary is that graph. The graph convention,
including the requirement that the domain occupy exactly the one-sided
subgraph, is the one of
[[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]]; the
regularity $h\in C^k$ is the only strengthening here, and connectedness is not
required.

Write $R(p)=(y,s)$. The **flattening chart** is
$$\Phi:W\longrightarrow\Phi(W)\subseteq B\times\mathbb R,\qquad \Phi(p)=(y,s-h(y)),$$
with inverse $\Phi^{-1}(y,t)=R^{-1}(y,t+h(y))$ on $\Phi(W)$. Thus
$\Phi(\Omega\cap W)=\Phi(W)\cap\{t<0\}$. Both maps are of class $C^k$; the
coordinate shear $(y,s)\mapsto(y,s-h(y))$ has Jacobian determinant one. If
$B'\subset\overline{B'}\subset B$ is a compactly contained concentric ball,
then every derivative $D^\beta h$ with $|\beta|\le k$ is continuous on
$\overline{B'}$, hence bounded there, and consequently the derivatives
through order $k$ of $\Phi$ and of $\Phi^{-1}$ are bounded on the corresponding
compact patch. This is the precise sense in which a boundary chart is said to
have bounded derivatives through order $k$ on the compact patches used; it
does not assert any bound uniform in the chart, the point, or a boundary
atlas.

In dimension $n=1$, the bounded sets satisfying this local one-sided condition
are finite disjoint unions of bounded open intervals. Each endpoint has an
interval neighbourhood on which the domain occupies one side; the coordinate
is the identity or its reflection, and the graph function and derivative
bounds are vacuous. General bounded open subsets of $\mathbb R$ need not have
this property. A bounded $C^1$ domain in the
sense of [[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]] is a
bounded $C^1$ domain in this sense when $n\ge2$.

This definition asserts no extension theorem, no trace operator, and no
uniformity of chart constants: it fixes only the regularity of the boundary
and the exact one-sided graph convention that later local statements use.
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every smooth manifold with boundary has a smooth collar.
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every open cover of a smooth manifold with boundary admits a smooth partition of unity subordinate to it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $(M,g)$ be a compact connected smooth Riemannian domain with nonempty smooth boundary and no orientability assumption, and let $\gamma\in C^\infty(M,\mathbb R)$ satisfy $\gamma>0$. There is a constant $C_P>0$ such that $\|w\|_{L^2(M)}\leq C_P\|
abla_gw\|_{L^2(M)}$ for every $w\in H_0^1(M)$. For every $h\in L^2(M)$ and $f\in H^{1/2}(\partial M)$ there is a unique $v\in H^1(M)$ with trace $f$ satisfying $\int_M\gamma\,g(
abla_gv,
abla_g\overline z)\,dV_g=-\int_Mh\overline z\,dV_g$ for every $z\in H_0^1(M)$. If $h$ and $f$ are smooth, this weak solution is smooth up to the boundary.

Assume Countable Choice.

Let $(M,g)$ be a compact smooth Riemannian manifold with smooth boundary, with no orientability assumption. Fix a finite smooth atlas of interior and boundary charts and a smooth partition of unity subordinate to it. For an integer $k\geq0$, define $H^k(M)$ as the completion of $C^\infty(M)$ in the sum of the Euclidean $W^{k,2}$ norms of the localized coordinate representatives; derivatives in a boundary chart are taken on the corresponding half-space. Define $H_0^1(M)$ as the closure of $C_c^\infty(M^\circ)$ in $H^1(M)$. Define $H^{1/2}(\partial M)$ by the fixed finite boundary atlas and partition of unity, using the Euclidean fractional Slobodeckij space $W^{1/2,2}(\mathbb R^{n-1})$ for each localized representative. Define $H^{-1/2}(\partial M)$ as the continuous dual of $H^{1/2}(\partial M)$ with the Riemannian boundary density pairing. These are the fixed-atlas norms used on this page; no atlas-independence assertion is part of this definition.

derivations.claim: Choose boundary normal coordinates $(y,x_n)$ near $x_0$, with $x_n=\operatorname{dist}(x,\partial\Omega)$ and inward unit normal $\partial_{x_n}$. The induced metric on the boundary is smooth. Choose a smooth hypersurface $S$ in $\partial\Omega$ through $x_0$, orthogonal there to $\xi_0$ (if $n=2$, take $S=\{x_0\}$). The boundary geodesics starting normally from $S$ give, by smooth dependence of the geodesic ODE and the inverse function theorem, coordinates $(s,z)$ near $x_0$; define $\phi(s,z)=s$. Gauss' lemma gives $|d\phi|_{g_{\partial\Omega}}=1$ and $d\phi(x_0)=\xi_0$. Shrink the patch so these coordinates and $\chi$ are supported inside it.

In boundary normal coordinates, $g^{nn}=1$ and $g^{n\alpha}=0$ at the boundary. Set $\Phi|_{x_n=0}=\phi$ and $\partial_n\Phi|_{x_n=0}=i$. Then $g^{ij}\partial_i\Phi\partial_j\Phi=0$ at $x_n=0$ because $|d\phi|=1$. Differentiate this eikonal equation successively in $x_n$. At each order the newest unknown normal jet $\partial_n^{j+1}\Phi|_{x_n=0}$ occurs linearly with coefficient $2i g^{nn}=2i\ne0$; all other terms use already assigned jets and derivatives of $g$. Solve recursively for every normal jet. Realize the resulting jet sequence by the following local Borel construction: if $c_j(y)$ is the prescribed $j$th normal derivative, choose a fixed smooth cutoff $\theta$ equal to one near zero and supported in $(-1,1)$, and set
$$\Phi(y,x_n)=\sum_{j\geq0}\frac{c_j(y)}{j!}x_n^j\theta(x_n/\varepsilon_j).$$
For all sufficiently large $j$, choose $\varepsilon_j<2^{-j}$ so that every derivative of order at most $j/2$ of the $j$th summand has sup norm at most $2^{-j}$; this is possible because those derivatives are bounded by constants times $\varepsilon_j^{j-m}$ with $m\leq j/2$. Choose any positive $\varepsilon_j$ for the finitely many smaller $j$. For each fixed derivative order, the tail then converges uniformly, so $\Phi$ is smooth and has the prescribed jets. In particular, the eikonal expression vanishes to infinite order at the boundary. Since $\partial_n\operatorname{Im}\Phi=1$ there, shrinking the collar gives $\operatorname{Im}\Phi\geq x_n/2$.

For $P_\gamma=\operatorname{div}(\gamma\nabla)$, direct differentiation gives
$$P_\gamma(e^{i\lambda\Phi}b)=e^{i\lambda\Phi}\big[-\lambda^2p_\gamma b+i\lambda L_\gamma b+P_\gamma b\big],$$
where $p_\gamma=\gamma g^{ij}\partial_i\Phi\partial_j\Phi$ and
$L_\gamma b=2\gamma g^{ij}(\partial_i\Phi)(\partial_jb)+\operatorname{div}(\gamma\nabla\Phi)b$.
The phase is common to both conductivities and $p_\gamma=\gamma p_1$ vanishes to infinite order on the boundary by step 1.2. Prescribe $b_{0,\gamma}|_{\partial\Omega}=\chi$ and $b_{-j,\gamma}|_{\partial\Omega}=0$ for $j\geq1$. In boundary normal coordinates the coefficient of the new normal derivative in $L_\gamma b$ is $2i\gamma$, which is nonzero. Therefore the normal derivatives of $b_{0,\gamma}$ can be chosen successively so that $L_\gamma b_{0,\gamma}=0$ to infinite order at the boundary; after choosing $b_{0,\gamma},\ldots,b_{-(j-1),\gamma}$, the same recursion chooses all jets of $b_{-j,\gamma}$ so that $iL_\gamma b_{-j,\gamma}+P_\gamma b_{-(j-1),\gamma}=0$ to infinite order. Realize each sequence by the Borel series in step 1.2 and multiply by a fixed collar cutoff equal to one near the boundary support. Repeat for $\widetilde\gamma$.

Let $b_{\lambda,\gamma}=\sum_{j=0}^K\lambda^{-j}b_{-j,\gamma}$, with the same construction for $\widetilde\gamma$. The order-$\lambda^2$ eikonal term and the order-$\lambda,\ldots,\lambda^{1-K}$ transport terms in step 2.1 vanish to infinite order at $x_n=0$. Thus each remaining coefficient is $O(x_n^R)$ for every prescribed integer $R$. On the collar, $|e^{i\lambda\Phi}|\leq e^{-\lambda x_n/2}$. For every fixed $a,R$, direct integration gives
$$\|\lambda^a x_n^R e^{-\lambda x_n/2}\|_{L^2(0,\delta)}=O(\lambda^{a-R-1/2}).$$
Choose $R$ and then $K$ large enough to make every residual term $O(\lambda^{-N})$. Derivatives of the collar cutoff are supported where $x_n\geq c>0$ and hence contribute $O(e^{-c\lambda})$. The same Gaussian integration shows $\|v_{\lambda,\gamma}\|_{L^2}=O(\lambda^{-1})$ and bounds its gradient norm above. Thus the $H^1$ norms are bounded above and the residual bounds hold for the arbitrary prescribed $N$.

Let $r_\lambda=u_{\lambda,\gamma}-v_{\lambda,\gamma}\in H_0^1(\Omega)$. Its weak equation is $P_\gamma r_\lambda=-P_\gamma v_{\lambda,\gamma}$. Test with $r_\lambda$, use $\gamma\geq\gamma_*>0$, and use the Poincare inequality in [F3]:
$$\gamma_*\|\nabla r_\lambda\|_2^2\leq\|P_\gamma v_{\lambda,\gamma}\|_2\|r_\lambda\|_2 \leq C_P\|P_\gamma v_{\lambda,\gamma}\|_2\|\nabla r_\lambda\|_2.$$
If the last gradient norm is zero then $r_\lambda=0$ by [F3]; otherwise divide by it. This proves $\|r_\lambda\|_{H^1}=O(\lambda^{-N})$. The same argument applies to $\widetilde\gamma$.

In the collar, write $J(y,x_n)dS(y)dx_n$ for Euclidean volume in boundary normal coordinates, with $J(y,0)=1$. Since $\Phi=\phi+ix_n+O(x_n^2)$, $\operatorname{Im}\Phi=x_n+O(x_n^2)$ and $g(d\Phi,\overline{d\Phi})=2+O(x_n)$. The boundary values of both leading amplitudes are $\chi$, and lower amplitudes vanish there. Differentiating $v_{\lambda,\gamma}$ and $v_{\lambda,\widetilde\gamma}$ therefore gives
$$\nabla v_{\lambda,\gamma}\cdot\overline{\nabla v_{\lambda,\widetilde\gamma}} =2\lambda e^{-2\lambda x_n}|\chi(y)|^2+e^{-2\lambda x_n}O(1)+ e^{-2\lambda x_n}O(\lambda x_n),$$
uniformly for $0\leq x_n\leq\lambda^{-1/2}$. On this shrinking collar $\lambda x_n^2\leq1$, so after $t=\lambda x_n$ the phase remainder factor is uniformly bounded; boundedness of $F,J,\chi$ gives an integrable majorant $C t^ke^{-t}$ for the rescaled leading term. For each fixed $t$, the rescaled leading term tends to $2t^ke^{-2t}F(y,0)|\chi(y)|^2$. Each displayed remainder has an additional factor $\lambda^{-1}$ after scaling and is dominated by $C\lambda^{-1}(t^k+t^{k+1}+t^{k+2})e^{-t}$, including the phase error $e^{O(t^2/\lambda)}-1=O(t^2/\lambda)$; its integral tends to zero. On the rest of the fixed collar, $\operatorname{Im}\Phi\geq x_n/2$ gives exponential decay $e^{-\lambda x_n}\leq e^{-\sqrt{\lambda}}$; every polynomial prefactor is therefore negligible. The cutoff region away from the collar is also exponentially small. Thus the limit for approximate beams is
$$2\int_0^\infty t^ke^{-2t}\,dt\int_{\partial\Omega}F|\chi|^2\,dS,$$
whose constant is strictly positive.

Taking equal conductivities, $F=1$, and $k=0$ in step 3.1 gives $\lim_{\lambda\to\infty}\int_\Omega|\nabla v_{\lambda,\gamma}|^2dx=c_0\int_{\partial\Omega}|\chi|^2dS>0$. Together with the upper bound in step 2.2 this proves the asserted two-sided $H^1$ norm bound.

The exact corrections satisfy $H^1$ errors $O(\lambda^{-N})$ by step 2.3, while both approximate beams have uniformly bounded $H^1$ norms by step 2.2. Cauchy-Schwarz bounds the change in the weighted product integral, after multiplication by $\lambda^k$, by $C\lambda^k\lambda^{-N}$ because $0\leq\operatorname{dist}(x,\partial\Omega)^k\leq C$ on the bounded domain. Choose $N>k$. The error tends to zero, so the same limit holds for the exact solutions.
