citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice.

Let $(M,g)$ be a compact smooth Riemannian manifold with smooth boundary, with no orientability assumption. Fix a finite smooth atlas of interior and boundary charts and a smooth partition of unity subordinate to it. For an integer $k\geq0$, define $H^k(M)$ as the completion of $C^\infty(M)$ in the sum of the Euclidean $W^{k,2}$ norms of the localized coordinate representatives; derivatives in a boundary chart are taken on the corresponding half-space. Define $H_0^1(M)$ as the closure of $C_c^\infty(M^\circ)$ in $H^1(M)$. Define $H^{1/2}(\partial M)$ by the fixed finite boundary atlas and partition of unity, using the Euclidean fractional Slobodeckij space $W^{1/2,2}(\mathbb R^{n-1})$ for each localized representative. Define $H^{-1/2}(\partial M)$ as the continuous dual of $H^{1/2}(\partial M)$ with the Riemannian boundary density pairing. These are the fixed-atlas norms used on this page; no atlas-independence assertion is part of this definition.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $n\ge1$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be a
bounded open set and let $1\le p<\infty$. Then $W^{1,p}_0(\Omega)$ is
compactly embedded in $L^p(\Omega)$: the inclusion is bounded, and every
sequence bounded in $W^{1,p}_0(\Omega)$ has a subsequence converging in
$L^p(\Omega)$. No regularity of $\partial\Omega$ is needed.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space, let $a$ be a bounded coercive sesquilinear form on $H$ with constants $M,\alpha$ ([[def-bounded-coercive-and-symmetric-sesquilinear-forms]]), and let $F:H\to\mathbb K$ be a bounded conjugate-linear functional with norm $\|F\|=\sup_{\|v\|\le1}|F(v)|$. Then there is a unique $u\in H$ with $$a(u,v)=F(v)\qquad\text{for every }v\in H,$$ and it satisfies $\alpha\|u\|\le\|F\|$, that is $\|u\|\le\|F\|/\alpha$. The real bilinear case is the same statement with $a$ symmetric or not, $F$ a bounded linear functional, and the conjugation read as the identity.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$, be a
bounded $C^1$ domain in the graph sense of
[[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]], let $\partial\Omega$ carry the
chart-independent surface measure of
[[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]] and
[[lem-surface-integral-is-independent-of-c-one-boundary-charts]], let
$1\le p<\infty$ and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then there is a
unique bounded linear operator
$$T:W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)\longrightarrow L^p(\partial\Omega;\mathbb K)$$
with $Tu=u|_{\partial\Omega}$ for every
$u\in C(\overline\Omega)\cap W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$, and it satisfies
$\|Tu\|_{L^p(\partial\Omega)}\le C(\Omega,p)\|u\|_{W^{1,p}(\Omega)}$. On each
boundary chart the operator is the flat half-space trace of
[[thm-trace-estimate-on-the-half-space]] transported by the flattening
diffeomorphism, and the chartwise definitions agree on overlaps; uniqueness
holds because two bounded operators agreeing on the dense subspace
$C(\overline\Omega)\cap W^{1,p}(\Omega)$ are equal.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$, be a
bounded $C^1$ domain, $1<p<\infty$, $\theta=1-1/p$, and let $T$ be the trace
operator of [[thm-lp-trace-operator-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]]. Then there is
a bounded linear operator
$$R:W^{\theta,p}(\partial\Omega;\mathbb K)\longrightarrow W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$$
with $T\circ R=\mathrm{id}_{W^{\theta,p}(\partial\Omega)}$ and
$\|Rg\|_{W^{1,p}(\Omega)}\le C(\Omega,p)\|g\|_{W^{\theta,p}(\partial\Omega)}$.
Moreover, for every open neighbourhood $U$ of $\partial\Omega$ in
$\mathbb R^n$ there is such an operator $R_U$ whose image is contained in the
classes vanishing a.e. outside $U$, with
$\|R_Ug\|_{W^{1,p}(\Omega)}\le C(\Omega,p,U)\|g\|_{W^{\theta,p}(\partial\Omega)}$.
The right inverse is not unique and no canonical choice is claimed.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a bounded
$C^{k+2}$ domain, $n\ge2$, $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, let
$k\ge0$, let $L,a$ be as in
[[def-uniformly-elliptic-divergence-form-operator]] with
$a^{ij}\in W^{k+1,\infty}(\Omega)$, $b^i,c\in W^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$ and all
coefficient derivatives bounded, and let $f\in H^k(\Omega)$. If
$u\in H^1_0(\Omega)$ is a weak solution of $Lu=f$ with zero boundary values
([[def-weak-dirichlet-solution-for-a-divergence-form-operator]]), then
$u\in H^{k+2}(\Omega)$ and
$$\|u\|_{H^{k+2}(\Omega)}\le C\big(\|f\|_{H^k(\Omega)}+\|u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\big),$$
with $C$ depending only on $n,k,\Omega$ and the coefficient bounds. The
derivative gain is exactly two orders; the boundary regularity required at
order $k$ is $C^{k+2}$, the coefficient regularity one order above the data
order, and the companion page records the sharp two-derivative example. For
$k=0$ the theorem is
[[thm-global-h-two-dirichlet-regularity]].

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $n\ge2$, let $\Omega$ be a bounded $W^{k,p}$-extension domain, $k\ge1$ and $1\le p<\infty$. Let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and $u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Then:

1. if $kp<n$, $\|u\|_{L^q(\Omega)}\le C\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$ for every $q$ with $\frac1q\ge\frac1p-\frac kn$ (equivalently $1\le q\le\frac{np}{n-kp}$);
2. if $kp=n$, $\|u\|_{L^q(\Omega)}\le C(q)\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$ for every finite $q$;
3. if $kp>n$, then for every integer $m\ge0$ and every $0<\alpha<1$ with $m+\alpha<k-\frac np$ there is a representative in $C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$ with $\|u\|_{C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)}\le C\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$; when $k-\frac np\notin\mathbb Z$ one may take $m=\lfloor k-\frac np\rfloor$ and $\alpha=k-\frac np-m$.

Here $C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$ uses the continuous derivatives of the constructed representative on an ambient neighbourhood of $\overline\Omega$, with norm
$$\|g\|_{C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)}:=\sum_{|\beta|\le m}\sup_{\overline\Omega}|D^\beta g|+\sum_{|\beta|=m}\sup_{\substack{x,y\in\overline\Omega\\x\ne y}}\frac{|D^\beta g(x)-D^\beta g(y)|}{|x-y|^\alpha}.$$
For $\Omega=\varnothing$ set these norm values to $0$. The proof supplies such an ambient representative, so no boundary differentiability or regularity of $\partial\Omega$ is assumed.
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every smooth manifold with boundary has a smooth collar.

derivations.claim: There is a constant $C_P$ such that $\|w\|_{L^2(M)}\leq C_P\|\nabla w\|_{L^2(M)}$ for $w\in H_0^1(M)$. Otherwise choose $w_j\in H_0^1(M)$ with $\|w_j\|_{L^2}=1$ and $\|\nabla w_j\|_{L^2}\to0$. The sequence is bounded in $H^1$. A finite chart partition and [F2] give an $L^2$-convergent subsequence; a further subsequence converges weakly in the Hilbert space $H^1$, so its limit $w$ belongs to the weakly closed subspace $H_0^1(M)$, has weak gradient zero, and has $L^2$ norm one. In each connected coordinate ball, convolution of a function with zero weak gradient is constant on smaller balls; overlapping balls force the constants to agree, so connectedness makes $w$ constant on $M^\circ$. Its trace is zero by [F4], whereas the trace of a nonzero constant is that same nonzero constant on the nonempty boundary. This contradiction proves the inequality.

Compactness of $M$ and positivity of $\gamma$ give $\gamma_*:=\min_M\gamma>0$. Thus $a_\gamma(w,z)=\int_M\gamma\,g(\nabla w,\nabla\bar z)\,dV_g$ is bounded on $H_0^1(M)$ and $a_\gamma(w,w)\geq c\|w\|_{H^1(M)}^2$ by step 1.1 and $\gamma_*$. By [F3], for any bounded conjugate-linear functional $G$ on $H_0^1(M)$ there is a unique $w\in H_0^1(M)$ with $a_\gamma(w,z)=G(z)$ for all $z$.

Flatten each boundary chart, apply the local half-space trace lift, and patch the finitely many chart lifts with a smooth partition. The resulting $Ef\in H^1(M)$ has trace $f$ and norm bounded by $C\|f\|_{H^{1/2}(\partial M)}$ by [F5]. For $h\in L^2(M)$ take $G(z)=-\int_Mh\overline z\,dV_g-a_\gamma(Ef,z)$ in step 2.1 and set $v=Ef+w$. Then $v$ has trace $f$ and satisfies the weak equation. If $v_1,v_2$ are two such solutions, their difference $w$ lies in $H_0^1$ and $a_\gamma(w,w)=0$; since $\gamma\geq\gamma_*>0$, $\nabla w=0$, and step 1.1 gives $w=0$.

Suppose $h$ and $f$ are smooth. By [F8], extend $f$ smoothly from the boundary into a collar and multiply by a cutoff to obtain a smooth extension $Ef$ on $M$. Then $w=v-Ef$ has zero trace and solves $\operatorname{div}_g(\gamma\nabla_gw)=h-\operatorname{div}_g(\gamma\nabla_gEf)$, whose right-hand side is smooth. In each boundary chart, flatten the boundary and write the principal matrix as $|g|^{1/2}\gamma g^{ij}$; it is smooth and uniformly elliptic because $g$ is positive definite and $\gamma$ has a positive minimum. For the base case, localize $w$ by a cutoff; its equation has an $L^2$ right-hand side since $w\in H^1$, so [F6] gives local $H^2$ regularity. If $w\in H^{m+1}$, each cutoff commutator contains derivatives of $w$ of order at most $m+1$ with smooth bounded coefficients, hence lies in $H^m$; the localized right-hand side is therefore in $H^m$, and [F6] gives $H^{m+2}$ regularity. Induction over $m$ and a finite chart cover give $w\in H^m(M)$ for every integer $m$. By [F7], $w$ and hence $v=Ef+w$ are smooth up to the boundary.

citations.quote:
A **Riemannian metric** on a Hausdorff second-countable smooth manifold $M$ is a smooth symmetric covariant two-tensor $g$ such that $g_p(v,v)>0$ for every point $p$ and every nonzero $v\in T_pM$. A **Riemannian manifold** is the pair $(M,g)$.

This is a [[def-smooth-tensor-field]] giving a [[def-smooth-bundle-metric]] on $TM$. Dimension zero is allowed: its zero bilinear form is positive definite because there are no nonzero vectors. The empty manifold has its unique empty metric. Boundaries are allowed where stated, with smoothness understood up to the boundary.

Let $X$ be a smooth vector field on $M$ and let $p\in M$. Then there exist
$h>0$, an open neighbourhood $U$ of $p$, and a smooth map

$$ \Phi:(-h,h)\times U\to M $$

such that for every $q\in U$, the curve $t\mapsto \Phi(t,q)$ is the unique
integral curve of $X$ on $(-h,h)$ with initial value $\Phi(0,q)=q$.

derivations.claim: Embed the segment in a collar extension across $\partial M_0$ and cover it by finitely many coordinate neighborhoods. On an embedded subsegment, parallel transport an orthonormal normal frame and set $F(t,y)=\exp_{\gamma(t)}(\sum_\alpha y_\alpha E_\alpha(t))$. The inverse function theorem gives local Fermi coordinates with $g_{jk}(t,0)=\delta_{jk}$ and $\partial_i g_{jk}(t,0)=0$. This construction is along an interval and uses no orientation of $M_0$.

In one such chart, seek $v_s=e^{is\Theta}a$, $s=\tau+i\lambda$, with $\Theta(t,0)=t$ and $\operatorname{Im}\Theta(t,y)\geq c|y|^2$. Expand $\Theta$ into homogeneous transverse Taylor polynomials. The quadratic polynomial is $\frac12H(t)y\cdot y$; substituting into $g(d\Theta,d\Theta)=1$ gives the matrix Riccati equation $H'+H^2=F(t)$, where $F$ is determined by the second transverse Taylor coefficient of the inverse metric. An initial complex symmetric $H(t_0)$ with positive-definite imaginary part yields a smooth solution with positive imaginary part on a short subsegment. Each higher homogeneous phase term then solves a linear first-order ODE along $t$, because its newest coefficient occurs linearly in the eikonal equation.

Substituting $a=\tau^{(m-1)/4}\sum_{j=0}^N s^{-j}a_{-j}$ into $(-\Delta_{g_0}-s^2)e^{is\Theta}a$ cancels successive powers of $s$ by linear transport ODEs for the transverse Taylor coefficients of each $a_{-j}$. The leading coefficient solves $a_0(t,0)=c_0\exp(-\frac12\int_{t_0}^t\operatorname{tr}H(r)\,dr)$. A finite Taylor realization to the order required for the fixed $K$ and a transverse cutoff produce a smooth local beam; Gaussian integration gives bounded $L^2$ norm and a residual that tends to zero faster than any prescribed power after increasing the Taylor order.

On an oriented transversal of dimension at least two, apply [F3] to complete the finite overlap matching and eliminate all distinct-branch cross terms. This gives the stated global family and limit; steps 1.1--2.1 describe its local ingredients, without claiming a new proof of the imported global estimates.

For a nonorientable transversal let $\pi:\widetilde M_0\to M_0$ be its orientation double cover, with deck involution $\sigma$, and lift $\gamma$ to $\widetilde\gamma$. Let $w_s$ be the oriented beam from [F3] along that lift. Define the descended function by $\pi^*v_s=w_s+\sigma^*w_s$. The residual and norm bounds follow by a finite sum and the covering integral formula. The two lifted segments have no common tangent branch: equality of position and velocity at different times would make the geodesic periodic, contrary to its nontangential boundary exit; opposite velocities at a repeated point would force a zero midpoint velocity by geodesic uniqueness. There are only finitely many crossing branches, by compactness and local uniqueness. The distinct-branch estimate in [F3], applied to these two lifts, therefore gives a zero mixed-term limit. For every continuous $\psi$ the covering formula is
$$\int_{M_0}|v_s|^2\psi\,dV=\int_{\widetilde M_0}|w_s|^2(\psi\circ\pi)\,dV+\operatorname{Re}\int_{\widetilde M_0}w_s\overline{\sigma^*w_s}(\psi\circ\pi)\,dV.$$
The first term has precisely the required ray limit and the second tends to zero. In particular there is no extra factor two in the normalization. The same argument works if the cover is disconnected.

If the transversal has dimension one, the component containing the segment is an interval with arclength coordinate $t$ beginning at its incoming endpoint. Set $v_s=e^{ist}$ on this component and zero on all other components. The residual is zero and the asserted integral formula is exact. In dimension zero the given unit-speed segment cannot exist. This covers the dimensions not needed in the CTA application as well.

citations.quote: A transversally anisotropic product domain of dimension $n\geq3$ is a compact connected smooth $n$-dimensional Riemannian domain $(M,g)$ with smooth boundary, together with a compact connected smooth $(n-1)$-dimensional Riemannian manifold with boundary $(M_0,g_0)$ and an isometric embedding of $(M,g)$ as a smooth domain compactly contained in $(\mathbb R\times M_0^\circ,dx_1^2\oplus g_0)$. The coordinate $x_1$ on $\mathbb R$ is the distinguished Euclidean coordinate; $M_0$ is the transversal manifold. All Laplacians use $\Delta_g=\operatorname{div}_g\nabla_g$. Neither $M$ nor $M_0$ is assumed orientable. A positive smooth conformal factor is not included in this definition; claims using a conformally related metric must state and prove the required conformal transformation separately.

Assume Countable Choice.

Let $(M,g)$ be a compact smooth Riemannian manifold with smooth boundary, with no orientability assumption. Fix a finite smooth atlas of interior and boundary charts and a smooth partition of unity subordinate to it. For an integer $k\geq0$, define $H^k(M)$ as the completion of $C^\infty(M)$ in the sum of the Euclidean $W^{k,2}$ norms of the localized coordinate representatives; derivatives in a boundary chart are taken on the corresponding half-space. Define $H_0^1(M)$ as the closure of $C_c^\infty(M^\circ)$ in $H^1(M)$. Define $H^{1/2}(\partial M)$ by the fixed finite boundary atlas and partition of unity, using the Euclidean fractional Slobodeckij space $W^{1/2,2}(\mathbb R^{n-1})$ for each localized representative. Define $H^{-1/2}(\partial M)$ as the continuous dual of $H^{1/2}(\partial M)$ with the Riemannian boundary density pairing. These are the fixed-atlas norms used on this page; no atlas-independence assertion is part of this definition.

Let $(M,g)$ be a Riemannian manifold, possibly with boundary, and let
$f:M\to\mathbb R$ be smooth. At each interior point, the
**Laplace–Beltrami operator** of $g$ is defined by the metric trace of the Hessian,
$$\Delta_gf(p):=\operatorname{tr}_g(\operatorname{Hess}f)_p:=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{Hess}f(e_i,e_i),$$
where $n=\dim M$ and $e_1,\dots,e_n$ is any $g_p$-orthonormal basis of $T_pM$; the
trace of a bilinear form with respect to a positive-definite inner product does not
depend on that choice, so $\Delta_gf$ is well-defined and smooth in the interior;
when $f$ is smooth up to the boundary, it has the usual one-sided extension there.
Here
$\operatorname{Hess}f(X,Y)=g(\nabla_X\operatorname{grad}f,Y)$ is the Levi-Civita
Hessian of
[[prop-gradient-hessian-and-divergence-connection-formulas]].

Equivalently, and with the **positive-divergence convention** of this library,
$$\Delta_gf=\operatorname{div}_g(\operatorname{grad}f),$$
where $\operatorname{div}_gX=\operatorname{tr}(v\mapsto\nabla_vX)$ is the Riemannian
divergence of [[def-riemannian-divergence]] as computed in
[[prop-gradient-hessian-and-divergence-connection-formulas]]. The equivalence is the
pointwise computation
$$\sum_i\operatorname{Hess}f(e_i,e_i)=\sum_i g(\nabla_{e_i}\operatorname{grad}f,e_i)=\operatorname{tr}(v\mapsto\nabla_v\operatorname{grad}f),$$
the middle sum being the endomorphism trace of $v\mapsto\nabla_v\operatorname{grad}f$
in the orthonormal basis $(e_i)$, which the same supplier identifies with
$\operatorname{div}_g(\operatorname{grad}f)$; no local coordinates are needed and no
analytic regularity beyond the smoothness of $f$ is used. On a zero-dimensional manifold
both sides are the empty sum $0$, and on a manifold with boundary the operator is defined
at interior points, with the usual one-sided extension at boundary points when $f$ is
smooth up to the boundary.

**This definition is the pointwise geometric operator only.** It records the trace
formula, the divergence form and the sign convention
$\Delta_g=\operatorname{div}_g\circ\operatorname{grad}$ fixed by
[[def-riemannian-divergence]]. It does not assert any analytic conclusion about
harmonic functions on manifolds — no maximum principle, no Harnack inequality, no
boundary-value solvability, no spectral theory, and no Liouville theorem. Those are
separate results with their own hypotheses, and their Euclidean forms are not licensed
on a general Riemannian manifold merely by writing down this definition.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X$ be a complex normed space, let $M \subseteq X$ be a linear subspace, and
let $f_0:M \to \mathbb{C}$ be a bounded complex linear functional. Then there
exists a bounded complex linear functional $F:X \to \mathbb{C}$ such that
$F|_M=f_0$ and $\|F\|=\|f_0\|$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space and let $f$ be a bounded linear functional on $H$ ([[def-dual-space-of-a-normed-space]]). Then there is a unique $y\in H$ with

$$f(x)=\langle x,y\rangle\qquad\text{for every }x\in H,$$

and $\|f\|=\|y\|$, where $\|f\|$ is the dual norm ([[def-operator-norm]]). Under the first-variable-linear convention the representing vector depends conjugate-linearly and isometrically on $f$: if $f_i$ is represented by $y_i$ and $a,b$ are scalars, then $af_1+bf_2$ is represented by $\overline a\,y_1+\overline b\,y_2$.

derivations.claim:
Put $s=\varphi$ and first set $q=0$. For a real smooth weight $\psi$, direct differentiation gives
$$P_{\psi,h,0}=e^{\psi/h}(-h^2\Delta_g)e^{-\psi/h} =-h^2\Delta_g-|
abla_g\psi|^2+2h
abla_g\psi\cdot
abla_g+h\Delta_g\psi.$$
For $\psi=s$, $|
abla s|=1$ and $\Delta s=0$, so $P_{s,h,0}=A+C$ with $A=-h^2\Delta_g-1$ self-adjoint and $C=2h\partial_s$ skew-adjoint on compactly supported functions.

Convexify by $\psi=f(s)=s+\frac{h}{2\varepsilon}s^2$, where $\varepsilon>0$ is fixed small and then $h/\varepsilon$ is small. Since $M$ is compact, choose $h$ so $f'=1+hs/\varepsilon>1/2$ on $M$. The conjugated operator is $P_{\psi,h,0}=A_\varepsilon+C_\varepsilon$ with
$$A_\varepsilon=-h^2\Delta_g-(f')^2,\qquad C_\varepsilon=2hf'\partial_s+hf'',\qquad f''=h/\varepsilon.$$
Here $A_\varepsilon$ is self-adjoint and $C_\varepsilon$ is skew-adjoint. Product independence of $s$ makes $-\Delta_g=-\partial_s^2-\Delta_{g_0}$, with $\Delta_{g_0}$ commuting with $C_\varepsilon$. Direct differentiation in the $s$ coordinate therefore gives the exact commutator
$$[A_\varepsilon,C_\varepsilon]=4h(f')^2f''-4h^3f''\partial_s^2.$$
For compactly supported $w$, integration by parts yields
$$\|P_{\psi,h,0}w\|_2^2 =\|A_\varepsilon w\|_2^2+\|C_\varepsilon w\|_2^2+ 4h f''\|(f')w\|_2^2+4h^3f''\|\partial_sw\|_2^2 \geq c h^2\varepsilon^{-1}\|w\|_2^2.$$
The same identity implies $\|A_\varepsilon w\|_2\leq\|P_{\psi,h,0}w\|_2$. Since
$\|h\nabla w\|_2^2=\langle A_\varepsilon w,w\rangle+\|f'w\|_2^2$,
the $L^2$ bound just obtained gives $\|w\|_2+\|h\nabla w\|_2\leq C_\varepsilon h^{-1}\|P_{\psi,h,0}w\|_2$.

The convexified and unconvexified weights are related by multiplication with $m=e^{s^2/(2\varepsilon)}$: $P_{\psi,h,0}(mw)=mP_{s,h,0}w$. On compact $M$, $m$ and $m^{-1}$ are bounded, so step 1.2 yields $\|w\|_2\leq C h^{-1}\|P_{s,h,0}w\|_2$. Adding the potential changes the conjugated operator by $h^2q$. Its norm on $w$ is at most $h^2\|q\|_\infty\|w\|_2$, which is absorbed in the preceding estimate for sufficiently small $h$. Replacing $s$ by either sign of $x_1$ proves the a priori estimate in the statement.

Let $P=P_{\varphi,h,q}$ and apply the a priori estimate also to $P^*=P_{-\varphi,h,q}$, which has the same real potential and the opposite allowed sign. On $E=P^*(C_c^\infty(M^\circ))\subset L^2(M)$ define the complex-linear functional $\ell(P^*w)=\int_M\bar Fw\,dV_g$. The estimate makes this well-defined: $P^*w=0$ implies $w=0$. It also gives $|\ell(P^*w)|\leq\|F\|_2\|w\|_2\leq Ch^{-1}\|F\|_2\|P^*w\|_2$. By [A1] extend $\ell$ to $L^2(M)$ with the same bound; by [A2] there is $R\in L^2(M)$ with $\ell(z)=\int_Mz\bar R\,dV_g$ and $\|R\|_2\leq Ch^{-1}\|F\|_2$. Taking complex conjugates gives $\int_MR\overline{P^*w}\,dV_g=\int_MF\bar w\,dV_g$ for every test $w$, which is precisely $PR=F$ distributionally on $M^\circ$.

Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space, let $a$ be a bounded coercive sesquilinear form on $H$ with constants $M,\alpha$ ([[def-bounded-coercive-and-symmetric-sesquilinear-forms]]), and let $F:H\to\mathbb K$ be a bounded conjugate-linear functional with norm $\|F\|=\sup_{\|v\|\le1}|F(v)|$. Then there is a unique $u\in H$ with $$a(u,v)=F(v)\qquad\text{for every }v\in H,$$ and it satisfies $\alpha\|u\|\le\|F\|$, that is $\|u\|\le\|F\|/\alpha$. Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $n\ge1$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be a
bounded open set and let $1\le p<\infty$. Then $W^{1,p}_0(\Omega)$ is
compactly embedded in $L^p(\Omega)$: the inclusion is bounded, and every
sequence bounded in $W^{1,p}_0(\Omega)$ has a subsequence converging in
$L^p(\Omega)$. No regularity of $\partial\Omega$ is needed.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $X$ be a Banach space
over a fixed field $F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, let $K:X\to X$ be a compact operator
([[def-compact-linear-operator]]) and put $A:=I-K$. Then:

1. $A$ is injective if and only if it is surjective, and in that case $A$ is
   boundedly invertible;
2. for every $y\in X$ the equation $Ax=y$ has a solution if and only if
   $\varphi(y)=0$ for every $\varphi\in\ker A^*$, the transpose
   $A^*=I-K^*$ acting on $X^*$
   ([[def-transpose-of-a-bounded-operator]]);
3. $\ker A$ and the cokernel $X/\operatorname{ran}A$
   ([[def-quotient-vector-space-coset-notation]]) are finite dimensional with
   equal dimensions over $F$ ([[def-dimension]]).

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$, be a
bounded $C^1$ domain, $1<p<\infty$, $\theta=1-1/p$, and let $T$ be the trace
operator of [[thm-lp-trace-operator-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]]. Then there is
a bounded linear operator
$$R:W^{\theta,p}(\partial\Omega;\mathbb K)\longrightarrow W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$$
with $T\circ R=\mathrm{id}_{W^{\theta,p}(\partial\Omega)}$ and
$\|Rg\|_{W^{1,p}(\Omega)}\le C(\Omega,p)\|g\|_{W^{\theta,p}(\partial\Omega)}$.
Moreover, for every open neighbourhood $U$ of $\partial\Omega$ in
$\mathbb R^n$ there is such an operator $R_U$ whose image is contained in the
classes vanishing a.e. outside $U$, with
$\|R_Ug\|_{W^{1,p}(\Omega)}\le C(\Omega,p,U)\|g\|_{W^{\theta,p}(\partial\Omega)}$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a bounded
$C^{k+2}$ domain, $n\ge2$, $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, let
$k\ge0$, let $L,a$ be as in
[[def-uniformly-elliptic-divergence-form-operator]] with

$u\in H^1_0(\Omega)$ is a weak solution of $Lu=f$ with zero boundary values
([[def-weak-dirichlet-solution-for-a-divergence-form-operator]]), then

$$\|u\|_{H^{k+2}(\Omega)}\le C\big(\|f\|_{H^k(\Omega)}+\|u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\big),$$

derivative gain is exactly two orders; the boundary regularity required at
order $k$ is $C^{k+2}$, the coefficient regularity one order above the data
order, and the companion page records the sharp two-derivative example. For
$k=0$ the theorem is
[[thm-global-h-two-dirichlet-regularity]].

derivations.claim: Choose a real constant $Q>1+\|q\|_{L^\infty(M)}$ and let $A=-\Delta_g+Q$ on $H_0^1(M)$, with form $a(w,z)=\int_M(g(\nabla w,\nabla\bar z)+Qw\bar z)\,dV_g$. The form is bounded and coercive in the chartwise $H^1$ norm, so [F2] gives a bounded inverse $A_D^{-1}:(H_0^1(M))^*\to H_0^1(M)$.

Multiplication by $Q-q$ maps $H_0^1(M)$ boundedly to $L^2(M)$, and the inclusion $H_0^1(M)\hookrightarrow L^2(M)$ is compact: localize with the finite atlas and partition, apply [F3] on each bounded chart piece (using zero extension at a boundary face), then extract a finite diagonal subsequence and sum the localized limits. Hence $K:=A_D^{-1}(Q-q)$ is compact on $H_0^1(M)$.

For $w\in H_0^1(M)$, $(I-K)w=0$ is equivalent, after applying $A$, to $(-\Delta_g+q)w=0$. The latter has only the zero solution by hypothesis, so $I-K$ is injective. By [F4], $I-K$ is boundedly invertible. This gives a unique weak zero-trace solution for every bounded functional on $H_0^1(M)$, in particular for every $F\in L^2(M)$ after subtracting any fixed boundary lift.

A finite collection of flattened boundary charts, the collar neighborhood, and [F5] give a bounded extension $E:H^{1/2}(\partial M)\to H^1(M)$ with trace $f$. Set $u=Ef+w$ and solve for $w\in H_0^1(M)$ with weak right-hand-side functional $z\mapsto\int_MF\bar z\,dV_g-a_q(Ef,z)$ by step 2.1. This proves existence for the stated data. The difference of any two solutions has zero trace and lies in the assumed trivial kernel, proving uniqueness.

First take zero boundary data and $F\in L^2$. In each interior chart the operator has smooth uniformly elliptic divergence-form coefficients $|g|^{1/2}g^{ij}$; in each boundary chart the collar flattens the boundary and the pulled-back coefficients remain smooth and uniformly elliptic. Applying the $m=0$ case of [F6] to localized zero-trace equations gives $u\in H^2$ and the estimate with the additional $L^2$ term. If $f$ is smooth, extend it smoothly in a boundary collar by keeping its chart representative constant in the normal variable near the boundary and multiplying by a cutoff; a finite partition patches these extensions to a smooth $Ef$. Then $w=u-Ef$ has zero trace and solves an equation with smooth datum, so the same local estimates apply to $w$.

If $u\in H^{k+1}$ and $F\in H^k$, differentiating the localized zero-trace equation $k$ times leaves the same uniformly elliptic principal part; each commutator contains a bounded derivative of a smooth coefficient and a derivative of $u$ of order at most $k+1$, so it belongs to $L^2$. Tangential derivatives retain zero trace. Applying [F6] at order $k$ on each boundary patch and the corresponding interior estimate gives $u\in H^{k+2}$ and $\|u\|_{H^{k+2}}\leq C_k(\|F\|_{H^k}+\|u\|_{L^2})$. The bounded inverse in step 2.1 controls $\|u\|_{H^1}$ by $\|F\|_{L^2}$ for zero trace; hence the local estimate and this inverse bound give $\|u\|_{H^{k+2}}\leq C_k\|F\|_{H^k}$. Induction gives the claimed zero-trace estimate; for smooth nonzero $f$ apply the same induction to $u-Ef$.

Define $H^{1/2}(\partial M)$ by the fixed finite boundary atlas and partition of unity, using the Euclidean fractional Slobodeckij space $W^{1/2,2}(\mathbb R^{n-1})$ for each localized representative. Define $H^{-1/2}(\partial M)$ as the continuous dual of $H^{1/2}(\partial M)$ with the Riemannian boundary density pairing. These are the fixed-atlas norms used on this page; no atlas-independence assertion is part of this definition.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$, be a
bounded $C^1$ domain and $1\le p<\infty$. Then the kernel of the trace
operator of [[thm-lp-trace-operator-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]] equals the
zero-boundary Sobolev space:
$$\{u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K):Tu=0\}=W_0^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K),$$
the $W^{1,p}$-closure of $C_c^\infty(\Omega)$
([[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]]).

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $(M,g)$ be a compact connected smooth Riemannian domain with nonempty smooth boundary and no orientability assumption, and let $\gamma\in C^\infty(M,\mathbb R)$ satisfy $\gamma>0$. There is a constant $C_P>0$ such that $\|w\|_{L^2(M)}\leq C_P\|
abla_gw\|_{L^2(M)}$ for every $w\in H_0^1(M)$. For every $h\in L^2(M)$ and $f\in H^{1/2}(\partial M)$ there is a unique $v\in H^1(M)$ with trace $f$ satisfying $\int_M\gamma\,g(
abla_gv,
abla_g\overline z)\,dV_g=-\int_Mh\overline z\,dV_g$ for every $z\in H_0^1(M)$. If $h$ and $f$ are smooth, this weak solution is smooth up to the boundary.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $(M,g)$ be a compact smooth Riemannian domain with smooth boundary and no orientability assumption, let $q\in C^\infty(M,\mathbb R)$, and suppose the only $w\in H_0^1(M)$ satisfying $(-\Delta_g+q)w=0$ weakly is $w=0$. For every $F\in L^2(M)$ and $f\in H^{1/2}(\partial M)$ there is a unique weak solution $u\in H^1(M)$ of $(-\Delta_g+q)u=F$ with trace $f$. If $f=0$, $F\in H^m(M)$ and $m\geq0$ is an integer, then $u\in H^{m+2}(M)$ and $\|u\|_{H^{m+2}}\leq C_m\|F\|_{H^m}$. If $F$ and $f$ are smooth, this solution belongs to $H^m(M)$ for every integer $m\geq0$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$, be a
bounded $C^1$ domain, $1<p<\infty$, $p'=p/(p-1)$,
$u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$, $v\in W^{1,p'}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$, and let
$T$ be the trace of [[thm-lp-trace-operator-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]] with
$\nu$ the outward normal of
[[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]]. Then for
every $i=1,\dots,n$,
$$\int_\Omega u\,\partial_iv\,dx=-\int_\Omega(\partial_iu)v\,dx+\int_{\partial\Omega}(Tu)(Tv)\,\nu_i\,dS,$$
and all three integrals are finite. If $u,v\in C^1(\overline\Omega)$, the
boundary term is the classical $\int_{\partial\Omega}uv\,\nu_i\,dS$ of the
divergence theorem
[[thm-divergence-theorem-for-bounded-c-one-euclidean-domains]] applied to the
field $uv\,e_i$; if in addition $Tu=\partial_\nu w$ on $\partial\Omega$ for a specified $w\in C^1(\overline\Omega)$, the boundary term is $\int_{\partial\Omega}(\partial_\nu w)(Tv)\nu_i\,dS$. The normal derivative of [[def-classical-normal-derivative]] is defined on the boundary, and this extra identity is an assumption, not an interior substitution.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$, be a
bounded $C^1$ domain, $1<p<\infty$, $\theta=1-1/p$, and let $T$ be the trace
operator of [[thm-lp-trace-operator-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]]. Then there is
a bounded linear operator
$$R:W^{\theta,p}(\partial\Omega;\mathbb K)\longrightarrow W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$$
with $T\circ R=\mathrm{id}_{W^{\theta,p}(\partial\Omega)}$ and
$\|Rg\|_{W^{1,p}(\Omega)}\le C(\Omega,p)\|g\|_{W^{\theta,p}(\partial\Omega)}$.
Moreover, for every open neighbourhood $U$ of $\partial\Omega$ in
$\mathbb R^n$ there is such an operator $R_U$ whose image is contained in the
classes vanishing a.e. outside $U$, with
$\|R_Ug\|_{W^{1,p}(\Omega)}\le C(\Omega,p,U)\|g\|_{W^{\theta,p}(\partial\Omega)}$.
The right inverse is not unique and no canonical choice is claimed.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$, be a
bounded $C^1$ domain, $1\le p<\infty$, and let $T$ be the trace operator of
[[thm-lp-trace-operator-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]].

(i) If $\eta\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$, then
$T(\eta u)=(\eta|_{\partial\Omega})\,Tu$ in $L^p(\partial\Omega)$ for every
$u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$, and

$\partial\Omega\cap\partial\Omega'$ is relatively open in $\partial\Omega$,
then $(Tu)|_{\partial\Omega\cap\partial\Omega'}=T_{\Omega'}(u|_{\Omega'})$
a.e. for every $u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega)$, where $T_{\Omega'}$ is the trace
operator relative to $\Omega'$; in particular the trace is local and
compatible with restrictions to subdomains.

(iii) If a boundary chart $\Phi$ flattens a neighbourhood of a boundary point,
then for $u$ supported in a compact ambient patch inside that chart the transported trace
equals $T_+$ of the zero-extended flattened function after reflecting $t\mapsto-t$ and the corresponding boundary $L^p$ norms
agree up to the chart Jacobian.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$, be a
bounded $C^1$ domain in the graph sense of
[[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]], let $\partial\Omega$ carry the
chart-independent surface measure of
[[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]] and
[[lem-surface-integral-is-independent-of-c-one-boundary-charts]], let

unique bounded linear operator
$$T:W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)\longrightarrow L^p(\partial\Omega;\mathbb K)$$
with $Tu=u|_{\partial\Omega}$ for every
$u\in C(\overline\Omega)\cap W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$, and it satisfies
$\|Tu\|_{L^p(\partial\Omega)}\le C(\Omega,p)\|u\|_{W^{1,p}(\Omega)}$. On each
boundary chart the operator is the flat half-space trace of
[[thm-trace-estimate-on-the-half-space]] transported by the flattening

holds because two bounded operators agreeing on the dense subspace
$C(\overline\Omega)\cap W^{1,p}(\Omega)$ are equal.

derivations.claim: Their difference $W=V_h^{(1)}-V_h^{(2)}$ has zero trace. Localize $W$ by the fixed finite partition in [F1]. On each boundary chart, [F7] shows that the localized function has zero Euclidean trace after flattening; [F2] then approximates it in $H^1$ by compactly supported interior smooth functions. On interior charts, ordinary compactly supported mollification gives the same approximation. Pulling back and summing the finitely many approximations shows $W\in H_0^1(M)$.

For the conductivity pairing, [F3] gives $\int_M\gamma\,g(
abla_gv_f,
abla_g\overline W)\,dV_g=0$, since $W\in H_0^1(M)$. Therefore replacing $V_h^{(1)}$ by $V_h^{(2)}$ changes the displayed pairing by zero. For the Schrödinger pairing, the same argument with the weak equation in [F4] gives $\int_M(g(
abla_gu_f,
abla_g\overline W)+qu_f\overline W)\,dV_g=0$. Thus both definitions are independent of the chosen extension and are well-defined.

By [F3] and [F4], smooth boundary data yield solutions smooth up to $\partial M$. For smooth test data $h$, choose a smooth collar extension $V_h$ by [F8]. In a boundary chart, write $\operatorname{div}_g(\gamma\nabla_gv)=|g|^{-1/2}\partial_i(|g|^{1/2}\gamma g^{ij}\partial_jv)$ and $\Delta_gu=|g|^{-1/2}\partial_i(|g|^{1/2}g^{ij}\partial_ju)$. Apply the Euclidean Gauss-Green identity [F5] to the coordinate fluxes; summing over the finite partition gives the Riemannian boundary flux, while artificial chart boundaries cancel and the density transforms to $dS_g$. For the conductivity equation it yields
$$\langle\Lambda_\gamma f,h\rangle=\int_{\partial M}\gamma\,\partial_{\nu_{\rm out}}v_f\,\overline h\,dS_g,$$
since $\operatorname{div}_g(\gamma\nabla_gv_f)=0$. For the Schrödinger equation it yields
$$\langle\Lambda_qf,h\rangle=\int_{\partial M}\partial_{\nu_{\rm out}}u_f\,\overline h\,dS_g,$$
since $(-\Delta_g+q)u_f=0$. The extensions required for the weak pairings exist by [F6], and smooth test extensions exist by [F8].

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice.

Let $(M,g)$ be a compact smooth Riemannian manifold with smooth boundary, with no orientability assumption. Fix a finite smooth atlas of interior and boundary charts and a smooth partition of unity subordinate to it. For an integer $k\geq0$, define $H^k(M)$ as the completion of $C^\infty(M)$ in the sum of the Euclidean $W^{k,2}$ norms of the localized coordinate representatives; derivatives in a boundary chart are taken on the corresponding half-space. Define $H_0^1(M)$ as the closure of $C_c^\infty(M^\circ)$ in $H^1(M)$. Define $H^{1/2}(\partial M)$ by the fixed finite boundary atlas and partition of unity, using the Euclidean fractional Slobodeckij space $W^{1/2,2}(\mathbb R^{n-1})$ for each localized representative. Define $H^{-1/2}(\partial M)$ as the continuous dual of $H^{1/2}(\partial M)$ with the Riemannian boundary density pairing. These are the fixed-atlas norms used on this page; no atlas-independence assertion is part of this definition.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $(M,g)$ be a compact connected smooth Riemannian domain with nonempty smooth boundary and no orientability assumption, and let $\gamma\in C^\infty(M,\mathbb R)$ satisfy $\gamma>0$. There is a constant $C_P>0$ such that $\|w\|_{L^2(M)}\leq C_P\|
abla_gw\|_{L^2(M)}$ for every $w\in H_0^1(M)$. For every $h\in L^2(M)$ and $f\in H^{1/2}(\partial M)$ there is a unique $v\in H^1(M)$ with trace $f$ satisfying $\int_M\gamma\,g(
abla_gv,
abla_g\overline z)\,dV_g=-\int_Mh\overline z\,dV_g$ for every $z\in H_0^1(M)$. If $h$ and $f$ are smooth, this weak solution is smooth up to the boundary.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $(M,g)$ be a compact smooth Riemannian domain with smooth boundary and no orientability assumption, let $q\in C^\infty(M,\mathbb R)$, and suppose the only $w\in H_0^1(M)$ satisfying $(-\Delta_g+q)w=0$ weakly is $w=0$. For every $F\in L^2(M)$ and $f\in H^{1/2}(\partial M)$ there is a unique weak solution $u\in H^1(M)$ of $(-\Delta_g+q)u=F$ with trace $f$. If $f=0$, $F\in H^m(M)$ and $m\geq0$ is an integer, then $u\in H^{m+2}(M)$ and $\|u\|_{H^{m+2}}\leq C_m\|F\|_{H^m}$. If $F$ and $f$ are smooth, this solution belongs to $H^m(M)$ for every integer $m\geq0$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $n\ge2$, let $\Omega$ be a bounded $W^{k,p}$-extension domain, $k\ge1$ and $1\le p<\infty$ with $kp>n$. Then there is $C(n,p,k,\Omega)$ with
$$\|uv\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}\le C\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}\|v\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}\qquad(u,v\in W^{k,p}(\Omega)),$$
so $W^{k,p}(\Omega)$ is a Banach algebra; the constants and the conclusion may depend on the choice of equivalent Sobolev norm only through $C$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $n\ge2$, let $\Omega$ be a bounded $W^{k,p}$-extension domain, $k\ge1$ and $1\le p<\infty$. Let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and $u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Then:

1. if $kp<n$, $\|u\|_{L^q(\Omega)}\le C\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$ for every $q$ with $\frac1q\ge\frac1p-\frac kn$ (equivalently $1\le q\le\frac{np}{n-kp}$);
2. if $kp=n$, $\|u\|_{L^q(\Omega)}\le C(q)\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$ for every finite $q$;
3. if $kp>n$, then for every integer $m\ge0$ and every $0<\alpha<1$ with $m+\alpha<k-\frac np$ there is a representative in $C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$ with $\|u\|_{C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)}\le C\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$; when $k-\frac np\notin\mathbb Z$ one may take $m=\lfloor k-\frac np\rfloor$ and $\alpha=k-\frac np-m$.

Here $C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$ uses the continuous derivatives of the constructed representative on an ambient neighbourhood of $\overline\Omega$, with norm
$$\|g\|_{C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)}:=\sum_{|\beta|\le m}\sup_{\overline\Omega}|D^\beta g|+\sum_{|\beta|=m}\sup_{\substack{x,y\in\overline\Omega\\x\ne y}}\frac{|D^\beta g(x)-D^\beta g(y)|}{|x-y|^\alpha}.$$
For $\Omega=\varnothing$ set these norm values to $0$. The proof supplies such an ambient representative, so no boundary differentiability or regularity of $\partial\Omega$ is assumed.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $X$, $Y$, $Z$ be real
Banach spaces, let $U \subseteq X \times Y$ be open for the product metric, let
$F : U \to Z$ be of class $C^k$ with $k \ge 1$
([[def-c-k-map-between-banach-spaces]]), and let $(a,b) \in U$ with
$F(a,b) = 0$. Let $D_XF(a,b) := DF(a,b)\circ i_X$ and
$D_YF(a,b) := DF(a,b)\circ i_Y$ be the partial derivatives, where
$i_X(x) := (x,0)$ and $i_Y(y) := (0,y)$. If $D_YF(a,b) : Y \to Z$ is a bounded
linear isomorphism, then there are open neighbourhoods $A \subseteq X$ of $a$
and $B \subseteq Y$ of $b$ and a unique map $g : A \to B$ of class $C^k$ such
that

$$\{\,(x,y) \in A \times B : F(x,y) = 0\,\} = \{\,(x,g(x)) : x \in A\,\},$$

and along the graph $Dg$ satisfies
$$Dg(x) = -\,D_YF\bigl(x,g(x)\bigr)^{-1}\,D_XF\bigl(x,g(x)\bigr) \qquad (x \in A).$$
In particular $g(a) = b$.
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every smooth manifold with boundary has a smooth collar.

derivations.claim: For $q=0$, the Dirichlet kernel of $-\Delta_g$ is trivial: if $w\in H_0^1(M)$ is weakly harmonic, testing with $w$ gives $\int_M|\nabla w|^2dV_g=0$, and the zero-trace Poincare inequality in [F2] gives $w=0$. Thus [F3] supplies the zero-boundary inverse $G=(-\Delta_g)^{-1}:H^{s-2}(M)\to X_s$, where $X_s=\{w\in H^s(M):w\in H_0^1(M)\}$. The high-order estimate in [F3], together with its bounded $H^1$ inverse, makes $G$ bounded.

Since $s>n/2+2$, [F4] makes $H^s(M)$ an algebra by localizing to finitely many smooth charts, extending each localized representative to a bounded Euclidean chart domain, applying the Euclidean algebra estimate, and summing the finite norms. Thus the map $(\epsilon,w)\mapsto q(Ef_\epsilon+w)^3$ is a continuous polynomial from $\mathbb R^m\times X_s$ into $H^{s-2}(M)$, where $f_\epsilon=\sum_j\epsilon_jh_j$ and $Ef_\epsilon$ is the smooth collar extension from [F7]. Define
$$\mathcal F(\epsilon,w)=w-G\big[\Delta_g(Ef_\epsilon)-q(Ef_\epsilon+w)^3\big]\in X_s.$$
It is $C^3$ (indeed polynomial plus bounded linear maps) and $\mathcal F(0,0)=0$.

At $(0,0)$, the derivative $D_w\mathcal F(0,0)$ is the identity on $X_s$, because the derivative of $u\mapsto q u^3$ at $u=0$ vanishes. By [F6], there is a neighborhood of $\epsilon=0$ and a unique $C^3$ map $w(\epsilon)\in X_s$ near zero such that $\mathcal F(\epsilon,w(\epsilon))=0$. The fixed-point equation is exactly $-\Delta_g(Ef_\epsilon+w)+q(Ef_\epsilon+w)^3=0$ with boundary trace $f_\epsilon$, so $u_\epsilon=Ef_\epsilon+w(\epsilon)$ gives the unique small solution.

By [F5], $u_\epsilon\in C^2(\overline M)$ and the outward normal derivative has a continuous boundary trace. The trace map from $C^1(\overline M)$ to $C^0(\partial M)$ is bounded in the chartwise norms, so composing the $C^3$ map $\epsilon\mapsto u_\epsilon$ with this bounded linear trace of $\partial_{\nu_{\rm out}}$ proves $C^3$ dependence of the nonlinear DN data.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable) has a choice function.

A transversally anisotropic product domain of dimension $n\geq3$ is a compact connected smooth $n$-dimensional Riemannian domain $(M,g)$ with smooth boundary, together with a compact connected smooth $(n-1)$-dimensional Riemannian manifold with boundary $(M_0,g_0)$ and an isometric embedding of $(M,g)$ as a smooth domain compactly contained in $(\mathbb R\times M_0^\circ,dx_1^2\oplus g_0)$. The coordinate $x_1$ on $\mathbb R$ is the distinguished Euclidean coordinate; $M_0$ is the transversal manifold. All Laplacians use $\Delta_g=\operatorname{div}_g\nabla_g$. Neither $M$ nor $M_0$ is assumed orientable. A positive smooth conformal factor is not included in this definition; claims using a conformally related metric must state and prove the required conformal transformation separately.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $(M,g)$ be a transversally anisotropic product domain, let $q\in C^\infty(\overline M,\mathbb R)$, and let $\varphi=\sigma x_1$ for $\sigma\in\{-1,1\}$. For $0<h\leq h_0$ define
$$P_{\varphi,h,q}=e^{\varphi/h}h^2(-\Delta_g+q)e^{-\varphi/h}.$$
There is a constant $C$ such that every $w\in C_c^\infty(M^\circ)$ satisfies
$$\|w\|_{L^2(M)}\leq Ch^{-1}\|P_{\varphi,h,q}w\|_{L^2(M)}.$$
Moreover, for every $F\in L^2(M)$ there is an $R\in L^2(M)$ solving $P_{\varphi,h,q}R=F$ in distributions on $M^\circ$ and satisfying
$$\|R\|_{L^2(M)}\leq Ch^{-1}\|F\|_{L^2(M)}.$$
No boundary trace is prescribed for $R$.

For a smooth real function $f$, its **Riemannian gradient** is $\operatorname{grad}_g f=(df)^\sharp$.

[[prop-exterior-derivative-of-a-function-is-its-differential]] identifies $df(X)=Xf$. The smooth bundle isomorphism in [[thm-the-musical-maps-are-smooth-inverse-bundle-isomorphisms]] therefore makes the gradient a smooth vector field. In coordinates $(\operatorname{grad}_g f)^i=\sum_jg^{ij}\partial_jf$. Constants, and all functions in dimension zero, have zero gradient.

Let $(M,g)$ be a Riemannian manifold, possibly with boundary, and let
$f:M\to\mathbb R$ be smooth. At each interior point, the
**Laplace–Beltrami operator** of $g$ is defined by the metric trace of the Hessian,
$$\Delta_gf(p):=\operatorname{tr}_g(\operatorname{Hess}f)_p:=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{Hess}f(e_i,e_i),$$
where $n=\dim M$ and $e_1,\dots,e_n$ is any $g_p$-orthonormal basis of $T_pM$; the
trace of a bilinear form with respect to a positive-definite inner product does not
depend on that choice, so $\Delta_gf$ is well-defined and smooth in the interior;
when $f$ is smooth up to the boundary, it has the usual one-sided extension there.
Here
$\operatorname{Hess}f(X,Y)=g(\nabla_X\operatorname{grad}f,Y)$ is the Levi-Civita
Hessian of
[[prop-gradient-hessian-and-divergence-connection-formulas]].

Equivalently, and with the **positive-divergence convention** of this library,
$$\Delta_gf=\operatorname{div}_g(\operatorname{grad}f),$$
where $\operatorname{div}_gX=\operatorname{tr}(v\mapsto\nabla_vX)$ is the Riemannian
divergence of [[def-riemannian-divergence]] as computed in
[[prop-gradient-hessian-and-divergence-connection-formulas]]. The equivalence is the
pointwise computation
$$\sum_i\operatorname{Hess}f(e_i,e_i)=\sum_i g(\nabla_{e_i}\operatorname{grad}f,e_i)=\operatorname{tr}(v\mapsto\nabla_v\operatorname{grad}f),$$
the middle sum being the endomorphism trace of $v\mapsto\nabla_v\operatorname{grad}f$
in the orthonormal basis $(e_i)$, which the same supplier identifies with
$\operatorname{div}_g(\operatorname{grad}f)$; no local coordinates are needed and no
analytic regularity beyond the smoothness of $f$ is used. On a zero-dimensional manifold
both sides are the empty sum $0$, and on a manifold with boundary the operator is defined
at interior points, with the usual one-sided extension at boundary points when $f$ is
smooth up to the boundary.

**This definition is the pointwise geometric operator only.** It records the trace
formula, the divergence form and the sign convention
$\Delta_g=\operatorname{div}_g\circ\operatorname{grad}$ fixed by
[[def-riemannian-divergence]]. It does not assert any analytic conclusion about
harmonic functions on manifolds — no maximum principle, no Harnack inequality, no
boundary-value solvability, no spectral theory, and no Liouville theorem. Those are
separate results with their own hypotheses, and their Euclidean forms are not licensed
on a general Riemannian manifold merely by writing down this definition.

derivations.claim:
Put $\Phi=x_1+i\psi$. By [F1] and $|d\psi|_{g_0}=1$,
$$g(d\Phi,d\Phi)=1+i^2|d\psi|_{g_0}^2=0.$$
Direct conjugation gives
$$(-\Delta_g+q)(e^{-\tau\Phi}a) =e^{-\tau\Phi}\left[\tau^2g(d\Phi,d\Phi)a+ \tau\left(2g(\nabla_g\Phi,\nabla_ga)+(\Delta_g\Phi)a\right) +(-\Delta_g+q)a\right].$$
The $\tau^2$ term vanishes by the eikonal equality, and the coefficient of $\tau$ is exactly the transport equation in the statement. Hence the residual is $e^{-\tau\Phi}(-\Delta_g+q)a$.

Set $h=\tau^{-1}$ and conjugate by the real weight $e^{-\tau x_1}$. The equation for the correction is
$$P_{x_1,h,q}r_\tau=-h^2e^{-i\tau\psi}(-\Delta_g+q)a.$$
The right side is in $L^2$ and has norm $h^2\|(-\Delta_g+q)a\|_2$. By [F4]--[F5], with the equation divided by $h^2$, there is an $H^1$ correction (and hence a distributional) $r_\tau\in L^2(M)$ with
$$\|r_\tau\|_2\leq Ch^{-1}h^2\|(-\Delta_g+q)a\|_2 =C\tau^{-1}\|(-\Delta_g+q)a\|_2.$$
Thus the asserted remainder estimate and the equation hold distributionally.

Choose the $H^1$ correction from step 1.2. Multiplication by the smooth exponentials preserves $H^1(M)$ for each fixed $\tau$, and the correction equation cancels the residual computed in step 1.1. Thus $u_\tau$ is exact, has the stated remainder bound, and has no imposed correction boundary value. The additional boundary regularity is the external input [F4], rather than a consequence asserted for the $L^2$ solver [F2].

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice.

Let $(M,g)$ be a nonempty compact connected smooth Riemannian domain with nonempty smooth boundary. For a real-valued $\gamma\in C^\infty(M)$ with $\gamma(x)>0$ at every $x\in M$, let $v_f\in H^1(M)$ be the unique weak solution of $\operatorname{div}_g(\gamma\nabla_gv_f)=0$ with trace $f\in H^{1/2}(\partial M)$, whose existence is supplied by the positive-conductivity solvability lemma. Define the full-data physical conductivity Dirichlet-to-Neumann map $\Lambda_\gamma:H^{1/2}(\partial M)\to H^{-1/2}(\partial M)$ by
$$\langle\Lambda_\gamma f,h\rangle=\int_M\gamma\,g(\nabla_gv_f,\nabla_g\overline{V_h})\,dV_g,$$
where $V_h\in H^1(M)$ is any extension of $h\in H^{1/2}(\partial M)$. The weak equation makes this value independent of the extension. For smooth data, $\Lambda_\gamma f=\gamma\partial_{\nu_{\rm out}}v_f|_{\partial M}$; this is the full physical flux convention. When $M=\overline\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ with the Euclidean metric, this is the scalar Euclidean conductivity DN map.

For a real $q\in C^\infty(M)$ such that the only $w\in H_0^1(M)$ satisfying $(-\Delta_g+q)w=0$ weakly is $w=0$, let $u_f\in H^1(M)$ be the unique weak solution of $(-\Delta_g+q)u_f=0$ with trace $f$, whose existence follows from the nonresonant regularity lemma. Define the Schrödinger DN map $\Lambda_q:H^{1/2}(\partial M)\to H^{-1/2}(\partial M)$ by
$$\langle\Lambda_qf,h\rangle=\int_M\big(g(\nabla_gu_f,\nabla_g\overline{V_h})+qu_f\overline{V_h}\big)\,dV_g.$$
For smooth data this is $\partial_{\nu_{\rm out}}u_f|_{\partial M}$. Equality of these operators means equality on all of $H^{1/2}(\partial M)$, not equality for a restricted set of boundary inputs.

abla_gw\|_{L^2(M)}$ for every $w\in H_0^1(M)$. For every $h\in L^2(M)$ and $f\in H^{1/2}(\partial M)$ there is a unique $v\in H^1(M)$ with trace $f$ satisfying $\int_M\gamma\,g(
abla_gv,
abla_g\overline z)\,dV_g=-\int_Mh\overline z\,dV_g$ for every $z\in H_0^1(M)$. If $h$ and $f$ are smooth, this weak solution is smooth up to the boundary.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $(M,g)$ be a compact smooth Riemannian domain with smooth boundary and no orientability assumption, let $q\in C^\infty(M,\mathbb R)$, and suppose the only $w\in H_0^1(M)$ satisfying $(-\Delta_g+q)w=0$ weakly is $w=0$. The matrix is that of [[prop-coordinate-criterion-for-a-riemannian-metric]], so its determinant is positive and smooth. derivations.claim: Write $a_{\gamma_j}(v,w)=\int_M\gamma_jg(\nabla v,\nabla\bar w)\,dV_g$. By [F1], $\langle\Lambda_{\gamma_1}f_1,f_2\rangle=a_{\gamma_1}(u_1,u_2)$, since $u_2$ is an extension of $f_2$. Let $\widetilde u_1$ solve the $\gamma_2$ equation with boundary value $f_1$, which exists by [F2]. Then $\langle\Lambda_{\gamma_2}f_1,f_2\rangle=a_{\gamma_2}(\widetilde u_1,u_2)$. Since $u_1-\widetilde u_1\in H_0^1(M)$ and $u_2$ solves the $\gamma_2$ weak equation, Hermitian symmetry gives $a_{\gamma_2}(u_1-\widetilde u_1,u_2)=\overline{a_{\gamma_2}(u_2,u_1-\widetilde u_1)}=0$. Write $a_{q_j}(v,w)=\int_M(g(\nabla v,\nabla\bar w)+q_jv\bar w)\,dV_g$. By [F1], $\langle\Lambda_{q_1}f_1,f_2\rangle=a_{q_1}(u_1,u_2)$ because $u_2$ extends $f_2$. Subtract the identities in step 2.1. The gradient terms cancel and the remaining volume term is $\int_M(q_1-q_2)u_1\overline{u_2}\,dV_g$, which proves the Schrödinger identity.

when $f$ is smooth up to the boundary, it has the usual one-sided extension there.
Here
$\operatorname{Hess}f(X,Y)=g(\nabla_X\operatorname{grad}f,Y)$ is the Levi-Civita
Hessian of
[[prop-gradient-hessian-and-divergence-connection-formulas]].

Equivalently, and with the **positive-divergence convention** of this library,
$$\Delta_gf=\operatorname{div}_g(\operatorname{grad}f),$$
where $\operatorname{div}_gX=\operatorname{tr}(v\mapsto\nabla_vX)$ is the Riemannian
divergence of [[def-riemannian-divergence]] as computed in
[[prop-gradient-hessian-and-divergence-connection-formulas]]. The equivalence is the
pointwise computation
$$\sum_i\operatorname{Hess}f(e_i,e_i)=\sum_i g(\nabla_{e_i}\operatorname{grad}f,e_i)=\operatorname{tr}(v\mapsto\nabla_v\operatorname{grad}f),$$
the middle sum being the endomorphism trace of $v\mapsto\nabla_v\operatorname{grad}f$
in the orthonormal basis $(e_i)$, which the same supplier identifies with
$\operatorname{div}_g(\operatorname{grad}f)$; no local coordinates are needed and no
analytic regularity beyond the smoothness of $f$ is used. On a zero-dimensional manifold
both sides are the empty sum $0$, and on a manifold with boundary the operator is defined
at interior points, with the usual one-sided extension at boundary points when $f$ is
smooth up to the boundary.

**This definition is the pointwise geometric operator only.** It records the trace
formula, the divergence form and the sign convention
$\Delta_g=\operatorname{div}_g\circ\operatorname{grad}$ fixed by
[[def-riemannian-divergence]]. It does not assert any analytic conclusion about
harmonic functions on manifolds — no maximum principle, no Harnack inequality, no
boundary-value solvability, no spectral theory, and no Liouville theorem. Those are
separate results with their own hypotheses, and their Euclidean forms are not licensed
on a general Riemannian manifold merely by writing down this definition.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$, be a
bounded $C^1$ domain, $1<p<\infty$, $p'=p/(p-1)$,
$u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$, $v\in W^{1,p'}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$, and let
$T$ be the trace of [[thm-lp-trace-operator-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]] with
$\nu$ the outward normal of
[[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]]. Then for
every $i=1,\dots,n$,
$$\int_\Omega u\,\partial_iv\,dx=-\int_\Omega(\partial_iu)v\,dx+\int_{\partial\Omega}(Tu)(Tv)\,\nu_i\,dS,$$
and all three integrals are finite. If $u,v\in C^1(\overline\Omega)$, the
boundary term is the classical $\int_{\partial\Omega}uv\,\nu_i\,dS$ of the
divergence theorem
[[thm-divergence-theorem-for-bounded-c-one-euclidean-domains]] applied to the
field $uv\,e_i$; if in addition $Tu=\partial_\nu w$ on $\partial\Omega$ for a specified $w\in C^1(\overline\Omega)$, the boundary term is $\int_{\partial\Omega}(\partial_\nu w)(Tv)\nu_i\,dS$. The normal derivative of [[def-classical-normal-derivative]] is defined on the boundary, and this extra identity is an assumption, not an interior substitution.

derivations.claim: Differentiate $-\Delta_g u_\epsilon+q u_\epsilon^3=0$ once in $\epsilon_j$ at $\epsilon=0$. Since $u_0=0$, the derivative $v_j=\partial_{\epsilon_j}u_\epsilon|_0$ solves $-\Delta_gv_j=0$ with trace $h_j$. Differentiating twice in distinct parameters gives $-\Delta_g(\partial_{\epsilon_i}\partial_{\epsilon_j}u_\epsilon|_0)=0$ with zero trace, so this second derivative vanishes by [F2].

The third mixed derivative of $u_\epsilon^3$ at zero has exactly the six permutations of $v_1v_2v_3$, hence equals $6v_1v_2v_3$; all other chain-rule terms contain $u_0$ or one of the vanishing second derivatives from step 1.1. Differentiating the equation gives $-\Delta_gw_{123}+6qv_1v_2v_3=0$, with zero boundary trace. By [F1], the third derivative of the nonlinear DN data is $\partial_{\nu_{\rm out}}w_{123}|_{\partial M}$.

Since $v_4$ is harmonic and $w_{123}$ has zero trace, chartwise Green's formula and a finite partition of unity give
$$\int_{\partial M}(\partial_{\nu_{\rm out}}w_{123})\overline{h_4}\,dS_g =\int_M(\Delta_gw_{123})\overline{v_4}\,dV_g.$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable) has a choice function.

Let $(M,g)$ be a compact, connected, nonempty smooth two-dimensional Riemannian manifold with smooth boundary. For $x\in\partial M$, let $\nu_{\mathrm{out}}(x)$ be the outward unit normal. The boundary is **strictly convex** if
$$
g(\nabla_w\nu_{\mathrm{out}},w)>0
$$
for every $x\in\partial M$ and every nonzero $w\in T_x\partial M$. A **Jacobi field** along a unit-speed geodesic $\gamma$ is a smooth vector field $J$ along $\gamma$ satisfying
$$
D_t^2J+R(J,\dot\gamma)\dot\gamma=0,
$$
where $R(X,Y)Z=\nabla_X\nabla_YZ-\nabla_Y\nabla_XZ-\nabla_{[X,Y]}Z$. The manifold has **no conjugate points** if, on every unit-speed geodesic segment $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$, a Jacobi field with $J(a)=J(b)=0$ must be identically zero. It is **nontrapping** if every maximal unit-speed geodesic starting in $M^\circ$ reaches $\partial M$ in finite forward and backward time. The pair $(M,g)$ is a **simple surface** if its boundary is strictly convex, it has no conjugate points, and it is nontrapping.

The unit tangent bundle is $SM=\{(x,v):x\in M,\ v\in T_xM,\ g_x(v,v)=1\}$. Write $\nu_{\mathrm{in}}=-\nu_{\mathrm{out}}$ and
$$
\partial_+SM=\{(x,v)\in SM:x\in\partial M,\ g_x(v,\nu_{\mathrm{in}})>0\}
$$
for inward-pointing unit boundary vectors. For $(x,v)\in\partial_+SM$, let $\gamma_{x,v}$ be the unit-speed geodesic with $\gamma_{x,v}(0)=x$ and $\dot\gamma_{x,v}(0)=v$, and let $\tau_+(x,v)$ be its first positive exit time from $M$. For $f\in C^\infty(M)$, its scalar **geodesic X-ray transform** is the function on $\partial_+SM$ defined by
$$
I_0f(x,v)=\int_0^{\tau_+(x,v)} f(\gamma_{x,v}(t))\,dt.
$$
The geodesic equation is interpreted up to first boundary exit; local smooth extensions of the metric are used only to solve the coordinate ODE at boundary initial data.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice.

Let $(M,g)$ be a transversally anisotropic product domain, let $q\in C^\infty(\overline M,\mathbb R)$, and let $\psi\in C^\infty$ be real on a neighborhood of the transversal projection of $M$, with $|d\psi|_{g_0}=1$. Suppose $a\in C^\infty(\overline M,\mathbb C)$ satisfies
$$2\partial_{x_1}a+2i\,g_0(\nabla_{g_0}\psi,\nabla_{g_0}a)+i(\Delta_{g_0}\psi)a=0.$$
Then, for all sufficiently large $\tau$, there is an exact solution
$$u_\tau=e^{-\tau(x_1+i\psi)}a+e^{-\tau x_1}r_\tau,\qquad (-\Delta_g+q)u_\tau=0\ \text{in }M^\circ,$$
with $r_\tau\in H^1(M)$ and $\|r_\tau\|_{L^2(M)}\leq C\tau^{-1}\|(-\Delta_g+q)a\|_{L^2(M)}$. No boundary value is prescribed for $r_\tau$.

derivations.claim: At $p$, choose two distinct non-tangential unit directions. Strict convexity and nontrapping extend them to maximal boundary-to-boundary segments. They meet transversely at $p$. If they met again at a distinct point $z$, the two different subsegments from $p$ to $z$ would violate uniqueness of geodesics on a simple surface. Thus the only intersection is $p$.

Fix unit tangent vectors $e_1,e_2$ at the crossing and their normal linear forms $\ell_1,\ell_2$ on the tangent plane. Their determinant has absolute value $|\sin\angle(e_1,e_2)|$. The normalized Gaussian
$$\frac{\tau}{\pi}e^{-\tau(\ell_1(y)^2+\ell_2(y)^2)}$$
has integral $c=|\sin\angle(e_1,e_2)|^{-1}>0$, by the linear substitution $z_j=\sqrt\tau\,\ell_j(y)$. Choose this unit Gaussian normalization for the constant in the statement. This calculation fixes $c$ and does not claim estimates for any exact-solution beam remainders.

Put $T=c\int_{I_p}e^{-i\xi x_1}Q(x_1,p)\,dx_1$, which is finite because $M$ is compact and $Q$ is bounded. If $Q=0$, four constant harmonic functions give the assertion. Otherwise [F3], by contraposition, gives smooth harmonic functions $w_1,w_2,w_3,w_4$ with $S=\int_M Qw_1w_2w_3w_4\,dV\ne0$. For every $\tau$ set
$$u_{\tau,1}^+=(T/S)w_1,\quad u_{\tau,1}^-=w_2,\quad u_{\tau,2}^+=w_3,\quad u_{\tau,2}^-=w_4.$$
They are exact harmonic smooth functions, hence belong to $H^1(M)$, with no prescribed boundary values. Their product integral equals $T$ for every $\tau$, so the required limit holds. This includes $T=0$. These are explicitly $Q$-dependent, constant-parameter witnesses; no estimate stronger than the unchanged statement is inferred from the $L^2$ CGO bound.

there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice.

Let $(M,g)$ be a compact smooth Riemannian domain with smooth boundary. If $\gamma_1,\gamma_2\in C^\infty(M,\mathbb R)$ are strictly positive and $u_j$ solves $\operatorname{div}_g(\gamma_j\nabla_gu_j)=0$ with smooth boundary value $f_j$, then
$$\langle(\Lambda_{\gamma_1}-\Lambda_{\gamma_2})f_1,f_2\rangle_{\partial M} =\int_M(\gamma_1-\gamma_2)g(\nabla_gu_1,\nabla_g\overline{u_2})\,dV_g.$$
If instead $q_1,q_2\in C^\infty(M,\mathbb R)$ have trivial Dirichlet kernels for $-\Delta_g+q_j$ and $u_j$ solves $(-\Delta_g+q_j)u_j=0$ with smooth boundary value $f_j$, then
$$\langle(\Lambda_{q_1}-\Lambda_{q_2})f_1,f_2\rangle_{\partial M} =\int_M(q_1-q_2)u_1\overline{u_2}\,dV_g.$$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\geq3$, let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a bounded smooth domain contained in a ball $B(0,R)$, and let $q\in L^\infty(\Omega,\mathbb C)$. There are constants $C>0$ and $\tau_0\geq1$, depending only on $n$, $R$, and $\|q\|_{L^\infty}$, such that for every $\zeta\in\mathbb C^n$ satisfying $\zeta\cdot\zeta=0$ and $|\zeta|\geq\tau_0$, there is $r_\zeta\in H^1(\Omega,\mathbb C)$ for which
$$u_\zeta(x)=e^{i\zeta\cdot x}(1+r_\zeta(x))$$
solves $(-\Delta+q)u_\zeta=0$ distributionally in $\Omega$, and
$$\|r_\zeta\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\leq C|\zeta|^{-1}\|q\|_{L^2(\Omega)},\qquad \|\nabla r_\zeta\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\leq C\|q\|_{L^2(\Omega)}.$$
The dot product in the null-phase condition is complex bilinear, and $|\zeta|=(\sum_{j=1}^n|\zeta_j|^2)^{1/2}$.
Assume AC. Finite complex Borel measures $\mu,\nu$ on $\mathbb R^n$ with $\widehat\mu=\widehat\nu$ are equal. Here finite means finite total variation, and $n\ge1$.

derivations.claim:
Set $Q=q_1-q_2$. By [F1],
$$\int_\Omega Q(x)u_1(x)\overline{u_2(x)}\,dx=0$$
for every exact $H^1$ solution pair of $(-\Delta+q_j)u_j=0$.

Fix $\xi\in\mathbb R^n$. Since $n\geq3$, choose orthonormal $\omega_1,\omega_2\in\mathbb R^n$ perpendicular to $\xi$; when $\xi=0$, choose any orthonormal pair. For $\tau\geq1$, set $\sigma_\tau=(\tau^2+|\xi|^2/4)^{1/2}$ and
$$\zeta_1=\tau\omega_1+i\sigma_\tau\omega_2+\xi/2,\qquad \zeta_2=-\tau\omega_1-i\sigma_\tau\omega_2+\xi/2.$$
The orthogonality gives $\zeta_j\cdot\zeta_j=\tau^2-\sigma_\tau^2+|\xi|^2/4=0$, $\zeta_1+\zeta_2=\xi$, and $|\zeta_j|\to\infty$. Apply [F2] to $q_1$ with phase $\zeta_1$ and to $q_2$ with phase $-\overline{\zeta_2}$; the latter is null, and reality of $q_2$ lets us conjugate the resulting solution. Thus
$$u_1=e^{i\zeta_1\cdot x}(1+r_1),\qquad u_2=e^{-i\overline{\zeta_2}\cdot x}(1+r_2),\qquad \|r_j\|_{L^2(\Omega)}=O(\tau^{-1}).$$
Substitute in step 1.1. Since $Q\in L^2(\Omega)\cap L^\infty(\Omega)$,
$$\left|\int_\Omega Qe^{i\xi\cdot x}\big(r_1+\overline{r_2}+r_1\overline{r_2}\big)\,dx\right| \leq \|Q\|_2(\|r_1\|_2+\|r_2\|_2)+\|Q\|_\infty\|r_1\|_2\|r_2\|_2=O(\tau^{-1}).$$
Taking $\tau\to\infty$ proves $\int_\Omega Qe^{i\xi\cdot x}\,dx=0$ for every $\xi\in\mathbb R^n$.

Define the finite complex Borel measure $\mu(E)=\int_{E\cap\Omega}Q(x)\,dx$ on $\mathbb R^n$. It has finite total variation because $\Omega$ is bounded and $Q$ is bounded. The identity in step 2.1 gives $\widehat\mu(\eta)=0$ for every $\eta\in\mathbb R^n$ (take $\xi=-2\pi\eta$). By [F3], $\mu=0$. Hence $\int_E\operatorname{Re}Q\,dx=\int_E\operatorname{Im}Q\,dx=0$ for every Borel $E$; applying this to the sets $\{\operatorname{Re}Q\geq1/m\}$, $\{\operatorname{Re}Q\leq-1/m\}$, and their imaginary-part analogues shows $Q=0$ almost everywhere. Continuity of $Q$ gives $Q=0$ throughout $\Omega$.

countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice.

Let $(M,g)$ be a nonempty compact connected smooth Riemannian domain with nonempty smooth boundary. For a real-valued $\gamma\in C^\infty(M)$ with $\gamma(x)>0$ at every $x\in M$, let $v_f\in H^1(M)$ be the unique weak solution of $\operatorname{div}_g(\gamma\nabla_gv_f)=0$ with trace $f\in H^{1/2}(\partial M)$, whose existence is supplied by the positive-conductivity solvability lemma. Define the full-data physical conductivity Dirichlet-to-Neumann map $\Lambda_\gamma:H^{1/2}(\partial M)\to H^{-1/2}(\partial M)$ by
$$\langle\Lambda_\gamma f,h\rangle=\int_M\gamma\,g(\nabla_gv_f,\nabla_g\overline{V_h})\,dV_g,$$
where $V_h\in H^1(M)$ is any extension of $h\in H^{1/2}(\partial M)$. The weak equation makes this value independent of the extension. For smooth data, $\Lambda_\gamma f=\gamma\partial_{\nu_{\rm out}}v_f|_{\partial M}$; this is the full physical flux convention. When $M=\overline\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ with the Euclidean metric, this is the scalar Euclidean conductivity DN map.

For a real $q\in C^\infty(M)$ such that the only $w\in H_0^1(M)$ satisfying $(-\Delta_g+q)w=0$ weakly is $w=0$, let $u_f\in H^1(M)$ be the unique weak solution of $(-\Delta_g+q)u_f=0$ with trace $f$, whose existence follows from the nonresonant regularity lemma. Define the Schrödinger DN map $\Lambda_q:H^{1/2}(\partial M)\to H^{-1/2}(\partial M)$ by
$$\langle\Lambda_qf,h\rangle=\int_M\big(g(\nabla_gu_f,\nabla_g\overline{V_h})+qu_f\overline{V_h}\big)\,dV_g.$$
For smooth data this is $\partial_{\nu_{\rm out}}u_f|_{\partial M}$. Equality of these operators means equality on all of $H^{1/2}(\partial M)$, not equality for a restricted set of boundary inputs.

$$\langle(\Lambda_{\gamma_1}-\Lambda_{\gamma_2})f_1,f_2\rangle_{\partial M} =\int_M(\gamma_1-\gamma_2)g(\nabla_gu_1,\nabla_g\overline{u_2})\,dV_g.$$

Choose a sufficiently small boundary patch and $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\partial\Omega)$ supported there with $\chi=1$ near $x_0$. For every integer $N\geq1$ there are a smooth complex phase $\Phi$ in a collar of the patch and amplitudes $b_{\lambda,\gamma}$, $b_{\lambda,\widetilde\gamma}$, defined for $\lambda\geq1$, such that
$$v_{\lambda,\gamma}=\lambda^{-1/2}e^{i\lambda\Phi}b_{\lambda,\gamma},\qquad v_{\lambda,\widetilde\gamma}=\lambda^{-1/2}e^{i\lambda\Phi}b_{\lambda,\widetilde\gamma},$$

$$\|\operatorname{div}(\gamma\nabla v_{\lambda,\gamma})\|_{L^2(\Omega)} +\|\operatorname{div}(\widetilde\gamma\nabla v_{\lambda,\widetilde\gamma})\|_{L^2(\Omega)} =O(\lambda^{-N}).$$
Here $\phi=\Phi|_{\partial\Omega}$ is real, $d\phi(x_0)=\xi_0$, and $\operatorname{Im}\Phi$ is comparable to the inward distance to the boundary on the collar. Let $u_{\lambda,\gamma}$ and $u_{\lambda,\widetilde\gamma}$ be the exact conductivity solutions with the same respective boundary values. Their corrections satisfy
$$\|u_{\lambda,\gamma}-v_{\lambda,\gamma}\|_{H^1(\Omega)} +\|u_{\lambda,\widetilde\gamma}-v_{\lambda,\widetilde\gamma}\|_{H^1(\Omega)} =O(\lambda^{-N}).$$
For every fixed integer $k\geq0$ and continuous $F$ on $\overline\Omega$, choosing $N>k$ gives
$$\lim_{\lambda\to\infty}\lambda^k \int_\Omega \operatorname{dist}(x,\partial\Omega)^k F(x) \nabla v_{\lambda,\gamma}\cdot\overline{\nabla v_{\lambda,\widetilde\gamma}}\,dx =c_k\int_{\partial\Omega}F|\chi|^2\,dS,\qquad c_k=2\int_0^\infty t^ke^{-2t}\,dt=\frac{k!}{2^k}>0.$$

Let $u_{\lambda,j}$ be their exact conductivity solutions. Equality of the DN maps and [F2] give
$$\int_\Omega(\gamma_1-\gamma_2)\nabla u_{\lambda,1}\cdot\overline{\nabla u_{\lambda,2}}\,dx=0.$$
Replacing each exact solution by its approximate beam changes this integral by $O(\lambda^{-N})$: the coefficient is bounded, the beam $H^1$ norms are uniformly bounded, and each exact correction is $O(\lambda^{-N})$ in $H^1$ by [F3].

Set $k=0$ in [F3] and let $\lambda\to\infty$ in step 1.1. Since $c_0>0$,
$$\int_{\partial\Omega}(\gamma_1-\gamma_2)|\chi|^2\,dS=0.$$
If $\gamma_1-\gamma_2$ were positive or negative at any boundary point, continuity would give a patch on which it has that strict sign; choosing $\chi$ supported in that patch and equal to one near the point would make this integral nonzero. Thus $\gamma_1=\gamma_2$ on $\partial\Omega$.

Fix an integer $k\geq1$ and suppose inductively that $\partial_{x_n}^j(\gamma_1-\gamma_2)=0$ on a boundary patch for every $j<k$. Taylor's formula with integral remainder in the inward normal coordinate gives
$$\gamma_1(y,x_n)-\gamma_2(y,x_n)=x_n^kF_k(y,x_n),\qquad F_k(y,0)=\frac{\partial_{x_n}^k(\gamma_1-\gamma_2)(y,0)}{k!},$$
for a smooth $F_k$. Apply [F2] to the exact beams from [F3], replace them by their approximate beams, and multiply the resulting integral identity by $\lambda^k$. The replacement error is $O(\lambda^{k-N})$, since the weight $x_n^k$ is bounded and the corrections are $O(\lambda^{-N})$ in $H^1$. Choose $N>k$ and apply the weighted limit in [F3]; then
$$c_k\int_{\partial\Omega}F_k(y,0)|\chi(y)|^2\,dS(y)=0.$$
Since $c_k>0$, the same localized sign argument as in step 1.2 gives $F_k(y,0)=0$ throughout the patch. Therefore the $k$th inward normal derivatives agree there.

Step 1.2 is the base case for the induction. Step 2.1 proves each subsequent order on a patch that may be chosen around any prescribed boundary point. Thus every boundary point has a neighborhood on which the order-$k$ normal derivative difference is zero for every integer $k\geq0$, proving the full boundary-jet assertion.
