The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable) has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice.

Let $(M,g)$ be a compact transversally anisotropic product domain of dimension $n\geq3$ and let $q\in C^\infty(M,\mathbb R)$. Fix an integer $s>n/2+2$ and a finite family $h_1,\ldots,h_m\in C^\infty(\partial M,\mathbb C)$. For $\epsilon=(\epsilon_1,\ldots,\epsilon_m)\in\mathbb R^m$ sufficiently near zero, the equation
$$-\Delta_g u+q u^3=0\quad\text{in }M^\circ,\qquad u|_{\partial M}=\sum_{j=1}^m\epsilon_jh_j$$
has a unique solution in a fixed small $H^s(M)$ ball. The parameter map $\epsilon\mapsto u_\epsilon$ is $C^3$ into $H^s(M)$, and the corresponding nonlinear Dirichlet-to-Neumann data $\partial_{\nu_{\rm out}}u_\epsilon|_{\partial M}$ is $C^3$ into $C^0(\partial M)$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice.

Let $(M,g)$ be a compact smooth Riemannian domain with smooth boundary, let $q\in C^\infty(M,\mathbb R)$, and let $\Lambda_q^{\rm NL}$ be the small-data nonlinear Dirichlet-to-Neumann map for $-\Delta_g u+qu^3=0$. For smooth boundary directions $h_1,h_2,h_3,h_4$, let $v_j$ be the harmonic solution with boundary value $h_j$. If
$$w_{123}=\left.\partial_{\epsilon_1}\partial_{\epsilon_2}\partial_{\epsilon_3}u_\epsilon\right|_{\epsilon=0},$$
where $u_\epsilon$ has boundary value $\epsilon_1h_1+\epsilon_2h_2+\epsilon_3h_3$, then
$$-\Delta_gw_{123}+6qv_1v_2v_3=0,\qquad w_{123}|_{\partial M}=0,$$
and
$$\left\langle (D^3\Lambda_q^{\rm NL})_0[h_1,h_2,h_3],h_4\right\rangle =6\int_Mq\,v_1v_2v_3\overline{v_4}\,dV_g.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice.

Let $M\Subset\mathbb R\times M_0^\circ$ be a three-dimensional transversally anisotropic product domain with compact connected simple surface transversal $(M_0,g_0)$. For every $p\in M_0^\circ$ choose two nontangential unit-speed geodesic segments $\gamma_1,\gamma_2$ meeting transversely at $p$ and nowhere else. For every $\xi\in\mathbb R$ and every $Q\in C^\infty(\overline M)$, there are four exact harmonic solutions $u_{\tau,1}^+,u_{\tau,1}^-,u_{\tau,2}^+,u_{\tau,2}^-\in H^1(M)$, with no prescribed boundary values, such that
$$\lim_{\tau\to\infty}\int_MQ(x_1,x')u_{\tau,1}^+u_{\tau,1}^-u_{\tau,2}^+u_{\tau,2}^-\,dV_g =c(p,\gamma_1,\gamma_2)\int_{I_p}e^{-i\xi x_1}Q(x_1,p)\,dx_1,$$
where $I_p=\{x_1\in\mathbb R:(x_1,p)\in M^\circ\}$ and $c(p,\gamma_1,\gamma_2)>0$ is the nonzero Gaussian normalization divided by $|\sin\angle(\dot\gamma_1(p),\dot\gamma_2(p))|$.
Assume countable choice. If $f,g\in L^1(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$ and $\widehat f=\widehat g$, then $f=g$ almost everywhere. Equality of the transforms almost everywhere already suffices.

Fix four smooth boundary directions $h_1,h_2,h_3,h_4$. Equality of the finite-parameter DN maps for $q_1$ and $q_2$ implies equality of their mixed third derivatives at the origin. Applying [F2] to each coefficient and subtracting gives
$$\int_M(q_1-q_2)v_1v_2v_3\overline{v_4}\,dV_g=0$$
for every four harmonic functions $v_j$ arising from smooth boundary data.

The identity in step 1.1 holds also for complex smooth harmonic functions: write their boundary values as real and imaginary parts and expand the separately linear or conjugate-linear expression. Since the Laplacian has real coefficients, conjugation preserves harmonicity; replacing the fourth function by its conjugate therefore gives $\int_M Qw_1w_2w_3w_4\,dV=0$ for every four smooth complex harmonic functions, where $Q=q_1-q_2$.

Fix $p\in M_0^\circ$ and $\xi\in\mathbb R$. Apply [F3] with $Q=q_1-q_2$. Its witnesses are smooth by [F5], so their product integral is zero for every $\tau$ by step 1.2. Taking their stated limit gives
$$c(p,\gamma_1,\gamma_2)\int_{I_p}e^{-i\xi x_1}(q_1-q_2)(x_1,p)\,dx_1=0,$$
where $c>0$ is the crossing normalization. The coefficient transform therefore vanishes for every $\xi$ and every $p$.

For each $p$, extend $x_1\mapsto(q_1-q_2)(x_1,p)$ by zero outside $I_p$. It is a compactly supported $L^1(\mathbb R)$ function. By step 2.1, [F4] makes this section zero almost everywhere; its smoothness in the interior of $M$ then makes $q_1-q_2=0$ on $M^\circ$, and continuity gives equality on $\overline M$. Thus the theorem follows.

> (Choice function).

there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable) has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice.

Let $(M,g)$ be a nonempty compact connected smooth Riemannian domain with nonempty smooth boundary. For a real-valued $\gamma\in C^\infty(M)$ with $\gamma(x)>0$ at every $x\in M$, let $v_f\in H^1(M)$ be the unique weak solution of $\operatorname{div}_g(\gamma\nabla_gv_f)=0$ with trace $f\in H^{1/2}(\partial M)$, whose existence is supplied by the positive-conductivity solvability lemma. Define the full-data physical conductivity Dirichlet-to-Neumann map $\Lambda_\gamma:H^{1/2}(\partial M)\to H^{-1/2}(\partial M)$ by
$$\langle\Lambda_\gamma f,h\rangle=\int_M\gamma\,g(\nabla_gv_f,\nabla_g\overline{V_h})\,dV_g,$$
where $V_h\in H^1(M)$ is any extension of $h\in H^{1/2}(\partial M)$. The weak equation makes this value independent of the extension. For smooth data, $\Lambda_\gamma f=\gamma\partial_{\nu_{\rm out}}v_f|_{\partial M}$; this is the full physical flux convention. When $M=\overline\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ with the Euclidean metric, this is the scalar Euclidean conductivity DN map.

For a real $q\in C^\infty(M)$ such that the only $w\in H_0^1(M)$ satisfying $(-\Delta_g+q)w=0$ weakly is $w=0$, let $u_f\in H^1(M)$ be the unique weak solution of $(-\Delta_g+q)u_f=0$ with trace $f$, whose existence follows from the nonresonant regularity lemma. Define the Schrödinger DN map $\Lambda_q:H^{1/2}(\partial M)\to H^{-1/2}(\partial M)$ by
$$\langle\Lambda_qf,h\rangle=\int_M\big(g(\nabla_gu_f,\nabla_g\overline{V_h})+qu_f\overline{V_h}\big)\,dV_g.$$
For smooth data this is $\partial_{\nu_{\rm out}}u_f|_{\partial M}$. Equality of these operators means equality on all of $H^{1/2}(\partial M)$, not equality for a restricted set of boundary inputs.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice.

Let $(M,g)$ be a compact smooth Riemannian domain with smooth boundary. If $\gamma_1,\gamma_2\in C^\infty(M,\mathbb R)$ are strictly positive and $u_j$ solves $\operatorname{div}_g(\gamma_j\nabla_gu_j)=0$ with smooth boundary value $f_j$, then
$$\langle(\Lambda_{\gamma_1}-\Lambda_{\gamma_2})f_1,f_2\rangle_{\partial M} =\int_M(\gamma_1-\gamma_2)g(\nabla_gu_1,\nabla_g\overline{u_2})\,dV_g.$$
If instead $q_1,q_2\in C^\infty(M,\mathbb R)$ have trivial Dirichlet kernels for $-\Delta_g+q_j$ and $u_j$ solves $(-\Delta_g+q_j)u_j=0$ with smooth boundary value $f_j$, then
$$\langle(\Lambda_{q_1}-\Lambda_{q_2})f_1,f_2\rangle_{\partial M} =\int_M(q_1-q_2)u_1\overline{u_2}\,dV_g.$$

Let $(M_0,g_0)$ be a compact connected smooth Riemannian manifold with smooth boundary. A nontangential maximal geodesic segment is a unit-speed geodesic $\gamma:[0,L]\to M_0$, with $L>0$, whose initial velocity points strictly inward at $\partial M_0$, whose terminal velocity points strictly outward at $\partial M_0$, and whose points for $0<t<L$ lie in $M_0^\circ$. For $f\in C_c^\infty(M_0^\circ,\mathbb R)$ define its geodesic ray transform by $I_{g_0}f(\gamma)=\int_0^L f(\gamma(t))\,dt$. The unweighted scalar ray transform is called injective on compactly supported smooth functions if $I_{g_0}f(\gamma)=0$ for every such segment implies $f=0$. For complex-valued $f$, injectivity means injectivity of its real and imaginary parts separately.
Assume countable choice. If $f,g\in L^1(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$ and $\widehat f=\widehat g$, then $f=g$ almost everywhere. Equality of the transforms almost everywhere already suffices.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice.

Let $(M,g)$ be a transversally anisotropic product domain, let $q\in C^\infty(\overline M,\mathbb R)$, and let $\psi\in C^\infty$ be real on a neighborhood of the transversal projection of $M$, with $|d\psi|_{g_0}=1$. Suppose $a\in C^\infty(\overline M,\mathbb C)$ satisfies
$$2\partial_{x_1}a+2i\,g_0(\nabla_{g_0}\psi,\nabla_{g_0}a)+i(\Delta_{g_0}\psi)a=0.$$
Then, for all sufficiently large $\tau$, there is an exact solution
$$u_\tau=e^{-\tau(x_1+i\psi)}a+e^{-\tau x_1}r_\tau,\qquad (-\Delta_g+q)u_\tau=0\ \text{in }M^\circ,$$
with $r_\tau\in H^1(M)$ and $\|r_\tau\|_{L^2(M)}\leq C\tau^{-1}\|(-\Delta_g+q)a\|_{L^2(M)}$. No boundary value is prescribed for $r_\tau$.

Let $(M_0,g_0)$ be a compact smooth Riemannian manifold with smooth boundary and let $\gamma:[0,L]\to M_0$ be a unit-speed nontangential geodesic segment. For every real $\lambda$ and every $K>0$, there is a family $v_{\tau+i\lambda}\in C^\infty(M_0)$, $\tau\geq1$, such that
$$\|(-\Delta_{g_0}-(\tau+i\lambda)^2)v_{\tau+i\lambda}\|_{L^2(M_0)}=O(\tau^{-K}),\qquad \|v_{\tau+i\lambda}\|_{L^2(M_0)}=O(1),$$
and for every $\psi\in C(M_0)$,
$$\lim_{\tau\to\infty}\int_{M_0}|v_{\tau+i\lambda}|^2\psi\,dV_{g_0} =\int_0^L e^{-2\lambda t}\psi(\gamma(t))\,dt.$$
The statement permits transversal manifolds without an orientability assumption and makes no boundary condition assertion for the quasimodes.

derivations.claim:
For any exact solutions $u_j\in H^1(M)$ with their respective equations, [F2] and the equality $\Lambda_{q_1}=\Lambda_{q_2}$ give
$$\int_M Q(x_1,x')u_1(x_1,x')\overline{u_2(x_1,x')}\,dV_g=0,\qquad Q=q_1-q_2.$$
Because $q_j\in C_c^\infty(M^\circ)$ and $M\Subset\mathbb R\times M_0^\circ$, extension of $Q$ by zero gives a smooth compactly supported function on $\mathbb R\times M_0$.

Fix $\lambda\in\mathbb R$, put $s=\tau+i\lambda$, and choose the beam $v_s$ of [F6] with residual $O(\tau^{-K})$. Use the signed real-weight solver [F5] to obtain exact solutions
$$u_1=e^{-s x_1}(v_s+r_1),\qquad u_2=e^{s x_1}(v_s+r_2)$$
for the respective potentials, with $r_j\in H^1(M)$ and $\|r_j\|_2=O(\tau^{-1})$. Indeed the conjugated residual is $(-\Delta_{g_0}-s^2)v_s+q_jv_s$, of bounded $L^2$ norm on a fixed product cylinder; multiplication by $e^{\pm i\lambda x_1}$ is bounded there. Correcting with the real-weight solver gives precisely this bound. Their product in step 1.1 is $e^{-2i\lambda x_1}(v_s+r_1)(\overline{v_s}+\overline{r_2})$. Every error integral tends to zero by Cauchy--Schwarz, the boundedness of $Q$, $\|v_s\|_2=O(1)$, and $\|r_j\|_2=o(1)$. Integrating first in $x_1$ gives the smooth compactly supported transversal test function $\widehat Q_\lambda$ below. Applying [F6] proves the attenuated ray identity for every $\lambda$ and every nontangential $\gamma$. This argument works on the base manifold; it does not assume injectivity of a ray transform on its orientation cover.

Step 2.1 supplies
$$\int_{\gamma}\widehat Q_\lambda(\gamma(t))e^{-2\lambda t}\,dt=0 \quad\text{for every real }\lambda\text{ and every nontangential geodesic }\gamma,$$
where $\widehat Q_\lambda(x')=\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-2i\lambda x_1}Q(x_1,x')\,dx_1$. At $\lambda=0$, [F3] gives $\widehat Q_0=0$. Assume inductively that $\partial_\lambda^j\widehat Q_0=0$ for every $j<k$. Differentiate the ray identity $k$ times at $\lambda=0$. Differentiation under the finite geodesic integral is valid because $Q$ is smooth with compact $x_1$ support. Leibniz' rule leaves the unweighted ray integral of $\partial_\lambda^k\widehat Q_0$; all other terms contain lower derivatives and vanish by the induction hypothesis. Thus [F3], applied to real and imaginary parts, gives $\partial_\lambda^k\widehat Q_0=0$. Induction proves that every Taylor coefficient of $\lambda\mapsto\widehat Q_\lambda(x')$ vanishes for each fixed $x'$.

For each fixed $x'$, compact $x_1$ support makes $\widehat Q_\lambda(x')$ entire in $\lambda$, so its zero Taylor series implies it vanishes for all real $\lambda$. This is the Fourier transform of the $L^1(\mathbb R)$ function $Q(\cdot,x')$ at every frequency $2\lambda$; [F4] gives $Q(\cdot,x')=0$ almost everywhere. Smoothness of $Q$ then yields $Q=0$ on $M$.

If their full physical conductivity Dirichlet-to-Neumann maps agree on all boundary data, then every inward boundary-normal derivative agrees:
$$\partial_{x_n}^k\gamma_1|_{\partial\Omega} =\partial_{x_n}^k\gamma_2|_{\partial\Omega} \qquad(k=0,1,2,\ldots),$$
where $x_n=\operatorname{dist}(x,\partial\Omega)$ in a boundary normal collar.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice.

Let $(M,g)$ be a compact smooth Riemannian domain with smooth boundary, let $\gamma\in C^\infty(M,\mathbb R)$ be strictly positive, put $\rho=\sqrt{\gamma}$, and define $q=(\Delta_g\rho)/\rho$. If $v$ solves $\operatorname{div}_g(\gamma\nabla_gv)=0$ and $u=\rho v$, then $u$ solves $(-\Delta_g+q)u=0$. The potential $q$ has trivial Dirichlet kernel. For boundary data $f=v|_{\partial M}$, with $\rho_b=\rho|_{\partial M}$ and the physical flux convention $\Lambda_\gamma f=\gamma\partial_{\nu_{\rm out}}v|_{\partial M}$, the exact boundary relation is
$$\Lambda_\gamma f=\rho_b\Lambda_q(\rho_b f)-\rho_b(\partial_{\nu_{\rm out}}\rho)|_{\partial M}f.$$

Let $n\geq3$, let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a bounded, nonempty, connected smooth domain, and let $q_1,q_2\in C^\infty(\overline\Omega,\mathbb R)$. Their Liouville boundary relations in [F2], together with $\Lambda_{\gamma_1}=\Lambda_{\gamma_2}$, now give $\Lambda_{q_1}g=\Lambda_{q_2}g$ for every $g\in H^{1/2}(\partial\Omega)$: substitute $f=g/\rho_b$ into the physical-flux relation, using the common positive boundary value $\rho_b$ and common $\partial_\nu\rho_j$. Multiplication and division by smooth positive $\rho_b$ preserve $H^{1/2}(\partial\Omega)$.

Each $q_j$ is nonresonant. If $w\in H_0^1(\Omega)$ solves $(-\Delta_g+q_j)w=0$, then $v=w/\rho_j\in H_0^1(\Omega)$ solves $-\operatorname{div}(\gamma_j\nabla v)=0$ by [F2]. Therefore $\rho_1=\rho_2$ and $\gamma_1=\rho_1^2=\rho_2^2=\gamma_2$ in $\Omega$; continuity extends this equality to $\overline\Omega$.

citations.quote: A transversally anisotropic product domain of dimension $n\geq3$ is a compact connected smooth $n$-dimensional Riemannian domain $(M,g)$ with smooth boundary, together with a compact connected smooth $(n-1)$-dimensional Riemannian manifold with boundary $(M_0,g_0)$ and an isometric embedding of $(M,g)$ as a smooth domain compactly contained in $(\mathbb R\times M_0^\circ,dx_1^2\oplus g_0)$. The coordinate $x_1$ on $\mathbb R$ is the distinguished Euclidean coordinate; $M_0$ is the transversal manifold. All Laplacians use $\Delta_g=\operatorname{div}_g\nabla_g$. Neither $M$ nor $M_0$ is assumed orientable. A positive smooth conformal factor is not included in this definition; claims using a conformally related metric must state and prove the required conformal transformation separately.

Let $(M,g)$ be a compact, connected, nonempty smooth two-dimensional Riemannian manifold with smooth boundary. For $x\in\partial M$, let $\nu_{\mathrm{out}}(x)$ be the outward unit normal. The boundary is **strictly convex** if
$$
g(\nabla_w\nu_{\mathrm{out}},w)>0
$$
for every $x\in\partial M$ and every nonzero $w\in T_x\partial M$. A **Jacobi field** along a unit-speed geodesic $\gamma$ is a smooth vector field $J$ along $\gamma$ satisfying
$$
D_t^2J+R(J,\dot\gamma)\dot\gamma=0,
$$
where $R(X,Y)Z=\nabla_X\nabla_YZ-\nabla_Y\nabla_XZ-\nabla_{[X,Y]}Z$. The manifold has **no conjugate points** if, on every unit-speed geodesic segment $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$, a Jacobi field with $J(a)=J(b)=0$ must be identically zero. It is **nontrapping** if every maximal unit-speed geodesic starting in $M^\circ$ reaches $\partial M$ in finite forward and backward time. The pair $(M,g)$ is a **simple surface** if its boundary is strictly convex, it has no conjugate points, and it is nontrapping.

The unit tangent bundle is $SM=\{(x,v):x\in M,\ v\in T_xM,\ g_x(v,v)=1\}$. Write $\nu_{\mathrm{in}}=-\nu_{\mathrm{out}}$ and
$$
\partial_+SM=\{(x,v)\in SM:x\in\partial M,\ g_x(v,\nu_{\mathrm{in}})>0\}
$$
for inward-pointing unit boundary vectors. For $(x,v)\in\partial_+SM$, let $\gamma_{x,v}$ be the unit-speed geodesic with $\gamma_{x,v}(0)=x$ and $\dot\gamma_{x,v}(0)=v$, and let $\tau_+(x,v)$ be its first positive exit time from $M$. For $f\in C^\infty(M)$, its scalar **geodesic X-ray transform** is the function on $\partial_+SM$ defined by
$$
I_0f(x,v)=\int_0^{\tau_+(x,v)} f(\gamma_{x,v}(t))\,dt.
$$
The geodesic equation is interpreted up to first boundary exit; local smooth extensions of the metric are used only to solve the coordinate ODE at boundary initial data.

derivations.claim: The boundary of $M$ is the level set $x_1^2+4|x'|^2=1$. Its defining function has gradient $(2x_1,8x_2,8x_3)$, which cannot vanish on that level set, so $M$ is a compact smooth three-dimensional domain. Every point of $M$ has $|x'|\leq1/2<1$, hence $M\Subset\mathbb R\times D^\circ$; the ambient metric is exactly $dx_1^2\oplus g_D$. By [F1], this is a transversally anisotropic product domain.

The disk has strictly convex boundary: its outward unit normal is $x'$ on $|x'|=1$ and $g(\nabla_w\nu_{\rm out},w)=|w|^2>0$ for every nonzero tangent $w$. Its curvature is zero, so a normal Jacobi field has scalar coefficient $a+bt$; if it vanishes at two distinct times then $a=b=0$, proving no conjugate points. Every unit-speed straight line exits the bounded disk in finite forward and backward time, and the segment between two points in the disk is unique. Thus $D$ is simple by [F2].

Apply [F3] to this simple surface. Its unweighted scalar geodesic ray transform is injective on the stated compactly supported smooth real functions. This verifies the injective-transversal condition for $M$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice.

Let $(M,g)$ be a nonempty compact connected smooth Riemannian domain with nonempty smooth boundary. For a real-valued $\gamma\in C^\infty(M)$ with $\gamma(x)>0$ at every $x\in M$, let $v_f\in H^1(M)$ be the unique weak solution of $\operatorname{div}_g(\gamma\nabla_gv_f)=0$ with trace $f\in H^{1/2}(\partial M)$, whose existence is supplied by the positive-conductivity solvability lemma. Define the full-data physical conductivity Dirichlet-to-Neumann map $\Lambda_\gamma:H^{1/2}(\partial M)\to H^{-1/2}(\partial M)$ by
$$\langle\Lambda_\gamma f,h\rangle=\int_M\gamma\,g(\nabla_gv_f,\nabla_g\overline{V_h})\,dV_g,$$
where $V_h\in H^1(M)$ is any extension of $h\in H^{1/2}(\partial M)$. The weak equation makes this value independent of the extension. For smooth data, $\Lambda_\gamma f=\gamma\partial_{\nu_{\rm out}}v_f|_{\partial M}$; this is the full physical flux convention. When $M=\overline\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ with the Euclidean metric, this is the scalar Euclidean conductivity DN map.

For a real $q\in C^\infty(M)$ such that the only $w\in H_0^1(M)$ satisfying $(-\Delta_g+q)w=0$ weakly is $w=0$, let $u_f\in H^1(M)$ be the unique weak solution of $(-\Delta_g+q)u_f=0$ with trace $f$, whose existence follows from the nonresonant regularity lemma. Define the Schrödinger DN map $\Lambda_q:H^{1/2}(\partial M)\to H^{-1/2}(\partial M)$ by
$$\langle\Lambda_qf,h\rangle=\int_M\big(g(\nabla_gu_f,\nabla_g\overline{V_h})+qu_f\overline{V_h}\big)\,dV_g.$$
For smooth data this is $\partial_{\nu_{\rm out}}u_f|_{\partial M}$. Equality of these operators means equality on all of $H^{1/2}(\partial M)$, not equality for a restricted set of boundary inputs.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice.

Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$, $n\geq2$, be a bounded smooth domain, and let $\gamma_1,\gamma_2\in C^\infty(\overline\Omega,\mathbb R)$ be strictly positive. If their full physical conductivity Dirichlet-to-Neumann maps agree on all boundary data, then every inward boundary-normal derivative agrees:
$$\partial_{x_n}^k\gamma_1|_{\partial\Omega} =\partial_{x_n}^k\gamma_2|_{\partial\Omega} \qquad(k=0,1,2,\ldots),$$
where $x_n=\operatorname{dist}(x,\partial\Omega)$ in a boundary normal collar.

derivations.claim: For every integer $m\geq0$, differentiation gives $\frac{d^m}{dt^m}e^{-1/t}=P_m(1/t)e^{-1/t}$ on $t>0$ for a polynomial $P_m$, by induction on $m$. For every polynomial $P$, $P(s)e^{-s}\to0$ as $s\to\infty$; for each power $s^N$, this follows from $e^s\geq s^{N+1}/(N+1)!$. Thus every right derivative tends to zero at $t=0$, so extension by zero to $t\leq0$ is smooth and flat there. Composition with $t=1-4|x|^2$ proves $\psi\in C_c^\infty(B(0,1))$, with compact support in $\overline{B(0,1/2)}$. It is nonzero at $x=0$, and $\|\psi\|_\infty<\infty$.

The bound $|\epsilon|\|\psi\|_\infty<1$ gives $\gamma_2(x)\geq1-|\epsilon|\|\psi\|_\infty>0$, so [F1] applies. Since $\psi$ vanishes on a neighborhood of $\partial\Omega$, $\gamma_1$ and $\gamma_2$ agree on that neighborhood and all their boundary derivatives agree. At the origin, $\gamma_2(0)-\gamma_1(0)=\epsilon e^{-1}\ne0$. Thus identical boundary jets do not force interior equality.

It is proper because the south pole is not in it. A nonzero smooth bump supported in a small lower cap defines boundary data outside $C_c^\infty(\Gamma)$, so the allowed inputs form a proper subset of the full boundary-data space.

By [F1] and [F2], the full-data theorem requires the map on every $H^{1/2}(\partial\Omega)$ input and the corresponding full boundary output. This classifies the configuration as outside the theorem's scope and asserts no uniqueness or nonuniqueness conclusion.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice.

Let $(M,g)$ be a compact smooth Riemannian manifold with smooth boundary, with no orientability assumption. Fix a finite smooth atlas of interior and boundary charts and a smooth partition of unity subordinate to it. For an integer $k\geq0$, define $H^k(M)$ as the completion of $C^\infty(M)$ in the sum of the Euclidean $W^{k,2}$ norms of the localized coordinate representatives; derivatives in a boundary chart are taken on the corresponding half-space. Define $H_0^1(M)$ as the closure of $C_c^\infty(M^\circ)$ in $H^1(M)$. Define $H^{1/2}(\partial M)$ by the fixed finite boundary atlas and partition of unity, using the Euclidean fractional Slobodeckij space $W^{1/2,2}(\mathbb R^{n-1})$ for each localized representative. Define $H^{-1/2}(\partial M)$ as the continuous dual of $H^{1/2}(\partial M)$ with the Riemannian boundary density pairing. These are the fixed-atlas norms used on this page; no atlas-independence assertion is part of this definition.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) and the boundary
conventions of
[[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]]. Let
$\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$, be a bounded $C^1$ domain, let
$0<s<1$, $1\le p<\infty$ and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Fix a
finite family of boundary charts: for each $j$ let $W_j\subseteq\mathbb R^n$
be open and $\Phi_j:W_j\to\Phi_j(W_j)\subseteq B_j\times\mathbb R$ a
flattening chart as in
[[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]], so that
$\Phi_j(\Omega\cap W_j)=\Phi_j(W_j)\cap\{t<0\}$ and the boundary corresponds
to the graph $\{t=0\}$; write $\Psi_j:=\pi\circ\Phi_j|_{\partial\Omega\cap W_j}$
for the induced parametrisation of $\partial\Omega\cap W_j$ by an open subset
$V_j:=\Psi_j(\partial\Omega\cap W_j)\subseteq\mathbb R^{n-1}$, and assume the
$\partial\Omega\cap W_j$ cover $\partial\Omega$. Fix a subordinate finite
ambient partition: nonnegative $\chi_j\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n)$ with
$\operatorname{supp}\chi_j\subseteq W_j$ and $\sum_j\chi_j=1$ on a
neighbourhood of $\partial\Omega$
([[lem-finite-ambient-partitions-for-euclidean-boundary-integration]]).
Finally let $\partial\Omega$ carry the chart-independent surface measure of
[[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]], which fixes the
meaning of almost-everywhere equality and of $L^p(\partial\Omega;\mathbb K)$
([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]).

For a Borel function $g:\partial\Omega\to\mathbb K$ put
$$\|g\|_{W^{s,p}(\partial\Omega)}:=\sum_j\bigl\|(\chi_jg)\circ\Psi_j^{-1}\bigr\|_{W^{s,p}(\mathbb R^{n-1})},$$
where the chart representation $(\chi_jg)\circ\Psi_j^{-1}$ is read in graph
coordinates and extended by zero off $V_j$, and the norm on the right is that
of [[def-fractional-slobodeckij-space-on-euclidean-space]]. The **fractional
Sobolev space of the boundary** is
$$W^{s,p}(\partial\Omega;\mathbb K):=\{g\in L^p(\partial\Omega;\mathbb K):\|g\|_{W^{s,p}(\partial\Omega)}<\infty\}.$$
The right-hand side is a finite sum of finite norms of compactly supported
chart representations, so $W^{s,p}(\partial\Omega;\mathbb K)$ is exactly the
set of $L^p(\partial\Omega)$ classes whose chart representations all lie in
the Euclidean space of
[[def-fractional-slobodeckij-space-on-euclidean-space]]; that the resulting
space and the topology of the norm do not depend on the choices of atlas and
partition, up to equivalence of norms, is proved in
[[lem-fractional-boundary-norm-is-independent-of-atlas]] and is not assumed
here.

Three conventions belong to the definition. First, membership is a property of
the $L^p(\partial\Omega)$ class: $g$ is an almost-everywhere class with respect
to the surface measure, and the chart representations are classes in
$W^{s,p}(\mathbb R^{n-1})$; representative independence for the Euclidean
factor is established together with the well-definedness lemma on this page
and is not presupposed here. Second, the norm is a finite sum
over a finite atlas, and each $\chi_jg$ is supported in the interior of the
chart, so the localisations are compactly supported and no boundary behaviour
of $\Psi_j^{-1}$ outside $V_j$ enters. Third, on this page the exponent used
is the trace exponent $s=\theta=1-1/p$ for $1<p<\infty$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$, be a bounded
$C^1$ domain, $0<s<1$ and $1\le p<\infty$.

(i) If $\Psi:V\to V'$ is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism between open subsets of
$\mathbb R^{d}$, $d\ge1$, which is bi-Lipschitz and whose derivatives in both directions are bounded,
then for every measurable $u:V'\to\mathbb K$,
$$\|u\circ\Psi\|_{W^{s,p}(V)}\le C(\Psi,s,p)\,\|u\|_{W^{s,p}(V')}$$
and symmetrically with $\Psi^{-1}$; in particular the Slobodeckij norm
$\|\cdot\|_{W^{s,p}}$ of [[def-fractional-slobodeckij-space-on-euclidean-space]]
is preserved up to equivalence by such coordinate changes. Here the norm on an open set uses the same double integral restricted to that set, with its $L^p$ term. Bounded derivatives alone on arbitrary open sets do not imply the bi-Lipschitz hypothesis.

(ii) Consequently two finite boundary chart families with subordinate
partitions, as in
[[def-fractional-sobolev-space-on-a-compact-c-one-boundary]], define
equivalent norms on $\partial\Omega$: the sum norms differ by multiplicative
constants depending only on the two atlases, the dimension and $s,p$, so
$W^{s,p}(\partial\Omega)$ is well defined as a set and its topology is
atlas-independent.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $k\ge1$, $1\le p\le\infty$ and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Let $U,V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open
and let $\Phi:U\to V$ be a $C^k$ diffeomorphism with inverse
$\Psi:=\Phi^{-1}:V\to U$. Fix open sets $U_0\subset\subset U$ and
$V_0\subset\subset V$ with $\Phi(U_0)\subseteq V_0$, and suppose that on
$\overline{U_0}$ the derivatives of $\Phi$ through order $k$ are bounded and
that on $\overline{V_0}$ the derivatives of $\Psi$ through order $k$ are
bounded; in the situation of
[[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]] these are exactly the compact
patches on which the flattening chart and its inverse have bounded derivatives
through order $k$. Then:

1. for every $u\in W^{k,p}(V_0;\mathbb K)$ the composition
$u\circ\Phi$ belongs to $W^{k,p}(U_0;\mathbb K)$, and for every
$1\le|\alpha|\le k$ its weak derivatives satisfy, almost everywhere on
$U_0$,
$$D^\alpha(u\circ\Phi)=\sum_{1\le|\beta|\le|\alpha|}\bigl((D^\beta u)\circ\Phi\bigr)\,P_{\alpha\beta}\bigl(D\Phi,\dots,D^k\Phi\bigr),$$
where $P_{\alpha\beta}$ is a universal polynomial with integer coefficients,
whose values on $\overline{U_0}$ are bounded by a constant depending only on
$n,k$ and the stated bounds for $\Phi$;

2. there is a constant $C$, depending only on $n$, $k$, $p$ and the two sets of
chart bounds, with
$$\|u\circ\Phi\|_{W^{k,p}(U_0)}\le C\,\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(V_0)}\qquad\text{for all }u\in W^{k,p}(V_0;\mathbb K).$$
If in addition $\Psi(V_0)\subseteq U_0$ (equivalently, under the stated
$\Phi(U_0)\subseteq V_0$, $\Phi(U_0)=V_0$), the same assertion holds for
composition with $\Psi$ from $W^{k,p}(U_0)$ to $W^{k,p}(V_0)$.

For $k=1$ only the first derivatives of $\Phi$ and $\Psi$ enter, so bounded
$C^1$ chart and inverse data suffice; no $C^1$-only claim is made for $k>1$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and let
$\eta\in C^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and
$u\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. For
$\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$, suppose that for every $\gamma\le\alpha$ there is
$v_\gamma\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with
$D^\gamma u=v_\gamma$ weakly. Then $\eta u$ has a weak $\alpha$-derivative,
and its almost-everywhere class is
$$D^\alpha(\eta u)=\sum_{\beta\le\alpha}\binom{\alpha}{\beta}(D^\beta\eta)D^{\alpha-\beta}u\quad\text{in }L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
where $D^\beta\eta$ is the classical derivative and products are pointwise
products of representatives. The resulting class does not depend on the
representatives.

For $k\in\mathbb N_0$ and $1\le p\le\infty$, if
$u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and $D^\beta\eta\in L^\infty(\Omega)$ for
every $|\beta|\le k$, then $\eta u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and the same
formula holds in $L^p$ for every $|\alpha|\le k$. In particular,
$\eta\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ is a sufficient condition on the
multiplier for this global conclusion.

For $\Omega=\varnothing$ all classes are zero and the identity holds. The
pairing convention is bilinear, with no complex conjugation.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $k\ge1$, $1\le p<\infty$,
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a
bounded $C^k$ domain in the graph sense of
[[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]]. Then the set of restrictions
to $\Omega$ of functions in $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ is dense in
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$: for every $u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and
every $\delta>0$ there is $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ with
$\|\varphi|_\Omega-u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}<\delta$.

The exponent range is $1\le p<\infty$; the result asserts no density in the
$W^{k,\infty}$ norm, and it does not hold on arbitrary open sets, as the
companion examples page shows.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, used to invoke the published real and complex
$L^p$ completeness results through their Countable-Choice interface. Let
$\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$,
$1\le p\le\infty$, and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$, equipped with the displayed norm of

$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.

Every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ belongs to

hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ for every exponent in range, and each of

Define the **zero-boundary Sobolev space**
$$W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K):=\overline{C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)},$$
the closure taken in the normed space
$(W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K),\|\cdot\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)})$ of
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]. The norm is a genuine norm on classes

derivations.claim: On the common smooth core, the identity between the fixed-atlas and Euclidean $W^{1,2}$ norms is bounded in both directions. Indeed, each fixed chart representative is obtained by multiplying by a fixed smooth cutoff and composing with a smooth flattening chart, so [F3] bounds the finite fixed-atlas sum by the Euclidean norm. Conversely, the finite partition of unity writes $u$ as the sum of its localized chart pieces; pull each piece back and use [F3] to bound the Euclidean $W^{1,2}$ norm by the fixed-atlas sum. The constants are finite because the atlas and partition are finite. By the density and completeness in [F3], the identity extends to bounded inverse maps on the completions. Since the two norms are equivalent on $C_c^\infty(\Omega)$, their closures give the same zero-boundary subspace.

For $u\in H^1_{\rm fix}$, take its localized boundary-chart representatives in the fixed-atlas definition. Apply [F4] to each representative (reflecting $t<0$ to $t>0$ when required), and sum the finitely many resulting local traces. The fixed-atlas norm [F1] gives a bounded map $T:H^1_{\rm fix}\to H^{1/2}_{\rm fix}$. For smooth $u$ this sum is the classical boundary restriction because the partition equals one near the boundary and the half-space traces agree with classical restriction. As an $L^2$-valued map, this trace agrees with the Euclidean trace [F5]: the maps are bounded into $L^2$ by [F2] and [F5], and the Euclidean and fixed $H^1$ norms are equivalent by step 1.1, so equality on the dense smooth core extends to all of $H^1$.

If $Tu=0$ in $H^{1/2}_{\rm fix}$, it is zero as an $L^2$ class by [F2]; the $L^2$ trace agreement of step 1.2 and [F6] imply $u\in H^1_{0,\rm E}$. Step 1.1 identifies this with $H^1_{0,\rm fix}$. Conversely, if $u\in H^1_{0,\rm fix}$, approximate it in the fixed $H^1$ norm by interior compactly supported smooth functions. Each has zero classical trace, so continuity of $T$ gives $Tu=0$. Therefore $\ker T=H^1_{0,\rm fix}$.

By [F7] and the boundary-norm equivalence [F2], the Euclidean $L^2$ trace has a bounded right inverse $R:H^{1/2}_{\rm fix}(\partial\Omega)\to H^1_{\rm E}(\Omega)$. The norm equivalence of step 1.1 makes $R$ bounded into $H^1_{\rm fix}$ as well. For every boundary class $f$, the Euclidean trace of $Rf$ is $f$; by step 1.2 the fixed trace agrees with it in $L^2$, hence as an $H^{1/2}_{\rm fix}$ class. So $T$ is onto. The kernel identity of step 2.1 induces a bounded bijection $\bar T:H^1_{\rm fix}/H^1_{0,\rm fix}\to H^{1/2}_{\rm fix}$. For any representative $u+v$ with $v\in H^1_{0,\rm fix}$, step 1.2 gives $\|Tu\|_{H^{1/2}}\le C\|u+v\|_{H^1_{\rm fix}}$; taking the infimum shows $\bar T$ is bounded. Also $\|\bar T^{-1}f\|\le\|Rf\|_{H^1_{\rm fix}}\le C_R\|f\|_{H^{1/2}}$, so its inverse is bounded. Composing with the quotient identity isomorphism of step 1.1 proves the asserted Euclidean quotient identification.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $n\ge2$ and let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a bounded connected open set with smooth boundary. Write $H^1(\Omega)=W^{1,2}(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ and let $H_0^1(\Omega)$ be the $H^1$-closure of $C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R)$. Define the boundary trace-data space $\mathcal B_\Omega:=H^1(\Omega)/H_0^1(\Omega)$ with quotient norm; the trace-quotient lemma identifies this quotient with the fixed-atlas $H^{1/2}(\partial\Omega)$ boundary data convention of the scalar conductivity map. Let $\gamma\in C^\infty(\overline\Omega;\operatorname{Sym}_n(\mathbb R))$ be uniformly positive definite, so some $0<c\le C<\infty$ satisfy $c|\xi|^2\le \xi^T\gamma(x)\xi\le C|\xi|^2$ for all $x\in\overline\Omega$ and $\xi\in\mathbb R^n$. For $f=[U]\in\mathcal B_\Omega$, a weak solution with boundary datum $f$ is a class $u_{\gamma,f}\in H^1(\Omega)$ with $[u_{\gamma,f}]=f$ and

$$\int_\Omega \gamma\nabla u_{\gamma,f}\cdot\nabla\varphi\,dx=0\qquad(\varphi\in H_0^1(\Omega)).$$

The weak anisotropic Dirichlet-to-Neumann map is the bilinear-form candidate $\Lambda_\gamma:\mathcal B_\Omega\times\mathcal B_\Omega\to\mathbb R$ given, whenever the weak solution exists, by

$$\langle\Lambda_\gamma f,h\rangle:=\int_\Omega\gamma\nabla u_{\gamma,f}\cdot\nabla V_h\,dx,$$

where $V_h\in H^1(\Omega)$ is any representative of $h$. The local anisotropic conductivity well-posedness lemma proves existence and uniqueness for every boundary class, independence of the representative $V_h$, and boundedness on $\mathcal B_\Omega\times\mathcal B_\Omega$; it therefore makes this candidate a bounded bilinear map. The map is the boundary energy form for the equation $\operatorname{div}(\gamma\nabla u)=0$. Under the trace-quotient isomorphism and the local boundedness result, this form gives the usual weak map into the dual $H^{-1/2}(\partial\Omega)$ with the scalar convention.

abla v\cdot
abla w\,dx$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $D\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded Lebesgue-measurable set, let $M:=|D|$, let $q\in L^\infty(D;\mathbb C)$, and let $k\in\mathbb R$. Here $L^2$ and $L^\infty$ are equivalence classes modulo null functions ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), and $L^\infty$ means essentially bounded with respect to Lebesgue measure ([[def-essential-supremum-with-respect-to-a-measure]]). We regard $q$ as zero off $D$. The convention is the volume equation
$$u=f+K_k u,\qquad K_k u(x):=\int_D G_k(x-y)q(y)u(y)\,dy,\qquad G_k(z):=\frac{e^{ik|z|}}{4\pi|z|}\quad(z\ne0).$$
Set $G_k(0):=0$; when $M>0$ the diagonal in $D\times D$ is product-null, so this value is only a representative convention. The input and unknown are classes in complex $L^2(D)$, and the displayed equation is interpreted as an equality of those classes. Its formula is well defined by [[lem-volume-integral-operator-well-defined-and-bounded]].

The associated far-field map is
$$\mathcal F_k[v](\theta):=\frac1{4\pi}\int_D e^{-ik\theta\cdot y}q(y)v(y)\,dy,\qquad \theta\in S^2.$$
Here $S^2$ has the surface measure of [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]]. The map is well defined as a continuous function of $\theta$ by [[lem-volume-far-field-map-is-bounded]].

For $x\notin\overline D$, the exterior volume potential is
$$V_kv(x):=\int_D G_k(x-y)q(y)v(y)\,dy.$$
For each $v\in L^2(D;\mathbb C)$, the essential-supremum result gives $|q|\le\|q\|_\infty$ almost everywhere, and Cauchy--Schwarz gives $\|qv\|_{L^1(D)}\le\|q\|_\infty\sqrt M\,\|v\|_2$. Thus, for $x\notin\overline D$, the exterior volume-potential integral is absolutely convergent: $\overline D$ is closed, so its complement contains a ball about $x$ disjoint from $D$.

If $M=0$, define $L^2(D)=\{0\}$ and $K_k=0$; all solution and far-field statements on that space are the zero-space statements. The substantive operator results below assume $0<M<\infty$.

This is a stipulated integral-equation model with the sign convention $(-\Delta-k^2)(u-f)=q u$ when the corresponding distributional Helmholtz equation is used. In the acoustic notation of Scherzer–Mindrinos, their equation $u=u_i-k^2\Phi*((1-n)u)$ corresponds to $q=k^2(n-1)$. No existence or uniqueness for all contrasts is asserted by this definition.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $D$ have finite Lebesgue measure. For every product-measurable kernel $a\in L^2(D\times D;\mathbb C)$, the formula $T_av(x)=\int_Da(x,y)v(y)dy$ defines a representative-independent complex-linear map $L^2(D;\mathbb C)\to L^2(D;\mathbb C)$ and $\|T_a\|\le\|a\|_{L^2(D\times D)}$. Consequently, under [[def-volume-integral-scattering-model]] with $0<|D|<\infty$,
$$\|K_k\|_{L^2\to L^2}\le\|G_k(\cdot-\cdot)q(\cdot)\|_{L^2(D\times D)}\le\|q\|_\infty\sqrt{\frac{|D|\,\operatorname{diam}(D)}{4\pi}}.$$
For $|D|=0$ the operator is zero.

Assume Countable Choice and the data of [[def-volume-integral-scattering-model]] with $0<|D|<\infty$. If $\rho:=\|K_k\|_{L^2\to L^2}<1$, then for every $f\in L^2(D;\mathbb C)$ the equation $u=f+K_ku$ has a unique solution. For each integer $m\ge0$, define the Born partial sum $u_m:=\sum_{j=0}^{m}K_k^jf$. Then
$$\|u-u_m\|_2\le\frac{\rho^{m+1}}{1-\rho}\|f\|_2.$$

$$\widehat f(\xi)=\mathcal Ff(\xi):=\int_{\mathbb R^n}f(x)\exp(-2\pi i x\cdot\xi)\,dx,\qquad \xi\in\mathbb R^n.$$
Here $x\cdot\xi=\sum_{j=1}^n x_j\xi_j$, Lebesgue measure is used, and the exponential is [[def-complex-exponential]]. Its unit modulus follows from [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]]. The integral is evaluated using any measurable representative. derivations.claim: The integral operator depends linearly on $q$, so $K_{q,k}-K_{q',k}=K_{q-q',k}$ for any $q,q'\in L^\infty(D;\mathbb C)$. By [F2], $\|K_{q,k}-K_{q',k}\|\le C_D\|q-q'\|_\infty$. The operator-norm triangle inequality then gives $|\rho_k(q)-\rho_k(q')|\le C_D\|q-q'\|_\infty$. Thus $q\mapsto\rho_k(q)$ is continuous, $\mathcal U_{D,k}=\{\rho_k<1\}$ is open, and $0\in\mathcal U_{D,k}$ because $K_{0,k}=0$.

By [F3], $f_{k,d}(x)=e^{ikd\cdot x}$ belongs to $L^2(D;\mathbb C)$ and has norm $\sqrt M$. Since $q\in\mathcal U_{D,k}$, [F4] applies with $f=f_{k,d}$ and gives exactly one $u_{q,k,d}\in L^2(D;\mathbb C)$.

By [F7], $qu_{q,k,d}\in L^2(D)$ with norm at most $\|q\|_\infty\|u_{q,k,d}\|_2$, while [F3] puts $e^{ik\theta\cdot y}$ in $L^2(D)$. Their pairing in [F5] is the stated integral, so it is absolutely convergent and independent of the representatives. Cauchy–Schwarz gives its absolute value at most $\|q\|_\infty\sqrt M\|u_{q,k,d}\|_2$.

By [F7], $\|q\|_2\le\sqrt M\|q\|_\infty$; pairing $|q|$ with $1_D$ in [F5] then gives $\int_D|q(y)|\,dy\le M\|q\|_\infty$. Hence $q_0\in L^1(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$. By [F6], its transform is finite and representative-independent. Since $e^{-ik\theta\cdot y}e^{ikd\cdot y}=e^{-2\pi i y\cdot(k(\theta-d)/(2\pi))}$, the Fourier and integral formulas for $\mathcal B_kq$ agree and are well-defined. This proves the assertion for both data families.

Apply [F8] to $v=u_{q,k,d}$, whose existence is established in step 1.2. It supplies continuity in observation direction and the stated uniform outgoing-wave limit estimate, so the defined data are the physical far-field amplitude for this volume branch.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $D\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded Lebesgue-measurable set with $0<M:=|D|<\infty$, and let $k>0$. Write $S^2:=\{v\in\mathbb R^3:|v|=1\}$ and $C_D:=\sqrt{M\,\operatorname{diam}(D)/(4\pi)}$. For $q\in L^\infty(D;\mathbb C)$, extended by zero off $D$, set $G_k(z):=e^{ik|z|}/(4\pi|z|)$ for $z\ne0$ and $G_k(0):=0$, and let
$$K_{q,k}v(x):=\int_D G_k(x-y)q(y)v(y)\,dy,\qquad \rho_k(q):=\|K_{q,k}\|_{L^2(D)\to L^2(D)}.$$
The **small-norm contrast class** is
$$\mathcal U_{D,k}:=\{q\in L^\infty(D;\mathbb C):\rho_k(q)<1\}.$$
For $d\in S^2$, put $f_{k,d}(x):=e^{ikd\cdot x}$ on $D$. For $q\in\mathcal U_{D,k}$, let $u_{q,k,d}\in L^2(D;\mathbb C)$ denote the unique solution of $u=f_{k,d}+K_{q,k}u$. For $q\in\mathcal U_{D,k}$, define the exact far-field data family by
$$\mathcal S_k(q)(\theta,d):=\frac1{4\pi}\int_D e^{-ik\theta\cdot y}q(y)u_{q,k,d}(y)\,dy,\qquad (\theta,d)\in S^2\times S^2.$$

For $h\in L^\infty(D;\mathbb C)$, define its first Born data by
$$\mathcal B_k h(\theta,d):=\frac1{4\pi}\int_D e^{-ik\theta\cdot y}h(y)e^{ikd\cdot y}\,dy=\frac1{4\pi}\widehat{h_0}\!\left(\frac{k}{2\pi}(\theta-d)\right),$$
where $h_0$ is the zero extension of $h$ to $\mathbb R^3$ and $\widehat g(\xi):=\int_{\mathbb R^3}g(y)e^{-2\pi i y\cdot\xi}\,dy$ for $g\in L^1(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$. No uniqueness or stability outside $\mathcal U_{D,k}$ is asserted.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $D$ have finite Lebesgue measure. For every product-measurable kernel $a\in L^2(D\times D;\mathbb C)$, the formula $T_av(x)=\int_Da(x,y)v(y)dy$ defines a representative-independent complex-linear map $L^2(D;\mathbb C)\to L^2(D;\mathbb C)$ and $\|T_a\|\le\|a\|_{L^2(D\times D)}$. Consequently, under [[def-volume-integral-scattering-model]] with $0<|D|<\infty$,
$$\|K_k\|_{L^2\to L^2}\le\|G_k(\cdot-\cdot)q(\cdot)\|_{L^2(D\times D)}\le\|q\|_\infty\sqrt{\frac{|D|\,\operatorname{diam}(D)}{4\pi}}.$$
For $|D|=0$ the operator is zero.

Assume Countable Choice and the data of [[def-volume-integral-scattering-model]] with $0<|D|<\infty$. If $\rho:=\|K_k\|_{L^2\to L^2}<1$, then for every $f\in L^2(D;\mathbb C)$ the equation $u=f+K_ku$ has a unique solution. For each integer $m\ge0$, define the Born partial sum $u_m:=\sum_{j=0}^{m}K_k^jf$. Then
$$\|u-u_m\|_2\le\frac{\rho^{m+1}}{1-\rho}\|f\|_2.$$
No compactness, analytic continuation, or physical uniqueness hypothesis is used in this small-norm branch.

On every measure space the pairing $\langle f,g\rangle=\int f\overline g$ on complex $L^2$ is representative-independent, linear in the first variable, conjugate-linear in the second, conjugate symmetric and positive definite, with $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$. Moreover,
$$|\langle f,g\rangle|\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$
If $g\ne0$ as a class, equality holds iff $f=cg$ a.e. for some $c\in\mathbb C$. If $g=0$, equality holds for every $f$.

For each finite $m\ge0$, the same conclusions hold on tuples $F=(f_j)_{j<m}$, with pairing $B(F,G)=\sum_{j<m}\langle f_j,g_j\rangle$ and $\|F\|^2=\sum_{j<m}\|f_j\|_2^2$. For $G\ne0$, equality means $f_j=cg_j$ a.e. for every $j$, with one common scalar $c$.

Let $n\ge1$ and $f\in L^1(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$, with the componentwise integral and quotient conventions of [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]], [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]. Define
$$\widehat f(\xi)=\mathcal Ff(\xi):=\int_{\mathbb R^n}f(x)\exp(-2\pi i x\cdot\xi)\,dx,\qquad \xi\in\mathbb R^n.$$
Here $x\cdot\xi=\sum_{j=1}^n x_j\xi_j$, Lebesgue measure is used, and the exponential is [[def-complex-exponential]]. Its unit modulus follows from [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]]. The integral is evaluated using any measurable representative. Absolute convergence and representative independence are the obligations discharged by [[lem-l-one-fourier-transform-is-well-defined]]. The output is a function defined at every frequency, not merely an almost-everywhere class. At frequency zero the formula reads $\widehat f(0)=\int f$. No choice selection of representatives for a family of classes is part of this definition.

Assume countable choice. For every measure space and $1\le p\le\infty$, $L^p(\mu;\mathbb C)$ is complete. Every sequence converging in this norm has a subsequence of measurable representatives converging a.e. to a measurable representative of its norm limit. For finite $p$ no pointwise convergence of the whole sequence is asserted.

Let $(V,N)$ be a complex normed space and define $d_N(u,v):=N(u-v)$ for $u,v\in V$. On the realification $V_{\mathbb R}$, the same function $N$ is a real norm. The underlying set, addition, norm values, and induced metric $d_N$ are unchanged.

On this page the scalar field is the field $\mathbb R$ of real numbers: $X$, $Y$
and $Z$ always denote real Banach spaces ([[def-banach-space]]) and $U
\subseteq X$ always denotes an open subset of $X$, in the metric topology of the
norm ([[def-metric-topology]]).

Let $f : U \to Y$ be a map and let $x \in U$. For a bounded linear operator
$T \in \mathcal B(X,Y)$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]],
[[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]]) write

$$r(h) := f(x+h) - f(x) - Th \qquad (h \in X,\ x+h \in U).$$

Then $f$ is **Fréchet differentiable at $x$** when there is
$T \in \mathcal B(X,Y)$ with

$$\lim_{\substack{h \to 0 \\ h \ne 0}} \frac{\|f(x+h)-f(x)-Th\|}{\|h\|} = 0 ,$$

the limit being taken over those $h$ with $x + h \in U$. Such an operator $T$ is
a **Fréchet derivative of $f$ at $x$**, written $T = Df(x)$, and $\|T\|$ is its
operator norm ([[def-operator-norm]]). When $f$ is Fréchet differentiable at
every point of $U$, $f$ is **differentiable on $U$** and the **derivative** is
the map $Df : U \to \mathcal B(X,Y)$, $x \mapsto Df(x)$.

Let $V$ be a normed space over $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] for $\mathbb R$ and [[def-complex-norm-and-complex-normed-space]] for $\mathbb C$, with
induced metric $d(x,y)=\|x-y\|$ (in the complex case supplied by [[lem-complex-norm-realification-is-a-real-norm]]). Then $V$ is a **Banach space** when this
metric space is complete in the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]].

Equivalently: every Cauchy sequence in $V$ for the norm metric converges to a
point of $V$.

For real $x,y$, $\exp(x+iy)=e^x(\cos y+i\sin y)$ and $|\exp(x+iy)|=e^x$. In particular $e^{i\pi}+1=0$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-eulers-formula]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]], [[thm-pythagorean-and-parity-identities-for-all-six-trigonometric-functions]], [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]].

Let $f:X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable on a measure space $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$,
and suppose $\|f\|_\infty<\infty$. Then

$$|f|\le\|f\|_\infty\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

Moreover, if $M\ge0$ and $|f|\le M$ almost everywhere, then

$$\|f\|_\infty\le M.$$

So $\|f\|_\infty$ is the least essential bound of $|f|$.

Assume Countable Choice and the hypotheses and notation of the definition of fixed-frequency far-field data. For each $q\in\mathcal U_{D,k}$ there is an $\varepsilon>0$ such that $\|q'-q\|_\infty<\varepsilon$ implies $q'\in\mathcal U_{D,k}$; in particular this metric neighborhood condition holds at zero. For every $q\in\mathcal U_{D,k}$ and every $d,\theta\in S^2$, the solution $u_{q,k,d}$ exists uniquely in $L^2(D;\mathbb C)$, the integrals defining $\mathcal S_k(q)(\theta,d)$ and $\mathcal B_kq(\theta,d)$ are absolutely convergent and independent of representatives, and $\mathcal S_k(q)(\cdot,d)$ is continuous. If $R_0>\sup_{y\in D}|y|$ and $r\ge2R_0$, then
$$\sup_{\theta\in S^2}\left|r e^{-ikr}V_k u_{q,k,d}(r\theta)-\mathcal S_k(q)(\theta,d)\right|\le\frac{2R_0+|k|R_0^2}{4\pi r}\|q\|_\infty\sqrt M\,\|u_{q,k,d}\|_2.$$
Thus $\mathcal S_k(q)(\cdot,d)$ is the uniform outgoing far-field amplitude in the stated convention.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: For any $h\in L^\infty(D;\mathbb C)$, [F8] gives $|e^{-ik\theta\cdot y}e^{ikd\cdot y}|=1$ and [F9] gives $\int_D|h|\le M\|h\|_\infty$. The integral definition therefore yields $|\mathcal B_kh(\theta,d)|\le M\|h\|_\infty/(4\pi)$. By [F5] and the Fourier formula in [F1], this integral is the stated Born functional. It is complex-linear in $h$, hence bounded and real-linear for every fixed pair of directions.
Let $f=f_{k,d}$. By the definition and [F8], $|f|=1$ on $D$, so $\|f\|_2=\sqrt M$. The case $N=0$ of [F3] gives $\|u_{q,k,d}-f\|_2\le\rho\sqrt M/(1-\rho)$.

Subtracting the integral formulas in [F1] yields $\mathcal S_k(q)(\theta,d)-\mathcal B_kq(\theta,d)=\frac1{4\pi}\int_D e^{-ik\theta\cdot y}q(y)\bigl(u_{q,k,d}(y)-f(y)\bigr)\,dy.$ By [F9], $q(u_{q,k,d}-f)$ has $L^2$ norm at most $\|q\|_\infty\|u_{q,k,d}-f\|_2$. The same unit-modulus calculation as step 1.2, with $d$ replaced by $\theta$, gives $\|e^{ik\theta\cdot(\cdot)}\|_2=\sqrt M$. By [F4], the integral's absolute value is at most $\|q\|_\infty\sqrt M\,\|u_{q,k,d}-f\|_2/(4\pi)$; then [F3] and step 1.2 give the first bound, uniformly in the directions.

By [F2], $\rho\le C_D\|q\|_\infty$. When $C_D\|q\|_\infty<1$, monotonicity of $t\mapsto t/(1-t)$ on $[0,1)$ gives $\rho/(1-\rho)\le C_D\|q\|_\infty/(1-C_D\|q\|_\infty)$. Substitution into step 2.1 proves the second bound.

For nonzero $q$ with $C_D\|q\|_\infty<1$, divide the second bound by $\|q\|_\infty$; the quotient is at most $\frac{M C_D}{4\pi}\frac{\|q\|_\infty}{1-C_D\|q\|_\infty}$, which tends to zero as $\|q\|_\infty\to0$. Since [F10] makes zero an interior point, the bounded real-linear map from step 1.1 satisfies the Fréchet remainder criterion [F7], with the Banach-space hypotheses in [F6]. Also $\mathcal S_k(0)=0$ by its definition. Thus $D\mathcal S_k(0)(\theta,d)h=\mathcal B_kh(\theta,d)$ for each fixed pair, with the same remainder estimate uniformly over the full direction family.

Assume Countable Choice and the hypotheses and notation of the fixed-frequency far-field definition. For $q\in\mathcal U_{D,k}$ put $\rho=\rho_k(q)$. Uniformly over all incident and observation directions,
$$\sup_{\theta,d\in S^2}\left|\mathcal S_k(q)(\theta,d)-\mathcal B_kq(\theta,d)\right|\le\frac{M}{4\pi}\|q\|_\infty\frac{\rho}{1-\rho}.$$
Whenever $C_D\|q\|_\infty<1$, this implies

For each fixed $(\theta,d)$, the scalar map $q\mapsto\mathcal S_k(q)(\theta,d)$ on the open domain $\mathcal U_{D,k}$, with $L^\infty(D;\mathbb C)$ and $\mathbb C$ viewed as real Banach spaces, is Fréchet differentiable at $q=0$ and has derivative $h\mapsto\mathcal B_kh(\theta,d)$. Let $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, let
$A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$ have singular value decomposition
$A=U\Sigma V^*$, and let $\tau\ge0$ be a declared threshold. The
**truncated singular-value pseudoinverse at threshold $\tau$** is

$$ A_\tau^+ := V\Sigma_\tau^+U^*, $$

where $\Sigma_\tau^+\in M_{n\times m}(\mathbb F)$ is the transposed-shape
diagonal matrix whose $i$th diagonal entry is $\sigma_i^{-1}$ when
$\sigma_i>\tau$ and is $0$ when $\sigma_i\le\tau$; every off-diagonal entry is
$0$.

The threshold is part of the definition, exactly as in
[[def-numerical-rank-relative-to-a-norm-scale-and-tolerance]]: changing
$\tau$ changes which singular directions are retained.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $K:X\to Y$ be a compact linear map
between real or complex Hilbert spaces, with Hilbert adjoint $K^*:Y\to X$.
Write $\mathbb N_{>0}:=\{1,2,3,\ldots\}$. If $R(K)$ has finite dimension
$r\in\mathbb N$, put $J=\{1,\ldots,r\}$, interpreted as empty when $r=0$;
if $R(K)$ is infinite-dimensional, put $J=\mathbb N_{>0}$. Thus $J$ indexes
exactly the positive singular values $s_j>0$ in nonincreasing order. Let
$(v_j)_{j\in J}$ and $(u_j)_{j\in J}$ be complete
orthonormal families in $N(K)^\perp$ and $\overline{R(K)}$, respectively,
with $Kv_j=s_ju_j$ and $K^*u_j=s_jv_j$. The empty sum is zero, finite $J$
uses a finite sum, and infinite $J$ uses the norm-convergent series whenever
the stated square-summability condition holds. Use inner products linear in the
first argument. Define the Picard sum
$$P_K(y):=\sum_{j\in J}\frac{|\langle y,u_j\rangle_Y|^2}{s_j^2},\qquad y\in Y.$$
Then:

1. The exact equation $Kx=y$ is solvable if and only if
   $y\perp N(K^*)$ and $P_K(y)<\infty$.

2. The domain of the Hilbert-space Moore–Penrose inverse is
   $$D(K^\dagger)=R(K)\oplus R(K)^\perp=\{y\in Y:P_K(y)<\infty\},$$
   and for every $y\in D(K^\dagger)$,
   $$K^\dagger y=\sum_{j\in J}\frac{\langle y,u_j\rangle_Y}{s_j}v_j.$$
   Thus the orthogonal component in $R(K)^\perp=N(K^*)$ is discarded by
   $K^\dagger$; exact range membership additionally requires that component
   to be zero.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $D\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded Lebesgue-measurable set, let $M:=|D|$, let $q\in L^\infty(D;\mathbb C)$, and let $k\in\mathbb R$. Here $L^2$ and $L^\infty$ are equivalence classes modulo null functions ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), and $L^\infty$ means essentially bounded with respect to Lebesgue measure ([[def-essential-supremum-with-respect-to-a-measure]]). We regard $q$ as zero off $D$. The convention is the volume equation
$$u=f+K_k u,\qquad K_k u(x):=\int_D G_k(x-y)q(y)u(y)\,dy,\qquad G_k(z):=\frac{e^{ik|z|}}{4\pi|z|}\quad(z\ne0).$$
Set $G_k(0):=0$; when $M>0$ the diagonal in $D\times D$ is product-null, so this value is only a representative convention. The input and unknown are classes in complex $L^2(D)$, and the displayed equation is interpreted as an equality of those classes. Its formula is well defined by [[lem-volume-integral-operator-well-defined-and-bounded]].

The associated far-field map is
$$\mathcal F_k[v](\theta):=\frac1{4\pi}\int_D e^{-ik\theta\cdot y}q(y)v(y)\,dy,\qquad \theta\in S^2.$$
Here $S^2$ has the surface measure of [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]]. The map is well defined as a continuous function of $\theta$ by [[lem-volume-far-field-map-is-bounded]].

For $x\notin\overline D$, the exterior volume potential is
$$V_kv(x):=\int_D G_k(x-y)q(y)v(y)\,dy.$$
For each $v\in L^2(D;\mathbb C)$, the essential-supremum result gives $|q|\le\|q\|_\infty$ almost everywhere, and Cauchy--Schwarz gives $\|qv\|_{L^1(D)}\le\|q\|_\infty\sqrt M\,\|v\|_2$. Thus, for $x\notin\overline D$, the exterior volume-potential integral is absolutely convergent: $\overline D$ is closed, so its complement contains a ball about $x$ disjoint from $D$.

If $M=0$, define $L^2(D)=\{0\}$ and $K_k=0$; all solution and far-field statements on that space are the zero-space statements. The substantive operator results below assume $0<M<\infty$.

This is a stipulated integral-equation model with the sign convention $(-\Delta-k^2)(u-f)=q u$ when the corresponding distributional Helmholtz equation is used. In the acoustic notation of Scherzer–Mindrinos, their equation $u=u_i-k^2\Phi*((1-n)u)$ corresponds to $q=k^2(n-1)$. No existence or uniqueness for all contrasts is asserted by this definition.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $D$ have finite Lebesgue measure. For every product-measurable kernel $a\in L^2(D\times D;\mathbb C)$, the formula $T_av(x)=\int_Da(x,y)v(y)dy$ defines a representative-independent complex-linear map $L^2(D;\mathbb C)\to L^2(D;\mathbb C)$ and $\|T_a\|\le\|a\|_{L^2(D\times D)}$. Consequently, under [[def-volume-integral-scattering-model]] with $0<|D|<\infty$,
$$\|K_k\|_{L^2\to L^2}\le\|G_k(\cdot-\cdot)q(\cdot)\|_{L^2(D\times D)}\le\|q\|_\infty\sqrt{\frac{|D|\,\operatorname{diam}(D)}{4\pi}}.$$
For $|D|=0$ the operator is zero.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write

$$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$

([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and
$\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every**
set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue
measurable with

$$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$

In particular this covers the four one-dimensional face conventions in each
coordinate — the open box, the closed box $[a,b]$, the half-open box
$B(a,b) = \prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i]$ of [[def-half-open-box]], and every mixture of
them, in any combination of coordinates — and it gives measure $0$ to all of them
whenever $a_i = b_i$ for some $i<n$. For a half-open box with infinite
parameters the value is already
$\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]).

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

For real $x,y$, $\exp(x+iy)=e^x(\cos y+i\sin y)$ and $|\exp(x+iy)|=e^x$. In particular $e^{i\pi}+1=0$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-eulers-formula]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]], [[thm-pythagorean-and-parity-identities-for-all-six-trigonometric-functions]], [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]].

The complex exponential is entire, and

$$ \exp'(z)=\exp z $$

for every $z\in\mathbb C$.

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$ and let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$.

1. **Fundamental theorem, second part, in $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be differentiable at every point of $[a,b]$ as
   a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]), and
   suppose $f' : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ is integrable. Then
   $$\int_a^b f' \;=\; f(b) - f(a).$$
2. **A bounded derivative gives a Lipschitz function.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable at
   every point of $(a,b)$, and let $M \ge 0$ satisfy
   $\lVert f'(t)\rVert_2 \le M$ for every $t \in (a,b)$. Then
   $$\lVert f(t) - f(s)\rVert_2 \;\le\; M\,|t-s| \qquad \text{for all } s,t \in [a,b],$$
   that is, $f$ is Lipschitz with constant $M$ as a map
   $([a,b], d_{\mathbb{R}}) \to (\mathbb{R}^{m}, d_2)$
   ([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]], [[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]],
   [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]).

On every measure space the pairing $\langle f,g\rangle=\int f\overline g$ on complex $L^2$ is representative-independent, linear in the first variable, conjugate-linear in the second, conjugate symmetric and positive definite, with $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$. Moreover,
$$|\langle f,g\rangle|\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$
If $g\ne0$ as a class, equality holds iff $f=cg$ a.e. for some $c\in\mathbb C$. If $g=0$, equality holds for every $f$.

For each finite $m\ge0$, the same conclusions hold on tuples $F=(f_j)_{j<m}$, with pairing $B(F,G)=\sum_{j<m}\langle f_j,g_j\rangle$ and $\|F\|^2=\sum_{j<m}\|f_j\|_2^2$. For $G\ne0$, equality means $f_j=cg_j$ a.e. for every $j$, with one common scalar $c$.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field, and let
$T:X\to Y$ be bounded in the sense of [[def-bounded-linear-operator]]. The
**operator norm** of $T$ is

$$\|T\| := \sup\{\|Tx\| : x \in X,\ \|x\| \le 1\}.$$

The set on the right contains $0$ and every bound $C$ for $T$ bounds it
above. Thus its finite real supremum exists by the proved least-upper-bound
property of the library's real field ([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]).
In particular every number strictly below the supremum is exceeded by a
member of this set; otherwise it would be a smaller upper bound. No choice
principle is used for this assertion.

The same number is the least bound of $T$:

$$\|T\| = \inf\{C \ge 0 : \|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \text{ for all } x \in X\}.$$

If $X \ne \{0\}$, positive homogeneity also gives

$$\|T\| = \sup\{\|Tx\| : \|x\| = 1\}.$$

When $X = \{0\}$, the unit sphere is empty and the unit-ball supremum is $0$,
so $\|T\| = 0$.

Let $\gamma$ be the unique smallest positive zero of cosine supplied by [[thm-cosine-has-a-smallest-positive-zero]]. Define
$$\pi:=2\gamma.$$

Thus $\pi>0$ and $\pi/2=\gamma$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $D\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded Lebesgue-measurable set with $0<M:=|D|<\infty$, and let $k>0$. Write $S^2:=\{v\in\mathbb R^3:|v|=1\}$ and $C_D:=\sqrt{M\,\operatorname{diam}(D)/(4\pi)}$. For $q\in L^\infty(D;\mathbb C)$, extended by zero off $D$, set $G_k(z):=e^{ik|z|}/(4\pi|z|)$ for $z\ne0$ and $G_k(0):=0$, and let
$$K_{q,k}v(x):=\int_D G_k(x-y)q(y)v(y)\,dy,\qquad \rho_k(q):=\|K_{q,k}\|_{L^2(D)\to L^2(D)}.$$
The **small-norm contrast class** is
$$\mathcal U_{D,k}:=\{q\in L^\infty(D;\mathbb C):\rho_k(q)<1\}.$$
For $d\in S^2$, put $f_{k,d}(x):=e^{ikd\cdot x}$ on $D$. For $q\in\mathcal U_{D,k}$, let $u_{q,k,d}\in L^2(D;\mathbb C)$ denote the unique solution of $u=f_{k,d}+K_{q,k}u$. For $q\in\mathcal U_{D,k}$, define the exact far-field data family by
$$\mathcal S_k(q)(\theta,d):=\frac1{4\pi}\int_D e^{-ik\theta\cdot y}q(y)u_{q,k,d}(y)\,dy,\qquad (\theta,d)\in S^2\times S^2.$$

For $h\in L^\infty(D;\mathbb C)$, define its first Born data by
$$\mathcal B_k h(\theta,d):=\frac1{4\pi}\int_D e^{-ik\theta\cdot y}h(y)e^{ikd\cdot y}\,dy=\frac1{4\pi}\widehat{h_0}\!\left(\frac{k}{2\pi}(\theta-d)\right),$$
where $h_0$ is the zero extension of $h$ to $\mathbb R^3$ and $\widehat g(\xi):=\int_{\mathbb R^3}g(y)e^{-2\pi i y\cdot\xi}\,dy$ for $g\in L^1(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$. No uniqueness or stability outside $\mathcal U_{D,k}$ is asserted.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: By [F2], $M=|D|=1/64$. By [F3], every distance in $D$ is at most $\sqrt3/4$, and opposite corners attain this value, so $d:=\operatorname{diam}(D)=\sqrt3/4<1/2$. The indicator $1_D$ is a nonzero $L^2$ class.

For $0\le r\le d$, the curve $\gamma(s)=e^{irs}$ on $[0,1]$ has derivative $\gamma'(s)=ir e^{irs}$, whose modulus is $r$ by [F4]. Fact [F5] gives $|e^{ir}-1|\le r$, and hence $\operatorname{Re}(e^{ir})\ge1-r\ge1-d>1/2$.

For almost every $x\in D$, the kernel integral in [F1] represents $K_{q,1}1_D(x)$. For such an $x$, almost every $y\in D$ has $r=|x-y|$ in $(0,d]$ by step 1.1, and [F1] gives $\operatorname{Re}G_1(x-y)=\frac{\operatorname{Re}(e^{ir})}{4\pi r}>\frac{1}{8\pi d}.$ Integrating this pointwise lower bound against the positive constant $q=512\pi$ yields $\operatorname{Re}(K_{q,1}1_D)(x)>qM/(8\pi d)=1/d=4/\sqrt3>2$ for almost every $x\in D$; the last inequality follows by squaring the positive sides of $\sqrt3<2$.

By step 3.1, $g:=|K_{q,1}1_D|^2-4$ is positive almost everywhere on $D$; [F1] and [A1] put $K_{q,1}1_D$ in $L^2(D)$, so $g$ is integrable. Since $M>0$ by step 1.1, the sets $\{x\in D:g(x)>1/n\}$ cannot all be null, as their countable union contains the positive-measure set where $g>0$. Thus for some $n$, the set $\{x\in D:g(x)>1/n\}$ has positive measure, so $\int_D g\ge |\{g>1/n\}|/n>0$; hence $\|K_{q,1}1_D\|_2^2>4M=4\|1_D\|_2^2$. The unit-ball supremum in [F7] gives $\|K_{q,1}\|>2$. By [F9] the contrast lies outside $\mathcal U_{D,1}$, so the small-norm model branch does not apply; no nonexistence or nonuniqueness conclusion follows.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $D$ have finite Lebesgue measure. Assume Countable Choice and the hypotheses and notation of the fixed-frequency far-field definition. For $q\in\mathcal U_{D,k}$ put $\rho=\rho_k(q)$. Uniformly over all incident and observation directions,
$$\sup_{\theta,d\in S^2}\left|\mathcal S_k(q)(\theta,d)-\mathcal B_kq(\theta,d)\right|\le\frac{M}{4\pi}\|q\|_\infty\frac{\rho}{1-\rho}.$$

$$\sup_{\theta,d\in S^2}\left|\mathcal S_k(q)(\theta,d)-\mathcal B_kq(\theta,d)\right|\le\frac{M C_D}{4\pi}\frac{\|q\|_\infty^2}{1-C_D\|q\|_\infty}.$$

Let $\mathbb{R}$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]).
For every $a \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \ge 0$ and every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with
$n \ge 1$ there is a **unique** $s \in \mathbb{R}$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^n = a$
([[def-integer-power]]); we write

$$s = a^{1/n} = \sqrt[n]{a}.$$

Moreover $a^{1/n} > 0$ when $a > 0$, and $a^{1/1} = a$.

**This generalises the published [[thm-of-square-roots]], and the case $n = 2$ is
not new.** That theorem already produces the unique $\sqrt{a} \ge 0$ with
$(\sqrt{a})^2 = a$, and it is cited as such throughout the library; the notation
$a^{1/2}$ introduced here is the same number. What is new is the passage to
general $n$: the completed square that drives the $n = 2$ argument has no direct
analogue, and its place is taken by the factorisation of $b^n - a^n$ and the
resulting Lipschitz estimate ([[lem-power-difference-factorisation]]).

derivations.claim: By [F4], $M=|D|=\ell^3$. The coordinate formula [F5] shows that the largest distance in the cube is attained by opposite corners and is $\operatorname{diam}(D)=\sqrt3\,\ell$. Also $\|q\|_\infty=1$.

Substituting the values from step 1.1 into [F2] gives $\rho_1(q)\le C_D=\sqrt{\frac{\ell^3\sqrt3\ell}{4\pi}}=\sqrt{\frac{\sqrt3\ell^4}{4\pi}}=\frac1{2\sqrt2}<1.$ The final strict inequality follows from $\sqrt2>1$. Hence $q\in\mathcal U_{D,1}$ by [F1].

Apply [F3] with $M=\ell^3$, $\|q\|_\infty=1$, and $C_D=1/(2\sqrt2)$. Since $C_D<1$, it gives the uniform error bound $\sup_{\theta,d\in S^2}|\mathcal S_1(q)(\theta,d)-\mathcal B_1q(\theta,d)|\le\frac{\ell^3}{4\pi}\frac{C_D}{1-C_D}=\frac{\ell^3}{4\pi(2\sqrt2-1)}.$ This verifies the claimed Born-regime example.
