citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a bounded Lipschitz domain, $V=H^1_0(\Omega;\mathbb R)$, and $H=L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R)$. Use the real integral pairing on $H$. Equip $V$ with the standard full Sobolev inner product and norm
$$(v,w)_V=(v,w)_H+\sum_{i=1}^d(D_i v,D_i w)_H,\qquad \|v\|_V^2=\|v\|_H^2+\sum_{i=1}^d\|D_i v\|_H^2.$$
Here $H^1_0=W^{1,2}_0$ is the closure of $C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ in the $W^{1,2}$ norm of [[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]]. Under Countable Choice, $H$ and $V$ are real Hilbert spaces; the local proof of completeness of $V$ is included in [[thm-linear-elliptic-control-state-and-adjoint-wellposedness]]. The inclusion $J:V\to H$ is continuous with $\|J\|\le1$.

Let $E\subseteq\Omega$ be bounded and measurable, $U=L^2(E;\mathbb R)$ with its real integral inner product, and let $Q_{ad}\subset U$ be the pointwise box of [[def-pde-box-control-set]]. Under Countable Choice, $U$ is a real Hilbert space by [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]. Let $a:V\times V\to\mathbb R$ be bilinear, bounded with constant $M$, and coercive with constant $\beta>0$ in the stated $V$ norm; symmetry is not assumed. Let $B:U\to V^*$ be bounded and linear, and fix $f\in V^*$, $u_d\in H$, and $\alpha>0$.

For every $q\in U$, the **state** $u(q)\in V$ is required to satisfy
$$
a(u(q),v)=\langle f+Bq,v\rangle_{V^*,V}\qquad(v\in V).
$$
The reduced objective, defined on all of $U$ and minimized over $Q_{ad}$, is
$$
\widehat J(q)=\frac12\|Ju(q)-u_d\|_H^2+\frac\alpha2\|q\|_U^2.
$$
A spatially varying coefficient, boundary control, variational crimes, finite-element control discretization, and parabolic evolution are separate hypotheses or branches; none is implicit in this definition. The state well-definedness is supplied by [[thm-linear-elliptic-control-state-and-adjoint-wellposedness]].

Assume Countable Choice and the setting of [[def-linear-elliptic-pde-constrained-control-problem]]. For every $q\in U$, there is a unique state $u(q)\in V$ satisfying
$$
a(u(q),v)=\langle f+Bq,v\rangle\qquad(v\in V),
$$
and
$$
\|u(q)\|_V\le \beta^{-1}\|f+Bq\|_{V^*}.
$$
For every $q\in U$, there is also a unique adjoint $p(q)\in V$ satisfying
$$
a(v,p(q))=(Ju(q)-u_d,Jv)_H\qquad(v\in V),
$$
with
$$
\|p(q)\|_V\le \beta^{-1}\|J\|\,\|Ju(q)-u_d\|_H.
$$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega$ be a bounded polyhedral open set with a finite matching
affine simplicial mesh, let $1\le p<\infty$, and let $v$ be a real-valued
conforming piecewise polynomial whose polynomial trace vanishes on every boundary
facet. Then
$$v\in W^{1,p}_0(\Omega),\qquad \|v\|_{L^p(\Omega)}\le C_\Omega\|\nabla v\|_{L^p(\Omega)}.$$
Here $W^{1,p}_0$ is the norm closure of $C_c^\infty(\Omega)$; no C1
trace characterization is used.

Fix an integer $d\ge2$. The underlying coordinate index set of $\mathbb R^d$
is $I_d=\{0,\ldots,d-1\}$. In this definition the conventional labels
$1\le i\le d$ are relabeled by $i\mapsto i-1$: write
$\widehat x_i:=\widehat x(i-1)$, and let $e_i\in\mathbb R^d$ be the function
on $I_d$ with $e_i(i-1)=1$ and $e_i(k)=0$ for $k\ne i-1$.
The vertex and barycentric labels $0,\ldots,d$ are distinct from these
underlying coordinate indices. The **reference open simplex** is
$$\widehat S_d:=\{\widehat x\in\mathbb R^d:\widehat x_i>0\ (1\le i\le d),\ \sum_{i=1}^d\widehat x_i<1\},$$
with closure $\overline{\widehat S_d}=\operatorname{conv}\{0,e_1,\ldots,e_d\}$.

A **matching affine simplicial mesh** of a bounded polyhedral open set
$\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ is a finite set $\mathcal T$ of closed,
nondegenerate $d$-simplices such that their union is $\overline\Omega$,
their interiors are pairwise disjoint, $\Omega$ is the interior of their
union, and the intersection of two distinct cells is either empty or a
whole face of each. Thus no lower-dimensional crack is omitted from
$\Omega$ while its surrounding cells are retained. Every interior facet is
incident to exactly two cells and every boundary facet to one. The faces of
a cell are the convex hulls of its vertex subsets. A facet means a face of
dimension $d-1$.

For each cell $K\in\mathcal T$, an affine bijection
$$F_K:\overline{\widehat S_d}\to K,\qquad F_K(\widehat x)=b_K+A_K\widehat x,$$
with invertible $A_K\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ is a **reference map**.
Choose the vertex order so $\det A_K>0$; this is the orientation convention
used for Piola formulas. Write $h_K:=\operatorname{diam}(K)$ and let
$\rho_K$ be the radius of the largest Euclidean ball contained in $K$.
A family $\{\mathcal T_h\}_{h\in H}$ is **shape regular** if there is a
finite $\sigma$ such that $h_K/\rho_K\le\sigma$ for every
$h\in H$ and $K\in\mathcal T_h$. This universal condition is vacuous for
an empty family.
This definition uses radius; references using the diameter of the inscribed
ball differ by a factor of two.

An affine image of the reference square is a parallelogram. A general
quadrilateral requires a nonaffine map and is outside this affine definition;
curved-cell approximation is not included here.

Let $d\ge1$, let $\widehat K\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a nonempty bounded open
reference cell, let $q\ge1$ be an integer, and let
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. A **reference finite element** is a
triple $(\widehat K,\widehat P,\widehat\Sigma)$ where $\widehat P$ is an
$N$-dimensional subspace of $[C(\overline{\widehat K};\mathbb K)]^q$ for
$N\in\mathbb N_0$ and
$\widehat\Sigma=(\widehat\sigma_1,\ldots,\widehat\sigma_N)$ is a list of
linear functionals on $\widehat P$ for which
$$J_{\widehat\Sigma}:\widehat P\to\mathbb K^N,\qquad J_{\widehat\Sigma}(p):=(\widehat\sigma_1(p),\ldots,\widehat\sigma_N(p)),$$
is bijective. The functionals are the **degrees of freedom** and the triple
is **unisolvent**. Its **shape functions** are the unique dual basis
$\widehat\phi_1,\ldots,\widehat\phi_N\in\widehat P$ satisfying
$\widehat\sigma_i(\widehat\phi_j)=\delta_{ij}$.

If $X$ is a normed vector space of functions on $\widehat K$ containing
$\widehat P$, fix for each $i$ a bounded linear extension of
$\widehat\sigma_i$ to $X$, and denote this chosen extension by the same
symbol. The **reference interpolation operator** associated with these
chosen extensions is
$$\widehat I:X\to\widehat P,\qquad \widehat I v:=\sum_{i=1}^N\widehat\sigma_i(v)\widehat\phi_i.$$
The definition of a reference finite element does not assert that any
particular list of functionals is unisolvent or bounded on a given Sobolev
space; those are separate proof obligations. For $N=0$, $\widehat P=\{0\}$,
$\mathbb K^0=\{0\}$, the empty list gives the unique bijection between these
zero spaces, and the shape-function list is empty. The corresponding
interpolation formula is the empty sum, hence the zero map into $\{0\}$.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be real Hilbert spaces, let $D\subseteq X$ be a nonempty domain, and let $F:D\to Y$ be a forward map. For a regularization parameter $\alpha>0$, reference element $x_0\in X$, and datum $y\in Y$, the **nonlinear Tikhonov functional** is the map $J_{\alpha,y,x_0}:D\to[0,\infty)$ defined by

$$
J_{\alpha,y,x_0}(x):=\frac12\|F(x)-y\|_Y^2+\frac{\alpha}{2}\|x-x_0\|_X^2\qquad(x\in D).
$$

A **global minimizer** is a point $x_\alpha\in D$ such that $J_{\alpha,y,x_0}(x_\alpha)\le J_{\alpha,y,x_0}(x)$ for every $x\in D$. This definition asserts neither existence nor uniqueness.

Assume a finite-element PDE model satisfying the admissibility and certificate contract, with nonempty closed convex coefficient set $Q_h$, discrete Tikhonov objective $\Phi_h$ using reference coefficient $q_0$, a state/adjoint solve routine, an exact projection routine, an objective interval routine, and finite solve and evaluation budgets. Let the input be an initial coefficient $q_{\rm init}\in Q_h$, data $y^\delta\in Y_h$, noise bound $\delta\ge0$, penalty $\alpha>0$, state and adjoint residual tolerances $\tau_u,\tau_p\ge0$, discrepancy factor $\kappa\ge1$, stationarity tolerance $\tau_g\ge0$, scaling parameter $L>0$, and positive integer budgets $N_{\rm iter}$, $N_{\rm solve}$, $N_{\rm eval}$, and $N_{\rm backtrack}$. The global budget $N_{\rm solve}$ counts state and adjoint solves; $N_{\rm eval}$ counts exact projections and objective-interval evaluations. The scaling parameter $L$ is only a positive step-size scale; it is not assumed to be a Lipschitz constant. The algorithm returns a coefficient, one status from `converged`, `discrepancy-stopped`, `linear-solve-failed`, `inadmissible`, or `budget-exhausted`, and any diagnostics certified at that coefficient.

1. If $q_{\rm init}\notin Q_h$ or the model's exact admissibility predicate is false at $q_{\rm init}$, return status `inadmissible` without solving a PDE. Otherwise set $q:=q_{\rm init}$.

2. For $k=0,\ldots,N_{\rm iter}$, first check the finite-time admissibility predicate, which includes membership in $Q_h$. If it is false, return `inadmissible`. If no global solve or evaluation budget remains, return `budget-exhausted`.

3. Call the state/adjoint solver at $q$ with tolerances $\tau_u,\tau_p$ and the remaining solve budget. If it returns `failure`, if either certified residual bound exceeds its declared tolerance, or if any required state/adjoint error estimate or derivative bound is missing or invalid, return `linear-solve-failed`. Otherwise receive $\widetilde g_h$, $\widetilde F_h$, $\eta_u,\eta_p,P,L_{J,u},L_{R,u},M_q,L_{G,u}$ and set $\varepsilon_g=(L_{J,u}+L_{R,u}P)\eta_u+M_q\eta_p$ and $\varepsilon_F=L_{G,u}\eta_u$.

4. Use the exact projection routine to compute $P_{Q_h}(q-\widetilde g_h/L)$. If the routine fails or the evaluation budget is exhausted, return `budget-exhausted`. Set $\widetilde\rho:=L\|q-P_{Q_h}(q-\widetilde g_h/L)\|_2$. If $\widetilde\rho+\varepsilon_g\le\tau_g$, return `converged` with stationarity upper bound $\widetilde\rho+\varepsilon_g$. This status means only that the exact projected-gradient residual of the discrete objective is within tolerance; it is not a claim that an iterate sequence converges or that $q$ is a global minimizer.

5. Compute $d^+:=\|\widetilde F_h-y^\delta\|_{Y_h}+\varepsilon_F$. If $d^+\le\kappa\delta$, return `discrepancy-stopped` with data-residual upper bound $d^+$. This status certifies only the discrete model's data discrepancy.

6. If $k=N_{\rm iter}$, return `budget-exhausted` at the current coefficient with its current diagnostics. Otherwise, evaluate the current objective using its certified interval $[\ell_h(q),u_h(q)]$. If the evaluation fails because a required state or adjoint solve fails its contract, return `linear-solve-failed`; if the global solve or evaluation budget is exhausted, return `budget-exhausted`.

7. For $j=0,\ldots,N_{\rm backtrack}-1$, set $t_j=2^{-j}/L$ and use the exact projection routine to compute $q_j=P_{Q_h}(q-t_j\widetilde g_h)$. If projection fails or the evaluation budget is exhausted, return `budget-exhausted`. Reject this trial and continue to the next $j$ if $q_j=q$ or its admissibility predicate is false. Otherwise evaluate a certified interval $[\ell_h(q_j),u_h(q_j)]$. If evaluation fails because a required linear solve fails its contract, return `linear-solve-failed`; if it only exhausts the finite evaluation budget, return `budget-exhausted`. Accept the first trial with $u_h(q_j)\le\ell_h(q)$, set $q:=q_j$, and continue to the next outer iteration. This interval test guarantees $\Phi_h(q_j)\le\Phi_h(q)$.

8. If no trial is accepted within the backtracking budget, return `budget-exhausted` at the current coefficient. Each accepted trial uses one of the at most $N_{\rm iter}$ updates; the inclusive outer loop evaluates the final coefficient before returning budget exhaustion.

The global solve budget counts all primal and adjoint solves used both at iterates and in objective trials. The evaluation budget counts every projection and objective-interval call. Each status is returned after finitely many tests because all four budgets are finite and every model routine returns in finite time or reports failure. Any continuous-to-discrete mesh bound is reported separately by the model contract and is never inferred from the algebraic state or adjoint residuals.

Fix an integer $d\ge2$, a bounded polyhedral open set $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$, a finite matching affine simplicial mesh $\mathcal T_h$ of $\Omega$, and unisolvent reference finite elements assembled on that mesh. Thus the mesh is a finite face-to-face cover by nondegenerate affine simplices with disjoint interiors, and each local finite-element degree-of-freedom map is bijective on its polynomial space. Fix coefficient spaces $\Theta_h=\mathbb R^m$, $V_h=\mathbb R^n$, and $Y_h=\mathbb R^s$ with their standard Euclidean inner products, where $m,n,s\ge1$. Let $Q_h\subseteq\Theta_h$ be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let $O_h\subseteq\Theta_h$ be open with $Q_h\subseteq O_h$.

A **finite-element PDE model** in this contract consists of a continuously differentiable residual map $R_h:O_h\times V_h\to V_h$ and a continuously differentiable observation map $G_h:O_h\times V_h\to Y_h$. It must supply a continuously differentiable state branch $S_h:O_h\to V_h$ satisfying $R_h(q,S_h(q))=0$ for every $q\in O_h$. For every $q\in Q_h$, this branch must be the specified unique admissible state and the matrix $D_uR_h(q,S_h(q))$ must be invertible. The discrete forward map is $F_h(q):=G_h(q,S_h(q))$. The unisolvent finite-element degrees of freedom identify $V_h$ with its coefficient space; all matrix transposes below are in the fixed Euclidean coefficient inner products.

For data $y^\delta\in Y_h$, reference parameter $q_0\in\Theta_h$, and $\alpha>0$, the discrete nonlinear Tikhonov objective is
$$
\Phi_h(q):=\frac12\|F_h(q)-y^\delta\|_{Y_h}^2+\frac\alpha2\|q-q_0\|_{\Theta_h}^2\qquad(q\in Q_h).
$$
Define the finite-dimensional objective before eliminating the state by
$$
J_h(q,u):=\frac12\|G_h(q,u)-y^\delta\|_{Y_h}^2+\frac\alpha2\|q-q_0\|_{\Theta_h}^2.
$$
The symbols $\nabla_uJ_h$ and $\nabla_qJ_h$ denote the Euclidean gradient vectors representing the two partial derivative functionals. At an admissible $q$, the **exact discrete adjoint** $p_h(q)\in V_h$ is the unique solution of
$$
\bigl(D_uR_h(q,S_h(q))\bigr)^T p_h(q)=\nabla_uJ_h(q,S_h(q)).
$$
The associated discrete-adjoint gradient vector is
$$
g_h(q):=\nabla_qJ_h(q,S_h(q))-\bigl(D_qR_h(q,S_h(q))\bigr)^T p_h(q).
$$
The next lemma proves that this vector is the gradient of $\Phi_h$; the definition itself asserts no minimizer exists and no gradient iteration converges.

An **admissibility predicate** is a specified finite-time test $\operatorname{adm}_h(q)$ that decides whether $q\in Q_h$ and checks the model's stated coefficient, boundary, mesh, and time-step hypotheses before a PDE solve. For an explicit time discretization, a Courant–Friedrichs–Lewy condition (CFL condition) is a method-specific bound relating the time step to the mesh and the discrete evolution operator; no universal CFL threshold is part of this definition. A true predicate result certifies that the declared model hypotheses hold for that input, not merely that a heuristic check passed.

The model must also supply an exact finite-dimensional projection routine which returns $P_{Q_h}(z)$ for a queried $z\in\Theta_h$ in finite time or reports failure only when its declared finite call budget is exhausted. The unique nearest point exists because $Q_h$ is nonempty, closed, and convex, but an operational routine for computing it is an additional part of this contract.

A solver routine with declared nonnegative state and adjoint tolerances $\tau_u,\tau_p$ and a finite solve budget must return either `failure` or approximate state and adjoint vectors $\widetilde u,\widetilde p$ together with certified finite bounds $\rho_u,\rho_p,\eta_u,\eta_p,P,L_{J,u},L_{R,u},M_q,L_{G,u}$. The residual bounds have the exact-system meaning $\|R_h(q,\widetilde u)\|_{V_h}\le\rho_u$ and $\|(D_uR_h(q,u))^T\widetilde p-\nabla_uJ_h(q,u)\|_{V_h}\le\rho_p$, where $u=S_h(q)$; both must satisfy $\rho_u\le\tau_u$ and $\rho_p\le\tau_p$. In particular, an adjoint residual evaluated at $\widetilde u$ alone does not certify $\rho_p$ unless the model also bounds the resulting state and derivative-data defects. With $u=S_h(q)$ and $p=p_h(q)$, the model must certify
$$
\|u-\widetilde u\|_{V_h}\le\eta_u,\qquad \|p-\widetilde p\|_{V_h}\le\eta_p,\qquad \|p\|_{V_h}\le P,
$$
$$
\|\nabla_qJ_h(q,u)-\nabla_qJ_h(q,\widetilde u)\|_{\Theta_h}\le L_{J,u}\eta_u,
$$
$$
\|(D_qR_h(q,u))^T-(D_qR_h(q,\widetilde u))^T\|\le L_{R,u}\eta_u,\qquad \|(D_qR_h(q,\widetilde u))^T\|\le M_q,
$$
and $\|G_h(q,u)-G_h(q,\widetilde u)\|_{Y_h}\le L_{G,u}\eta_u$. It then returns
$$
\widetilde g:=\nabla_qJ_h(q,\widetilde u)-(D_qR_h(q,\widetilde u))^T\widetilde p,\qquad \widetilde F:=G_h(q,\widetilde u),
$$
All constants and state/adjoint error bounds must be justified for the chosen model with every derivative-data, geometry, quadrature, and algebraic-solve defect retained. Certified residual bounds $\rho_u,\rho_p$ do not by themselves imply $\eta_u,\eta_p$; a separate model-valid stability estimate is required. The proposition below derives the resulting $\varepsilon_g$ and $\varepsilon_F$ bounds. An objective-evaluation routine must return in its finite budget either `failure` or an interval $[\ell_h(q),u_h(q)]$ containing the exact value $\Phi_h(q)$; `failure` is permitted only when a required state/adjoint solve fails its contract or the evaluation-call budget is exhausted. Exact evaluation is the degenerate-interval case. Projection and objective-evaluation calls consume the algorithm's finite evaluation budget. Each routine must return within its declared budget or report failure.

If a continuous model $F$ is also supplied, an optional mesh certificate $\varepsilon_{\rm mesh}$ must separately bound the claimed continuous-to-discrete error, such as $\|F_h(q)-F(q)\|$ or $\|\nabla\Phi_h(q)-\nabla\Phi(q)\|$. The state and adjoint algebraic residual certificates do not imply this mesh certificate.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

For any finite-element PDE model satisfying its solver and admissibility contract, the finite-budget Tikhonov algorithm returns after finitely many operations one of `converged`, `discrepancy-stopped`, `linear-solve-failed`, `inadmissible`, or `budget-exhausted`. A `converged` return satisfies the exact discrete projected-gradient bound $\|G_L(q)\|_2\le\tau_g$; a `discrepancy-stopped` return satisfies $\|F_h(q)-y^\delta\|_{Y_h}\le\kappa\delta$. Every accepted safeguarded step has nonincreasing exact discrete objective $\Phi_h$. `inadmissible` and `linear-solve-failed` are returned only on the corresponding failed predicate or solver-certificate checks. `budget-exhausted` asserts no optimizer or continuous-model accuracy.

derivations.claim: The four triangles have area $1/4$. On each triangle $\phi$ is the barycentric coordinate of $O$. For $k=1,2,3$, integration on the reference triangle gives $\int_K\phi^k=|K|\,2/((k+1)(k+2))$; this follows by integrating $(1-x-y)^k$ over $0\le x\le1$, $0\le y\le1-x$. Hence $\int_\Omega\phi=1/3$, $\int_\Omega\phi^2=1/6$, and $\int_\Omega\phi^3=1/10$. Each cell's base is a unit square edge and its altitude from $O$ is $1/2$, so the affine barycentric coordinate has gradient magnitude $2$; therefore $\int_\Omega|\nabla\phi|^2=4$. By [F2], $w=\phi^2\in H^1_0(\Omega)$. Since $|\Omega|=1$, [F6] gives $|\int_\Omega q|\le\|q\|_{L^2}$, and it also gives $|a(w,z)|\le\|w\|_V\|z\|_V$; hence $B$ is a bounded linear map into $V^*$. The same inequality gives $|\int_\Omega v|\le\|v\|_{L^2}\le\|v\|_V$, so the observation is bounded. The form has $a(v,v)=\|v\|_V^2$ and continuity constant $1$, so [F1] applies and gives a unique state.

The exact state is $u(\gamma)=\gamma w$, since substituting it gives $a(u(\gamma),z)=\gamma a(w,z)$ for every $z\in V$; uniqueness from [F1] identifies this as the state map. Therefore $F(\gamma)=\gamma\int_\Omega\phi^2=\gamma/6$.

Write the Galerkin state as $u_h(\gamma)=c\gamma\phi$. Testing its weak equation with $\phi$ gives $c\,a(\phi,\phi)=a(\phi^2,\phi)$. Here $a(\phi,\phi)=\int(\phi^2+|\nabla\phi|^2)=1/6+4=25/6$, while $a(\phi^2,\phi)=\int(\phi^3+2\phi|\nabla\phi|^2)=1/10+2\cdot4\cdot(1/3)=83/30$. Thus $c=(83/30)/(25/6)=83/125$, and $F_h(\gamma)=c\gamma\int_\Omega\phi=83\gamma/375$. The scalar Galerkin stiffness $25/6$ is positive, so this state solve is unique and its exact algebraic residual is zero.

The exact objective is $\Phi(\gamma)=\frac12(\gamma/6-1/6)^2+\frac12\gamma^2$. Its derivative is $(1/36+1)\gamma-1/36$, so its unique minimizer is $\gamma_*=1/37\in[0,1]$. The discrete objective is $\Phi_h(\gamma)=\frac12(83\gamma/375-1/6)^2+\frac12\gamma^2$. Its derivative is $((83/375)^2+1)\gamma-(83/375)(1/6)$. Since $(83/375)(1/6)=83/2250$ and $(83/375)^2+1=147514/140625$, its unique zero is $\gamma_h=(83/2250)(140625/147514)=10375/295028\in[0,1]$. Both second derivatives are positive, so these stationary points are the unique minimizers on the interval. Moreover $10375\cdot37=383875>295028$, hence $\gamma_h>1/37=\gamma_*$.

For every $\gamma\in[0,1]$, $|F(\gamma)-F_h(\gamma)|=|\gamma|\,|1/6-83/375|\le41/750$, with equality at $\gamma=1$. Thus the forward mesh discrepancy has the explicit bound $41/750$. The scalar Galerkin state matrix is $25/6>0$, and the scalar adjoint matrix is its transpose, so both equations can be solved exactly with zero algebraic residuals. By [F4], [F5] and [F7], the exact discrete reduced gradient at $\gamma_h$ is $\Phi_h'(\gamma_h)=0$. With the algorithm inputs specified in the Example, $\gamma_h$ is interior and $P_{[0,1]}(\gamma_h-\Phi_h'(\gamma_h))=\gamma_h$, so the projected-gradient residual is zero and the algorithm returns `converged` before its discrepancy check. This status certifies only discrete stationarity while the continuous model has the different minimizer proved in step 3.1; the mesh bound remains separate.

citations.quote: Assume countable choice and let $n\ge1$. Fourier transformation on Schwartz space extends uniquely to a surjective complex-linear isometry $\mathcal F_2:L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)\to L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$. It preserves the first-variable-linear inner product, and hence is unitary.

Assume countable choice. The negative-sign, $2\pi$-normalized Fourier transform is continuous $\mathcal F:\mathcal S\to\mathcal S$, and
$$\mathcal F(\partial^\alpha f)(\xi)=(2\pi i\xi)^\alpha\widehat f(\xi),\qquad \partial^\beta\widehat f=\mathcal F((-2\pi ix)^\beta f).$$
Assume countable choice. The Fourier transform is a topological automorphism of $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$, with $\mathcal F^2=R$ and $\mathcal F^{-1}=R\mathcal F$, where $Rf(x)=f(-x)$.

Assume countable choice. For $f,g\in L^1(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$ with $\widehat f\in L^1$, use the continuous representative $f_c(x)=\int\widehat f(\eta)e^{2\pi ix\cdot\eta}\,d\eta$. Then $f_cg\in L^1$ and, for every $\xi$,
$$\widehat{fg}(\xi)=\int\widehat f(\eta)\widehat g(\xi-\eta)\,d\eta.$$
The product class is unchanged by other representatives; the symmetric variant holds when $\widehat g\in L^1$ instead.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n \ge 1$,
let $S^{n-1} \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be the unit sphere, and let $\sigma$ be the
set function of [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]]. Then $\sigma$
is a finite Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$, and for every Borel measurable
$f : \mathbb R^n \to [0,\infty]$,
$$\int_{\mathbb R^n} f(x)\,d\lambda_n(x) = \int_0^\infty \int_{S^{n-1}} f(r\omega) r^{n-1}\,d\sigma(\omega)\,dr.$$
Moreover, $\sigma$ is the unique Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$ with this
property.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Rotate coordinates so the two given vectors are the first coordinate vectors. Write $\xi=(a,se_2'+r\omega)$ with $a\in\mathbb R$, $r\ge0$, and $\omega\in S^{d-2}$ in the remaining coordinates. Then $p_\zeta(\xi)=s^2-a^2-r^2+2isa$, and its zero set is $\Sigma=\{a=0,r=s\}$. The exact distance to this sphere is $D(\xi)=\sqrt{a^2+(r-s)^2}$. For each fixed $K$, on $|\xi|\le Ks$ one has $|p_\zeta(\xi)|\asymp_K sD(\xi)$. To check the lower bound, if $|a|\ge D/4$, use the imaginary part. Otherwise $|r-s|>D/2$ and $|a|\le|r-s|/2$; since $|r-s|\le r+s$, $|s^2-r^2-a^2|\ge(s+r)|s-r|-a^2\ge(3/4)(s+r)|s-r|\ge(3/8)sD$. The upper bound follows by expanding $s^2-a^2-r^2$ and using $|a|+r+s\le C_Ks$. Also, if $|\xi|\ge8s$, the triangle inequality gives $|p_\zeta(\xi)|\asymp|\xi|^2$. Therefore $s/|p_\zeta(\xi)|\le C(1+D(\xi)^{-1})$ everywhere away from $\Sigma$.

For $N>d+3$, the integral $\int\langle\xi-\etaangle^{-N}D(\xi)^{-1}\,d\xi$ is bounded uniformly in $s\ge1$ and $\eta\in\mathbb R^d$, where $\langle xangle=(1+|x|^2)^{1/2}$. Off $D<1/4$ this follows from $D^{-1}\le4$ and integrability of the bracket power. On $D<1/4$, write $\eta=(b,se_2'+t
u)$ with $t\ge0$ and any unit $
u$ if $t=0$. The inequality $|r\omega-t
u|\ge(r/2)|\omega-
u|$ follows from $(r-t)^2+rt|\omega-
u|^2$ by minimizing in $t\ge0$. Hence the angular integral of $\langle\xi-\etaangle^{-N}$ is at most $C r^{-(d-2)}$ for $r\ge3/4$. Indeed, in polar angle $	heta$ from $
u$, split at $	heta=1/r$ and use $|\omega-
u|=2\sin(	heta/2)\ge2	heta/\pi$ and the spherical measure bound $C	heta^{d-3}d	heta$; the two integrals are bounded by $Cr^{-(d-2)}$. This cancels the radial Jacobian $r^{d-2}$. The remaining integral over $|a|,|r-s|<1/4$ of $(a^2+(r-s)^2)^{-1/2}$ is finite with an absolute bound by planar polar integration. This proves the uniform assertion, including all centers $\eta$.

Put $h=\xi-\eta$. The identity $p_\zeta(\eta)-p_\zeta(\xi)=|\xi|^2-|\eta|^2-2i\zeta\cdot h$ and the bound $|\xi|\le C(s+\sqrt{|p_\zeta(\xi)|})$ imply $$s+|p_\zeta(\eta)|\le C(s+|p_\zeta(\xi)|)\langle h\rangle^2.$$ For the auxiliary bound, use $|\xi|^2\le|p_\zeta(\xi)|+2\sqrt2s|\xi|$ and solve this quadratic inequality. In the difference identity, the terms $s|h|$, $\sqrt{|p_\zeta(\xi)|}|h|$, and $|h|^2$ are absorbed by the displayed right side using $s\ge1$ and $2ab\le a^2+b^2$. Since $\widehat\phi$ is rapidly decreasing, steps 1.1–2.1 now give $$\sup_\eta\int |\widehat\phi(\xi-\eta)|\frac{s+|p_\zeta(\eta)|}{|p_\zeta(\xi)|}\,d\xi\le C_\phi.$$ Indeed the integrand is bounded by $C_\phi\langle\xi-\eta\rangle^{-N}(1+D(\xi)^{-1})$ after choosing sufficiently many Schwartz powers.

For nonnegative weights $v,w$ positive almost everywhere and an integrable kernel $K$, Cauchy–Schwarz and Tonelli yield $$\int w(\xi)|(K*f)(\xi)|^2d\xi\le\|K\|_1\left(\sup_\eta\int |K(\xi-\eta)|\frac{w(\xi)}{v(\eta)}d\xi\right)\int v(\eta)|f(\eta)|^2d\eta.$$ To see this directly, bound $|K*f|^2$ by $\|K\|_1\int|K(\xi-\eta)||f(\eta)|^2d\eta$, multiply by $w$, and interchange nonnegative integrals. Apply this with $K=(2\pi)^{-d/2}\widehat\phi$, $v=(s+|p_\zeta|)^{-1}$ and $w=|p_\zeta|^{-1}$. Step 3.1 and [F2] prove the negative-half cutoff bound. The locally integrable singularity proved in step 2.1 and the quadratic large-frequency growth show that every Schwartz function has finite negative-half norm.

The positive-half estimate is the dual of step 4.1. More explicitly, use the same negative-half bound for the cutoff $\overline\phi$ and the Fourier $L^2$ pairing. Cauchy–Schwarz with reciprocal weights gives $|(\phi u,v)_{L^2}|=|(u,\overline\phi v)_{L^2}|\le\|u\|_{\dot X^{1/2}_\zeta}\|\overline\phi v\|_{\dot X^{-1/2}_\zeta}\le C\|u\|_{\dot X^{1/2}_\zeta}\|v\|_{X^{-1/2}_\zeta}$. The supremum over Schwartz $v$ of the left side divided by its negative-half norm equals $\|\phi u\|_{X^{1/2}_\zeta}$. For this equality, truncate the weighted dual extremizer to a ball and away from $\Sigma$, approximate it by smooth compactly supported frequency functions there, and use ordinary $L^2$ density where the weights are bounded above and below; monotone truncation recovers the full weighted integral. Thus the claimed supremum uses no unattained extremizer.

The positive-half weight is at least $s$, so step 5.1 immediately gives $\|\phi u\|_2\le Cs^{-1/2}\|u\|_{\dot X^{1/2}_\zeta}$. Split the gradient Fourier integral into $|\xi|\le8s$ and its complement. The first part has norm at most $8s\|\phi u\|_2$, hence at most $Cs^{1/2}\|u\|_{\dot X^{1/2}_\zeta}$. On the complement $|\xi|^2\le C|p_\zeta(\xi)|$, so its norm is at most $C\|\phi u\|_{X^{1/2}_\zeta}\le C\|u\|_{\dot X^{1/2}_\zeta}$. Since $s\ge1$, their sum gives the gradient bound. A bounded map sends norm-Cauchy sequences to norm-Cauchy sequences, with the same bound; passing to equivalence classes therefore extends each map uniquely to the stated completions.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Fix an integer $k\ge0$ and $0<\alpha<1$. Write $D_r:=\{z\in\mathbb C:|z|<r\}$ and $\overline D_r:=\{z\in\mathbb C:|z|\le r\}$. Let
$$X_{k,\alpha}:=\{q\in C^{k,\alpha}(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C):\operatorname{supp}q\subseteq\overline D_2\},$$
where derivatives are in the real coordinates and the complex-valued Hölder norm is that of [[def-holder-spaces-c-k-alpha-and-their-scaled-norms]] ([[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]). Put $\Gamma(z)=-(2\pi)^{-1}\log|z|$ and let $Nq=\Gamma*q$ be the Newtonian potential of [[def-laplace-fundamental-solution-with-positive-minus-laplacian-sign]] and [[def-newtonian-potential]]. Using the Wirtinger derivatives of [[def-wirtinger-derivatives]], define
$$Tq(z):=-4\,\partial_zNq(z),\qquad Sq(z):=\partial_zTq(z)=-4\,\partial_z^2Nq(z).$$

(i) **The Cauchy transform.** For every $q\in X_{k,\alpha}$ and $z\in\mathbb C$,
$$Tq(z)=\frac1\pi\int_{\mathbb C}\frac{q(\zeta)}{z-\zeta}\,dA(\zeta),$$
and this integral is absolutely convergent. The function $Tq$ is smooth on $\mathbb C\setminus\overline D_2$, satisfies $\partial_{\bar z}Tq=q$ pointwise, and for every $R>0$ obeys
$$\|Tq\|_{C^{k+1,\alpha}(D_R)}\le C_{k,\alpha,R}\,\|q\|_{C^{k,\alpha}(\mathbb R^2)}.$$

(ii) **The derivative.** The function $Sq$ lies in $C^{k,\alpha}(\mathbb R^2)$ and has the principal-value representation
$$Sq(z)=-\frac1\pi\,\operatorname{p.v.}\!\int_{\mathbb C}\frac{q(\zeta)}{(z-\zeta)^2}\,dA(\zeta),$$
where the principal value uses circular truncations. Equivalently, it is the absolutely convergent subtracted integral
$$Sq(z)=-\frac1\pi\left[\int_{|\zeta-z|<1}\frac{q(\zeta)-q(z)}{(z-\zeta)^2}\,dA(\zeta)+\int_{|\zeta-z|\ge1}\frac{q(\zeta)}{(z-\zeta)^2}\,dA(\zeta)\right].$$
The subtraction is only over the unit disk; no globally absolutely convergent subtraction of $q(z)$ is asserted.

(iii) **Bound on the fixed-support space.** There is $M_{k,\alpha}<\infty$, depending only on $k$ and $\alpha$, such that
$$\|Sq\|_{C^{k,\alpha}(\mathbb R^2)}\le M_{k,\alpha}\,\|q\|_{C^{k,\alpha}(\mathbb R^2)},\qquad q\in X_{k,\alpha}.$$
No global $L^p$ mapping property of $S$ is asserted.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb C$ be open for $d_{\mathbb C}$ ([[def-complex-metric-convergence-and-continuity]]). Put $V=\Phi[U]$, where $\Phi(a+bi)=(a,b)$ is the bijection of [[thm-complex-numbers-are-the-real-coordinate-plane]]. Then $V$ is open by [[thm-complex-coordinate-isometry-and-topology-transport]]. For $f:U\to\mathbb C$ define $\widetilde f=\Phi\circ f\circ\Phi^{-1}:V\to\mathbb R^2$, with component functions $u=\operatorname{Re}(f\circ\Phi^{-1})$ and $v=\operatorname{Im}(f\circ\Phi^{-1})$ ([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). All real partial derivatives below are those of $\widetilde f$ on $V$ in [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], evaluated at the coordinate point in question. Write $\partial_x f=u_x+iv_x$ and $\partial_y f=u_y+iv_y$ after transport back to $U$.

At a point where the four real partial derivatives exist, define

$$ \partial_z f:=\frac12(\partial_x f-i\partial_y f)=\frac12(u_x+v_y)+\frac{i}{2}(v_x-u_y), $$

$$ \partial_{\bar z}f:=\frac12(\partial_x f+i\partial_y f)=\frac12(u_x-v_y)+\frac{i}{2}(v_x+u_y). $$

Real total differentiability means total differentiability of $\widetilde f$ under [[def-total-derivative-in-euclidean-space]], with a real-linear derivative as in [[def-euclidean-linear-map]]. Its transported real-linear map $Df$ is supplied by [[thm-complex-coordinate-map-preserves-real-total-differentiability]]. If $f$ is real totally differentiable, put $A=\partial_x f$ and $B=\partial_y f$. The remainder definition along the two coordinate axes gives $Df(1)=A$ and $Df(i)=B$. Real linearity then gives $Df(s+it)=sA+tB$ for real $s,t$, whereas direct expansion of $\frac12(A-iB)(s+it)+\frac12(A+iB)(s-it)$ gives the same expression. Thus

$$ Df(h)=(\partial_z f)h+(\partial_{\bar z}f)\overline h. $$

A real-differentiable map is **antiholomorphic** on $U$ when $\partial_z f=0$ at every point of $U$. Thus its differential is conjugate-linear at every point; no complex differentiability is asserted unless the other Wirtinger derivative also vanishes.

Assume countable choice and let $n\ge1$. Fourier transformation on Schwartz space extends uniquely to a surjective complex-linear isometry $\mathcal F_2:L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)\to L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$. It preserves the first-variable-linear inner product, and hence is unitary.

On every measure space, complex finite simple functions with finite-measure nonzero sets are dense in $L^p(\mu;\mathbb C)$ for $1\le p<\infty$. Assuming countable choice, $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$, and consequently $C_c(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$, is dense in Euclidean Lebesgue $L^p$ for $n\ge1$ and the same finite exponents. The $L^\infty$ closure of complex $C_c$ consists exactly of classes with a complex $C_0$ representative. Neither assertion claims density of finite-measure-supported tests or smooth functions in all of $L^\infty$.

Assume countable choice. For every measure space and $1\le p\le\infty$, $L^p(\mu;\mathbb C)$ is complete. Every sequence converging in this norm has a subsequence of measurable representatives converging a.e. to a measurable representative of its norm limit. For finite $p$ no pointwise convergence of the whole sequence is asserted.

Fix an integer $n\ge1$; Lebesgue measure, the Euclidean norm, and the complex
test-function conventions are those of
[[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. A **Calderón–Zygmund
kernel** with constants $A_1,A_2$ is a pair consisting of a measurable function
$k:\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}\to\mathbb C$ that is integrable on compact subsets of
$\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}$ ([[def-locally-integrable-function-on-r-n]]) and finite
numbers $0\le A_1,A_2<\infty$ such that
$$\sup_{R>0}\int_{R\le|x|\le2R}|k(x)|\,dx\le A_1 \qquad (1)$$
and
$$\sup_{y\ne0}\int_{|x|\ge2|y|}|k(x-y)-k(x)|\,dx\le A_2. \qquad (2)$$
Condition (1) is an annular **size condition**: it bounds the $L^1$ mass of every
dyadic annulus $R\le|x|\le2R$ by $A_1$, uniformly in the scale $R>0$. It is an
integral, not a pointwise, bound: the pointwise estimate $|k(x)|\le A|x|^{-n}$
implies (1) with $A_1=A\,|S^{n-1}|\log 2$, and not conversely. Since every compact
subset of $\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}$ lies in $\{a\le|x|\le b\}$ with
$0<a\le b<\infty$, and the latter is covered by the finitely many annuli
$2^ja\le|x|\le2^{j+1}a$ for $0\le j\le m$ with $2^ma\ge b$, condition (1) also
implies the local integrability listed above. Condition (2) is **Hörmander's
condition**: an integral smoothness bound at scale $|y|$. It is translation
invariant, in that substituting $x-c$ for $x$ and leaving $y$ unchanged leaves the
value of the integral unchanged, so it may be applied with the origin replaced by
any centre $c$.

A linear map $T:L^2(\mathbb R^n)\to L^2(\mathbb R^n)$ with finite operator norm
$B=\|T\|_{L^2\to L^2}$ is a **Calderón–Zygmund operator with kernel $k$** when for
every compactly supported $f\in L^2(\mathbb R^n)$ the integral
$\int_{\mathbb R^n}k(x-y)f(y)\,dy$ converges absolutely for almost every
$x\notin\operatorname{supp}f$ and satisfies
$$Tf(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}k(x-y)f(y)\,dy \qquad\text{for almost every }x\notin\operatorname{supp}f. \qquad (3)$$
Here $\operatorname{supp}f=\operatorname{ess\,supp}f$ is the essential support
defined in [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]; compact
support means that this closed set is compact. These conditions depend only on
the almost-everywhere class of $f$. Thus the
only link between the operator and the kernel is the off-support representation
(3): the action of $T$ on $L^1$ functions, on general bounded functions, or off
the diagonal is not presupposed, and $T$ need not be convolution with any
distribution. In the mean-zero applications below the absolute convergence in (3)
is recovered from Hörmander's condition (2) by Tonelli's theorem; it is automatic
whenever $k$ is locally square-integrable on $\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}$.

A **principal-value distribution for $k$** is a tempered distribution $W$ on
$\mathbb R^n$ ([[def-tempered-distribution]],
[[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]]) that agrees with $k$ on
$\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}$, in the sense that
$\langle W,\varphi\rangle=\int_{\mathbb R^n}k(x)\varphi(x)\,dx$ for every
$\varphi\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$ supported in $\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}$, and
for which some sequence $\delta_j\downarrow0$ satisfies
$$\langle W,\varphi\rangle=\lim_{j\to\infty}\int_{|x|\ge\delta_j}k(x)\varphi(x)\,dx$$
for every $\varphi\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$.

Neither the existence of a principal-value distribution nor the existence of any
truncation limit is part of the definition of a Calderón–Zygmund kernel: a kernel
may fail to have one, and the operator $T$ of (3) need not arise from one. Only
the annular size condition (1), Hörmander's condition (2), the $L^2$ bound, and
the off-support representation (3) are assumed. No choice principle is used in
this definition.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

Let $T$ be a Calderón–Zygmund operator with kernel constants $A_1,A_2$ and $L^2$
norm $B$. Then for every $1<p<\infty$, $T$ extends uniquely to a bounded operator
on $L^p(\mathbb R^n)$ with
$$\|Tf\|_p\le C_{n,p}(A_2+B)\max\bigl(p,(p-1)^{-1}\bigr)\|f\|_p,$$
where $C_{n,p}$ depends only on $n$ and $p$. In fact $C_{n,p}$ may be chosen to be a dimensional constant $C_n$ independent of $p$.

Assume countable choice. Work with complex-valued $L^p$ spaces and a complex-linear operator.
Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be measure spaces. Let
$1\le p_0,p_1<\infty$, let $1<q_0,q_1<\infty$, let $0<\theta<1$, and define
$$\frac1{p_\theta}:=\frac{1-\theta}{p_0}+\frac{\theta}{p_1}, \qquad \frac1{q_\theta}:=\frac{1-\theta}{q_0}+\frac{\theta}{q_1},$$

Suppose $T$ is a complex-linear map from the almost-everywhere classes of complex finite simple functions with finite-measure nonzero set on $X$ to measurable complex almost-everywhere classes on $Y$, and suppose $M_0,M_1\ge0$ satisfy
$$\|Tf\|_{q_0}\le M_0\|f\|_{p_0}, \qquad \|Tf\|_{q_1}\le M_1\|f\|_{p_1}$$
for every such $f$. Then $T$ extends uniquely to a bounded linear operator
$$\widetilde T:L^{p_\theta}(\mu;\mathbb C)\to L^{q_\theta}(\nu;\mathbb C)$$
satisfying
$$\|\widetilde T f\|_{q_\theta}\le M_0^{1-\theta}M_1^\theta\|f\|_{p_\theta} \qquad(f\in L^{p_\theta}(\mu)).$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n \ge 1$,
let $S^{n-1} \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be the unit sphere, and let $\sigma$ be the
set function of [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]]. Then $\sigma$
is a finite Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$, and for every Borel measurable
$f : \mathbb R^n \to [0,\infty]$,
$$\int_{\mathbb R^n} f(x)\,d\lambda_n(x) = \int_0^\infty \int_{S^{n-1}} f(r\omega) r^{n-1}\,d\sigma(\omega)\,dr.$$
Moreover, $\sigma$ is the unique Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$ with this
property.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: For $f\in C_c^\infty$, [F1] shows that $Sf:=\partial\mathcal Cf$ is bounded locally and decays as $O(|z|^{-2})$, hence is in $L^2$. Distributional commutation gives $\bar\partial Sf=\partial f$. Fourier transformation gives $(i\xi_1-\xi_2)\widehat{Sf}=(i\xi_1+\xi_2)\widehat f$, so almost everywhere off the origin $\widehat{Sf}=((\xi_1-i\xi_2)/(\xi_1+i\xi_2))\widehat f$. The multiplier has modulus one. [F2] extends $S$ uniquely to the isometry $\mathcal B$ on $L^2$. Multiplication by the translation character commutes with this multiplier, giving translation commutation there.

The kernel $K(z)=-1/(\pi z^2)$ has annular integral $2\log2$. Its gradient is bounded by $C|z|^{-3}$, so for $|z|\ge2|h|$, the segment estimate gives $|K(z-h)-K(z)|\le C|h||z|^{-3}$. Polar integration from $2|h|$ to infinity bounds its integral by an absolute constant. The off-support representation for compactly supported $L^2$ inputs follows by approximating them by smooth inputs in one fixed compact neighborhood of their support: on any compact set at positive distance from that neighborhood the kernel integrals converge uniformly by Cauchy–Schwarz, while the operator outputs converge in $L^2$ by step 1.1. Exhausting the complement of the essential support by compact sets and shrinking the neighborhoods gives the representation almost everywhere off the essential support. Thus [F3] applies. Let $A=\max\{1,\|\mathcal B\|_{4\to4}\}$. Interpolating the norm-one $L^2$ bound and the $L^4$ bound gives $\|\mathcal B\|_{p\to p}\le A^\theta$ with $1/p=(1-\theta)/2+\theta/4$, that is $\theta=2-4/p$. Density makes all extensions compatible and carries translation commutation to every finite $p$.

Let $p>2$, let $q=p/(p-1)<2$, and let $f$ have support in $D_R$. Hölder gives absolute convergence of $\mathcal Cf$ at every $z$: the singularity $|z-w|^{-q}$ is locally integrable, and the support is bounded. For $\delta=|z-z'|>0$, split its kernel difference into the union of the two disks of radius $2\delta$ about $z,z'$ and its complement. On the first region, integrating the two singularities with Hölder bounds their contributions by $C_p\|f\|_p\delta^{1-2/p}$. On the complement, $|(z-w)^{-1}-(z'-w)^{-1}|\le C\delta|z-w|^{-2}$; its $L^q$ norm is at most $C_p\delta(\int_{2\delta}^\infty r^{1-2q}dr)^{1/q}=C_p\delta^{1-2/p}$. This proves the global Hölder bound. On $|z|\le2R$, the same singular-kernel estimate gives $|\mathcal Cf(z)|\le C_{p,R}\|f\|_p$; on $|z|>2R$, the bound is $C\|f\|_1/|z|\le C_R\|f\|_p/|z|$. The latter is $L^p$ because $p>2$, proving $\|\mathcal Cf\|_p\le C_{p,R}\|f\|_p$ and the stated decay. Approximate $f$ in $L^p$ by smooth functions supported in $D_{R+1}$. Their Cauchy transforms converge in $L^p$, and their two weak derivatives converge to $f$ and $\mathcal Bf$ by step 2.1. Passing the derivative identities against tests proves the two weak identities and the $W^{1,p}$ bound.

If $\kappa=0$, the final operator is the identity. Otherwise choose $2<p_\kappa\le4$ so close to $2$ that $\kappa A^{2-4/p_\kappa}\le(1+\kappa)/2<1$; this is possible by continuity and the value $1$ of the bound at $p=2$. For $2\le p\le p_\kappa$, the operator $Tf=\mu\mathcal Bf+\nu\overline{\mathcal Bf}$ has pointwise modulus at most $(|\mu|+|\nu|)|\mathcal Bf|$, and therefore norm at most $(1+\kappa)/2$. Regard $L^p(\mathbb C;\mathbb C)$ as a real Banach space. The norm-convergent series $\sum_{j=0}^\infty T^j$ is a two-sided inverse to $I-T$, since the finite geometric-series remainder has norm tending to zero. Its norm is at most $1/(1-(1+\kappa)/2)=2/(1-\kappa)$, proving the assertion.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\ge3$, $s\ge1$, and let $e_1,e_2\in\mathbb R^d$ be orthonormal. Put $\zeta=s(e_1-ie_2)$ and
$$p_\zeta(\xi)=-|\xi|^2+2i\zeta\cdot\xi.$$
Use the unitary angular-frequency Fourier transform $\widehat u(\xi)=(2\pi)^{-d/2}\int e^{-ix\cdot\xi}u(x)\,dx$, and set
$$\|u\|_{\dot X_\zeta^b}^2=\int_{\mathbb R^d}|p_\zeta(\xi)|^{2b}|\widehat u(\xi)|^2\,d\xi,\qquad \|u\|_{X_\zeta^b}^2=\int_{\mathbb R^d}(s+|p_\zeta(\xi)|)^{2b}|\widehat u(\xi)|^2\,d\xi.$$
For every fixed Schwartz function $\phi$, a constant $C=C(d,\phi)$ independent of $s,e_1,e_2$ satisfies, for all Schwartz $u$,
$$\|\phi u\|_{\dot X_\zeta^{-1/2}}\le C\|u\|_{X_\zeta^{-1/2}},\qquad \|\phi u\|_{X_\zeta^{1/2}}\le C\|u\|_{\dot X_\zeta^{1/2}}.$$
Consequently
$$\|\phi u\|_2\le Cs^{-1/2}\|u\|_{\dot X_\zeta^{1/2}},\qquad \|\nabla(\phi u)\|_2\le Cs^{1/2}\|u\|_{\dot X_\zeta^{1/2}}.$$
The norms are finite on Schwartz space; the values of the weights on the measure-zero characteristic sphere do not affect them. All four maps extend continuously to the completions in the respective input norms.

Assume countable choice and let $n\ge1$. Fourier transformation on Schwartz space extends uniquely to a surjective complex-linear isometry $\mathcal F_2:L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)\to L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$. It preserves the first-variable-linear inner product, and hence is unitary.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $1 \le p,q,r \le \infty$ satisfy

$$ \frac1r = \frac1p + \frac1q - 1. $$

If $f \in L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$ and $g \in L^q(\mathbb{R}^n)$, then the
convolution $f*g$ is defined almost everywhere and satisfies

$$ \|f*g\|_r \le \|f\|_p\|g\|_q. $$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Direct expansion gives $\zeta_\pm\cdot\zeta_\pm=0$, $|\zeta_\pm|^2=2s^2$, and $\zeta_++\zeta_-=ik$. For either sign, writing $a=\xi\cdot\eta$, $b=\xi\cdot\eta^\perp$, the symbol satisfies $|p_\zeta(\xi)|\asymp\bigl||\xi|^2+k\cdot\xi\pm2r(s)b\bigr|+2s|a|$, with absolute constants. Put $R=|\xi|$, $A=|\Pi_P\xi|$, and $W(s,\eta,\xi)=R^2/(s+|p_\zeta(\xi)|)$. We prove the uniform kernel bound $\lambda^{-1}\int_{S^1}\int_\lambda^{2\lambda}W\,ds\,d\eta\le C(1+(1+|k|^2)/\lambda)$. If $R\le100\sqrt{1+|k|^2}$, the pointwise bound $W\le R^2/\lambda$ proves it. Otherwise $|k\cdot\xi|\le R^2/100$. If $A\le R^2/(100\lambda)$, then $2r(s)|b|\le4\lambda A\le R^2/25$ and the real part has absolute value at least $R^2/2$, giving $W\le2$. Thus only the case $A>R^2/(100\lambda)$ remains; here $R^2/A<100\lambda$.

In this last case, on $|a|\ge A/2$ the imaginary part gives $W\le R^2/(\lambda A)\le100$. On the remaining angular set, partition into shells $E_j=\{2^{-j-2}A<|a|\le2^{-j-1}A\}$, $j\ge0$, ignoring the measure-zero set $a=0$. Each shell has arclength at most $C2^{-j}$, since $a=A\cos\theta$ and $|\sin\theta|\ge\sqrt3/2$ there. On each shell, $|b|\ge\sqrt3 A/2$ and the denominator is bounded below, up to an absolute constant, by $|B\pm2r(s)b|+\lambda(1+2^{-j-1}A)$, where $B=R^2+k\cdot\xi$ is independent of $s,\eta$. Since $dr/ds=s/r\ge1$ and the $r$-interval is contained in $[\lambda/2,2\lambda]$, integration in $s$ is bounded by integration in $r$ over this latter interval. For any interval $I$ of length at most $2\lambda$ and $c>0$, splitting at the zero of the affine function gives $\int_I(|B+2br|+c)^{-1}dr\le C|b|^{-1}\log(1+\lambda|b|/c)$. Therefore $\int_\lambda^{2\lambda}W\,ds\le C(R^2/A)\log(1+C A/(1+2^{-j-1}A))\le C\lambda(j+1)$. Multiplying by the shell measure and summing $\sum_{j\ge0}(j+1)2^{-j}<\infty$ proves the kernel bound of step 1.1. This proof treats all $A$, including $A=0$ via its earlier case, and its constants are independent of $k,P$.

Initially let $f$ be Schwartz. By [F1], $\|\phi\operatorname{div}f\|_{\dot X^{-1/2}_\zeta}^2\le C\int |\xi\cdot\widehat f(\xi)|^2/(s+|p_\zeta(\xi)|)\,d\xi\le C\int W(s,\eta,\xi)|\widehat f(\xi)|^2d\xi$. Interchange the nonnegative integrals using [F2] and apply step 2.1 and Plancherel. This proves the first estimate. For $f\in H^1$, the simpler denominator bound $s+|p_\zeta|\ge s\ge\lambda$ gives $\|\phi\operatorname{div}f\|_{\dot X^{-1/2}_\zeta}^2\le C\lambda^{-1}\|\nabla f\|_2^2$; averaging over the parameter interval of length $\lambda$ and circle length $2\pi$ proves the second estimate. The same estimates hold for general $L^2$ and $H^1$ fields by Fourier truncation and smooth approximation. The limits match the distribution $\phi\operatorname{div}f$: convergence in the weighted negative space implies distributional convergence when tested against Schwartz functions, by reciprocal-weight Cauchy–Schwarz, and $L^2$ convergence of $f$ already implies distributional convergence of its derivative.

Write $f=f_h+(f-f_h)$ with $f_h=\rho_h*f$. Differentiation under the convolution, first for smooth fields and then by $L^2$ approximation, gives $\|\nabla f_h\|_2\le\|\nabla\rho_h\|_1\|f\|_2=C_\rho h^{-1}\|f\|_2$ by [F3]. Also $\|f-f_h\|_2\le\omega_2(f,h)$: at each $x$ apply the integral Cauchy–Schwarz inequality to the probability density $\rho_h(y)dy$, then integrate in $x$ and interchange nonnegative integrals to bound the squared norm by $\int\rho_h(y)\|f-f(\cdot-y)\|_2^2dy$. The support of $\rho_h$ is inside $|y|\le h$. Since $\|v+w\|^2\le2\|v\|^2+2\|w\|^2$, apply the $H^1$ estimate of step 3.1 to $f_h$ and its $L^2$ estimate to $f-f_h$. This yields the claimed mollified estimate after enlarging the constant.

is an isometry and extends boundedly to every $L^p$, $1<p<\infty$. It commutes with translations. There is a finite constant $A\ge1$ such that, for $2\le p\le4$,
$$\|\mathcal B\|_{L^p\to L^p}\le A^{2-4/p}.$$
For $p>2$ and $f\in L^p$ supported in a fixed disk $D_R$, the absolutely convergent integral
$$\mathcal Cf(z):=\frac1\pi\int_{\mathbb C}\frac{f(w)}{z-w}\,dA(w)$$
belongs to $W^{1,p}(\mathbb C)$, satisfies $\bar\partial\mathcal Cf=f$, $\partial\mathcal Cf=\mathcal Bf$, and obeys
$$\|\mathcal Cf\|_{W^{1,p}}\le C_{p,R}\|f\|_p,\qquad |\mathcal Cf(z)-\mathcal Cf(z')|\le C_p\|f\|_p|z-z'|^{1-2/p}.$$

$$I-\mu\mathcal B-\nu\overline{\mathcal B},\qquad \overline{\mathcal B}(f):=\overline{\mathcal Bf},$$
is invertible on $L^p(\mathbb C;\mathbb C)$, with inverse norm at most $2/(1-\kappa)$.

u\|_q)\|\mathcal BG\|_r+\|	au_hH-H\|_2]$. All terms are in $L^2$: the differentiated cutoff has compact support, $G\in L^r$, and the coefficient translation differences are in $L^q$ because the coefficients are bounded with fixed bounded support.

abla(f\psi)\|_2$ for smooth inputs; smooth approximation in [F2] gives the same inequality for this Sobolev function. Expand each coefficient product in $H$ by $	au_h(\mu f\psi)-\mu f\psi=(	au_h\mu-\mu)	au_h(f\psi)+\mu(	au_h(f\psi)-f\psi)$, and the analogous expression with $
u\overline f$. Hölder gives $\|	au_hH-H\|_2\le CU(\|	au_h\mu-\mu\|_q+\|	au_h
u-
u\|_q+|h|)$. Step 1.1 also gives $\|\mathcal BG\|_r\le CU$. Substitution in step 2.1, followed by the supremum over $|h|\le t$, proves the desired bound for $G$. Finally $\phi ar\partial f=G-f ar\partial\phi$, and the just-proved translation bound for $f\psi$ yields the second bound.

Average $\|\tau_hG-G\|_2^2$ over the square $[-2/T,2/T]^2$ with normalized Lebesgue measure. Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mu$ be a Beltrami coefficient on the Riemann sphere with $\|\mu\|_\infty\le k<1$ ([[def-measurable-beltrami-coefficient]]), and let $0,1,\infty$ denote the standard points in the finite and infinity charts ([[def-riemann-sphere-holomorphic-charts]], [[rem-riemann-sphere-one-point-compactification]]). Then:

(i) **Existence.** There is an orientation-preserving quasiconformal homeomorphism $f:\widehat{\mathbb C}\to\widehat{\mathbb C}$ whose Beltrami coefficient is $\mu$ almost everywhere ([[def-acl-sobolev-quasiconformal-homeomorphism]], [[def-geometric-quasiconformal-homeomorphism]], [[def-beltrami-coefficient-and-maximal-dilatation]]); equivalently, $f$ is a weak solution of $f_{\bar z}=\mu f_z$ ([[def-weak-solution-beltrami-equation]]). Its maximal dilatation is $K_f=K(\mu)\le(1+k)/(1-k)$.

(ii) **Uniqueness up to Möbius maps.** If $f$ and $g$ are two such solutions, then $g\circ f^{-1}$ is a Möbius transformation of $\widehat{\mathbb C}$ ([[def-mobius-transformation]]). Thus the solutions are exactly $\{M\circ f:M\text{ is Möbius}\}$, and there is a unique solution fixing $0,1,\infty$.

(iii) **Any normalization.** For every ordered triple $(a,b,c)$ of distinct sphere points, there is exactly one solution with $f(0)=a$, $f(1)=b$, and $f(\infty)=c$ ([[thm-three-point-transitivity-mobius-transformations]]). In particular the solution normalized by $f(0)=0$, $f(1)=1$, $f(\infty)=\infty$ is unique; denote it by $f^\mu$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\Omega,\Omega'\subseteq\mathbb C$ be complex domains ([[def-complex-domain]]) and $f:\Omega\to\Omega'$ a homeomorphism. The following are equivalent.

(a) $f$ is $1$-quasiconformal, in either the geometric or the analytic sense ([[def-geometric-quasiconformal-homeomorphism]], [[def-acl-sobolev-quasiconformal-homeomorphism]], [[thm-geometric-and-analytic-quasiconformality-equivalent]]).

(b) $f\in W^{1,2}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ and its weak Wirtinger derivative satisfies $\partial_{\bar z}f=0$ almost everywhere; under this Sobolev hypothesis this is equivalent to $\mu_f=0$ almost everywhere together with $\partial_{\bar z}f=0$ almost everywhere on $\{\partial_zf=0\}$ ([[def-acl-sobolev-quasiconformal-homeomorphism]], [[def-beltrami-coefficient-and-maximal-dilatation]]).

(c) $f$ is holomorphic; equivalently, it is a biholomorphism of $\Omega$ onto $\Omega'$ ([[def-biholomorphic-map]]).

Thus the conformal maps in this library's orientation-preserving sense are exactly the $1$-quasiconformal homeomorphisms; in particular, they preserve angles.

An injective holomorphic map on a complex domain has nowhere-zero derivative and is biholomorphic onto its open image.

Precisely, if $f:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is holomorphic and injective on a complex domain, then $f'(a)\ne0$ for every $a\in\Omega$, the set $f[\Omega]$ is a complex domain, and $f:\Omega\to f[\Omega]$ is biholomorphic ([[def-biholomorphic-map]]).

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $f:\Omega\to\Omega'$ be an analytically $K$-quasiconformal homeomorphism ([[def-acl-sobolev-quasiconformal-homeomorphism]]) with Beltrami coefficient $\mu_f$ ([[def-beltrami-coefficient-and-maximal-dilatation]]). Then $g=f^{-1}:\Omega'\to\Omega$ is analytically $K$-quasiconformal, $K_g=K_f$, and
$$\mu_g(f(z))=-\mu_f(z)\,\frac{f_z(z)}{\overline{f_z(z)}}\quad\text{for almost every }z\in\Omega.$$
Consequently $|\mu_g|\circ f=|\mu_f|$ almost everywhere, and $f$ is analytically quasiconformal exactly when $f^{-1}$ is, with the same maximal dilatation.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $f:\Omega\to\Omega'$ be a homeomorphism of complex domains which is $K$-quasiconformal in the analytic sense, with $K\ge1$, and let $\lambda,\mu$ denote the extremal length and reciprocal curve-family modulus of [[def-extremal-length-and-curve-family-modulus]].

(i) **Quadrilaterals.** Let $Q$ be a quadrilateral with $\overline Q\subset\Omega$ and marked opposite sides $E_0,E_1$, as in [[def-geometric-quasiconformal-homeomorphism]], and let $\Gamma(Q;E_0,E_1)$ consist of paths in $Q$ joining those sides. Then $f\Gamma(Q;E_0,E_1)=\Gamma(f(Q);f(E_0),f(E_1))$ and
$$K^{-1}\mu\bigl(\Gamma(Q;E_0,E_1)\bigr)\le \mu\bigl(\Gamma(f(Q);f(E_0),f(E_1))\bigr)\le K\mu\bigl(\Gamma(Q;E_0,E_1)\bigr),$$
equivalently
$$K^{-1}\lambda\bigl(\Gamma(Q;E_0,E_1)\bigr)\le \lambda\bigl(\Gamma(f(Q);f(E_0),f(E_1))\bigr)\le K\lambda\bigl(\Gamma(Q;E_0,E_1)\bigr).$$
The same inequalities hold with the other pair of opposite marked sides.

(ii) **Annuli.** Let $\widetilde A\subset\Omega$ be a doubly connected domain, meaning that $\widehat{\mathbb C}\setminus\widetilde A$ has exactly two connected components ([[rem-riemann-sphere-one-point-compactification]]), and put $A=f(\widetilde A)$. Let $\Gamma(\widetilde A)$ and $\Gamma(A)$ be the path families joining the two annular ends. Then
$$K^{-1}\mu(\Gamma(\widetilde A))\le\mu(\Gamma(A))\le K\mu(\Gamma(\widetilde A)),\qquad K^{-1}\lambda(\Gamma(\widetilde A))\le\lambda(\Gamma(A))\le K\lambda(\Gamma(\widetilde A)).$$
For a round annulus $A(r,R)$ the connecting-family extremal length is the conformal parameter $(2\pi)^{-1}\log(R/r)$ and the reciprocal modulus is $2\pi/\log(R/r)$, by [[thm-modulus-rectangle-and-annulus]] and [[thm-round-annulus-conformal-parameter-is-complete-invariant]].

(iii) **Area and null sets.** For every relatively compact Borel set $E\subset\Omega$,
$$\operatorname{area}(f(E))=\int_EJ_f\,dA.$$
In particular, $f^{-1}$ maps Lebesgue-null Borel subsets of $\Omega'$ to null subsets of $\Omega$.

**Annular end-path convention.** In (ii), paths have parameter interval (0,1), are proper, and their tails escape into different ends, defined by the two-collar exhaustion proved below. Local rectifiability means rectifiability on each compact parameter interval. Their nonnegative Borel weighted length is the increasing supremum of those compact-restriction arc-length integrals; a nonrectifiable restriction has infinite length. The displayed extremal-length supremum over finite positive-area densities and reciprocal modulus convention are unchanged. The proof verifies compatibility with ordinary finite-boundary families and transport of the two ends, including punctured and infinite rings.

Assume Countable Choice. Identify $\mathbb C$ with $\mathbb R^2$, use angular-frequency unitary Fourier transformation, and put $\partial=(\partial_x-i\partial_y)/2$, $\bar\partial=(\partial_x+i\partial_y)/2$. The Beurling transform $\mathcal B$ defined on $L^2(\mathbb C)$ by
$$\widehat{\mathcal Bf}(\xi)=\frac{\xi_1-i\xi_2}{\xi_1+i\xi_2}\widehat f(\xi)\qquad(\xi\ne0)$$
is an isometry and extends boundedly to every $L^p$, $1<p<\infty$. It commutes with translations. There is a finite constant $A\ge1$ such that, for $2\le p\le4$,
$$\|\mathcal B\|_{L^p\to L^p}\le A^{2-4/p}.$$
For $p>2$ and $f\in L^p$ supported in a fixed disk $D_R$, the absolutely convergent integral
$$\mathcal Cf(z):=\frac1\pi\int_{\mathbb C}\frac{f(w)}{z-w}\,dA(w)$$
belongs to $W^{1,p}(\mathbb C)$, satisfies $\bar\partial\mathcal Cf=f$, $\partial\mathcal Cf=\mathcal Bf$, and obeys
$$\|\mathcal Cf\|_{W^{1,p}}\le C_{p,R}\|f\|_p,\qquad |\mathcal Cf(z)-\mathcal Cf(z')|\le C_p\|f\|_p|z-z'|^{1-2/p}.$$
It is $O(1/|z|)$ at infinity. For every $0\le\kappa<1$ there is $p_\kappa>2$ such that, whenever $2\le p\le p_\kappa$ and $\mu,\nu$ are measurable with $\||\mu|+|\nu|\|_\infty\le\kappa$, the real-linear map
$$I-\mu\mathcal B-\nu\overline{\mathcal B},\qquad \overline{\mathcal B}(f):=\overline{\mathcal Bf},$$
is invertible on $L^p(\mathbb C;\mathbb C)$, with inverse norm at most $2/(1-\kappa)$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$.

If $T\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ and $\Delta T=0$, there is a unique smooth harmonic $h$ with $T=T_h$.

Every bounded entire function is constant.

More explicitly, if $f:\mathbb C\to\mathbb C$ is holomorphic and there is a real $M\ge0$ such that $|f(z)|\le M$ for every $z\in\mathbb C$, then $f$ is constant.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $1 \le p,q,r \le \infty$ satisfy

$$ \frac1r = \frac1p + \frac1q - 1. $$

If $f \in L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$ and $g \in L^q(\mathbb{R}^n)$, then the
convolution $f*g$ is defined almost everywhere and satisfies

$$ \|f*g\|_r \le \|f\|_p\|g\|_q. $$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Take a solution from [F1] fixing infinity. Outside $D_R$ its coefficient is zero, so it is conformal there. In the infinity chart it is an injective holomorphic map fixing zero with nonzero derivative. Its Taylor expansion there gives $az+b+O(1/z)$ in the original chart, with $a\ne0$. Postcomposition by $(w-b)/a$ gives the principal normalization. Any two principal solutions differ by a Möbius map by [F1]; since both fix infinity this map is affine, and their leading and constant Laurent coefficients force it to be the identity. This proves existence and uniqueness of $\Phi$.

Set $h=\bar\partial\Phi$, which is in $L^2$ and has support in $\overline D_R$ by local quasiconformal Sobolev regularity and the zero coefficient outside. The Cauchy integral for compact $L^2$ data is locally $L^2$: on a fixed target disk the kernel restricted to all differences with $D_R$ is in $L^1$, so [F4] applies; outside a larger disk its bound is $C\|h\|_1/|z|$. Approximating $h$ by smooth functions in a fixed support disk yields distributionally $\bar\partial\mathcal Ch=h$ and $\partial\mathcal Ch=\mathcal Bh$, the latter by Beurling $L^2$ boundedness. Thus $\bar\partial(\Phi-z-\mathcal Ch)=0$. Applying $\partial$ and [F4] makes this distribution smooth harmonic; the original Cauchy–Riemann equation makes its representative holomorphic. It tends to zero at infinity by the principal normalization and the exterior Cauchy bound. Liouville gives $\Phi-z=\mathcal Ch$. Therefore $\partial\Phi=1+\mathcal Bh$, and the Beltrami equation says $(I-\mu\mathcal B)h=\mu$.

Let $h_r=(I-\mu\mathcal B)^{-1}\mu$ in $L^r$. Its norm is at most $C_\kappa\|\mu\|_r\le C_{\kappa,R,r}$ by [F3]. The equation gives $h_r=0$ outside $D_R$, hence $h_r\in L^2$ by Hölder on that disk. Compatibility of the $L^2$ and $L^r$ Beurling actions and uniqueness of the $L^2$ inverse imply $h_r=h$ from step 2.1. Apply the Cauchy bounds in [F3] to $\Phi-z=\mathcal Ch$. This proves its $W^{1,r}$, supremum and Hölder bounds. In particular $\Phi(D_S)$ lies in a disk of radius $S+C_{\kappa,R,r}$, uniformly in $\mu$.

By [F2], $\Psi=\Phi^{-1}$ has coefficient bounded by $\kappa$, supported in $\Phi(\overline D_R)$, and has the same principal expansion at infinity. Step 3.1 puts that support inside a fixed disk; applying step 3.1 to $\Psi$ therefore gives a uniform $L^r$ bound for $\partial\Psi$ on every fixed disk. At common differentiability points, the derivative inverse formula gives $|\partial\Psi(\Phi(z))|=1/[(1-|\mu(z)|^2)|\partial\Phi(z)|]$. Thus $|\partial\Phi(z)|^{-\sigma}\le|\partial\Psi(\Phi(z))|^\sigma$. Change variables with $z=\Psi(w)$ using [F2]; the bound $J_\Psi\le|\partial\Psi|^2$ gives $\int_{D_S}|\partial\Phi|^{-\sigma}\le\int_{\Phi(D_S)}|\partial\Psi(w)|^{\sigma+2}dA(w)$. Since $\sigma+2=r$, step 3.1 and the uniform disk containing $\Phi(D_S)$ bound the right side. Null-set preservation in [F2] justifies all inverse identities and negative powers on common full-measure sets.

On $D_S$, $|\Phi|\le S+C_{\kappa,R,r}$. For $|k|=1$, the exponential and its derivative therefore have bounded modulus above and away from zero. Smooth composition, first for smooth approximations on this bounded range and then by Sobolev convergence, gives $\partial f=ik e^{ik\Phi}\partial\Phi$ and the corresponding $\bar\partial$ formula. Step 3.1 supplies the $W^{1,r}$ bound, while $|\partial f|^{-\sigma}\le e^{\sigma(S+C)}|\partial\Phi|^{-\sigma}$ and step 4.1 supply the negative-power bound. This proves the final assertion, including the case $\sigma<1$ with its stated integral convention.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Fix an integer $k\ge0$ and $0<\alpha<1$. Write $D_r:=\{z\in\mathbb C:|z|<r\}$ and $\overline D_r:=\{z\in\mathbb C:|z|\le r\}$. Let
$$X_{k,\alpha}:=\{q\in C^{k,\alpha}(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C):\operatorname{supp}q\subseteq\overline D_2\},$$
where derivatives are in the real coordinates and the complex-valued Hölder norm is that of [[def-holder-spaces-c-k-alpha-and-their-scaled-norms]] ([[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]). Put $\Gamma(z)=-(2\pi)^{-1}\log|z|$ and let $Nq=\Gamma*q$ be the Newtonian potential of [[def-laplace-fundamental-solution-with-positive-minus-laplacian-sign]] and [[def-newtonian-potential]]. Using the Wirtinger derivatives of [[def-wirtinger-derivatives]], define
$$Tq(z):=-4\,\partial_zNq(z),\qquad Sq(z):=\partial_zTq(z)=-4\,\partial_z^2Nq(z).$$

(i) **The Cauchy transform.** For every $q\in X_{k,\alpha}$ and $z\in\mathbb C$,
$$Tq(z)=\frac1\pi\int_{\mathbb C}\frac{q(\zeta)}{z-\zeta}\,dA(\zeta),$$
and this integral is absolutely convergent. The function $Tq$ is smooth on $\mathbb C\setminus\overline D_2$, satisfies $\partial_{\bar z}Tq=q$ pointwise, and for every $R>0$ obeys
$$\|Tq\|_{C^{k+1,\alpha}(D_R)}\le C_{k,\alpha,R}\,\|q\|_{C^{k,\alpha}(\mathbb R^2)}.$$

(ii) **The derivative.** The function $Sq$ lies in $C^{k,\alpha}(\mathbb R^2)$ and has the principal-value representation
$$Sq(z)=-\frac1\pi\,\operatorname{p.v.}\!\int_{\mathbb C}\frac{q(\zeta)}{(z-\zeta)^2}\,dA(\zeta),$$
where the principal value uses circular truncations. Equivalently, it is the absolutely convergent subtracted integral
$$Sq(z)=-\frac1\pi\left[\int_{|\zeta-z|<1}\frac{q(\zeta)-q(z)}{(z-\zeta)^2}\,dA(\zeta)+\int_{|\zeta-z|\ge1}\frac{q(\zeta)}{(z-\zeta)^2}\,dA(\zeta)\right].$$
The subtraction is only over the unit disk; no globally absolutely convergent subtraction of $q(z)$ is asserted.

(iii) **Bound on the fixed-support space.** There is $M_{k,\alpha}<\infty$, depending only on $k$ and $\alpha$, such that
$$\|Sq\|_{C^{k,\alpha}(\mathbb R^2)}\le M_{k,\alpha}\,\|q\|_{C^{k,\alpha}(\mathbb R^2)},\qquad q\in X_{k,\alpha}.$$
No global $L^p$ mapping property of $S$ is asserted.

derivations.claim: Set $\lambda=|\ell|$ and choose $R=\max\{1,(8C/\lambda)^{1/b}\}$. Then for $|k|\ge R$, $|g(k)-\ell k|\le(\lambda/8)|k|$, so $g$ is nonzero there and its restriction to $|k|=R$ has winding one, by the straight homotopy to $\ell k$. Choose a smooth real cutoff $\chi_R$ equal to $1$ on $D_R$, supported in $D_{2R}$, with derivative bounded by $C/R$, and set $s=\mathcal C(\sigma\chi_R)$. Direct integration of its kernel gives $\|s\|_\infty\le C_B R$. The $L^4$ Cauchy estimate in [F1] gives a one-half Hölder bound at most $C_B R^{1/2}$. These estimates hold independently of the regularity of $\sigma$.

Put $H=e^{-s}E\chi_R$ and $S=\mathcal CH-\mathcal CH(0)$. On $D_{2R}$ the hypotheses give $\|E\|_\infty\le C\delta e^{2CR}$ and $\operatorname{Lip}(E)\le Ce^{C(1+2R)}$. The elementary estimate $|E(x)-E(y)|\le\min\{2\|E\|_\infty,\operatorname{Lip}(E)|x-y|\}$ implies $[E]_{C^{0,1/2}}\le C\delta^{1/2}e^{C'R}$ on that disk. Combine this with step 1.1 and the cutoff product estimate to get $\|H\|_{C^{0,1/2}(\mathbb C)}\le C\delta^{1/2}e^{C'R}$; the smooth cutoff vanishes before leaving $D_{2R}$, so extension by zero retains this bound after increasing the constant. By [F1] and dilation, $\|\nabla S\|_\infty\le C\delta^{1/2}e^{C_1R}$, absorbing polynomial powers of $R$ into the exponential. Also $S(0)=0$, so $|S(k)|\le C\delta^{1/2}e^{C_1R}|k|$. If $E=0$, take $S=0$ and these bounds hold with zero right side.

Define $F=e^{-s}g-S$. The distributional product rule, justified by the locally Sobolev Cauchy gauge and smooth approximation, gives $\bar\partial F=e^{-s}(1-\chi_R)(\sigma g+E)$, hence $F$ is holomorphic on $D_R$ by [F2], and $F(0)=0$. Suppose $C\delta^{1/2}e^{(C_1+C_B)R}\le\lambda/8$. On $|k|=R$, step 1.1 gives $|e^{-s}g|\ge(7/8)\lambda R e^{-C_BR}$ and step 2.1 makes $|S|\le(1/8)\lambda R e^{-C_BR}$. Thus $F$ is homotopic there to $e^{-s}g$, whose winding is one: $e^{-s}$ has a continuous logarithm on the disk, so contributes winding zero. By [F2], $F$ has precisely one zero counted with multiplicity in $D_R$. Since $F(0)=0$, it is simple and there are no others. Consequently $F(k)/k$ extends holomorphically and nonvanishingly to $D_R$ and its boundary, where its modulus is at least $(3/4)\lambda e^{-C_BR}$. The minimum-modulus principle gives the same lower bound throughout. Step 2.1 now yields $|F(k)+S(k)|\ge(5/8)\lambda e^{-C_BR}|k|$ for $0<|k|<R$. Hence $g=e^s(F+S)$ has no zero except zero inside this disk, and step 1.1 excludes all the exterior zeros. If $E=0$, the same proof works for every $\lambda>0$.

It remains to ensure the displayed smallness condition. Write $L=\log(1/\delta)$. If $\lambda\ge DL^{-b}$, then $R\le1+(8C/D)^{1/b}L$. Choose $D$ large enough that $(C_1+C_B)(8C/D)^{1/b}\le1/4$. Since $e^{-L/4}L^b\to0$, there is a fixed $L_0$ for which the condition holds whenever $L\ge L_0$. Put $\delta_0=\min\{1/4,e^{-L_0}\}$. Step 3.1 then proves the asserted implication and its zero-error version.
