Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $u\in L^1(\Omega;\mathbb R)$, where elements of $L^1$ are almost-everywhere equivalence classes. For each $i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}$, its distributional derivative $D_i u$ acts on $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ by
$$\langle D_i u,\varphi\rangle:=-\int_\Omega u\,\partial_i\varphi\,dx.$$
The function $u$ is in $BV(\Omega)$ when each $D_i u$ is represented by a finite signed Radon measure and the resulting vector-valued measure $Du=(D_1u,\ldots,D_nu)$ has finite total variation. Here a finite vector-valued Radon measure means that its partition variation is a finite Radon measure. For a Borel set $A\subseteq\Omega$, define
$$|Du|(A):=\sup\left\{\sum_{j=1}^\infty |Du(A_j)|:\ (A_j)_{j\ge1}\text{ is a Borel partition of }A\right\},$$
using the Euclidean norm on each vector value. Define the spatial total variation by $TV(u;\Omega):=|Du|(\Omega)$. A Lebesgue-measurable set $E\subseteq\Omega$ of finite measure has finite perimeter relative to $\Omega$ when $\chi_E\in BV(\Omega)$; its relative perimeter is $P(E;\Omega):=TV(\chi_E;\Omega)$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $m\ge1$, let $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $h:Q\to\mathbb R$ be locally Lipschitz. Then $h$ is differentiable almost everywhere, its partial derivatives are measurable and are its weak derivatives. On every open region where $h$ is $L$-Lipschitz, $|Dh|\le L$ almost everywhere. Let $H^m$ denote the repository's unnormalised Hausdorff measure, put $c_m=H^m((0,1]^m)$, and write $\sigma_m=c_m^{-1}H^m$ also on Euclidean spaces containing $m$-dimensional subsets. The graph map $F(y)=(y,h(y))$ satisfies, for every nonnegative Borel $a$,
$$\int_{F(Q)}a(x)\,d\sigma_m(x)=\int_Qa(F(y))\sqrt{1+|Dh(y)|^2}\,dy.$$
For the epigraph $G=\{(y,z):y\in Q,\ z>h(y)\}$, a smooth vector field compactly supported away from the chart sides satisfies
$$\int_G\operatorname{div}\phi\,dx=\int_Q\phi(y,h(y))\cdot(Dh(y),-1)\,dy.$$
Thus its outward normal is $(Dh,-1)/\sqrt{1+|Dh|^2}$ almost everywhere. The sign reverses for a subgraph. The graph surface measure is locally finite and Radon on $F(Q)$ with its relative topology, and its null sets coincide with graph images of Lebesgue-null subsets of the base.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable
$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. If $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ are measurable, then
$$\int(f+g)\,d\mu=\int f\,d\mu+\int g\,d\mu.$$

Assume the $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ convention of [[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]]. Let S be a compact embedded $C^1$ hypersurface in $\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$. Choose finitely many regular injective $C^1$ parametrizations $X_j:V_j\to S\cap O_j$ with $C^1$ coordinate transitions, and an ambient partition $\chi_j$ from [[lem-finite-ambient-partitions-for-euclidean-boundary-integration]], with supports compactly contained in the corresponding chart neighborhoods. Put $J_{X_j}=\sqrt{\det(DX_j^TDX_j)}$, using [[def-gram-matrix-and-gram-determinant]].

For a nonnegative Borel f on S define $\int_S f\,dS=\sum_j\int_{V_j}(\chi_j f)(X_j(y))J_{X_j}(y)\,dy$, where the integrals on the right are those of [[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]] and $0\cdot\infty=0$. Set $S(A)=\int_S\mathbf1_A\,dS$ for Borel A. For signed f with $\int_S|f|\,dS<\infty$ use the difference of the positive and negative integrals. The same chart formula restricts to a compact Borel face contained in a regular patch. The empty surface has zero integral. Independence and finiteness are established by the following chart-independence lemma.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every regular chart density is continuous and strictly positive. The chart integral on a compact embedded $C^1$ hypersurface defines a finite Borel measure independent of the finite charts and subordinate partitions. In graph coordinates $X(y)=(y,h(y))$ its density is $\sqrt{1+|Dh|^2}$. On a one-sided domain boundary the outward unit normal agrees on chart overlaps and is continuous.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Put $B=B(0,1)$ and first prove its flux formula directly from [F2]. Cover $\partial B$ by finitely many graph neighborhoods, each expressing $B$ locally as an epigraph or subgraph of a smooth function, and add an interior open set compactly contained in $B$ to cover $\overline B$. Rigid changes of coordinates preserve volume, divergence and normal flux by [F3]–[F5], so the graph identities apply in these coordinates. Choose smooth nonnegative functions $\eta_i$ compactly supported in those sets and with $\sum_i\eta_i>0$ on $\overline B$: finitely many smaller balls cover this compact set, and ordinary Euclidean smooth bumps positive on those balls supply the functions. Normalize their sum on a neighborhood of $\overline B$, using one additional smooth cutoff equal to one near $\overline B$ and supported where that sum is positive. This gives functions $\chi_i$ subordinate to the same sets with $\sum_i\chi_i=1$ near $\overline B$. For any smooth compactly supported vector field $\psi$, apply [F2] to $\chi_i\psi$ in each boundary graph patch. Its divergence integral over $B$ is its outward flux over $\partial B$ by [F4], because the graph domain and $B$ agree on the support. The interior piece has divergence integral zero: its support is compact inside $B$, so choose a horizontal line below that support and apply [F2] on the half-plane above that line. The field vanishes on the line and its half-plane integral equals its whole-space integral, which equals its integral over $B$. Summing the finitely many identities, the derivatives of the partition cancel since its sum is one near $\overline B$. Consequently $\int_B\operatorname{div}\psi=\int_{\partial B}\psi\cdot\nu_B\,d\mathcal H^1$. This proves the required unit-disk identity without using a B-example or a stronger-choice divergence theorem.

Let $T(y)=x_0+ry$ and, for arbitrary $\phi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb R^2)$, put $\psi=\phi\circ T$. By [F5], $\operatorname{div}_y\psi(y)=r\,\operatorname{div}_x\phi(T(y))$. Applying [F3] to the positive and negative parts of $\operatorname{div}\phi$, whose integrals are finite because $\phi$ is smooth and compactly supported, gives
$$\int_E\operatorname{div}\phi(x)\,dx=r^2\int_B\operatorname{div}\phi(T(y))\,dy=r\int_B\operatorname{div}\psi(y)\,dy.$$
By step 1.1 this is $r\int_{\partial B}\psi\cdot
u_B\,d\mathcal H^1$. The circle parametrization in [F4] has outward normal $(\cos	heta,\sin	heta)$ and arclength element $r\,d	heta$, so this last expression equals $\int_{\partial E}\phi\cdot
u_E\,d\mathcal H^1$. Thus $\int_E\operatorname{div}\phi=\int_{\partial E}\phi\cdot
u_E\,d\mathcal H^1$ for every test field; [F1] yields $D\chi_E=-
u_E\mathcal H^1|_{\partial E}$.

By [F4], the circle is parametrized with speed $r$, so $\mathcal H^1(\partial E)=2\pi r$. For any Borel partition $(A_j)$ of $\partial E$, [F1] and $|\nu_E|=1$ give $\sum_j|D\chi_E(A_j)|=\sum_j|\int_{A_j}\nu_E\,d\mathcal H^1|\le2\pi r$. For the reverse bound, partition the circle into $N$ equal arcs and their finitely many endpoints. The endpoints have zero arclength; on each arc, direct integration of $(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)r$ gives a vector of norm $2r\sin(\pi/N)$. Thus the partition sum is $2rN\sin(\pi/N)$, which tends to $2\pi r$ as $N\to\infty$. By the partition definition in [F1], $TV(\chi_E;\mathbb R^2)=2\pi r$. This finite variation proves $\chi_E\in BV(\mathbb R^2)$.
Because $\overline E\subset D$, the full derivative measure in step 1.2 is supported inside $D$. Hence $TV(\chi_E;D)=|D\chi_E|(D)=|D\chi_E|(\mathbb R^2)=2\pi r$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\ge3$, $s\ge1$, and let $e_1,e_2\in\mathbb R^d$ be orthonormal. Put $\zeta=s(e_1-ie_2)$ and
$$p_\zeta(\xi)=-|\xi|^2+2i\zeta\cdot\xi.$$
Use the unitary angular-frequency Fourier transform $\widehat u(\xi)=(2\pi)^{-d/2}\int e^{-ix\cdot\xi}u(x)\,dx$, and set
$$\|u\|_{\dot X_\zeta^b}^2=\int_{\mathbb R^d}|p_\zeta(\xi)|^{2b}|\widehat u(\xi)|^2\,d\xi,\qquad \|u\|_{X_\zeta^b}^2=\int_{\mathbb R^d}(s+|p_\zeta(\xi)|)^{2b}|\widehat u(\xi)|^2\,d\xi.$$
For every fixed Schwartz function $\phi$, a constant $C=C(d,\phi)$ independent of $s,e_1,e_2$ satisfies, for all Schwartz $u$,
$$\|\phi u\|_{\dot X_\zeta^{-1/2}}\le C\|u\|_{X_\zeta^{-1/2}},\qquad \|\phi u\|_{X_\zeta^{1/2}}\le C\|u\|_{\dot X_\zeta^{1/2}}.$$
Consequently
$$\|\phi u\|_2\le Cs^{-1/2}\|u\|_{\dot X_\zeta^{1/2}},\qquad \|\nabla(\phi u)\|_2\le Cs^{1/2}\|u\|_{\dot X_\zeta^{1/2}}.$$
The norms are finite on Schwartz space; the values of the weights on the measure-zero characteristic sphere do not affect them. All four maps extend continuously to the completions in the respective input norms.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\ge3$, $k\in\mathbb R^d$, and fix an oriented two-plane $P\perp k$. For a unit vector $\eta\in P$, let $\eta^\perp$ be its positive quarter turn. For $s\ge|k|/2$, put $r(s)=\sqrt{s^2-|k|^2/4}$ and
$$\zeta_\pm(s,\eta)=\pm s\eta+i(k/2\pm r(s)\eta^\perp).$$
These phases are null, have length $\sqrt2s$, and sum to $ik$. Use the unitary angular Fourier convention and the norms $\dot X_\zeta^b,X_\zeta^b$ with inhomogeneous weight $s+|p_\zeta|$, where $p_\zeta(\xi)=-|\xi|^2+2i\zeta\cdot\xi$. For a fixed $\phi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$, define
$$\mathcal A_{\lambda,k}(f):=\frac1\lambda\int_{S^1(P)}\int_\lambda^{2\lambda}\|\phi\operatorname{div}f\|_{\dot X_{\zeta_\pm(s,\eta)}^{-1/2}}^2\,ds\,d\eta.$$
Here $d\eta$ is arclength, either sign can be used, and the derivative is distributional. For $\lambda\ge100\sqrt{1+|k|^2}$ and $f\in L^2(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C^d)$,
$$\mathcal A_{\lambda,k}(f)\le C\left(1+\frac{1+|k|^2}{\lambda}\right)\|f\|_2^2,$$
where $C$ depends only on $d,\phi$. If $f\in H^1$, also
$$\mathcal A_{\lambda,k}(f)\le\frac C\lambda\|\nabla f\|_2^2.$$
Let $\rho\in C_c^\infty(B(0,1))$ be nonnegative with integral $1$, put $\rho_h(x)=h^{-d}\rho(x/h)$, and define $\omega_2(f,h)=\sup_{|y|\le h}\|f(\cdot-y)-f\|_2$. For $h>0$ one consequently has
$$\mathcal A_{\lambda,k}(f)\le C_\rho\left[\frac{\|f\|_2^2}{\lambda h^2}+\left(1+\frac{1+|k|^2}{\lambda}\right)\omega_2(f,h)^2\right].$$

Assume countable choice and let $n\ge1$. Fourier transformation on Schwartz space extends uniquely to a surjective complex-linear isometry $\mathcal F_2:L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)\to L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$. It preserves the first-variable-linear inner product, and hence is unitary.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $1 \le p,q,r \le \infty$ satisfy

$$ \frac1r = \frac1p + \frac1q - 1. $$

If $f \in L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$ and $g \in L^q(\mathbb{R}^n)$, then the
convolution $f*g$ is defined almost everywhere and satisfies

$$ \|f*g\|_r \le \|f\|_p\|g\|_q. $$

For a distribution $u\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ in the convention of [[def-distribution]] and a multi-index $\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$, its **distributional derivative** is
$$\langle\partial^\alpha u,\varphi\rangle=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\langle u,\partial^\alpha\varphi\rangle\qquad(\varphi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)).$$
The test derivative is a continuous linear endomorphism by [[thm-test-function-operations-are-continuous]]. Its composition with $u$, multiplied by the indicated sign, is therefore a continuous complex-linear functional, so this definition produces a distribution. The pairing is bilinear, with no complex conjugation. For $\alpha=0$ the operation is the identity; for one coordinate derivative its sign is minus. Every derivative of the zero distribution is zero, including on the empty domain. No choice axiom enters this construction. Compatibility with classical derivatives requires an integration-by-parts argument where it is used; it is not part of the definition.

statement.

derivations.claim: Fix $\phi\in C_c^\infty$ equal to $1$ on the ball consisting of points of distance at most $2$ from $B$. For Schwartz $u,v$, the integrands defining $m_q$ are supported where $\phi=1$, so they can be written using $u_B=\phi u,v_B=\phi v$. By [F1], $\|u_Bv_B\|_1\le Cs^{-1}\|u\|_{\dot X^{1/2}_\zeta}\|v\|_{\dot X^{1/2}_\zeta}$ and $\|\nabla(u_Bv_B)\|_1\le C\|u\|_{\dot X^{1/2}_\zeta}\|v\|_{\dot X^{1/2}_\zeta}$, the latter from the product rule and the two combinations $s^{1/2}s^{-1/2}$. Thus a bounded coefficient multiplying $u_Bv_B$ costs $Cs^{-1}$, whereas a bounded vector coefficient multiplying its gradient costs $C$. The same estimates hold when $u,v$ have any two null phases of the same length, because [F1] is uniform in the phase directions. These bounds also prove continuity of the bilinear form on the weighted completions and local $H^1$ representatives.

Choose a nonnegative smooth mollifier $\rho$ of integral $1$ supported in the unit ball and put $a_h=\rho_h*a$ for $0<h\le1$. The bounds $\|\operatorname{div}a_h\|_\infty\le C_\rho h^{-1}\|a\|_\infty$ and $\|a-a_h\|_\infty\le[a]_{C^{0,\alpha}}h^\alpha$ follow, respectively, by differentiation of the kernel and integration of $|a(x)-a(x-y)|\le K|y|^\alpha$. The support of $a_h$ stays inside the region where $\phi=1$. Split the derivative term of $m_q$ into $a_h$ and $a-a_h$, and integrate the former by parts. Step 1.1 gives $|\langle m_qu,v\rangle|\le C[s^{-1}K^2+s^{-1}h^{-1}K+Kh^\alpha]\|u\|_{\dot X^{1/2}}\|v\|_{\dot X^{1/2}}$. Take $h=s^{-1/(1+\alpha)}$; since $s\ge1$, this is bounded by $Cs^{-\alpha/(1+\alpha)}$ times the product of norms. Weighted Fourier duality identifies the bounded bilinear form with a map to $\dot X^{-1/2}$: in Fourier coordinates the dual weight is $|p_\zeta(-\xi)|^{-1}$ for a bilinear pairing, and reflection changes the test phase to $-\zeta$; the cutoff bounds of step 1.1 are identical for $\zeta$ and $-\zeta$. Therefore the same proof with $v$ measured in $\dot X_{-\zeta}^{1/2}$ gives exactly the asserted map norm. Enlarge $s_0$ until this norm is at most $1/2$.

The weighted completions are realized as the Fourier $L^2$ spaces with weights $|p_\zeta|^{\pm1}$: smooth functions supported away from the characteristic set and inside a bounded frequency ball are dense by truncation and ordinary $L^2$ approximation there. They define tempered distributions because reciprocal-weight Cauchy–Schwarz controls their pairing with a Schwartz test; the only new local singularity is $|p_\zeta|^{-1}$, integrable by the codimension-two computation in [F1]. Multiplication of the Fourier transform by $p_\zeta^{-1}$ is consequently an isometry $G_\zeta:\dot X^{-1/2}_\zeta\to\dot X^{1/2}_\zeta$ and is a distributional right inverse of $\Delta+2\zeta\cdot\nabla$. The characteristic set has measure zero, so its values need not be assigned. Also $q\in\dot X^{-1/2}_\zeta$: its compactly supported divergence part follows from [F1] applied to $\operatorname{div}a\in X^{-1/2}_\zeta$, and its bounded compactly supported zero-order part follows from the same cutoff bound. For the former, $|\xi|^2/(s+|p_\zeta(\xi)|)$ is bounded for fixed $s$, so $a\in L^2$ suffices; for the latter, the inhomogeneous negative norm is at most $s^{-1/2}$ times its $L^2$ norm.

By steps 2.1–3.1, the series $r_\zeta=\sum_{j=0}^\infty(G_\zeta m_q)^jG_\zeta q$ converges in $\dot X^{1/2}_\zeta$, has norm at most $2\|q\|_{\dot X^{-1/2}_\zeta}$, and satisfies $(\Delta+2\zeta\cdot\nabla)r_\zeta=q+m_qr_\zeta$. For a cutoff equal to $1$ on any fixed compact set, [F1] gives convergence in $H^1$ there, so $r_\zeta\in H^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$. The product-form definition agrees with the distributional equation by this local convergence. Conjugating $-\Delta$ by $e^{x\cdot\zeta}$ gives $-\Delta-2\zeta\cdot\nabla-\zeta\cdot\zeta$; the last term vanishes. Hence the displayed remainder equation is exactly $(-\Delta+q)e^{x\cdot\zeta}(1+r_\zeta)=0$. This proves existence and the remainder bound.

Since $a$ is supported in $\overline B$, for $0<h\le1$ its translation difference has support in a fixed bounded ball and absolute value at most $Kh^\alpha$. Consequently $\omega_2(a,h)\le C_BKh^\alpha$ and $\|a\|_2\le C_BK$. Apply [F2] to $a$ with a cutoff equal to $1$ near its support. The zero-order part $|a|^2$ has squared negative-half norm at most $Cs^{-1}\||a|^2\|_2^2\le Cs^{-1}C_BK^4$ by [F1]. The inequality $\|v+w\|^2\le2\|v\|^2+2\|w\|^2$ therefore bounds the average squared norm of $q$ by $C[\lambda^{-1}+\lambda^{-1}h^{-2}+(1+(1+|k|^2)/\lambda)h^{2\alpha}]$. Set $h=\lambda^{-1/(2+2\alpha)}$. Both $\lambda^{-1}h^{-2}$ and $h^{2\alpha}$ equal $\lambda^{-\alpha/(1+\alpha)}$, and $\lambda^{-1}$ is no larger. The pointwise remainder bound from step 4.1 then gives the asserted average for $q$ and $r$ together. The parameterized norms and integrals are measurable: first for Fourier-truncated smooth data this follows directly from the measurable weights; the Neumann partial sums are measurable as iterated multipliers and fixed coefficient forms, and their norm limits retain measurability.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $D_j=\{z\in\mathbb C:|z|<j\}$, let $0\le\kappa<1$, and let $2<r\le p_\kappa$, where $p_\kappa$ is a near-two inverse exponent. Put $q=2r/(r-2)$, so $1/2=1/q+1/r$. Let $\mu,\nu$ be measurable, supported in $D_3$, and satisfy $\||\mu|+|\nu|\|_\infty\le\kappa$. Suppose $f\in W^{1,r}(D_3;\mathbb C)$ satisfies
$$\bar\partial f=\mu\partial f+\nu\overline{\partial f}$$
almost everywhere. Fix a real $\phi\in C_c^\infty(D_2)$ and extend $F=\phi f$ by zero. Then
$$\|\bar\partial F\|_r+\|\partial F\|_r\le C_{\kappa,r}\|f\nabla\phi\|_r.$$
For $\omega_p(g,t):=\sup_{|h|\le t}\|g(\cdot-h)-g\|_p$, $G=\bar\partial F$, and $U=\|f\|_{W^{1,r}(D_3)}$, one has, when $0<t\le1/2$,
$$\omega_2(G,t)+\omega_2(\phi\bar\partial f,t)\le C_{\kappa,r,\phi}U\bigl(\omega_q(\mu,t)+\omega_q(\nu,t)+t\bigr).$$
For the unitary angular Fourier transform and $T\ge6$, this implies
$$\|\mathbf1_{\{|\xi|\ge T\}}\widehat G\|_2\le C_{\kappa,r,\phi}U\bigl(\omega_q(\mu,3/T)+\omega_q(\nu,3/T)+T^{-1}\bigr).$$

Assume Countable Choice. Identify $\mathbb C$ with $\mathbb R^2$, use angular-frequency unitary Fourier transformation, and put $\partial=(\partial_x-i\partial_y)/2$, $\bar\partial=(\partial_x+i\partial_y)/2$. The Beurling transform $\mathcal B$ defined on $L^2(\mathbb C)$ by
$$\widehat{\mathcal Bf}(\xi)=\frac{\xi_1-i\xi_2}{\xi_1+i\xi_2}\widehat f(\xi)\qquad(\xi\ne0)$$
is an isometry and extends boundedly to every $L^p$, $1<p<\infty$. It commutes with translations. There is a finite constant $A\ge1$ such that, for $2\le p\le4$,
$$\|\mathcal B\|_{L^p\to L^p}\le A^{2-4/p}.$$
For $p>2$ and $f\in L^p$ supported in a fixed disk $D_R$, the absolutely convergent integral
$$\mathcal Cf(z):=\frac1\pi\int_{\mathbb C}\frac{f(w)}{z-w}\,dA(w)$$
belongs to $W^{1,p}(\mathbb C)$, satisfies $\bar\partial\mathcal Cf=f$, $\partial\mathcal Cf=\mathcal Bf$, and obeys
$$\|\mathcal Cf\|_{W^{1,p}}\le C_{p,R}\|f\|_p,\qquad |\mathcal Cf(z)-\mathcal Cf(z')|\le C_p\|f\|_p|z-z'|^{1-2/p}.$$
It is $O(1/|z|)$ at infinity. For every $0\le\kappa<1$ there is $p_\kappa>2$ such that, whenever $2\le p\le p_\kappa$ and $\mu,\nu$ are measurable with $\||\mu|+|\nu|\|_\infty\le\kappa$, the real-linear map
$$I-\mu\mathcal B-\nu\overline{\mathcal B},\qquad \overline{\mathcal B}(f):=\overline{\mathcal Bf},$$
is invertible on $L^p(\mathbb C;\mathbb C)$, with inverse norm at most $2/(1-\kappa)$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

derivations.claim: Fix $\phi$ from [F3], put $F=\phi(f_1-f_2)$ and $G=\bar\partial F$. At frequencies $|\xi|<T$, the Wirtinger multiplier has magnitude $|\xi|/2$, so $\|\mathbf1_{\{|\xi|<T\}}\widehat G\|_2\le(T/2)\|F\|_2\le C T\varepsilon$. At higher frequencies, apply [F1] to each $f_j$ and use $\theta\le1$ to get $\|\mathbf1_{\{|\xi|\ge T\}}\widehat G\|_2\le CU(A+1)T^{-\theta}$ for $T\ge6$. Therefore $\|G\|_2\le C[T\varepsilon+T^{-\theta}]$. For $0<\varepsilon\le1$, choose $T=\max\{6,\varepsilon^{-1/(1+\theta)}\}$ to obtain $\|G\|_2\le C\varepsilon^{\theta/(1+\theta)}$; the range where $T=6$ is absorbed into $C$. For $\varepsilon=0$, let $T\to\infty$ to obtain $G=0$. Since $\phi=1$ on $D_1$, [F2] implies $\|\partial(f_1-f_2)\|_{L^2(D_1)}+\|\bar\partial(f_1-f_2)\|_{L^2(D_1)}\le2\|G\|_2$.

The negative-power hypothesis makes $\partial f_2\ne0$ almost everywhere. Subtract the two Beltrami equations in the form $\bar\partial(f_1-f_2)=\mu_1\overline{\partial(f_1-f_2)}+(\mu_1-\mu_2)\overline{\partial f_2}$. Thus $|\mu_1-\mu_2|\le(|\bar\partial(f_1-f_2)|+\kappa|\partial(f_1-f_2)|)|\partial f_2|^{-1}$ almost everywhere. Put $s=2\sigma/(2+\sigma)$, so $0<s<2$ and $1/s=1/2+1/\sigma$. Apply Hölder to the $s$-th powers with conjugate exponents $2/s$ and $\sigma/s$, both greater than one. This gives $(\int_{D_1}|\mu_1-\mu_2|^s)^{1/s}\le C V\|G\|_2$, without needing a triangle inequality when $s<1$. Step 1.1 consequently bounds this quantity by $C\varepsilon^{\theta/(1+\theta)}$, including $\varepsilon=0$.

If $\kappa=0$, both coefficients are zero and the conclusion is immediate. Otherwise $|\mu_1-\mu_2|\le2\kappa$, and hence $\int|\mu_1-\mu_2|^2\le(2\kappa)^{2-s}\int|\mu_1-\mu_2|^s$. Step 2.1 and the square root yield $\|\mu_1-\mu_2\|_2\le C\varepsilon^{\theta s/(2+2\theta)}=C\varepsilon^\eta$. The scalar map $x\mapsto(1-x)/(1+x)$ has derivative bounded by $2/(1-\kappa)^2$ on $[-\kappa,\kappa]$. The mean value theorem therefore gives the same estimate for the two conductivities. Substitution of the stated logarithmic bound for $\varepsilon$ gives exponent $b\eta$ for sufficiently small data, and $\varepsilon=0$ gives equality by step 2.1.

Assume Countable Choice. Identify $\mathbb C$ with $\mathbb R^2$, use angular-frequency unitary Fourier transformation, and put $\partial=(\partial_x-i\partial_y)/2$, $\bar\partial=(\partial_x+i\partial_y)/2$. The Beurling transform $\mathcal B$ defined on $L^2(\mathbb C)$ by
$$\widehat{\mathcal Bf}(\xi)=\frac{\xi_1-i\xi_2}{\xi_1+i\xi_2}\widehat f(\xi)\qquad(\xi\ne0)$$
is an isometry and extends boundedly to every $L^p$, $1<p<\infty$. It commutes with translations. There is a finite constant $A\ge1$ such that, for $2\le p\le4$,
$$\|\mathcal B\|_{L^p\to L^p}\le A^{2-4/p}.$$
For $p>2$ and $f\in L^p$ supported in a fixed disk $D_R$, the absolutely convergent integral
$$\mathcal Cf(z):=\frac1\pi\int_{\mathbb C}\frac{f(w)}{z-w}\,dA(w)$$
belongs to $W^{1,p}(\mathbb C)$, satisfies $\bar\partial\mathcal Cf=f$, $\partial\mathcal Cf=\mathcal Bf$, and obeys
$$\|\mathcal Cf\|_{W^{1,p}}\le C_{p,R}\|f\|_p,\qquad |\mathcal Cf(z)-\mathcal Cf(z')|\le C_p\|f\|_p|z-z'|^{1-2/p}.$$
It is $O(1/|z|)$ at infinity. For every $0\le\kappa<1$ there is $p_\kappa>2$ such that, whenever $2\le p\le p_\kappa$ and $\mu,\nu$ are measurable with $\||\mu|+|\nu|\|_\infty\le\kappa$, the real-linear map
$$I-\mu\mathcal B-\nu\overline{\mathcal B},\qquad \overline{\mathcal B}(f):=\overline{\mathcal Bf},$$
is invertible on $L^p(\mathbb C;\mathbb C)$, with inverse norm at most $2/(1-\kappa)$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Fix $0\le\kappa<1$ and $R,S>0$. For every measurable $\mu$ supported in $D_R=\{|z|<R\}$ with $\|\mu\|_\infty\le\kappa$, there is a unique quasiconformal homeomorphism $\Phi:\mathbb C\to\mathbb C$ satisfying
$$\bar\partial\Phi=\mu\partial\Phi,\qquad \Phi(z)=z+O(1/z)\quad(z\to\infty).$$
Choose any fixed $2<r\le p_\kappa$ from the near-two inversion result, and put $\sigma=r-2>0$. Uniformly over all these coefficients,
$$\|\Phi-z\|_{W^{1,r}(\mathbb C)}+\|\Phi-z\|_\infty+[\Phi-z]_{C^{0,1-2/r}}\le C_{\kappa,r,R},\qquad \int_{D_S}|\partial\Phi|^{-\sigma}\,dA\le C_{\kappa,r,R,S}.$$
The Jacobian and $\partial\Phi$ are positive and nonzero almost everywhere, respectively, so the negative power is well-defined almost everywhere. In particular, for any $|k|=1$ and $f(z)=e^{ik\Phi(z)}$,
$$\|f\|_{W^{1,r}(D_S)}+\bigl\||\partial f|^{-1}\bigr\|_{L^\sigma(D_S)}\le C_{\kappa,r,R,S}.$$
For $0<\sigma<1$ the displayed $L^\sigma$ quantity means $(\int|\partial f|^{-\sigma})^{1/\sigma}$, without asserting a norm triangle inequality.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $f:\Omega\to\Omega'$ be an analytically $K$-quasiconformal homeomorphism ([[def-acl-sobolev-quasiconformal-homeomorphism]]) with Beltrami coefficient $\mu_f$ ([[def-beltrami-coefficient-and-maximal-dilatation]]). Then $g=f^{-1}:\Omega'\to\Omega$ is analytically $K$-quasiconformal, $K_g=K_f$, and
$$\mu_g(f(z))=-\mu_f(z)\,\frac{f_z(z)}{\overline{f_z(z)}}\quad\text{for almost every }z\in\Omega.$$
Consequently $|\mu_g|\circ f=|\mu_f|$ almost everywhere, and $f$ is analytically quasiconformal exactly when $f^{-1}$ is, with the same maximal dilatation.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $f:\Omega\to\Omega'$ be a homeomorphism of complex domains which is $K$-quasiconformal in the analytic sense, with $K\ge1$, and let $\lambda,\mu$ denote the extremal length and reciprocal curve-family modulus of [[def-extremal-length-and-curve-family-modulus]].

(i) **Quadrilaterals.** Let $Q$ be a quadrilateral with $\overline Q\subset\Omega$ and marked opposite sides $E_0,E_1$, as in [[def-geometric-quasiconformal-homeomorphism]], and let $\Gamma(Q;E_0,E_1)$ consist of paths in $Q$ joining those sides. Then $f\Gamma(Q;E_0,E_1)=\Gamma(f(Q);f(E_0),f(E_1))$ and
$$K^{-1}\mu\bigl(\Gamma(Q;E_0,E_1)\bigr)\le \mu\bigl(\Gamma(f(Q);f(E_0),f(E_1))\bigr)\le K\mu\bigl(\Gamma(Q;E_0,E_1)\bigr),$$
equivalently
$$K^{-1}\lambda\bigl(\Gamma(Q;E_0,E_1)\bigr)\le \lambda\bigl(\Gamma(f(Q);f(E_0),f(E_1))\bigr)\le K\lambda\bigl(\Gamma(Q;E_0,E_1)\bigr).$$
The same inequalities hold with the other pair of opposite marked sides.

(ii) **Annuli.** Let $\widetilde A\subset\Omega$ be a doubly connected domain, meaning that $\widehat{\mathbb C}\setminus\widetilde A$ has exactly two connected components ([[rem-riemann-sphere-one-point-compactification]]), and put $A=f(\widetilde A)$. Let $\Gamma(\widetilde A)$ and $\Gamma(A)$ be the path families joining the two annular ends. Then
$$K^{-1}\mu(\Gamma(\widetilde A))\le\mu(\Gamma(A))\le K\mu(\Gamma(\widetilde A)),\qquad K^{-1}\lambda(\Gamma(\widetilde A))\le\lambda(\Gamma(A))\le K\lambda(\Gamma(\widetilde A)).$$
For a round annulus $A(r,R)$ the connecting-family extremal length is the conformal parameter $(2\pi)^{-1}\log(R/r)$ and the reciprocal modulus is $2\pi/\log(R/r)$, by [[thm-modulus-rectangle-and-annulus]] and [[thm-round-annulus-conformal-parameter-is-complete-invariant]].

(iii) **Area and null sets.** For every relatively compact Borel set $E\subset\Omega$,
$$\operatorname{area}(f(E))=\int_EJ_f\,dA.$$
In particular, $f^{-1}$ maps Lebesgue-null Borel subsets of $\Omega'$ to null subsets of $\Omega$.

**Annular end-path convention.** In (ii), paths have parameter interval (0,1), are proper, and their tails escape into different ends, defined by the two-collar exhaustion proved below. Local rectifiability means rectifiability on each compact parameter interval. Their nonnegative Borel weighted length is the increasing supremum of those compact-restriction arc-length integrals; a nonrectifiable restriction has infinite length. The displayed extremal-length supremum over finite positive-area densities and reciprocal modulus convention are unchanged. The proof verifies compatibility with ordinary finite-boundary families and transport of the two ends, including punctured and infinite rings.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $X$ be a Banach space
over a fixed field $F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, let $K:X\to X$ be a compact operator
([[def-compact-linear-operator]]) and put $A:=I-K$. Then:

1. $A$ is injective if and only if it is surjective, and in that case $A$ is
   boundedly invertible;
2. for every $y\in X$ the equation $Ax=y$ has a solution if and only if
   $\varphi(y)=0$ for every $\varphi\in\ker A^*$, the transpose
   $A^*=I-K^*$ acting on $X^*$
   ([[def-transpose-of-a-bounded-operator]]);
3. $\ker A$ and the cokernel $X/\operatorname{ran}A$
   ([[def-quotient-vector-space-coset-notation]]) are finite dimensional with
   equal dimensions over $F$ ([[def-dimension]]).

**Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) and the Axiom
of Dependent Choice ([[def-dependent-choice]]).** Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space
([[def-metric-space]]). Then the following five conditions are equivalent.

- **(a)** $(X,d)$ is compact ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
- **(b)** $(X,d)$ is countably compact ([[def-metric-compactness-variants]]).
- **(c)** $(X,d)$ is limit point compact.
- **(d)** $(X,d)$ is sequentially compact.
- **(e)** $(X,d)$ is complete ([[def-complete-metric-space]]) and totally bounded
  ([[def-totally-bounded]]).

**The two hypotheses are not needed everywhere, and the statement should not be
read as if they were.** Of the implications assembled below, all but two are
theorems of ZF. Dependent choice is used only for "sequentially compact implies
totally bounded" ([[thm-sequentially-compact-implies-totally-bounded]]), and
countable choice only for "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]). Each is an upper bound on
the cost of the proof given in this library and not a claim of necessity; the
implication-by-implication account is
[[rem-compactness-choice-ledger-metric]].

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$.

If $T\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ and $\Delta T=0$, there is a unique smooth harmonic $h$ with $T=T_h$.

Every bounded entire function is constant.

More explicitly, if $f:\mathbb C\to\mathbb C$ is holomorphic and there is a real $M\ge0$ such that $|f(z)|\le M$ for every $z\in\mathbb C$, then $f$ is constant.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p<\infty$ and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then the compactly supported smooth
functions $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ are dense in
$W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$: for every
$u\in W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ and every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ with
$$\|\varphi-u\|_{W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n)}<\delta.$$
No such norm-density assertion is made for $p=\infty$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

We first establish the factorization needed below. If a continuous $G\in W^{1,2}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb C)$ satisfies $ ar\partial G=
u\partial G$ with $
u$ compactly supported and $|
u|\le\kappa$, let $\Psi$ be the principal homeomorphic solution for $
u$ from [F2]. Then $H=G\circ\Psi^{-1}$ is locally $H^1$ and holomorphic. Here are the Sobolev details: on compact sets, mollifications $G_n$ converge uniformly to $G$ and in $H^1$. The classical composition chain rule with the Sobolev inverse, first by smooth approximation of that inverse, gives $D(G_n\circ\Psi^{-1})=(DG_n\circ\Psi^{-1})D\Psi^{-1}$. The area formula and inverse distortion bound give $\int|D((G_n-G_m)\circ\Psi^{-1})|^2\le K\int|D(G_n-G_m)|^2$ over corresponding compact neighborhoods. Thus these compositions converge locally in $H^1$, with the chain rule in the limit. At common differentiability points, the two Beltrami equations and the inverse derivative identity cancel the $ ar\partial$ derivative of $H$. Null-set preservation makes these identities valid on a full-measure target set. Hence $ ar\partial H=0$ distributionally; apply $\partial$ and [F4] to make $H$ smooth harmonic, and then its Cauchy–Riemann equation gives holomorphy.

Suppose a bounded continuous $F\in W^{1,r}_{\mathrm{loc}}$ satisfies $| ar\partial F|\le\kappa\mathbf1_{D_1}|\partial F|+\gamma|F|$, with $\gamma\in L^r$ supported in $D_1$. It can be written $ ar\partial F=
u\partial F+AF$ with $
u,A$ supported in $D_1$, $|
u|\le\kappa$, and $|A|\le\gamma$. To construct them measurably, if $| ar\partial F|\le\kappa|\partial F|$, take $
u= ar\partial F/\partial F$ and $A=0$, using zero at zero denominators. Otherwise choose $
u\partial F$ of length $\kappa|\partial F|$ in the direction of $ ar\partial F$, and put $A=( ar\partial F-
u\partial F)/F$; in this branch $F
e0$ wherever the numerator is nonzero, by the assumed inequality. Set both coefficients to zero outside $D_1$. Let $h=(I-
u\mathcal B)^{-1}A$ and $\eta=\mathcal Ch$. The equation for $h$ implies its support lies in $\overline D_1$. By [F1], $ ar\partial\eta-
u\partial\eta=A$ and $\|\eta\|_\infty+\|\eta\|_{W^{1,r}}\le C_{\kappa,r}\|\gamma\|_r$, with $\eta=O(1/z)$. The product rule gives $ ar\partial(e^{-\eta}F)=
u\partial(e^{-\eta}F)$. This bounded continuous function factors as an entire bounded holomorphic function after a principal change of variables by step 1.1, so it is constant. Thus $F=c e^\eta$; if $F	o c_\infty$ at infinity, then $c=c_\infty$. In particular a solution of this inequality tending to zero is identically zero.

Put $e_{-k}(z)=e^{-i(kz+\overline k\overline z)}$, $
u=e_{-k}\mu$ and $\alpha=-i\overline k e_{-k}\mu$. The ansatz $f=e^{ikz}(1+\eta)$ gives exactly $ ar\partial\eta-
u\overline{\partial\eta}=\alpha\overline\eta+\alpha$. Define the real-linear operator $K g=\mathcal C(I-
u\overline{\mathcal B})^{-1}(\alpha\overline g)$ on $L^r(\mathbb C;\mathbb C)$, regarded as a real Banach space. The data to its inverse have support in $\overline D_1$, with norm at most $C_{\kappa,r}|k|\|g\|_r$. Its inverse output has the same support, by its defining equation. The Cauchy map on such data is compact into $L^r$: on the unit ball of data, [F1] gives uniform boundedness and a common Hölder modulus, and gives a uniform $C/|z|$ bound outside $D_2$. To obtain a finite $\epsilon$-net, first make the $L^r$ norm of this exterior tail small by taking a large disk, then partition that disk into sufficiently small squares and quantize the uniformly bounded complex values at their centers to a finite mesh; the Hölder modulus bounds the $L^r$ approximation error inside. Completeness and [F3] turn total boundedness into relative compactness. Thus $K$ is compact.

If $g=Kg$, then $g\in W^{1,r}$ is continuous and bounded by [F1], is $O(1/z)$ at infinity, and satisfies $\bar\partial g-\nu\overline{\partial g}=\alpha\overline g$. Therefore $|\bar\partial g|\le\kappa|\partial g|+|\alpha||g|$, so step 2.1 implies $g=0$. By [F3], $I-K$ is invertible. The equation $\eta-K\eta=\mathcal C(I-\nu\overline{\mathcal B})^{-1}\alpha=K\mathbf1_{D_1}$ has a unique $L^r$ solution. The equation itself and [F1] put $\eta\in W^{1,r}$, continuous with $O(1/z)$ decay. Reversing the ansatz calculation proves existence of $f_\mu$ and the asserted normalization. For any other solution, density of compact smooth functions in global $W^{1,r}$ gives $\partial\eta=\mathcal B\bar\partial\eta$; applying the inverse in [F1] and then $\mathcal C$ recovers the same integral equation, since its holomorphic residual vanishes at infinity. It therefore gives the same $\eta$. When $k=0$, $\alpha=0$, so $\eta=0$ and $f_\mu=1$.

Write $M=1+\eta$ from step 4.1. Its equation is $ ar\partial M=
u\overline{\partial M}+\alpha\overline M$, so $| ar\partial M|\le\kappa|\partial M|+|\alpha||M|$. Step 2.1 gives $M=e^a$, where $a=\mathcal Ch$ for data $h$ supported in $\overline D_1$ with $\|h\|_r\le C_{\kappa,r}\|\alpha\|_r\le C_{\kappa,r}|k|$. Thus $M$ never vanishes and $\|a\|_\infty+\|a\|_{W^{1,r}}\le C_{\kappa,r}|k|$. The bounds $|e^a-1|\le e^{\|a\|_\infty}|a|$ and $|
abla e^a|\le e^{\|a\|_\infty}|
abla a|$ prove the quantitative bound on $M-1$. The same Cauchy integral gives $|a(z)|\le C_{\kappa,r}|k|/|z|$ for $|z|>2$.

If $k\ne0$, set $\Phi=z+a/(ik)$. Then $f=e^{ik\Phi}$, $\Phi=z+O(1/z)$ and the asserted uniform deformation estimates follow from step 5.1. Since the exponential has no zeros, the chain rule in the Beltrami equation for $f$ gives $|\bar\partial\Phi|\le\kappa|\partial\Phi|$, with $\bar\partial\Phi=0$ outside $\overline D_1$. Define its complex coefficient by $\bar\partial\Phi/\partial\Phi$, using zero where both vanish, and take the principal homeomorphic solution $\Psi$ for that coefficient from [F2]. Step 1.1 gives $\Phi=H\circ\Psi$ with $H$ entire holomorphic. Both maps have the principal expansion, so $H(w)-w\to0$ at infinity. Liouville in [F4] gives $H(w)=w$, hence $\Phi=\Psi$ is a principal quasiconformal homeomorphism. Multiplication and composition with the exponential on $D_S$ now give the stated solution $W^{1,r}$ bound, while for $|k|=1$ the last clause of [F2] gives the inverse-gradient estimate. This completes all claims.

The probability form of Hölder, followed by integration, gives $\|v-v_h\|_p\le\omega_p(v,h)\le Ah^\theta$. Also $\|v_h\|_\infty\le B$, $\|\nabla v_h\|_\infty\le C_\rho B/h$, and its support is contained in $\overline D_{R+1}$. The latter derivative bound follows by differentiating the smooth convolution kernel and taking its derivative's $L^1$ norm. All supports involved in $v_h\circ\Psi$ and $v\circ\Psi$ lie in $\Phi(\overline D_{R+1})$, hence inside one fixed disk by [F1]. Null-set preservation of $\Phi$ makes composition with $\Psi$ independent of the representative of $v$.

Apply the weighted area formula with $w=\Phi(z)$ and then Hölder. Since $J_\Phi\le|\partial\Phi|^2$, its $L^a$ norm on $D_{R+1}$ is uniformly bounded by [F1]. Thus $\|(v-v_h)\circ\Psi\|_q^q=\int|v-v_h|^qJ_\Phi\,dA\le\|v-v_h\|_{qa'}^q\|J_\Phi\|_{a}\le C A^qh^{q\theta}$, using $qa'=p$. Therefore the translation difference of this error has $L^q$ norm at most $2CAh^\theta$, by translation invariance of Lebesgue measure.

For $|y|\le t\le1$, the inverse deformation estimate gives $|\Psi(w-y)-\Psi(w)|\le|y|+C|y|^{\theta_0}\le C t^{\theta_0}$. The Lipschitz bound for $v_h$ therefore bounds $|v_h(\Psi(w-y))-v_h(\Psi(w))|$ by $CBh^{-1}t^{\theta_0}$. $$\widehat{\mathcal Bf}(\xi)=\frac{\xi_1-i\xi_2}{\xi_1+i\xi_2}\widehat f(\xi)\qquad(\xi\ne0)$$
is an isometry and extends boundedly to every $L^p$, $1<p<\infty$. It commutes with translations. There is a finite constant $A\ge1$ such that, for $2\le p\le4$,
$$\|\mathcal B\|_{L^p\to L^p}\le A^{2-4/p}.$$
For $p>2$ and $f\in L^p$ supported in a fixed disk $D_R$, the absolutely convergent integral
$$\mathcal Cf(z):=\frac1\pi\int_{\mathbb C}\frac{f(w)}{z-w}\,dA(w)$$
belongs to $W^{1,p}(\mathbb C)$, satisfies $\bar\partial\mathcal Cf=f$, $\partial\mathcal Cf=\mathcal Bf$, and obeys
$$\|\mathcal Cf\|_{W^{1,p}}\le C_{p,R}\|f\|_p,\qquad |\mathcal Cf(z)-\mathcal Cf(z')|\le C_p\|f\|_p|z-z'|^{1-2/p}.$$
It is $O(1/|z|)$ at infinity. For every $0\le\kappa<1$ there is $p_\kappa>2$ such that, whenever $2\le p\le p_\kappa$ and $\mu,\nu$ are measurable with $\||\mu|+|\nu|\|_\infty\le\kappa$, the real-linear map
$$I-\mu\mathcal B-\nu\overline{\mathcal B},\qquad \overline{\mathcal B}(f):=\overline{\mathcal Bf},$$
is invertible on $L^p(\mathbb C;\mathbb C)$, with inverse norm at most $2/(1-\kappa)$.

$$\bar\partial\Phi=\mu\partial\Phi,\qquad \Phi(z)=z+O(1/z)\quad(z\to\infty).$$
Choose any fixed $2<r\le p_\kappa$ from the near-two inversion result, and put $\sigma=r-2>0$. Uniformly over all these coefficients,
$$\|\Phi-z\|_{W^{1,r}(\mathbb C)}+\|\Phi-z\|_\infty+[\Phi-z]_{C^{0,1-2/r}}\le C_{\kappa,r,R},\qquad \int_{D_S}|\partial\Phi|^{-\sigma}\,dA\le C_{\kappa,r,R,S}.$$

$$\|f\|_{W^{1,r}(D_S)}+\bigl\||\partial f|^{-1}\bigr\|_{L^\sigma(D_S)}\le C_{\kappa,r,R,S}.$$

This is a translation-invariant Fourier multiplier, and $\|T_n\|_{p	o p}=\|\mathcal B\|_{p	o p}$, since the two modulation factors have modulus one.

Put $\ell=2q/(q-2)$, so $1/2=1/q+1/\ell$, and $M=2+\|\mathcal B\|_{\ell\to\ell}$. Iteration of the product norm gives $\|f_n\|_\ell\le C_R\kappa^{n+1}\|\mathcal B\|_{\ell\to\ell}^n$. Induction therefore yields $\omega_2(f_n,t)\le C_RA\kappa^nM^nt^\theta$ for $0<t\le1$: the two induction contributions are bounded by $M^{n-1}$ and $\|\mathcal B\|_{\ell\to\ell}^n$, whose sum is at most $M^n$ after increasing the fixed constant.

On $|\xi|\ge T$, one sinc factor has absolute value at most $1/\sqrt2$; the multiplier is bounded below by a positive absolute constant. Hence $\|\mathbf1_{\{|\xi|\ge T\}}\widehat f\|_2\le C\omega_2(f,3/T)$. Since $\widehat h_n$ is the shifted transform of $f_n$ by $(n+1)v$, the disk $|\xi|\le K/2$ samples $\widehat f_n$ only at frequencies at least $K/2$. Step 2.1 therefore gives, when $K\ge6$, $\|\widehat g_N\|_{L^2(D_{K/2})}\le C A M^{N+1}K^{-\theta}$, by summing the geometric upper bounds and discarding the beneficial factors $\kappa^n$.

Choose $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb C)$ equal to one on $|z|\le 2R+1$, and set $P(z)=\chi(z)/(\pi z)$ for $z\ne0$, with arbitrary value at zero. Thus $P$ is compactly supported and belongs to $L^1\cap L^{r\prime}$ for every $1<r\prime<2$, although it is singular at zero. On $D_R$, convolution $P*h_v$ equals $\mathcal Ch_v$. The tail $P*b_N$ has supremum at most $C\|b_N\|_r\le Cc^{N+1}$, and $(P-P_\delta)*g_N$ has supremum at most $C\delta^{\theta_0}$, by step 4.1 and the $L^r$ bounds of step 1.1. Fix an integer $d\ge2$. Let $\Omega\subset(0,1)^d$ be a nonempty bounded connected open domain with $C^\infty$ boundary, and let $\Omega'\subset\Omega$ be an open domain whose closure is compact and contained in $\Omega$. Fix real parameters $m>0$, $M\ge\max\{1,m\}$, $R>0$, and $0<\alpha<1$. Define
$$\Gamma_{m,M}(\Omega):=\{\gamma\in L^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R):m\le\gamma(x)\le M\text{ for almost every }x\in\Omega\}$$
and
$$\Gamma'_{m,M}(\Omega,\Omega'):=\{\gamma\in\Gamma_{m,M}(\Omega):\gamma=1\text{ almost everywhere on }\Omega\setminus\Omega'\}.$$
For $\gamma\in BV(\Omega)$ set $\|\gamma\|_{BV(\Omega)}:=\max\{\|\gamma\|_{L^1(\Omega)},TV(\gamma;\Omega)\}$. For a continuously differentiable function on $\overline\Omega$ whose first derivatives are $\alpha$-Hölder continuous, set
$$\|\gamma\|_{C^{1,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)}:=\max\left\{\max_{|\beta|\le1}\sup_{x\in\overline\Omega}|\partial^\beta\gamma(x)|,\ \max_{|\beta|=1}\sup_{\substack{x,y\in\overline\Omega\\x\ne y}}\frac{|\partial^\beta\gamma(x)-\partial^\beta\gamma(y)|}{|x-y|^\alpha}\right\}.$$
Define
$$X_d(R):=\begin{cases}\{\gamma\in\Gamma'_{m,M}(\Omega,\Omega')\cap BV(\Omega):\|\gamma\|_{BV(\Omega)}\le R\},&d=2,\\[2mm]\{\gamma\in\Gamma'_{m,M}(\Omega,\Omega')\cap C^{1,\alpha}(\overline\Omega):\|\gamma\|_{C^{1,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)}\le R\},&d\ge3.\end{cases}$$
For $\gamma\in\Gamma'_{m,M}(\Omega,\Omega')$, define its measurable background extension $\gamma_e:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ by $\gamma_e=\gamma$ almost everywhere on $\Omega$ and $\gamma_e=1$ on $\mathbb R^d\setminus\Omega$. Then $\gamma_e-1$ vanishes almost everywhere outside $\Omega'$. No pointwise continuity of $\gamma_e$ is asserted. The classes $X_d(R)$ are not assumed nonempty.

derivations.claim: Since $\overline{\Omega'}$ is compact in $\Omega$, every boundary point of $\Omega$ has a neighborhood disjoint from $\overline{\Omega'}$. On the open set $\Omega\setminus\overline{\Omega'}$, continuity and the almost-everywhere background condition force $\gamma=1$ everywhere: otherwise a sufficiently small ball would have positive measure and $|\gamma-1|$ bounded below by a positive number. Thus $\gamma_e$ is identically $1$ in a neighborhood of every boundary point and is $C^1$ globally. Its derivatives vanish off $\Omega$ and near $\partial\Omega$. The same continuity argument promotes the almost-everywhere ellipticity bounds to pointwise bounds in $\Omega$, and the extension gives the claimed global value and derivative bounds. It also shows $\gamma_e-1=0$ outside $\overline{\Omega'}$.

For $x,y\in\Omega$, the Hölder estimate for each derivative follows from [F1]. For $x,y\notin\Omega$, both derivatives are zero. In the remaining case take $x\in\Omega$ and $y\notin\Omega$. The segment from $x$ to $y$ has a first exit point $z\in\partial\Omega$, with $|x-z|\le|x-y|$. By step 1.1, $\partial_j\gamma_e(z)=\partial_j\gamma_e(y)=0$. Applying the original Hölder estimate on $\overline\Omega$ to $x,z$ gives $|\partial_j\gamma_e(x)-\partial_j\gamma_e(y)|\le R|x-z|^\alpha\le R|x-y|^\alpha$. These cases exhaust all pairs, establishing the global seminorm and hence $C^{1,\alpha}$ regularity.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $n\ge2$ and let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a nonempty bounded connected open set whose boundary is covered by finitely many $C^1$ graph charts. Define $\mathcal D(\Omega):=H^1(\Omega;\mathbb K)/H_0^1(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with its quotient norm. The trace induces a bounded linear bijection $\overline T:\mathcal D(\Omega)\to W^{1/2,2}(\partial\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with bounded inverse, so these two norms are equivalent under the induced identification. The induced map after quotienting by constants is also a bounded linear bijection $\mathcal D(\Omega)/\mathbb K\mathbf1\to W^{1/2,2}(\partial\Omega;\mathbb K)/\mathbb K$, with equivalent quotient norms. A continuous linear functional on $W^{1/2,2}(\partial\Omega;\mathbb K)$ descends to the constant quotient exactly when it annihilates constants, and its descended functional has the quotient dual norm.

Define the **zero-boundary Sobolev space** $$W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K):=\overline{C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)},$$ the closure taken in the normed space $(W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K),\|\cdot\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)})$ of [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]. The norm is a genuine norm on classes by [[lem-sobolev-norm-is-well-defined-and-definite]], so this is the usual metric closure of a subset of a normed space: $u\in W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ if and only if for every $\delta>0$ there is $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with $\|u-\varphi\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}<\delta$. Let $\gamma:[0,1]\to\mathbb C^\times$ be a closed rectifiable loop with
$\gamma(0)=\gamma(1)=1$, and define

$$\alpha(t)=\frac{\gamma(t)}{|\gamma(t)|}\in\{z\in\mathbb C:|z|=1\}.$$

Under the standard homeomorphism $[s]\mapsto(\cos 2\pi s,\sin 2\pi s)$ from
$\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ to the unit circle, the loop $\alpha$ determines a based
loop in $\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ at $[0]$, and

$$n(\gamma,0)=\deg(\alpha).$$

Equivalently, the winding number of $\gamma$ about $0$ is exactly the integer
that classifies the normalized circle loop of $\gamma$.

For a based loop $\gamma:[0,1]\to\mathbb C^\times$ at $1$, let
$r(z)=z/|z|$ and define

$$W([\gamma]):=\deg(r\circ\gamma).$$

Then $W$ is the standard isomorphism

$$\pi_1(\mathbb C^\times,1)\cong(\mathbb Z,+).$$

If $\gamma$ is rectifiable, then

$$W([\gamma])=n(\gamma,0).$$

Thus the analytic winding number of any rectifiable representative is the
integer classifying its loop class.

For every real $t$, the combination $G=M_+-itM_-$ satisfies the same displayed equation with its plus coefficient, because conjugation changes $-it$ to $it$. The continuous ratio $M_+/M_-$ tends to $1$ at infinity and never meets the imaginary axis: a value $it$ would give a zero of $G$. If its real part were nonpositive anywhere, continuity along a path to a sufficiently large point would force such an imaginary-axis value. Hence its real part is strictly positive everywhere. Equality of the mixed weak derivatives of $b$ implies $\operatorname{div}(\gamma\nabla a)=0$. The same computation for $f_-$, with coefficient $-\mu$, shows that its imaginary part solves the $\gamma$ equation. Thus their stated complex combination $u_\gamma$ solves that equation. Setting $A=f_++f_-$ and $B=f_+-f_-$ gives $u_\gamma=(A+\overline B)/2$. Step 1.1 is equivalent to $|B|<|A|$, so $u_\gamma\ne0$. Its normalized remainder is $R_\gamma=\tfrac12[M_++M_-+e^{-i(kz+\overline k\overline z)}(\overline M_+-\overline M_-)]-1$. The multiplier bounds in [F1] and differentiation of the unit-modulus exponential give $R_\gamma\in W^{1,r}$ and its $O(1/z)$ normalization; the case $k=0$ follows from $f_\pm=1$.

For every constant $|\lambda|=1$, uniqueness of the CGO solution gives $f_{\lambda\mu}=\tfrac12[(1+\lambda)f_++(1-\lambda)f_-]=(A+\lambda B)/2$. To check its equation, the constants $a=(1+\lambda)/2$, $b=(1-\lambda)/2$ satisfy $a=\lambda\overline a$ and $-b=\lambda\overline b$; substitution proves the required real-linear Beltrami equation, and $a+b=1$ gives the normalization. At a point where $B\ne0$, choose $\lambda(z,k)=\overline B/B$; where $B=0$, choose any unit value. Then $u_\gamma(z,k)=f_{\lambda(z,k)\mu}(z,k)$. Each right side is $e^{ik\Phi_{\lambda\mu}(z,k)}$.

For fixed $k\ne0$, the phases $\Phi_{\lambda\mu}$ depend continuously on $\lambda$ and $z$. Indeed, the coefficients in the Fredholm construction of [F1] depend continuously on $\lambda$ in operator norm; the resolvent identity gives continuity of its solution locally in $\lambda$, hence on the compact parameter circle. Its nonvanishing normalized multiplier admits the uniquely determined logarithm tending to zero at infinity. That logarithm depends continuously on $\lambda$ on compact sets: start at a uniformly large base point where all multipliers are close to $1$, use the principal logarithm there, and extend along a finite covering of any fixed compact path by disks where the multipliers stay away from zero. The resulting phase is the normalized principal phase in [F2]. Therefore $\widetilde\delta(z)=ik\Phi_{\lambda(z,k)\mu}(z,k)$ is continuous where $B\ne0$. If $B(z_0,k)=0$, all values $f_{\lambda\mu}(z_0,k)$ coincide. Their phases have equal exponentials and vary continuously with $\lambda$, so their differences belong to the discrete set $2\pi i\mathbb Z$ and are constant; they are thus all equal. Compactness of the rotation circle and joint continuity then give continuity of $\widetilde\delta$ also at $z_0$. Its exponential is $u_\gamma$ by step 3.1, and [F2] gives its required normalization and bounds. Uniqueness follows because any two continuous logarithms on the connected plane differ by a constant $2\pi i n$, which the normalization forces to be zero.

The phase $\delta_\gamma=\widetilde\delta$ differs from $ikz$ by a bounded function. For any target $w$, choose a large circle $|z|=R$ on which $|\delta_\gamma(z)-ikz|+|w|<|k|R$. The straight homotopy between $\delta_\gamma(z)-w$ and $ikz$ avoids zero on this circle, so their winding numbers are both one. If $\delta_\gamma-w$ had no zero in the disk, its boundary loop would extend to a loop through a disk in $\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}$ and would have winding zero, a contradiction. Thus the phase is onto. Finally the Hölder and supremum bounds on $M_\pm$ in [F1]–[F2], combined with the smooth exponential on a fixed disk, give the asserted Hölder estimate for $f_\pm$ and hence for their real and imaginary combination $u_\gamma$.

derivations.claim: Let $n=|k|$, $s=r/a$, and $\sigma=1+\beta$. In polar coordinates $\rho=|x-x_0|$, seek a solution with angular mode $e^{ik\theta}$, using $u_i=A\rho^ne^{ik\theta}$ for $\rho<r$ and $u_o=(B\rho^n+C\rho^{-n})e^{ik\theta}$ for $r<\rho<a$. Continuity of $u$ and continuity of $\gamma\partial_\rho u$ at $\rho=r$ give $C r^{-2n}=-\eta B$ because $(\sigma-1)/(\sigma+1)=\eta$. The boundary condition $u_o(a,\theta)=e_k(\theta)$ then gives $Ba^n=(1-\eta s^{2n})^{-1}$.

Each piece is harmonic on its subdomain, and its value and conductivity-weighted normal derivative agree at $\rho=r$ by step 1.1. Both pieces and their classical gradients are bounded up to the interface because $r>0$. Testing a distributional first derivative against $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(D)$ and integrating by parts on the inner disk and annulus produces interface terms equal to the jump in $u$ times $\varphi$; the matching values cancel these terms, leaving the bounded piecewise classical derivatives. By [F7] the glued function belongs to $H^1(D)$. For any $z\in C_c^\infty(D)$, integration by parts on the inner disk and outer annulus cancels the interface flux terms and proves the weak equation. Since $C_c^\infty(D)$ is dense in $H_0^1(D)$ by [F1] and the energy form is continuous, the equation holds for every $z\in H_0^1(D)$. By [F1] the function is the unique solution for trace $e_k$. At $\rho=a$, the conductivity is $1$, so the outward flux is
$$\partial_\rho u_o(a,\theta)=\frac{n}{a}\frac{1+\eta s^{2n}}{1-\eta s^{2n}}e_k(\theta).$$
The Gauss–Green identity [F3] identifies this flux with the weak DN functional. For $\gamma_1\equiv1$, the harmonic extension $(\rho/a)^n e_k(\theta)$ gives flux $(n/a)e_k$, and the constant solution has zero flux.

For each angle $\theta$, define $(R_\theta U)(x)=U(x_0+Q_\theta(x-x_0))$ on $D$, where $Q_\theta$ is the planar rotation matrix, and define $P_kU=(2\pi)^{-1}\int_0^{2\pi}e^{-ik\theta}R_\theta U\,d\theta$. By density [F5] and the rotation isometries, $\theta\mapsto R_\theta U$ is strongly continuous in $H^1(D)$ for every $U$, so this integral is the $H^1$ limit of its Riemann sums. Rotations preserve the $H^1(D)$ inner product; Minkowski's inequality makes $P_k$ a contraction, and character orthogonality [F2] makes it a self-adjoint projection with pairwise orthogonal ranges. For $w\in C_c^\infty(D)$, the map $\theta\mapsto R_\theta w$ is continuous in $H^1$ and every Riemann sum of the displayed integral is in $C_c^\infty(D)$, so $P_kw\in H_0^1(D)$; contraction and density in the definition of $H_0^1$ extend this invariance to all of $H_0^1(D)$. For a smooth restriction $U$, the polar-coordinate chain rule gives the $H^1$ norm as the integral of $|U|^2+|\partial_\rho U|^2+\rho^{-2}|\partial_\theta U|^2$ against $\rho\,d\rho d\theta$. Parseval [F2] for these three terms and monotone convergence [F6] in the radial integral show that the finite orthogonal sums $S_N:=\sum_{|k|\le N}P_k$ converge to $U$ in $H^1(D)$. For a general $U\in H^1(D)$, approximate by smooth restrictions using [F5]; on each annulus $\epsilon<\rho<a$ the polar map is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism, so the polar norm and Fourier identities pass to the limit there, and monotone convergence [F6] as $\epsilon\downarrow0$ gives the full-disk identities. Each $S_N$ is an orthogonal projection and hence a contraction; density [F5] therefore extends $S_NU\to U$ to every $U\in H^1(D)$. The induced quotient modes are thus a complete orthogonal family in $\mathcal D(D)$, and the constant mode is orthogonal to every nonzero mode. Since the trace is bounded and rotation-equivariant on smooth functions, [F4] and [F5] extend commutation to all of $H^1(D)$; the trace-kernel identity in [F4] then shows that each projected boundary class is a scalar multiple of one mode. For any $H^1$ representative $U$ of the boundary mode $e_k$, let $v(\rho)$ be its $k$th angular Fourier coefficient. Parseval gives
$$\|U\|_{H^1(D)}^2\ge 2\pi\int_0^a\left(|v'(\rho)|^2\rho+\frac{n^2|v(\rho)|^2}{\rho}\right)d\rho.$$
The trace condition gives $v(a)=1$. On every interval $[\epsilon,a]$, the one-dimensional Sobolev representative of $v$ is absolutely continuous, and expansion of the square yields
$$\int_\epsilon^a\left(|v'|^2\rho+\frac{n^2|v|^2}{\rho}\right)d\rho=\int_\epsilon^a\left|v'-\frac n\rho v\right|^2\rho\,d\rho+n|v(a)|^2-n|v(\epsilon)|^2.$$
The full energy being finite implies $\int_0^a|v(\rho)|^2\rho^{-1}d\rho<\infty$, so there is a sequence $\epsilon_j\downarrow0$ with $v(\epsilon_j)\to0$; otherwise $|v|$ would be bounded below near zero and this integral would diverge. Letting $\epsilon=\epsilon_j$ and using nonnegativity of the square proves that the radial energy is at least $n$. Thus every representative has squared $H^1$ norm at least $2\pi n$, so [F4] gives $Q_n^{\mathcal D}:=\|e_k\|_{\mathcal D(D)}^2\ge2\pi n$. The harmonic lift $(\rho/a)^ne_k$ has squared $H^1$ norm $2\pi n+\pi a^2/(n+1)$ by direct radial integration, so [F4] gives $Q_n^{\mathcal D}\le2\pi n+\pi a^2/(n+1)$. Orthogonality of the constant mode to $e_k$ gives $\|e_k+c\mathbf1\|_{\mathcal D}^2=Q_n^{\mathcal D}+|c|^2\|\mathbf1\|_{\mathcal D}^2$; the constant class has positive norm by the trace isomorphism [F4]. Taking the infimum over $c$ shows that the statement's further quotient norm satisfies $Q_n=Q_n^{\mathcal D}$.

The weak DN map is diagonal on the complete orthogonal quotient modes from step 2.1; the constant mode is orthogonal to all nonzero modes, so quotienting by constants leaves $Q_n$ unchanged: angular integration makes the pairing of mode $e_k$ with any distinct mode zero, and step 1.2 gives its diagonal coefficient. For finite sums, the dual norm of the difference applied to $\sum a_ke_k$ is $\bigl(\sum_{k\ne0}|a_k|^2(2\pi a|\lambda_n(r)-n/a|)^2/Q_n\bigr)^{1/2}$; boundedness [F1] and density extend this formula to all inputs. Therefore
$$\|\dot{\Lambda}_{\gamma_r}-\dot{\Lambda}_{\gamma_1}\|=\sup_{k\ne0}\frac{2\pi a\,|\lambda_n(r)-n/a|}{Q_n},\qquad \lambda_n(r)-\frac na=\frac{2n}{a}\frac{\eta s^{2n}}{1-\eta s^{2n}}.$$
Using $Q_n\ge2\pi n$, $0<s\le1/2$, and $0<\eta<1$, this is at most
$$\sup_{n\ge1}\frac{2\eta s^{2n}}{1-\eta s^{2n}}\le\frac{2\eta}{1-\eta}s^2.$$
This proves all asserted eigenvalue and operator-norm formulas.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Let $v$ be the weak $\gamma_2$ solution with trace class $f_1$, available by [F2]. The difference $u_1-v$ belongs to $H_0^1$. The real-valuedness of $\gamma_2$ makes $a_2$ Hermitian, so $a_2(u_1-v,u_2)=\overline{a_2(u_2,u_1-v)}=0$. By the representative independence in [F1], $((\Lambda_{\gamma_1}-\Lambda_{\gamma_2})f_1)(f_2)=a_1(u_1,u_2)-a_2(v,u_2)=a_1(u_1,u_2)-a_2(u_1,u_2)$. Subtraction of these two integrals is precisely the asserted conductivity identity. All integrals are absolutely convergent since the coefficients are bounded and the solution gradients are square integrable.

Set $T=\Lambda_{\gamma_1}-\Lambda_{\gamma_2}$ and $b(f,g)=(Tf)(g)$. By [F2], $b(f+c\mathbf1,g+c'\mathbf1)=b(f,g)$ for all constants $c,c'$. If $N=\|T\|_{\mathcal L(\mathcal D,\mathcal D^*)}$, then $|b(f,g)|\le N\|f+c\mathbf1\|_{\mathcal D}\|g+c'\mathbf1\|_{\mathcal D}$. Taking the two infima independently gives $|b(f,g)|\le N\|[f]\|_E\|[g]\|_E$, including zero quotient norms. Thus the descended form has norm at most $N$. Conversely, the quotient map has norm at most one, so a bound $|b(f,g)|\le N'\|[f]\|_E\|[g]\|_E$ implies $|b(f,g)|\le N'\|f\|_{\mathcal D}\|g\|_{\mathcal D}$. Taking suprema over the two unit balls gives $N\le N'$. The operator norm into a conjugate-linear dual is exactly this supremum of absolute form values by the definition of the dual norm. Hence the two operator norms are equal.

The descended form in step 1.2 is exactly the difference of the two induced DN maps, so its norm is the stated $\delta$. Applying its form bound to step 1.1 proves the first integral bound. Since $u_j$ represents $f_j$, the two successive quotient infima give $\|[f_j]\|_E\le\|f_j\|_{\mathcal D}\le\|u_j\|_{H^1}$. Multiplying these inequalities proves the second bound, with no coefficient-dependent norm conversion factor.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Fix $0\le\kappa<1$ and $2<r\le p_\kappa$ from the near-two inverse. Let $\mu\in L^\infty(\mathbb C;\mathbb C)$ be supported in $D_1$, with $\|\mu\|_\infty\le\kappa$. For each $k\in\mathbb C$ there is a unique solution
$$f_\mu(z,k)=e^{ikz}M_\mu(z,k),\qquad M_\mu(\cdot,k)-1\in W^{1,r}(\mathbb C),\qquad M_\mu(z,k)=1+O(1/z)$$
of $\bar\partial f_\mu=\mu\overline{\partial f_\mu}$, with $f_\mu(\cdot,0)=1$. The function $M_\mu$ never vanishes and
$$\|M_\mu(\cdot,k)-1\|_{W^{1,r}(\mathbb C)}\le C_{\kappa,r} |k|e^{C_{\kappa,r}|k|}.$$
When $k\ne0$, it has a representation
$$f_\mu(z,k)=e^{ik\Phi_\mu(z,k)},$$
where $\Phi_\mu(\cdot,k)$ is a principal $K$-quasiconformal homeomorphism, $K=(1+\kappa)/(1-\kappa)$, conformal outside $\overline D_1$, and
$$\|\Phi_\mu(\cdot,k)-z\|_{W^{1,r}(\mathbb C)}+\sup_z(1+|z|)|\Phi_\mu(z,k)-z|\le C_{\kappa,r}.$$
Consequently $\|f_\mu(\cdot,k)\|_{W^{1,r}(D_S)}\le C_{\kappa,r,S}(1+|k|)e^{C_{\kappa,r,S}|k|}$; for $|k|=1$, the inverse-gradient bound $\int_{D_S}|\partial f_\mu|^{-(r-2)}\le C_{\kappa,r,S}$ also holds uniformly.

Assume Countable Choice. Identify $\mathbb C$ with $\mathbb R^2$, use angular-frequency unitary Fourier transformation, and put $\partial=(\partial_x-i\partial_y)/2$, $\bar\partial=(\partial_x+i\partial_y)/2$. The Beurling transform $\mathcal B$ defined on $L^2(\mathbb C)$ by
$$\widehat{\mathcal Bf}(\xi)=\frac{\xi_1-i\xi_2}{\xi_1+i\xi_2}\widehat f(\xi)\qquad(\xi\ne0)$$
is an isometry and extends boundedly to every $L^p$, $1<p<\infty$. It commutes with translations. There is a finite constant $A\ge1$ such that, for $2\le p\le4$,
$$\|\mathcal B\|_{L^p\to L^p}\le A^{2-4/p}.$$
For $p>2$ and $f\in L^p$ supported in a fixed disk $D_R$, the absolutely convergent integral
$$\mathcal Cf(z):=\frac1\pi\int_{\mathbb C}\frac{f(w)}{z-w}\,dA(w)$$
belongs to $W^{1,p}(\mathbb C)$, satisfies $\bar\partial\mathcal Cf=f$, $\partial\mathcal Cf=\mathcal Bf$, and obeys
$$\|\mathcal Cf\|_{W^{1,p}}\le C_{p,R}\|f\|_p,\qquad |\mathcal Cf(z)-\mathcal Cf(z')|\le C_p\|f\|_p|z-z'|^{1-2/p}.$$
It is $O(1/|z|)$ at infinity. For every $0\le\kappa<1$ there is $p_\kappa>2$ such that, whenever $2\le p\le p_\kappa$ and $\mu,\nu$ are measurable with $\||\mu|+|\nu|\|_\infty\le\kappa$, the real-linear map
$$I-\mu\mathcal B-\nu\overline{\mathcal B},\qquad \overline{\mathcal B}(f):=\overline{\mathcal Bf},$$
is invertible on $L^p(\mathbb C;\mathbb C)$, with inverse norm at most $2/(1-\kappa)$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Fix $0\le\kappa<1$ and $2<r\le p_\kappa$. Let $\nu,\alpha,E$ be measurable and supported in $D_1$, with $\|\nu\|_\infty\le\kappa$, $\|\alpha\|_\infty\le B$ and $E\in L^r$. If $F\in W^{1,r}(\mathbb C)$ is continuous, tends to zero at infinity, and satisfies
$$\bar\partial F=\nu\overline{\partial F}+\alpha\overline F+E,$$
then
$$\|F\|_{W^{1,r}(\mathbb C)}+\|F\|_\infty\le C_{\kappa,r}e^{C_{\kappa,r}(1+B)}\|E\|_r.$$
The constants do not depend on the measurable coefficients or on the particular solution.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $\mu$ be real, supported in $D_1$ and bounded by $0<\kappa<1$, and put $\gamma=(1-\mu)/(1+\mu)$. Let $f_\pm=f_{\pm\mu}$ be the measurable Beltrami CGO solutions. Then
$$\operatorname{Re}\frac{f_+(z,k)}{f_-(z,k)}>0,\qquad u_\gamma(z,k):=\operatorname{Re}f_+(z,k)+i\operatorname{Im}f_-(z,k)\ne0.$$
The function $u_\gamma$ solves $\operatorname{div}(\gamma\nabla u_\gamma)=0$ weakly, has the form $e^{ikz}(1+R_\gamma)$ with $R_\gamma\in W^{1,r}(\mathbb C)$ and $R_\gamma(z,k)=O(1/z)$, and $u_\gamma(\cdot,0)=1$. For $k\ne0$ there is a continuous logarithmic phase $\delta_\gamma(\cdot,k)$, uniquely normalized by
$$u_\gamma(z,k)=e^{\delta_\gamma(z,k)},\qquad \delta_\gamma(z,k)-ikz=O(1/z)\quad(z\to\infty).$$
It maps $\mathbb C$ onto $\mathbb C$. If the power-modulus hypotheses of the Beltrami phase-decay result hold, uniformly for unimodular multiples of $\mu$, then for some $C,b>0$,
$$|\delta_\gamma(z,k)-ikz|\le C|k|\min\{(1+|z|)^{-1},|k|^{-b}\}\qquad(|k|\ge1).$$
For each fixed $k$, $u_\gamma$ is uniformly Hölder continuous on every fixed disk, with an exponent $1-2/r>0$ and a constant depending only on that disk, $\kappa,r,|k|$.

Let $f:\mathbb D\to\mathbb D$ be holomorphic and satisfy $f(0)=0$. Then

$$|f(z)|\le|z|\qquad(z\in\mathbb D),\qquad |f'(0)|\le1.$$

Moreover, if either $|f(z_0)|=|z_0|$ for some $z_0\in\mathbb D\setminus\{0\}$
or $|f'(0)|=1$, then

$$f(z)=e^{i\theta}z$$

for some real $\theta$; conversely every rotation $z\mapsto e^{i\theta}z$
satisfies equality in both conclusions.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Put $e_k(z)=e^{i(kz+\overline k\overline z)}$, $A_k=\partial_z+ik$, and define the complex-antilinear operator $L_k g=\mathcal C[\mu e_{-k}\overline{A_k g}]$ on the real Banach space $Y=W^{1,r}(\mathbb C)\oplus\mathbb C$. It is bounded into $W^{1,r}$ and smooth in the two real coordinates of $k$, because its coefficient derivatives are bounded multiplications on the fixed disk. Both $I-L_k$ and $I+L_k$ are invertible on $Y$. To verify surjectivity rather than assume it, prescribe a right side $h+c\in Y$, put the desired unknown equal to $h+c+j$, and differentiate the equation for $j$. Its derivative equation is $(I-\mu e_{-k}\overline{\mathcal B})\bar\partial j=\alpha\overline j+E$, with $\alpha=-i\overline k\mu e_{-k}$ and compact forcing $E=\mu e_{-k}\overline{\partial h}+\alpha(\overline h+\overline c)$. It reduces to the same compact Fredholm operator as [F1], with arbitrary compact $L^r$ forcing, so gives a unique $j\in W^{1,r}$. Replacing $\mu$ by $-\mu$ proves the other sign. The bounded inverse follows from this Fredholm solution formula. Resolvent identities therefore imply that $M_\pm=(I\mp L_k)^{-1}1$ depend smoothly on $k$ in $Y$, with constant component always $1$.

Differentiating the multiplier equation with respect to either real coordinate of $k$ gives an equation for $W=\partial_{k_j}M_\pm$ with principal coefficient of modulus at most $\kappa$, lower-order coefficient bounded by $C|k|$, and compact forcing bounded in $L^r$ by $C(1+|k|)(1+\|M_\pm-1\|_{W^{1,r}})$. Coefficient derivatives contribute only bounded factors $z,\overline z$ on $D_1$. By [F1] this forcing is at most $Ce^{C(1+|k|)}$. The derivatives $W$ are continuous, in $W^{1,r}$, and tend to zero at infinity by the compact Cauchy representation and its differentiated data. Apply [F2] to get the claimed derivative bounds. The integral identity $\overline{b_\pm}=\pi^{-1}\int(\pm\mu)\partial_z(e_kM_\pm)\,dA$ follows by integrating the compact Cauchy data for $M_\pm-1$ and conjugating, using that $\mu$ is real. Differentiation under this compact integral, justified by the just-proved $W^{1,r}$ bounds, gives the stated derivative bound on $\tau$.

Define $F_+=(M_++M_-)/2$, $J=(M_+-M_-)/2$, and $F_-=i e_{-k}\overline J$. Adding and subtracting the multiplier equations gives $F_+=1+L_kJ$ and $J=L_kF_+$, hence $(I-L_k^2)F_+=1$. The square is complex-linear and $I-L_k^2=(I-L_k)(I+L_k)$ is invertible. Put $Q_k h=e_{-k}\overline{\mathcal C}(e_kh)$, where $\overline{\mathcal C}$ has kernel $1/(\pi(\overline z-\overline w))$. Direct kernel differentiation gives, for fixed compact data $h$, $\bar\partial_kQ_kh=-i e_{-k}\pi^{-1}\int e_kh\,dA$: the derivative of the exponential cancels the kernel denominator. Composing the two antilinear factors of $L_k$ gives $L_k^2g=\mathcal C\mu\bar\partial_zQ_k\mu A_kg$. Since $\bar\partial_k A_k=0$, it follows for fixed $g\in Y$ that $\bar\partial_k(L_k^2)g=-i t(g;k)\mathcal C(\mu\bar\partial_ze_{-k})$, where $t(g;k)=\pi^{-1}\int\mu\partial_z(e_kg)dA$. All these identities hold first for smooth compact data by the displayed integrals and then by $L^r$ approximation and boundedness of the composed operators.

The coefficient identity in step 2.1 gives $t(F_+;k)=\tfrac12(\overline b_+-\overline b_-)=\tau$. Also $J=L_k1+L_k^2J$ and $J=i e_{-k}\overline F_-$ imply $(I-L_k^2)(e_{-k}\overline F_-)=-i\mathcal C(\mu\bar\partial_ze_{-k})$. Differentiate $(I-L_k^2)F_+=1$ with respect to $\overline k$ and apply step 3.1 and complex linearity of the inverse. Uniqueness yields $\bar\partial_kF_+=\tau e_{-k}\overline F_-$. The definitions further give $F_+=1-i\mathcal C(\mu\bar\partial_zF_-)$ and $F_-=iQ_k\mu A_kF_+$. Differentiating the latter identity, using the rank-one formula of step 3.1 and the first derivative identity just proved, gives $\bar\partial_kF_-=\tau e_{-k}[1+i\overline{\mathcal C}(\mu\partial_z\overline F_-)]=\tau e_{-k}\overline F_+$. Since $u_\gamma=e^{ikz}(F_+-iF_-)$, these two identities give $\bar\partial_ku_\gamma=-i\tau\overline{u_\gamma}$. Division by the nonzero solution in [F3] gives the displayed phase equation.

By [F3], $|J/F_+|<1$. Outside $\overline D_1$ this quotient is holomorphic, and it tends to zero at infinity. Thus $w\mapsto J(1/w)/F_+(1/w)$ extends to a holomorphic disk self-map vanishing at zero. Its derivative there is $(b_+-b_-)/2$, so Schwarz's lemma in [F3] gives $|\tau|\le1$. At $k=0$, $M_+=M_-=1$, giving $\tau(0)=0$. For $z\in D_S$, the pointwise rotated-coefficient representation in [F3] and the uniform principal deformation bound in [F1] give $|u_\gamma(z,k)|\ge e^{-C_S|k|}$. Step 2.1 bounds $|\nabla_ku_\gamma|$ by $Ce^{C_S(1+|k|)}$. Dividing gives the asserted derivative bound for $\delta_\gamma$. The normalized multipliers tend to $1$ as $k\to0$ by [F1], so the phase continues smoothly there with value zero. This completes all claims.
