citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
[[def-measurable-rectangle]].

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with **conjugation** $z\mapsto\overline z$
the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of [[def-inner-product-space]]: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

**Induced length.** The **induced length**, or inner-product norm, of $v$ is

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

which is exactly the published [[def-inner-product-norm]]: positive definiteness
makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square
root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$.

**The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or
complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.
In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of
$\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex
modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either
scalar field.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

A topological space $X$ is **separable** if some at most countable subset $D\subseteq X$ is dense in $X$ ([[def-dense-top]], [[def-countable]]). Equivalently, every nonempty open subset of $X$ meets $D$.

A **real Hilbert space** is a real inner-product space $H$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]) whose induced-length metric is complete in the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]]: every Cauchy sequence in $H$ for the norm $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ ([[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]) converges to a point of $H$. A **complex Hilbert space** is a complex inner-product space with the same completeness property, so that a Hilbert space is exactly a real or complex inner-product space that is a Banach space for its induced norm ([[def-banach-space]]).

**The completion convention is the Cauchy-sequence one.**
[[def-banach-space]] defines completeness by convergence of Cauchy sequences, and this page keeps that convention throughout. It is weaker than $\sigma$-completeness — the assertion that every decreasing sequence of nonempty closed subsets with diameters tending to zero has a nonempty intersection. The two agree in ZFC, but Blackadar, Farah and Karagila note that the closest-point theorem on a $\sigma$-complete inner-product space is provable in ZF, whereas the Cauchy-complete form used below consumes the Axiom of Countable Choice; nothing here silently imports the stronger notion.

Let $H$ be a real or complex inner-product space ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]), with inner
product linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second, and
with the induced length $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$. The definitions below
do not require completeness. When the term *Hilbert basis* is used, $H$ is
additionally assumed complete ([[def-hilbert-space]]).

**Orthonormal indexed family.** Let $I$ be any set. An indexed family
$(e_i)_{i\in I}$ of vectors of $H$ is **orthonormal** when

$$\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=\delta_{ij}:=\begin{cases}1,&i=j,\\0,&i\ne j,\end{cases} \qquad\text{for all } i,j\in I .$$Because $1\ne 0$ in the scalar field, the family contains no zero vector: $\|e_i\|^2=\langle e_i,e_i\rangle=1$, so $\|e_i\|=1$ for every $i$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]); and the index map is injective, since $e_i=e_j$ with $i\ne j$ would give $0=\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=1$. Thus an orthonormal family is the same thing as an orthonormal set together with a labelling of it, and in the sequel no choice is hidden in passing between the two descriptions. **Orthonormal set.** A subset $S\subseteq H$ is **orthonormal** when every $s\in S$ has $\|s\|=1$ and $\langle s,t\rangle=0$ for all distinct $s,t\in S$. For such an $S$ the family $(e_s)_{s\in S}$ with $e_s:=s$ is orthonormal in the indexed sense, and the image of an orthonormal indexed family is an orthonormal set. Orthogonal means $\langle s,t\rangle=0$ ([[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]). **Independence and unique coefficients.** Let $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ be orthonormal, let $F\subseteq I$ be finite, and let scalars $c_i$ satisfy $\sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i=0$. For each fixed $j\in F$, linearity in the first argument gives$$0=\Bigl\langle \sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i,\;e_j\Bigr\rangle=\sum_{i\in F}c_i\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=c_j ,$$

so every finite subfamily of an orthonormal family is linearly independent. In
particular the coefficients in a finite expansion are unique: if
$\sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i=\sum_{i\in F}d_ie_i$, then applying the computation to
$c-d$ gives $c_i=d_i$ for every $i\in F$.

**Closed linear span and completeness.** The **span** of an indexed family is
the set of all finite linear combinations $\sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i$ with $F\subseteq I$
finite and scalars $c_i$; it is the smallest linear subspace of $H$ containing
every $e_i$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]). Its closure in the induced norm is the
**closed linear span** of the family, the smallest closed linear subspace of $H$
containing every $e_i$. The family is **complete**, or is a **complete
orthonormal system**, when its closed linear span is all of $H$. A
**Hilbert basis**, or **orthonormal basis**, of $H$ is a complete orthonormal
family in $H$.

**The empty family.** The span of the empty family is $\{0\}$, which is already
closed, so the empty family is complete exactly when $H=\{0\}$. Thus the zero
Hilbert space always has a Hilbert basis, namely the empty one.

**Not a Hamel basis, and no order is assumed.** A Hilbert basis is a basis only
in the sense of closed linear span: for an infinite-dimensional $H$ the vectors
of $H$ are in general **not** finite linear combinations of a Hilbert basis, and
the expansion of an arbitrary vector is a norm limit of finite partial sums, not
a finite sum. No enumeration, ordering or countability of the index set is part
of the definition; the partial sums are indexed by the finite subsets of $I$,
ordered by inclusion, and that is the convention used on this page.

**Coefficient notation.** For orthonormal $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ and $x\in H$ the
scalars $\langle x,e_i\rangle$ are the **coefficients** of $x$ with respect to
the family. They are well defined for every $x$, without any assumption that
the family is complete.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(e_i)_{i\in I}$ be an orthonormal family in a real or complex Hilbert space $H$
([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]), and
for $x\in H$ and finite $F\subseteq I$ put

$$P_Fx:=\sum_{i\in F}\langle x,e_i\rangle e_i .$$

Then the following four assertions are equivalent:

1. **(completeness)** the closed linear span of $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ is $H$;
2. **(zero complement)** the only vector orthogonal to every $e_i$ is $0$;
3. **(Parseval)** $\displaystyle\sum_{i\in I}|\langle x,e_i\rangle|^2=\|x\|^2$
   for every $x\in H$, the sum being the supremum of the finite subsums
   ([[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]]);
4. **(net convergence)** the finite-subset net $(P_Fx)_{F\in\operatorname{Fin}(I)}$
   converges to $x$ for every $x\in H$.

Assertion 2 is the statement
$\operatorname{span}\{e_i : i\in I\}^\perp=\{0\}$
([[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]).

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space, $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ a sub-sigma-algebra, and $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ integrable. A **conditional-expectation version of $X$ given $\mathcal G$** is a real, $\mathcal G$-measurable, integrable function $Y$ such that $\int_A Y\,dP=\int_A X\,dP$ for every $A\in\mathcal G$. No completeness of $\mathcal G$ is assumed.

Expectation means the integral of [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]. Integrable representatives use [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]; quotient notation is introduced after uniqueness.

Assume AC. Real $L^2(\Omega,\mathcal G,P|_{\mathcal G})$ embeds isometrically as a closed subspace of real $L^2(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$. For $X\in L^2(P)$, $U=E[X\mid\mathcal G]$ is its orthogonal projection onto this subspace. It uniquely minimizes $E[(X-Z)^2]$ over $Z\in L^2(\mathcal G)$ as an almost-sure class.

Let K be a finite kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$, in particular a probability kernel, or a uniformly sigma-finite kernel with the specified exhaustion of the kernel definition. For every nonnegative $\Sigma\otimes\Tau$-measurable function $f:S\times T\to[0,\infty]$, the function
$$I_f(s)=\int_T f(s,t)\,K(s,dt)$$
is $\Sigma$-measurable, with infinity allowed. For a real product-measurable f, the set $D=\{s:I_{|f|}(s)<\infty\}$ is measurable, and its signed integral on D, extended by zero on $S\setminus D$, is a measurable real function. No assertion here is made for a general kernel lacking a common measurable finite-mass exhaustion.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ have a supplied posterior probability kernel $\Pi_y$, let $(\mathsf A,\mathcal G)$ be a measurable action space, and let $L:\Theta\times\mathsf A\to[0,\infty]$ be a measurable function on the product measurable space [[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]], in the sense of [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]. This strengthens the section-measurability convention in [[def-loss-function-and-risk]] so that posterior integrals vary measurably with measurable action rules.

For a fixed data fiber $y$ and action $a$, define the **posterior risk** only when
$$\rho_y(a):=\int_\Theta L(\theta,a)\,\Pi_y(d\theta)<\infty.$$
A **pointwise Bayes action** at $y$ is a finite-risk action attaining the minimum among all finite-risk actions. On a declared measurable data domain $D$, a **Bayes action rule** is a measurable map $\delta:D\to\mathsf A$ whose finite posterior risk attains that minimum at every $y\in D$. This definition makes no assertion that finite-risk actions or measurable minimizing rules always exist. It therefore does not infer a Bayes action merely from the existence of an infimum. The sampling risk in [[def-loss-function-and-risk]] is a different integral, taken over the data law at a fixed parameter.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\to(E,\mathcal S)$ and $Y:(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\to(T,\mathcal T)$ be measurable random elements. A **conditional law of X given Y** is a probability kernel $K:(T,\mathcal T)\to(E,\mathcal S)$ such that $\omega\mapsto K(Y(\omega),\cdot)$ is a regular conditional distribution of X given $\sigma(Y)$ in [[def-regular-conditional-distribution]]. Thus for every $A\in\mathcal S$ and $H\in\sigma(Y)$,
$$\int_H K(Y(\omega),A)\,dP=P(H\cap\{X\in A\}).$$

Composition with Y makes each evaluation $\sigma(Y)$-measurable, and every section remains a probability by [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]. The notation $P(X\in A\mid Y=y)=K(y,A)$ refers to a chosen kernel; it is not a ratio involving the possibly zero probability $P(Y=y)$.

Write $P_Y(B)=P(Y^{-1}(B))$ for the law in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]. If a specified countable family $\mathcal C\subseteq\mathcal S$ determines probability measures, two conditional laws K,L agree as measures outside a single $\mathcal T$-measurable $P_Y$-null set. Indeed for each $A\in\mathcal C$ the measurable discrepancy $D_A=\{y:K(y,A)\ne L(y,A)\}$ has null inverse image under Y by [[lem-conditional-expectation-is-unique-almost-surely]]. > Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

$$\int_H K(Y(\omega),A)\,dP=P(H\cap\{X\in A\}).$$

Write $P_Y(B)=P(Y^{-1}(B))$ for the law in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]. Indeed for each $A\in\mathcal C$ the measurable discrepancy $D_A=\{y:K(y,A)\ne L(y,A)\}$ has null inverse image under Y by [[lem-conditional-expectation-is-unique-almost-surely]]. Hence $P_Y(D_A)=0$ by the law definition; the countable union $D$ is null by [[thm-finite-and-countable-subadditivity-of-measures]], and off D the determining property gives equality of measures. This uses a supplied determining family and makes no AC assertion about obtaining one.

Empty-event evaluations remain zero and whole-target evaluations remain one. Existence on standard-Borel spaces is proved separately; the definition alone does not assert a conditional kernel exists.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ be a measurable data space, let $H$ be a separable real Hilbert space, and fix a complete orthonormal basis $(e_j)_{j\in J}$, where $J$ is either finite with its supplied ordering or $J=\mathbb N$. A complex Hilbert signal space is included by viewing it as a real Hilbert space with inner product the real part of its complex inner product and supplying a real orthonormal basis. Let $\Pi$ be a probability kernel from $\mathsf Y$ to $H$ with its norm Borel sigma-algebra. Define
$$D_2:=\left\{y\in\mathsf Y:\int_H\|h\|_H^2\,\Pi_y(dh)<\infty\right\}.$$
For every $y\in D_2$ and $j\in J$, define
$$m_j(y):=\int_H\langle h,e_j\rangle_H\,\Pi_y(dh),\qquad \mu(y):=\sum_{j\in J}m_j(y)e_j,$$
where the last sum is the norm limit of its finite partial sums. Then $D_2\in\mathcal Y$, the sum defining $\mu(y)$ exists for every $y\in D_2$, and $\mu:D_2\to H$ is measurable. For every $y\in D_2$ and every action $a\in H$,
$$\int_H\|h-a\|_H^2\,\Pi_y(dh)=\int_H\|h-\mu(y)\|_H^2\,\Pi_y(dh)+\|a-\mu(y)\|_H^2.$$
Thus $\mu(y)$ is the unique finite-risk action minimizing posterior squared-error risk over all of $H$, and it is a measurable Bayes action rule on $D_2$. The minimization is over the full Hilbert space: the mean need not belong to a nonconvex admissible signal subset, and no perceptual-representativeness claim is made. For a probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$, let $Y:\Omega\to(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ and $T:\Omega\to H$ be measurable random elements with $E\|T\|_H^2<\infty$. If the same $\Pi$ is a supplied regular conditional law of $T$ given $Y$, write $P_Y(B)=P(Y\in B)$ for the law of $Y$. Then $D_2$ has full $P_Y$-measure. Extend $\mu$ by zero to a measurable map $\bar\mu:\mathsf Y\to H$; the coordinates of $\bar\mu(Y)$ are versions of $E[\langle T,e_j\rangle_H\mid\sigma(Y)]$, and $\bar\mu(Y)$ is square-integrable. Any square-integrable $H$-valued random variable whose basis coordinates are versions of those same conditional expectations equals $\bar\mu(Y)$ almost surely. The RCD's values on $P_Y$-null data sets remain version choices.

Let $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ and $(Q,\mathcal Q)$ be measurable data and target spaces, with $\mathcal Q$ the Borel sigma-algebra of the target metric space. Let $P$ be a probability measure on the product space $(\mathsf Y\times Q,\mathcal Y\otimes\mathcal Q)$, and let $\ell:Q\times Q\to[0,+\infty]$ be product-measurable, where $\ell(t,a)$ is the loss for target $t$ and action $a$. For a Borel point reconstruction rule $g:\mathsf Y\to Q$, its risk under $P$ is the extended nonnegative integral
$$R_P(g):=\int_{\mathsf Y\times Q}\ell(t,g(y))\,P(dy,dt).$$
For a randomized reconstruction rule given by a probability kernel $K$ from $\mathsf Y$ to $Q$, define
$$R_P(K):=\int_{\mathsf Y\times Q}\!\left(\int_Q\ell(t,a)\,K(y,da)\right)P(dy,dt).$$
The inner integral is measurable in $(y,t)$ by kernel integration; a deterministic rule is the special case $K_y=\delta_{g(y)}$. When $P_{\rm train}$ and $P_{\rm test}$ are specified joint laws on the same input-target space, the corresponding training-law risk and test-law risk are $R_{P_{\rm train}}(K)$ and $R_{P_{\rm test}}(K)$. Either value may be $+\infty$. This definition imposes no inequality between the two risks: any such comparison requires an additional assumption relating the joint laws or the rule's behavior under them.

For every $a\in\mathbb R$, $\int(t-a)^2\Pi_0(dt)=\tfrac12(-1-a)^2+\tfrac12(1-a)^2=1+a^2$. The unique minimizer over $\mathbb R$ is $0$; on the restricted set $S$, both values $a=\pm1$ have risk $2$. Let $(X,d_X)$ and $(Y,d_Y)$ be metric spaces, called the **parameter space** and the **data space**. Let $U\subseteq X$ be a nonempty set of **admissible truths**, and let $F:U\to Y$ be a **forward map**. For $x\in U$, the datum $F(x)$ is its exact observation. For $y\in Y$, define the exact solution set

$$S_F(y):=\{x\in U:F(x)=y\}.$$

The datum $y$ is exactly solvable on $U$ when $S_F(y)\ne\varnothing$.

Let $\sim$ be an equivalence relation on $U$, meaning it is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive; truths equivalent under $\sim$ represent the same recovery target. A **metric solution-class space** for $(U,\sim)$ consists of a metric space $(Q,d_Q)$ and a function $q:U\to Q$ whose image is all of $Q$ and such that $q(x)=q(x')$ if and only if $x\sim x'$. The loss between two target classes is their metric distance $d_Q$. Exact recovery of the truth itself is the special case $Q=U$, $q(x)=x$, and $d_Q=d_X$ restricted to $U$.

Let $(X,d_X)$ and $(Y,d_Y)$ be metric parameter and data spaces, let $U\subseteq X$ be a nonempty admissible truth class, let $F:U\to Y$ be a forward map, and let $(Q,d_Q)$ be a metric target space with a measurable target map $q:U\to Q$. The target $q(x)$ is the recovery object assigned to truth $x$; $Q$ may be the parameter space itself or a quotient solution-class space. All metric spaces in this definition carry their Borel sigma-algebras. A **point reconstruction rule** is a Borel map $g:Y\to Q$, and its output at data $y$ is $g(y)$. A **learned point estimator** is such a map $\widehat q_\phi$ with a fitted parameter $\phi$ in a specified parameter set. A complete training description names the probability law $P_{\rm fit}$ of all variables used to fit $\phi$; those variables may be paired or unpaired. A complete test description names a probability law $P_{\rm test}$ for evaluation pairs $(Y,q(X))$. No equality between fitting and test laws is assumed.

A finite **unrolled learned update** consists of an integer $K\geq1$, a Borel initialization $u_0:Y\to Q$, and Borel maps $T_{\phi,k}:Q\times Y\to Q$ for $0\leq k<K$, with $u_{k+1}(y)=T_{\phi,k}(u_k(y),y)$. Its output $u_K(y)$ is a point reconstruction rule. An **amortized inverse map** is a learned point estimator applied to multiple data inputs after a single fit; this term adds a reuse convention, not an accuracy guarantee.

For a real Hilbert signal space $H$, a **denoiser** is a Borel map $D_\phi:H\to H$ trained under a specified signal-corruption law and used to transform a corrupted signal into a signal estimate or an update. A denoiser is the exact minimum mean-square error map only when it equals the conditional mean for the specified signal and corruption laws. A **learned prior** is a supplied Borel probability measure $\rho_\phi$ on $H$; one construction is the pushforward law $\rho_\phi(A)=\nu(G_\phi^{-1}(A))$ of a specified probability $\nu$ under a Borel generator $G_\phi:Z\to H$. A **posterior sampler** is a probability kernel $S:Y\to Q$; relative to a supplied posterior target kernel $\Pi_y$, it is exact on a data domain $D$ when $S_y=\Pi_y$ as probability measures for every $y\in D$. A draw from $S_y$ is random; obtaining a point estimate from it requires an additional summary rule. A finite **unrolled learned update** consists of an integer $K\geq1$, a Borel initialization $u_0:Y\to Q$, and Borel maps $T_{\phi,k}:Q\times Y\to Q$ for $0\leq k<K$, with $u_{k+1}(y)=T_{\phi,k}(u_k(y),y)$. Its output $u_K(y)$ is a point reconstruction rule. An **amortized inverse map** is a learned point estimator applied to multiple data inputs after a single fit; this term adds a reuse convention, not an accuracy guarantee.

For a real Hilbert signal space $H$, a **denoiser** is a Borel map $D_\phi:H\to H$ trained under a specified signal-corruption law and used to transform a corrupted signal into a signal estimate or an update. A denoiser is the exact minimum mean-square error map only when it equals the conditional mean for the specified signal and corruption laws. A **learned prior** is a supplied Borel probability measure $\rho_\phi$ on $H$; one construction is the pushforward law $\rho_\phi(A)=\nu(G_\phi^{-1}(A))$ of a specified probability $\nu$ under a Borel generator $G_\phi:Z\to H$. The law or generator alone is not a data-to-target estimator.

In a finite-dimensional signal space $\mathbb R^d$, a **score field model** is a Borel map $s_\phi:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ intended to approximate $\nabla_x\log p_t(x)$ for a specified family of positive continuously differentiable densities $p_t$. A score field is not itself a posterior law, posterior sample, or point reconstruction rule. A **posterior sampler** is a probability kernel $S:Y\to Q$; relative to a supplied posterior target kernel $\Pi_y$, it is exact on a data domain $D$ when $S_y=\Pi_y$ as probability measures for every $y\in D$. A draw from $S_y$ is random; obtaining a point estimate from it requires an additional summary rule. The name “learned” by itself asserts no exact recovery, stability, convergence, calibration, or train-to-test guarantee.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ be a measurable data space, let $H$ be a separable real Hilbert space, and fix a complete orthonormal basis $(e_j)_{j\in J}$, where $J$ is either finite with its supplied ordering or $J=\mathbb N$. A complex Hilbert signal space is included by viewing it as a real Hilbert space with inner product the real part of its complex inner product and supplying a real orthonormal basis. Let $\Pi$ be a probability kernel from $\mathsf Y$ to $H$ with its norm Borel sigma-algebra. Define
$$D_2:=\left\{y\in\mathsf Y:\int_H\|h\|_H^2\,\Pi_y(dh)<\infty\right\}.$$
For every $y\in D_2$ and $j\in J$, define
$$m_j(y):=\int_H\langle h,e_j\rangle_H\,\Pi_y(dh),\qquad \mu(y):=\sum_{j\in J}m_j(y)e_j,$$
where the last sum is the norm limit of its finite partial sums. Then $D_2\in\mathcal Y$, the sum defining $\mu(y)$ exists for every $y\in D_2$, and $\mu:D_2\to H$ is measurable. For every $y\in D_2$ and every action $a\in H$,
$$\int_H\|h-a\|_H^2\,\Pi_y(dh)=\int_H\|h-\mu(y)\|_H^2\,\Pi_y(dh)+\|a-\mu(y)\|_H^2.$$
Thus $\mu(y)$ is the unique finite-risk action minimizing posterior squared-error risk over all of $H$, and it is a measurable Bayes action rule on $D_2$. The minimization is over the full Hilbert space: the mean need not belong to a nonconvex admissible signal subset, and no perceptual-representativeness claim is made. For a probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$, let $Y:\Omega\to(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ and $T:\Omega\to H$ be measurable random elements with $E\|T\|_H^2<\infty$. If the same $\Pi$ is a supplied regular conditional law of $T$ given $Y$, write $P_Y(B)=P(Y\in B)$ for the law of $Y$. Then $D_2$ has full $P_Y$-measure. Extend $\mu$ by zero to a measurable map $\bar\mu:\mathsf Y\to H$; the coordinates of $\bar\mu(Y)$ are versions of $E[\langle T,e_j\rangle_H\mid\sigma(Y)]$, and $\bar\mu(Y)$ is square-integrable. Any square-integrable $H$-valued random variable whose basis coordinates are versions of those same conditional expectations equals $\bar\mu(Y)$ almost surely. The RCD's values on $P_Y$-null data sets remain version choices.

Let $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ and $(Q,\mathcal Q)$ be measurable data and target spaces, with $\mathcal Q$ the Borel sigma-algebra of the target metric space. Let $P$ be a probability measure on the product space $(\mathsf Y\times Q,\mathcal Y\otimes\mathcal Q)$, and let $\ell:Q\times Q\to[0,+\infty]$ be product-measurable, where $\ell(t,a)$ is the loss for target $t$ and action $a$. For a Borel point reconstruction rule $g:\mathsf Y\to Q$, its risk under $P$ is the extended nonnegative integral
$$R_P(g):=\int_{\mathsf Y\times Q}\ell(t,g(y))\,P(dy,dt).$$
For a randomized reconstruction rule given by a probability kernel $K$ from $\mathsf Y$ to $Q$, define
$$R_P(K):=\int_{\mathsf Y\times Q}\!\left(\int_Q\ell(t,a)\,K(y,da)\right)P(dy,dt).$$
The inner integral is measurable in $(y,t)$ by kernel integration; a deterministic rule is the special case $K_y=\delta_{g(y)}$. When $P_{\rm train}$ and $P_{\rm test}$ are specified joint laws on the same input-target space, the corresponding training-law risk and test-law risk are $R_{P_{\rm train}}(K)$ and $R_{P_{\rm test}}(K)$. Either value may be $+\infty$. This definition imposes no inequality between the two risks: any such comparison requires an additional assumption relating the joint laws or the rule's behavior under them.

derivations.claim: Because $Y=0$ with probability one, the constant kernel $\Pi_0=\tfrac12\delta_{-1}+\tfrac12\delta_1$ satisfies the conditional-law identity for the empty event and the whole sample space, so it is a posterior version.
The sampler kernel is $S_0=\Pi_0$, hence $\mathcal L(\widetilde T\mid Y=0)=\Pi_0$ and exact posterior calibration holds by [F2]. Its mean is $\tfrac12(-1)+\tfrac12(1)=0$.
Under posterior risk, the action $0$ has loss expectation $\tfrac12(-1-0)^2+\tfrac12(1-0)^2=1$. By [F3], whose AC hypothesis is stated in the Example, it is the unique Bayes point action.

Conditional independence gives probability $1/2$ to equal draws, with squared difference $0$, and probability $1/2$ to unequal draws, with squared difference $4$. Therefore $E[(T-\widetilde T)^2\mid Y=0]=\tfrac12(0)+\tfrac12(4)=2$, which is the randomized rule risk under [F4].

The exact posterior sample has conditional law $\Pi_0$, but its random squared-error risk $2$ exceeds the posterior mean action's risk $1$; therefore posterior calibration of a sample does not make the sample the point Bayes action.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by

> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

derivations.claim: The local graph charts of the smooth boundary form an open cover. Shrinking them gives graph-chart neighborhoods whose coordinate images have compact closure inside Euclidean balls; compactness selects a finite subcover. Rescale each coordinate ball affinely into $(1/4,3/4)^{d-1}$. On each compact chart closure, the map and inverse have bounded derivatives, so the restricted coordinate maps are bi-Lipschitz. Apply [F1] to the finite cover and combine partition functions sharing one chart to obtain nonnegative smooth $\theta_j$ compactly supported in $U_j$, with $\sum_j\theta_j=1$. Since $\sum_j\theta_j^2\ge J^{-1}$, $\psi_j=\theta_j/(\sum_i\theta_i^2)^{1/2}$ is smooth, has the same support, and satisfies $\sum_j\psi_j^2=1$.

For each pair set $\Phi_{jk}(x,y)=(\phi_j(x),\phi_k(y))$ and $\chi_{jk}(x,y)=\psi_j(x)\psi_k(y)$. Define $(Gh)_{jk}(z)=(\chi_{jk}h)(\Phi_{jk}^{-1}z)$ on $\Phi_{jk}(U_j\times U_k)$ and zero elsewhere, and define $(Lv)(x,y)=\sum_{j,k}\chi_{jk}(x,y)v_{jk}(\Phi_{jk}(x,y))$ on the chart pairs, zero outside. These are finite sums. The chart Jacobians and surface-density factors are bounded above and below on compact supports by bi-Lipschitz regularity and [F2]–[F3], with Fubini [F5] for the product chart factors. Thus the pullbacks, zero extensions and smooth multiplications are bounded on $L^2$, so $G$ and $L$ are bounded linear maps.
Substitution in the finite sum gives $(LGh)(x,y)=\sum_{j,k}\chi_{jk}(x,y)^2h(x,y)=(\sum_j\psi_j(x)^2)(\sum_k\psi_k(y)^2)h(x,y)=h(x,y)$ almost everywhere. Thus $LG=I$ as maps on $L^2(M)$.

For smooth $h$, the product and chain rules show that first derivatives of $(Gh)_{jk}$ are bounded chart coefficients times $h$ and its first tangential derivatives. The Jacobian bounds in step 2.1 give $\|Gh\|_{\oplus H^1}\le C\|h\|_{H^1(M)}$ and $\|Lv\|_{H^1(M)}\le C\|v\|_{\oplus H^1}$. Since the weights vanish near patch edges, zero extension remains smooth. Density in the completion definition extends these maps boundedly to $H^1$.

By [F4], $P_N$ is a contraction on the finite direct sum and converges strongly to the identity. The image $G(C)$ is compact by step 2.1. For $\varepsilon>0$, take a finite $\varepsilon/3$-net $v_1,\ldots,v_s$ for $G(C)$ and then take $N$ large enough that $\|P_Nv_i-v_i\|<\varepsilon/3$ for all $i$. For any $v\in G(C)$ choose $v_i$ with $\|v-v_i\|<\varepsilon/3$; contraction gives $\|P_Nv-v\|\le\|P_N(v-v_i)\|+\|P_Nv_i-v_i\|+\|v_i-v\|<\varepsilon$. This proves compact-uniform convergence.

For $w\in H^1(\mathbb T^n)$, weak integration by parts against a character gives $\widehat{\partial_\ell w}(k)=2\pi i k_\ell\widehat w(k)$. Parseval [F4] yields $\|(I-P_N)w\|_2^2=\sum_{\|k\|_\infty>N}|\widehat w(k)|^2\le(2\pi N)^{-2}\sum_k|2\pi k|^2|\widehat w(k)|^2\le(2\pi N)^{-2}\|\nabla w\|_2^2$ for $N\ge1$. Apply this to each component of $Gh$ and use step 3.2. For $N=0$, $\|Gh\|_2\le\|Gh\|_{H^1}\le C\|h\|_{H^1}$; enlarging $C_1$ proves the stated tail estimate.

derivations.claim: Fix an integer $m\ge1$ and $a\in\mathbb R^n$. Since $\sigma$ is not a polynomial, $\sigma^{(m)}$ is not identically zero; choose $b_m$ with $\sigma^{(m)}(b_m)\ne0$. For $h\ne0$ define $R_{m,h}(x):=\frac{1}{\sigma^{(m)}(b_m)h^m}\sum_{j=0}^{m}(-1)^{m-j}\binom mj\sigma(b_m+jh(a\cdot x))$. This is a finite linear combination of permitted units. The repeated-integral formula for the $m$th forward difference gives $R_{m,h}(x)=\frac{(a\cdot x)^m}{\sigma^{(m)}(b_m)}\int_{[0,1]^m}\sigma^{(m)}(b_m+h(a\cdot x)(t_1+\cdots+t_m))\,dt$. Because $a\cdot x$ is bounded on compact $K$ and $\sigma^{(m)}$ is uniformly continuous on a compact interval around $b_m$, $R_{m,h}\to(a\cdot x)^m$ uniformly on $K$ as $h\to0$.

For $m\ge1$ and arbitrary real $x_1,\ldots,x_m$, the polarization identity $x_1\cdots x_m=\frac{1}{2^m m!}\sum_{\epsilon\in\{-1,1\}^m}(\prod_{j=1}^m\epsilon_j)(\sum_{j=1}^m\epsilon_jx_j)^m$ expresses each monomial of total degree $m$ in $n$ variables as a finite linear combination of powers of linear forms. The network closure contains them by step 2.1 and is therefore all of $C(K,\mathbb R)$.

citations.quote: Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space, let $C\subseteq H$ be nonempty, closed and convex, and let $x\in H$. Then there is exactly one point $p\in C$ with $\|x-p\|=\inf_{c\in C}\|x-c\|$, that is, a unique nearest point of $C$ to $x$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space, let $C\subseteq H$ be closed and convex with $x\in H$, and let $p\in C$. Then $p$ is the nearest point of $C$ to $x$ if and only if

$$\operatorname{Re}\langle x-p,\ y-p\rangle\le0 \qquad \text{for every } y\in C .$$

In particular, for the nearest point the inequality holds, and conversely any $p\in C$ satisfying the inequality is nearest.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: For a nonnegative function $\delta$ with $\delta(0)=0$, consider the finite weighted inequality $\sum_{i,j}a_ia_j[\delta(\|v_i\|)^2+\delta(\|v_j\|)^2-\delta(\|v_i-v_j\|)^2]\ge0$ for Hilbert vectors $v_i$ and nonnegative scalars $a_i$. The function $\delta(t)=t$ satisfies it, since the sum is $2\|\sum_i a_iv_i\|^2$. Each truncated function $\delta_A(t)=\min\{t,A\}$, $A>0$, also satisfies it. Indeed, for the subsum with BOTH $\|v_i\|,\|v_j\|<A$, replacing the negative truncated-distance square by the negative full-distance square can only decrease the sum, and this subsum is then $2\|\sum_{\|v_i\|<A}a_iv_i\|^2\ge0$. Every remaining summand is separately nonnegative, because at least one of its two positive squares is $A^2$ while its negative square is at most $A^2$. The property is closed under pointwise limits, and under taking $\delta=(\sum_{k=1}^N c_k\delta_k^2)^{1/2}$ with $c_k\ge0$, since the weighted expression is linear in $\delta^2$.

The function $\eta(t)=\omega(\sqrt t)^2$ is nondecreasing, continuous, zero at zero and concave. Here is a proof that covers nonsmooth moduli. Interpolate $\omega$ on grids $0,1/n,2/n,\ldots,n$ and extend constantly after $n$; these concave nondecreasing polygonal functions converge pointwise to $\omega$. On each affine piece $\omega_n(r)=a+br$, its slope $b$ is nonnegative and its intercept $a$ is nonnegative because concavity and $\omega_n(0)=0$ imply $\omega_n(r)\ge r\omega_n'(r)$. Thus $\omega_n(\sqrt t)^2=a^2+2ab\sqrt t+b^2t$ is concave on that piece. At a junction its one-sided derivatives are $\omega_n(r)b/r$, so the slope drops when $b$ drops. Continuity at zero then proves global concavity for $\eta_n$, and passing to the pointwise limit proves it for $\eta$. Interpolate $\eta$ on the same type of grids and flatten the final slope to zero. Every such polygonal $\eta_n$ is a finite sum $\sum_k c_k\min\{t,t_k\}$ with $c_k\ge0$: take $c_k$ to be the decrease of slope at the breakpoint $t_k$. Hence $\sqrt{\eta_n(t^2)}=(\sum_k c_k\min\{t,\sqrt{t_k}\}^2)^{1/2}$ has step 1.1's property. Passing to the limit gives that property for $\omega(t)=\sqrt{\eta(t^2)}$.

First suppose the index set is finite and nonempty. If $\omega$ is identically zero, the pairwise hypothesis makes all the $y_i$ equal and their common value works. Otherwise $\omega(t)>0$ for every $t>0$: if $\omega(t_*)=0$ with $t_*>0$, monotonicity makes it zero on $[0,t_*]$, and concavity bounds every subsequent slope by zero, forcing it to be identically zero. If some $x_i=x$, then $y=y_i$ works directly by the pairwise hypothesis. In the remaining case all $r_i=\|x_i-x\|$ and $b_i=\omega(r_i)$ are positive. In the finite-dimensional affine span of the $y_i$, minimize $h(y)=\max_i\|y-y_i\|^2/b_i^2$. A minimum exists because this continuous function tends to infinity with $\|y\|$ in that span; its perpendicular projection from $H_2$ never increases any distance. Let $y$ be a minimizer and let $J$ be its active set. The origin belongs to the convex hull of $(y-y_i)/b_i^2$, $i\in J$: otherwise that finite convex hull has a nonzero nearest point $z$, whose variational inequality gives $\langle z,(y-y_i)/b_i^2\rangle\ge\|z\|^2>0$ for every active $i$. Moving a sufficiently small distance in direction $-z$ strictly decreases all active functions and keeps the finitely many inactive ones below the old maximum, a contradiction.

Choose nonnegative coefficients $\beta_i$, summing to one over $J$, with $\sum_{i\in J}\beta_i(y-y_i)/b_i^2=0$, and normalize $a_i=(\beta_i/b_i^2)/(\sum_{j\in J}\beta_j/b_j^2)$. Then $\sum a_i=1$ and $y=\sum a_iy_i$. Write $h(y)=\lambda^2$; every active index has $\|y-y_i\|^2=\lambda^2b_i^2$. The Hilbert variance identity gives $\sum_{i,j\in J}a_ia_j\|y_i-y_j\|^2=2\sum_{i\in J}a_i\|y_i-y\|^2=2\lambda^2\sum_i a_ib_i^2$. Apply the pairwise hypothesis and step 2.1's weighted inequality to $v_i=x_i-x$. They bound that same sum above by $\sum_{i,j}a_ia_j\omega(\|v_i-v_j\|)^2\le2\sum_i a_i\omega(\|v_i\|)^2=2\sum_i a_ib_i^2$. The latter scalar is positive, so $\lambda\le1$. The minimizer therefore belongs to EVERY target ball, proving finite intersection.

Now let $I$ be arbitrary and nonempty, and fix $i_0\in I$. For every finite $J\subset I$ containing $i_0$, the set $C_J=\bigcap_{i\in J}\overline B(y_i,b_i)$ is nonempty by step 4.1, closed and convex. Let $p_J$ be its nearest point to zero by [F1]. Since $C_J$ lies in the fixed ball with center $y_{i_0}$ and radius $b_{i_0}$, the numbers $\|p_J\|^2$ have a finite supremum $D$. By [A1], choose finite $J_n$ with $\|p_{J_n}\|^2>D-1/n$ and replace them by their cumulative unions, preserving this inequality. They are increasing. For $m\ge n$, [F1] gives $\|p_{J_m}-p_{J_n}\|^2\le\|p_{J_m}\|^2-\|p_{J_n}\|^2\le D-\|p_{J_n}\|^2$, so they form a Cauchy sequence and converge to a point $p\in H_2$.

For any fixed $i\in I$, let $q_n=p_{J_n\cup\{i\}}$. Again [F1] gives $\|q_n-p_{J_n}\|^2\le\|q_n\|^2-\|p_{J_n}\|^2\le D-\|p_{J_n}\|^2\to0$. Hence $q_n\to p$; since every $q_n$ lies in the closed ball $\overline B(y_i,b_i)$, so does $p$. This works for each $i$ without enumerating $I$, and proves the required full intersection. If $I$ is empty, zero belongs to its intersection by convention. This proves all cases.

citations.quote: Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space, let $a$ be a bounded coercive sesquilinear form on $H$ with constants $M,\alpha$ ([[def-bounded-coercive-and-symmetric-sesquilinear-forms]]), and let $F:H\to\mathbb K$ be a bounded conjugate-linear functional with norm $\|F\|=\sup_{\|v\|\le1}|F(v)|$. Then there is a unique $u\in H$ with $$a(u,v)=F(v)\qquad\text{for every }v\in H,$$ and it satisfies $\alpha\|u\|\le\|F\|$, that is $\|u\|\le\|F\|/\alpha$. The real bilinear case is the same statement with $a$ symmetric or not, $F$ a bounded linear functional, and the conjugation read as the identity.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be a compact self-adjoint operator
([[def-compact-linear-operator]],
[[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]],
[[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). Let

$$\Sigma:=\{\lambda:\lambda\ \text{is an eigenvalue of}\ T,\ \lambda\ne0\}$$

be its set of nonzero eigenvalues
([[def-eigenvalue-eigenvector-eigenspace-and-spectrum]]), with eigenspaces
$E_\lambda=\ker(T-\lambda I)$ for $\lambda\in\Sigma$. Then:

1. $\Sigma$ is a finite or countably infinite set of **real** numbers, each
   eigenvalue has finite multiplicity in the sense $\dim E_\lambda<+\infty$, and
   for every real $\varepsilon>0$ there are only finitely many
   $\lambda\in\Sigma$ with $|\lambda|\ge\varepsilon$; in particular every point
   of $\mathbb F\setminus\{0\}$ has a neighbourhood containing only finitely
   many elements of $\Sigma$, so the only possible accumulation point of
   $\Sigma$ is $0$;
2. the closed linear span $M$ of $\bigcup_{\lambda\in\Sigma}E_\lambda$ satisfies
   $$M=(\ker T)^\perp=\overline{\operatorname{ran}T}$$
   ([[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]), and $H=M\oplus M^\perp$
   with $M^\perp\subseteq\ker T$;
3. for every $x\in H$ the finite-subset net of $\sum_{\lambda\in\Sigma}\lambda P_\lambda x$
   over the orthogonal projections $P_\lambda$ onto $E_\lambda$ converges in
   norm and
   $$Tx=\sum_{\lambda\in\Sigma}\lambda P_\lambda x ;$$
4. if in addition $H$ is a complex Hilbert space, then the nonzero spectrum
   agrees with the nonzero eigenvalues,
   $$\sigma(T)\cap\{\mu\in\mathbb C:\mu\ne0\}=\Sigma .$$

No Hilbert basis of $\ker T$ is selected anywhere: only the orthonormal bases of
the finite-dimensional eigenspaces $E_\lambda$, $\lambda\ne0$, are used.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n\ge1$
and let $e_k(x)=\exp(2\pi i\,k\cdot x)$, $k\in\mathbb Z^n$, be the coordinate
characters on $\mathbb T^n$
([[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]],
[[def-fourier-coefficients-and-trigonometric-polynomials]]). Then:

1. $(e_k)_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}$ is an orthonormal family in the complex Hilbert
   space $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$;
2. it is an orthonormal basis: its closed linear span is $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$;
3. consequently the Fourier expansion
   $f=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}\widehat f(k)e_k$ and Parseval's identity
   $$\|f\|_2^2=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}|\widehat f(k)|^2,\qquad \langle f,g\rangle=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}\widehat f(k)\overline{\widehat g(k)}$$
   hold for all $f,g\in L^2(\mathbb T^n)$, in the finite-subset-net sense; and
4. the Fourier coefficient map is a surjective linear isometry of
   $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$ onto $\ell^2(\mathbb Z^n,\mathbb C)$.

No Hilbert tensor-product identification is used anywhere.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Use the finite boundary charts and square partition from [F1] to define $\mathcal Gf=((\psi_jf)\circ\phi_j^{-1})_j$ on each chart and zero elsewhere, and $\mathcal L(v)=\sum_j\psi_j(v_j\circ\phi_j)$, extended by zero off the charts. The identity $\sum_j\psi_j^2=1$ gives $\mathcal L\mathcal G=I$. Change of variables and the product/chain rules on the compact chart supports make the maps bounded on $L^2$ and $H^1$. Fourier Parseval yields $\|f-\mathcal L P_N\mathcal Gf\|_2\le C(1+N)^{-1}\|f\|_{H^1(M)}$. The finite Fourier sums $\mathcal L P_N\mathcal Gf$ are smooth chartwise functions and converge in $L^2$, so smooth functions are dense in $L^2(M)$.

The estimate in step 1.1 proves $H^1(M)\hookrightarrow L^2(M)$ is compact: the finite-rank maps $\mathcal L P_N\mathcal G$ approximate the identity uniformly on the $H^1$ unit ball, and their images are bounded subsets of finite-dimensional spaces, hence have finite nets of every positive radius. Thus the unit ball is totally bounded in the complete space $L^2(M)$.

Put $q(u,v)=\int_M(u\overline v+\nabla_Mu\cdot\overline{\nabla_Mv})\,dS$ on $H^1(M)$. For $f\in L^2(M)$, [F2] gives a unique $u=\widetilde Kf\in H^1(M)$ with $q(u,v)=\langle f,v\rangle$ for every $v\in H^1(M)$ and $\|u\|_{H^1}\le\|f\|_2$. Let $J:H^1(M)\hookrightarrow L^2(M)$ and $K=J\widetilde K$. By step 2.1, $K$ is compact. Hermitian symmetry of $q$ gives $\langle Kf,g\rangle=\langle f,Kg\rangle$ and $\langle Kf,f\rangle=q(\widetilde Kf,\widetilde Kf)\ge0$. If $Kf=0$, the weak equation and smooth density from step 1.1 imply $\langle f,v\rangle=0$ for every $v\in L^2(M)$, so $f=0$. Thus $K$ is compact, positive, self-adjoint and injective.

By [F3], $K$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis $e_j$ with positive eigenvalues $\mu_j	o0$; order these so that $\mu_j$ is nonincreasing. Put $\lambda_j=\mu_j^{-1}-1$. From $Ke_j=\mu_je_j$ and the weak equation, $\int_M
abla_Me_j\cdot\overline{
abla_Mv}\,dS=\lambda_j\langle e_j,vangle$ for every $v\in H^1(M)$. Taking $v=e_j$ gives $\lambda_j=\int_M|
abla_Me_j|^2\,dS\ge0$, and these are the eigenvectors of the stated weak Laplace–Beltrami operator. In the form inner product $q$, the vectors $(1+\lambda_j)^{-1/2}e_j$ are orthonormal and complete: a vector $v$ orthogonal to every $e_j$ in $q$ satisfies $(1+\lambda_j)\langle v,e_jangle=0$ for every $j$, hence vanishes in $L^2$. Form Parseval gives $q(v,v)=\sum_j(1+\lambda_j)|\langle v,e_jangle|^2$, proving the $s=1$ norm identity.

Let $E_\Lambda=\operatorname{span}\{e_j:\lambda_j\le\Lambda\}$. For $u\in E_\Lambda$, step 4.1 gives $\|u\|_{H^1}^2\le(1+\Lambda)\|u\|_2^2$. If $\dim E_\Lambda$ exceeded the rank of $P_N\mathcal G|_{E_\Lambda}$, rank-nullity would give nonzero $u\in E_\Lambda$ with $P_N\mathcal Gu=0$. The left inverse and Fourier tail estimate from [F1] then give $\|u\|_2\le C(1+N)^{-1}\|u\|_{H^1}\le C\sqrt{1+\Lambda}(1+N)^{-1}\|u\|_2$. Choose $N\ge2C\sqrt{1+\Lambda}$ to contradict $u\ne0$. Thus $N_M(\Lambda)=\dim E_\Lambda\le\operatorname{rank}(P_N\mathcal G)\le J(2N+1)^n\le C'(1+\Lambda)^{n/2}$.

For $p=n/2+\tau$, group eigenvalues into $[2^k,2^{k+1})$. The bound from step 5.1 gives $\sum_j(1+\lambda_j)^{-p}\le C\sum_{k\ge0}2^{-kp}N_M(2^{k+1})\le C'\sum_{k\ge0}2^{-k(p-n/2)}<\infty$; the finitely many eigenvalues below $1$ contribute finitely. This proves the stated summability for every $\tau>0$. Defining $H^s_\Delta(M)$ by the weighted coefficient norm in the Statement completes the spectral-scale claim.

Let $M\subset\mathbb R^{d_a}$ be a compact smooth manifold of dimension $n\ge d$, let $\Omega\subset(0,1)^d$ be a bounded domain, and let $\sigma\in C^\infty(\mathbb R)$ be globally Lipschitz and nonpolynomial. Fix finite input and output channel dimensions. A generalized Fourier neural operator is a map $\Psi:L^2(M;\mathbb R^{d_{in}})\to L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^{d_{out}})$ of the form
$$\Psi=Q\circ R\circ F\circ L_L\circ\cdots\circ L_1\circ E\circ S.$$
Here $S$ is a pointwise finite-dimensional affine network, $S(h)(x)=s(x,h(x))$; $E$ is a continuous linear chart-lifting map from manifold functions to multichannel functions on $\mathbb T^n$; each $L_\ell$ acts on periodic channel fields by a fixed matrix channel map plus a continuous periodic channel bias $b_\ell(x)$ and a finite Fourier-multiplier convolution, followed coordinatewise by $\sigma$; $F:L^2(\mathbb T^n;\mathbb R^{c})\to L^2(\mathbb T^d;\mathbb R^{r})$ is a continuous linear dimension-reduction layer
$$ (Fv)(x_1,\ldots,x_d)=\int_{\mathbb T^{n-d}}K(z)v(x_1,\ldots,x_d,z)\,dz,$$
with a finite-dimensional matrix kernel $K$; $R$ is restriction of periodic fields to $\Omega$; and $Q$ is a pointwise finite-dimensional output network. For the EIT boundary manifold $M=\partial\Omega\times\partial\Omega$, the chart-lifting map $E$ may be taken to be the map $G$ of the chart-lifting lemma, with its finite chart-pair array treated as input channels. The finite Fourier multiplier at a layer is $\widehat{\mathcal K v}(k)=R_k\widehat v(k)$ for finitely many $k\in\mathbb Z^n$, with real-valued outputs enforced by conjugate-symmetric coefficients. When $n=d$, $F$ is the identity layer.

This is an architecture definition only. It asserts no approximation, training, statistical, discretization, or computational-cost guarantee.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$
and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure spaces
([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]), let $\mu\times\nu$ be
their product measure
([[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]]),
let $\overline{\mu\times\nu}$ be its completion
([[def-completed-product-measure]]), and let $k$ be a class in
$L^2(\overline{\mu\times\nu};\mathbb C)$. Write $L^2(\nu;\mathbb C)$ and
$L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ for the complex $L^2$ spaces of the original measures,
with $\langle f,g\rangle=\int f\overline g$ linear in the first variable
([[thm-complex-l-two-inner-product-is-well-defined-and-cauchy-schwarz]],
[[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]). Then:

1. **(representative of finite norm)** there is a
   $(\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal B)$-measurable representative $k_0$ of $k$ with
   $\int|k_0|^2\,d(\mu\times\nu)<+\infty$, and its norm equals $\|k\|_2$;
2. **(the kernel operator)** for every $f\in L^2(\nu;\mathbb C)$ the section
   integral $(T_kf)(x):=\int_Yk_0(x,y)f(y)\,d\nu(y)$ converges for
   $\mu$-almost every $x$, agrees almost everywhere with a $\mu$-measurable
   function, and its class in $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ depends only on the classes
   of $f$ and $k$; the resulting map $T_k:L^2(\nu;\mathbb C)\to
   L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ is linear and bounded with
   $\|T_k\|\le\|k\|_2$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]],
   [[def-operator-norm]]);
3. **(exact Hilbert–Schmidt norm)** every Hilbert space admits a Hilbert basis
   under the Axiom of Choice
   ([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]),
   and for every Hilbert basis $E$ of $L^2(\nu;\mathbb C)$ and every Hilbert
   basis $F$ of $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$,
   $$\sum_{e\in E}\|T_ke\|^2=\sum_{f\in F}\|T_k^*f\|^2=\|k\|_2^2,$$
   the sums being finite-subset suprema
   ([[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]]); consequently
   $T_k$ is Hilbert–Schmidt relative to every such basis and
   $\|T_k\|_{HS}=\|k\|_2$ ([[def-hilbert-schmidt-operator]],
   [[thm-hilbert-schmidt-norm-is-basis-independent]]).

The operator is interpreted through the representative $k_0$ of claim 1, and
claim 2 asserts that no other choice of representative changes the resulting
classes; this is the sense in which a kernel of the completed product defines
an operator on the $L^2$ spaces of the original factors.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Let $c_0=|M|^{-1/2}\mathbf1$ and choose a countable orthonormal basis $(c_j)_{j\ge1}$ of $L^2_0(M)$, using [A1] and separability [F1]. Extend $T$ by $\widetilde T c_0=0$ and $\widetilde T c_j=Tc_j$. The Hilbert–Schmidt condition means $\sum_{j\ge1}\|Tc_j\|_2^2<\infty$. Choose measurable representatives and define $\kappa_N(x,y)=\sum_{j=1}^{N}(Tc_j)(x)\overline{c_j(y)}$. For $i\ne j$, the summands are orthogonal in $L^2(M\times M)$ because their $y$-factors are orthogonal; Fubini [F3] gives $\|\kappa_N-\kappa_{N'}\|_2^2=\sum_{j=N'+1}^{N}\|Tc_j\|_2^2$ for $N>N'$. Thus $(\kappa_N)$ is Cauchy and converges to $\kappa_T\in L^2(M\times M)$ with $\|\kappa_T\|_2^2=\sum_{j\ge1}\|Tc_j\|_2^2=\|T\|_{\mathrm{HS}}^2$.

For a finite linear combination $f=\sum_{j=0}^{m}a_jc_j$, orthonormality and the definition of $\kappa_N$ give $\int_M\kappa_N(x,y)f(y)\,dS_y=\sum_{j=1}^{\min(N,m)}a_jTc_j(x)$. Passing to the limit in $N$ gives $\widetilde T f$ in $L^2(M)$. By [F2], the integral operator $K_{\kappa_T}$ is bounded on $L^2(M)$ with norm at most $\|\kappa_T\|_2$; finite linear combinations of the basis are dense, so continuity of $K_{\kappa_T}$ and $\widetilde T$ extends the equality to every $f\in L^2(M)$.

Since $\widetilde T c_0=0$, step 2.1 with $f=c_0$ yields $\int_M\kappa_T(x,y)\,dS_y=0$ for almost every $x$. Since the range of $\widetilde T$ lies in $L^2_0(M)$, for every $f\in L^2(M)$ Fubini gives $0=\int_M\widetilde T f(x)\,dS_x=\int_M f(y)(\int_M\kappa_T(x,y)\,dS_x)\,dS_y$. The inner section is in $L^2(M)$ by Cauchy–Schwarz and [F3]; its pairing with every $f$ vanishes, so it is zero almost everywhere. This proves the two zero-mean properties.

If $\kappa'$ is another $L^2$ kernel for $\widetilde T$, let $q=\kappa_T-\kappa'$. For every pair of basis vectors $c_i,c_j$, the coefficient $\int_{M\times M}q(x,y)c_j(y)\overline{c_i(x)}\,dS_xdS_y$ is zero because both kernels represent the same operator. If $q$ is orthogonal to all products $c_i(x)\overline{c_j(y)}$, Fubini makes each section coefficient $\int_Mq(x,y)\overline{c_j(y)}dS_y$ vanish for almost every $x$; Countable Choice gives one conull set for all $j$, and completeness of $(c_j)$ then gives $q(x,\cdot)=0$ there. Hence $q=0$ in $L^2(M\times M)$, proving uniqueness.

The kernel is unique, has the prescribed zero-mean convention, and has the exact norm in step 1.1. This establishes the claimed kernel representation without relying on the reverse implication of [F2].

Fix an integer $d\ge2$. Let $\Omega\subset(0,1)^d$ be a nonempty bounded connected open domain with $C^\infty$ boundary, and let $\Omega'\subset\Omega$ be an open domain whose closure is compact and contained in $\Omega$. Fix real parameters $m>0$, $M\ge\max\{1,m\}$, $R>0$, and $0<\alpha<1$. Define
$$\Gamma_{m,M}(\Omega):=\{\gamma\in L^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R):m\le\gamma(x)\le M\text{ for almost every }x\in\Omega\}$$
and
$$\Gamma'_{m,M}(\Omega,\Omega'):=\{\gamma\in\Gamma_{m,M}(\Omega):\gamma=1\text{ almost everywhere on }\Omega\setminus\Omega'\}.$$
For $\gamma\in BV(\Omega)$ set $\|\gamma\|_{BV(\Omega)}:=\max\{\|\gamma\|_{L^1(\Omega)},TV(\gamma;\Omega)\}$. For a continuously differentiable function on $\overline\Omega$ whose first derivatives are $\alpha$-Hölder continuous, set
$$\|\gamma\|_{C^{1,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)}:=\max\left\{\max_{|\beta|\le1}\sup_{x\in\overline\Omega}|\partial^\beta\gamma(x)|,\ \max_{|\beta|=1}\sup_{\substack{x,y\in\overline\Omega\\x\ne y}}\frac{|\partial^\beta\gamma(x)-\partial^\beta\gamma(y)|}{|x-y|^\alpha}\right\}.$$
Define
$$X_d(R):=\begin{cases}\{\gamma\in\Gamma'_{m,M}(\Omega,\Omega')\cap BV(\Omega):\|\gamma\|_{BV(\Omega)}\le R\},&d=2,\\[2mm]\{\gamma\in\Gamma'_{m,M}(\Omega,\Omega')\cap C^{1,\alpha}(\overline\Omega):\|\gamma\|_{C^{1,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)}\le R\},&d\ge3.\end{cases}$$
For $\gamma\in\Gamma'_{m,M}(\Omega,\Omega')$, define its measurable background extension $\gamma_e:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ by $\gamma_e=\gamma$ almost everywhere on $\Omega$ and $\gamma_e=1$ on $\mathbb R^d\setminus\Omega$. Then $\gamma_e-1$ vanishes almost everywhere outside $\Omega'$. No pointwise continuity of $\gamma_e$ is asserted. The classes $X_d(R)$ are not assumed nonempty.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $n\ge1$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be a
nonempty bounded connected extension domain, and let $1\le p<\infty$. Then there is
$C=C(\Omega,p)$ such that every $u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ satisfies
$$\|u-u_\Omega\|_{L^p(\Omega)}\le C\|Du\|_{L^p(\Omega)},\qquad u_\Omega:=|\Omega|^{-1}\int_\Omega u(x)\,dx.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $n\ge2$ and let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a nonempty bounded connected open set whose boundary is covered by finitely many $C^1$ graph charts. Give $H^1(\Omega;\mathbb K)=W^{1,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ its Sobolev norm, let $H_0^1(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ be the $H^1$-closure of $C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$, and let $W^{1/2,2}(\partial\Omega;\mathbb K)$ have the finite-chart Slobodeckij norm. Define $\mathcal D(\Omega):=H^1(\Omega;\mathbb K)/H_0^1(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with its quotient norm. The trace induces a bounded linear bijection $\overline T:\mathcal D(\Omega)\to W^{1/2,2}(\partial\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with bounded inverse, so these two norms are equivalent under the induced identification. The induced map after quotienting by constants is also a bounded linear bijection $\mathcal D(\Omega)/\mathbb K\mathbf1\to W^{1/2,2}(\partial\Omega;\mathbb K)/\mathbb K$, with equivalent quotient norms. A continuous linear functional on $W^{1/2,2}(\partial\Omega;\mathbb K)$ descends to the constant quotient exactly when it annihilates constants, and its descended functional has the quotient dual norm.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space, let $a$ be a bounded coercive sesquilinear form on $H$ with constants $M,\alpha$ ([[def-bounded-coercive-and-symmetric-sesquilinear-forms]]), and let $F:H\to\mathbb K$ be a bounded conjugate-linear functional with norm $\|F\|=\sup_{\|v\|\le1}|F(v)|$. Then there is a unique $u\in H$ with $$a(u,v)=F(v)\qquad\text{for every }v\in H,$$ and it satisfies $\alpha\|u\|\le\|F\|$, that is $\|u\|\le\|F\|/\alpha$. The real bilinear case is the same statement with $a$ symmetric or not, $F$ a bounded linear functional, and the conjugation read as the identity.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $k\ge1$, $1\le p\le\infty$,
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a
bounded $C^k$ domain in the graph sense of
[[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]]. Then for every open set
$V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $\overline\Omega\subseteq V$ there is a bounded
linear extension operator
$$E:W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)\longrightarrow W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K),\qquad (Eu)|_\Omega=u\ \text{a.e. on }\Omega,$$
such that $\operatorname{supp}(Eu)$ is a compact subset of $V$ for every
$u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. In particular each bounded $C^k$ domain is a
$W^{k,p}$-extension domain, with an operator whose output is supported in any
prescribed neighbourhood of $\overline\Omega$. For $k=0$, extension by zero
is an isometric $L^p$ extension on any open $\Omega$; its output is supported
in the compact set $\overline\Omega\subseteq V$ when $\Omega$ is bounded.

Assume the $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ convention of [[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]]. Let S be a compact embedded $C^1$ hypersurface in $\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$. Choose finitely many regular injective $C^1$ parametrizations $X_j:V_j\to S\cap O_j$ with $C^1$ coordinate transitions, and an ambient partition $\chi_j$ from [[lem-finite-ambient-partitions-for-euclidean-boundary-integration]], with supports compactly contained in the corresponding chart neighborhoods. Put $J_{X_j}=\sqrt{\det(DX_j^TDX_j)}$, using [[def-gram-matrix-and-gram-determinant]].

For a nonnegative Borel f on S define $\int_S f\,dS=\sum_j\int_{V_j}(\chi_j f)(X_j(y))J_{X_j}(y)\,dy$, where the integrals on the right are those of [[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]] and $0\cdot\infty=0$. Set $S(A)=\int_S\mathbf1_A\,dS$ for Borel A. For signed f with $\int_S|f|\,dS<\infty$ use the difference of the positive and negative integrals. The same chart formula restricts to a compact Borel face contained in a regular patch. The empty surface has zero integral. Independence and finiteness are established by the following chart-independence lemma.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every regular chart density is continuous and strictly positive. The chart integral on a compact embedded $C^1$ hypersurface defines a finite Borel measure independent of the finite charts and subordinate partitions. In graph coordinates $X(y)=(y,h(y))$ its density is $\sqrt{1+|Dh|^2}$. On a one-sided domain boundary the outward unit normal agrees on chart overlaps and is continuous.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $V=\{v\in H^1(\Omega):\int_\Omega v\,dx=0\}$, a closed Hilbert subspace of $H^1(\Omega)$. By [F2], $\|v\|_{H^1}\le C_0\|
abla v\|_2$ on $V$, where $C_0=(1+C^2)^{1/2}$. By [F1], the form $a_\gamma(u,v)=\int_\Omega\gamma
abla u\cdot\overline{
abla v}$ is bounded on $V$ and $a_\gamma(v,v)\ge m\|
abla v\|_2^2\ge mC_0^{-2}\|v\|_{H^1}^2$. Thus it is bounded and coercive on $V$.

Define $\ell_F(v)=F([\operatorname{Tr}v])$ for $v\in V$. By [F3], the quotient trace norm of $[\operatorname{Tr}v]$ is at most $C_1\|v\|_{H^1}$, so $|\ell_F(v)|\le C_1\|F\|\|v\|_{H^1}$; hence $\ell_F$ is bounded on $V$. Applying [F4] to step 1.1 gives a unique $u_0\in V$ with $a_\gamma(u_0,v)=\ell_F(v)$ for every $v\in V$.

For arbitrary $v\in H^1(\Omega)$ write $v=v_0+c$ with $v_0=v-v_\Omega\in V$ and $c=v_\Omega$. Gradients are unchanged by adding $c$, and $F$ acts on the trace quotient by constants, so the equation for $u_0$ on $V$ implies it for every $v\in H^1$. If $u_1$ is another solution class, subtract its volume mean to obtain $w\in V$ with $a_\gamma(w,v)=0$ for all $v\in V$; setting $v=w$ and using coercivity from step 1.1 gives $w=0$. Thus the solution is unique modulo constants.

The estimate in [F4] and step 2.1 give $\|u_0\|_{H^1}\le C_0^2C_1m^{-1}\|F\|$. The bounded trace map [F3] therefore makes the solution class in $\dot{\mathcal D}$ a bounded linear function of $F$. By [F5], the compact smooth boundary has finite positive surface measure. Subtracting the surface mean of $\operatorname{Tr}u_0$ selects one representative with boundary mean zero; this constant shift preserves the weak equation and is the only such shift. For mean-zero $f\in L^2(\partial\Omega)$, Cauchy–Schwarz and the trace bound show $F_f$ is continuous, and its zero mean makes it independent of the representative modulo constants. This proves the final assertion.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $H$ be the Hilbert transform of
[[cor-hilbert-transform-is-an-ltwo-isometry-and-squares-to-minus-identity|the line]]
and, for $1\le j\le n$, let $R_j$ be the Riesz transform of
[[def-riesz-transforms-on-euclidean-space]]. Then $H$ and each $R_j$ are
Calderon-Zygmund operators with the kernels $k(x)=1/(\pi x)$ and
$K_j(x)=c_nx_j/|x|^{n+1}$: they are $L^2$-bounded with norm at most $1$, and
for every compactly supported $f\in L^2$ and almost every
$x\notin\operatorname{supp}f$ one has $Tf(x)=\int k(x-y)f(y)\,dy$ with the
kernel of $T$. Moreover both kernels are standard $1$-Holder Calderon-Zygmund
kernels with the published constants ($A_2'=2/\pi$ and
$C_n=c_n2^{n+1}(3n+4)$, respectively).

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

Let $T$ be a Calderón–Zygmund operator with kernel constants $A_1,A_2$ and $L^2$
norm $B$. Then for every $1<p<\infty$, $T$ extends uniquely to a bounded operator
on $L^p(\mathbb R^n)$ with
$$\|Tf\|_p\le C_{n,p}(A_2+B)\max\bigl(p,(p-1)^{-1}\bigr)\|f\|_p,$$
where $C_{n,p}$ depends only on $n$ and $p$. In fact $C_{n,p}$ may be chosen to be a dimensional constant $C_n$ independent of $p$.

Assume countable choice. Work with complex-valued $L^p$ spaces and a complex-linear operator.
Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be measure spaces. Let
$1\le p_0,p_1<\infty$, let $1<q_0,q_1<\infty$, let $0<\theta<1$, and define
$$\frac1{p_\theta}:=\frac{1-\theta}{p_0}+\frac{\theta}{p_1}, \qquad \frac1{q_\theta}:=\frac{1-\theta}{q_0}+\frac{\theta}{q_1},$$

Suppose $T$ is a complex-linear map from the almost-everywhere classes of complex finite simple functions with finite-measure nonzero set on $X$ to measurable complex almost-everywhere classes on $Y$, and suppose $M_0,M_1\ge0$ satisfy
$$\|Tf\|_{q_0}\le M_0\|f\|_{p_0}, \qquad \|Tf\|_{q_1}\le M_1\|f\|_{p_1}$$
for every such $f$. Then $T$ extends uniquely to a bounded linear operator
$$\widetilde T:L^{p_\theta}(\mu;\mathbb C)\to L^{q_\theta}(\nu;\mathbb C)$$
satisfying
$$\|\widetilde T f\|_{q_\theta}\le M_0^{1-\theta}M_1^\theta\|f\|_{p_\theta} \qquad(f\in L^{p_\theta}(\mu)).$$

Assume countable choice and let $n\ge1$. Fourier transformation on Schwartz space extends uniquely to a surjective complex-linear isometry $\mathcal F_2:L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)\to L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$. It preserves the first-variable-linear inner product, and hence is unitary.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $n\ge2$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be a bounded $W^{1,p}$-extension domain with a bounded extension operator $E$, and let $1\le p<n$, $p\le q\le p^{*}=\frac{np}{n-p}$. Then $W^{1,p}(\Omega)\hookrightarrow L^q(\Omega)$ continuously:
$$\|u\|_{L^q(\Omega)}\le C(n,p,q,\Omega)\|u\|_{W^{1,p}(\Omega)}\qquad(u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)).$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $n\ge2$ and let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be nonempty, open, bounded and a $W^{1,p}$-extension domain for every $p\in(n/2,n)$ (the extension operator may depend on $p$). For every $1\le q<\infty$ there is $C(n,q,\Omega)$ with
$$\|u\|_{L^q(\Omega)}\le C(n,q,\Omega)\|u\|_{W^{1,n}(\Omega)}\qquad(u\in W^{1,n}(\Omega;\mathbb K));$$
that is, $W^{1,n}(\Omega)\hookrightarrow L^q(\Omega)$ continuously for every finite $q$. The constant necessarily blows up as $q\to\infty$, so no $L^\infty$ bound is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $n\ge1$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be a
nonempty bounded connected extension domain, and let $1\le p<\infty$. Then there is
$C=C(\Omega,p)$ such that every $u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ satisfies
$$\|u-u_\Omega\|_{L^p(\Omega)}\le C\|Du\|_{L^p(\Omega)},\qquad u_\Omega:=|\Omega|^{-1}\int_\Omega u(x)\,dx.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $d\ge2$, let $\Omega\subset(0,1)^d$ be nonempty, bounded, connected and $C^1$, and let $\gamma\in L^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ satisfy $0<m\le\gamma\le M<\infty$ almost everywhere. Let $\mathcal D(\Omega)=H^1(\Omega)/H_0^1(\Omega)$ be the trace quotient and write $\dot{\mathcal D}=\mathcal D(\Omega)/\mathbb R\mathbf1$. For each $F\in\dot{\mathcal D}^{*}$ there is a unique weak solution class $[u]\in H^1(\Omega)/\mathbb R\mathbf1$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega\gamma\nabla u\cdot\overline{\nabla v}\,dx=F([\operatorname{Tr}v])\qquad(v\in H^1(\Omega)).$$
The resulting solution operator $\mathscr R_\gamma:\dot{\mathcal D}^{*}\to\dot{\mathcal D}$ is bounded. Its unique representative whose boundary trace has surface mean zero solves the same weak equation. In particular, for $f\in L^2(\partial\Omega)$ with $\int_{\partial\Omega}f\,dS=0$, the functional $F_f([g])=\int_{\partial\Omega}f\overline g\,dS$ is admissible and defines the mean-zero Neumann-to-Dirichlet map on mean-zero $L^2$ fluxes.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $1 \le p,q,r \le \infty$ satisfy

$$ \frac1r = \frac1p + \frac1q - 1. $$

If $f \in L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$ and $g \in L^q(\mathbb{R}^n)$, then the
convolution $f*g$ is defined almost everywhere and satisfies

$$ \|f*g\|_r \le \|f\|_p\|g\|_q. $$

Assume Countable Choice and $n\ge2$. With $\omega_{n-1}=|S^{n-1}|>0$ in the published chart/polar convention, set $\Phi(x)=|x|^{2-n}/((n-2)\omega_{n-1})$ for $n\ge3$ and $\Phi(x)=-(2\pi)^{-1}\log|x|$ for $n=2$, $x\ne0$. Extend it as a locally integrable function at the pole. The one-dimensional analogue is $-\tfrac12|x|$; the subsequent $n\ge2$ Green theory does not silently include it.

Assume Countable Choice and let $n\ge2$. The locally integrable kernel $\Phi$ of [[def-laplace-fundamental-solution-with-positive-minus-laplacian-sign]] defines a regular distribution $T_\Phi\in\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^n)$ and satisfies $-\Delta T_\Phi=\delta_0$. For every $y\in\mathbb R^n$, the regular distribution associated with $x\mapsto\Phi(x-y)$ satisfies $-\Delta_x T_{\Phi(\cdot-y)}=\delta_y$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.
