Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $d\ge2$, let $\Omega\subset(0,1)^d$ be nonempty, bounded, connected and $C^1$, and let $\gamma\in L^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ satisfy $0<m\le\gamma\le M<\infty$ almost everywhere. Let $\mathcal D(\Omega)=H^1(\Omega)/H_0^1(\Omega)$ be the trace quotient and write $\dot{\mathcal D}=\mathcal D(\Omega)/\mathbb R\mathbf1$. For each $F\in\dot{\mathcal D}^{*}$ there is a unique weak solution class $[u]\in H^1(\Omega)/\mathbb R\mathbf1$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega\gamma\nabla u\cdot\overline{\nabla v}\,dx=F([\operatorname{Tr}v])\qquad(v\in H^1(\Omega)).$$
The resulting solution operator $\mathscr R_\gamma:\dot{\mathcal D}^{*}\to\dot{\mathcal D}$ is bounded. Its unique representative whose boundary trace has surface mean zero solves the same weak equation. In particular, for $f\in L^2(\partial\Omega)$ with $\int_{\partial\Omega}f\,dS=0$, the functional $F_f([g])=\int_{\partial\Omega}f\overline g\,dS$ is admissible and defines the mean-zero Neumann-to-Dirichlet map on mean-zero $L^2$ fluxes.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $n\ge2$ and let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a nonempty bounded connected open set whose boundary is covered by finitely many $C^1$ graph charts. Give $H^1(\Omega;\mathbb K)=W^{1,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ its Sobolev norm, let $H_0^1(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ be the $H^1$-closure of $C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$, and let $W^{1/2,2}(\partial\Omega;\mathbb K)$ have the finite-chart Slobodeckij norm. Define $\mathcal D(\Omega):=H^1(\Omega;\mathbb K)/H_0^1(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with its quotient norm. The trace induces a bounded linear bijection $\overline T:\mathcal D(\Omega)\to W^{1/2,2}(\partial\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with bounded inverse, so these two norms are equivalent under the induced identification. The induced map after quotienting by constants is also a bounded linear bijection $\mathcal D(\Omega)/\mathbb K\mathbf1\to W^{1/2,2}(\partial\Omega;\mathbb K)/\mathbb K$, with equivalent quotient norms. A continuous linear functional on $W^{1/2,2}(\partial\Omega;\mathbb K)$ descends to the constant quotient exactly when it annihilates constants, and its descended functional has the quotient dual norm.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge1$,
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and $\Omega'\Subset\Omega$;
write $\delta_hu=(\delta_h^1u,\dots,\delta_h^nu)$ and
$Du=(D_1u,\dots,D_nu)$ for the difference-quotient and gradient vectors, with
$$\|\delta_hu\|_{L^p(\Omega')}:=\Big\|\Big(\sum_{i=1}^n|\delta_h^iu|^2\Big)^{1/2}\Big\|_{L^p(\Omega')},\qquad \|Du\|_{L^p(\Omega)}:=\Big\|\Big(\sum_{i=1}^n|D_iu|^2\Big)^{1/2}\Big\|_{L^p(\Omega)} .$$
(1) If $1\le p\le\infty$ and $u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$, then for every
$0<|h|<\operatorname{dist}(\Omega',\partial\Omega)$ and every coordinate
direction $i$,
$$\|\delta_h^iu\|_{L^p(\Omega')}\le\|D_iu\|_{L^p(\Omega)},\qquad \|\delta_hu\|_{L^p(\Omega')}\le n^{|1/p-1/2|}\|Du\|_{L^p(\Omega)} .$$
At $p=2$ the vector estimate has constant one. The coordinate bound also
holds on any open $U\subseteq\Omega$ for a fixed $i,h$ for which every
segment $[x,x+he_i]$, $x\in U$, stays in $\Omega$; compact containment
is unnecessary. In particular, $\|\delta_h^iu\|_{L^p(H)}\le
\|D_iu\|_{L^p(H)}$ for tangential directions on a half-space $H$.
(2) Conversely, if $1<p<\infty$, $u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and there is $C$
with $\|\delta_h^iu\|_{L^p(\Omega')}\le C$ for every coordinate $i$ and all
$0<|h|<\operatorname{dist}(\Omega',\partial\Omega)/2$, then
$u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega')$ with $D_iu\in L^p(\Omega')$,
$\|D_iu\|_{L^p(\Omega')}\le C$, and
$\delta_h^iu\rightharpoonup D_iu$ weakly in $L^p(\Omega')$ as $h\to0$.
For $1\le p<\infty$, tangential quotients on $H$ also converge strongly:
$\delta_h^iu\to D_iu$ in $L^p(H)$ as $h\to0$.
Both parts are identities of classes and hold without any regularity of
$\partial\Omega$. At $p=1$ the converse in (2) is deliberately not asserted;
the companion remark records why only a measure derivative survives there.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge1$,
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, let $k\ge0$, and let $L,a$ be as in
[[def-uniformly-elliptic-divergence-form-operator]] with
$a^{ij}\in W^{k+1,\infty}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$,
$b^i,c\in W^{k,\infty}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$, all derivatives bounded by
constants $M_\ell$; let $f\in H^k_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ and let
$u\in H^1(\Omega)$ be a local weak solution of $Lu=f$
([[def-local-weak-solution-for-a-divergence-form-operator]]). Then
$u\in H^{k+2}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$, and for all open sets
$\Omega'\Subset\Omega''\Subset\Omega$ there is
$C=C(n,\theta,k,M_0,\dots,M_{k+1},\Omega',\Omega'')$ with
$$\|u\|_{H^{k+2}(\Omega')}\le C\big(\|f\|_{H^k(\Omega'')}+\|u\|_{L^2(\Omega'')}\big).$$
The gain is exactly two derivatives; the coefficient regularity required is
one order above the data order. For $k=0$ the theorem reduces to
[[thm-interior-h-two-regularity-for-divergence-form-equations]]. The
scaffold wrote $\|f\|_{H^k(\Omega)}+\|u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}$ on the right-hand
side, which is ill-posed for locally Sobolev data on an unbounded $\Omega$;
the nested formulation is the well-posed local statement.

Assume countable choice and let $n\ge1$. Fourier transformation on Schwartz space extends uniquely to a surjective complex-linear isometry $\mathcal F_2:L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)\to L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$. It preserves the first-variable-linear inner product, and hence is unitary.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Here is the needed half-order identification, without assuming an unproved equivalence for the full spectral scale. For a Hilbert pair $(E_0,E_1)$ use $K(t,f)^2=\inf_{f=f_0+f_1}(\|f_0\|_{E_0}^2+t^2\|f_1\|_{E_1}^2)$. In the spectral $L^2,H^1$ pair, independent minimization of each coefficient gives $K(t,f)^2=\sum_j|f_j|^2t^2w_j/(1+t^2w_j)$. Integration against $t^{-2}\,dt$ yields a fixed positive multiple of $\sum_jw_j^{1/2}|f_j|^2$, by substituting $t\sqrt{w_j}$ and Tonelli. Use the single-boundary versions of the chart maps: $Gf=((\psi_jf)\circ\phi_j^{-1})_j$ and $L(v)=\sum_j\psi_j(v_j\circ\phi_j)$, with zero extension. The finite chart Jacobian bounds and product rule give their $L^2,H^1$ bounds, while $\sum_j\psi_j^2=1$ gives $LG=I$, exactly as in [F3] with one chart factor. These maps bound the respective $K$ functionals in both directions (apply either map to every decomposition, using its endpoint bounds and its left inverse). For a compactly supported chart function the identical Fourier calculation gives weight $(1+|\xi|^2)^{1/2}$. This is equivalent to its Slobodeckij norm: Parseval applied to $f(\cdot+h)-f$ and integration against $|h|^{-n-1}\,dh$ give the homogeneous weight $c_n|\xi|$, with $0<c_n<\infty$ by splitting $|h|\le1$ and $|h|>1$. Smooth compact chart cutoffs and bi-Lipschitz changes of coordinates preserve this norm by the difference definition, using $|\psi(x)-\psi(y)|\le C|x-y|$ for the product term. Thus [F2] identifies the trace quotient with $H^{1/2}_\Delta/\mathbb R$, and duality identifies its mean-zero dual with $H^{-1/2}_\Delta$. Subtracting the total surface mean is bounded in every norm here, even when the boundary is disconnected.

We record the local homogeneous-Neumann estimate used below. In boundary normal coordinates $(y,t)$ on a fixed collar, the Laplace equation is $\partial_i(a^{ij}\partial_jv)=0$ with smooth positive coefficients, $a^{t\ell}=0$ for every tangential index $\ell$, and homogeneous conormal condition $\partial_tv=0$ on $t=0$. For a compactly supported collar cutoff $\eta$, tangential testing with $-\delta_{-h}(\eta^2\delta_hv)$ gives $c\|\eta
abla\delta_hv\|_2^2\le C\|v\|_{H^1}^2+(c/2)\|\eta
abla\delta_hv\|_2^2$: the coefficient difference is bounded by $C|h|$ before division by $h$, the cutoff terms by $C\|v\|_{H^1}$, and $2ab\le\epsilon a^2+\epsilon^{-1}b^2$ absorbs them. There is no boundary term because these are admissible weak Neumann tests. Applying [F4] gives all second derivatives with at least one tangential derivative. The equation then solves for $\partial_{tt}v$, since $a^{tt}\ge c>0$. Iterating with nested cutoffs proves $\|v\|_{H^k(V)}\le C_k\|v\|_{H^1(V_0)}$ for every integer $k$, with $V$ a smaller collar. In detail, tangentially differentiating $r$ times introduces only terms $\partial_i((D_y^ eta a^{ij})\partial_jD_y^{r- eta}v)$ with $| eta|\ge1$; their energy pairings are bounded by the already known derivatives of total order at most $r$, leaving $
abla D_y^rv$ on the left. Derivatives with two or more normal indices are recovered successively by differentiating the equation and isolating $a^{tt}D^\alpha\partial_{tt}v$; every other derivative of the same total order has fewer normal indices, while differentiated coefficient terms have lower total order. This induction proves the asserted estimate, rather than importing a Neumann boundary theorem. For a smooth forcing the same induction includes its finitely many derivatives on the right; a smooth nonzero normal datum can first be subtracted using a smooth collar function $t f(y)$ with cutoff and the appropriate normal sign.

It suffices first to treat real fluxes; real and imaginary parts give the complexified estimates with the same uniform dependence. Choose a smooth vector field $X$ supported in the fixed harmonic collar with $X=
u$ on the boundary. For smooth mean-zero flux $f$, the weak solution is smooth in a smaller collar: subtract the smooth normal-data lifting in step 1.2 and apply that step's inhomogeneous induction. For its harmonic part, direct differentiation gives $\operatorname{div}(X|
abla u|^2-2(X\cdot
abla u)
abla u)=(\operatorname{div}X)|
abla u|^2-2\partial_iX_j\partial_iu\partial_ju$. Integrate on the collar, where $X$ vanishes near its inner edge. The outer flux is $|
abla_Mu|^2-|f|^2$, so $\|
abla_Mu\|_2^2\le\|f\|_2^2+C\|
abla u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2$. With the trace normalized to surface mean zero, [F1], the bounded $L^2$-to-quotient-flux inclusion from [F2], and the trace $L^2$ estimate bound $\|u|_M\|_{H^1}\le C\|f\|_2$. Approximate an arbitrary mean-zero $L^2$ flux by smooth mean-zero fluxes. Apply the same estimate to their differences with the SAME conductivity and use [F1] for convergence of the weak solutions; their traces converge in $H^1$, proving the displayed uniform bound by [F3].

For an arbitrary weak flux $F$, put $v=u_{\gamma,F}-u_{1,F}$. Its $H^1/\mathbb R$ norm is at most $C\|F\|$ by [F1], and it is harmonic with ZERO normal derivative throughout the fixed collar. Apply step 1.2 to a representative of bounded $H^1$ norm. Tangential boundary derivatives are controlled by collar derivatives: for each smooth $z(y,t)$, the one-dimensional fundamental theorem applied to $|z|^2$ between $0$ and a fixed interior slice, averaged over that slice, gives $\|z(\cdot,0)\|_2^2\le C(\|z\|_2^2+\|z\|_2\|\partial_tz\|_2)$; apply this to all tangential derivatives. Thus all integer chart norms of the trace are bounded by $C_q\|F\|$. Applying the tangential differential operator $(1-\Delta_M)^k$ to this smooth trace and using [F5] gives $\sum_jw_j^{2k}|v_j|^2\le C_k\|F\|^2$; integration by parts against the weak eigenfunctions is justified by their local smoothness from [F4] in boundary charts. Smaller spectral exponents follow from $w_j\ge1$. Finally subtract the boundary mean, a bounded operation, and use step 1.1 to obtain the second displayed estimate.

The weak energy identity makes $\mathscr R_\gamma$ self-adjoint on mean-zero $L^2$: $\langle\mathscr R_\gamma f,g\rangle=\int\gamma\nabla u_f\cdot\overline{\nabla u_g}$. Hence $b_{ij}=\overline{b_{ji}}$. By step 1.1 the quotient flux norm of $e_j$ is at most $Cw_j^{-1/4}$; step 2.2 applied twice gives $|b_{ij}|\le C_q w_i^{-q/2}w_j^{-1/4}$. Symmetry gives also $|b_{ij}|\le C_q w_j^{-q/2}w_i^{-1/4}$. Their geometric mean is $C_q(w_iw_j)^{-q/4-1/8}$. Choose an integer $q$ with $q/4+1/8\ge L$ to obtain the asserted two-sided estimate, uniformly for every pair of conductivities. This also covers additional mean-zero zero eigenmodes caused by a disconnected boundary, since all $w_j\ge1$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $d\ge2$, let $\Omega\subset(0,1)^d$ be nonempty, bounded, connected and $C^\infty$, and let $\gamma\in X_d(R)$ be a real conductivity. Write $M=\partial\Omega$, let $dS$ be surface measure, and set
$$L^2_0(M)=\left\{f\in L^2(M):\int_M f\,dS=0\right\},\qquad P_0f=f-|M|^{-1}\int_Mf\,dS.$$
The mean-zero Neumann-to-Dirichlet operator $\mathscr R_\gamma:L^2_0(M)\to L^2_0(M)$ sends $f$ to the mean-zero boundary trace of the weak solution of $\nabla\cdot(\gamma\nabla u)=0$ with outward conormal flux $f$, as defined by the weak Neumann problem. Let $-\Delta_M$ be the nonnegative Laplace–Beltrami operator on the compact boundary manifold, with eigenpairs $(e_j,\lambda_j)$ on $L^2_0(M)$ from its spectral resolution. For $\tau=1/2$ when $d=2$ and any fixed $\tau>0$ when $d\ge3$, put
$$r_d:=\frac{d-1}{2}-1+\tau,\qquad C_M^{r_d/2}e_j=(1+\lambda_j)^{-r_d/2}e_j.$$
The smoothed observation is the bounded operator $A_\gamma:=\mathscr R_\gamma C_M^{r_d/2}:L^2_0(M)\to L^2_0(M)$. Its extension to all of $L^2(M)$ is $\widetilde A_\gamma f=\iota_0A_\gamma(P_0f)$, where $\iota_0:L^2_0(M)\hookrightarrow L^2(M)$ is inclusion. Thus its integral kernel, when it exists in $L^2(M\times M)$, is fixed to have zero mean in each variable. No assertion of a kernel's existence or Hilbert–Schmidt regularity is part of this definition.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $M=\partial\Omega$ be the compact smooth boundary in the boundary spectral setting, let $P_0$ be projection onto $L^2_0(M)$, and let $T:L^2_0(M)\to L^2_0(M)$ be Hilbert–Schmidt. Extend $T$ to $\widetilde T:L^2(M)\to L^2(M)$ by $\widetilde T=\iota_0TP_0$, where $\iota_0$ is inclusion. Then there is a unique $\kappa_T\in L^2(M\times M)$ such that
$$\widetilde T f(x)=\int_M\kappa_T(x,y)f(y)\,dS_y\quad\text{for almost every }x\text{ and every }f\in L^2(M),$$
and
$$\|\kappa_T\|_{L^2(M\times M)}=\|T\|_{\mathrm{HS}}.$$
The kernel has zero mean in each variable: $\int_M\kappa_T(x,y)\,dS_y=0$ for almost every $x$, and $\int_M\kappa_T(x,y)\,dS_x=0$ for almost every $y$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$
and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure spaces
([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]), let $\mu\times\nu$ be
their product measure
([[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]]),
let $\overline{\mu\times\nu}$ be its completion
([[def-completed-product-measure]]), and let $k$ be a class in
$L^2(\overline{\mu\times\nu};\mathbb C)$. Write $L^2(\nu;\mathbb C)$ and
$L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ for the complex $L^2$ spaces of the original measures,
with $\langle f,g\rangle=\int f\overline g$ linear in the first variable
([[thm-complex-l-two-inner-product-is-well-defined-and-cauchy-schwarz]],
[[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]). Then:

1. **(representative of finite norm)** there is a
   $(\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal B)$-measurable representative $k_0$ of $k$ with
   $\int|k_0|^2\,d(\mu\times\nu)<+\infty$, and its norm equals $\|k\|_2$;
2. **(the kernel operator)** for every $f\in L^2(\nu;\mathbb C)$ the section
   integral $(T_kf)(x):=\int_Yk_0(x,y)f(y)\,d\nu(y)$ converges for
   $\mu$-almost every $x$, agrees almost everywhere with a $\mu$-measurable
   function, and its class in $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ depends only on the classes
   of $f$ and $k$; the resulting map $T_k:L^2(\nu;\mathbb C)\to
   L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ is linear and bounded with
   $\|T_k\|\le\|k\|_2$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]],
   [[def-operator-norm]]);
3. **(exact Hilbert–Schmidt norm)** every Hilbert space admits a Hilbert basis
   under the Axiom of Choice
   ([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]),
   and for every Hilbert basis $E$ of $L^2(\nu;\mathbb C)$ and every Hilbert
   basis $F$ of $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$,
   $$\sum_{e\in E}\|T_ke\|^2=\sum_{f\in F}\|T_k^*f\|^2=\|k\|_2^2,$$
   the sums being finite-subset suprema
   ([[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]]); consequently
   $T_k$ is Hilbert–Schmidt relative to every such basis and
   $\|T_k\|_{HS}=\|k\|_2$ ([[def-hilbert-schmidt-operator]],
   [[thm-hilbert-schmidt-norm-is-basis-independent]]).

The operator is interpreted through the representative $k_0$ of claim 1, and
claim 2 asserts that no other choice of representative changes the resulting
classes; this is the sense in which a kernel of the completed product defines
an operator on the $L^2$ spaces of the original factors.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $\Omega$ be a bounded connected smooth domain, let $\Omega'\Subset\Omega$, let $0<m\le1\le M<\infty$, and let $m\le\gamma\le M$ be measurable with $\gamma=1$ outside $\Omega'$. Put $M_\partial=\partial\Omega$ and give the NtD maps their total-boundary-mean-zero representatives. The spectral space $H^{1/2}_\Delta(M_\partial)$ is equivalent to the chart trace space $H^{1/2}(M_\partial)$, including their quotients by constants and mean-zero duals. Uniformly in $\gamma$,
$$\|\mathscr R_\gamma f\|_{H^1_\Delta(M_\partial)}\le C\|f\|_{L^2(M_\partial)}\quad\left(\int_{M_\partial}f=0\right).$$
For every integer $q\ge0$ there is $C_q$ such that
$$\|(\mathscr R_\gamma-\mathscr R_1)F\|_{H^q_\Delta(M_\partial)}\le C_q\|F\|_{H^{-1/2}_\Delta(M_\partial)}$$
for every mean-zero weak Neumann flux $F$. If $w_j=1+\lambda_j$ and $(e_j)$ is any orthonormal boundary Laplace–Beltrami basis on the total-mean-zero subspace, the matrix $b_{ij}=\langle(\mathscr R_\gamma-\mathscr R_{\gamma_0})e_j,e_i\rangle$ of any two such conductivities satisfies, for every $L>0$,
$$|b_{ij}|\le C_L(w_iw_j)^{-L}.$$
The constants depend only on the displayed fixed data and $q$ or $L$. More generally, any $v\in H^1$ harmonic with zero weak normal derivative on a fixed smooth boundary collar has $\|v|_{M_\partial}\|_{H^q_\Delta}\le C_q\|v\|_{H^1(\text{collar})}$ for every integer $q\ge0$, using a fixed smaller collar for the boundary estimate.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $d\ge2$, let $\Omega\subset(0,1)^d$ be a nonempty bounded connected $C^1$ domain, let $0<m\le M<\infty$, and let $\gamma\in L^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ satisfy $m\le\gamma\le M$ almost everywhere. Define $\mathcal D(\Omega):=H^1(\Omega;\mathbb C)/H_0^1(\Omega;\mathbb C)$ with its quotient norm. For every boundary trace class $f\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$ there is a unique $u_{\gamma,f}\in f$ such that
$$\int_\Omega\gamma\,
abla u_{\gamma,f}\cdot\overline{
abla z}\,dx=0\qquad	ext{for every }z\in H_0^1(\Omega;\mathbb C).$$
For every $g\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$, the value $\int_\Omega\gamma
abla u_{\gamma,f}\cdot\overline{
abla V_g}\,dx$ is independent of the representative $V_g\in g$ and defines a bounded linear map $\Lambda_\gamma:\mathcal D(\Omega)	o\mathcal D(\Omega)^*$. Constants are in its kernel and its range functionals annihilate constants.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be a compact self-adjoint operator
([[def-compact-linear-operator]],
[[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]],
[[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). Let

$$\Sigma:=\{\lambda:\lambda\ \text{is an eigenvalue of}\ T,\ \lambda\ne0\}$$

be its set of nonzero eigenvalues
([[def-eigenvalue-eigenvector-eigenspace-and-spectrum]]), with eigenspaces
$E_\lambda=\ker(T-\lambda I)$ for $\lambda\in\Sigma$. Then:

1. $\Sigma$ is a finite or countably infinite set of **real** numbers, each
   eigenvalue has finite multiplicity in the sense $\dim E_\lambda<+\infty$, and
   for every real $\varepsilon>0$ there are only finitely many
   $\lambda\in\Sigma$ with $|\lambda|\ge\varepsilon$; in particular every point
   of $\mathbb F\setminus\{0\}$ has a neighbourhood containing only finitely
   many elements of $\Sigma$, so the only possible accumulation point of
   $\Sigma$ is $0$;
2. the closed linear span $M$ of $\bigcup_{\lambda\in\Sigma}E_\lambda$ satisfies
   $$M=(\ker T)^\perp=\overline{\operatorname{ran}T}$$
   ([[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]), and $H=M\oplus M^\perp$
   with $M^\perp\subseteq\ker T$;
3. for every $x\in H$ the finite-subset net of $\sum_{\lambda\in\Sigma}\lambda P_\lambda x$
   over the orthogonal projections $P_\lambda$ onto $E_\lambda$ converges in
   norm and
   $$Tx=\sum_{\lambda\in\Sigma}\lambda P_\lambda x ;$$
4. if in addition $H$ is a complex Hilbert space, then the nonzero spectrum
   agrees with the nonzero eigenvalues,
   $$\sigma(T)\cap\{\mu\in\mathbb C:\mu\ne0\}=\Sigma .$$

No Hilbert basis of $\ker T$ is selected anywhere: only the orthonormal bases of
the finite-dimensional eigenspaces $E_\lambda$, $\lambda\ne0$, are used.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that

itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most

derivations.claim: Write $r=r_d\ge0$, $n=d-1$ and $w_j=1+\lambda_j$ on the total-mean-zero subspace. The counting estimate [F1] implies $w_j^{-1/2}\le C(1+j)^{-1/n}$, after enlarging the constant for finitely many low modes. By [F5], $R=\mathscr R_\gamma$ maps the $L^2$ unit ball into a uniformly bounded $H^1_\Delta$ ball. If $P_J$ is the first $J$-mode projection, then $R_J=P_JR$ has rank at most $J$ and $\|R-R_J\|\le C(1+J)^{-1/n}$. Likewise $S=C_M^{r/2}$ has the rank-$J$ approximation $S_J=P_JS$ with $\|S-S_J\|\le C(1+J)^{-r/n}$; for $r=0$ this means the bound one and does not assert that $S$ is compact.

The rank-at-most-$2J$ map $R_JS+(R-R_J)S_J$ approximates $RS$ with error $(R-R_J)(S-S_J)$, bounded by $C(1+J)^{-(1+r)/n}$. The compact operator $RS$ therefore has singular values $s_j\le C(1+j)^{-(1+r)/n}$. To justify this implication, apply [F7] to $(RS)^*(RS)$: truncating its orthogonal singular expansion gives a rank-$k$ approximation with error $s_{k+1}$, and any other rank-$k$ approximation has a kernel vector in the span of the first $k+1$ right singular vectors, so its error is at least $s_{k+1}$. Since $2(1+r)>n$ by the actual dimension-dependent choice of $r$, $\sum_js_j^2<\infty$ uniformly. Thus $A_\gamma=RS$ and its zero extension are Hilbert–Schmidt. Apply [F3] to obtain the unique $L^2$ kernel and norm equality. Input and output annihilation of the constant mode mean that its integral in either variable is zero, by testing the integral operator and its adjoint on the constant function.

Put $B=\mathscr R_\gamma-\mathscr R_{\gamma_0}$ and $s=\|\kappa_\gamma-\kappa_{\gamma_0}\|_2$. By [F4], $s^2=\sum_{i,j}|b_{ij}|^2w_j^{-r}$. Choose $L$ so large that both $\sum_iw_i^{1-2L}$ and $\sum_jw_j^{r+1-2L}$ converge by [F1]. Then [F5] gives $T:=\sum_{i,j}|b_{ij}|^2w_iw_j^{r+1}\le C$, uniformly over every conductivity pair. Cauchy–Schwarz now yields $\sum_{i,j}w_i^{1/2}w_j^{1/2}|b_{ij}|^2\le (\sum|b_{ij}|^2w_j^{-r})^{1/2}(\sum|b_{ij}|^2w_iw_j^{r+1})^{1/2}\le C s$. The left side is the squared Hilbert–Schmidt norm from $H^{-1/2}_\Delta$ to $H^{1/2}_\Delta$: the normalized input basis is $w_j^{1/4}e_j$. Taking square roots and [F5]'s quotient norm equivalence gives $\|B\|_{\mathcal L(\dot{\mathcal D}^*,\dot{\mathcal D})}\le C s^{1/2}$, also when $s=0$.

For clarity, the inverse assertion in [F6] uses no boundary pointwise differentiability: the Dirichlet weak solution with boundary class $g$ has Neumann functional $\dot\Lambda_\gamma g$, and uniqueness of the weak Neumann problem gives $\mathscr R_\gamma\dot\Lambda_\gamma g=g$; conversely the weak Neumann solution satisfies its own Dirichlet problem, giving $\dot\Lambda_\gamma\mathscr R_\gamma F=F$. Therefore $\dot\Lambda_\gamma-\dot\Lambda_{\gamma_0}=\dot\Lambda_\gamma(\mathscr R_{\gamma_0}-\mathscr R_\gamma)\dot\Lambda_{\gamma_0}$. Uniform DN operator bounds in [F6] and step 3.1 prove the displayed square-root comparison. Together with step 2.1 this establishes all assertions.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $\Omega$ be a bounded connected smooth domain, let $\Omega'\Subset\Omega$, let $0<m\le1\le M<\infty$, and let $m\le\gamma\le M$ be measurable with $\gamma=1$ outside $\Omega'$. Put $M_\partial=\partial\Omega$ and give the NtD maps their total-boundary-mean-zero representatives. The spectral space $H^{1/2}_\Delta(M_\partial)$ is equivalent to the chart trace space $H^{1/2}(M_\partial)$, including their quotients by constants and mean-zero duals. Uniformly in $\gamma$,
$$\|\mathscr R_\gamma f\|_{H^1_\Delta(M_\partial)}\le C\|f\|_{L^2(M_\partial)}\quad\left(\int_{M_\partial}f=0\right).$$
For every integer $q\ge0$ there is $C_q$ such that
$$\|(\mathscr R_\gamma-\mathscr R_1)F\|_{H^q_\Delta(M_\partial)}\le C_q\|F\|_{H^{-1/2}_\Delta(M_\partial)}$$
for every mean-zero weak Neumann flux $F$. If $w_j=1+\lambda_j$ and $(e_j)$ is any orthonormal boundary Laplace–Beltrami basis on the total-mean-zero subspace, the matrix $b_{ij}=\langle(\mathscr R_\gamma-\mathscr R_{\gamma_0})e_j,e_i\rangle$ of any two such conductivities satisfies, for every $L>0$,
$$|b_{ij}|\le C_L(w_iw_j)^{-L}.$$
The constants depend only on the displayed fixed data and $q$ or $L$. More generally, any $v\in H^1$ harmonic with zero weak normal derivative on a fixed smooth boundary collar has $\|v|_{M_\partial}\|_{H^q_\Delta}\le C_q\|v\|_{H^1(\text{collar})}$ for every integer $q\ge0$, using a fixed smaller collar for the boundary estimate.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $d\ge2$, let $\Omega$ be a bounded connected smooth domain, let $U\Subset\Omega$ be open, and fix $0<m\le M<\infty$. There are $p\in(2,4)$ and $C<\infty$, depending only on $d,m,M,\Omega,U$, such that every real measurable $\gamma$ with $m\le\gamma\le M$ and every weak solution $u\in H^1(\Omega)$ of $\operatorname{div}(\gamma
abla u)=0$ satisfy
$$\|
abla u\|_{L^p(U)}\le C\|
abla u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}.$$
In particular, for a weak Neumann solution with quotient flux $F\in\dot{\mathcal D}^{*}$, the right side is at most $C\|F\|_{\dot{\mathcal D}^{*}}$, uniformly in $\gamma$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $d\ge2$, let $\Omega\subset(0,1)^d$ be nonempty, bounded, connected and $C^1$, and let $\gamma\in L^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ satisfy $0<m\le\gamma\le M<\infty$ almost everywhere. Let $\mathcal D(\Omega)=H^1(\Omega)/H_0^1(\Omega)$ be the trace quotient and write $\dot{\mathcal D}=\mathcal D(\Omega)/\mathbb R\mathbf1$. For each $F\in\dot{\mathcal D}^{*}$ there is a unique weak solution class $[u]\in H^1(\Omega)/\mathbb R\mathbf1$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega\gamma\nabla u\cdot\overline{\nabla v}\,dx=F([\operatorname{Tr}v])\qquad(v\in H^1(\Omega)).$$
The resulting solution operator $\mathscr R_\gamma:\dot{\mathcal D}^{*}\to\dot{\mathcal D}$ is bounded. Its unique representative whose boundary trace has surface mean zero solves the same weak equation. In particular, for $f\in L^2(\partial\Omega)$ with $\int_{\partial\Omega}f\,dS=0$, the functional $F_f([g])=\int_{\partial\Omega}f\overline g\,dS$ is admissible and defines the mean-zero Neumann-to-Dirichlet map on mean-zero $L^2$ fluxes.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space, let $a$ be a bounded coercive sesquilinear form on $H$ with constants $M,\alpha$ ([[def-bounded-coercive-and-symmetric-sesquilinear-forms]]), and let $F:H\to\mathbb K$ be a bounded conjugate-linear functional with norm $\|F\|=\sup_{\|v\|\le1}|F(v)|$. Then there is a unique $u\in H$ with $$a(u,v)=F(v)\qquad\text{for every }v\in H,$$ and it satisfies $\alpha\|u\|\le\|F\|$, that is $\|u\|\le\|F\|/\alpha$. The real bilinear case is the same statement with $a$ symmetric or not, $F$ a bounded linear functional, and the conjugation read as the identity.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice and let $d=2$ with the conductivity class $X_2(R)$ of the Calderón admissible class. For $\gamma\in X_2(R)$ let $\widetilde{\gamma-1}$ be the zero extension of $\gamma-1$ from $\Omega$ to $\mathbb R^2$ and set $\gamma_e:=1+\widetilde{\gamma-1}$. Define $B:=\max\{1,M,m^{-1}\}$. There is a constant $C_1$ depending only on $\Omega,m,M,R$ such that
$$\|\gamma_e(\cdot+h)-\gamma_e\|_{L^1(\mathbb R^2)}\le C_1|h|\qquad(h\in\mathbb R^2).$$
For every finite $p>2B$ there is $C_p<\infty$, depending only on $\Omega,m,M,R,p$, such that
$$\sup_{\gamma\in X_2(R)}\ \sup_{|h|\le t}\|\gamma_e(\cdot+h)-\gamma_e\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^2)}\le C_p t^{1/p}\qquad(t\ge0).$$
The extension is an almost-everywhere measurable class; no pointwise continuity is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Dependent Choice. Let
$1\le p<\infty$ and let $\mathcal F\subseteq L^p(\mathbb R^n)$. In each of the
three displayed nonnegative suprema, take the value $0$ if $\mathcal F=\varnothing$.
Assume $\mathcal F$ satisfies:
(i) $\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}\|f\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n)}<\infty$; (ii) for every
$\varepsilon>0$ there is $R>0$ with
$\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}\bigl(\int_{|x|>R}|f|^p\bigr)^{1/p}<\varepsilon$; and
(iii) for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $\delta>0$ with
$\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}\|\tau_hf-f\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n)}<\varepsilon$ whenever
$|h|<\delta$. Then $\mathcal F$ is totally bounded in $L^p(\mathbb R^n)$, the
closure of $\mathcal F$ is compact, and every sequence in $\mathcal F$ has a
subsequence converging in $L^p(\mathbb R^n)$.

Let $1\le p<\infty$, let $E\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be bounded and let
$\mathcal F\subseteq L^p(\mathbb R^n)$ be a family such that every
$f\in\mathcal F$ vanishes Lebesgue-almost everywhere outside $E$. In the
displayed nonnegative supremum, take the value $0$ if $\mathcal F=\varnothing$.
Then for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $R>0$ with
$$\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}\int_{|x|>R}|f(x)|^p\,dx<\varepsilon.$$
In particular the tightness hypothesis of the Fr\'echet--Kolmogorov criterion
is automatic for families supported in one bounded set.

**Assume the Axiom of Choice.** Let $X$ be a nonempty compact metric space and let $n\in\mathbb N$ with $n\geq1$. For $Z=\mathbb R$ and for $Z=\mathbb R^n$ with its Euclidean metric:

1. A family $\mathcal F\subseteq C(X,Z)$ is compact in the uniform topology if and only if it is uniformly closed, equicontinuous, and pointwise bounded.
2. Every pointwise bounded equicontinuous sequence in $C(X,Z)$ has a uniformly convergent subsequence with limit in $C(X,Z)$.

For real-valued families, equicontinuity is uniform over the compact domain, and equicontinuity together with pointwise boundedness gives one bound for all values. The same one-bound conclusion holds for Euclidean-valued families.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $d\ge2$, let $\Omega\subset(0,1)^d$ be a nonempty bounded connected $C^1$ domain, let $0<m\le M<\infty$, and let $\gamma\in L^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ satisfy $m\le\gamma\le M$ almost everywhere. Define $\mathcal D(\Omega):=H^1(\Omega;\mathbb C)/H_0^1(\Omega;\mathbb C)$ with its quotient norm. For every boundary trace class $f\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$ there is a unique $u_{\gamma,f}\in f$ such that
$$\int_\Omega\gamma\,
abla u_{\gamma,f}\cdot\overline{
abla z}\,dx=0\qquad	ext{for every }z\in H_0^1(\Omega;\mathbb C).$$
For every $g\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$, the value $\int_\Omega\gamma
abla u_{\gamma,f}\cdot\overline{
abla V_g}\,dx$ is independent of the representative $V_g\in g$ and defines a bounded linear map $\Lambda_\gamma:\mathcal D(\Omega)	o\mathcal D(\Omega)^*$. Constants are in its kernel and its range functionals annihilate constants.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $d\ge2$, let $\Omega\subset(0,1)^d$ be nonempty, bounded, connected and $C^\infty$, and let $\gamma\in X_d(R)$ be a real conductivity. Write $M=\partial\Omega$, let $dS$ be surface measure, and set
$$L^2_0(M)=\left\{f\in L^2(M):\int_M f\,dS=0\right\},\qquad P_0f=f-|M|^{-1}\int_Mf\,dS.$$
The mean-zero Neumann-to-Dirichlet operator $\mathscr R_\gamma:L^2_0(M)\to L^2_0(M)$ sends $f$ to the mean-zero boundary trace of the weak solution of $\nabla\cdot(\gamma\nabla u)=0$ with outward conormal flux $f$, as defined by the weak Neumann problem. Let $-\Delta_M$ be the nonnegative Laplace–Beltrami operator on the compact boundary manifold, with eigenpairs $(e_j,\lambda_j)$ on $L^2_0(M)$ from its spectral resolution. For $\tau=1/2$ when $d=2$ and any fixed $\tau>0$ when $d\ge3$, put
$$r_d:=\frac{d-1}{2}-1+\tau,\qquad C_M^{r_d/2}e_j=(1+\lambda_j)^{-r_d/2}e_j.$$
The smoothed observation is the bounded operator $A_\gamma:=\mathscr R_\gamma C_M^{r_d/2}:L^2_0(M)\to L^2_0(M)$. Its extension to all of $L^2(M)$ is $\widetilde A_\gamma f=\iota_0A_\gamma(P_0f)$, where $\iota_0:L^2_0(M)\hookrightarrow L^2(M)$ is inclusion. Thus its integral kernel, when it exists in $L^2(M\times M)$, is fixed to have zero mean in each variable. No assertion of a kernel's existence or Hilbert–Schmidt regularity is part of this definition.

For every open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and real-valued $u\in BV(\Omega)$, $$TV(u;\Omega)=\sup\left\{\int_\Omega u\,\operatorname{div}\varphi\,dx:\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^n),\ |\varphi(x)|\le1\right\}.$$ If $u_k,u\in BV(\Omega)$ are real-valued and $u_k\to u$ in $L^1(\Omega)$, then $TV(u;\Omega)\le\liminf_kTV(u_k;\Omega)$. In addition, assuming Countable Choice, for any real-valued $u\in L^1(\Omega)$ the displayed supremum is finite if and only if $u\in BV(\Omega)$, with equality to $TV(u;\Omega)$; under the same assumption, an $L^1$ limit of real-valued BV functions with bounded liminf total variation belongs to $BV(\Omega)$ and satisfies the same lower-semicontinuity inequality.

For every open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and real-valued $u\in BV(\Omega)$, $$TV(u;\Omega)=\sup\left\{\int_\Omega u\,\operatorname{div}\varphi\,dx:\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^n),\ |\varphi(x)|\le1\right\}.$$ If $u_k,u\in BV(\Omega)$ are real-valued and $u_k\to u$ in $L^1(\Omega)$, then $TV(u;\Omega)\le\liminf_kTV(u_k;\Omega)$. In addition, assuming Countable Choice, for any real-valued $u\in L^1(\Omega)$ the displayed supremum is finite if and only if $u\in BV(\Omega)$, with equality to $TV(u;\Omega)$; under the same assumption, an $L^1$ limit of real-valued BV functions with bounded liminf total variation belongs to $BV(\Omega)$ and satisfies the same lower-semicontinuity inequality.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Fix a smooth bounded connected domain $\Omega$, an open $\Omega'\Subset\Omega$, and $0<m\le1\le M<\infty$. Let $\gamma,\gamma_0$ range over all measurable conductivities between $m$ and $M$ equal to one outside $\Omega'$. Let $(e_j,\lambda_j)$ be the mean-zero boundary spectral basis and put $w_j=1+\lambda_j$. There is $p\in(2,4)$ such that for every $L>0$,
$$\|\nabla u_{\gamma,e_j}\|_{L^p(\Omega')}\le C_Lw_j^{-L}.$$
Put $q=p/(p-2)>2$. For any fixed smoothing exponent $r\ge0$, the difference $(\mathscr R_\gamma-\mathscr R_{\gamma_0})(1-\Delta_{\partial\Omega})^{-r/2}$, extended to kill constants, is Hilbert–Schmidt and satisfies
$$\| (\mathscr R_\gamma-\mathscr R_{\gamma_0})(1-\Delta_{\partial\Omega})^{-r/2}\|_{\mathrm{HS}}\le C_r\|\gamma-\gamma_0\|_{L^q(\Omega)}.$$
It also satisfies the same bound with the coefficient $L^\infty$ norm in place of $L^q$. Constants depend only on the displayed fixed geometry, ellipticity and exponents.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. For each fixed integer $d\ge2$, let $\Omega\subset(0,1)^d$ be a nonempty bounded connected smooth domain, let $\Omega'\Subset\Omega$, fix $m>0$, $M\ge\max\{1,m\}$, $R>0$ and $0<\alpha<1$, and let $\gamma,\gamma_0\in X_d(R)$. Set
$$\delta:=\|\dot{\Lambda}_\gamma-\dot{\Lambda}_{\gamma_0}\|_{\mathcal L(\mathcal D(\Omega)/\mathbb C\mathbf1,(\mathcal D(\Omega)/\mathbb C\mathbf1)^*)}.$$
There exist constants $C>0$, $\rho>0$ and $t_0\in(0,1)$, depending only on $d,\alpha,\Omega,\Omega',m,M,R$, such that
$$\|\gamma-\gamma_0\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\le C\,\omega(\delta),\qquad \omega(0):=0,\qquad \omega(t):=\left[\log\!\left(\frac1{\min\{t,t_0\}}\right)\right]^{-\rho}\quad(t>0).$$
Here $X_d(R)$ is the BV class when $d=2$ and the bounded $C^{1,\alpha}$ class when $d\ge3$, and $\dot\Lambda_\gamma$ is the induced weak conductivity Dirichlet-to-Neumann map on the trace quotient by constants.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H_1,H_2$ be real Hilbert spaces, let $I$ be any set, let $x\in H_1$, and let $(x_i)_{i\in I}\subset H_1$ and $(y_i)_{i\in I}\subset H_2$. Let $\omega:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ be continuous, nondecreasing and concave, with $\omega(0)=0$. If
$$\|y_i-y_j\|\le\omega(\|x_i-x_j\|)\qquad(i,j\in I),$$
then
$$\bigcap_{i\in I}\overline B\bigl(y_i,\omega(\|x_i-x\|)\bigr)\ne\varnothing.$$
The intersection over an empty index set means all of $H_2$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice, let $d\ge2$, let $\Omega\subset(0,1)^d$ be nonempty, bounded, connected and $C^\infty$, and let $\gamma\in X_d(R)$. Write $M=\partial\Omega$, $n=d-1$, and let $A_\gamma$ and $\widetilde A_\gamma$ be the mean-zero smoothed NtD observation and its extension from the preceding definition. Then $\widetilde A_\gamma$ is Hilbert–Schmidt on $L^2(M)$ and has a unique zero-mean-in-each-variable kernel $\kappa_\gamma\in L^2(M\times M)$, with
$$\|\kappa_\gamma\|_{L^2(M\times M)}=\|\widetilde A_\gamma\|_{\mathrm{HS}}.$$
The Hilbert–Schmidt norms are uniformly bounded over $X_d(R)$. Moreover, there is $C<\infty$, depending only on the fixed class and domain, such that
$$\|\dot\Lambda_\gamma-\dot\Lambda_{\gamma_0}\|_{\mathcal L(\dot{\mathcal D},\dot{\mathcal D}^{*})}\le C\|\kappa_\gamma-\kappa_{\gamma_0}\|_{L^2(M\times M)}^{1/2}\qquad(\gamma,\gamma_0\in X_d(R)).$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $(P, \le)$ be a
nonempty poset in which **every chain has an upper bound**. Then $P$ has a
maximal element ([[def-maximal-element]]).

Note the hypothesis asks only for an upper bound, not a least upper bound, and
the conclusion asserts only that a maximal element exists, never that a greatest
one does.

Order it by graph inclusion. It is nonempty, since $(A,g)$ is in it. Every nonempty chain has as upper bound the union of its graphs: every two of its domain points occur together in one member of the chain, so the same modulus inequality holds for their union. The empty chain has $(A,g)$ as an upper bound. By [F4] and [A1] there is a maximal pair $(B,h)$.

For the EIT application first arrange $t_0\le e^{-(\rho+1)}$. If the original IP-45 constants have a larger cutoff, decrease it and enlarge $C_0$ if needed: the uniform class diameter is at most $2M|\Omega|^{1/2}$, so taking $C_0\ge2M|\Omega|^{1/2}[\log(1/t_0)]^\rho$ covers all DN distances above the new cutoff, while increasing $C_0$ preserves the old small-distance estimate. For $0<s<(t_0/C_1)^2$, put $L(s)=\log(1/(C_1\sqrt{s}))$ and $\varphi(s)=C_0L(s)^{-\rho}$. Then $\varphi'(s)=C_0\rho/(2sL(s)^{\rho+1})>0$ and $\varphi''(s)=C_0\rho[\rho+1-2L(s)]/(4s^2L(s)^{\rho+2})\le0$. At the cutoff it joins continuously to a constant and its derivative drops to zero; at zero it tends to zero. Thus the displayed $\omega_\star$ is continuous, nondecreasing and concave on the entire nonnegative half-line.

If $B\ne H_1$, fix $x\in H_1\setminus B$. Apply [F2] to the source family $(u)_{u\in B}$ and target family $(h(u))_{u\in B}$. It gives a point $y\in H_2$ satisfying $\|y-h(u)\|\le\omega_\star(\|x-u\|)$ for every $u\in B$. Adding $h(x)=y$ gives a strictly larger admissible graph, contradicting maximality. This also covers $B=\varnothing$, since [F2]'s empty intersection is $H_2$, which contains zero. Thus $B=H_1$ and $\widetilde g=h$ proves the full same-modulus extension theorem for arbitrary real Hilbert spaces and arbitrary subsets.

For an exact conductivity pair put $s=\|\kappa_\gamma-\kappa_{\gamma_0}\|_2$. $$L^2_0(M)=\left\{f\in L^2(M):\int_M f\,dS=0\right\},\qquad P_0f=f-|M|^{-1}\int_Mf\,dS.$$
The mean-zero Neumann-to-Dirichlet operator $\mathscr R_\gamma:L^2_0(M)\to L^2_0(M)$ sends $f$ to the mean-zero boundary trace of the weak solution of $\nabla\cdot(\gamma\nabla u)=0$ with outward conormal flux $f$, as defined by the weak Neumann problem. Let $-\Delta_M$ be the nonnegative Laplace–Beltrami operator on the compact boundary manifold, with eigenpairs $(e_j,\lambda_j)$ on $L^2_0(M)$ from its spectral resolution. For $\tau=1/2$ when $d=2$ and any fixed $\tau>0$ when $d\ge3$, put
$$r_d:=\frac{d-1}{2}-1+\tau,\qquad C_M^{r_d/2}e_j=(1+\lambda_j)^{-r_d/2}e_j.$$
The smoothed observation is the bounded operator $A_\gamma:=\mathscr R_\gamma C_M^{r_d/2}:L^2_0(M)\to L^2_0(M)$. Its extension to all of $L^2(M)$ is $\widetilde A_\gamma f=\iota_0A_\gamma(P_0f)$, where $\iota_0:L^2_0(M)\hookrightarrow L^2(M)$ is inclusion. Thus its integral kernel, when it exists in $L^2(M\times M)$, is fixed to have zero mean in each variable. No assertion of a kernel's existence or Hilbert–Schmidt regularity is part of this definition.

Fix an integer $d\ge2$. Let $\Omega\subset(0,1)^d$ be a nonempty bounded connected open domain with $C^\infty$ boundary, and let $\Omega'\subset\Omega$ be an open domain whose closure is compact and contained in $\Omega$. Fix real parameters $m>0$, $M\ge\max\{1,m\}$, $R>0$, and $0<\alpha<1$. Define
$$\Gamma_{m,M}(\Omega):=\{\gamma\in L^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R):m\le\gamma(x)\le M\text{ for almost every }x\in\Omega\}$$
and
$$\Gamma'_{m,M}(\Omega,\Omega'):=\{\gamma\in\Gamma_{m,M}(\Omega):\gamma=1\text{ almost everywhere on }\Omega\setminus\Omega'\}.$$
For $\gamma\in BV(\Omega)$ set $\|\gamma\|_{BV(\Omega)}:=\max\{\|\gamma\|_{L^1(\Omega)},TV(\gamma;\Omega)\}$. For a continuously differentiable function on $\overline\Omega$ whose first derivatives are $\alpha$-Hölder continuous, set
$$\|\gamma\|_{C^{1,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)}:=\max\left\{\max_{|\beta|\le1}\sup_{x\in\overline\Omega}|\partial^\beta\gamma(x)|,\ \max_{|\beta|=1}\sup_{\substack{x,y\in\overline\Omega\\x\ne y}}\frac{|\partial^\beta\gamma(x)-\partial^\beta\gamma(y)|}{|x-y|^\alpha}\right\}.$$
Define
$$X_d(R):=\begin{cases}\{\gamma\in\Gamma'_{m,M}(\Omega,\Omega')\cap BV(\Omega):\|\gamma\|_{BV(\Omega)}\le R\},&d=2,\\[2mm]\{\gamma\in\Gamma'_{m,M}(\Omega,\Omega')\cap C^{1,\alpha}(\overline\Omega):\|\gamma\|_{C^{1,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)}\le R\},&d\ge3.\end{cases}$$
For $\gamma\in\Gamma'_{m,M}(\Omega,\Omega')$, define its measurable background extension $\gamma_e:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ by $\gamma_e=\gamma$ almost everywhere on $\Omega$ and $\gamma_e=1$ on $\mathbb R^d\setminus\Omega$. Then $\gamma_e-1$ vanishes almost everywhere outside $\Omega'$. No pointwise continuity of $\gamma_e$ is asserted. The classes $X_d(R)$ are not assumed nonempty.

For every open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and real-valued $u\in BV(\Omega)$, $$TV(u;\Omega)=\sup\left\{\int_\Omega u\,\operatorname{div}\varphi\,dx:\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^n),\ |\varphi(x)|\le1\right\}.$$ If $u_k,u\in BV(\Omega)$ are real-valued and $u_k\to u$ in $L^1(\Omega)$, then $TV(u;\Omega)\le\liminf_kTV(u_k;\Omega)$. In addition, assuming Countable Choice, for any real-valued $u\in L^1(\Omega)$ the displayed supremum is finite if and only if $u\in BV(\Omega)$, with equality to $TV(u;\Omega)$; under the same assumption, an $L^1$ limit of real-valued BV functions with bounded liminf total variation belongs to $BV(\Omega)$ and satisfies the same lower-semicontinuity inequality.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $u\in L^1(\Omega;\mathbb R)$, where elements of $L^1$ are almost-everywhere equivalence classes. For each $i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}$, its distributional derivative $D_i u$ acts on $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ by
$$\langle D_i u,\varphi\rangle:=-\int_\Omega u\,\partial_i\varphi\,dx.$$
The function $u$ is in $BV(\Omega)$ when each $D_i u$ is represented by a finite signed Radon measure and the resulting vector-valued measure $Du=(D_1u,\ldots,D_nu)$ has finite total variation. Here a finite vector-valued Radon measure means that its partition variation is a finite Radon measure. For a Borel set $A\subseteq\Omega$, define
$$|Du|(A):=\sup\left\{\sum_{j=1}^\infty |Du(A_j)|:\ (A_j)_{j\ge1}\text{ is a Borel partition of }A\right\},$$
using the Euclidean norm on each vector value. Define the spatial total variation by $TV(u;\Omega):=|Du|(\Omega)$. A Lebesgue-measurable set $E\subseteq\Omega$ of finite measure has finite perimeter relative to $\Omega$ when $\chi_E\in BV(\Omega)$; its relative perimeter is $P(E;\Omega):=TV(\chi_E;\Omega)$.

derivations.claim: The square $[7/16,9/16]^2$ has side $1/8$ and lies in $\Omega'$ because its corner radius from $(1/2,1/2)$ is $\sqrt2/16<1/8$. The grid spacing is $s_N=1/(8q)$ and $r_N=s_N/4$. Distinct cell centers are separated by at least $s_N>2r_N$, and each disk lies inside its cell; hence the disks are disjoint and contained in $\Omega'$. Thus $1\le\gamma_N\le1+a=5/4<3/2$ and $\gamma_N=1$ on $\Omega\setminus\Omega'$.

For a disk $B(c,r)$ and a smooth compactly supported vector field $\varphi$, polar coordinates give $\int_{B(c,r)}\operatorname{div}\varphi\,dx=r\int_0^{2\pi}\varphi(c+r(\cos\theta,\sin\theta))\cdot(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)\,d\theta$. Indeed, in polar variables $\operatorname{div}\varphi=\rho^{-1}\partial_\rho(\rho\varphi_r)+\rho^{-1}\partial_\theta\varphi_\theta$; integrating against $\rho\,d\rho\,d\theta$ makes the angular derivative integrate to zero and the inner radial term vanish. The distributional definition therefore gives $D\mathbf1_{B(c,r)}=-\nu\,\mathcal H^1|_{\partial B(c,r)}$, whose variation has mass $2\pi r$. Summing these measures over the disjoint disks shows $D\mathbf1_{E_N}$ is finite with variation mass $2\pi r_NN$, so [F3] gives $\mathbf1_{E_N}\in BV(\Omega)$ and [F2] gives the stated upper bound.

The annuli of radii $(r_N/2,3r_N/2)$ about the chosen centers are pairwise disjoint: their outer radii sum to $3r_N=3s_N/4<s_N$, while distinct centers are at least $s_N$ apart. They lie in $\Omega$, since each center is within $\sqrt2/16$ of $(1/2,1/2)$ and $\sqrt2/16+3r_N/2\le\sqrt2/16+3/64<1/4$. On each annulus choose a smooth radial cutoff equal to one at radius $r_N$, vanishing outside the annulus and between zero and one. The sum of the corresponding radial unit-vector fields is smooth, compactly supported in $\Omega$, has norm at most one, and equals the outward normal on every circle. Its flux is $2\pi r_NN$, so [F2] gives the matching lower bound. Since $D\gamma_N=aD\mathbf1_{E_N}$ by [F3] and $a>0$, step 1.2 gives $TV(\mathbf1_{E_N};\Omega)=2\pi r_NN$ and $TV(\gamma_N;\Omega)=2\pi a r_NN=\pi aN/(16q)$.

Since $q=\lceil\sqrt N\rceil\le2\sqrt N$, step 2.1 gives $TV(\gamma_N;\Omega)\ge(\pi a/32)\sqrt N$. The value and collar bounds were checked in step 1.1, and every finite union of disks has the finite perimeter computed in step 2.1. Thus each conductivity is individually finite-BV while the total variations diverge, so no fixed $R$ contains the whole family in $X_2(R)$.

citations.quote:
Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval and let $f:X\times I\to\mathbb C$
be such that:

1. for every $t\in I$, the function $x\mapsto f(x,t)$ is integrable;
2. for almost every $x$, the map $t\mapsto f(x,t)$ is differentiable on $I$;
3. for every $t\in I$, the function
   $$x\mapsto \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(x,t),$$
   extended by zero where the derivative is undefined, is measurable;
4. there are a measurable null set $N$ and a nonnegative measurable function
   $g$ with
   $$\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$$
   and
   $$\left|\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(x,t)\right|\le g(x)$$
   for every $t\in I$ and every $x\in X\setminus N$.

Then
$$F(t):=\int f(x,t)\,d\mu(x)$$
is differentiable on $I$, and
$$F'(t)=\int \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(x,t)\,d\mu(x),$$
with the same zero extension in the last integral.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $k\in\mathbb N$. Finite componentwise sums and products of $C^k$ Euclidean maps are $C^k$, and a composite of composable $C^k$ Euclidean maps is $C^k$. Scalar multiples are included among the finite componentwise operations. The assertions remain valid on an empty open domain.

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $m,q\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$. A map $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is of class $C^k$ when each component is of class $C^k$. Each scalar component uses the word-derivative convention of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], whose source dimension is positive. The map is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, when it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $U,V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. A bijection $f:U\to V$ is a **$C^k$ diffeomorphism** when both $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are $C^k$. For $k\ge1$, a **local $C^k$ diffeomorphism at $a\in U$** is a restriction $f|_P:P\to Q$ between open neighbourhoods of $a$ and $f(a)$ that is a $C^k$ diffeomorphism. At $k=1$ this agrees with [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]: continuous first partial derivatives give the required total derivative by [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]], while continuity of the total derivative gives continuity of its matrix entries and hence of the first partial derivatives.

In ZF, let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be smooth, and let $a\in U$. If $Df(a)$ is invertible, then there are open neighbourhoods $a\in V\subseteq U$ and $f(a)\in W$ such that $f|_V:V\to W$ is a diffeomorphism. Writing $g=(f|_V)^{-1}$,
$$Dg(y)=Df(g(y))^{-1}\qquad(y\in W).$$
No choice axiom is used.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Let $m\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$. A **multi-index** is $\alpha=(\alpha_0,\ldots,\alpha_{m-1})\in\mathbb N^m$. Put

$$|\alpha|:=\sum_{i<m}\alpha_i,\qquad \alpha!:=\prod_{i<m}\alpha_i!,\qquad h^\alpha:=\prod_{i<m}h_i^{\alpha_i}\quad(h\in\mathbb R^m).$$

Here $|\alpha|$ and $\alpha!$ use the natural-number sum and product of [[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]], and $n!$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]]. By contrast, $h^\alpha$ is the finite product in $\mathbb R$ of [[def-finite-sum]], with the natural exponents interpreted by [[def-integer-power]]. For the zero multi-index $0$, set $D^0f:=f$. For nonzero $\alpha$, write

$$D^\alpha f:=\partial_0^{\alpha_0}\cdots\partial_{m-1}^{\alpha_{m-1}}f$$

for this displayed, canonical order whenever it exists. Coordinate partial derivatives have the meaning fixed in [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

For $k\in\mathbb N$, $f$ is of class $C^k$ on $U$ when, for every word $(i_1,\ldots,i_r)$ of coordinate indices with $0\le r\le k$, the iterated derivative $\partial_{i_r}\cdots\partial_{i_1}f$ exists and is continuous on $U$; the word of length $0$ denotes $f$. Thus this definition does **not** presuppose that differently ordered derivatives are equal. Equality of their values is a later theorem under these regularity hypotheses.

derivations.claim: Since $0<\rho_\sigma(z-u)\le1$, $p_\sigma(z)\le1$. For fixed $z$, the measurable sets $E_k=\{u:\rho_\sigma(z-u)\ge1/k\}$, $k\ge1$, cover $\mathbb R^n$. By [F2] and countable subadditivity, some $E_k$ has positive $\mu$-measure; hence $p_\sigma(z)\ge\mu(E_k)/k>0$. For $j=1,2$, the function $u\mapsto\|u\|_2^j\rho_\sigma(z-u)$ is bounded because a polynomial factor is dominated at infinity by the Gaussian exponential, so its $\mu$-integral is finite. Thus $\nu_{\sigma,z}$ is a probability measure with finite second moment and $D_\sigma(z)$ is well-defined.

Let $\alpha\in\mathbb N^n$ be a multi-index as in [F13]. At order zero, $\partial^\alpha\rho_\sigma=\rho_\sigma$. If $\partial^\alpha\rho_\sigma(w)=P(w)\rho_\sigma(w)$ for a polynomial $P$, then $\partial_j(P(w)\rho_\sigma(w))=(\partial_jP(w)-w_jP(w)/\sigma^2)\rho_\sigma(w)$, again a polynomial times $\rho_\sigma$. Induction on $|\alpha|$ proves the stated form for every finite derivative. On each compact set of $z$ values, both $|\partial^\alpha\rho_\sigma(z-u)|$ and $|u_i\partial^\alpha\rho_\sigma(z-u)|$ are bounded uniformly in $u$, since every polynomial times the Gaussian tends to zero at infinity. Apply [F3] coordinate by coordinate to $p_\sigma$ and to each numerator $N_i(z)=\int u_i\rho_\sigma(z-u)\,\mu(du)$; the uniform bounds supply an integrable majorant and [F4] justifies passage of each derivative limit through the integral. The same bounds for derivatives of order $|\alpha|+1$ give a uniform bound $M$ for the first derivatives of each resulting derivative on any compact ball $K$. For $z,w\in K$, apply [F12] to that derivative along $z+t(w-z)$, $0\le t\le1$, to obtain a difference bound $\sqrt n M\|z-w\|_2$; thus each resulting derivative is continuous. Iterating over $\alpha$ makes $p_\sigma$ and every $N_i$ smooth. Since $p_\sigma>0$, the reciprocal $r(s)=1/s$ is smooth on $(0,\infty)$: its first derivative is $-r(s)^2$ by the difference quotient, and repeated use of [F8] shows every higher derivative is a polynomial in $r$. Thus [F9] makes $D_\sigma=(N_i/p_\sigma)_{i<n}$ smooth; [F6], [F8], and positivity of $p_\sigma$ also make $q_\sigma=-\log p_\sigma$ smooth.

For $a\in\mathbb R^n$, expand $u-a=(u-D_\sigma(z))+(D_\sigma(z)-a)$ and integrate. The cross term vanishes because $\int(u-D_\sigma(z))\,
u_{\sigma,z}(du)=0$, giving $$\int\|u-a\|_2^2\,
u_{\sigma,z}(du)=\int\|u-D_\sigma(z)\|_2^2\,
u_{\sigma,z}(du)+\|a-D_\sigma(z)\|_2^2.$$ Thus $D_\sigma(z)$ is the unique posterior squared-error minimizer. Differentiating $N_i/p_\sigma$ using [F3], [F5], [F7], [F8], and [F9] gives $$\partial_jD_{\sigma,i}(z)= rac1{\sigma^2}\left(\int u_i u_j\,
u_{\sigma,z}(du)-D_{\sigma,i}(z)D_{\sigma,j}(z)ight),$$ because the terms containing $z_j$ cancel. This is exactly the stated symmetric covariance formula.

For each coordinate $j$, $\partial_jho_\sigma(z-u)=(u_j-z_j)ho_\sigma(z-u)/\sigma^2$. Differentiating under the integral by [F3] and using step 1.1 gives $
abla p_\sigma(z)=p_\sigma(z)(D_\sigma(z)-z)/\sigma^2$. Since $p_\sigma(z)>0$, [F6] gives $
abla\log p_\sigma=
abla p_\sigma/p_\sigma$, proving both Tweedie identities in the Statement.

For nonzero $v\in\mathbb R^n$, $$v^{\mathsf T}J D_\sigma(z)v=\sigma^{-2}\int\langle v,u-D_\sigma(z)angle^2\,
u_{\sigma,z}(du).$$ If this were zero, then for each $k\ge1$ the set where $|\langle v,u-D_\sigma(z)angle|\ge1/k$ would have $
u_{\sigma,z}$-measure zero; their union is the complement of the affine hyperplane $\{u:\langle v,uangle=\langle v,D_\sigma(z)angle\}$. Hence that hyperplane has full $
u_{\sigma,z}$-measure. The density $ho_\sigma(z-u)/p_\sigma(z)$ is strictly positive, so $
u_{\sigma,z}$ and $\mu$ have the same null sets: if $
u_{\sigma,z}(E)=0$, then each set $E\cap\{ho_\sigma(z-u)/p_\sigma(z)\ge1/k\}$ has zero $\mu$-measure, and these sets cover $E$. Thus the hyperplane has full $\mu$-measure, contradicting the hypothesis. Therefore $J D_\sigma(z)$ is positive definite.

Fix $z$ and write $$\Psi_z(u)= rac12\|D_\sigma(u)-z\|_2^2- rac12\|D_\sigma(u)-u\|_2^2+\sigma^2q_\sigma(u).$$ By the definition of $h_{\sigma,\gamma}$, this equals $ rac12\|D_\sigma(u)-z\|_2^2+\gamma h_{\sigma,\gamma}(D_\sigma(u))$. Differentiate using [F7] and the symmetry of $J D_\sigma$ from step 3.1: $$
abla\Psi_z(u)=J D_\sigma(u)(D_\sigma(u)-z)-(J D_\sigma(u)-I)(D_\sigma(u)-u)+\sigma^2
abla q_\sigma(u)=J D_\sigma(u)(u-z),$$ where the last equality uses $D_\sigma(u)-u=-\sigma^2

Let $n\ge1$, let $\mu$ be a Borel probability measure on $\mathbb R^n$ that is not concentrated on any affine hyperplane, and let $\sigma,\gamma>0$. Put
$$\rho_\sigma(w)=\exp\!\left(-\frac{\|w\|_2^2}{2\sigma^2}\right),\qquad p_\sigma(z)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}\rho_\sigma(z-u)\,\mu(du),$$
and define the normalized posterior measure and its mean by
$$\nu_{\sigma,z}(E)=\frac{\int_E\rho_\sigma(z-u)\,\mu(du)}{p_\sigma(z)}\quad(E\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R^n)),\qquad D_\sigma(z)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}u\,\nu_{\sigma,z}(du).$$
The omitted normalizing constant of the $N(0,\sigma^2I)$ likelihood is independent of $u$ and cancels in $\nu_{\sigma,z}$. Writing $U(u)=u$ for the identity random vector under $\nu_{\sigma,z}$, its covariance matrix is
$$\operatorname{Cov}_{\nu_{\sigma,z}}(U)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}(u-D_\sigma(z))(u-D_\sigma(z))^{\mathsf T}\,\nu_{\sigma,z}(du).$$
Then $p_\sigma$ is positive and smooth, each $\nu_{\sigma,z}$ has finite second moment, and $D_\sigma(z)$ uniquely minimizes the posterior squared-error risk $a\mapsto\int\|u-a\|_2^2\,\nu_{\sigma,z}(du)$. Moreover, $D_\sigma$ is smooth and
$$J D_\sigma(z)=\sigma^{-2}\operatorname{Cov}_{\nu_{\sigma,z}}(U)$$
is symmetric positive definite. Hence $D_\sigma$ is injective with open image $X_\sigma=D_\sigma(\mathbb R^n)$ and smooth inverse on $X_\sigma$. Put $q_\sigma=-\log p_\sigma$ and, for $x\in X_\sigma$, define
$$h_{\sigma,\gamma}(x)=-\frac{\|x-D_\sigma^{-1}(x)\|_2^2}{2\gamma}+\frac{\sigma^2}{\gamma}q_\sigma(D_\sigma^{-1}(x));$$
set $h_{\sigma,\gamma}(x)=+\infty$ outside $X_\sigma$. The restriction of $h_{\sigma,\gamma}$ to $X_\sigma$ is smooth. For any extended-real $h:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$, define
$$\operatorname{prox}^{\mathrm{glob}}_{\gamma h}(z)=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{x\in\mathbb R^n}\left\{\frac12\|x-z\|_2^2+\gamma h(x)\right\},$$
where the argmin is the set of global minimizers and $h$ need not be convex. Then
$$D_\sigma(z)=z+\sigma^2\nabla\log p_\sigma(z)=z-\sigma^2\nabla q_\sigma(z),\qquad \operatorname{prox}^{\mathrm{glob}}_{\gamma h_{\sigma,\gamma}}(z)=\{D_\sigma(z)\}\quad(z\in\mathbb R^n).$$

Let $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be continuously differentiable and suppose $\nabla f$ is Lipschitz with constant $L\ge0$ in the Euclidean norm. Then
$$f(y)\le f(x)+\langle\nabla f(x),y-x\rangle+\frac{L}{2}\|y-x\|_2^2\qquad(x,y\in\mathbb R^n).$$

Let $(X,d_X)$ and $(Y,d_Y)$ be metric spaces ([[def-metric-space]]) and let
$f : X \to Y$ be a function. Recall that a metric takes nonnegative real values
([[lem-metric-nonnegativity]]).

- $f$ is **Lipschitz** with **constant** $L$, where $L \in \mathbb{R}$ and
  $L \ge 0$, if
  $$d_Y\big(f(x), f(x')\big) \;\le\; L \, d_X(x,x') \qquad \text{for all } x, x' \in X .$$
  $f$ is *Lipschitz* if it is Lipschitz with some such constant.
- Let $\alpha \in \mathbb{Q}$ with $0 < \alpha \le 1$ ([[def-rat-order]]). $f$ is
  **$\alpha$-Hölder** with **constant** $C$, where $C \in \mathbb{R}$ and
  $C \ge 0$, if
  $$d_Y\big(f(x), f(x')\big) \;\le\; C \, d_X(x,x')^{\alpha} \qquad \text{for all } x, x' \in X ,$$
  the power being the rational power of a nonnegative base
  ([[def-rational-power]]). $f$ is *$\alpha$-Hölder* if it is so with some such
  constant, and *Hölder* if it is $\alpha$-Hölder for some rational
  $\alpha \in (0,1]$.
- $f$ is a **contraction** with constant $q$ if it is Lipschitz with constant $q$
  and $0 \le q < 1$. The number $q$ is then called a **contraction constant** for
  $f$.

**The power $d_X(x,x')^{\alpha}$ is defined at every pair, including $x = x'$.**
The base $d_X(x,x')$ is a nonnegative real, and [[def-rational-power]] defines
$a^{\alpha}$ for every $a > 0$ and, by its supplementary clause, sets
$0^{\alpha} = 0$ for every rational $\alpha > 0$. Since $\alpha > 0$ is required
here, the displayed inequality at $x = x'$ reads $0 \le C \cdot 0$, which holds;
so no separate clause and no restriction to $x \ne x'$ is needed. Note that this
does not by itself explain the strict inequality $\alpha>0$: if one extended the
formula to $\alpha=0$ using the convention $0^0=1$ of [[def-integer-power]], the
equal-point inequality would still be the automatic $0\le C$. Globally, however,
that extension would reduce to the bounded-diameter condition
$d_Y(f(x),f(x'))\le C$, outside the standard Hölder range adopted here.

**Why the exponent is rational on this page and why it is at most $1$.** At this
point in the reading order only rational powers are available
([[def-rational-power]]), so $\alpha$ ranges over the rationals. The upper
bound $\alpha \le 1$ is the standard convention, and it is where the notion is
useful: the classical theory reserves the name for $\alpha \in (0,1]$, and
nothing in this library uses an exponent outside that range. No claim is made
here about what an exponent $\alpha > 1$ would do.

**Constants are not unique and are not part of the data.** If $f$ is Lipschitz
with constant $L$ it is Lipschitz with every constant $L' \ge L$, and likewise
for Hölder constants; the adjectives above are existential statements. A
*contraction*, by contrast, requires a constant strictly below $1$, and that is a
real restriction: exhibiting the constant is part of exhibiting a contraction, and
a map that shrinks every distance without admitting one uniform constant is not a
contraction here.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

For $t\ge2$, $x_t$ is a global minimizer of $\mu_s$ and belongs to the open set $X_\sigma$, where $\mu_s$ is differentiable. For every direction $v$, the global minimum gives nonnegative directional difference quotients along $v$ and $-v$ for small positive increments; taking limits gives $\langle

set $h_{\sigma,\gamma}(x)=+\infty$ outside $X_\sigma$. The restriction of $h_{\sigma,\gamma}$ to $X_\sigma$ is smooth. For any extended-real $h:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$, define
$$\operatorname{prox}^{\mathrm{glob}}_{\gamma h}(z)=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{x\in\mathbb R^n}\left\{\frac12\|x-z\|_2^2+\gamma h(x)\right\},$$
where the argmin is the set of global minimizers and $h$ need not be convex. Then
$$D_\sigma(z)=z+\sigma^2\nabla\log p_\sigma(z)=z-\sigma^2\nabla q_\sigma(z),\qquad \operatorname{prox}^{\mathrm{glob}}_{\gamma h_{\sigma,\gamma}}(z)=\{D_\sigma(z)\}\quad(z\in\mathbb R^n).$$

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

$$\delta_{x_0}(E):=\begin{cases}1,&x_0\in E,\\0,&x_0\notin E,\end{cases}\qquad E\in\mathcal A.$$

For $x_0\in X$, the Dirac set function $\delta_{x_0}$ is a probability measure on every sigma-algebra on $X$.
