Let $n\ge1$, let $\mu$ be a Borel probability measure on $\mathbb R^n$ that is not concentrated on any affine hyperplane, and let $\sigma,\gamma>0$. Put
$$\rho_\sigma(w)=\exp\!\left(-\frac{\|w\|_2^2}{2\sigma^2}\right),\qquad p_\sigma(z)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}\rho_\sigma(z-u)\,\mu(du),$$
and define the normalized posterior measure and its mean by
$$\nu_{\sigma,z}(E)=\frac{\int_E\rho_\sigma(z-u)\,\mu(du)}{p_\sigma(z)}\quad(E\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R^n)),\qquad D_\sigma(z)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}u\,\nu_{\sigma,z}(du).$$
The omitted normalizing constant of the $N(0,\sigma^2I)$ likelihood is independent of $u$ and cancels in $\nu_{\sigma,z}$. Writing $U(u)=u$ for the identity random vector under $\nu_{\sigma,z}$, its covariance matrix is
$$\operatorname{Cov}_{\nu_{\sigma,z}}(U)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}(u-D_\sigma(z))(u-D_\sigma(z))^{\mathsf T}\,\nu_{\sigma,z}(du).$$
Then $p_\sigma$ is positive and smooth, each $\nu_{\sigma,z}$ has finite second moment, and $D_\sigma(z)$ uniquely minimizes the posterior squared-error risk $a\mapsto\int\|u-a\|_2^2\,\nu_{\sigma,z}(du)$. Moreover, $D_\sigma$ is smooth and
$$J D_\sigma(z)=\sigma^{-2}\operatorname{Cov}_{\nu_{\sigma,z}}(U)$$
is symmetric positive definite. Hence $D_\sigma$ is injective with open image $X_\sigma=D_\sigma(\mathbb R^n)$ and smooth inverse on $X_\sigma$. Put $q_\sigma=-\log p_\sigma$ and, for $x\in X_\sigma$, define
$$h_{\sigma,\gamma}(x)=-\frac{\|x-D_\sigma^{-1}(x)\|_2^2}{2\gamma}+\frac{\sigma^2}{\gamma}q_\sigma(D_\sigma^{-1}(x));$$
set $h_{\sigma,\gamma}(x)=+\infty$ outside $X_\sigma$. The restriction of $h_{\sigma,\gamma}$ to $X_\sigma$ is smooth. For any extended-real $h:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$, define
$$\operatorname{prox}^{\mathrm{glob}}_{\gamma h}(z)=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{x\in\mathbb R^n}\left\{\frac12\|x-z\|_2^2+\gamma h(x)\right\},$$
where the argmin is the set of global minimizers and $h$ need not be convex. Then
$$D_\sigma(z)=z+\sigma^2\nabla\log p_\sigma(z)=z-\sigma^2\nabla q_\sigma(z),\qquad \operatorname{prox}^{\mathrm{glob}}_{\gamma h_{\sigma,\gamma}}(z)=\{D_\sigma(z)\}\quad(z\in\mathbb R^n).$$

derivations.claim: By [F1]–[F2], $\mu=\frac12\delta_{-a}+\frac12\delta_a$ is a probability measure: for pairwise-disjoint Borel sets each of the two atoms occurs in at most one set, and $\mu(\mathbb R)=1$. Since $a>0$, its two atoms are distinct and each has positive mass; every affine hyperplane in $\mathbb R$ is a singleton, so $\mu$ is not concentrated on any affine hyperplane. The posterior weights at $a$ and $-a$ are proportional to $\rho_\sigma(z-a)$ and $\rho_\sigma(z+a)$, hence $D_\sigma(z)=a\frac{\rho_\sigma(z-a)-\rho_\sigma(z+a)}{\rho_\sigma(z-a)+\rho_\sigma(z+a)}$.

Factoring $\exp(-(z^2+a^2)/(2\sigma^2))$ from numerator and denominator and using [F3] yields $D_\sigma(z)=a(\exp(az/\sigma^2)-\exp(-az/\sigma^2))/(\exp(az/\sigma^2)+\exp(-az/\sigma^2))$, which is the stated hyperbolic-tangent formula.

Fact [F4] applies to this nondegenerate two-point prior, so the posterior mean is the unique squared-error minimizer and the lemma's $h_{\sigma,\gamma}$ makes $D_\sigma(z)$ the unique global minimizer of the displayed proximal objective for every $z$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

Assume AC. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma>0$, the normal law $N(m,\sigma^2)$
of [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]] has Lebesgue density
$$g_{m,\sigma}(y)=\frac1\sigma\frac{e^{-((y-m)/\sigma)^2/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}=\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}}e^{-(y-m)^2/(2\sigma^2)}.$$

derivations.claim: Since $\nabla g(x)=x-\varepsilon$, [F3] gives $z_1=\varepsilon/2$, $x_1=\varepsilon^2/4$, and $z_2=x_1-\frac12(x_1-\varepsilon)=\varepsilon^2/8+\varepsilon/2=(\varepsilon+2)^2/8-1/2$. Thus $z_2\ge-1/2$ almost surely.

The event $-1/2<\varepsilon<1/2$ has positive probability by [A1, F1] and gives $-7/32<z_2<9/32$. The event $-5/2<\varepsilon<-3/2$ also has positive probability and gives $-1/2\le z_2<-15/32$. These disjoint output intervals show that $z_2$ is not almost surely constant.

A nondegenerate Gaussian law has positive probability below $-1/2$ by [A1, F2], whereas $z_2$ has none by step 1.1; a degenerate Gaussian is a point mass, whereas step 2.1 shows $z_2$ is not. Therefore $z_2$ is not Gaussian and the universal iterative-AWGN claim is false.

Input a real matrix $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$, data $b\in\mathbb R^m$,
and a strictly increasing finite grid $0<\lambda_1<\cdots<\lambda_q$ with
$q\ge3$. For each grid point, compute the unique Tikhonov minimizer
$$x_j=(A^TA+\lambda_j I)^{-1}A^Tb,$$
and the residual $r_j=\|Ax_j-b\|$ and solution norm $s_j=\|x_j\|$.
Discard any index with $r_j=0$ or $s_j=0$. If fewer than three indices
remain, return failure status `insufficient-valid-points`.

For consecutive retained indices $i_0<i_1<i_2$, set
$p_k=(\log r_{i_k},\log s_{i_k})\in\mathbb R^2$, $u=p_1-p_0$,
and $v=p_2-p_1$. Define their discrete curvature by
$$\kappa=\begin{cases} \dfrac{2|\det(u,v)|}{\|u\|\,\|v\|\,\|u+v\|},&\|u\|\,\|v\|\,\|u+v\|>0,\\ 0,&\text{otherwise}. \end{cases}$$
Assign this curvature to the middle retained index. Among the resulting
$q'-2$ values, return the original grid parameter whose curvature is largest;
if there is a tie, return the tied parameter with the smallest original index.
No uniform-grid spacing is assumed in log parameter. This is a finite-grid
heuristic and carries no universal optimality claim.

The output is either a selected $\lambda_j$ with its discrete curvature and
index, or the stated failure status. Every step uses a finite loop over the
input grid.

The three grid points therefore have positive residual and solution coordinates $(1/10,9/10)$, $(1/2,1/2)$, and $(9/10,1/10)$.

The logarithmic points have increments $u=(\log 5,-\log(9/5))$ and $v=(\log(9/5),-\log 5)$. Their determinant is $-\log^2 5+\log^2(9/5)\ne0$, their norms are positive, and $u+v=(\log9,-\log9)\ne0$, so the algorithm's discrete curvature is well-defined and positive.

Exactly three indices remain, so the only consecutive triple assigns its curvature to the middle index 2. That is the only candidate for the largest curvature; the returned parameter is $\lambda_2=1$ and no tie-break is needed.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Let $X,Y$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces over the same scalar field, and let
$K:X\to Y$ be a compact linear operator. The associated compact linear inverse
model has parameter space $X$, data space $Y$, forward map $K$, and admissible
truth class $X$: for a true parameter $x^\dagger\in X$, the exact datum is
$y=Kx^\dagger\in Y$. Given an exact datum $y\in Y$, solving this inverse
problem means finding a parameter $x\in X$ such that $Kx=y$. No injectivity,
surjectivity, or closed-range assumption is included in the model.

Define the Hilbert-space Moore–Penrose inverse $K^\dagger$ to have domain $$D(K^\dagger):=R(K)\oplus R(K)^\perp$$ and, for the unique decomposition $y=r+z$ with $r\in R(K)$ and $z\in R(K)^\perp$, set $$K^\dagger y:=\widetilde K^{-1}r.$$ Thus $K^\dagger y$ is the unique minimum-norm solution of $Kx=r$, and the orthogonal-range component is mapped to zero.

It is **noise-level-free** (also called **heuristic**) when the value $\alpha(z)$ for an observed datum $z\in Y$ uses only $K$, the fixed family, and $z$; it does not take the exact datum or a noise bound $\delta$ as input.

derivations.claim: For fixed $y\in D(K^\dagger)$, the output $T(y)=R_{\alpha(y)}y$ is independent of $\delta$. The exact datum $y$ belongs to every ball of radius $\delta>0$, so its error is at most $E_y(\delta)$ for every $\delta$. The assumed limit therefore forces $T(y)=K^\dagger y$.

For any $y\in D(K^\dagger)$ and $\varepsilon>0$, choose $r>0$ with $E_y(r)<\varepsilon$. Every $z\in D(K^\dagger)$ satisfying $\|z-y\|_Y\le r$ lies in that noise ball, and step 1.1 makes the reconstruction at $z$ equal $K^\dagger z$. Hence $\|K^\dagger z-K^\dagger y\|_X<\varepsilon$, proving continuity at $y$ and contradicting the hypothesis.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

Let $(X,\mathcal T)$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]). The
**Borel sigma-algebra of $X$** is the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets:

$$\mathcal B(X):=\sigma_X(\mathcal T).$$

Its members are the **Borel subsets** of $X$. The generated sigma-algebra exists
and is minimal by [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]].

derivations.claim: For $v=x-u$, $\partial_i\varphi_\sigma(v)=-v_i\varphi_\sigma(v)/\sigma^2$ and $\partial_j\partial_i\varphi_\sigma(v)=(v_iv_j/\sigma^4-\delta_{ij}/\sigma^2)\varphi_\sigma(v)$. Each second derivative is bounded, so for every coordinate direction the difference quotient of $\varphi_\sigma(x-u)$ converges to its derivative uniformly in $u$: by the one-variable fundamental theorem of calculus, its error is at most $|h|\sup_v|\partial_{ii}\varphi_\sigma(v)|/2$. Integrating this uniform bound against $\mu$ proves $\partial_i p_\sigma(x)=\int\partial_i\varphi_\sigma(x-u)\,\mu(du)$. The bounded Hessian also makes this derivative continuous in $x$. Boundedness and [F3] give $p_\sigma(x)<\infty$, while strict positivity of $\varphi_\sigma$ and total mass one give $p_\sigma(x)>0$.

Tonelli and normalization give $P_\sigma(\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R^d)=\int\mu(du)\int\varphi_\sigma(x-u)\,dx=1$, so $P_\sigma$ is a probability law. For each Borel $A\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, the numerator $x\mapsto\int_A\varphi_\sigma(x-u)\,\mu(du)$ is continuous because the first derivative of $\varphi_\sigma$ is bounded. Dividing by the positive continuous $p_\sigma$ makes $Q_\sigma(x,A)$ Borel; for fixed $x$, $Q_\sigma(x,\cdot)$ is a probability measure by its defining ratio. Thus $Q_\sigma$ is a probability kernel by [F1]. Tonelli gives $P_\sigma(A\times B)=\int_B p_\sigma(x)Q_\sigma(x,A)\,dx$ for Borel $A,B$, so it is the conditional law of the clean coordinate given $x$. The numerator defining $m_\sigma(x)$ is finite because $\|u\|\varphi_\sigma(x-u)$ is bounded as a function of $u$.

Substituting the first derivative from step 1.1 gives $\nabla p_\sigma(x)=\int (u-x)\varphi_\sigma(x-u)\,\mu(du)/\sigma^2$. Dividing by $p_\sigma(x)>0$ yields $\nabla\log p_\sigma(x)=(m_\sigma(x)-x)/\sigma^2$. Applying the same Gaussian-convolution calculation to the posterior probability $\mu_y$ shows that $p_\sigma(x\mid y)$ is positive and continuously differentiable. The definitions give $Z_y p_\sigma(x\mid y)=\int\varphi_\sigma(x-u)\ell_y(u)\mu(du)=p_\sigma(x)r_\sigma(y\mid x)$. Taking logarithms and differentiating in $x$, with $Z_y$ independent of $x$, gives the conditional-score decomposition.

By step 2.1, $R(h)=\int p_\sigma(x)\int\|h(x)-u\|^2Q_\sigma(x,du)\,dx$, with the iterated-integral identity justified by [F2]. Nonnegativity of $\int\|u-m_\sigma(x)\|^2Q_\sigma(x,du)$ gives $\|m_\sigma(x)\|^2\le\int\|u\|^2Q_\sigma(x,du)$; integrating and using [F2] proves $m_\sigma\in L^2(p_\sigma)$ under the finite-second-moment hypothesis. Expanding about $m_\sigma(x)$ makes the cross term vanish because $\int u\,Q_\sigma(x,du)=m_\sigma(x)$, so $R(h)=R(m_\sigma)+\int\|h(x)-m_\sigma(x)\|^2p_\sigma(x)\,dx$. The last term is nonnegative and vanishes exactly for the same $p_\sigma$-almost-everywhere class.

The conditional mean of $(u-x)/\sigma^2$ under $Q_\sigma(x,du)$ is $(m_\sigma(x)-x)/\sigma^2=
abla\log p_\sigma(x)$ by step 3.1. The noise target has finite second moment because $\int\|v\|^2\varphi_\sigma(v)\,dv<\infty$; the conditional-mean square bound then puts $
abla\log p_\sigma$ in $L^2(p_\sigma)$. Expanding the squared score risk around that conditional mean gives $J(s)=J(
abla\log p_\sigma)+\int\|s(x)-
abla\log p_\sigma(x)\|^2p_\sigma(x)\,dx$, so the unique score-risk minimizer is the stated score. Under the finite-second-moment hypothesis of step 3.2, $x$ and $m_\sigma(x)$ are in $L^2(p_\sigma)$; then $s\mapsto h(x)=x+\sigma^2s(x)$ is a bijection between the two predictor classes and $R(h)=\sigma^4J(s)$, proving the claimed denoiser/score minimizer equivalence.

Let $d\ge1$, let $\sigma>0$, and let $\mu$ be a probability measure on the Borel subsets of $\mathbb R^d$. Write $\varphi_\sigma(v)=c_{\sigma,d}\exp(-\|v\|^2/(2\sigma^2))$ for the normalized Gaussian density with respect to Lebesgue measure $dx$, define $P_\sigma(du,dx)=\mu(du)\varphi_\sigma(x-u)\,dx$, and set $p_\sigma(x)=\int\varphi_\sigma(x-u)\,\mu(du)$. Define $Q_\sigma(x,du)=\varphi_\sigma(x-u)\mu(du)/p_\sigma(x)$ and $m_\sigma(x)=\int u\,Q_\sigma(x,du)$; under $P_\sigma$, write $X_0(u,x)=u$ and $X_\sigma(u,x)=x$ for the coordinate random vectors. For Borel maps $h,s:\mathbb R^d	o\mathbb R^d$ that are square-integrable with respect to $p_\sigma(x)dx$, define $R(h)=\int\|h(x)-u\|^2P_\sigma(du,dx)$ and $J(s)=\int\|s(x)-(u-x)/\sigma^2\|^2P_\sigma(du,dx)$. Then $p_\sigma$ is positive and continuously differentiable, $Q_\sigma$ is the conditional law of $X_0$ given $X_\sigma=x$, and $
abla\log p_\sigma(x)=(m_\sigma(x)-x)/\sigma^2$ for every $x\in\mathbb R^d$. If $\int\|u\|^2\,\mu(du)<\infty$, $m_\sigma$ uniquely minimizes $R$ up to $p_\sigma$-almost-everywhere equality. The unique minimizer of $J$ is $
abla\log p_\sigma$, also up to $p_\sigma$-almost-everywhere equality. Under the same Gaussian noising, suppose that for the fixed observation $y$, $\ell_y:\mathbb R^d	o(0,\infty)$ is a bounded Borel likelihood-density function relative to a fixed sigma-finite observation measure, and assume $0<Z_y=\int\ell_y(u)\,\mu(du)<\infty$. Let $\mu_y(du)=\ell_y(u)\mu(du)/Z_y$ and $p_\sigma(x\mid y)=\int\varphi_\sigma(x-u)\,\mu_y(du)$. Then, for $r_\sigma(y\mid x)=\int\ell_y(u)\,Q_\sigma(x,du)$, the conditional score satisfies $
abla_x\log p_\sigma(x\mid y)=
abla_x\log p_\sigma(x)+
abla_x\log r_\sigma(y\mid x)$. No absolute-continuity or bounded-support assumption on $\mu$ is required; $\sigma>0$ supplies the full-support smoothing density.

Let $p_\sigma$, $Q_\sigma$, $m_\sigma$, and $r_\sigma(y\mid x)$ be formed under the hypotheses of the conditional-score and Tweedie identities for Gaussian smoothing. The **diffusion prior score** is $s_\sigma(x)=
abla_x\log p_\sigma(x)$, the exact score of the smoothed prior density. The **measurement score** is $g_\sigma(x,y)=
abla_x\log r_\sigma(y\mid x)$, the score in the noisy state of the likelihood density averaged over $Q_\sigma(x,du)$. The **conditional score** is $c_\sigma(x,y)=
abla_x\log p_\sigma(x\mid y)$; it equals $s_\sigma(x)+g_\sigma(x,y)$, and the clean-state conditional mean is $m_\sigma(x)=x+\sigma^2s_\sigma(x)$. A learned field $\widehat s_	heta$ is an estimate of $s_\sigma$ and is exact only when it agrees with $s_\sigma$ almost everywhere under $p_\sigma(x)dx$. Replacing $r_\sigma(y\mid x)$ by the likelihood evaluated at $m_\sigma(x)$ is a plug-in likelihood approximation, not part of the exact measurement-score definition.

derivations.claim: For $x\in\mathbb R$, Bayes' formula gives $\displaystyle\frac{P(X_0=1\mid X_\sigma=x)}{P(X_0=-1\mid X_\sigma=x)}=\frac{\varphi_\sigma(x-1)}{\varphi_\sigma(x+1)}=\exp(2x/\sigma^2)$. Therefore the posterior mean is $(e^{2x/\sigma^2}-1)/(e^{2x/\sigma^2}+1)=\tanh(x/\sigma^2)$, agreeing with the conditional-mean version in [F1].

At $y=0$, both possible clean states have the same likelihood density: $\varphi_\tau(0-1)=\varphi_\tau(0+1)=\varphi_\tau(1)$. Averaging these equal values over the conditional law from [F2] gives $r_\sigma(0\mid x)=\varphi_\tau(1)$ for every $x$, so its logarithmic derivative and the exact measurement score are zero.

The plug-in log density is $\log\varphi_\tau(-m_\sigma(x))=-\log(\sqrt{2\pi}\tau)-m_\sigma(x)^2/(2\tau^2)$. Differentiating the quotient expression in step 1.1 gives $m_\sigma'(x)=4e^{2x/\sigma^2}/(\sigma^2(e^{2x/\sigma^2}+1)^2)>0$. Hence the plug-in score is $-m_\sigma(x)m_\sigma'(x)/\tau^2$, which is nonzero whenever $x\ne0$.

The exact score in step 1.2 and the plug-in score in step 2.1 disagree for every nonzero $x$. Thus the exact posterior mean does not, in general, make likelihood-at-the-mean guidance equal to the exact measurement score. The calculation permits special cases of equality but refutes a general identity.

Let $d\ge1$, let $\sigma>0$, and let $\mu$ be a probability measure on the Borel subsets of $\mathbb R^d$. Write $\varphi_\sigma(v)=c_{\sigma,d}\exp(-\|v\|^2/(2\sigma^2))$ for the normalized Gaussian density with respect to Lebesgue measure $dx$, define $P_\sigma(du,dx)=\mu(du)\varphi_\sigma(x-u)\,dx$, and set $p_\sigma(x)=\int\varphi_\sigma(x-u)\,\mu(du)$. Define $Q_\sigma(x,du)=\varphi_\sigma(x-u)\mu(du)/p_\sigma(x)$ and $m_\sigma(x)=\int u\,Q_\sigma(x,du)$; under $P_\sigma$, write $X_0(u,x)=u$ and $X_\sigma(u,x)=x$ for the coordinate random vectors. For Borel maps $h,s:\mathbb R^d	o\mathbb R^d$ that are square-integrable with respect to $p_\sigma(x)dx$, define $R(h)=\int\|h(x)-u\|^2P_\sigma(du,dx)$ and $J(s)=\int\|s(x)-(u-x)/\sigma^2\|^2P_\sigma(du,dx)$. Then $p_\sigma$ is positive and continuously differentiable, $Q_\sigma$ is the conditional law of $X_0$ given $X_\sigma=x$, and $
abla\log p_\sigma(x)=(m_\sigma(x)-x)/\sigma^2$ for every $x\in\mathbb R^d$. If $\int\|u\|^2\,\mu(du)<\infty$, $m_\sigma$ uniquely minimizes $R$ up to $p_\sigma$-almost-everywhere equality. The unique minimizer of $J$ is $
abla\log p_\sigma$, also up to $p_\sigma$-almost-everywhere equality. Under the same Gaussian noising, suppose that for the fixed observation $y$, $\ell_y:\mathbb R^d	o(0,\infty)$ is a bounded Borel likelihood-density function relative to a fixed sigma-finite observation measure, and assume $0<Z_y=\int\ell_y(u)\,\mu(du)<\infty$. Let $\mu_y(du)=\ell_y(u)\mu(du)/Z_y$ and $p_\sigma(x\mid y)=\int\varphi_\sigma(x-u)\,\mu_y(du)$. Then, for $r_\sigma(y\mid x)=\int\ell_y(u)\,Q_\sigma(x,du)$, the conditional score satisfies $
abla_x\log p_\sigma(x\mid y)=
abla_x\log p_\sigma(x)+
abla_x\log r_\sigma(y\mid x)$. No absolute-continuity or bounded-support assumption on $\mu$ is required; $\sigma>0$ supplies the full-support smoothing density.

Let $K$ be a probability kernel on a measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$
([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]), and let $\pi$ be a
probability measure on $(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). The
probability measure $\pi$ is **invariant** for $K$, and $\pi$ is a
**stationary distribution** of $K$, when

$$(\pi K)(A):=\int_E K(x,A)\,\pi(dx)=\pi(A)\qquad\text{for every }A\in\mathcal E .$$

The set function $\pi K$ is again a probability measure: for fixed $A$ the map
$x\mapsto K(x,A)$ is measurable and lies in $[0,1]$, so the integral exists in
$[0,1]$; for pairwise disjoint $A_n\in\mathcal E$ the identity
$K(x,\bigcup_nA_n)=\sum_nK(x,A_n)$ of the measure $K(x,\cdot)$ and the
monotone convergence theorem for nonnegative functions
([[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]) give
$\sigma$-additivity of $\pi K$; and $K(x,E)=1$ for every $x$ gives
$(\pi K)(E)=1$. Thus $(\pi K)(A)=\pi(A)$ is an identity between two probability
measures evaluated at $A$.

A $K$-chain whose initial law is $\pi$ is called **stationary** when
$\pi K=\pi$. Stationarity of the process is a statement about all of its
finite-dimensional laws and is proved, not assumed, from $\pi K=\pi$; see
[[thm-invariant-initial-law-makes-the-chain-stationary]].

On a countable state space $E$ with sigma-algebra $2^E$ and transition matrix
$p(x,y)=K(x,\{y\})$ ([[def-transition-matrix-and-n-step-transition-probabilities]]),
a measure on $E$ is its weighted sum of Dirac masses at singletons
([[thm-measures-on-countable-discrete-spaces-are-weighted-dirac-sums]]), so
invariance is equivalent to the matrix identity

$$\pi(y)=\sum_{x\in E}\pi(x)\,p(x,y)\qquad\text{for every }y\in E .$$

The definition fixes no irreducibility, aperiodicity or uniqueness hypothesis,
and it selects no conditional-expectation versions; the display defines a
single measure $\pi K$ and asserts an identity for it. A transient, periodic or
reducible chain may have several invariant probability measures or none.

Thus the variational output law is its selected $q$; it is the target law in the exact case $q=\pi_y$, and it differs from the target precisely when the induced probability measures differ, equivalently when the densities disagree on a set of positive $\lambda$-measure.

Under [A4], repeated execution of the deterministic latent optimizer returns the single value $G(\widehat z)$, so its output law is $\delta_{G(\widehat z)}$. If $\pi_y$ is not a point mass, this point mass is not $\pi_y$. The stated objective contains only the measurement residual; it does not specify the negative log posterior or a global optimizer of that posterior objective, so the given inputs establish no MAP conclusion.

If a Markov chain starts with law $\pi_y$, one transition has law $\pi_yK_y=\pi_y$ by [F3]; induction gives the same marginal after every finite number of transitions. In contrast, on $\{0,1\}$ let $\pi=(\delta_0+\delta_1)/2$ and let $K(x,B)=\mathbf 1_B(x)$. Then $\pi K=\pi$, but a chain starting at $\delta_0$ remains $\delta_0$ after each finite step and is never $\pi$.

To check the failure boundary, take $d=1$, target $\pi_y=(\delta_0+\delta_1)/2$ (prior equal to this law and likelihood one), and a two-step path with $X_2=0$, $X_1\sim\pi_y$, and $X_0=X_1$. Its exact reverse kernels draw $X_1$ from $\pi_y$ and then set $X_0=X_1$. Initialize at zero and use these same kernels, but declare correction failure in the last step exactly when $X_1=1$. All operations have finite budgets. Completed status then has probability $1/2$ and its conditional output law is $\delta_0$, not $\pi_y$. Thus allowing the failure branches in [F2] invalidates an unconditional exactness inference from the reverse kernels alone.

A realized weighted empirical particle measure $\widehat\pi_K=\sum_{j=1}^K w_j\delta_{x_j}$ is supported on the finite set $S=\{x_1,\ldots,x_K\}$. By [A5] and finite additivity, $\pi_y(S)\le\sum_{j=1}^K\pi_y(\{x_j\})=0$, while $\widehat\pi_K(S)=1$, so the finite empirical measure is not the target. This does not determine the marginal law of a randomly selected particle; that exactness is a separate algorithm-specific claim.

derivations.claim: Sort the distinct sample sites together with endpoints $0$ and $1$. The at most $N+1$ consecutive gaps have total length one, so one open gap $(a,b)$ has length $\ell=b-a\ge1/(N+1)$. Let $x_*=(a+b)/2$, $r=\ell/2$, $f_0(x)=0$, and $f_1(x)=\max\{0,r-|x-x_*|\}$. The tent has slopes of magnitude at most one, vanishes at every sample site, and has height $r\ge1/(2(N+1))$ at $x_*$. Thus $f_0,f_1$ are both $1$-Lipschitz and yield identical training pairs.

Because the training pairs are identical, the deterministic rule returns the same value $g(x_*)$ for both target functions. Since $|g(x_*)-f_0(x_*)|+|g(x_*)-f_1(x_*)|\ge|f_1(x_*)-f_0(x_*)|=r$, one of the two errors is at least $r/2\ge1/(4(N+1))$. Their uniform distance is $r\ge1/(2(N+1))$, proving both claims.

derivations.claim: Completing the square in $e^{-u^2/2}e^{-(Y-u)^2/2}$ gives posterior $N(Y/2,1/2)$, so its exact credible interval is $[Y/2-r,Y/2+r]$. Under truth $\theta\in[-1,1]$, $Y=\theta+G$ and the exact coverage is $c(\theta)=P\{|\theta/2-G/2|\le r\}$. This is a continuous strictly positive function of $\theta$, and is at most one. By compactness of $[-1,1]$ it has a positive minimum $c_*>0$. Therefore $\delta^0_{1,1/4}\le\max\{q-c_*,1-q\}<q$.

Put $h=1/K$ and let $\mathcal G_K=\{1-kh:0\le k<K\}$. Away from this finite set of times, use the exact noised-posterior score. At each $t\in\mathcal G_K$ set $s_t^Y(x)=(1-x)/h-x/2$. This finite-valued jointly Borel field has zero integrated score error: its discrepancy from the exact score is supported on the finite, Lebesgue-null set $\mathcal G_K$ in time. The noised posterior has mean $e^{-t/2}Y/2$ and variance $1-e^{-t}/2$: the integrating-factor solution of the linear forward equation is $e^{-t/2}X_0+e^{-t/2}\int_0^te^{u/2}\,dW_u$, whose independent Gaussian integral has variance $1-e^{-t}$ (use dyadic Brownian-increment sums and pass their Gaussian characteristic functions to the mean-square limit). Its exact score is therefore affine in $x$, so the inner Gaussian error integral is finite at every time. The zero-error conclusion holds for every observation and hence uniformly over all truths.

The variable $\theta/2-G/2$ has a density bounded by $2/\sqrt{2\pi}$ uniformly in $\theta$. The event $\bigl||\theta/2-G/2|-r\bigr|\le u$ is contained in two intervals of total length at most $4u$. Thus its probability is at most $8u/\sqrt{2\pi}$. The required margin holds, for example with $\kappa=1$, $u_0=1$ and $C_{\mathrm{ac}}=8/\sqrt{2\pi}$.

At every Euler step the deterministic update becomes $x+h(x/2+s_t^Y(x))=1$. Thus each new state is $1+\sqrt h\,\zeta_k$, independently of its input and of $Y$, and the terminal law is $N(1,h)$. For $M=K$, write the independent terminal draws as $1+K^{-1/2}G_i$. If $V_K=\max_{i\le K}|G_i|$, then the empirical center differs from one by at most $K^{-1/2}V_K$ and every empirical distance to that center is at most $2K^{-1/2}V_K$. Hence the empirical radius has that same upper bound.

The Gaussian density gives $P\{|G|>v\}\le2e^{-v^2/2}$ for $v\ge1$: integrate $x\phi(x)/v$ on $[v,\infty)$ and use $1/(v\sqrt{2\pi})\le1$. The union bound then gives $P\{V_K>K^{1/4}\}\le2K e^{-\sqrt K/2}\to0$. On the complementary event the center is at least $1-K^{-1/4}$ and the radius at most $2K^{-1/4}$, so for all sufficiently large $K$ the empirical interval excludes truth zero. Its coverage therefore tends to zero, and its deviation from $q$ tends to $q>\delta^0_{1,1/4}$. Since both error norms are zero and $K^{-1},M^{-1/2}\to0$, a uniformly vanishing $\Phi$ would contradict this strict gap.

derivations.claim: The zero estimator gives risk at most $R^2$ for every allowed law and operator. If $\sigma<R$, put $t=(R/\sigma)^{2/(2s+2p+1)}>1$ and $k=\lfloor t\rfloor\ge1$. Use the Borel finite-coordinate estimator $\widehat\theta_j=j^pY_j$ for $j\le k$ and zero otherwise; it ignores the training data. Under any test truth its retained error is $P_kE\theta+(\sigma j^p\xi_j)_{j\le k}$ and its omitted error is $-(I-P_k)\theta$. These components are orthogonal, and the centered noise is independent of the truth. Hence its expected squared error is at most $R^2\rho_A^2+R^2(k+1)^{-2s}+\sigma^2\sum_{j=1}^k j^{2p}$. Because $k+1>t$ and $\sum_{j\le k}j^{2p}\le k^{2p+1}\le t^{2p+1}$, the last two terms are at most $2R^2t^{-2s}=2Q_{p,s}$. If $\sigma\ge R$, $Q_{p,s}=R^2$ and the zero estimator already gives the asserted upper bound. Taking the better of the zero and cutoff rules proves the displayed upper bound uniformly over both shift classes.

For the noise lower bound first suppose $\sigma\ge R$. Set $E=0$ and $\mu=\mu_0=(\delta_{Re_1}+\delta_{-Re_1})/2$. These laws have Wasserstein distance zero and are admissible at every $\rho_X$. The training sample is independent of the fresh test sign, and all other test coordinates are independent pure noise. Given those ancillary variables, testing the fresh sign reduces to [A1] with $\delta=R$. Thus any prediction of its first coordinate has squared error at least $R^2$ whenever its induced sign test is wrong, and its integrated risk is at least $R^2\Phi(-R/\sigma)\ge bR^2=bQ_{p,s}$. At a zero predicted coordinate, choose either sign; the squared error is still $R^2$.

Put $r=\rho_A$. If $r>0$, define $a=R/(1+r)$, $b_0=R$ and take the same source and test law $\mu_0=\mu=(\delta_{ae_1}+\delta_{b_0e_1})/2$. Compare the two allowed operators $E_1=0$ and $E_2=-r(1+r)^{-1}P_1$, whose norms are at most $r$. In the first world, the test truth $ae_1$ has observation mean $ae_1$; in the second, truth $b_0e_1$ has the same mean because $(I+E_2)b_0e_1=ae_1$. The joint law of the full training sample and this conditional test observation is identical in the two cases, including every noisy coordinate. Calling that common law $H$, the corresponding two full test risks satisfy $R_1\ge\tfrac12E_H\|G-ae_1\|^2$ and $R_2\ge\tfrac12E_H\|G-b_0e_1\|^2$. Therefore [A2] gives $\max(R_1,R_2)\ge(b_0-a)^2/8=R^2r^2/[8(1+r)^2]\ge R^2r^2/18$. This holds for every Borel learner and all training sizes. If $r=0$, the asserted zero operator lower bound is immediate.

If $\sigma<R$, use $t$ from step 1.1 and $k=\lceil t\rceil\le2t$. On the coordinate block $k\le j<2k$, put $a=2^{-s-1}Rk^{-s-1/2}$ and let $\mu_0=\mu$ be the uniform law on the $2^k$ vectors having independent coordinates $\theta_j=\pm a$ on this block and zero elsewhere. Each such vector lies in the ellipsoid because $\sum_jj^{2s}\theta_j^2\le k(2k)^{2s}a^2=R^2/4$. Again choose $E=0$. For every block coordinate, its test sign is independent of the whole training sample and of all other test coordinates. Its signal amplitude is $j^{-p}a\le k^{-p}a\le\sigma$, by the definition of $t$ and $k\ge t$. Applying the density-crossing argument in [A1], conditional on all ancillary data, gives sign error at least $b$. Summing the coordinate squared errors gives risk at least $bka^2=b2^{-2s-2}R^2k^{-2s}\ge b2^{-4s-2}Q_{p,s}$. Finite averaging over the sign prior and integration over the independent ancillary observations suffice; no choice of an unknown prior by the learner is being assumed.

Steps 1.2 and 2.1 give $\mathfrak R_N\ge c_0Q_{p,s}$ with $c_0=b\min\{1,2^{-4s-2}\}>0$, and step 1.3 gives $\mathfrak R_N\ge R^2\rho_A^2/18$. The maximum of these bounds is at least $\tfrac12\min\{c_0,1/18\}(Q_{p,s}+R^2\rho_A^2)$, proving the lower bound with that explicit positive $c_{p,s}$. For fixed $p,s,R>0$, the upper bound tends to zero when $\sigma,\rho_A\to0$, and the lower bound forces both limits whenever the risk tends to zero. Both lower constructions have $\mu=\mu_0$, so they remain admissible even at zero truth-law shift; the upper construction ignores the training law entirely. This explains why $N$ and $\rho_X$ do not enter the matching-order rate for this worst-law formulation.

derivations.claim: Use the exact score at all grid times before the last two updates. All those states have finite first moment because each exact-score drift has linear growth by [A1]. Let $U$ be the state before the penultimate update, corresponding to ideal time $2h$. Its law has a strictly positive continuous density $\rho$: for $J=2$ it is exactly $p_T$, and otherwise the last preceding nondegenerate Euler noise gives [A2]. Since $p_{2h}$ is also positive and continuous, the density ratio $\rho/p_{2h}$ has positive minimum $c$ and finite maximum $C$ on $[-1,1]$.

For every sufficiently small $q>0$, choose the centered interval $A_q\subseteq[-1,1]$ with $\int_{A_q}p_{2h}(x)\,dx=q$. Such an interval exists by continuity and positivity of that density. Then $cq\le P\{U\in A_q\}\le Cq$. Put $b_q=\varepsilon_s/(2\sqrt q)$ and add $b_q\mathbf1_{A_q}$ to the score at time $2h$. Its squared ideal-marginal error is exactly $\varepsilon_s^2/4$. Set $f(x)=(1+h/2)x+hs_{2h}(x)$ and $H=\sup_{|x|\le1}|f(x)|<\infty$. After this update the state is $V=f(U)+hb_q\mathbf1_{A_q}(U)+\sqrt h\,G$.

Let $I_q=[hb_q-H-\sqrt h,hb_q+H+\sqrt h]$, and let $r_q=\int_{I_q}p_h(x)\,dx>0$. On $\{U\in A_q,|G|\le1\}$ the state $V$ lies in $I_q$, so $P\{V\in I_q\}\ge cqP\{|G|\le1\}$. The ideal density $p_h$ is a fixed Gaussian mixture. Since the interval width is constant and its center $hb_q$ tends to infinity, its Gaussian density formula gives constants $C_1,c_1>0$, independent of small $q$, such that $r_q\le C_1e^{-c_1b_q^2}$. For example, once $hb_q\ge2(H+\sqrt h+a)$, every point of the interval is at distance at least $hb_q/2$ from either component mean; use the largest fixed variance in its Gaussian exponent and the constant interval length.

At the final evaluation time $h$ add $d_q\mathbf1_{I_q}$ to the exact score, where $d_q=\varepsilon_s/(2\sqrt{r_q})$. This second squared ideal-marginal error is also $\varepsilon_s^2/4$. At all other times use the exact score. These modifications at two distinct times define a jointly Borel finite-valued field with the original supremum-in-time score bound. Every individual field has finite first moments at all Euler steps: it is an affine-growth exact score plus two bounded, finite-amplitude additions.

The first moment of $V$ is bounded uniformly as $q\downarrow0$: the added term has expectation at most $hb_qCq= hC\varepsilon_s\sqrt q/2$, while $E|f(U)|$ and $E|\sqrt hG|$ are fixed and finite. The terminal state is $X=(1+h/2)V+hs_h(V)+hd_q\mathbf1_{I_q}(V)+\sqrt hG'$. By [A1] the absolute expectation of the first two terms is uniformly bounded; $EG'=0$. Therefore $EX\ge h\varepsilon_scqP\{|G|\le1\}/(2\sqrt{r_q})-C_2\to+\infty$, because $b_q^2=\varepsilon_s^2/(4q)$ and the exponential bound in step 3.1 dominates every power of $q$.

Every coupling of two finite-first-moment probabilities satisfies $|EX-EY|\le E|X-Y|$ by the integral triangle inequality. Thus $W_1(\widehat\pi_{J,M},\pi)\ge|M^{-1}\sum_iX^{(i)}|$ because the target mean is zero. Taking expectations gives $EW_1\ge|EX|$, which tends to infinity by step 5.1 for every finite $M$. The other two terms in the requested fidelity loss are nonnegative. Its supremum is consequently infinite despite fixed positive score-error allowance and fixed admissible target parameters.

derivations.claim: Each Fourier multiplier commutes with translation because the kth translated Fourier coefficient is multiplied by the scalar $e^{-ik\alpha}$, which commutes with its channel matrix. Every constant channel matrix, constant bias and coordinatewise scalar activation also commutes with translation. By induction through the lift, all layers and output map, the realized scalar output field is translation-equivariant. The layer fields are in $L^2$: a globally Lipschitz activation has linear growth, the pointwise weights are finite and the finite Fourier multipliers are bounded. For odd $m$, projection onto the first m coefficients commutes with translation by [A1]. Hence the zero-extended output map $F=I_m\Psi_m$ satisfies $F(U_\alpha x)=T_\alpha F(x)$, where $U_\alpha$ is the orthogonal translation matrix on the retained coefficients. This holds for every individual parameter array, also after data-dependent selection.

Put $a=R3^{-(p+s)}$, choose $\theta_c=a2^pe_2$ and $\theta_s=a3^pe_3$, and let $\mu=(\delta_{\theta_c}+\delta_{\theta_s})/2$. These truths lie in the ellipsoid because their weighted squared norms are at most $a^23^{2(p+s)}=R^2$. Their forward coefficient vectors are respectively $ae_2$ and $ae_3$, related by $U=U_{\pi/2}$. Conditional on any training sample, the test truth is still an independent equal-probability draw from these two values. Couple the corresponding test noises as $\eta$ and $U\eta$; by [A2] both have the required $N(0,\sigma^2m^{-1}I_m)$ law.

To see unrestricted vanishing without training, put $k_m=\min\{m,\max\{1,\lfloor m^{1/(2(2p+1))}\rfloor\}\}$. Output $j^pX_{m,j}$ for $j\le k_m$ and zero otherwise. Its risk for every truth is at most $\sigma^2m^{-1}\sum_{j\le k_m}j^{2p}+R^2(k_m+1)^{-2s}\le\sigma^2m^{-1}k_m^{2p+1}+R^2(k_m+1)^{-2s}\to0$. It is a Borel predictor and is allowed in the unrestricted class. This proves the contrast with the positive odd-mesh architecture floor.

For fixed training data, let $F$ be its selected predictor. By step 1.1, $F(ae_3+U\eta)=T_{\pi/2}F(ae_2+\eta)$. Translating the first output and truth preserves their norm. Consequently the conditional average of the two squared risks is $\tfrac12E[\|T_{\pi/2}F(ae_2+\eta)-T_{\pi/2}\theta_c\|^2+\|T_{\pi/2}F(ae_2+\eta)-\theta_s\|^2]$, which is at least $\|T_{\pi/2}\theta_c-\theta_s\|^2/4=a^2(3^p-2^p)^2/4$ by [A3]. This lower bound is independent of the training sample. Integrating over it, taking the worst law and then the infimum over selectors proves the stated floor.

The mismatch arises because the diagonal inverse rescales the first cosine and sine by different factors $2^p$ and $3^p$, while the coordinate-free architecture must respect translation between them. It is independent of finite training or parameter-size limitations. The proof deliberately uses odd $m$ so both the input noise law and retained output subspace are translation-invariant; it supplies no identical assertion for even $m$, whose last frequency pair is incomplete.

citations.quote: $\mathbb{R} = \mathcal{C}/\mathcal{N}$ ([[def-real-numbers]]) is a field.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring. Define polynomial rings in finitely many commuting indeterminates recursively by

$$ R[x_1,\ldots,x_0]:=R,\qquad R[x_1,\ldots,x_{n+1}]:=R[x_1,\ldots,x_n][x_{n+1}]. $$

At each stage the coefficient ring embeds as the constant polynomials ([[thm-polynomial-ring-is-a-commutative-ring]]), so all preceding indeterminates remain present. The new indeterminate commutes with every coefficient by the commutativity built into [[def-polynomial-ring-over-a-commutative-ring]], and consequently all $x_i$ commute. This iterated ring is denoted $R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$.
If $R$ is an integral domain, then $R[x]$ is an integral domain.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $n\ge1$, and let $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(R)$. Its **determinant** is
$$\det(A):=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\prod_{i<n}a_{\sigma(i),i}.$$
The sum is finite because $S_n$ has $n!$ elements. The product is taken in $R$, so the signs $1$ and $-1$ act through the ring identities. The formula uses columns indexed by $i<n$ and rows indexed by $\sigma(i)$.

When $A$ is real, $|\det A|$ means the ordinary real absolute value of its real determinant. It is not alternate notation for the determinant itself.
For $n\ge1$ and every commutative ring $R$, the Leibniz determinant $\det:M_n(R)\to R$ is column-multilinear, alternating and normalized.

Let $R,S$ be commutative rings, let $\varphi\colon R\to S$ be a unital ring homomorphism, and let $s\in S$. There is a unique unital ring homomorphism

$$ \operatorname{ev}_{\varphi,s}\colon R[x]\to S $$

that extends $\varphi$ on constant polynomials and sends $x$ to $s$. It is given by $\operatorname{ev}_{\varphi,s}(\sum_i a_i x^i)=\sum_i\varphi(a_i)s^i$.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $a\in R$, and $f\in R[x]$. Then $f(a)=0$ if and only if $x-a$ divides $f$ in $R[x]$.

More precisely, there is a unique $q\in R[x]$ such that $f=q(x-a)+f(a)$.

For every $n\ge1$ and every real matrix $A\in M_n(\mathbb R)$,
$$A\text{ is invertible}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\det(A)\ne0.$$

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]). As in
[[def-linear-combination-and-span]], a **finite list** of vectors is a function
$v : n \to V$ on a von Neumann natural $n = \{0, \dots, n-1\}$
([[def-natural-numbers]], [[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), written
$v_i := v(i)$, and

$$\sum_{i<n} \lambda_i v_i$$

is the finite sum of [[def-monoid-finite-product]] read additively in the abelian
group $(V,+,0_V)$, applied to the list $i \mapsto \lambda_i v_i$. No second notion
of finite sum is introduced here.

### Independence of a list

A finite list $v : n \to V$ is **linearly independent** when, for every list of
scalars $\lambda : n \to F$,

$$\sum_{i<n} \lambda_i v_i = 0_V \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \lambda_i = 0_F \text{ for every } i < n,$$

and **linearly dependent** otherwise, that is, when some $\lambda : n \to F$ has
$\sum_{i<n}\lambda_i v_i = 0_V$ while $\lambda_j \ne 0_F$ for at least one
$j < n$. Such a $\lambda$ is called a **witness** to the dependence of $v$.

### Independence of a subset

A subset $S \subseteq V$ is **linearly independent** when **every injective**
finite list $v : n \to S$ ([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]) is linearly
independent, and **linearly dependent** otherwise, that is, when some injective
finite list into $S$ is linearly dependent.

**The injectivity clause is not decoration.** A linear combination in
[[def-linear-combination-and-span]] is indexed by an arbitrary list $v : n \to S$,
which is **not** required to be injective. If the definition above quantified
over all such lists, then for any $w \in S$ the list $v : 2 \to S$ with
$v_0 = v_1 = w$ and the scalars $\lambda_0 = 1_F$, $\lambda_1 = -1_F$ would give

$$\sum_{i<2}\lambda_i v_i = (0_V + 1_F w) + (-1_F)w = w + (-w) = 0_V$$

with $\lambda_0 = 1_F \ne 0_F$ ([[def-field]],
[[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]]), so **every** nonempty subset of
$V$ would be dependent and the notion would be empty. Quantifying over injective
lists is what makes the subset notion the intended one. It costs nothing for
lists: [[lem-independent-list-is-injective]] shows that the vanishing condition
above already forces a list to be injective, so no injectivity hypothesis has to
be carried alongside independence of a list.

### The boundary cases are genuine cases

$\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]), so both of the following are
instances of the definitions and neither is a convention.

- **The empty list is independent.** For $n = 0$ the only list of scalars is the
  empty one, and the condition "$\lambda_i = 0_F$ for every $i < 0$" holds
  vacuously.
- **$\varnothing \subseteq V$ is independent.** The only function $v : n \to
  \varnothing$ is the empty one, with $n = 0$, and it is independent by the
  previous point.
- **$\{0_V\}$ is dependent.** The list $v : 1 \to \{0_V\}$ with $v_0 = 0_V$ is
  injective, and taking $\lambda_0 = 1_F$ gives
  $\sum_{i<1}\lambda_i v_i = 0_V + 1_F 0_V = 0_V$ by the recursion of
  [[def-monoid-finite-product]] and $\lambda 0_V = 0_V$
  ([[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]]), while $1_F \ne 0_F$ in a field
  ([[def-field]]). So $\{0_V\}$, and hence every subset of $V$ containing $0_V$,
  is linearly dependent.

derivations.claim: Let $N=d(d-1)/2$. By [F2], every Leibniz term of $\det V_d$ is a signed monomial that assigns the exponents $0,1,\ldots,d-1$ once each to $t_1,\ldots,t_d$, so every term has total degree $N$. With lexicographic order $t_d>t_{d-1}>\cdots>t_1$, the unique largest exponent tuple assigns exponent $d-1$ to $t_d$, exponent $d-2$ to $t_{d-1}$, and so on; it is the identity-permutation term $\prod_{q=1}^d t_q^{q-1}$ with coefficient $1$.

If $d=1$, then $V_d=[1]$ and both sides of the displayed formula are $1$. Suppose henceforth $d\ge2$. For each pair $p<q$, specializing $t_q=t_p$ makes columns $p$ and $q$ equal, so alternation in [F2] gives $\det V_d=0$ after that substitution. Apply [F3] with coefficient ring $C=\mathbb R[t_j:j\ne q]$ to get $t_q-t_p\mid\det V_d$.

For a fixed pair $p<q$, the substitution map $\phi_{pq}:P\to\mathbb R[t_j:j\ne q]$ sending $t_q$ to $t_p$ and fixing the other indeterminates is a surjective ring homomorphism by [F3]. Its kernel is generated by $t_q-t_p$ by the factor-theorem clause of [F3]. The target is an integral domain by [F1]; therefore $t_q-t_p$ is prime: if it divides a product, applying $\phi_{pq}$ makes one factor zero, and the kernel description makes $t_q-t_p$ divide that factor. Distinct pairs $p<q$ give nonassociate linear polynomials, since their coefficient vectors have different nonzero coordinates.

List the finitely many factors $t_q-t_p$ in any fixed order. They all divide $\det V_d$ by step 1.2. Inductively suppose the product of the first $k$ factors divides the determinant. The next prime factor divides the determinant, so primality makes it divide one of the first $k$ factors or the remaining quotient. It cannot divide an earlier factor, since both have degree one and are nonassociate. Thus it divides the remaining quotient. This proves that the full product $\Delta_d:=\prod_{p<q}(t_q-t_p)$ divides $\det V_d$.

The product $\Delta_d$ has total degree $N$, and step 1.1 shows $\det V_d$ also has total degree $N$. Since $P$ is an integral domain and $\Delta_d$ divides $\det V_d$, their quotient is a constant. Under the same lexicographic order, the leading monomial of every factor $t_q-t_p$ is $t_q$, so $\Delta_d$ has leading monomial $\prod_q t_q^{q-1}$ with coefficient $1$. Step 1.1 gives the same leading monomial and coefficient for $\det V_d$. Hence the constant quotient is $1$, proving the determinant formula.

For distinct real nodes $s_1,\ldots,s_d$, substitution into the formula gives $\det V_d(s_1,\ldots,s_d)=\prod_{p<q}(s_q-s_p)\ne0$. By [F4], the square matrix with these moment-curve vectors as columns is invertible, hence has trivial coefficient kernel and linearly independent columns by [F5].

Let $d\ge1$, $m\ge0$, and $\Phi=(a_i)_{i\in[m]}$ be a finite family in $\mathbb R^d$, allowing zero measurement vectors and not assuming that $\Phi$ spans. Here $[m]=\{1,\ldots,m\}$ and $[0]=\varnothing$; measurement labels are one-based, while coordinates in $\mathbb R^d$ use the library's zero-based convention $k<d$. Write $\mathbb R^{[m]}=\{y:[m]\to\mathbb R\}$. Use the Euclidean inner product $\langle u,v\rangle=\sum_{k<d}u_kv_k$ and norm $\|u\|_2=\sqrt{\langle u,u\rangle}$. Define the signal equivalence relation $x\sim z$ by $z=x$ or $z=-x$, let $Q_d=\mathbb R^d/\sim$, and write $q(x)=[x]$. Its quotient distance is
$$d_{\pm}([x],[z]):=\min\{\|x-z\|_2,\|x+z\|_2\}.$$

Use data space $Y_m=\{b:[m]\to[0,\infty)\}$ with metric
$$\rho_m(b,c)=\begin{cases}\sqrt{\sum_{k<m}(b_{k+1}-c_{k+1})^2},&m\ge1,\\0,&m=0.\end{cases}$$
The fixed relabeling $i\mapsto i-1$ identifies $[m]$-indexed data with the library's zero-based $\mathbb R^m$; $Y_0$ is a singleton. Define the real analysis map $T_\Phi:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^{[m]}$ by
$$T_\Phi x=(\langle a_i,x\rangle)_{i\in[m]}.$$
The amplitude map is $\mathcal M_\Phi([x])=(|\langle a_i,x\rangle|)_{i\in[m]}$, while the intensity map is
$$\mathcal I_\Phi([x])=(\langle a_i,x\rangle^2)_{i\in[m]}\in Y_m.$$
A finite real measurement family performs **phase retrieval** when $\mathcal I_\Phi:Q_d\to Y_m$ is injective, equivalently when the induced amplitude map is injective. The quotient distance, both induced maps, and the data metric are well defined as verified below.

The diagram records the identity $\mathcal I_\Phi\circ q=S\circ T_\Phi$, where $S(y)=(y_i^2)_{i\in[m]}$ is coordinatewise squaring. It distinguishes signed linear measurements, amplitudes, and intensities; no proof relies on the diagram.

```tikzcd
\mathbb R^d \arrow[r,"T_\Phi"] \arrow[d,"q"'] & \mathbb R^{[m]} \arrow[d,"S"] \\
Q_d \arrow[r,"\mathcal I_\Phi"'] & [0,\infty)^m
```

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$. A von Neumann natural is the set of its
predecessors, $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]), so it can be
used directly as an index set. Define

$$\mathbb{R}^n := \{\, x : x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\},$$

and write $x_k$ for $x(k)$, $k < n$. Two elements of $\mathbb{R}^n$ are equal
exactly when they agree at every $k < n$, functions being equal when they have
the same values. For $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^n$ put

$$d_1(x,y) := \sum_{k<n} |x_k - y_k|, \qquad d_2(x,y) := \sqrt{\ \sum_{k<n} (x_k - y_k)^2\ }, \qquad d_\infty(x,y) := \max\{\, |x_k - y_k| : k < n \,\}.$$

All three are well defined: the finite sums are those of [[def-finite-sum]]; the
sum of squares is nonnegative ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]], [[lem-of-square-positive]])
so it has a unique nonnegative square root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]); and
$\{|x_k - y_k| : k < n\}$ is a nonempty finite subset of $\mathbb{R}$, because
$n \ge 1$, so it has a maximum ([[lem-finite-set-has-max]], [[def-max-min]]).

**Then $d_1$, $d_2$ and $d_\infty$ are metrics on $\mathbb{R}^n$**
([[def-metric-space]]).

**Why $n \ge 1$.** For $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^0$ has exactly one element,
the empty function, and $d_1$ and $d_2$ are the empty sum $0$ and its root; but
$d_\infty$ would be the maximum of the empty set, which does not exist. The
hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is therefore not decoration, and it is carried by every
statement about $d_\infty$ in this library.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]) constructed in this
library ([[def-real-numbers]]) and carrying its order ([[def-real-order]]).

Let $X$ be a set. A **metric** on $X$ is a function
$d : X \times X \to \mathbb{R}$ such that for all $x, y, z \in X$:

- **(M1) Separation.** $d(x,y) = 0$ if and only if $x = y$.
- **(M2) Symmetry.** $d(x,y) = d(y,x)$.
- **(M3) Triangle inequality.** $d(x,z) \le d(x,y) + d(y,z)$.

A **metric space** is a pair $(X,d)$ consisting of a set $X$ and a metric $d$ on
it. The elements of $X$ are its **points** and $d(x,y)$ is the **distance** from
$x$ to $y$. When only one metric is in play we write $X$ for $(X,d)$; when
several are, the metric is always named.

**The values of a metric are real numbers.** The codomain is $\mathbb{R}$, so
$d(x,y)$ is an honest element of the complete ordered field and every
inequality above is an inequality there. No infinite value is permitted;
[[rem-metric-axiom-conventions]] records why extended metrics are not treated in
this library.

**Nonnegativity is deliberately absent from the axiom list.** Many texts add a
fourth axiom $d(x,y) \ge 0$. It is redundant: (M1), (M2) and (M3) already force
it, as [[lem-metric-nonnegativity]] proves. Nothing below assumes it before that
lemma is available.

**Pseudometric.** A **pseudometric** on $X$ is a function
$p : X \times X \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfying (M2), (M3) and the weakening

- **(M1') Reflexivity.** $p(x,x) = 0$ for every $x \in X$

of (M1). A pseudometric may therefore assign distance $0$ to two distinct
points. Every metric is a pseudometric, and a pseudometric is a metric exactly
when $p(x,y) = 0$ forces $x = y$.

**Ultrametric.** An **ultrametric** on $X$ is a metric $d$ that in addition
satisfies

- **(M3') Strong triangle inequality.** $d(x,z) \le \max\{d(x,y), d(y,z)\}$

for all $x, y, z \in X$, where the maximum is that of a two-element subset of
$\mathbb{R}$, which exists and is one of the two elements
([[def-max-min]], [[lem-finite-set-has-max]]). An **ultrametric space** is a pair
$(X,d)$ with $d$ an ultrametric.

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]). The **absolute value** of
$x \in F$ is

$$|x| \;:=\; \begin{cases} x & \text{if } x \ge 0, \\ -x & \text{if } x < 0. \end{cases}$$

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) and let $x, y \in F$, with
$|x|$ the absolute value ([[def-abs-value]]). Then

$$|x| \ge 0; \quad |x| = 0 \iff x = 0; \quad -|x| \le x \le |x|; \quad |-x| = |x|; \quad |xy| = |x|\,|y|;$$

and, for every $c > 0$, one has $|x| < c \iff -c < x < c$.

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Then every
$a \in F$ with $a \ge 0$ has a **unique** $s \in F$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^2 = a$;
we write $s = \sqrt{a}$. Consequently the positive elements of $F$ are exactly the
nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) with positive cone $P$. For
every $a \in F$ with $a \neq 0$ we have $a^2 > 0$, where $a^2 = a \cdot a$. In
particular, every nonzero square is positive.

An **ordered field** is a field $F$ ([[def-field]]) together with a subset
$P \subseteq F$, the set of **positive** elements (the *positive cone*),
satisfying:

- **(O1) Trichotomy.** For each $x \in F$, exactly one of the following holds:
  $x \in P$, or $x = 0$, or $-x \in P$.
- **(O2) Closure.** If $x, y \in P$ then $x + y \in P$ and $x \cdot y \in P$.

We write $x > 0$ for $x \in P$ (read "$x$ is positive"), and define the order by

$$a < b \;:\Longleftrightarrow\; b - a \in P, \qquad a \le b \;:\Longleftrightarrow\; a < b \text{ or } a = b.$$

Thus $a > b$ means $b < a$, and $a \ge b$ means $b \le a$. An element $x$ with
$-x \in P$ (equivalently $x < 0$) is called **negative**.

Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ and $m \in \mathbb{R}$.

- $m$ is a **maximum** (or *greatest element*) of $S$ if $m \in S$ and $s \le m$
  for every $s \in S$.
- $m$ is a **minimum** (or *least element*) of $S$ if $m \in S$ and $m \le s$
  for every $s \in S$.

A set has at most one maximum: if $m_1$ and $m_2$ are both maxima then
$m_1 \in S$ gives $m_1 \le m_2$ and $m_2 \in S$ gives $m_2 \le m_1$, so
$m_1 = m_2$ by antisymmetry of the order, which is immediate from the trichotomy
axiom of an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]], [[def-complete-ordered-field]]).
The same argument applies to minima, so we may write $\max S$ and $\min S$.

derivations.claim: The relation $\sim$ is reflexive because $x=x$, symmetric because $z=x$ implies $x=z$ and $z=-x$ implies $x=-z$, and transitive because multiplying the two signs in $z=\epsilon x$ and $w=\delta z$ gives $w=(\delta\epsilon)x$ with $\delta\epsilon\in\{1,-1\}$. Thus $Q_d$ is the quotient set and $q(x)=[x]$ is onto by the definition of equivalence classes.

If $m\ge1$, the relabeling $J:Y_m\to[0,\infty)^m$ given by $J(b)_k=b_{k+1}$ is a bijection and $\rho_m(b,c)=d_2(Jb,Jc)$, so the metric axioms of [F2] restrict to $Y_m$. If $m=0$, $Y_0$ has one element and the zero function separates its only pair and is symmetric and triangular. Hence $Y_m$ is a metric space in both cases.

Replacing representatives by $x'=\epsilon x$ and $z'=\delta z$, with $\epsilon,\delta\in\{1,-1\}$, changes the pair $(\|x-z\|_2,\|x+z\|_2)$ only by possibly interchanging its two entries, since $\|x'-z'\|_2=\|x-(\epsilon\delta)z\|_2$ and $\|x'+z'\|_2=\|x+(\epsilon\delta)z\|_2$. By [F7] the minimum is attained, so its value is independent of representatives.

Replacing $x$ by $-x$ changes each amplitude coordinate from $|\langle a_i,x\rangle|$ to $|-\langle a_i,x\rangle|=|\langle a_i,x\rangle|$, and changes each intensity coordinate from $\langle a_i,x\rangle^2$ to $(-\langle a_i,x\rangle)^2=\langle a_i,x\rangle^2$. Every intensity coordinate is nonnegative by [F6], so both maps have the stated codomain and are well defined on $Q_d$, including zero rows and the zero signal. For $m=0$ both are the unique map to the empty tuple.

Choose signs $\epsilon,\delta\in\{1,-1\}$ attaining the two minima for $d_{\pm}([x],[y])$ and $d_{\pm}([y],[z])$; [F7] ensures these minima exist, and the choices are from finite two-element sets. The Euclidean triangle inequality and sign-invariance of the norm give $d_{\pm}([x],[z])\le\|x-\epsilon\delta z\|_2\le\|x-\epsilon y\|_2+\|y-\delta z\|_2=d_{\pm}([x],[y])+d_{\pm}([y],[z])$. Thus the triangle inequality holds.

Both candidate norms are nonnegative by the nonnegative-root convention [F5], and their minimum is symmetric under interchanging $x$ and $z$. The minimum is zero exactly when $x=z$ or $x=-z$, which is exactly $[x]=[z]$ by [F1] and separation of the Euclidean metric in [F2]. Together with the triangle inequality in step 2.2, this proves that $d_{\pm}$ is a metric.

Each amplitude coordinate is nonnegative and its square is the corresponding intensity coordinate. If two nonnegative amplitudes have the same square, uniqueness of nonnegative square roots [F5] makes the amplitudes equal; conversely equal amplitudes have equal squares. Coordinatewise, the amplitude and intensity maps therefore have the same fibers and are injective simultaneously.
