citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Fix a design $d$ in a design-indexed dominated inverse experiment, with prior $\mu_0$, likelihood density $p_d(y\mid\theta)$ relative to the common sigma-finite measure $\nu$, predictive density $p_d(y)$, and posterior $\mu_d^y$ on $G_d=\{y:0<p_d(y)<\infty\}$. Let $P_d$ be the joint law of $(\theta,Y)$, so on measurable rectangles
$$P_d(A\times B)=\int_B\int_Ap_d(y\mid\theta)\,\mu_0(d\theta)\,\nu(dy),$$
let $P_{Y\mid d}(B)=\int_Bp_d(y)\,\nu(dy)$, and let $Q_d=\mu_0\otimes P_{Y\mid d}$. Then
$$\operatorname{EIG}(d)=D(P_d\|Q_d)\in[0,+\infty].$$
On $G_d$, the Radon–Nikodym density $dP_d/dQ_d$ is $p_d(y\mid\theta)/p_d(y)$ almost everywhere. The identity is valid as an extended integral: its negative part is finite, its positive part may be infinite, and no subtraction of two infinite entropies occurs.

Assume AC. Let $n,m\ge1$, $m_0\in\mathbb R^n$, and let
$C_0\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be symmetric with $v^TC_0v\ge0$ for every
$v\in\mathbb R^n$. Let
$A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$ and let
$\Gamma\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$ be symmetric positive definite, meaning
$u^T\Gamma u>0$ for every nonzero $u\in\mathbb R^m$. Suppose
$X$ and $\eta$ are independent random vectors with laws
$X\sim N_n(m_0,C_0)$ and $\eta\sim N_m(0,\Gamma)$, and set
$Y=AX+\eta$. Define $\mu_0(E)=\mathbb P(X\in E)$ for Borel
$E\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, and set
$S=AC_0A^T+\Gamma$. Then $S$ is positive definite. For each
$y\in\mathbb R^m$, define
$$ \Phi_y(x)=\tfrac12(y-Ax)^T\Gamma^{-1}(y-Ax),\qquad Z(y)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}e^{-\Phi_y(x)}\,\mu_0(dx). $$
For every $y$, $0<Z(y)<\infty$, so the normalized potential update
$$ \Pi^y(E)=\frac{\int_E e^{-\Phi_y(x)}\,\mu_0(dx)}{Z(y)} \quad(E\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R^n)) $$
is a probability measure and equals the conditional-law version obtained by
conditioning the observation model at $y$. Its Gaussian formula, defined for
every $y$, is
$$ N_n\!\left( m_0+C_0A^TS^{-1}(y-Am_0),\ C_0-C_0A^TS^{-1}AC_0 \right). $$
Let $P_Y(B)=\mathbb P(Y\in B)$ for Borel $B\subseteq\mathbb R^m$.
Conditional-law versions are unique only $P_Y$-almost surely. The displayed
mean and covariance formulas invert only $S$, not $C_0$; $C_0$ and the
posterior covariance may be singular. The prior support is
$m_0+\operatorname{Ran}(C_0)$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $m\ge1$ be finite, let $d_j\ge1$, and let
$Z_j$ for $1\le j\le m$ be mutually independent random elements of
$\mathbb R^{d_j}$. Suppose $Z_j\sim N_{d_j}(a_j,\Sigma_j)$, where each
$\Sigma_j$ is symmetric positive semidefinite. Put
$D=\sum_{j=1}^m d_j$, $Z=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_m)$,
$a=(a_1,\ldots,a_m)$, and
$\Sigma=\operatorname{diag}(\Sigma_1,\ldots,\Sigma_m)$. Then
$$Z\sim N_D(a,\Sigma).$$
No covariance block needs to be invertible.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Assume AC. Let $d\ge1$, $m\in\mathbb R^d$, and let $\Sigma$ be a real symmetric positive-definite $d\times d$ matrix. If $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$, then its law has Lebesgue density
$$f_{m,\Sigma}(x)=(2\pi)^{-d/2}\det(\Sigma)^{-1/2} \exp\!\left(-\tfrac12(x-m)^T\Sigma^{-1}(x-m)\right), \qquad x\in\mathbb R^d.$$

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be non-negative. Then there exists a unique non-negative operator
$R:V\to V$ such that

$$R^2=T.$$

For $n\ge1$ and $A,B\in M_n(R)$ over a commutative ring,
$$\det(AB)=\det(A)\det(B).$$

derivations.claim: For every nonzero $v\in\mathbb R^m$, $v^TSv=(A^Tv)^TC(A^Tv)+v^T\Gamma v>0$ because $C\succeq0$ and $\Gamma\succ0$. Thus $S\succ0$ and both observation covariances have positive determinants. The same conclusion is recorded in [F2].

By [F3], $(\theta,\eta)$ is jointly Gaussian, so its linear image $Y=A\theta+\eta$ is Gaussian with mean $Am_0$ and covariance $S$. Conditional on $\theta$, $Y$ is a translate of $\eta$ and has covariance $\Gamma$. Since both $S$ and $\Gamma$ are positive definite, [F4] gives the positive conditional and predictive densities needed in [F1].

Write $z=Y-Am_0$ and $e=Y-A\theta=\eta$. By [F4], the log likelihood ratio in [F1] is $\log\frac{p(Y\mid\theta)}{p_Y(Y)}=\frac12\log\frac{\det S}{\det\Gamma}-\frac12e^T\Gamma^{-1}e+\frac12z^TS^{-1}z$. The two quadratic terms have finite expectations: expanding each finite sum and using $\mathbb E[ee^T]=\Gamma$ and $\mathbb E[zz^T]=S$ gives $\mathbb E[e^T\Gamma^{-1}e]=\operatorname{tr}(\Gamma^{-1}\Gamma)=m$ and $\mathbb E[z^TS^{-1}z]=\operatorname{tr}(S^{-1}S)=m$. Their expectations cancel, so [F1] yields $\operatorname{EIG}=\frac12\log(\det S/\det\Gamma)$.

Let $W=\Gamma^{-1/2}$. Since $\Gamma^{1/2}W=I_m$, matrix multiplication gives $S=\Gamma^{1/2}(I_m+WACA^TW)\Gamma^{1/2}$. The middle matrix is positive definite because $ACA^T\succeq0$. By [F5], $\det S=\det(\Gamma^{1/2})^2\det(I_m+WACA^TW)=\det\Gamma\,\det(I_m+WACA^TW)$. Substitution in step 2.1 proves the formula. No inverse or determinant of $C$ was used, so singular $C$ is included; centering by $m_0$ in $z$ proves the mean cancellation.

supplier_interfaces.quote:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $n,m\ge1$, let $m_0\in\mathbb R^n$, let $C\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be symmetric positive semidefinite, let $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$, and let $\Gamma\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$ be symmetric positive definite. Suppose $\theta\sim N_n(m_0,C)$ and $\eta\sim N_m(0,\Gamma)$ are independent, and observe $Y=A\theta+\eta$. With $S=ACA^T+\Gamma$, the expected information gain of this experiment is
$$\operatorname{EIG}=\frac12\log\det\!\left(I_m+\Gamma^{-1/2}ACA^T\Gamma^{-1/2}\right).$$
Here $\Gamma^{-1/2}$ is the inverse of the unique symmetric positive-definite square root of $\Gamma$, and $\log$ is the natural logarithm. The matrix inside the log determinant is positive definite. This formula permits singular $C$ and never uses differential entropy of $\theta$; the mean $m_0$ cancels. Noise depending on $\theta$ is outside the hypotheses and need not satisfy the formula.
supplier_interfaces.use: The exact linear-Gaussian EIG is a log determinant, including singular state covariance.

supplier_interfaces.quote:
Let $D$ be a finite set of design indices, let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ and $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ be measurable spaces, let $\mu_0$ be a probability measure on $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$, and let $\nu$ be a sigma-finite measure on $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$. For each $d\in D$, let $Q_d$ be a probability kernel from $\Theta$ to $\mathsf Y$ with a specified nonnegative jointly measurable density $p_d(y\mid\theta)$ relative to $\nu$, so
$$Q_d(\theta,B)=\int_B p_d(y\mid\theta)\,\nu(dy)\qquad(\theta\in\Theta,\ B\in\mathcal Y).$$
Define the prior-predictive density $p_d(y)=\int_\Theta p_d(y\mid\theta)\,\mu_0(d\theta)$. For each datum $y$ with $0<p_d(y)<\infty$, define the posterior probability measure
$$\mu_d^y(A)=\frac{\int_A p_d(y\mid\theta)\,\mu_0(d\theta)}{p_d(y)}\qquad(A\in\mathcal T).$$
The dominated-kernel Bayes formula makes $p_d\,d\nu$ the observation law and identifies $\mu_d^y$ as a posterior version on these positive finite evidence fibers. No posterior formula is assigned on fibers with zero or infinite evidence; their prior-predictive probability is zero.
supplier_interfaces.use: Each candidate's Gaussian model is a singleton design in the dominated-experiment convention.

supplier_interfaces.quote:
Assume the Axiom of Choice for the library's Kullback–Leibler divergence convention. For a design $d$ in a design-indexed dominated inverse experiment, let $G_d=\{y:0<p_d(y)<\infty\}$ be its positive finite evidence fibers. The **expected information gain** is
$$\operatorname{EIG}(d):=\int_{G_d}D(\mu_d^y\|\mu_0)\,p_d(y)\,\nu(dy)\in[0,+\infty],$$
where the integrand is defined to be zero outside $G_d$. Here $D(P\|Q)$ is the directional Kullback–Leibler divergence of probability measures, with natural logarithms.
supplier_interfaces.use: EIG is the extended prior-predictive posterior-to-prior KL integral.

supplier_interfaces.quote:
Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be non-negative. Then there exists a unique non-negative operator

$$R^2=T.$$
supplier_interfaces.use: A positive-semidefinite prior covariance has a positive-semidefinite square root for the Gram representation.

supplier_interfaces.quote:
Let $n\ge 1$ and $A\in M_n(\mathbb C)$; over $\mathbb R$ the same definition uses transpose
instead of conjugate transpose.

The matrix $A$ is **Hermitian positive definite** if $A=A^*$ and

$$x^*Ax>0$$for every nonzero vector $x\in \mathbb C^n$. A **Cholesky factorisation with positive diagonal** of $A$ is a factorisation$$A=LL^*,$$

where $L$ is lower triangular and every diagonal entry of $L$ is a positive real
number.

The Hermitian terminology matches
[[def-sesquilinear-and-hermitian-forms-over-a-field-with-involution]], and the
triangular terminology matches
[[def-triangular-and-diagonal-matrices-over-a-commutative-ring]].
supplier_interfaces.use: Cholesky factors are lower triangular with positive diagonal.

supplier_interfaces.quote:
Let $n\ge 1$ and let $A\in M_n(\mathbb C)$, with the real case obtained by
restricting scalars to $\mathbb R$. Then the following are equivalent:

1. $A$ has a Cholesky factorisation $A=LL^*$ with $L$ lower triangular and
   positive real diagonal.
2. $A$ is Hermitian positive definite.

When these conditions hold, the factor $L$ is unique.
supplier_interfaces.use: Every symmetric positive-definite matrix has a unique positive-diagonal Cholesky factor.

supplier_interfaces.quote:
Let $A\in M_n(\mathbb C)$ be Hermitian positive definite and let
$A=LL^*$ be its Cholesky factorisation with positive diagonal.

1. For every right-hand side $b\in\mathbb C^n$, the system $Ax=b$ is solved by
   first solving $Ly=b$ and then solving $L^*x=y$.
2. The two triangular solves cost $2n^2+O(n)$ scalar operations altogether, and
   the dense Cholesky factorisation costs
   $$\frac{1}{3}n^3+O(n^2)$$
   scalar operations, compared with
   $$\frac{2}{3}n^3+O(n^2)$$
   for dense LU factorisation without exploiting symmetry.
supplier_interfaces.use: Cholesky triangular solves evaluate positive-definite systems without forming an inverse.

supplier_interfaces.quote:
If $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(R)$ is upper or lower triangular over a commutative ring, with $n\ge1$, then
$$\det(A)=\prod_{i<n}a_{ii}.$$
supplier_interfaces.use: The determinant of a triangular matrix is the product of its diagonal entries.

supplier_interfaces.quote:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $n\ge1$, and let $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(R)$. Its **determinant** is
$$\det(A):=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\prod_{i<n}a_{\sigma(i),i}.$$
The sum is finite because $S_n$ has $n!$ elements. The product is taken in $R$, so the signs $1$ and $-1$ act through the ring identities. The formula uses columns indexed by $i<n$ and rows indexed by $\sigma(i)$.

When $A$ is real, $|\det A|$ means the ordinary real absolute value of its real determinant. It is not alternate notation for the determinant itself.
supplier_interfaces.use: The log-determinant score uses the usual determinant of a finite square matrix.

supplier_interfaces.quote:
For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.
supplier_interfaces.use: The logarithm in the score is the natural logarithm.

supplier_interfaces.quote:
Input a Hermitian positive-definite matrix $A\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$, $n\ge1$, whose real and imaginary components are in the floating-point system, using the convention of [[def-cholesky-factorisation-with-positive-diagonal]]; real matrices are included. Initialize every entry of $\widehat L$ to zero. Process columns $j=1,\ldots,n$ in increasing order. For the diagonal, initialize $s=0$ and, for $k=1,\ldots,j-1$ in increasing order, compute
$$r_k=\operatorname{fl}(\Re(\widehat l_{jk})^2),\quad t_k=\operatorname{fl}(\Im(\widehat l_{jk})^2),\quad q_k=\operatorname{fl}(r_k+t_k),\quad s=\operatorname{fl}(s+q_k),$$
in that order. Then compute $p_j=\operatorname{fl}(a_{jj}-s)$. If an operation fails, or if $p_j$ is not positive and normal, return `failure` with pivot $j$ and the first failing operation location. Otherwise compute $\widehat l_{jj}=\operatorname{fl}(\sqrt{p_j})$; if it is not positive and normal, return `failure` at pivot $j$.

For each $i=j+1,\ldots,n$ in increasing order, initialize the complex accumulator $c_{ij}=0$. For $k=1,\ldots,j-1$ in increasing order, compute the complex product $w_{ik}=\widehat l_{ik}\overline{\widehat l_{jk}}$ using exactly the six real operations of the complex-product convention in [[def-operationwise-real-complex-floating-point-model-with-sqrt-and-fma]], then update
$$\Re(c_{ij})\gets\operatorname{fl}(\Re(c_{ij})+\Re(w_{ik})),\qquad \Im(c_{ij})\gets\operatorname{fl}(\Im(c_{ij})+\Im(w_{ik})).$$
After this dot product, compute $r_{ij}=a_{ij}-c_{ij}$ by one rounded real subtraction for each component, then compute each component of $\widehat l_{ij}=r_{ij}/\widehat l_{jj}$ by one rounded real division. The empty dot product is zero. On any failure return `failure` with pivot $j$ and its first failing operation location (stage, column, row, inner index, component, and operation where applicable), with the diagonal and row loops ordered as stated. If all columns finish, return `success(\widehat L)`. By [[thm-cholesky-factorisation-exists-iff-hermitian-positive-definite-and-is-unique]], exact positive definiteness ensures an exact factor exists, but does not ensure the rounded algorithm succeeds.
supplier_interfaces.use: The floating-point factorization reports success or its first pivot/operation failure.

supplier_interfaces.quote:
Let $R\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be upper triangular with stored floating-point entries and nonzero diagonal, and let $y\in\mathbb R^n$ have stored floating-point entries, where $n\ge1$ and $(n+3)u<1$. Use the operationwise arithmetic model of [[def-operationwise-real-complex-floating-point-model-with-sqrt-and-fma]] at unit roundoff $u$. Compute descending substitution by the sequential rounded dot $s_i=\operatorname{fl}(\sum_{j>i}R_{ij}\widehat x_j)$ (empty sum zero), $t_i=\operatorname{fl}(y_i-s_i)$, and $\widehat x_i=\operatorname{fl}(t_i/R_{ii})$. Assume each exact intermediate is zero or normal and each rounded result is finite, so every operation succeeds under that model. Then there is upper triangular $\Delta R$ with
$$(R+\Delta R)\widehat x=y,\qquad |\Delta R|\le\gamma_{n+3}|R|,\qquad \|\Delta R\|_F\le\gamma_{n+3}\|R\|_F.$$
In particular $\widehat x=0$ forces $y=0$. Forward substitution has the transposed conclusion.
supplier_interfaces.use: Successful rounded triangular solves have the stated componentwise backward error.

supplier_interfaces.quote:
Let $n\ge1$ and let $A=A^*$ be positive definite in $\mathbb C^{n\times n}$. Suppose the rounded Cholesky algorithm succeeds with $\widehat L$. Put $m=20n+20$ and $g=\gamma_m=\frac{m u}{1-m u}$; assume $m u<1/5$. For $E=\widehat L\widehat L^*-A$, which is Hermitian, and with $|M|$ denoting entrywise absolute value for matrices,
$$|E|\le100g\,|\widehat L|\,|\widehat L|^*\quad\hbox{entrywise},\qquad \|E\|_F\le100g\|\widehat L\|_F^2,\qquad \|E\|_2\le100g\|\widehat L\|_F^2.$$
Thus $c_n(u)u=\frac{100m u}{1-m u}$. If also $100\sqrt n\,g\le1/2$, then
$$\|E\|_F\le200\sqrt n\,g\|A\|_F,\qquad \|E\|_2\le200\sqrt n\,g\|A\|_F.$$
These bounds apply on success only; positive definiteness does not guarantee rounded success.
supplier_interfaces.use: Successful rounded Cholesky gives the stated factorization residual bounds.

supplier_interfaces.quote:
Use the finite observation designs of [[def-nonlinear-experimental-design-and-local-identifiability]]. Suppose uniformly over $x\in\mathcal X$ that $\|J_x\|_2\le K$, $\|J_{h,x}-J_x\|_2\le\eta$, and $\|W_x\|_2\le w$, where $K,\eta,w\ge0$. For every approximate design $\xi$,
$$\|M_h(\xi)-M(\xi)\|_2\le\delta:=w(2K\eta+\eta^2),$$
where $M_h(\xi)=\sum_x\xi_xJ_{h,x}^TW_xJ_{h,x}$. If $M(\xi)$ satisfies $v^TM(\xi)v\ge\alpha\|v\|_2^2$ for every $v$ with some $\alpha>\delta$, then
$$v^TM_h(\xi)v\ge(\alpha-\delta)\|v\|_2^2$$
for every $v$, so the computed information matrix remains positive definite.
supplier_interfaces.use: Uniform factor and solve errors imply the stated information-matrix perturbation bound.

supplier_interfaces.quote:
Let $p\ge1$, let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ be open, and let $\mathcal X$ be a finite nonempty set of experimental conditions. For each $x\in\mathcal X$, let $q_x\ge1$, let $F_x:\Theta\to\mathbb R^{q_x}$ be $C^1$ in the sense of [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]], and let $W_x\in\mathbb R^{q_x\times q_x}$ be a symmetric positive-definite weight matrix, meaning $z^T W_x z>0$ for every nonzero $z\in\mathbb R^{q_x}$.

An **approximate design** is a function $\xi:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$ with $\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}\xi_x=1$, as in [[def-approximate-linear-model-design-and-optimality-criteria]]. Its support is $\operatorname{supp}(\xi)=\{x\in\mathcal X:\xi_x>0\}$. Define the joint observation map by
$$F_\xi(\theta)=(F_x(\theta))_{x\in\operatorname{supp}(\xi)},$$
where the finite product is ordered by any fixed listing of $\operatorname{supp}(\xi)$. Its **stacked sensitivity Jacobian** at $\theta$ is the vertical concatenation $J_\xi(\theta)$ of the matrices $J_x(\theta)=DF_x(\theta)$ for $x\in\operatorname{supp}(\xi)$. The associated **weighted information matrix** is
$$M_\theta(\xi)=\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}\xi_x J_x(\theta)^T W_x J_x(\theta).$$
The matrix is symmetric positive semidefinite because each summand has nonnegative quadratic form.

Because the support is finite, $F_\xi$ is $C^1$ with derivative $J_\xi(\theta)$: the finite collection of component first-order remainders has a stacked Euclidean norm that is still $o(\|h\|_2)$, and the stacked derivative is continuous because each $DF_x$ is continuous.

For a fixed design $\xi$, the observation map is **locally identifiable at $\theta_0\in\Theta$** if it is injective on some open neighborhood of $\theta_0$ in $\Theta$. It is **globally identifiable on $\Theta$** if it is injective on all of $\Theta$. A matrix $J:\mathbb R^p\to\mathbb R^m$ has full column rank when $Jv=0$ implies $v=0$. Its smallest singular value is $\sigma_{\min}(J)=\inf_{\|v\|_2=1}\|Jv\|_2$; thus $\sigma_{\min}(J)\ge\mu$ means $\|Jv\|_2\ge\mu\|v\|_2$ for every $v$.
supplier_interfaces.use: A one-point approximate design with a linear sensitivity map and weight matrix $W=I$ satisfies the finite-design setting.

supplier_interfaces.quote:
Let $p\ge1$ and let $A,B\in\mathbb R^{p\times p}$ be symmetric. Put $E=B-A$ and $A_t=(1-t)A+tB$ for $0\le t\le1$. Suppose there is $\alpha>0$ such that $v^T A_t v\ge\alpha\|v\|_2^2$ for every $v\in\mathbb R^p$ and every $t\in[0,1]$. Then $A_t$ is positive definite and
$$|\log\det B-\log\det A|\le\frac{p\|E\|_2}{\alpha}.$$
supplier_interfaces.use: A positive eigenvalue floor controls log-determinant perturbation.

supplier_interfaces.quote:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $n,m\ge1$, let $m_0\in\mathbb R^n$, let $C\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be symmetric positive semidefinite, let $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$, and let $\Gamma\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$ be symmetric positive definite. Suppose $\theta\sim N_n(m_0,C)$ and $\eta\sim N_m(0,\Gamma)$ are independent, and observe $Y=A\theta+\eta$. With $S=ACA^T+\Gamma$, the expected information gain of this experiment is
$$\operatorname{EIG}=\frac12\log\det\!\left(I_m+\Gamma^{-1/2}ACA^T\Gamma^{-1/2}\right).$$
Here $\Gamma^{-1/2}$ is the inverse of the unique symmetric positive-definite square root of $\Gamma$, and $\log$ is the natural logarithm. The matrix inside the log determinant is positive definite. This formula permits singular $C$ and never uses differential entropy of $\theta$; the mean $m_0$ cancels. Noise depending on $\theta$ is outside the hypotheses and need not satisfy the formula.
supplier_interfaces.use: The exact log-determinant formula applies to the linear-Gaussian model stated there.

supplier_interfaces.quote:

Assume each exact intermediate is zero or normal and each rounded result is finite, so every operation succeeds under that model. Then there is upper triangular $\Delta R$ with
$$(R+\Delta R)\widehat x=y,\qquad |\Delta R|\le\gamma_{n+3}|R|,\qquad \|\Delta R\|_F\le\gamma_{n+3}\|R\|_F.$$
In particular $\widehat x=0$ forces $y=0$. Forward substitution has the transposed conclusion.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC for the library KL/EIG convention. Input a prior covariance $C\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ with $n\ge1$ symmetric positive semidefinite, a finite ordered list of raw candidate records $(A_d,\Gamma_d,c_d)_{d=1}^N$, and a real budget $B$. Each stored $A_d$ and $\Gamma_d$ is a finite real matrix, with its dimensions part of the input, and each declared cost $c_d$ is finite and real. A candidate is dimension-valid when $A_d$ has at least one row and exactly $n$ columns and $\Gamma_d$ is a symmetric square matrix whose dimension equals the row count of $A_d$; for a dimension-valid candidate write that common positive dimension as $m_d$. The prior mean is immaterial to the score.

Interpret each admissible candidate $d$ (dimension-valid with $\Gamma_d$ positive definite) as a separate singleton-design dominated inverse experiment with prior $\theta\sim N_n(m_0,C)$ for any $m_0\in\mathbb R^n$, observation space $\mathbb R^{m_d}$ with Lebesgue measure, and observation $Y_d=A_d\theta+\eta_d$, where $\eta_d\sim N_{m_d}(0,\Gamma_d)$ is independent of $\theta$. Here $\operatorname{EIG}(d)$ is the expected information gain from the preceding definition for that singleton experiment. Different candidates may have different $m_d$ because each is evaluated on its own observation space. The score is independent of $m_0$.

In exact-real arithmetic, process the list in order. Mark a candidate inadmissible if it is not dimension-valid or if its noise covariance $\Gamma_d$ is not positive definite. For each remaining candidate with $c_d\le B$, compute the Cholesky factor $\Gamma_d=L_dL_d^T$ with positive diagonal, solve $L_dV_d=A_d$ by forward substitution, and form the symmetric positive-semidefinite matrix $Z_d=V_dCV_d^T$. Set $H_d=I_{m_d}+Z_d$ and compute its Cholesky factor $H_d=R_dR_d^T$. Assign the utility
$$U_d=\sum_{j=1}^{m_d}\log (R_d)_{jj}-c_d=\tfrac12\log\det(H_d)-c_d.$$
Initialize the stored best candidate as unset. For each admissible candidate meeting the budget, set it if unset; otherwise replace it exactly when the new utility is strictly greater than the stored utility. After the scan, return the stored candidate. This update rule preserves the first index in any tie. If every candidate is inadmissible, return `all-inadmissible`; if at least one candidate is admissible but none meets the budget, return `budget-exhausted`.

In floating-point mode, use the failure-aware Cholesky and triangular-solve procedures. Certify the positive-definiteness status of every dimension-valid $\Gamma_d$; a failed rounded factorization alone is not evidence that $\Gamma_d$ is not positive definite. If any candidate's admissibility cannot be certified, return `numerically-unresolved`. Once admissibility is certified, return `all-inadmissible` if none is admissible and `budget-exhausted` if none meets the budget. Otherwise require a certified interval $[\widehat U_d-\varepsilon_d,\widehat U_d+\varepsilon_d]$ for each feasible candidate's exact utility. One admissible score certificate supplies a positive-semidefinite computed matrix $\widehat Z_d$ with $\|\widehat Z_d-Z_d\|_2\le\delta_d$, a successful computed Cholesky factor $\widehat R_d$ with $\|\widehat R_d\widehat R_d^T-(I+\widehat Z_d)\|_2\le\rho_d<1$, and a remaining log/summation/cost evaluation radius $\lambda_d$. It sets
$$\varepsilon_d=\frac{m_d}{2}\left(\delta_d+\frac{\rho_d}{1-\rho_d}\right)+\lambda_d.$$
The matrix radius may be certified by the published information-matrix perturbation bound in its single-design, unit-weight $W=I$ case. Factor $C$ as $C^{1/2}C^{1/2}$ and set $J_d=C^{1/2}V_d^T$; for a computed solve $\widehat V_d$, set $\widehat J_d=C^{1/2}\widehat V_d^T$. Then $Z_d=J_d^TJ_d$ and $\widehat Z_d=\widehat J_d^T\widehat J_d$. The lemma's finite-design hypotheses hold for the one-point sensitivity maps $z\mapsto J_dz$ and $z\mapsto\widehat J_dz$ on $\mathbb R^{m_d}$, with weight $W=I$ and design weight $1$. If $\|J_d\|_2\le K_d$ and $\|\widehat J_d-J_d\|_2\le\eta_d$, then $\delta_d$ may be any verified bound at least $2K_d\eta_d+\eta_d^2$, enlarged by any separate matrix-formation residual. A rounded triangular-solve backward-error bound must be converted to the required forward matrix bound using verified conditioning; any rounding in the covariance-root multiply is included in $\eta_d$ or the formation residual. The published rounded-Cholesky and log-determinant perturbation results supply their stated components under their own hypotheses. A missing or failed certificate returns `numerically-unresolved` and no optimum claim. Given a comparison tolerance $\tau\ge0$, compute $M=\max_{d\text{ feasible}}\widehat U_d$ and return the first feasible candidate with $\widehat U_d\ge M-\tau$. Its true utility gap is at most $\tau+2\max_d\varepsilon_d$. If the selected candidate's lower interval endpoint exceeds every earlier candidate's upper endpoint and is at least every later candidate's upper endpoint, return it as the certified first exact maximizer. The algorithm makes no bit-complexity claim for exact-real comparisons.

Let $n\ge 1$ and let $A\in M_n(\mathbb C)$, with the real case obtained by
restricting scalars to $\mathbb R$. Then the following are equivalent:

1. $A$ has a Cholesky factorisation $A=LL^*$ with $L$ lower triangular and
   positive real diagonal.
2. $A$ is Hermitian positive definite.

When these conditions hold, the factor $L$ is unique.

Let $A\in M_n(\mathbb C)$ be Hermitian positive definite and let
$A=LL^*$ be its Cholesky factorisation with positive diagonal.

1. For every right-hand side $b\in\mathbb C^n$, the system $Ax=b$ is solved by
   first solving $Ly=b$ and then solving $L^*x=y$.
2. The two triangular solves cost $2n^2+O(n)$ scalar operations altogether, and
   the dense Cholesky factorisation costs
   $$\frac{1}{3}n^3+O(n^2)$$
   scalar operations, compared with
   $$\frac{2}{3}n^3+O(n^2)$$
   for dense LU factorisation without exploiting symmetry.

If $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(R)$ is upper or lower triangular over a commutative ring, with $n\ge1$, then
$$\det(A)=\prod_{i<n}a_{ii}.$$

For $n\ge1$ and $A,B\in M_n(R)$ over a commutative ring,
$$\det(AB)=\det(A)\det(B).$$

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be non-negative. Then there exists a unique non-negative operator
$R:V\to V$ such that

$$R^2=T.$$

Its smallest singular value is $\sigma_{\min}(J)=\inf_{\|v\|_2=1}\|Jv\|_2$; thus $\sigma_{\min}(J)\ge\mu$ means $\|Jv\|_2\ge\mu\|v\|_2$ for every $v$.

Use the finite observation designs of [[def-nonlinear-experimental-design-and-local-identifiability]]. Suppose uniformly over $x\in\mathcal X$ that $\|J_x\|_2\le K$, $\|J_{h,x}-J_x\|_2\le\eta$, and $\|W_x\|_2\le w$, where $K,\eta,w\ge0$. For every approximate design $\xi$,

where $M_h(\xi)=\sum_x\xi_xJ_{h,x}^TW_xJ_{h,x}$. If $M(\xi)$ satisfies $v^TM(\xi)v\ge\alpha\|v\|_2^2$ for every $v$ with some $\alpha>\delta$, then

Let $p\ge1$ and let $A,B\in\mathbb R^{p\times p}$ be symmetric. Put $E=B-A$ and $A_t=(1-t)A+tB$ for $0\le t\le1$. Suppose there is $\alpha>0$ such that $v^T A_t v\ge\alpha\|v\|_2^2$ for every $v\in\mathbb R^p$ and every $t\in[0,1]$. Then $A_t$ is positive definite and
$$|\log\det B-\log\det A|\le\frac{p\|E\|_2}{\alpha}.$$

Let $n\ge1$ and let $A=A^*$ be positive definite in $\mathbb C^{n\times n}$. Suppose the rounded Cholesky algorithm succeeds with $\widehat L$. Put $m=20n+20$ and $g=\gamma_m=\frac{m u}{1-m u}$; assume $m u<1/5$. For $E=\widehat L\widehat L^*-A$, which is Hermitian, and with $|M|$ denoting entrywise absolute value for matrices,

In particular $\widehat x=0$ forces $y=0$. Forward substitution has the transposed conclusion.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

derivations.claim: For a valid candidate, $\Gamma_d=L_dL_d^T$ and $V_d=L_d^{-1}A_d$, so $Z_d=V_dCV_d^T$ is symmetric positive semidefinite. Hence $H_d=I_{m_d}+Z_d$ is positive definite and has the Cholesky factor used by the exact algorithm.

Put $Q_d=A_dCA_d^T$ and $W_d=\Gamma_d^{-1/2}$. The square-root identity [F5] gives $\Gamma_d+Q_d=\Gamma_d^{1/2}(I_{m_d}+W_dQ_dW_d)\Gamma_d^{1/2}$. By [F4], $\det(\Gamma_d+Q_d)=\det(\Gamma_d^{1/2})^2\det(I_{m_d}+W_dQ_dW_d)=\det(\Gamma_d)\det(I_{m_d}+W_dQ_dW_d)$. Also step 1.1 gives $\Gamma_d+Q_d=L_dH_dL_d^T$, so [F3]–[F4] give $\det(\Gamma_d+Q_d)=\det(\Gamma_d)\det(H_d)$ with $\det(\Gamma_d)=(\det L_d)^2>0$. Dividing proves $\det(I_{m_d}+W_dQ_dW_d)=\det(H_d)$. By [F2], the exact EIG is $\tfrac12\log\det(H_d)$. By [F3], $\det(H_d)=\det(R_dR_d^T)=(\prod_j(R_d)_{jj})^2$; all Cholesky diagonal entries are positive, so [F10] gives $\tfrac12\log\det(H_d)=\sum_j\log(R_d)_{jj}$. Thus the algorithm's exact score equals $U_d$.

For the exact scan, after the first feasible candidate the stored candidate is the first maximum of that one-element prefix. When the next candidate is processed, [F1] says a strictly larger score replaces it; an equal or smaller score leaves it in place, preserving the earliest maximizing index. Repeating this finite comparison through the ordered feasible list proves the final stored candidate is the first global maximizer. The validity and budget tests likewise make `all-inadmissible` and `budget-exhausted` exactly the two stated empty-feasible-set cases.

In floating-point mode, when $\widehat Z_d=\widehat J_d^T\widehat J_d$ and $Z_d=J_d^TJ_d$, [F6] supplies $\delta_d\ge2K_d\eta_d+\eta_d^2$ from certified bounds $\|J_d\|_2\le K_d$ and $\|\widehat J_d-J_d\|_2\le\eta_d$; any rounded matrix-formation residual is included in the supplied $\delta_d$. Both $I+Z_d$ and $I+\widehat Z_d$ have eigenvalues at least $1$, and every matrix on their segment does too. Applying [F7] gives $|\log\det(I+\widehat Z_d)-\log\det(I+Z_d)|\le m_d\delta_d$.

Put $E_d=\widehat R_d\widehat R_d^T-(I+\widehat Z_d)$. Every matrix $I+\widehat Z_d+tE_d$ has quadratic form at least $(1-t\rho_d)\|v\|_2^2\ge(1-\rho_d)\|v\|_2^2$, since $I+\widehat Z_d\succeq I$ and $\|E_d\|_2\le\rho_d<1$. Applying [F7] on this segment yields $|\log\det(\widehat R_d\widehat R_d^T)-\log\det(I+\widehat Z_d)|\le m_d\rho_d/(1-\rho_d)$. Under the successful rounded-factorization hypotheses, [F8] provides such a residual radius. [F9] supplies only a backward-error constraint for triangular solves; any forward matrix error used in $\delta_d$ must additionally account for conditioning.

The certificate's $\lambda_d$ bounds the remaining rounded log, summation, and cost evaluation. Combining it with steps 3.1–3.2, the log-determinant perturbation [F7], and the factor $1/2$ in the EIG formula gives $|\widehat U_d-U_d|\le\varepsilon_d$.

Let $d^*$ maximize exact utility and let $\widehat d$ be the selected computed $\tau$-maximizer. By [F1] and the hypothesis, $\widehat U_{\widehat d}\ge\max_d\widehat U_d-\tau$. Then $U_{d^*}\le\widehat U_{d^*}+\varepsilon_{d^*}\le\max_d\widehat U_d+\varepsilon_{d^*}$, while $U_{\widehat d}\ge\widehat U_{\widehat d}-\varepsilon_{\widehat d}\ge\max_d\widehat U_d-\tau-\varepsilon_{\widehat d}$. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Fix a design $d$ in a design-indexed dominated inverse experiment, with prior $\mu_0$, likelihood density $p_d(y\mid\theta)$ relative to the common sigma-finite measure $\nu$, predictive density $p_d(y)$, and posterior $\mu_d^y$ on $G_d=\{y:0<p_d(y)<\infty\}$. Let $P_d$ be the joint law of $(\theta,Y)$, so on measurable rectangles
$$P_d(A\times B)=\int_B\int_Ap_d(y\mid\theta)\,\mu_0(d\theta)\,\nu(dy),$$
let $P_{Y\mid d}(B)=\int_Bp_d(y)\,\nu(dy)$, and let $Q_d=\mu_0\otimes P_{Y\mid d}$. Then
$$\operatorname{EIG}(d)=D(P_d\|Q_d)\in[0,+\infty].$$
On $G_d$, the Radon–Nikodym density $dP_d/dQ_d$ is $p_d(y\mid\theta)/p_d(y)$ almost everywhere. The identity is valid as an extended integral: its negative part is finite, its positive part may be infinite, and no subtraction of two infinite entropies occurs.

Assume the Axiom of Choice for the library's Kullback–Leibler divergence convention. For a design $d$ in a design-indexed dominated inverse experiment, let $G_d=\{y:0<p_d(y)<\infty\}$ be its positive finite evidence fibers. The **expected information gain** is
$$\operatorname{EIG}(d):=\int_{G_d}D(\mu_d^y\|\mu_0)\,p_d(y)\,\nu(dy)\in[0,+\infty],$$
where the integrand is defined to be zero outside $G_d$. Here $D(P\|Q)$ is the directional Kullback–Leibler divergence of probability measures, with natural logarithms.

Assume AC and use the directional convention of
[[def-kullback-leibler-divergence]]. For probability measures $P,Q$ on one
measurable space, $D(P\|Q)\ge0$, and $D(P\|Q)=0$ if and only if $P=Q$.

There is also the following normalized-density identity. Let
$(\mathsf X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a sigma-finite measure space: it is a set
with a sigma-algebra and measure ([[def-measure-space]]), and there is a
countable measurable cover by sets of finite $\mu$-measure
([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]). Let
$\gamma:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ be a finite-valued measurable function with
$Z:=\int\gamma\,d\mu\in(0,\infty)$, and put $\pi=\gamma/Z$. Let
$q:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ be a finite-valued measurable probability density,
so $\int q\,d\mu=1$, and suppose $q=0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on
$\{\gamma=0\}$. Assume
$$\int q\bigl(|\log\gamma|+|\log q|\bigr)\,d\mu<\infty,$$
where each term with $q=0$ is defined to be zero. Then
$$\log Z =\int q(\log\gamma-\log q)\,d\mu +D(q\,\mu\|\pi\,\mu).$$
In particular, the first integral is at most $\log Z$. This identity concerns
normalized densities only; it does not assert posterior existence for an
unspecified statistical model.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

Let $P,Q$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
([[def-probability-measure]]). Absolute continuity $P\ll Q$ has the convention
of [[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]]. If
$P\not\ll Q$, define $D(P\|Q)=+\infty$. If $P\ll Q$, assume AC
([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) as in [[def-likelihood-ratio-as-rn-derivative]] and
let $r=dP/dQ$ be a finite-valued nonnegative measurable representative of its
Radon–Nikodym class; such a representative exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].
On $\{r=0\}$ set $\ell=0$, and on $\{r>0\}$ set $\ell=\log r$. This
function is measurable: for $a\ge0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r>\exp(a)\}$, and for
$a<0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r=0\}\cup\{r>\exp(a)\}$, by the inverse and
monotonicity properties of the natural logarithm
([[def-natural-logarithm]], [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]). These are
measurable sets by [[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Since
$P(\{r=0\})=\int_{\{r=0\}}r\,dQ=0$ by
[[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]], the value chosen there does not
affect $\int\ell\,dP$. Define
$$D(P\|Q):=\int \ell\,dP,$$
where $\log$ is the natural logarithm ([[def-natural-logarithm]]).

The definition is independent of the representative: two representatives
agree $Q$-almost everywhere, hence $P$-almost everywhere. Put
$$\psi(0):=0,\qquad \psi(t):=t\log t\quad(t>0).$$
The function $\psi$ is continuous at zero: for $s\ge1$,
$$0\le \frac{\log s}{s}=\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{u}\le\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{\sqrt u}\le\frac2{\sqrt s}.$$
Thus $t\log t\to0$ as $t\downarrow0$; here $L=\log$ by
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]] and
[[def-integral-logarithm]]. On $(0,\infty)$, $\psi$ is a product of continuous
functions by [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and
[[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], so $\psi$ is continuous on
$[0,\infty)$ and $\psi(r)$ is measurable by
[[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Its signed integral is
defined by the positive and negative parts
([[def-positive-and-negative-parts-of-a-function]],
[[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]).

For $0<t\le1$, the function $-t\log t$ has derivative $-\log t-1$ and
maximum $1/e$ at $t=1/e$: $e=\exp(1)>1$ by
[[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]] and
[[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]], $1/e=\exp(-1)$ by
[[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], and $\log(1/e)=-1$ by
[[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and the inverse definition. The mean value
theorem gives increase before and decrease after this point
([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-integral-logarithm-derivative-and-normalisation]],
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]], [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]).
At $t=0$ the negative part is zero. Since $Q$ is a probability measure,
$$\int \psi(r)^-\,dQ\le\frac1e.$$
The change-of-measure identity of [[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]],
applied to $\ell^-$ gives $\int\ell^-\,dP=\int\psi(r)^-\,dQ\le1/e$,
so $\int\ell\,dP$ is well-defined; applying it to both positive and negative
parts gives
$$D(P\|Q)=\int\ell\,dP=\int\psi(r)\,dQ=\int r\log r\,dQ,$$
with $0\log0:=0$ and a finite negative part. Therefore the extended integral
is well-defined without an $\infty-\infty$ ambiguity.

This convention is directional: the first argument must be absolutely
continuous with respect to the second for the integral formula to apply.

Let $S\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be an embedded smooth submanifold. Using the
Euclidean inner product, define its **orthogonal normal bundle** by
$$ N^\perp S:=\{(p,v)\in S\times\mathbb R^m:v\perp T_pS\}. $$
Local slice charts and orthogonal projection onto $T_pS$ give this set its
standard smooth rank-$(m-\dim S)$ vector-bundle structure. The **normal
addition map** is
$$ E:N^\perp S\to\mathbb R^m,\qquad E(p,v):=p+v. $$
It restricts on the zero section to the inclusion $S\hookrightarrow\mathbb R^m$
and is the basic model map used to build Euclidean tubular neighbourhoods.

Let $S\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be an embedded smooth submanifold, and let
$E:N^\perp S\to\mathbb R^m$ be its normal addition map. For every $p\in S$ the
differential
$$ dE_{(p,0)}:T_{(p,0)}(N^\perp S)\to T_p\mathbb R^m\cong\mathbb R^m $$
is an isomorphism. Consequently, $E$ is a local diffeomorphism at every point
of the zero section.

Let $(X,d)$ be a compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $\mathcal{U}$ be an open cover of $X$. Then there
is a real $\delta > 0$, a **Lebesgue number** for $\mathcal{U}$, such that every
nonempty $A \subseteq X$ with $\operatorname{diam}(A) < \delta$
([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]) satisfies $A \subseteq U$ for some
$U \in \mathcal{U}$.

Diameters of nonempty subsets of $X$ are defined because a compact space is
bounded ([[thm-compact-subset-is-closed-and-bounded]]) and a subset of a bounded
set is bounded. No choice principle is used.

Let $A\subseteq X$ carry the subspace topology, and let $i:A\hookrightarrow X$ be the inclusion ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]).

A continuous map $r:X\to A$ is a **retraction of $X$ onto $A$** if

$$r\circ i=\operatorname{id}_A,$$

equivalently, if $r(a)=a$ for every $a\in A$. When such an $r$ exists, $A$ is a **retract** of $X$.

The subspace $A$ is a **deformation retract** of $X$ if there are a retraction $r:X\to A$ and a homotopy

$$H:\operatorname{id}_X\simeq_A i\circ r.$$

Thus $H(x,0)=x$, $H(x,1)=i(r(x))$, and $H(a,t)=a$ for all $a\in A$ and $t\in I$ ([[def-homotopy-relative-and-path-homotopy]]). The pair $(r,H)$ is a **deformation retraction**.

Some sources call the pointwise-fixed condition a *strong deformation retract*. In this library the word *deformation retract* always includes it.

Work with smooth oriented knots in the standard oriented three-sphere; a knot is a one-component oriented link. A **finite planar code for an oriented knot diagram** consists of finite vertex and edge sets, incidence data, a cyclic order of the four half-edges at every crossing vertex, a pairing of opposite half-edges into the two local branches, an orientation of each edge, and a choice of which branch is over at each crossing. Every other vertex is a bend vertex of valence two. The code includes a finite plane-drawing certificate: rational coordinates for the vertices and bends, and a finite polygonal path for every edge. The certificate must realize the incidences and cyclic orders, have no edge self-intersection, and have pairwise disjoint edge interiors except at the specified bend and crossing vertices; at a crossing the two branches must be transverse. These conditions are checked by finitely many exact segment-intersection tests. Edge orientations must join coherently across each paired branch and each bend vertex, and following the edges through the crossing pairings and the degree-two bend vertices must give one oriented circle. Thus an admissible code represents a connected regular oriented diagram of a single knot. If there are no crossing vertices, the code is one oriented polygonal circle and has one arc. Smooth each bend in a small disk disjoint from all crossings and other edges; the resulting smooth diagram has the same crossing data.

An **under-arc** is a maximal portion of the oriented circle between consecutive points where the knot passes under at a crossing; the over branch is not cut. With no crossings the entire circle is the unique under-arc. A **positive meridian** of an oriented branch is the oriented boundary of a small normal disk, with disk orientation chosen so that the oriented tangent to the branch followed by the disk orientation agrees with the ambient orientation of $S^3$. Planarity, incidence, orientation consistency, one-component tracing and the over/under data are input validity conditions; a procedure receiving an invalid finite record must report invalid input rather than repair it. The code stores no algebraic crossing sign: the oriented plane and the direction of the over branch determine which incident under branch is on its left and which is on its right.

Let $K\subset\mathbb R^3$ be the image of a compact smooth embedded circle, and let $E:N^\perp K\to\mathbb R^3$ be the Euclidean normal-addition map $E(p,v)=p+v$. There is a real $\varepsilon>0$ such that $E$ restricts to a diffeomorphism from $\{(p,v):\|v\|<\varepsilon\}$ onto an open neighborhood $N_\varepsilon$ of $K$. Moreover, $\mathbb R^3\setminus K$ strongly deformation retracts onto $\mathbb R^3\setminus N_\varepsilon$ by pushing each nonzero normal vector radially to length $\varepsilon$. The construction uses only a finite cover of the compact circle and no choice axiom.

If $A\subset X$ is a CW subcomplex and its inclusion is a homotopy equivalence, then $X$ strongly deformation retracts onto $A$. Moreover, if $(Y,B)$ is a CW pair and $u_0,u_1:B\to Z$ are homotopic, then the adjunction spaces $Z\cup_{u_0}Y$ and $Z\cup_{u_1}Y$ are homotopy equivalent relative to their common subspace $Z$.

Let $(X,A)$ be a CW pair with $A\ne\varnothing$ and supplied characteristic maps. The ordinary quotient $X/A$ is a CW complex, with one vertex $*$ replacing $A$ and one cell of the same dimension for every cell of $X\setminus A$.

If $A$ admits a contraction $H:A\times I\to A$, $H(-,0)=\mathrm{id}_A$, $H(-,1)=a\in A$, then the quotient map $q:X\to X/A$ is a homotopy equivalence and a weak homotopy equivalence. If $H(a,t)=a$ for every $t$, the constructed inverse and inverse homotopies are based at $a$ and $*$. No choice principle is required; a contraction is one witness, not a family of selected contractions.

If $P\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ is a polygon, then $\mathbb R^2\setminus P$ has exactly two regions, one bounded and one unbounded, and

$$\operatorname{Fr}(U)=P$$

for each of them. Regions and frontiers are from [[def-plane-region-and-frontier]]. The proof uses the finite simple edge cycle of [[def-polygonal-arc-and-polygon]] and polygonal crossing parity from [[lem-polygonal-crossing-parity-is-locally-constant]].

Let $Q=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ be pointed at $[0]$, and for $r\in\mathbb N$ put

$$W_r:=\bigvee_{j<r}(Q,[0]).$$

Then $\pi_1(W_r,w)$ is the free group on the $r$ standard loops, one traversing each circle summand once. In particular it has rank $r$ ([[def-rank-of-a-finite-rank-free-group]]). For $r=0$, $W_0$ is a point and the basis is empty.
For every natural number $n\ge2$, the unit sphere $S^n\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+1}$ is simply connected ([[def-simply-connected]]).

Let $X=U\cup V$, where $U$ and $V$ are open path-connected subsets of $X$, let $U\cap V$ be path-connected, and fix $x_0\in U\cap V$. For the inclusion-induced maps in the diagram

$$\pi_1(U,x_0)\longleftarrow\pi_1(U\cap V,x_0)\longrightarrow\pi_1(V,x_0),$$

the group $\pi_1(X,x_0)$, together with the two inclusion-induced homomorphisms, is a pushout ([[def-pushout-of-group-homomorphisms]]). Equivalently, the canonical homomorphism from any pushout $P$ of the displayed diagram to $\pi_1(X,x_0)$ is an isomorphism. No injectivity of either map from the overlap group is assumed.

Apply the finite compact-tube construction [F2] to the flat curve $(\gamma(s),0)$: the planar slice of its normal tube is an injective strip $\Psi(s,r)=\gamma(s)+r n(s)$, with $n$ the positive unit planar normal. The fibre maps $r\mapsto r+t\chi(r)f(s)$ are strictly increasing homeomorphisms fixing the strip boundary; extended by the identity, they give an ambient planar isotopy carrying $\gamma$ to this polygon. Its product with the identity in $z$ is an ambient three-dimensional isotopy. All subdivisions and bounds use a finite cover and one sufficiently large subdivision number. Take the lower arc to be the two straight segments from its two interior top-face endpoints to one interior point of $C_i$. This replacement of the underpass is realized by vertical interpolation of its negative graph, fixing its endpoints. Each $C_i$ is a product neighborhood of that arc: radial coordinates from the interior vertex identify $C_i$ with a ball; on its boundary send two disjoint disks around the endpoints of a diameter to small disks around the two top endpoints, and extend radially. Such a boundary map is constructed by joining the disk centers by simple polygonal arcs, taking rectangular strips around those arcs, and using affine maps on a finite common triangulation; outside the strips it is the identity. Thus it identifies a standard cylinder core with the two-segment arc and its two end disks with the designated exits. Attach product tubes along the disjoint upper arcs to those exits. The resulting neighborhood $N_*$ has one cap and one upper tube per underpass, joined in the same single cycle as $K$; its coordinates are a disk bundle around $K$, not an assumption about an arbitrary regular neighborhood. Corners and the core bends can be rounded inside disjoint smaller charts; retain the polygonal cap boundary, which is only used topologically.

The polygon's bounded side is supplied by [F6]. Triangulate it by diagonals: at a convex vertex use its neighbor triangle if it contains no other vertex; otherwise join it to a vertex in that triangle farthest from the opposite side. The smaller open triangle contains no intervening vertex, so the diagonal is internal; induction on the vertex count yields a finite triangulation. A leaf of its triangle-adjacency tree is an ear $uvw$, with ear tip $v$ and base $uw$. Remove any collinear vertices before this step. Put $q$ in the interior of $uw$. Choose $z_+=q+(1+\eta)(v-q)$ and $z_-=q-\epsilon(v-q)$, with small positive $\eta,\epsilon$, so the convex quadrilateral $Q=(u,z_+,w,z_-)$ meets the rest of the polygon only at $u,w$. At $t=1$ it sends the two ear edges $uv,vw$ onto $uq,qw$, while fixing all other polygon edges. This is an ambient straightening, not a collapse of a triangle to its base. Inductively remove the ears until a triangle remains. From an interior point of that triangle its boundary has a continuous positive radial-distance function $R(\theta)$; the plane homeomorphism multiplying each ray's radius by $1/R(\theta)$ sends it to a round circle. The products of these plane maps with the identity in $z$ identify the actual knot complement with the round-circle complement.

Let $K\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a smooth oriented knot with a regular diagram represented by a valid finite planar code, and let $c$ be its number of crossings. Choose a sufficiently small closed normal tube $N(K)$ and set $E_K=\mathbb R^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$. If $c>0$, there is a subspace $Y\subset E_K$, fixed pointwise by a strong deformation retraction of $E_K$, with a finite relative-open cover
$$Y=U\cup V_1\cup\cdots\cup V_c.$$
The space $U$ deformation retracts to a wedge of $c$ circles. With a common basepoint in the collar above the diagram and access paths in that collar extended into the arc charts, the positive under-arc meridians are its free basis. Each $V_i$ is contractible, $U\cap V_i$ is an open annulus around the $i$-th crossing attachment, and distinct $V_i$ are disjoint. Thus $V_i$ meets $U$ and any previously attached crossing pieces precisely in $U\cap V_i$.

For $c=0$, the Euclidean complement has homotopy type $S^1\vee S^2$, with the circle represented by the positive meridian. In particular its fundamental group is infinite cyclic; the extra sphere at infinity must not be discarded. In all cases the punctured normal tube retracts radially to its boundary, giving a strong deformation retraction $\mathbb R^3\setminus K\to E_K$. These constructions require only finitely many charts and no choice axiom.

Let $X$ be a topological space and let $x_0\in X$. A **based loop at $x_0$**
is a path $\alpha:I\to X$ with $\alpha(0)=x_0=\alpha(1)$
([[def-path-connected]]). Two based loops are equivalent when they are
path-homotopic relative to the endpoints. This is an equivalence relation by
[[cor-homotopy-relative-and-path-homotopy-are-equivalence-relations]].

The **fundamental group set** of $X$ at $x_0$ is

$$\pi_1(X,x_0):=\{\,[\alpha]:\alpha\text{ is a based loop at }x_0\,\}.$$

For composable paths, write

$$(\alpha*\beta)(s):=\begin{cases}\alpha(2s),&0\leq s\leq\tfrac12,\\ \beta(2s-1),&\tfrac12\leq s\leq1.\end{cases}$$

The finite closed-pasting argument already carried out in
[[def-path-connected]] shows that this is a path. The multiplication proposed
on loop classes is

$$[\alpha][\beta]:=[\alpha*\beta].$$

**Order convention.** The product $[\alpha][\beta]$ traverses $\alpha$ first
and $\beta$ second. Every product on this page uses this convention.

The constant loop at $x_0$ is denoted $c_{x_0}$, and the reversed loop is
$\bar\alpha(s):=\alpha(1-s)$. The next theorem proves that multiplication is
independent of representatives and that $[c_{x_0}]$ and $[\bar\alpha]$ are the
identity and inverse required by the group axioms.

For every pointed topological space $(X,x_0)$, the product

$$[\alpha][\beta]=[\alpha*\beta]$$

is well defined and makes $\pi_1(X,x_0)$ a group. Its identity is the class of
the constant loop $c_{x_0}$, and $[\alpha]^{-1}=[\bar\alpha]$.

Let $X=U\cup V$, where $U$ and $V$ are open path-connected subsets of $X$, let $U\cap V$ be path-connected, and fix $x_0\in U\cap V$. For the inclusion-induced maps in the diagram

$$\pi_1(U,x_0)\longleftarrow\pi_1(U\cap V,x_0)\longrightarrow\pi_1(V,x_0),$$

the group $\pi_1(X,x_0)$, together with the two inclusion-induced homomorphisms, is a pushout ([[def-pushout-of-group-homomorphisms]]). Equivalently, the canonical homomorphism from any pushout $P$ of the displayed diagram to $\pi_1(X,x_0)$ is an isomorphism. No injectivity of either map from the overlap group is assumed.

For homomorphisms $f:K\to G$ and $h:K\to H$, let $N$ be the normal closure in $G\ast H$ of $$\{j_G(f(k))j_H(h(k))^{-1}:k\in K\}.$$ Then $(G\ast H)/N$, with the induced factor maps $j_G$ and $j_H$, is a pushout of $f$ and $h$.

derivations.claim: Take ambient coordinates $(x,y,z)$ with overstrand tangent $+\partial_x$, viewing normal $+\partial_z$, and positive projection basis $(\partial_x,\partial_y)$. Source has $y<0$ and target $y>0$, with the understrand below the overstrand. Choose its oriented product tube $\Phi(u,v)$, where $v\in\mathbb R^2$ is the normal-disk coordinate, and choose a small positive radius $r$ and a fixed angle $\theta_0=0$, taking the first normal-frame vector toward the upper side of the understrand. The path used here is the push-off $\beta(u)=\Phi(u,r(\cos\theta_0,\sin\theta_0))$, from source to target; it never lies on the knot core. The two meridian loops are the boundaries $\mu_u(\tau)=\Phi(u,r(\cos(\theta_0+2\pi\tau),\sin(\theta_0+2\pi\tau)))$, based at the endpoints of $\beta$. For exterior paths take $r$ at least the removed tube radius; shrink that radius first if necessary. Choose the product tube disjoint from the overstrand and other arc pieces, and $r$ smaller than the crossing-chart separation bounds. Choose upper-collar paths $\alpha_s,\alpha_t$ to these actual boundary points. In the normal $(y,z)$ plane of the overstrand, their concatenation $\alpha_s\beta\alpha_t^{-1}$ follows a small perturbation of the polygon $(0,H),(-d,-h),(d,-h),(0,H)$, which has positive signed area. The polygon and a sufficiently small surrounding strip avoid the origin; the chosen radius makes the perturbation lie in that strip, so its winding is still $+1$. For explicit complement control, straighten the local under-core to $x=0,z=-h$ in the product chart and take its upper push-off at $z=-h+r$. The access triangle is then entirely above $z=-h$, while the over-core projects to the origin. Radial interpolation of its positive polar-distance function to a sufficiently small circle about the origin stays inside that triangle minus the origin, hence above the under-core as well. Retain the positive-radius angular access in the under-tube until reaching these straightened paths. Thus the resulting homotopy is to one counterclockwise over-meridian and avoids both strands throughout. Thus all paths and homotopies lie in the complement, the loop represents $m_o$, and $\alpha_t\simeq m_o^{-1}\alpha_s\beta$ rel endpoints there.

The positive-radius cylinder $(u,\tau)\mapsto\Phi(u,r(\cos(\theta_0+2\pi\tau),\sin(\theta_0+2\pi\tau)))$ transports the boundary meridians, with its basepoint edge equal to $\beta$. Its image misses the knot core and, by the separated tube choice, the overstrand and every other arc. Reading the boundary of this cylinder gives $\beta\mu_t\beta^{-1}\simeq\mu_s$ in the complement; its disk orientation is transported continuously even when the source-to-target direction opposes the knot orientation. Therefore $[\alpha_t\mu_t\alpha_t^{-1}]=m_o^{-1}[\alpha_s\beta\mu_t\beta^{-1}\alpha_s^{-1}]m_o=m_o^{-1}m_sm_o$. Equivalently the annular-core word $m_o^{-1}m_sm_om_t^{-1}$ bounds the cap of [F1], consistently with [F3]. Reversing the understrand orientation inverts both its meridians, so inversion gives the same side-based equation, rather than a switch of the conjugating direction.

The under-tangent follows $n_o$ exactly when incoming is source and outgoing is target, giving the first incoming/outgoing equation. Otherwise solve the same equation for $m_s$ to obtain the second. A reversed meridian is the inverse loop by [F2]. If a common access path $\alpha$ is replaced by $\lambda\alpha$, the class $[\alpha\mu\alpha^{-1}]$ becomes $[\lambda][\alpha\mu\alpha^{-1}][\lambda]^{-1}$; this holds for each of the three meridians. These observations prove all remaining assertions.

For every natural number $n\ge2$, the unit sphere $S^n\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+1}$ is simply connected ([[def-simply-connected]]).

A topological space $X$ is **simply connected** when it is nonempty and
path-connected ([[def-path-connected]]) and, for every $x_0\in X$, the group
$\pi_1(X,x_0)$ has exactly one element.

Requiring every basepoint avoids presuming a change-of-basepoint theorem. For a
path-connected space that later theorem shows that checking one basepoint is
equivalent, but no such result is needed for this definition. The empty space
is path-connected under the published convention, but it is not simply
connected here because nonemptiness is explicit.

Let $X=U\cup V$, where $U$ and $V$ are open path-connected subsets of $X$, let $U\cap V$ be path-connected, and fix $x_0\in U\cap V$. For the inclusion-induced maps in the diagram

$$\pi_1(U,x_0)\longleftarrow\pi_1(U\cap V,x_0)\longrightarrow\pi_1(V,x_0),$$

the group $\pi_1(X,x_0)$, together with the two inclusion-induced homomorphisms, is a pushout ([[def-pushout-of-group-homomorphisms]]). Equivalently, the canonical homomorphism from any pushout $P$ of the displayed diagram to $\pi_1(X,x_0)$ is an isomorphism. No injectivity of either map from the overlap group is assumed.

$$f_*:\pi_1(X,x_0)\longrightarrow\pi_1(Y,f(x_0)),\qquad f_*([\alpha]):=[f\circ\alpha].$$

that it is a group homomorphism in the sense of [[def-group-homomorphism]], and
that induced maps respect identities, composition and homotopies that fix the
basepoint.

Let $f:(X,x_0)\to(Y,y_0)$ be a continuous map with $f(x_0)=y_0$. Then

$$f_*([\alpha])=[f\circ\alpha]$$

is a well-defined group homomorphism. For pointed continuous maps,

$$\operatorname{id}_*=\operatorname{id},\qquad (g\circ f)_*=g_*\circ f_*.$$

Work with smooth oriented knots in the standard oriented three-sphere; a knot is a one-component oriented link. A **finite planar code for an oriented knot diagram** consists of finite vertex and edge sets, incidence data, a cyclic order of the four half-edges at every crossing vertex, a pairing of opposite half-edges into the two local branches, an orientation of each edge, and a choice of which branch is over at each crossing. Every other vertex is a bend vertex of valence two. The code includes a finite plane-drawing certificate: rational coordinates for the vertices and bends, and a finite polygonal path for every edge. The certificate must realize the incidences and cyclic orders, have no edge self-intersection, and have pairwise disjoint edge interiors except at the specified bend and crossing vertices; at a crossing the two branches must be transverse. These conditions are checked by finitely many exact segment-intersection tests. Edge orientations must join coherently across each paired branch and each bend vertex, and following the edges through the crossing pairings and the degree-two bend vertices must give one oriented circle. Thus an admissible code represents a connected regular oriented diagram of a single knot. If there are no crossing vertices, the code is one oriented polygonal circle and has one arc. Smooth each bend in a small disk disjoint from all crossings and other edges; the resulting smooth diagram has the same crossing data.

An **under-arc** is a maximal portion of the oriented circle between consecutive points where the knot passes under at a crossing; the over branch is not cut. With no crossings the entire circle is the unique under-arc. A **positive meridian** of an oriented branch is the oriented boundary of a small normal disk, with disk orientation chosen so that the oriented tangent to the branch followed by the disk orientation agrees with the ambient orientation of $S^3$. Planarity, incidence, orientation consistency, one-component tracing and the over/under data are input validity conditions; a procedure receiving an invalid finite record must report invalid input rather than repair it. The code stores no algebraic crossing sign: the oriented plane and the direction of the over branch determine which incident under branch is on its left and which is on its right.

Orient the projection plane by the viewing normal and the ambient orientation. At an oriented crossing let $o$ be the over-arc, and let $n_o$ be its positive in-plane normal: the ordered pair consisting of the over-tangent and $n_o$ is positive. Call the under-side from which $n_o$ points the source $s$, and the side toward which it points the target $t$. A positive meridian is the oriented boundary of a small normal disk whose orientation, preceded by the oriented knot tangent, is the ambient orientation. With the common upper-collar basing paths, the based positive meridians satisfy
$$m_t=m_o^{-1}m_s m_o.$$
This side-based equation is independent of the direction of the understrand. In an oriented chart with over-tangent rightward, the target is the upper side $L$ and source the lower side $R$, so equivalently $m_R=m_o m_Lm_o^{-1}$. In incoming/outgoing notation, the outgoing under-meridian is $m_o^{-1}m_{\rm in}m_o$ if the under-tangent points along $n_o$, and is $m_om_{\rm in}m_o^{-1}$ otherwise. Reversing a chosen meridian loop inverts its class. Changing every common access path by the same based loop conjugates all three classes simultaneously.

Let $F(X)$ be a free group and let $R\subseteq F(X)$ be a set of words, called
**relations**. The group with presentation

$$\langle X\mid R\rangle:=F(X)/\langle\!\langle R\rangle\!\rangle_{F(X)}$$

is the quotient by the normal closure of $R$. The members of $X$ are its
**generators**. In this quotient, every relation in $R$ becomes the identity,
as do all consequences forced by normality.

The crossing scan visits each crossing exactly once. The positive normal names its source and target without conflating them with incoming and outgoing. By [F2], its relator is exactly $x_o^{-1}x_sx_ox_t^{-1}$; solving that relation for outgoing gives the two equivalent incoming/outgoing formulas in the procedure. No other relation is appended. The resulting generator and relator lists are finite, so [F3] defines the returned presentation; its generator assignment is the meridian assignment stated in the procedure.

Let $K\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a smooth oriented knot with a regular diagram represented by a valid finite planar code, and let $c$ be its number of crossings. Choose a sufficiently small closed normal tube $N(K)$ and set $E_K=\mathbb R^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$. If $c>0$, there is a subspace $Y\subset E_K$, fixed pointwise by a strong deformation retraction of $E_K$, with a finite relative-open cover
$$Y=U\cup V_1\cup\cdots\cup V_c.$$
The space $U$ deformation retracts to a wedge of $c$ circles. With a common basepoint in the collar above the diagram and access paths in that collar extended into the arc charts, the positive under-arc meridians are its free basis. Each $V_i$ is contractible, $U\cap V_i$ is an open annulus around the $i$-th crossing attachment, and distinct $V_i$ are disjoint. Thus $V_i$ meets $U$ and any previously attached crossing pieces precisely in $U\cap V_i$.

For $c=0$, the Euclidean complement has homotopy type $S^1\vee S^2$, with the circle represented by the positive meridian. In particular its fundamental group is infinite cyclic; the extra sphere at infinity must not be discarded. In all cases the punctured normal tube retracts radially to its boundary, giving a strong deformation retraction $\mathbb R^3\setminus K\to E_K$. These constructions require only finitely many charts and no choice axiom.

Orient the projection plane by the viewing normal and the ambient orientation. At an oriented crossing let $o$ be the over-arc, and let $n_o$ be its positive in-plane normal: the ordered pair consisting of the over-tangent and $n_o$ is positive. Call the under-side from which $n_o$ points the source $s$, and the side toward which it points the target $t$. A positive meridian is the oriented boundary of a small normal disk whose orientation, preceded by the oriented knot tangent, is the ambient orientation. With the common upper-collar basing paths, the based positive meridians satisfy
$$m_t=m_o^{-1}m_s m_o.$$
This side-based equation is independent of the direction of the understrand. In an oriented chart with over-tangent rightward, the target is the upper side $L$ and source the lower side $R$, so equivalently $m_R=m_o m_Lm_o^{-1}$. In incoming/outgoing notation, the outgoing under-meridian is $m_o^{-1}m_{\rm in}m_o$ if the under-tangent points along $n_o$, and is $m_om_{\rm in}m_o^{-1}$ otherwise. Reversing a chosen meridian loop inverts its class. Changing every common access path by the same based loop conjugates all three classes simultaneously.

Let $X=U\cup V$, where $U$ and $V$ are open path-connected subsets of $X$, let $U\cap V$ be path-connected, and fix $x_0\in U\cap V$. For the inclusion-induced maps in the diagram

$$\pi_1(U,x_0)\longleftarrow\pi_1(U\cap V,x_0)\longrightarrow\pi_1(V,x_0),$$

the group $\pi_1(X,x_0)$, together with the two inclusion-induced homomorphisms, is a pushout ([[def-pushout-of-group-homomorphisms]]). Equivalently, the canonical homomorphism from any pushout $P$ of the displayed diagram to $\pi_1(X,x_0)$ is an isomorphism. No injectivity of either map from the overlap group is assumed.

For homomorphisms $f:K\to G$ and $h:K\to H$, let $N$ be the normal closure in $G\ast H$ of $$\{j_G(f(k))j_H(h(k))^{-1}:k\in K\}.$$ Then $(G\ast H)/N$, with the induced factor maps $j_G$ and $j_H$, is a pushout of $f$ and $h$.

Let $Q=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ be pointed at $[0]$, and for $r\in\mathbb N$ put

$$W_r:=\bigvee_{j<r}(Q,[0]).$$

Then $\pi_1(W_r,w)$ is the free group on the $r$ standard loops, one traversing each circle summand once. In particular it has rank $r$ ([[def-rank-of-a-finite-rank-free-group]]). For $r=0$, $W_0$ is a point and the basis is empty.

A **free group on a set $X$** is a group $F(X)$ together with a map
$i:X\to F(X)$ such that, for every group $G$ and every function $u:X\to G$,
there is a unique group homomorphism $\widehat u:F(X)\to G$ satisfying

$$\widehat u\circ i=u.$$

The reduced-word construction supplies such a group; the construction and its
universal property are established in [[thm-reduced-words-form-the-free-group]].
When no ambiguity arises, $x\in X$ is identified with its image $i(x)$.

Let $F(X)$ be a free group and let $R\subseteq F(X)$ be a set of words, called
**relations**. The group with presentation

$$\langle X\mid R\rangle:=F(X)/\langle\!\langle R\rangle\!\rangle_{F(X)}$$

is the quotient by the normal closure of $R$. The members of $X$ are its
**generators**. In this quotient, every relation in $R$ becomes the identity,
as do all consequences forced by normality.

A homomorphism that kills a normal subgroup factors uniquely through the quotient group.

If $N\mathrel{\trianglelefteq}G$, $f:G\to H$ is a homomorphism, and
$N\subseteq\ker f$, then there is a unique homomorphism $\bar f:G/N\to H$
such that $\bar f(gN)=f(g)$ and $f=\bar f\circ\pi$.

Let $K\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a compact smooth knot and let $b\in\mathbb R^3\setminus K$. The inclusion $\mathbb R^3\setminus K\hookrightarrow S^3\setminus K$ induces an isomorphism
$$\pi_1(\mathbb R^3\setminus K,b)\xrightarrow{\ \cong\ }\pi_1(S^3\setminus K,b).$$

Define a finite procedure $\mathsf{Wirtinger}(D,a_0)$ on a finite planar code $D$ for one oriented knot and a designated under-arc $a_0$ as follows. First check all incidence, valence, branch-pairing, crossing over/under, edge-orientation, and one-component conditions in the code. For each pair of rational line segments in the drawing certificate, compute the determinant of their direction vectors. If it is nonzero, solve the two-coordinate linear intersection equations and check whether the solution lies on both closed segments. If the determinant is zero, test collinearity and overlap by exact rational determinant and endpoint-order comparisons. Accept an intersection only when it is a shared declared bend or crossing vertex with the recorded incidence, and at a crossing verify that the two branch direction vectors have nonzero determinant. Reject self-intersections and all unrecorded intersections. If any check fails, return `invalid-input`. Otherwise traverse the oriented knot once starting at $a_0$, label the maximal under-arcs $a_1,\ldots,a_m$, and introduce one symbol $x_i$ for the positive meridian of each $a_i$. For each crossing $v$, read its oriented over-tangent and positive in-plane normal. Let $a_s$ be the under-side from which that normal points and $a_t$ the side toward which it points, and read the over-arc $a_o$. Append exactly the relator $x_o^{-1}x_sx_ox_t^{-1}$. Equivalently, if the incoming under-tangent follows that normal, append $x_o^{-1}x_{\rm in}x_ox_{\rm out}^{-1}$; otherwise append $x_ox_{\rm in}x_o^{-1}x_{\rm out}^{-1}$. The orientation of a positive meridian is fixed locally by requiring the knot tangent followed by the normal-disk orientation to give the ambient orientation. Once a complement basepoint and basing paths to the meridians are fixed, interpret $x_i$ as the corresponding based positive meridian. Return the finite group presentation with generators $x_1,\ldots,x_m$ and this one relator per crossing. The procedure uses only finite scans and terminates.

$\operatorname{Deg}:\pi_1(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z,[0])\to(\mathbb Z,+)$ is an isomorphism. Its inverse is

$$n\longmapsto[\omega_n].$$

derivations.claim: By [F10], the constructor terminates and has exactly one generator per under-arc and one relator per crossing. If $c=0$, the explicit punctured-product model in [F1] gives its fundamental group as infinite cyclic on the positive meridian (the sphere factor is simply connected), while [F6]–[F8] identify the returned one-generator empty-relator presentation with the same free cyclic group. If $c>0$, [F1] and [F5] give the free meridian basis for the meridian region.

Assume $c>0$ and add the crossing pieces in any fixed order. The ordered-intersection condition in [F1] makes the intersection at each attachment precisely its annular core. By [F3] and [F4], van Kampen kills the normal closure of that core's image; [F2] identifies this image with the relator emitted at that crossing. Repeating over the finite crossing set yields the quotient of the free meridian group by exactly the constructor's relator normal closure.

By [F6] and [F7], the quotient in step 2.1 is the returned presentation group; [F8] identifies the quotient map with the homomorphism sending each symbol to its positive meridian. It is an isomorphism onto the group of the covered exterior by the pushout construction.

For $c=0$, step 1.1 already identifies the returned cyclic presentation with the Euclidean complement group on the positive meridian. For $c>0$, step 3.1 identifies the presentation with the covered exterior group, and the compact-tube retraction identifies that group with $\pi_1(\mathbb R^3\setminus K)$. In both cases [F9] then gives the isomorphism to $\pi_1(S^3\setminus K)$, with exactly the stated positive-meridian assignment.

By [F2], replacing the common basing path conjugates every generator image by the same element. Simultaneous conjugation is an inner automorphism of the target group, so the resulting presentation group remains isomorphic to $\pi_1(S^3\setminus K)$.

Changing the designated start arc reindexes the same finite list of under-arcs. The induced bijection of generator symbols carries each crossing's over/under labels, and therefore each constructor relator, to the corresponding relator in the new indexing. It extends to an isomorphism of the free groups and carries one relator normal closure onto the other; [F7] and [F8] give an isomorphism of the presented quotients.

The trefoil panels give the crossing triples $(b,c,a)$, $(c,a,b)$, and $(a,b,c)$. Applying [F2] gives the three crossing relations in the statement. The crossing with overarc $a$ gives $c=aba^{-1}$. Substituting this into $a=bcb^{-1}$ gives $a=bab a^{-1}b^{-1}$. Right multiplication by $ba$ yields $aba=bab$. Under that braid relation, $cac^{-1}=a b a b^{-1}a^{-1}=b$, so the third crossing equation follows from the first two. Thus eliminating $c$ gives exactly $\langle a,b\mid aba=bab\rangle$.

The side triples $(o,L,R)$ are $(x_1,x_2,x_3)$, $(x_4,x_2,x_1)$, $(x_2,x_4,x_3)$, and $(x_3,x_4,x_1)$. Substitution, and reversal of the written equality when needed, gives exactly the four equations in the statement. The under-arrow direction does not select a different conjugation rule.

In $S_3$, the two words $(12)(23)(12)$ and $(23)(12)(23)$ both equal $(13)$, so the assignment respects the trefoil relation. The transpositions $(12)$ and $(23)$ generate all six permutations $e,(12),(23),(12)(23),(23)(12),(13)$, hence the homomorphism is surjective by [F4] and [F6].
