The Seifert smoothing may merge two circles into one or split one circle into
two at a crossing, so its number of circles is a new invariant of the picture
and is not in general the number of components of the link.

The **Seifert picture** of $D$ is the smoothed picture together with one signed
short arc at each former crossing $v$, drawn transversely to the two smoothed
strands and joining the two distinct Seifert circles that passed through $v$; the sign of the arc is the sign of the
crossing, positive or negative. The signed arcs lie in the complement of the
Seifert circles and meet the circles only at their endpoints
([[def-embedded-submanifold-and-slice-chart]]); every crossing is recorded exactly once. The two smoothed arcs at a crossing
are parallel and equally directed. They cannot belong to the same oriented
Jordan circle: the connecting strip is on opposite local sides of its two
equally directed boundary arcs, whereas a fixed complementary side of an
oriented Jordan circle is consistently on one local side. Thus each signed
arc joins distinct circles, coherently oriented in their common annulus. The orientation of each Seifert circle is the one induced by the
Smoothed strands, and the collection of circles and signed arcs is the object
to which the coherence and height definitions
([[def-coherence-of-seifert-circles-and-the-height-of-a-diagram]]) are applied.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $D$ be a finite regular oriented link diagram with exactly one component, and let $c$ be its number of crossings. Perform the following construction in its projection sphere $S^2$.

1. Choose a point $q\in S^2$ outside the finite diagram. In pairwise disjoint small disks about the crossings, replace each crossing by the unique noncrossing smoothing compatible with the strand orientations. Let the resulting oriented circles be the Seifert circles and let $s$ be their number.
2. For each Seifert circle $C$, take the closure of the component of $S^2\setminus C$ that does not contain $q$. Under the stated choice axiom, each such region is an embedded compact disk. The finite family of disk regions is nested or disjoint. Orient each disk to induce the given orientation of its boundary circle, then place nested disks at distinct nearby heights ordered by inclusion; the resulting disk interiors are pairwise disjoint in $S^3$.
3. For every original crossing, attach one rectangular band along short boundary intervals on the two smoothing arcs. A half-twist means a single $180$-degree turn of the band across the crossing neighborhood. Choose its direction, endpoint orientations, and over/under order to match the original crossing.
4. Return the finite disk-and-band construction data together with $(s,c)$.

The returned data are a finite attached two-dimensional complex. This algorithm's definition alone does not assert that the resulting image is embedded, is a surface, is connected, or has the original knot as boundary; the separate correctness lemma establishes those properties.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $D$ be a finite regular oriented diagram of a single knot, and let the Seifert algorithm supply its finite disk-and-band construction data. These disks and bands can be realized in $S^3$ as a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface $F$ with exactly one boundary component, whose oriented boundary is the knot represented by $D$. The bands can be chosen mutually disjoint and disjoint from disk interiors except at their attaching intervals.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. If a connected compact oriented disk-and-band surface $F$ is built from $s$ disjoint disks by attaching $c$ rectangular bands along boundary intervals and has one boundary component, then $\chi(F)=s-c$ and $g(F)=(1-s+c)/2$. In particular, if the Seifert algorithm on an oriented knot diagram $D$ has $s$ Seifert circles and $c$ crossings, its output surface has genus $(1-s+c)/2$ and the knot genus satisfies $g(K)\le (1-s+c)/2$. This is an upper bound from one spanning surface, not a minimality assertion.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. For an oriented smooth knot $K\subset S^3$, define

$$\mathcal G(K):=\{n\in\mathbb N_0: \text{there is a Seifert surface }F\text{ for }K\text{ with }g(F)=n\}.$$

Every element of $\mathcal G(K)$ is the genus of a connected compact oriented surface. The existence theorem makes $\mathcal G(K)$ nonempty, and the well-ordering of $\mathbb N_0$ gives its least element. The **smooth knot genus** is $g(K):=\min\mathcal G(K)$. This genus is the minimum over embedded spanning surfaces; it is not the number of Seifert circles or the genus of every surface produced from a diagram.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice-principle-for-foliation-pair]]). Let $S$ be an oriented Hausdorff $C^2$ surface without boundary, possibly disconnected. Then:

1. Every compact subset $K\subset S$ lies in the interior of a compact finitely cellulated $C^2$ subsurface $N$. If $K$ is contained in one connected component of $S$, $N$ can be chosen connected. A specified finite embedded regular $C^2$ graph contained in $\operatorname{Int}N$ can be included in its one-skeleton.
2. Every connected closed compact subsurface has an oriented genus normal form: the sphere for $g=0$, or the polygon word $\prod_{i=1}^g a_i b_i a_i^{-1}b_i^{-1}$ for $g\ge1$, with $\chi=2-2g$. A connected compact subsurface with $b>0$ boundary circles has a free fundamental group; capping its boundaries defines genus $g$ and gives $\chi=2-2g-b$ and free rank $2g+b-1$.
3. The fundamental group of every connected component of $S$ is torsion-free.
4. Every regular embedded $C^2$ nullhomotopic circle $c$ bounds an embedded compact disk region in $S$. Here a disk region is a compact subsurface homeomorphic to the closed disk, with boundary exactly $c$; its inherited surface structure and boundary are $C^2$. It is unique unless the **connected component containing $c$** is a sphere; in that component the two complementary disk regions are the two possibilities.

The normal forms in clause 2 are homeomorphism normal forms. No general differentiable smoothing theorem or arbitrary-surface triangulation-existence theorem is a premise of this item.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$ and let $Q=(q_1,\dots,q_n)$ be the base configuration of
[[def-geometric-braid-with-setwise-endpoints]], with $h=\frac{1}{4(n+1)}$ and
$q_j=((2j-n-1)h,0)$. Fix an index $i$ with $1\le i\le n-1$. The two adjacent
base points are

$$q_i=\bigl((2i-n-1)h,0\bigr),\qquad q_{i+1}=\bigl((2i+1-n)h,0\bigr),$$

their **midpoint** is $m_i:=(q_i+q_{i+1})/2=((2i-n)h,0)=q_i+(h,0)$, and their
**support disc** is the open disc

$$U_i:=\bigl\{w\in\mathbb R^2:\lVert w-m_i\rVert_2<\tfrac32h\bigr\}.$$

The support disc contains the two base points $q_i,q_{i+1}$, whose distance from
$m_i$ is $h$, and it contains no other base point: for $k<i$ one has
$\lVert q_k-m_i\rVert_2=(2(i-k)+1)h\ge 3h$ and for $k>i+1$ one has
$\lVert q_k-m_i\rVert_2=(2(k-i)-1)h\ge3h$, both exceeding $\tfrac32h$. Moreover
$U_i\subseteq D^\circ$, because every point of $U_i$ has norm at most
$\lVert m_i\rVert_2+\tfrac32h\le(n-2)h+\tfrac32h<(n+1)h<1$. Finally
$U_i\cap U_j=\varnothing$ whenever $|i-j|>1$, since then the midpoints are at
distance $2|i-j|h\ge4h>3h$, twice the radius.

**The positive half twist.** Define $\rho\colon I\to\mathbb R^2$, the
**anticlockwise diamond path**, by

$$\rho(t):=\begin{cases}\bigl(2th-h,\,-2th\bigr),&0\le t\le \tfrac12,\\[2pt] \bigl(2th-h,\,2th-2h\bigr),&\tfrac12\le t\le1.\end{cases}$$

Thus $\rho(0)=(-h,0)$, $\rho(\tfrac12)=(0,-h)$, $\rho(1)=(h,0)$, and $\rho$ is
continuous, piecewise linear, and satisfies $\lVert\rho(t)\rVert_2\le h$ for all
$t$ with $\rho(t)\neq0$ throughout. The **elementary half twist at $i$**, written
$\sigma_i$, is the tuple of motions

$$(\sigma_i)_i(t):=m_i+\rho(t),\qquad (\sigma_i)_{i+1}(t):=m_i-\rho(t),\qquad (\sigma_i)_k(t):=q_k\ \ (k\notin\{i,i+1\}).$$

It is a braid based at $Q$
([[def-geometric-braid-with-setwise-endpoints]],
[[def-continuous-map-top]]): the two moving points stay in $U_i$ and are
antipodal about $m_i$, so they are distinct; every other point is fixed and lies
outside $U_i$; and the endpoint permutation is the transposition of $i$ and
$i+1$, since $(\sigma_i)_i(1)=m_i+(h,0)=q_{i+1}$ and
$(\sigma_i)_{i+1}(1)=m_i-(h,0)=q_i$.

The words *positive* and *anticlockwise* refer to the fixed orientation of the
plane of the disc and to the fixed planar projection whose horizontal axis
contains $Q$: the moving pair turns through the half turn anticlockwise, the
label $i$ passing below its midpoint and the label $i+1$ above. Together with
the first-under-second stacking convention of
[[prop-stacking-of-geometric-braids-is-well-defined]] this fixes the sign
convention for every signed crossing on this page and its companion.

**The opposite half twist.** The **opposite** (clockwise) half twist at $i$ is
defined by the reflected path

$$\rho^{-}(t):=\bigl(\rho_1(t),-\rho_2(t)\bigr),$$

through the motions $(\sigma_i^{-})_i(t):=m_i+\rho^{-}(t)$,
$(\sigma_i^{-})_{i+1}(t):=m_i-\rho^{-}(t)$ and
$(\sigma_i^{-})_k(t):=q_k$ for $k\notin\{i,i+1\}$. It is again a braid supported
in $U_i$ with endpoint permutation the transposition of $i$ and $i+1$; its pair
turns through the same half turn clockwise, the label $i$ passing above the
midpoint. The two motions are not equal, and they are not related by a
reparametrisation of the height: they are the two signed crossings of the pair.

**The opposite motion is the group inverse.** For a braid $\beta$ the reversed
braid $\overline\beta_j(t)=z_{\pi(\beta)^{-1}(j)}(1-t)$ represents
$[\beta]^{-1}$ in the group $G_n$
([[thm-geometric-braids-form-a-group]]). For $\beta=\sigma_i$ one computes
$\overline{\sigma_i}=\sigma_i^{-}$: reversing the height and relabelling by the
transposition of $i$ and $i+1$ sends $\rho(t)=m_i+(\rho_1,\rho_2)$ to the
motion with relative path $-\rho(1-t)$, which is the reflected path
$\rho^-$ traversed from $t=0$ to $t=1$. Hence

$$[\sigma_i^{-}]=[\sigma_i]^{-1}\qquad\text{in }G_n .$$

**Elementary cases.** For $n\le1$ there is no index $i$ with $1\le i\le n-1$,
and there are no elementary half twists; the assertions above are vacuous. For
$n\ge2$ and $1\le i\le n-1$ both $[\sigma_i]$ and $[\sigma_i^{-}]$ are
nonidentity elements of $G_n$, since their endpoint permutations are
transpositions, which are not the identity permutation.

**Two letters do not commute in general.** For adjacent indices the supports
$U_i$ and $U_{i+1}$ overlap and no commutation is asserted;
[[lem-geometric-far-commutativity]] proves commutativity only for disjoint
supports.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$ and let $Q=(q_1,\dots,q_n)$ be the base configuration of
[[def-geometric-braid-with-setwise-endpoints]]. Write

$$G_n:=\{[\beta]:\beta\ \text{a braid based at}\ Q\}$$

for the set of braid isotopy classes relative to the top and bottom
([[def-braid-isotopy-relative-top-and-bottom]]), and let $[\gamma][\beta]:
=[\gamma\star\beta]$ be the stacking of
[[prop-stacking-of-geometric-braids-is-well-defined]]. Then:

**(a)** $G_n$ is a group ([[def-group]]) with this operation. Its identity is
the class $[e]$ of the trivial braid $e_j(t):=q_j$, and the inverse of
$[\beta]$, for $\beta=(z_1,\dots,z_n)$ with endpoint permutation $\pi(\beta)$,
is the class of the **reversed braid**

$$\overline\beta_j(t):=z_{\pi(\beta)^{-1}(j)}(1-t)\qquad(t\in I,\ 1\le j\le n).$$

**(b)** The endpoint permutation map

$$\pi\colon G_n\longrightarrow S_n,\qquad[\beta]\longmapsto\pi(\beta),$$

is a well-defined group homomorphism
([[def-finite-symmetric-group-and-permutation-notation]]).

The construction is choice-free: all motions and reparametrisations used are
given by explicit formulas.

Let $n\ge0$ and let $\beta=(z_1,\ldots,z_n)$ be a geometric braid with
the fixed real basepoints $q_j=((2j-n-1)/(4(n+1)),0)$ and endpoint
permutation $\pi$, as in [[def-geometric-braid-with-setwise-endpoints]].
Identify the disk with $\{x\in\mathbb C:|x|<1\}$ and put
$$V=(D^\circ\times[0,1])/((x,1)\sim(x,0)).$$
The quotient and its topology use [[def-product-topology]] and the circle
$\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ of [[def-circle-as-real-line-mod-integers]].
The interval images
$$s_j=\{[(z_j(t),t)]:0\le t\le1\},\qquad \operatorname{cl}(\beta)=\bigcup_{j=1}^n s_j$$
are the **closure in the open solid torus**. In general an individual
$s_j$ is an interval image, not a closed circle: its last point is the
first point of $s_{\pi(j)}$.

**Components and orientation.** For a cycle
$(j,\pi(j),\ldots,\pi^{k-1}(j))$ concatenate these $k$ strand maps in
that order, with parameter in $[0,k]$. Their endpoints agree in $V$,
so the concatenation factors through $\mathbb R/k\mathbb Z$.
It is injective on this circle: points at distinct nonintegral heights
can agree only when their parameters have the same fractional part,
and the distinct strands at that height have distinct disk coordinates;
at integral heights only the specified adjacent endpoints agree.
Thus each cycle gives an embedded circle. Different cycles give
disjoint circles, and every strand belongs to exactly one cycle.
These circles are precisely the connected components of the closure.
The orientation is increasing concatenation parameter. In particular
the number of components equals the number of cycles of $\pi$.

**The standard axis and fixed framing.** In
$S^3=\{(z,w)\in\mathbb C^2:|z|^2+|w|^2=1\}$, as in
[[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]], set
$$A=\{(0,w):|w|=1\},\qquad P_\theta=\{(z,w)\in S^3:z\ne0,\ \arg z=\theta\}.$$
Fix the following particular diffeomorphism, including its disk framing:
$$\varphi([(x,t)])=  \bigl(\sqrt{1-|x|^2}\,e^{2\pi it},x\bigr):  V\longrightarrow S^3\setminus A.$$
Its inverse has disk coordinate $x=w$ and circle coordinate
$[t]=[\arg z/(2\pi)]$. Every $P_\theta$ is consequently an open disk.
The **raw topological oriented closure** is
$$\widehat\beta_{\mathrm{top}}=\varphi(\operatorname{cl}(\beta)).$$
This explicit $\varphi$ is part of the construction; the definition
does not allow an arbitrary page-preserving change of framing.

**Page intersections and smooth representatives.** The whole closure
meets every page in exactly $n$ points. A component belonging to a
$\pi$-cycle of length $k$ meets each page in exactly $k$ points:
at any fractional height it uses exactly those $k$ distinct strands.
The page coordinate of its concatenation is $[t]$, for
$t\in\mathbb R/k\mathbb Z$, so its oriented degree is $+k$.
If all disk-coordinate strand maps are smooth and have all positive-order derivatives
zero at their endpoints, their cycle concatenations have matching jets
at every seam. The page coordinate has nonzero derivative, so the
result is a smooth embedding of disjoint oriented circles, in the
sense of [[def-smooth-embedding]]. For an endpoint-flat smooth braid, its literal $\varphi$-image is therefore a smooth oriented link and is denoted $\widehat\beta$.

**Closure in the smooth oriented-link category.** The raw image need not be smooth, even if individual strands are smooth but their endpoint jets fail to match at the cycle seams. For an arbitrary continuous braid, assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]) and choose a smooth representative $\beta_s$ by [[lem-every-geometric-braid-is-braid-isotopic-to-a-smooth-braid]]. Make it endpoint-flat by composing all disk-coordinate strands with a fixed smooth nondecreasing $\psi:I\to I$, equal to $0$ near $0$ and $1$ near $1$. Interpolation of height maps $(1-u)t+u\psi(t)$ is an endpoint-fixed braid isotopy, because every strand is evaluated at the same height. The smooth-category closure of $\beta$ is the oriented-link isotopy class of this chosen model's literal $\varphi$-image; when a subset is needed, use that chosen closed-braid representative. Independence of the representative is proved by [[lem-closure-depends-only-on-the-braid-isotopy-class]]. Page and cycle properties refer to the chosen constructed closed braid, with the same number of strands and endpoint permutation as $\beta$.

If $\beta$ already has smooth strands with matching cycle-seam jets, in particular if it is endpoint-flat, its literal raw image is a smooth link and is retained as $\widehat\beta$. The raw quotient, fixed $\varphi$, finite cycles, page counts and trivial closures remain choice-free. Finite elementary words have explicit smooth endpoint-flat models, so forming their literal closures also requires no choice assumption; $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is used for the general continuous-representative convention and its independence theorem.

**The trivial closure.** For the constant braid its circles are
$\{(\sqrt{1-q_j^2}e^{2\pi it},q_j):[t]\in\mathbb R/\mathbb Z\}$.
They are latitudes of the sphere
$S=\{(z,w)\in S^3:\operatorname{Im}w=0\}$, with
$\operatorname{Re}w=q_j$. Each northern cap
$C_j=\{p\in S:\operatorname{Re}w(p)\ge q_j\}$ is a smooth disk:
stereographic coordinates on $S$ give radius
$\sqrt{(1-q_j)/(1+q_j)}$ for this cap. To make their spanning disks
disjoint, let $e$ be the unit vector in the $\operatorname{Im}w$
direction, set $\varepsilon=\pi/16$ and
$f_j(p)=\varepsilon(\operatorname{Re}w(p)-q_j)$ on $C_j$, and use
$$F_j(p)=\cos(f_j(p))p+\sin(f_j(p))e.$$
The boundary is fixed. The tubular parametrization
$(p,s)\mapsto\cos(s)p+\sin(s)e$ is injective for $|s|<\pi/2$,
and $0\le f_j<\pi/8$. On overlapping caps, if $q_i<q_j$ then
$f_i-f_j=\varepsilon(q_j-q_i)>0$, so their graphs are disjoint.
Thus these are pairwise disjoint smooth spanning disks. The trivial
$n$-braid closes to the oriented $n$-component unlink; for $n=1$
this is the unknot.

At $n=0$ all strand and cycle unions are empty, every page has zero intersections,
and the closure is the empty link. The basepoint list and disk constructions
above then have no entries.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most

In ZF, let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be smooth, and let $a\in U$. If $Df(a)$ is invertible, then there are open neighbourhoods $a\in V\subseteq U$ and $f(a)\in W$ such that $f|_V:V\to W$ is a diffeomorphism. Writing $g=(f|_V)^{-1}$,
$$Dg(y)=Df(g(y))^{-1}\qquad(y\in W).$$
No choice axiom is used.

If $P\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ is a polygon, then $\mathbb R^2\setminus P$ has exactly two regions, one bounded and one unbounded, and

$$\operatorname{Fr}(U)=P$$

for each of them. Regions and frontiers are from [[def-plane-region-and-frontier]]. The proof uses the finite simple edge cycle of [[def-polygonal-arc-and-polygon]] and polygonal crossing parity from [[lem-polygonal-crossing-parity-is-locally-constant]].
Every simple polygon admits a triangulation.

If a connected plane graph has vertex, edge and face sets $V,E,F$ ([[def-plane-graph-face-and-boundary]]), then

$$|V|-|E|+|F|=2.$$

Deletion is as in [[def-graph-deletion-contraction-minor-and-subdivision]], the tree boundary case uses [[prop-plane-forest-has-one-face]], and the finite induction is [[thm-induction-principle]].

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $N$ be a connected smooth $n$-manifold with
nonempty boundary and let $D\subseteq\partial N$ be an embedded closed disk.
Then the boundary connected sum $N\natural D^n$, obtained by gluing an $n$-disk
along $D$, is diffeomorphic to $N$ by a diffeomorphism equal to the identity
outside a collar neighbourhood of $D$.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $V$ be a compact
smooth $n$-manifold with boundary and let $N$ be a smooth $n$-manifold without
boundary ([[def-smooth-manifold]]). Let $F:V\times I\to N$ be a smooth map such
that $F_t:=F(\cdot,t)$ is a smooth embedding for every $t\in I$
([[def-smooth-embedding]]), and suppose $F$ is constant near the ends: for some
$\varepsilon\in(0,\tfrac12)$ one has $F(x,t)=F(x,0)$ for $t\le\varepsilon$ and
$F(x,t)=F(x,1)$ for $t\ge1-\varepsilon$, for all $x\in V$.

Then for every open neighbourhood $W\subseteq N$ of the compact image
$F(V\times I)$ there is a smooth map $H:N\times I\to N$ such that
$H_0=\operatorname{id}_N$, every $H_t$ is a diffeomorphism of $N$
([[def-diffeomorphism-and-local-diffeomorphism-of-manifolds]]),
$$H_t\circ F_0=F_t\quad\text{for every }t\in I,$$
$H_t=\operatorname{id}_N$ outside $W$ for every $t$, $H_t=\operatorname{id}_N$
for $t\le\varepsilon/2$, and $H_t=H_1$ for $t\ge1-\varepsilon/2$.

derivations.claim: Parametrize the circle by a smooth regular embedding $\gamma:S^1\to\mathbb R^2$, and let $n$ be its smooth unit normal obtained by rotating and normalizing its tangent. The map $T(s,r)=\gamma(s)+rn(s)$ has invertible derivative at $r=0$. By [F1] and compactness it is a local diffeomorphism on a common strip $|r|<a$. It is injective after shrinking $a$: otherwise collisions for widths tending to zero would have a subsequence of their circle parameters converging; equality of the limiting images and injectivity of $\gamma$ give the same limiting parameter, contrary to a local inverse there. Thus $T$ is a smooth two-sided annular coordinate.

We prove that a rounded polygonal region is a smooth disk. Take the finite triangulation in [F3]. The dual adjacency graph of its triangles, with an exterior root adjacent across every boundary edge, is connected. Indeed the triangles at any one vertex form a consecutive cyclic fan or a consecutive interval fan, so all their sectors are joined through shared edges, and connectedness of the triangulated region joins all fans. Choose a finite spanning tree of this dual graph rooted at the exterior. Process triangles in increasing distance from that root. Remove each triangle and its edge toward its parent: this edge is free, since its only other incident triangle has already been removed or is exterior. Removing a triangle with its free side leaves its two other sides and vertices, preserves connectedness, and preserves $V-E+F$. Plane Euler in [F3], with the exterior counted as one extra face, gives initial value $V-E+F=1$. At the end the remaining connected graph $K$ therefore has $V-E=1$, so it is a tree: a spanning tree already has $V-1$ edges, leaving no edge outside that spanning tree.

Inscribe a polygon with a sufficiently fine cyclic mesh in $\gamma$. Uniform continuity of $\gamma'$ gives positive scalar product of each chord direction with the tangent at every nearby normal projection, and the chord error tends uniformly to zero. Hence the normal projection of each chord is strictly increasing in its cyclic coordinate; the whole polygon has degree one under normal projection and is a normal graph. In particular it is embedded. Smooth its finitely many corners in disjoint small graph charts: convolution of the local graph function with a smooth compactly supported kernel on a smaller interval, joined by a smooth cutoff on a larger interval, leaves it unchanged outside that chart and can be made arbitrarily small in height and tangent direction. The smoothed curve $P'$ is still a normal graph $r=f(s)$, with $f$ smooth and arbitrarily small. Choose a smooth cutoff $\chi$ supported in $(-a,a)$ and equal to one near zero. For $\|f\|_\infty\|\chi'\|_\infty<1$, the map $(s,r)\mapsto(s,r+\chi(r)f(s))$ is a diffeomorphism, because its normal derivative is positive, and equals the identity near the ends of the strip. It extends by the identity to a smooth plane diffeomorphism carrying $\gamma$ onto the rounded polygon $P'$. The same graph construction compares any two sufficiently small choices of corner rounding. By [F2], the polygon has bounded and unbounded regions; rounding preserves them by local graph homeomorphisms: in a graph chart, a continuous vertical displacement, cut off in the transverse direction with positive transverse derivative, carries the original piecewise affine graph to the rounded graph, and transporting them by the displayed plane diffeomorphism proves the corresponding separation and smooth boundary charts for $\gamma$.

Realize these finite collapses on smooth rounded neighborhoods. In affine coordinates on a triangle whose free side is to be removed, retain thin strips along its other two sides and a rounded disk at their common vertex. The missing sector can be chosen as a convex triangle with its corners rounded. Its attaching part runs along the inner sides of the two retained strips, joined around their common vertex, and is one boundary interval. Near the other two vertices use disjoint vertex disks and the corresponding short collar intervals; outside this triangle the neighborhood is unchanged. No other simplex meets its open interior. These choices give compatible rounded neighborhoods before and after the collapse whose difference is one smooth disk attached along one embedded boundary interval. To check that this added piece is a standard disk, a convex rounded triangle has a positive smooth radial boundary function $a(\theta)$ about any interior center. On the standard disk the radial map $r\mapsto r\exp(\eta(\log r)\log a(\theta))$ is smooth and linear near zero when $\eta=0$ there, agrees with $r\mapsto ra(\theta)$ near $r=1$ when $\eta=1$ there, and has positive radial derivative if $|\eta'|\,\|\log a\|_\infty<1$; choose its transition over a sufficiently long interval of $\log r$. Thus it is a disk parametrization. The corner models match the retained strip collars before [F4] is applied. Consequently each collapse preserves the smooth diffeomorphism type of the rounded neighborhood. A rounded neighborhood of the final tree is a disk: remove a leaf disk and its band successively, each a disk attached along one interval, until one vertex disk remains. Applying [F4] finitely often proves the assertion for the initial rounded polygon. Step 2.1 then proves it for the original smooth circle.

Choose orientation-preserving disk parametrizations $p_i:\overline B(0,1)\to D_i$. The boundary map $p_1^{-1}bp_0$ has a smooth increasing angular lift $g:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$, with $g(\theta+2\pi)=g(\theta)+2\pi$. Let $\rho(r)$ be smooth, zero near zero and one near one. The map $(r,\theta)\mapsto(r,\theta+\rho(r)(g(\theta)-\theta))$ is the identity near the center and has angular derivative $1+\rho(r)(g'(\theta)-1)>0$. It is consequently a smooth disk diffeomorphism extending the boundary map, and is a product in the radial collars. Conjugate by $p_0,p_1$ to obtain a preliminary extension.

We can replace either radial collar by its prescribed collar without changing the boundary. More generally, express two collars with the same boundary parametrization in the normal coordinates of step 1.1. Their relative coordinate map is $(s,r)\mapsto(S(s,r),R(s,r))$, where $S(s,0)=s$, $R(s,0)=0$, and $\partial_rR(s,0)>0$. Use the periodic lift of $S-s$ and interpolate to the identity by $(s+u(S-s),(1-u)r+uR)$ for $0\le u\le1$. At $r=0$ the Jacobian is triangular with positive diagonal entries $1,(1-u)+u\partial_rR(s,0)$. Smooth collar maps extend across $r=0$ in the normal chart, by their local smooth-extension convention and finitely many chart cutoffs. Compactness and the local-inverse and separation argument of step 1.1 give a common narrow two-sided closed annulus on which every interpolated map is an embedding. Reparametrize $u$ smoothly to be constant near its endpoints. Apply [F5] to this compact two-dimensional annulus and the ambient plane, with support in a thin boundary neighborhood. The prescribed isotopy fixes its middle circle, so its ambient extension fixes every boundary point and preserves the bounded side. Its final diffeomorphism identifies the two collar germs exactly. Perform this correction on both sides of the preliminary extension of step 4.1. The resulting extension agrees with $c_0(p,r)\mapsto c_1(b(p),r)$ on a common smaller collar. Its smooth inverse and orientation follow from the same properties of all the factors.

For the interior prescription, first move $B(p_0)$ to $p_1$ by a diffeomorphism supported in $\operatorname{int}D_1$. A smooth path exists there by the disk parametrization of step 3.1. Cover it by finitely many interior coordinate balls and subdivide it so each successive pair lies in one smaller convex coordinate ball. For each pair, translation of a sufficiently small closed coordinate disk along their segment is an isotopy of full-dimensional disk embeddings whose track lies in that ball. Apply [F5], with a time parameter constant near its ends, and compose the resulting supported ambient diffeomorphisms. This moves the point as stated and leaves a neighborhood of the boundary fixed. Rename the resulting extension $B$. The germ $k=q\circ B^{-1}$ at $p_1$ fixes $p_1$ and preserves orientation. In centered coordinates its rescalings $k_t(x)=k(tx)/t$ for $t>0$ extend smoothly at $t=0$ to $Ax$, where $A=Dk(0)$, since $k(tx)/t=\int_0^1Dk(stx)x\,ds$. Each positive linear matrix $A$ is smoothly joined to the identity: write $A=RP$ with $P$ positive definite and $R$ a rotation, interpolate $P$ linearly to the identity and the rotation angle linearly to zero. Concatenate the resulting path from the identity to $A$ with $k_t$ from $A$ to $k$, and make the time parameter constant near the endpoints and all joins. On one common sufficiently small closed disk all slices are embeddings with track in an interior coordinate ball, by compactness and the inverse-function and separation argument of step 1.1. [F5] extends this disk isotopy to an ambient isotopy supported in that ball. Its terminal map $K$ agrees with $k$ near $p_1$, so $K\circ B=q$ near $p_0$. The boundary collars stay fixed. Only [F4] and [F5] use Countable Choice; all selections and compositions are finite.

For e_G=R^G_alpha z-y^dagger, the residual representation is e_G=-|G|^nu p^G_alpha(G*G)v. Hence its source witness norm is at most S_G rho. The first discrepancy inequality and the noise bound give ||G e_G|| <= (tau_G+S_G)delta; interpolation yields an exact-data first-stage error of order rho^(1/(nu+1))delta^(nu/(nu+1)).

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $f:M\to N$ be smooth. Then there exist an open ball
$$ B\subseteq\mathbb R^m $$
containing $0$ and a smooth family of maps
$$ \mathcal F:M\times B\to N $$
such that $\mathcal F_0=f$ and, for every $p\in M$, the parameter map
$$ \mathcal F_p:B\to N,\qquad a\longmapsto \mathcal F(p,a), $$
is a submersion. In particular, the evaluation map $\mathcal F$ is a
submersion, so it is transverse to every closed embedded submanifold
$Z\subseteq N$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\mathcal F:M\times S\to N$ be a smooth family of maps and let $Z\subseteq N$
be an embedded submanifold. If $\mathcal F\pitchfork Z$, then the set of
parameters $s\in S$ for which the slice $\mathcal F_s:M\to N$ fails to be
transverse to $Z$ is a null subset of $S$.
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every smooth manifold with boundary has a smooth collar.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$.

1. **Compact main case.** Let $M$ be a compact smooth manifold, possibly with boundary, let $N$ be a smooth manifold without boundary, let $F:M\times I\to N$ be a smooth isotopy of embeddings that is constant near the ends of $I$, and let $W$ be an open neighbourhood of $F(M\times I)$ in $N$. Then there is an ambient isotopy $H:N\times I\to N$ with $H_0=\mathrm{id}_N$, every $H_t$ a diffeomorphism, $H_t\circ F_0=F_t$ for all $t\in I$, $H_t=\mathrm{id}_N$ outside $W$ for every $t$, and $H_t$ stationary near the ends; if $F$ is constant near the ends with parameter $\varepsilon$, then $H_t=\mathrm{id}_N$ for $t\le\varepsilon/2$ and $H_t=H_1$ for $t\ge1-\varepsilon/2$.
2. **Relative form.** Let $N$ be boundaryless, $U\subseteq N$ open, $A\subseteq U$ compact, and let $F:U\times I\to N$ be a smooth isotopy of embeddings whose track image is open in $N\times I$. Then there is a compactly supported ambient isotopy $H$ of $N$ with $H_t\circ F_0=F_t$ on a neighbourhood of $A$ for every $t$.
3. **Boundary stratum.** If $N$ has boundary and $F(M\times I)\subseteq\partial N$, then the ambient isotopy of clause 1 can be chosen with every $H_t$ carrying $\partial N$ onto itself; if $F(M\times I)\subseteq N\setminus\partial N$, it can be chosen compactly supported in $N\setminus\partial N$.
4. **General isotopies.** For the same compact source (possibly with boundary) and boundaryless target as in clause 1, every smooth isotopy extends with support in a compact subset of any prescribed neighbourhood $W$ of $F(M\times I)$. The endpoint-constancy hypothesis and the stationary-end conclusion are both omitted; all other conclusions of clause 1 hold.

Thus $i$ is transverse to $S$ along $\partial F$. Transversality is open in the point of the source, and $\partial F$ is compact, so there is a collar neighbourhood $U$ of $\partial F$ on which $i$ is transverse to $S$.

Choose a smooth collar coordinate $s$ on $U$ and a smooth function $\gamma:F\to[0,1]$ that vanishes on a smaller boundary collar and equals $1$ outside $U$. Such a function is obtained by composing the collar coordinate with a smooth one-variable cutoff and extending by $1$. Put $\tau=\gamma^2$. Then $d\tau=0$ wherever $\tau=0$, and the zero set of $\tau$ lies inside $U$.

Apply [F1] to the boundaryless interior $F^\circ$ and the map $i|_{F^\circ}$, obtaining a smooth family $\mathcal F:F^\circ\times B\to M$ with $\mathcal F(p,0)=i(p)$ and each parameter map a submersion. On $F^\circ$ define $G(p,a)=\mathcal F(p,\tau(p)a)$, restricting $B$ if necessary so $\tau(p)a\in B$. Where $\tau>0$, the parameter derivative of $G$ is surjective. Where $\tau=0$, $d\tau=0$, so $G(p,a)=i(p)$ and its source derivative is $di_p$; [F5] and step 1.1 make it transverse to $S$. Since $\tau=0$ on a boundary collar, setting $G=i$ on $\partial F$ extends $G$ smoothly to $F\times B$, fixed near the boundary. Thus the total family is transverse to $S$.

Apply [F2] to $G|_{F^\circ\times B}$. Its good parameters are dense, because the bad set is null and every open parameter ball has positive measure. For each good parameter $a$, $G_a$ is transverse on $F^\circ$; near $\partial F$ it equals $i$, which is transverse by step 1.1. Hence $G_a$ is transverse on all of $F$.

Choose compatible Riemannian metrics on $F$ and $M$ using [F6]. At each $x\in F$, choose coordinate charts and a linear projection $P_x$ to a two-dimensional tangent plane so that $D(P_x\circ i)$ at $x$ is invertible. By [F5], shrink to a convex coordinate neighbourhood $U_x$ on which this derivative stays within one quarter of the least singular value of its value at $x$. Every sufficiently $C^1$-close map $j$ then has $P_x\circ j$ injective on $U_x$: integrate its derivative along the coordinate segment between two points to obtain a lower bound of one half that least singular value times their coordinate distance. Compactness gives a finite cover by such $U_x$ and a Lebesgue number $\delta>0$. For pairs at source distance at least $\delta$, compactness and injectivity of $i$ give a positive minimum target distance, which persists under sufficiently small $C^0$ perturbations. The differential of $i$ has a positive minimum norm on the compact unit tangent bundle, so immersion also persists under sufficiently small $C^1$ perturbations. Thus all sufficiently $C^1$-close maps are injective immersions; compactness of $F$ and the Hausdorff property of $M$ make them embeddings. By the density in step 4.1 choose a good $a$ in that ball; then $t\mapsto G_{ta}$ is an isotopy through embeddings fixed near $\partial F$. Apply [F4] to extend it to an ambient isotopy. Its endpoint carries $i(F)$ to a surface transverse to $S$, as required.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $V$ be a compact
smooth $n$-manifold with boundary and let $N$ be a smooth $n$-manifold without
boundary ([[def-smooth-manifold]]). Let $F:V\times I\to N$ be a smooth map such
that $F_t:=F(\cdot,t)$ is a smooth embedding for every $t\in I$
([[def-smooth-embedding]]), and suppose $F$ is constant near the ends: for some
$\varepsilon\in(0,\tfrac12)$ one has $F(x,t)=F(x,0)$ for $t\le\varepsilon$ and
$F(x,t)=F(x,1)$ for $t\ge1-\varepsilon$, for all $x\in V$.

Then for every open neighbourhood $W\subseteq N$ of the compact image
$F(V\times I)$ there is a smooth map $H:N\times I\to N$ such that
$H_0=\operatorname{id}_N$, every $H_t$ is a diffeomorphism of $N$
([[def-diffeomorphism-and-local-diffeomorphism-of-manifolds]]),
$$H_t\circ F_0=F_t\quad\text{for every }t\in I,$$
$H_t=\operatorname{id}_N$ outside $W$ for every $t$, $H_t=\operatorname{id}_N$
for $t\le\varepsilon/2$, and $H_t=H_1$ for $t\ge1-\varepsilon/2$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Shrink the parametrized ball without collapsing it: $e_t(x)=e(r(t)x)$, where $r$ decreases smoothly from $1$ to a fixed positive $\varepsilon$ and is constant near both ends. Every slice is an embedding. For sufficiently small $\varepsilon$, its last image lies in one coordinate chart centered at $e(0)$. Write the chart representative of $e$ near $0$ as $f$, with $f(0)=0$ and $L=Df(0)$ invertible. Let $m>0$ satisfy $|Lv|\ge m|v|$. Choose $\varepsilon$ so that $\|Df(y)-L\|<m/2$ for $|y|\le\varepsilon$. The interpolation $f_s(x)=\varepsilon Lx+(1-s)(f(\varepsilon x)-\varepsilon Lx)$ has invertible differential and is injective: its difference from $\varepsilon L$ is Lipschitz with constant less than $\varepsilon m/2$, so $|f_s(x)-f_s(y)|\ge\varepsilon m|x-y|/2$. All images lie in the chart after a further shrink. This is an isotopy from the small ball to a linear ellipsoid.

Write $L=QP$ with $Q$ orthogonal and $P$ positive definite. The positive definite path $(1-s)P+s\lambda I$, for small $\lambda>0$, gives an isotopy from that ellipsoid to a coordinate round ball. Reparametrize and concatenate the finite paths smoothly with stationary endpoints. By [F1] the resulting embedding isotopy extends to an ambient isotopy carrying $e(D^n)$ to that round ball. A coordinate ball can be moved along any prescribed finite chain of overlapping charts, shrinking it inside each overlap before the next move; a path between its center and any prescribed target center has such a finite chart subdivision. Within a chart, translation and positive dilation of a sufficiently small round ball are embedding isotopies. Hence any two sufficiently small coordinate balls in the same connected component are ambient isotopic.

Parametrize the given $3$-ball $B$ by $D^3$. Its boundary is thereby the standard $S^2$. Apply steps 1.1–2.1 in dimension two to a parametrization of its disk window $W\subset S^2$, then move and enlarge the resulting small round disk to a hemisphere by latitude disks. The endpoint parametrization in step 2.1 is linear orthogonal followed by a positive scalar; its orthogonal factor is the restriction of a fixed orthogonal symmetry of $S^2$. Consequently the standardization can retain the specified disk parametrization, up to that fixed symmetry, rather than only its image. Thus there is an isotopy $h_t$ of $S^2$, starting at the identity, that carries $W$ to a hemisphere, and, if needed, a fixed orthogonal symmetry makes its endpoint agree with the specified standard disk coordinates. This isotopy extends over $D^3$ explicitly: in a radial annulus use $(r,x)\mapsto(r,h_{\alpha(r)t}(x))$, where $\alpha=0$ near the inner edge and $\alpha=1$ near $r=1$, and use the identity on the smaller ball. Each slice is a diffeomorphism, with inverse $(r,y)\mapsto(r,h_{\alpha(r)t}^{-1}(y))$. It is smooth across the inner edge because it is the identity there; the fixed orthogonal symmetry also extends linearly over $D^3$. This proves standardization of the ball-window pair with its disk coordinates, without extending an arbitrary sphere diffeomorphism.

Standardize the added ball's window using its actual attaching parametrization, as permitted by step 3.1. Its collar map is then the product $(x,t)\mapsto(x,t)$ in the receiving disk coordinates. The standard ball-window pair can be represented as a cap over a flat disk: its remaining boundary is a dome meeting the window at its edge. This representation follows by viewing a round ball as two hemispherical graphs and flattening one graph in its collar; the strictly positive normal-coordinate derivative makes the flattening a diffeomorphism. Making the cap thinner is a positive rescaling of its normal coordinate. Therefore in the collar of a disk $D$ in the receiving boundary the attached ball may be represented as a thin cap, with its attaching map retained. A coordinate neighborhood of the whole closed disk exists: extend its full-rank parametrization across the boundary circle using finitely many boundary charts; the extensions agree with it on the disk, and sufficiently small extensions remain injective by compactness and the inverse function theorem.

In these coordinates the receiving manifold is $t\ge0$. After rounding the edge, its union with the thin cap is $t\ge\gamma(x)$, where $\gamma\le0$ is smooth and compactly supported in the disk coordinate neighborhood. Take a smooth cutoff $\rho(t)$ equal to one near the cap and zero beyond the chosen receiving collar. Choose the cap thin enough that $\|\gamma\rho'\|_\infty<1$. Then $(x,t)\mapsto(x,t-\gamma(x)\rho(t))$ sends $t\ge\gamma(x)$ diffeomorphically to $t\ge0$: its normal derivative is $1-\gamma(x)\rho'(t)>0$, its boundary value is zero, and it is the identity at the far end of each collar fiber. It is the identity outside this neighborhood, so it pastes to the identity elsewhere. This proves disk absorption. Applying the inverse construction proves disk removal, with the same support assertion.

The first assertion is established by steps 1.1–2.1, the window assertion by step 3.1, and both attachment assertions by step 5.1. In particular two balls glued along one boundary disk form a ball; and a boundary-attached ball indented into a ball can be removed leaving a ball. Every use of isotopy extension is in dimensions two or three with compact source and stationary endpoints, as required by [F1].

Work in the smooth category ([[def-smooth-manifold]]). Fix once and for all the
three-sphere as the one-point compactification

$$S^3:=\mathbb R^3\cup\{\infty\}$$

of Euclidean three-space, carrying its standard smooth structure, and fix the
standard orientation of $S^3$: the orientation induced by the standard
orientation of $\mathbb R^3$ under the one-point compactification, so that the
charts of the standard atlas away from $\infty$ are orientation-preserving and
the orientation is that of a connected oriented $3$-manifold in the sense of
[[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]]. For $r>0$ write
$\overline B_r:=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:\lVert x\rVert_2\le r\}$, the closed ball of
[[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]] with the following restriction convention. Smoothness on a closed ball means
local extension to a smooth map on an open neighborhood in Euclidean space;
smoothness on $M\times I$, for a smooth manifold $M$ without boundary, means
local extension across $t=0,1$ in $M\times\mathbb R$. Thus these closed domains
are not asserted to be manifolds without boundary in the cited definition.

**Links.** The **standard oriented circle** is the circle
$S^1=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ with its standard counterclockwise orientation,
regarded as a smooth $1$-manifold; a
**finite disjoint union of oriented circles** is a smooth manifold
$C=S^1\sqcup\dots\sqcup S^1$ ($k$ summands, $k\in\mathbb N$)
diffeomorphic to the disjoint union of $k$ standard oriented circles. An
**oriented link** (with $k$ components) is a smooth embedding

$$L\colon C\longrightarrow S^3$$

of such a disjoint union in the sense of [[def-smooth-embedding]]. So $L$ is
injective, is an immersion, and is a homeomorphism onto its image with the
subspace topology, and its image $L(C)$ is a finite disjoint union of smoothly
embedded circles. Thus every link considered here is finite and tame: the
smoothness of $L$ is exactly the standing convention, and no polygonal or other
tame model is used. The **components** of $L$ are the images of the individual
summands, and the number of components is $k$.

**Ambient isotopy.** Let $I=[0,1]$. An **ambient isotopy** of $S^3$ is a smooth
map

$$H\colon S^3\times I\longrightarrow S^3$$

such that $H_0=\mathrm{id}_{S^3}$, each $H_t\colon S^3\to S^3$,
$H_t(x):=H(x,t)$, is a diffeomorphism ([[def-diffeomorphism-and-local-diffeomorphism-of-manifolds]]),
and each $H_t$ is orientation-preserving with respect to the fixed orientation.
The last clause is in fact automatic: $t\mapsto H_t$ is continuous in the
$C^\infty$ topology of the diffeomorphism group, the orientation sign is locally
constant in $t$, and $H_0=\mathrm{id}$ is orientation-preserving, so it is kept
only for emphasis.

**Equivalence of links.** Two oriented links $L_0\colon C_0\to S^3$ and
$L_1\colon C_1\to S^3$ are **equivalent** (written $L_0\sim L_1$), or
**ambient isotopic**, when there are an ambient isotopy $H$ and an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism $f:C_0\to C_1$ with
$H_1\circ L_0=L_1\circ f$. Thus parametrizations and component labels are
irrelevant, while the induced orientation of each image component is preserved. The relation is an equivalence relation on links:
it is reflexive with $H=\mathrm{id}$, transitive by composing isotopies, and
symmetric because a smooth family of diffeomorphisms has a smooth family of
inverses. An equivalence class is an **(oriented) link type**.

**Moving off $\infty$.** Because the definition of equivalence allows the
isotopy to move a link through $\infty$, the standard practice of this page is
to first apply an ambient isotopy that carries a given link into the open ball,
and only then to project; every projection and every Reidemeister move below is
read after moving the link off $\infty$ into $\mathbb R^3$ in this way. The
orientation-preserving clause in the definition of ambient isotopy is exactly
what the oriented Reidemeister moves and the oriented closure construction must
respect. The unoriented theory uses the same ambient isotopies but forgets
the orientations of the link components.

**Links in the three-sphere versus links in $\mathbb R^3$.** A link contained in
$\mathbb R^3\subset S^3$ is a link in $S^3$; conversely every link may be
assumed after isotopy to lie in $\mathbb R^3$, by choosing a point outside the compact one-dimensional image and moving that
point to $\infty$ by a smooth rotation of the standard sphere. When comparing
links already in $\mathbb R^3$, an isotopy can also be arranged to avoid
$\infty$ throughout; the track-avoidance argument is given in
[[thm-oriented-reidemeister-equivalence-theorem]].

Fix a coordinate orientation-reversing reflection $r:S^3\to S^3$ for the mirror convention. Let $K$ and $J$ be smooth oriented knots in the standard oriented three-sphere. A connected-sum datum consists of one smoothly embedded closed three-ball around a short subarc of $K$ and one around a short subarc of $J$, each meeting its knot in a single trivial properly embedded arc, together with the fixed standard orientation-reversing boundary identification of the two standard oriented ball boundaries that joins the oriented arcs into one circle. Choose this standard map once in the standard two-ball model so that it commutes with $r$ and an orientation-preserving half-turn interchanging the two balls preserves the joining convention. Here a trivial arc is an embedded interval in a ball that is carried by an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism of ball-arc pairs to a straight diameter. Remove the interiors of the two balls and glue the remaining boundary spheres using this fixed identification; the resulting oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere is a connected sum of $K$ and $J$, denoted $K\#J$ for the specified datum.

The **standard unknot** is the oriented unit circle in a fixed coordinate two-plane of $S^3\subset\mathbb R^4$. A knot is **nontrivial** if it is not ambient isotopic through orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms of $S^3$ to the standard unknot. A nontrivial knot is **prime** if it has no connected-sum presentation whose two summand knots are both nontrivial.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$.

1. **Compact main case.** Let $M$ be a compact smooth manifold, possibly with boundary, let $N$ be a smooth manifold without boundary, let $F:M\times I\to N$ be a smooth isotopy of embeddings that is constant near the ends of $I$, and let $W$ be an open neighbourhood of $F(M\times I)$ in $N$. Then there is an ambient isotopy $H:N\times I\to N$ with $H_0=\mathrm{id}_N$, every $H_t$ a diffeomorphism, $H_t\circ F_0=F_t$ for all $t\in I$, $H_t=\mathrm{id}_N$ outside $W$ for every $t$, and $H_t$ stationary near the ends; if $F$ is constant near the ends with parameter $\varepsilon$, then $H_t=\mathrm{id}_N$ for $t\le\varepsilon/2$ and $H_t=H_1$ for $t\ge1-\varepsilon/2$.
2. **Relative form.** Let $N$ be boundaryless, $U\subseteq N$ open, $A\subseteq U$ compact, and let $F:U\times I\to N$ be a smooth isotopy of embeddings whose track image is open in $N\times I$. Then there is a compactly supported ambient isotopy $H$ of $N$ with $H_t\circ F_0=F_t$ on a neighbourhood of $A$ for every $t$.
3. **Boundary stratum.** If $N$ has boundary and $F(M\times I)\subseteq\partial N$, then the ambient isotopy of clause 1 can be chosen with every $H_t$ carrying $\partial N$ onto itself; if $F(M\times I)\subseteq N\setminus\partial N$, it can be chosen compactly supported in $N\setminus\partial N$.
4. **General isotopies.** For the same compact source (possibly with boundary) and boundaryless target as in clause 1, every smooth isotopy extends with support in a compact subset of any prescribed neighbourhood $W$ of $F(M\times I)$. The endpoint-constancy hypothesis and the stationary-end conclusion are both omitted; all other conclusions of clause 1 hold.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: A change of knot representative already comes with an oriented ambient isotopy by [F1]. Applying that isotopy to its ball-arc data carries the cut complement and its boundary collars to the new data, so the standard gluing produces an ambient-isotopic sum. A change of radius in one local straightening chart is the isotopy that rescales the standard ball radially while preserving its oriented diameter. This is an isotopy of compact ball-arc embeddings, so [A1] and [F3] extend it to an ambient isotopy of the knot sphere.

For two local oriented ball-arc charts centered at the same point, express them in one smooth coordinate chart. Their transition germ fixes the center, carries the positive tangent line of the knot to itself, and has positive determinant. Shrink to a common ball and use the smooth rescaling homotopy $G_s(x)=s^{-1}(G(sx)-G(0))$ for $s>0$, with $G_0(x)=DG_0(x)$. Taylor's formula gives the smooth extension at $s=0$. On a sufficiently small common ball the differentials stay uniformly close to the injective linear map $DG_0$, so every $G_s$ is an embedding and preserves the oriented diameter. The subgroup of invertible linear maps preserving that oriented line and the ambient orientation is path-connected: in line-normal coordinates its diagonal blocks lie in $(0,\infty)$ and $GL^+(2,\mathbb R)$, and the shear block contracts linearly to zero. Thus the chart germ is isotopic through oriented ball-arc embeddings to the fixed standard chart.

If the marked points differ, move the parameter point along the knot circle by a smooth isotopy of that circle. The resulting family of knot embeddings carries the short oriented subarc along a finite chain of local straightening charts; compactness of the parameter interval gives a common sufficiently small ball radius. Apply [F3] to this isotopy and to the chart isotopies of steps 1.1 and 1.2. The resulting ambient isotopies identify the cut complements with their boundary collars and preserve the fixed endpoint pairing in the standard gluing. Hence they induce an oriented ambient isotopy between the two connected-sum outputs.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice-principle-for-foliation-pair]]). Let $S$ be an oriented Hausdorff $C^2$ surface without boundary, possibly disconnected. Then:

1. Every compact subset $K\subset S$ lies in the interior of a compact finitely cellulated $C^2$ subsurface $N$. If $K$ is contained in one connected component of $S$, $N$ can be chosen connected. A specified finite embedded regular $C^2$ graph contained in $\operatorname{Int}N$ can be included in its one-skeleton.
2. Every connected closed compact subsurface has an oriented genus normal form: the sphere for $g=0$, or the polygon word $\prod_{i=1}^g a_i b_i a_i^{-1}b_i^{-1}$ for $g\ge1$, with $\chi=2-2g$. A connected compact subsurface with $b>0$ boundary circles has a free fundamental group; capping its boundaries defines genus $g$ and gives $\chi=2-2g-b$ and free rank $2g+b-1$.
3. The fundamental group of every connected component of $S$ is torsion-free.
4. Every regular embedded $C^2$ nullhomotopic circle $c$ bounds an embedded compact disk region in $S$. Here a disk region is a compact subsurface homeomorphic to the closed disk, with boundary exactly $c$; its inherited surface structure and boundary are $C^2$. It is unique unless the **connected component containing $c$** is a sphere; in that component the two complementary disk regions are the two possibilities.

The normal forms in clause 2 are homeomorphism normal forms. No general differentiable smoothing theorem or arbitrary-surface triangulation-existence theorem is a premise of this item.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. A compact $C^2$ surface, with regular $C^2$ boundary allowed, is $C^2$ diffeomorphic to a compact smooth surface with smooth boundary. For a compact cooriented embedded surface in a smooth three-manifold, the diffeomorphism can be obtained by arbitrarily small local ambient displacements. This also applies to a compact intrinsic subsurface of a $C^2$ leaf: compactness is in the leaf topology, and its boundary is regular in that topology.

A connected oriented closed such surface with Euler characteristic zero is $C^2$ diffeomorphic to $T^2$. A compact regular surface region homeomorphic to a closed disk is $C^2$ diffeomorphic to $D^2$, and any prescribed $C^2$ diffeomorphism of its boundary circle can be realized by the disk parametrization.

Two disjoint regular closed disk regions in a $C^2$ sphere can simultaneously be carried to the standard two disk windows by a $C^2$ diffeomorphism, with compatible prescribed boundary parametrizations. A $C^2$ scalar function defined on a neighborhood of a compact set in $\mathbb R^2$ admits smooth approximations uniformly with its derivatives through order two on that compact set.

Finally let $L$ be a $C^2$ surface and $u:D^2\to L$ an **intrinsically continuous** map which is $C^2$ on an open boundary collar. On any smaller closed boundary collar contained in that open collar, $u$ has arbitrarily close $C^2$ approximations agreeing with $u$ on a neighborhood of the smaller collar, and a homotopy to each approximation fixed there. Closeness is uniform for any fixed compatible metric on $L$. No injectivity or immersion of the cap map is required.

Let $f:M\to\mathbb R$ be smooth, let $p$ be a nondegenerate critical point of
$f$, and let $\lambda$ be the index of $p$. If $n=\dim M$, then there are local
coordinates $(x^1,\dots,x^n)$ centered at $p$ in which

$$f=f(p)-\sum_{i=1}^{\lambda}(x^i)^2+\sum_{i=\lambda+1}^{n}(x^i)^2.$$

For $n=0$, both sums are empty.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$.

1. **Compact main case.** Let $M$ be a compact smooth manifold, possibly with boundary, let $N$ be a smooth manifold without boundary, let $F:M\times I\to N$ be a smooth isotopy of embeddings that is constant near the ends of $I$, and let $W$ be an open neighbourhood of $F(M\times I)$ in $N$. Then there is an ambient isotopy $H:N\times I\to N$ with $H_0=\mathrm{id}_N$, every $H_t$ a diffeomorphism, $H_t\circ F_0=F_t$ for all $t\in I$, $H_t=\mathrm{id}_N$ outside $W$ for every $t$, and $H_t$ stationary near the ends; if $F$ is constant near the ends with parameter $\varepsilon$, then $H_t=\mathrm{id}_N$ for $t\le\varepsilon/2$ and $H_t=H_1$ for $t\ge1-\varepsilon/2$.
2. **Relative form.** Let $N$ be boundaryless, $U\subseteq N$ open, $A\subseteq U$ compact, and let $F:U\times I\to N$ be a smooth isotopy of embeddings whose track image is open in $N\times I$. Then there is a compactly supported ambient isotopy $H$ of $N$ with $H_t\circ F_0=F_t$ on a neighbourhood of $A$ for every $t$.

The endpoint-constancy hypothesis and the stationary-end conclusion are both omitted; all other conclusions of clause 1 hold.

Assume countable choice. For $n=2$ or $3$, a smoothly embedded closed $n$-ball in a connected boundaryless smooth $n$-manifold can be carried to a sufficiently small coordinate round ball by a smooth ambient isotopy. Consequently, a smooth closed disk in the boundary of a smooth $3$-ball is a standard disk window: the pair consisting of the ball and that disk is diffeomorphic to a round ball with a hemispherical boundary disk. Attaching a smooth $3$-ball to a smooth manifold along one such disk window does not change the diffeomorphism type, after smoothing the corner. The same conclusion holds in reverse, when a ball meeting the boundary in one disk is removed; the diffeomorphism is supported near the attached or removed ball and its attaching collar.

statement.

> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: On a compact height band without critical points, the restriction of height to the surface has a smooth field $X$ with $dz(X)=1$: in any surface chart divide a coordinate field by its nonzero height derivative, and combine finitely many such fields by a smooth partition near the compact band. Its flow carries the level circles through the band. Existence for the entire height interval follows by covering the compact band by finitely many flow charts, choosing a common positive short time, and restarting; the trajectory remains in the band until its height reaches an endpoint. Projecting each moving circle to its horizontal plane gives a smooth isotopy of disjoint plane curves. Its velocity has a smooth planar extension near the circles by their normal collar charts; finitely many cutoffs give a compactly supported extension. Its planar flow therefore straightens these curves simultaneously, level by level. In ambient coordinates use $(x,z)\mapsto(g_z(x),z)$ for these plane diffeomorphisms, cutting it off beyond the end levels. Consequently every regular end of the piece can be made vertical. The construction can be made fixed near its attachment to a critical neighborhood.

Move the horizontal caps toward the critical level, stopping in a sufficiently thin slab about that level; in a regular collar this is exactly shortening a vertical cylinder and translating its cap. With nested caps perform the move on the innermost disk first and keep the stopping heights distinct in the order imposed by disjointness. This prevents intersections: outside the moving collar the only possible obstruction is another cap over a nested planar disk, and that cap has already been moved to a nearer stopping height or is kept beyond the moving one. Use positive, strictly monotone changes of the height coordinate along each cylinder, constant near its fixed end, to implement these moves; on the cap use the corresponding translation. Smooth corner rounding is done in disjoint collar neighborhoods. These are isotopies of the capped surface, and [F2] extends them ambiently. The same shortening applies in a component with no critical point, using any intermediate level.

At a saddle use the chart $z=z(p)+u^2-v^2$. Outside a small rectangle about the saddle the regular sheets can be made vertical by step 1.1. Viewed in the horizontal plane, the two circles on the two-component side are joined by the projected saddle rectangle; its interior misses those circles. There are exactly two possibilities: their bounded disks are disjoint, or one disk lies inside the other. To justify completeness, each circle bounds the unique disk in the plane by [F1]. The connected second circle avoids the first and hence lies entirely in its disk interior or its exterior; applying the same argument with the two interchanged gives precisely disjoint or nested disks. The rectangle lies in the region adjacent to both of its attaching arcs: outside both disks in the disjoint case and in the annulus between them in the nested case. A different region would force it to cross one of the two circles. The saddle's other level circle is the boundary obtained by the band reconnection. Reverse height if necessary so this is the one-component side.

With no critical point the connected uncapped piece is a cylinder: the flow in step 1.1 identifies it with one level circle times an interval. After shortening and straightening it is the vertical wall over a plane circle, with one disk cap at each end. Its bounded region is $D^2\times I$ in the disk coordinates from [F1]. This is a ball after rounding: replace the product corners in the disk-radius/height half-plane by circular arcs; the rounded solid is a smooth convex cylinder with rounded ends, radially parametrizable from its center. If there is a maximum or a minimum, the critical chart in [F2] is a paraboloid disk. The regular part is a cylinder attached to its boundary, by step 1.1. Shorten that cylinder into the chart. The paraboloid and its opposite planar cap bound a region $\{(u,v,t):0\le t\le c-u^2-v^2\}$, or its reflection. It is a ball, since rounding its edge gives a convex solid with a smooth radial parametrization; a radial rescaling is constant linear near the center and adjusted near the boundary. Thus these three cases give standard balls.

In the disjoint-disk case, straighten the two attaching arcs in the boundary collars of their planar disks. The projected union of the two disks and the connecting rectangle is a disk: shrink the disks in their parametrizations to end caps, straighten the rectangle in its product coordinates, and round to a stadium. All remaining interval parametrizations extend over their collars by increasing interpolation, so this is an actual disk parametrization. The capped saddle bounds the solid made from the two short disk cylinders by a single thickened rectangle joining one disk window of each. Indeed, away from the rectangle its boundary is exactly the two vertical walls and their horizontal caps; across the rectangle its boundary has the reconnection prescribed by $u^2-v^2$. Rounding the rectangle's two lower or upper edges produces that saddle chart, and rounding the other edges gives precisely the cap collars. The two cylinders are balls by step 3.1. The thickened rectangle is a ball meeting the first cylinder in one disk, and its union with that cylinder meets the second cylinder in one disk. > $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Choose a point of $S^3$ outside $S$ and use its stereographic chart to regard $S$ as a compact smoothly embedded sphere in $\mathbb R^3$. By [F1] choose a direction whose restricted height is Morse, and rotate it to the $z$ direction. Separate its finitely many critical values by the finite small perturbation in [F1]. Realize that perturbation geometrically by retaining the $x,y$ coordinates and changing only $z$. A sufficiently small $C^1$ perturbation and its straight interpolation are embeddings: finitely many graph charts retain a nonzero rank-two minor and local injectivity, while pairs of source points outside those chart neighborhoods have a positive image-separation minimum by compactness. Choose the perturbation below both bounds. By [F5] this is an ambient isotopy of $S^3$, supported away from the stereographic point. It therefore suffices to prove that the resulting sphere, with excellent Morse height, bounds a smooth standard ball in $\mathbb R^3$.

Choose finitely many regular heights between consecutive critical values. A level meets the sphere in finitely many smooth disjoint circles: its preimage is a compact regular one-manifold, and finitely many connected local interval charts cover it. Each circle bounds a planar smooth disk by [F2]. Choose an innermost circle, so that this disk's interior misses every other level circle and hence misses the sphere. In a sufficiently thin regular band around the level remove the sphere's annular collar of that circle and replace it by the two horizontal disks at the band's ends. The level curves vary smoothly, so their disks at nearby heights remain disjoint from the rest of the surface after a sufficiently small band shrink. Round the two seams in that band. This is surgery on the sphere along a disk whose interior misses the surface.

Every such surgery replaces one smooth sphere by two smooth spheres. Indeed its circle splits that sphere into two disk regions by [F2], and each region, with the added cap, is a smooth sphere: the boundary gluing is a smooth circle map and extends over a disk by the angular interpolation used in [F2]'s normal-form construction. Now repeat step 1.2 on each remaining circle of that regular level, always innermost among the remaining circles and with a new sufficiently small collar width. Earlier horizontal caps are kept at distinct nearby levels, and the new width is chosen smaller than their positive distances from the chosen level. There are finitely many circles. Then repeat at the finitely many other chosen regular levels, with disjoint level neighborhoods. The outcome is a finite disjoint collection of smooth spheres, each made from a connected piece of the original sphere between successive cutting levels, together with horizontal caps. Each such piece contains at most one height critical point.

By [F3] each final sphere bounds a smooth embedded standard ball. We shall reverse the surgeries and prove inductively that each sphere then present bounds a smooth embedded standard ball. No assertion that all their chosen balls are disjoint is needed: balls bounded by disjoint spheres may be nested.

Consider the reverse of the last unreversed surgery, whose two output spheres bound balls $A$ and $B$ by the inductive assertion. In its product disk neighborhood the two added cap disks can be moved toward each other until both occupy the original surgery disk $D$; equivalently shrink the normal coordinate of the deleted annular collar to zero. Their remaining boundaries are disjoint. The move is an isotopy up to its endpoint on each individual ball, because the cap has a product collar and its boundary annulus is shortened monotonically; at the endpoint it merely meets the other ball's boundary in $D$. An arbitrarily small corner rounding reverses this motion and recovers the pre-surgery sphere. The balls now have either disjoint interiors and intersection exactly $D$, or one is contained in the other, with their boundaries meeting exactly in $D$. To check that these alternatives exhaust the possibilities, first take their disjoint cap positions. The complement of a known embedded ball in $\mathbb R^3$ is connected: [F4] carries that ball to a round one by a compactly supported ambient isotopy. Hence each connected sphere disjoint from the other's boundary lies wholly inside or wholly outside its ball. If neither ball contains the other's boundary, their interiors are disjoint; otherwise one ball is inside the other. The product cap motion preserves the corresponding alternative and makes their boundary contact exactly $D$.

In the disjoint-interior case the pre-surgery sphere is the rounded boundary of $A\cup_D B$. This union is a ball by disk absorption [F4]. In the nested case, relabel so that $B\subset A$; the pre-surgery sphere is the rounded boundary of $A\setminus\operatorname{Int}B$, where $B$ meets $\partial A$ in the disk $D$. Disk removal [F4] says that this too is a ball. These boundary identifications can be checked in $D\times[-\varepsilon,\varepsilon]$: the pre-surgery annular wall is the side $\partial D\times[-\varepsilon,\varepsilon]$, whereas surgery inserts the faces $D\times\{-\varepsilon,\varepsilon\}$; all surfaces agree outside that neighborhood. Thus the induction gives a smooth standard ball bounded by the original excellent-height sphere. Undoing the initial small ambient isotopy gives a smooth embedded standard ball bounded by the given $S$.

Apply [F4] to that parametrized embedded ball, using the stereographic chart, to carry it by an ambient isotopy to a small Euclidean round ball. Translation and positive dilation in $\mathbb R^3$ extend smoothly across its compactifying point: they are the usual stereographic conformal transformations of $S^3$, and their parameter paths give smooth ambient isotopies. They carry the round boundary sphere to the unit sphere, the standard equator in this stereographic convention. Concatenate with the preceding isotopies, using smooth stationary reparametrizations. This gives the claimed $H_t$, starting at the identity. The two components and both ball diffeomorphisms are now the inverse images of the two standard open hemispheres and their closures under $H_1$. The two restrictions agree on $S$ because they restrict one ambient diffeomorphism, and pulling back the standard equator's two-sided collar gives a common collar with the same property.
