citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume full AC. Every compact topological three-manifold $M$, with boundary allowed, is homeomorphic to the realization of a finite combinatorial three-manifold triangulation, with boundary allowed (the empty complex when $M=\varnothing$). Its boundary is the realization of a subcomplex. Thus $M$ admits a finite compatible PL structure, without any previously supplied smooth or PL structure on its interior.

If a TOP product collar of the boundary, together with a finite PL structure on its boundary surface, has already been supplied, the new PL structure may be chosen equal to that product PL structure on a smaller boundary neighborhood. No smooth marking or smooth ambient isotopy is asserted. Full AC remains the hypothesis of this theorem; no choice-free theorem is obtained by omitting that premise.

Assume full AC. Put $B^j=[-1,1]^j$. Let $k+n=3$, $0\le k\le3$, and let $h:B^k\times\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^3$ be a topological embedding which is PL on a neighborhood of $\partial B^k\times\mathbb R^n$. There is an isotopy of embeddings $h_t$, $0\le t\le1$, starting at $h$, such that $h_1$ is PL on a neighborhood of $B^k\times B^n$, and
$$h_t=h\quad\text{on}\quad(\partial B^k\times\mathbb R^n)\cup\bigl(B^k\times(\mathbb R^n\setminus\operatorname{Int}(2B^n))\bigr).$$
For $n=0$ this means a boundary-relative straightening of the whole three-ball. More precisely $h_t=hP_t$ for an ambient TOP isotopy of the source with jointly continuous inverses and the displayed fixed set. No smooth isotopy is asserted.

This is a full-AC-qualified TOP-to-PL handle statement, including handles whose interior was only topologically parametrized. It does not by itself provide a finite triangulation of an arbitrary compact TOP manifold or discharge an original choice-free consumer.

Let $M$ be a compact connected orientable PL three-manifold supplied with a finite PL triangulation, possibly with nonempty boundary. There are finitely many compact connected orientable PL three-manifolds $P_1,\ldots,P_q$, $q\ge1$, each **prime**, and a finite PL connected-sum presentation
$$M\cong P_1\mathbin\#\cdots\mathbin\# P_q.$$
Here prime means that a PL connected-sum factorization has a standard PL three-sphere as one factor. Connected sum removes interiors of parametrized PL balls and glues their boundary spheres by supplied finite PL maps. The presentation supplies the cut spheres, cap-ball parameters and gluing maps, and identifies every original boundary component of $M$ with its boundary component in exactly one factor. Original sphere boundary components are allowed; their ball factors are not discarded. The presentation can be chosen with non-irreducible factors only standard $S^1\times S^2$; every other prime factor is PL irreducible.

This is existence in an already supplied finite PL manifold. No uniqueness, TOP triangulation, TOP-to-PL compatibility, Poincare conjecture, or statement that an arbitrary TOP ball is a PL ball is asserted. No choice axiom is required.

A supplied finite PL embedding of the standard PL two-sphere in $\mathbb R^3$ bounds a compact parametrized PL three-ball; its two complementary components are the bounded ball interior and a connected unbounded exterior. A supplied finite PL embedding of the standard PL two-sphere in the standard PL three-sphere bounds two parametrized PL three-balls, and a PL homeomorphism of that three-sphere carries it to the common boundary in a standard double of a convex three-ball. All parameters and homeomorphisms are finite PL on the compact spaces in question. No choice hypothesis is introduced.

This is a PL assertion in already supplied standard PL ambient spaces. It does not assert triangulability of arbitrary topological three-manifolds or tame arbitrary wild sphere embeddings.

Here a parametrized PL ball means a finite polyhedron supplied with a piecewise linear homeomorphism, with piecewise linear inverse, to a convex polyhedral ball of the stated dimension. All subpolyhedra and maps in the following assertions are finite.

(a) Let $B_1,B_2$ be parametrized PL three-balls and $D_i\subset\partial B_i$ parametrized PL two-disks. Every PL homeomorphism $f:D_1\to D_2$ extends to a PL homeomorphism $B_1\to B_2$.

(b) The space obtained by gluing two parametrized PL three-balls along parametrized PL two-disks in their boundaries, by a specified PL homeomorphism, is a parametrized PL three-ball.

(c) Let $B$ and $A\subset B$ be parametrized PL three-balls, with $A\ne B$. Suppose $A\cap\partial B=\partial A\cap\partial B=D$ is a parametrized PL two-disk and $A\setminus D\subset\operatorname{Int}B$. Impose the following standard boundary-window condition at $C=\partial D$: every point of $C$ has a PL coordinate neighborhood in which
$$B=\{(u,v,w):w\ge0\},\qquad A=\{(u,v,w):w\ge0,\ v\le0\},\qquad D=\{w=0,\ v\le0\}.$$
The equalities are understood after intersection with the coordinate neighborhood, and $C$ corresponds to $v=w=0$. Then $Q=\overline{B\setminus A}$, with closure in $B$, is a parametrized PL three-ball.

No assertion about a sphere in an arbitrary PL three-manifold is assumed. In (c) the closure of the set difference is essential: $B\setminus\operatorname{Int}_{\mathbb R^3}A$ would retain the interior of the contact disk as an extra sheet. These statements introduce no choice hypothesis.

Every finite convex cell complex has a compatible finite simplicial triangulation. Choose one relative interior point in each nonempty cell; triangulate the boundary in increasing dimension and cone from that point. This construction agrees on every common face and preserves each cell as a subpolyhedron.

Let $M$ be a compact topological three-manifold with boundary $P$. Suppose a finite combinatorial PL surface $P_0$ and a homeomorphism $P_0\to P$ are given. Then there is a TOP embedding $c:P\times[0,1]\to M$ with $c(x,0)=x$ such that $c(P\times[0,1))$ is a relatively open neighborhood of $P$ in $M$. If $P$ is empty the empty embedding has this property.

The boundary PL structure is used to organize finitely many local pushes only. No PL structure on $M$, and no PL or smooth property of the resulting collar, is asserted or assumed.

For every simplicial complex $K$ and abelian group $G$, there is a canonical
natural isomorphism $H_n^{\mathrm{simp}}(K;G)\cong H_n(|K|;G)$ for all $n$.
When the vertex set has a supplied total order, it is induced by the
simplicial-to-singular chain map of [[def-simplicial-to-singular-chain-map]],
extended $G$-linearly. Different supplied orders induce the same homology map.
For an arbitrary vertex set, the isomorphism is defined compatibly on its
finite subcomplexes and requires no choice principle.

For an open cover $X=U\cup V$, the sequence
$$\cdots\to H_n(U\cap V;G)\to H_n(U;G)\oplus H_n(V;G)\to H_n(X;G)\xrightarrow{\delta}H_{n-1}(U\cap V;G)\to\cdots$$
is exact, with middle map $(u,v)\mapsto u+v$.

derivations.claim: Fix the finite PL structure on $M$ supplied by [F1]. We give the compatibility operation needed below, rather than assume that an arbitrary TOP sphere was PL in this structure. For a finite disjoint locally flat sphere system, cut along its spheres using their local flat charts. The orientation of each sphere and of $M$ labels the two local sides consistently; the cut space is therefore a compact TOP manifold with two boundary copies of each sphere, and its old boundary unchanged. Assign the standard finite sphere PL parameter to one copy and the identical parameter under the cutting identification to the other. These finitely many new boundary components have collars by [F5]; keep also the old PL boundary collar of $M$, choosing all collars disjoint. Apply the relative assertion of [F1] to each cut component. On the smaller new boundary collars the cutting identification is the identity in the assigned sphere parameters, so gluing the collars gives an actual PL product across each seam. Finite product-cell subdivisions give a finite PL structure $\Sigma'$ on the original $M$ in which every sphere of the system is PL. It agrees with the original structure $\Sigma$ near $\partial M$. This operation also applies to any finite TOP connected-sum presentation: each gluing sphere receives matching parameters, and its cap balls have the cone parameters of [F4].

Two such finite PL structures $\Sigma,\Sigma'$ on $M$ agreeing near its boundary are related by a homeomorphism $u:(M,\Sigma)\to(M,\Sigma')$ TOP isotopic to the identity, fixed on a smaller boundary collar. Here is the needed relative comparison construction. Cover the compact remainder of that collar by $\Sigma'$ coordinate domains. Subdivide the finite $\Sigma$ triangulation so finely that the closed thirty-two-fold star of each simplex meeting the remainder is in one of these domains; finite cover shrinking and the geometric mesh decrease give this subdivision. Form the vertex, edge, face and tetrahedron handles of [F1], Proof1.1, with all transverse extensions inside these stars. At each index straighten the current identity map in the chosen $\Sigma'$ coordinate chart using [F2]. Its source parameter is a $\Sigma$ PL handle; for positive index its attaching band lies in the already straightened region. Protect smaller earlier core neighborhoods and trim the attaching bands exactly as in [F1], Proof2.1. Here the coordinate control is finite and explicit. Choose the transverse extensions inside the closed two-fold star of their core simplex; at a fixed index their nonidentity supports are disjoint, after trimming the protected attaching bands. A correction can therefore carry a point only between simplices at most four adjacency steps apart, and at most one correction of that index moves it. Before the last index there have been at most three such stages. Consequently the current image of a handle and its transverse extension stays in the closed thirty-two-fold star of its core simplex, inside its chosen target coordinate domain. A sufficiently fine subdivision has this property because each fixed finite iterate of the star has mesh tending to zero. Thus every coordinate embedding to which [F2] is applied really has its whole domain in the chosen chart; no PL compatibility of the original TOP transition maps is assumed. Each correction is the identity on its attaching boundary and outside its own compact twice-core, so extends to all of $M$. Subsequent widths are chosen inside the remaining PL neighborhoods. The index-zero through index-three cores and their protected bands cover the remainder, just as in [F1], Proof2.1. At the endpoint the map is locally PL everywhere, including the unchanged boundary collar. Its inverse is locally PL on the same finite image subdivisions, hence it is a PL homeomorphism. Concatenating the finitely many supported isotopies gives $u$ and its TOP ambient isotopy. In particular, pulling the system of step1.1 back by $u$ makes it a PL sphere system in the ORIGINAL structure by an actual TOP ambient isotopy; this statement does not assert a smooth isotopy.

Consequently PL primeness and PL irreducibility for a finite PL manifold agree with their TOP tame versions. One recognition detail is needed in the reverse direction: if a closed finite PL manifold is TOP homeomorphic to $S^3$, pull its PL structure to standard $S^3$ and apply step2.1 (there is no boundary collar condition) to obtain a PL homeomorphism to standard PL $S^3$. If a finite PL manifold with sphere boundary is a TOP ball, its PL double is TOP $S^3$; the preceding recognition and [F4] make each half a PL ball. Thus neither a TOP sphere factor nor a TOP ball side is silently being recognized as PL without the comparison construction. Indeed a TOP splitting sphere can be moved to a PL sphere by steps1.1 and2.1, and the ambient homeomorphism identifies its two cut components. If its PL side is a parametrized ball, its TOP side is a parametrized TOP ball; conversely every PL splitting is an admitted TOP splitting. The same argument compares every finite TOP connected-sum presentation with a finite PL presentation. Capping choices do not affect the homeomorphism types: conjugate any boundary identification to a sphere map and extend by the cone formula $[x,t]\mapsto[f(x),t]$, which is a homeomorphism even when $f$ is only TOP. No assertion that a TOP ball parameter was PL in the old structure is used. Now apply [F3] to the fixed finite triangulation of $M$. It gives a finite connected sum of factors prime in the full tame TOP sense, with boundary allowed and every original boundary mark retained. This proves existence. It also proves the asserted prime-but-not-irreducible exception: [F3] proves $S^1\times S^2$ PL prime, hence TOP prime by this step, and $\{*\}\times S^2$ is nonseparating and cannot bound a ball. Every other prime is irreducible by [F3] and this same compatibility operation.

We prove uniqueness first for finite PL presentations in one fixed PL manifold. A system $S$ will be said to reduce $M$ to a list $P_1,\ldots,P_k$ if cutting along $S$ and capping its cut faces gives precisely these manifolds together with some standard three-spheres having no original boundary marks. All original boundary components remain assigned to their cut component. Each $P_i$ is irreducible and is not $S^3$; balls and other factors with original boundary are retained. Given a prime presentation, take its separating connected-sum spheres and add one standard nonseparating sphere in each $S^1\times S^2$ summand. Their finite collars and the marked model in [F3], Proof3.1, show that they reduce $M$ to its irreducible nonspherical prime factors: cutting and capping the added sphere turns that summand into $S^3$. The cap-ball avoidance construction [F3], Proof1.1, realizes all these spheres disjointly in the original manifold. Conversely, if $S$ reduces to this list, adding any finite PL spheres disjoint from $S$ leaves the list unchanged. In a capped irreducible component each new sphere bounds a ball. Its cut-and-cap operation leaves that component and an unmarked $S^3$; in a capped $S^3$ this follows from [F4]. Move cap balls off the sphere as in [F3], Proof1.1, to carry out the cutting, or equivalently keep track of the cap balls as punctures on their respective sides. They introduce only extra punctures and do not erase an original boundary component. Induction over the finite added spheres proves the assertion.

Let $S$ and $T$ be systems reducing $M$ to the irreducible lists from two prime presentations. Make their intersection transverse by a finite PL perturbation of one system. To see the finiteness and the local condition, take finite common subdivisions of their surface charts and ambient stars, and move their vertices by sufficiently small generic displacements in the finite linear charts. Avoid the finitely many affine incidences giving coincident vertices, tangencies or edge/face degeneracies; choose them one at a time outside these proper affine subsets. Finite compact disjoint simplices retain their positive separation, and the transverse link disks retain their embedding under such small moves. Use the boundary-fixed face-cone extensions in the ambient little stars to realize the moves, or just keep the parametrized perturbed surfaces; no factor changes. The intersection is now a compact one-manifold with a finite triangulation, hence finitely many disjoint polygonal circles. If there are no circles, keep the two systems. Otherwise choose a circle innermost on a component of $T$, bounding a PL disk $D$ whose interior misses $S$. The disk exists because a polygonal circle on a PL sphere bounds two parametrized disks by [F4]'s sphere boundary-disk construction.

Suppose $\partial D\subset S_j$. Surger $S_j$ along $D$: its two complementary disks capped by two close parallel copies of $D$ give spheres $S'_j,S''_j$. Small product pushes make both disjoint from $S_j$ and from all the other spheres of $S$. These are actual finite PL surfaces: in the finite disk and circle collar charts take two levels, triangulate the product strips, and flatten their quadrant corners by finite face-cone maps. The three spheres $S_j,S'_j,S''_j$ bound a parametrized three-punctured sphere $P$. For its parameter, take the collar of $S_j$ on the $D$ side and the narrow disk prism thickening $D$; it is the standard collar with a disk two-handle on one end. Cut the sphere parameter along the common circle into its two parametrized disks. The two disk prisms and their circle strip give, by the marked window gluing of [F4], a ball with two disjoint parametrized interior balls removed. This verifies the three-punctured-sphere description with its three specified boundary components, not just its homology. Add both new spheres to $S$. By step4.1 this enlarged system reduces to the same list. Then delete $S_j$. This attaches $P$ to the component on the other side of $S_j$ along exactly that one boundary sphere; the other two boundary spheres stay cut. After capping these two faces, the operation just fills the old $S_j$ face by a parametrized ball. Thus the capped component is unchanged, and all other capped components are unchanged. This remains true if the two sides belonged to the same component before adding the new spheres, since $P$ is an isolated component AFTER the two new cuts. The new system therefore reduces to the same list.

The surgery reduces the number of intersections with $T$. Choose its disk levels on opposite sides of $D\subset T$ and the circle collar so that the two cap disks miss $T$. Every remaining old intersection circle lies in one of the two complementary disks of $S_j$ and is merely carried to the corresponding new sphere. The chosen circle disappears, and no new one is created; all other members of $S$ are unchanged. Repeat step6.1 until the finite nonnegative intersection count is zero. The resulting $S^*$ is disjoint from $T$ and reduces to precisely the original $P_i$ list. Their union is now an enlargement both of $S^*$ and of $T$. Step4.1 says its capped components consist of the $P_i$ together with unmarked $S^3$'s and also of the $Q_i$ together with unmarked $S^3$'s. Hence the nonspherical irreducible factors occur with identical multiplicity and homeomorphism types, up to permutation. Original boundary marks may be retained throughout, though the Statement does not require that stronger marking.

The remaining number of $S^1\times S^2$ factors is also determined. Work over $\mathbb Q$. The finite triangulation and [F6] make $b_1(M)=\dim H_1(M;\mathbb Q)$ finite. For a separating connected-sum sphere, use its collar to form an open two-set cover; the intersection retracts to $S^2$. This sphere has $H_1=0$ and connected $H_0=\mathbb Q$, and its map to the two connected sides' $H_0$ groups is $a\mapsto(a,-a)$, injective. Exactness in [F6] gives $H_1(M;\mathbb Q)\cong H_1(P;\mathbb Q)\oplus H_1(Q;\mathbb Q)$; filling the boundary spheres has no effect on $H_1$ by the same cover sequence with a ball. For $S^1\times S^2$ use two proper overlapping open circle arcs whose intersection has two interval components, and multiply by $S^2$. Each of the two open sets retracts to $S^2$ and the overlap retracts to two copies of $S^2$. The sphere has zero $H_1$ by its finite boundary-of-a-tetrahedron chain complex in [F6]. The degree-zero map $\mathbb Q^2\to\mathbb Q^2$ sends both component generators to $(1,-1)$, so its kernel is one-dimensional. The same exact sequence gives $b_1(S^1\times S^2)=1$. Thus a presentation with irreducible list $P_i$ and $\ell$ such factors satisfies $b_1(M)=\sum_i b_1(P_i)+\ell$. Step7.1 identifies the sum for the two presentations, so their numbers $\ell$ are equal.

Finally take any two admitted finite tame TOP prime presentations of the original $M$. By steps1.1 and2.1 move each of their finite cutting systems to a PL system in the fixed structure. Their capped factors are homeomorphic to the original factors by step3.1. TOP prime factors become PL prime, so [F3]'s prime-versus-irreducible assertion applies; the explicit nonseparating handle model identifies the possible $S^1\times S^2$ factors. Steps4.1–8.1 therefore compare these two presentations and give precisely the required equality of prime factors up to order and insertion or deletion of $S^3$. A single-factor presentation and $M=S^3$ are included: the reducing system may be empty and its only capped component may be an unmarked $S^3$; the same refinement argument forces every nonspherical irreducible list to be empty, and step8.1 forces zero handle factors. Existence and the exceptional prime factor were proved in step3.1. All boundary cuts and cap maps used actual parameters, the only TOP-to-PL compatibility used the explicit relative operation of steps1.1 and2.1, and full AC entered through [A1], [F1] and [F2] exactly as declared.

citations.quote: Assume countable choice. Let $S\subset S^3$ be the image of a smooth embedding of the standard $S^2$. There is a smooth ambient isotopy $H_t:S^3\to S^3$, with $H_0=\operatorname{id}$, such that $H_1(S)$ is the standard equatorial sphere $E$. In particular $S^3\setminus S$ has exactly two components. Their closures $B_+$ and $B_-$ are smoothly embedded standard closed $3$-balls with common boundary $S$. If $D_+$ and $D_-$ denote the standard closed hemispheres bounded by $E$, the labels can be chosen so that the restrictions $H_1:B_\pm\to D_\pm$ are diffeomorphisms with the same boundary restriction $H_1|_S:S\to E$. Thus the ball identifications are compatible on their boundary and on a common two-sided collar of that boundary.

Fix a coordinate orientation-reversing reflection $r:S^3\to S^3$ for the mirror convention. Let $K$ and $J$ be smooth oriented knots in the standard oriented three-sphere. derivations.claim: If $K$ is ambient isotopic to the standard unknot, carry its planar spanning disk through the isotopy. This is a genus-zero spanning surface, and nonnegativity gives $g(K)=0$.

Conversely, use [F1] to let a smooth embedding $e:D^2\to S^3$ parametrize a genus-zero spanning surface with oriented boundary $K$. For $0<r\le1$ the circles $x\mapsto e(rx)$, $x\in S^1$, are embedded and form a smooth isotopy from $K$ to a sufficiently small circle about $e(0)$. This contracts circles inside the embedded disk; it does not contract the final circle to a point. Choose a point outside this spanning disk and the fixed standard disk; their union has empty interior, since finitely many surface slice charts cover each compact disk. Its stereographic complement is one common positive chart $\mathbb R^3$ containing both disks. Write $p$ for the chart image of $e(0)$ and $E$ for the expression of $e$ translated by $-p$, so $E(0)=0$. For small fixed $r>0$, the maps $x\mapsto E(trx)/t$ for $0<t\le1$, continued at $t=0$ by $r\,dE_0(x)$, are an isotopy of embedded circles in that chart. Indeed Taylor's formula gives the smooth extension and, on a small disk, the derivatives are uniformly close to the injective linear map $r\,dE_0$; projection onto its image plane gives a uniform injectivity estimate by integration along line segments. Their images lie in the chart after decreasing $r$.

The final linear ellipse is isotopic to an oriented round circle in its plane: use the positive square root of its two-dimensional Gram matrix to deform its ordered independent spanning vectors to an orthonormal pair. Complete that pair by its positive normal to a positive ambient frame. Apply the same shrinking and linearization to the fixed standard disk in the common stereographic chart, obtaining an oriented round circle about its interior point $q$. Join the two round circles explicitly in this $\mathbb R^3$: move the center along the segment from $p$ to $q$, interpolate their positive radii, and rotate the first positive frame to the second through rotations in $SO(3)$ (successive rotations about coordinate axes suffice). Each intermediate circle is embedded, and the whole finite track is compact in the chart. A half-turn about a diameter reverses a circle orientation if required while preserving the ambient orientation. Reverse the standard disk shrinking to finish at the fixed standard unknot. Extend the concatenated circle isotopies by [F2]; each ambient diffeomorphism preserves orientation since it starts at the identity. Thus $K$ is the standard oriented unknot.

Such a surface exists by [F1], [F3], and well-ordering of the nonnegative integers. The intersection is a compact one-manifold whose boundary is the two points $(K\#J)\cap S$, hence consists of one arc $\alpha$ and finitely many circles.

If circles occur, choose one innermost on $S$. Since the intersection circles are disjoint and the arc $\alpha$ is connected and misses them, finite nesting gives a disk side of some circle containing neither $\alpha$ nor another intersection component. By [F4] this is an embedded disk $D\subset S$, disjoint from $K$.

If the selected circle $c$ is nonseparating on $F$, cut $F$ along $c$ and cap the two new boundary copies by parallel copies of $D$, rounded in a product neighbourhood of $c$. The caps are disjoint and the boundary remains the original knot. Cutting along a circle preserves Euler characteristic and the two caps add $2$, so by [F2] the new genus is $g(F)-1$, contradicting minimality.

Let $D$ be a disk in one region of the complement of $\mathcal S$, with interior disjoint from that system and boundary a circle $c$ on a single sphere $A\in\mathcal S$. The circle misses the marks. Surgery on $A$ replaces it by the two spheres obtained by attaching parallel copies of $D$ to the two disks of $A\setminus c$, rounded and slightly pushed apart. The three spheres bound a standard sphere with three holes: take a product collar of $A$ and attach the thickened disk. Consequently the region on the other side of $A$ is unchanged after capping, except for extra punctures; all actual changes of capped knot occur in the one region containing the interior of $D$. Its other cap balls and arcs are untouched. This gives a precise local model in which the following cases are checked.

If $D$ has no mark, parity forces $c$ to leave both marks of $A$ in one disk of $A\setminus c$. Indeed otherwise one of the surgery spheres would meet the closed knot once, whereas a separating sphere has an even number of transverse intersections with a closed curve. Thus one surgery sphere is unmarked and the other has two marks. After capping the affected region, the unmarked sphere misses its closed knot. By [F2] its ball side not containing that connected knot is an empty ball. Filling or removing this empty ball and the adjoining product collars changes no capped knot. Discard the unmarked sphere and retain the twice-marked sphere. Hence this replacement preserves every nontrivial factor. The same argument covers empty ball and nested ball positions: it uses the side avoiding the capped knot, rather than a prespecified inside side.

If $D$ has one mark, parity instead forces each disk of $A\setminus c$ to have one mark. Both surgery spheres then have two marks. Let $C$ be the cap ball attached to $A$ on the affected region. Construct a proper disk $E\subset C$ with $\partial E=c$ by pushing one of the disks of $A\setminus c$ into the cap collar, fixing its boundary and rounding there. This disk is boundary parallel. Choose a simple boundary arc joining the two marks and crossing $c$ exactly once; a thin rectangular strip about that arc gives a boundary-parallel cap arc $\beta$ in $C$ meeting $E$ transversely exactly once. Explicitly the strip passes from the side of $E$ next to the first marked boundary disk to the side next to the other one, with a single normal crossing; away from that crossing it stays in disjoint boundary collars. Thus $\beta$ is trivial, and changing the original cap to $\beta$ is allowed by [F1]. Now $D\cup E$, rounded at $c$, meets the capped knot exactly twice: once on $D$ and once on $\beta$. It is the required marked decomposing sphere in the capped affected region. By [F1] the old factor $P$ is the sum $P'\#P''$ of the two new capped factors, with orientations inherited from the original knot. Since $P$ is prime, exactly one is the unknot and the other is $P$, by [F3]. Retain both new spheres temporarily and then delete the sphere separating that trivial region from its other neighbour. Deletion merges the neighbour with an unknot, so leaves its oriented knot class unchanged by [F3]. The net result is again a prime system with exactly the same unordered prime factors. The disk $E$ and the cap change lie entirely in $C$, disjoint from every other cap ball of the affected region. On the opposite region the three-holed-sphere collar of step 1.1 replaces only the cap at $A$: the short pieces of that cap become the caps on the two new spherical boundaries with the same endpoint pairing and orientation. Its other cap balls and their arcs stay pointwise fixed outside this collar. Therefore, even when that neighbour has several boundary spheres, deleting the sphere next to the trivial new region changes its capped knot precisely by oriented connected sum with the unknot, without changing any other attachment or factor.

To compare intersecting systems, choose a sphere of $\mathcal T$ that meets $\mathcal S$ and an innermost intersection disk on it containing at most one mark. Such a disk always exists: if there is one intersection circle, its two complementary disks have at most two marks in total, so choose a side with at most one. If there are several circles, the circle nesting tree has at least two leaf disks with disjoint interiors; since there are only two marks, one leaf contains at most one. Its interior misses $\mathcal S$. Use this disk in step 2.1 or step 2.2. The surgery copies can be pushed off $\mathcal T$ in its product neighbourhood and rounded near $c$; they introduce no new intersection circles, while $c$ disappears. Deleting a redundant sphere only decreases the count further. Thus the finite total number of intersection circles strictly decreases. Iterating makes the first system disjoint from $\mathcal T$, preserving its prime factor list throughout.

Add the spheres of $\mathcal T$ one at a time to the disjoint first system, initially allowing trivial capped regions. Let $D$ be an oriented link diagram ([[def-regular-oriented-link-diagram]]),
regarded as a decorated immersed oriented $4$-valent planar graph, and let
$V$ be its finite set of double points. At each $v\in V$ the two branches of
the diagram cross; the local **Seifert smoothing** of $D$ at $v$ replaces the
crossing by the unique pair of non-crossing arcs in a small disk about $v$ that
joins the four half-edges in the orientation-respecting way: entering along a
strand, one follows the smoothing turn that keeps the travelling direction
consistently on the same side, so that the two oriented arcs through $v$ are
reconnected without crossing. Performing this replacement in pairwise disjoint
small disks, one for each crossing, and leaving the rest of the diagram
unchanged produces the **Seifert smoothing of $D$**: a finite disjoint union of
oriented simple closed curves in $S^2$, its **Seifert circles**. At each
crossing the smoothing reconnects the four half-edges in one of the two
possible non-crossing ways, and exactly one of the two respects the
orientations; hence the smoothing is a well-defined operation on the diagram.
The Seifert smoothing may merge two circles into one or split one circle into
two at a crossing, so its number of circles is a new invariant of the picture
and is not in general the number of components of the link.

The **Seifert picture** of $D$ is the smoothed picture together with one signed
short arc at each former crossing $v$, drawn transversely to the two smoothed
strands and joining the two distinct Seifert circles that passed through $v$; the sign of the arc is the sign of the
crossing, positive or negative. The signed arcs lie in the complement of the
Seifert circles and meet the circles only at their endpoints
([[def-embedded-submanifold-and-slice-chart]]); every crossing is recorded exactly once. The two smoothed arcs at a crossing
are parallel and equally directed. They cannot belong to the same oriented
Jordan circle: the connecting strip is on opposite local sides of its two
equally directed boundary arcs, whereas a fixed complementary side of an
oriented Jordan circle is consistently on one local side. Thus each signed
arc joins distinct circles, coherently oriented in their common annulus. The orientation of each Seifert circle is the one induced by the
Smoothed strands, and the collection of circles and signed arcs is the object
to which the coherence and height definitions
([[def-coherence-of-seifert-circles-and-the-height-of-a-diagram]]) are applied.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $D$ be a finite regular oriented link diagram with exactly one component, and let $c$ be its number of crossings. Perform the following construction in its projection sphere $S^2$.

1. Choose a point $q\in S^2$ outside the finite diagram. In pairwise disjoint small disks about the crossings, replace each crossing by the unique noncrossing smoothing compatible with the strand orientations. Let the resulting oriented circles be the Seifert circles and let $s$ be their number.
2. For each Seifert circle $C$, take the closure of the component of $S^2\setminus C$ that does not contain $q$. Under the stated choice axiom, each such region is an embedded compact disk. The finite family of disk regions is nested or disjoint. Orient each disk to induce the given orientation of its boundary circle, then place nested disks at distinct nearby heights ordered by inclusion; the resulting disk interiors are pairwise disjoint in $S^3$.
3. For every original crossing, attach one rectangular band along short boundary intervals on the two smoothing arcs. A half-twist means a single $180$-degree turn of the band across the crossing neighborhood. Choose its direction, endpoint orientations, and over/under order to match the original crossing.
4. Return the finite disk-and-band construction data together with $(s,c)$.

The returned data are a finite attached two-dimensional complex. This algorithm's definition alone does not assert that the resulting image is embedded, is a surface, is connected, or has the original knot as boundary; the separate correctness lemma establishes those properties.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $D$ be a finite regular oriented diagram of a single knot, and let the Seifert algorithm supply its finite disk-and-band construction data. These disks and bands can be realized in $S^3$ as a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface $F$ with exactly one boundary component, whose oriented boundary is the knot represented by $D$. The bands can be chosen mutually disjoint and disjoint from disk interiors except at their attaching intervals.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. If a connected compact oriented disk-and-band surface $F$ is built from $s$ disjoint disks by attaching $c$ rectangular bands along boundary intervals and has one boundary component, then $\chi(F)=s-c$ and $g(F)=(1-s+c)/2$. In particular, if the Seifert algorithm on an oriented knot diagram $D$ has $s$ Seifert circles and $c$ crossings, its output surface has genus $(1-s+c)/2$ and the knot genus satisfies $g(K)\le (1-s+c)/2$. This is an upper bound from one spanning surface, not a minimality assertion.
Assume AC. The trefoil knot does not bound a smooth properly embedded disk in $B^4$.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice-principle-for-foliation-pair]]). Let $S$ be an oriented Hausdorff $C^2$ surface without boundary, possibly disconnected. Then:

1. Every compact subset $K\subset S$ lies in the interior of a compact finitely cellulated $C^2$ subsurface $N$. If $K$ is contained in one connected component of $S$, $N$ can be chosen connected. A specified finite embedded regular $C^2$ graph contained in $\operatorname{Int}N$ can be included in its one-skeleton.
2. Every connected closed compact subsurface has an oriented genus normal form: the sphere for $g=0$, or the polygon word $\prod_{i=1}^g a_i b_i a_i^{-1}b_i^{-1}$ for $g\ge1$, with $\chi=2-2g$. A connected compact subsurface with $b>0$ boundary circles has a free fundamental group; capping its boundaries defines genus $g$ and gives $\chi=2-2g-b$ and free rank $2g+b-1$.
3. The fundamental group of every connected component of $S$ is torsion-free.
4. Every regular embedded $C^2$ nullhomotopic circle $c$ bounds an embedded compact disk region in $S$. Here a disk region is a compact subsurface homeomorphic to the closed disk, with boundary exactly $c$; its inherited surface structure and boundary are $C^2$. It is unique unless the **connected component containing $c$** is a sphere; in that component the two complementary disk regions are the two possibilities.

The normal forms in clause 2 are homeomorphism normal forms. No general differentiable smoothing theorem or arbitrary-surface triangulation-existence theorem is a premise of this item.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. A compact $C^2$ surface, with regular $C^2$ boundary allowed, is $C^2$ diffeomorphic to a compact smooth surface with smooth boundary. For a compact cooriented embedded surface in a smooth three-manifold, the diffeomorphism can be obtained by arbitrarily small local ambient displacements. This also applies to a compact intrinsic subsurface of a $C^2$ leaf: compactness is in the leaf topology, and its boundary is regular in that topology.

A connected oriented closed such surface with Euler characteristic zero is $C^2$ diffeomorphic to $T^2$. A compact regular surface region homeomorphic to a closed disk is $C^2$ diffeomorphic to $D^2$, and any prescribed $C^2$ diffeomorphism of its boundary circle can be realized by the disk parametrization.

Two disjoint regular closed disk regions in a $C^2$ sphere can simultaneously be carried to the standard two disk windows by a $C^2$ diffeomorphism, with compatible prescribed boundary parametrizations. A $C^2$ scalar function defined on a neighborhood of a compact set in $\mathbb R^2$ admits smooth approximations uniformly with its derivatives through order two on that compact set.

Finally let $L$ be a $C^2$ surface and $u:D^2\to L$ an **intrinsically continuous** map which is $C^2$ on an open boundary collar. On any smaller closed boundary collar contained in that open collar, $u$ has arbitrarily close $C^2$ approximations agreeing with $u$ on a neighborhood of the smaller collar, and a homotopy to each approximation fixed there. Closeness is uniform for any fixed compatible metric on $L$. No injectivity or immersion of the cap map is required.
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every smooth manifold with boundary has a smooth collar.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. For an oriented smooth knot $K\subset S^3$, define

$$\mathcal G(K):=\{n\in\mathbb N_0: \text{there is a Seifert surface }F\text{ for }K\text{ with }g(F)=n\}.$$

Every element of $\mathcal G(K)$ is the genus of a connected compact oriented surface. The existence theorem makes $\mathcal G(K)$ nonempty, and the well-ordering of $\mathbb N_0$ gives its least element. The **smooth knot genus** is $g(K):=\min\mathcal G(K)$. This genus is the minimum over embedded spanning surfaces; it is not the number of Seifert circles or the genus of every surface produced from a diagram.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

derivations.claim: Use the standard right-trefoil diagram, the closure of the positive two-strand braid $\sigma_1^3$, with both braid strands directed downward and the closing arcs directed back to the top. It has exactly three crossings. At each crossing the oriented smoothing pairs each upper endpoint with the lower endpoint in the same vertical position, rather than the diagonal pairing. Smoothing all three crossings therefore leaves two vertical strands; each joins its own closing arc to form one circle. Thus $s=2$ and $c=3$. The unsmoothed braid has the transposition permutation (three interchanges), so its closure has one knot component. The algorithm attaches three half-twisted bands between the two disk records, with twist directions restoring these three positive crossings. By [F1] and [A2] the result is a connected compact smooth oriented embedded spanning surface for $T$, and its genus is $(1-2+3)/2=1$ (equivalently $\chi=2-3=-1$). Hence the nonnegative minimum in [F5] satisfies $g(T)\le1$.

If $g(T)=0$, a minimizing surface exists by [F5], and [F3] makes it a smooth disk $D\subset S^3$. Let $c:S^3\times[0,\epsilon)\to B^4$ be a collar from [F4]. A boundary collar of $D$ gives a smooth function $h:D\to[0,\epsilon)$ that equals the inward collar coordinate near $\partial D$, is positive on $\operatorname{Int}D$, and vanishes exactly on $\partial D$. The map $x\mapsto c(x,h(x))$ is injective because the collar projection is $x$, and its differential is injective because its first coordinate is the inclusion of $D$; at $\partial D$, the positive derivative of $h$ in the inward conormal makes the disk proper and transverse to $\partial B^4$. Thus it is a smooth proper disk in $B^4$ with boundary $T$, contradicting [F2]. Hence $g(T)\ne0$.
A nonnegative integer at most $1$ and not equal to $0$ is $1$. Hence $g(T)=1$.

By [F1], $g(J),g(L)\ge1$ and $g(J)+g(L)=g(K)$, so both genera are strictly smaller. The induction hypothesis gives each factor a finite prime decomposition; concatenate these lists using [F3]. For genus one the nonsimple case is impossible by the same inequalities. This establishes finite existence for every positive genus.

Realize any finite connected-sum presentation by its standard separating spheres: take the gluing sphere in each two-ball construction, and place later summand constructions away from earlier small gluing collars. The resulting finite disjoint sphere system cuts the knot into arcs whose capped knots are exactly the original factors by [F2]. Conversely successive leaf regions of such a system give its connected-sum presentation, again by [F2] and associativity. Thus every prime presentation gives a prime sphere system with the same oriented factors.

For two prime presentations of $K$, use step 2.1 to obtain their two prime sphere systems in the same oriented knot sphere, transporting the standard constructions through the given ambient isotopies. Apply [F2]'s marked cut-and-paste comparison. Its replacements preserve oriented capped factors and reduce intersections until a common disjoint refinement compares the two lists. Therefore the lists have the same length and the same oriented prime knot classes, up to permutation. This is the full existence and uniqueness assertion.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

Assume the full Axiom of Choice. A positive Hopf band is an oriented annulus whose two boundary components, with their induced orientations, have linking number $+1$. Let $F$ be the genus-one Seifert surface obtained by plumbing two positive Hopf bands in a square, with oriented core curves $a,b$ forming a positive handle basis, and choose the plumbing side so that $a^+$ bounds a disk in $S^3$ disjoint from $b$. The oriented boundary of this standard positive two-band plumbing is the right-handed trefoil. In the positive-push convention $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$ with ordered basis $(a,b)$, the Seifert matrix is
$$
V=\begin{pmatrix}-1&0\\-1&-1\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Assume full AC. Use the canonical geometric Artin half twist in the oriented chart $(x,y,t)$, the canonical crossing sign $\det_P(v_{\rm over},v_{\rm under})$, and the Seifert convention $\theta(u,v)=\operatorname{lk}(u^+,v)$. Let $F$ be the oriented braid Seifert surface consisting of two Seifert disks and the three crossing bands of the closure of $\sigma_1^3$. Label the bands in braid order $e_1,e_2,e_3$, oriented as edges from the first disk to the second. The cycle classes $a=e_1-e_2$ and $b=e_2-e_3$ form an integral basis. Order these two classes as $(u,v)$ so that $u\cdot_Fv=1$. Then
$$V_{(u,v)}=\begin{pmatrix}-1&1\\0&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad V+V^T=\begin{pmatrix}-2&1\\1&-2\end{pmatrix}.$$
In particular the signature is $-2$. The three pair-of-band annuli have core self-pairing $-1$, so they are positive Hopf bands when positive refers to the positively linked oriented boundary, rather than to core self-pairing $+1$.

Assume the full Axiom of Choice. Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot, and let $F\subset S^3$ be a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface whose oriented boundary is $K$, with $\chi(F)=1-2g$. Choose an ordered integral basis $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$ and use the positive normal convention $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. Let $A_K$ be the first homology of the infinite cyclic cover of $S^3\setminus K$ classified by total linking, with $t$ acting by the positive-meridian deck transformation. Let $\Delta_K(t)$ be the generator of the zeroth elementary ideal $E_0(A_K)$ in $\Lambda=\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$, and write $p\doteq q$ when $p$ and $q$ differ by a unit $\pm t^k$ of $\Lambda$. Then for every such $F$ and basis,

$$\det(V-tV^T)\doteq\Delta_K(t).$$

The determinant is $1$ for the empty $0\times0$ matrix when $g=0$. This formula concerns the polynomial $\Delta_K$; the existing knot-normalized fraction $D_K=\Delta_K/(1-t)$ is a separate invariant.

Assume the full Axiom of Choice. Let $K,J\subset S^3$ be smooth oriented knots, and let $K\#J$ be their oriented connected sum for a connected-sum datum using the fixed gluing convention. Then

$$\Delta_{K\#J}(t)\doteq \Delta_K(t)\Delta_J(t),$$

where each $\Delta$ is the generator of the zeroth elementary ideal of the one-variable Alexander module and $\doteq$ means equality up to multiplication by a unit $\pm t^k$ of $\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$. The statement is independent of the local connected-sum choices and of the Seifert surfaces and bases used to compute the polynomials.

Assume full AC. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in the oriented standard $3$-sphere, let $F$ be a connected compact smooth oriented surface with oriented boundary $K$, let $V$ be the matrix of the Seifert pairing $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$ in an ordered integral basis, and let $\omega\in S^1\setminus\{1\}$. Define the **Levine–Tristram Hermitian matrix** by
$$H_\omega(V)=(1-\omega)V+(1-\bar\omega)V^T.$$
It is Hermitian because $V$ is real and $\bar\omega=\omega^{-1}$. Its signature is the number of positive eigenvalues minus the number of negative eigenvalues, both counted with multiplicity and with zero eigenvalues omitted. When $\Delta_K(\omega)\ne0$, define $\sigma_\omega(K)$ to be this signature. At a root $\omega_0\ne1$ of $\Delta_K$, define $\sigma_{\omega_0}(K)$ to be the arithmetic mean of the two one-sided limits of $\sigma_{e^{i\theta}}(K)$ as $\theta$ approaches an argument of $\omega_0$ from below and above. The invariance and one-sided-existence lemmas justify treating these values as independent of the chosen surface and basis.

Assume full AC. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in the oriented standard $3$-sphere, and let $F,F'$ be any connected compact smooth oriented spanning surfaces for $K$. For any ordered integral bases of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$ and $H_1(F';\mathbb Z)$, the matrices of the positive-push Seifert pairing are related by a finite sequence of integral unimodular congruences and the two rank-two elementary Seifert enlargements or their reverses.

Assume full AC. For every $\omega\in S^1\setminus\{1\}$, changing an ordered basis by an integral unimodular congruence or changing a knot Seifert matrix by either elementary enlargement or reduction preserves the signature of $H_\omega$. Consequently, the nonroot Levine–Tristram signature and its one-sided-average value at every Alexander root are independent of the spanning surface and basis.
Assume full AC. The standard right-handed trefoil is a prime oriented knot.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. If a smooth oriented knot $K$ is nontrivial and prime, then its mirror image under the fixed reflection from the connected-sum convention, with the image orientation, is also nontrivial and prime.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Every nontrivial smooth oriented knot in $S^3$ is ambient isotopic to a finite connected sum of prime knots, and the prime factors are unique up to permutation and orientation-preserving ambient isotopy of the oriented factors.

Fix a coordinate orientation-reversing reflection $r:S^3\to S^3$ for the mirror convention. Let $K$ and $J$ be smooth oriented knots in the standard oriented three-sphere. A connected-sum datum consists of one smoothly embedded closed three-ball around a short subarc of $K$ and one around a short subarc of $J$, each meeting its knot in a single trivial properly embedded arc, together with the fixed standard orientation-reversing boundary identification of the two standard oriented ball boundaries that joins the oriented arcs into one circle. Choose this standard map once in the standard two-ball model so that it commutes with $r$ and an orientation-preserving half-turn interchanging the two balls preserves the joining convention. Here a trivial arc is an embedded interval in a ball that is carried by an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism of ball-arc pairs to a straight diameter. Remove the interiors of the two balls and glue the remaining boundary spheres using this fixed identification; the resulting oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere is a connected sum of $K$ and $J$, denoted $K\#J$ for the specified datum.

The **standard unknot** is the oriented unit circle in a fixed coordinate two-plane of $S^3\subset\mathbb R^4$. A knot is **nontrivial** if it is not ambient isotopic through orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms of $S^3$ to the standard unknot. A nontrivial knot is **prime** if it has no connected-sum presentation whose two summand knots are both nontrivial.

derivations.claim:
By [F1] and [F2],
$$\Delta_T(t)\doteq\det(V-tV^T)=\det\begin{pmatrix}t-1&t\\-1&t-1\end{pmatrix}=(t-1)^2+t=t^2-t+1.$$
For $-T^*$ use the reflected spanning surface with its surface orientation reversed, so its boundary is the reversed reflected knot. Its positive normal is the reflected original positive normal: ambient reflection and surface reversal each negate the orientation, so their effects cancel in the normal-first convention. Reflection negates linking. The transported homology basis on this actual surface consequently has matrix $-V$. Its determinant is $\det(-V+tV^T)=\det(V-tV^T)$, since the matrix size is two. The two determinants evaluate to $3$ at $t=-1$, so this parameter is nonroot and [F3] applies directly, with no root-average ambiguity.

By [F2], the actual boundary connected-sum surfaces of $G=T\#T$ and $Q=T\#(-T^*)$ have matrices $V\oplus V$ and $V\oplus(-V)$. Their block determinants both equal $(t^2-t+1)^2$, proving the two Alexander-polynomial identities up to units. Also
$$H_{-1}(V)=2(V+V^T)=\begin{pmatrix}-4&-2\\-2&-4\end{pmatrix}.$$
Its eigenvalues on the vectors $(1,1)$ and $(1,-1)$ are $-6$ and $-2$, respectively. Thus $\sigma_{-1}(T)=-2$ and $\sigma_{-1}(-T^*)=2$. The corresponding block forms give $\sigma_{-1}(G)=-4$ and $\sigma_{-1}(Q)=-2+2=0$. These are actual knot-invariant values by [F3], since the sum polynomials at $-1$ equal $9\ne0$. In particular $|\sigma_{-1}(G)|=4$ as stated.

By [F4], $T$ and $T^*$ are nontrivial prime oriented knots. Reversal of knot orientation also preserves these properties: reverse both factors and the two local oriented arcs in any purported nontrivial connected-sum presentation of $-T^*$ to obtain a nontrivial presentation of $T^*$; reversing again is the inverse operation, and the unknot remains the unknot. Thus $-T^*$ is prime. The signatures in step2.1 show that $T$ and $-T^*$ are distinct oriented knot types, since an oriented ambient isotopy would preserve [F3]'s signature. Therefore the displayed two-prime decompositions have respective multisets $\{T,T\}$ and $\{T,-T^*\}$, which are different. By [F4]'s actual oriented Schubert uniqueness they are the prime-factor multisets of $G$ and $Q$, independent of a chosen decomposition. Together with their equal Alexander polynomials, this proves the entire original refutation. No planned matrix interface or conditional prime/invariant premise remains.

citations.quote: Let $P$ and $Q$ be compact piecewise-linear polyhedra. A **piecewise-linear map** $f:P\to Q$ is a map that is simplicial after suitable finite subdivisions of triangulations of $P$ and $Q$. A **subpolyhedron** $A$ of $Q$ is a subset represented by the realization of a subcomplex in some finite linear triangulation of $Q$. A map $f:P\to Q$ is a **piecewise-linear embedding** if it is piecewise-linear, its image $f(P)$ is a subpolyhedron of $Q$, and $f:P\to f(P)$ is a piecewise-linear homeomorphism. A finite simplicial triangulation of a closed piecewise-linear $n$-manifold is **combinatorial** if the link of every $k$-simplex is a piecewise-linear sphere of dimension $n-k-1$. Thus in a closed combinatorial $3$-manifold every triangular face has link $S^0$ and is incident to exactly two tetrahedra.

Two finite linear simplicial subdivisions $K_1,K_2$ of a fixed finite Euclidean simplicial complex have a common finite linear simplicial refinement. This asserts refinement of triangulations of the same embedded polyhedron, not of arbitrary abstractly homeomorphic triangulations.

Let $(V,K)$ be an abstract simplicial complex.

A **subcomplex** of $K$ is a subfamily $L \subseteq K$ that is itself closed
under taking subsets.

If $\sigma \in K$, its **closure** is the subcomplex
$$\overline{\sigma}:=\{\tau \in K : \tau \subseteq \sigma\}.$$
More generally, if $A \subseteq K$, its closure is
$$\overline{A}:=\{\tau \in K : \tau \subseteq \sigma \text{ for some } \sigma \in A\}.$$

For a simplex $\sigma \in K$, the **closed star** of $\sigma$ in $K$ is
$$\operatorname{St}_K(\sigma):=\{\tau \in K : \sigma \cup \tau \in K\},$$
and the **open star** is the union, after realization, of the relative
interiors of simplices $\rho\in K$ with $\sigma\subseteq\rho$.

The **link** of $\sigma$ in $K$ is
$$\operatorname{Lk}_K(\sigma):=\{\tau \in K : \tau \cap \sigma=\varnothing \text{ and } \sigma \cup \tau \in K\}.$$

Let $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ and $(Y, \mathcal{T}_Y)$ be topological spaces and let
$f : X \to Y$ be a function. Continuity is as in [[def-continuous-map-top]],
injections, surjections and bijections as in
[[def-injection-surjection-bijection]].

- $f$ is an **open map** if $f[U]$ is open in $Y$ for every open $U \subseteq X$.
- $f$ is a **closed map** if $f[F]$ is closed in $Y$ for every closed
  $F \subseteq X$.
- $f$ is a **homeomorphism** if $f$ is a continuous bijection whose inverse
  $f^{-1} : Y \to X$ is also continuous. The spaces are **homeomorphic**, written
  $X \cong Y$, when a homeomorphism $X \to Y$ exists.
- $f$ is an **embedding** if $f$ is injective and the corestriction
  $f_0 : X \to f[X]$, $f_0(x) = f(x)$, is a homeomorphism onto $f[X]$ carrying
  the subspace topology inherited from $Y$ ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]).

**The inverse in the third clause exists because $f$ is a bijection**, and it is
the unique two-sided inverse ([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]); no choice
principle is involved. Continuity of $f^{-1}$ is a genuine additional demand: a
continuous bijection need not be a homeomorphism, and this page records that
failure as a false statement with a two-point witness.

**Open, closed and homeomorphism are three different conditions.** A
homeomorphism is continuous by definition, but an open map need not be continuous
and a closed map need not be continuous; and continuity implies neither openness
nor closedness. An open map need
not be closed and a closed map need not be open, and Sierpinski space
$S = \{a,b\}$ with open point $b$ ([[def-standard-topologies]]) witnesses both
failures at once: the constant map $S \to S$ with value $b$ is open, since the
image of every nonempty set is the open set $\{b\}$, and is not closed, since the
image of the closed set $\{a\}$ is $\{b\}$, whose complement $\{a\}$ is not open;
the constant map with value $a$ is closed and not open by the same computation
read the other way. What is true
is that for a **continuous bijection** the three notions collapse: it is a
homeomorphism exactly when it is open, exactly when it is closed. That is proved
in the next item and is not assumed here.

**Topological properties.** A **property of topological spaces** is a condition
$P$ that is either true or false of each space. $P$ is a **topological property**
(one is also said to be *preserved by homeomorphism*, or *invariant*) when
$X \cong Y$ implies that $P(X)$ and $P(Y)$ have the same truth value. Since
$\cong$ is an equivalence relation on spaces — the identity is a homeomorphism,
inverses and composites of homeomorphisms are homeomorphisms, all three verified
in the next item — a topological property is exactly one that is constant on each
$\cong$-class.

**What a homeomorphism transports.** If $h : X \to Y$ is a homeomorphism then
$U \mapsto h[U]$ is a bijection from $\mathcal{T}_X$ onto $\mathcal{T}_Y$, with
inverse $V \mapsto h^{-1}[V]$: both maps are well defined because $h$ and
$h^{-1}$ are continuous, and they are mutually inverse because $h$ is a
bijection. So a homeomorphism is an isomorphism of the structure "a set together
with a distinguished family of subsets", and every notion defined from the open
sets alone — closed, closure, interior, boundary, dense, convergence of
sequences, continuity of maps into and out of the space — is carried across by
it. Anything defined from extra data, such as a metric or an order, is not, and
that distinction is exactly what the phrase *topological property* is for.

Write $I=[0,1]$ with its usual subspace topology, as in [[def-path-connected]]. Let $X$ and $Y$ be topological spaces, and let $f,g:X\to Y$ be continuous maps ([[def-continuous-map-top]]).

A **homotopy from $f$ to $g$** is a continuous map

$$H:X\times I\longrightarrow Y$$

from the product space ([[def-product-topology]]) such that $H(x,0)=f(x)$ and $H(x,1)=g(x)$ for every $x\in X$. When such an $H$ exists, $f$ and $g$ are **homotopic**, written $f\simeq g$.

Let $A\subseteq X$ carry the subspace topology ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]). The homotopy $H$ is a **homotopy relative to $A$**, or a homotopy **rel $A$**, when

$$H(a,t)=f(a)=g(a)\qquad(a\in A,\ t\in I).$$

Thus a homotopy rel $A$ can exist only when $f|_A=g|_A$, and every ordinary homotopy is a homotopy rel $\varnothing$. We write $f\simeq_A g$ when a homotopy rel $A$ exists.

If $\alpha,\beta:I\to Y$ are paths with the same initial point and the same terminal point ([[def-path-connected]]), a **path homotopy from $\alpha$ to $\beta$ relative to the endpoints** is a homotopy $H:I\times I\to Y$ rel $\{0,1\}$. Explicitly,

$$H(s,0)=\alpha(s),\quad H(s,1)=\beta(s),\quad H(0,t)=\alpha(0)=\beta(0),\quad H(1,t)=\alpha(1)=\beta(1).$$

The first coordinate $s$ parametrises the path and the second coordinate $t$ parametrises the deformation.

derivations.claim: Choose $R>1$ so large that $K\cup f(K)$ lies in the open radius-$R$ ball; this is possible because the continuous image of a compact set is compact, and compact Euclidean sets are bounded. Set $L=R+1$. Define an increasing homeomorphism $\rho:[0,\infty)\to[0,L)$ by $\rho(r)=r$ for $r\le R$ and $\rho(r)=R+(r-R)/(1+r-R)$ for $r\ge R$. The radial map $y(0)=0$, $y(x)=\rho(\lVert x\rVert)x/\lVert x\rVert$ for $x\ne0$, is a homeomorphism from $\mathbb R^n$ onto the open radius-$L$ ball, and it is the identity on the closed radius-$R$ ball. On the open radius-$L$ ball put $g=y\circ f\circ y^{-1}$. This is a homeomorphism there.

Extend $g$ by the identity on the radius-$L$ sphere. To verify continuity there, put $r=\lVert x\rVert$ and $s=\lVert f(x)\rVert$. The displacement bound gives $s\ge r-C$. For $r>C$, insert $f(x)/r$ between the two unit vectors to obtain
$$\left\lVert\frac{f(x)}{s}-\frac{x}{r}\right\rVert\le\frac{|s-r|}{r}+\frac{C}{r}\le\frac{2C}{r}.$$
Consequently
$$\lVert y(f(x))-y(x)\rVert\le |\rho(s)-\rho(r)|+\rho(r)\frac{2C}{r}\le (L-\rho(s))+(L-\rho(r))+\frac{2LC}{r}.$$
The right side tends to zero as $r\to\infty$, uniformly over directions, since $s\ge r-C$ and $\rho$ is increasing with limit $L$. For an interior point $z=y(x)$ approaching a boundary point $b$, the equality $\lVert z\rVert=\rho(r)$ forces $r\to\infty$, and $\lVert g(z)-b\rVert\le\lVert g(z)-z\rVert+\lVert z-b\rVert$ tends to zero by this bound. This proves continuity directly. The inverse $f^{-1}$ has the same displacement bound: if $z=f(x)$ then $\lVert f^{-1}(z)-z\rVert=\lVert x-f(x)\rVert\le C$. Applying the same calculation to $f^{-1}$ gives the continuous inverse extension. Extend once more by the identity outside the closed radius-$L$ ball to obtain a homeomorphism $G$ of $\mathbb R^n$. The formulas and their inverse formulas agree on the joining sphere.

The set $U=\{x:\lVert x\rVert<R,\ \lVert f(x)\rVert<R\}$ is an open neighborhood of $K$. On $U$ both $y^{-1}(x)=x$ and $y(f(x))=f(x)$, so $G(x)=f(x)$. Thus any piecewise linearity of $f$ on an open neighborhood of $K$ is retained after intersecting that neighborhood with $U$. This is an equality of actual local maps, rather than an approximation statement about their images.

For $0<t\le1$ define $G_t(x)=tG(x/t)$ when $\lVert x\rVert\le tL$, and $G_t(x)=x$ when $\lVert x\rVert\ge tL$; put $G_0(x)=x$. The branches agree at $\lVert x\rVert=tL$ because $G$ fixes the radius-$L$ sphere. Each $G_t$ is a homeomorphism, with inverse given by the same formula using $G^{-1}$; it fixes every point outside the radius-$tL$ ball. The formulas give joint continuity for $t>0$. At $t=0$, both $x$ and its image lie in the radius-$tL$ ball whenever a point moves, so $\lVert G_t(x)-x\rVert\le2tL$. This proves joint continuity at zero, uniformly in $x$. The identical estimate applies to the inverse family, hence $(x,t)\mapsto(G_t(x),t)$ is a homeomorphism with continuous inverse $(x,t)\mapsto(G_t^{-1}(x),t)$. Therefore $G_t$ is an ambient isotopy, supported in the radius-$L$ ball, from the identity to $G$. Together with step 2.1 this proves all conclusions.

citations.quote: Every finite convex cell complex has a compatible finite simplicial triangulation. Choose one relative interior point in each nonempty cell; triangulate the boundary in increasing dimension and cone from that point. This construction agrees on every common face and preserves each cell as a subpolyhedron.

Let $Q$ be a compact piecewise-linear polyhedron with a fixed finite linear triangulation $T$. If $f:P\to Q$ is a piecewise-linear embedding of a compact piecewise-linear polyhedron, then some finite subdivision $T'$ of $T$ contains $f(P)$ as the realization of a subcomplex.

derivations.claim: Attach an external collar and denote the resulting polyhedron by $Q^+=(Q\times\{1\})\cup(P\times[0,1])$, identifying $P\subset Q$ with $P\times\{1\}$. This is a polyhedron: triangulate the compact marked part of $Q$ with $P$ a subcomplex, triangulate its product prisms compatibly, and glue the equal marked faces. Outside this compact part keep the original locally finite triangulation. A local collar chart about $a\in P$, shrunk to the closed star $S_a=a*L_a$ of a vertex in a finite triangulation of $P$, identifies $S_a\times[1,2]$ with a neighborhood in $Q$ of that star. Combining it with the external collar gives $S_a\times[0,2]\subset Q^+$. The product is the cone from $(a,1)$ over $(L_a\times[0,2])\cup(S_a\times\{0,2\})$. Triangulate that boundary and cone it to $(a,1)$. Moving the cone vertex to $(a,1/2)$ and extending linearly on the cone simplices defines a piecewise linear homeomorphism of this product fixed on the displayed cone base, which is the relative frontier of the local neighborhood in $Q^+$. The remaining sides, if the star meets the boundary of $P$, may move along the boundary of $Q^+$. Both cone decompositions cover the product: on every radial line in the star factor the product has a single interval in each height direction, so each ray from either vertex has a unique final boundary point. Extend this map by the identity to $Q^+$ and call it $h_a$.

On the external collar, $h_a$ preserves the $P$ coordinate and decreases the height weakly. In a cone simplex this follows directly from affine coordinates: only the cone vertex changes, by the vertical displacement $-1/2$, so a point with cone-vertex coefficient $\lambda$ has the same first coordinate and height reduced by $\lambda/2$. The decrease is strict for points over the relative interior $S_a\setminus L_a$ with height strictly between $0$ and $2$. Compactness provides finitely many such star interiors covering $P$. Compose their pushes in any fixed order to obtain a piecewise linear homeomorphism $h'$ of $Q^+$. Every point $(x,1)$ is then sent to $(x,t(x))$ with $0<t(x)<1$: at least one selected star contains $x$ in its interior, that push strictly decreases the height, subsequent pushes cannot increase it, and all pushes fix height zero and are injective. Since each push preserves the ordered vertical intervals in the external collar, $h'(Q)\cap(P\times[0,1])$ is exactly the region $T=\{(x,s):t(x)\le s\le1\}$. Also $h'(Q)$ contains all of $Q\times\{1\}$, since the inverse of every push increases height on any point at height at least one in its local chart.

The function $t$ is piecewise linear on a finite subdivision of $P$: the graph $h'(P)$ is a finite polyhedron projecting bijectively to $P$, and subdividing the projection gives an affine bijection on every simplex with affine inverse on its image. Refine its projected cells compatibly using [F1]. For each simplex $A$ in this subdivision, $T\cap(A\times[0,1])$ is a convex prism cut out by the affine bottom $s=t(x)$ and the constant top $s=1$. Its faces correspond exactly to the faces of $A\times[0,1]$. Construct compatible piecewise linear homeomorphisms between these prisms by induction over their faces: prescribe the identity on the top, the projection $(x,t(x))\mapsto(x,0)$ on the bottom, use the already constructed face maps on the vertical sides, and cone from interior points to extend over each remaining cell. The finite convex cell triangulation argument in [F1] verifies bijectivity and a piecewise linear inverse. These maps paste to $g:T\to P\times[0,1]$, fixed on the top and sending the graph to the bottom by its first coordinate. Extend $g$ by the identity on $Q\times\{1\}$ to obtain a piecewise linear homeomorphism $h'(Q)\to Q^+$.

The composite $h=g\circ h'|_Q:Q\to Q^+$ is a piecewise linear homeomorphism and sends each $x\in P$ to $(x,0)$. Pull back the external collar by $h$: put $c(x,s)=h^{-1}(x,s)$. This is a piecewise linear embedding with the required bottom restriction, and its half-open image is an open neighborhood because $P\times[0,1)$ is an open neighborhood of $P\times\{0\}$ in $Q^+$. A piecewise linear boundary chart is a local product chart of the required kind, so the manifold assertion follows. Only the finite local cover and finite subdivisions were selected; no countable or arbitrary-index choice assumption is used.

For a finite Euclidean simplicial complex $K$ define its simplex mesh $m(K)$ to be the maximum diameter of its nonempty simplices, with the separate convention $m(K)=0$ if there are none. If $\dim K=n\geq1$, then
$$m(\operatorname{sd}^rK)\leq\left(\frac n{n+1}\right)^r m(K)\longrightarrow0.$$
Every nonempty vertex star has diameter at most $2m(K)$. Zero-dimensional and vertex-free complexes have mesh zero. The metric is the original Euclidean metric transported through barycentric realization, not a new unit-edge metric at each subdivision.

Let $(X,d)$ be a compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $\mathcal{U}$ be an open cover of $X$. Then there
is a real $\delta > 0$, a **Lebesgue number** for $\mathcal{U}$, such that every
nonempty $A \subseteq X$ with $\operatorname{diam}(A) < \delta$
([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]) satisfies $A \subseteq U$ for some
$U \in \mathcal{U}$.

Diameters of nonempty subsets of $X$ are defined because a compact space is
bounded ([[thm-compact-subset-is-closed-and-bounded]]) and a subset of a bounded
set is bounded. No choice principle is used.

derivations.claim: If $P$ is empty, take $V$ empty, with the empty triangulation and homotopy; all assertions hold. Otherwise subdivide $K$ sufficiently finely that the closed union of its simplices meeting $P$ lies in $W$. To see this, when $M\setminus W$ is nonempty its compactness and that of $P$ give a positive distance between them in the finite realization metric; take the mesh smaller than that distance. If $W=M$, there is no restriction. After one further barycentric subdivision, the subdivided $P$ is a full subcomplex: vertices of a simplex are a chain of faces of the preceding triangulation, so if all those vertices belong to the subdivided $P$, every face in the chain belongs to $P$, and the whole chain simplex belongs to it. Denote this final triangulation again by $K$. For each vertex $v$ put $a_v=1$ when $v\in P$ and $a_v=0$ otherwise, and extend linearly on simplices to a function $r:M\to[0,1]$. Fullness gives $r^{-1}(1)=P$. Set $V=\{r\ge1/2\}$. This is compact, contains the relatively open neighborhood $\{r>1/2\}$ of $P$, and lies in $W$: every simplex meeting $V$ has a vertex in $P$ and hence belongs to the closed union chosen above.

On a simplex with barycentric coordinates $(\lambda_v)$ and with $r\ge1/2$, define a homotopy by replacing each coordinate at a vertex of $P$ by $\lambda_v(r+t(1-r))/r$ and each other coordinate by $(1-t)\lambda_v$, for $0\le t\le1$. The new coordinates are nonnegative and sum to one; their sum at the vertices of $P$ is $r+t(1-r)\ge1/2$. The formulas agree on common faces and have denominator bounded below by $1/2$, so they give a continuous homotopy of $V$ into itself. At time zero it is the identity, at time one it maps into the face spanned by the $P$ vertices, which lies in $P$ by fullness, and it fixes every point of $P$ throughout. This is the required strong deformation retraction. It also gives a path in $V$ from each point to $P$, so $V$ is connected when $P$ is.

The cuts of each simplex by $r=1/2$ are convex polyhedral cells and agree on common faces. Their finite collection has a compatible triangulation by [F2], including their faces in $P$ and in $\partial M$. Thus $V$, its level frontier $L=\{r=1/2\}$, and its boundary trace $A=V\cap\partial M$ are finite subpolyhedra. It remains to verify the manifold and surface assertions, rather than inferring them merely from this triangulation.

Let $x\in L$, and let $\sigma$ be the unique simplex whose relative interior contains $x$. Since its barycentric coordinates are all positive and their weighted sum is $1/2$, $\sigma$ has both a vertex of $P$ and one outside $P$. Choose a vector $d$ in its affine span with coordinate sum zero and with $dr(d)=1$, for example the difference between such two vertices. In every coface of $\sigma$, translation a sufficiently small distance along $d$ changes only the coordinates of vertices of $\sigma$; these remain positive near $x$, all other coordinates remain unchanged, and $r$ changes by exactly that distance. The translations agree on shared faces. Consequently the maps $z\mapsto(z-(r(z)-1/2)d,r(z)-1/2)$ and $(w,s)\mapsto w+sd$ give inverse local piecewise linear product coordinates with $w\in L$. The simplex-link hypothesis supplies the usual local manifold chart for the remaining coordinates. If $x$ is in the interior of $M$, these coordinates identify $V$ locally with a half-space and $L$ with its boundary plane. If $x\in\partial M$, the vector $d$ is tangent to the boundary simplex and these coordinates also preserve $\partial M$; $V$ is locally a quadrant times a line, with its two faces equal to $A$ and $L$.

A quadrant times a line is a piecewise linear half-space: in its two-dimensional factor send the two boundary rays to the positive and negative horizontal rays and send the diagonal ray to the positive vertical ray, extending linearly on the two intervening cones. This is a piecewise linear homeomorphism with piecewise linear inverse, and take its product with the remaining line coordinate. Away from $L$, a point of $V$ has $r>1/2$ and hence inherits the ordinary manifold or boundary chart of $M$. Together with step 3.1 these charts prove that $V$ is a compact piecewise linear three-manifold, $A$ is a subsurface of $\partial M$, and $L$ is a proper piecewise linear surface. At their common points the quadrant model identifies their boundaries with the same line, so their common boundary is exactly $A\cap L$. The finite triangulation of step 2.2 and the deformation retraction of step 2.1 finish the proof. All subdivision, triangulation and coordinate selections are finite.
