derivations.claim: Choose a bicollar of $T_K$ in $S^3$ and thicken $E_K$ and $N(K)$ slightly to an open cover. The two sets deformation-retract to $E_K$ and $N(K)$, and their intersection deformation-retracts to $T_K$. By [F1] and [F2], the segment $H_2(S^3;\mathbb Z)\to H_1(T_K;\mathbb Z)\to H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)\oplus H_1(N(K);\mathbb Z)\to H_1(S^3;\mathbb Z)$ has zero groups at both ends, so the middle map is an isomorphism.

Let $M=E_K(p/q)$, write $\alpha=p\mu+q\lambda$, and choose $\beta=r\mu+s\lambda$ with $ps-qr=1$, so $\alpha,\beta$ form a basis of $H_1(T_K;\mathbb Z)$. In the Mayer–Vietoris map for $M$, $\alpha$ maps to $(p[\mu],0)$ because it bounds the attached solid-torus meridian disk, and $\beta$ maps to $(r[\mu],\pm v)$ where $v$ generates the first homology of the attached solid torus; the coefficient is $\pm1$ because $\beta$ intersects $\alpha$ once. The spaces $E_K$, $T_K$, and the attached solid torus are connected, so the following $H_0$ map is injective and $H_1(M;\mathbb Z)$ is the cokernel of this map.

By [F3], $H_1(T_K;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z^2$, and by [F4] and [F2] the solid torus $N(K)\simeq S^1$ has $H_1(N(K);\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$. Since $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)\oplus\mathbb Z\cong\mathbb Z^2$, the direct summand $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$ is free of rank one. Under the isomorphism in step 1.1, $\mu$ maps to $([\mu],0)$ because it bounds a disk in $N(K)$, while $\lambda$ maps to $(0,\pm1)$ by [A1]. Since the map is an isomorphism, $[\mu]$ is a generator of $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$ and $[\lambda]=0$.

Thus $H_1(M;\mathbb Z)$ has generators $[\mu],v$ and relations $p[\mu]=0$ and $r[\mu]\pm v=0$. Eliminating $v$ leaves $\mathbb Z\langle[\mu]\rangle/\langle p[\mu]\rangle$. If $p\ne0$, this is $\mathbb Z/|p|\mathbb Z$; if $p=0$, coprimality gives $q=\pm1$ and the group is $\mathbb Z$.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$ and let $Q=(q_1,\dots,q_n)$ be the base configuration of
[[def-geometric-braid-with-setwise-endpoints]], with $h=\frac{1}{4(n+1)}$ and
$q_j=((2j-n-1)h,0)$. Fix an index $i$ with $1\le i\le n-1$. The two adjacent
base points are

$$q_i=\bigl((2i-n-1)h,0\bigr),\qquad q_{i+1}=\bigl((2i+1-n)h,0\bigr),$$

their **midpoint** is $m_i:=(q_i+q_{i+1})/2=((2i-n)h,0)=q_i+(h,0)$, and their
**support disc** is the open disc

$$U_i:=\bigl\{w\in\mathbb R^2:\lVert w-m_i\rVert_2<\tfrac32h\bigr\}.$$

The support disc contains the two base points $q_i,q_{i+1}$, whose distance from
$m_i$ is $h$, and it contains no other base point: for $k<i$ one has
$\lVert q_k-m_i\rVert_2=(2(i-k)+1)h\ge 3h$ and for $k>i+1$ one has
$\lVert q_k-m_i\rVert_2=(2(k-i)-1)h\ge3h$, both exceeding $\tfrac32h$. Moreover
$U_i\subseteq D^\circ$, because every point of $U_i$ has norm at most
$\lVert m_i\rVert_2+\tfrac32h\le(n-2)h+\tfrac32h<(n+1)h<1$. Finally
$U_i\cap U_j=\varnothing$ whenever $|i-j|>1$, since then the midpoints are at
distance $2|i-j|h\ge4h>3h$, twice the radius.

**The positive half twist.** Define $\rho\colon I\to\mathbb R^2$, the
**anticlockwise diamond path**, by

$$\rho(t):=\begin{cases}\bigl(2th-h,\,-2th\bigr),&0\le t\le \tfrac12,\\[2pt] \bigl(2th-h,\,2th-2h\bigr),&\tfrac12\le t\le1.\end{cases}$$

Thus $\rho(0)=(-h,0)$, $\rho(\tfrac12)=(0,-h)$, $\rho(1)=(h,0)$, and $\rho$ is
continuous, piecewise linear, and satisfies $\lVert\rho(t)\rVert_2\le h$ for all
$t$ with $\rho(t)\neq0$ throughout. The **elementary half twist at $i$**, written
$\sigma_i$, is the tuple of motions

$$(\sigma_i)_i(t):=m_i+\rho(t),\qquad (\sigma_i)_{i+1}(t):=m_i-\rho(t),\qquad (\sigma_i)_k(t):=q_k\ \ (k\notin\{i,i+1\}).$$

It is a braid based at $Q$
([[def-geometric-braid-with-setwise-endpoints]],
[[def-continuous-map-top]]): the two moving points stay in $U_i$ and are
antipodal about $m_i$, so they are distinct; every other point is fixed and lies
outside $U_i$; and the endpoint permutation is the transposition of $i$ and
$i+1$, since $(\sigma_i)_i(1)=m_i+(h,0)=q_{i+1}$ and
$(\sigma_i)_{i+1}(1)=m_i-(h,0)=q_i$.

The words *positive* and *anticlockwise* refer to the fixed orientation of the
plane of the disc and to the fixed planar projection whose horizontal axis
contains $Q$: the moving pair turns through the half turn anticlockwise, the
label $i$ passing below its midpoint and the label $i+1$ above. Together with
the first-under-second stacking convention of
[[prop-stacking-of-geometric-braids-is-well-defined]] this fixes the sign
convention for every signed crossing on this page and its companion.

**The opposite half twist.** The **opposite** (clockwise) half twist at $i$ is
defined by the reflected path

$$\rho^{-}(t):=\bigl(\rho_1(t),-\rho_2(t)\bigr),$$

through the motions $(\sigma_i^{-})_i(t):=m_i+\rho^{-}(t)$,
$(\sigma_i^{-})_{i+1}(t):=m_i-\rho^{-}(t)$ and
$(\sigma_i^{-})_k(t):=q_k$ for $k\notin\{i,i+1\}$. It is again a braid supported
in $U_i$ with endpoint permutation the transposition of $i$ and $i+1$; its pair
turns through the same half turn clockwise, the label $i$ passing above the
midpoint. The two motions are not equal, and they are not related by a
reparametrisation of the height: they are the two signed crossings of the pair.

**The opposite motion is the group inverse.** For a braid $\beta$ the reversed
braid $\overline\beta_j(t)=z_{\pi(\beta)^{-1}(j)}(1-t)$ represents
$[\beta]^{-1}$ in the group $G_n$
([[thm-geometric-braids-form-a-group]]). For $\beta=\sigma_i$ one computes
$\overline{\sigma_i}=\sigma_i^{-}$: reversing the height and relabelling by the
transposition of $i$ and $i+1$ sends $\rho(t)=m_i+(\rho_1,\rho_2)$ to the
motion with relative path $-\rho(1-t)$, which is the reflected path
$\rho^-$ traversed from $t=0$ to $t=1$. Hence

$$[\sigma_i^{-}]=[\sigma_i]^{-1}\qquad\text{in }G_n .$$

**Elementary cases.** For $n\le1$ there is no index $i$ with $1\le i\le n-1$,
and there are no elementary half twists; the assertions above are vacuous. For
$n\ge2$ and $1\le i\le n-1$ both $[\sigma_i]$ and $[\sigma_i^{-}]$ are
nonidentity elements of $G_n$, since their endpoint permutations are
transpositions, which are not the identity permutation.

**Two letters do not commute in general.** For adjacent indices the supports
$U_i$ and $U_{i+1}$ overlap and no commutation is asserted;
[[lem-geometric-far-commutativity]] proves commutativity only for disjoint
supports.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$ and let $Q=(q_1,\dots,q_n)$ be the base configuration of
[[def-geometric-braid-with-setwise-endpoints]], with $h:=\frac{1}{4(n+1)}$ and
$q_j=((2j-n-1)h,0)$. Let $\beta=(z_1,\dots,z_n)$ and $\gamma=(w_1,\dots,w_n)$
be braids based at $Q$ with endpoint permutations $\pi(\beta)$ and $\pi(\gamma)$
([[def-geometric-braid-with-setwise-endpoints]]), and let $\sim$ denote braid
isotopy relative to the top and bottom
([[def-braid-isotopy-relative-top-and-bottom]]).

**(a) The stacked tuple is a braid.** Define $\gamma\star\beta$ by

$$(\gamma\star\beta)_j(t):=\begin{cases}z_j(2t),&0\le t\le\tfrac12,\\[2pt] w_{\pi(\beta)(j)}(2t-1),&\tfrac12\le t\le1.\end{cases}$$

Then $\gamma\star\beta$ is a braid based at $Q$. It is the stacking of $\beta$
below $\gamma$: the motion $\beta$ runs during the first half of the height
interval and the motion $\gamma$ during the second half, after the strand of
label $\pi(\beta)(j)$ has been joined.

**(b) The endpoint permutation multiplies.** $\pi(\gamma\star\beta)
=\pi(\gamma)\circ\pi(\beta)$, with $(\pi\circ\sigma)(j)=\pi(\sigma(j))$.

**(c) The operation descends to isotopy classes.** If $\beta\sim\beta'$ and
$\gamma\sim\gamma'$ then $\gamma\star\beta\sim\gamma'\star\beta'$.

**(d) The operation is associative.** If $\delta$ is a further braid based at
$Q$, then $(\delta\star\gamma)\star\beta\sim\delta\star(\gamma\star\beta)$.

**(e) The endpoint permutation is constant along isotopies.** If
$\beta\sim\beta'$ then $\pi(\beta)=\pi(\beta')$; equivalently $\pi$ is constant
on each braid isotopy class, so that $\pi$ is a function of the class $[\beta]$
alone.

Consequently the stacking of isotopy classes,
$[\gamma]\,[\beta]:=[\gamma\star\beta]$, is a well-defined associative binary
operation on the set of braid isotopy classes based at $Q$, with
$\pi(\delta\star\gamma\star\beta)=\pi(\delta)\pi(\gamma)\pi(\beta)$ for any
three braids.

Let $n\ge0$ and let $\beta=(z_1,\ldots,z_n)$ be a geometric braid with
the fixed real basepoints $q_j=((2j-n-1)/(4(n+1)),0)$ and endpoint
permutation $\pi$, as in [[def-geometric-braid-with-setwise-endpoints]].
Identify the disk with $\{x\in\mathbb C:|x|<1\}$ and put
$$V=(D^\circ\times[0,1])/((x,1)\sim(x,0)).$$
The quotient and its topology use [[def-product-topology]] and the circle
$\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ of [[def-circle-as-real-line-mod-integers]].
The interval images
$$s_j=\{[(z_j(t),t)]:0\le t\le1\},\qquad \operatorname{cl}(\beta)=\bigcup_{j=1}^n s_j$$
are the **closure in the open solid torus**. In general an individual
$s_j$ is an interval image, not a closed circle: its last point is the
first point of $s_{\pi(j)}$.

**Components and orientation.** For a cycle
$(j,\pi(j),\ldots,\pi^{k-1}(j))$ concatenate these $k$ strand maps in
that order, with parameter in $[0,k]$. Their endpoints agree in $V$,
so the concatenation factors through $\mathbb R/k\mathbb Z$.
It is injective on this circle: points at distinct nonintegral heights
can agree only when their parameters have the same fractional part,
and the distinct strands at that height have distinct disk coordinates;
at integral heights only the specified adjacent endpoints agree.
Thus each cycle gives an embedded circle. Different cycles give
disjoint circles, and every strand belongs to exactly one cycle.
These circles are precisely the connected components of the closure.
The orientation is increasing concatenation parameter. In particular
the number of components equals the number of cycles of $\pi$.

**The standard axis and fixed framing.** In
$S^3=\{(z,w)\in\mathbb C^2:|z|^2+|w|^2=1\}$, as in
[[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]], set
$$A=\{(0,w):|w|=1\},\qquad P_\theta=\{(z,w)\in S^3:z\ne0,\ \arg z=\theta\}.$$
Fix the following particular diffeomorphism, including its disk framing:
$$\varphi([(x,t)])=  \bigl(\sqrt{1-|x|^2}\,e^{2\pi it},x\bigr):  V\longrightarrow S^3\setminus A.$$
Its inverse has disk coordinate $x=w$ and circle coordinate
$[t]=[\arg z/(2\pi)]$. Every $P_\theta$ is consequently an open disk.
The **raw topological oriented closure** is
$$\widehat\beta_{\mathrm{top}}=\varphi(\operatorname{cl}(\beta)).$$
This explicit $\varphi$ is part of the construction; the definition
does not allow an arbitrary page-preserving change of framing.

**Page intersections and smooth representatives.** The whole closure
meets every page in exactly $n$ points. A component belonging to a
$\pi$-cycle of length $k$ meets each page in exactly $k$ points:
at any fractional height it uses exactly those $k$ distinct strands.
The page coordinate of its concatenation is $[t]$, for
$t\in\mathbb R/k\mathbb Z$, so its oriented degree is $+k$.
If all disk-coordinate strand maps are smooth and have all positive-order derivatives
zero at their endpoints, their cycle concatenations have matching jets
at every seam. The page coordinate has nonzero derivative, so the
result is a smooth embedding of disjoint oriented circles, in the
sense of [[def-smooth-embedding]]. For an endpoint-flat smooth braid, its literal $\varphi$-image is therefore a smooth oriented link and is denoted $\widehat\beta$.

**Closure in the smooth oriented-link category.** The raw image need not be smooth, even if individual strands are smooth but their endpoint jets fail to match at the cycle seams. For an arbitrary continuous braid, assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]) and choose a smooth representative $\beta_s$ by [[lem-every-geometric-braid-is-braid-isotopic-to-a-smooth-braid]]. Make it endpoint-flat by composing all disk-coordinate strands with a fixed smooth nondecreasing $\psi:I\to I$, equal to $0$ near $0$ and $1$ near $1$. Interpolation of height maps $(1-u)t+u\psi(t)$ is an endpoint-fixed braid isotopy, because every strand is evaluated at the same height. The smooth-category closure of $\beta$ is the oriented-link isotopy class of this chosen model's literal $\varphi$-image; when a subset is needed, use that chosen closed-braid representative. Independence of the representative is proved by [[lem-closure-depends-only-on-the-braid-isotopy-class]]. Page and cycle properties refer to the chosen constructed closed braid, with the same number of strands and endpoint permutation as $\beta$.

If $\beta$ already has smooth strands with matching cycle-seam jets, in particular if it is endpoint-flat, its literal raw image is a smooth link and is retained as $\widehat\beta$. The raw quotient, fixed $\varphi$, finite cycles, page counts and trivial closures remain choice-free. Finite elementary words have explicit smooth endpoint-flat models, so forming their literal closures also requires no choice assumption; $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is used for the general continuous-representative convention and its independence theorem.

**The trivial closure.** For the constant braid its circles are
$\{(\sqrt{1-q_j^2}e^{2\pi it},q_j):[t]\in\mathbb R/\mathbb Z\}$.
They are latitudes of the sphere
$S=\{(z,w)\in S^3:\operatorname{Im}w=0\}$, with
$\operatorname{Re}w=q_j$. Each northern cap
$C_j=\{p\in S:\operatorname{Re}w(p)\ge q_j\}$ is a smooth disk:
stereographic coordinates on $S$ give radius
$\sqrt{(1-q_j)/(1+q_j)}$ for this cap. To make their spanning disks
disjoint, let $e$ be the unit vector in the $\operatorname{Im}w$
direction, set $\varepsilon=\pi/16$ and
$f_j(p)=\varepsilon(\operatorname{Re}w(p)-q_j)$ on $C_j$, and use
$$F_j(p)=\cos(f_j(p))p+\sin(f_j(p))e.$$
The boundary is fixed. The tubular parametrization
$(p,s)\mapsto\cos(s)p+\sin(s)e$ is injective for $|s|<\pi/2$,
and $0\le f_j<\pi/8$. On overlapping caps, if $q_i<q_j$ then
$f_i-f_j=\varepsilon(q_j-q_i)>0$, so their graphs are disjoint.
Thus these are pairwise disjoint smooth spanning disks. The trivial
$n$-braid closes to the oriented $n$-component unlink; for $n=1$
this is the unknot.

At $n=0$ all strand and cycle unions are empty, every page has zero intersections,
and the closure is the empty link. The basepoint list and disk constructions
above then have no entries.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the smooth normal-bundle structure used in the
framing clause. For a knot component $K$, its normal bundle is the fibrewise
quotient $\nu K=TS^3|_K/TK$, and a normal section is a smooth section of this
bundle.

Let $D$ be a regular oriented link diagram in a projection plane $P$ of an
oriented $3$-sphere, after moving the link off the point at infinity. Fix the
unit viewing normal $n$ pointing toward the viewer. Orient $P$ by the rule that
an ordered basis $(u,v)$ of $P$ is positive exactly when $(n,u,v)$ is a positive
basis of the ambient $3$-space. At a crossing $c$, let $v_{\rm over}$ and
$v_{\rm under}$ be the nonzero projected tangent vectors following the
orientations of the overpassing and underpassing strands. Define
$$\operatorname{sgn}(c):=\operatorname{sgn}\det_P(v_{\rm over},v_{\rm under})\in\{+1,-1\}.$$
Reversing the orientation of $P$ reverses every crossing sign.

This convention makes the positive geometric Artin half twist positive. In
the braid chart $(x,y,t)$ with ambient orientation $(x,y,t)$, view along $+y$;
the induced positive orientation of the $(x,t)$ projection plane is the ordered
basis $(\partial_t,\partial_x)$. For the positive half twist, label $i$ moves
from $x=-h$ to $x=h$ below the midpoint, while label $i+1$ moves from $x=h$ to
$x=-h$ above it, with $h>0$. Thus the over and under projected tangent vectors
in coordinates $(t,x)$ are $(1,-2h)$ and $(1,2h)$, whose determinant is
$4h>0$.

The **writhe** of $D$ is
$$\operatorname{wr}(D):=\sum_{c\text{ a crossing of }D}\operatorname{sgn}(c).$$
For a link component $K_i$, its **self-writhe**
$\operatorname{wr}_i(D)$ is the sum over crossings whose two branches belong to
$K_i$; the total writhe also includes all mixed crossings between distinct
components.

The **blackboard framing** of a component of $D$ is the homotopy class of the
normal section represented by the positive quarter-turn in $P$ of the projected
oriented tangent. The projection is an immersion, so this vector never
vanishes; it is perpendicular to the projected tangent, hence also to the
spatial tangent, and therefore represents a nonzero normal section of the
component in the ambient $3$-sphere.

```tikz
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.8,>=stealth]
  \draw[->] (-1,0) -- (1,0) node[right] {$v_{\rm over}$};
  \draw[->] (0,-1) -- (0,1) node[above] {$v_{\rm under}$};
  \node[above left] at (0,0) {$+1$};
\end{tikzpicture}
```

In the displayed local chart, the over tangent is the positive horizontal
vector and the under tangent is the positive vertical vector, so the determinant
is $+1$. This figure illustrates the determinant rule only; no proof below
depends on a picture.

Orient the projection plane by the viewing normal and the ambient orientation. At an oriented crossing let $o$ be the over-arc, and let $n_o$ be its positive in-plane normal: the ordered pair consisting of the over-tangent and $n_o$ is positive. Call the under-side from which $n_o$ points the source $s$, and the side toward which it points the target $t$. A positive meridian is the oriented boundary of a small normal disk whose orientation, preceded by the oriented knot tangent, is the ambient orientation. With the common upper-collar basing paths, the based positive meridians satisfy
$$m_t=m_o^{-1}m_s m_o.$$
This side-based equation is independent of the direction of the understrand. In an oriented chart with over-tangent rightward, the target is the upper side $L$ and source the lower side $R$, so equivalently $m_R=m_o m_Lm_o^{-1}$. In incoming/outgoing notation, the outgoing under-meridian is $m_o^{-1}m_{\rm in}m_o$ if the under-tangent points along $n_o$, and is $m_om_{\rm in}m_o^{-1}$ otherwise. Reversing a chosen meridian loop inverts its class. Changing every common access path by the same based loop conjugates all three classes simultaneously.

Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot, let $D$ be a valid finite planar code for a regular diagram of $K$, choose a basepoint $b$ in the complement, and designate a starting under-arc. The finite procedure $\mathsf{Wirtinger}(D,a_0)$ terminates and returns a presentation with one positive-meridian generator for each under-arc and one crossing conjugacy relator for each crossing. For the based meridians determined by the diagram's common upper-collar paths from $b$, the homomorphism from the presented group to $\pi_1(S^3\setminus K,b)$ that sends each generator to its corresponding based positive meridian is an isomorphism. Changing the designated starting under-arc only relabels the same finite cyclic arc set and gives an isomorphic presentation. If all basing paths are changed by prepending the same based loop, every generator image is conjugated by the same element, so the isomorphism type is unchanged.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $D$ be a regular oriented diagram
of a knot $K$ with blackboard framing $b_D$. The self-linking number of the
framed knot $(K,b_D)$ equals the diagram writhe:
$$\operatorname{sl}(K,b_D)=\operatorname{wr}(D).$$
For a link component $K_i$, the corresponding self-linking number is its
self-writhe $\operatorname{wr}_i(D)$. Total writhe of a link still includes
the signs of mixed crossings, while the sum of component self-linking numbers
uses only self-crossings.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. For an oriented smooth knot
$K:S^1\hookrightarrow S^3$, its normal bundle is
$\nu K=TS^3|_K/TK$, oriented so that a positive tangent to $K$ followed by a
positive basis of a normal fibre gives the ambient orientation. A **framing**
of $K$ is a homotopy class through smooth nowhere-zero sections of $\nu K$.
The normal bundle is made a smooth vector bundle under this axiom; a framed
knot includes the section class as data, not a choice made afterwards. For the
relative integer use the round metric transferred from the unit sphere in
$\mathbb R^4$ by the explicit diffeomorphism
$$x\longmapsto\left(\frac{2x}{1+\lVert x\rVert^2},\frac{\lVert x\rVert^2-1}{1+\lVert x\rVert^2}\right),\qquad\infty\longmapsto(0,0,0,1).$$
It induces a smooth bundle metric on $\nu K$. The resulting winding number is
independent of the metric: any two smooth fibre metrics interpolate through
positive metrics and the corresponding angle maps are homotopic.

Given a reference framing $[s_0]$ and another framing $[s_1]$, use a bundle
metric and the positive quarter-turn $J$ on each oriented normal plane to write
the normalized representative of $s_1$ as
$$s_1(x)=\cos\theta(x)s_0(x)+\sin\theta(x)Js_0(x).$$
The resulting map $S^1\to S^1$ has a continuous angle lift along a parameter
interval $[0,1]$: subdivide into finitely many intervals whose images lie in
open semicircles and choose consecutive local arguments agreeing at endpoints.
Since the map is closed, the lift changes by $2\pi m$ for some $m\in\mathbb Z$;
different lifts differ by a constant multiple of $2\pi$, and homotopies keep
$m$ fixed. This integer $m$ is the **relative framing integer** of $[s_1]$
with respect to $[s_0]$. Thus, once a reference framing is supplied, the
framing classes are an integer torsor; no absolute integer is assigned before
choosing a reference.

The **self-linking number** of a framed knot $(K,[s])$ is the linking number
of $K$ with a sufficiently small push-off along $s$, oriented parallel to $K$.
The push-off and its integer are independent of the representative section,
small radius, and normalized tubular chart by the preceding well-definedness
result.

If a compact oriented surface $\Sigma$ is supplied with boundary $K$, its
**Seifert framing relative to $\Sigma$** is the homotopy class of the inward
unit conormal to $K$ in $\Sigma$, viewed as a nonzero normal section to $K$ in
$S^3$. This definition is relative to the supplied surface; it neither asserts
that every knot bounds such a surface nor asserts the self-linking-zero result.

Assume countable choice as in the chosen tubular-neighbourhood data. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot with chosen exterior $E_K$ and boundary torus $T_K=\partial E_K$, and let $p:T_K\to K$ be the projection of the chosen normal-disk tube. Orient each normal disk so that its positive tangent direction followed by its oriented normal basis agrees with the orientation of $S^3$. A **meridian** $\mu$ is the oriented boundary of one such normal disk. A **degree-one parallel curve** is a simple closed curve $\lambda$ in $T_K$ for which $p|_\lambda:\lambda\to K$ has degree $+1$. A **preferred longitude** is a degree-one parallel curve satisfying $i_*[\lambda]=0$ in $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$, where $i:T_K\hookrightarrow E_K$ is inclusion. This is a condition on a curve; this definition alone asserts neither existence nor uniqueness. Reversing the orientation of $K$ reverses the orientations of both $\mu$ and any degree-one parallel curve. If a subgroup $P\le\pi_1(E_K,x)$ is specified using a path from $x$ to $T_K$, record it only up to replacing it by $gPg^{-1}$ for $g\in\pi_1(E_K,x)$.

For every path-connected topological space $X$ and $x_0\in X$, the Hurewicz map
$$h:\pi_1(X,x_0)\longrightarrow H_1(X;\mathbb Z)$$
is surjective and has kernel $[\pi_1(X,x_0),\pi_1(X,x_0)]$. Hence it induces a natural isomorphism
$$\pi_1(X,x_0)^{\mathrm{ab}}\cong H_1(X;\mathbb Z).$$
The proof is choice-free and requires no CW, separation, local path-connectivity or local simple-connectivity assumption.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in the oriented $3$-sphere, let $N(K)$ be a chosen closed tubular solid-torus neighborhood, let $E_K=\overline{S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)}$, and let $T_K=\partial E_K=\partial N(K)$. Let $\mu$ be the positive oriented meridian, meaning the boundary of a positive normal disk in $N(K)$, and let $\lambda$ be a preferred longitude, meaning a degree-one parallel of the core $K$ in $N(K)$ that is null-homologous in $E_K$. Assume that $[\mu],[\lambda]$ are an ordered basis of $H_1(T_K;\mathbb Z)$, with the boundary-orientation convention $\mu\cdot\lambda=-1$. A slope is the unoriented isotopy class of an essential simple closed curve on $T_K$ whose homology class is $p[\mu]+q[\lambda]$ for coprime integers $p,q$ not both zero; $(p,q)$ and $(-p,-q)$ represent the same slope. For a slope represented by $p[\mu]+q[\lambda]$, the Dehn filling $E_K(p/q)$ is obtained by gluing an oriented solid torus $D^2\times S^1$ to $E_K$ by an orientation-reversing boundary homeomorphism that sends $[\partial D^2\times\{1\}]$ to that slope; the filled orientation agrees with the fixed orientation on $E_K$. If $q\ne0$, the coefficient is written $p/q$; the meridional slope is $1/0$, and integer $n$-framed filling means slope $n[\mu]+[\lambda]$. The oriented homeomorphism type is independent of the gluing map once its meridian image is fixed.

Let $X=U\cup V$, where $U$ and $V$ are open path-connected subsets of $X$, let $U\cap V$ be path-connected, and fix $x_0\in U\cap V$. For the inclusion-induced maps in the diagram

$$\pi_1(U,x_0)\longleftarrow\pi_1(U\cap V,x_0)\longrightarrow\pi_1(V,x_0),$$

the group $\pi_1(X,x_0)$, together with the two inclusion-induced homomorphisms, is a pushout ([[def-pushout-of-group-homomorphisms]]). Equivalently, the canonical homomorphism from any pushout $P$ of the displayed diagram to $\pi_1(X,x_0)$ is an isomorphism. No injectivity of either map from the overlap group is assumed.

derivations.claim: In [F1], for $0<t<1/2$ the left-starting motion is $(2ht-h,-2ht)$ and the right-starting motion its negative. At the crossing the latter has greater $y$, hence is over when viewed along $+y$. Their projected tangents in coordinates $(t,x)$ are $(1,-2h)$ and $(1,2h)$, with determinant $4h>0$. Rounding the diamond corners and flattening endpoints preserves this strict sign. The downward three-crossing diagram therefore has three positive crossings. The diagram agrees with the fixed geometric closure: the change from stacked diamonds to rounded diagonal strands is a height-preserving interpolation with nonzero pair difference, followed by the fixed closure map. In particular it is not the mirror braid.

Label the initial left and right meridians $a,b$. At a positive crossing the right input is over, and the left input follows the positive over-normal to become the right output. Successive rows of the braid have input/output pairs $\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}\text{row}&\text{input }(L,R)&\text{output }(L,R)&\text{underpass relation}\\\hline1&(a,b)&(b,c)&c=b^{-1}ab\\2&(b,c)&(c,a)&a=c^{-1}bc\\3&(c,a)&(a,b)&b=a^{-1}ca\end{array}$ Here the last two output labels use the closure identifications of bottom and top positions. These are all crossing relations by [F3]. Substituting $c=b^{-1}ab$ into $b=a^{-1}ca$ gives $aba=bab$; the remaining relation follows because $b^{-1}ab=aba^{-1}$ and then $c^{-1}bc=a$. Thus $\pi_1(S^3\setminus T)=\langle a,b\mid aba=bab\rangle$, with the stated positive meridians. In the chosen tube, the radial normal homotopy from positive radius $r<\epsilon$ to $(1-s)r+s\epsilon$ identifies this group with $\pi_1(E_T)$.

Trace a small parallel starting at the initial left arc. Along the oriented component its underpasses occur in row order $1,3,2$, with over-meridians $b,a,c$; it passes over the intervening crossings. This order follows directly from the input/output table: $a$ becomes $c$ on the right in row 1, passes over in row 2, becomes $b$ in row 3, closes to the initial right position, passes over in row 1, becomes $a$ in row 2 and closes after passing over in row 3. At each underpass the access-path calculation in [F3] is $\alpha_{\rm in}\beta=g_o\alpha_{\rm out}$, where $\beta$ is the path along the small parallel; thus the three successive factors are $b,a,c$, with positive exponents. At an overpass the access path slides through its upper product chart and contributes no factor. On the crossing-free exterior closure arcs use the same product charts, again contributing no factor. Concatenating gives the based parallel word $w=bac$. These path identities can be made on the upper side of the normal circles. The upper normal section and the blackboard section are homotopic without zero: in the normal quotient the blackboard vector and viewing vector form a positively oriented basis, so the interpolation rotating the former through a fixed quarter-turn to the latter is everywhere nonzero. This proves that the traced parallel has the blackboard framing and oriented degree $+1$, rather than identifying a peripheral word only from its exponent sum. By [F4] and step 1.1 its self-linking is $+3$.

The boundary torus has product coordinates from this actual parallel: its degree-one section is $w$ and its positive fibre is $a$. A section making three negative fibre turns is an embedded degree-one curve with based word $w a^{-3}$; the torus rectangle homotopy makes the fibre and section commute. In the abelianization of step 2.1 the relation $aba=bab$ gives $[a]=[b]$, and sending each to $1$ supplies an inverse to the cyclic generator map. Thus $H_1(E_T)=\mathbb Z$ on $[a]$ by [F6], and $[w]=[b]+[a]+[c]=3[a]$. Therefore $\lambda=w a^{-3}$ has zero exterior homology and degree $+1$, precisely [F5]. Moreover $c=aba^{-1}$, so $w a^3=b a^2b a^2=b a(bab)a=(ba)^3=(ab)^3.$ Both last cubes equal $(aba)^2$, which commutes with $a,b$ because conjugation by $aba$ exchanges them. This proves $\lambda=(ab)^3a^{-6}$ with the fixed positive meridian and the correct sign.

The $+1$ slope is the primitive boundary curve $\lambda\mu$, since its coefficients in the oriented meridian/longitude basis are $(1,1)$. In [F7] the solid torus has cyclic fundamental group; a complementary boundary generator identifies its core generator and eliminates it, while its meridian kills precisely $\lambda\mu$. Thus filling adds $w a^{-2}=1$. Substituting $w=bac$ and $c=b^{-1}ab$ gives $bab^{-1}aba^{-2}=1$. Equivalently step 4.1 gives $(ab)^3=a^5$. These are the asserted presentations of the same positive-trefoil $+1$ filling.

citations.quote:
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in the oriented $3$-sphere with a chosen connected exterior $E_K$ and boundary torus $T_K$. Let $(\mu,\lambda)$ be its positive meridian and preferred longitude, assume $([\mu],[\lambda])$ is a basis of $H_1(T_K;\mathbb Z)$, and assume $[\mu]$ generates $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$ and $[\lambda]=0$. For coprime integers $p,q$ not both zero, let $E_K(p/q)$ be the filling whose attached solid-torus meridian maps to $p[\mu]+q[\lambda]$. Then
$$H_1(E_K(p/q);\mathbb Z)\cong\begin{cases}\mathbb Z/|p|\mathbb Z,&p\ne0,\\[2pt]\mathbb Z,&p=0.\end{cases}$$

For $g\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$, an **orientable handlebody of genus $g$** is a compact connected orientable smooth $3$-manifold obtained from a $3$-ball by attaching $g$ smooth $1$-handles along orientation-compatible pairs of disjoint boundary disks and rounding the corners. A $1$-handle here is a copy of $D^2\times[-1,1]$ attached by its two end disks to those boundary disks. Its boundary is a connected closed orientable surface of genus $g$. A **Heegaard splitting** of a closed connected oriented smooth $3$-manifold $M$ is a decomposition
$$
M=H_-\cup_{\varphi}H_+
$$
in which $H_-$ and $H_+$ are orientable handlebodies of the same genus, their common boundary is a connected closed surface $\Sigma=\partial H_-=\partial H_+$, and $\varphi:\partial H_-\to\partial H_+$ is an orientation-reversing diffeomorphism whose gluing gives $M$. The surface $\Sigma$ is the **Heegaard surface** of the splitting.

derivations.claim: By [A1] and [F1], choose a finite triangulation $\mathcal T$ of $M$. Its $1$-skeleton is connected: if it were disconnected, each simplex would have all its vertices in a single graph component because every pair of vertices of a simplex is joined by an edge; the realization would therefore be a disjoint union of nonempty subcomplexes, contrary to connectedness of $M$.

In the barycentric subdivision, thicken the finite embedded $1$-skeleton by taking disjoint small $3$-balls at its vertices and disjoint narrow tubes around the edge interiors, each tube meeting its endpoint balls in end disks. The vertex balls joined by the tubes along a spanning tree form a $3$-ball: adding a leaf ball and its joining tube joins two balls along a tube and again gives a ball. Each remaining edge tube attaches along two disks to this connected boundary and is one $1$-handle. There are $|E|-|V|+1$ such edges; the cycles formed by each non-tree edge with its spanning-tree path form a basis of the graph's first homology, so this number is $b_1$. The resulting connected orientable manifold is a handlebody of genus $b_1$ by the definition.

In the barycentric dual cell structure, put one vertex in each tetrahedron and join two such vertices through the barycentre of each common triangular face. This dual graph is connected: choose a piecewise-linear path between interior points of any two tetrahedra and perturb its finitely many segments inside simplex stars so it avoids the primal $1$-skeleton and meets triangular faces transversely. Each crossing then passes between tetrahedra sharing that face, producing a finite path in the dual graph.

Take the vertex balls and edge tubes in step 2.1 as the primal barycentric blocks, so their complement is made of the dual blocks. In each tetrahedron the complementary block is a $3$-ball about its barycentre; across each common triangular face, the two balls join by a tube about the dual edge through that face. Thus the dual balls and tubes form the closure of $M\setminus\operatorname{int}H_-$. The dual graph is connected by step 2.2; joining its vertex balls along a spanning tree gives a $3$-ball, and each other dual edge contributes one $1$-handle. Thus the complementary closure is a handlebody $H_+$. Since $M$ is closed, its boundary is the same surface $\Sigma=\partial H_-$ as the boundary of $H_+$.

Both boundaries are $\Sigma$, so the handlebodies have equal genus by the definition of genus as the genus of their boundary. Their induced boundary orientations are opposite because they are the two sides of the oriented manifold $M$; the gluing map is therefore orientation-reversing. By [F2], $M=H_-\cup_\Sigma H_+$ is a Heegaard splitting.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $M$ be a smooth
$m$-manifold, let $0\le p\le m-1$ and $q=m-p$, so that $q\ge1$, and let
$\varphi:S^p\times D^q\hookrightarrow M$ be a framed embedded surgery sphere
with image in the interior of $M$ ([[def-framed-embedded-surgery-sphere]]). The
**$p$-surgery on $M$ along $\varphi$**, also called a spherical modification of
type $(p+1,q)$, is the smooth $m$-manifold $M_\varphi$ obtained by removing the
open tubular piece $\varphi(S^p\times\operatorname{int}D^q)$ and gluing in
$D^{p+1}\times S^{q-1}$ along the common boundary, using the identification
induced by $\varphi$ on $S^p\times S^{q-1}$:
$$M_\varphi=\bigl(M\setminus\varphi(S^p\times\operatorname{int}D^q)\bigr)\cup_{\varphi|_{S^p\times S^{q-1}}}\bigl(D^{p+1}\times S^{q-1}\bigr).$$

The two pieces are smooth manifolds with boundary sharing the boundary component
$S^p\times S^{q-1}$ under the identification induced by $\varphi$; the complement
also retains $\partial M$. They are glued along collars of the shared component and the seam is
smoothed by the signed collar charts also used along the boundary of a smooth handle attachment
([[def-attaching-a-smooth-handle-with-corner-rounding]],
[[thm-collar-neighborhood-theorem]]). The smooth structure produced this way is
independent of the auxiliary collar and smoothing choices up to a
diffeomorphism supported near the seam; this is proved by the gluing lemma of
this page, and it is the sense in which the construction is
well defined ([[lem-surgery-gluing-has-a-canonical-smooth-structure-up-to-diffeomorphism]]).

The **core sphere** is $\varphi_0:S^p\to M$, $\varphi_0(x)=\varphi(x,0)$; it
lies in the removed piece and is not a submanifold of $M_\varphi$. The **belt sphere** is
$\{0\}\times S^{q-1}\subseteq
D^{p+1}\times S^{q-1}\subseteq M_\varphi$, a closed embedded $(q-1)$-sphere with
the normal data of the disk-factor decomposition
([[def-k-handle-core-cocore-attaching-region-and-belt-sphere]]). The glued-in
disk factor has dimension $p+1$, while the whole piece has dimension
$(p+1)+(q-1)=m$. The disk dimension is the index shift recorded by the trace
construction of this page.

The boundary identification is the restriction of the supplied product
embedding $\varphi$, whose derivative along the core induces the normal
framing. Changing that embedding or its framing can change the surgery, but
distinct normal framings need not give distinct boundary identifications or
distinct diffeomorphism types. Nothing in the definition
asserts that a framing exists for a given embedded sphere; that condition is the
content of the framing lemma of this page.

When $\partial M\ne\varnothing$ the construction takes place in the interior of
$M$ and leaves $\partial M$ unchanged: the removed piece lies in the interior
and the glued-in piece meets $\partial M$ in no point. The case $p=m-1$ (so $q=1$)

A diagram is considered up to orientation-preserving ambient isotopy carrying each component framing; a planar projection is only a way of drawing the link.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For an integral framed link diagram, **Kirby move equivalence** is the equivalence relation generated by the following operations.

1. Apply an orientation-preserving ambient isotopy to the framed link in $S^3$.

2. **Handle slide:** choose distinct components $K_i,K_j$, a parallel $K_j^+$ determined by the framing of $K_j$, and an embedded band whose ends attach to $K_i$ and $K_j^+$ and whose interior misses every link component. Replace $K_i$ by the band sum of $K_i$ with $K_j^+$ and keep the framing obtained by carrying the normal framing across the band. Orient the new component by the band-sum orientation.

3. **Stabilization or destabilization:** add or remove an unknot with framing $+1$ or $-1$ that lies in a $3$-ball disjoint from all the other components.

The integer framing of a component is measured from its preferred longitude as in the integral surgery definition. A planar link projection is not part of the move data; any drawing below is schematic.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $W$ be a compact smooth $n$-manifold with collared boundary, let $M\subseteq\partial_+W$ be a connected boundary region, and let $h_1,h_2$ be $k$-handles attached to $M$ by embeddings $f_1,f_2$ with disjoint images, where $1\le k\le n-2$. A **slide of $h_1$ over $h_2$** is determined by a band datum: points $x_i$ in the attaching spheres $f_i(S^{k-1}\times\{0\})$, trivializations of the normal bundles of the attaching spheres near $x_i$ compatible with the framings of $f_i$, and an embedded band $\beta$ whose rank-$(n-k-1)$ normal framing matches the sphere framings after quotienting out the transverse band direction, as supplied by the band lemma. The datum also includes the full framing gluing convention described below; quotient compatibility alone is insufficient. The slid handle $h_1'$ is the $k$-handle attached to $M$ by the embedding $f_1'$ whose core sphere is obtained from $f_1(S^{k-1}\times\{0\})\setminus\operatorname{int}\beta_0$ and from $f_2(S^{k-1}\times\{0\})\setminus\operatorname{int}\beta_1$ pushed off along the band framing, where $\beta_0,\beta_1$ are the two end discs, together with the side $\partial D^{k-1}\times I$ of the band, smoothed along the gluing circles; the framing of $f_1'$ is built from the framing of $f_1$, the signed framing of the parallel copy of $f_2$, and the band framing, and extends to an embedding of the attaching region. Equivalently, in the band-sum picture, the attaching sphere of $h_1'$ is the connected sum of the attaching sphere of $h_1$ with a signed framed parallel copy of the attaching sphere of $h_2$ along the band, so that the slid attachment is disjoint from the attachment of $h_2$. Different band data may give different slides; all of them are called slides of $h_1$ over $h_2$. For $k=1$ the general formula is read in the $0$-dimensional sense: the band is an arc joining a point of the first attaching $0$-sphere to a framed parallel point of the second, and the slid attaching $0$-sphere is obtained from the first by replacing that point with a parallel copy of the other point of the second attaching $0$-sphere.

For $k\ge2$, write the old ordered normal framings as $(v_{i1},\ldots,v_{iq})$, $q=n-k$, choosing the first normal line to be the transverse band line at each end. The band framing matches the classes of $(v_{i2},\ldots,v_{iq})$. Round the seams in the two-dimensional plane formed by the end disk's radial direction and the transverse band direction. The first normal to the rounded sphere is the complementary normal in this plane; choose its sign to match $v_{11}$ on the first sphere. At the other end it agrees with $\sigma v_{21}$ for a uniquely determined $\sigma\in\{1,-1\}$. Use $(\sigma v_{21},v_{22},\ldots,v_{2q})$ on the entire parallel copy of the second sphere. Equivalently, when $\sigma=-1$, precompose its normal disk coordinate with $(z_1,z_2,\ldots,z_q)\mapsto(-z_1,z_2,\ldots,z_q)$. This reflection concerns the copy used in the band sum; the retained handle $h_2$ keeps its original attaching embedding. Require these full ordered frames to glue across the rounded seams, rather than requiring agreement with both unreflected old frames. In an oriented boundary, this is the usual condition that the orientations induced on the two removed end disks by the framed spheres and the band have opposite boundary-gluing signs. Both addition and subtraction are allowed by the choice of band-end coordinates and this sign convention.

The seam rotation in the indicated plane, together with the remaining band normal vectors, gives a full framing agreeing with the first old framing and the signed second-copy framing. A sufficiently thin normal thickening is then an attaching embedding; take the parallel copy outside the retained attaching region and the thickening small enough to be disjoint from it. For $k=1$, use the full normal framing transported when the chosen foot is pushed along the band and across the parallel interval core of $h_2$ to its other foot; this fixes the analogous sign convention without using a positive-dimensional seam. The band lemma supplies the embedded band and its quotient framing, while the full-frame convention supplies the additional gluing data. No uniqueness of the slide is asserted. Countable Choice is inherited through the band-existence and smooth-attachment conventions.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $h_1,h_2$ be $k$-handles attached to $M\subseteq\partial_+W$ as in the slide definition, with $1\le k\le n-2$, and let $h_1'$ be a slide of $h_1$ over $h_2$ (the slid handle attached to $M$ by the band move). Then $W\cup_{f_1}h_1\cup_{f_2}h_2$ and $W\cup_{f_1'}h_1'\cup_{f_2}h_2$ are diffeomorphic relative to $\partial_0W$; more precisely there is a diffeomorphism supported in a neighbourhood of the two handles and the band region carrying the first presentation to the second. Consequently a handle slide does not change the diffeomorphism type of the presented manifold and may be performed on any of two equal-index handles.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $M$ be a closed
smooth $m$-manifold, $0\le p\le m-1$, $q=m-p$, and let
$\varphi:S^p\times D^q\hookrightarrow M$ be a framed embedded surgery sphere
([[def-framed-embedded-surgery-sphere]]). Regard $\varphi$ in the upper face
$M\times\{1\}$ of the cylinder $M\times[0,1]$ as the embedding
$\varphi\times\{1\}$, whose image is contained in the interior of that face. The
**surgery trace cobordism** of $\varphi$ is the compact smooth
$(m+1)$-manifold
$$W_\varphi=(M\times[0,1])\cup_{\varphi\times\{1\}}(D^{p+1}\times D^q),$$
that is, the cylinder $M\times[0,1]$ with the standard $(p+1)$-handle
$D^{p+1}\times D^q$ attached along the framed sphere, the corner along
$\varphi(S^p\times\partial D^q)$ being rounded in the standard way
([[def-attaching-a-smooth-handle-with-corner-rounding]]). The index shift is
part of the construction: a surgery datum of sphere dimension $p$ produces a
handle of index $p+1$, whose attaching region is $S^p\times D^q$ and whose
outgoing region is $D^{p+1}\times S^{q-1}$
([[def-k-handle-core-cocore-attaching-region-and-belt-sphere]]).

The cylinder is the product cobordism with the empty handle presentation, whose
incoming face is $M_0=M\times\{0\}$ and whose outgoing face is
$M\times\{1\}$; the product presentation and its, possibly empty, collar
structure are those of
[[lem-product-cobordisms-have-critical-point-free-presentations]], and the
collar of the incoming face is the one used whenever the trace is recorded as a
cobordism ([[def-smooth-collar-of-a-manifold-boundary]],
[[def-smooth-cobordism-triad-for-morse-theory]]).

The trace carries the following fixed pieces of structure, which are not
choices made afterwards:

- the **incoming face** $M\times\{0\}$, identified with $M$ by the product
  structure;
- the **core disk** $D^{p+1}\times\{0\}$ of the attached handle;
- the **cocore disk** $\{0\}\times D^q$ of the attached handle;
- the **belt sphere** $\{0\}\times S^{q-1}\subseteq D^{p+1}\times S^{q-1}$,
  a copy of which lies in the outgoing face of $W_\varphi$.

When $M$ is oriented, an oriented trace additionally requires compatibility
of the framing with the orientation: choose the handle orientation so its
attaching identification reverses the induced boundary orientations of the
handle and the cylinder. The orientation then glues, and $W_\varphi$ is an oriented
bordism from $M$ to its outgoing face, the outgoing face carrying the induced
boundary orientation and the incoming face the negative of the orientation of
$M$, in the outward-normal-first convention of
[[def-induced-boundary-orientation]]; this is the oriented bordism relation of
[[def-oriented-smooth-cobordism]], and the orientation of $M$ determines the extending orientation when this compatibility
holds. For $p\ge1$ the attaching region is connected, so the handle
orientation can always be chosen to match it. For $p=0$ its two components
must both match that one handle orientation; an arbitrary pair of interval
framings need not do so, and the unoriented trace remains defined in that case.
The supplied orientation is the only ambient orientation used ([[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]]).

Nothing is proved here. In particular, the identification of the outgoing face
with the surgered manifold $M_\varphi$ of
[[def-p-surgery-on-a-smooth-m-manifold]] is the content of the upper-boundary
theorem of this page, and the deformation retractions of the trace are not part
of the definition.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $M$ be a closed
smooth $m$-manifold, $0\le p\le m-1$, $q=m-p$, let $\varphi$ be a framed
embedded surgery sphere in $M$, let $W_\varphi$ be its trace and let
$M_\varphi$ be the $p$-surgery on $M$ along $\varphi$. Then:

(i) $\partial W_\varphi$ is the disjoint union of the two closed faces
$M\times\{0\}\cong M$ (the incoming face) and the outgoing face, and the
outgoing face is diffeomorphic to $M_\varphi$, with compatible collar choices the identification
being the identity on $M\setminus\varphi(S^p\times\operatorname{int}D^q)$ and
carrying the belt sphere of the handle to the belt sphere of the surgery;

(ii) there are homotopy equivalences of pairs relative to the indicated faces,
$$(W_\varphi,M)\simeq(M\cup_{\varphi_0}D^{p+1},M),\qquad (W_\varphi,M_\varphi)\simeq(M_\varphi\cup_{\beta}D^q,M_\varphi),$$
where $\beta$ is the belt-sphere embedding. The characteristic disks in these
models include the collar paths from the attaching spheres to the respective
faces; the raw core disk in the upper handle does not have boundary in the
incoming face;

(iii) in particular the trace is a bordism from $M$ to $M_\varphi$, as the
definition of the trace asserts.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in the oriented $3$-sphere, let $N(K)$ be a chosen closed tubular solid-torus neighborhood, let $E_K=\overline{S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)}$, and let $T_K=\partial E_K=\partial N(K)$. Let $\mu$ be the positive oriented meridian, meaning the boundary of a positive normal disk in $N(K)$, and let $\lambda$ be a preferred longitude, meaning a degree-one parallel of the core $K$ in $N(K)$ that is null-homologous in $E_K$. Assume that $[\mu],[\lambda]$ are an ordered basis of $H_1(T_K;\mathbb Z)$, with the boundary-orientation convention $\mu\cdot\lambda=-1$. A slope is the unoriented isotopy class of an essential simple closed curve on $T_K$ whose homology class is $p[\mu]+q[\lambda]$ for coprime integers $p,q$ not both zero; $(p,q)$ and $(-p,-q)$ represent the same slope. For a slope represented by $p[\mu]+q[\lambda]$, the Dehn filling $E_K(p/q)$ is obtained by gluing an oriented solid torus $D^2\times S^1$ to $E_K$ by an orientation-reversing boundary homeomorphism that sends $[\partial D^2\times\{1\}]$ to that slope; the filled orientation agrees with the fixed orientation on $E_K$. If $q\ne0$, the coefficient is written $p/q$; the meridional slope is $1/0$, and integer $n$-framed filling means slope $n[\mu]+[\lambda]$. The oriented homeomorphism type is independent of the gluing map once its meridian image is fixed.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: For an ambient isotopy, carry each component neighbourhood, meridian, and preferred longitude along the isotopy. The endpoint diffeomorphism of $S^3$ therefore maps every filling meridian to the same framed slope on the corresponding endpoint torus. Extend it over each attached solid torus by the product identification used in the filling. The resulting map is an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism of the filled manifolds.

Applying [A1] to the family of values of any sequence $(X_n)$ in [F8] gives a choice function on that range; composing it with $n\mapsto X_n$ supplies the choice function required by [F8]. Thus the $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ hypothesis of [F3]–[F6] holds. Form the $4$-dimensional surgery trace from a $4$-ball by attaching one $2$-handle for each framed link component. The product collar on the outgoing boundary of the $4$-ball lets these handles be attached successively; by repeated use of [F5]–[F6], the outgoing boundary is the simultaneous surgery result. The link slide of [F2] is exactly the $k=2$ handle slide of [F3], including its full transported normal framing. Since $1\le2\le4-2$, [F4] supplies a diffeomorphism of the two traces relative to the incoming $4$-ball. Its restriction to the outgoing boundaries is the required orientation-preserving diffeomorphism.

Suppose a split unknot is added with coefficient $\varepsilon\in\{1,-1\}$ in a ball disjoint from the rest of the link. The separating sphere shows that the filled manifold is the connected sum of the old surgery result with the filling of the unknot exterior along $\varepsilon[\mu_U]+[\lambda_U]$. For the standard unknot, take $E_U=\{|z_2|\ge1/\sqrt2\}\subset S^3\subset\mathbb C^2$, identified with $D^2\times S^1$ by $(z_1,z_2)\mapsto(z_1,z_2/|z_2|)$. Its preferred longitude $\lambda_U$ is the meridian of this solid torus, and $\mu_U$ is its core longitude. The diffeomorphism $g_\varepsilon(z,w)=(w^{-\varepsilon}z,w)$ of $D^2\times S^1$ preserves orientation, fixes $[\lambda_U]$, and sends $[\mu_U]$ to $[\mu_U]-\varepsilon[\lambda_U]$; hence it sends the slope $\varepsilon[\mu_U]+[\lambda_U]$ to the unoriented meridional slope $[\mu_U]$. Choose the $S^3$ gluing with meridian $[\mu_U]$ and the $\varepsilon$-filling gluing as its pullback by $g_\varepsilon^{-1}$. The map $g_\varepsilon$ on the exterior and the identity on the attached solid torus then give an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism between the two fillings. Filling along $[\mu_U]$ restores the original unknot neighbourhood, so the $\varepsilon$-framed unknot filling is orientation-preservingly diffeomorphic to $S^3$. Hence the connected sum is the original manifold: deleting a ball and regluing the complementary ball of $S^3$ restores the same manifold. Removing a split $\varepsilon$-framed unknot is the inverse operation.

Each allowed move preserves the oriented surgery manifold by steps 1.1–1.3. Composing the finitely many orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms along a move sequence proves the assertion for Kirby-move-equivalent diagrams.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. It supplies countable choice for the chosen tubular data: for any sequence of nonempty sets, apply full choice to its range and compose with the index map. Let $L=\bigcup_{i\in I}K_i$ be a finite oriented link in the standard oriented $3$-sphere, where $I$ is a finite index set. For each component $K_i$, include a chosen closed tubular neighbourhood $N(K_i)$, its exterior $E_{K_i}=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K_i)$, the positive meridian $\mu_i$, and the preferred longitude $\lambda_i$; the longitude is the degree-one parallel class in $H_1(\partial E_{K_i};\mathbb Z)$ that maps to zero in $H_1(E_{K_i};\mathbb Z)$. For each $i\in I$, choose an integer $n_i$. The resulting **integral framed-link surgery diagram** is this link and integer family, with the surgery result defined by removing the interiors of all $N(K_i)$ and gluing an oriented solid torus to each boundary torus so that its meridian maps to $n_i[\mu_i]+[\lambda_i]$. If $I=\varnothing$, the surgery result is $S^3$. A diagram is considered up to orientation-preserving ambient isotopy carrying each component framing; a planar projection is only a way of drawing the link.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in the oriented $3$-sphere, let $N(K)$ be a chosen closed tubular solid-torus neighborhood, let $E_K=\overline{S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)}$, and let $T_K=\partial E_K=\partial N(K)$. Let $\mu$ be the positive oriented meridian, meaning the boundary of a positive normal disk in $N(K)$, and let $\lambda$ be a preferred longitude, meaning a degree-one parallel of the core $K$ in $N(K)$ that is null-homologous in $E_K$. Assume that $[\mu],[\lambda]$ are an ordered basis of $H_1(T_K;\mathbb Z)$, with the boundary-orientation convention $\mu\cdot\lambda=-1$. A slope is the unoriented isotopy class of an essential simple closed curve on $T_K$ whose homology class is $p[\mu]+q[\lambda]$ for coprime integers $p,q$ not both zero; $(p,q)$ and $(-p,-q)$ represent the same slope. For a slope represented by $p[\mu]+q[\lambda]$, the Dehn filling $E_K(p/q)$ is obtained by gluing an oriented solid torus $D^2\times S^1$ to $E_K$ by an orientation-reversing boundary homeomorphism that sends $[\partial D^2\times\{1\}]$ to that slope; the filled orientation agrees with the fixed orientation on $E_K$. If $q\ne0$, the coefficient is written $p/q$; the meridional slope is $1/0$, and integer $n$-framed filling means slope $n[\mu]+[\lambda]$. The oriented homeomorphism type is independent of the gluing map once its meridian image is fixed.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. An oriented lens space is an oriented closed $3$-manifold obtained by gluing two solid tori by an orientation-reversing boundary homeomorphism. For coprime integers $p>0$ and $q$, let $L(p,q)$ denote the oriented union of the exterior of the unknot in the oriented $3$-sphere and a solid torus whose meridian is identified with the slope $p[\mu_U]+q[\lambda_U]$ on the unknot exterior. Thus this library uses the convention $L(p,q)=E_U(p/q)$; no symbol $L(0,q)$ is assigned.

Assume countable choice as in the chosen tubular-neighbourhood data. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot with chosen exterior $E_K$ and boundary torus $T_K=\partial E_K$, and let $p:T_K\to K$ be the projection of the chosen normal-disk tube. Orient each normal disk so that its positive tangent direction followed by its oriented normal basis agrees with the orientation of $S^3$. A **meridian** $\mu$ is the oriented boundary of one such normal disk. A **degree-one parallel curve** is a simple closed curve $\lambda$ in $T_K$ for which $p|_\lambda:\lambda\to K$ has degree $+1$. A **preferred longitude** is a degree-one parallel curve satisfying $i_*[\lambda]=0$ in $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$, where $i:T_K\hookrightarrow E_K$ is inclusion. This is a condition on a curve; this definition alone asserts neither existence nor uniqueness. Reversing the orientation of $K$ reverses the orientations of both $\mu$ and any degree-one parallel curve. If a subgroup $P\le\pi_1(E_K,x)$ is specified using a path from $x$ to $T_K$, record it only up to replacing it by $gPg^{-1}$ for $g\in\pi_1(E_K,x)$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K:S^1	o S^3$ be a smooth oriented embedding and write its quotient normal bundle as $
u_K=K^*TS^3/dK(TS^1)$. Choose an orientation-preserving trivialization $
u_K\cong S^1	imes\mathbb R^2$ and a tubular map $\Phi:\Omega	o S^3$, meaning a smooth embedding from an open neighbourhood $\Omega\subseteq
u_K$ of the zero section onto an open neighbourhood of $K(S^1)$ with $\Phi(s,0)=K(s)$, such that in these product coordinates $\Omega$ contains $S^1	imes D^2_{2\epsilon}$ for some $\epsilon>0$. Here $D^2_r=\{z\in\mathbb R^2:\|z\|\le r\}$. Set $N(K)=\Phi(S^1	imes D^2_\epsilon)$, $E_K=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$, $T_K=\partial E_K$, and let $i:T_K\hookrightarrow E_K$ be inclusion, $p:T_K	o S^1$ the product projection, and $\mu$ the positive boundary of a normal disk, using the normal-plane orientation determined by the orientations of $K$ and $S^3$. A class is primitive if it is not $m$ times another class for any integer $|m|>1$. Then $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$ is generated by $[\mu]$. The kernel of $i_*:H_1(T_K;\mathbb Z)	o H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$ is a primitive rank-one direct summand generated by a unique class $[\lambda]$ with $p_*[\lambda]=1\in H_1(S^1;\mathbb Z)$. It has a simple closed representative, is the preferred longitude, and $([\mu],[\lambda])$ is a basis of $H_1(T_K;\mathbb Z)$.

derivations.claim: Applying [A1] to the range of any sequence $(X_n)$ in [A2] and composing the resulting choice function with $n\mapsto X_n$ gives the countable-choice function required by [A2]. Thus the chosen tubular and slope interfaces used below are available.
For the empty link there are no tubular neighbourhoods to remove and no solid tori to attach. The definition [F1] therefore leaves the standard oriented $S^3$ unchanged.

Use $N(U)=\{|z_2|\le 1/\sqrt2\}$; its exterior is the solid torus $E_U=\{|z_2|\ge1/\sqrt2\}\cong D^2\times S^1$, with disk coordinate $z_1$ and core coordinate $\arg z_2$. The loop in the $z_1$ direction has degree one and bounds a disk in $E_U$, so [F4]–[F5] identify it with $\lambda_U$; the positive meridian $\mu_U$ runs once around the exterior core. For $0$-surgery, [F2] sends the attached meridian to $\lambda_U$, the meridian of $E_U$. The gluing-map convention in the slope definition permits the product gluing: the two disk factors glue to $S^2$ and the core circles glue to $S^1$, giving $S^1\times S^2$ with the induced surgery orientation.
For $p>0$, [F2] identifies the $p$-framed unknot filling with the filling of $E_U$ along $p[\mu_U]+[\lambda_U]$. This is exactly $L(p,1)$ by [F3]. The case $p=1$ is included.

Step 2.1 includes p=1.

No interval parameter occurs.

Work in the smooth category ([[def-smooth-manifold]]). Fix once and for all the
three-sphere as the one-point compactification

$$S^3:=\mathbb R^3\cup\{\infty\}$$

of Euclidean three-space, carrying its standard smooth structure, and fix the
standard orientation of $S^3$: the orientation induced by the standard
orientation of $\mathbb R^3$ under the one-point compactification, so that the
charts of the standard atlas away from $\infty$ are orientation-preserving and
the orientation is that of a connected oriented $3$-manifold in the sense of
[[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]]. For $r>0$ write
$\overline B_r:=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:\lVert x\rVert_2\le r\}$, the closed ball of
[[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]] with the following restriction convention. Smoothness on a closed ball means
local extension to a smooth map on an open neighborhood in Euclidean space;
smoothness on $M\times I$, for a smooth manifold $M$ without boundary, means
local extension across $t=0,1$ in $M\times\mathbb R$. Thus these closed domains
are not asserted to be manifolds without boundary in the cited definition.

**Links.** The **standard oriented circle** is the circle
$S^1=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ with its standard counterclockwise orientation,
regarded as a smooth $1$-manifold; a
**finite disjoint union of oriented circles** is a smooth manifold
$C=S^1\sqcup\dots\sqcup S^1$ ($k$ summands, $k\in\mathbb N$)
diffeomorphic to the disjoint union of $k$ standard oriented circles. An
**oriented link** (with $k$ components) is a smooth embedding

$$L\colon C\longrightarrow S^3$$

of such a disjoint union in the sense of [[def-smooth-embedding]]. So $L$ is
injective, is an immersion, and is a homeomorphism onto its image with the
subspace topology, and its image $L(C)$ is a finite disjoint union of smoothly
embedded circles. Thus every link considered here is finite and tame: the
smoothness of $L$ is exactly the standing convention, and no polygonal or other
tame model is used. The **components** of $L$ are the images of the individual
summands, and the number of components is $k$.

**Ambient isotopy.** Let $I=[0,1]$. An **ambient isotopy** of $S^3$ is a smooth
map

$$H\colon S^3\times I\longrightarrow S^3$$

such that $H_0=\mathrm{id}_{S^3}$, each $H_t\colon S^3\to S^3$,
$H_t(x):=H(x,t)$, is a diffeomorphism ([[def-diffeomorphism-and-local-diffeomorphism-of-manifolds]]),
and each $H_t$ is orientation-preserving with respect to the fixed orientation.
The last clause is in fact automatic: $t\mapsto H_t$ is continuous in the
$C^\infty$ topology of the diffeomorphism group, the orientation sign is locally
constant in $t$, and $H_0=\mathrm{id}$ is orientation-preserving, so it is kept
only for emphasis.

**Equivalence of links.** Two oriented links $L_0\colon C_0\to S^3$ and
$L_1\colon C_1\to S^3$ are **equivalent** (written $L_0\sim L_1$), or
**ambient isotopic**, when there are an ambient isotopy $H$ and an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism $f:C_0\to C_1$ with
$H_1\circ L_0=L_1\circ f$. Thus parametrizations and component labels are
irrelevant, while the induced orientation of each image component is preserved. The relation is an equivalence relation on links:
it is reflexive with $H=\mathrm{id}$, transitive by composing isotopies, and
symmetric because a smooth family of diffeomorphisms has a smooth family of
inverses. An equivalence class is an **(oriented) link type**.

**Moving off $\infty$.** Because the definition of equivalence allows the
isotopy to move a link through $\infty$, the standard practice of this page is
to first apply an ambient isotopy that carries a given link into the open ball,
and only then to project; every projection and every Reidemeister move below is
read after moving the link off $\infty$ into $\mathbb R^3$ in this way. The
orientation-preserving clause in the definition of ambient isotopy is exactly
what the oriented Reidemeister moves and the oriented closure construction must
respect. The unoriented theory uses the same ambient isotopies but forgets
the orientations of the link components.

$\mathbb R^3\subset S^3$ is a link in $S^3$; conversely every link may be
assumed after isotopy to lie in $\mathbb R^3$, by choosing a point outside the compact one-dimensional image and moving that
point to $\infty$ by a smooth rotation of the standard sphere. When comparing
links already in $\mathbb R^3$, an isotopy can also be arranged to avoid
$\infty$ throughout; the track-avoidance argument is given in
[[thm-oriented-reidemeister-equivalence-theorem]].

Give $S^3$ its unit-sphere model in $\mathbb C^2$ and let $U(t)=(e^{2\pi i t},0)$. With $N(U)=\{|z_2|\le1/\sqrt2\}$, the exterior is $D^2\times S^1$ with disk coordinate $z_1$ and core coordinate $w=z_2/|z_2|$. The preferred longitude $\lambda_U$ is the disk-meridian class and $\mu_U$ is the core-longitude class by [F2]–[F3]. The diffeomorphism $g(z,w)=(w^{-1}z,w)$ preserves orientation and sends $[\mu_U]+[\lambda_U]$ to $[\mu_U]$. Let $f_0$ be the original $S^3$ gluing, which sends the meridian of the removed unknot neighbourhood to $[\mu_U]$, and choose the $+1$-filling map $f_1=g^{-1}\circ f_0$. It sends the attached meridian to $[\mu_U]+[\lambda_U]$, the required slope by [F1]. The map equal to $g$ on the exterior and the identity on the attached solid torus is well-defined because $g\circ f_1=f_0$; it is a smooth orientation-preserving diffeomorphism to the original $S^3$. Thus $D_1$ also presents $S^3$.

The diagrams are not ambient isotopic: $D_0$ has zero components and $D_1$ has one, while [F5] implies ambient isotopy preserves component count. Yet they have the same oriented surgery result by steps 1.1–1.2. Moreover [F4] identifies their difference as a permitted stabilization. Hence the false claim fails.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. It supplies countable choice for the chosen tubular data: for any sequence of nonempty sets, apply full choice to its range and compose with the index map. Let $L=\bigcup_{i\in I}K_i$ be a finite oriented link in the standard oriented $3$-sphere, where $I$ is a finite index set. For each component $K_i$, include a chosen closed tubular neighbourhood $N(K_i)$, its exterior $E_{K_i}=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K_i)$, the positive meridian $\mu_i$, and the preferred longitude $\lambda_i$; the longitude is the degree-one parallel class in $H_1(\partial E_{K_i};\mathbb Z)$ that maps to zero in $H_1(E_{K_i};\mathbb Z)$. For each $i\in I$, choose an integer $n_i$. The resulting **integral framed-link surgery diagram** is this link and integer family, with the surgery result defined by removing the interiors of all $N(K_i)$ and gluing an oriented solid torus to each boundary torus so that its meridian maps to $n_i[\mu_i]+[\lambda_i]$. If $I=\varnothing$, the surgery result is $S^3$. A diagram is considered up to orientation-preserving ambient isotopy carrying each component framing; a planar projection is only a way of drawing the link.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For an integral framed link diagram, **Kirby move equivalence** is the equivalence relation generated by the following operations.

1. Apply an orientation-preserving ambient isotopy to the framed link in $S^3$.

2. **Handle slide:** choose distinct components $K_i,K_j$, a parallel $K_j^+$ determined by the framing of $K_j$, and an embedded band whose ends attach to $K_i$ and $K_j^+$ and whose interior misses every link component. Replace $K_i$ by the band sum of $K_i$ with $K_j^+$ and keep the framing obtained by carrying the normal framing across the band. Orient the new component by the band-sum orientation.

3. **Stabilization or destabilization:** add or remove an unknot with framing $+1$ or $-1$ that lies in a $3$-ball disjoint from all the other components.

The integer framing of a component is measured from its preferred longitude as in the integral surgery definition. A planar link projection is not part of the move data; any drawing below is schematic.

derivations.claim: **Framing bookkeeping from bands.** For oriented components $A,B$ with integers $a,b$ and linking number $l$, a slide of $A$ over $sB$, $s=\pm1$, has framing $a+b+2sl$. Indeed choose small framed parallels and the parallel band. The linking of the new curve with its parallel is the sum of the old self-linkings $a,b$ and the two cross-linkings $sl,sl$; the two bands have disjoint interiors and contribute no further crossing. Its linking with a third component $C$ is $\operatorname{lk}(A,C)+s\operatorname{lk}(B,C)$. These are consequences of the actual parallel-and-band construction, not permissions to replace a geometric link by a matrix. We use bands with no added full twist; an existing twist of any component is carried with its strip.

**The zero-meridian crossing operation.** A slide over $U$ can switch a crossing of a selected strand with the strand of $K$ encircled by $U$. Here is the local construction. Take the disk of $U$ transverse to the latter strand, and take a thin band from the selected strand to a disk-parallel copy of $U$. Put the interior of the band off the disk and all the link. In a cross-section perpendicular to the encircled strand, the band sum replaces a short detour on one side of the origin by that detour followed by one signed circuit about the origin. Round its two band corners. The result is the detour on the other side: the region between the circuit with its return segment and this detour is a disk in the punctured cross-section, so pushing across its product with the short strand interval is an ambient isotopy relative to the ends. Thus precisely the chosen crossing changes. Use the opposite band side for the opposite crossing. The disk-parallel framing of $U$ has no twist, so the strip is the transported framing of this operation, including any change of self-linking prescribed by step 1.1. The operation is valid when the selected strand is another part of $K$: use distinct disjoint short arcs as the two band ends. The encircled arc is unchanged, so $U$ remains its small zero-framed meridian. To use a different arc, move this meridian along a thin tubular neighbourhood of $K$; a meridional disk slides along the product tube, so this is an isotopy of $U$ in the complement of $K\cup L$, with its disk framing. The bands and their corners have smooth rounded product neighbourhoods; the disk pushes extend by a cutoff in those neighbourhoods to smooth orientation-preserving ambient isotopies.

**Signed-unit blowdown as allowed moves.** Suppose an unknotted component $J$ has framing $\varepsilon=\pm1$ and a spanning disk $D$ transverse to the other strands. At a piercing of sign $d$, slide that strand over $-\varepsilon d$ times the oriented framed parallel of $J$. Route its band beside $D$. The parallel makes exactly $\varepsilon$ full turns around the disk-normal direction, so this banded detour removes that piercing and gives one signed twist of the remaining disk-piercing strands. This is a geometric disk operation: cut the strands at their small piercing intervals, carry their cut ends along disjoint narrow radial strips of $D$ to its boundary, and use the framed parallel there to join the ends on the same side of $D$. Nested radial strips are used one at a time; corners are rounded in the disk-normal product. After all piercings have been removed, $J$ bounds a disk missing the remaining link, so a small neighbourhood of that disk is a ball separating $J$. Delete it by [F2]. The remaining strands have acquired $-\varepsilon$ full twist about $D$; reversing this construction gives the corresponding blowup. The framing/linking updates are $a_i'=a_i-\varepsilon l_i^2$ and $l_{ij}'=l_{ij}-\varepsilon l_il_j$, where $l_i=\operatorname{lk}(A_i,J)$: apply step 1.1 successively to the signed slides, or count the crossings of the parallel strips in the displayed full twist. In the applications below each remaining component crosses $D$ only once. A full twist of one such strand is a curl of an unknotted arc; of two such strands it is their two-strand full twist. Thus this operation has an explicit geometric meaning, as well as the displayed integer update.

**Splitting the pair from the old link.** Choose a regular finite projection of the compact smooth link, keeping a small meridional arc marked. Such a projection can be obtained by replacing finitely many short arcs inside disjoint tubular charts by polygonal arcs and rounding, followed by a small generic change of direction; the replacements are isotopies in their product tubes, and finitely many nonadjacent projected line segments have only finitely many transverse intersections after that change. At every mixed crossing of $K$ with $L$, use step 2.1 on the strand of $L$ to put $K$ above that strand. Its framing does not change: that component has linking zero with the small meridian $U$, and $U$ has framing zero, so step 1.1 gives the same integer. The local replacement changes no crossing between two strands of $L$. Consequently the old framed link, considered by itself, is still its original framed isotopy class. Once $K$ is above $L$ at every mixed crossing, lift $K$ and its very small meridian in the projection direction above a slab containing $L$, and move them into a ball disjoint from $L$. This lift has no obstruction at a mixed crossing because their height order was chosen precisely this way. From now on all operations are in that ball.

**Unknotting the companion.** Fix a base point away from the meridional arc. Switch self-crossings of $K$ by step 2.1 until its based diagram is descending: on traversing from the base point, the first encounter with each crossing is the overpass. A descending diagram is an unknot by the following explicit disk construction. Cut at the base point, and straighten the arc in traversal order, lifting each initial segment above all later segments; each lift is possible because the initial segment is the overpass at every first encounter. Join the endpoints by the short base-point arc outside the projection. This gives a simple planar circle after a final height isotopy, hence an embedded spanning disk. There are finitely many crossings, so these are finitely many moves and disk pushes. Keep $U$ tiny at an unchanged arc during each crossing operation and carry it by the subsequent isotopies. The result is the standard Hopf pair $K_n,U_0$ in the disjoint ball, for some integer $n$. Changes of $n$ have been carried by the strips; we do not assert that crossing changes preserve $n$.

**Reducing the Hopf framing.** Orient the Hopf components to have linking $+1$. Sliding $K$ over either signed disk-parallel of $U$ changes $n$ by $+2$ or $-2$ by step 1.1. Choose the band in the standard Hopf solid torus $S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(U)=D^2\times S^1$, where $K$ is a core. A disk-framed parallel of $U$ is a meridian of this exterior solid torus. The band running radially from the core to that meridian makes the new curve, after pushing slightly inside, $(r w^{\pm1},w)$, $w\in S^1$, for small fixed $r>0$: the added meridian is the single turn of its disk coordinate. The curves $((1-t)r w^{\pm1},w)$, $0\le t\le1$, are embedded for every $t$, since the second coordinate is $w$. They give an isotopy to the core, supported away from the exterior boundary and hence away from $U$. Extend its velocity in a small tube by a cutoff to obtain an ambient isotopy; the full normal strip is transported. Thus the pair is again a Hopf pair, rather than merely having the same linking matrix. Repeating gives $K_0,U_0$ if $n$ is even and $K_1,U_0$ if $n$ is odd. Negative $n$ is covered by choosing the increasing sign.

**The odd Hopf pair.** In $K_1,U_0$, the disk of $K$ has just one piercing, by $U$. Apply step 2.2 with $J=K$ and $\varepsilon=1$. The remaining component is the unknot $U$ with framing $-1$: the single strand receives one curl, which is removed by an ambient isotopy while retaining its changed normal framing. It is split from $L$, so delete it. This removes the odd pair by allowed moves alone.

**The even Hopf pair.** In $K_0,U_0$, introduce a split $+1$ unknot $V$ in the same otherwise empty ball. Slide $U$ over $V$ along the untwisted band between their spanning disks, orienting the band so the new linking of $U$ and $V$ is $+1$. The band sum of these two unknots is still an unknot: its spanning disk is the band sum of their disjoint disks. Its framing is $1$. The three components are now the standard chain $K_0,U_1,V_1$, with adjacent linkings $+1$ and with $K,V$ unlinked. The disk of the middle component meets each end component once in separate straight product arcs. Blow down $U_1$ by step 2.2. Its two-strand twist makes the ends a standard Hopf pair of linking $-1$, with framings $K_{-1},V_0$. Each end remains unknotted, since its own arc has only received a curl; their mixed two crossings are the Hopf clasp. Blow down $K_{-1}$. The remaining $V$ is the unknot with framing $0-(-1)(-1)^2=1$, again with only a single-arc curl. Delete this split $+1$ unknot. Thus the even pair also disappears. The disk, band and full-twist descriptions identify every intermediate knot and not just its algebraic linking data.

Steps 3.1 and 4.1 reduce the original configuration to the original framed $L$ and an isolated Hopf pair. Steps 5.1 and 6.1 and 6.2 remove that pair. All bands, disk pushes and lists are finite, and every deletion was a split signed-unit unknot deletion or its explicitly proved slide expansion. Orientations of components and their normal strips are transported at each move. Reversing the finite list proves the insertion assertion.

A real isonormal Gaussian process on $H$ is a family $Z(g)$ of real random variables with finite second moments, indexed by $g\in H$, such that $g\mapsto[Z(g)]$ is linear into $L^2(\mathbb P)$, $\mathbb E Z(g)=0$, and $\mathbb E[Z(g)Z(h)]=\langle g,h\rangle_H$.
