For any finite list of vectors, expressing them in an orthonormal basis of their finite-dimensional span shows that their process values have the corresponding linear-image Gaussian law. Here $L^2(\mathbb P)$ identifies square-integrable random variables that agree almost surely. containing every $e_i$. The family is **complete**, or is a **complete
orthonormal system**, when its closed linear span is all of $H$. A
**Hilbert basis**, or **orthonormal basis**, of $H$ is a complete orthonormal
family in $H$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $t>0$. Then
$$\mu(\{f\ge t\})\le\frac1t\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ be measurable sets in a measure space. If the nonnegative extended sum satisfies

$$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k)<+\infty,$$

then

$$\mu\left(\limsup_{k\to\infty}E_k\right)=0.$$

No independence hypothesis and no finiteness hypothesis on the whole space are required.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ be a measurable space and let
$f_n : X \to \overline{\mathbb{R}}$ be measurable for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.
Then the functions

$$\sup_n f_n,\qquad \inf_n f_n,\qquad \limsup_n f_n,\qquad \liminf_n f_n$$

are measurable. The set

$$\{\, x : \lim_n f_n(x) \text{ exists in } \overline{\mathbb{R}} \,\}$$

is measurable. In particular, if $f_n \to f$ pointwise, then $f$ is measurable.

Centering and the covariance identity in [F1] give $\mathbb E Z(r_N)=0$ and $\mathbb E[Z(r_N)^2]=\|r_N\|_H^2$; expanding the square therefore shows that the squared mean-square error is $|\langle Kx,r_N\rangle_H|^2+\epsilon^2\|r_N\|_H^2$. Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$.

1. **Compact main case.** Let $M$ be a compact smooth manifold, possibly with boundary, let $N$ be a smooth manifold without boundary, let $F:M\times I\to N$ be a smooth isotopy of embeddings that is constant near the ends of $I$, and let $W$ be an open neighbourhood of $F(M\times I)$ in $N$. Then there is an ambient isotopy $H:N\times I\to N$ with $H_0=\mathrm{id}_N$, every $H_t$ a diffeomorphism, $H_t\circ F_0=F_t$ for all $t\in I$, $H_t=\mathrm{id}_N$ outside $W$ for every $t$, and $H_t$ stationary near the ends; if $F$ is constant near the ends with parameter $\varepsilon$, then $H_t=\mathrm{id}_N$ for $t\le\varepsilon/2$ and $H_t=H_1$ for $t\ge1-\varepsilon/2$.
2. **Relative form.** Let $N$ be boundaryless, $U\subseteq N$ open, $A\subseteq U$ compact, and let $F:U\times I\to N$ be a smooth isotopy of embeddings whose track image is open in $N\times I$. Then there is a compactly supported ambient isotopy $H$ of $N$ with $H_t\circ F_0=F_t$ on a neighbourhood of $A$ for every $t$.
3. **Boundary stratum.** If $N$ has boundary and $F(M\times I)\subseteq\partial N$, then the ambient isotopy of clause 1 can be chosen with every $H_t$ carrying $\partial N$ onto itself; if $F(M\times I)\subseteq N\setminus\partial N$, it can be chosen compactly supported in $N\setminus\partial N$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere $S^3$. A **Seifert surface** for $K$ is a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface $F\subset S^3$ with boundary set equal to $K$. Orient each boundary component so that an outward-pointing conormal in $F$, followed by a positive boundary tangent, is a positive basis of $TF$; the oriented boundary of $F$ must agree with the given orientation of $K$. For such a surface, its genus $g(F)$ is the unique nonnegative integer satisfying $\chi(F)=2-2g(F)-b$, where $b$ is the number of boundary components; here $b=1$, so $\chi(F)=1-2g(F)$. At longitudinal angle $u\in\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ in the first coordinate, the knot meets this disk at the $p$ points with second-coordinate angles $2\pi q(u+k)/p$, $k=0,\ldots,p-1$. Place these points at the vertices of a regular $p$-gon. A counterclockwise rotation by $2\pi/p$, tapered to fix the disk boundary, carries each point to the next and crosses consecutive points once in the order $\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_{p-1}$; each $\sigma_i$ is the positive half twist of adjacent points. Thus one such increment is the braid block $\delta=\sigma_1\cdots\sigma_{p-1}$, and the rotation through $2\pi q/p$ gives $\delta^q$. The lifted curve has winding vector $(p,q)$ in the fixed Heegaard-torus coordinates, exactly the parameterization in [F1]. The braid block permutes the points by a $p$-cycle, so its $q$th power has one cycle because $\gcd(p,q)=1$.

At each positive crossing replace the crossing by the orientation-compatible smoothing and then attach one half-twisted rectangle in the original crossing ball; this is the oriented braid Seifert-surface construction. It gives $p$ disks joined by $q(p-1)$ positively half-twisted bands, one for each crossing. The first block has one band between each adjacent pair of disks, so its incidence graph is a path; attaching bands along a tree joins the disks to a disk. Each of the remaining $q-1$ blocks has $p-1$ bands.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

the group $\pi_1(X,x_0)$, together with the two inclusion-induced homomorphisms, is a pushout ([[def-pushout-of-group-homomorphisms]]). derivations.claim: The primitive slope $p\alpha+q\beta$ is essential on the Heegaard torus. Removing a small annular neighborhood of $K$ from that torus leaves a closed annulus $A$. On either side, removing the corresponding half of the tube from a solid torus only removes a boundary collar, so the two pieces retract to solid tori $W_x,W_y$ and their overlap retracts to $A$. Thicken the pieces by half-collars to obtain path-connected open sets covering $E_K$ whose intersection retracts to $A$. The core of $A$ winds $p$ times around the core generator $x$ on one side and $q$ times around $y$ on the other. Full AC [A1] supplies the countable-choice hypothesis of [F2] by [L1].

The action $\rho_t$ is isometric for the round metric. Its generic orbits have slope $(p,q)$ and trivial stabilizer because $\gcd(p,q)=1$; hence the metric tube chosen in the Statement is invariant. The coordinate circles $z_1=0$ and $z_2=0$ have stabilizer orders $|q|$ and $|p|$ respectively. The orbit space is a sphere: on each torus $|z_1|=r$ with $0<r<1$, quotienting by the primitive circle orbit leaves a circle, and the two end circles collapse to the two coordinate-orbit points. Removing the invariant tube removes a disk from the orbit sphere, so the exterior is fibered over a disk with the stated multiplicities. Multiplicity one is the regular local model; multiplicity greater than one is exceptional.

The three fundamental groups in this cover are $\pi_1(W_x)=\langle x\rangle\cong\mathbb Z$, $\pi_1(W_y)=\langle y\rangle\cong\mathbb Z$, and $\pi_1(A)=\langle a\rangle\cong\mathbb Z$, with inclusion maps $a\mapsto x^p$ and $a\mapsto y^q$. By [F4], $\pi_1(E_K)$ is their pushout. A group receiving maps from the two cyclic factors is determined by images of $x,y$; the maps agree on the intersection exactly when $x^p=y^q$. Hence the pushout has presentation $\langle x,y\mid x^p=y^q\rangle$.

A regular orbit parallel to $K$ represents the annulus core $x^p=y^q=h$. This element commutes with $x$ because it is $x^p$, and commutes with $y$ because it is $y^q$; as $x,y$ generate the group from step 2.1, $h$ is central.

Choose integers $c,d$ with $pd-qc=1$ and let $L=c\alpha+d\beta$ be the corresponding simple curve on the Heegaard torus; its algebraic intersection with $K$ is one. At the intersection, the boundary $m$ of a small normal disk splits into arcs $\gamma_x,\gamma_y$ on the two solid-torus sides, while $L$ splits into its crossing arc and complementary arc $L_1$. Inserting $L_1L_1^{-1}$ into $m=\gamma_x\gamma_y$ gives $m=(\gamma_xL_1)(L_1^{-1}\gamma_y)$. The first factor winds $c$ times around the $x$ core and the second winds $-d$ times around the $y$ core, hence $m=x^c y^{-d}$. Its abelianization under $x\mapsto q$, $y\mapsto p$ is $cq-dp=-1$, so it is opposite the positive normal-disk meridian, whose class is the positive generator by [F3]. Thus $\mu=m^{-1}=y^d x^{-c}$. Setting $\alpha=d$ and $\beta=-c$ gives $p\alpha+q\beta=1$ and the stated word; another Bezout solution changes the exponents by $(qk,-pk)$, so the word is unchanged because $y^{qk}=h^k=x^{pk}$ and $h$ is central.

Abelianizing the presentation in step 2.1 gives the relation $p[x]=q[y]$. The map $x\mapsto q$, $y\mapsto p$ is surjective because $\gcd(p,q)=1$, and its kernel in $\mathbb Z^2$ is generated by $(p,-q)$, exactly the relation vector; hence it identifies this quotient with $\mathbb Z$. Step 3.2 sends the positive meridian to $1$, so by [F3] it is the positive generator of $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$. Thus $[h]=p[x]=pq[\mu]$. The regular orbit $h$ is a degree-one parallel of $K$ on $\partial E_K$, and $\mu$ has degree zero there, so $\lambda=h\mu^{-pq}$ has degree one and zero image in $H_1(E_K)$. Uniqueness in [F3] identifies it with the preferred longitude; [F3] also proves that $[\mu],[\lambda]$ form a basis of $H_1(\partial E_K;\mathbb Z)$, so each is primitive.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the full Axiom of Choice. Let $p,q$ be coprime nonzero integers, let $K=T(p,q)$ be the oriented primitive slope curve in the standard Heegaard torus, and let $\rho_t(z_1,z_2)=(e^{2\pi i p t}z_1,e^{2\pi i q t}z_2)$ be the weighted circle action on the unit $S^3\subset\mathbb C^2$. Choose $N(K)$ to be a sufficiently small closed metric tube around the orbit $K$ for the round metric; this tube is invariant because $\rho_t$ is isometric and preserves $K$. Set $E_K=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$. Let $x$ and $y$ be based generators of the fundamental groups of the two solid-torus pieces obtained by cutting $E_K$ along the annulus left on the Heegaard torus, oriented so that the annulus core maps to $x^p$ and $y^q$. Then

$$\pi_1(E_K)=\langle x,y\mid x^p=y^q\rangle.$$

The common element $h=x^p=y^q$ is central and represents a regular fiber of a Seifert fibration of $E_K$ over a disk. The fibration has two distinguished core fibers of multiplicities $|p|$ and $|q|$; a fiber of multiplicity one is regular, and a fiber of multiplicity greater than one is exceptional. Thus there are exactly two exceptional fibers when $|p|,|q|>1$, and one is regular when one absolute parameter is $1$.

For any integers $\alpha,\beta$ with $p\alpha+q\beta=1$, compatible based paths identify the positive normal-disk meridian and preferred longitude in the peripheral system as

$$\mu=y^\alpha x^\beta,\qquad \lambda=h\mu^{-pq}.$$

Here the positive meridian is the oriented boundary of a normal disk, and the preferred longitude has degree one around $K$ and maps to zero in $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$. Their homology classes form a basis of $H_1(\partial E_K;\mathbb Z)$, so both classes are primitive.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K:S^1	o S^3$ be a smooth oriented embedding and write its quotient normal bundle as $
u_K=K^*TS^3/dK(TS^1)$. Choose an orientation-preserving trivialization $
u_K\cong S^1	imes\mathbb R^2$ and a tubular map $\Phi:\Omega	o S^3$, meaning a smooth embedding from an open neighbourhood $\Omega\subseteq
u_K$ of the zero section onto an open neighbourhood of $K(S^1)$ with $\Phi(s,0)=K(s)$, such that in these product coordinates $\Omega$ contains $S^1	imes D^2_{2\epsilon}$ for some $\epsilon>0$. Here $D^2_r=\{z\in\mathbb R^2:\|z\|\le r\}$. Set $N(K)=\Phi(S^1	imes D^2_\epsilon)$, $E_K=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$, $T_K=\partial E_K$, and let $i:T_K\hookrightarrow E_K$ be inclusion, $p:T_K	o S^1$ the product projection, and $\mu$ the positive boundary of a normal disk, using the normal-plane orientation determined by the orientations of $K$ and $S^3$. A class is primitive if it is not $m$ times another class for any integer $|m|>1$. Then $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$ is generated by $[\mu]$. The kernel of $i_*:H_1(T_K;\mathbb Z)	o H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$ is a primitive rank-one direct summand generated by a unique class $[\lambda]$ with $p_*[\lambda]=1\in H_1(S^1;\mathbb Z)$. It has a simple closed representative, is the preferred longitude, and $([\mu],[\lambda])$ is a basis of $H_1(T_K;\mathbb Z)$.

Assume countable choice. For every smooth oriented knot $K$ in $S^3$, there are an oriented normal-bundle trivialization, a tubular map $\Phi$ defined on an open neighbourhood containing $S^1\times D^2_{2\epsilon}$ for some $\epsilon>0$, and a closed tubular neighbourhood $N(K)=\Phi(S^1\times D^2_\epsilon)$. This $N(K)$ is diffeomorphic to $S^1\times D^2$, its boundary $T_K$ is diffeomorphic to $S^1\times S^1$, and its exterior $E_K=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$ is a compact smooth oriented three-manifold with boundary $T_K$. The open complement $S^3\setminus K$ strongly deformation retracts onto $E_K$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $L=K_1\cup\cdots\cup K_r\subset S^3$ be an
oriented link with $r\ge1$ components and complement $X_L$,
([[def-oriented-link-in-s-three-and-ambient-isotopy]]), and let
$$\varphi:H_1(X_L;\mathbb Z)\longrightarrow\mathbb Z$$
be the **total linking homomorphism**, defined as the composite
$$H_1(X_L;\mathbb Z)\xrightarrow[\ \sim\ ]{\mathrm{Alex}}\widetilde H^1(L;\mathbb Z)\cong\bigoplus_{i=1}^rH^1(K_i;\mathbb Z)\xrightarrow{\text{sum}}\mathbb Z,$$
where the first arrow is Alexander duality
([[thm-alexander-duality-for-compact-locally-contractible-subsets-of-a-sphere]]),
each $H^1(K_i;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$ is the orientation-induced
identification, and the last map sums the $r$ coordinates. By
[[prop-the-first-hurewicz-map-in-degree-one-is-abelianization]] the map $\varphi$
may again be written $\pi_1(X_L)\to H_1(X_L)\xrightarrow{\varphi}\mathbb Z$; we
denote both composites by $\varphi$ and set $K:=\ker\varphi$.

The **one-variable Alexander module** of $L$ is
$$A_L:=H_1(\widetilde{X_L};\mathbb Z),$$
the first singular homology of the connected infinite cyclic cover
$p:\widetilde{X_L}\to X_L$ classified by $K$
([[thm-classification-of-connected-covering-spaces]],
[[lem-subgroup-quotient-of-universal-cover]],
[[def-covering-map-and-evenly-covered-neighbourhoods]]), equipped with its
structure of module over $\Lambda=\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$
([[def-the-laurent-polynomial-ring]]) in which $t$ acts by the deck
transformation corresponding to the positive generator of
$\operatorname{Deck}(\widetilde{X_L}/X_L)\cong\mathbb Z$.

**Caveats.** The cover is the one classified by $K=\ker\varphi$; since $K$ is
normal the cover is regular and its deck group is
$\pi_1(X_L)/K\cong\mathbb Z$
([[def-regular-covering]], [[thm-regular-covering-characterizations]], [[cor-deck-group-of-a-regular-covering]],
[[def-deck-transformation-and-deck-group]]). The module $A_L$ is ordinary
integral homology of the cover, with the deck action as its module structure;
no twisting by a representation of the link group is used. The total linking
homomorphism satisfies $\varphi(\mu_i)=1$ for a meridian $\mu_i$ of any one
component, so $r\ge1$ is needed for $\varphi$ to be interesting and $A_L$
depends on the orientations of all components through this map.

For every CW complex $X$, abelian group $G$, and $n\geq0$, the cellular complex has an
isomorphism $H_n^{\mathrm{cell}}(X;G)\cong H_n(X;G)$, natural with respect to
cellular maps.

For every path-connected topological space $X$ and $x_0\in X$, the Hurewicz map
$$h:\pi_1(X,x_0)\longrightarrow H_1(X;\mathbb Z)$$
is surjective and has kernel $[\pi_1(X,x_0),\pi_1(X,x_0)]$. Hence it induces a natural isomorphism
$$\pi_1(X,x_0)^{\mathrm{ab}}\cong H_1(X;\mathbb Z).$$
The proof is choice-free and requires no CW, separation, local path-connectivity or local simple-connectivity assumption.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring ([[def-commutative-ring]]) and let $M$ be a
finitely presented $R$-module ([[def-finitely-presented-module-and-algebra]]),
so that there are $m,n\in\mathbb N$ and a presentation

$$R^m\xrightarrow{\ A\ }R^n\xrightarrow{\ \beta\ }M\longrightarrow0 .$$

Fix the standard bases $e_1,\dots,e_m$ of $R^m$ and $f_1,\dots,f_n$ of $R^n$
([[def-finitely-presented-module-and-algebra]]) and let $A=(a_{ij})$ be the
$n\times m$ matrix of the $R$-linear map $\alpha$ with respect to them: the
$j$-th column of $A$ is the coordinate vector of $\alpha(e_j)$, so
$\alpha(e_j)=\sum_{i=1}^n a_{ij}f_i$. Such a matrix is called a **presentation
matrix** of $M$ (for the chosen presentation). A **minor** of $A$ of size
$r\times r$ is the determinant $\det(a_{i_sj_t})_{s,t=1}^r$
([[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]]) of the square submatrix obtained by
choosing rows $i_1<\dots<i_r$ and columns $j_1<\dots<j_r$; determinants of
$1\times1$ and $0\times0$ submatrices are allowed, with the empty determinant
equal to $1$.

For $k\ge0$ the **$k$-th elementary ideal** $E_k(M)$ of the presented module $M$
is the ideal of $R$ generated by the determinants of **all**
$(n-k)\times(n-k)$ minors of $A$ ([[def-generated-and-principal-ideals]],
[[def-left-right-and-two-sided-ideal]]): if $n-k>n$ or $n-k>m$ there is no such
minor, and the ideal generated by the empty set is $0$. In particular no minor
is nonzero-by-convention: the conventions are
$$E_k(M)=R\quad\text{for }k\ge n,\qquad E_k(M)=0\quad\text{for }k<n-m .$$
For $0\le k\le\min(n,m)$ the ideal $E_k(M)$ is the ideal generated by the
$(n-k)\times(n-k)$ minors; e.g. $E_1(M)$ is generated by the
$(n-1)\times(n-1)$ minors of $A$, and $E_n(M)=R$ because the $0\times0$ minor
is $1$. This is the $k$-th **Fitting ideal** $\operatorname{Fit}_k(M)$ of the
Stacks Project (Tag 07Z6, Lemma 15.8.2 and Definition 15.8.3), which is
indexed by the size $n-k$ of the complementary minors; the two conventions
$0=E_{-1}\subset E_0\subset\cdots$ agree on the range $0\le k\le\min(n,m)$.

**Caveats.** (i) The notation $E_k(M)$ suppresses the chosen presentation; the
ideal defined here is a priori attached to the presentation and it is the
content of [[lem-elementary-ideals-are-independent-of-the-presentation]] that
it is in fact an invariant of $M$. (ii) The conventions in the degenerate
ranges are conventions, not theorems; they are the ones compatible with the
Stacks numbering and with independence of the presentation.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, so that the Alexander module $A_L$ of an oriented
nonempty link $L$ is defined and finitely presented over
$\Lambda=\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$
([[def-one-variable-alexander-module-of-an-oriented-link]],
[[lem-the-alexander-module-of-a-link-complement-is-finitely-presented]]). Let
$r$ be the number of components of $L$. Define the **one-variable Alexander
polynomial** $\Delta_L(t)\in\Lambda$ to be a greatest common divisor of the zeroth
elementary ideal $E_0(A_L)$
([[def-elementary-ideals-of-a-finitely-presented-module]]), i.e. a generator of
the smallest principal ideal of $\Lambda$ containing $E_0(A_L)$
([[lem-the-laurent-polynomial-ring-is-noetherian-and-a-unique-factorisation-domain]],
[[def-unique-factorisation-domain]]); it is well defined up to multiplication
by a unit $\pm t^k$ of $\Lambda$
([[lem-units-and-powers-of-the-laurent-polynomial-ring]]). The **Alexander
invariant** is the normalisation
$$D_L(t):=\begin{cases}\Delta_L(t),&r>1,\\[2pt] \dfrac{\Delta_L(t)}{1-t},&r=1,\end{cases}$$
understood for a knot as an element of the fraction field of $\Lambda$ when
$(1-t)\nmid\Delta_L(t)$; for the integer-valued link formulas of this page the
distinction matters and is stated with each use.

**Caveats.** The ideal $E_0(A_L)$ is a well-defined invariant of $L$ because
$A_L$ is finitely presented and elementary ideals are independent of the
presentation
([[lem-elementary-ideals-are-independent-of-the-presentation]]); a greatest
common divisor in a unique factorisation domain is well defined up to units, and
the units of $\Lambda$ are $\pm t^k$. For every link the absolute one-variable Alexander module admits a square
presentation, so $E_0(A_L)$ is principal, generated by its determinant (the
standard link fact recorded in [F3]). For a knot ($r=1$), every gcd
representative satisfies $\Delta_L(1)=\pm1$. These standard presentation and
normalisation facts are recorded here; the gcd definition itself uses only
finite presentability and unique factorisation.

The Laurent polynomial ring $\Lambda=\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$ of
[[def-the-laurent-polynomial-ring]] is Noetherian, hence every ideal of
$\Lambda$ is finitely generated, and $\Lambda$ is a unique factorisation
domain; its units are $\pm t^k$, $k\in\mathbb Z$, and $t$ is prime in $\mathbb Z[t]$ but becomes a unit in $\Lambda$.

derivations.claim: Abelianizing the presentation in [F1] gives the relation $p[x]=q[y]$. The map $\phi(x)=q$, $\phi(y)=p$ is onto because $\gcd(p,q)=1$; its kernel in $\mathbb Z^2$ is generated by $(p,-q)$, exactly the abelianized relation vector, so the abelianization is $\mathbb Z$. The meridian in [F1] maps to $p\alpha+q\beta=1$, so the epimorphism $\phi$ in the Statement is precisely the positive total-linking homomorphism that classifies the cover in [F4].

For every integer $n$, $(z^n-1)/(z-1)$ is a finite Laurent sum; for $n<0$ it equals $-(z^{-1}+\cdots+z^n)$. In the lifted attaching word, a positive edge contributes the current deck translate and a negative edge contributes the negative of the preceding translate. The $x^p$ block therefore contributes $(x^p-1)/(x-1)$ to the $x$-edge coordinate. The following $y^{-q}$ block starts after the $x^p$ translate and contributes $x^p(y^{-q}-1)/(y-1)$ to the $y$-edge coordinate. These are the complete signed edge contributions of the two-cell in $\widetilde P_\phi$.

The cyclic cover in the Statement has cellular chain groups $C_2=\Lambda$, $C_1=\Lambda^2$, $C_0=\Lambda$. Its first boundary is $d_1=(t^q-1,\ t^p-1)$ because lifted $x$- and $y$-edges end $q$ and $p$ deck steps from their starts. Evaluating the two edge contributions in step 1.2 at $x=t^q$, $y=t^p$ gives the second boundary column; the $y$-coordinate is $t^{pq}(t^{-pq}-1)/(t^p-1)=-(t^{pq}-1)/(t^p-1)$:
$$d_2(1)=\left(\frac{t^{pq}-1}{t^q-1},\ -\frac{t^{pq}-1}{t^p-1}\right)^T.$$
This is the cellular boundary of the lifted two-cell.

In $\Lambda$, $\gcd(t^p-1,t^q-1)\doteq t-1$: for positive exponents the Euclidean algorithm gives this because $\gcd(|p|,|q|)=1$, and negative exponents differ from the positive ones by units. Hence $a=(t^q-1)/(t-1)$ and $b=(t^p-1)/(t-1)$ are coprime. The kernel of $d_1$ is the free rank-one submodule generated by $(b,-a)^T$: if $au+bv=0$, unique factorization implies $a\mid v$, and then $(u,v)$ is a multiple of $(b,-a)$. The column in step 2.1 is $\delta_{p,q}(b,-a)^T$. To show $\delta_{p,q}\in\Lambda$, replace signed exponents by $m=|p|$, $n=|q|$, which changes each factor only by a unit. Set $A=(t^m-1)/(t-1)$ and $B=(t^n-1)/(t-1)$. They are coprime; since $m,n$ divide $mn$, both divide $(t^{mn}-1)/(t-1)$. Unique factorization gives $AB\mid(t^{mn}-1)/(t-1)$, hence $\delta_{m,n}=((t^{mn}-1)/(t-1))/(AB)\in\Lambda$, and the signed quotient is a unit multiple. If $|p|=1$ or $|q|=1$, this quotient is a unit, so the same cyclic presentation gives $A_K=0$.

By [F5], $H_1$ of the cyclic cover of $P_{p,q}$ is $\ker d_1/\operatorname{im}d_2\cong\Lambda/(\delta_{p,q})$. The presentation complex and $E_K$ have the same fundamental group and the same homomorphism $\phi$; the fundamental groups of their cyclic covers are the corresponding kernels, and the deck action on their abelianizations is conjugation by a preimage of $1\in\mathbb Z$. Hurewicz therefore identifies their first-homology $\Lambda$-modules. Full AC [A1] supplies the countable-choice hypothesis of [F3] by [L1]; the deformation retraction then identifies the cyclic-cover homology of $E_K$ with that of $S^3\setminus K$. Thus $A_K\cong\Lambda/(\delta_{p,q})$.

The one-by-one presentation $[\delta_{p,q}]$ of $\Lambda/(\delta_{p,q})$ has $E_0$ generated by its sole $1\times1$ minor, namely $\delta_{p,q}$. Isomorphism invariance of the Alexander module and the definition [F6] give $E_0(A_K)=(\delta_{p,q})$ and hence $\Delta_K\doteq\delta_{p,q}$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Identify the standard oriented three-sphere with $S^3=\{(z_1,z_2)\in\mathbb C^2:|z_1|^2+|z_2|^2=1\}$ and choose $0<r<1$. The standard unknotted Heegaard torus is $T_r=\{|z_1|=r,\ |z_2|=\sqrt{1-r^2}\}$; its two sides are solid tori. In the angular coordinates $(u,v)\in(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)^2$ given by $(u,v)\mapsto(r e^{2\pi i u},\sqrt{1-r^2}e^{2\pi i v})$, let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be the first and second coordinate classes in $H_1(T_r;\mathbb Z)$. For coprime nonzero integers $p,q$, the **oriented torus knot** $T(p,q)$ is the image of $s\mapsto(r e^{2\pi i p s},\sqrt{1-r^2}e^{2\pi i q s})$, for $s\in\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$, oriented by increasing $s$; it represents the primitive slope $p\alpha+q\beta$. The mirror convention is the reflection $(z_1,z_2)\mapsto(z_1,\overline{z_2})$, which sends $T(p,q)$ to $T(p,-q)$ with image orientation, and reversing the knot orientation gives $T(-p,-q)$. For nonzero $p,q$ with $d=\gcd(|p|,|q|)>1$, the corresponding torus link is the union of $d$ disjoint parallel copies of the primitive slope $(p/d,q/d)$; it is not a single embedded curve of class $p\alpha+q\beta$. The exterior is $E_K=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$ for a chosen closed tubular neighborhood. A positive meridian is the oriented boundary of a normal disk, and a preferred longitude is a degree-one class on $\partial E_K$ whose image in $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$ is zero; this definition alone asserts neither existence nor uniqueness.

Assume the full Axiom of Choice. Let $p,q$ be coprime nonzero integers, let $K=T(p,q)$ be the oriented primitive slope curve in the standard Heegaard torus, and let $\rho_t(z_1,z_2)=(e^{2\pi i p t}z_1,e^{2\pi i q t}z_2)$ be the weighted circle action on the unit $S^3\subset\mathbb C^2$. Choose $N(K)$ to be a sufficiently small closed metric tube around the orbit $K$ for the round metric; this tube is invariant because $\rho_t$ is isometric and preserves $K$. Set $E_K=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$. Let $x$ and $y$ be based generators of the fundamental groups of the two solid-torus pieces obtained by cutting $E_K$ along the annulus left on the Heegaard torus, oriented so that the annulus core maps to $x^p$ and $y^q$. $$\pi_1(E_K)=\langle x,y\mid x^p=y^q\rangle.$$

The common element $h=x^p=y^q$ is central and represents a regular fiber of a Seifert fibration of $E_K$ over a disk. The fibration has two distinguished core fibers of multiplicities $|p|$ and $|q|$; a fiber of multiplicity one is regular, and a fiber of multiplicity greater than one is exceptional. Thus there are exactly two exceptional fibers when $|p|,|q|>1$, and one is regular when one absolute parameter is $1$.

For any integers $\alpha,\beta$ with $p\alpha+q\beta=1$, compatible based paths identify the positive normal-disk meridian and preferred longitude in the peripheral system as

$$\mu=y^\alpha x^\beta,\qquad \lambda=h\mu^{-pq}.$$

Let $A_K=H_1(\widetilde{S^3\setminus K};\mathbb Z)$ be the one-variable Alexander module for the infinite cyclic cover classified by total linking, with $t$ acting by the deck transformation of the positive meridian. Put $\Lambda=\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$ and define
$$\delta_{p,q}(t)=\frac{(t^{pq}-1)(t-1)}{(t^p-1)(t^q-1)}.$$
Then $\delta_{p,q}(t)$ is a Laurent polynomial, $A_K\cong\Lambda/(\delta_{p,q})$, and the Alexander polynomial $\Delta_K$, defined as a generator of the zeroth elementary ideal $E_0(A_K)$, satisfies $\Delta_K(t)\doteq\delta_{p,q}(t)$, where $f\doteq g$ means $f=\pm t^k g$ for some integer $k$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. If $p,q$ are coprime nonzero integers and $|p|=1$ or $|q|=1$, then the oriented torus knot $T(p,q)$ is ambient isotopic in $S^3$ to the standard unknot with its standard orientation.

Assume Countable Choice. For coprime nonzero integers $p,q$, the fixed orientation-reversing reflection used for the mirror convention sends the oriented curve $T(p,q)$ to the image-oriented curve $T(p,-q)$, and reversing the orientation of $T(p,q)$ gives $T(-p,-q)$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in $S^3$, and let $r:S^3\to S^3$ be an orientation-reversing reflection. Give $r(K)$ the image orientation, and let $-K$ denote reversal of the knot orientation. Then $g(K)=g(r(K))=g(-K)=g(-r(K))$.

It can be constructed from a disk by plumbing $(p-1)(q-1)$ positive Hopf bands: a positive Hopf band is the oriented annulus spanning the positively linked Hopf link, and plumbing along a square glues square neighborhoods of properly embedded arcs in two surfaces on opposite sides of a 3-ball, with the four boundary edges alternating between the surfaces and with orientations agreeing on the square. Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. For an oriented smooth knot $K\subset S^3$, define

$$\mathcal G(K):=\{n\in\mathbb N_0: \text{there is a Seifert surface }F\text{ for }K\text{ with }g(F)=n\}.$$

The existence theorem makes $\mathcal G(K)$ nonempty, and the well-ordering of $\mathbb N_0$ gives its least element. The **smooth knot genus** is $g(K):=\min\mathcal G(K)$. Its defining rational function is finite at $t=0$, because numerator and denominator both have constant term $1$; a Laurent polynomial finite at $0$ has no negative powers. Thus $\delta_{a,b}\in\mathbb Z[t]$, and $\Delta_K\doteq\delta_{a,b}$.
By [F6], $T(a,b)$ bounds a connected oriented surface of genus $g_0=(a-1)(b-1)/2$, so the minimum in [F7] satisfies $g(K)=g(T(a,b))\le g_0$.

If $a=1$ or $b=1$, the quotient defining $\delta_{a,b}$ cancels to $1$. By [F4], $K$ is ambient isotopic to the standard unknot, which bounds a disk; an ambient isotopy carries spanning surfaces to spanning surfaces of the same genus in both directions. Since genus is nonnegative by [F7], the minimum is $g(K)=0=(a-1)(b-1)/2$.

Since $\delta_{a,b}\in\mathbb Z[t]$, its degree is $ab+1-a-b=(a-1)(b-1)$: the numerator and denominator have leading coefficient $1$, and the quotient is polynomial by step 2.1. Its constant coefficient is $1$, since the numerator and denominator both have constant term $1$. Hence its exponent width is $(a-1)(b-1)=2g_0$, and multiplication by a unit does not change width.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

citations.quote: Let $M$ be a compact smooth $3$-manifold. A properly embedded surface is **two-sided** if it has a product neighbourhood $F\times[-1,1]$ in $M$. A **compressing disk** for a two-sided surface $F$ is an embedded disk $D\subset M$ with $\operatorname{int}(D)\cap F=\varnothing$ and $\partial D$ an essential simple closed curve in $F$; $F$ is **incompressible** if it has no compressing disk. A **boundary-compressing disk** is an embedded disk $D$ with $\partial D=\alpha\cup\beta$, where $\alpha=D\cap F$ is an arc not cutting off a disk in $F$, $\beta=D\cap\partial M$, and $\operatorname{int}(D)$ misses $F\cup\partial M$; $F$ is **boundary-incompressible** if it has no such disk. A surface is **boundary-parallel** if it cobounds a product with a subsurface of $\partial M$, and it is **essential** if it is incompressible, boundary-incompressible, and not boundary-parallel. $M$ is **irreducible** if every embedded $2$-sphere in its interior bounds an embedded $3$-ball in $M$. An incompressible torus is boundary-parallel if it cobounds a product $T^2\times[0,1]$ with a component of $\partial M$; $M$ is **atoroidal** if every incompressible torus is boundary-parallel. A **Seifert fibration** is a decomposition into circles with local models given by fibered solid tori; in the model $(D^2\times S^1)/\langle(z,w)\mapsto(e^{2\pi i/q}z,e^{2\pi ip/q}w)\rangle$, where $\gcd(p,q)=1$, the core fiber has multiplicity $q$. Fibers of multiplicity $1$ are **regular** and those of multiplicity greater than $1$ are **exceptional**. A finite family of pairwise disjoint incompressible tori is a **JSJ system** if every component obtained by cutting $M$ along the family is atoroidal or Seifert-fibered. It is **inclusion-minimal** if no proper subfamily is a JSJ system. Atoroidal does not mean hyperbolic.

An essential smooth embedded circle in the standard torus $T=\mathbb R^2/\mathbb Z^2$ represents a nonzero primitive integral homology class. A finite disjoint family of essential smooth circles can be carried by a jointly smooth ambient isotopy of $T$ to parallel affine circles. Two essential circles with the same primitive unoriented class are smoothly ambient isotopic. The components between disjoint essential circles have smooth annulus parameters, with prescribed product collars on their boundary circles. No choice axiom is assumed.

Likewise two smooth spanning arcs of a parametrized annulus with the same endpoints and relative winding number are smoothly ambient isotopic relative to any collars on which they already agree. When disjoint, they have a smooth disk-strip parameter; disjoint essential circles in a parametrized annulus have smooth annulus-strip parameters. All isotopies may be stationary near their time endpoints.

For $n=2,3$, a given smooth ball embedding $e:D^n\to N$ into a connected boundaryless smooth $n$-manifold is isotopic through embeddings to a small coordinate round ball, and that embedding isotopy extends ambiently with compact support. For a parametrized smooth $n$-ball $B$ and a parametrized smooth boundary $(n-1)$-disk $W$, the pair $(B,W)$ is diffeomorphic to the standard ball with a hemispherical window. The diffeomorphism can retain the specified window parameter, using stereographic parameters on the standard hemisphere and allowing the necessary orientation of that parameter. No choice axiom is assumed.

Consequently, attaching a parametrized smooth $n$-ball to a smooth $n$-manifold along such a window does not change its diffeomorphism type, provided an attaching collar and corner rounding are supplied. The resulting diffeomorphism is supported in the added ball and an arbitrarily small receiving collar. The inverse assertion holds for removing a ball that meets the boundary in exactly one such window with the supplied collar charts. In dimension two the windows are intervals.

Let $M$ be a compact smooth three-manifold, possibly nonorientable and with boundary, and let $f:F\to M$ be a smooth embedding of a compact smooth surface with $f^{-1}(\partial M)=\partial F$. Transversality to $\partial M$ is not assumed. Given an open neighborhood $U$ of $C=f(\partial F)$, there is a jointly smooth map $(x,t)\mapsto f_t(x)$ such that each $f_t$ is an embedding, $f_0=f$, every $f_t$ agrees with $f$ on $\partial F$ and outside $f^{-1}(U)$, and $f_t$ is neatly proper for every $t>0$. Time may instead be reparametrized to be stationary near both endpoints; in that version neatness holds after the initial stationary interval.

There is also a jointly continuous ambient isotopy of homeomorphisms $H_t:M\to M$, starting at the identity, supported in $U$, fixing $\partial M$ pointwise, and satisfying $H_t f=f_t$. The construction makes $H_t$ jointly smooth on $(M\setminus C)\times[0,1]$. If $f$ is already neat, the same $f_t$ alternatively admits a jointly smooth ambient extension fixing $\partial M$. No smooth ambient extension at an original tangency is asserted.

Let $F_0=f(F)$ be a compact two-sided smoothly embedded surface in a compact smooth three-manifold, with $f^{-1}(\partial M)=\partial F$, and let $F_1,H_1$ be its angular neatification from [[lem-compact-smooth-boundary-preimage-surfaces-admit-neat-embedding-isotopies]]. The ambient manifold may be nonorientable. If $F_1$ has a smooth compressing disk or smooth boundary-compressing disk, then $F_0$ has a disk of the same type. Boundary-compressing disks can also be transported in the opposite direction: if $F_0$ has one, then $F_1$ has one. Consequently absence of either kind of smooth disk passes from $F_0$ to $F_1$.

Here the boundary-compressing witness has one boundary arc in the surface and the other in $\partial M$, its interior missing both. The construction allows the broader convention of ordinary smooth disk embeddings with tangential endpoint contact, and also gives smooth corner-disk witnesses with transverse surface arcs when that convention is used. No smooth ambient removal of an original surface tangency is asserted.

derivations.claim: First apply [F9] to the given surface, fixed pointwise on its boundary. The resulting surface is neat. Incompressibility passes to it, and a boundary-compressing witness passes in either direction; absence of boundary compressions therefore passes as well. Work with this neat representative for the following smooth collar constructions. The boundary-fixing topological ambient extension pulls any resulting boundary-parallel product back to the actual original surface. Thus this preparation does not add a neatness hypothesis to the Statement. Write $\partial D=\alpha\cup\beta$, where $\alpha$ is the essential proper arc in $A$ and $\beta$ lies in a boundary torus $T$. In an annulus every essential proper arc joins its two boundary circles: cut along a radial spanning arc and use a lift to the strip; an arc returning to the same boundary cuts off a disk there. Consequently both boundary circles of $A$ lie on this same $T$. They are essential on $T$: otherwise choose an innermost disk bounded by one of them in $T$, push it inward off the annulus collar, and obtain a compression of $A$. By [F2] the two circles cut $T$ into two parametrized annuli. The interior of $\beta$ misses them and joins them, so it spans one of these annuli, denoted $A_0$.

Push the interior of $A_0$ a little into its inward collar, keeping its rim on $A$, and round the rim. The union $S=A\cup A_0$ is a torus with a displayed corner before rounding. The curve $\alpha\cup\beta$ on it meets a core of $A$ once algebraically, not merely modulo two: $\alpha$ is a spanning arc of the annulus. It is therefore a nonseparating essential circle. Compress $S$ along $D$, taking two parallel copies of $D$ in its disk neighborhood; the result is a sphere. Irreducibility supplies a parametrized ball bounded by it. The disk neighborhood lies outside this ball: its strip along $\beta$ is joined to $\partial M$ through the gap left when that strip was removed from $A_0$, without crossing the compressed sphere. A ball in the interior cannot contain that boundary collar. Restoring the disk neighborhood therefore attaches one marked $1$-handle to the ball, rather than removing a possibly knotted handle from it. Its two attaching disk windows have the actual parallel-copy parameters of $D$. They can be put in standard positions by [F3]: standardize one window, shrink the other in the connected complement of the first on the boundary sphere, and move it to the opposite standard disk by the finite supported construction in [F3]'s Proof 1.1–2.1, fixing the first. Thus the restored region $U$ is a smooth solid torus with meridian disk the cocore of this handle. Its boundary is the displayed $S$; all corner changes are restored by the original quadrant collars.

The marking is essential. In the product coordinates $U=D^2\times S^1$ supplied by that ball and handle, let $(\mu,\lambda)$ denote the meridian-longitude basis of its boundary. Each rim circle of $A$ meets the cocore boundary once algebraically, because it meets $\alpha\cup\beta$ once. Hence its slope is $p\mu+q\lambda$ with $q=\pm1$. By [F2] normalize the two rim circles to affine circles of that slope. The entire boundary isotopy extends into a radial annulus of $D^2\times S^1$: in the boundary radial coordinate use the same formula $(r,x)\mapsto(r,h_{\eta(r)t}(x))$ as [F3], identity near the inner solid torus. The product diffeomorphism $(z,e^{i\theta})\mapsto(e^{ip\theta}z,e^{iq\theta})$, with inverse $(z,e^{i\varphi})\mapsto(e^{-ipq\varphi}z,e^{iq\varphi})$, carries longitudinal circles to that slope, up to replacing $p$ by its negative according to the chosen inverse. Apply its inverse. The two complementary boundary annuli now correspond to the two arcs between two points on $\partial D^2$, times $S^1$. The disk with one of these marked arcs is a rectangle with its bottom edge marked, with the usual rounded-corner interpretation, by [F3] in dimension two. Taking its product with $S^1$ gives a product between the corresponding annuli: the first is $A\times\{0\}$, and $A\times\{1\}\cup\partial A\times[0,1]$ is the second annulus $A_0$. Restore the retained quadrant collars to get this product for the actual original $A$ and boundary annulus in $\partial M$. This proves boundary-parallelity in [F1]'s precise sense. The winding-one condition from $D$ is what justifies this product; complementary annuli in an arbitrary solid torus do not suffice. All selected charts, windows and curve moves were finite, and [F2]–[F3] require no choice.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable) has a choice function.

Let $M$ be a compact smooth $3$-manifold. A properly embedded surface is **two-sided** if it has a product neighbourhood $F\times[-1,1]$ in $M$. A **compressing disk** for a two-sided surface $F$ is an embedded disk $D\subset M$ with $\operatorname{int}(D)\cap F=\varnothing$ and $\partial D$ an essential simple closed curve in $F$; $F$ is **incompressible** if it has no compressing disk. A **boundary-compressing disk** is an embedded disk $D$ with $\partial D=\alpha\cup\beta$, where $\alpha=D\cap F$ is an arc not cutting off a disk in $F$, $\beta=D\cap\partial M$, and $\operatorname{int}(D)$ misses $F\cup\partial M$; $F$ is **boundary-incompressible** if it has no such disk. A surface is **boundary-parallel** if it cobounds a product with a subsurface of $\partial M$, and it is **essential** if it is incompressible, boundary-incompressible, and not boundary-parallel. $M$ is **irreducible** if every embedded $2$-sphere in its interior bounds an embedded $3$-ball in $M$. An incompressible torus is boundary-parallel if it cobounds a product $T^2\times[0,1]$ with a component of $\partial M$; $M$ is **atoroidal** if every incompressible torus is boundary-parallel. A **Seifert fibration** is a decomposition into circles with local models given by fibered solid tori; in the model $(D^2\times S^1)/\langle(z,w)\mapsto(e^{2\pi i/q}z,e^{2\pi ip/q}w)\rangle$, where $\gcd(p,q)=1$, the core fiber has multiplicity $q$. Fibers of multiplicity $1$ are **regular** and those of multiplicity greater than $1$ are **exceptional**. A finite family of pairwise disjoint incompressible tori is a **JSJ system** if every component obtained by cutting $M$ along the family is atoroidal or Seifert-fibered. It is **inclusion-minimal** if no proper subfamily is a JSJ system. Atoroidal does not mean hyperbolic.

Assume countable choice. Let $S\subset S^3$ be the image of a smooth embedding of the standard $S^2$. There is a smooth ambient isotopy $H_t:S^3\to S^3$, with $H_0=\operatorname{id}$, such that $H_1(S)$ is the standard equatorial sphere $E$. In particular $S^3\setminus S$ has exactly two components. Their closures $B_+$ and $B_-$ are smoothly embedded standard closed $3$-balls with common boundary $S$. If $D_+$ and $D_-$ denote the standard closed hemispheres bounded by $E$, the labels can be chosen so that the restrictions $H_1:B_\pm\to D_\pm$ are diffeomorphisms with the same boundary restriction $H_1|_S:S\to E$. Thus the ball identifications are compatible on their boundary and on a common two-sided collar of that boundary.

Every orientation-preserving smooth diffeomorphism $g:S^2\to S^2$ is joined to the identity by a jointly smooth isotopy of orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms, stationary near its time endpoints. Consequently every smooth diffeomorphism $b:\partial B_0\to\partial B_1$ between the boundaries of two parametrized smooth $3$-balls extends to a smooth diffeomorphism $B_0\to B_1$. In the radial boundary collars supplied by their parametrizations, the extension can be required to have the product form $(x,r)\mapsto(b(x),r)$ on one smaller collar. Its orientation agrees with the orientation of $b$ on the boundaries, using the outward-normal convention.

This asserts existence of an isotopy for each given map; it does not assert a deformation retraction parametrized by the entire diffeomorphism group.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. The bounded region of a smooth embedded
circle in the oriented plane, together with its boundary, is a smooth manifold
with boundary diffeomorphic to the closed standard disk. Let $D_0,D_1$ be two
such closed regions. Every orientation-preserving smooth boundary
diffeomorphism $b:\partial D_0\to\partial D_1$ extends to an
orientation-preserving diffeomorphism $B:D_0\to D_1$. More precisely, for
specified smooth inward collars $c_i:\partial D_i\times[0,\epsilon)\to D_i$
with $c_i(p,0)=p$, the extension may be required to satisfy
$B(c_0(p,r))=c_1(b(p),r)$ for every sufficiently small $r\ge0$. In addition, given interior points $p_i\in D_i$ and an orientation-preserving smooth diffeomorphism $q$ from a neighborhood of $p_0$ onto a neighborhood of $p_1$, the extension can agree with $q$ near $p_0$ while retaining the prescribed boundary collars.

All isotopies below are jointly smooth diffeotopies, stationary near the time endpoints.

1. On $A=(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)\times[0,1]$, every smooth diffeomorphism fixing both boundary circles pointwise is isotopic relative to the boundary to exactly one twist
$$D_k(\theta,u)=(\theta+k\rho(u),u),\qquad k\in\mathbb Z,$$
where $\rho$ is a fixed smooth function equal to zero near $0$ and one near $1$. If the map initially fixes a boundary collar, a common smaller collar can be fixed throughout this isotopy. Without fixing the boundary, every annulus diffeomorphism is isotopic to one of the four maps $(\theta,u)\mapsto(\varepsilon\theta,u)$ or $(\theta,u)\mapsto(\varepsilon\theta,1-u)$, with $\varepsilon=\pm1$.
2. Every smooth diffeomorphism of $T^2=\mathbb R^2/\mathbb Z^2$ inducing the identity on $H_1(T^2;\mathbb Z)$ is smoothly isotopic to the identity. Consequently every torus diffeomorphism is smoothly isotopic to the linear torus map inducing its integral unimodular matrix on $H_1$.

Assume countable choice. Let $M$ be a compact orientable smooth three-manifold and let $\mathcal A$ be a finite disjoint family of properly embedded two-sided annuli. Suppose each map $\pi_1(A)\to\pi_1(M)$ is injective and every component of the cut-open manifold $M\mathbin{\|}\mathcal A$, with its boundary corners rounded, is irreducible. Then $M$ is irreducible. The family may be empty, and its annuli need not be separating or boundary-incompressible.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $F$ be a compact smooth surface with boundary, let $M$ be a smooth three-manifold without boundary, and let $S\subset M$ be a closed embedded smooth surface. If $i:F\to M$ is a smooth embedding whose boundary restriction $i|_{\partial F}$ is transverse to $S$, then there is a smooth isotopy $i_t:F\to M$ through embeddings, fixed on a neighbourhood of $\partial F$, such that $i_1(F)$ is transverse to $S$.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$.

1. **Compact main case.** Let $M$ be a compact smooth manifold, possibly with boundary, let $N$ be a smooth manifold without boundary, let $F:M\times I\to N$ be a smooth isotopy of embeddings that is constant near the ends of $I$, and let $W$ be an open neighbourhood of $F(M\times I)$ in $N$. Then there is an ambient isotopy $H:N\times I\to N$ with $H_0=\mathrm{id}_N$, every $H_t$ a diffeomorphism, $H_t\circ F_0=F_t$ for all $t\in I$, $H_t=\mathrm{id}_N$ outside $W$ for every $t$, and $H_t$ stationary near the ends; if $F$ is constant near the ends with parameter $\varepsilon$, then $H_t=\mathrm{id}_N$ for $t\le\varepsilon/2$ and $H_t=H_1$ for $t\ge1-\varepsilon/2$.
2. **Relative form.** Let $N$ be boundaryless, $U\subseteq N$ open, $A\subseteq U$ compact, and let $F:U\times I\to N$ be a smooth isotopy of embeddings whose track image is open in $N\times I$. Then there is a compactly supported ambient isotopy $H$ of $N$ with $H_t\circ F_0=F_t$ on a neighbourhood of $A$ for every $t$.
3. **Boundary stratum.** If $N$ has boundary and $F(M\times I)\subseteq\partial N$, then the ambient isotopy of clause 1 can be chosen with every $H_t$ carrying $\partial N$ onto itself; if $F(M\times I)\subseteq N\setminus\partial N$, it can be chosen compactly supported in $N\setminus\partial N$.
4. **General isotopies.** For the same compact source (possibly with boundary) and boundaryless target as in clause 1, every smooth isotopy extends with support in a compact subset of any prescribed neighbourhood $W$ of $F(M\times I)$. The endpoint-constancy hypothesis and the stationary-end conclusion are both omitted; all other conclusions of clause 1 hold.

Let $M$ be a compact connected orientable smooth three-manifold, let $F$ be a compact connected smooth subsurface of $\partial M$, and let $N\lhd\pi_1(F)$ be normal. If a continuous disk map into $M$ has its boundary in $\operatorname{Int}F$ with class outside $N$, there is a smoothly properly embedded disk in $M$ whose boundary lies in $\operatorname{Int}F$ and has class outside $N$. No pointwise preservation of the original boundary loop is asserted.

Consequently a compact neatly properly embedded two-sided smooth surface $S$ in such a compact orientable smooth three-manifold is incompressible if and only if its inclusion induces an injection on fundamental groups, component by component. Here incompressibility means absence of a smooth embedded compressing disk, with the conventions of the indicated definition.

Let $M$ be a compact smooth three-manifold, possibly nonorientable and with boundary, and let $f:F\to M$ be a smooth embedding of a compact smooth surface with $f^{-1}(\partial M)=\partial F$. Transversality to $\partial M$ is not assumed. Given an open neighborhood $U$ of $C=f(\partial F)$, there is a jointly smooth map $(x,t)\mapsto f_t(x)$ such that each $f_t$ is an embedding, $f_0=f$, every $f_t$ agrees with $f$ on $\partial F$ and outside $f^{-1}(U)$, and $f_t$ is neatly proper for every $t>0$. Time may instead be reparametrized to be stationary near both endpoints; in that version neatness holds after the initial stationary interval.

There is also a jointly continuous ambient isotopy of homeomorphisms $H_t:M\to M$, starting at the identity, supported in $U$, fixing $\partial M$ pointwise, and satisfying $H_t f=f_t$. The construction makes $H_t$ jointly smooth on $(M\setminus C)\times[0,1]$. If $f$ is already neat, the same $f_t$ alternatively admits a jointly smooth ambient extension fixing $\partial M$. No smooth ambient extension at an original tangency is asserted.

Let $F_0=f(F)$ be a compact two-sided smoothly embedded surface in a compact smooth three-manifold, with $f^{-1}(\partial M)=\partial F$, and let $F_1,H_1$ be its angular neatification from [[lem-compact-smooth-boundary-preimage-surfaces-admit-neat-embedding-isotopies]]. The ambient manifold may be nonorientable. If $F_1$ has a smooth compressing disk or smooth boundary-compressing disk, then $F_0$ has a disk of the same type. Boundary-compressing disks can also be transported in the opposite direction: if $F_0$ has one, then $F_1$ has one. Consequently absence of either kind of smooth disk passes from $F_0$ to $F_1$.

Here the boundary-compressing witness has one boundary arc in the surface and the other in $\partial M$, its interior missing both. The construction allows the broader convention of ordinary smooth disk embeddings with tangential endpoint contact, and also gives smooth corner-disk witnesses with transverse surface arcs when that convention is used. No smooth ambient removal of an original surface tangency is asserted.

Assume full AC. Every compact topological three-manifold $M$, with boundary allowed, is homeomorphic to the realization of a finite combinatorial three-manifold triangulation, with boundary allowed (the empty complex when $M=\varnothing$). Its boundary is the realization of a subcomplex. Thus $M$ admits a finite compatible PL structure, without any previously supplied smooth or PL structure on its interior.

If a TOP product collar of the boundary, together with a finite PL structure on its boundary surface, has already been supplied, the new PL structure may be chosen equal to that product PL structure on a smaller boundary neighborhood. No smooth marking or smooth ambient isotopy is asserted. Full AC remains the hypothesis of this theorem; no choice-free theorem is obtained by omitting that premise.

Let $M$ be a compact connected orientable piecewise linear three-manifold with a given finite compatible manifold triangulation and with boundary a subcomplex. Let $F\subset\partial M$ be a connected compact piecewise linear subsurface and $N\trianglelefteq\pi_1(F)$ a normal subgroup. Suppose there is a continuous map $f:(D^2,\partial D^2)\to(M,F)$ whose boundary lies in the relative interior of $F$ and has class outside $N$. Then there is a properly embedded piecewise linear disk in $M$, with boundary in the relative interior of $F$, whose boundary class is outside $N$.

In particular, if a connected boundary component has noninjective induced fundamental-group map into $M$, it contains an essential simple closed curve bounding a properly embedded piecewise linear disk in $M$. Boundary classes outside $N$ are understood up to conjugation by a basepath in $F$.

Let $X=U\cup V$, where $U$ and $V$ are open path-connected subsets of $X$, let $U\cap V$ be path-connected, and fix $x_0\in U\cap V$. For the inclusion-induced maps in the diagram

$$\pi_1(U,x_0)\longleftarrow\pi_1(U\cap V,x_0)\longrightarrow\pi_1(V,x_0),$$

the group $\pi_1(X,x_0)$, together with the two inclusion-induced homomorphisms, is a pushout ([[def-pushout-of-group-homomorphisms]]). Equivalently, the canonical homomorphism from any pushout $P$ of the displayed diagram to $\pi_1(X,x_0)$ is an isomorphism. No injectivity of either map from the overlap group is assumed.

Every element of $G\ast_KH$ has a unique normal form $s_1\cdots s_nk$ relative to fixed transversals. A normal word of positive length is nonidentity. The represented group and these conclusions are independent of the chosen transversals.

Fix an HNN extension in associated-subgroup notation and choose transversal data
$(S_-,S_+)$ as in [[def-choice-of-transversals-for-hnn-normal-forms]]. Then
every element of the HNN extension is represented by a unique transversal normal
form

$$a_0t^{\varepsilon_1}a_1\cdots t^{\varepsilon_n}a_n.$$

In particular, the identity has the unique normal form with $n=0$ and
$a_0=e_A$.

$\operatorname{Deg}:\pi_1(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z,[0])\to(\mathbb Z,+)$ is an isomorphism. Its inverse is

$$n\longmapsto[\omega_n].$$

For pointed topological spaces $(X,x_0)$ and $(Y,y_0)$, the coordinate projections induce a natural group isomorphism

$$\Theta:\pi_1(X\times Y,(x_0,y_0))\longrightarrow\pi_1(X,x_0)\times\pi_1(Y,y_0),\qquad [\gamma]\longmapsto([\pi_X\gamma],[\pi_Y\gamma]).$$

Its inverse sends $([\alpha],[\beta])$ to the class of the paired loop $s\mapsto(\alpha(s),\beta(s))$.

derivations.claim: The solid torus is irreducible. Embed it as a standard unknotted solid torus in $S^3$. A sphere in its interior has two ball sides by [F2]. Its exterior solid torus is connected and misses the sphere, so lies entirely on one side; the other ball is contained in $V$. We will use the following disk-push consequence with its smooth interpretation. If two smooth disks meet just along their common boundary and bound such a ball, their faces admit a common-boundary disk sweep through the ball. To retain the actual faces, take a thin rim collar first. At a transverse rim its normal section is a quadrant; at a previously shared collar first separate the two faces by a small normal graph. Parametrize the two faces by smooth disks with their prescribed rim collars, using [F3]. Round and truncate the rim; the remaining boundary is a smooth sphere with these marked disk and collar portions. The two disk maps and the intervening product annulus give a smooth boundary diffeomorphism to the corresponding standard rounded lens; [F3] extends it over the ball. Restore the quadrant rim using those same product collars. This gives a lens parameter retaining both faces and their rim coordinates. In this parameter use [F4]'s spherical-cap sweep; in the rim section its inward tangent runs between the two face tangents and stays nonzero. The sweep is jointly smooth, including at the disk center, by [F4]'s displayed formulas. It can be continued just past either face in its normal collar and extended ambiently by [F5]. If another surface misses the ball except in one face, the push removes that face's intersections and creates none. The support can be restricted to the ball and arbitrarily thin face and rim collars.

For the classification first replace $F$ by its neat representative using [F9]; both disk-obstruction hypotheses pass to it. Its boundary and abstract surface are unchanged. The topological ambient extension pulls a boundary-parallel product back to the original surface, and no smooth product at an original tangency is asserted. In the rest of the classification denote this neat representative again by $F$. The surface $F$ is compact, since its inclusion is proper and $V$ is compact, and it is orientable, since it is two-sided in oriented $V$. If some component $c$ of $\partial F$ is nullhomotopic on $\partial V$, choose one with an innermost boundary disk $Q$ whose interior misses all of $\partial F$. A short inward push gives a disk with boundary $c$ on $F$ and interior disjoint from $F$. If $F$ is not a disk, $c$ is essential on $F$: a boundary circle of a connected surface can bound a disk in that surface only when that disk is the entire surface, by the local half-disk charts and connectedness. The pushed disk would therefore compress $F$. Thus in this case $F$ is a disk. For the rest of the classification suppose $F$ is not a disk; then every boundary circle is essential on $\partial V$. Disjoint essential circles on a torus have the same primitive unoriented slope, as the strip reductions of [F4] show. Use those reductions for the finite family and extend into a boundary collar by [F5] to make them parallel affine circles in coordinates $(\mu,\phi)\in(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)^2$, where $\phi$ is the longitude coordinate of $V$. If the slope is meridional, choose a standard meridian disk $D_0$ with boundary disjoint from them. Otherwise the affine circles have nonzero $\phi$ derivative and meet $\partial D_0=\{\phi=0\}$ transversely.

Put the interiors of $F$ and $D_0$ in finite transverse position. An innermost intersection circle on $D_0$ bounds a disk $D$ with interior missing $F$. Incompressibility makes its boundary bound a disk $D'$ on $F$. The sphere $D\cup D'$ bounds a ball in $V$ by step 1.1, with the corner interpreted there. The connected surface $F\setminus\operatorname{Int}D'$ reaches $\partial V$, misses the sphere off its rim, and hence lies on the exterior side of that ball. The disk push of step 1.1 replaces $D'$ by a disk just past $D$. It removes this circle and any additional circles in $D'$, and creates none. After finitely many pushes no circle remains. The isotopies have interior support and retain the normalized boundary curves.

Suppose an intersection arc remains. An outermost arc $\alpha$ cuts off a disk $D$ in $D_0$, with other boundary arc $\beta\subset\partial D_0$ and interior missing $F$. Boundary-incompressibility implies that $\alpha$ cuts off a disk $D'$ on $F$, with other boundary arc $\gamma$ contained in one component of $\partial F$. If the slope were meridional there would be no arc endpoints, by the chosen disjoint boundaries. Otherwise $\gamma$ is a nonconstant subarc of an affine boundary circle whose longitude coordinate is strictly monotone on its lift. Both its endpoints have $\phi=0$, so its lifted longitude displacement is a nonzero integer. But $\beta$ has constant longitude. The union $D\cup D'$, pushed a little along its common edge if necessary, gives a continuous disk cap for the loop $\beta\cup\gamma$ in $V$. Its longitude degree would therefore be zero, contradicting that nonzero integer. Thus there are no arcs. If the slope were nonmeridional, the affine boundary curves would necessarily meet $\partial D_0$, so this case is impossible. We have made $F$ disjoint from $D_0$. Cutting $V$ along $D_0$ leaves a ball. An innermost boundary circle of $F$ on its boundary sphere has a disk there with interior missing all boundary circles of $F$. Push it inward. Unless $F$ is a disk it is a compressing disk, by the boundary-circle argument of step 2.1. This contradicts our supposition that $F$ was not a disk.

Let $D_1,D_2$ be meridian disks with the same boundary $C$. If either disk is not neat, first neatify each separately by [F9], fixing $C$. Apply the following neat-disk argument and then reverse the second embedding path. This gives a smooth embedding isotopy for the broad inputs; their two explicit topological ambient extensions and the middle smooth ambient path give a topological ambient extension. For neat inputs no preliminary change is necessary, and the entire argument below is smooth ambient. Now suppose both disks neat. In coordinates along $C$, use a small normal graph to separate their interior collars while fixing $C$ pointwise: with inward boundary coordinate $q\ge0$ and a transverse coordinate $y$ on $\partial V$, the two collars can be arranged as $y=\pm\varepsilon q$ on a common smaller strip. First each neat disk is straightened to such a graph by its full-rank collar coordinates; interpolation of the positive inward derivative gives an embedding path on a common compact strip, extended by [F5]. This keeps every boundary point fixed. General position relative to those collars then leaves only finitely many interior intersection circles. An innermost one on $D_1$ and its subdisk on $D_2$ bound a ball by irreducibility. The complement of that subdisk in $D_2$ reaches $C$ outside the ball, so the disk push from step 1.1 removes the circle and any circles inside that subdisk. Repeat until the interiors are disjoint. The resulting disks bound a ball with rim $C$, again by step 1.1 after the rim is rounded. Its common-boundary cap sweep carries one disk to the other, fixing $C$ throughout; at the rim every intermediate tangent is an inward direction between the two collar tangents, so the family remains neat in $V$. Undo the preliminary isotopies of $D_2$ and concatenate with stationary time changes. This gives a jointly smooth isotopy relative to $C$; The velocity vanishes on $C$ throughout this neat path. In a neat boundary chart it is $q$ times a smooth coefficient, as in [F9] and its neatification supplier Proof 5.2. Extend that coefficient and retain the factor $q$; the finite compact flow gives a smooth ambient isotopy fixing all of $\partial V$, not only $C$.

We have proved that $F$ is a disk. If $\partial F$ is essential on $\partial V$, it is a primitive class in the kernel of $\pi_1(\partial V)=\mathbb Z\mu\oplus\mathbb Z\phi\to\pi_1(V)=\mathbb Z\phi$, since $F$ caps it. It is therefore $\pm\mu$, so $F$ is a meridian disk. If $\partial F$ is inessential, let $Q$ be its disk on $\partial V$. The sphere $F\cup Q$, pushed slightly into the interior and rounded, bounds a ball there. Restore the boundary collar as in step 1.1 to get a ball with these two disk faces. Its marked lens parameter gives the boundary-parallel product: extend $Q$ a short distance beyond its rim in $\partial V$ and retain a smaller collar on $F$; in the normal section the two disk faces are separated by a rectangle, with its outer edge on $\partial V$. The lens parameter away from that rim and this rectangle near it identify the region with $D^2\times[0,1]$, with $D^2\times\{0\}=F$ and the other disk and lateral annulus in $\partial V$. Thus $F$ is boundary-parallel in exactly [F1]'s product sense. Finally allow the torus $T\subset\operatorname{Int}V$ to be TOP two-sided with its given product neighborhood, without assuming it smooth. Cut along that TOP collar. The cut pieces are compact orientable TOP3-manifolds; there are either two connected pieces with one torus face each, or one connected piece with two torus faces. Indeed every piece meets a face, and each face is connected. If any face map has nontrivial fundamental-group kernel, [F10] gives a proper disk in that cut piece whose boundary has nontrivial class on the face. Its image in $V$ is an embedded TOP compression of $T$ contained in $\operatorname{Int}V$, since its interior misses every cut boundary face and its boundary lies on only the chosen copy of $T$. Suppose therefore all face maps inject. In the two-piece case, [F11] embeds $\pi_1(T)$ in their amalgam $\pi_1(V)$. In the one-piece case choose a path in the cut piece joining the two face basepoints. Adjoining a thin copy of this path to the collar makes its overlap connected; van Kampen gives the presentation $\langle\pi_1(W),t\mid t i_+(a)t^{-1}=i_-(a),\ a\in\pi_1(T)\rangle$. One torus-overlap group maps to the collar's torus group and the other to its conjugate by the new path letter, which is exactly the displayed HNN relation. The two injected face groups are its associated subgroups, so HNN normal form [F11] again embeds $\pi_1(T)$ in $\pi_1(V)$. Both alternatives would inject $\mathbb Z^2$ into $\mathbb Z$, impossible: if the two basis images are $a,b$, then $(b,-a)$ is a nonzero kernel vector when either image is nonzero, and otherwise the whole group is the kernel. Thus some face kernel is nontrivial and the TOP compression exists. This closes the original unqualified torus clause without converting its input or its resulting disk to the smooth category. The preceding smooth classification and meridian-isotopy arguments are unchanged; their original convention/disposition remains owned by the parent assembly.
