The **satellite knot** $P(K)$ is $e(P)$, with chosen exterior $E_{P(K)}=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}e(N(P))$; the image $e(\partial V)$ is its **companion torus**. The outer torus is **incompressible** when it bounds no properly embedded disk in $X_P$ with essential boundary on $\partial V$. It is **product-parallel** to the inner torus when $X_P$ is a product $T^2\times[0,1]$ with those tori as its ends. This definition alone asserts neither incompressibility nor essentiality of the companion torus.

Let $M$ be a compact smooth $3$-manifold. A properly embedded surface is **two-sided** if it has a product neighbourhood $F\times[-1,1]$ in $M$. A **compressing disk** for a two-sided surface $F$ is an embedded disk $D\subset M$ with $\operatorname{int}(D)\cap F=\varnothing$ and $\partial D$ an essential simple closed curve in $F$; $F$ is **incompressible** if it has no compressing disk. A **boundary-compressing disk** is an embedded disk $D$ with $\partial D=\alpha\cup\beta$, where $\alpha=D\cap F$ is an arc not cutting off a disk in $F$, $\beta=D\cap\partial M$, and $\operatorname{int}(D)$ misses $F\cup\partial M$; $F$ is **boundary-incompressible** if it has no such disk. A surface is **boundary-parallel** if it cobounds a product with a subsurface of $\partial M$, and it is **essential** if it is incompressible, boundary-incompressible, and not boundary-parallel. $M$ is **irreducible** if every embedded $2$-sphere in its interior bounds an embedded $3$-ball in $M$. An incompressible torus is boundary-parallel if it cobounds a product $T^2\times[0,1]$ with a component of $\partial M$; $M$ is **atoroidal** if every incompressible torus is boundary-parallel. A **Seifert fibration** is a decomposition into circles with local models given by fibered solid tori; in the model $(D^2\times S^1)/\langle(z,w)\mapsto(e^{2\pi i/q}z,e^{2\pi ip/q}w)\rangle$, where $\gcd(p,q)=1$, the core fiber has multiplicity $q$. Fibers of multiplicity $1$ are **regular** and those of multiplicity greater than $1$ are **exceptional**. A finite family of pairwise disjoint incompressible tori is a **JSJ system** if every component obtained by cutting $M$ along the family is atoroidal or Seifert-fibered. It is **inclusion-minimal** if no proper subfamily is a JSJ system. Atoroidal does not mean hyperbolic.

derivations.claim: The companion embedding sends the core $S^1\times\{0\}$ to $K$, so the satellite knot $P(K)$ is exactly $K$ with the specified smaller tubular neighbourhood. The companion torus is the boundary of the larger neighbourhood.

The shell between the two concentric tubular neighbourhoods is explicitly $T^2\times[0,1]$, by radial interpolation in the $D^2$ coordinate. It lies in the satellite exterior and has the companion torus and the satellite exterior boundary as its end tori. Thus the companion torus is boundary-parallel and, by [F2], is not essential. This refutes the unrestricted statement.

citations.quote: Let $V=S^1\times D^2$ be the standard oriented solid torus, with oriented core $S^1\times\{0\}$. A **pattern** is a smooth oriented knot $P$ contained in the interior of $V$, together with a chosen closed tubular neighbourhood $N(P)$ contained in the interior of $V$. Its **winding number** $w(P)$ is the integer by which the homology class $[P]$ maps to $H_1(V;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$ under the isomorphism that sends the oriented core to $1$. The **pattern exterior** is $X_P=V\setminus\operatorname{int}N(P)$; its **outer torus** is $\partial V$ and its **inner torus** is $\partial N(P)$. A **companion** is a smooth oriented knot $K\subset S^3$ with a specified orientation-preserving tubular embedding $e:V\to S^3$ that sends the core to $K$ and identifies the solid-torus meridian and product longitude with the positive meridian and preferred longitude of $K$. The **satellite knot** $P(K)$ is $e(P)$, with chosen exterior $E_{P(K)}=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}e(N(P))$; the image $e(\partial V)$ is its **companion torus**. The outer torus is **incompressible** when it bounds no properly embedded disk in $X_P$ with essential boundary on $\partial V$. It is **product-parallel** to the inner torus when $X_P$ is a product $T^2\times[0,1]$ with those tori as its ends. This definition alone asserts neither incompressibility nor essentiality of the companion torus.

Assume the full Axiom of Choice. Let $p,q$ be coprime nonzero integers, let $K=T(p,q)$ be the oriented primitive slope curve in the standard Heegaard torus, and let $\rho_t(z_1,z_2)=(e^{2\pi i p t}z_1,e^{2\pi i q t}z_2)$ be the weighted circle action on the unit $S^3\subset\mathbb C^2$. Choose $N(K)$ to be a sufficiently small closed metric tube around the orbit $K$ for the round metric; this tube is invariant because $\rho_t$ is isometric and preserves $K$. Set $E_K=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$. Let $x$ and $y$ be based generators of the fundamental groups of the two solid-torus pieces obtained by cutting $E_K$ along the annulus left on the Heegaard torus, oriented so that the annulus core maps to $x^p$ and $y^q$. Then

$$\pi_1(E_K)=\langle x,y\mid x^p=y^q\rangle.$$

The common element $h=x^p=y^q$ is central and represents a regular fiber of a Seifert fibration of $E_K$ over a disk. The fibration has two distinguished core fibers of multiplicities $|p|$ and $|q|$; a fiber of multiplicity one is regular, and a fiber of multiplicity greater than one is exceptional. Thus there are exactly two exceptional fibers when $|p|,|q|>1$, and one is regular when one absolute parameter is $1$.

For any integers $\alpha,\beta$ with $p\alpha+q\beta=1$, compatible based paths identify the positive normal-disk meridian and preferred longitude in the peripheral system as

$$\mu=y^\alpha x^\beta,\qquad \lambda=h\mu^{-pq}.$$

Here the positive meridian is the oriented boundary of a normal disk, and the preferred longitude has degree one around $K$ and maps to zero in $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$. Their homology classes form a basis of $H_1(\partial E_K;\mathbb Z)$, so both classes are primitive.

Let $X=U\cup V$, where $U$ and $V$ are open path-connected subsets of $X$, let $U\cap V$ be path-connected, and fix $x_0\in U\cap V$. For the inclusion-induced maps in the diagram

$$\pi_1(U,x_0)\longleftarrow\pi_1(U\cap V,x_0)\longrightarrow\pi_1(V,x_0),$$

the group $\pi_1(X,x_0)$, together with the two inclusion-induced homomorphisms, is a pushout ([[def-pushout-of-group-homomorphisms]]). Equivalently, the canonical homomorphism from any pushout $P$ of the displayed diagram to $\pi_1(X,x_0)$ is an isomorphism. No injectivity of either map from the overlap group is assumed.

Every element of $G\ast_KH$ has a unique normal form $s_1\cdots s_nk$ relative to fixed transversals. A normal word of positive length is nonidentity. The represented group and these conclusions are independent of the chosen transversals.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Every nonempty compact
connected boundaryless topological $2$-manifold is homeomorphic to exactly one
of the following types: the sphere $S^2$, a connected sum of $g\geq1$ tori,
or a connected sum of $k\geq1$ real projective planes. The connected sums here
are the explicit polygonal models with their chosen disk removals and boundary
gluings ([[def-connected-sum-of-compact-surfaces]]). The integer is unique
within its type. Equivalently, two such surfaces are homeomorphic if and only
if they have the same integral orientability and Euler characteristic.

The canonical one-face words are respectively the sphere digon $aa^{-1}$
(whose *reduced notation* is empty), the $g$-fold commutator word
$\prod_{i=1}^g a_i b_i a_i^{-1} b_i^{-1}$, and the $k$-fold square word
$\prod_{j=1}^k c_jc_j$. The empty notation is not an empty polygonal schema.

Assume full AC. Let $M$ be a compact connected irreducible Seifert-fibered $3$-manifold, and let $F\subset M$ be a connected, two-sided essential annulus or torus, neatly embedded at its boundary (the condition is vacuous for a torus). Then $F$ is ambient isotopic to either a vertical surface, meaning a union of regular fibers, or a horizontal surface, meaning a surface transverse to every fiber. For a horizontal surface $F$ with $n$ sheets over the base orbifold $B$ and exceptional-fiber multiplicities $q_1,\ldots,q_m$, the Euler characteristics satisfy
$$
\frac{\chi(F)}{n}=\chi(B)-\sum_{i=1}^m\left(1-\frac1{q_i}\right).
$$
If $F$ is two-sided and horizontal, cutting $M$ along $F$ gives an interval bundle over a surface.

For a smooth boundary-preimage embedding without the neatness condition, the same vertical-or-horizontal normal form is attained by a smooth isotopy of embeddings, fixed on the original boundary during its preliminary neatification, and by a topological ambient isotopy. The Euler count and interval-bundle conclusions apply to the resulting horizontal representative. A smooth ambient isotopy is asserted for the neat inputs above.

Assume full AC. Let $K$ be a nontrivial smooth knot with a specified companion solid torus $V=e(S^1\times D^2)$, let $P\subset\operatorname{int}(S^1\times D^2)$ be a pattern, and assume the outer torus of its pattern exterior $X_P$ has no compressing disk and is not product-parallel to the inner pattern torus. Let $T_c=\partial V=e(\partial(S^1\times D^2))\subset E_{P(K)}$ be the companion torus. Then $T_c$ is incompressible and is not boundary-parallel in $E_{P(K)}$; hence it is essential.

Assume full AC. Let $M=E_{P(K)}$ be a satellite knot exterior with companion torus $T_c$. Suppose the pattern hypotheses of the essential-companion-torus lemma hold, both components of $M$ cut along $T_c$ are atoroidal or Seifert-fibered, and $M$ itself is neither atoroidal nor Seifert-fibered. Then the inclusion-minimal JSJ system of $M$ consists of a torus ambient isotopic to $T_c$. Cutting along that torus identifies the companion exterior $E_K$ as the component on the outside of the embedded companion solid torus. No conclusion is made for an essential companion torus that is absorbed into a Seifert-fibered union.

Assume full AC. Let $K:S^1\to S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot with a chosen compact exterior $E_K$. There exists a finite inclusion-minimal collection $\mathcal T$ of pairwise disjoint incompressible tori in the interior of $E_K$ such that every component of $E_K$ cut along $\mathcal T$ is atoroidal or Seifert-fibered. Any two such inclusion-minimal collections are ambient isotopic in $E_K$. Atoroidal pieces in this statement are not asserted to be hyperbolic.

Let $M$ be a compact connected orientable smooth Seifert-fibered three-manifold and let $T$ be a boundary torus whose inclusion induces an injection on fundamental groups. Fix one Seifert fibration and a based regular fiber $h\in\pi_1(T)\subset\pi_1(M)$. Suppose the quotient $\pi_1(M)/\langle h\rangle$ is isomorphic to a finite free product of at least two nontrivial groups, excluding the free product of two groups of order two. Then every Seifert fibration of $M$ has the same unoriented regular-fiber slope on $T$ as the fixed fibration. No choice hypothesis is introduced. The notation $\langle h\rangle$ denotes the cyclic subgroup, which is normal as proved below.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice as an ambient hypothesis; the finite construction and
the ODE interfaces below use no additional choice, so this hypothesis is
dispensable. A smooth manifold with corners here is Hausdorff and second
countable, with charts in relatively open subsets of $[0,\infty)^c\times\mathbb R^{n-c}$
and transition maps smoothly extendible with invertible derivative at corner
points; transitions preserve the local depth and its face germs. Let $M$ be
compact. Then $M$ has a finite corner-adapted whole-star smooth triangulation.
Corner faces are locally subpolyhedra, and any specified finite union of
closed faces is a subpolyhedron.

If the total boundary already has a finite piecewise smooth triangulation
$f:L\to\partial M$ compatible on all local face intersections, with its
differential fan giving a homeomorphism onto the union of boundary faces of the
tangent orthant at each point, the triangulation extends to $M$, pointwise
preserving $f$ with compatible subdivisions allowed. In the resulting finite
union construction all intersections may be made full subcomplexes. The same
relative conclusion applies to a fixed corner-adapted triangulated closed neighbourhood piece
whose smaller protected subcomplex lies in its relative interior: fitting is
performed away from that protected subcomplex. No extension of arbitrary
incompatible boundary data is asserted.

Let $G=G_1*\cdots*G_k$, where $2\le k<\infty$ and every factor is nontrivial. If $k=2$, assume the two factors are not both cyclic of order two. Then every cyclic normal subgroup of $G$ is trivial. No choice hypothesis is required.

derivations.claim: The circle action $t\cdot(z,w)=(e^{4\pi i t}z,e^{2\pi i t}w)$ on $S^1\times D^2$ has generic orbit slope $2\lambda_V+\mu_V$. The given pattern is one such orbit. The core $S^1\times\{0\}$ has stabilizer of order $2$, while generic points have trivial stabilizer. Removing a tube about the regular orbit $P_{2,1}$ therefore gives a Seifert fibration of $X_{P_{2,1}}$ over an annulus with one exceptional point of multiplicity $2$. On the outer torus its regular-fiber slope is $2\lambda_V+\mu_V$.

Remove a small neighborhood of the exceptional point from the annulus base. The remaining pair of pants has fundamental group freely generated by a loop $a$ around the outer boundary and a loop $c$ around the removed cone point; its third boundary loop is $(ac)^{-1}$. The circle bundle over this pair of pants has a section: it retracts to a graph, and a section over that graph is obtained by choosing one point in the fiber at the vertex and extending over each edge. Thus its group has generators $a,c,h$, with $h$ the fiber and $[a,h]=[c,h]=1$. The order-two local model $(z,w)\mapsto(-z,-w)$ around the exceptional core identifies the filled meridian with $c^2h$ after replacing $c$ by $ch^k$ if necessary: one circuit of the cone-point boundary lifts from $(z,w)$ to $(-z,-w)$, so two circuits equal one inverse fiber turn, and the twisting coefficient is odd. Filling that neighborhood kills this meridian. By [F3],
$$
\pi_1(X_{P_{2,1}})=\langle a,c,h\mid [a,h]=[c,h]=1,\ c^2h=1\rangle.
$$
Its quotient by $\langle h\rangle$ is $\mathbb Z*C_2$, which is nonabelian by reduced normal forms [F4]; hence $X_{P_{2,1}}$ is not $T^2\times I$. Its outer boundary subgroup is generated by $a,h$. The abelianization is free on $[a],[c]$ with $[h]=-2[c]$, so $a^m h^n=1$ implies $m=0$ and $n=0$. Thus the outer torus group injects into $\pi_1(X_{P_{2,1}})$ and has no compressing disk.

For the trefoil, [F2] gives $\pi_1(E_K)=\langle x,y\mid x^2=y^3\rangle$ and regular fiber $h_K=x^2=y^3$. Its quotient by $\langle h_K\rangle$ is $C_2*C_3$, nonabelian by [F4], and $h_K$ is infinite because its abelianization is $6$ times the generator of $H_1(E_K)\cong\mathbb Z$. The group maps onto $S_3$ by $x\mapsto(12)$ and $y\mapsto(123)$, so it is nonabelian and $K$ is not the unknot, whose exterior group is $\mathbb Z$.

The peripheral formula in [F2] gives $h_K=\lambda_K+6\mu_K$. The companion embedding identifies $(\mu_V,\lambda_V)$ with $(\mu_K,\lambda_K)$. Therefore the two Seifert fibrations on the cut sides induce slopes $2\lambda+\mu$ and $\lambda+6\mu$ on the companion torus. Their determinant in the ordered basis $(\mu,\lambda)$ is $\det\begin{pmatrix}1&6\\2&1\end{pmatrix}=-11$, so the slopes are not parallel.
By [F7], the companion torus $T_c$ is essential. Hence the whole exterior $M=E_{P_{2,1}(K)}$ is not atoroidal. Both pieces cut along $T_c$ are Seifert-fibered by steps 1.1 and 1.3.

The horizontal case is impossible. The interval-bundle bases inherit smooth transverse charts from the horizontal surface and the fiber charts. For any such compact connected surface with nonempty boundary, [F10] gives a finite triangulation. Root a spanning tree of its triangle-adjacency graph at a boundary edge. Delete each triangle across its exposed parent edge, starting at the root; this collapses the surface to a finite connected graph. Its group is therefore free, with rank equal to the rank of its abelianization, by collapsing a graph spanning tree. For a closed surface, the polygon models of [F5] give abelianization $\mathbb Z^{2g}$ in the orientable genus $g$ case and $\mathbb Z^{k-1}\oplus\mathbb Z/2$ in the nonorientable genus $k$ case, by adding the signed edge occurrences in its single face word. Hence a compact surface group with torsion-free rank-two abelianization is either the torus group $\mathbb Z^2$ or the free group of rank two; with torsion-free rank-one abelianization it is infinite cyclic. The cable group has abelianization $\mathbb Z^2$, is nonabelian because its quotient is $\mathbb Z*C_2$, and has the nonidentity central element $h$ since $[h]=-2[c]$ in its abelianization. It is neither $\mathbb Z^2$ nor the free group of rank two, whose center is trivial by [F11]. The trefoil group has abelianization $\mathbb Z$ and is nonabelian by step 1.3, so it too is not a surface group with that abelianization. Thus neither cut piece can be an interval bundle over a surface.

Suppose $M$ had a Seifert fibration. It is irreducible by [[lem-knot-exterior-is-irreducible]], so [F6] makes $T_c$ ambient isotopic to a vertical or horizontal torus. Isotopy preserves the homeomorphism types of the cut pieces. In the horizontal case, cutting along $T_c$ gives interval bundles over compact connected surfaces, so each side group is a surface group.

Suppose instead that $T_c$ is vertical after isotopy. Pull the hypothetical fibration back by that ambient isotopy, so the original $T_c$ is vertical and the original cut-piece markings are retained. Restriction gives a Seifert fibration on each cut piece with one common regular-fiber slope on $T_c$. Their boundary groups inject independently of any general knot-boundary incompressibility theorem. For the cable side this was proved in step 1.2. For the trefoil side, the peripheral formula of [F2], with $2(-1)+3(1)=1$, gives $\mu=y^{-1}x$ and $\lambda=h_K\mu^{-6}$. Thus $(\mu,h_K)$ is also a basis for its boundary-torus group. In the quotient $C_2*C_3$ the word $y^{-1}x$ is cyclically reduced of length two, so all its nonzero powers are nonidentity by [F4]. If $\mu^a h_K^b=1$, quotienting forces $a=0$, and the infinite order of $h_K$ from step 1.3 forces $b=0$. This proves injectivity of that boundary group. The two original fiber quotients are $\mathbb Z*C_2$ and $C_2*C_3$, respectively, by steps 1.2 and 1.3; neither is the two-order-two exception. Apply [F9] separately to the restricted hypothetical fibration on each side. Its common boundary-fiber slope must equal both original slopes, contradicting their determinant $-11$ in step 2.1. This rules out the vertical case; together with step 2.3 it proves that $M$ is not Seifert-fibered.

Steps 2.2 and 4.1 verify the nonamalgamation hypotheses of [F8], so the companion torus is a JSJ torus and the component outside the companion solid torus is $E_K$. The smooth ambient uniqueness in [F8] carries the original marked outside component to the outside component for any isotopic minimal JSJ torus.

citations.quote:
An essential smooth embedded circle in the standard torus $T=\mathbb R^2/\mathbb Z^2$ represents a nonzero primitive integral homology class. A finite disjoint family of essential smooth circles can be carried by a jointly smooth ambient isotopy of $T$ to parallel affine circles. Two essential circles with the same primitive unoriented class are smoothly ambient isotopic. The components between disjoint essential circles have smooth annulus parameters, with prescribed product collars on their boundary circles. No choice axiom is assumed.

Likewise two smooth spanning arcs of a parametrized annulus with the same endpoints and relative winding number are smoothly ambient isotopic relative to any collars on which they already agree. When disjoint, they have a smooth disk-strip parameter; disjoint essential circles in a parametrized annulus have smooth annulus-strip parameters. All isotopies may be stationary near their time endpoints.

derivations.claim: Choose a smooth parametrization $h:T\to\mathbb R^2/\mathbb Z^2$, as supplied by saying that $T$ is a smooth torus. It preserves essentiality, and its induced integral homology isomorphism preserves primitivity and equality up to sign. Apply [F1] to $h(c)$ to obtain primitivity of $[c]$. This is one supplied finite-dimensional parametrization, not a set-indexed choice.

If $[c]=\pm[d]$, apply [F1] to their images and conjugate its ambient isotopy by $h$. This gives the required ambient isotopy in $T$. If the original curves are disjoint and distinct, the two complementary annulus parameters in [F1] pull back by $h$; either supplies an embedded annulus with exactly those original curves as boundary. No annulus is inferred for intersecting original curves, and no choice axiom is introduced.

e0$, commutation forces the affine multiplier to be one. Thus $A$ consists of translations. In fact every element of $P$ is a translation. Write such an element as $z\mapsto az+b$. If $|a|
e1$, its conjugation action multiplies translation vectors by $a$, so conjugating $z\mapsto z+\lambda$ by positive or negative powers gives nontrivial translations tending to the identity. If $|a|=1$ and $a

The matrix bound treats c=0 separately as the ideal-point stabilizer and proves |c|>=1 only when c is nonzero. Proof, step 4.2: Rescale the finite boundary coordinate so that $T:z\mapsto z+1$ belongs to $\Gamma$. If $g=\left[\begin{smallmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{smallmatrix}\right]\in\Gamma$ has $c\ne0$, then $|c|\ge1$. To prove this, suppose $0<|c|<1$ and choose a determinant-one lift $g_0$. Define $g_{n+1}=g_nTg_n^{-1}$ using the lift $T=\left[\begin{smallmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right]$. Matrix multiplication gives $$ g_{n+1}=\begin{pmatrix}1-a_nc_n&a_n^2\\-c_n^2&1+a_nc_n\end{pmatrix},\qquad c_{n+1}=-c_n^2. $$ Put $r=|c_0|<1$. Then $|c_n|=r^{2^n}$ and $|a_{n+1}|\le1+r|a_n|$, so $|a_n|\le\max\{|a_0|,(1-r)^{-1}\}$. Consequently $a_{n+1}\to1$, $a_n^2\to1$ and $g_n\to T$. Their nonzero lower-left entries have distinct absolute values, so these are distinct projective matrices. This contradicts discreteness and proves the bound. [given, L1, step 3.1, algebra]

Exactly one topological end is needed only for the compact-complement corollary, not for the general embedded horocusp. Proof, step 8.1: The quotient $M$ is complete: a geodesic lifts locally to $\mathbb H^3$ and its lifted geodesic is defined for all real time, so it projects to a global extension. Hence [F1] makes $M$ proper. Let $C$ be the embedded closed horocusp and $S=\partial C$. Its interior is a connected component of $M\setminus S$: it is open there, and it is closed there by properness in step 6.1. The other side is connected. Indeed, the outward collar of the connected torus $S$ belongs to a single component; any other component of the complement of $C$ would have no frontier in $M$ and would be both open and closed, contradicting connectedness of $M$. If that other side had noncompact closure, both sides of the compact separator $S$ would be nonrelatively compact components. This contradicts the one-end hypothesis, since in an interior of a compact collared manifold the definition of one end says that exactly one component of the complement of any sufficiently large compact set is nonrelatively compact. More generally this follows from the usual exhaustion definition of one end, applied after adding a compact connected set containing $S$. Thus the other side has compact closure. This proves the last assertion; it does not assert that arbitrary many-ended quotients have compact complement of a single horocusp. [A1, F1, given, step 6.1, construct] ∎

A loxodromic centralizer has torsion-free discrete cyclic subgroups, so it cannot contain the rank-two input. Proof, step 2.1: Suppose that an abelian subgroup contains a loxodromic element. Every matrix commuting with it preserves its two distinct eigenlines individually: interchanging them would conjugate its eigenvalue ratio to its inverse, which is different because its modulus is not one. Its centralizer is therefore the diagonal group, identified with $\mathbb C^*$. Every discrete torsion-free subgroup $D$ of this group is cyclic. For each $B>0$, the annulus $e^{-B}\le|z|\le e^B$ is compact, so contains only finitely many elements of $D$ by [L1]. The kernel of $z\mapsto\log|z|$ is a finite subgroup of the unit circle and hence trivial. If $D$ is nontrivial, this map therefore has a smallest positive value $b$: choose one positive value $B$, and minimize among the finitely many in $(0,B]$. Division with remainder by $b$ shows that every value is an integer multiple of $b$, proving the cyclic assertion. Thus $A$ cannot contain a loxodromic element. [given, L1, step 1.1, algebra]

ChooseR>1 strictly, giving disjoint closed horoballs even in the sharp |c|=1 case. Proof, step 5.1: The extension of a Möbius matrix to upper half-space has height coordinate $$ y(g(z,y))=\frac{y}{|cz+d|^2+|c|^2y^2}. $$ This follows by composing translations, rotations and dilations with inversion; these generate the determinant-one matrices by Gaussian elimination. For $c\ne0$ and $y\ge R$, step 4.2 therefore gives $y(g(z,y))\le1/R$. Choose $R>1$. Then every translate of the closed horoball by an element outside $P$ is disjoint from that horoball, whereas translations in $P$ preserve it. Thus $\{y\ge R\}$ is precisely invariant under $P$, and its quotient injects into $M$. The strict inequality $1/R<R$ gives an embedded boundary collar as well. [step 3.1, step 4.2, algebra]

Shortest lattice vectors exist by compact finiteness; AC is retained for the global metric suppliers. Proof, step 4.1: A discrete additive subgroup $\Lambda$ of $\mathbb C\cong\mathbb R^2$ has rank at most two. Here are the needed elementary details. Choose a shortest nonzero vector $v$, whose existence follows from finiteness in bounded disks. If every vector is collinear with $v$, division with remainder along that line proves $\Lambda=\mathbb Zv$. Otherwise subtract integer multiples of $v$ to put the parallel component of every vector in $[0,|v|)$. Among vectors with positive perpendicular component, a least such component exists: below any fixed positive candidate and with that normalized parallel component, there are finitely many vectors in a compact rectangle. Choose a vector $w$ realizing it. Division with remainder in the perpendicular direction, followed by division along $v$, shows that every vector is in $\mathbb Zv+\mathbb Zw$. Since $A$ has rank two, the collinear case is impossible. Therefore the translation vectors of $P$ form a rank-two lattice $\Lambda$. An element centralizing $A$ must centralize its chosen parabolic and hence belong to $P$ by step 3.1; since $P$ is abelian, it is the unique maximal abelian subgroup containing $A$. [given, L1, step 3.1, algebra]

The rank-two input produces a proper embedded standard horocusp, with positive finite cross-sectional area. Proof, step 6.1: This quotient map is a proper embedding. A closed horoball quotient has the coordinates $(\mathbb C/\Lambda)\times[R,\infty)$. If a sequence escapes every compact subset of this product, its heights tend to infinity after passing to a subsequence, because the horizontal factor is compact. For a fixed nonzero $\lambda\in\Lambda$, the distance between $(z,y)$ and $(z+\lambda,y)$ is $2\operatorname{arsinh}(|\lambda|/(2y))$, as follows by the hyperbolic distance formula in a vertical half-plane. Hence the injectivity radii of their images in $M$ tend to zero. On every compact subset of $M$ the injectivity radius is bounded below by a positive constant: each point has an evenly covered small metric ball, and finitely many smaller such balls cover a compact set. Thus this escaping sequence cannot have its image in a compact set. Sequential compactness in metric spaces proves properness. An injective proper local embedding is an embedding, giving the assertion. [given, step 4.1, step 5.1, algebra]

The converse identification of arbitrary topological ends is not asserted; only the explicit quotient cusp and the one-end corollary are proved. Proof, step 7.1: The volume density is $y^{-3}\,dx_1dx_2dy$. Integrating over one Euclidean fundamental parallelogram and $y\ge R$ gives $\operatorname{area}(\mathbb C/\Lambda)\int_R^\infty y^{-3}dy=\operatorname{area}(\mathbb C/\Lambda)/(2R^2)$. This also identifies the compact boundary as a torus and the open interior as its product with a half-line. [step 4.1, step 6.1, algebra]

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $(M,g)$ be a **nonempty**, connected,
boundaryless Riemannian manifold, and let $d=d_g$ be its Riemannian distance.
The following conditions are equivalent.

1. The metric space $(M,d)$ is complete.
2. The Riemannian manifold $(M,g)$ is geodesically complete.
3. For every $p\in M$, the fibre exponential domain is all of the tangent
   space: $\mathcal E_p=T_pM$.
4. There is a point $p_0\in M$ for which $\mathcal E_{p_0}=T_{p_0}M$.
5. Every closed bounded subset of the metric space $(M,d)$ is compact.

Whenever these conditions hold, every $x,y\in M$ are joined by a minimizing
geodesic. More exactly, there is $v\in T_xM$ with
$$
\exp_x(v)=y,\qquad |v|_{g_x}=d(x,y),
$$
and $t\mapsto\exp_x(tv)$ on $[0,1]$ has length $d(x,y)$.

The nonemptiness hypothesis is essential for this formulation: on the empty
manifold conditions 1--3 and 5 are vacuous, whereas condition 4 is false.

boundaries.evidence: Finite positive quotient measure is assumed, so the bounded Beltrami lift is a genuineL2 vector. Proof, step 2.2: Outside the Haar-null set where $g(0)=\infty$, define $F(g)=\mu(g(0))\overline{g'(0)}/g'(0)$, and put it equal to zero on that exceptional set. This is bounded and measurable. Step 1.2 and the holomorphic chain rule give $F(\gamma g)=F(g)$ for almost every $g$, for each $\gamma$. Because $\Gamma$ is countable, remove the union of the exceptional sets and all their $\Gamma$ translates; this is an invariant Haar-null set. Redefining $F$ as zero on it gives an exactly left-$\Gamma$-invariant representative. It descends to a measurable bounded function on $X$: on each quotient chart use a local section of the covering projection, and exact invariance makes the resulting definitions agree. Finite measure gives $F\in L^2(X,\nu)$. [A1, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

Rotation bypi/2 forces the constant lifted Beltrami coefficient equal to its negative and hence zero. Proof, step 6.1: In the finite source coordinate, $a_t(z)=e^tz$, so $a_t$ fixes $0$ and has positive real derivative there. Consequently $F(ga_t)=F(g)$ for Haar-almost every $g$, for every $t$; the redefinition in step 2.2 changes this only on a null set and its right translate. Thus $R_{a_t}F=F$ in $L^2(X)$, and steps 3.1–5.1 imply $F=c$ almost everywhere for a complex constant $c$. Now let $m_\theta(z)=e^{i\theta}z$. The same computation gives $F(gm_\theta)=e^{-2i\theta}F(g)$ almost everywhere. Right translation preserves the measure class, so the constant satisfies $c=e^{-2i\theta}c$ for every $\theta$. Taking $\theta=\pi/2$ gives $c=-c$, hence $c=0$. [step 3.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, step 2.2, algebra]

The resulting1-quasiconformal map is holomorphic and therefore Mobius on the sphere. Proof, step 7.1: Since the derivative ratio in step 2.2 has modulus one, $F=0$ Haar-almost everywhere implies $\mu\circ p=0$ Haar-almost everywhere. The positive-area converse in step 1.2 forces $\mu=0$ area-almost everywhere. By [F4], $h$ is holomorphic in every finite source and target chart. The finitely many omitted chart points cause no issue: use alternate source and target charts there and the conformal coefficient transformation law [F3]; their exceptional sets remain null. Thus $h$ is a biholomorphic sphere homeomorphism and is Möbius by [F4]. [F3, F4, step 1.2, step 2.2, step 6.1, algebra] ∎

Sphere chart singularities and pullbacks of area-null exceptional sets are treated through submersion coordinates and Fubini. Proof, step 1.2: Let $\mu$ be the Beltrami coefficient of $h$ in the standard finite source coordinate, defined arbitrarily on its null exceptional set, with $|\mu|\le k<1$. Finite source and target charts suffice outside at most finitely many points. Since holomorphic coordinate changes obey [F3], the conjugacy identity gives $\mu(\gamma z)\overline{\gamma'(z)}/\gamma'(z)=\mu(z)$ almost everywhere, for every $\gamma\in\Gamma$. Consider the evaluation map $p:G\to\widehat{\mathbb C}$, $p(g)=g(0)$. It is a smooth submersion: infinitesimal translations span the tangent plane at $0$, and left translation transports that statement to every $g$. Its local coordinates are a product of a sphere chart and a four-dimensional fiber chart; Haar measure has a smooth positive density in these coordinates. Thus inverse images under $p$ of area-null sets are Haar null by Fubini; conversely a positive-area set has inverse image of positive Haar measure in some such product chart. [A1, F2, F3, given, algebra]

The two opposite limits t→±infinity contract the two unipotent groups separately. Proof, step 3.1: Put $a_t=\left[\begin{smallmatrix}e^{t/2}&0\\0&e^{-t/2}\end{smallmatrix}\right]$, $n_+(z)=\left[\begin{smallmatrix}1&z\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right]$ and $n_-(z)=\left[\begin{smallmatrix}1&0\\z&1\end{smallmatrix}\right]$. For $n=n_+(z)$ the conjugate is $n_+(e^tz)$ and tends to the identity as $t\to-\infty$; for $n=n_-(z)$ it is $n_-(e^{-t}z)$ and tends to the identity as $t\to+\infty$. Strong continuity from step 2.1 forces $R_nv=v$ in both cases. [step 2.1, algebra]

Proof, step 7.1: Since the derivative ratio in step 2.2 has modulus one, $F=0$ Haar-almost everywhere implies $\mu\circ p=0$ Haar-almost everywhere. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\Omega\xrightarrow{\,g\,}\Omega''\xrightarrow{\,f\,}\Omega'$ be analytically quasiconformal homeomorphisms, with $g$ $K_1$-quasiconformal and $f$ $K_2$-quasiconformal ([[def-acl-sobolev-quasiconformal-homeomorphism]]).

(i) **Composition.** The composite $f\circ g$ is analytically $K_1K_2$-quasiconformal, with $K_{f\circ g}\le K_1K_2$, and almost everywhere
$$\mu_{f\circ g}(z)= \frac{g_{\bar z}(z)+\mu_f(g(z))\,\overline{g_z(z)}} {g_z(z)+\mu_f(g(z))\,\overline{g_{\bar z}(z)}}.$$

(ii) **Inverse.** The inverse $f^{-1}$ is $K_2$-quasiconformal, $K_{f^{-1}}=K_f$, and
$$\mu_{f^{-1}}(f(z))=-\mu_f(z)\frac{f_z(z)}{\overline{f_z(z)}}\quad\text{for almost every }z.$$

Consequently quasiconformal homeomorphisms are closed under inverses and composition, and the $1$-quasiconformal self-maps of a domain form a group.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\Omega,\Omega'\subseteq\mathbb C$ be complex domains ([[def-complex-domain]]) and $f:\Omega\to\Omega'$ a homeomorphism. The following are equivalent.

(a) $f$ is $1$-quasiconformal, in either the geometric or the analytic sense ([[def-geometric-quasiconformal-homeomorphism]], [[def-acl-sobolev-quasiconformal-homeomorphism]], [[thm-geometric-and-analytic-quasiconformality-equivalent]]).

(b) $f\in W^{1,2}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ and its weak Wirtinger derivative satisfies $\partial_{\bar z}f=0$ almost everywhere; under this Sobolev hypothesis this is equivalent to $\mu_f=0$ almost everywhere together with $\partial_{\bar z}f=0$ almost everywhere on $\{\partial_zf=0\}$ ([[def-acl-sobolev-quasiconformal-homeomorphism]], [[def-beltrami-coefficient-and-maximal-dilatation]]).

(c) $f$ is holomorphic; equivalently, it is a biholomorphism of $\Omega$ onto $\Omega'$ ([[def-biholomorphic-map]]).

Thus the conformal maps in this library's orientation-preserving sense are exactly the $1$-quasiconformal homeomorphisms; in particular, they preserve angles.
Every biholomorphic self-map of the Riemann sphere is Möbius.

derivations.claim: The quotient $X$ is a second-countable smooth manifold: left translation by a discrete subgroup is free, and each point of $G$ has a small open neighborhood disjoint from its nontrivial left translates. The projection restricts to a diffeomorphism there, giving the quotient charts. The subgroup is countable, since a discrete subgroup of the second-countable manifold $G$ is discrete and closed and its distinct points can be assigned distinct elements of a countable neighborhood basis. A Borel set in $X$ is $\nu$-null exactly when its full inverse image is Haar null, by the local quotient definition of $\nu$, countable quotient charts and countability of $\Gamma$. Both measures are sigma-finite: $G$ and $X$ have countable relatively compact chart covers, and their Radon measures are finite on compact sets.

Let $\mu$ be the Beltrami coefficient of $h$ in the standard finite source coordinate, defined arbitrarily on its null exceptional set, with $|\mu|\le k<1$. Finite source and target charts suffice outside at most finitely many points. Since holomorphic coordinate changes obey [F3], the conjugacy identity gives $\mu(\gamma z)\overline{\gamma'(z)}/\gamma'(z)=\mu(z)$ almost everywhere, for every $\gamma\in\Gamma$. Consider the evaluation map $p:G\to\widehat{\mathbb C}$, $p(g)=g(0)$. It is a smooth submersion: infinitesimal translations span the tangent plane at $0$, and left translation transports that statement to every $g$. Its local coordinates are a product of a sphere chart and a four-dimensional fiber chart; Haar measure has a smooth positive density in these coordinates. Thus inverse images under $p$ of area-null sets are Haar null by Fubini; conversely a positive-area set has inverse image of positive Haar measure in some such product chart.

Define $R_g f(x)=f(xg)$ on $L^2(X,\nu)$. Right invariance of $\nu$ makes every $R_g$ unitary, and $R_gR_k=R_{gk}$. This representation is strongly continuous. Indeed, if $f\in C_c(X)$ and $g$ stays in a compact identity neighborhood, the supports of $R_gf-f$ lie in one compact subset of $X$. Joint continuity of the action and compactness give uniform convergence $R_gf\to f$ there as $g\to e$, so convergence holds in $L^2$. For a general $v\in L^2$, approximate by $f\in C_c(X)$ using [F1] and use $\|R_gv-v\|_2\le2\|v-f\|_2+\|R_gf-f\|_2$.

Outside the Haar-null set where $g(0)=\infty$, define $F(g)=\mu(g(0))\overline{g'(0)}/g'(0)$, and put it equal to zero on that exceptional set. This is bounded and measurable. Step 1.2 and the holomorphic chain rule give $F(\gamma g)=F(g)$ for almost every $g$, for each $\gamma$. Because $\Gamma$ is countable, remove the union of the exceptional sets and all their $\Gamma$ translates; this is an invariant Haar-null set. Redefining $F$ as zero on it gives an exactly left-$\Gamma$-invariant representative. It descends to a measurable bounded function on $X$: on each quotient chart use a local section of the covering projection, and exact invariance makes the resulting definitions agree. Finite measure gives $F\in L^2(X,\nu)$.

Put $a_t=\left[\begin{smallmatrix}e^{t/2}&0\\0&e^{-t/2}\end{smallmatrix}\right]$, $n_+(z)=\left[\begin{smallmatrix}1&z\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right]$ and $n_-(z)=\left[\begin{smallmatrix}1&0\\z&1\end{smallmatrix}\right]$. If $v\in L^2(X)$ satisfies $R_{a_t}v=v$ for every $t$, then $\|R_nv-v\|_2=\|R_{a_tna_{-t}}v-v\|_2$ by unitarity and this invariance. For $n=n_+(z)$ the conjugate is $n_+(e^tz)$ and tends to the identity as $t\to-\infty$; for $n=n_-(z)$ it is $n_-(e^{-t}z)$ and tends to the identity as $t\to+\infty$. Strong continuity from step 2.1 forces $R_nv=v$ in both cases.

These two unipotent subgroups generate $G$. To check this without any structural rigidity theorem, define $w(\lambda)=n_+(\lambda)n_-(-\lambda^{-1})n_+(\lambda)=\left[\begin{smallmatrix}0&\lambda\\-\lambda^{-1}&0\end{smallmatrix}\right]$ for $\lambda\ne0$. Then $w(\lambda)w(-1)=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda,\lambda^{-1})$. Every determinant-one matrix with upper left entry $a\ne0$ factors as $n_-(c/a)\operatorname{diag}(a,a^{-1})n_+(b/a)$, where $b,c$ are its other off-diagonal entries. If $a=0$, its lower left entry is nonzero, so left multiplication by $n_+(1)$ makes that upper left entry nonzero. The factorization descends to $G$. Thus every vector in step 3.1 is invariant under every $R_g$.

A vector invariant under all $R_g$ is constant almost everywhere. Take a Borel representative $v$ and its lift $\widetilde v$ to $G$. For each fixed $k\in G$, right invariance in $L^2(X)$ and the null-set equivalence in step 1.1 give $\widetilde v(gk)=\widetilde v(g)$ for Haar-almost every $g$. Tonelli on compact exhaustions of $G\times G$ gives this equality for almost every pair $(g,k)$. The smooth change of variables $(g,k)\mapsto(g,y=gk)$ preserves the Haar product measure class, since for fixed $g$ left translation preserves Haar measure. Hence $\widetilde v(y)=\widetilde v(g)$ for almost every $(g,y)$. Fubini supplies one $g$ whose section has full measure, proving $\widetilde v$, and therefore $v$, almost everywhere constant. Steps 3.1–5.1 have proved the complete contraction assertion needed below.

In the finite source coordinate, $a_t(z)=e^tz$, so $a_t$ fixes $0$ and has positive real derivative there. Consequently $F(ga_t)=F(g)$ for Haar-almost every $g$, for every $t$; the redefinition in step 2.2 changes this only on a null set and its right translate. Thus $R_{a_t}F=F$ in $L^2(X)$, and steps 3.1–5.1 imply $F=c$ almost everywhere for a complex constant $c$. Now let $m_\theta(z)=e^{i\theta}z$. The same computation gives $F(gm_\theta)=e^{-2i\theta}F(g)$ almost everywhere. Right translation preserves the measure class, so the constant satisfies $c=e^{-2i\theta}c$ for every $\theta$. Taking $\theta=\pi/2$ gives $c=-c$, hence $c=0$.

Since the derivative ratio in step 2.2 has modulus one, $F=0$ Haar-almost everywhere implies $\mu\circ p=0$ Haar-almost everywhere. The positive-area converse in step 1.2 forces $\mu=0$ area-almost everywhere. By [F4], $h$ is holomorphic in every finite source and target chart. The finitely many omitted chart points cause no issue: use alternate source and target charts there and the conformal coefficient transformation law [F3]; their exceptional sets remain null. Thus $h$ is a biholomorphic sphere homeomorphism and is Möbius by [F4].

Proof, step 2.1: For $x\in V$ and $0<|t|<\operatorname{dist}(V,\partial U)/2$, use step 1.1 with radius $2|t|$ to obtain $|h(x+te_i)-h(x)|^2\le(H^2/\pi)\omega(B(x,2|t|))$. These balls lie in $U$. Tonelli, applied to their incidence indicator, gives $\int_V\omega(B(x,2|t|))\,dx=\int_U|V\cap B(y,2|t|)|\,d\omega(y)\le4\pi t^2\omega(U)$. Combining the two inequalities proves the explicit difference-quotient estimate. [A1, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

The zero derivative is allowed and satisfies every asserted Beltrami inequality. Proof, step 4.1: By the general-homeomorphism interface [F3], $h$ is totally differentiable almost everywhere. At such a point $x$, write $h(x+v)=h(x)+Av+o(|v|)$; the remainder is uniform over $|v|=r$ after division by $r$. If $A$ has rank one, there are unit vectors $u,v$ with $Au=0$ and $|Av|>0$. citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge1$,
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and $\Omega'\Subset\Omega$;
write $\delta_hu=(\delta_h^1u,\dots,\delta_h^nu)$ and
$Du=(D_1u,\dots,D_nu)$ for the difference-quotient and gradient vectors, with
$$\|\delta_hu\|_{L^p(\Omega')}:=\Big\|\Big(\sum_{i=1}^n|\delta_h^iu|^2\Big)^{1/2}\Big\|_{L^p(\Omega')},\qquad \|Du\|_{L^p(\Omega)}:=\Big\|\Big(\sum_{i=1}^n|D_iu|^2\Big)^{1/2}\Big\|_{L^p(\Omega)} .$$
(1) If $1\le p\le\infty$ and $u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$, then for every
$0<|h|<\operatorname{dist}(\Omega',\partial\Omega)$ and every coordinate
direction $i$,
$$\|\delta_h^iu\|_{L^p(\Omega')}\le\|D_iu\|_{L^p(\Omega)},\qquad \|\delta_hu\|_{L^p(\Omega')}\le n^{|1/p-1/2|}\|Du\|_{L^p(\Omega)} .$$
At $p=2$ the vector estimate has constant one. The coordinate bound also
holds on any open $U\subseteq\Omega$ for a fixed $i,h$ for which every
segment $[x,x+he_i]$, $x\in U$, stays in $\Omega$; compact containment
is unnecessary. In particular, $\|\delta_h^iu\|_{L^p(H)}\le
\|D_iu\|_{L^p(H)}$ for tangential directions on a half-space $H$.
(2) Conversely, if $1<p<\infty$, $u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and there is $C$
with $\|\delta_h^iu\|_{L^p(\Omega')}\le C$ for every coordinate $i$ and all
$0<|h|<\operatorname{dist}(\Omega',\partial\Omega)/2$, then
$u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega')$ with $D_iu\in L^p(\Omega')$,
$\|D_iu\|_{L^p(\Omega')}\le C$, and
$\delta_h^iu\rightharpoonup D_iu$ weakly in $L^p(\Omega')$ as $h\to0$.
For $1\le p<\infty$, tangential quotients on $H$ also converge strongly:
$\delta_h^iu\to D_iu$ in $L^p(H)$ as $h\to0$.
Both parts are identities of classes and hold without any regularity of
$\partial\Omega$. At $p=1$ the converse in (2) is deliberately not asserted;
the companion remark records why only a measure derivative survives there.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, used through the cited Countable-Choice and
Dependent-Choice interfaces (completed-product Fubini, approximate identities,
the fundamental theorem of calculus for absolutely continuous functions), for
the countable selections of cutoffs and mollifier scales below, and through the
earlier ACL reconstruction lemma. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be
open, $n\ge1$, let $1\le p<\infty$, and let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.
For an almost-everywhere class $u$ on $\Omega$ the following are equivalent:

1. $u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$;
2. $u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and $u$ has one measurable ACL representative
   $u^*$ whose classical coordinate derivatives $\partial_i u^*$ exist almost
   everywhere, are measurable, and belong to $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$.

In that case $\partial_i u^*$ is a representative of $D_i u$ for every
$i$, that is, $D_i u=\partial_i u^*$ almost everywhere.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, there is only the zero class, its representative
$u^*=0$ is ACL, and every displayed assertion holds vacuously.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $f:\Omega\to\Omega'$ be an orientation-preserving analytically $K$-quasiconformal homeomorphism, $K\ge1$, in the sense of [[def-acl-sobolev-quasiconformal-homeomorphism]]. For every Jordan quadrilateral $Q\Subset\Omega$ with either pair of opposite marked sides, write $\Gamma_Q$ for its joining family and $\Gamma_{f(Q)}$ for the corresponding image family ([[def-geometric-quasiconformal-homeomorphism]]). Then
$$K^{-1}\mu(\Gamma_Q)\le\mu(\Gamma_{f(Q)})\le K\mu(\Gamma_Q),$$
equivalently
$$K^{-1}\lambda(\Gamma_Q)\le\lambda(\Gamma_{f(Q)})\le K\lambda(\Gamma_Q).$$
This result supplies quadrilateral bounds; no inverse regularity, inverse null-set property or arbitrary-ring comparison is assumed.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), and let
$\overline{\mu 	imes 
u}$ be the completed product of two sigma-finite
measure spaces.

1. If $f : X 	imes Y 	o [0,\infty]$ is $\overline{\mu 	imes 
u}$-measurable, there are measurable null sets $A\subseteq X$ and $B\subseteq Y$ such that $f_x$ is $\overline{\mathcal B}$-measurable for $x
otin A$ and $f^y$ is $\overline{\mathcal A}$-measurable for $y
otin B$. Define $I_f(x)=\int_Y f_x\,d\overline
u$ for $x
otin A$ and $I_f(x)=0$ on $A$; define $J_f(y)=\int_X f^y\,d\overline\mu$ for $y
otin B$ and $J_f(y)=0$ on $B$. Then $I_f,J_f$ are measurable and
$$\int f\,d\overline{\mu 	imes 
u}=\int_X I_f\,d\mu=\int_Y J_f\,d
u.$$
2. If $f \in L^1(\overline{\mu 	imes 
u})$, there are measurable null sets $A\subseteq X$ and $B\subseteq Y$ such that the sections are measurable and integrable outside them. Define $I_f,J_f$ by the same section integrals outside $A,B$ and by zero on $A,B$. They are measurable and integrable, and the same equality holds.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb C$ be open for $d_{\mathbb C}$ ([[def-complex-metric-convergence-and-continuity]]). Put $V=\Phi[U]$, where $\Phi(a+bi)=(a,b)$ is the bijection of [[thm-complex-numbers-are-the-real-coordinate-plane]]. Then $V$ is open by [[thm-complex-coordinate-isometry-and-topology-transport]]. For $f:U\to\mathbb C$ define $\widetilde f=\Phi\circ f\circ\Phi^{-1}:V\to\mathbb R^2$, with component functions $u=\operatorname{Re}(f\circ\Phi^{-1})$ and $v=\operatorname{Im}(f\circ\Phi^{-1})$ ([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). All real partial derivatives below are those of $\widetilde f$ on $V$ in [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], evaluated at the coordinate point in question. Write $\partial_x f=u_x+iv_x$ and $\partial_y f=u_y+iv_y$ after transport back to $U$.

At a point where the four real partial derivatives exist, define

$$ \partial_z f:=\frac12(\partial_x f-i\partial_y f)=\frac12(u_x+v_y)+\frac{i}{2}(v_x-u_y), $$

$$ \partial_{\bar z}f:=\frac12(\partial_x f+i\partial_y f)=\frac12(u_x-v_y)+\frac{i}{2}(v_x+u_y). $$

Real total differentiability means total differentiability of $\widetilde f$ under [[def-total-derivative-in-euclidean-space]], with a real-linear derivative as in [[def-euclidean-linear-map]]. Its transported real-linear map $Df$ is supplied by [[thm-complex-coordinate-map-preserves-real-total-differentiability]]. If $f$ is real totally differentiable, put $A=\partial_x f$ and $B=\partial_y f$. The remainder definition along the two coordinate axes gives $Df(1)=A$ and $Df(i)=B$. Real linearity then gives $Df(s+it)=sA+tB$ for real $s,t$, whereas direct expansion of $\frac12(A-iB)(s+it)+\frac12(A+iB)(s-it)$ gives the same expression. Thus

$$ Df(h)=(\partial_z f)h+(\partial_{\bar z}f)\overline h. $$

A real-differentiable map is **antiholomorphic** on $U$ when $\partial_z f=0$ at every point of $U$. Thus its differential is conjugate-linear at every point; no complex differentiability is asserted unless the other Wirtinger derivative also vanishes.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $\Omega,\Omega'\subseteq\mathbb C$ be complex domains ([[def-complex-domain]]) and $f:\Omega\to\Omega'$ a homeomorphism ([[def-homeomorphism-and-open-maps]]). Read $f$ as a map into $\mathbb R^2$; continuity makes its components locally square integrable. Recall that $W^{1,2}_{\rm loc}(\Omega)$ ([[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]) means that the components of $f$ admit weak first partial derivatives ([[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]) in $L^2_{\rm loc}$; equivalently, their almost-everywhere classes have ACL representatives in both coordinate directions whose measurable classical coordinate derivatives belong to $L^2_{\rm loc}$ ([[def-absolute-continuity-on-almost-every-coordinate-line]], [[thm-acl-characterisation-of-w-one-p]]). ACL alone does not assert this derivative integrability. Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) is included in AC for the completed-product Fubini interfaces. On almost every coordinate line the continuous map $f$ agrees almost everywhere with its ACL representative, hence everywhere by continuity of both restrictions; its classical line derivatives then represent its weak derivatives.

Let $K\ge1$ and put $k=(K-1)/(K+1)\in[0,1)$. The homeomorphism $f$ is **$K$-quasiconformal in the analytic sense** when

(A1) $f\in W^{1,2}_{\rm loc}(\Omega)$; and

(A2) its weak Wirtinger derivatives $\partial_zf,\partial_{\bar z}f$ ([[def-wirtinger-derivatives]]) lie in $L^2_{\rm loc}(\Omega)$ and satisfy
$$|\partial_{\bar z}f(z)|\le k|\partial_zf(z)|\qquad\text{for almost every }z\in\Omega.$$

The inequality is a statement about $L^2_{\rm loc}$ classes: it is independent of the choice of representative of $f$ and of the Borel representatives of its weak Wirtinger derivatives, since each such representative agrees almost everywhere with its class ([[lem-weak-derivative-is-independent-of-lp-representatives]]). The map is **analytically quasiconformal** if it is $K$-analytically quasiconformal for some finite $K$. Its minimal constant is recovered from the Beltrami coefficient defined later on this page.

**Orientation and the regularity requirement.** Inequality (A2) gives $J_f=|\partial_zf|^2-|\partial_{\bar z}f|^2\ge(1-k^2)|\partial_zf|^2\ge0$ almost everywhere, with respect to planar Lebesgue measure ([[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]). A classical derivative inequality alone does not replace (A1): on $(0,1)^2$, the map $f(x+iy)=x+g(x)+iy$, where $g$ is the Cantor function, is a homeomorphism onto $(0,2)\times(0,1)$ ([[lem-x-plus-the-cantor-function-is-a-homeomorphism-from-zero-one-onto-zero-two]]). The Cantor function is continuous, nonconstant, and locally constant off the null Cantor set, so $g'=0$ almost everywhere ([[thm-cantor-function-properties]], [[cor-cantor-set-is-an-uncountable-lebesgue-null-set]]). Thus the classical Wirtinger derivatives are $\partial_zf=1$ and $\partial_{\bar z}f=0$ almost everywhere. But $g$ cannot be absolutely continuous on every compact subinterval of $(0,1)$: the fundamental theorem would make it constant there, and then continuity would contradict $g(0)=0$, $g(1)=1$ ([[thm-fundamental-theorem-of-calculus-for-absolutely-continuous-functions]]). Subtracting the identity shows that $f$ fails ACL on every horizontal line and therefore fails (A1). Its classical inequality is not the weak-derivative assertion (A2). Orientation preservation follows from (A1) together with (A2), as proved by the equivalence theorem on this page.

derivations.claim: Define the locally finite Borel measure $\omega(E)=\operatorname{area}(h(E))$. This is a measure because a homeomorphism maps disjoint Borel sets to disjoint Borel sets and respects unions. It is Radon because it is the pushforward of planar area by the homeomorphism $h^{-1}$; compact and open approximation transport through that homeomorphism. The open image $h(B(x,r))$ contains $B(h(x),l(x,r))$: otherwise a segment from $h(x)$ to a point of that smaller disk outside the image would first meet the boundary $h(\partial B(x,r))$, contradicting the definition of $l$. The maximum distance from $h(x)$ in $h(\overline{B(x,r)})$ occurs on its boundary, because distance from a fixed point has no maximum in a nonempty open set. Hence $|h(y)-h(x)|\le L(x,r)\le H l(x,r)$ for $y\in\overline{B(x,r)}$, and $\pi l(x,r)^2\le\omega(B(x,r))$.

For $x\in V$ and $0<|t|<\operatorname{dist}(V,\partial U)/2$, use step 1.1 with radius $2|t|$ to obtain $|h(x+te_i)-h(x)|^2\le(H^2/\pi)\omega(B(x,2|t|))$. These balls lie in $U$. Tonelli, applied to their incidence indicator, gives $\int_V\omega(B(x,2|t|))\,dx=\int_U|V\cap B(y,2|t|)|\,d\omega(y)\le4\pi t^2\omega(U)$. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Consequently [F2]'s extension is exactly the ideal-boundary homeomorphism, and $x_n\to a$ ideally implies $f(x_n)\to h(a)$ whenever $(x_n)$ runs to infinity along a geodesic ray. An isometry with identity boundary action fixes intersections of complete geodesics and is the identity. Proof, step 1.1: We first give the model geometry used below. Translations, complex rotations and positive dilations act by $(z,s)\mapsto(az+b,|a|s)$ and preserve the metric by substitution. Euclidean inversion in the unit sphere, followed by reflection in a vertical plane, is $(z,s)\mapsto(-\overline z/(|z|^2+s^2),s/(|z|^2+s^2))$ and extends $z\mapsto-1/z$. These maps generate all Möbius transformations: a matrix with nonzero lower-left entry gives a translation, an inversion, a complex dilation and a translation by elementary fraction division; a zero lower-left entry gives an affine map. Thus every boundary Möbius transformation extends to an isometry. The Cayley map $T(z,s)=(2\operatorname{Re}z,2\operatorname{Im}z,|z|^2+s^2-1)/(|z|^2+(s+1)^2)$ is a bijection onto the unit ball, with inverse $z=2(u_1+iu_2)/Q$, $s=(1-|u|^2)/Q$, $Q=u_1^2+u_2^2+(1-u_3)^2$. It carries $(0,1)$ to the origin and gives metric $4|du|^2/(1-|u|^2)^2$: its Euclidean length factor is $2/(|z|^2+(s+1)^2)$ and $1-|T|^2=4s/(|z|^2+(s+1)^2)$. Radial integration in the ball, together with $|(|u|)'|\le|u'|$ on every competing path, gives distance $2\operatorname{artanh}|u|$ from the origin. Applying the affine normalization of a general basepoint yields $\cosh d((z,s),(w,t))=\frac{|z-w|^2+s^2+t^2}{2st}.$ Equality in that radial length argument characterizes the radial segment. Its inverse Cayley image shows that geodesics are the vertical lines and the Euclidean semicircles orthogonal to the boundary. In particular geodesics are unique, closed bounded hyperbolic balls are compact by the displayed formula, and the ideal endpoints of a complete geodesic are its distinct Euclidean boundary endpoints. A complete geodesic is uniquely determined by those endpoints. Consequently an isometry with identity boundary action preserves every complete geodesic and fixes the intersection of two distinct complete geodesics through each point; it is the identity. Thus the Möbius extension constructed above is unique. [given, algebra]

The exact equal-circle source-center comparison uses arcosh(5/3)=log3 and includes all positive radii. Proof, step 7.1: Postcompose $f$ by the isometry extending a Möbius transformation that sends $h(\infty)$ to $\infty$; its quasi-isometry constants do not change. The normalized boundary map restricts to a plane homeomorphism. For distinct finite $z,a$, the center of $(z,a,\infty)$ is $c(z,a)=((z+a)/2,\sqrt3|a-z|/2),$ by the affine isometry in step 1.1. If $|a-z|=|b-z|=r$, these two source centers have equal height $\sqrt3r/2$ and horizontal separation at most $r$. Their distance is at most $\operatorname{arcosh}(5/3)=\log3$ by the distance formula. Step 6.1 and the quasi-isometry inequality give $d(c(hz,ha),c(hz,hb))\le2C(D)+\lambda\log3+\varepsilon$. Height logarithms differ by at most hyperbolic distance, so $\left|\log\frac{|h(a)-h(z)|}{|h(b)-h(z)|}\right|\le2C(D)+\lambda\log3+\varepsilon.$ The compact source circle maps injectively to a compact curve missing $h(z)$, so its maximum and positive minimum exist. Taking them in this inequality proves the claimed all-circle bound with $H=\exp(2C(D)+\lambda\log3+\varepsilon)$. This establishes a bounded equal-radius distortion, not merely a Hölder bound. [step 1.1, step 6.1, algebra]

To see this, send one vertex to the center of the ball by the isometries in step 1.1; the two other vertices and that center lie in a Euclidean plane through the center. Reflection in that plane is a ball isometry, and uniqueness of geodesics makes its fixed plane totally geodesic. In its upper-half-plane coordinates $(x,y)$, the Christoffel formula [F3] gives $\Gamma^x_{xy}=\Gamma^x_{yx}=-1/y$, $\Gamma^y_{xx}=1/y$, $\Gamma^y_{yy}=-1/y$, and all other symbols zero. Thus for the global positive orthonormal frame $e_1=y\partial_x$, $e_2=y\partial_y$, one has $
abla_{e_1}e_1=e_2$, $
abla_{e_1}e_2=-e_1$, $
abla_{e_2}e_1=
abla_{e_2}e_2=0$ and $[e_1,e_2]=-e_1$. Consequently $R(e_1,e_2)e_2=-e_1$ and $K=-1$. Finally equivariance follows either by taking ideal limits along rays or by the composition property in [F2]; the exact equality $f\gamma=\theta(\gamma)f$ implies $h\gamma=\theta(\gamma)h$. No converse extension theorem for an arbitrary boundary quasiconformal map is asserted. citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC for the projection-family proof below. For $\lambda\ge1$, $\varepsilon\ge0$ and $\delta\ge0$, the image of every possibly discontinuous $(\lambda,\varepsilon)$-quasi-geodesic map of a nonempty compact real interval into a geodesic $\delta$-slim space has Hausdorff distance at most
$$M=92\lambda^2(\varepsilon+3\delta)$$
from every geodesic with the same endpoints. No properness is assumed.

Assume AC for the Morse/coarse-inverse proof. A quasi-isometry between geodesic hyperbolic spaces induces a homeomorphism of their Gromov-sequence boundaries; bounded-distance maps induce the same map and extensions respect composition. Properness is needed for the compact ray-boundary package, not imposed on this sequence statement.

Assume AC. Let $X$ be a nonempty proper geodesic space with a product hyperbolicity constant $\kappa\ge0$, and fix $o\in X$. Proper means every closed ball of positive finite radius is compact. Every Gromov-sequence class has a geodesic ray representative $r:[0,\infty)\to X$ with $r(0)=o$, represented by $(r(n))_{n\ge1}$. The quotient of these rays by finite Hausdorff distance, with the topology induced from uniform convergence on bounded parameter intervals, is homeomorphic to the Gromov-sequence boundary with its product topology. In particular the boundary is compact, including when it is empty.

In coordinates for a Riemannian metric with matrix $(g_{ij})$ and inverse $(g^{ij})$, its Levi–Civita symbols are
$$\Gamma^k{}_{ij}=\tfrac12\sum_\ell g^{k\ell}(\partial_i g_{j\ell}+\partial_j g_{i\ell}-\partial_\ell g_{ij}).$$

Assume the axiom of choice. Let $(M,g,J)$ be an oriented Riemannian surface and let $T\subseteq M$ be a
compact regular oriented disk region with exactly three vertices whose boundary
is the cyclic concatenation of three regular $C^2$ embedded geodesic segments
of the interior metric; at each vertex the incoming and outgoing one-sided unit
tangents are not antipodal. Suppose that a neighbourhood of $T$ carries a
smooth positive orthonormal frame and that $T$ is positively oriented as a disk
region. If $\alpha,\beta,\gamma\in(0,2\pi)$ are the interior sector angles at
the three vertices, then

$$\int_TK\,dA=\alpha+\beta+\gamma-\pi .$$

The boundary orientation is the outward-normal-first orientation of
[[def-regular-oriented-surface-region-with-piecewise-smooth-boundary]], and no
claim is made about the existence of such a triangle on a general surface.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $h:\mathbb C\to\mathbb C$ be an orientation-preserving homeomorphism. For $x\in\mathbb C$ and $r>0$, put $L(x,r)=\max_{|y-x|=r}|h(y)-h(x)|$ and $l(x,r)=\min_{|y-x|=r}|h(y)-h(x)|$. Suppose $L(x,r)\le H l(x,r)$ for every $x,r$, with one fixed $1\le H<\infty$. Then $h\in W^{1,2}_{\mathrm{loc}}$, its continuous representative is ACL, and it is analytically $H$-quasiconformal:
$$|h_{\bar z}|\le\frac{H-1}{H+1}|h_z|\quad\hbox{almost everywhere}.$$
For relatively compact open sets $V\Subset U\Subset\mathbb C$, a coordinate unit vector $e_i$ and $0<|t|<\operatorname{dist}(V,\partial U)/2$, one has the explicit estimate
$$\int_V\left|\frac{h(x+te_i)-h(x)}t\right|^2\,dx\le4H^2\operatorname{area}(h(U)).$$

The same argument applies to every fixed $x\in\ell$.

citations.quote: Use the upper half-space model $$ \mathbb H^3=\{(x+iy,t):x,y\in\mathbb R,\ t>0\},\qquad ds^2=t^{-2}(dx^2+dy^2+dt^2), $$ whose ideal boundary is $\mathbb C\cup\{\infty\}$. An oriented ideal tetrahedron in normalized position has ideal vertices $0,1,\infty,z$, where $\operatorname{Im}z>0$. Its three edge-shape parameters are $$ z,\qquad z'=\frac1{1-z},\qquad z''=\frac{z-1}{z}, $$ each assigned to one pair of opposite edges; the parameter at a corner of a truncated ideal vertex triangle is the parameter of the incident edge. For an oriented path $\gamma$ in a triangulated torus link of ideal vertices, its cusp multiplier $H(\gamma)$ is the product of the corner parameters encountered along $\gamma$, using the parameter when the path cuts off that corner on its left and its reciprocal when it cuts off the corner on its right.

For an oriented ideal tetrahedron with normalized vertices $0,1,\infty,z$ and $\operatorname{Im}z>0$, its three edge-shape parameters are $z$, $z'=1/(1-z)$, and $z''=(z-1)/z$. They satisfy $zz'z''=-1$, and their arguments in $(0,\pi)$ are the three dihedral angles, whose sum is $\pi$. For $\omega=e^{i\pi/3}$, the choice $z=\omega$ gives $z=z'=z''=\omega$ and all six dihedral angles equal to $\pi/3$.

derivations.claim: The positive shapes determine nondegenerate ideal tetrahedra. The face maps are hyperbolic isometries. Around each finite edge, the edge product $1$ makes the accumulated complex similarity the identity, and the $2\pi$ angle sum removes a cone angle. Thus the tetrahedra glue to a smooth hyperbolic metric away from the ideal vertex. Horospherical truncations give Euclidean triangles on the torus link; their face identifications are Euclidean similarities, maps of the form $x\mapsto aRx+b$ with $a>0$, $R$ a rotation, and have no cone singularities. They define a Euclidean similarity structure: an atlas with these transition maps. Its linear holonomy, the product $aR$ accumulated around a loop, need not yet be trivial.

For a loop $\gamma$ on the link, the linear part of its similarity holonomy is $H(\gamma)$: transporting a tangent vector across each corner multiplies it by the corner parameter or its reciprocal according to the side used. The basis loops have multiplier $1$, so the linear holonomy is trivial on $\pi_1(T)$, since every loop is a word in that basis.

Trivial linear holonomy lets a Euclidean metric in one similarity chart be transported consistently to every chart: two transport paths differ by a loop, whose linear holonomy is the identity by step 1.2. An oriented ideal tetrahedron in normalized position has ideal vertices $0,1,\infty,z$, where $\operatorname{Im}z>0$. Its three edge-shape parameters are $$ z,\qquad z'=\frac1{1-z},\qquad z''=\frac{z-1}{z}, $$ each assigned to one pair of opposite edges; the parameter at a corner of a truncated ideal vertex triangle is the parameter of the incident edge. For an oriented path $\gamma$ in a triangulated torus link of ideal vertices, its cusp multiplier $H(\gamma)$ is the product of the corner parameters encountered along $\gamma$, using the parameter when the path cuts off that corner on its left and its reciprocal when it cuts off the corner on its right.
For real $\theta$, define the Lobachevsky function $$ \Lambda(\theta)=-\int_0^\theta \log|2\sin u|\,du, $$ where the integral is interpreted improperly at zeros of $\sin u$.

For every real $\theta$, $\Lambda$ is continuous, odd, and $\pi$-periodic, with $\Lambda(\pi/2)=0$ and $$ \Lambda(2\theta)=2\Lambda(\theta)+2\Lambda(\theta+\pi/2). $$ For $0\le\theta\le\pi$, $$ \Lambda(\theta)=\frac12\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{\sin(2n\theta)}{n^2}. $$ In particular, $$ \Lambda(\pi/3)=\frac{\sqrt3}{4}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \left(\frac1{(3k+1)^2}-\frac1{(3k+2)^2}\right). $$ For every integer $N\ge1$, the positive remainder after the terms $k=0,\ldots,N$ is at most $\sqrt3/(72N^2)$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the inherited Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let
$(M,g)$ be a connected, boundaryless, finite-dimensional Riemannian manifold
that is complete and whose sectional curvature satisfies $K\le0$ at every
tangent two-plane. Then for every $p\in M$:

1. the exponential map $\exp_p:T_pM\to M$ is a smooth covering map when its
   domain carries the pulled-back metric $\tilde g:=\exp_p^*g$;
2. $(T_pM,\tilde g)$ is complete and $T_pM$ is simply connected, so $\exp_p$ is
   a **universal cover** of $M$;
3. if in addition $M$ is simply connected, then $\exp_p$ is a diffeomorphism
   for every $p$, and $M$ is diffeomorphic to the Euclidean space $T_pM$.

The curvature sign is the one of [[def-sectional-curvature]], so $K\le0$
includes the flat case; no lower bound on curvature, no compactness and no
dimension restriction (other than finiteness) are assumed. The completeness of
$(T_pM,\tilde g)$ is a conclusion, not a hypothesis: without it the pulled-back
metric need not be complete even for a local diffeomorphism of a complete
manifold.

Assume exactly $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $(M,g)$ be a smooth Riemannian
manifold without boundary, let $p\in M$, let $v\in\mathcal E_p$ be in the
domain of $\exp_p$, and let $w\in T_pM$. Define
$$\gamma:[0,1]\to M,\qquad \gamma(t)=\exp_p(tv).$$
There is a unique Jacobi field $J$ along $\gamma$ with
$$J(0)=0,\qquad D_tJ(0)=w,$$
where the derivative at $0$ is one-sided. For every $t\in[0,1]$,
$$J(t)=d(\exp_p)_{tv}(tw),$$
using the canonical identification $T_{tv}(\mathcal E_p)\cong T_pM$,
and in particular $d(\exp_p)_v(w)=J(1)$. The exponential differential is
evaluated at points $tv\in\mathcal E_p$, as ensured by the geodesic-time
scaling property. Constant central geodesics, zero initial data, and dimension
zero are included. No completeness hypothesis is imposed.

This item assumes $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, namely [[def-countable-choice|countable choice]]. In the propagated dependency chain, that assumption is required through [[def-constant-sectional-curvature-and-space-form]]; the tensor-determination argument is choice-free.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ as inherited through
[[def-constant-sectional-curvature-and-space-form]]; the algebraic proof below
uses no additional choice. A Riemannian manifold has constant sectional
curvature $K$ if and only if

$$R(X,Y)Z=K\bigl(g(Y,Z)X-g(X,Z)Y\bigr).$$

Equivalently,

$$\operatorname{Rm}(X,Y,Z,W)=K\bigl(g(Y,Z)g(X,W)-g(X,Z)g(Y,W)\bigr).$$

Let $\gamma:I\to M$ be smooth on an interval, with smooth one-sided data at included endpoints. For every $t_0\in I$ and $v_0\in E_{\gamma(t_0)}$ there is exactly one parallel section $V$ on all of $I$ with $V(t_0)=v_0$. The same holds for a piecewise smooth curve on a compact interval, with continuity at its finitely many corners. A singleton carries its prescribed vector. No AC is required for a supplied connection and curve.

Let $(M,g)$ be an $n$-dimensional Riemannian manifold, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$
be an interval with nonempty interior, and let $\gamma:I\to M$ be an
affinely parametrized geodesic. For every $a\in I$ and every
$v,w\in T_{\gamma(a)}M$, there is exactly one smooth Jacobi field $J$ along
all of $\gamma$ such that
$$J(a)=v,\qquad D_tJ(a)=w.$$
If $a$ is an included endpoint, $D_tJ(a)$ is interpreted one-sided. Constant
geodesics and dimension zero are included. The result requires no completeness,
compactness of $I$, or axiom of choice.

Levi–Civita parallel transport preserves inner products, lengths, angles of nonzero vectors, and Riemannian volume density. If the manifold is oriented, it also preserves its oriented Riemannian volume form. Without a supplied global orientation only density preservation is claimed.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. On $\mathbb H^3=\{(z,s):z\in\mathbb C,\ s>0\}$ use the metric $s^{-2}(|dz|^2+ds^2)$. Suppose $f:\mathbb H^3\to\mathbb H^3$ is a quasi-isometry with constants $\lambda\ge1$, $\varepsilon\ge0$:
$$\lambda^{-1}d(x,y)-\varepsilon\le d(f(x),f(y))\le\lambda d(x,y)+\varepsilon,$$
and with coarsely dense image. Then it induces an ideal-boundary homeomorphism $h:\widehat{\mathbb C}\to\widehat{\mathbb C}$. There is $H=H(\lambda,\varepsilon)<\infty$ such that, after postcomposition by any Möbius transformation carrying $h(\infty)$ to $\infty$, its plane restriction satisfies
$$\max_{|a-z|=r}|h(a)-h(z)|\le H\min_{|a-z|=r}|h(a)-h(z)|\qquad(z\in\mathbb C,\ r>0).$$
Here $h$ in that inequality denotes the normalized map. If the boundary homeomorphism preserves orientation, it is analytically quasiconformal in sphere charts, with constant at most $H$. If it reverses orientation, postcomposition with complex conjugation is quasiconformal with that constant. If $f$ is equivariant for a homomorphism between groups of hyperbolic isometries, its boundary map is equivariant for their boundary actions.

For an oriented ideal tetrahedron with normalized vertices $0,1,\infty,z$ and $\operatorname{Im}z>0$, its three edge-shape parameters are $z$, $z'=1/(1-z)$, and $z''=(z-1)/z$. They satisfy $zz'z''=-1$, and their arguments in $(0,\pi)$ are the three dihedral angles, whose sum is $\pi$. For $\omega=e^{i\pi/3}$, the choice $z=\omega$ gives $z=z'=z''=\omega$ and all six dihedral angles equal to $\pi/3$.

For $0<\zeta<\pi/2$, let $$ \mathcal O_\zeta= \{(x+iy,t)\in\mathbb H^3: 0\le x\le\cos\zeta,\quad 0\le y\le x\tan\zeta,\quad t\ge\sqrt{1-x^2-y^2}\}. $$ Its hyperbolic volume in the upper half-space metric is $\frac12\Lambda(\zeta)$.

For every real $\theta$, $\Lambda$ is continuous, odd, and $\pi$-periodic, with $\Lambda(\pi/2)=0$ and $$ \Lambda(2\theta)=2\Lambda(\theta)+2\Lambda(\theta+\pi/2). $$ For $0\le\theta\le\pi$, $$ \Lambda(\theta)=\frac12\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{\sin(2n\theta)}{n^2}. $$ In particular, $$ \Lambda(\pi/3)=\frac{\sqrt3}{4}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \left(\frac1{(3k+1)^2}-\frac1{(3k+2)^2}\right). $$ For every integer $N\ge1$, the positive remainder after the terms $k=0,\ldots,N$ is at most $\sqrt3/(72N^2)$.

derivations.claim: Apply a Euclidean similarity of the boundary plane, extended by the same scaling of height, sending the circumcircle of the three finite ideal vertices to the unit circle centered at $0$; this upper half-space isometry fixes $\infty$. The three vertices become points $p,q,r$ on that circle and remain equilateral. Hence $(0,0)$ lies in the interior of their triangle, so the vertical ray from $(0,0,1)$ to $\infty$ lies inside the tetrahedron.

On the unit-hemisphere face, draw the perpendicular arcs from $(0,0,1)$ to its three edges and the arcs from $(0,0,1)$ to $p,q,r$. Cone the six resulting sectors to $\infty$. Because the vertical ray lies in the tetrahedron, the six simplices have disjoint interiors and cover the tetrahedron; their common faces have three-dimensional volume zero. Each simplex has two finite vertices and two ideal vertices. Its three right dihedral angles come from the perpendicular cuts; among its other angles, two equal the corresponding original tetrahedron edge angle $\zeta$ and the third is $\pi/2-\zeta$. The tetrahedron is regular, so [F2] gives $\zeta=\pi/3$ for each of the six simplices.

Normalize one simplex by a hyperbolic isometry so its ideal vertices are $\infty$ and $(\cos\zeta,\sin\zeta)$ and one finite vertex is $(0,0,1)$. The three right angles place the projected right-angle vertex at $(\cos\zeta,0)$: the two legs are horizontal and vertical. The angle at the origin is $\zeta$, so the other ideal point has coordinates $(\cos\zeta,\sin\zeta)$. The projected triangle is the intersection of the half-planes $x\ge0$, $y\ge0$, $x\le\cos\zeta$ and $y\le x\tan\zeta$. The unit hemisphere through $(0,0,1)$ has equation $x^2+y^2+t^2=1$, and the tetrahedral side is above it. Thus the simplex is exactly $\mathcal O_\zeta$ from [F3] with $\zeta=\pi/3$.

By [F3], each of the six simplices has volume $\frac12\Lambda(\pi/3)$. Their interiors are disjoint and their union is the tetrahedron up to faces of volume zero, so additivity gives $\operatorname{Vol}=6\cdot\frac12\Lambda(\pi/3)=3\Lambda(\pi/3)$. Substitution of the absolutely convergent series in [F4] gives the second displayed expression; absolute convergence follows by comparison with $\sum_{n\ge1}n^{-2}$.
