The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Every nonempty connected oriented complete Riemannian three-manifold of constant sectional curvature $-1$ is isometric to $\Gamma\backslash\mathbb H^3$ for a discrete torsion-free subgroup $\Gamma\le\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb C)$. The covering is a universal Riemannian covering and identifies $\Gamma$ with the fundamental group up to the usual basepoint conjugacies. Its completeness and quotient presentation are conclusions from the stated metric hypotheses. The orientation-preserving isometry group of the model is $\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb C)$ with its usual Möbius boundary action.

Assume AC. Use the upper half-space model $\mathbb H^3=\{(z,y):z\in\mathbb C,y>0\}$ with metric $(|dz|^2+dy^2)/y^2$. Let $\Gamma\le\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb C)$ be discrete and torsion-free, and suppose that it contains a subgroup $A\cong\mathbb Z^2$. Then $A$ fixes a unique ideal point. After conjugating that point to infinity, its full stabilizer $P=\operatorname{Stab}_\Gamma(\infty)$ consists of translations by a lattice $\Lambda\le\mathbb C$ of rank two. It is the unique maximal abelian subgroup containing $A$.

For a sufficiently large $R$, the quotient of the closed horoball $\{y\ge R\}$ by $P$ embeds properly in $M=\Gamma\backslash\mathbb H^3$. Its boundary is a compact torus, its interior is a cusp, and its volume is $\operatorname{area}(\mathbb C/\Lambda)/(2R^2)$. If $M$ has exactly one topological end, the complement of the open cusp has compact closure.

No finite-volume thin decomposition, abstract peripheral recognition, or rigidity theorem is assumed or concluded here. The rank-two subgroup and the quotient presentation of $M$ are hypotheses.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $(M,g)$ be a **nonempty**, connected,
boundaryless Riemannian manifold, and let $d=d_g$ be its Riemannian distance.
The following conditions are equivalent.

1. The metric space $(M,d)$ is complete.
2. The Riemannian manifold $(M,g)$ is geodesically complete.
3. For every $p\in M$, the fibre exponential domain is all of the tangent
   space: $\mathcal E_p=T_pM$.
4. There is a point $p_0\in M$ for which $\mathcal E_{p_0}=T_{p_0}M$.
5. Every closed bounded subset of the metric space $(M,d)$ is compact.

Whenever these conditions hold, every $x,y\in M$ are joined by a minimizing
geodesic. More exactly, there is $v\in T_xM$ with
$$
\exp_x(v)=y,\qquad |v|_{g_x}=d(x,y),
$$
and $t\mapsto\exp_x(tv)$ on $[0,1]$ has length $d(x,y)$.

The nonemptiness hypothesis is essential for this formulation: on the empty
manifold conditions 1--3 and 5 are vacuous, whereas condition 4 is false.

The **Riemannian volume density** is $\mu_g=\sqrt{\det G_x}\,|dx^1\cdots dx^n|$ in coordinates.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a $C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable $f : V \to [0,\infty]$, $$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then $$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

A compact orientable three-manifold $M$ is **irreducible** if every embedded $2$-sphere in its interior bounds an embedded $3$-ball in $M$. A properly embedded surface is **incompressible** if it admits no embedded disk whose interior misses the surface and whose boundary is an essential simple closed curve in it. A boundary subsurface is **$\pi_1$-injective** if the inclusion of each component induces an injection on fundamental groups. A **pared pair** is a pair $(M,P)$ in which $M$ is compact, orientable and irreducible, and $P$ is a possibly empty compact subsurface of $\partial M$ whose pairwise disjoint components are $\pi_1$-injective annuli or tori, every noncyclic abelian subgroup of $\pi_1(M)$ is conjugate into $\pi_1$ of a component of $P$ up to base-path conjugacy, and every map of pairs $$ (S^1\times I,S^1\times\partial I)\longrightarrow(M,P) $$ that induces injections on fundamental groups is homotopic through maps of pairs into $P$, so its boundary remains in $P$ during the homotopy. Write $\partial_0M=\partial M\setminus\operatorname{int}P$. A **horoball** is a region bounded by a horosphere, a Euclidean plane or sphere tangent to the ideal boundary at one point. The **peripheral subgroup** for a component of $P$ is the image of its fundamental group in $\pi_1(M)$, recorded up to conjugacy. A **hyperbolic structure** on $(M,P)$ is a curvature $-1$ metric on $\operatorname{int}M$ described by an atlas of charts into $\mathbb H^3$ whose transition maps are in $\operatorname{Isom}^+(\mathbb H^3)$. Its developing map $\operatorname{dev}$ from the universal cover and holonomy homomorphism $\rho:\pi_1(M)\to\operatorname{Isom}^+(\mathbb H^3)$ satisfy $\operatorname{dev}(gx)=\rho(g)\operatorname{dev}(x)$. The metric is **complete** when it is geodesically complete. A **cusp** corresponding to a component of $P$ is a quotient of a horoball by the associated peripheral subgroup. The hyperbolic volume is the integral of the Riemannian volume density over $\operatorname{int}M$; the structure has **finite volume** when this integral is finite.

derivations.claim: Since $f$ is an isometry, $f^*g_N=g_M$. In any coordinate charts, if $J=Df$ is the coordinate derivative, then the metric matrices satisfy $G_M=J^{\mathsf T}(G_N\circ f)J$. Taking determinants gives $\sqrt{\det G_M}=|\det J|\sqrt{\det(G_N\circ f)}$. Thus $f$ pulls the Riemannian volume density of $N$ back to that of $M$, regardless of whether it preserves orientation.

For each point of $M$, choose a coordinate neighborhood $U_j$ whose image under $f$ lies in a coordinate neighborhood $V_j$ of $N$. Second countability and [A1] give a countable such cover $(U_j)_{j\ge1}$. Make it disjoint by setting $A_1=U_1$ and $A_j=U_j\setminus\bigcup_{i<j}U_i$; these are Borel, disjoint and cover $M$. In coordinates on $U_j,V_j$, apply [F2] to the nonnegative measurable function equal to the target density times the indicator of $f(A_j)$. The Jacobian identity in step 1.1 yields $\operatorname{Vol}_M(A_j)=\operatorname{Vol}_N(f(A_j))$. The sets $f(A_j)$ are disjoint and cover $N$.

The indicators of the finite unions $\bigcup_{j\le n}A_j$ increase to $1_M$. By [F3] and [F4], the volume of $M$ is the limit of the sums $\sum_{j\le n}\operatorname{Vol}_M(A_j)$, and the same holds for $N$ and the sets $f(A_j)$. These finite sums agree term by term by step 2.1; their limits therefore agree in $[0,\infty]$. If one volume is finite, their common value is finite.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable) has a choice function.

Assume countable choice. Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth knot with a chosen closed tubular neighborhood $N(K)$, and let $E_K=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$. Every smoothly embedded two-sphere in the interior of $E_K$ bounds a smoothly embedded closed three-ball contained in $E_K$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth knot that is not ambient isotopic to the standard unknot, let $E_K$ be its chosen compact exterior, and let $T_K=\partial E_K$. There is no properly embedded disk $D\subset E_K$ whose boundary is a simple closed curve in $T_K$ that is not null-homotopic in $T_K$.

citations.quote: The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

Let $M$ be a compact smooth $3$-manifold. A properly embedded surface is **two-sided** if it has a product neighbourhood $F\times[-1,1]$ in $M$. A **compressing disk** for a two-sided surface $F$ is an embedded disk $D\subset M$ with $\operatorname{int}(D)\cap F=\varnothing$ and $\partial D$ an essential simple closed curve in $F$; $F$ is **incompressible** if it has no compressing disk. A **boundary-compressing disk** is an embedded disk $D$ with $\partial D=\alpha\cup\beta$, where $\alpha=D\cap F$ is an arc not cutting off a disk in $F$, $\beta=D\cap\partial M$, and $\operatorname{int}(D)$ misses $F\cup\partial M$; $F$ is **boundary-incompressible** if it has no such disk. A surface is **boundary-parallel** if it cobounds a product with a subsurface of $\partial M$, and it is **essential** if it is incompressible, boundary-incompressible, and not boundary-parallel. $M$ is **irreducible** if every embedded $2$-sphere in its interior bounds an embedded $3$-ball in $M$. An incompressible torus is boundary-parallel if it cobounds a product $T^2\times[0,1]$ with a component of $\partial M$; $M$ is **atoroidal** if every incompressible torus is boundary-parallel. A **Seifert fibration** is a decomposition into circles with local models given by fibered solid tori; in the model $(D^2\times S^1)/\langle(z,w)\mapsto(e^{2\pi i/q}z,e^{2\pi ip/q}w)\rangle$, where $\gcd(p,q)=1$, the core fiber has multiplicity $q$. Fibers of multiplicity $1$ are **regular** and those of multiplicity greater than $1$ are **exceptional**. A finite family of pairwise disjoint incompressible tori is a **JSJ system** if every component obtained by cutting $M$ along the family is atoroidal or Seifert-fibered. It is **inclusion-minimal** if no proper subfamily is a JSJ system. Atoroidal does not mean hyperbolic.
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following statement.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K:S^1\to S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot with a chosen product tubular neighbourhood $N(K)$, and set $E_K=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$ and $T_K=\partial E_K$. If $K$ is not ambient isotopic through orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms to the standard unknot, then every smoothly embedded $2$-sphere in $\operatorname{int}E_K$ bounds an embedded $3$-ball in $E_K$, and there is no smoothly embedded disk $D\subset E_K$ whose interior misses $T_K$ and whose boundary is an essential simple closed curve in $T_K$.

If $\pi_1(T)\to\pi_1(M)$ had nontrivial kernel, [F1] would supply an essential simple curve in $T$ bounding a proper disk in $M$, contradicting boundary incompressibility. Hence $\pi_1(M)$ contains the injected group $\pi_1(T)\cong\mathbb Z^2$ and is infinite.

The given embedded-torus atoroidality and the hypothesis that $M$ is not Seifert-fibered allow [F2] to be applied. Therefore every $\pi_1$-injective torus map is homotopic into $\partial M$. All hypotheses of [F3] now hold for this actual $M$, so $\operatorname{int}(M)$ admits a complete finite-volume metric of constant sectional curvature $-1$. This applies to fibered knot exteriors as well as nonfibered ones; no additional non-interval-bundle assumption has been introduced.

The interior of a compact connected manifold with one connected boundary component has one end: a boundary collar gives a cofinal family of connected complements of compact subsets, namely $T\times(0,\epsilon)$. By [F4], every end of the metric from step 1.2 is a rank-two horoball quotient, so there is exactly one torus cusp. It belongs to the unique original boundary end. The action identifies $G$ with the oriented orthonormal frame bundle: in the ball model an orientation-preserving isometry can send the center to any point by an upper half-space affine map after Cayley conjugation, and its stabilizer acts as every rotation; an isometry fixing a frame fixes each geodesic with its initial velocity and is the identity. Give $K$ normalized bi-invariant volume from the Ad-invariant inner product $-\operatorname{tr}(XY)$ on $\mathfrak{so}(3)$. Integrating this probability measure on each frame fiber against hyperbolic volume defines a smooth positive measure on $G$. It is independent of the local frame section, since changes of section are rotations, and is left-$G$-invariant, since $G$ acts isometrically on the base and by rotations on the fibers. citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Every nonempty connected oriented complete Riemannian three-manifold of constant sectional curvature $-1$ is isometric to $\Gamma\backslash\mathbb H^3$ for a discrete torsion-free subgroup $\Gamma\le\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb C)$. The covering is a universal Riemannian covering and identifies $\Gamma$ with the fundamental group up to the usual basepoint conjugacies. Its completeness and quotient presentation are conclusions from the stated metric hypotheses. The orientation-preserving isometry group of the model is $\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb C)$ with its usual Möbius boundary action.

Assume AC. Let $M$ be a nonempty connected oriented complete Riemannian three-manifold of constant curvature $-1$ and finite volume. Then $M$ is a compact core together with finitely many pairwise disjoint standard torus cusp ends. Each end is an embedded quotient $\{y>R_i\}/\Lambda_i$ of a horoball by a rank-two translation lattice, and the complement of these open ends is compact. The number of cusps may be zero. In particular, the standard cusp decomposition in the general rigidity construction follows from the complete finite-volume metric, with no knot or triangulation assumption.

Assume AC. Let $M=\Gamma\backslash\mathbb H^3$ and $N=\Gamma'\backslash\mathbb H^3$ be connected orientable hyperbolic manifolds, with discrete torsion-free groups. Suppose each is a compact core together with finitely many disjoint standard torus cusp ends: an end is an embedded quotient $\{y>R_i\}/\Lambda_i$ by a rank-two translation lattice, and the complement of the union of these ends is compact. Zero ends are allowed, in which case the manifold is compact.

Every group isomorphism $\theta:\Gamma\to\Gamma'$ permutes the conjugacy classes of the peripheral cusp groups. There is a smooth $\theta$-equivariant quasi-isometry $F:\mathbb H^3\to\mathbb H^3$ which on every sufficiently deep lifted cusp is affine in its horizontal coordinates and preserves cusp depth after a constant height rescaling. It has a smooth equivariant quasi-inverse with inverse affine cusp maps. On quotient manifolds these maps are proper homotopy equivalences.

The standard cusp decomposition is a supplied hypothesis here; this lemma does not derive it merely from finite volume.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. On $\mathbb H^3=\{(z,s):z\in\mathbb C,\ s>0\}$ use the metric $s^{-2}(|dz|^2+ds^2)$. Suppose $f:\mathbb H^3\to\mathbb H^3$ is a quasi-isometry with constants $\lambda\ge1$, $\varepsilon\ge0$:
$$\lambda^{-1}d(x,y)-\varepsilon\le d(f(x),f(y))\le\lambda d(x,y)+\varepsilon,$$
and with coarsely dense image. Then it induces an ideal-boundary homeomorphism $h:\widehat{\mathbb C}\to\widehat{\mathbb C}$. There is $H=H(\lambda,\varepsilon)<\infty$ such that, after postcomposition by any Möbius transformation carrying $h(\infty)$ to $\infty$, its plane restriction satisfies
$$\max_{|a-z|=r}|h(a)-h(z)|\le H\min_{|a-z|=r}|h(a)-h(z)|\qquad(z\in\mathbb C,\ r>0).$$
Here $h$ in that inequality denotes the normalized map. If the boundary homeomorphism preserves orientation, it is analytically quasiconformal in sphere charts, with constant at most $H$. If it reverses orientation, postcomposition with complex conjugation is quasiconformal with that constant. If $f$ is equivariant for a homomorphism between groups of hyperbolic isometries, its boundary map is equivariant for their boundary actions.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $G=\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb C)$ act on the Riemann sphere by Möbius transformations. Let $\Gamma\le G$ be discrete, with finite nonzero Haar quotient measure $\nu$ on $X=\Gamma\backslash G$. Here Haar quotient measure means the right invariant Radon measure obtained by locally transporting Haar measure through the covering projection $G\to X$; its normalization is immaterial. Let $\theta:\Gamma\to G$ be a homomorphism, and let $h:\widehat{\mathbb C}\to\widehat{\mathbb C}$ be an orientation-preserving quasiconformal homeomorphism satisfying $h\circ\gamma=\theta(\gamma)\circ h$ for every $\gamma\in\Gamma$. Then $h$ is Möbius.

This statement assumes the existence of the quasiconformal boundary conjugacy. It does not assert that an abstract group isomorphism or a quasi-isometry produces one.

Assume countable choice. Let $M$ and $N$ be second-countable oriented hyperbolic three-manifolds, and let $f:M\to N$ be an isometry. Then
$$
\int_M d\operatorname{vol}_M=\int_N d\operatorname{vol}_N.
$$
In particular, if either volume is finite, then both are finite and the values agree.

A relatively compact open disk in that plane with disjoint nontrivial translates gives an embedded positive-area product disk times all $r>0$, or both sides identified by a possible side reversal; either way its volume is infinite. Both alternatives contradict finite volume. Thus the full centralizer is trivial. Two isometries inducing the same outer isomorphism have lifts whose induced isomorphisms agree after a target deck transformation. Their quotient then centralizes $\Gamma$, so they are equal.

The descended $F$ and $I$ are properly homotopic. Indeed, every point of $\mathbb H^3$ is the center of an ordered ideal triangle: take the center of $(0,1,\infty)$ and send it to the point by an isometry. By the uniform triangle-center bound in [F2], $F$ is at bounded distance from $\widetilde I$ on every point, because the latter sends each such center exactly to its boundary-image center. Unique geodesics give an equivariant homotopy with bounded tracks. On the quotients this is proper: $F$ is proper by [F1], and a track meeting a compact set has its initial point in a fixed compact metric neighborhood of that set. The quotient hyperbolic manifolds are complete and proper, as in [F1]'s proof.

Let $g:M\to N$ be any proper homotopy equivalence inducing the same outer isomorphism. Choose a lift $\widetilde g$ inducing $\theta$. On every sufficiently deep source cusp, properness puts its image outside any prescribed compact target core, hence in a single target cusp component. The induced injection of its peripheral group is $\theta(P_i)$, so the peripheral recognition in [F1] identifies that component as the same one used by $I$. The lift of that connected tail consequently lies in the corresponding target horoball; its boundary ideal point is the one fixed by $\theta(P_i)$. For any deeper target horoball, properness gives a still deeper source tail with image in it: avoidance of the enlarged compact target core is uniform on the compact source torus cross-sections. The isometry $I$ has the same property. Horoballs are geodesically convex, so the pointwise geodesic homotopy from $\widetilde g$ to $\widetilde I$ stays inside that arbitrarily deep target horoball on sufficiently deep source tails. On the remaining compact source core the homotopy has compact image by continuity. Thus the homotopy descends and is proper. This includes zero cusps, when both manifolds are compact and every homotopy is proper.

A proper homotopy preserves the degree on locally finite top homology, or equivalently on compactly supported top cohomology: pulling back a compactly supported orientation class through a proper homotopy gives the same class by the prism homotopy with compact preimage. For a homotopy equivalence of connected oriented manifolds that degree is $+1$ or $-1$ and detects its orientation. Thus step 3.2 gives the asserted agreement of orientation. Finally apply [F4] to the isometry from step 2.1; its countable-choice premise follows from AC. The two Riemannian volume integrals agree.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume AC. Let $M$ and $N$ be nonempty connected oriented complete finite-volume Riemannian three-manifolds of constant curvature $-1$. There is no knot, compactness, or cusp-number restriction. Every isomorphism $\theta:\pi_1(M)\to\pi_1(N)$, up to conjugacy from basepoint changes, is induced by a unique isometry $I:M\to N$. The isometry is properly homotopic to every proper homotopy equivalence inducing that outer isomorphism. Its orientation agrees with that of such an equivalence, and the two Riemannian volumes are equal.

Assume countable choice, as required for the smooth normal-bundle structure in the tubular-neighbourhood interface. Let $K:S^1	o S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot, let $
u(K)=TS^3|_K/TK$ be its quotient normal bundle, and let $\Phi:\Omega	o S^3$ be a tubular-neighbourhood map from an open neighbourhood $\Omega$ of the zero section in $
u(K)$ that restricts to the inclusion of $K$. Choose a radius $\epsilon>0$ whose closed disk subbundle $D_\epsilon
u(K)$ is contained in $\Omega$, and set $N(K)=\Phi(D_\epsilon
u(K))$. The **exterior** of this chosen tube is $$ E_K:=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}_{S^3}N(K). $$ Retain its boundary $T_K:=\partial E_K=\partial N(K)$, orient $E_K$ by restriction of the fixed orientation of $S^3$, and orient $T_K$ as the boundary of $E_K$. The choice of tubular map and radius is part of the input to this definition.

Let $M$ be a compact smooth $3$-manifold. A properly embedded surface is **two-sided** if it has a product neighbourhood $F\times[-1,1]$ in $M$. A **compressing disk** for a two-sided surface $F$ is an embedded disk $D\subset M$ with $\operatorname{int}(D)\cap F=\varnothing$ and $\partial D$ an essential simple closed curve in $F$; $F$ is **incompressible** if it has no compressing disk. A **boundary-compressing disk** is an embedded disk $D$ with $\partial D=\alpha\cup\beta$, where $\alpha=D\cap F$ is an arc not cutting off a disk in $F$, $\beta=D\cap\partial M$, and $\operatorname{int}(D)$ misses $F\cup\partial M$; $F$ is **boundary-incompressible** if it has no such disk. A surface is **boundary-parallel** if it cobounds a product with a subsurface of $\partial M$, and it is **essential** if it is incompressible, boundary-incompressible, and not boundary-parallel. $M$ is **irreducible** if every embedded $2$-sphere in its interior bounds an embedded $3$-ball in $M$. An incompressible torus is boundary-parallel if it cobounds a product $T^2\times[0,1]$ with a component of $\partial M$; $M$ is **atoroidal** if every incompressible torus is boundary-parallel. A **Seifert fibration** is a decomposition into circles with local models given by fibered solid tori; in the model $(D^2\times S^1)/\langle(z,w)\mapsto(e^{2\pi i/q}z,e^{2\pi ip/q}w)\rangle$, where $\gcd(p,q)=1$, the core fiber has multiplicity $q$. Fibers of multiplicity $1$ are **regular** and those of multiplicity greater than $1$ are **exceptional**. A finite family of pairwise disjoint incompressible tori is a **JSJ system** if every component obtained by cutting $M$ along the family is atoroidal or Seifert-fibered. It is **inclusion-minimal** if no proper subfamily is a JSJ system. Atoroidal does not mean hyperbolic.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $E_K$ be the compact connected orientable exterior of a smooth knot in $S^3$, with one torus boundary component. If $E_K$ is irreducible, its boundary is incompressible, $E_K$ is atoroidal, and $E_K$ is not Seifert-fibered, then $\operatorname{int}(E_K)$ admits a complete finite-volume Riemannian metric of constant sectional curvature $-1$ with one torus cusp. No conclusion is asserted for a torus or satellite knot unless its exterior satisfies all four topological hypotheses.

derivations.claim: The action preserves $|z|^2+|w|^2$, so it acts smoothly on $S^3$. The orbit of $(2^{-1/2},2^{-1/2})$ is exactly $K$. A group element stabilizes this point only if $3\theta$ and $2\theta$ are both multiples of $2\pi$; coprimality of $2$ and $3$ makes the stabilizer trivial. The regions $|z|\le|w|$ and $|w|\le|z|$ are solid tori, parametrized respectively by $(z,w)=(z,\sqrt{1-|z|^2}\eta)$ and $(z,w)=(\sqrt{1-|w|^2}\eta,w)$ with the disk coordinate bounded by $2^{-1/2}$ and $\eta\in S^1$. The $w$ coordinate is the core direction of the first solid torus and winds twice along $K$; the $z$ coordinate is the core direction of the second and winds three times. This proves the claimed $(3,2)$ torus-knot type. On the axis $z=0$ the stabilizer has order $2$, and on the axis $w=0$ it has order $3$.

On $zw\ne0$, write $\alpha=\arg z$ and $\beta=\arg w$ modulo $2\pi$. The integer coordinate change $\theta=\alpha-\beta$, $\phi=2\alpha-3\beta$ has determinant $-1$ and is invertible on the phase torus. The circle action changes $\theta$ by its parameter and fixes $\phi$, while $r=|z|\in(0,1)$ is fixed; thus the quotient of this open set is the cylinder with coordinates $(r,\phi)$, and the inverse image of any disk $D$ around $q(K)$ in it is explicitly $S^1_\theta\times D$. At $r=0$ and $r=1$ the phase circle collapses to one point at each end, so the full orbit space is a sphere; the two axis orbits have stabilizer orders $2$ and $3$. The complement of $D$ is a disk with those two cone points. Its orbits give the fibers of $E_K$, and [F2] identifies the axis fibers as exceptional of orders $2$ and $3$.

Choose a basepoint $x$ on a regular fiber, let $h$ be that fiber loop, and let $\gamma$ be any loop in $E_K$ based at $x$. The map $F:[0,1]^2\to E_K$ defined by $F(s,t)=g_{2\pi s}(\gamma(t))$ is well-defined because the tube is invariant. Its boundary represents $h\gamma h^{-1}\gamma^{-1}$: the two vertical sides are $\gamma$ and $\gamma^{-1}$ since $g_0=g_{2\pi}=\operatorname{id}$, and the horizontal sides are the fiber loop and its reverse. The square contracts its boundary, so $h$ commutes with $[\gamma]$. Since $\gamma$ was arbitrary, the regular fiber class is central in $\pi_1(E_K)$.

By [F3], a Seifert-fibered exterior does not satisfy the required non-Seifert-fibered hypothesis. Step 2.1 establishes that $E_K$ is Seifert-fibered, so this example refutes the statement that every knot exterior is non-Seifert-fibered and also fails that hypothesis of the hyperbolization contract.

Define the standard figure-eight knot $K_8$ to be the oriented closure of the three-strand geometric braid $(\sigma_1\sigma_2^{-1})^2$. Its endpoint permutation is a $3$-cycle, so this closure has one component.

Let $\Delta_0=[0,1,2,3]$ and $\Delta_1=[0',1',2',3']$ be oriented ideal tetrahedra with orientation-reversing affine face maps
$$
[0,1,2]\to[3',1',2'],\quad
[0,1,3]\to[0',1',2'],\quad
[0,2,3]\to[0',1',3'],\quad
[1,2,3]\to[0',2',3'].
$$
This is the two-tetrahedron ideal triangulation obtained from the standard four-crossing figure-eight diagram by cutting along crossing arcs, identifying upper and lower polyhedron faces with equal region labels, and collapsing the two bigon faces. Its edge classes are
$$
\{01,02,23,0'1',1'3',2'3'\},\qquad
\{12,03,13,1'2',0'2',0'3'\};
$$
each has valence six, and the unique ideal vertex link is a torus. Put shape $z_1$ on $01,23$, shape $z_2$ on $03,12$, and shape $z_3$ on $02,13$ in $\Delta_0$; put shape $w_1$ on $0'1',2'3'$, shape $w_2$ on $0'3',1'2'$, and shape $w_3$ on $0'2',1'3'$ in $\Delta_1$. Unfold the eight cusp-link triangles by the face maps into the standard rectangular strip, and label them $a,b,c,d,e,f,g,h$ from left to right; identify the strip boundary sides as prescribed by those same maps. Let $\alpha$ be the edge path across the strip from the left side of $a$ on the left boundary to the left side of $a$ on the right boundary, and let $\beta$ be the edge path on the left boundary from the base of $a$ to the top of $h$. Their ordered corner factors are respectively $z_3,w_2^{-1},z_2,w_3^{-1},z_3,w_2^{-1},z_2,w_3^{-1}$ and $z_2^{-1},w_1$. The face-pairing incidence check gives one positive transverse intersection, so their homology classes form a basis of $H_1$ and the loops form a basis of $\pi_1$ of the torus link. The two edge products are $z_1^2z_3w_1^2w_3$ and $z_2^2z_3w_2^2w_3$, while
$$
H(\alpha)=\left(\frac{z_2z_3}{w_2w_3}\right)^2,\qquad H(\beta)=\frac{w_1}{z_2}.
$$
For $\omega=e^{i\pi/3}$, assigning $z_1=z_2=z_3=w_1=w_2=w_3=\omega$ makes both edge products and both cusp multipliers equal to $1$ and gives total angle $2\pi$ around each edge. The gluing therefore gives the figure-eight complement a complete finite-volume curvature $-1$ metric with one peripheral torus cusp.

Every regular ideal tetrahedron in hyperbolic three-space has volume
$$
v_3=3\Lambda(\pi/3)
=\frac{3\sqrt3}{4}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}
\left(\frac1{(3k+1)^2}-\frac1{(3k+2)^2}\right).
$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $M$ and $N$ be interiors of compact connected oriented knot exteriors carrying complete finite-volume hyperbolic metrics. Every isomorphism $\pi_1(M)\to\pi_1(N)$, considered up to the conjugacy induced by basepoint changes, is realized by a unique isometry in the corresponding proper homotopy class. If the isomorphism is induced by an orientation-preserving proper homotopy equivalence, the isometry preserves orientation. In particular, the two metrics have equal volume, where volume is the integral of their Riemannian volume densities.

For every real $\theta$, $\Lambda$ is continuous, odd, and $\pi$-periodic, with $\Lambda(\pi/2)=0$ and
$$
\Lambda(2\theta)=2\Lambda(\theta)+2\Lambda(\theta+\pi/2).
$$
For $0\le\theta\le\pi$,
$$
\Lambda(\theta)=\frac12\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{\sin(2n\theta)}{n^2}.
$$
In particular,
$$
\Lambda(\pi/3)=\frac{\sqrt3}{4}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}
\left(\frac1{(3k+1)^2}-\frac1{(3k+2)^2}\right).
$$
For every integer $N\ge1$, the positive remainder after the terms $k=0,\ldots,N$ is at most $\sqrt3/(72N^2)$.

derivations.claim: Let $p,q\in\mathbb Z$ satisfy $\gcd(p,q)=1$. Bézout's identity gives $r,s\in\mathbb Z$ with $ps-qr=1$. The matrix with columns $(p,q)$ and $(r,s)$ lies in $\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb Z)$, so it induces a homeomorphism of $\mathbb R^2/\mathbb Z^2$. The image of the first coordinate circle is embedded, essential, and represents $p[\mu]+q[\lambda]$. Reversing its parameter negates both coefficients, so the unoriented curve is unchanged.

If $\gamma$ is an essential simple closed curve on $T$, it is nonseparating; cutting along it gives an annulus. An arc joining the two annulus boundary circles closes to a simple curve $\delta$ meeting $\gamma$ once, so the algebraic intersection is $[\gamma]\cdot[\delta]=\pm1$. Writing $[\gamma]=p[\mu]+q[\lambda]$ and $[\delta]=a[\mu]+b[\lambda]$ gives $pb-qa=\pm1$ because the ordered basis has intersection form $\pm1$. Any common divisor of $p,q$ would divide $pb-qa$, so $\gcd(p,q)=1$.

Suppose $\gamma_0,\gamma_1$ are essential simple closed curves whose primitive classes agree up to sign. Reverse one orientation if necessary so their classes agree, and isotope them to be transverse. Let $v$ be their common primitive class and let $A=\mathbb R^2/\langle T_v\rangle$ be the cyclic cover of $T$ corresponding to the subgroup generated by $v$. A lift of each curve to $A$ is an embedded essential circle representing the generator of $H_1(A;\mathbb Z)$. Their algebraic intersection in the annulus $A$ is zero, so if they meet the signed crossing count in a fundamental period has both signs. Lift these circles to the universal cover $\mathbb R^2$ of $A$. Their chosen lifts are proper lines invariant under the same translation $T_v$; they have the same two ends at infinity. Opposite-sign crossings on this pair of lines have a bounded complementary disk between subarcs, by the Jordan curve theorem. Among all such disks choose one with the fewest interior intersections with lifted curves, and among ties one of least transverse width modulo the deck translations. Any lifted arc entering its interior cuts off a disk with fewer interior intersections; any nontrivial translate meeting it yields a disk of smaller transverse width. Thus its interior misses every lift and translate, so it projects injectively to an embedded bigon in $T$. Isotoping one curve across this bigon removes exactly two intersections and creates none. Since the original intersection set is finite, repetition terminates and makes the curves disjoint. Cutting $T$ along $\gamma_0$ gives an annulus, and the disjoint essential curve $\gamma_1$ is parallel to its core, so the two curves cobound a subannulus. Isotopy across that annulus carries $\gamma_0$ to $\gamma_1$. Thus the primitive class modulo simultaneous sign determines exactly one unoriented isotopy class.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume countable choice, as required for the smooth normal-bundle structure in the tubular-neighbourhood interface. Let $K:S^1\to S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot, let $\nu(K)=TS^3|_K/TK$ be its quotient normal bundle, and let $\Phi:\Omega\to S^3$ be a tubular-neighbourhood map from an open neighbourhood $\Omega$ of the zero section in $\nu(K)$ that restricts to the inclusion of $K$. Choose a radius $\epsilon>0$ whose closed disk subbundle $D_\epsilon\nu(K)$ is contained in $\Omega$, and set $N(K)=\Phi(D_\epsilon\nu(K))$. The **exterior** of this chosen tube is
$$
E_K:=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}_{S^3}N(K).
$$
Retain its boundary $T_K:=\partial E_K=\partial N(K)$, orient $E_K$ by restriction of the fixed orientation of $S^3$, and orient $T_K$ as the boundary of $E_K$. The choice of tubular map and radius is part of the input to this definition.

Work in the smooth category ([[def-smooth-manifold]]). Fix once and for all the
three-sphere as the one-point compactification

$$S^3:=\mathbb R^3\cup\{\infty\}$$

of Euclidean three-space, carrying its standard smooth structure, and fix the
standard orientation of $S^3$: the orientation induced by the standard
orientation of $\mathbb R^3$ under the one-point compactification, so that the
charts of the standard atlas away from $\infty$ are orientation-preserving and
the orientation is that of a connected oriented $3$-manifold in the sense of
[[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]]. For $r>0$ write
$\overline B_r:=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:\lVert x\rVert_2\le r\}$, the closed ball of
[[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]] with the following restriction convention. Smoothness on a closed ball means
local extension to a smooth map on an open neighborhood in Euclidean space;
smoothness on $M\times I$, for a smooth manifold $M$ without boundary, means
local extension across $t=0,1$ in $M\times\mathbb R$. Thus these closed domains
are not asserted to be manifolds without boundary in the cited definition.

**Links.** The **standard oriented circle** is the circle
$S^1=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ with its standard counterclockwise orientation,
regarded as a smooth $1$-manifold; a
**finite disjoint union of oriented circles** is a smooth manifold
$C=S^1\sqcup\dots\sqcup S^1$ ($k$ summands, $k\in\mathbb N$)
diffeomorphic to the disjoint union of $k$ standard oriented circles. An
**oriented link** (with $k$ components) is a smooth embedding

$$L\colon C\longrightarrow S^3$$

of such a disjoint union in the sense of [[def-smooth-embedding]]. So $L$ is
injective, is an immersion, and is a homeomorphism onto its image with the
subspace topology, and its image $L(C)$ is a finite disjoint union of smoothly
embedded circles. Thus every link considered here is finite and tame: the
smoothness of $L$ is exactly the standing convention, and no polygonal or other
tame model is used. The **components** of $L$ are the images of the individual
summands, and the number of components is $k$.

**Ambient isotopy.** Let $I=[0,1]$. An **ambient isotopy** of $S^3$ is a smooth
map

$$H\colon S^3\times I\longrightarrow S^3$$

such that $H_0=\mathrm{id}_{S^3}$, each $H_t\colon S^3\to S^3$,
$H_t(x):=H(x,t)$, is a diffeomorphism ([[def-diffeomorphism-and-local-diffeomorphism-of-manifolds]]),
and each $H_t$ is orientation-preserving with respect to the fixed orientation.
The last clause is in fact automatic: $t\mapsto H_t$ is continuous in the
$C^\infty$ topology of the diffeomorphism group, the orientation sign is locally
constant in $t$, and $H_0=\mathrm{id}$ is orientation-preserving, so it is kept
only for emphasis.

**Equivalence of links.** Two oriented links $L_0\colon C_0\to S^3$ and
$L_1\colon C_1\to S^3$ are **equivalent** (written $L_0\sim L_1$), or
**ambient isotopic**, when there are an ambient isotopy $H$ and an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism $f:C_0\to C_1$ with
$H_1\circ L_0=L_1\circ f$. Thus parametrizations and component labels are
irrelevant, while the induced orientation of each image component is preserved. The relation is an equivalence relation on links:
it is reflexive with $H=\mathrm{id}$, transitive by composing isotopies, and
symmetric because a smooth family of diffeomorphisms has a smooth family of
inverses. An equivalence class is an **(oriented) link type**.

**Moving off $\infty$.** Because the definition of equivalence allows the
isotopy to move a link through $\infty$, the standard practice of this page is
to first apply an ambient isotopy that carries a given link into the open ball,
and only then to project; every projection and every Reidemeister move below is
read after moving the link off $\infty$ into $\mathbb R^3$ in this way. The
orientation-preserving clause in the definition of ambient isotopy is exactly
what the oriented Reidemeister moves and the oriented closure construction must
respect. The unoriented theory uses the same ambient isotopies but forgets
the orientations of the link components.

**Links in the three-sphere versus links in $\mathbb R^3$.** A link contained in
$\mathbb R^3\subset S^3$ is a link in $S^3$; conversely every link may be
assumed after isotopy to lie in $\mathbb R^3$, by choosing a point outside the compact one-dimensional image and moving that
point to $\infty$ by a smooth rotation of the standard sphere. When comparing
links already in $\mathbb R^3$, an isotopy can also be arranged to avoid
$\infty$ throughout; the track-avoidance argument is given in
[[thm-oriented-reidemeister-equivalence-theorem]].

derivations.claim: In $S^3=\{(z_1,z_2)\in\mathbb C^2:|z_1|^2+|z_2|^2=1\}$, the standard Hopf link is $H=\{z_1z_2=0\}$. On its complement, $f(z_1,z_2)=z_1z_2/|z_1z_2|$ is a submersion to $S^1$. Writing $r=|z_1|^2$, $\theta=\arg z_1$, and $\phi=\arg z_2$, a fiber is $0<r<1$, $\phi=-\theta+\text{constant}$, hence an annulus. For base angle $s\in[0,2\pi]$, transport by $\theta_s=\theta+\chi(r)s$, $\phi_s=\phi+(1-\chi(r))s$, where $\chi=1$ near $r=0$ and $\chi=0$ near $r=1$, fixes both boundary circles at $s=2\pi$ and makes one full annular twist between them. The sign is determined by the signed linking of the positive normal push-off of the core with the core: changing the handedness of the Hopf band reverses the twist. With $a\cdot_F b=+1$, the positive twist about $a$ acts by $b\mapsto a+b$, while the negative twist about $b$ acts by $a\mapsto a+b$. Hence the two band monodromies have the stated actions $R_a$ and $L_b$.

Cutting a fibered exterior open along its page gives page $\times[0,1]$, with the two ends reidentified by the monodromy. In the square plumbing, the two annulus pages meet in the plumbing square $D$ and their product collars meet in $D\times[0,1]$. The interval coordinates agree on this product, so gluing the cut-open product pieces gives $(A\mathbin{\natural_D}B)\times[0,1]=F\times[0,1]$, where $A\mathbin{\natural_D}B$ denotes the surface obtained by gluing the two annuli along $D$. Reidentifying the interval ends extends each band map by the identity outside its annulus. The first return map is the composition in the stipulated plumbing order; choosing the positive band first gives $R_a\circ L_b$. The boundary knot is the standard figure-eight isotopy class by the specified plumbing presentation and [F2], and the chosen exterior is formed by deleting the binding neighborhood as in [F1]. Thus the exterior is the mapping torus of $F$ with that monodromy.

Each annulus has Euler characteristic $0$, and the plumbing square has Euler characteristic $1$, so $\chi(F)=0+0-1=-1$. The plumbing is connected, oriented, and has one boundary component by the stated gluing; hence $\chi(F)=1-2g(F)$ gives $g(F)=1$. Thus $F$ is a once-punctured torus.

In the ordered basis $([a],[b])$, the columns of $R_a$ are $(1,0)$ and $(1,1)$, while the columns of $L_b$ are $(1,1)$ and $(0,1)$. Their product is $\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1&1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$. Inclusion of the once-punctured torus into the torus obtained by capping its sole boundary induces an isomorphism on $H_1$, since attaching a disk along the boundary adds no 1-cycle or 2-cycle relation in degree one. Extending the boundary-fixing monodromy by the identity on that disk therefore has the same displayed action.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in the oriented $3$-sphere, let $N(K)$ be a chosen closed tubular solid-torus neighborhood, let $E_K=\overline{S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)}$, and let $T_K=\partial E_K=\partial N(K)$. Let $\mu$ be the positive oriented meridian, meaning the boundary of a positive normal disk in $N(K)$, and let $\lambda$ be a preferred longitude, meaning a degree-one parallel of the core $K$ in $N(K)$ that is null-homologous in $E_K$. Assume that $[\mu],[\lambda]$ are an ordered basis of $H_1(T_K;\mathbb Z)$, with the boundary-orientation convention $\mu\cdot\lambda=-1$. A slope is the unoriented isotopy class of an essential simple closed curve on $T_K$ whose homology class is $p[\mu]+q[\lambda]$ for coprime integers $p,q$ not both zero; $(p,q)$ and $(-p,-q)$ represent the same slope. For a slope represented by $p[\mu]+q[\lambda]$, the Dehn filling $E_K(p/q)$ is obtained by gluing an oriented solid torus $D^2\times S^1$ to $E_K$ by an orientation-reversing boundary homeomorphism that sends $[\partial D^2\times\{1\}]$ to that slope; the filled orientation agrees with the fixed orientation on $E_K$. If $q\ne0$, the coefficient is written $p/q$; the meridional slope is $1/0$, and integer $n$-framed filling means slope $n[\mu]+[\lambda]$. The oriented homeomorphism type is independent of the gluing map once its meridian image is fixed.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K:S^1	o S^3$ be a smooth oriented embedding and write its quotient normal bundle as $
u_K=K^*TS^3/dK(TS^1)$. Choose an orientation-preserving trivialization $
u_K\cong S^1	imes\mathbb R^2$ and a tubular map $\Phi:\Omega	o S^3$, meaning a smooth embedding from an open neighbourhood $\Omega\subseteq
u_K$ of the zero section onto an open neighbourhood of $K(S^1)$ with $\Phi(s,0)=K(s)$, such that in these product coordinates $\Omega$ contains $S^1	imes D^2_{2\epsilon}$ for some $\epsilon>0$. Here $D^2_r=\{z\in\mathbb R^2:\|z\|\le r\}$. Set $N(K)=\Phi(S^1	imes D^2_\epsilon)$, $E_K=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$, $T_K=\partial E_K$, and let $i:T_K\hookrightarrow E_K$ be inclusion, $p:T_K	o S^1$ the product projection, and $\mu$ the positive boundary of a normal disk, using the normal-plane orientation determined by the orientations of $K$ and $S^3$. A class is primitive if it is not $m$ times another class for any integer $|m|>1$. Then $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$ is generated by $[\mu]$. The kernel of $i_*:H_1(T_K;\mathbb Z)	o H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$ is a primitive rank-one direct summand generated by a unique class $[\lambda]$ with $p_*[\lambda]=1\in H_1(S^1;\mathbb Z)$. It has a simple closed representative, is the preferred longitude, and $([\mu],[\lambda])$ is a basis of $H_1(T_K;\mathbb Z)$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice for the chosen smooth knot-exterior data. Let $K_8$ be the standard figure-eight knot, presented as the boundary of the square plumbing of one positive and one negative Hopf band, with one boundary component. A positive Hopf band is an oriented annulus whose positive normal push-off of its core has linking number $+1$ with the core; a negative Hopf band has linking number $-1$. A square plumbing identifies a square in the boundary collars of the annuli with the four boundary edges alternating between the annuli, then smooths corners. Let $F$ be this plumbed surface, and choose the compact exterior by deleting the interior of the binding neighborhood $N(K_8)\cong\partial F\times D^2$ supplied by the open book; on every page this neighborhood meets the page in an annular collar of $\partial F$. Let $a,b$ be the core curves, ordered so that $a$ is the positive-band core and $a\cdot_F b=+1$. The exterior $E_{K_8}$ fibers over $S^1$ with fiber $F$. With the twist convention that the positive twist $R_a$ sends $a\mapsto a$, $b\mapsto a+b$, and the negative twist $L_b$ sends $a\mapsto a+b$, $b\mapsto b$, the monodromy is $R_a\circ L_b$. After capping $\partial F$ by a disk, its action on the ordered homology basis $([a],[b])$ is represented by $\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$.

Let $\overline M$ be a compact connected oriented three-manifold whose boundary is a disjoint union of tori $T_1,\ldots,T_k$. Choose an ordered integral basis $([\mu_i],[\lambda_i])$ for each $H_1(T_i;\mathbb Z)$. A **slope** on $T_i$ is an unoriented isotopy class of essential simple closed curves whose homology class is $p_i[\mu_i]+q_i[\lambda_i]$ for a primitive pair $(p_i,q_i)\in\mathbb Z^2$; simultaneous negation gives the same unoriented slope. The primitive-pair correspondence gives exactly one such slope for each primitive pair modulo sign. The **ordinary Dehn filling** along a tuple of slopes indexed by $J\subseteq\{1,\ldots,k\}$ attaches an oriented solid torus $D^2\times S^1$ to each $T_i$, $i\in J$, by an orientation-reversing boundary homeomorphism that sends $[\partial D^2\times\{*\}]$ to the chosen slope. The gluing maps are part of the filling data; $i\notin J$ means that the cusp is left unfilled, denoted by the parameter $\infty$.

For a hyperbolic deformation, the **generalized cone-filling parameter space** at each cusp is the one-point compactification $\mathbb R^2\cup\{\infty\}$ of the real coefficient plane, with $\infty$ denoting the complete cusp. A primitive integral pair $(p_i,q_i)$ is an ordinary smooth filling coefficient. If a realized generalized parameter lies on the ray $g_i=r_i(p_i,q_i)$ with $r_i>0$ and $(p_i,q_i)$ primitive integral, its topological core direction is the ordinary slope $(p_i,q_i)$ and its cone angle is $2\pi/r_i$. Only $r_i=1$ is the ordinary smooth filling; $r_i>1$ describes a cone or orbifold completion and does not turn the nonprimitive vector $g_i$ into a slope.

derivations.claim: By [F2] and [A1], the needed countable-choice hypothesis [F1] holds. Let $F$ be the fiber from [F5]. Cutting the exterior along $F$ gives $F\times[0,1]$, with its interval ends reidentified by the monodromy $\varphi$; because $\varphi$ fixes $\partial F$ pointwise, the boundary torus is identified with $\partial F\times S^1$.

The curve $\partial F$ on the peripheral torus is an essential parallel of the knot and bounds the fiber in the exterior, so its homology class maps to zero in $H_1(E_{K_8};\mathbb Z)$. It is primitive because it is a simple essential curve. By uniqueness in [F4], it represents $\lambda$ up to orientation, hence it is exactly the unoriented filling slope $0$ by [F3].

Write the filling solid torus as $D^2\times S^1$, using its second coordinate for the mapping-torus direction. Its meridian disk boundary is identified with $\partial F\times\{t\}$ by [F3] and step 2.1. The filling is therefore the mapping torus of $\overline F=F\cup_{\partial F}D^2$: extend $\varphi$ over the added disk by the identity. This extension is continuous and fixes the seam because $\varphi|_{\partial F}=\mathrm{id}$. If the chosen boundary gluing differs by a twist along the meridian slope, that twist extends over $D^2\times S^1$ by rotating the disk as the second coordinate varies, so it does not change the resulting bundle up to homeomorphism.

The surface $\overline F$ is obtained from a once-punctured torus by capping its sole boundary component with a disk, so it is a closed torus. The mapping torus of the extended homeomorphism $\overline\varphi$ is consequently a torus bundle over $S^1$. Inclusion $F\hookrightarrow\overline F$ induces an isomorphism on first homology, and the extension is the identity on the cap, so its matrix remains the matrix in [F5].

A compact orientable three-manifold $M$ is **irreducible** if every embedded $2$-sphere in its interior bounds an embedded $3$-ball in $M$. A properly embedded surface is **incompressible** if it admits no embedded disk whose interior misses the surface and whose boundary is an essential simple closed curve in it. A boundary subsurface is **$\pi_1$-injective** if the inclusion of each component induces an injection on fundamental groups. A **pared pair** is a pair $(M,P)$ in which $M$ is compact, orientable and irreducible, and $P$ is a possibly empty compact subsurface of $\partial M$ whose pairwise disjoint components are $\pi_1$-injective annuli or tori, every noncyclic abelian subgroup of $\pi_1(M)$ is conjugate into $\pi_1$ of a component of $P$ up to base-path conjugacy, and every map of pairs
$$
(S^1\times I,S^1\times\partial I)\longrightarrow(M,P)

Assume the inherited Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let
$(M,g)$ be a connected, boundaryless, finite-dimensional Riemannian manifold
that is complete and whose sectional curvature satisfies $K\le0$ at every
tangent two-plane. Then for every $p\in M$:

1. the exponential map $\exp_p:T_pM\to M$ is a smooth covering map when its
   domain carries the pulled-back metric $\tilde g:=\exp_p^*g$;
2. $(T_pM,\tilde g)$ is complete and $T_pM$ is simply connected, so $\exp_p$ is
   a **universal cover** of $M$;
3. if in addition $M$ is simply connected, then $\exp_p$ is a diffeomorphism
   for every $p$, and $M$ is diffeomorphic to the Euclidean space $T_pM$.

The curvature sign is the one of [[def-sectional-curvature]], so $K\le0$
includes the flat case; no lower bound on curvature, no compactness and no
dimension restriction (other than finiteness) are assumed. The completeness of
$(T_pM,\tilde g)$ is a conclusion, not a hypothesis: without it the pulled-back
metric need not be complete even for a local diffeomorphism of a complete
manifold.

Assume exactly $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ through the declared constant-curvature
interface. Let $(M,g)$ be a finite-dimensional Riemannian manifold without boundary
of constant sectional curvature $K\in\mathbb R$, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a
nondegenerate interval containing $0$, and let
$\gamma:I\to M$ be a unit-speed affinely parametrized geodesic. Put
$T=\dot\gamma$ and define
$$
s_K(t)=\begin{cases}\sin(\sqrt K\,t)/\sqrt K,&K>0,\\ t,&K=0,\\ \sinh(\sqrt{-K}\,t)/\sqrt{-K},&K<0.\end{cases}
$$
Then the normal Jacobi fields $J$ with $J(0)=0$ are exactly
$$J(t)=s_K(t)E(t),$$
where $E$ is a unique parallel normal field along $\gamma$. The tangential
Jacobi fields are exactly
$$J(t)=(at+b)\dot\gamma(t),\qquad a,b\in\mathbb R.$$

are one-sided.

A **universal covering space** of $B$ is a covering map $p:\widetilde B\to B$ whose total space $\widetilde B$ is simply connected ([[def-covering-map-and-evenly-covered-neighbourhoods]], [[def-simply-connected]]).

For a covering $p:E\to B$, a **deck transformation** is an isomorphism $h:E\to E$ over $B$, so $p\circ h=p$ ([[def-map-and-isomorphism-of-covering-spaces]]). Deck transformations form the **deck group** $\operatorname{Deck}(p)$ under composition, and this group acts on $E$ by evaluation ([[def-group]], [[def-group-action]]).

For a path-connected, locally path-connected, semilocally simply connected base $B$, the deck group of a universal cover is isomorphic to $\pi_1(B,b_0)$. With the library's traversal-order path product the monodromy action is a right action, and the assignment carrying a loop class to the deck transformation that moves the chosen point of the fibre to the corresponding lifted endpoint is itself an isomorphism; no path reversal is inserted.

An **isometry** $F:(M,g)\to(N,h)$ is a diffeomorphism with $F^*h=g$. A **local isometry** is a smooth local diffeomorphism with $F^*h=g$. An **isometric immersion** is a smooth immersion satisfying that same pullback identity.

Use [[def-pullback-riemannian-metric]] and [[def-diffeomorphism-and-local-diffeomorphism-of-manifolds]]. Positivity forces injective differential by [[prop-pullback-of-a-riemannian-metric-is-riemannian-exactly-for-immersions]]. In equal dimensions on boundaryless manifolds, the inverse function theorem as applied in the next proposition makes a metric-preserving smooth map a local isometry. At a boundary the definition retains the local-diffeomorphism requirement. An isometric immersion need not have equal source and target dimensions.

$$df\bigl(\nabla^M_XY\bigr)=\nabla^N_{f_*X}(f_*Y)\circ f$$
for all smooth vector fields $X,Y$ on $U$, where $\nabla^M$ and $\nabla^N$ are the Levi-Civita connections.

Consequently, if $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ is an interval with nonempty interior, $\gamma:I\to M$ is smooth, and $W$ is a smooth vector field along $\gamma$, then
$$D_t^N\bigl(dF_{\gamma(t)}W(t)\bigr)=dF_{\gamma(t)}\bigl(D_t^M W(t)\bigr).$$
In particular, $F\circ\gamma$ is an affinely parametrized geodesic whenever $\gamma$ is. No completeness, connectedness, surjectivity, or length-minimizing hypothesis is required.

Let $p:E\to B$ be a covering, let $\alpha:I\to B$ be a path, and let $e_0\in E$ satisfy $p(e_0)=\alpha(0)$. There is a unique path $\widetilde\alpha:I\to E$ with $\widetilde\alpha(0)=e_0$ and $p\circ\widetilde\alpha=\alpha$.

derivations.claim: The lift of the complete metric to $\widetilde M$ is complete: every geodesic upstairs projects by [F4] to a geodesic downstairs, which extends for all time; path lifting extends the original geodesic upstairs, and a local isometry preserves its geodesic equation.

By [F2], the complete simply connected universal cover $\widetilde M$ is diffeomorphic to $\mathbb R^3$. Along each radial unit-speed geodesic from a fixed point, [F3] says the differential of the exponential map multiplies angular vectors by $\sinh r$, while its radial differential preserves length. Thus in polar coordinates the pulled-back metric is $dr^2+\sinh^2(r)g_{S^2}$, the standard hyperbolic metric; the exponential map identifies $\widetilde M$ isometrically with $\mathbb H^3$. By [F4], $\Gamma=\pi_1(M)$ acts freely and properly discontinuously by deck isometries; compactness of $M$ makes the action cocompact.

Every nonidentity element of $\Gamma$ is loxodromic. A Möbius map $z\mapsto(az+b)/(cz+d)$ has fixed-point equation $cz^2+(d-a)z-b=0$ on the boundary sphere. If there are two distinct fixed points, conjugate them to $0,\infty$; the map then has form $z\mapsto \lambda z$. If $|\lambda|=1$ and $\lambda
e1$, its extension fixes the axis joining $0$ to $\infty$, contrary to the free deck action [F4]. If $|\lambda|
e1$, it preserves that axis and translates it nontrivially. If the fixed-point equation has a double root, conjugate it to $\infty$; the map has form $z\mapsto az+b$, and its only fixed point is $\infty$ precisely when $a=1$ and $b
e0$. This is parabolic: the upper-half-space distance formula gives $\cosh d((0,t),(b,t))=1+|b|^2/(2t^2)$, so its displacement tends to zero as $t	o\infty$. To exclude such a parabolic in a cocompact deck group, choose compact $K$ with $\Gamma K=\mathbb H^3$ and points $y_n$ whose displacement tends to zero. Choose $h_n\in\Gamma$ so $x_n=h_ny_n\in K$ and put $\gamma_n=h_n\gamma h_n^{-1}$. The points $x_n$ and $\gamma_nx_n$ lie in a fixed compact neighborhood of $K$, so proper discontinuity permits only finitely many $\gamma_n$. Along a subsequence this element is constant and $x_n$ converges in $K$; the displacement limit makes it fix the limit point, contradicting freeness. Hence every nonidentity element has two fixed endpoints and preserves a unique axis with nonzero translation.

Fix $\gamma\ne1$ and let $C_\Gamma(\gamma)=\{\delta\in\Gamma:\delta\gamma=\gamma\delta\}$. Commutation preserves the attracting and repelling endpoints of $\gamma$ individually, hence preserves its axis and acts there by a signed translation. The signed translation map $\tau:C_\Gamma(\gamma)\to\mathbb R$ is a homomorphism. It is injective: an element in its kernel fixes every point on the axis, and [F4] makes it the identity. Its image is discrete: if infinitely many elements had bounded signed translations, their images of a fixed point on the axis would lie in a compact segment, contradicting proper discontinuity in [F4]. Every discrete subgroup of $(\mathbb R,+)$ is cyclic, so $C_\Gamma(\gamma)$ is cyclic.

If $H\le\Gamma$ were isomorphic to $\mathbb Z^2$, choose $\gamma\in H\setminus\{1\}$. Since $H$ is abelian, $H\subseteq C_\Gamma(\gamma)$, contradicting step 4.1 because a cyclic group has no subgroup isomorphic to $\mathbb Z^2$. Therefore no such $H$ exists.

derivations.claim: For each tetrahedron, [F1] supplies a nondegenerate ideal simplex, and the assigned face maps are hyperbolic isometries because their three corresponding ideal vertices have the same cross-ratio shape. Around a finite edge, the product equation makes the accumulated complex similarity the identity, while the angle sum $2\pi$ makes the total rotation one full turn. Thus the simplices glue to a smooth curvature $-1$ metric away from the ideal vertices.

Truncate the ideal vertices by sufficiently small horospheres. Each link triangle is Euclidean, and face identifications restrict to Euclidean similarities. Around each vertex, the same edge conditions remove the truncation singularities; the two basis multipliers being $1$ imply trivial linear holonomy on its torus link, since every loop is a word in that basis. Apply [F3] to the neighborhood of each vertex separately: each end is a complete rank-two horoball quotient. There are finitely many vertices, so this proves completeness at every end.

A horospherical truncation of each ideal tetrahedron is compact and has finite volume because its smooth hyperbolic volume density is bounded on that compact region. Each removed vertex tail is contained in a rank-two horocusp and has finite volume by [F4]. There are finitely many tetrahedra and vertices, so the glued manifold has finite total volume.

The part remaining after all cusp neighborhoods are removed is a compact union of truncated tetrahedra. Let $(x_n)$ be a Cauchy sequence. If infinitely many terms lie in that compact part, a subsequence converges there and the Cauchy property forces the whole sequence to the same limit. Otherwise the sequence eventually lies in the union of the finitely many disjoint cusp ends; sufficiently deep points in distinct ends have positive separation through the compact core, so the Cauchy property forces it eventually into one end, where it converges by step 2.1. Thus the full metric is complete. Together with step 3.1 and the curvature $-1$ charts from step 1.1, this is a complete finite-volume hyperbolic structure as defined in [F5].

derivations.claim: In cylindrical coordinates $(r,\theta,z)$ about a geodesic in $\mathbb H^3$, the metric is $ds^2=dr^2+\sinh^2(r)\,d\theta^2+\cosh^2(r)\,dz^2$. The full-turn condition makes $\theta$ have period $2\pi$, while the axial translation identifies $z$ with $z+L$. Thus the developed tube quotient is $(0,\varepsilon)\times(\mathbb R/2\pi\mathbb Z)\times(\mathbb R/L\mathbb Z)$, and its meridian is exactly the $\theta$ circle representing $\mu$.

Set $x=r\cos\theta$ and $y=r\sin\theta$. Then $dr^2+\sinh^2(r)d\theta^2=dx^2+dy^2+\frac{(\sinh^2r-r^2)}{r^4}(x\,dy-y\,dx)^2$. The coefficient has the convergent even-power expansion $1/3+O(r^2)$ at $r=0$, and $\cosh^2(r)$ is smooth in $x^2+y^2$. Hence the metric extends smoothly across $x=y=0$; the added set is the circle $\mathbb R/L\mathbb Z$ and is the core of a solid torus. The extended metric has curvature $-1$ on the dense punctured tube by [F2], so its smooth curvature tensor has curvature $-1$ on the core by continuity.

By [F1], attaching a solid torus with meridian $\mu$ is precisely the ordinary filling specified by the angular circle in step 1.1. The local extension in step 2.1 agrees with the original metric on the overlap, so it defines a smooth hyperbolic metric on the filled manifold. For finitely many ends the tube neighborhoods are disjoint, and the same local extension can be performed independently at each one.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

Assume AC. Every nonempty connected oriented complete Riemannian three-manifold of constant sectional curvature $-1$ is isometric to $\Gamma\backslash\mathbb H^3$ for a discrete torsion-free subgroup $\Gamma\le\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb C)$. The covering is a universal Riemannian covering and identifies $\Gamma$ with the fundamental group up to the usual basepoint conjugacies. Its completeness and quotient presentation are conclusions from the stated metric hypotheses. The orientation-preserving isometry group of the model is $\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb C)$ with its usual Möbius boundary action.

Assume AC. Let $M$ be a nonempty connected oriented complete Riemannian three-manifold of constant curvature $-1$ and finite volume. Then $M$ is a compact core together with finitely many pairwise disjoint standard torus cusp ends. Each end is an embedded quotient $\{y>R_i\}/\Lambda_i$ of a horoball by a rank-two translation lattice, and the complement of these open ends is compact. The number of cusps may be zero. In particular, the standard cusp decomposition in the general rigidity construction follows from the complete finite-volume metric, with no knot or triangulation assumption.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $M=\Gamma\backslash\mathbb H^3$ be a connected oriented complete finite-volume hyperbolic three-manifold, with a compact smooth core $N$ and $k\ge1$ standard rank-two torus cusp ends. Thus $M$ is the interior of $N$ and each end has metric $dt^2+e^{-2t}g_i$, where $g_i$ is a flat torus metric. Let $\rho_0:\pi_1(N)\to G=\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb C)$ be its holonomy. Choose a positively oriented basis $(\mu_i,\lambda_i)$ for each oriented horotorus, so its translation lattice can be normalized to $\langle1,\tau_i^0\rangle$ with $\operatorname{Im}\tau_i^0>0$.

The germ of representations modulo conjugacy at $[\rho_0]$ is a smooth complex manifold of dimension $k$. The functions $s_i(\rho)=\operatorname{tr}^2\rho(\mu_i)$ are local holomorphic coordinates near their values $s_i=4$. Trace squared is well defined in $G$, independently of an $SL_2$ lift.

Augment a nearby representation by choosing one common invariant line for each peripheral subgroup, and quotient these data by simultaneous conjugacy. The germ of this augmented space at the complete representation and its unique peripheral fixed lines is a smooth complex $k$-manifold. It has holomorphic coordinates $u=(u_1,\ldots,u_k)$, where $u_i$ is the eigenvalue-ratio logarithm for $\mu_i$ on the selected line, and the forgetful map is
$$s_i=4\cosh^2(u_i/2).$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Apply [F1] to the given complete metric. Its one cusp has the standard quotient description needed by [F2]. First choose a positively oriented basis. Specializing [F2] to $k=1$ gives the smooth ordinary curve with coordinate $s$, the smooth augmented curve with coordinate $u$, $s=4\cosh^2(u/2)$, and the holomorphic factorization $v(u)=u\tau(u)$ with $\operatorname{Im}\tau(0)>0$. Holomorphy gives $\tau(u)=\tau(0)+O(u)$, hence the asserted first-order expansion. This uses no ideal triangulation.

For an arbitrary supplied basis, keep its first element $\mu$. If its orientation is negative, replace $\lambda$ by $-\lambda$ temporarily to apply step 1.1, then return to the supplied basis by $v\mapsto-v$ and $\tau\mapsto-\tau$. This preserves $u$, the ordinary trace coordinate, the branched forgetful map, and all deformations. It proves precisely the signed nonreal assertion for every ordered basis. A holomorphic logarithm coordinate on the ordinary curve cannot replace this augmentation: differentiating $s=4\cosh^2(u/2)$ at $u=0$ gives $ds=0$ if $u$ were a holomorphic function on that curve, contradicting that $s$ is its local coordinate.

The coefficient equation has unique real coefficients when $u\ne0$, because $1,\tau(u)$ are real-linearly independent; $u=0$ is the complete parameter. Apply [F3] for the small-solution assertion. For a negatively oriented supplied basis, the simultaneous equation is unchanged after replacing $q$ by $-q$ and $v$ by $-v$, so [F4] supplies the same geometric completion after returning to the positive basis. By [F5], primitivity is exactly the ordinary meridian convention and nonprimitive multiples do not become ordinary slopes. Thus the full analytic and ordinary-filling conclusions hold for the entire given one-cusped class.
