The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $M$ be the interior of a compact connected orientable three-manifold with $k\ge1$ torus cusps and a complete finite-volume hyperbolic metric. Choose a peripheral basis $(\mu_i,\lambda_i)$ on each cusp. On the augmented holonomy space obtained by selecting one common invariant line on each peripheral subgroup, near the complete structure write $u_i$ and $v_i$ for the logarithms of the eigenvalue ratios of the peripheral holonomies of $\mu_i$ and $\lambda_i$, with branches chosen so $u_i=v_i=0$ at the complete structure. There is a neighborhood of the complete point in the $k$ generalized parameter spheres such that primitive integral filling data $(p_i,q_i)$ in that neighborhood satisfying $p_i u_i+q_i v_i=2\pi i$ at every filled cusp produce a complete finite-volume hyperbolic structure on the ordinary filled manifold. The peripheral full-turn equations are solved simultaneously across the $k$ cusps; unfilled cusps retain their complete parabolic holonomy. No universal numeric length threshold is asserted.

Let $\overline M$ be a compact connected oriented three-manifold whose boundary is a disjoint union of tori $T_1,\ldots,T_k$. Choose an ordered integral basis $([\mu_i],[\lambda_i])$ for each $H_1(T_i;\mathbb Z)$. A **slope** on $T_i$ is an unoriented isotopy class of essential simple closed curves whose homology class is $p_i[\mu_i]+q_i[\lambda_i]$ for a primitive pair $(p_i,q_i)\in\mathbb Z^2$; simultaneous negation gives the same unoriented slope. The primitive-pair correspondence gives exactly one such slope for each primitive pair modulo sign. The **ordinary Dehn filling** along a tuple of slopes indexed by $J\subseteq\{1,\ldots,k\}$ attaches an oriented solid torus $D^2\times S^1$ to each $T_i$, $i\in J$, by an orientation-reversing boundary homeomorphism that sends $[\partial D^2\times\{*\}]$ to the chosen slope. The gluing maps are part of the filling data; $i\notin J$ means that the cusp is left unfilled, denoted by the parameter $\infty$.

For a hyperbolic deformation, the **generalized cone-filling parameter space** at each cusp is the one-point compactification $\mathbb R^2\cup\{\infty\}$ of the real coefficient plane, with $\infty$ denoting the complete cusp. A primitive integral pair $(p_i,q_i)$ is an ordinary smooth filling coefficient. If a realized generalized parameter lies on the ray $g_i=r_i(p_i,q_i)$ with $r_i>0$ and $(p_i,q_i)$ primitive integral, its topological core direction is the ordinary slope $(p_i,q_i)$ and its cone angle is $2\pi/r_i$. Only $r_i=1$ is the ordinary smooth filling; $r_i>1$ describes a cone or orbifold completion and does not turn the nonprimitive vector $g_i$ into a slope.

A compact orientable three-manifold $M$ is **irreducible** if every embedded $2$-sphere in its interior bounds an embedded $3$-ball in $M$. A properly embedded surface is **incompressible** if it admits no embedded disk whose interior misses the surface and whose boundary is an essential simple closed curve in it. A boundary subsurface is **$\pi_1$-injective** if the inclusion of each component induces an injection on fundamental groups. A **pared pair** is a pair $(M,P)$ in which $M$ is compact, orientable and irreducible, and $P$ is a possibly empty compact subsurface of $\partial M$ whose pairwise disjoint components are $\pi_1$-injective annuli or tori, every noncyclic abelian subgroup of $\pi_1(M)$ is conjugate into $\pi_1$ of a component of $P$ up to base-path conjugacy, and every map of pairs
$$
(S^1\times I,S^1\times\partial I)\longrightarrow(M,P)
$$
that induces injections on fundamental groups is homotopic through maps of pairs into $P$, so its boundary remains in $P$ during the homotopy. Write $\partial_0M=\partial M\setminus\operatorname{int}P$. A **horoball** is a region bounded by a horosphere, a Euclidean plane or sphere tangent to the ideal boundary at one point. The **peripheral subgroup** for a component of $P$ is the image of its fundamental group in $\pi_1(M)$, recorded up to conjugacy. A **hyperbolic structure** on $(M,P)$ is a curvature $-1$ metric on $\operatorname{int}M$ described by an atlas of charts into $\mathbb H^3$ whose transition maps are in $\operatorname{Isom}^+(\mathbb H^3)$. Its developing map $\operatorname{dev}$ from the universal cover and holonomy homomorphism $\rho:\pi_1(M)\to\operatorname{Isom}^+(\mathbb H^3)$ satisfy $\operatorname{dev}(gx)=\rho(g)\operatorname{dev}(x)$. The metric is **complete** when it is geodesically complete. A **cusp** corresponding to a component of $P$ is a quotient of a horoball by the associated peripheral subgroup. The hyperbolic volume is the integral of the Riemannian volume density over $\operatorname{int}M$; the structure has **finite volume** when this integral is finite.

Let $M$ be the interior of a compact connected orientable three-manifold with a complete finite-volume hyperbolic metric and torus cusps $C_1,\ldots,C_k$. For a chosen cusp $C_i$, choose a horospherical section $T_i$ and identify its Euclidean universal cover with $\mathbb R^2$ so its deck group is a rank-two translation lattice. A slope on $T_i$ is represented by a primitive lattice vector $v$ modulo sign. Its **Euclidean slope length on the chosen section** is $\ell_{T_i}(v)=\lVert v\rVert$ in the induced Euclidean metric. In upper half-space coordinates, if the section is the quotient of the horosphere of height $h>0$ by lattice $\Lambda$, then $\ell_{T_i}(p,q)=|p u+q w|/h$, where $u,w$ are the translation vectors representing the chosen basis. Replacing height $h$ by $h'>0$ multiplies every slope length by $h/h'$; therefore the length depends on the chosen section and is not an intrinsic number until that section is fixed.

derivations.claim: Apply [F1] to the entire given $k$-cusped metric. It supplies a product neighborhood $U$ of $(\infty,\ldots,\infty)$ and the required complete finite-volume metric for every tuple with primitive finite coordinates. Coordinates $\infty$ retain their complete translation cusps, so the conclusion includes every partial filling and the unchanged complete manifold. These are the ordinary fillings of [F2], including their supplied gluing data, rather than just representations solving the peripheral equations.

Choose cuspwise open neighborhoods $U_i$ of $\infty$ with $\prod_iU_i\subseteq U$; one may use the product neighborhood in [F1] itself. The complement $S_i\setminus U_i$ is a closed subset of the compact sphere $S_i$ missing $\infty$, hence a compact subset of $\mathbb R^2$ and therefore bounded. A bounded set contains only finitely many integer lattice points: if its norm is at most $B$, each coordinate is one of the finitely many integers between $-\lceil B\rceil$ and $\lceil B\rceil$. Restricting to primitive pairs and quotienting by simultaneous sign cannot increase their number. This proves the finite-exception assertion at every cusp and hence the simultaneous conclusion.

By [F3], any sequence of primitive slopes whose chosen-section lengths tend to infinity leaves every bounded coefficient set, so it eventually lies in its $U_i$. Rescaling a horotorus multiplies all these lengths by one positive constant and does not alter this conclusion. A nonprimitive ray parameter does not specify an ordinary primitive meridian; by [F2] its cone-angle convention is separate from the smooth fillings proved here. All neighborhoods are allowed to depend on the given manifold and its metric, so the proof asserts neither a universal numeric threshold nor a universal number of exceptions.

derivations.claim: The coordinates $(2,0)$ have greatest common divisor $2$, so they are not primitive. By [F1], they therefore do not represent an ordinary slope or the meridian class of an ordinary smooth filling. The primitive pair on the same ray is $(1,0)$.

Write $(2,0)=2(1,0)$, so the radial factor is $r=2$. The generalized parameter convention in [F1] assigns cone angle $2\pi/2=\pi$ to this ray parameter. This differs from the ordinary smooth filling along slope $(1,0)$, which uses the primitive parameter with $r=1$ and full angle $2\pi$. Hence the nonprimitive pair is a cone/orbifold completion parameter, not an ordinary slope.

Define the standard figure-eight knot $K_8$ to be the oriented closure of the three-strand geometric braid $(\sigma_1\sigma_2^{-1})^2$. Its endpoint permutation is a $3$-cycle, so this closure has one component.

Let $\Delta_0=[0,1,2,3]$ and $\Delta_1=[0',1',2',3']$ be oriented ideal tetrahedra with orientation-reversing affine face maps
$$
[0,1,2]\to[3',1',2'],\quad
[0,1,3]\to[0',1',2'],\quad
[0,2,3]\to[0',1',3'],\quad
[1,2,3]\to[0',2',3'].
$$
This is the two-tetrahedron ideal triangulation obtained from the standard four-crossing figure-eight diagram by cutting along crossing arcs, identifying upper and lower polyhedron faces with equal region labels, and collapsing the two bigon faces. Its edge classes are
$$
\{01,02,23,0'1',1'3',2'3'\},\qquad
\{12,03,13,1'2',0'2',0'3'\};
$$
each has valence six, and the unique ideal vertex link is a torus. Put shape $z_1$ on $01,23$, shape $z_2$ on $03,12$, and shape $z_3$ on $02,13$ in $\Delta_0$; put shape $w_1$ on $0'1',2'3'$, shape $w_2$ on $0'3',1'2'$, and shape $w_3$ on $0'2',1'3'$ in $\Delta_1$. Unfold the eight cusp-link triangles by the face maps into the standard rectangular strip, and label them $a,b,c,d,e,f,g,h$ from left to right; identify the strip boundary sides as prescribed by those same maps. Let $\alpha$ be the edge path across the strip from the left side of $a$ on the left boundary to the left side of $a$ on the right boundary, and let $\beta$ be the edge path on the left boundary from the base of $a$ to the top of $h$. Their ordered corner factors are respectively $z_3,w_2^{-1},z_2,w_3^{-1},z_3,w_2^{-1},z_2,w_3^{-1}$ and $z_2^{-1},w_1$. The face-pairing incidence check gives one positive transverse intersection, so their homology classes form a basis of $H_1$ and the loops form a basis of $\pi_1$ of the torus link. The two edge products are $z_1^2z_3w_1^2w_3$ and $z_2^2z_3w_2^2w_3$, while
$$
H(\alpha)=\left(\frac{z_2z_3}{w_2w_3}\right)^2,\qquad H(\beta)=\frac{w_1}{z_2}.
$$
For $\omega=e^{i\pi/3}$, assigning $z_1=z_2=z_3=w_1=w_2=w_3=\omega$ makes both edge products and both cusp multipliers equal to $1$ and gives total angle $2\pi$ around each edge. The gluing therefore gives the figure-eight complement a complete finite-volume curvature $-1$ metric with one peripheral torus cusp.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K_8$ be the standard figure-eight knot with compact exterior obtained by deleting the binding neighborhood from its open-book presentation and peripheral basis $(\mu,\lambda)$, where $\mu$ is the positive meridian and $\lambda$ is the preferred zero-homology longitude. The exterior fibers over $S^1$ with fiber a once-punctured torus and monodromy fixing its boundary pointwise. Filling along the slope $\lambda$ produces a torus bundle over $S^1$. For the fiber and ordered core basis in the figure-eight plumbing convention, the induced action on the capped torus homology is $\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. If $M$ is a closed connected orientable three-manifold with a complete Riemannian metric of constant sectional curvature $-1$, then its fundamental group contains no subgroup isomorphic to $\mathbb Z^2$.

Let $\overline M$ be a compact connected oriented three-manifold whose boundary is a disjoint union of tori $T_1,\ldots,T_k$. Choose an ordered integral basis $([\mu_i],[\lambda_i])$ for each $H_1(T_i;\mathbb Z)$. A **slope** on $T_i$ is an unoriented isotopy class of essential simple closed curves whose homology class is $p_i[\mu_i]+q_i[\lambda_i]$ for a primitive pair $(p_i,q_i)\in\mathbb Z^2$; simultaneous negation gives the same unoriented slope. The primitive-pair correspondence gives exactly one such slope for each primitive pair modulo sign. The **ordinary Dehn filling** along a tuple of slopes indexed by $J\subseteq\{1,\ldots,k\}$ attaches an oriented solid torus $D^2\times S^1$ to each $T_i$, $i\in J$, by an orientation-reversing boundary homeomorphism that sends $[\partial D^2\times\{*\}]$ to the chosen slope. The gluing maps are part of the filling data; $i\notin J$ means that the cusp is left unfilled, denoted by the parameter $\infty$.

For a hyperbolic deformation, the **generalized cone-filling parameter space** at each cusp is the one-point compactification $\mathbb R^2\cup\{\infty\}$ of the real coefficient plane, with $\infty$ denoting the complete cusp. A primitive integral pair $(p_i,q_i)$ is an ordinary smooth filling coefficient. If a realized generalized parameter lies on the ray $g_i=r_i(p_i,q_i)$ with $r_i>0$ and $(p_i,q_i)$ primitive integral, its topological core direction is the ordinary slope $(p_i,q_i)$ and its cone angle is $2\pi/r_i$. Only $r_i=1$ is the ordinary smooth filling; $r_i>1$ describes a cone or orbifold completion and does not turn the nonprimitive vector $g_i$ into a slope.

A **covering map** is a continuous surjection $p:E\to B$ such that every $b\in B$ has an open neighbourhood $U$ for which $p^{-1}(U)$ is a disjoint union of open sets $V_j$, called **sheets**, and each restriction $p|_{V_j}:V_j\to U$ is a homeomorphism ([[def-continuous-map-top]], [[def-homeomorphism-and-open-maps]], [[def-disjoint-union-topology]]). Such a $U$ is **evenly covered**, and $p^{-1}(b)$ is the **fibre** over $b$. A covering is **trivial** when it is isomorphic over $B$ to a product projection $B\times F\to B$ with $F$ discrete.
For a covering $p:(E,e_0)\to(B,b_0)$, the induced homomorphism $p_*:\pi_1(E,e_0)\to\pi_1(B,b_0)$ is injective.

derivations.claim: By [A1] and [F2], the countable-choice premise [F1] holds. The face gluing and regular-shape assignment in [F3] give the complete finite-volume metric and its two-tetrahedron volume. By [F4] and [F6], the zero filling along the preferred longitude is the stated torus bundle.

Write the bundle as the mapping torus of its torus monodromy. Pull it back along the explicit universal cover $t\mapsto e^{2\pi i t}$ of $S^1$; its total space is $T^2\times\mathbb R$, and the pullback projection is a covering because it is trivial over each lifted bundle chart. Its fundamental group is $\pi_1(T^2)\cong\mathbb Z^2$. By [F8], this subgroup injects into the fundamental group of the filled manifold.

If the filled manifold admitted a complete hyperbolic metric, it would be a closed connected three-manifold with curvature $-1$. By [F5] its fundamental group could contain no $\mathbb Z^2$ subgroup, contradicting step 2.1. Hence the zero filling is nonhyperbolic. The original complete structure has volume $2v_3=6\Lambda(\pi/3)$ by step 1.1.

Let $d\ge1$ and let $f:S^{d-1}\to S^{d-1}$ be a homeomorphism of the unit
sphere $S^{d-1}\subseteq\mathbb R^d$. Then $f$ extends to a homeomorphism
$F:D^d\to D^d$ of the closed unit disk, given by
$$F(0)=0,\qquad F(rx)=r\,f(x)\quad\text{for }0<r\le1,\ x\in S^{d-1}.$$
The extension need not be smooth at the origin.

derivations.claim: Let $c((e^{i\theta},w),s)=((1-s/8)e^{i\theta},w)$ for $(e^{i\theta},w)\in\partial V'$ and $s\in[0,2]$; this is a collar because its radial coordinate ranges from $1$ to $3/4$. Set $\rho(s)=1-s$ for $0\le s\le1$ and $\rho(s)=0$ for $1\le s\le2$. The map $J(c(x,s))=c(H_{\rho(s)}(x),s)$ on the collar, extended by the identity outside it, is a homeomorphism: its inverse replaces $H_{\rho(s)}$ with $H_{\rho(s)}^{-1}$. It restricts to $H_1$ at the boundary and is isotopic to the identity through the same formula with $H_{u\rho(s)}$ for $u\in[0,1]$. Thus $h_0=J|_{\partial V'}\circ h$ sends $\mu$ exactly to $\mu'$, and extending $h_0$ suffices because postcomposition with $J^{-1}$ recovers an extension of $h$ without changing its orientation sign.

Cut $V$ and $V'$ along the product meridian disks $D=D^2\times\{1\}$ and $D'=D^2\times\{1\}$. Each cut-open solid torus is $D^2\times[0,1]$. After centering the interval at $0$, this convex cylinder is homeomorphic to the unit ball by radial rescaling: in direction $u=(u_1,u_2,u_3)\in S^2$ its boundary radius is $R(u)=\min\{(u_1^2+u_2^2)^{-1/2},(2|u_3|)^{-1}\}$, with a zero denominator interpreted as $+\infty$, and $(r,u)\mapsto rR(u)u$ gives the homeomorphism. The boundary of each cut-open torus consists of the annulus obtained by cutting the boundary torus along the meridian and two disk faces. The restriction of $h_0$ maps the annular portions to one another. Its common restriction to $\mu$ extends over each disk face by [F1], using the same disk map on both copies. The radial disk maps send the center of each disk face to the center of its target face. These maps assemble to a homeomorphism $\psi:\partial B\to\partial B'$ between the sphere boundaries of the cut-open balls, carrying the pair of disk-face centers to that pair in the target.

Identify each cut-open ball with the unit ball in $\mathbb R^3$. Apply [F1] with $d=3$ to extend $\psi$ radially over the ball. The cylinder-to-ball radial rescaling of step 2.1 carries the central product arc $\{0\}\times[0,1]$ to the diameter joining the two disk-face center points. Since $\psi$ carries those endpoints to the target pair, its radial extension carries this entire diameter to the corresponding target diameter. Thus the ball extension preserves the product core arc. The extension has orientation sign equal to the degree sign of $\psi$. On the open annulus away from the disk faces, $\psi$ is exactly $h_0$; cutting does not change the local boundary orientation there, so this degree sign is the orientation sign of $h_0$.

The two copies of each meridian disk receive the same disk map from [F1], so the ball extension agrees on their identified faces. It therefore descends after regluing to a homeomorphism $V\to V'$ extending $h_0$ and carrying the product core circle to the target core circle. Composing with $J^{-1}$ extends the original $h$; this collar-supported map fixes the core and keeps the same orientation sign because $J$ is isotopic to the identity.

e0$, so the final limiting assertion is vacuous. This proves the Statement in that case. Henceforth suppose $k\ge1$. Composition of the two affine maps shows that commutativity is exactly $a_i(e^{v_i}-1)=b_i(e^{u_i}-1)$. Let $E(t)=(e^t-1)/t$ for $t
e0$ and $E(0)=1$; its convergent series is $\sum_{n\ge0}t^n/(n+1)!$, so it is holomorphic and nonzero near zero. Since $a_i(o)
e0$, the holomorphic function $	au_i=(b_i/a_i)E(u_i)/E(v_i)$ is defined near $o$. The commutativity equation becomes exactly $v_i=	au_i u_i$, and $	au_i(o)=b_i(o)/a_i(o)$. The finitely many nonreal values permit one common neighborhood on which all $\operatorname{Im}	au_i$ are nonzero. Thus all $	au_i$ are nonzero, proving the equivalence of their zero logarithms and the asserted quotient limit. The argument is an identity of holomorphic functions on $Z$, so singular points cause no difficulty.

e0$, real linear independence of $u_i$ and $v_i=	au_i u_i$ follows from $\operatorname{Im}	au_i

e0$, the denominator $p_i+q_i	au_i^0$ cannot vanish: if it did, its imaginary part would give $q_i=0$, then its real part $p_i=0$, contrary to the full-turn equation. citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $M$ be a closed linear subspace of a real or complex Hilbert space $H$. Then every $x\in H$ has a unique decomposition

$$x=m+n,\qquad m\in M,\quad n\in M^\perp ,$$

so that $H=M\oplus M^\perp$ as a direct sum of the subspace $M$ and its orthogonal complement.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space and let $f$ be a bounded linear functional on $H$ ([[def-dual-space-of-a-normed-space]]). Then there is a unique $y\in H$ with

$$f(x)=\langle x,y\rangle\qquad\text{for every }x\in H,$$

and $\|f\|=\|y\|$, where $\|f\|$ is the dual norm ([[def-operator-norm]]). Under the first-variable-linear convention the representing vector depends conjugate-linearly and isometrically on $f$: if $f_i$ is represented by $y_i$ and $a,b$ are scalars, then $af_1+bf_2$ is represented by $\overline a\,y_1+\overline b\,y_2$.

derivations.claim: Put $G=\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb C)$, $K=\mathrm{PSU}(2)$ and $V=\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb C)$. Choose $X_1=\tfrac12\left(\begin{smallmatrix}i&0\\0&-i\end{smallmatrix}\right)$, $X_2=\tfrac12\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ and $X_3=\tfrac12\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&i\\i&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ in $\mathfrak k$, and put $Y_j=iX_j$. These $Y_j$ are an orthonormal tangent basis for curvature $-1$ hyperbolic space; for example $\exp(tY_1)$ moves the basepoint distance $|t|$, and the $K$ action rotates this basis. The matrix commutators give $[X_i,X_j]=\epsilon_{ijk}X_k$ and $[Y_i,Y_j]=i\epsilon_{ijk}Y_k$. On $V$ let $R_j=\operatorname{ad}Y_j$. Each $Y_j$ is Hermitian, so $R_j$ is self-adjoint for $\langle A,B\rangle=\operatorname{tr}(AB^*)$, by cyclicity of trace. The $K$ action is unitary for this product.

Represent $E$-valued forms by horizontal $K$-equivariant $V$-valued forms on $Q=\Gamma\backslash G$, expressing their coefficients in the left Maurer–Cartan frame. Indeed a frame $g$ identifies the fiber over $gK$ with $V$ by $\operatorname{Ad}g$, and replacing $g$ by $gk$ changes these coefficients by $\operatorname{Ad}k^{-1}$ and rotates the tangent indices. In these coefficients write $\varepsilon_j$ for exterior multiplication by the dual of $Y_j$ and $\iota_j$ for contraction by $Y_j$. The ordinary covariant differential of the $K$ connection is $D=\sum_j\varepsilon_jY_j$, because the horizontal part of $[Y_i,Y_j]$ is zero. Differentiating the fiber change $\operatorname{Ad}g$ gives $d_E=D+T$, where $T=\sum_j\varepsilon_jR_j$. These are actual coefficient formulas on all degrees, not definitions of a different connection.

The invariant volume on $Q$ is the product of hyperbolic volume and normalized compact-fiber volume. Integration in a local bundle chart and then a partition of unity shows that integration of a $K$-invariant coefficient norm on $Q$ equals its integration on $M$. The left invariant fields $Y_j$ have zero divergence for this volume: $G$ is unimodular, since $\operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{ad}Z)=0$ for the displayed Lie algebra basis, hence for all $Z$, and $\det\operatorname{Ad}(\exp Z)=1$. Right translation therefore preserves its Haar volume. Integration by parts on compact supports now gives $D^*=-\sum_j\iota_jY_j$ and $T^*=\sum_j\iota_jR_j$. The relations $\varepsilon_i\iota_j+\iota_j\varepsilon_i=\delta_{ij}$ show that $DT^*+T^*D+TD^*+D^*T=0$: the two anticommutator sums are respectively $\sum_jR_jY_j$ and its negative, since coefficient differentiation commutes with the constant matrices $R_j$. Thus $d_E\delta_E+\delta_Ed_E=DD^*+D^*D+H$, where $H=TT^*+T^*T$. All statements are $K$-equivariant and descend from $Q$ to $M$.

On one-form coefficients $a=(a_1,a_2,a_3)\in V^3$, the exterior-contraction relations give $(Ha)_i=\sum_jR_j^2a_i+\sum_j[R_i,R_j]a_j$. This finite-dimensional self-adjoint operator is positive definite. If $Ha=0$, positivity of $TT^*+T^*T$ gives $Ta=0$, namely $R_ia_j=R_ja_i$ for all $i,j$. Since $[R_i,R_j]=i\epsilon_{ijk}R_k$, the commutator sum in the displayed formula is a multiple of $R_ka_j-R_ja_k$ and vanishes. Consequently $0=\langle Ha,a\rangle=\sum_{i,j}\|R_ja_i\|^2$. Each $a_i$ commutes with all $Y_j$, which span $\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb C)$ over $\mathbb C$. A matrix commuting with all traceless matrices is scalar, and a traceless scalar is zero. Thus $a=0$. Compactness of the unit sphere in $V^3$ supplies $c>0$ with $H\ge cI$.

For a compactly supported smooth one-form, integration by parts in step 3.1 and step 4.1 give $\|d_E\alpha\|_2^2+\|\delta_E\alpha\|_2^2=\|D\alpha\|_2^2+\|D^*\alpha\|_2^2+(H\alpha,\alpha)\ge c\|\alpha\|_2^2$. We next extend this inequality to the joint weak graph domain. On each cusp choose a smooth cutoff equal to one for $t\le R$, zero for $t\ge2R$, with derivative bounded by $C/R$, and set it equal to one on the compact core. These cutoffs $\chi_R$ have compact support and $|d\chi_R|\le C/R$. For a weak graph-domain form $v$, the product formulas $d_E(\chi_Rv)=\chi_Rd_Ev+d\chi_R\wedge v$ and $\delta_E(\chi_Rv)=\chi_R\delta_Ev-\iota_{\nabla\chi_R}v$ show convergence to $v$ in the joint graph norm. The same conclusion holds separately for each differential and codifferential and for forms of every degree. In the compact case take the cutoff identically one.

Here are the local smoothing details needed to finish that graph-density argument. In a finite collection of trivializing charts around the support of $\chi_Rv$, every differential or codifferential is a first-order matrix operator $P=\sum_jA_j(x)\partial_j+B(x)$ with smooth coefficients. Multiplication by a subordinate smooth partition reduces to forms supported inside individual charts. For convolution with a smooth unit-mass kernel $\rho_\epsilon$, the difference $P(v*\rho_\epsilon)-(Pv)*\rho_\epsilon$ is a sum of integral operators with kernels $(A_j(x)-A_j(y))\partial_j\rho_\epsilon(x-y)+(\partial_jA_j)(y)\rho_\epsilon(x-y)$ and a zero-order coefficient commutator. The $L^1$ kernel bounds are uniform on the compact chart, by the mean-value bound for $A_j$ and scaling of $\rho_\epsilon$; thus these commutators are uniformly bounded on $L^2$. They tend to zero on smooth functions by differentiation of convolutions, hence on all $L^2$ functions by smooth approximation and the uniform bound. Therefore local mollification converges in each asserted graph norm, also for the direct sum operator $(d_E,\delta_E)$. The partition contributes only fixed zero-order commutators, so a finite sum completes the approximation by compactly supported smooth forms. Together with step 5.1 this proves the coercive inequality on the maximal joint graph domain. It also proves that maximal differentials are the adjoints of maximal formal codifferentials, since their compact-support integration-by-parts identities extend by this graph density.

Let $\mathcal H_p=L^2(\Lambda^pT^*M\otimes E)$ and let $d_p$ be the maximal weak differential. It is closed: convergence of a form and its differential in $L^2$ preserves the weak test-function identity. Flatness gives $d_1d_0=0$ distributionally. Put $Z=\ker d_1$, a closed subspace of $\mathcal H_1$, and $\delta=d_0^*$. Every $w\in Z^\perp$ belongs to $\operatorname{Dom}\delta$ with $\delta w=0$, because it is orthogonal to $\operatorname{ran}d_0\subseteq Z$. Hence the orthogonal projection $P_Z$ maps $\operatorname{Dom}\delta$ into itself and $\delta P_Zv=\delta v$. On $Z\cap\operatorname{Dom}\delta$, steps 5.1 and 6.1 give $\|v\|_2\le c^{-1/2}\|\delta v\|_2$. In particular $A=\delta|_{Z\cap\operatorname{Dom}\delta}$ is injective with closed range: a Cauchy sequence of its images is, by this estimate, the image under the closed operator $\delta$ of a convergent sequence in $Z$.

Fix a weakly closed $\alpha\in\mathcal H_1$, so $\alpha\in Z$. On the closed range of $A$ define $\ell(Av)=\langle v,\alpha\rangle$. It is well defined and bounded, with norm at most $c^{-1/2}\|\alpha\|_2$, by step 7.1. Extend it to $\mathcal H_0$ by zero on the orthogonal complement of that range and use [F1] to obtain $b\in\mathcal H_0$ with $\langle Av,b\rangle=\langle v,\alpha\rangle$ and $\|b\|_2\le c^{-1/2}\|\alpha\|_2$. For arbitrary $v\in\operatorname{Dom}\delta$, replace $v$ by $P_Zv$; its $\delta$ image is unchanged and its pairing with $\alpha$ is unchanged. Thus $\langle\delta v,b\rangle=\langle v,\alpha\rangle$ on the full domain of $\delta$. By the adjoint definition and the graph-density conclusion of step 6.1, $b\in\operatorname{Dom}d_0$ and $d_0b=\alpha$. This proves the primitive assertion in the weak sense without an external closed-range or harmonic-representative theorem.

If $\alpha$ is smooth, the primitive $b$ is smooth. In a flat parallel frame on a coordinate ball, $d_Eb=\alpha$ is the ordinary componentwise distributional equation $db=\alpha$. A smooth closed one-form on a smaller star-shaped coordinate ball has a smooth primitive $b_0$, given by integrating along straight radial segments; differentiating the integral and using closedness verifies $db_0=\alpha$. Then $d(b-b_0)=0$ distributionally. Mollification on still smaller balls makes this difference a sequence of constants, so its distributional limit is constant as well. Thus $b=b_0+\text{constant}$ is smooth locally and hence globally. Its $L^2$ norm and the bound from step 8.1 remain unchanged.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $M=\Gamma\backslash\mathbb H^3$ be an oriented hyperbolic three-manifold with compact complement to finitely many standard torus cusp ends, each isometric to $(T^2\times[0,\infty),dt^2+e^{-2t}g_T)$ for a flat metric $g_T$. The compact case is allowed. Let $E=\mathbb H^3\times_\Gamma\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb C)$ be the adjoint flat bundle. Give its fiber at a basepoint the Hilbert–Schmidt Hermitian product and transport this product by the homogeneous $\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb C)/\mathrm{PSU}(2)$ construction. Write $d_E$ for its flat differential and $\delta_E$ for the metric formal adjoint.

There is $c>0$, depending only on the model normalization, such that every compactly supported smooth $E$-valued one-form satisfies
$$\|d_E\alpha\|_2^2+\|\delta_E\alpha\|_2^2\ge c\|\alpha\|_2^2.$$
Every smooth $E$-valued one-form $\alpha$ with $d_E\alpha=0$ and $\|\alpha\|_2<\infty$ has a smooth square-integrable primitive $b$, with $d_Eb=\alpha$ and $\|b\|_2\le c^{-1/2}\|\alpha\|_2$.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every compact smooth manifold, with boundary
allowed, has the homotopy type of a finite CW complex. If its boundary is a
supplied finite CW manifold, the collar may be retained in a finite relative CW
model.

For $A\subseteq X$ and a local system $\mathcal L$ on $X$, restriction to $A$ gives natural exact sequences
$$\cdots\to H_n(A;\mathcal L|_A)\to H_n(X;\mathcal L)\to H_n(X,A;\mathcal L)\xrightarrow{\partial}H_{n-1}(A;\mathcal L|_A)\to\cdots$$
and
$$\cdots\to H^n(X,A;\mathcal L)\to H^n(X;\mathcal L)\to H^n(A;\mathcal L|_A)\xrightarrow{\delta}H^{n+1}(X,A;\mathcal L)\to\cdots.$$
The homology connector sends a relative cycle represented by $c$ to $[\partial c]$. The cohomology connector sends a cocycle $a$ on $A$ to $[\delta\widetilde a]$, where $\widetilde a$ is its extension by zero to simplices not contained in $A$. Naturality uses the variances of the preceding functoriality proposition.

Assume AC. Let $M$ be a compact $n$-manifold and let $A=\partial M$; let $R$ be a commutative unital ring and $\mathcal L$ an $R$-module local system on $M$. Cap with the canonical relative twisted fundamental class gives isomorphisms, for every integer $k$,
$$H^k(M;\mathcal L)\xrightarrow{\sim}H_{n-k}(M,A;\mathcal O_M^R\otimes_R\mathcal L),\qquad H^k(M,A;\mathcal L)\xrightarrow{\sim}H_{n-k}(M;\mathcal O_M^R\otimes_R\mathcal L).$$
Here $\mathcal O_M^R$ is the collar extension of the interior orientation system. The statement is for the actual boundary $A$, not an arbitrary subspace of $M$.

Let $m,n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb C^m\times\mathbb C^n$ be open, let
$f:U\to\mathbb C^n$ be holomorphic, and let $(a,b)\in U$ satisfy $f(a,b)=0$.
Assume the complex Jacobian with respect to the second block is invertible:

$$\det\left(\frac{\partial f_j}{\partial w_k}(a,b)\right)_{1\le j,k\le n}\ne0.$$

Then there are neighbourhoods $A$ of $a$ and $B$ of $b$, and a unique
holomorphic map $\varphi:A\to B$, such that

$$f(z,\varphi(z))=0\qquad(z\in A),$$

and, after shrinking $A\times B$ if needed,

$$f(z,w)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad w=\varphi(z).$$

Let $Z$ be a reduced complex analytic space with point $o$, and suppose $u_i,v_i,a_i,b_i$ are holomorphic germs on $Z$ for $1\le i\le k$, with $k<\infty$, $u_i(o)=v_i(o)=0$, $a_i(o)\ne0$ and $\tau_i^0=b_i(o)/a_i(o)\notin\mathbb R$. Suppose the affine maps
$$L_i(w)=e^{u_i}w+a_i,\qquad P_i(w)=e^{v_i}w+b_i$$
commute at every parameter point. Then, after shrinking around $o$, there are holomorphic germs $\tau_i$ such that $v_i=\tau_i u_i$, $\tau_i(o)=\tau_i^0$ and $\operatorname{Im}\tau_i\ne0$ throughout. In particular $u_i=0$ if and only if $v_i=0$, and $v_i/u_i\to\tau_i^0$ as the parameter tends to $o$ through $u_i\ne0$. No smoothness, dimension or rank hypothesis on $Z$ is required.

For $u_i\ne0$, there is a unique real pair $(p_i,q_i)$ solving $p_iu_i+q_iv_i=2\pi i$. With
$$\widetilde u_i=\frac{2\pi i}{p_i+\tau_i^0q_i},$$
one has
$$|\widetilde u_i-u_i|\le\frac{|\tau_i-\tau_i^0|}{|\operatorname{Im}\tau_i^0|}|u_i|.$$
Set $\widetilde u_i=0$ when $u_i=0$. The functions $\widetilde u_i$ are continuous at such points, and $\|\widetilde u-u\|=o(\|u\|)$ as the parameter tends to $o$ through $u\ne0$.

derivations.claim: The complete holonomy is irreducible and its adjoint invariants vanish. Indeed one cusp subgroup is a rank-two translation lattice fixing $\infty$. If all of $\Gamma$ fixed $\infty$, its elements would be similarities $z\mapsto az+b$. An element with $|a|\ne1$ would conjugate a fixed nonzero lattice translation to translations tending to the identity, contradicting discreteness. An element with $|a|=1$ and $a\ne1$ is elliptic about a vertical line, impossible in a torsion-free discrete group. Hence all elements would be translations, and the quotient would have infinite volume as height tends to zero. This contradicts the finite-volume hypothesis. Thus some element does not fix $\infty$. A traceless matrix invariant under the cusp group is a multiple of $E=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$, by direct commutation with a nontrivial unipotent. A nonzero such matrix invariant under all of $\Gamma$ would force preservation of its kernel line, hence of $\infty$, a contradiction. Thus $H^0(M;E_{\operatorname{Ad}\rho_0})=0$. The same argument excludes a common invariant line for the holonomy matrices. The group centralizer in $G$ is trivial as well: a Möbius map commuting with the cusp translations fixes $\infty$ and is itself a translation, by its affine formula; a nonidentity such translation has unique fixed point $\infty$, so commuting with the entire group would force the whole group to fix $\infty$.

We specify the cohomology comparisons being used. The flat adjoint bundle has local parallel frames, obtained on simply connected balls by trivializing its defining covering construction. In such frames its differential is the componentwise ordinary exterior differential; integration of forms over simplices is compatible with the constant transition matrices and with Stokes. The usual local Poincaré contraction is explicit: integrate contraction by the radial vector along radial coordinate segments. A locally finite good cover by sufficiently small strongly convex metric balls therefore gives a Čech double complex whose form columns resolve the parallel local sections. Its positive Čech rows are contracted by $(hc)_{i_0\ldots i_{r-1}}=\sum_j\phi_jc_{ji_0\ldots i_{r-1}}$, for a subordinate partition of unity. The small-singular-cochain double complex has the same degree-zero columns, since every intersection is contractible; subdivision makes singular simplices subordinate to the cover, and the Čech rows contract by assigning a containing index to each small simplex. The two edge comparisons identify flat de Rham cohomology with singular cohomology with this local system, naturally for restrictions. These constructions also apply to compact support and to collars, so relative classes are represented by forms supported away from the ends. Finally $M$ is aspherical, with universal cover $\mathbb H^3$ contractible. Its lifted cellular or singular chains form a free resolution of $\mathbb C$ as a $\mathbb C\Gamma$-module; comparison of free resolutions by successive lifts gives the same cohomology as group cocycles. In degree one, this comparison is concretely integration of an equivariant closed form along a lifted group loop. These arguments establish the coefficient comparisons, rather than invoking an unproved twisted de Rham theorem.

The representation scheme of a torus is smooth near its noncentral complete peripheral pair. Use local $SL_2$ lifts $A,B$ of the two generators, both near nontrivial commuting unipotents; their commutator is $I$ because its sign is locally constant and is positive at the basepoint. Choose a fixed vector $v$ with $v,Av$ independent at that point and hence nearby. For a commuting matrix $B$, write $Bv=av+bAv$; commutation then forces $B=aI+bA$ by applying both sides to the basis $v,Av$. This argument works over truncated power-series rings too, because the basis determinant is a unit. Put $C=A-(\operatorname{tr}A)I/2$ and write $B=\alpha I+\beta C$. Its determinant condition is $\alpha^2-\beta^2((\operatorname{tr}A)^2/4-1)=1$. At the complete pair $\alpha=1$, so [F3] solves uniquely for $\alpha$ in terms of $A$ and $\beta$. Thus the commuting-pair scheme is locally a smooth four-dimensional space, parametrized by the three coordinates of $A$ and one of $\beta$. In particular every representation over $\mathbb C[t]/(t^{n+1})$ near this pair extends one order further.

Write $E_0=E_{\operatorname{Ad}\rho_0}$. The restriction $r_1:H^1(N;E_0)\to H^1(\partial N;E_0)$ is injective. If a closed smooth form represents a class in its kernel, on each cusp tail it equals $d_{E_0}b_i$ for a smooth section, by step 1.2. Subtract $d_{E_0}(\chi_i b_i)$ using a cutoff equal to one sufficiently far along that end and zero near the core. The resulting cohomologous closed form is compactly supported, hence square integrable, and is exact by [F1]. Thus the original class is zero. Equivalently the map $H^1(N,\partial N;E_0)\to H^1(N;E_0)$ vanishes. By [F2], its transpose, up to the harmless cap-boundary sign, is the map $H^2(N,\partial N;E_0)\to H^2(N;E_0)$, so that map also vanishes. The pair sequence therefore gives $r_2:H^2(N;E_0)\to H^2(\partial N;E_0)$ injective. It is onto because its cokernel embeds in $H^3(N,\partial N;E_0)$, which is dual to $H^0(N;E_0)=0$ by step 1.1.

We give the full obstruction construction. Suppose $\rho^{(n)}$ is a representation over $\mathbb C[t]/(t^{n+1})$ with constant term $\rho_0$. Choose arbitrary one-order lifts $\widetilde\rho(\gamma)$ of its values. The defect is uniquely $\widetilde\rho(\gamma)\widetilde\rho(\delta)\widetilde\rho(\gamma\delta)^{-1}=I+t^{n+1}c(\gamma,\delta)$ modulo $t^{n+2}$, with $c$ in the adjoint Lie algebra; this expression is read in the identity chart of $G$. Associativity gives $c(\gamma,\delta)+c(\gamma\delta,\epsilon)=\operatorname{Ad}_{\rho_0(\gamma)}c(\delta,\epsilon)+c(\gamma,\delta\epsilon)$, exactly the group two-cocycle relation. Replacing the lift at $\gamma$ by $(I+t^{n+1}b(\gamma))\widetilde\rho(\gamma)$ changes $c$ by $b(\gamma)+\operatorname{Ad}_{\rho_0(\gamma)}b(\delta)-b(\gamma\delta)$. Hence a one-order extension exists if and only if the class $[c]\in H^2(\Gamma;\operatorname{Ad}\rho_0)$ vanishes. The formulas commute with restriction to every subgroup.

At a cusp the adjoint invariants are $\mathbb CE$, of dimension one. Torus duality and the Euler characteristic of a finite cellular local system give $\dim H^0(T_i;E_0)=\dim H^2(T_i;E_0)=1$ and $\dim H^1(T_i;E_0)=2$. Indeed every cell contributes three coefficient dimensions, so the alternating chain dimension is $3\chi(T_i)=0$. The pair sequence and step 2.1 give a short exact sequence $0\to H^1(N;E_0)\to H^1(\partial N;E_0)\to H^2(N,\partial N;E_0)\to0$. The last group is dual to the first by [F2]. Consequently $\dim H^1(N;E_0)=k$, while $r_2$ identifies $H^2(N;E_0)$ with $\mathbb C^k$. All these spaces are finite dimensional by the finite CW model in [F2].

On each peripheral subgroup the obstruction in step 2.2 is zero by the smooth formal chart of step 1.3. The map on $H^2$ restricting to all peripheral subgroups is injective by step 2.1 and the comparisons in step 1.2, so the global obstruction vanishes. Starting with any first-order cocycle, repeat step 2.2 and choose corrections at each order. AC supplies this countable recursive sequence. Every first-order representation tangent vector therefore has a full formal representation curve with that tangent. No convergence assertion about this curve is needed.

We compute the cusp classes and trace derivatives. Normalize the cusp lattice as $z=x+\tau_i^0 y$, with deck translations $x\mapsto x+1$ and $y\mapsto y+1$, and put $F=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&0\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$, $H=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)$ and $n(z)=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&z\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$. The forms $\eta_i=dx\otimes E$ and $\omega_i=dz\otimes\operatorname{Ad}_{n(z)}F$ are equivariant and closed: $E$ is translation invariant and the polynomial $\operatorname{Ad}_{n(z)}F=F+zH-z^2E$ depends only on $z$, so its derivative wedges to zero with $dz$. Their trace-paired cup product is $\operatorname{tr}(\eta_i\wedge\omega_i)=\tau_i^0dx\wedge dy$, while each self-pairing is zero. Thus these two classes are independent and form a basis by step 3.1. The form $\eta_i$ is square integrable on its cusp: at height $t$, $|dx|$ grows as $e^t$ and the homogeneous norm of $E$ decays as $e^{-t}$, whereas volume decays as $e^{-2t}$.

Let $L$ be the span of the $k$ classes $\eta_i$ in $H^1(\partial N;E_0)$. The image of $r_1$ meets $L$ only in zero. If a global closed form restricts cohomologically to a combination of these $\eta_i$, subtract exact cutoff terms on the ends as in step 2.1 to arrange equality with that combination on each tail. The resulting global form is square integrable by step 4.1 and compactness of the remaining core, hence exact by [F1]. Since both $H^1(N;E_0)$ and the span of the $\omega_i$ have dimension $k$, there is a global cohomology basis whose boundary images are $\omega_i+\sum_jc_{ij}\eta_j$.

A group one-cocycle $a$ represents the infinitesimal representation $(I+\epsilon a(\gamma))\rho_0(\gamma)$ modulo $\epsilon^2$, as direct multiplication verifies; infinitesimal conjugacies are precisely coboundaries. Thus representation tangent vectors modulo infinitesimal conjugacy are $H^1(N;E_0)$. For the positive local lift of the normalized cusp meridian, $\rho_0(\mu_i)=n(1)$, integration in step 1.2 gives $a_{\eta_i}(\mu_i)=E$ and $a_{\omega_i}(\mu_i)=\int_0^1(F+xH-x^2E)\,dx=F+H/2-E/3$. Therefore $d\operatorname{tr}_{\mu_i}(\eta_i)=\operatorname{tr}(En(1))=0$ and $d\operatorname{tr}_{\mu_i}(\omega_i)=1$. For trace squared the latter derivative is $4$, since the complete trace is $2$. Classes supported at other cusps contribute only their own restrictions. By the basis in step 5.1, $(ds_1,\ldots,ds_k)$ is an isomorphism from $H^1(N;E_0)$ to $\mathbb C^k$. This is a tangent calculation; smoothness is proved next.

Here is why formal integrability implies analytic smoothness in this setting, without an approximation theorem for formal solutions. Take a finite presentation from [F2] and express its relators near $\rho_0$ as an analytic map $R:\mathbb C^{3g}\to\mathbb C^{3r}$ by using local coordinates on $G$ for the generators and the identity logarithm for each relator. Put $K_0=\ker dR_0$, choose a complement $W$ in the source and a projection $\pi$ onto $\operatorname{im}dR_0$ in the target. By [F3], the equation $\pi R(z,w)=0$ has the unique solution $w=\psi(z)$, with $z\in K_0$, $\psi(0)=0$ and $d\psi_0=0$. Thus the representation germ is the zero set of $\kappa(z)=(I-\pi)R(z,\psi(z))$. If $\kappa$ were nonzero, let $P_d$ be its first nonzero homogeneous Taylor term. A formal representation curve of arbitrary tangent $a\in K_0$, supplied by step 3.2, has $z(t)=ta+O(t^2)$ and $w(t)=\psi(z(t))$; the latter identity follows recursively from the invertible partial Jacobian defining $\psi$. Its relators then give $P_d(a)=0$. This holds for every $a\in K_0$, contradicting that $P_d$ is a nonzero polynomial. Hence $\kappa$ vanishes identically by convergence of its analytic Taylor series. The representation scheme is smooth with tangent $K_0=Z^1(\Gamma;\operatorname{Ad}\rho_0)$ and dimension $k+3$: $H^1$ has dimension $k$, and the coboundaries have dimension three because the invariants vanish in step 1.1.

To pass to ordinary conjugacy, choose three linear coordinate conditions transverse to the conjugation orbit at $\rho_0$. The orbit derivative is injective by step 1.1. The analytic inverse theorem, equivalently [F3] applied to the conjugation map, gives a local product of a three-dimensional identity neighborhood in $G$ and a slice $S$ of dimension $k$. This slice represents the actual conjugacy quotient germ. To exclude extra identifications by large conjugations, suppose instead that arbitrarily near $\rho_0$ there were conjugate pairs requiring conjugators away from the identity in $G$. Choose such a sequence, lift its conjugators to nonzero matrices and normalize their Euclidean matrix norms to one. After a subsequence the normalized matrices have a nonzero limit $P$. Choose local lifts of the finitely many generator matrices. Their intertwining equations have signs $\pm1$; after another subsequence each sign is fixed. If $P$ had rank one, these equations would make its kernel a common invariant line of the limiting holonomy matrices, contradicting step 1.1. Thus $P$ is invertible, and its projective class centralizes the complete holonomy. That projective centralizer is trivial by step 1.1, so the conjugators tend projectively to the identity, a contradiction. The local product uniqueness therefore excludes all extra slice identifications after shrinking. This proves smoothness of the ordinary quotient germ. By step 6.1 the trace-squared map on $S$ has invertible differential, and [F3] makes $(s_1,\ldots,s_k)$ its holomorphic coordinates.

Let $u\in\mathbb C^k$ be small. Step 8.1 gives a unique slice representation $\rho(u)$ whose trace-squared coordinates are $s_i=4\cosh^2(u_i/2)$; it depends holomorphically on $u$. Choose local $SL_2$ lifts $A_i(u)$ of $\rho(u)(\mu_i)$ with trace near $2$. Their traces equal $2\cosh(u_i/2)$, because their squares agree and the near-$2$ branch is unique. Thus $e^{u_i/2}$ is an eigenvalue. The matrix $A_i(u)-e^{u_i/2}I$ has rank one throughout a small neighborhood, including $u_i=0$, since it has zero determinant and stays near a nonzero rank-one matrix. A fixed nonzero column of its adjugate gives a holomorphic kernel line $\ell_i(u)$ after shrinking. This line is invariant under the whole peripheral subgroup by commutation. Conversely, given a nearby slice representation with a chosen peripheral line, its meridian eigenvalue on that line is holomorphic and near $1$; its unique near-zero ratio logarithm defines $u_i$. The trace relation forces precisely the representation just constructed, and the rank-one kernel forces precisely its chosen line. Both constructions are holomorphic: the eigenvalue is read by applying the matrix to a local nonzero vector of the line. They are inverse maps on the augmented germ. Hence that germ is smooth of dimension $k$ with coordinates $u$.

The local lift of $\rho(u)(\lambda_i)$ commutes with $A_i(u)$: the commutator sign is locally constant and positive at the complete point. It acts on $\ell_i(u)$ by a nonzero holomorphic eigenvalue near its complete value; choose its sign to make this value $1$, and define $v_i$ as twice its near-zero logarithm. Choose a holomorphic change of frame sending $\ell_i(u)$ to $\mathbb Ce_1$, by adjoining a fixed complementary vector and normalizing the determinant locally. The resulting peripheral Möbius maps fix $\infty$ and act on its finite complement as $z\mapsto e^{u_i}z+a_i(u)$ and $z\mapsto e^{v_i}z+b_i(u)$. At $u=0$, their translations satisfy $a_i(0)\ne0$ and $b_i(0)/a_i(0)=\tau_i^0$. Apply [F4] to get $v_i=\tau_i(u)u_i$ with $\tau_i$ holomorphic and $\tau_i(0)=\tau_i^0$. Positivity of the imaginary part persists on a sufficiently small common neighborhood. For one cusp the holomorphic Taylor expansion gives $v(u)=\tau^0u+O(u^2)$. All constructions used representation matrices and cusp models; none used an ideal triangulation, or a positivity assumption about tetrahedra.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty complete metric space ([[def-complete-metric-space]])
and let $f : X \to X$ be a contraction with constant $q$, so
$d(f(u),f(v)) \le q\,d(u,v)$ for all $u,v \in X$ and $0 \le q < 1$
([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]]). Then:

1. There is exactly one $x^{*} \in X$ with $f(x^{*}) = x^{*}$.
2. For every $x_0 \in X$ the sequence of **iterates**, defined by recursion
   ([[thm-recursion]]) by $x_{n+1} := f(x_n)$, converges to $x^{*}$ in $(X,d)$
   ([[def-metric-convergence]]). In particular the limit does not depend on
   $x_0$.
3. For all $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge n$,
   $$d(x_m, x_n) \;\le\; \frac{q^{\,n}\, d(x_1,x_0)}{1-q},$$
   with the integer power of [[def-integer-power]].

Claim 3 is the quantitative form of the argument that proves claims 1 and 2, and
it is recorded in the statement because the error estimates
([[cor-banach-error-estimates]]) are read off from it.

derivations.claim: Shrink to a closed convex polydisc $B_\epsilon=\{\|u\|_\infty\le\epsilon\}$ inside the holomorphy domain. Its compactness and continuity of the derivatives give a common Lipschitz constant $L$ for all $\tau_i$ there, by integrating their derivatives along line segments. Put $A=\max_i|\operatorname{Im}\tau_i(0)|^{-1}$ and shrink $\epsilon$ so that $AL\epsilon\le1/4$ and every $\operatorname{Im}\tau_i(u)$ stays nonzero on $B_\epsilon$. For any nonzero real pair $(p,q)$, $p+q\tau_i(0)\ne0$ and $|q/(p+q\tau_i(0))|\le A$. Moreover $|p+q\tau_i(0)|\ge c\sqrt{p^2+q^2}$ for one common $c>0$: the real-linear maps $(p,q)\mapsto p+q\tau_i(0)$ are invertible, and their moduli have a positive minimum on the unit circle.

For a parameter tuple with finite pairs outside a sufficiently large radius $R$, define $a_i=q_i/(p_i+q_i\tau_i(0))$ and the $w_i$ in the Statement. At an infinite coordinate put $a_i=w_i=0$. On $B_\epsilon$ define $T_i(u)=w_i/[1+a_i(\tau_i(u)-\tau_i(0))]$. Step 1.1 makes every denominator have modulus at least $3/4$, hence $\|T(u)\|_\infty\le(4/3)\|w\|_\infty$. Also $\|T(u)-T(u')\|_\infty\le(16/9)AL\|w\|_\infty\|u-u'\|_\infty$. Since step 1.1 makes $\|w\|_\infty\le2\pi/(cR)$, choose $R$ so large that $\|w\|_\infty\le\epsilon/2$ and $(16/9)AL\|w\|_\infty\le1/2$. The closed polydisc is nonempty and complete, and $T$ maps it into itself, so [F1] supplies its unique fixed point. Its defining equations are exactly the simultaneous full-turn equations at finite coordinates, and $u_i=0$ at infinite ones. At a finite coordinate $w_i\ne0$, so its solution $u_i$ cannot vanish. Every solution in $B_\epsilon$ is such a fixed point and is therefore this one.

The fixed-point bound in step 2.1 gives $\|u\|_\infty\le(4/3)\|w\|_\infty$. Its coordinate equation also gives $|u_i-w_i|\le(4/3)A|w_i|\,|\tau_i(u)-\tau_i(0)|\le(16/9)AL|w_i|\|w\|_\infty$. This proves the stated uniform expansion, including every $w_i=0$ coordinate exactly.

Define the coefficient map $\Phi$ on the open polydisc by the equations in the Statement. If $u_i\ne0$, the real-linear equation $p_i+q_i\tau_i(u)=2\pi i/u_i$ has a unique real pair, continuously depending on $u$. If $u_i\to0$, the norms of these pairs tend to infinity uniformly with the other coordinates in $B_\epsilon$: boundedness of $\tau_i$ gives $2\pi/|u_i|=|p_i+q_i\tau_i(u)|\le C\sqrt{p_i^2+q_i^2}$. Thus $\Phi$ is continuous also at its infinite coordinates, with $\Phi(0)=(\infty,\ldots,\infty)$. Let $V$ be the product neighborhood specified using $R$ in step 2.1, and put $U=\Phi^{-1}(V)$ inside the open polydisc. This is an open neighborhood of $0$. Every parameter in $V$ has its unique solution in the interior by step 2.1, so $\Phi:U\to V$ is bijective.

Its inverse is continuous on the whole product neighborhood, including partially unfilled tuples. If parameter tuples converge, their fixed-point maps $T$ from step 2.1 converge uniformly on $B_\epsilon$. For a finite limiting coordinate, $a_i,w_i$ converge in the displayed rational formulas. For an infinite limiting coordinate, $w_i\to0$ while $|a_i|\le A$, so the corresponding $T_i$ tends uniformly to zero by the $3/4$ denominator bound, regardless of the directions of the real pairs. If $u,u'$ are the two fixed points and $T,T'$ their maps, then $\|u-u'\|_\infty\le\tfrac12\|u-u'\|_\infty+\sup_{B_\epsilon}\|T-T'\|_\infty$, proving continuity. This establishes the homeomorphism. No primitivity was used in this analytic proof; primitivity enters only when a later geometric construction identifies a smooth solid-torus meridian.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $M=\Gamma\backslash\mathbb H^3$ be a connected oriented complete finite-volume hyperbolic three-manifold, with a compact smooth core $N$ and $k\ge1$ standard rank-two torus cusp ends. Thus $M$ is the interior of $N$ and each end has metric $dt^2+e^{-2t}g_i$, where $g_i$ is a flat torus metric. Let $\rho_0:\pi_1(N)\to G=\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb C)$ be its holonomy. Choose a positively oriented basis $(\mu_i,\lambda_i)$ for each oriented horotorus, so its translation lattice can be normalized to $\langle1,\tau_i^0\rangle$ with $\operatorname{Im}\tau_i^0>0$.

The germ of representations modulo conjugacy at $[\rho_0]$ is a smooth complex manifold of dimension $k$. The functions $s_i(\rho)=\operatorname{tr}^2\rho(\mu_i)$ are local holomorphic coordinates near their values $s_i=4$. Trace squared is well defined in $G$, independently of an $SL_2$ lift.

Augment a nearby representation by choosing one common invariant line for each peripheral subgroup, and quotient these data by simultaneous conjugacy. The germ of this augmented space at the complete representation and its unique peripheral fixed lines is a smooth complex $k$-manifold. It has holomorphic coordinates $u=(u_1,\ldots,u_k)$, where $u_i$ is the eigenvalue-ratio logarithm for $\mu_i$ on the selected line, and the forgetful map is
$$s_i=4\cosh^2(u_i/2).$$
The corresponding logarithms $v_i$ for $\lambda_i$ are holomorphic and satisfy
$$v_i(u)=\tau_i(u)u_i,\qquad \tau_i(0)=\tau_i^0,\qquad \operatorname{Im}\tau_i(u)>0$$
on a sufficiently small neighborhood. In particular $u_i=0$ if and only if $v_i=0$, and for $k=1$ one has $v(u)=\tau^0u+O(u^2)$. No positive or nondegenerate ideal triangulation is assumed. The statement concerns the augmented space, not a single-valued eigenvalue logarithm on the ordinary conjugacy quotient.
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every open cover of a smooth manifold admits a smooth partition of unity subordinate to it.

Let $F:M\to N$ be a smooth map and let $p\in M$. If $dF_p:T_pM\to T_{F(p)}N$ is
an isomorphism, then there are open neighbourhoods $U$ of $p$ and $V$ of
$F(p)$ such that $F|_U:U\to V$ is a diffeomorphism.

Assume AC. Every nonempty connected oriented complete Riemannian three-manifold of constant sectional curvature $-1$ is isometric to $\Gamma\backslash\mathbb H^3$ for a discrete torsion-free subgroup $\Gamma\le\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb C)$. The covering is a universal Riemannian covering and identifies $\Gamma$ with the fundamental group up to the usual basepoint conjugacies. Its completeness and quotient presentation are conclusions from the stated metric hypotheses. The orientation-preserving isometry group of the model is $\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb C)$ with its usual Möbius boundary action.

Let $\overline M$ be a compact connected oriented three-manifold whose boundary is a disjoint union of tori $T_1,\ldots,T_k$. Choose an ordered integral basis $([\mu_i],[\lambda_i])$ for each $H_1(T_i;\mathbb Z)$. A **slope** on $T_i$ is an unoriented isotopy class of essential simple closed curves whose homology class is $p_i[\mu_i]+q_i[\lambda_i]$ for a primitive pair $(p_i,q_i)\in\mathbb Z^2$; simultaneous negation gives the same unoriented slope. The primitive-pair correspondence gives exactly one such slope for each primitive pair modulo sign. The **ordinary Dehn filling** along a tuple of slopes indexed by $J\subseteq\{1,\ldots,k\}$ attaches an oriented solid torus $D^2\times S^1$ to each $T_i$, $i\in J$, by an orientation-reversing boundary homeomorphism that sends $[\partial D^2\times\{*\}]$ to the chosen slope. The gluing maps are part of the filling data; $i\notin J$ means that the cusp is left unfilled, denoted by the parameter $\infty$.

For a hyperbolic deformation, the **generalized cone-filling parameter space** at each cusp is the one-point compactification $\mathbb R^2\cup\{\infty\}$ of the real coefficient plane, with $\infty$ denoting the complete cusp. A primitive integral pair $(p_i,q_i)$ is an ordinary smooth filling coefficient. If a realized generalized parameter lies on the ray $g_i=r_i(p_i,q_i)$ with $r_i>0$ and $(p_i,q_i)$ primitive integral, its topological core direction is the ordinary slope $(p_i,q_i)$ and its cone angle is $2\pi/r_i$. Only $r_i=1$ is the ordinary smooth filling; $r_i>1$ describes a cone or orbifold completion and does not turn the nonprimitive vector $g_i$ into a slope.

Let $V=D^2\times S^1$ and $V'=D^2\times S^1$ be solid tori, with meridian curves $\mu=\partial D^2\times\{1\}$ and $\mu'=\partial D^2\times\{1\}$. Suppose $h:\partial V\to\partial V'$ is a homeomorphism and there is an isotopy $H_t:\partial V'\to\partial V'$ through homeomorphisms, with $H_0=\mathrm{id}$, such that $H_1(h(\mu))=\mu'$. Then $h$ extends to a homeomorphism $\overline h:V\to V'$. The extension may be chosen to carry the product core $\{0\}\times S^1$ onto the product core of $V'$, and has the same orientation sign as $h$ with respect to the boundary orientations.

derivations.claim: We first give an isometry-equivariant way of blending maps into $\mathbb H^3$. Use the Lorentz form $\langle X,X\rangle=X_1^2+X_2^2+X_3^2-X_4^2$ and embed upper half-space by $\Phi(Z,Y)=(\operatorname{Re}Z/Y,\operatorname{Im}Z/Y,(|Z|^2+Y^2-1)/(2Y),(|Z|^2+Y^2+1)/(2Y))$. Direct substitution gives $\langle\Phi,\Phi\rangle=-1$, positive last coordinate, and differentiation gives the upper half-space metric $(|dZ|^2+dY^2)/Y^2$. Its coordinate matrix in $(\operatorname{Re}Z,\operatorname{Im}Z,Y)$ is $Y^{-2}I_3$, so its volume coefficient is the positive square root of $Y^{-6}$, namely $Y^{-3}$. The action of $G=\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb C)$ is linear on these Lorentz coordinates. Indeed the equivalent Hermitian-matrix coordinate is $Y^{-1}\left(\begin{smallmatrix}|Z|^2+Y^2&Z\\\overline Z&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$; it is positive definite with determinant one, and $X\mapsto AXA^*$, for $A\in SL_2(\mathbb C)$, is linear on the four real Hermitian coordinates, preserves determinant and positivity, and is unchanged by replacing $A$ by $-A$. For positive weights summing to one, a weighted sum $S$ of future unit timelike vectors is future timelike: writing each vector as $(x,t)$ gives $t>|x|$, and the triangle inequality gives this strict inequality for the sum. Thus $B(S)=S/\sqrt{-\langle S,S\rangle}$ is well defined and smooth. It commutes with every $G$ action. If every input equals $X$, its value is $X$. This is a normalized Lorentz sum, rather than an undefined linear average inside a manifold.

Fix an end and omit its index temporarily. Choose the frames in [F1] so that at zero its original developing map is $(x,y,t)\mapsto(a(0)(x+\tau(0)y),e^t)$ on $\mathbb R^2\times[0,\infty)$. The deck generators add one to $x$ and $y$. Such a normalization is obtained by a fixed translation and dilation of a lift of the original horoball; it only fixes the origin and the level called $t=0$. Write $\zeta=x+\tau(u)y$, $L=u\zeta$, $w=(1-e^u)/a(u)$ and $B=\sqrt{(1+|w|^2)/(1+e^{2t}|w|^2)}$, choosing the positive square root. Put $E(z)=(e^z-1)/z$ with $E(0)=1$. Define an end map $\Psi_u=(Z_u,Y_u)$ by $Y_u=e^t|e^L|B$ and $Z_u=a(u)\zeta E(L)/E(u)+e^L(e^{2t}-1)\overline w/((1+e^{2t}|w|^2)(1+B))$. All these formulas are smooth in $(x,y,t,\operatorname{Re}u,\operatorname{Im}u)$, and in the other deformation coordinates: $a,\tau$ are holomorphic, $a$ and $E(u)$ are nonzero after shrinking, and every real denominator is positive. At $u=0$ they give precisely $(a(u)(x+\tau(u)y),e^t)$, including when other deformation coordinates are nonzero. At the complete parameter they give the original developing map. Consequently their convergence, with every derivative, is uniform on each fixed compact coordinate collar.

Choose product coordinates $T_i^2\times[0,\infty)$ on the ends, and include their collars through $t=2$ in a compact set $K$. The given complete developing map identifies the universal cover of $M$ with $\mathbb H^3$, with deck action $\rho_0$. Cover $K$ by finitely many simply connected evenly covered coordinate sets $U_j$ and choose one lift $\widetilde U_j$ for each. On an open neighborhood $V$ of $K$ covered by these sets, use [F2] to choose a subordinate smooth partition $\phi_j$. Pull each function to each component $\rho_0(\gamma)\widetilde U_j$ and extend it by zero; denote this lifted function by $\phi_{\gamma j}$. Its support stays inside that component. These functions are locally finite and sum to one on the inverse image of $V$. Put $D_{\gamma j}(x,u)=\rho_u(\gamma)\rho_0(\gamma)^{-1}x$ and let $D^{\mathrm{core}}_u(x)$ be the Lorentz blend of the points $D_{\gamma j}(x,u)$ with weights $\phi_{\gamma j}(x)$. The sums are locally finite and smooth. The deck identities for the weights and $D_{\delta\gamma,j}(\rho_0(\delta)x,u)=\rho_u(\delta)D_{\gamma j}(x,u)$ show exact $\rho_u$ equivariance. At zero every input is $x$, so $D^{\mathrm{core}}_0(x)=x$.

When $u\ne0$, put $c=1/w=a/(1-e^u)$ and $C=|c|$. The identity $(1-B)/w=(e^{2t}-1)\overline w/((1+e^{2t}|w|^2)(1+B))$ rewrites the preceding formula as $Z_u=c(1-Be^L)$, $Y_u=e^t|e^L|B$. On adding one to $x$, these become $Z\mapsto e^uZ+a$, $Y\mapsto e^{\operatorname{Re}u}Y$. Commutativity gives $a(e^v-1)=b(e^u-1)$, so $c(1-e^v)=b$; adding one to $y$ gives the other peripheral isometry. When $u=0$, the translation formula in step 1.2 gives the same equivariance because $v=0$ and $b=a\tau$. Compose $\Psi_u$ with the inverse of the frame from [F1]; this gives a map $D^{\mathrm{end}}_u$ on a chosen lifted end, equivariant under its peripheral subgroup. Extend to all its deck translates by $D^{\mathrm{end}}_u(\rho_0(\gamma)x)=\rho_u(\gamma)D^{\mathrm{end}}_u(x)$. This is well defined because two descriptions differ by a peripheral deck transformation.

On the compact quotient $K$, the last construction converges to the identity in every derivative as $u\to0$, in fixed local lift charts. To see uniformity without an assertion about infinitely many deck transformations, cover $K$ by finitely many smaller relatively compact chart pieces and lift each piece once. Only finitely many of the locally finite functions $\phi_{\gamma j}$ meet those compact lifts. Only these finitely many matrices $\rho_u(\gamma)\rho_0(\gamma)^{-1}$ enter the derivative estimates there, and each converges smoothly to the identity. Invertibility of a matrix is open; compactness and [F2] therefore give one neighborhood of zero on which $D^{\mathrm{core}}_u$ is a local diffeomorphism at all points over $K$. Its pullback metric descends by equivariance, is hyperbolic, and converges smoothly to the original metric on $K$.

The end map is a local diffeomorphism on its entire domain. For $u=0$ this follows directly from the translation formula and $\operatorname{Im}\tau>0$. For $u\ne0$ introduce Fermi coordinates about the vertical geodesic with endpoints $c,\infty$: $Z=c+e^s\tanh r\,e^{i\theta}$, $Y=e^s/\cosh r$. Direct differentiation using [F3] gives $dr^2+\sinh^2r\,d\theta^2+\cosh^2r\,ds^2$. The map in step 2.2 is precisely $r(t)=\operatorname{arsinh}(Ce^{-t})$, $s=\log\sqrt{C^2+1}+\operatorname{Re}L$, $\theta=\arg(-c)+\operatorname{Im}L$. The choice of the constant argument is immaterial modulo $2\pi$. The real linear map $(x,y)\mapsto(\operatorname{Re}L,\operatorname{Im}L)$ has determinant $\operatorname{Im}(\overline u v)=|u|^2\operatorname{Im}\tau>0$, and $r'(t)\ne0$. Thus the differential is invertible everywhere for finite $t$. For $t\ge T$ its image is the whole punctured tube $0<r\le R(T)$, where $R(T)=\operatorname{arsinh}(Ce^{-T})$, and $(s,\theta)$ before angular reduction range over all $\mathbb R^2$. No discreteness of the full peripheral image is required for this local assertion.

We now join the core and the end maps. Take a fixed smooth function $\beta(t)$ equal to zero near $t=0$ and one for $t\ge1$. On the end collar $0\le t\le1$, Lorentz blend $D^{\mathrm{core}}_u$ and $D^{\mathrm{end}}_u$ with weights $1-\beta$ and $\beta$; use the core map below this collar and the end map above it. Both maps have the same $\rho_u$ equivariance, so the blend does too. The lifted end components are disjoint; their deck translates give the construction on all of the universal cover. At the complete parameter both inputs are the identity, and steps 3.1 and 1.2 show smooth convergence on the compact transition collars. Therefore, after one common shrinking for the finitely many ends, the blended differential is invertible throughout these collars. Above them step 3.2 applies; below them step 3.1 applies. We have constructed a global smooth equivariant local diffeomorphism $D_u:\widetilde M\to\mathbb H^3$. Its pullback of the hyperbolic metric is invariant under the original deck group and hence defines $g_u$ on $M$, with holonomy $\rho_u$. Local inverses from [F2] give its hyperbolic charts. The construction is smooth in parameters on compact subsets and gives $g_0$ exactly.

If $u_i=0$, the metric above the collar is the translation-cusp metric $dt^2+e^{-2t}|a_i(u)|^2|dx+\tau_i(u)dy|^2$. It has volume $|a_i(u)|^2\operatorname{Im}\tau_i(u)e^{-2T}/2$ for $t\ge T\ge1$, by integration on $[0,1]^2\times[T,\infty)$. Its end is complete: the length of any path dominates the total change in $t$, so reaching arbitrarily large $t$ requires unbounded length. This proves all assertions about unfilled ends, independently of what happens at the other cusps.

Fix a filled cusp, so $u\ne0$ by its full-turn equation. Let $m=(p,q)$ be its primitive filling vector and choose integers $p',q'$ with $pq'-qp'=1$, using the integer Euclidean algorithm. Put $d=(p',q')$ and $W=p'u+q'v=A+iB_0$. Under the Fermi linear map in step 3.2, $m$ maps to $(0,2\pi)$ and $d$ to $(A,B_0)$. The determinant identity gives $-2\pi A=|u|^2\operatorname{Im}\tau>0$. In particular $A\ne0$ and $|A|=|u|^2\operatorname{Im}\tau/(2\pi)$. The vectors $m,d$ are an integral basis, so the image of the deck lattice is exactly the lattice generated by $(0,2\pi)$ and $(A,B_0)$. It follows that the end $t\ge T\ge1$ with its actual metric is isometric to the punctured radius-$R(T)$ hyperbolic tube modulo the screw motion $(r,\theta,s)\mapsto(r,\theta+B_0,s+A)$. This is a bijective local isometry: the real linear map is invertible, $t\mapsto r$ is one-to-one onto $(0,R(T)]$, and its only identifications after reducing $\theta$ modulo $2\pi$ and then by the screw are precisely the original integral deck lattice. This checks the global quotient, beyond the local developing map.

Add the axis $r=0$ to this tube before taking its screw quotient. Its smooth structure and metric are ordinary hyperbolic ones. Explicitly, with $X=r\cos\theta$, $Y'=r\sin\theta$, the upper-half-space formula becomes $Z=c+e^s(\tanh r/r)(X+iY')$ and $Y=e^s/\cosh r$. The even smooth functions $\tanh r/r$ and $1/\cosh r$ extend at $r=0$ with value one. The map has invertible differential there and gives standard hyperbolic coordinates across the axis. The screw extends smoothly, freely and properly: it translates $s$ by the nonzero number $A$, so no nonidentity power fixes a point and only finitely many powers move one compact set to meet another. Its closed radius-$R(T)$ quotient is compact, as a closed disk times an $s$ interval of length $|A|$ with its ends identified by a rotation. More explicitly $(r,\theta,s)\mapsto(r e^{i(\theta-B_0s/A)},e^{2\pi i s/A})$ identifies the quotient smoothly with a product solid torus, including at $r=0$. The angular vector $m$, which changes $\theta$ by exactly $2\pi$ while fixing $s$, is its meridian. Thus the boundary identification furnished in step 5.2 attaches an ordinary solid torus with meridian $p\mu+q\lambda$, exactly as in [F4]. Its metric agrees on a whole punctured collar with $g_u$, so the attachment is smooth. The core is a geodesic of length $|A|=\ell_i$; no nonidentity screw power fixes a point on that core because the same screw has nonzero axial translation.

These constructions are simultaneous and give the required topology. Choose the same level $T\ge1$ in the finitely many disjoint end products. Retain the compact truncated core, and attach the solid tori of step 6.1 on the filled boundary components, using the explicit boundary diffeomorphisms of step 5.2. Retain the translation ends on the unfilled components. This produces the ordinary partial filling with the indicated meridians, with its orientation extended from the core. The boundary maps reverse the induced boundary orientations because they identify the two sides of the same product collar; the constructed metric agrees there and fixes the oriented structure. Equivalently the removed open punctured solid torus in each completed tube has exactly the original $T^2\times[T,\infty)$ marking. Thus no separate identification of slopes, covering degree or core topology is being inferred merely from trivial peripheral holonomy. For precision concerning arbitrary supplied attaching maps, write $f_i:\partial V_i\to T_i$ for our explicit attachment and $h_i:\partial W_i\to T_i$ for a supplied orientation-reversing boundary homeomorphism with the same meridian slope. By the ambient-isotopy convention in [F4], choose an ambient isotopy $J_{i,t}$ of $T_i$, starting at the identity, carrying $h_i(\partial D^2\times\{1\})$ onto $f_i(\partial D^2\times\{1\})$. For $e_i=f_i^{-1}h_i$, the conjugate isotopy $f_i^{-1}J_{i,t}f_i$ therefore satisfies exactly the meridian hypothesis of [F4]. Extend $e_i$ to a core-preserving homeomorphism $\overline e_i:W_i\to V_i$. It is orientation preserving because both $f_i,h_i$ reverse boundary orientation. The identity on the truncated manifold and these extensions glue to an orientation-preserving, core-preserving homeomorphism $P$ from the supplied filling to our constructed filling: on the attaching boundary, $f_i\overline e_i=h_i$. On the supplied topological filling declare charts to be $(P^{-1}U,\varphi\circ P)$ for every chart $(U,\varphi)$ of the constructed smooth filling. These charts have the same smooth transition functions as the constructed atlas; in this transported smooth structure $P$ is a diffeomorphism, and the metric defined by those same chart coefficients is $P^*g_u$. It makes $P$ an isometry. Because $P$ is the identity on the truncated original manifold, its original smooth structure and metric there are retained. Completeness, orientation, volume and core lengths are preserved by this isometry. This is transport of a smooth structure, not a claim that a given arbitrary boundary homeomorphism is smooth for some independently specified atlas. Smooth convergence on compact subsets of the marked original $M$ follows from step 4.1, since the explicit realized metrics agree with $g_u$ there.

The extended metric is complete and has finite volume. The union of the truncated core and the finitely many closed filled tubes is compact. The other ends are the explicit complete translation cusps of step 5.1. For metric completeness, define $f=0$ on that compact part and $f=t-T$ on each retained cusp. It is continuous and $1$-Lipschitz for the path metric: on cusp segments $|df|=1$, on the compact part it is zero, and splitting paths at the common boundary gives the global inequality. A Cauchy sequence has bounded $f$ and therefore stays in a compact union of that part and finitely many truncated cusps. A smooth Riemannian metric induces the manifold topology locally, since on a small relatively compact coordinate ball its positive-definite coefficients bound Euclidean lengths above and below; hence that compact union is metric compact. The sequence has a convergent subsequence, and being Cauchy converges. This proves completeness directly. The compact part has finite volume, each retained cusp has the finite volume in step 5.1, and each filled tube has finite volume: its Fermi density is $\sinh r\cosh r\,dr\,d\theta\,ds$, so its volume is $\pi|A|\sinh^2R(T)$. Curvature is $-1$ everywhere because the extension charts of step 6.1 are actual hyperbolic charts.

Finally the same formulas give convergence of volume, including for varying simultaneous slope tuples. On a filled end $\sinh^2R(T)=|c|^2e^{-2T}$ and $|A|=|u|^2\operatorname{Im}\tau/(2\pi)$, so its completed tail volume is exactly $|a(u)|^2\operatorname{Im}\tau(u)e^{-2T}/(2|E(u)|^2)$, since $|1-e^u|^2=|u|^2|E(u)|^2$. On an unfilled end this formula has the same value by step 5.1 and $E(0)=1$. Thus, for any fixed $T\ge1$, each tail volume tends to its original complete-cusp volume as the full parameter tends to zero. On the compact part $t\le T$, step 4.1 gives smooth metric convergence, hence convergence of volume densities and their integrals; finitely many coordinate charts and a partition of unity reduce this to uniform convergence of smooth positive determinants on compact sets. Adding the finitely many tail volumes proves convergence of total volume. The displayed core-length formula in step 5.2 tends to zero as well, because $\tau$ stays bounded. All assertions of the Statement follow.
