citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K$ and $J$ be disjoint oriented smooth
embedded circles in the oriented three-sphere, and let $\Sigma$ be a compact
oriented smooth surface embedded in the three-sphere with boundary $K$, whose
outward-normal-first boundary orientation is the specified orientation of $K$.
Here outward-normal-first means that an outward-pointing normal followed by a
positive boundary tangent gives the orientation of $\Sigma$. Assume
$J$ is transverse to $\Sigma$, and fix a regular oriented diagram $D$ of
$J\cup K$. Let $\eta$ be a positively oriented meridian of $K$ and let
$m\in\mathbb Z$ be the unique integer such that
$[J]=m[\eta]$ in $H_1(S^3\setminus K;\mathbb Z)$. Define the topological
linking number by $\operatorname{lk}(J,K):=m$. Let
$\operatorname{lk}_D(J,K)$ be the half-sum of the signs of the mixed crossings
of $D$. Orient the normal line of $\Sigma$ by the ambient orientation. A point
of $J\cap\Sigma$ has sign $+1$ if the oriented curve $J$ crosses from the
negative side of $\Sigma$ to its positive side, and sign $-1$ for the reverse
passage. Then
$$\operatorname{lk}_D(J,K)=\operatorname{lk}(J,K)=\sum_{p\in J\cap\Sigma}\operatorname{sign}_\Sigma(p).$$
The statement is conditional on a supplied spanning surface and regular
diagram; it asserts no surface- or diagram-existence theorem.
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Every smooth oriented knot $K\subset S^3$ bounds a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface $F\subset S^3$ whose oriented boundary is $K$.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $W$ be a compact oriented smooth $1$-manifold and give $\partial W$ the outward-normal-first orientation ([[def-induced-boundary-orientation]]). The boundary is a finite $0$-manifold, so its orientation at a boundary point $p$ is a sign $\varepsilon(p)\in\{+1,-1\}$; then $$\sum_{p\in\partial W}\varepsilon(p)=0.$$ On each closed-interval component the two boundary points carry opposite signs; circle components contribute nothing. With the standard orientation of $[a,b]$ the outward-normal-first convention gives $\partial[a,b]=\{b\}-\{a\}$.

If $X$ is a nonempty contractible topological space, then for every $n\geq 0$
and every abelian group $G$,
$$H_n^{\mathrm{sing}}(X;G)\cong H_n^{\mathrm{sing}}(\ast;G),$$
where $\ast$ denotes a one-point space.

Let $X$ be a compact oriented smooth $x$-manifold without boundary, let $M$ be an oriented smooth $n$-manifold without boundary, and let $Z\subseteq M$ be a closed oriented embedded $z$-submanifold with $x+z=n$ ([[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]]). For a smooth $f:X\to M$ transverse to $Z$, the **oriented intersection number** is the finite sum

$$I(f,Z):=\sum_{p\in f^{-1}(Z)}\varepsilon(p)\in\mathbb Z,$$

with the local signs of [[def-local-oriented-intersection-sign]]; the sum is finite by [[lem-compact-transverse-complementary-intersections-are-finite]]. For an arbitrary smooth $g:X\to M$, choose a transverse $f$ homotopic to $g$ ([[thm-transversality-homotopy-theorem]], under Countable Choice; the homotopy is a smooth family in the sense of [[def-smooth-family-of-maps-and-evaluation-map]]) and set $I(g,Z):=I(f,Z)$; independence of the choice is [[thm-oriented-intersection-number-is-homotopy-invariant]], not assumed here. For compact oriented complementary-dimensional submanifolds $A,B\subseteq M$, where one is compact and the other closed, one sets $I(A,B):=I(i_A,B)$ with $i_A$ the inclusion, so the first factor is the submanifold $A$. If the source is not compact, or the target submanifold is not closed, the sum may fail to be finite or invariant; the safe extension by properness with compact trace is recorded in the remark on properness later on this page. Countable Choice is assumed for selecting transverse representatives and for the classification used to prove independence of that selection; the signs, the finite sum and the empty case (which contributes $0$) are choice-free.

For transverse maps $f:X^x\to M$, $g:Z^z\to M$ with compact oriented boundaryless sources and $x+z=\dim M$, define $I(f,g)$ as the sum of the local signs of [[def-local-oriented-intersection-sign]] over $X\times_MZ$. This set is closed in the compact product because $M$ is Hausdorff, and discrete by [[def-transverse-complementary-dimensional-intersection-set]], so the sum is finite. If $g$ is an inclusion this recovers $I(f,Z)$. Ambient compactness is unnecessary in either construction.

Let $M$ be an oriented smooth $n$-manifold and let $f:X^x\to M$ and $g:Z^z\to M$ be smooth maps from oriented smooth manifolds, with $x+z=n$ and $f,g$ transverse in the sense of [[def-transverse-smooth-maps]]. Let $a\in X$, $b\in Z$ satisfy $f(a)=g(b)=y$. Then $T_aX\oplus T_bZ$ and $T_yM$ have the same dimension, and transversality says that

$$(df_a,dg_b):T_aX\oplus T_bZ\longrightarrow T_yM,\qquad (v,w)\mapsto df_a(v)+dg_b(w),$$

is surjective, hence a linear isomorphism ([[def-transverse-linear-subspaces]]); the sum is direct because the dimensions add up. The ordered direct sum $T_aX\oplus T_bZ$ carries the product orientation with the first factor $T_aX$ and the second factor $T_bZ$ ([[def-product-orientation]]), and the three tangent spaces carry their manifold orientations ([[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]]).

The **local oriented intersection sign** $\varepsilon(a,b)\in\{+1,-1\}$ is $+1$ when this isomorphism carries the product orientation of $T_aX\oplus T_bZ$ to the orientation of $T_yM$, and $-1$ otherwise; equivalently it is the orientation sign of the induced isomorphism of determinant lines ([[def-determinant-line-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]], [[def-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]).

For transverse oriented embedded submanifolds $A^a,B^b\subseteq M$ with $a+b=n$ one takes $f$ and $g$ to be the inclusion maps ([[def-transverse-embedded-submanifolds]]); the sign at $p\in A\cap B$ then compares $T_pA\oplus T_pB\to T_pM$ with $A$ first. The empty intersection is allowed and carries no signs. In dimension zero the sign compares the two orientation rays directly, and for $x=z=n=0$ it is $\varepsilon_X(a)\varepsilon_Z(b)\varepsilon_M(y)$, the product of the two source point signs and the ambient point sign. The factor order is part of the definition: with the two factors exchanged the signs are multiplied by $(-1)^{ab}$, exactly the graded-commutativity sign measured later on this page by the factor-interchange theorem. No compactness, closedness hypothesis or choice axiom is used in this local definition.

For an oriented manifold with boundary, orient $T_p\partial M$ by the **outward-normal-first** rule: an outward vector first, followed by a positive boundary determinant, is a positive determinant of $T_pM$.

For oriented vector spaces use the ordered determinant isomorphism $\det(V\oplus W)\cong\det V\otimes\det W$ and take the tensor product of the selected rays. Fibrewise this defines the product orientation.

derivations.claim: First consider disjoint oriented knots $\alpha,\beta$ and two admissible choices $P,P'$ bounding $\alpha$ with the same product collar, while $Q$ is fixed. Their difference $C=P-P'$ is a closed rational $2$-cycle supported in the interior of $B^4$, because the common boundary collars cancel. By [F3], $C=\partial Z$ for a finite rational $3$-chain $Z$ supported in the interior. Put $Z$ and $Q$ in general position relative to their boundary collars. The transverse intersection $Z\cap Q$ is a compact oriented $1$-chain. The product-orientation convention in [F4] makes its boundary count equal to the intersection count $(P-P')\cdot Q$ plus the term from $Z\cap\partial Q$; the latter is empty because $Z$ lies in the interior and $\partial Q=\beta\subset S^3$. By [F2], its signed boundary count is zero, so $P\cdot Q=P'\cdot Q$. The same argument with $Q-Q'$ shows independence of the second bounding chain. Bilinearity gives this independence for finite rational combinations of knots.

By [F5], choose an oriented Seifert surface $S_\beta\subset S^3$ for each knot component of $\beta$, and similarly choose a cap for each component of $\alpha$. It suffices by bilinearity to consider one knot component of each. Choose a collar depth $0<\epsilon$ in $B^4$. Make $Q$ a graph of $S_\beta$ in the boundary collar with depth zero on $\beta$ and strictly between $0$ and $\epsilon/2$ on its interior. Make $P$ consist of the product collar $\alpha\times[0,\epsilon]$ followed by a cap at depth $\epsilon$. Then $P$ and $Q$ intersect exactly above $\alpha\cap S_\beta$. At each such point, the oriented tangent basis of the collar of $P$ is $(n_{\mathrm{out}},a)$, where $a$ is the positive tangent to $\alpha$ and $n_{\mathrm{out}}$ is the outward normal of $B^4$; the tangent basis of $Q$ is a positive basis $(s_1,s_2)$ of $S_\beta$, up to radial components which do not change the determinant. By [F4], $(n_{\mathrm{out}},a,s_1,s_2)$ is positive exactly when $(a,s_1,s_2)$ is positive in the boundary orientation. Thus the $4$-dimensional intersection sign is exactly the $3$-dimensional sign of $\alpha\cap S_\beta$. Hence $P\cdot Q=\operatorname{lk}(\alpha,\beta)$ by [F1].

Step 1.1 shows the intersection number is independent of admissible collared bounding chains, and step 1.2 computes it for one convenient choice. Hence the equality holds for all such $P,Q$ when the boundaries are knots. Expanding finite rational cycles into their oriented knot components and using bilinearity of both signed intersection and linking proves the stated equality.

Let $J_F$ be the matrix of the algebraic intersection form on $F$, with a transverse intersection of oriented curves $u,v$ counted positively exactly when their ordered tangent vectors form a positive basis of $TF$. Then $V-V^T=J_F$. The matrix $J_F$ is skew-symmetric and unimodular; when $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ is a standard handle basis, it is a direct sum of blocks $\begin{psmallmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{psmallmatrix}$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K$ and $J$ be disjoint oriented smooth
embedded circles in the oriented three-sphere, and let $\Sigma$ be a compact
oriented smooth surface embedded in the three-sphere with boundary $K$, whose
outward-normal-first boundary orientation is the specified orientation of $K$.
Here outward-normal-first means that an outward-pointing normal followed by a
positive boundary tangent gives the orientation of $\Sigma$. Assume
$J$ is transverse to $\Sigma$, and fix a regular oriented diagram $D$ of
$J\cup K$. Let $\eta$ be a positively oriented meridian of $K$ and let
$m\in\mathbb Z$ be the unique integer such that
$[J]=m[\eta]$ in $H_1(S^3\setminus K;\mathbb Z)$. Define the topological
linking number by $\operatorname{lk}(J,K):=m$. Let
$\operatorname{lk}_D(J,K)$ be the half-sum of the signs of the mixed crossings
of $D$. Orient the normal line of $\Sigma$ by the ambient orientation. A point
of $J\cap\Sigma$ has sign $+1$ if the oriented curve $J$ crosses from the
negative side of $\Sigma$ to its positive side, and sign $-1$ for the reverse
passage. Then
$$\operatorname{lk}_D(J,K)=\operatorname{lk}(J,K)=\sum_{p\in J\cap\Sigma}\operatorname{sign}_\Sigma(p).$$

diagram; it asserts no surface- or diagram-existence theorem.

The linking number $\operatorname{lk}(J,L)$ is the integer determined by $[J]=\operatorname{lk}(J,L)[\mu_L]$ in $H_1(S^3\setminus L;\mathbb Z)$, using the Alexander-duality identification that sends $[\mu_L]$ to $1$. Extend linking additively over integral one-cycles. The Seifert pairing is $\theta_F(x,y)=\operatorname{lk}(x^+,y)$, and its matrix in the chosen basis is $V=(V_{ij})_{i,j=1}^{2g}$, where $V_{ij}=\theta_F(a_i,a_j)=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. derivations.claim: If $g=0$, $V$ is the empty matrix and a disk with its empty homology basis realizes it. Assume $g>0$. Put $J=V-V^T$ and $H=\mathbb Z^{2g}$. Choose a primitive vector $e\in H$. Since $J:H\to\operatorname{Hom}(H,\mathbb Z)$ is an isomorphism, the functional $J(e,-)$ is primitive, so Bezout's identity gives $f\in H$ with $J(e,f)=1$. For every $x\in H$, the vector $x'=x-J(x,f)e+J(x,e)f$ satisfies $J(x',e)=J(x',f)=0$. Thus $H=\langle e,f\rangle\oplus\langle e,f\rangle^\perp$, and the restricted alternating form on the second summand is unimodular. Induction gives a basis with matrix $J_0=\bigoplus_{k=1}^g\begin{psmallmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{psmallmatrix}$. Let $P\in\mathrm{GL}_{2g}(\mathbb Z)$ be the corresponding change of basis and put $W=P^TVP$; then $W-W^T=J_0$.

Start with a disk and attach $2g$ oriented bands in the standard one-boundary handle pattern. Their core curves form an integral basis with intersection matrix $J_0$. The result is a connected compact smooth oriented surface with one boundary component. Write $W_0$ for its positive-push matrix; by [F1], $W_0-W_0^T=J_0$.

For each band core, inserting an integer number of full twists in a small subarc changes only its self-linking entry by the chosen integer. The twist box is disjoint from the other core arcs, and the surface intersection matrix is unchanged. Perform these finitely many modifications to make every diagonal entry of $W_0$ equal the corresponding diagonal entry of $W$.

For each pair $i<j$, choose subarcs of bands $i$ and $j$ in a ball disjoint from every other core and every earlier modification. Insert the oriented local clasp whose two new mixed crossings between $a_i^+$ and $a_j$ have the same sign $\varepsilon\in\{+1,-1\}$. By [F2], their signed sum changes by $2\varepsilon$, so $W_{ij}$ changes by $\varepsilon$. The clasp preserves the abstract surface intersection form; by [F1], $W_{ij}-W_{ji}$ is unchanged, and therefore $W_{ji}$ also changes by $\varepsilon$. The move is supported away from every other core, so all other pair entries and all diagonal entries stay fixed. The target equation $W-W_0=(W-W_0)^T$ off the diagonal holds because both skew parts are $J_0$. A finite number of positive or negative clasps thus sets both entries to their target values for each pair, without changing previously treated pairs. The resulting surface has positive-push matrix exactly $W$.

The basis change $P^{-1}\in\mathrm{GL}_{2g}(\mathbb Z)$ on this surface changes its matrix from $W$ to $(P^{-1})^TW P^{-1}=V$. The constructed surface has one boundary component, so its boundary is an oriented knot and the matrix is a Seifert matrix for that knot.

Assume the full Axiom of Choice when a knot's Seifert pairing is formed. The rank-zero lattice is allowed, with the determinant of its empty skew matrix equal to $1$. A metabolizer is a primitive direct summand $M\subset H$ of rank $g$ such that $V(x,y)=0$ for every $x,y\in M$; the lattice is metabolic when it has a metabolizer. A chosen Seifert surface of an oriented knot gives such a lattice through the positive-push pairing. Its form is algebraically slice when that lattice is metabolic.

An isomorphism of integral Seifert lattices $(H,V)$ and $(H',V')$ is an integral group isomorphism $P:H\to H'$ satisfying $V'(Px,Py)=V(x,y)$ for all $x,y\in H$. Let $\mathcal S$ be the commutative monoid of these isomorphism classes under orthogonal direct sum, where $(H,V)\oplus(H',V')$ has underlying group $H\oplus H'$ and pairing $V\oplus V'$, with the rank-zero lattice as identity. The integral algebraic concordance group $G_{\mathbb Z}$ is the abelian group generated by symbols $[V]$ for $[V]\in\mathcal S$, subject to $[V\oplus W]=[V]+[W]$ and $[M]=0$ for every metabolic lattice $M$. Two selected Seifert forms are algebraically concordant when they represent the same element of $G_{\mathbb Z}$. This form relation does not assert the existence of a smooth or locally flat topological concordance annulus between the knots.

derivations.claim: In $(H,V)\oplus(H,-V)$, the diagonal subgroup $\Delta H=\{(x,x):x\in H\}$ is a direct summand: it is the kernel of the surjection $(x,y)\mapsto x-y$ and that surjection has section $z\mapsto(z,0)$. Its rank is $\operatorname{rank}H$, half the rank of $H\oplus H$. For $x,y\in H$, $(V\oplus(-V))((x,x),(y,y))=V(x,y)-V(x,y)=0$, so $\Delta H$ is a metabolizer.
By [F1], the metabolic direct sum in step 1.1 represents zero, while the direct-sum relation identifies its class with $[V]+[-V]$. Hence $[-V]=-[V]$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $V$ be an even-order square matrix with integer entries, of size $n=2g$. A unimodular congruence replaces $V$ by $P^TVP$ for an integer matrix $P$ with determinant $+1$ or $-1$. For $x,y\in\mathbb Z^n$ as column vectors and $z\in\mathbb Z$, the two elementary enlargements of $V$ are
$$
E_0(V;x,y,z)=\begin{pmatrix}V&x&0\\y^T&z&0\\0^T&1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad
E_1(V;x,y,z)=\begin{pmatrix}V&x&0\\y^T&z&1\\0^T&0&0\end{pmatrix}.
$$
Two even-order integral matrices are **S-equivalent** if one can be obtained from the other by a finite sequence of unimodular congruences, elementary enlargements, and reverse elementary enlargements.

Assume the full Axiom of Choice when a knot's Seifert pairing is formed. An integral Seifert lattice is a pair $(H,V)$ in which $H$ is a free abelian group of rank $2g$ for some $g\geq0$, and $V:H\times H\to\mathbb Z$ is bilinear with $V-V^T$ unimodular. The rank-zero lattice is allowed, with the determinant of its empty skew matrix equal to $1$. A metabolizer is a primitive direct summand $M\subset H$ of rank $g$ such that $V(x,y)=0$ for every $x,y\in M$; the lattice is metabolic when it has a metabolizer. A chosen Seifert surface of an oriented knot gives such a lattice through the positive-push pairing. Its form is algebraically slice when that lattice is metabolic.

An isomorphism of integral Seifert lattices $(H,V)$ and $(H',V')$ is an integral group isomorphism $P:H\to H'$ satisfying $V'(Px,Py)=V(x,y)$ for all $x,y\in H$. Let $\mathcal S$ be the commutative monoid of these isomorphism classes under orthogonal direct sum, where $(H,V)\oplus(H',V')$ has underlying group $H\oplus H'$ and pairing $V\oplus V'$, with the rank-zero lattice as identity. The integral algebraic concordance group $G_{\mathbb Z}$ is the abelian group generated by symbols $[V]$ for $[V]\in\mathcal S$, subject to $[V\oplus W]=[V]+[W]$ and $[M]=0$ for every metabolic lattice $M$. Two selected Seifert forms are algebraically concordant when they represent the same element of $G_{\mathbb Z}$. This form relation does not assert the existence of a smooth or locally flat topological concordance annulus between the knots.

Assume full AC when the form is obtained from a knot. For every integral Seifert lattice $(H,V)$, the class represented by $(H,-V)$ is the additive inverse of the class represented by $(H,V)$ in $G_{\mathbb Z}$.

For each displayed enlargement, its skew part has block form
$$
E_i-E_i^T=\begin{pmatrix}J&u&0\\-u^T&0&s_i\\0^T&-s_i&0\end{pmatrix},
$$
where $J=V-V^T$, $u=x-y$, $s_0=-1$, and $s_1=1$. If $V$ is knot-derived, [A1] is the choice hypothesis for its Seifert-pairing convention; the following lattice calculation itself is choice-free. Since $J$ is unimodular, choose the integral vector $c=-J^{-1}u$ and replace the penultimate basis vector by itself plus the old-basis combination $c$. This integral basis change removes the $u$ block and leaves $J\oplus\begin{psmallmatrix}0&s_i\\-s_i&0\end{psmallmatrix}$. Both blocks are unimodular, so each enlargement is an integral Seifert lattice.

In $E_i\oplus(-V)$, take the subgroup generated by $(e_j; e_j)$ for the old basis vectors $e_1,\ldots,e_{2g}$ and by $(b;0)$, where $b$ is the last basis vector of the enlarged lattice. Its rank is $2g+1$, half the total rank. The two displayed enlargement matrices have zero old-to-$b$, $b$-to-old, and $b$-to-$b$ entries. The $V$ and $-V$ blocks cancel on the diagonal generators, while all pairings involving $(b;0)$ vanish. Therefore the form vanishes on this subgroup.

The subgroup in step 1.2 is a direct summand: its generators, together with $(a;0)$ and $(0;e_j)$ for every old basis vector, form an integral basis because subtracting $(0;e_j)$ from $(e_j;e_j)$ gives $(e_j;0)$. It is therefore a metabolizer. By [F2], $[E_i]+[-V]=0$, and [F3] gives $[E_i]=[V]$ in $G_{\mathbb Z}$.

For an integral Seifert lattice $(H,V)$, its integral Witt class is its class in $G_{\mathbb Z}$ from the definition of metabolic Seifert form and algebraic knot concordance. An isomorphism $(W,B,T)\to(W',B',T')$ of rational isometric structures is a rational-linear bijection $P:W\to W'$ such that $B'(Px,Py)=B(x,y)$ and $PT=T'P$. Define the rational Witt group $G_{\mathbb Q}$ by direct sum of isomorphism classes, with metabolic structures set equal to zero. derivations.claim: The matrix $B=V+V^T$ is symmetric. Modulo $2$, $V+V^T\equiv V-V^T$; by [F1] the determinant of $V-V^T$ is odd, so $\det B$ is odd and in particular nonzero. Thus $B$ is nonsingular over $\mathbb Q$.

Since $V$ and $V^T$ are invertible over $\mathbb Q$, $T=V^{-1}V^T$ is invertible. Direct multiplication gives
$$
T^TBT=V(V^T)^{-1}(V+V^T)V^{-1}V^T=V+V^T=B,
$$
because the two summands in the middle expression simplify respectively to $V$ and $V^T$. Therefore $T$ is a $B$-isometry.
Finally $I-T=V^{-1}(V-V^T)$, which is invertible by invertibility of $V$ and [F1]. The three defining conditions in [F2] hold, proving the claim.

The image of a group homomorphism is a subgroup, so it also contains the negative of every such generator. Every element of the presented integral group is a finite sum of signed generators, hence is in the image. This proves the entire smooth surjective-homomorphism assertion.

In the locally flat category, [F10] supplies the group law and inverse needed for descent. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the full Axiom of Choice when a knot's Seifert pairing is formed. An integral Seifert lattice is a pair $(H,V)$ in which $H$ is a free abelian group of rank $2g$ for some $g\geq0$, and $V:H\times H\to\mathbb Z$ is bilinear with $V-V^T$ unimodular. The rank-zero lattice is allowed, with the determinant of its empty skew matrix equal to $1$. A metabolizer is a primitive direct summand $M\subset H$ of rank $g$ such that $V(x,y)=0$ for every $x,y\in M$; the lattice is metabolic when it has a metabolizer. A chosen Seifert surface of an oriented knot gives such a lattice through the positive-push pairing. Its form is algebraically slice when that lattice is metabolic.

An isomorphism of integral Seifert lattices $(H,V)$ and $(H',V')$ is an integral group isomorphism $P:H\to H'$ satisfying $V'(Px,Py)=V(x,y)$ for all $x,y\in H$. Let $\mathcal S$ be the commutative monoid of these isomorphism classes under orthogonal direct sum, where $(H,V)\oplus(H',V')$ has underlying group $H\oplus H'$ and pairing $V\oplus V'$, with the rank-zero lattice as identity. The integral algebraic concordance group $G_{\mathbb Z}$ is the abelian group generated by symbols $[V]$ for $[V]\in\mathcal S$, subject to $[V\oplus W]=[V]+[W]$ and $[M]=0$ for every metabolic lattice $M$. Two selected Seifert forms are algebraically concordant when they represent the same element of $G_{\mathbb Z}$. This form relation does not assert the existence of a smooth or locally flat topological concordance annulus between the knots.

Assume the full Axiom of Choice when an integral Seifert lattice comes from a knot's positive-push pairing. For an integral Seifert lattice $(H,V)$, its integral Witt class is its class in $G_{\mathbb Z}$ from the definition of metabolic Seifert form and algebraic knot concordance. An isomorphism $(W,B,T)\to(W',B',T')$ of rational isometric structures is a rational-linear bijection $P:W\to W'$ such that $B'(Px,Py)=B(x,y)$ and $PT=T'P$. A rational isometric structure is a triple $(W,B,T)$ in which $W$ is a finite-dimensional even-dimensional $\mathbb Q$-vector space, $B:W\times W\to\mathbb Q$ is a nonsingular symmetric bilinear form, $T:W\to W$ is an invertible linear map satisfying $B(Tx,Ty)=B(x,y)$ for all $x,y\in W$, and $I-T$ is invertible. Such a structure is metabolic if it has a $T$-invariant subspace $L\subset W$ with $\dim_{\mathbb Q}L=\frac12\dim_{\mathbb Q}W$ and $B|_{L\times L}=0$. Define the rational Witt group $G_{\mathbb Q}$ by direct sum of isomorphism classes, with metabolic structures set equal to zero. For a nonsingular integral Seifert matrix $V$, the associated matrix pair is $(B,T)=(V+V^T,V^{-1}V^T)$; whether this pair is a rational isometric structure is established separately.

The definition concerns finite-rank bilinear forms and isometry data. It does not identify the unrelated Witt Lie algebra with either $G_{\mathbb Z}$ or $G_{\mathbb Q}$.

Every element of the integral algebraic concordance group has an invertible integral Seifert-matrix representative, allowing the empty matrix for the zero-rank representative. If $V$ is any such representative, the rule
$$
[V]\longmapsto[(\mathbb Q^{\operatorname{rank}V},V+V^T,V^{-1}V^T)]
$$
defines an injective homomorphism into the rational isometric Witt group. An integral Seifert form represents zero in the integral group if and only if it is itself metabolic. These are finite algebraic assertions and require no choice principle; knot-derived forms retain their separately stated choice assumptions.

For a monic irreducible polynomial $p\in\mathbb Q[t]$ with $p(0)\ne0$, put $p^*(t)=p(0)^{-1}t^{\deg p}p(t^{-1})$. For each such self-reciprocal polynomial $p=p^*$ other than $t-1$, let $G_p$ be the subgroup of the rational isometric Witt group generated by structures whose characteristic polynomial is a power of $p$. Then restriction to the generalized primary subspaces induces an isomorphism
$$
G_{\mathbb Q}\longrightarrow\bigoplus_{p=p^*,\ p\ne t-1}G_p.
$$
A pair of distinct reciprocal primary factors contributes a metabolic structure and therefore contributes zero. Only finitely many components of any given class are nonzero. No choice principle is needed.

Let $p\in\mathbb Q[t]$ be monic, irreducible, and self-reciprocal, with $p(0)
e0$ and $p
e t-1$. Put $E=\mathbb Q[t]/(p)$, write $\alpha=t+(p)$, and give $E$ the involution $\iota(\alpha)=\alpha^{-1}$. If $p
e t+1$, the primary component $G_p$ of the rational isometric Witt group is isomorphic to the hermitian Witt group of $E$ with this involution. Here the latter group is generated by finite-dimensional nonsingular hermitian forms, with orthogonal direct sum as addition and forms having an isotropic half-dimensional $E$-subspace set to zero. If $p=t+1$, the same conclusion holds with the group generated by even-dimensional nonsingular symmetric forms over $\mathbb Q$, modulo metabolic forms. For a semisimple primary isometry, the comparison sends a hermitian form $h$ to $(\operatorname{Tr}_{E/\mathbb Q}h,\alpha)$ on its underlying rational vector space. These comparisons require no choice principle.

Let $E/F$ be a quadratic extension of number fields with its nontrivial involution. In the hermitian Witt group $W(E/F)$, the kernel of all signatures is killed by $4$. The joint signature image is a free abelian subgroup of $\mathbb Z^s$ of rank at most $s$, where $s$ is the number of real places of $F$ at which $E$ becomes complex. No choice principle is required.

Let $W(\mathbb Q)$ denote the Witt group of nonsingular symmetric bilinear forms over $\mathbb Q$, with orthogonal sum as addition and metabolic forms set to zero. For every such form $q$, four times its Witt class equals its signature times the class of the four-dimensional identity form. In particular, the kernel of the signature is killed by $4$, including its restriction to the subgroup of even-dimensional classes. The signature image is $\mathbb Z$ on the full group and $2\mathbb Z$ on the even-dimensional subgroup.

In the integral algebraic concordance group put
$$
F_b=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&b\end{pmatrix},\qquad P_n=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&-n^2\end{pmatrix},\qquad Q_q=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&-(3q-1)/4\end{pmatrix},
$$
where $b,n$ range over positive integers and $q$ ranges over primes congruent to $3$ modulo $4$ other than $3$. The classes $[F_b]$ are independent of infinite order, each $[P_n]$ has exact order two, and each $[Q_q]$ has exact order four. The three families together generate their direct sum, isomorphic to
$$
\mathbb Z^{(\mathbb N)}\oplus(\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z)^{(\mathbb N)}\oplus(\mathbb Z/4\mathbb Z)^{(\mathbb N)}.
$$
Moreover the classes $[P_n]$ have linearly independent images in $G_{\mathbb Z}/2G_{\mathbb Z}$. These are pure algebraic assertions about the displayed forms; no choice principle is required.

Assume full AC. Let $G$ be a countable abelian group and $s:G\to\bigoplus_{n\ge1}\mathbb Z$ a homomorphism whose kernel $K$ satisfies $4K=0$. Then $K$ is precisely the torsion subgroup of $G$, and for cardinals $r,u,v\le\aleph_0$,
$$G\cong\mathbb Z^{(r)}\oplus(\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z)^{(u)}\oplus(\mathbb Z/4\mathbb Z)^{(v)}.$$
If $G$ contains elements $f_i,p_i,q_i$, indexed by positive integers, such that the $f_i$ are integer-linearly independent, the order-two elements $p_i$ have linearly independent images in $G/2G$, and the $2q_i$ are linearly independent order-two elements with $4q_i=0$, then $r=u=v=\aleph_0$.

derivations.claim: Both groups in [F1] are countable. A rational structure is specified, after one finite basis choice, by its dimension and two finite rational matrices; the isometry and nonsingularity conditions select a subset of this countable set. An integral Seifert lattice is likewise specified by a finite integer matrix. The corresponding presented groups are quotients of the countable sets of finite signed lists of these matrices: finite lists of rationals or integers have explicit natural-number codes, so a countable union over their lengths is countable. Quotients are countable by the surjection from these codes. This argument does not identify the two types of object. Use the injection [F2] to regard $G_{\mathbb Z}$ as a subgroup of $G_{\mathbb Q}$ for the rest of the proof.

For each primary group of [F3] other than $t+1$, the involution on $E$ is nontrivial. Indeed if its distinguished generator equalled its inverse, its irreducible polynomial would divide $t^2-1$; $t-1$ is excluded by invertibility of $I-T$ and $t+1$ was separated. If $F=E^{\sigma}$, choose $0\ne\delta$ with $\sigma\delta=-\delta$. Every $z\in E$ has the unique decomposition $(z+\sigma z)/2+\delta(z-\sigma z)/(2\delta)$ with coefficients in $F$, so $E/F$ is quadratic. Take all hermitian signatures at real places of $F$ where $E$ becomes complex, and take the ordinary rational signature on the $t+1$ component. These form a homomorphism $s:G_{\mathbb Q}\to\bigoplus_{j\in J}\mathbb Z$. The index set $J$ is at most countable: there are countably many rational irreducible polynomials and finitely many real places for each number field. Each individual class has only finitely many primary components, so its total signature has finite support. With [A1] fix an enumeration of this index set, adding zero coordinates if needed, to put the target inside $\bigoplus_{n\ge1}\mathbb Z$.

If $s(x)=0$, each of the finitely many nonzero primary components of $x$ has all its signatures zero. By [F4] four times each such component is zero; the primary direct-sum isomorphism [F3] gives $4x=0$. Thus $4\ker s=0$. The same holds for the kernel of $s\iota$ on $G_{\mathbb Z}$, since $\iota$ is injective. Applying [F6] separately to these two countable groups gives decompositions of each with at most countable free, order-two and order-four multiplicities. In particular every torsion class has order dividing four; the proof has used signatures to identify all torsion, rather than merely exhibiting some finite-order classes.

In either group, the elements $F_b,P_n,Q_q$ of [F5] meet the three infinitude tests of [F6]. A finite nonzero integer combination of the $F_b$ cannot be torsion: if some nonzero multiple vanished, projection to each distinct primary factor would contradict the infinite order of its $F_b$. The $2Q_q$ are independent order-two elements, by distinct primary factors and exact order four. For the rational quotient by doubles, project to the quadratic primary factor of $P_n$, identified with a hermitian Witt group by [F3], and then take hermitian rank modulo two. This is a homomorphism because metabolic hermitian forms have even rank. The two-dimensional rational structure of $P_n$ has rank one over its quadratic field, so the homomorphism takes value one there; it vanishes on the other $P_m$ by their distinct primary factors, and on every double by its target $\mathbb Z/2$. Hence the $P_n$ are independent modulo doubles in $G_{\mathbb Q}$ as well as in $G_{\mathbb Z}$, the latter also following directly from [F5]. Thus the $P_n$ are independent in the quotient by doubles in each group. This last condition forces independent order-two summands after splitting; independent order-two elements alone would not suffice, since doubles of order-four elements also have order two. There are infinitely many indicated primes $q$ by the finite Euclidean argument in [F5].

By [F6] and step 4.1, all three multiplicities in both decompositions from step 3.1 are infinite, and their countable upper bounds make them precisely $\aleph_0$. This is the displayed abstract group isomorphism for each of $G_{\mathbb Q}$ and $G_{\mathbb Z}$. The integral result here follows from its proved injection, the shared exponent bound, the splitting argument and the actual integral families. No assertion that primary summands split integrally, no identification of the rational group with its integral subgroup, and no unspecified integral localization or coupling theorem is needed for this abstract isomorphism. In particular the allowed $t+1$ component of the original rational Definition has been retained throughout.

derivations.claim: The disk has $H_1=0$, so its Seifert matrix is the empty matrix. The subgroup $M=0$ has rank zero, is a direct summand, and the pairing vanishes on it. By [F1], this is metabolic and represents the identity class.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the full Axiom of Choice. A positive Hopf band is an oriented annulus whose core has self-linking $+1$ in the positive-push convention. Let $F$ be the genus-one Seifert surface obtained by plumbing two positive Hopf bands in a square, with oriented core curves $a,b$ forming a positive handle basis, and choose the plumbing side so that $a^+$ bounds a disk in $S^3$ disjoint from $b$. The oriented boundary of this standard positive two-band plumbing is the right-handed trefoil. In the positive-push convention $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$ with ordered basis $(a,b)$, the Seifert matrix is
$$
V=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\-1&1\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Fix the orientation-reversing reflection $r:S^3\to S^3$ chosen for the mirror convention in the oriented connected-sum definition. If $K$ is a smooth oriented knot, its mirror $r(K)$ carries the orientation induced from $K$ by $r$. The reverse mirror of $K$, denoted $K^\dagger$, is the image $r(K)$ with its knot orientation reversed. Thus $K^\dagger$ changes both the ambient orientation convention and the orientation of the knot.

Fix a coordinate orientation-reversing reflection $r:S^3\to S^3$ for the mirror convention. Let $K$ and $J$ be smooth oriented knots in the standard oriented three-sphere. A connected-sum datum consists of one smoothly embedded closed three-ball around a short subarc of $K$ and one around a short subarc of $J$, each meeting its knot in a single trivial properly embedded arc, together with the fixed standard orientation-reversing boundary identification of the two standard oriented ball boundaries that joins the oriented arcs into one circle. Choose this standard map once in the standard two-ball model so that it commutes with $r$ and an orientation-preserving half-turn interchanging the two balls preserves the joining convention. Here a trivial arc is an embedded interval in a ball that is carried by an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism of ball-arc pairs to a straight diameter. Remove the interiors of the two balls and glue the remaining boundary spheres using this fixed identification; the resulting oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere is a connected sum of $K$ and $J$, denoted $K\#J$ for the specified datum.

The **standard unknot** is the oriented unit circle in a fixed coordinate two-plane of $S^3\subset\mathbb R^4$. A knot is **nontrivial** if it is not ambient isotopic through orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms of $S^3$ to the standard unknot. A nontrivial knot is **prime** if it has no connected-sum presentation whose two summand knots are both nontrivial.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. For two smooth oriented knots, changing either representative by oriented ambient isotopy, changing the sufficiently small coordinate ball and trivial subarc used for either knot, or changing the positive local frame used to identify that ball with the standard oriented ball does not change the oriented ambient-isotopy class of the connected-sum knot, when the boundary gluing map is the fixed standard orientation-reversing map from the definition.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. For every smooth oriented knot $K\subset S^3$, let $B^4=\{x\in\mathbb R^4:\lVert x\rVert^2\le1\}$ with boundary $S^3$. The oriented connected sum $K\#K^\dagger$ bounds a smooth properly embedded disk $D\subset B^4$ for which the squared radial function $\rho(x)=\lVert x\rVert^2$ restricts to a Morse function on the interior of $D$ with all critical points of index $0$ or $1$.

Assume the full Axiom of Choice. Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot, and let $F\subset S^3$ be a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface whose oriented boundary is $K$, with $\chi(F)=1-2g$. Choose an ordered integral basis $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$ and use the positive normal convention $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. Let $A_K$ be the first homology of the infinite cyclic cover of $S^3\setminus K$ classified by total linking, with $t$ acting by the positive-meridian deck transformation. Let $\Delta_K(t)$ be the generator of the zeroth elementary ideal $E_0(A_K)$ in $\Lambda=\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$, and write $p\doteq q$ when $p$ and $q$ differ by a unit $\pm t^k$ of $\Lambda$. Then for every such $F$ and basis,

$$\det(V-tV^T)\doteq\Delta_K(t).$$

The determinant is $1$ for the empty $0\times0$ matrix when $g=0$. This formula concerns the polynomial $\Delta_K$; the existing knot-normalized fraction $D_K=\Delta_K/(1-t)$ is a separate invariant.

derivations.claim: By [F1], the stated full-AC hypothesis supplies $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Apply [F5] to $T$; its conclusion gives the required smooth proper disk for $S=T\#T^\dagger$ and the stated radial critical-point indices.

Let $a_1,a_2$ be the ordered Hopf-core basis for $T$. The surface for the reverse mirror is the oppositely oriented reflected surface. Reflection reverses linking number, and the positive normal for the reverse-mirror surface is the reflected negative normal of the original. Thus its matrix entries are $-\operatorname{lk}(a_i^-,a_j)$. The identity $\operatorname{lk}(a_i^-,a_j)=\operatorname{lk}(a_j^+,a_i)$ follows by symmetry of linking and pushing the two curves to the common positive side without crossing; hence the reverse-mirror matrix is $-V^T$.

Form the boundary-connected-sum Seifert surface in the two summand balls. Cycles from different summands have zero linking because each bounds a $2$-chain in its own ball, disjoint from the other summand. The combined basis therefore has matrix $W=\operatorname{diag}(V,-V^T)$.

Let $P=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$. Direct multiplication gives $P^TV^TP=V$. The graph $M=\{(x,Px):x\in\mathbb Z^2\}$ is spanned by $e_1+e_4$ and $e_2+e_3$; projection onto the first factor identifies it with $\mathbb Z^2$, so it is a rank-$2$ direct summand. For any $x,y\in\mathbb Z^2$, $(x,Px)^TW(y,Py)=x^T(V-P^TV^TP)y=0$. Thus $M$ is a metabolizer.

The two blocks give $\det(V-tV^T)=(1-t)^2+t=t^2-t+1$ and $\det(-V^T+tV)=(t-1)^2+t=t^2-t+1$. Hence $\det(W-tW^T)=(t^2-t+1)^2$. For $f(t)=t^2-t+1$, one has $f(t^{-1})=t^{-2}f(t)$, so $\det(W-tW^T)=t^2f(t)f(t^{-1})$. By [F6], this is the claimed Fox–Milnor norm factorization of $\Delta_S$.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the full Axiom of Choice. A positive Hopf band is an oriented annulus whose two boundary components, with their induced orientations, have linking number $+1$. Let $F$ be the genus-one Seifert surface obtained by plumbing two positive Hopf bands in a square, with oriented core curves $a,b$ forming a positive handle basis, and choose the plumbing side so that $a^+$ bounds a disk in $S^3$ disjoint from $b$. The oriented boundary of this standard positive two-band plumbing is the right-handed trefoil. In the positive-push convention $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$ with ordered basis $(a,b)$, the Seifert matrix is
$$
V=\begin{pmatrix}-1&0\\-1&-1\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Assume the full Axiom of Choice. Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot, and let $F\subset S^3$ be a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface whose oriented boundary is $K$, with $\chi(F)=1-2g$. Choose an ordered integral basis $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$ and use the positive normal convention $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. Let $A_K$ be the first homology of the infinite cyclic cover of $S^3\setminus K$ classified by total linking, with $t$ acting by the positive-meridian deck transformation. Let $\Delta_K(t)$ be the generator of the zeroth elementary ideal $E_0(A_K)$ in $\Lambda=\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$, and write $p\doteq q$ when $p$ and $q$ differ by a unit $\pm t^k$ of $\Lambda$. Then for every such $F$ and basis,

$$\det(V-tV^T)\doteq\Delta_K(t).$$

The determinant is $1$ for the empty $0\times0$ matrix when $g=0$. This formula concerns the polynomial $\Delta_K$; the existing knot-normalized fraction $D_K=\Delta_K/(1-t)$ is a separate invariant.

Assume full AC. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in the oriented standard $3$-sphere, let $F$ be a connected compact smooth oriented surface with oriented boundary $K$, let $V$ be the matrix of the Seifert pairing $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$ in an ordered integral basis, and let $\omega\in S^1\setminus\{1\}$. Define the **Levine–Tristram Hermitian matrix** by
$$H_\omega(V)=(1-\omega)V+(1-\bar\omega)V^T.$$
It is Hermitian because $V$ is real and $\bar\omega=\omega^{-1}$. Its signature is the number of positive eigenvalues minus the number of negative eigenvalues, both counted with multiplicity and with zero eigenvalues omitted. When $\Delta_K(\omega)\ne0$, define $\sigma_\omega(K)$ to be this signature. At a root $\omega_0\ne1$ of $\Delta_K$, define $\sigma_{\omega_0}(K)$ to be the arithmetic mean of the two one-sided limits of $\sigma_{e^{i\theta}}(K)$ as $\theta$ approaches an argument of $\omega_0$ from below and above. The invariance and one-sided-existence lemmas justify treating these values as independent of the chosen surface and basis.

Assume full AC. Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot, let $F$ be a connected compact smooth oriented Seifert surface of genus $g$, and let $V$ be the positive-push Seifert matrix in an ordered integral basis. Suppose the integral Seifert lattice has a rank-$g$ direct summand $M$ on which $V$ vanishes identically. For every $\omega\in S^1\setminus\{1\}$ with $\Delta_K(\omega)\ne0$, the Levine–Tristram signature $\sigma_\omega(K)$ is zero. The assertion concerns only points away from Alexander roots; no value at a root is asserted here.

Assume the full Axiom of Choice. Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot, let $F\subset S^3$ be a connected compact smooth oriented Seifert surface of genus $g$, and let $V$ be its positive-push Seifert matrix, with entries $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$ in an ordered integral basis of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$. Let $\Delta_K(t)$ be the Alexander polynomial normalized by $\Delta_K(t)\doteq\det(V-tV^T)$, where $p\doteq q$ means $p=\pm t^kq$ for some $k\in\mathbb Z$. If the integral Seifert lattice is metabolic, then there is an $f(t)\in\mathbb Z[t]$ such that $\Delta_K(t)\doteq f(t)f(t^{-1})$. The same factorization is necessary if $K$ bounds a locally flat properly embedded disk in the standard four-ball $B^4$. This is a necessary condition for either algebraic or locally flat sliceness, not a sufficient condition. The factorization concerns the Alexander polynomial $\Delta_K$, not the separate knot-normalized fraction $D_K(t)=\Delta_K(t)/(1-t)$.

Assume full AC. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in the oriented standard $3$-sphere, let $F\subset S^3$ be a connected compact smooth oriented Seifert surface of genus $g$, and let $D\subset B^4$ be a locally flat properly embedded disk with oriented boundary $K$. Then the positive-push Seifert lattice $(H_1(F;\mathbb Z),V)$ is metabolic: it has a rank-$g$ primitive direct summand on which $V$ vanishes identically.

Assume the full Axiom of Choice. Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot and let $\Delta_K(t)$ be its Alexander polynomial in the determinant normalization, with $p\doteq q$ meaning $p=\pm t^kq$ for some $k\in\mathbb Z$. If there is no Laurent polynomial $f(t)\in\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$ such that $\Delta_K(t)\doteq f(t)f(t^{-1})$, then $K$ does not bound a locally flat properly embedded disk in the standard four-ball $B^4$. This is a necessary obstruction only; factorization alone does not assert sliceness.

derivations.claim: By [F1] and [F2], $\Delta_T(t)\doteq\det(V-tV^T)=(1-t)^2+t=t^2-t+1$. Thus $|\Delta_T(-1)|=3$, since every Laurent unit $\pm t^k$ evaluates to $\pm1$ at $-1$.

If $\Delta_T(t)\doteq f(t)f(t^{-1})$ for some $f\in\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$, then evaluating at $t=-1$ gives $3=f(-1)^2$ or $-3=f(-1)^2$. Neither is possible because an integer square is nonnegative and $3$ is not an integer square. Hence the trefoil polynomial is not an integral reciprocal norm.

At $\omega=-1$, one has $H_{-1}(V)=2(V+V^T)=\begin{pmatrix}-4&-2\\-2&-4\end{pmatrix}$, whose eigenvalues are $-2$ and $-6$. Since $\Delta_T(-1)\ne0$, its Levine–Tristram signature is $-2$. By [F4], a metabolic Seifert form would have signature $0$ there, so the trefoil Seifert form is not metabolic.

By [F6] and step2.1, the trefoil does not bound a locally flat properly embedded disk in the standard four-ball. Independently, if such a disk existed then [F5] would give a metabolic Seifert form, contradicting the signature calculation in step2.2 and [F4]. Thus the original locally flat sliceness claim is refuted by both necessary tests, with their TOP geometric inputs supplied rather than inferred from the numbers alone.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Let $M$ be a compact $R$-oriented $n$-manifold with boundary $A$, for a commutative unital ring $R$. Cap with its relative fundamental class gives isomorphisms, for every integer $p$,
$$S_p:H^p(M;R)\xrightarrow{\sim}H_{n-p}(M,A;R),\qquad T_p:H^p(M,A;R)\xrightarrow{\sim}H_{n-p}(M;R).$$
Here both maps send a class $a$ to $a\cap[M,A]$ in the displayed target. Empty boundary recovers Poincaré duality. Disconnected and empty manifolds are included. AC is inherited only from the exhaustion and local universal-coefficient arguments in Poincaré duality.

For $A\subseteq X$ there is an exact sequence
$$\cdots\to H_n(A;G)\to H_n(X;G)\to H_n(X,A;G)\xrightarrow{\delta}H_{n-1}(A;G)\to H_{n-1}(X;G)\to\cdots.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $R$ be a PID, $C$ a chain complex of free
$R$-modules, and $G$ an $R$-module. Then naturally
$$0\to\operatorname{Ext}^1_R(H_{n-1}C,G)\to H^n\operatorname{Hom}_R(C,G)\xrightarrow{\operatorname{ev}_n}\operatorname{Hom}_R(H_nC,G)\to0$$
is exact.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every compact smooth manifold, with boundary
allowed, has the homotopy type of a finite CW complex. If its boundary is a
supplied finite CW manifold, the collar may be retained in a finite relative CW
model.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Thus $Y$ is a rational homology sphere. By [F4] and [A1], both $W$ and its smooth boundary $Y$ have finite CW type, so their integral homology groups are finitely generated; their positive-degree rationalizations vanish and are therefore finite.

Put $A=H_1(Y;\mathbb Z)$, $B=H_1(W;\mathbb Z)$, and $C=H_2(W;\mathbb Z)$. Since $A$ is finite by step 1.1, the universal coefficient sequence [F3] gives $H^1(Y;\mathbb Z)=0$; [F7] then gives $H_2(Y;\mathbb Z)=0$. Also $H_3(W;\mathbb Z)=0$: [F1] identifies $H_4(W,Y)$ with $H^0(W)=\mathbb Z$, and its fundamental-class boundary maps to the generator of $H_3(Y)=\mathbb Z$; since $H_3(W,Y)\cong H^1(W)=0$, exactness forces $H_3(W)=0$.

By [F3], $H^2(W;\mathbb Z)\cong\operatorname{Ext}(B,\mathbb Z)$ and $H^3(W;\mathbb Z)\cong\operatorname{Ext}(C,\mathbb Z)$, because $B,C$ are finite and $H_3(W)=0$. Their orders are $|B|$ and $|C|$. Under [F1], these are the orders of $H_2(W,Y)$ and $H_1(W,Y)$, respectively. The pair sequence [F2] shows that $P=\ker(A\to B)$ is the cokernel of the injective map $H_2(W)\to H_2(W,Y)$, while $B\to H_1(W,Y)$ is onto because the next map $H_0(Y)\to H_0(W)$ is an isomorphism. Hence $|P|=|B|/|C|$ and $|A/P|=|B|/|C|$, so $|A|=|P|^2$.

To prove isotropy, [F2] and the naturality in [F7] identify $P$ under Poincaré duality with the image of $H^2(W;\mathbb Z)\to H^2(Y;\mathbb Z)$. For $x,y\in P$, choose lifts $\widetilde x,\widetilde y\in H^2(W;\mathbb Z)$. Since $W$ is a rational homology ball, the coefficient Bockstein $H^1(W;\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z)\to H^2(W;\mathbb Z)$ is onto by [F8]: the adjacent groups $H^1(W;\mathbb Q)$ and $H^2(W;\mathbb Q)$ vanish. Choose $\gamma\in H^1(W;\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z)$ with Bockstein $\widetilde y$. By [F5], $\lambda_Y(x,y)$ is the evaluation on $[Y]$ of the restriction of $\gamma\smile\widetilde x$. This class extends over $W$, and the inclusion sends $[Y]$ to zero in $H_3(W)$ because $Y=\partial W$. Thus $\lambda_Y(x,y)=0$.
The isotropy from step 3.2 gives $P\subseteq P^\perp$. Nonsingularity [F5] implies $|P^\perp|=|A|/|P|=|P|$ by step 3.1. Therefore $P=P^\perp$, so $P$ is a metabolizer by [F6].

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot bounding a smooth proper disk $D\subset B^4$, and let $q\ge2$. Write $X_D$ for the compact disk exterior and let the positive meridian induce $\pi_1(X_D)\to H_1(X_D;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z/q$. Let $X_{D,q}$ be the connected cover classified by the kernel of this map. Attach $D^2\times D^2$ to $X_{D,q}$ along the connected cover of $D^2\times S^1$ using the normal-disk map $z\mapsto z^q$. The resulting compact oriented $4$-manifold $W_{D,q}$ is the $q$-fold cyclic cover of $B^4$ branched along $D$; its boundary is $\Sigma_q(K)$, and the local branched model is $(x,z)\mapsto(x,z^q)$.

Assume AC. Let $D\subset B^4$ be a smooth proper disk, let $p$ be prime, $q=p^k$ with $k\ge1$, and let $\mathbb F_p$ be the field with $p$ elements. For the connected $q$-fold cyclic cover $X_{D,q}$ of the disk exterior, $H_0(X_{D,q};\mathbb F_p)\cong\mathbb F_p$, $H_1(X_{D,q};\mathbb F_p)\cong\mathbb F_p$, and $H_i(X_{D,q};\mathbb F_p)=0$ for every $i\ge2$.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every compact smooth manifold, with boundary
allowed, has the homotopy type of a finite CW complex. If its boundary is a
supplied finite CW manifold, the collar may be retained in a finite relative CW
model.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: The core circle of $D^2\times S^1$ is the lift of $\mu^q$. Lift that loop to the infinite cyclic cover $X_{D,\infty}$: it is a path from a point $\widetilde x$ to $t^q\widetilde x$. The connecting map of the chain sequence for the $q$-fold quotient sends its homology class to $[\widetilde x]\in H_0(X_{D,\infty};\mathbb F_p)$. By the proof of [F2], this connecting map is an isomorphism in degree one, so the overlap map $H_1(D^2\times S^1;\mathbb F_p)\to H_1(X_{D,q};\mathbb F_p)$ is an isomorphism.

The filling piece $D^2\times D^2$ is contractible and the overlap has homology only in degrees zero and one. The Mayer–Vietoris sequence [F4], using the isomorphism from step 1.1, gives $H_i(W_{D,q};\mathbb F_p)=0$ for every $i>0$. The two glued pieces and their overlap are connected, so $W_{D,q}$ is connected; orientation is inherited from the cyclic branched covering map away from the branch set and extends over the local model.

By [F3], each integral homology group $H_i(W_{D,q};\mathbb Z)$ is finitely generated. The injection $H_i(W_{D,q};\mathbb Z)\otimes\mathbb F_p\hookrightarrow H_i(W_{D,q};\mathbb F_p)$ from [F5] makes that tensor product zero for $i>0$. A finitely generated abelian group with zero tensor product with $\mathbb F_p$ has rank zero; hence $H_i(W_{D,q};\mathbb Q)=0$. Its boundary is $\Sigma_q(\partial D)$ by [F1], proving the statement.

derivations.claim: Choose a Seifert surface for $K$ by [F4] and remove its boundary collar to obtain a properly embedded surface $F_0$ in the knot exterior. Its boundary is a degree-one longitude curve, hence represents the preferred longitude by [F3]. Each element of $\pi_1(F_0)$ has a smooth loop representative. Push that loop slightly to one side of the Seifert surface; the push is homotopic in the exterior and disjoint from the surface, so [F5] gives meridian coordinate zero. Thus $\ell_K\bmod q$ vanishes on $\pi_1(F_0)$, and [F7] lifts $F_0$ to each sheet of $E_q$. Each lifted copy has one boundary component over the preferred longitude, proving that every lifted longitude is nullhomologous in $E_q$.

In the branched filling, $\widetilde\mu$ bounds the attached solid torus's meridian disk and a longitude lift maps to its core generator. The same Mayer–Vietoris cokernel calculation [F6] gives $H_1(\Sigma_q(K);\mathbb Z)\cong H_1(E_q;\mathbb Z)/\langle[\widetilde\mu]\rangle$.

In the zero-surgery filling, the boundary-torus basis consists of the closed meridian lift $\widetilde\mu$ and a longitude lift $\widetilde\lambda$. The latter bounds a meridian disk in the attached solid torus and the former maps to its core generator. The Mayer–Vietoris cokernel in [F6] therefore eliminates the core generator and gives $H_1(M_{0,q};\mathbb Z)\cong H_1(E_q;\mathbb Z)/\langle[\widetilde\lambda]\rangle$. Step 1.1 makes this quotient $H_1(E_q;\mathbb Z)$.

The cover subgroup is $\ker(\ell_K\bmod q)$ by [F7]. Thus $\ell_K(g)$ is divisible by $q$ for every $g\in\pi_1(E_q)$, and $g\mapsto\ell_K(g)/q$ is a homomorphism $\pi_1(E_q)\to\mathbb Z$. It descends to $r:H_1(E_q;\mathbb Z)\to\mathbb Z$ and satisfies $r([\widetilde\mu])=1$, since $\widetilde\mu$ projects to $\mu^q$. Therefore $\mathbb Z[\widetilde\mu]$ is a direct summand and $H_1(E_q)\cong H_1(E_q)/\langle[\widetilde\mu]\rangle\oplus\mathbb Z[\widetilde\mu]$. Using step 1.2 and then step 2.1 proves the statement.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere and let $B^4$ be the standard four-ball with boundary $S^3$. Let $\mathcal S_{\mathrm{sm}}(K)$ be the set of genera of connected compact orientable smooth properly embedded surfaces $F\subset B^4$ with oriented boundary $K$. Let $\mathcal S_{\mathrm{top}}(K)$ be the set of genera of connected compact orientable locally flat topologically properly embedded surfaces $F\subset B^4$ with oriented boundary $K$. $$
g_4^{\mathrm{sm}}(K):=\min\mathcal S_{\mathrm{sm}}(K),\qquad g_4^{\mathrm{top}}(K):=\min\mathcal S_{\mathrm{top}}(K).
$$

the ODE interfaces below use no additional choice, so this hypothesis is
dispensable. A smooth manifold with corners here is Hausdorff and second
countable, with charts in relatively open subsets of $[0,\infty)^c\times\mathbb R^{n-c}$
and transition maps smoothly extendible with invertible derivative at corner
points; transitions preserve the local depth and its face germs. Let $M$ be
compact. Then $M$ has a finite corner-adapted whole-star smooth triangulation.
Corner faces are locally subpolyhedra, and any specified finite union of
closed faces is a subpolyhedron.

If the total boundary already has a finite piecewise smooth triangulation
$f:L\to\partial M$ compatible on all local face intersections, with its
differential fan giving a homeomorphism onto the union of boundary faces of the
tangent orthant at each point, the triangulation extends to $M$, pointwise
preserving $f$ with compatible subdivisions allowed. In the resulting finite
union construction all intersections may be made full subcomplexes. The same
relative conclusion applies to a fixed corner-adapted triangulated closed neighbourhood piece

Assume AC. If a smooth oriented knot $K$ bounds a smooth proper disk $D$ in $B^4$ and $q$ is a prime power, then
$$P_D=\ker\bigl(H_1(\Sigma_q(K);\mathbb Z)\to H_1(W_{D,q};\mathbb Z)\bigr)$$
is a metabolizer for the torsion linking form of $\Sigma_q(K)$.

Assume AC. Let $D\subset B^4$ be a smooth proper disk, let $p$ be prime, and let $q=p^k$ with $k\ge1$. The $q$-fold cyclic cover $W_{D,q}$ of $B^4$ branched along $D$ is a compact connected oriented $4$-manifold with $H_i(W_{D,q};\mathbb Q)=0$ for every $i>0$ and boundary $\Sigma_q(\partial D)$.

Assume AC. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot, let $q\ge2$, and let $M=\Sigma_q(K)$ be its $q$-fold cyclic branched cover. A character is a homomorphism $\chi:H_1(M;\mathbb Z)\to\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z$. Its order is its order in $\operatorname{Hom}(H_1(M;\mathbb Z),\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z)$; it is finite-order when this order is finite and has prime-power order when its order is $p^e$ for a prime $p$ and $e\ge1$. It vanishes on a subgroup $P$ when $\chi(x)=0$ for every $x\in P$.

derivations.claim: If $\chi$ extends to $\widetilde\chi:H_1(W_{D,q};\mathbb Z)\to\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z$, then for every $x\in P_D$ one has $i(x)=0$, so $\chi(x)=\widetilde\chi(i(x))=0$. The extension has finite image because its domain is finite.

Conversely, suppose $\chi(P_D)=0$. Then $\chi$ factors uniquely through the subgroup $I=i(H_1(\Sigma_q(\partial D)))$ of the finite group $B=H_1(W_{D,q})$. Let $p$ be the prime underlying the order of $\chi$ as in [F2]. Every element of order coprime to $p$ maps to zero, since its image is killed both by a power of $p$ and by an integer coprime to $p$. Thus the factored map restricts to the $p$-primary subgroup $I_p\le B_p$.

A homomorphism from a subgroup $J$ of a finite abelian $p$-group $B_p$ into $\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z[p^\infty]$ extends when one adjoins one element $b\in B_p$: if $p^k$ is the order of $b+J$, choose $c\in\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z[p^\infty]$ with $p^kc=f(p^kb)$, which exists because multiplication by $p^k$ is surjective on this Prüfer group. Set $f'(j+rb)=f(j)+rc$. If $j+rb=j'+r'b$, then $(r-r')b\in J$, so $r-r'$ is divisible by $p^k$; the chosen equation makes the two values equal. The extension is therefore well-defined. Repeating this finite step extends the character from $I_p$ to $B_p$.

Set the extension to zero on the complementary primary summand of $B$ and combine it with the extension on $B_p$. The resulting character on $B$ extends $\chi$ and has finite $p$-power image because $B$ is finite and the values are $p$-primary. This proves the reverse implication.

$$\rho(g)=\zeta_{p^a}^{c(g)}t^{\psi(g)},\qquad \bar t=t^{-1}.$$
Then $H_*(X_q;\mathbb C(t)_\rho)=0$. The same conclusion holds for a trivial finite character.

Thus its regular cover $Y$ is not a finite-sheeted cover: the free coordinate takes the boundary meridian to one and gives arbitrarily many different sheets. By [F2], $H_i(\partial W;F)=0$ in every degree. The actual pair sequence therefore identifies $H_2(W;F)$ with $H_2(W,\partial W;F)$. By [F3] the latter is its conjugate dual, with this map exactly the intersection pairing. It follows that the pairing is nonsingular. The involution in [F2] is precisely complex conjugation with $t\mapsto t^{-1}$, so the pairing is Hermitian in the stated convention.

To spell out the boundary cap, split each finite-dimensional boundary chain group into its cycles and a complement; the differential on that complement is an isomorphism to the preceding boundary space. Its inverses give a contraction of the acyclic boundary complex. The quotient from absolute to relative chains consequently has contractible kernel and preserves the absolute middle homology. This algebraic Poincare cap is enough for the Witt construction; it changes neither its module nor its pairing. The ordinary form, which need not be nonsingular on all ordinary $H_2$, instead uses [F3]'s quotient by its boundary radical. These are distinct operations, and no nonexistent finite $G$-cover or geometric attachment preserving a singular ordinary form has been assumed.

This conclusion concerns the entire Witt class, not just its signature. No arbitrary-group analytic index theorem is required.

If the bounding multiplicities are $r_0,r_1$, take $r_1$ disjoint copies of $W_0$ and $r_0$ copies of $W_1$. Their whole marked boundaries are the same $r_0r_1$ copies. citations.quote: Assume AC. Let $D\subset B^4$ be a smooth proper disk, let $p$ be prime, and let $q=p^k$ with $k\ge1$. The $q$-fold cyclic cover $W_{D,q}$ of $B^4$ branched along $D$ is a compact connected oriented $4$-manifold with $H_i(W_{D,q};\mathbb Q)=0$ for every $i>0$ and boundary $\Sigma_q(\partial D)$.

Assume AC. If a smooth oriented knot $K$ bounds a smooth proper disk $D$ in $B^4$ and $q$ is a prime power, then
$$P_D=\ker\bigl(H_1(\Sigma_q(K);\mathbb Z)\to H_1(W_{D,q};\mathbb Z)\bigr)$$
is a metabolizer for the torsion linking form of $\Sigma_q(K)$.

Assume AC. Let $D\subset B^4$ be a smooth proper disk with boundary K, let q be a prime power, and let $W_{D,q}$ be its branched cover. Put
$$P_D=\ker\bigl(H_1(\Sigma_q(\partial D);\mathbb Z)\to H_1(W_{D,q};\mathbb Z)\bigr).$$
If $\chi:H_1(\Sigma_q(\partial D);\mathbb Z)\to\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z$ has prime-power order, then $\chi$ vanishes on $P_D$ if and only if it extends to a character of prime-power order on $H_1(W_{D,q};\mathbb Z)$.

Assume AC. Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot bounding a smooth proper disk $D\subset B^4$, and let $q\ge2$. Write $X_D$ for the compact disk exterior and let the positive meridian induce $\pi_1(X_D)\to H_1(X_D;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z/q$. Let $X_{D,q}$ be the connected cover classified by the kernel of this map. Attach $D^2\times D^2$ to $X_{D,q}$ along the connected cover of $D^2\times S^1$ using the normal-disk map $z\mapsto z^q$. The resulting compact oriented $4$-manifold $W_{D,q}$ is the $q$-fold cyclic cover of $B^4$ branched along $D$; its boundary is $\Sigma_q(K)$, and the local branched model is $(x,z)\mapsto(x,z^q)$.

Assume AC. Let $X_D$ be the exterior of a smooth proper disk, with positive-meridian isomorphism $H_1(X_D;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$. Let $X_{D,\infty}$ be the connected cover classified by the kernel of $\pi_1(X_D)\to H_1(X_D;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$, and let $t$ denote the deck transformation represented by the positive meridian. For $q\ge2$, define $X_{D,q}=X_{D,\infty}/\langle t^q\rangle$.

Let $\mathcal L$ be one local system on $X$.

1. If $Z\subseteq A\subseteq X$ and $\overline Z\subseteq\operatorname{int}_X(A)$, inclusion induces excision isomorphisms in both local homology and local cohomology between $(X\setminus Z,A\setminus Z)$ and $(X,A)$, using the restrictions of $\mathcal L$.
2. For an open cover $X=U\cup V$, there are natural exact sequences
   $$\cdots\to H_n(U\cap V;\mathcal L)\to H_n(U;\mathcal L)\oplus H_n(V;\mathcal L)\to H_n(X;\mathcal L)\to\cdots$$
   and
   $$\cdots\to H^n(X;\mathcal L)\to H^n(U;\mathcal L)\oplus H^n(V;\mathcal L)\to H^n(U\cap V;\mathcal L)\to\cdots,$$
   where all systems are restrictions and the middle difference map in cohomology is $u|_{U\cap V}-v|_{U\cap V}$.

The same conclusions hold for the standard excisive-cover condition after replacing the cover by interiors. A local system given only on a subspace is not silently assumed to extend to $X$.

Assume AC. Let $X$ be a smooth knot exterior or the exterior of a smooth proper disk in the standard four-ball. Its meridian-coordinate homomorphism is $\ell:\pi_1X\to\mathbb Z$. Let $X_q$ be its connected $q$-fold cyclic cover, for any $q\ge1$, and put $\psi=\ell/q$ on its group. For any homomorphism $c:\pi_1X_q\to C_{p^a}$, where $p$ is prime and $a\ge1$, give $\mathbb C(t)$ the rank-one unitary coefficient system
$$\rho(g)=\zeta_{p^a}^{c(g)}t^{\psi(g)},\qquad \bar t=t^{-1}.$$
Then $H_*(X_q;\mathbb C(t)_\rho)=0$. The same conclusion holds for a trivial finite character.

If $M_{0,q}$ is the $q$-fold cover of zero surgery on a smooth knot, and $c$ is any prime-power-order character on its first homology, the same conclusion holds on $M_{0,q}$ with its meridian free coordinate. In particular every smooth four-bordism whose boundary consists of such data has a nonsingular twisted middle Hermitian form, with no change to its absolute twisted $H_2$. The regular $C_{p^a}\times\mathbb Z$ cover in this assertion is generally infinite; the assertion concerns its specified rank-one localization.

Assume AC. For a fixed prime-power cover degree and prime-power order character, the rationalized difference between the twisted and untwisted Casson–Gordon intersection-form Witt classes, divided by the bounding multiplicity $r$, is independent of the chosen multiple and bounding pair. It defines a class in $W(\mathbb C(t))\otimes\mathbb Q$.

Assume AC. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot, let $q$ be a prime power, and let $\chi:H_1(\Sigma_q(K);\mathbb Z)\to\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z$ have prime-power order $d$. Choose a Casson–Gordon bordism datum $(M_{0,q},\eta,r,W)$. Write $G=\mathbb Z/d\oplus\mathbb Z$, let $Y\to W$ be the regular cover determined by $\eta$, and give $\mathbb C(t)$ the $G$-action $(a,n)z=\exp(2\pi ia/d)t^n z$ and involution $\overline{t}=t^{-1}$ with complex conjugation on constants. Define
$$H_2^t(W;\mathbb C)=H_2(Y;\mathbb C)\otimes_{\mathbb C[G]}\mathbb C(t).$$
The Casson–Gordon Witt class is
$$\tau(\Sigma_q(K),\chi)=\frac{1}{r}\bigl([H_2^t(W;\mathbb C)]-[Q_0(W)\otimes_{\mathbb C}\mathbb C(t)]\bigr)\in W(\mathbb C(t))\otimes\mathbb Q,$$
using the nonsingular twisted form and the ordinary nonsingular image form. Precisely, put $Q_0(W)=H_2(W;\mathbb C)/\operatorname{rad}(\lambda_W)$ with its induced form; the untwisted term in the display is understood as $Q_0(W)\otimes_{\mathbb C}\mathbb C(t)$. The twisted boundary complex is acyclic, so its algebraic Poincare cap preserves the absolute twisted module. This does not assert that an arbitrary ordinary absolute intersection form is nonsingular. Here $W(\mathbb C(t))$ is the Witt group of nonsingular Hermitian forms over the field with involution, modulo hyperbolic forms. Its signature defect is $\sigma(K,\chi)=\sigma_1(\tau(\Sigma_q(K),\chi))$, where $\sigma_1$ evaluates a Hermitian representative at $t=e^{i\theta}$ and takes the one-sided limit as $\theta\to0^+$. This is the specified Casson–Gordon invariant and signature homomorphism; it is not an arbitrary rho invariant or an unspecified difference of signatures.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere and let $B^4$ be the standard four-ball with boundary $S^3$. Let $\mathcal S_{\mathrm{sm}}(K)$ be the set of genera of connected compact orientable smooth properly embedded surfaces $F\subset B^4$ with oriented boundary $K$. Let $\mathcal S_{\mathrm{top}}(K)$ be the set of genera of connected compact orientable locally flat topologically properly embedded surfaces $F\subset B^4$ with oriented boundary $K$. For each such surface, its genus $g(F)$ is the nonnegative integer determined by $\chi(F)=1-2g(F)$. Define the smooth slice genus and the locally flat topological slice genus by

$$
g_4^{\mathrm{sm}}(K):=\min\mathcal S_{\mathrm{sm}}(K),\qquad g_4^{\mathrm{top}}(K):=\min\mathcal S_{\mathrm{top}}(K).
$$

derivations.claim: By [F1], choose an extending character $\widetilde\chi$ on the branched disk cover, and write its exact order as $D=p^a$. If the original nontrivial character has order $d=p^b$, then $d\mid D$. Restrict $\widetilde\chi$ to $H_1(X_{D,q})$ and pair it with $\ell/q$. Its finite coordinate vanishes on the lifted meridian because that circle bounds the branch-tube disk in the filled cover. Its infinite coordinate takes that circle to one. On the exterior of the boundary knot the finite coordinate is the original $\chi$; on the zero-filling solid torus it is zero. Thus its boundary is precisely the original $\eta$ followed by the inclusion $C_d\times\mathbb Z\to C_D\times\mathbb Z$, with the root representation unchanged.

The actual oriented boundary of $X_{D,q}$ is $M_{0,q}$. Indeed the product disk tube at the base disk gives a longitude filling of the knot exterior: its framing is zero, since a parallel disk is disjoint and its boundary has linking zero with $K$. Passing to the meridional $q$-cover lifts the same longitude slope, while its normal circle is the closed lift of $\mu^q$. These are the zero-surgery cover coordinates in [F2], with the positive boundary orientation retained. Mayer–Vietoris in the rational homology ball $W_{D,q}=X_{D,q}\cup(D^2\times D^2)$, whose overlap is $D^2\times S^1$, gives $H_2(X_{D,q};\mathbb Q)=0$ and $H_1(X_{D,q};\mathbb Q)=\mathbb Q$ on that overlap circle. The higher groups vanish as well. In particular its ordinary middle nonsingular image form is zero.

The character in step 1.1 is of prime-power order on the actual exterior cover. Hence [F3] gives $H_2(X_{D,q};\mathbb C(t))=0$, so its twisted form is also zero. The difference of the two Witt forms of this actual single-boundary smooth filling is therefore zero. By [F4]'s larger-target comparison it computes the original rationalized class even when $D>d$: compare any original multiple bounding datum, viewed over $C_D\times\mathbb Z$, with the same number of copies of this filling and use the closed fourth-bordism ambiguity calculation. Thus $\tau(\Sigma_q(K),\chi)=0$ in $W(\mathbb C(t))\otimes\mathbb Q$. Applying the specified one-sided signature homomorphism gives $\sigma(K,\chi)=0$, as claimed. This proves the full prime-power extension case rather than assuming extension with unchanged finite order.
