citations.quote: Let $X$ be a compact connected oriented topological $4$-manifold with nonempty boundary, let $x_0\in X$, and put $G=\pi_1(X,x_0)$. A **finite relative disk-embedding datum** consists of proper generic immersions $f_i:(D^2,S^1)\looparrowright(X,\partial X)$, $1\le i\le n$, whose boundary circles are embedded and pairwise disjoint, together with framed immersed spheres $g_i:S^2\looparrowright\operatorname{int}X$ that are algebraically dual to the disks. Here a generic immersion is locally a topological embedding except at finitely many double points, each with exactly two preimages whose image sheets are the coordinate planes $\mathbb R^2\times\{0\}$ and $\{0\}\times\mathbb R^2$ in a chart of $X$; proper means that the inverse image of $\partial X$ is exactly the domain boundary; and framed means that the normal microbundle has a chosen trivialization extending the specified boundary framing. Choose paths from $x_0$ to the immersed surfaces and orient the surfaces. Each transverse intersection $p$ of two surfaces contributes $\epsilon(p)g_p$ to $\lambda$, where $\epsilon(p)\in\{1,-1\}$ compares their induced local orientation with the chosen orientation of $X$, and $g_p\in G$ is the loop that travels along the chosen path to the first surface, then to $p$, and returns along the second surface and its chosen path. Thus $\lambda$ is a signed equivariant intersection sum in $\mathbb Z[G]$. Wall's self-intersection sum $\mu$ is the signed sum over self-double points in $\mathbb Z[G]/\langle g-g^{-1}:g\in G\rangle$, because interchanging the two sheets replaces a label by its inverse. The normal framing is a separate datum; its relative normal Euler or boundary-framing obstruction is zero precisely when the specified framing extends over the immersion. The spheres are **algebraically dual** when $\lambda(f_i,g_j)=\delta_{ij}$, $\lambda(g_i,g_j)=0$ for every $i,j$, and $\mu(g_i)=0$ for every $i$. The disk data are **algebraically unobstructed** when also $\lambda(f_i,f_j)=0$ for $i\ne j$ and $\mu(f_i)=0$ for every $i$.

Let $\Gamma$ be a group. Say that $\Gamma$ is **good for the Freedman disk-embedding theorem** when it has the $\pi_1$-null disk property: for every disk-like capped grope $G^c$ of height $1.5$ with a chosen basepoint and every homomorphism $\phi:\pi_1(G^c)\to\Gamma$, there is an immersed disk whose framed boundary is the attaching region of $G^c$, such that each double-point loop of the disk, regarded after basing as an element of $\pi_1(G^c)$, is sent to the identity by $\phi$. This definition of a good group is a hypothesis on $\Gamma$; it does not assert that any particular group is good.

Use the framed four-dimensional block and stage conventions for gropes in the cited definitions. A **capped grope** is a staged thickening whose bottom surface stage is joined along curves in a symplectic basis to higher surface stages, with the final tip circles capped by framed immersed disks. A **disk-like capped grope** has one connected bottom surface stage with exactly one attaching circle. Its **height** is the number of successive surface stages on each side of the symplectic basis, with caps terminating the stages. A disk-like capped grope has **height one and one-half**, written $1.5$, when its two sides have heights $(1,0)$ or $(0,1)$ in the asymmetric convention; equivalently, one half of the first-stage basis has one additional surface stage and the other half is capped immediately. The **attaching region** is the framed solid-torus neighborhood of the single attaching circle. For an immersed disk, a **double-point loop** is the image of a path in the domain disk joining the two preimages of a transverse self-intersection. In the disk-embedding property for an input capped grope, this loop is read as the corresponding element of the grope's fundamental group; choosing a basing path from the grope basepoint fixes that based element.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable) has a choice function.
Assume countable choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $F:M\to N$ be a continuous map between smooth manifolds. Then there exists a smooth map $\widetilde F:M\to N$ homotopic to $F$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\mathcal F:M\times S\to N$ be a smooth family of maps and let $Z\subseteq N$
be an embedded submanifold. If $\mathcal F\pitchfork Z$, then the set of
parameters $s\in S$ for which the slice $\mathcal F_s:M\to N$ fails to be
transverse to $Z$ is a null subset of $S$.

derivations.claim: **Section1: Finite contraction and cyclic-label cancellation.** The following finite construction and its limiting steps use the supplied framed data.

A finite framed four-dimensional capped-grope neighborhood is supplied, with its usual product collars and self-plumbing charts. Its body is embedded; only cap interiors have generic double points. An integer labeling means a homomorphism from the fundamental group of this actual neighborhood to Z. Paths to individual cap sheets are fixed once. Conjugating a based loop does not change its integer label. No arbitrary locally flat surface is given a tubular neighborhood by this hypothesis: the actual grope's framed block neighborhood is input.

Contract one top surface stage. Designate a finite subset of cap double points to be pushed off at that contraction, and choose a first and second sheet at each designated point. Then the resulting shorter capped grope has the same lower body, attaching circle and framing. Every old intersection not designated has parallel descendants with its old label. No designated old intersection remains. Every new cap intersection is a descendant of two designated intersections removed across dual caps at this same contraction, and its label is a difference of their labels, up to overall sign. Consequently, if all designated labels lie in an interval [a,b], every new label has absolute value at most b−a.

Cut the top surface at each pair of symplectic attaching curves. Replace the cut part by two small parallel copies of each of its two caps and the small central square at their unique attaching-curve intersection. Cutting a genus-g one-boundary surface along its complete symplectic system leaves the disk region with paired edges; the four parallel cap sectors and this square fill each pair of edges. Thus this replaces the surface with its contracted disk. All replacements take place in the supplied framed block. Parallel copies are made in its chosen normal coordinate; the central square uses the untwisted product collar, so the external attaching framing is unchanged. The result may be immersed, which is allowed.

For a designated point, take an embedded path on its second cap from that point to its attaching boundary, with interior avoiding all other double-point preimages. Finitely many paths on one cap can be chosen with disjoint interiors by an embedded finite tree and small parallel offsets. The two parallel copies of that path, closed across the central square, bound a ribbon Whitney disk pairing the two intersections of the first sheet with the contracted cap. In a product rectangle around the path, this is just the rectangle between the two parallel copies, closed by the boundary square. Its interior is disjoint from the old body and all unmodified sheets. A generic sufficiently small choice of the finitely many product widths is possible because their unwanted incidences are finitely many closed disjoint compact sets. No appeal to a normal bundle over an arbitrary TOP surface occurs.

Push the first sheet across this ribbon. This removes precisely the two paired intersections. The only ribbons that can meet are ones running across dual cap sectors: their boundary paths cross in the central square. Resolving those crossings by the prescribed order of the pushes creates intersections between the pushed first sheets. Ribbons on the same cap have been chosen parallel and disjoint, and ribbons belonging to different handles have disjoint block neighborhoods. Therefore every new intersection has exactly the stated two designated ancestors. Repeating for all parallel descendants removes the designated old point altogether. This is a finite sequence of ordinary finger/Whitney operations in explicit smooth block charts; a small relative perturbation makes the resulting intersections transverse.

Here is the label calculation, including the path issue. Let the two designated points have based first-to-second loops g,h. A path to the new intersection follows the first pushed sheet along the ribbon to its second-sheet cap, crosses the common central square, and returns along the other ribbon in reverse. Cancel the common paths in the old body. The resulting word is g h^{-1}; changing starting path conjugates it and exchanging the two resulting sheets inverts it. This is a calculation in the original supplied neighborhood, since every ribbon and push lies there. Its Z label is consequently ±(phi(g)−phi(h)). An old point copied to parallel sheets has its old loop with a small contractible product strip added, so its label is unchanged. The construction, classification of new intersections and claimed bound follow.
**Section2: The finite asymmetric bootstrap.** The following finite construction and its limiting steps use the supplied framed data.

Start with one symplectic pair above the bottom surface: on the positive side a framed capped surface R of positive genus, on the negative side a framed immersed cap W. The same construction is repeated for the finitely many pairs; their body blocks are disjoint, and interactions between cap systems are allowed. All operations fix a neighborhood of the original bottom surface and its attaching region.

Take two small framed parallel copies of R, at negative and positive normal coordinate, and join their boundary circles by the normal annulus crossing the attaching curve of W once. The result is an embedded closed surface of genus twice that of R. Its caps are the corresponding parallel copies of the caps of R. This is a sphere-like capped surface F: compressing its symplectic system gives a sphere. Its body meets W in one point and is disjoint from R; its cap intersections with all the old caps are unrestricted. The annulus and the single crossing are read in the supplied symplectic handle block, not in a hypothetical neighborhood of an arbitrary locally flat surface.

Construct a small parallel copy of F and contract its top stage to an immersed framed sphere T. During contraction, push every other cap sheet off T by the ribbons of Section1, excluding the one prescribed body intersection T with W. This includes the original caps of F, the caps of R and the remaining parts of W. All intersections newly produced by those pushes are between those cap sheets. The sphere T is therefore disjoint from both R and the body/caps of F, and from the caps of R, and meets W at its one prescribed point only. Self-intersections of T are allowed. The ribbons have support near cap arcs and their central squares, away from the lower body, so they do not alter any of the displayed body intersections.

Use T as a Norman sphere to remove every intersection of W with a cap of R or F: for each such point, choose a path in W from that point to the unique point W meets T. Remove a small disk from the intersecting cap and connect it by an untwisted tube, along a parallel copy of that path, to T with a small disk removed. The second endpoint consumes the one intersection of that parallel T with W. The two disks removed and the tube are the boundary of a product neighborhood of the path, so the resulting cap misses W at the chosen point and has the same boundary and framing. Choose the finitely many paths as branches of a tree in the abstract disk W, with separate parallel approach paths at their common endpoint; their interiors avoid all other double-point preimages. Normal widths are chosen successively small. The added copies of T are framed immersed spheres; their self- and mutual intersections belong entirely to the modified CAPS. Thus they may create cap intersections but no body intersections. Their original intersections with R or the body of F are empty, and sufficiently small parallel copies retain that property. After this finite operation W is disjoint from every other part except its own self-intersections and the single point on the body of F. In particular F remains a proper capped surface transverse to W.

For each self-intersection of W, tube one of its sheets to a separate small parallel copy of the BODY of F, along the other sheet and then along a chosen arc in W to the transverse point. This is the same local Norman cancellation, now using a capped surface instead of the contracted sphere. The new body consists of W with that sheet disk deleted, the punctured closed body of F, and their connecting annulus. It is a one-boundary surface with additional genus, with the old W boundary/framing. The caps of the added F provide the symplectic caps for its new handles. Its body is embedded: before the tubing, distinct body copies were disjoint and met W only at their distinct transverse endpoints; the tube arcs avoid every other double-point preimage. Choose disjoint parallel branches of a finite tree in W and nested normal widths. The tube neighborhoods consequently miss all other body sheets. Every old self-intersection of W is removed once, and none is introduced into the new body. Its new caps may intersect each other or the old caps, but they miss every body: the prior operation made the old caps disjoint from W, and properness of F makes its caps disjoint from all the parallel body sheets. At the attaching collars this assertion is the defining product chart. Consequently W has become an actual proper framed capped surface, not merely a surface with unaccounted body intersections.

This changes the side heights (1,0) to (1,1), preserving the original bottom stage. All choices and moves were finite. The scorecard is: R/body(F) embedded and mutually disjoint throughout; T immersed auxiliary, intersecting W once; old caps arbitrary among themselves; after the Norman cancellations all old caps miss W; after the final tubing every new intersection lies among caps. The auxiliary T is discarded after its copies have been inserted into caps. No disjointness of its parallel copies is needed, because their intersections are allowed cap intersections.
**Section3: Finite bootstrap to height three.** The following finite construction and its limiting steps use the supplied framed data.

Here the two side heights count stages ABOVE the fixed bottom surface. Section2 gives (1,0) to (1,1). The following side extension, used only finitely often in this bootstrap, supplies (1,1) to (2,1) to (2,3). Let P be the side to be raised and Q its other side, of heights p,q at least one. Construct F transverse to the bottom surface of P by taking two normal parallels of Q and closing their rims with the normal annulus. It is sphere-like of height q. Its body is embedded, meets P only at the specified first-stage point, and misses all other body stages; intersections of its caps with the old caps are allowed.

First make a contracted parallel sphere T transverse to the bottom of P, using Section1 and pushing off all original cap sheets and the caps of F. Its only body intersection is that prescribed transverse point. To make the caps of F disjoint from the old P caps, push an F-cap sheet at each intersection down the old P cap to its attaching stage and then down successive P stages to its bottom. A finger across one attaching collar replaces one intersection with two on the immediately lower stage; this is two parallel paths around the two ends of that collar. After p stages there are finitely many points on the bottom of P. Tube them off over parallel copies of T. These changes affect only caps of F. They cannot reintroduce intersections with old P caps because T misses those caps and the finger paths on the old caps avoid the other finitely many double-point preimages. The new intersections are among caps of F and possibly the old Q caps, which are still caps. All old body stages are fixed.

Now for an intersection of an old P cap with a Q cap, push the Q-cap sheet down the P stages and tube it off over T. The Q cap is still an immersed disk; its boundary and framing are fixed. It may acquire self/intersections with other caps, which are allowed. It remains disjoint from the old P caps and all body stages: the punctured T used in the tubing has had its unique bottom-P intersection removed. Crucially T is also disjoint from the body of F, so the Q caps miss every body piece to be added in the next step.

Finally treat every self/mutual intersection among the old P caps by pushing one of its P sheets down the P stages and tubing it off over copies of the full F, rather than T. This replaces each old P cap by a capped grope: its first added stage is the old disk with punctured bodies of F attached, followed by the higher stages of those copies of F. Orient each added copy so its transverse intersection cancels the chosen point, and use the untwisted framed tubes. All old P-cap intersections have been removed; the added bodies are embedded and disjoint from each other because distinct body parallels of F are disjoint, and the tube paths avoid all other old preimages. The new caps are copies of F's caps. Those were made disjoint from ALL old P caps before this step, and properness makes them disjoint from F's parallel bodies. Consequently every new intersection is among caps, not on a new body. A cap with no intersections may be regarded as a genus-zero stage with no attached higher surface, as in the disk-like model. We have obtained side heights at least (p+q,q), with the previous body and its attaching framing preserved. The first and second steps are needed: merely asserting that tubing adds height would leave the old cap intersections on the new body.

All choices involve finite paths, parallels and normal widths in supplied framed blocks. Use the move first with p=q=1, then exchange the two sides and use p=1,q=2. Both sides then have height at least two, so the entire grope has height at least three. The induced integer labels on its finite plumbing generators are obtained by following their actual paths back to the original neighborhood; let B be the maximum of their absolute values. B exists without any growth estimate for this finite bootstrap.
**Section4: Efficient symmetric raising and the word bound.** The following finite construction and its limiting steps use the supplied framed data.

Once both sides have height at least two, there is an efficient variant which contracts only the TOP stage of a transverse grope. For the side P to be extended, form the transverse grope from the opposite side Q. Its height is that of Q. Contract its top stage and push the old caps off that contraction by Section1. The transverse grope now has height one less and its caps are disjoint from all old caps. Push each intersection on a P cap down the P stages, and at the bottom tube off over this transverse grope. The same body/cap scorecard as Section3 applies: new bodies consist of separate parallel copies of the old embedded opposite-side bodies, and all cap intersections have been removed from the new body before it is declared a body. This replaces each old P cap by a capped grope with the height of the contracted transverse grope. In terms of full path heights a,b INCLUDING the shared bottom, the updated path height is a+b−2. Alternate the sides. Starting with a_{−1}=a_0=3, the successive updated path heights obey a_n=a_{n−1}+a_{n−2}−2. The uniform height is the smaller of the two current path heights. Writing a_n−2 as a Fibonacci recursion gives, after 2k steps, uniform height at least 2^k: consecutive pairs increase the smaller Fibonacci term by at least a factor two. Additional initial height only improves the bound.

For clarity, the required estimate concerns WORDS, not numbers of double points. Base every old cap-point loop by a path in the old grope. Body-stage paths contribute no new plumbing generator. Contraction copies an old point without changing its generator. A push off a contraction creates the difference loop of Section1, a word of length at most two in the OLD cap-point generators. A new intersection among caps of the parallel transverse grope has length one, since its sheets are old parallel sheets. The only remaining type is a loop using a newly pushed-down finger: follow its first sheet across at most two old cap-point loops to the parallel transverse copy, cross its new cap intersection (one old generator), and return across at most two old loops on the other finger. The two bottom-stage paths cancel, as do the parallel collar paths. This is a concatenation of at most 2+1+2 old generators or inverses. These exhaust the new intersections: they occur on unchanged parallels, on a contraction push, or between two inserted fingers. Thus each step sends every NEW generator to a word of length at most five in the PRECEDING generators. Induction gives length at most 5^(2k) after 2k steps, and absolute Z label at most 5^(2k)B. No count of the possibly much larger number of points is substituted for this word bound.
**Section5: The special relative disk-to-disk operation in standardness.** The following finite construction and its limiting steps use the supplied framed data.

This is the operation of FQ4.6, with the actual relative data made explicit. Let f:B^4→B^4 be continuous and onto, with a homeomorphic boundary restriction. Its point-inverse collection is null (only finitely many fibres have diameter at least any positive epsilon), its singular IMAGE is nowhere dense, and E is a closed subset of the target containing the whole boundary. Suppose f:f^−1(E)→E is a homeomorphism. Then there is a homeomorphism h:B^4→B^4 equal to f on f^−1(E). Here E CONTAINS the boundary; it is not merely a subset of that boundary. The latter misreading would make the relative assertion too weak for the collared-tower application.

Use the following intermediate configuration. W is compact metrizable; e,f:B^4→W and g:W→B^4 are onto. The composites ge,gf are identity on the boundary. The fibres of g,ge,gf are null; their relevant singular images Sigma_g, g(Sigma_e),g(Sigma_f) are nowhere dense and pairwise well separated: neither set meets the closure of another. A protected closed set E_0 containing the boundary is disjoint from all three, and the relation e^−1 f is fixed there. Nullity makes each singular image countable (group the nontrivial fibres by diameter at least1/m). We will decrease both e- and f-fibre diameters while controlling the relations e^−1 f and f^−1 e between the TWO fixed domain balls.

Here is the local replacement. Choose a closed round ball B in the TARGET of g, disjoint from E_0,Sigma_g,g(Sigma_f), and a smaller concentric ball B_0 whose boundary misses g(Sigma_e). The restrictions over B for g and over the sphere boundary of B_0 for ge are homeomorphisms: they are continuous bijections of compact spaces to Hausdorff spaces. We require no open neighborhood of that sphere free of e singular values, which may accumulate on it. Replace g^−1(int B_0) in W by (ge)^−1(B_0), gluing their boundaries by e. The result is W'. On the inserted piece define e' to be the identity and g' to be ge; outside use the old e,g. These maps match at the gluing and satisfy g'e'=ge. The map e' is a homeomorphism over the inserted piece, so every e-fibre with g-image in B_0 has been eliminated. This is a finite compact adjunction, not a claim that W' is already a manifold.

To transfer f, take a homeomorphism w:B→B^4 fixed on B_0. Such a map exists by radial extension from the center of these convex balls. On g^−1 B define
H=g^−1 w^−1 g e w g,

where g^−1 is single-valued on B because B misses Sigma_g. Outside use the identity. On the boundary of B the definitions agree because ge is identity on the outer sphere. In the part whose image lies in g^−1 B_0, the first g^−1 w^−1 cancels the g before e; the remaining map e w g lifts to the inserted piece as w g. Thus H has a continuous lift H':W→W', and put f'=H'f. This gives f'=f outside the region with gf-image in B. On the inserted piece its formula is wgf. On the remaining annular region its fibres are the transported fibres of ge. Since gf is a homeomorphism over B, these new fibres are coordinate copies of a null family, so they remain null. The other fibres are unchanged. For g' the outside fibres are subsets of old g fibres, and the inside fibres are old ge fibres in the inserted compact piece. Both coordinate inclusions are uniformly continuous on their compact domains; a finite union of the corresponding null collections is null. For g'f', outside B nothing changes; in the inner piece it equals ge composed with the homeomorphism wgf, and in the annular piece it equals w^−1 ge wgf. Thus its nontrivial fibres are homeomorphic coordinate images of ge fibres. This is the actual nullity argument; composition of arbitrary null maps is not being asserted to preserve nullity.

The only possible failure of the separation condition is between the transported countable singular image and the retained image of ge. Choose w so these are well separated off B_0. This choice needs no unproved Baire assertion under the original countable-choice branch. Fix one radial reference map w_0:B→B^4. Enumerate the two countable singular sets. For each point condition require that its image avoid the CLOSED closure of the other singular set, and for each inverse-point condition require the analogous inverse avoidance. Each requirement is open and dense among homeomorphisms with the fixed inner/outer boundary data: a small coordinate ball around the free point lies off those fixed boundaries, and a compactly supported translation moves that point off the prescribed nowhere-dense closed set. Explicitly use x→x+rho(x)v with |v|Lip(rho)<1; the contraction inverse proves it is a homeomorphism. The required target complement is open dense, so a least satisfactory rational v in a fixed enumeration exists. At step m choose the translation and its inverse uniformly smaller than2^−m times every currently protected avoidance margin. Later changes then preserve all earlier requirements. Choose supports and rational radii from a fixed coordinate enumeration. The forward and inverse maps converge uniformly, and their limits are inverse by uniform continuity. The limit homeomorphism meets every avoidance requirement. This is a definable countable recursion with explicit finite rational searches, not dependent choice for arbitrary nonempty sets of homeomorphisms. It gives the required local configuration e',f',g'.

For the global iteration, first normalize the boundary: let e_0 be the radial cone on the given boundary homeomorphism, let W_0=B^4, g_0=e_0^−1 and f_0=f. Protect E_0=g_0(E). All conditions hold; the other singular sets are empty. Rescale the two fixed source metrics initially to diameter<1. Suppose all e_n- and f_n-fibres have diameter less than2^−n. There are only finitely many fibres of either map with diameter at least2^−n−1. Their g-images avoid Sigma_g; the separation condition makes the OTHER composite a local homeomorphism there. Around each large e-fibre choose a ball B, and then B_0, so that (ge)^−1 B has diameter less than2^−n while (gf)^−1 B has diameter less than2^−n−1. These choices follow from compactness: if inverse images of shrinking neighborhoods did not enter a prescribed neighborhood of a fibre, a convergent countersequence would give a point outside that fibre mapping to its center. Choose these finite balls disjoint and away from the protected set and the irrelevant singular images. Their boundary radii can avoid the countably many singular points.

Apply the local replacement. It kills the chosen large e-fibres, and all new f-fibres lie in the small (gf)^−1 B regions, hence have diameter less than2^−n−1. Reverse e and f and do the same to the remaining large f-fibres. The newly introduced e-fibres are now small by the analogous local-homeomorphism condition. The finite two-pass step therefore makes ALL fibres smaller than2^−n−1. It changes e^−1 f only within domains and ranges of diameter less than2^−n, and gives the same bound for the inverse relation. Make these bounds strictly summable, for instance use2^−n−3 after reindexing. On the protected set the relation stays e_0^−1 f_0 exactly. No source or target manifold classification is used in these replacements.

The relations R_n=e_n^−1 f_n and their inverses are thus uniformly Cauchy in the fibrewise Hausdorff distance. Their values have diameter tending to zero, so their limits are single-valued continuous maps R,S of the fixed balls. For completeness, continuity is not inferred from continuity of the set-valued R_n. Given x_j→x, fix n and select y_(n,j) in R_n(x_j) within the uniform tail bound of R(x_j). A subsequence of these selections converges to y_n in R_n(x), by compactness and the closed graph of R_n. The distance from y_n to R(x) is at most the tail bound plus diam R_n(x). Thus every subsequential limit of R(x_j) is within twice the tail bound plus diam R_n(x) of R(x). Letting n→infinity proves continuity. The identical argument applies to the inverse relations. Passing to the inverse graphs shows SR=RS=identity. Hence R is a homeomorphism. The fixed relation on the protected set yields R=e_0^−1 f on f^−1(E). Then h=e_0 R is the asserted homeomorphism agreeing with f there.

This proves the needed relative disk-to-disk replacement operation. It does NOT by itself prove that a tower is a disk: that application still needs the actual dual-handle/design/common-quotient construction, including the other approximation whose fibres are explicit disk-with-boundary-neighborhood pieces. No general4D cell-like approximation theorem is imported.
**Section6: From a null grope to the first actual tower story.** The following finite construction and its limiting steps use the supplied framed data.

This step has an exact input which the cyclic construction must supply: an actual properly immersed framed disk-like capped grope A of height at least three, whose entire image has trivial fundamental-group image in the smooth ambient four-manifold, together with framed geometric transverse spheres, each missing A except for its one prescribed bottom-stage point. It does not start with vanishing algebraic intersections alone. All modifications below take place in supplied plumbing charts and finitely many immersed disk charts; the ambient manifold is smooth at this stage.

First raise the height as far as needed by Section4, reserving one more full stage than the desired number of stages in the story. Because the raising maps factor through the previous grope neighborhood, its image remains group-null. Order the finitely many components of the extra top stage. Contract the first one, and push the cap sheets of every other component off that contraction by the ribbon Whitney disks of Section1. Contract the second and push all still uncontracted cap sheets off it; continue. The resulting grope caps are pairwise disjoint. They need not be embedded, but every self-intersection is part of the finger-pair model, with a specified Whitney disk. Here is the local pairing check: pushing a sheet off a contraction replaces its old cap intersection by the two parallel intersections with the opposite cap through the central square. Their signs are opposite, and the ribbon between the two parallel cap copies, continued along the chosen arc on the dual cap, is the Whitney disk. At an old cap self-intersection the four parallel-sheet intersections split into two such opposite-sign pairs. Order the pushes so each newly contracted component is protected from all later cap sheets. Distinct ribbon arcs are disjoint except at their prescribed central-square crossings; any interior crossings are among the disks which will be declared top caps, rather than intersections among the remaining grope caps. This is the actual disk-with-finger-pairs model, not the assertion that zero algebraic self-intersection supplies embedded Whitney disks.

For each finger pair choose an accessory circle: start at its chosen double point, follow one sheet to the Whitney arc and return on the other sheet. It is a loop in the image of the contracted grope. It is therefore nullhomotopic in the ambient manifold by the input nullness; no conclusion about the fundamental group of the complement is needed. A nullhomotopy relative to this fixed embedded boundary arc can be put in general position as an immersed disk with its prescribed boundary collar. The boundary collar is the accessory collar in the standard finger model. Its extending normal framing is corrected, if necessary, by interior twists in that disk together with boundary twists in the model collar; interior twists change the relative Euler number by two, and one boundary twist changes its parity. The latter creates an intersection with the grope cap, which is permitted temporarily. The boundary-circle germ itself and the original bottom attaching framing are fixed. The accessory disks and the previously specified ribbon Whitney disks are now the TOP caps. All finger pairs and their accessory boundary collars have the same finite plumbing model as an ordinary disk finger move followed by its Whitney and accessory disks. Thus the thickening is a one-story tower model before properness is imposed.

Only top-cap intersections with the lower grope remain to be removed. At such an intersection, modify the TOP-cap sheet, pushing it along the lower grope sheet through its successive attaching collars down to the first stage. At one attaching collar the two sides of the push produce two points on the preceding stage; after finitely many stages this produces finitely many points on the bottom. All paths avoid the other finitely many preimages. Remove each resulting bottom point by tubing the top cap over a separate parallel of the corresponding geometric transverse sphere, choosing its orientation to cancel the point. The punctured transverse sphere has no other intersection with the grope. Hence this operation changes only top caps, makes them disjoint from every grope stage including the grope caps, and may create intersections only among top caps. Tubing to a sphere preserves the top-cap disk topology. Its framing extends by the untwisted tube and the supplied sphere framing. Top caps are allowed to have mutual and self-plumbings. The bottom attaching circle, all its framing data, and every reserved lower stage are fixed.

We have obtained an ACTUAL proper one-story capped tower of the chosen finite grope height. Its model has an embedded lower body, grope caps with the prescribed finger-pair singularities, and arbitrary plumbings only among the top Whitney/accessory caps. The finite framed neighborhoods glue by their stipulated product collars, so the conclusion is a framed neighborhood of that tower, not only a map of its underlying two-complex. This is the first-story operation needed before replication and convergence. It has not constructed additional stories or identified any tower neighborhood with a standard two-handle.
**Section7: Replication of a tower, with the body and top caps kept distinct.** The following finite construction and its limiting steps use the supplied framed data.

Write G for a story's grope body, C for its grope caps with their paired finger points, and D for the top Whitney/accessory caps. Thus G union C is the story body; intersections among D are allowed, whereas D misses G union C. When another story replaces D, the new story bodies, and not their eventual top caps, must be disjoint and embedded in the stipulated plumbing model. This distinction is essential in the following replication.

First describe the transverse grope operation in the actual finite model. A surface attached at a positive curve of a symplectic pair has a sphere-like transverse capped grope formed from two parallels of the negative branch and the annulus joining their boundaries. Its bottom meets that positive surface once. Its caps are parallels of the original grope caps. At their intersections with the original grope caps, the two parallel sheets give the ribbon Whitney pairs of Section1. If a further story is present, the corresponding Whitney disk is the bottom of the next story's disk-like grope. Replace the affected band of the transverse grope by two parallels of that Whitney grope and the boundary band along its Whitney arc. This is the grope version of the ordinary Whitney move: cutting the band removes the two old intersection points, and all new intersections lie in the top caps of the inserted Whitney grope. Its body misses every lower story, since that next-story body does. Repeat through the finite list of stories. Stop with its caps parallel to the LAST GROPE caps C, so their possible intersections with the original tower are only with its top caps D. Do not take the additional contraction through the final Whitney/accessory caps: that would give geometric transverse gropes whose nullness is no longer guaranteed. The transverse grope then meets the original tower only at its single specified transverse body point and at the TOP caps D. Its body AND caps use only parallels of pieces of the original tower BODY strictly above the first surface stage.

The group-nullness used here is a direct model calculation. Collapse each surface stage to its symplectic attaching curves and connecting arcs, and each paired-finger grope cap to its double-point graph. The stage-curve generators bound the next stages after contraction. The double-point graph generators bound the specified accessory disks; the Whitney disk identifies the generator at the mate point with the same generator or its inverse according to the sheet orientation. Accordingly every loop in the body strictly above the first stage is null in the entire tower neighborhood. Only the plumbing generators among the TOP caps can remain in that neighborhood's fundamental group. Thus the transverse grope just constructed has trivial group image there. This calculation concerns its actual body and cap paths through the model; it makes no assertion that arbitrary top-cap plumbings are null.

Suppose now a proper tower has first-story grope height at least four. Apply the preceding operation to the second-stage surfaces, contract parallel transverse gropes, and push the old top-cap sheets off those contractions. This supplies framed geometric transverse spheres for the disk-like components remaining after the first surface stage and its fixed collar are removed. Work in that complement. The first-stage collar will be fixed throughout what follows.

Choose the positive side of the top story to be replicated. For its second-stage surfaces construct transverse gropes from the opposite, negative branches. Arrange their caps to meet only the negative-side top caps, as in the preceding Whitney-grope procedure. Contract one top surface stage of the transverse gropes and push the negative-side top caps off those contractions. The resulting transverse gropes and the changed negative cap sheets still have trivial group image whenever that assertion is made of the new BODY: their new body loops run in the old body neighborhood just analyzed, and contraction/push-off changes a loop only by a product of old body loops. Top-cap plumbing generators have not been declared trivial. The negative lower body is unchanged. The height-four hypothesis leaves enough height to raise these transverse gropes to any prescribed finite height by Section4.

Make the needed transverse gropes disjoint near-parallels by ordering their constructions. Contract a parallel, then push all still unused cap sheets off it, using separate ribbon arcs. Repeat for the finite number of copies needed. This is why merely taking many geometric parallels of an immersed capped grope would not suffice: their caps could intersect the old body to be added. The ordered contraction/push-off produces copies whose bodies are disjoint and whose caps miss those old body sheets. Each copy is still null by the model calculation.

At every mutual or self-intersection of POSITIVE top caps, push one sheet down that positive branch to its second-stage surface. A push through one stage doubles the number of points; there are finitely many stages, so only finitely many points result. At every resulting point tube over a separate full transverse grope, not its contraction. The punctured transverse bottom surface removes the point; its higher stages and caps become the higher stages and caps on the changed positive top sheet. The original positive top caps are now properly immersed capped gropes of the chosen height. Their new bodies are disjoint: all their former mutual/self-points were treated, the transverse bodies are disjoint near-parallels, and their caps were cleared off the former top sheets before the tubing. Intersections which remain are among the new caps. The negative branch body has stayed fixed.

There is also the necessary group check for the NEW body. A double-point loop in a changed cap comes from a single selected transverse-grope copy and from the fingers used for that one former top-cap point. The two paths down the original positive branch are parallel, so their whisker words cancel. What remains is a loop in that transverse copy, which is null by the preceding model calculation. Copies used for DIFFERENT former points are distinct near-parallels; their body pieces do not meet and cannot create additional body generators. Thus the new positive body has trivial group image in the complement being used. The retained negative body already has that property, since all its generators are killed by its old Whitney/accessory scaffold. No conclusion is taken about either collection's as-yet-unassigned top-cap plumbing loops.

Raise the new top grope by one extra stage, contract its top components successively and push all the later caps off each contraction. As in Section6, this gives mutually disjoint grope caps with canonical finger-pair Whitney disks. Their accessory loops lie in the just verified null BODY, so they admit immersed accessory disks in the working complement. Correct their framings and push their intersections with the lower body down to the lowest surfaces, then tube over the geometric transverse spheres constructed after deleting the first stage. This produces legitimate new top caps disjoint from the full body. The positive side now has one additional story. Interchange positive and negative and repeat. The original lower body and its framed attaching product are fixed, and both sides now have one additional story, with any prescribed finite height in the new top story.

This is a finite replication inside an arbitrarily small supplied neighborhood of the old tower together with the required accessory-disk images. The latter are not automatically small from the word estimate; localization is exactly the issue separated in the additional localization hypotheses for a controlled application. For the uncontrolled single-component standardness construction, the model nullhomotopies above lie in the tower neighborhood itself, so that neighborhood supplies their support. The source calculation checked here is the full FQ3.4–3.5, printed53–56. Its statement and the present operation require the actual framed tower model and first-story height at least four, not only a collection of algebraically unobstructed immersed disks.
**Section8: Squeezing and convergence, retaining only a pinched neighborhood.** The following finite construction and its limiting steps use the supplied framed data.

Replicate twice by Section7, obtaining three stories with as many stages as desired in the second story. Delete the top caps and contract each component of the third-story grope completely. The contractions supply caps for the second story. Distinct such caps are disjoint, since the distinct third-story BODIES were disjoint; the discarded top-cap intersections have not been retained. The old top caps give nullhomotopies of the generators of each upper-story body, in the complement of the retained first-story body. This is again the model generator calculation: each stage generator is killed by its cap and each finger generator by its accessory cap. All these killing disks lie above the retained first story. Thus the upper-story regular neighborhoods are group-null there. We need to move their finite spines, rather than assert that an arbitrary embedded two-complex can be shrunk by isotopy.

For each upper-story component collapse its regular neighborhood to a finite graph K. One can see the collapse directly: cut a surface stage to its attaching curves and arcs joining the curves; repeat upward; a cap with self-plumbings collapses to its double-point graph and connecting arcs. The disks of the preceding first story which enter this neighborhood consist of strips ending on K. More precisely, relative to their portions C outside the neighborhood, they are a mapping cylinder L times I whose inner ends are mapped into K. This description is obtained in the same finite surface cuts and normal disk blocks. It provides the regular neighborhood of the PAIR C union (L times I) union K, not a claim that the first-story cap disks are fixed pointwise while their attaching ends move.

Choose distinct small smooth coordinate balls, one for each upper-story component, in the complement of the retained first-story body. The null graph map is homotopic there to an embedding of the same abstract graph in the chosen ball: collapse a maximal tree and use the actual generator nullhomotopies, then reverse a contraction of a tiny standard graph in the ball. Perturb this graph homotopy relative to its initial end and its final small-ball end to a one-parameter family of embeddings. The dimension calculation is useful here: two nonincident moving graph points and their common time form a three-dimensional parameter space, less than four, so general position removes equal-image pairs at the SAME time. Preserve the finite vertex stars by translations in small vertex charts, and perturb edge interiors with the endpoints fixed. This gives an isotopy of the graph. Intersections of its TRACE at different times need not disappear; they do not obstruct a graph isotopy and are not being used as a Whitney-disk theorem.

The first-story grope body is avoided by the whole homotopy. Arrange its finitely many intersections with the remaining cap sheets C and the mapping-cylinder strips transversely. Push those sheet intersections along the homotopy toward its free final end and past the final graph. In a normal coordinate ball this is the ordinary finger push of a two-sheet off a terminal one-dimensional arc; its support is a narrow neighborhood of the chosen trace path. Each push modifies only a grope-cap sheet, not the retained grope body. Intersections it creates are among those cap sheets. At their finitely many crossings choose different narrow parallel paths, so the changes do not meet the initial graph or the retained body. The result is an isotopy of K disjoint from C and from the interiors of the mapping-cylinder strips, with their prescribed common inner endpoints allowed in the pair model. The outer ends of those strips on C are fixed. No claim of an embedded homotopy TRACE of a graph in four-space is required.

An isotopy of this finite smooth graph extends to an ambient isotopy of a sufficiently small regular neighborhood, fixed outside a neighborhood of its track and fixed on C and the retained grope body. Here is the elementary extension in the present setting. Near each moving vertex use its small translated coordinate ball. Subdivide time so the vertex balls remain disjoint and each moving edge segment lies in a fixed product chart. On the interior of such an edge, extend its velocity by a cutoff in the normal three-disk, agreeing with the chosen vertex translations at its ends. A finite partition of unity along the edge pieces gives a compactly supported smooth vector field agreeing with the velocity on the graph. Integrate for that short time interval; in the compact support the solution exists throughout the interval. Compose the finitely many intervals. The supports avoid the fixed pair pieces just cleared from the track. Transport the graph regular neighborhood by this isotopy; make its final normal widths small enough that the ENTIRE upper-story neighborhood, not just its spine, lies in the selected small ball. Transport the attaching mapping cylinders at the same time, retaining their outer ends. This proves the required squeezing without using a topological half-space unknotting assertion or a general TOP smoothing theorem.

Now iterate within the resulting upper-story neighborhoods. At stage n choose disjoint closed coordinate four-balls B_(n,j), of diameter<2^−n, containing precisely the next replacement components; choose their closures in the interiors of their parent balls. The old body and its marked attaching product lie outside their interiors. All subsequent modifications for a descendant are required to lie in that same ball. Section7 supplies the next finite story and the preceding squeezing supplies such balls of the next diameter, so the induction uses only the finite operations already specified. Heights can be prescribed in advance at every story; in particular the first story retains height at least four, sufficient for the standardness construction.

We spell out why this gives an embedded LIMIT OBJECT and why it gives less than an ordinary open neighborhood at its ends. Away from the nested balls every point is fixed after finitely many stages, so its map is the finite-stage framed embedding there. An infinite descending branch of balls has a unique intersection point: the balls are nested nonempty compact sets in a compact first-stage neighborhood and their diameters tend to zero. Distinct branches separate in disjoint balls at some finite level, so their points are distinct. Such a limit point cannot equal an old finite-stage body point: a deeper descendant closure lies in the interior of its parent, whereas that finite body point is excluded from all sufficiently deep replacement interiors. The topology at a branch is given by the descendant balls. These observations show injectivity and continuity of the natural map from the end-compactified model to the ambient space. Its domain is compact: an open cover first covers the compact set of branches by finitely many cylinder neighborhoods in the finite-branching tree, then covers the remaining finite-stage compact body by finitely many sets. A continuous injection from that compact domain to the Hausdorff ambient manifold is a homeomorphism onto its image.

For the NEIGHBORHOOD make the same construction with the framed four-dimensional model blocks, not just their spines. At each stage modify the previous block so it meets each chosen ball in the ordinary neighborhood of the disk being replaced; later replacement blocks are contained in that ball. Repeat the preceding compactness and shrinking-ball argument for these blocks and their ends. The result is an embedded PINCHED regular neighborhood, with the prescribed attaching solid torus and framing unchanged. At an end it may have no ambient interior and no locally flat boundary. Nothing in the argument identifies it with a two-handle or supplies a TOP normal bundle there. That identification is exactly the separate parameterization obligation. The construction can be supported in any prescribed open neighborhood containing the actual input tower and the finite nullhomotopies used in the replication, by choosing all balls and normal widths with closures in that open set. This is the support guarantee needed by the additional localization hypotheses for a controlled application once its localized inputs are supplied.
**Section9: The explicit radial collapse used on the model side.** The following finite construction and its limiting steps use the supplied framed data.

The model-side shrinking needs more than the assertion that a compact set is contractible. Its nontrivial fibers have supplied neighborhood coordinates of two particular kinds: a closed ball, or an embedded framed disk together with a regular neighborhood of its boundary circle. In the second case that regular neighborhood overlaps the disk in an ANNULAR COLLAR. Treating the overlap as just the core circle would give the wrong quotient model. We describe the collapse in those coordinates.

First let E be a closed starlike subset in the interior of a Euclidean ball, with center0. Its radial extent e(u)=max{r:ru is in E} is upper semicontinuous: if u_j→u and r_j≤e(u_j) converge to r, closedness gives ru in E. Given an open neighborhood U of E, compactness permits a continuous positive radial function v(u)>e(u) whose radial closed ball V lies in U. To construct v, take for each direction a small angular neighborhood on which e is below a chosen strict radial bound; take finitely many of these neighborhoods and a partition of unity, and use their strict upper bounds. Refine the angular cover enough that the resulting radial set stays in U. A sequence of such V_i can therefore be chosen with V_(i+1) in int V_i and intersection E.

Let {T_j} be a null collection of closed sets disjoint from E, and fix delta>0. Choose V_0 so any T_j meeting V_0 has diameter<delta/2; only finitely many exceptions must be avoided. Choose positive radii b_i decreasing to0, with b_0 the radius of the ambient ball and b_i−b_(i+1)<delta/8. Inductively choose V_i in int V_(i−1), within distance2^−i of E, so any T_j meeting V_i misses the complement of V_(i−1). This is possible: any T_j meeting arbitrarily close to E and also outside the fixed V_(i−1) has diameter bounded below by half the positive distance from E to that complement. There are only finitely many such T_j, all disjoint from E. Avoid them in V_i. Put W_i=V_i union the centered ball B_(b_i). These remain starlike with continuous positive radius functions, are nested, and intersect in E.

On each ray map the interval W_i minus int W_(i+1) affinely to the interval B_(b_i) minus int B_(b_(i+1)), and send E to0. Adjacent formulas agree at their endpoints; continuous radial functions give continuity away from E, and b_i→0 gives continuity at E. The result k is identity on the outer boundary, collapses exactly E, and is a homeomorphism off E. One must check its effect on the OTHER T_j, not merely the distinguished collapse. If x is outside V_i in the shell between W_i and W_(i+1), then k moves x by at most b_i−b_(i+1)<delta/8. Any T_j meeting V_i is contained in V_(i−1), so the whole part which may be moved a large distance lies at most one such radial level apart. If both x,y in T_j lie outside all relevant V levels, their displacements are<delta/8. Otherwise take the deepest level met by T_j and project x,y radially to the corresponding small sphere. Radial projection from points outside that sphere does not increase their distance; the two interpolation intervals change their distances by at most2delta/8 each. Hence, when diam T_j<delta/2, diam k(T_j)<delta. A T_j not meeting V_0 is unchanged except for the small radial displacements. Thus for every j either all its points move by<delta, or its entire image has diameter<delta. This is the control required for later null fibers.

Here is a concrete verification for the second fiber type. In its supplied framed disk chart write x=r exp(i theta) for the disk coordinate and y=s exp(i phi) for its normal coordinate. After a small radial adjustment of the boundary tube, the pair is
D={0≤r≤1,s=0},
E=D union {(r−1)^2+s^2≤a^2},   0<a<1,

with the angular identifications at r=0 and s=0. The neighborhood is rotational in both angles. Its two-dimensional orbit quadrant has a boundary interval [0,1] on s=0 representing D, and a half-disk about (1,0) representing the boundary tube. Collapse [0,1]. The quotient quadrant is again a quadrant, and the tube half-disk becomes a half-disk meeting the corner: this is an elementary planar construction, not a four-dimensional quotient theorem. To see it explicitly, first replace the two circular arcs by polygonal arcs using radial interpolation in disjoint annular neighborhoods. Triangulate the finite region between the arcs and the quadrant boundary. Collapsing the boundary interval merges its consecutive boundary vertices; the remaining region has the same cyclic boundary order as the quadrant with a half-disk based at its corner. Match these boundary orders, cut the remaining region along an arc joining its two boundary components, and extend the boundary maps by coning the resulting polygons from interior points. The maps agree on the two copies of the cut. Use the identity outside the chosen orbit neighborhood. This is a homeomorphism of the QUOTIENT quadrant to the ordinary quadrant, preserving its two distinguished axes.

Choose its target tube half-disk to be {(r−1)^2+s^2≤1,r≥0,s≥0}. Lift the orbit map by keeping theta and phi. Preservation of the axes ensures continuity across the angular collapses; its inverse has the same property. It is therefore an ambient homeomorphism from the four-dimensional disk quotient by D to the standard disk, supported in the supplied normal chart. The image of E is
E'={ (x,y): |x|^2+|y|^2≤2|x| }.

It is starlike about0: for 0≤t≤1, the displayed left side at (tx,ty) is t^2 times the old left side, whereas the right side is t times the old right side. The image contains0 and has precisely the intended overlapping-boundary-tube quotient topology. Thus E is EVENTUALLY starlike by two explicit collapses: first the framed disk D, then E'. This uses the supplied disk and boundary-tube coordinates, not a normal-bundle existence theorem for an arbitrary locally flat disk.

Apply the preceding starlike collapse first to D and then to E'. The other disjoint null sets still form a null collection after the first collapse, by uniform continuity on the compact source; the quotient images remain disjoint from the distinguished set. Choose the first collapse's control small enough for the second step's coordinate uniform-continuity tolerances. Finite sets whose coordinate diameters exceed the chosen tolerance can be excluded from the collapse neighborhoods because they are disjoint from the distinguished set. Pulling the radial operations back through the supplied coordinate maps proves the same movement-or-small-image conclusion in the original metric. The maps are identity on the boundary of the local ball throughout.

Finally suppose alpha:B^4→Q is an onto quotient with a null collection of nontrivial fibers, each of one of these two SUPPLIED coordinate types, Q compact metric, and alpha a homeomorphism on the outer boundary. We give the iteration with the correct inverse CONTROL MAP, rather than claiming the raw inverse relations converge to a function. A raw inverse fiber may remain large permanently when that original alpha fiber is collapsed.

Start with f_0 the identity. Maintain a continuous onto f_n:B^4→B^4 whose only nontrivial fibers are finitely many original alpha fibers, and such that every set f_n(alpha^−1(q)) has diameter<epsilon_n, where epsilon_n decreases summably to0. Because alpha is constant on every f_n fiber, it descends to a continuous map u_n:B^4→Q with u_n f_n=alpha. Continuity follows from the compact quotient property of f_n. Every current image E_q=f_n(alpha^−1(q)) is therefore a set on which u_n is constant. The uncollapsed E_q retain their original supplied neighborhood type, since f_n is a homeomorphism near each such compact set, disjoint from the finite already collapsed fibers.

There are finitely many current E_q of diameter at least epsilon_(n+1)/2: nullity follows from uniform continuity of f_n on the original null family. Choose mutually disjoint small coordinate neighborhoods U_q of these E_q so diam U_q<2epsilon_n and diam u_n(U_q)<epsilon_n in the chosen metric of Q. The first bound follows from diam E_q<epsilon_n and a small neighborhood; the second follows from continuity of u_n and its constancy on E_q. Choose a closed coordinate ball in each U_q carrying the prescribed fiber model. If there are N selected sets, apply each local collapse with the movement-or-small-image tolerance d=epsilon_(n+1)/(4N+4), treating the other current E sets as the null family. Other selected sets are outside its support. Every unselected set starts with diameter<epsilon_(n+1)/2. Over the N collapses its diameter either increases by at most2Nd, or, after the last small-image outcome, is at most d+2Nd. Both bounds are strictly below epsilon_(n+1). Thus no untreated current fiber image crosses the next size threshold. Compose these finitely many collapses to get g_n and put f_(n+1)=g_n f_n. Its newly nontrivial fibers are exactly the selected entire original alpha fibers, so u_n is constant on each g_n fiber. Hence it descends to a continuous u_(n+1) with u_(n+1)g_n=u_n and u_(n+1)f_(n+1)=alpha.

The changes of f_n occur in the coordinate U_q, so their uniform size is<2epsilon_n. For the inverse control maps, if y=g_n(z) is in such a neighborhood, then u_(n+1)(y)=u_n(z) and both z,y lie in U_q. Consequently d_Q(u_(n+1)(y),u_n(y))<epsilon_n. Outside those neighborhoods there is no change. Thus both f_n and u_n are uniformly Cauchy; write their continuous limits f_infinity and u. Passing to u_n f_n=alpha gives u f_infinity=alpha. Uniform convergence also implies that f_infinity is constant on every alpha fiber, since diam f_n(alpha^−1(q))→0.

To prove u injective, let u(y)=q and choose x_n with f_n(x_n)=y. Then alpha(x_n)=u_n(y)→q. A subsequence converges to x in the compact original ball. Uniform convergence gives f_infinity(x)=y and alpha(x)=q. Therefore EVERY y with u(y)=q lies in the singleton f_infinity(alpha^−1(q)). Conversely this singleton maps to q by u f_infinity=alpha. Thus u is bijective. It is a homeomorphism from compact B^4 to Hausdorff Q, agreeing with alpha on the outer boundary. This proves the model-side approximation without any assertion that the raw f_n inverse fibers shrink or that a uniform limit of set-valued inverses is automatically a homeomorphism.
**Section10: Why the collared singular model is an actual ball.** The following finite construction and its limiting steps use the supplied framed data.

There is a necessary reduction before Section5 can be applied to the tower model: its DOMAIN must be a standard ball. A map beta:C'→B^4 by itself does not prove that hypothesis. The special singular parameterization supplies extra structure which gives the reduction explicitly.

Suppose q on the OUTER boundary S^3 is a homeomorphism to the specified boundary of C'. Attach an exterior boundary collar S^3 times [1,2] to both domain and quotient, using that boundary homeomorphism. The enlarged domain is still the literal standard ball with an exterior product collar.

Choose j:S^3→[0,1] with zero set K, for example j(s)=min(1,dist(s,K)), with the empty-K case j=1. On the combined collar S^3 times [0,2] define
F(s,t)=(s,j(s)t)                         for 0≤t≤1,
F(s,t)=(s,j(s)+(t−1)(2−j(s)))            for 1≤t≤2.

On the complement of that collar use the identity, identifying its t=0 boundary by c. The formulas agree at t=1, fix t=0 and t=2, and vary continuously with s. If j(s)>0 they give a strictly increasing interval homeomorphism. If j(s)=0 their only nontrivial point inverse is [0,1], sent to0; the remainder maps strictly increasingly to[0,2]. The induced bijection from C' union its added collar to that enlarged ball is a homeomorphism by compactness and the Hausdorff target. In particular this is not an invocation of a four-dimensional Schoenflies theorem or a conclusion that the wild inner boundary is locally flat.

Now assume the actual common quotient construction has supplied beta:C'→Q with null fibers and nowhere-dense singular image, and Section9 has given a homeomorphism a:B^4→Q matching alpha on the boundary. Extend a^−1 beta over the added collar by its boundary product to the ordinary B^4 union exterior collar. Use the explicit homeomorphism just constructed to identify the DOMAIN with a standard ball. The extended map is an onto ball-to-ball map with null fibers and nowhere-dense singular image. Its restriction over the ENTIRE target exterior collar is a homeomorphism. Apply Section5 with that closed collar as protected E. The resulting homeomorphism agrees with the extended map on the whole preimage collar, so it takes its complementary inner C' exactly onto the complementary inner standard B^4, with the required boundary map. Its attaching solid torus inherits the specified original framing because that boundary map was protected, not subsequently adjusted by an arbitrary sphere homeomorphism.

This is the full reduction made in FQ4.6 printed80, including its paragraph between the proposition and the proof. That paragraph is indispensable: applying the ball-to-ball proposition directly to an unparameterized pinched neighborhood C' would be circular. It uses the special wild-COLLAR arc fibers, not merely arbitrary arc fibers. The actual dual-handle construction must therefore provide that precise singular parameterization, in addition to providing beta and its common quotient; those are still the geometric design obligations before the present operation can be used on the original disk problem.
**Section11: Dual model and the singular collar parameterization.** The following finite construction and its limiting steps use the supplied framed data.

Fix a FINITE model tower, before its extra plumbings are mapped into the ambient manifold. The entire disk-like capped model has regular neighborhood D^2 times D^2. Deleting the caps instead leaves the complement of disjoint dual two-handles H_m=(D^2 times D^2,D^2 times S^1). The latter convention for their attaching solid torus is the dual one; it is not the original attaching S^1 times D^2. This statement is checked at one elementary surface move: replace the disk by its self-tube along a short arc. Its complement acquires a one-handle, and the two caps supply its cancelling dual two-handle pair. Slice the tube by a normal three-disk. The two cap dual disks run on opposite sides of that slice; outside the tube they are two parallel strips, while inside it their strips pass once on opposite normal sides. Gluing the slice back gives the two linked solid tori in the original D^2 times S^1. Replacing one cap by another capped surface repeats exactly this operation INSIDE its own dual handle. Multiple handles on a surface give disjoint stacks of this pair. Finger moves on a cap, and its added Whitney/accessory disks, give further dual handles contained in those already present. Thus successive finite stories give nested finite families H_(n,m), and the neighborhood of their body is
(D^2 times D^2) minus union_m int H_(n,m).
The elementary pair of linked tori just described is the Bing pair in this argument; its specified strips, rather than a link name alone, determine the relevant pattern.

Here is the finite shortening operation on that pattern. Cut the longitude of the parent solid torus at a small box. After the first doubling each core has a long forward-and-return pair of strands, monotone in the longitude coordinate, with the remaining clasp confined to the cut box. A 'monotone loop of length r' means one strand runs monotonically through an interval of length r and the other returns through that same interval; the rest has longitude diameter<a. If r>a, place a doubling clasp a short distance a along the forward strand and its mate a short distance a from the far turn on the return strand. On either child the two middle opposite parallel runs bound an empty ribbon: they are the two sides of the same normal strip, with its clasp endpoints outside that ribbon. Cancel these two runs by pushing across this ribbon. The remaining child has one forward-and-return pair of longitude length at most r−a; its two short joining pieces and clasp have longitude diameter<a. Perform the cancellation for the two children in different normal levels of the parent strip. Their supports are disjoint, and the old single linked passage between the children stays in their short clasp boxes. This is an isotopy of the doubled pair inside the parent torus: the moving ribbon is in its product normal disk, its endpoints are fixed on the two clasp boxes, and at each intermediate time the strands remain in their prescribed separate normal levels. It does not cut a linked component or pass it through the other one.

Iterate the shortening. The initial forward-and-return length is less than the circumference of the longitude circle, say2pi. After more than2pi/a steps every child core has longitude diameter<a. Compress the transverse disk widths as well, with an isotopy in the solid-torus product coordinates. Hence sufficiently many grope stages put every boundary solid torus of the dual handles in a ball of arbitrarily small prescribed diameter about a point of the longitude core. Further Whitney/accessory handles lie inside the preceding dual handles, so also satisfy that bound. citations.quote: Let $X$ be a compact connected oriented topological $4$-manifold with nonempty boundary, let $x_0\in X$, and put $G=\pi_1(X,x_0)$. A **finite relative disk-embedding datum** consists of proper generic immersions $f_i:(D^2,S^1)\looparrowright(X,\partial X)$, $1\le i\le n$, whose boundary circles are embedded and pairwise disjoint, together with framed immersed spheres $g_i:S^2\looparrowright\operatorname{int}X$ that are algebraically dual to the disks. Here a generic immersion is locally a topological embedding except at finitely many double points, each with exactly two preimages whose image sheets are the coordinate planes $\mathbb R^2\times\{0\}$ and $\{0\}\times\mathbb R^2$ in a chart of $X$; proper means that the inverse image of $\partial X$ is exactly the domain boundary; and framed means that the normal microbundle has a chosen trivialization extending the specified boundary framing. Choose paths from $x_0$ to the immersed surfaces and orient the surfaces. Each transverse intersection $p$ of two surfaces contributes $\epsilon(p)g_p$ to $\lambda$, where $\epsilon(p)\in\{1,-1\}$ compares their induced local orientation with the chosen orientation of $X$, and $g_p\in G$ is the loop that travels along the chosen path to the first surface, then to $p$, and returns along the second surface and its chosen path. Thus $\lambda$ is a signed equivariant intersection sum in $\mathbb Z[G]$. Wall's self-intersection sum $\mu$ is the signed sum over self-double points in $\mathbb Z[G]/\langle g-g^{-1}:g\in G\rangle$, because interchanging the two sheets replaces a label by its inverse. The normal framing is a separate datum; its relative normal Euler or boundary-framing obstruction is zero precisely when the specified framing extends over the immersion. The spheres are **algebraically dual** when $\lambda(f_i,g_j)=\delta_{ij}$, $\lambda(g_i,g_j)=0$ for every $i,j$, and $\mu(g_i)=0$ for every $i$. The disk data are **algebraically unobstructed** when also $\lambda(f_i,f_j)=0$ for $i\ne j$ and $\mu(f_i)=0$ for every $i$.
