citations.quote: Let $\Gamma$ be a group. Say that $\Gamma$ is **good for the Freedman disk-embedding theorem** when it has the $\pi_1$-null disk property: for every disk-like capped grope $G^c$ of height $1.5$ with a chosen basepoint and every homomorphism $\phi:\pi_1(G^c)\to\Gamma$, there is an immersed disk whose framed boundary is the attaching region of $G^c$, such that each double-point loop of the disk, regarded after basing as an element of $\pi_1(G^c)$, is sent to the identity by $\phi$. This definition of a good group is a hypothesis on $\Gamma$; it does not assert that any particular group is good.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: **Section1: Precise input.** A finite framed four-dimensional capped-grope neighborhood is supplied, with its usual product collars and self-plumbing charts. Its body is embedded; only cap interiors have generic double points. An integer labeling means a homomorphism from the fundamental group of this actual neighborhood to Z. Paths to individual cap sheets are fixed once. Conjugating a based loop does not change its integer label. No arbitrary locally flat surface is given a tubular neighborhood by this hypothesis: the actual grope's framed block neighborhood is input.

**Operation.** Contract one top surface stage. Designate a finite subset of cap double points to be pushed off at that contraction, and choose a first and second sheet at each designated point. Then the resulting shorter capped grope has the same lower body, attaching circle and framing. Every old intersection not designated has parallel descendants with its old label. No designated old intersection remains. Every new cap intersection is a descendant of two designated intersections removed across dual caps at this same contraction, and its label is a difference of their labels, up to overall sign. Consequently, if all designated labels lie in an interval [a,b], every new label has absolute value at most b−a.

**Proof of the contraction operation.** Cut the top surface at each pair of symplectic attaching curves. Replace the cut part by two small parallel copies of each of its two caps and the small central square at their unique attaching-curve intersection. Cutting a genus-g one-boundary surface along its complete symplectic system leaves the disk region with paired edges; the four parallel cap sectors and this square fill each pair of edges. Thus this replaces the surface with its contracted disk. All replacements take place in the supplied framed block. Parallel copies are made in its chosen normal coordinate; the central square uses the untwisted product collar, so the external attaching framing is unchanged. The result may be immersed, which is allowed.

For a designated point, take an embedded path on its second cap from that point to its attaching boundary, with interior avoiding all other double-point preimages. Finitely many paths on one cap can be chosen with disjoint interiors by an embedded finite tree and small parallel offsets. The two parallel copies of that path, closed across the central square, bound a ribbon Whitney disk pairing the two intersections of the first sheet with the contracted cap. In a product rectangle around the path, this is just the rectangle between the two parallel copies, closed by the boundary square. Its interior is disjoint from the old body and all unmodified sheets. A generic sufficiently small choice of the finitely many product widths is possible because their unwanted incidences are finitely many closed disjoint compact sets. No appeal to a normal bundle over an arbitrary TOP surface occurs.

Push the first sheet across this ribbon. This removes precisely the two paired intersections. The only ribbons that can meet are ones running across dual cap sectors: their boundary paths cross in the central square. Resolving those crossings by the prescribed order of the pushes creates intersections between the pushed first sheets. Ribbons on the same cap have been chosen parallel and disjoint, and ribbons belonging to different handles have disjoint block neighborhoods. Therefore every new intersection has exactly the stated two designated ancestors. Repeating for all parallel descendants removes the designated old point altogether. This is a finite sequence of ordinary finger/Whitney operations in explicit smooth block charts; a small relative perturbation makes the resulting intersections transverse.

Here is the label calculation, including the path issue. Let the two designated points have based first-to-second loops g,h. A path to the new intersection follows the first pushed sheet along the ribbon to its second-sheet cap, crosses the common central square, and returns along the other ribbon in reverse. Cancel the common paths in the old body. The resulting word is g h^{-1}; changing starting path conjugates it and exchanging the two resulting sheets inverts it. This is a calculation in the original supplied neighborhood, since every ribbon and push lies there. Its Z label is consequently ±(phi(g)−phi(h)). An old point copied to parallel sheets has its old loop with a small contractible product strip added, so its label is unchanged. The construction, classification of new intersections and claimed bound follow.

**Section2: Halving and the finite stopping bound.** Suppose there are h top surface stages available for contraction and the absolute labels of all the actual cap-point generators are at most an integer N. Contract the top stage, designating all points whose labels are in [N/2,N]. Their new labels have absolute value at most N/2 by Section1. The unmodified old positive labels are less than N/2; old negative labels may still range to −N. Contract the next top stage and designate the labels in [−N,−N/2]. Again new labels have absolute value at most N/2. Old labels outside this interval already have absolute value at most N/2. Thus two contractions reduce the bound to N/2. The same construction works when N is odd, since inequalities refer to real bounds and labels remain integers.

After q pairs of contractions the bound is N/2^q. Choose the least integer q with 2^q>N; if N=0 take q=0. This is a finite integer algorithm. At that point every cap-point generator has label zero. The neighborhood group is generated by these loops: the abstract disk-like capped grope is simply connected (its symplectic basis loops are killed by its attached higher stages/caps), and each self-plumbing identifies two small simply connected sheet neighborhoods, adding its one double-point loop. Cutting the finite plumbing neighborhoods restores the abstract source. Van Kampen, adding them back one at a time, gives precisely these generators, with no assertion that an arbitrary ambient group is free. Hence the entire neighborhood image has zero Z label.

Contract the remaining body stages to a disk. Every operation stays in this neighborhood, so all double-point loops of the final framed immersed disk have zero image under the original homomorphism. Its boundary and framing are unchanged. This proves null-disk production **when sufficiently many actual stages have been constructed**; it does not yet manufacture those stages from height1.5.

In the symmetric height-raising construction, the precise quantitative target can be stated without the harmless factor-of-two compression in FQ2.9. If 2k raising steps give height at least 2^k and each resulting cap-point loop has word length at most 5^{2k} in the original finite cap-point generators, their absolute labels are at most 5^{2k}B. It suffices that
2^(−floor((2^k−1)/2)) · 5^(2k) · B < 1.

Reserve one bottom surface stage; the other stages supply the indicated number of contraction pairs. The displayed quantity tends to zero because its base-two logarithm is at most −2^(k−1)+O(k)+log2 B. Thus a least successful k is obtained by a terminating integer search. No infinite choice or convergence theorem is hidden in this numerical step. Sections3–4 prove the required height and word-length estimates starting from the asymmetric height1.5 input.

**Section3: The asymmetric bootstrap.** Start with one symplectic pair above the bottom surface: on the positive side a framed capped surface R of positive genus, on the negative side a framed immersed cap W. The same construction is repeated for the finitely many pairs; their body blocks are disjoint, and interactions between cap systems are allowed. All operations fix a neighborhood of the original bottom surface and its attaching region.

Take two small framed parallel copies of R, at negative and positive normal coordinate, and join their boundary circles by the normal annulus crossing the attaching curve of W once. The result is an embedded closed surface of genus twice that of R. Its caps are the corresponding parallel copies of the caps of R. This is a sphere-like capped surface F: compressing its symplectic system gives a sphere. Its body meets W in one point and is disjoint from R; its cap intersections with all the old caps are unrestricted. The annulus and the single crossing are read in the supplied symplectic handle block, not in a hypothetical neighborhood of an arbitrary locally flat surface.

Construct a small parallel copy of F and contract its top stage to an immersed framed sphere T. During contraction, push every other cap sheet off T by the ribbons of Section1, excluding the one prescribed body intersection T with W. This includes the original caps of F, the caps of R and the remaining parts of W. All intersections newly produced by those pushes are between those cap sheets. The sphere T is therefore disjoint from both R and the body/caps of F, and from the caps of R, and meets W at its one prescribed point only. Self-intersections of T are allowed. The ribbons have support near cap arcs and their central squares, away from the lower body, so they do not alter any of the displayed body intersections.

Use T as a Norman sphere to remove every intersection of W with a cap of R or F: for each such point, choose a path in W from that point to the unique point W meets T. Remove a small disk from the intersecting cap and connect it by an untwisted tube, along a parallel copy of that path, to T with a small disk removed. The second endpoint consumes the one intersection of that parallel T with W. The two disks removed and the tube are the boundary of a product neighborhood of the path, so the resulting cap misses W at the chosen point and has the same boundary and framing. Choose the finitely many paths as branches of a tree in the abstract disk W, with separate parallel approach paths at their common endpoint; their interiors avoid all other double-point preimages. Normal widths are chosen successively small. The added copies of T are framed immersed spheres; their self- and mutual intersections belong entirely to the modified CAPS. Thus they may create cap intersections but no body intersections. Their original intersections with R or the body of F are empty, and sufficiently small parallel copies retain that property. After this finite operation W is disjoint from every other part except its own self-intersections and the single point on the body of F. In particular F remains a proper capped surface transverse to W.

For each self-intersection of W, tube one of its sheets to a separate small parallel copy of the BODY of F, along the other sheet and then along a chosen arc in W to the transverse point. This is the same local Norman cancellation, now using a capped surface instead of the contracted sphere. The new body consists of W with that sheet disk deleted, the punctured closed body of F, and their connecting annulus. It is a one-boundary surface with additional genus, with the old W boundary/framing. The caps of the added F provide the symplectic caps for its new handles. Its body is embedded: before the tubing, distinct body copies were disjoint and met W only at their distinct transverse endpoints; the tube arcs avoid every other double-point preimage. Choose disjoint parallel branches of a finite tree in W and nested normal widths. The tube neighborhoods consequently miss all other body sheets. Every old self-intersection of W is removed once, and none is introduced into the new body. Its new caps may intersect each other or the old caps, but they miss every body: the prior operation made the old caps disjoint from W, and properness of F makes its caps disjoint from all the parallel body sheets. At the attaching collars this assertion is the defining product chart. Consequently W has become an actual proper framed capped surface, not merely a surface with unaccounted body intersections.

This changes the side heights (1,0) to (1,1), preserving the original bottom stage. All choices and moves were finite. The scorecard is: R/body(F) embedded and mutually disjoint throughout; T immersed auxiliary, intersecting W once; old caps arbitrary among themselves; after the Norman cancellations all old caps miss W; after the final tubing every new intersection lies among caps. The auxiliary T is discarded after its copies have been inserted into caps. No disjointness of its parallel copies is needed, because their intersections are allowed cap intersections.

**Section4: Height raising and word length.** Here the two side heights count stages ABOVE the fixed bottom surface. Section3 gives (1,0) to (1,1). The following side extension, used only finitely often in this bootstrap, supplies (1,1) to (2,1) to (2,3). Let P be the side to be raised and Q its other side, of heights p,q at least one. Construct F transverse to the bottom surface of P by taking two normal parallels of Q and closing their rims with the normal annulus. It is sphere-like of height q. Its body is embedded, meets P only at the specified first-stage point, and misses all other body stages; intersections of its caps with the old caps are allowed.

First make a contracted parallel sphere T transverse to the bottom of P, using Section1 and pushing off all original cap sheets and the caps of F. Its only body intersection is that prescribed transverse point. To make the caps of F disjoint from the old P caps, push an F-cap sheet at each intersection down the old P cap to its attaching stage and then down successive P stages to its bottom. A finger across one attaching collar replaces one intersection with two on the immediately lower stage; this is two parallel paths around the two ends of that collar. After p stages there are finitely many points on the bottom of P. Tube them off over parallel copies of T. These changes affect only caps of F. They cannot reintroduce intersections with old P caps because T misses those caps and the finger paths on the old caps avoid the other finitely many double-point preimages. The new intersections are among caps of F and possibly the old Q caps, which are still caps. All old body stages are fixed.

Now for an intersection of an old P cap with a Q cap, push the Q-cap sheet down the P stages and tube it off over T. The Q cap is still an immersed disk; its boundary and framing are fixed. It may acquire self/intersections with other caps, which are allowed. It remains disjoint from the old P caps and all body stages: the punctured T used in the tubing has had its unique bottom-P intersection removed. Crucially T is also disjoint from the body of F, so the Q caps miss every body piece to be added in the next step.

Finally treat every self/mutual intersection among the old P caps by pushing one of its P sheets down the P stages and tubing it off over copies of the full F, rather than T. This replaces each old P cap by a capped grope: its first added stage is the old disk with punctured bodies of F attached, followed by the higher stages of those copies of F. Orient each added copy so its transverse intersection cancels the chosen point, and use the untwisted framed tubes. All old P-cap intersections have been removed; the added bodies are embedded and disjoint from each other because distinct body parallels of F are disjoint, and the tube paths avoid all other old preimages. The new caps are copies of F's caps. Those were made disjoint from ALL old P caps before this step, and properness makes them disjoint from F's parallel bodies. Consequently every new intersection is among caps, not on a new body. A cap with no intersections may be regarded as a genus-zero stage with no attached higher surface, as in the disk-like model. The first and second steps are needed: merely asserting that tubing adds height would leave the old cap intersections on the new body.

All choices involve finite paths, parallels and normal widths in supplied framed blocks. Use the move first with p=q=1, then exchange the two sides and use p=1,q=2. Both sides then have height at least two, so the entire grope has height at least three. The induced integer labels on its finite plumbing generators are obtained by following their actual paths back to the original neighborhood; let B be the maximum of their absolute values. B exists without any growth estimate for this finite bootstrap.

For the side P to be extended, form the transverse grope from the opposite side Q. Its height is that of Q. Contract its top stage and push the old caps off that contraction by Section1. The transverse grope now has height one less and its caps are disjoint from all old caps. Push each intersection on a P cap down the P stages, and at the bottom tube off over this transverse grope. The same body/cap scorecard as Section4 applies: new bodies consist of separate parallel copies of the old embedded opposite-side bodies, and all cap intersections have been removed from the new body before it is declared a body. This replaces each old P cap by a capped grope with the height of the contracted transverse grope. In terms of full path heights a,b INCLUDING the shared bottom, the updated path height is a+b−2. Alternate the sides. Starting with a_{−1}=a_0=3, the successive updated path heights obey a_n=a_{n−1}+a_{n−2}−2. The uniform height is the smaller of the two current path heights. Writing a_n−2 as a Fibonacci recursion gives, after 2k steps, uniform height at least 2^k: consecutive pairs increase the smaller Fibonacci term by at least a factor two. Additional initial height only improves the bound.

Contraction copies an old point without changing its generator. A push off a contraction creates the difference loop of Section1, a word of length at most two in the OLD cap-point generators. A new intersection among caps of the parallel transverse grope has length one, since its sheets are old parallel sheets. The only remaining type is a loop using a newly pushed-down finger: follow its first sheet across at most two old cap-point loops to the parallel transverse copy, cross its new cap intersection (one old generator), and return across at most two old loops on the other finger. The two bottom-stage paths cancel, as do the parallel collar paths. This is a concatenation of at most 2+1+2 old generators or inverses. These exhaust the new intersections: they occur on unchanged parallels, on a contraction push, or between two inserted fingers. Thus each step sends every NEW generator to a word of length at most five in the PRECEDING generators. Induction gives length at most 5^(2k) after 2k steps, and absolute Z label at most 5^(2k)B. No count of the possibly much larger number of points is substituted for this word bound.

Choose the least k satisfying Section2's displayed stopping inequality (if B=0 no raising is needed). Height supplies the required number of contraction pairs, and the label estimate supplies their initial bound. Section2 then gives zero image on every cap-point loop, and final contraction produces a framed immersed disk with the original framed attaching circle. Everything occurs in the original supplied grope neighborhood. For an arbitrary homomorphism to Z this is the pi1-null disk property of the existing goodness Definition. The construction is finite for each input: no countable-stage choice, limiting disk, tower standardization or arbitrary TOP normal-bundle theorem has been used in this cyclic part.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K:S^1\hookrightarrow S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere, and let $F\subset S^3$ be a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface with boundary $K$, oriented so that its boundary orientation is the given orientation of $K$. Let $g$ be the nonnegative integer determined by $\chi(F)=1-2g$. Choose an ordered integral basis $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ of the first singular homology group $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$, represented by integral one-cycles on $F$. Orient the normal line of $F$ by requiring $(n,u,v)$ to be positively oriented in $S^3$ whenever $(u,v)$ is a positive tangent basis of $F$. The positive push-off $a_i^+$ is the cycle carried to a sufficiently small positive normal level in a bicollar of $F$.

For disjoint oriented closed curves $J,L\subset S^3$, orient a meridian $\mu_L$ of $L$ so that a positive tangent to $L$ followed by a positive basis of its normal disk gives the ambient orientation. The linking number $\operatorname{lk}(J,L)$ is the integer determined by $[J]=\operatorname{lk}(J,L)[\mu_L]$ in $H_1(S^3\setminus L;\mathbb Z)$, using the Alexander-duality identification that sends $[\mu_L]$ to $1$. Extend linking additively over integral one-cycles. The Seifert pairing is $\theta_F(x,y)=\operatorname{lk}(x^+,y)$, and its matrix in the chosen basis is $V=(V_{ij})_{i,j=1}^{2g}$, where $V_{ij}=\theta_F(a_i,a_j)=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. The surface and basis are part of the data; this definition asserts no knot-only matrix invariant.

Fix the orientation-reversing reflection $r:S^3\to S^3$ chosen for the mirror convention in the oriented connected-sum definition. If $K$ is a smooth oriented knot, its mirror $r(K)$ carries the orientation induced from $K$ by $r$. The reverse mirror of $K$, denoted $K^\dagger$, is the image $r(K)$ with its knot orientation reversed. Thus $K^\dagger$ changes both the ambient orientation convention and the orientation of the knot.

derivations.claim: Give the reflected surface $r(F)$ its transported orientation. Its boundary is $r(K)$ with the transported knot orientation. Therefore the Seifert surface for the specified reverse mirror is $F^\dagger=-r(F)$, with the opposite surface orientation. Let $(u,v)$ be a positive tangent frame of $F$ and let $n$ be its positive normal, so $(n,u,v)$ is ambient-positive by [F1]. A positive tangent frame for $F^\dagger$ is $(-dr(u),dr(v))$: reversing exactly one tangent reverses the surface orientation. Since $r$ reverses ambient orientation, the frame $(dr(n),-dr(u),dr(v))$ is ambient-positive. Consequently the positive normal of $F^\dagger$ is $dr(n)$, and the positive push of the image basis curve $r(a_i)$ is precisely $r(a_i^+)$. This computation includes both orientation reversals; reversing both tangent vectors instead would preserve the surface orientation.

Reflection negates linking. Indeed an oriented normal disk to an oriented curve $D$ is positive when its disk orientation follows the tangent of $D$ in the ambient orientation. The reflected disk has the opposite normal-disk orientation relative to $r(D)$, since $r$ reverses the ambient orientation. Thus $r$ takes the positive meridian class to minus the positive meridian class, and taking meridian coefficients in the complement gives $\operatorname{lk}(r(C),r(D))=-\operatorname{lk}(C,D)$. Using the actual positive pushes from step 1.1, the image-basis entries are therefore $\operatorname{lk}(r(a_i^+),r(a_j))=-\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)=-V_{ij}$. This proves the matrix is $-V$, including the empty matrix in genus zero.

Assume the full Axiom of Choice. Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot, and let $F\subset S^3$ be a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface whose oriented boundary is $K$, with $\chi(F)=1-2g$. Choose an ordered integral basis $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$ and use the positive normal convention $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. Let $A_K$ be the first homology of the infinite cyclic cover of $S^3\setminus K$ classified by total linking, with $t$ acting by the positive-meridian deck transformation. Let $\Delta_K(t)$ be the generator of the zeroth elementary ideal $E_0(A_K)$ in $\Lambda=\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$, and write $p\doteq q$ when $p$ and $q$ differ by a unit $\pm t^k$ of $\Lambda$. Then for every such $F$ and basis,

$$\det(V-tV^T)\doteq\Delta_K(t).$$

The determinant is $1$ for the empty $0\times0$ matrix when $g=0$. This formula concerns the polynomial $\Delta_K$; the existing knot-normalized fraction $D_K=\Delta_K/(1-t)$ is a separate invariant.

Let $V$ be an integral Seifert matrix in the positive-push convention $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. Two integral Seifert forms are **S-equivalent** when they are related by a finite sequence of integral unimodular basis changes and algebraic tube additions or their inverses. A basis change replaces $V$ by $P^T V P$ for $P\in\operatorname{GL}_m(\mathbb Z)$. A tube addition replaces $V$ by
$$
\begin{pmatrix}
V&0&\rho\\
0&0&1\\
\rho^T&0&0
\end{pmatrix},\qquad \rho\in\mathbb Z^m,
$$
where the two new basis elements are the short and long curves of the added tube. The **empty Seifert form** is the unique bilinear form on the zero module, represented by the $0\times0$ matrix.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented embedded circle in the oriented standard three-sphere, let $F$ be a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface with boundary $K$, and let $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ be any ordered integral basis of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$ with Seifert matrix $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. Let $J_F$ be the matrix of the algebraic intersection form on $F$, with a transverse intersection of oriented curves $u,v$ counted positively exactly when their ordered tangent vectors form a positive basis of $TF$. Then $V-V^T=J_F$. The matrix $J_F$ is skew-symmetric and unimodular; when $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ is a standard handle basis, it is a direct sum of blocks $\begin{psmallmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{psmallmatrix}$.

Let V be an integral 2g-by-2g matrix and J=V−V^T unimodular alternating. Suppose P(t)=det(V−tV^T) is a Laurent unit. Since P is a polynomial and P(t)=t^(2g)P(t^−1), it is t^g: a unit polynomial is ±t^m, reciprocity gives m=g, and P(1)=det J=1 fixes the sign. (The determinant of an integral unimodular alternating matrix is +1: choose any primitive vector, use the primitive row of J and Bezout to split off a symplectic pair, and repeat on its integral orthogonal direct summand. This determinant argument does not require a kernel vector of V, so it precedes the following deduction det V=0 without circularity.) For g>0 its constant coefficient det V is zero. Choose a nonzero rational kernel vector of V, clear denominators and divide by its coordinate gcd. This gives a primitive integral x with Vx=0.

The row x^T V equals x^T J, since x^T V^T=(Vx)^T=0. It is primitive because multiplication by the unimodular J preserves primitive vectors. Bezout therefore gives an integral y with x^T V y=1. Then omega(x,y)=x^T J y=1. Put L={z:omega(x,z)=omega(y,z)=0}. Every z decomposes uniquely as [F1, F2, F3, algebra]
z = omega(z,y)x + omega(x,z)y + z_0,  z_0 in L.

Thus Z^(2g)=Zx direct-sum Zy direct-sum L, and omega restricted to L is unimodular alternating. L is a free integral direct summand; its basis is obtained by applying the displayed integral projection to the coordinate generators and elementary Euclidean column operations. Repeating the primitive-vector/Bezout splitting in L gives an integral symplectic basis there. In that basis, followed by x,y, the Seifert matrix is [F1, F2, F3, algebra]
[[B,0,u],[0,0,1],[u^T,0,w]].

Indeed Vx=0 gives its zero x-column, and x^T V=x^T J gives the x-row. Orthogonality to y gives equality of the two old-to-y coupling vectors. Replace y by y−wx. This is a symplectic integral basis change and makes w zero, without changing B,u. We have exhibited exactly the algebraic tube enlargement in the ACTUAL S-equivalence Definition, not a rational enlargement.

Expanding det(tV−V^T) along the x-row and then x-column gives [F1, F2, F3, algebra]
det(tV−V^T)=t det(tB−B^T).

For even matrix size det(tV−V^T)=P(t) by transposition and multiplication by −1. Hence the reduced matrix B again has unit polynomial t^(g−1) and unimodular alternating skew part. Induct on g. This supplies a finite sequence of integral congruences and exact inverse tube additions down to the empty matrix. No stabilization theorem is assumed. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere $S^3$. A **Seifert surface** for $K$ is a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface $F\subset S^3$ with boundary set equal to $K$. Orient each boundary component so that an outward-pointing conormal in $F$, followed by a positive boundary tangent, is a positive basis of $TF$; the oriented boundary of $F$ must agree with the given orientation of $K$. For such a surface, its genus $g(F)$ is the unique nonnegative integer satisfying $\chi(F)=2-2g(F)-b$, where $b$ is the number of boundary components; here $b=1$, so $\chi(F)=1-2g(F)$. The compact-surface normal-form result supplies this integer under the stated choice axiom.
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Every smooth oriented knot $K\subset S^3$ bounds a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface $F\subset S^3$ whose oriented boundary is $K$.

Assume the full Axiom of Choice. Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot with Alexander polynomial $\Delta_K(t)\doteq1$, where $\doteq$ denotes equality up to multiplication by a unit $\pm t^k$ of $\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$. For every Seifert surface $F$ of $K$ and every integral Seifert matrix $V$ of $F$ in the positive-push convention, the form represented by $V$ is S-equivalent over $\mathbb Z$ to the empty Seifert form.

Let $V$ be an integral Seifert matrix in the positive-push convention $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. Two integral Seifert forms are **S-equivalent** when they are related by a finite sequence of integral unimodular basis changes and algebraic tube additions or their inverses. A basis change replaces $V$ by $P^T V P$ for $P\in\operatorname{GL}_m(\mathbb Z)$. A tube addition replaces $V$ by
$$
\begin{pmatrix}
V&0&\rho\\
0&0&1\\
\rho^T&0&0
\end{pmatrix},\qquad \rho\in\mathbb Z^m,
$$
where the two new basis elements are the short and long curves of the added tube. The **empty Seifert form** is the unique bilinear form on the zero module, represented by the $0\times0$ matrix.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice-principle-for-foliation-pair]]). Let $S$ be an oriented Hausdorff $C^2$ surface without boundary, possibly disconnected. Then:

1. Every compact subset $K\subset S$ lies in the interior of a compact finitely cellulated $C^2$ subsurface $N$. If $K$ is contained in one connected component of $S$, $N$ can be chosen connected. A specified finite embedded regular $C^2$ graph contained in $\operatorname{Int}N$ can be included in its one-skeleton.
2. Every connected closed compact subsurface has an oriented genus normal form: the sphere for $g=0$, or the polygon word $\prod_{i=1}^g a_i b_i a_i^{-1}b_i^{-1}$ for $g\ge1$, with $\chi=2-2g$. A connected compact subsurface with $b>0$ boundary circles has a free fundamental group; capping its boundaries defines genus $g$ and gives $\chi=2-2g-b$ and free rank $2g+b-1$.
3. The fundamental group of every connected component of $S$ is torsion-free.
4. Every regular embedded $C^2$ nullhomotopic circle $c$ bounds an embedded compact disk region in $S$. Here a disk region is a compact subsurface homeomorphic to the closed disk, with boundary exactly $c$; its inherited surface structure and boundary are $C^2$. It is unique unless the **connected component containing $c$** is a sphere; in that component the two complementary disk regions are the two possibilities.

The normal forms in clause 2 are homeomorphism normal forms. No general differentiable smoothing theorem or arbitrary-surface triangulation-existence theorem is a premise of this item.

derivations.claim: Full AC implies Countable Choice, so choose the actual connected smooth Seifert surface supplied by [F2]. The proved reduction [F3] splits its given lattice by symplectic pairs and the exact inverse tube enlargements of [F4].

Reversing these reductions also produces the claimed trivial Alexander block. Keep all short vectors first and all long vectors second. A reverse tube addition introduces a new short x with zero column and only the entry 1 in its own long column, and a new long y with zero diagonal. Its couplings to earlier short vectors occupy precisely the new LAST column of U, so U stays strictly upper triangular. Its couplings to earlier long vectors give a symmetric new row/column of W, with zero new diagonal. Starting from the empty matrix therefore gives [[0,I+U],[U^T,W]] with exactly the advertised conditions. This is an integral symplectic basis of the original lattice; the finite construction below realizes it geometrically rather than assuming that arbitrary integral basis changes are surface homeomorphisms.

Fix a standard geometric basis a_i,b_i on the actual compact oriented genus-g surface with one boundary circle. Its existence follows by cutting a finite disk-and-handle model of the surface, not from an arbitrary homology basis. Put omega(a_i,b_j)=delta_ij. An annular Dehn twist about an embedded curve v acts by the transvection T_v(z)=z+omega(z,v)v, choosing the twist sign accordingly. This formula is proved by cutting each transverse arc at the annulus: the twisted arc acquires one oriented copy of its core. Curves representing a_i+a_j, b_i+b_j and a_i+b_j for i≠j are embedded band sums on distinct handles. The joining arc lies in the complement of the other standard handles; the band gives the indicated homology class. Thus these transvections and their inverses are actual boundary-fixed surface homeomorphisms (smooth diffeomorphisms in the smooth model).

For orthogonal u,v, direct expansion gives
T_(u+v) T_u^−1 T_v^−1(z)
=z+omega(z,u)v+omega(z,v)u.

Taking u=a_i,v=b_j, i≠j, realizes the elementary block-GL operation a_j to a_j+a_i and b_i to b_i−b_j. Its powers realize arbitrary integral elementary additions. Handle permutations and simultaneous sign reversal of a_i,b_i are also realized; the latter is the square of the two-twist rotation on that handle. Euclidean elimination consequently realizes every block action (x,y) to (A x,A^−T y) for A in GL_g(Z). Likewise the a_i and a_i+a_j twists realize every symmetric upper shear, because the diagonal rank-one matrices and the identity (e_i+e_j)(e_i+e_j)^T−E_ii−E_jj=E_ij+E_ji generate all symmetric integral matrices; the b_i analogues realize every symmetric lower shear.

Here is a complete generation argument, so this is not an appeal to mapping-class surjectivity. Given a primitive vector v=(x,y), first interchange the a and b directions on a handle if necessary to make x nonzero. A block-GL operation makes x=(d,0,...,0), d>0. If some y_j is not divisible by d, reduce d strictly: for j=1 use the ordinary Euclidean two-twist SL_2 algorithm on (d,y_1); for j≠1 an upper diagonal shear inserts y_j in x_j, then block-GL Euclidean reduction replaces d by gcd(d,y_j). Repeat. The positive integer d decreases until every y_j is divisible by d; primitivity then forces d=1. A lower symmetric shear with first column −y clears y while keeping x=e_1. Thus an actual finite product of the specified twists takes every primitive vector to a_1.

Let A be an arbitrary symplectic integral matrix. Apply this procedure to its first column, so the resulting matrix fixes a_1. Its image of b_1 has the form b_1+c a_1+z, with z in the span W of the remaining handles. The displayed orthogonal-transvection combination for u=a_1 and each basis vector v of W fixes a_1. Its k-th power subtracts k v from that image of b_1 and only changes its a_1 coefficient in addition. Use these powers to clear all coordinates of z. Then a power of T_(a_1) clears c. The resulting matrix fixes both a_1,b_1, and hence restricts symplectically to W. Induct on g. We have reduced A to the identity by actual twists; reversing the finite list realizes A. In particular the symplectic lattice basis from the preceding primitive-vector/tube reduction is represented by an ACTUAL geometric basis, with disjoint short curves, disjoint long curves and exactly one transverse short–long intersection on each matching pair.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

Assume full AC. Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot with $\Delta_K(t)\doteq1$, where $\doteq$ denotes equality up to multiplication by a unit $\pm t^k$ of $\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$. Then $K$ has a connected compact smooth oriented Seifert surface $F$ and an ordered geometric basis, represented by embedded simple closed curves $s_1,\ldots,s_g,\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_g$ for $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$, such that $s_i\cdot_Fs_j=0=\ell_i\cdot_F\ell_j$ and $s_i\cdot_F\ell_j=\delta_{ij}$, and the Seifert matrix in this basis has block form
$$V=\begin{pmatrix}0&I_g+U\\U^T&W\end{pmatrix},$$
where $U$ is strictly upper triangular and $W$ is symmetric with zero diagonal. Such a geometric symplectic basis and block matrix are called a trivial Alexander basis.

Let $X$ be a compact connected oriented topological $4$-manifold with nonempty boundary, let $x_0\in X$, and put $G=\pi_1(X,x_0)$. A **finite relative disk-embedding datum** consists of proper generic immersions $f_i:(D^2,S^1)\looparrowright(X,\partial X)$, $1\le i\le n$, whose boundary circles are embedded and pairwise disjoint, together with framed immersed spheres $g_i:S^2\looparrowright\operatorname{int}X$ that are algebraically dual to the disks. Here a generic immersion is locally a topological embedding except at finitely many double points, each with exactly two preimages whose image sheets are the coordinate planes $\mathbb R^2\times\{0\}$ and $\{0\}\times\mathbb R^2$ in a chart of $X$; proper means that the inverse image of $\partial X$ is exactly the domain boundary; and framed means that the normal microbundle has a chosen trivialization extending the specified boundary framing. Choose paths from $x_0$ to the immersed surfaces and orient the surfaces. Each transverse intersection $p$ of two surfaces contributes $\epsilon(p)g_p$ to $\lambda$, where $\epsilon(p)\in\{1,-1\}$ compares their induced local orientation with the chosen orientation of $X$, and $g_p\in G$ is the loop that travels along the chosen path to the first surface, then to $p$, and returns along the second surface and its chosen path. Thus $\lambda$ is a signed equivariant intersection sum in $\mathbb Z[G]$. Wall's self-intersection sum $\mu$ is the signed sum over self-double points in $\mathbb Z[G]/\langle g-g^{-1}:g\in G\rangle$, because interchanging the two sheets replaces a label by its inverse. The normal framing is a separate datum; its relative normal Euler or boundary-framing obstruction is zero precisely when the specified framing extends over the immersion. The spheres are **algebraically dual** when $\lambda(f_i,g_j)=\delta_{ij}$, $\lambda(g_i,g_j)=0$ for every $i,j$, and $\mu(g_i)=0$ for every $i$. The disk data are **algebraically unobstructed** when also $\lambda(f_i,f_j)=0$ for $i\ne j$ and $\mu(f_i)=0$ for every $i$.

Let $\Gamma$ be a group. Say that $\Gamma$ is **good for the Freedman disk-embedding theorem** when it has the $\pi_1$-null disk property: for every disk-like capped grope $G^c$ of height $1.5$ with a chosen basepoint and every homomorphism $\phi:\pi_1(G^c)\to\Gamma$, there is an immersed disk whose framed boundary is the attaching region of $G^c$, such that each double-point loop of the disk, regarded after basing as an element of $\pi_1(G^c)$, is sent to the identity by $\phi$. This definition of a good group is a hypothesis on $\Gamma$; it does not assert that any particular group is good.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. The infinite cyclic group $\mathbb Z$ is good for the Freedman disk-embedding theorem, in the sense of the $\pi_1$-null disk property defined for a good fundamental group.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K:S^1\hookrightarrow S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere, and let $F\subset S^3$ be a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface with boundary $K$, oriented so that its boundary orientation is the given orientation of $K$. Let $g$ be the nonnegative integer determined by $\chi(F)=1-2g$. Choose an ordered integral basis $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ of the first singular homology group $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$, represented by integral one-cycles on $F$. Orient the normal line of $F$ by requiring $(n,u,v)$ to be positively oriented in $S^3$ whenever $(u,v)$ is a positive tangent basis of $F$. The positive push-off $a_i^+$ is the cycle carried to a sufficiently small positive normal level in a bicollar of $F$.

For disjoint oriented closed curves $J,L\subset S^3$, orient a meridian $\mu_L$ of $L$ so that a positive tangent to $L$ followed by a positive basis of its normal disk gives the ambient orientation. The linking number $\operatorname{lk}(J,L)$ is the integer determined by $[J]=\operatorname{lk}(J,L)[\mu_L]$ in $H_1(S^3\setminus L;\mathbb Z)$, using the Alexander-duality identification that sends $[\mu_L]$ to $1$. Extend linking additively over integral one-cycles. The Seifert pairing is $\theta_F(x,y)=\operatorname{lk}(x^+,y)$, and its matrix in the chosen basis is $V=(V_{ij})_{i,j=1}^{2g}$, where $V_{ij}=\theta_F(a_i,a_j)=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. The surface and basis are part of the data; this definition asserts no knot-only matrix invariant.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented embedded circle in the oriented standard three-sphere, let $F$ be a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface with boundary $K$, and let $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ be the ordered integral basis and positive normal push-off convention used to define the Seifert matrix $V$ above. Every class of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$ has a representative that is a finite integral sum of pairwise disjoint smooth oriented embedded circles in $F$. For such representatives $x$ and $y$, the sum of the pairwise linking numbers between the positive push-off of $x$ and $y$ depends only on $[x]$ and $[y]$, is independent of the sufficiently small positive push-off, and equals the bilinear extension of $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. The linking number of two disjoint oriented circle components is symmetric. In particular, the Seifert pairing is a well-defined bilinear map $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)\times H_1(F;\mathbb Z)\to\mathbb Z$.
Assume countable choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $F:M\to N$ be a continuous map between smooth manifolds. Then there exists a smooth map $\widetilde F:M\to N$ homotopic to $F$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\mathcal F:M\times S\to N$ be a smooth family of maps and let $Z\subseteq N$
be an embedded submanifold. If $\mathcal F\pitchfork Z$, then the set of
parameters $s\in S$ for which the slice $\mathcal F_s:M\to N$ fails to be
transverse to $Z$ is a null subset of $S$.

derivations.claim: Use [F1] to fix the actual geometric trivial Alexander basis. The following integral shear preserves its short–long intersection convention and makes its long–long block zero.

The current general disk carrier demands vanishing mutual/self Wall numbers for its dual spheres, not merely the triangular disk–sphere matrix in the short GT application. The following integral operation removes a potential extra obstruction rather than assuming those two interfaces coincide.

Suppose a supplied geometric trivial Alexander basis has matrix V=[[0,I+U],[U^T,W]], with U strictly upper triangular and W symmetric. Put N(C)=CU+U^T C on symmetric integral g-by-g matrices. Left multiplication by U^T and right multiplication by U commute and each has gth power zero. The binomial expansion therefore gives N^(2g−1)=0: in every summand one of the two exponents is at least g. Hence I+N has the integral inverse sum_{r=0}^{2g−2}(−N)^r (the g=0 case is empty). Set C=−(I+N)^(−1)W. This is an explicit symmetric INTEGRAL matrix, since N preserves symmetry. The block change S=[[I,C],[0,I]] is symplectic: its new long basis vectors are ell'_j=ell_j+sum_i s_i C_ij, and their intersections are −C_ij+C_ji=0; short–long intersections remain the identity. Direct multiplication gives
S^T V S = [[0,I+U],[U^T,W+C(I+U)+U^T C]]
= [[0,I+U],[U^T,0]].

Thus the same triangular block admits an entirely zero long–long Seifert block. This does NOT assert minimal Seifert rank: U may be nonzero. The initial basis is supplied by [F1]. This particular shear has an explicit geometric realization, so no general surjectivity assertion about the mapping-class group is needed for THIS step. For any vector v among e_i and e_i+e_j, realize its short-class sum by an embedded circle: use s_i for e_i; for e_i+e_j use a band sum of parallel copies of s_i,s_j along a simple arc avoiding all short curves. Such an arc exists because cutting along all the short curves leaves a connected surface. If that cut were disconnected, the oriented boundary of one complementary component would give a nontrivial integral relation among the independent short classes, a contradiction. The band sum and its small annular neighborhood can be chosen disjoint from every original short curve. A Dehn twist in that annulus, written in annular coordinates as (theta,r) to (theta+2pi rho(r),r), is a homeomorphism fixed on the annulus boundary; choose rho constant zero/one near its two ends. Tracking an oriented transverse arc gives on homology the transvection x to x+(x intersection v)v, with sign reversed by the inverse twist. It fixes every short class and sends the long classes by the symmetric rank-one shear vv^T, with the sign chosen according to the intersection convention. Now
E_ij+E_ji = (e_i+e_j)(e_i+e_j)^T−E_ii−E_jj.

Every symmetric integral C is a finite integer sum of these rank-one matrices. Compose the corresponding positive/negative twist powers. Each action fixes the short Lagrangian, so their shear matrices ADD even when their supporting annuli are not disjoint. The composition is an actual orientation-preserving boundary-fixed surface homeomorphism. Applying it to the entire original geometric basis preserves all its geometric intersection counts and realizes S. In the smooth category choose smooth annular cutoffs to obtain a diffeomorphism. Thus the zero-W basis is genuinely geometric and has exactly the same triangular U. The basis supplier [F1] supplies that initial input.

Apply the preceding shear to [F1]. We obtain a smooth geometric basis s_i,ell_i with V=[[0,I+U],[U^T,0]], not only the existential lattice statement. The following construction retains the ambient ball and all attaching data. It is stated before invoking any disk-embedding conclusion.

Use the literal ball of radius1.5 and its unit sphere. Place the original surface F in that unit sphere and add the exterior collar K times [1,1.5]. Round its junction with F, retaining the outer K product collar; call this proper smooth surface Sigma. Near F its normal coordinates are the radial coordinate x and the positive normal coordinate y of F in S3. Choose its open normal thickening there to be .9<x<1.1, |y|<epsilon, with the compatible product continuation near K. This is an ACTUAL smooth thickening, supplied by the radial product and the normal line of the oriented surface in S3. Put N=the complement of that open thickening, with corners rounded away from the marked circles. It is compact, connected, smooth, and the original ball/surface have not been replaced by an abstract four-manifold.

A disk-and-band handle decomposition of F has one disk and2g bands. Make its height increase from that disk across the bands to the boundary, and realize that height as a small radial displacement in the displayed collar. The complement has one0handle, one1handle from the surface minimum and2g2handles from its bands, with no higher handles. This local complement recipe follows by taking the product normal2disk to a surface0handle or1handle: its complement adds respectively the normal meridian1handle or the2handle whose core crosses the band. The product collars identify the attaching pieces; no arbitrary embedded4ball is identified with the standard ball. The resulting complement deformation retracts onto a2complex with one vertex, one1cell and2g2cells. Name the positive normal meridian of its one1handle a. The local2handle at an oriented surface band identifies its endpoint meridians by transport through the band: its attaching relation is m_1 w m_2^−1 w^−1. To see the signs, take the boundary of a normal2disk and transport it along the band core; the two boundary ends of the resulting normal-annulus strip have opposite induced boundary orientations. Both endpoint meridians come from the same original disk and represent a in the one-generator1skeleton. Any winding of a knotted band only changes the transport word w, which is a power of a there. Thus the attaching word is a a^k a^−1 a^−k=1, for every band. Consequently pi1(N)=Z, and the same2complex is homotopy equivalent to a circle wedge2g spheres. This is the actual group/attaching-word computation, not an inference from H1 alone.

Choose generic immersed disks Delta(s_i) in the inner unit ball with boundaries s_i-down. Run their boundary collars in the negative-y side of the marked normal strip, bending into the interior of N immediately off each boundary circle. Choose disks Delta(ell_i) bounding the long curves and trim their radial collars to x=.8; they then have boundaries ell_i at x=.8 and lie in the ball x<=.8. The short disks consist of disks in that inner ball and their mutually disjoint negative-y collars. Their union lies in a simply connected part of N: the inner ball together with those product collars retracts onto the inner ball. Thus all their equivariant intersection labels are1. Their ordinary intersections are the boundary linking numbers, which are V(s_i,s_j)=0. To justify this relative4-ball identity, compare one filling disk with a Seifert surface for the same boundary curve pushed into a thin boundary collar. Their difference is a two-cycle, null in the ball. Its intersection with the other proper disk is therefore zero, by the boundary-of-intersection identity for a bounding three-chain. The collar surface counts exactly the linking number on the boundary sphere, with the outward-normal-first orientation. This proves the identity for immersed fillings, rather than assuming disjoint embedded disk fillings. The boundary framings are the prescribed surface pushoffs. A generic filling disk with that zero longitude can be made framed: the parallel-intersection identity gives 0=2mu+e, so its relative normal Euler number e is even; an interior cusp changes e by2. Use finitely many cusps to make e0. The same identity then gives mu0. These changes are local in the inner ball and preserve the boundary circle/frame. Mutual intersection numbers are invariant under those rel-boundary homotopies. Accordingly lambda(Delta(s_i),Delta(s_j))=0 and mu(Delta(s_i))=0 in the precise integral group-ring convention, not merely after augmentation.

For each long curve construct the torus T_i=ell_i times the boundary of the normal rectangle [.8,1.2] times [−2epsilon,2epsilon]. The long curves are geometrically disjoint, so these tori are disjoint. They lie in N. A short disk meets T_i at the point of ell_i intersection s_j on its negative-y radial collar, hence with geometric signed count delta_ij. Remove an annular neighborhood of the long curve at x=.8,y=0 in T_i, and cap its two boundary circles by opposite oriented framed parallel copies of the trimmed Delta(ell_i). This is a smooth immersed sphere g_i in N. The long–long Seifert block is ZERO, so these long disks have zero boundary linking and can be chosen with the zero extending normal framing as above. The torus product framing matches both caps explicitly: along x=.8 the first common normal is the direction in F transverse to ell_i; the second rotates from the radial direction on the torus to the y-direction on each disk across the chosen rectangle corner. The opposite upper/lower cap orientations give opposite half-rotations, not an extra full twist. The long disk's extending zero frame supplies the remainder. Hence the untwisted attaching annuli give a trivial normal2plane bundle on g_i. Thus these are framed spheres, not tori called spheres without a framing check.

Fix orientations explicitly before the coefficient calculation. At a positive short–long intersection let u be the short tangent and v the long tangent, so (u,v) orients F. The ambient ball orientation is (x,y,u,v), with x outward radial and y the positive surface normal in S3. Orient the rectangle boundary counterclockwise in (x,y), and orient T_i by its rectangle tangent FIRST and its long tangent SECOND. At its x=.8 side the torus tangent basis is (−y,v), while the outward-radial collar of the short disk has basis(x,u); their ordered determinant relative to(x,y,u,v) is positive. Thus the old torus–short point contributes +delta_ij. Removing the annulus |y|<epsilon' at that side leaves its upper boundary oriented +ell_i and its lower boundary −ell_i. Consequently the surgery uses −Delta(ell_i) on the upper cap and +Delta(ell_i) on the lower cap.

Take t to be the counterclockwise meridian in the oriented (x,y) normal plane and base through the inner ball on the lower side. Traveling in the retained torus from the lower cap to the upper one goes around the rectangle's outer three sides counterclockwise; returning through the inner ball closes the positive meridian. Thus the upper cap path differs from the lower by t, with no arbitrary relabeling of the prescribed positive meridian. Use common basing paths through the inner ball. The old torus–short-disk point contributes delta_ij. Every intersection of the long disk with a short disk gives two sphere–short intersections of opposite signs. Their paths differ by precisely the short meridian, so
lambda(g_i,Delta(s_j))=delta_ij+(1−t)lk(ell_i,s_j-down)
=delta_ij+(1−t)(U^T)_ij.

For two DIFFERENT g spheres the tori and their annular surgery pieces contribute no points, because the long curves are geometrically disjoint. Each long-disk intersection contributes four points from the two cap parallels, with factors1,−t,−t^−1,1. Hence
lambda(g_i,g_j)=(1−t)lk(ell_i,ell_j-down)(1−t^−1)=0.

For a self-double point the same parallel-sheet accounting gives two identity-label contributions and the negative t,t^−1 contributions, modulo the sheet-exchange relation. The long disk has framed relative Euler number0 and self-intersection sum0, so mu(g_i)=0. No extra intersections occur at the surgery seam: its two parallel attaching annuli are disjoint in the explicit product torus, with their normal framings already matched. This verifies the additional dual-sphere vanishings demanded by the ACTUAL local disk-data Definition, not just the weaker duality assertion quoted in AppendixA.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

Assume full AC. Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot with $\Delta_K(t)\doteq1$. There is a connected compact smooth Seifert surface $F$ with a geometric symplectic basis $s_1,\ldots,s_g,\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_g$ whose positive-push matrix is
$$V=\begin{pmatrix}0&I_g+U\\ U^T&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad U\text{ strictly upper triangular}.$$
Place $F$ on the unit sphere in the literal radius-$3/2$ ball and join its boundary to the outer copy of $K$ by the radial product collar, rounding the inner junction away from that outer collar. Write $\Sigma$ for this proper surface. Its actual smooth normal thickening can be chosen so that the rounded complement
$$N=B^4_{3/2}\setminus\operatorname{int}\nu\Sigma$$
is compact, connected and smooth, with $\pi_1(N)\cong\mathbb Z$ generated by the positive normal meridian of $\Sigma$.

The fixed negative normal pushoffs of the short curves give disjoint framed circles $\delta_i\subset\partial N$. They bound proper framed smooth generic disks $\Delta_i$ in $N$ admitting framed smooth immersed spheres $f_i$ such that
$$\lambda(\Delta_i,f_j)=\delta_{ij},\quad \lambda(\Delta_i,\Delta_j)=0\ (i\ne j),\quad \mu(\Delta_i)=0,\quad \lambda(f_i,f_j)=0,\quad\mu(f_i)=0$$
in $\mathbb Z[\mathbb Z]$ with the specified Wall conventions. Along the fixed annuli from $\delta_i$ to $s_i\subset\Sigma$, their boundary framings agree with the normal directions of $s_i$ within $\Sigma$. Thus the data retain the actual ambient ball, complement, attaching circles and compression framings. The group is good when the infinite-cyclic good-group theorem is supplied. For $g=0$ the disk and sphere families are empty and the geometric complement assertion remains valid.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. The infinite cyclic group $\mathbb Z$ is good for the Freedman disk-embedding theorem, in the sense of the $\pi_1$-null disk property defined for a good fundamental group.

Assume Countable Choice. Assume $\pi_1(V)$ is good for disk embedding. Let $f_i:(D^2,S^1)\looparrowright(V,V\cap\partial X)$ be a finite proper smooth generic disk datum with pairwise disjoint embedded framed boundaries, and framed smooth immersed spheres $g_i$ satisfying $\lambda(f_i,g_j)=\delta_{ij}$, $\lambda(g_i,g_j)=0$, $\mu(g_i)=0$, $\lambda(f_i,f_j)=0$ for $i\ne j$, and $\mu(f_i)=0$, computed in $\mathbb Z[\pi_1(V)]$.

Their bodies extend to embedded convergent skyscraper pinched neighborhoods, each with a relative standard-two-handle parameterization preserving its attaching solid torus and framing. The corresponding embedded framed Whitney disks give pairwise disjoint proper locally flat disks $\bar f_i$ homotopic to $f_i$ rel boundary and framing. They carry product normal neighborhoods supplied by this construction and framed immersed geometric duals $\bar g_i$ homotopic in $V$ to $g_i$.

Let $X$ be a four-dimensional manifold with boundary and let $W$ be a compact surface with boundary. An embedding $e:(W,\partial W)\to(X,\partial X)$ is proper when $e^{-1}(\partial X)=\partial W$. It is locally flat at an interior point of $W$ when there are neighborhoods of the point and its image and a homeomorphism of pairs from those neighborhoods to $(\mathbb R^4,\mathbb R^2)$, with the standard linear plane $\mathbb R^2\subset\mathbb R^4$. It is locally flat at a boundary point when there are such neighborhoods and a homeomorphism of pairs to $(\mathbb R^4_+,\mathbb R^2_+)$, where $\mathbb R^4_+=\{x_4\geq0\}$ and $\mathbb R^2_+=\{x_2=x_3=0,\ x_4\geq0\}$; the line $\partial\mathbb R^2_+$ lies in $\partial\mathbb R^4_+$. Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented embedded circle in the oriented standard three-sphere, let $F$ be a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface with boundary $K$, and let $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ be the ordered integral basis and positive normal push-off convention used to define the Seifert matrix $V$ above. Every class of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$ has a representative that is a finite integral sum of pairwise disjoint smooth oriented embedded circles in $F$. For such representatives $x$ and $y$, the sum of the pairwise linking numbers between the positive push-off of $x$ and $y$ depends only on $[x]$ and $[y]$, is independent of the sufficiently small positive push-off, and equals the bilinear extension of $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. The linking number of two disjoint oriented circle components is symmetric. In particular, the Seifert pairing is a well-defined bilinear map $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)\times H_1(F;\mathbb Z)\to\mathbb Z$.

derivations.claim: For the unknot, the Seifert surface is a disk, so $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)=0$ and the empty determinant is $1$; the standard flat disk in $B^4$ proves sliceness. For the trefoil, [F1] and [F2] give $\det(V-tV^T)=t^2-t+1$, which is not a Laurent unit.

Construct the actual surface inside the preferred-longitude tube of $T$ from [F3]. Take a narrow annulus $A$ about its core with the zero product framing. In a small ball meeting $A$ in one square $Q$, plumb $A$ to a positive Hopf annulus $H$: identify their squares so the two annular core arcs are the two crossing coordinate axes in $Q$, and place the parts outside the square on opposite sides. Smooth the four square corners. Outside that ball the boundary is the two oppositely oriented zero-framed parallels of $T$; inside the ball the positive Hopf band joins them by its positive clasp. This is precisely the positive-clasped untwisted Whitehead pattern in the specified tube. The untwisted condition is the zero framing of $A$, and the construction uses the preferred longitude rather than an arbitrary longitude. It is also the $k=0$ surface of the cited Figure 2; that figure identifies the convention but is not a substitute for the following matrix calculation.

Let $a$ be the annulus core and $b$ the Hopf core, with orientations chosen so their sole square intersection has $a\cdot_F b=1$. The plumbed surface is connected and oriented. Its Euler characteristic is $0+0-1=-1$, and tracing the alternating four attaching edges gives one boundary component. The two annuli retract to their two core loops with the square intersection identified, so $(a,b)$ is an integral handle basis and the surface has genus one. Choose the plumbing side in which the positive push of the $a$-arc is above the square. The unknotted Hopf core $b$ has a spanning disk in the local ball lying below the square except for its boundary arc; use the lower side for the remainder of $H$. Thus this disk misses $a^+$, including the part of $a^+$ outside the ball. This is a local disk for $b$, and does not assert that the companion $a=T$ bounds a disk.

The positive push of $a$ is a small parallel with the product annulus framing; its linking with $a$ is zero because that product longitude is the preferred longitude. Equivalently move the push to the annular side direction through nonzero normal directions, keeping it disjoint from $a$. The local square does not add a twist to this annular framing. Hence $V_{11}=0$. The two boundary components of the positive Hopf annulus, with induced orientations, link $+1$. Equally oriented core parallels therefore link $-1$, since one induced boundary orientation is reversed. Moving one core parallel to the positive normal push preserves this linking, so $V_{22}=-1$. The local spanning disk from step 2.1 and symmetry of linking give $V_{12}=\operatorname{lk}(a^+,b)=0$. Finally [F5] gives $V_{21}=-1$. Thus the ACTUAL Whitehead double of $T$, not just the pattern applied to the unknot, has matrix $V_0=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\-1&-1\end{pmatrix}$.

Direct calculation gives $\det(V_0-tV_0^T)=t$. This is a Laurent unit, with inverse $t^{-1}$, so [F2] gives $\Delta_{Wh^+(T)}\doteq1$. Applying [F4] proves the stated locally flat proper slice disk in the standard $B^4$. The argument establishes the announced topological conclusion; it contains no smooth slice-disk construction and no inference that the trefoil is nonslice from its nonunit Alexander polynomial. Every claim in the example follows without a general satellite determinant theorem.

For every path-connected topological space $X$ and $x_0\in X$, the Hurewicz map
$$h:\pi_1(X,x_0)\longrightarrow H_1(X;\mathbb Z)$$
is surjective and has kernel $[\pi_1(X,x_0),\pi_1(X,x_0)]$. Hence it induces a natural isomorphism
$$\pi_1(X,x_0)^{\mathrm{ab}}\cong H_1(X;\mathbb Z).$$
The proof is choice-free and requires no CW, separation, local path-connectivity or local simple-connectivity assumption.

Assume AC. Let $M$ be an $R$-oriented boundaryless $n$-manifold, with $R$ commutative unital; manifolds are Hausdorff and second countable here. Then cap with the compatible compact orientation classes gives isomorphisms
$$D_M:H_c^p(M;R)\xrightarrow{\sim}H_{n-p}(M;R)$$
for every integer $p$, including disconnected, noncompact and empty $M$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $R$ be a PID, $C$ a chain complex of free
$R$-modules, and $G$ an $R$-module. Then naturally
$$0\to\operatorname{Ext}^1_R(H_{n-1}C,G)\to H^n\operatorname{Hom}_R(C,G)\xrightarrow{\operatorname{ev}_n}\operatorname{Hom}_R(H_nC,G)\to0$$
is exact.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $M$ be a closed smooth
manifold ([[def-smooth-manifold]]). Then $M$ has the homotopy type of a finite
CW complex ([[def-cw-complex-with-closure-finiteness-and-weak-topology]]).

Let $X$ be a closed connected oriented smooth four-manifold. Its integral intersection lattice is the abelian group $L_X=H_2(X;\mathbb Z)/\operatorname{Tor}H_2(X;\mathbb Z)$ with the integer-valued symmetric bilinear pairing $Q_X(\bar x,\bar y)=\langle \operatorname{PD}^{-1}(x)\smile\operatorname{PD}^{-1}(y),[X]\rangle$. Here $\operatorname{Tor}$ is the subgroup of elements of finite order, $[X]\in H_4(X;\mathbb Z)$ is the orientation class, and $\operatorname{PD}:H^2(X;\mathbb Z)\to H_2(X;\mathbb Z)$ is the Poincaré duality isomorphism. The rank is $b_2(X)=\dim_{\mathbb Q}H_2(X;\mathbb Q)$. The lattice is positive definite when $Q_X(x,x)>0$ for every nonzero $x\in L_X$; it is unimodular when a Gram matrix in an integral basis has determinant $1$ or $-1$.

derivations.claim: By [F1] and [A1], $H_1(X;\mathbb Z)=0$, so the Ext term in [F3] is zero and evaluation identifies $H^2(X;\mathbb Z)$ with $\operatorname{Hom}(H_2(X;\mathbb Z),\mathbb Z)$. [given, F1, F3, A1, algebra]

By [F4] and [A1], $H_2(X;\mathbb Z)$ is finitely generated. Its quotient $L=H_2(X;\mathbb Z)/\operatorname{Tor}$ is therefore free of finite rank, and every homomorphism from $H_2$ to $\mathbb Z$ factors uniquely through $L$. Thus $\operatorname{Hom}(H_2,\mathbb Z)=\operatorname{Hom}(L,\mathbb Z)$. [F4, A1, algebra]

Under the isomorphism [F2], the map $L\to\operatorname{Hom}(L,\mathbb Z)$ sending $\bar x$ to $(\bar y\mapsto Q_X(\bar x,\bar y))$ is the composite of the inverse Poincaré-duality map $H_2\to H^2$ with the evaluation map of [F3]; [F5] identifies that composite with the intersection pairing. Both component maps are isomorphisms by steps 1.1–1.2 and [F2]. Hence the pairing map is an isomorphism. [F2, F3, F5, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎
