derivations.claim: **The actual BPST bundle and almost solution.** Fix $p\in X$ and oriented normal coordinates, with $g_{ij}=\delta_{ij}+O(r^2)$. In quaternionic coordinates the regular BPST potential is $I_\lambda=\operatorname{Im}(q\,d\bar q)/(\lambda^2+|q|^2)$. Write $q=rv$, $|v|=1$, and $\theta=v\,d\bar v$, so $d\theta=-\theta\wedge\theta$. Differentiation gives $F_{I_\lambda}=\lambda^2(\lambda^2+r^2)^{-2}\operatorname{Im}(dq\wedge d\bar q)$, which is self-dual in the oriented Euclidean metric. Its Euclidean norm square is $48\lambda^4/(\lambda^2+r^2)^4$, with integral $8\pi^2$, and its three curvature components at zero span $\mathfrak{su}(2)$. Gauge transformation by $v$ gives the singular potential $\lambda^2(\lambda^2+r^2)^{-1}\bar v\,dv$, bounded by $C\lambda^2/r^3$ when $r\ge\lambda$. Fix a small coordinate radius $\rho$, independent of $\lambda$, cut off this singular potential on $\rho<r<2\rho$ to zero, and use the regular frame inside. The fixed transition $v$ on their overlap constructs one smooth bundle $P'$ independent of $\lambda$ and smooth connections $A_\lambda$ which equal the product connection outside the chart. It is this singular potential that is cut off; a cutoff of a regular potential is not assumed to commute with a gauge transformation.

**Small error for the given curved metric.** The Hodge projection differs from its Euclidean value by $O(r^2)$ in the inner ball. Thus $E_\lambda=F_{A_\lambda}^-$ satisfies $|E_\lambda|\le C\lambda^2r^2/(\lambda^2+r^2)^2\le C\lambda^2/(\lambda^2+r^2)$ there, and $|E_\lambda|\le C_\rho\lambda^2$ on the fixed cutoff annulus. Direct radial integration gives $\|E_\lambda\|_2\le C\lambda^2\sqrt{1+|\log\lambda|}$ and $\|F_{A_\lambda}\|_2\le\Lambda$ uniformly. For the Green norm use [F2]'s kernel bound. If the pole has $|x|\le2\lambda$, split at radius $4\lambda$; the inner contribution is $O(\lambda^2)$ and the outer shells contribute $C\lambda^2\int_\lambda^{2\rho}dr/r$. If $s=|x|>2\lambda$, split into $|x-y|<s/2$, $|y|<2s$ outside that set, and $|y|\ge2s$. The first integral is at most $C(\lambda^2/s^2)s^2=C\lambda^2$, the second at most $Cs^{-2}\lambda^2\int_0^{2s}r^3/(\lambda^2+r^2)dr\le C\lambda^2$, and the third is bounded by the same logarithmic shell integral. A pole outside the coordinate region only improves the bound, and the fixed annulus contributes $O(\lambda^2)$. The non-singular kernel term is smaller; metric volumes are uniformly comparable. Consequently $\|E_\lambda\|_\sharp\le C\lambda^2(1+|\log\lambda|)$ and $\|E_\lambda\|_B\to0$ in the actual fixed metric.

**The charge of the constructed bundle.** The bundle $P'$ and its transition map in step 1.1 are fixed as $\lambda$ varies. Its Chern–Weil integral is consequently an integer independent of $\lambda$. On the fixed inner ball, the explicit Euclidean self-dual BPST integral tends to $-1$ in the convention $c_2=(8\pi^2)^{-1}\operatorname{tr}(F\wedge F)$. On the cutoff annulus its curvature is $O_\rho(\lambda^2)$, so its Chern integral tends to zero. The integral is metric independent. Hence $c_2(P')[X]=-1$ exactly. This computes the charge of the actual fixed bundle used by the contraction, not merely that of an abstract model.

**Uniform spectral gap with no hidden inverse assumption.** From [F2]'s Weitzenböck formula, scalar Sobolev applied to $|\xi|$ using Kato, and $\|E_\lambda\|_2\to0$, absorb $C\|E_\lambda\|_2\|\xi\|_4^2$ to get $\|\nabla_{A_\lambda}\xi\|_2^2\le C(\langle P_{A_\lambda}\xi,\xi\rangle+\|\xi\|_2^2)$. If no uniform positive gap existed as $\lambda\downarrow0$, take $\|\xi_n\|_2=1$ and $\|(d_{A_{\lambda_n}}^-)^*\xi_n\|_2\to0$. The displayed estimate and Kato give a uniform $L^4$ bound, so the $L^2$ mass in every radius-$r$ ball is at most $Cr^2$. In the global singular/product frame away from $p$, $A_{\lambda_n}\to0$ smoothly by step 1.1. Local $H^1$ bounds and Rellich therefore give a strongly locally $L^2$ convergent subsequence to an ordinary adjoint-valued anti-self-dual two-form $\xi$ with $d^*\xi=0$. The small-ball bound shows $\|\xi\|_2=1$, with no lost mass. Lower semicontinuity on each punctured compact set gives a finite ordinary $H^1$ norm off $p$, uniformly as the deleted radius tends to zero. Multiply by cutoffs vanishing near $p$: their error is bounded in $L^2$ by the $L^4$ norm of $\xi$ on a shrinking annulus times the bounded $L^4$ norm of the cutoff gradient, and tends to zero by absolute continuity. Thus $\xi$ extends in $H^1$ with $d^*\xi=0$ globally. Anti-self-duality then gives $d\xi=0$, so [F3] makes it harmonic, contrary to $b_-=0$ and $\|\xi\|_2=1$. Hence a fixed gap $c>0$ exists for all sufficiently small $\lambda$. This was proved before choosing the correction threshold depending on $c$.

**Smooth solutions and actual irreducibility.** Steps 2.1–3.1 satisfy every hypothesis of [F2] for small $\lambda$. It produces smooth self-dual $A_\lambda+a_\lambda$ on the same $P'$, with $\|a_\lambda\|_4\to0$. If arbitrarily small members were reducible, choose unit parallel adjoint sections $u_\lambda$. Pull them back to the scale-$\lambda$ unit ball in the regular frame, where $A_\lambda$ is exactly $I_1$; four-dimensional $L^4$ norms of one-forms are invariant under this scaling and the fixed metric is uniformly comparable. Thus $\|\nabla_{I_1}u_\lambda\|_4\le C\|a_\lambda\|_4\to0$. Since $|u_\lambda|=1$, their ordinary $W^{1,4}$ norms are bounded in that fixed smooth frame. Rellich in $H^1\to L^2$, followed by $\|u_i-u_j\|_4^4\le C\|u_i-u_j\|_2^2$, gives a strongly $L^4$ convergent subsequence. Its limit is an $I_1$-parallel unit section; the first-order equation with smooth coefficients bootstraps it to a smooth section. Commuting derivatives at zero makes its value commute with all three curvature values of $I_1$. Those span $\mathfrak{su}(2)$, whose common centralizer in its Lie algebra is zero, a contradiction. Therefore sufficiently small corrected members are irreducible.

**Comparison with the specified bundle.** Use [F5]'s finite smooth triangulation of $X$. An $SU(2)$ bundle is the unit sphere bundle of its defining quaternionic line, since $SU(2)$ acts freely and transitively on its unit vectors. It is trivial on the three-skeleton: the obstruction groups $\pi_0,\pi_1,\pi_2$ of $SU(2)=S^3$ vanish. On each oriented four-cell a three-skeleton trivialization has a boundary unit-vector map $S^3\to S^3$, with integer degree. These degrees form its four-cochain obstruction; changing a three-cell trivialization changes it by that cellular coboundary, by [F5]. Here is the general Chern identification: in the pulled-back trivial bundle over one characteristic four-disk, extend the boundary unit section as a vector-valued map and make it transverse to zero in the interior, retaining its boundary homotopy class. The boundary degree is the sum of its local zero degrees, by excising disjoint small zero-balls and the boundary homology relation. Those local degrees are precisely the relative pullback of the oriented Thom class. Thus this cellular cocycle represents the Euler class of the underlying complex-oriented real four-plane bundle, and equals $c_2$ by [F4]. This is a general relative-cell computation, not an inference from the BPST calibration. For two bundles, the obstruction to extending a three-skeleton isomorphism over a four-cell is the difference of these two degrees; pointwise multiplication of the two boundary $S^3$ maps adds their degrees, by [F5]. By [F6] and step 2.2, $P$ and $P'$ have the same degree-four class. Adjusting the isomorphism on the three-cells kills the difference cochain by its coboundary, and degree classification then extends it over every four-cell. Smooth it as an everywhere nonzero section of the quaternionic homomorphism bundle, using finite smooth charts and a partition of unity, and normalize its quaternionic norm. Uniform approximation preserves nonvanishing; unit quaternionic maps are determinant-one unitary isomorphisms. Transfer the smooth irreducible self-dual connection of step 4.1 through this actual smooth bundle isomorphism to $P$. This proves the full given-metric, given-bundle conclusion.

citations.quote: Let $X$ be a closed oriented Riemannian four-manifold and let $P\to X$ be a smooth principal $SU(2)$-bundle with $c_2(P)[X]=-1$. The Hodge star on two-forms is $*$, and $F_A^-=(F_A-*F_A)/2$ denotes the anti-self-dual projection of the curvature of a connection $A$. The equation used in this item is $F_A^-=0$, so the curvature is self-dual; this convention and the negative second Chern number are fixed together for the positive-definite orientation. The self-dual moduli set is the set of smooth connections satisfying $F_A^-=0$, modulo the action of smooth gauge transformations of $P$. At a solution, the deformation complex is $0\to\Omega^0(X;\operatorname{ad}P)\xrightarrow{d_A}\Omega^1(X;\operatorname{ad}P)\xrightarrow{d_A^-}\Omega^-(X;\operatorname{ad}P)\to0$, and its gauge-fixed operator is $D_A=d_A^*\oplus d_A^-$. For index calculations, $D_A$ is completed from the first Sobolev space of one-forms to the direct sum of the zeroth Sobolev spaces of zero-forms and anti-self-dual two-forms.

Assume full AC. Let $X$ be a closed simply connected oriented smooth Riemannian four-manifold with positive-definite intersection form, and $E$ a Hermitian rank-two bundle with fixed unit determinant and $c_2(E)[X]=-1$. Use the equation $F_A^-=0$ and the unbased $H^3/H^4$ configuration quotient. The actual smooth reducible solution orbits are finite. Sending such a solution to its pair of parallel eigenlines gives an injection into the unordered pairs $\{x,-x\}$ in $H^2(X;\mathbb Z)$ with $x^2[X]=1$. Distinct pairs arising in this way are orthogonal, so there are at most $b_2(X)$ reducible solution orbits.

At each such orbit there are invariant Coulomb-slice coordinates with effective circle stabilizer. The finite obstruction map is a smooth circle-equivariant map $\phi:\mathbb C^{3+p}\to\mathbb C^p$, with $\phi(0)=D\phi(0)=0$ and scalar circle action of the same nonzero weight on both spaces. Arbitrarily small $C^1(H^3,H^2)$, bounded $H^3$-valued, equivariant perturbations supported near that orbit can be chosen so that their zero set near it, before taking the circle quotient, is equivariantly diffeomorphic to a neighborhood of $0$ in $\mathbb C^3$. After quotient it is a cone on $\mathbb{CP}^2$, with smooth irreducible punctured part. The finitely many constructions may have disjoint supports.

Deleting a smaller cone neighborhood leaves a smooth boundary link diffeomorphic to $\mathbb{CP}^2$. An orientation of the surrounding regular moduli manifold induces one of its two orientations; the result does not assert a common sign for distinct links. This is a local preparation operation and does not assert a small-instanton end or a global compactification.

Assume full AC. Let $X$ be a closed simply connected oriented Riemannian four-manifold with positive-definite intersection form, and let $P\to X$ be an $SU(2)$-bundle with $c_2(P)[X]=-1$. Complete the connections in $H^3$ and the gauge transformations in $H^4$, and use the unbased irreducible configuration quotient. The curvature section $\Phi([A])=F_A^-$ takes values in its $H^2$ equation bundle. Choose an open subset $U$ covered by finitely many bounded Coulomb slice balls centered at smooth irreducible connections, and an open $V$ whose closure is contained in the union of strictly smaller closed balls in these charts, their images lying in $U$.

Allow smooth gauge-equivariant perturbation sections supported in $U$, whose slice representatives are smooth $H^3$-valued maps with finite uniform $H^3$ norm on the specified chart balls. Interpret them in the $H^2$ equation bundle by inclusion. Give this class the topology of the uniform $H^3$ section norm on those finitely many balls together with convergence of the section and its slice derivative $H^3\to H^2$ uniformly on compact subsets. The perturbations for which $\Phi+\sigma$ is transverse to zero at every zero in $\overline V$ form an open dense subset. Their zero sets in $V$ are smooth orientable five-manifolds, and the real determinant line of the gauge-fixed deformation family is orientable on the irreducible quotient. The based quotient may be used to pull back this orientation; it carries an additional $SO(3)$ framing fiber and is not the unbased five-dimensional moduli space.

Assume full AC. Let $X$ be a closed oriented Riemannian four-manifold, let $P$ be a fixed principal $SU(2)$-bundle with charge $k=-\langle c_2(P),[X]\rangle$, and let $(A_j)$ be smooth connections satisfying $F_{A_j}^-=0$ and $\sup_j\int_X|F_{A_j}|^2\,d\mathrm{vol}<\infty$. Then a subsequence, bundle isomorphisms, and a finite set $S\subset X$ exist such that the transported connections converge in local Sobolev gauge on compact subsets of $X\setminus S$ to a self-dual connection on a possibly lower-charge bundle of charge $k_\infty$. For each $p\in S$ there is a positive integer bubble charge $m_p$, and $k=k_\infty+\sum_{p\in S}m_p$. The limiting connection extends smoothly across every puncture after gauge transformation, and the compactified moduli space is obtained by adjoining the lower-charge limits together with the finite bubble points and their integer charge labels.

Assume full AC. Let $X$ be a closed connected simply connected oriented smooth Riemannian four-manifold with positive-definite intersection form, and fix a smooth $SU(2)$ bundle $P$ with $c_2(P)[X]=-1$. The unperturbed self-dual moduli space has a neighborhood of its ideal stratum consisting precisely of the flat connection and one charge-one point, and this neighborhood, including the ideal stratum, is diffeomorphic in its interior and homeomorphic up to that stratum to $X\times[0,\lambda_0)$. Its interior consists of irreducible regular solutions. The parameter on the second factor is a smooth positive concentration scale tending to zero at the ideal stratum. Every sufficiently concentrating solution occurs, and occurs once. In particular this is a complete end theorem, not merely existence of a five-parameter family. It does not assert that arbitrary perturbations preserve this end.

Assume full AC. Let $P$ be a smooth principal $SU(2)$-bundle over a connected closed Riemannian four-manifold $X$. Fix a smooth reference connection and use the corresponding finite-chart Sobolev norms. Let $\mathcal A^3$ be its affine $H^3$ space of connections, and let $\mathcal G^4$ be the group of $H^4$ sections of the bundle with fiber $SU(2)$ and conjugation transition maps. A connection is called irreducible when its stabilizer in this group is precisely the two constant central transformations. The irreducible locus is open. Its quotient $\mathcal B^*=\mathcal A^{3,*}/(\mathcal G^4/\{\pm1\})$ is a Hausdorff, second-countable smooth Hilbert manifold. At each irreducible $A$, a neighborhood is represented uniquely by a sufficiently small ball in $\ker(d_A^*:H^3(\Lambda^1\otimes\operatorname{ad}P)\to H^2(\operatorname{ad}P))$.

The corresponding quotient of $H^2(\Lambda^-\otimes\operatorname{ad}P)$ is a smooth Hilbert bundle over $\mathcal B^*$, with smooth curvature section $[A]\mapsto F_A^-$. Its slice linearization is $a\mapsto d_A^-a$. Fixing a point of $P$ above $x_0\in X$, quotienting instead by transformations with value $1$ there gives a principal $SO(3)$-bundle over $\mathcal B^*$. In local product coordinates the curvature section is its pullback. In particular its linearization has three additional kernel directions and the same cokernel; framing must not be identified with the unbased deformation problem.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $M,E,P$ have exactly the compact, boundaryless, scalar-positive-symbol and formal symmetry hypotheses of [[thm-elliptic-differential-operators-on-compact-vector-bundles-have-parametrices-and-regularity]], with $\operatorname{dom}P=H^2(M,E)$. Write $\mathcal H=\ker P$.

Then $\mathcal H$ is finite dimensional and consists of smooth sections, $\operatorname{ran}P=\mathcal H^\perp$ is closed in $L^2$, and
$$L^2(M,E)=\mathcal H\mathbin{\oplus^\perp}\operatorname{ran}P.$$
Let $\Pi$ be the orthogonal projection onto $\mathcal H$. There is a unique linear operator $G:L^2\to H^2\cap\mathcal H^\perp$ with
$$PG=I-\Pi\quad\hbox{on }L^2,\qquad GP=I-\Pi\quad\hbox{on }H^2,\qquad G\Pi=\Pi G=0.$$
It is bounded from $H^k$ to $H^{k+2}$ for every integer $k\ge0$, compact and selfadjoint on $L^2$, and preserves smooth sections. For all such $k$,
$$H^k=\mathcal H\oplus P(H^{k+2}),\qquad C^\infty(M,E)=\mathcal H\oplus P(C^\infty(M,E)),$$
where the second summands are the corresponding intersections with $\mathcal H^\perp$, and the decompositions are topological. The projection is smoothing: for every integer $r\ge0$, $\|\Pi f\|_{C^r}\le C_r\|f\|_2$. Consequently $G$ is a two-sided parametrix with finite-rank smoothing remainders. If additionally $(Pu,u)_2\ge0$ for smooth $u$, then $P$ and $G$ are nonnegative on their respective domains.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: **Prepare precisely the actual reducibles.** Apply [F2] to their finite set and choose disjoint bounded invariant slice neighborhoods. Its constructed smoothing section $\sigma_r$ is supported in their union and vanishes at the central reducible points. On smaller neighborhoods its zeros are equivariant smooth graphs over $\mathbb C^3$; the punctured quotients are smooth oriented five-manifolds, and cutting their graph-radius gives projective links. There are no additional reducible solutions inside these slice neighborhoods: the stabilizer of a nearby orbit is a subgroup of the center's circle by the local slice construction; a reducible orbit must therefore be fixed by that circle. On its fixed diagonal subspace the equivariant off-diagonal perturbation is zero. The diagonal equation is the abelian self-dual equation, whose only local slice solution is the center because its $H^1$ is zero. Outside these neighborhoods the equation remains unperturbed, so [F2] lists all remaining reducibles. The construction is bounded and smooth into $H^3$ in these finitely many slices.

**Compactness for this prepared equation and a genuine middle region.** The supports in step 1.1 are in bounded $H^3$ slice balls. For a zero in such a ball the equation $d_{A_i}^-a=-F_{A_i}^--(a\wedge a)^--\sigma_r(a)$ has bounded $H^3$ right side, since $H^3$ is an algebra and the section is uniformly $H^3$ bounded. Together with $d_{A_i}^*a=0$, the Green estimate [F5] bounds $a$ in $H^4$. Thus zeros there have compact $H^3$ closure, including along the edges of the support. Any sequence of zeros outside these balls is unperturbed, so [F4] supplies its smooth or ideal subsequence. The bounded balls cannot approach an ideal point: their curvature has a uniform $L^4$ bound from the $H^3$ bound, so its energy on a ball of volume tending to zero tends uniformly to zero by Holder. Therefore a sufficiently small whole ideal collar from [F4] misses all the supports. The prepared equation is literally unperturbed there, retaining its entire regular end. Delete a smaller portion of that collar and smaller reducible cone neighborhoods. The remaining zero set is compact and irreducible, by the two sequence arguments just given. Cover this compact set by finitely many bounded irreducible Coulomb-slice collars, avoiding the protected smaller end and cone neighborhoods, and choose larger/smaller radii as in [F3].

**Relative middle transversality with all ends preserved.** Apply the finite-dimensional cokernel-direction and Sard proof of [F3] to $\Phi+\sigma_r$ on these middle collars, multiplying its new directions by bumps supported there. The fixed $\sigma_r$ is allowed in those charts: transition gauges on bounded chart sets have uniform $H^4$ bounds, and its original finite smooth target vectors and coordinate cutoffs consequently have uniformly bounded $H^3$ representatives. The derivative is a compact perturbation of the original Fredholm slice derivative, so its index remains five. The actual compact zero-container in [F3] and its positive-minimum argument exclude all new middle zeros outside the chosen smaller covering neighborhoods when the finite parameters are small. Around the protected cone and ideal collars the equation and its regularity remain exactly as in steps 1.1–2.1; on the compact transition overlaps, openness of surjectivity preserves their regularity. Thus a sufficiently small regular finite parameter makes every irreducible zero transverse. The same proof gives openness and density for all further allowed small middle sections. Both perturbations are zero outside the finite original and middle slice neighborhoods. For every resulting zero sequence in their union the same bounded-section $H^4$ estimate gives a converging $H^3$ subsequence; outside their union [F4] applies unchanged. This proves compactness of the full ideal completion and excludes any other ends, without applying an unperturbed compactness theorem to a nonzero perturbation.

**The actual smooth cut bordism.** The determinant line orients the transverse irreducible zero set by [F3], and its compact-derivative homotopy includes the fixed reducible preparation. At the ideal stratum, [F4]'s actual center-scale diffeomorphism and homeomorphic ideal extension provide a smooth collar $X\times[0,\lambda_0)$. At each reducible, [F2]'s graph-radius coordinate gives the smooth punctured cone collar $(0,\delta)\times\mathbb{CP}^2$. Delete its part of radius less than a smaller positive number. These finitely many collars are disjoint from each other and from the ideal collar. Step 3.1 makes the remaining interior compact up to the displayed collars, so the cut completion is a compact smooth five-manifold with exactly those boundary components. The induced boundary orientation on each projective link is its complex orientation or its negative. On the unique component meeting the connected ideal boundary choose the determinant orientation's global sign so this boundary orientation agrees with the given orientation of $X$; arbitrary other components cause no additional boundary strata. The number of links is exactly the number of actual reducibles, bounded by [F2]. This proves the compatible perturbation, compactified-strata and smooth cut-bordism assertions.

Its integral intersection lattice is the abelian group $L_X=H_2(X;\mathbb Z)/\operatorname{Tor}H_2(X;\mathbb Z)$ with the integer-valued symmetric bilinear pairing $Q_X(\bar x,\bar y)=\langle \operatorname{PD}^{-1}(x)\smile\operatorname{PD}^{-1}(y),[X]\rangle$. Here $\operatorname{Tor}$ is the subgroup of elements of finite order, $[X]\in H_4(X;\mathbb Z)$ is the orientation class, and $\operatorname{PD}:H^2(X;\mathbb Z)\to H_2(X;\mathbb Z)$ is the Poincaré duality isomorphism. The rank is $b_2(X)=\dim_{\mathbb Q}H_2(X;\mathbb Q)$. The lattice is positive definite when $Q_X(x,x)>0$ for every nonzero $x\in L_X$; it is unimodular when a Gram matrix in an integral basis has determinant $1$ or $-1$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X$ be a closed connected oriented smooth four-manifold with $\pi_1(X)=0$. Its integral intersection lattice on $H_2(X;\mathbb Z)/\operatorname{Tor}$ is a finite-rank free abelian group and its intersection pairing is unimodular.

Assume full AC. Let $X$ be a closed simply connected oriented smooth Riemannian four-manifold with positive-definite intersection form, and let $P\to X$ be an $SU(2)$ bundle with $c_2(P)[X]=-1$. Use the unbased $H^3/H^4$ quotient and the determinant-line orientation. There is a compatible perturbation procedure as follows: prepare the finitely many reducible circle-slice obstruction maps by arbitrarily small equivariant finite-rank smoothing perturbations, and make a further generic bounded smoothing perturbation on finitely many bounded irreducible slice collars in a middle region. The procedure is fixed near the prepared reducibles and vanishes on the entire small-instanton end. The further choices may be made arbitrarily small; they form a relatively open dense transverse class on the prescribed smaller middle collars.

The resulting regular irreducible zero set is an oriented five-manifold. Its ideal completion is compact, has one small-instanton boundary stratum identified with $X$, and has exactly the finitely many prepared reducible cone points, with no other strata. A neighborhood of each cone point is a cone on $\mathbb{CP}^2$. Delete smaller open cone neighborhoods and add the small-instanton boundary. The result is a smooth compact oriented five-manifold with boundary $X$ and one projective-plane link for each actual reducible orbit, with their induced orientations. Each projective link has one of the two complex-orientation signs; no common sign or numerical spectral-flow computation is asserted. The orientation on the component with the small-instanton end can be chosen so that this boundary is $X$ with its given orientation. The number of projective links is at most $b_2(X)$.

Assume AC. Let $Y$ be a compact oriented Hausdorff topological five-manifold with supplied boundary collar, and let $X=\partial Y$ have its boundary orientation. Supply a based homomorphism $\psi:\pi_1Y\to G$ on each component, where $G$ is an arbitrary discrete group, with the standard unitary regular coefficient systems. Then
$$\operatorname{sign}^{(2)}_G(X,\psi|_X)=0,\qquad \operatorname{sign}(X)=0.$$
In particular, when $X=X_1\sqcup(-X_0)$, the ordinary and $L^2$ signatures of these closed oriented four-manifolds agree across this actual coefficient-extending TOP bordism. The equality is unchanged under embedding the target group in a larger group. This theorem asserts bordism invariance and does not assert existence of a bordism between arbitrary closed coefficient manifolds.

Assume AC. For every $N\geq0$ identify
$\mathbb{CP}^N=\operatorname{Gr}_1(\mathbb C^{N+1})$, the space of complex
lines in $\mathbb C^{N+1}$, and let $\gamma$ be the tautological complex line
with $x=e(\gamma_{\mathbb R})\in H^2(\mathbb{CP}^N;\mathbb Z)$ its Euler class
in the complex orientation. Then, as a graded ring,
$$H^*(\mathbb{CP}^N;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z[x]/(x^{N+1}),$$
the class $x$ generating each even degree and the odd groups vanishing; for
$0\leq m\leq N$ the standard inclusion
$\mathbb{CP}^m\hookrightarrow\mathbb{CP}^N$, induced by

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if

derivations.claim: **An actual bordism rather than an assumed end.** If $b=0$ the free intersection group has rank zero and its empty integral basis gives the claim. Suppose $b>0$. A charge-minus-one bundle exists: glue a trivial bundle on a ball to the trivial bundle on its complement by the unit-quaternion clutching function on the common three-sphere, with the sign used by the explicit BPST construction in the Taubes proof. Its smooth model connection has $c_2[X]=-1$, by the displayed curvature integral $8\pi^2$ and the fixed sign convention. Apply [F2] on this actual bundle. It gives a compact oriented smooth five-manifold $W$ whose full boundary is $X$ together with $n$ oriented projective-plane links, where $n$ is the actual number of reducible solution orbits. The determinant orientation can be chosen so the $X$ boundary has its given orientation. Closed components of $W$ have empty boundary and do not affect this assertion.

**The signed boundary inequality forces enough reducibles.** Positive definiteness makes $\operatorname{sign}(X)=b$. Each projective link has signature $\varepsilon_i\in\{1,-1\}$ by [F4]. Additivity of the intersection form under finite disjoint union and [F3] give $0=b+\sum_{i=1}^n\varepsilon_i$, hence $b\le n$. The actual reducible classification in [F2] gives $n\le b$, since its $n$ distinct unordered norm-one pairs are mutually orthogonal and nonzero. Thus $n=b$ (and the boundary equation also forces every $\varepsilon_i=-1$ for this chosen orientation). No numerical spectral-flow label or prior common sign was assumed.

**The integral basis, not merely a real diagonalization.** Choose one representative $x_i$ from each of these $b$ unordered norm-one pairs in cohomology. They satisfy $x_i\cdot x_j=\delta_{ij}$ by [F2]. Let $L=H^2(X;\mathbb Z)/\operatorname{Tor}$. They are a real basis of $L\otimes\mathbb R$ because they are $b$ nonzero orthogonal vectors. For every $y\in L$, its real-basis expansion is $y=\sum_i(y\cdot x_i)x_i$. Every coefficient is an integer by integrality of [F1], so $y$ belongs to their integral span. Thus these vectors are an integral basis of the full lattice, not a proper finite-index sublattice. Integral Poincare duality identifies this lattice with the homological intersection lattice in [F1]. Transporting this basis gives the asserted identity matrix on $H_2(X;\mathbb Z)/\operatorname{Tor}$. The rank-zero case was already covered, and this proves the original diagonalization conclusion.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in the standard oriented $3$-sphere, choose its compact exterior $E_K$ with boundary torus $T_K$, and let $\mu$ and $\lambda$ be its positive meridian and preferred longitude. The exterior homology theorem gives $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z[\mu]$. Let $\phi:\pi_1(E_K)\to\mathbb Z$ be the composite of abelianization with the homomorphism $[\mu]\mapsto1$. For an integer $q\ge2$, let $\phi_q$ be the composite $\pi_1(E_K)\xrightarrow{\phi}\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z/q\mathbb Z$, and let $p_q:E_q\to E_K$ be the connected cover classified by $\ker\phi_q$. On $T_K$, the homomorphism sends $[\mu]\mapsto1$ and $[\lambda]\mapsto0$, so the preimage of $T_K$ is a connected torus cover whose fundamental group corresponds to $\langle\mu^q,\lambda\rangle$. Let $\widetilde\mu$ be the closed lift of $\mu^q$. Attach a solid torus to $E_q$ with its meridian identified with $\widetilde\mu$; the resulting oriented closed $3$-manifold is the $q$-fold cyclic branched cover $\Sigma_q(K)$. In tubular coordinates near $K$, the extended map to $S^3$ has local form $(s,w)\mapsto(s,w^q)$, and the deck group $\mathbb Z/q\mathbb Z$ acts by $w\mapsto e^{2\pi i/q}w$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $W$ be a compact connected oriented smooth four-manifold whose boundary $M$ is a rational homology three-sphere, meaning $H_*(M;\mathbb Q)\cong H_*(S^3;\mathbb Q)$. The boundary intersection lattice has underlying group $L_W=H_2(W;\mathbb Z)/\operatorname{Tor}H_2(W;\mathbb Z)$. Poincaré–Lefschetz duality identifies each $x\in H_2(W;\mathbb Z)$ with a class $\alpha_x\in H^2(W,M;\mathbb Z)$. Define $Q_W(\bar x,\bar y)=\langle\alpha_x\smile\alpha_y,[W,M]\rangle$, where $\smile$ is the relative cup product and $[W,M]\in H_4(W,M;\mathbb Z)$ is the relative orientation class; equivalently, this is the signed intersection number of interior two-cycle representatives. Its rank is $b_2(W)=\dim_{\mathbb Q}H_2(W;\mathbb Q)$. A nondegenerate positive-definite $Q_W$ is called a positive-definite filling lattice. The boundary identification in the statement permits the smooth oriented gluing $X=W\cup_M(-B_D)$; collars [F7] give a smooth closed oriented four-manifold. [given, F1, F2, F3, F7, A2, construct]

Applying [F5] to the collar-thickened union gives $\pi_1(X)=\pi_1(W)*_{\pi_1(M)}\pi_1(B_D)$. Since $\pi_1(W)=1$, this pushout is the quotient of $\pi_1(B_D)$ by the normal closure of the image of $\pi_1(M)$. That normal closure is all of $\pi_1(B_D)$ by [A1], so $\pi_1(X)=1$. [given, F5, A1, algebra]

In the rational Mayer–Vietoris sequence of [F6], $H_2(M;\mathbb Q)=H_1(M;\mathbb Q)=0$ and $H_i(B_D;\mathbb Q)=0$ for $i>0$ by [F1]. Thus inclusion induces an isomorphism $H_2(W;\mathbb Q)\cong H_2(X;\mathbb Q)$, so $b_2(X)=b_2(W)$. By [F8], $H_2(W;\mathbb Z)\otimes\mathbb Q\cong H_2(W;\mathbb Q)$, and the kernel of the integral-to-rational map is exactly the torsion subgroup. If an integral class maps to torsion in $H_2(X;\mathbb Z)$, its rational image vanishes; the isomorphism forces its rational class in $W$ to vanish, so it was torsion. Therefore the induced map on torsion-free quotients is injective and has full rank. [given, F1, F6, F8, A2, algebra]

Represent classes of $W$ by two-cycles in its interior and make two representatives transverse. Their signed intersection points are unchanged in the glued manifold, so the map of step 2.1 preserves the intersection form. Its rational extension is an isomorphism and transports the positive-definite form of $W$ to $X$; hence $Q_X$ is positive definite. [F4, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

citations.quote: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot such that its double branched cover $M=\Sigma_2(K)$ is a rational homology sphere. Let $D\subset B^4$ be a smooth proper embedded disk with boundary $K$, and let $B_D$ be the connected double cover of $B^4$ branched over $D$. Let $W$ be a compact connected smooth simply connected oriented four-manifold with boundary identified orientation-compatibly with $M$, and assume its boundary intersection form is positive definite. Assume also that the image of $\pi_1(M)\to\pi_1(B_D)$ normally generates $\pi_1(B_D)$, meaning its normal closure is the whole group. Then the oriented gluing $X=W\cup_M(-B_D)$ is a closed smooth simply connected positive-definite four-manifold, and inclusion induces an isometric full-rank embedding $Q_W\hookrightarrow Q_X$ of integral intersection lattices with $b_2(X)=b_2(W)$.

Assume full AC. Let $X$ be a compact connected smooth simply connected oriented four-manifold. If its integral intersection form is positive definite, then there is an integral basis of $H_2(X;\mathbb Z)/\operatorname{Tor}$ in which the form is the identity matrix. Equivalently, the integral intersection lattice is isometric to the standard diagonal lattice $\mathbb Z^{b_2(X)}$ with dot product.

derivations.claim: Suppose a smooth slice disk $D$ existed. The universal assumption [A1] supplies the normal-generation hypothesis for this actual $D$, so the proved conditional gluing implication [F1] gives a closed smooth simply connected positive-definite manifold $X$ and an isometric full-rank embedding $Q_W\hookrightarrow Q_X$. Its rank is $n$ by the same gluing result. This uses the explicit hypothesis and does not infer normal generation from rational homology.

By [F2], $Q_X$ is isometric to $\mathbb Z^n$ with its dot product. Composing that isometry with the embedding in step 1.1 contradicts the assumed absence of an isometric full-rank embedding $Q_W\hookrightarrow\mathbb Z^n$. Thus no smooth slice disk exists, proving precisely the conditional nonsliceness conclusion. No larger lower bound on the smooth four-ball genus is deduced.

citations.quote: Assume countable choice as required by the chosen tubular-neighborhood and peripheral-system data. Let K be a smooth oriented knot with compact exterior E_K, positive meridian mu_K, and preferred longitude lambda_K on the boundary torus. The zero-framed surgery manifold M(K) is the closed oriented 3-manifold obtained by gluing D²×S¹ to E_K so that the meridian boundary circle of D²×{1} is identified with lambda_K and the core {0}×S¹ is identified with mu_K. The orientation extends the orientation of E_K across the filling. Thus the filling slope is the preferred zero-linking longitude; the definition asserts no 4-manifold bounded by M(K).

Let $X$ be a four-dimensional manifold with boundary and let $W$ be a compact surface with boundary. An embedding $e:(W,\partial W)\to(X,\partial X)$ is proper when $e^{-1}(\partial X)=\partial W$. It is locally flat at an interior point of $W$ when there are neighborhoods of the point and its image and a homeomorphism of pairs from those neighborhoods to $(\mathbb R^4,\mathbb R^2)$, with the standard linear plane $\mathbb R^2\subset\mathbb R^4$. It is locally flat at a boundary point when there are such neighborhoods and a homeomorphism of pairs to $(\mathbb R^4_+,\mathbb R^2_+)$, where $\mathbb R^4_+=\{x_4\geq0\}$ and $\mathbb R^2_+=\{x_2=x_3=0,\ x_4\geq0\}$; the line $\partial\mathbb R^2_+$ lies in $\partial\mathbb R^4_+$. A collar of a boundary circle of $W$ is an embedding of that circle times $[0,\varepsilon)$ into $W$ that is the identity on the circle at parameter $0$; a concordance collar is required to agree with the corresponding product collar of the ambient end. A smooth proper surface has the analogous smooth charts and collars, which are also topological locally flat charts.

Let $\mathcal L$ be one local system on $X$.

1. If $Z\subseteq A\subseteq X$ and $\overline Z\subseteq\operatorname{int}_X(A)$, inclusion induces excision isomorphisms in both local homology and local cohomology between $(X\setminus Z,A\setminus Z)$ and $(X,A)$, using the restrictions of $\mathcal L$.
2. For an open cover $X=U\cup V$, there are natural exact sequences
   $$\cdots\to H_n(U\cap V;\mathcal L)\to H_n(U;\mathcal L)\oplus H_n(V;\mathcal L)\to H_n(X;\mathcal L)\to\cdots$$
   and
   $$\cdots\to H^n(X;\mathcal L)\to H^n(U;\mathcal L)\oplus H^n(V;\mathcal L)\to H^n(U\cap V;\mathcal L)\to\cdots,$$
   where all systems are restrictions and the middle difference map in cohomology is $u|_{U\cap V}-v|_{U\cap V}$.

The same conclusions hold for the standard excisive-cover condition after replacing the cover by interiors. A local system given only on a subspace is not silently assumed to extend to $X$.

Let $X=U\cup V$, where $U$ and $V$ are open path-connected subsets of $X$, let $U\cap V$ be path-connected, and fix $x_0\in U\cap V$. For the inclusion-induced maps in the diagram

$$\pi_1(U,x_0)\longleftarrow\pi_1(U\cap V,x_0)\longrightarrow\pi_1(V,x_0),$$

the group $\pi_1(X,x_0)$, together with the two inclusion-induced homomorphisms, is a pushout ([[def-pushout-of-group-homomorphisms]]). Equivalently, the canonical homomorphism from any pushout $P$ of the displayed diagram to $\pi_1(X,x_0)$ is an isomorphism. No injectivity of either map from the overlap group is assumed.

derivations.claim: Put $E=\overline{W\setminus N}$, $C=A\times S^1$, and $E_i=E\cap S_i^3$, $N_i=N\cap S_i^3$, $C_i=C\cap S_i^3$. The supplied product identifies $N$ with $S^1\times I\times D^2$, $N_i$ with $S^1\times\{i\}\times D^2$, $C$ with $S^1\times I\times S^1$, and $C_i$ with its endpoint torus. Attach $F=D^2\times S^1\times I$ along $C$, identifying its disk-boundary circle with the annulus longitude and its other circle with the normal meridian. Each endpoint boundary is then $E_i$ filled by $F_i=D^2\times S^1\times\{i\}$ along the preferred longitude, precisely $M(K_i)$ by [F1]. The common annular-side collar gives a manifold after gluing, with the same smooth or topological category as the supplied data; in the smooth case round the product corners. This constructs $V=E\cup_C F$ with the prescribed oriented ends.

Here is the relative chain comparison in every degree. Thicken the pieces slightly along their supplied common collars to make excisive covers, using the same thickening at the ends; the thickenings retract onto the indicated pieces and intersections as pairs. For either decomposition $X=P\cup_C Q$ with corresponding endpoint $X_i=P_i\cup_{C_i}Q_i$, the small-chain sequence underlying [F3], quotiented by the endpoint sequence, is degreewise exact: $0\to C_*(C,C_i;R)\to C_*(P,P_i;R)\oplus C_*(Q,Q_i;R)\to C_*^{\mathrm{small}}(X,X_i;R)\to0$, with maps $c\mapsto(c,-c)$ and $(p,q)\mapsto p+q$. Exactness follows simplex by simplex, and subdivision and its prism preserve the endpoint chains, so the last complex computes $H_*(X,X_i;R)$. Its connecting map sends a relative cycle $p+q$ to the class of $\partial p=-\partial q$ in the intersection quotient. Thus it supplies the relative exact sequence in all degrees, including degrees zero and one, rather than only a comparison of absolute ranks.

The endpoint inclusions $N_i\to N$ and $C_i\to C$ are deformation retractions up to inverse inclusion, by linearly contracting the $I$ coordinate to $i$. Their relative homology groups therefore vanish in every degree. Apply step 2.1 to $(W,S_i^3)=(E,E_i)\cup(N,N_i)$: the exact sequence gives $H_k(E,E_i;R)\cong H_k(W,S_i^3;R)$ for every $k$. The latter groups vanish because $S_i^3\to W$ induces homology isomorphisms in every degree, as follows directly from the long exact sequence of this pair. Next $F_i\to F$ is also a product deformation retraction. Applying the same exact sequence to $(V,M(K_i))=(E,E_i)\cup(F,F_i)$ gives $H_k(V,M(K_i);R)\cong H_k(E,E_i;R)=0$ for every $k$. The pair sequence now proves that each $M(K_i)\to V$ is an $R$-homology isomorphism, including in degree zero and the top degrees.

Suppose finally that $\pi_1(W)=1$. The exterior $E$ is connected: $W$ is connected, $N$ and its side $C$ are connected, and any other component of the manifold $E$ would be a component of $W$ disjoint from the gluing side. Choose basepoint paths in $C$ and write $\ell,m$ for its annulus and meridian circles. The map $\pi_1(C)\to\pi_1(N)$ is surjective with kernel normally generated by $m$. The pushout [F4] consequently identifies $\pi_1(W)$ with $\pi_1(E)/\langle\!\langle m\rangle\!\rangle$; this follows also directly by eliminating the generator $\ell$ of the second factor in its amalgamated presentation. Thus $m$ normally generates $\pi_1(E)$. For the second gluing, $\pi_1(C)\to\pi_1(F)$ is surjective with kernel generated by $\ell$, so the same elimination gives $\pi_1(V)=\pi_1(E)/\langle\!\langle\ell\rangle\!\rangle$. The image of $m$ still normally generates this quotient and lies in each endpoint knot-exterior group, hence in its zero-surgery group image. This proves the stated endpoint normal-generation conclusion. The proof uses the normal neighborhood already assumed in the Statement and makes no assertion that local flatness alone constructs it.

citations.quote: Let knots be smooth oriented knots in the standard oriented S³ and let I=[0,1]. Let C_sm be their smooth concordance classes, where equivalence is witnessed by a smooth proper annulus in S³×I. Let C_top be their locally flat topological concordance classes in that product. Let C_ex be their exotic-smooth concordance classes: equivalence is witnessed by a smooth proper annulus in a compact smooth oriented 4-manifold W together with an orientation-preserving homeomorphism of pairs (W,∂W)≅(S³×I,S³×{0,1}) matching the endpoint knots. For a nonzero integer n set R_n=Z[1/|n|]. Let C^{1/n} be the classes under equivalence witnessed by a smooth proper annulus in a compact smooth oriented 4-manifold W with boundary the two standard endpoint 3-spheres such that each boundary inclusion induces an isomorphism H_i(S³;R_n)→H_i(W;R_n) for every i. A knot is pseudo-slice if it bounds a smooth proper disk in a compact smooth oriented 4-manifold homeomorphic to B⁴, with its oriented boundary identified with the standard oriented S³. A knot is Z[1/|n|]-slice if it bounds a smooth proper disk in a compact smooth oriented 4-manifold B with its oriented boundary identified with the standard oriented S³ and with H_i(B;R_n)≅H_i(B⁴;R_n) for every i; such a B is an R_n-homology 4-ball. These are sets of equivalence classes; this definition alone asserts no group structure.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. For every smooth oriented knot $K\subset S^3$, let $B^4=\{x\in\mathbb R^4:\lVert x\rVert^2\le1\}$ with boundary $S^3$. The oriented connected sum $K\#K^\dagger$ bounds a smooth properly embedded disk $D\subset B^4$ for which the squared radial function $\rho(x)=\lVert x\rVert^2$ restricts to a Morse function on the interior of $D$ with all critical points of index $0$ or $1$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. On oriented ambient-isotopy classes of smooth knots in $S^3$, the connected-sum operation is associative and commutative, and the standard unknot is a two-sided identity. Here “commutative monoid” means a set with an associative binary operation, a two-sided identity, and equality after interchanging the two inputs.

Fix a coordinate orientation-reversing reflection $r:S^3\to S^3$ for the mirror convention. Let $K$ and $J$ be smooth oriented knots in the standard oriented three-sphere. A connected-sum datum consists of one smoothly embedded closed three-ball around a short subarc of $K$ and one around a short subarc of $J$, each meeting its knot in a single trivial properly embedded arc, together with the fixed standard orientation-reversing boundary identification of the two standard oriented ball boundaries that joins the oriented arcs into one circle. Choose this standard map once in the standard two-ball model so that it commutes with $r$ and an orientation-preserving half-turn interchanging the two balls preserves the joining convention. Here a trivial arc is an embedded interval in a ball that is carried by an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism of ball-arc pairs to a straight diameter. Remove the interiors of the two balls and glue the remaining boundary spheres using this fixed identification; the resulting oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere is a connected sum of $K$ and $J$, denoted $K\#J$ for the specified datum.

The **standard unknot** is the oriented unit circle in a fixed coordinate two-plane of $S^3\subset\mathbb R^4$. A knot is **nontrivial** if it is not ambient isotopic through orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms of $S^3$ to the standard unknot. A nontrivial knot is **prime** if it has no connected-sum presentation whose two summand knots are both nontrivial.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Specialize the TOP/exotic external assertion [F5] at each finite list of knot representatives and witnessing annuli actually used. For TOP these lie in the standard product; for exotic concordance the supplied boundary-marked homeomorphism to that product is part of the input code. The finite chart and pair-chart extraction in [F6] uses compactness, not a choice of an atlas for a countable family. Inside $L[r]$ use the ordinary CDR group operation, retain the actual output annulus and marked product homeomorphism, and export their compact forward/inverse and collar certificates. This proves the required finite compatibility and transitivity instances in $V$. Since each instance starts with its own given finite data, no simultaneous choice of representatives or witnesses for all classes is made. The quotient group operations and laws follow by universal quantification over these instances; the original $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ hypothesis is therefore respected, rather than inferred from the unqualified source assertion. The localized category is handled directly by steps2.1–2.2, with no TOP normal theorem needed.

The supplied connected-sum theorem gives associativity, commutativity and the unknot identity at the level of oriented knot types. The retained standard smooth boundary-sum construction on witnessing annuli gives concordance compatibility in the standard smooth product; the TOP/exotic compatibility is the external input [F5], and the localized ambient verification is given in steps2.1–2.2 below. The knot-type isotopies themselves are admissible annuli in every category.
The reverse-mirror construction in [F2] supplies an inverse annulus in the standard 4-ball, hence in the standard product, and so it is admissible in all four categories.

The external input [F5] supplies the TOP and exotic ambient gluing/compatibility assertions at exactly the definitions in [F1]. For the localized smooth category, transitivity is stacking along the marked $S^3$: Mayer–Vietoris and the two boundary homology isomorphisms give another $R_n$-homology $S^3\times I$. Reflection gives symmetry and a product gives reflexivity, all with their smooth annulus collars.

For localized connected sum choose a smooth product neighborhood $D^3\times I$ of a proper spanning arc inside each witnessing annulus, with the annulus strip in its standard local position, and remove its interior. If $Q$ is the remaining ambient piece, excision gives $H_j(W,Q;R_n)=R_n$ only for $j=3$. The map $H_3(W;R_n)\to H_3(W,Q;R_n)$ is an isomorphism: the boundary fundamental class meets the spanning arc once. The pair sequence therefore makes $Q$ an $R_n$-homology ball. Glue the two such complements on $S^2\times I$, joining the annulus strips. Mayer–Vietoris gives $R_n$ in degrees0 and3 and zero in other positive degrees; the endpoint connected-sum spheres give the degree3 generator, so each end inclusion is a homology isomorphism. The resulting smooth annulus witnesses connected-sum compatibility in the original localized category. These calculations use no homeomorphism-to-product assertion.

Thus connected sum is well defined in every category: the retained standard smooth construction handles $\mathcal C_{\mathrm{sm}}$, [F5] handles TOP/exotic, and step2.2 handles the localized case. The oriented knot connected-sum monoid [F3] descends to each quotient, giving associativity, commutativity and the unknot identity. The ribbon inverse in [F2], admissible in all four ambients, supplies the stated reverse-mirror inverse. All ambient and coefficient conditions are those of [F1].

Its winding number w(P) is its algebraic intersection with an oriented meridional disk, equivalently the coefficient of the core in [P]∈H₁(V;Z). For a smooth oriented knot K in S³, let e_K:V→S³ be a zero-framed tubular embedding carrying the core to K and carrying the meridian and product longitude to the positive meridian and preferred longitude of K. The satellite knot P(K) is e_K(P).

When concordance preservation has been established, the formula [K]↦[P(K)] defines a set map on each of C_sm, C_top, C_ex and C^{1/n}. The solid-torus meridian is strong winding number ±1 for P if, after V is embedded as the standard unknotted solid torus and P(U) denotes the resulting closure, that meridian normally generates π₁(S³\P(U)). Normal generation means that the smallest normal subgroup containing the element is the whole group. Strong winding number ±1 is a separate condition from ordinary winding number ±1. No additivity or homomorphism property is part of this definition.

Let $V=S^1\times D^2$ be the standard oriented solid torus, with oriented core $S^1\times\{0\}$. A **pattern** is a smooth oriented knot $P$ contained in the interior of $V$, together with a chosen closed tubular neighbourhood $N(P)$ contained in the interior of $V$. Its **winding number** $w(P)$ is the integer by which the homology class $[P]$ maps to $H_1(V;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$ under the isomorphism that sends the oriented core to $1$. The **pattern exterior** is $X_P=V\setminus\operatorname{int}N(P)$; its **outer torus** is $\partial V$ and its **inner torus** is $\partial N(P)$. A **companion** is a smooth oriented knot $K\subset S^3$ with a specified orientation-preserving tubular embedding $e:V\to S^3$ that sends the core to $K$ and identifies the solid-torus meridian and product longitude with the positive meridian and preferred longitude of $K$. The **satellite knot** $P(K)$ is $e(P)$, with chosen exterior $E_{P(K)}=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}e(N(P))$; the image $e(\partial V)$ is its **companion torus**. The outer torus is **incompressible** when it bounds no properly embedded disk in $X_P$ with essential boundary on $\partial V$. It is **product-parallel** to the inner torus when $X_P$ is a product $T^2\times[0,1]$ with those tori as its ends. This definition alone asserts neither incompressibility nor essentiality of the companion torus.

Fix a coordinate orientation-reversing reflection $r:S^3\to S^3$ for the mirror convention. Let $K$ and $J$ be smooth oriented knots in the standard oriented three-sphere. A connected-sum datum consists of one smoothly embedded closed three-ball around a short subarc of $K$ and one around a short subarc of $J$, each meeting its knot in a single trivial properly embedded arc, together with the fixed standard orientation-reversing boundary identification of the two standard oriented ball boundaries that joins the oriented arcs into one circle. Choose this standard map once in the standard two-ball model so that it commutes with $r$ and an orientation-preserving half-turn interchanging the two balls preserves the joining convention. Remove the interiors of the two balls and glue the remaining boundary spheres using this fixed identification; the resulting oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere is a connected sum of $K$ and $J$, denoted $K\#J$ for the specified datum.

A knot is **nontrivial** if it is not ambient isotopic through orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms of $S^3$ to the standard unknot. A nontrivial knot is **prime** if it has no connected-sum presentation whose two summand knots are both nontrivial.
Let $0<r<R$ and $n\ge 1$. Then there exists a smooth function $\rho:\mathbb R^n\to [0,1]$ such that $\rho=1$ on $\overline B_r(0)$ and $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)\subseteq B_R(0)$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be
$C^1$, and let $a\in U$.  If $Df(a)$ is invertible, then there are open sets
$V,W\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $a\in V\subseteq U$ and $f(a)\in W$ such that

derivations.claim: A transverse meridional disk exists for every smooth pattern, without a selection axiom. Parametrize $P$ by its supplied circle embedding and compose with the angular projection of the solid torus to obtain a smooth circle map $f$. Its angular derivative is a continuous real function on the parameter circle. For $0<\delta<1/2$, uniform continuity allows a partition into finitely many equal short intervals such that on any interval meeting the zero set of $f'$ one has $|f'|<\delta$. Make the intervals short enough to lift the map to real angular coordinates there. The images of these intervals have total arc length at most $\delta$, by integrating this derivative bound over intervals of total length at most one. Those finitely many image arcs cannot cover the target circle of length one: cutting at their finitely many endpoints and adding the lengths proves this finite covering inequality directly. Choose an angle outside them. Every preimage is regular, so its meridional disk is transverse; the case of empty preimage is allowed. Only one angle and finitely many intervals are selected. The specified transverse disk in the Statement may be any such disk.

Represent $K\#J$ by concatenating long representatives of $K$ and $J$, each constant in its endpoint product collars, and then closing by the fixed trivial outside arc. Use their zero-framed tubular products, glued by the identity on the two normal disk coordinates. This is the zero-framed product of the connected sum: a longitude and the core have linking zero on each of the two separated summand portions, their connecting parallel arcs are untwisted, and cross linking vanishes because those portions lie in disjoint balls. Their total linking is therefore zero. This checks the framing rather than introducing an unspecified meridional twist at the concatenation.

Let the disk meet $P$ in the finite transverse set $p_1,\ldots,p_m$. Finiteness follows because this inverse image is a compact discrete subset of the compact knot. Shrink the slab so that its intersection with $P$ consists of exactly $m$ arcs crossing from one disk face to the other. Indeed transversality gives each intersection a local graph over the slab coordinate; finitely many disjoint such neighborhoods suffice, and the compact remaining part of $P$ is disjoint from the central disk and hence from a sufficiently short slab. Straighten the graph arcs in disjoint small disks about the $p_j$. Explicitly, if the $j$th graph has disk coordinate $p_j(t)$, use $(q,t)\mapsto(q+\chi_j(q)(p_j(0)-p_j(t)),t)$, with $\chi_j=1$ near that graph and zero outside its disk. Work first in a slightly larger slab and multiply the displacement by a smooth time-coordinate cutoff $\tau(t)$ equal to one on the inner slab and zero near the larger slab faces. Thus the isotopy is the identity at the outside faces and glues to the identity off the larger slab. After shortening the slab its derivative in $q$ differs from the identity by norm less than $1/2$; the straight-line interpolation has the same bound and is an isotopy. Each disk map is a diffeomorphism: solve its inverse by the uniformly contracting iteration $q_{k+1}=z-\tau(t)\chi_j(q_k)(p_j(0)-p_j(t))$, and use [F3] at its everywhere invertible derivative to obtain smooth local inverses, which agree with this unique inverse. Thus the pattern can be represented as one remaining tangle joined to $m$ straight parallel strands across the chosen slab, with some of their orientations possibly reversed.

derivations.claim: Let λ denote the longitude of the pattern solid torus. Filling the outer boundary of the pattern exterior along λ produces S³∖P(U), so the induced epimorphism π₁(ST∖P)→π₁(S³∖P(U)) has kernel normally generated by λ. By [F1], the target is normally generated by the image of η; hence π₁(ST∖P) is normally generated by η and λ.

For a local connected sum with any knot J, the closure-complement group is the amalgamated product of the two knot groups along their common meridian, by cutting at the connected-sum sphere and applying van Kampen. Each knot-group factor is normally generated by its meridian.

Decompose the complement of P(K) along the companion torus into ST∖P and S³∖K. Van Kampen gives a generating set normally contained in the images of these two groups. The first is normally generated by η and λ by step 1.1; the second is normally generated by μ_K by [F3].

Under the torus gluing, λ is identified with λ_K and η with μ_K. Since μ_K normally generates the companion-knot group, λ becomes redundant, and η normally generates the entire satellite-complement group. The outer solid-torus meridian for the pattern P(K) is isotopic in the complement to η, so it too normally generates.

The solid-torus meridian normally generates the strong-winding factor by hypothesis; quotienting the amalgamated product by that meridian kills this factor and the common meridian. The other knot-group factor is then killed because its meridian normally generates it. Thus the whole closure-complement group is normally generated by the solid-torus meridian.

There is a compact oriented smooth cobordism $E$ with
$$\partial E=M(P)\sqcup M(K)\sqcup(-M(P(K))).$$
For any commutative unital coefficient ring $R$, it has $H_1(E;R)=R$ and $H_2(E;R)=R^2$. The two first boundary components induce the displayed basis in degree two. If $s_L=\alpha_L\cap[M(L)]$ where $\alpha_L\in H^1(M(L);R)$ evaluates as $1$ on the positive meridian, then, in those coordinates,
$$i_*s_{P(K)}=i_*s_P+w\,i_*s_K.$$
In degree one the meridians of $P$, $K$ and $P(K)$ map to $1,w,1$, respectively.

Likewise, for any finite nonempty list of knots $K_1,\ldots,K_q$ with the same supplied peripheral data, there is a compact oriented smooth cobordism $C$ from $\bigsqcup_j M(K_j)$ to $M(K_1\#\cdots\#K_q)$, with $H_1(C;R)=R$ and $H_2(C;R)=R^q$. The incoming degree-two classes are its coordinate basis and the outgoing class maps to their sum. In particular, for $X=E$ or $C$, the outgoing inclusions are injective on $H_1,H_2$ and the union of incoming components surjects onto $H_2(X;R)$.

The peripheral and framing data are supplied, rather than selected by an existence theorem. Their subsequent construction and the homology assertions use no additional choice principle. This is an ordinary-coefficient assertion; arbitrary twisted-coefficient boundary generation is not asserted.

No winding-number condition is needed. The inclusion-induced homomorphism is onto and induces
$$\pi_1(M(P(K)))/\langle\!\langle\lambda_K\rangle\!\rangle\ \cong\ \pi_1(E).$$
The marked companion meridian and pattern-axis core have the same image in $\pi_1(E)$, with the supplied base paths.

$$\pi_1(W)/\langle\!\langle i_*(\lambda_K)\rangle\!\rangle\ \cong\ \pi_1(W\cup_{M(P(K))}E).$$

Assume full AC, matching the chosen finite twisted-chain and maximal-abelian-cover conventions. Let K be a smooth oriented knot, M(K) its preferred-longitude zero-framed surgery, W a compact connected oriented smooth 4-manifold with boundary M(K), and π=π₁(W). Put π^(0)=π and π^(j+1)=[π^(j),π^(j)]. A right Zπ-chain complex with coefficients in a left Z[π/π^(j)]-module is formed by tensoring over Zπ with that module.

For n≥0, W is an integral n-solution for K when H₁(M(K);Z)→H₁(W;Z) is an isomorphism, H₂(W;Z) is free of rank 2r for some finite r, and there are classes x₁,…,x_r,y₁,…,y_r in H₂(W;Z[π/π^(n)]) whose equivariant intersection pairings satisfy λ_n(x_i,x_j)=0 and λ_n(x_i,y_j)=δ_ij. It is an integral (n+1/2)-solution when, in addition, each x_i is the image of a class x̃_i in H₂(W;Z[π/π^(n+1)]) and λ_{n+1}(x̃_i,x̃_j)=0 for all i,j. Here λ_j is the equivariant intersection pairing induced by the orientation of W.

For a commutative ring R with 1≠0, a group G belongs to Strebel's class D(R) if every homomorphism between projective RG-modules is injective whenever its tensor with the trivial G-module R is injective. In this page R is Q or F_p for a prime p. For a countable discrete group G, its group von Neumann algebra N G is the weak-operator closure of CG in the left regular representation on ℓ²(G), with trace τ_G(T)=⟨Tδ_e,δ_e⟩. The von Neumann dimension of a finitely generated projective N G-module represented by a projection E is τ_G(E); for an arbitrary module it is the supremum of the dimensions of its finitely generated projective submodules.

For a compact oriented 4-manifold W with boundary, sign(W) is the inertia difference of the symmetric intersection form on H₂(W;R) modulo its radical (the subspace pairing to zero with every class), equivalently on the image of H₂(W;R)→H₂(W,∂W;R). Given a closed oriented 3-manifold M, a homomorphism φ:π₁(M)→G, a compact oriented 4-manifold W with ∂W=M, and an extension ψ:π₁(W)→G of φ, the L²-signature sign_G^(2)(W,ψ) is the von Neumann signature of the nonsingular part of the N G-coefficient intersection form. When such a W and extension exist, the signature defect is sign_G^(2)(W,ψ)−sign(W). It is called the rho invariant of (M,φ) only after its independence of the bounding data is established by a separate bordism argument.

Assume AC. Let $G$ be a discrete group, let $A=\mathcal N G\subseteq\mathcal B(\ell^2(G))$ have its canonical faithful normal trace $\tau$, and give matrices the unnormalized trace $\tau_r((a_{ij}))=\sum_{i=1}^r\tau(a_{ii})$. For a projection $p\in M_r(A)$ put $\dim_A(pA^r)=\tau_r(p)$; for any right $A$-module take the supremum of dimensions of its finitely generated projective submodules. These dimensions are independent of the projective representation. If $L\subseteq pA^r$ is any submodule and $q$ is the projection onto its Hilbert closure in $p\ell^2(G)^r$, then $q\in M_r(A)$, $q\le p$, and
$$\dim_A L=\tau_r(q),\qquad \dim_A(pA^r/L)=\tau_r(p)-\tau_r(q).$$
In particular a Hilbert-dense submodule has dimension-zero quotient. Modules of dimension zero are closed under submodules, quotients, extensions and filtered colimits. For any matrix $B\in M_{r,s}(A)$, its kernel and Hilbert-closed image are projection modules, its algebraic image is isomorphic to its support projection module, and
$$\tau_s(P_{\ker B})+\tau_r(P_{\overline{\operatorname{im}B}})=s.$$

Work under the standing AC convention for finite von Neumann modules. Let $G$ be a countable discrete amenable group, so that for every finite $S\subseteq G$ and $\varepsilon>0$ there is a nonempty finite $F\subseteq G$ with $|SF\setminus F|<\varepsilon|F|$. Let $B\in M_{m,n}(\mathbb CG)$ act by left convolution on $\ell^2(G)^n$. The Hilbert closure of $\ker(B:(\mathbb CG)^n\to(\mathbb CG)^m)$ is the full Hilbert kernel of $B$. More precisely, if the finite coefficient support of $B$, together with the identity, is contained in $S$, and $K_F$ is the space of vectors in that kernel supported in $F$, then, writing $d=\tau_n(P_{\ker B})$ and $r=\tau_m(P_{\overline{\operatorname{im}B}})=n-d$,
$$n|F|-r|SF|\le\dim_{\mathbb C}K_F\le d|F|.$$
The closure of the right $\mathcal N G$-span of the algebraic kernel is therefore the full Hilbert kernel, and the quotient of the algebraic $\mathcal N G$-kernel by that span has dimension zero.

Let $A$ be a unital ring and $M$ a right $A$-module. Then the functor
$T_M=M\otimes_A-:A\text{-}\mathbf{Mod}\to\mathbf{Ab}$ is additive, preserves
cokernels (so it is right exact: every exact sequence
$X\xrightarrow fY\xrightarrow gZ\to0$ of left $A$-modules induces an exact
sequence $M\otimes_AX\xrightarrow{1\otimes f}M\otimes_AY\xrightarrow{1\otimes g}M\otimes_AZ\to0$),
and preserves arbitrary direct sums: the natural map
$\bigoplus_{i\in I}(M\otimes_AX_i)\to M\otimes_A(\bigoplus_{i\in I}X_i)$
induced by the coordinate inclusions is an isomorphism, including $I=\varnothing$.
If $M$ is a $(B,A)$-bimodule then $T_M$ takes values in left $B$-modules and all
the displayed maps are $B$-linear. No commutativity of $A$ or $B$ is assumed and
no choice is used.

For a right $R$-module $N$ with a specified projective resolution
$Q_\bullet\twoheadrightarrow N$ and a left $R$-module $M$, define the
right-resolution construction
$$\operatorname{Tor}^{R,Q}_n(N,M):=H_n(Q_\bullet\otimes_RM).$$
The datum $Q$ remains in the notation until the balance and change-of-resolution
results prove that it may be suppressed.

For every left $R$-module $M$, repeatedly taking the canonical free cover of the current kernel yields a functorial exact augmented complex of free modules $$\cdots\to F_2\to F_1\to F_0\to M\to0.$$ This construction is available in ZF because it uses only underlying sets and canonical free-module maps. Under the previously recorded choice boundary for free modules, the same complex is a projective resolution.

Assume the Axiom of Dependent Choice.

Any two projective resolutions of the same object are homotopy equivalent over that object.

derivations.claim: First let $K\subseteq R^n$ be generated by finitely many columns, and let $B:R^s\to R^n$ be the corresponding matrix map onto $K$. Right exactness of tensor products identifies $K\otimes_R A$ with $A^s/\operatorname{im}((\ker_R B)\otimes_R A)$. The kernel of its natural map to $A^n$ is therefore $\ker_A B/\operatorname{im}((\ker_R B)\otimes_R A)$. This quotient has dimension zero by [F3]. The tensor-product identifications follow directly from the presentation $\ker_R B\to R^s\to K\to0$: relations among the chosen generators are exactly the elements of $\ker_R B$.

For an arbitrary submodule $K\subseteq R^n$, take its directed union of finitely generated submodules $K_j$. A tensor is a finite sum, so every element of $K\otimes_R A$ comes from some $K_j\otimes_R A$. If its image in $A^n$ is zero, its representative already lies in the kernel of the natural map $K_j\otimes_R A\to A^n$. Thus the kernel for $K$ is the directed union of images of the zero-dimensional kernels from step 1.1; it has dimension zero by [F2]. This also proves the assertion if relations identify different representatives, since images are quotients of those kernels.

Let $F=\bigoplus_{i\in I}R$ be any free module and $K\subseteq F$. Every finite tensor in $K\otimes_R A$ involves finitely many vectors of $K$, each of finite coordinate support in $F$. Their supports lie in one finite free summand $R^n\subseteq F$. A kernel element is therefore the image of a kernel for a submodule of that finite free summand, handled by step 2.1. Taking the directed union over those submodules and finite supports, and applying [F2], proves that $\ker(K\otimes_R A\to F\otimes_R A)$ has dimension zero for every free $F$.

Choose a free presentation $0\to K\to F\to M\to0$. In the resolution-dependent definition of Tor, first use a free resolution beginning with this presentation. For any other chosen projective resolution, [F5] gives chain maps inverse up to chain homotopy. Additive tensoring preserves the homotopy equation $f-g=dh+hd$, since tensoring respects sums and composition. Thus the tensor complexes are homotopy equivalent and their homology modules are isomorphic; the calculation below therefore applies to every retained resolution datum. A free resolution beginning with this presentation computes $\operatorname{Tor}_1^R(M,A)$ as $\ker(K\otimes_R A\to F\otimes_R A)$: resolving $K$ and splicing onto $F\to M$ gives this equality by right exactness at the last differential. Thus step 3.1 proves the assertion for degree one. For $q>1$, successively apply the same construction to the kernels in a free resolution of $M$; the positive-degree homology after splicing shifts by one, giving $\operatorname{Tor}_q^R(M,A)\cong\operatorname{Tor}_1^R(K_{q-1},A)$ for the appropriate syzygy $K_{q-1}$. The degree-one argument applies to every such module, so every asserted higher Tor group has dimension zero. No claim that these algebraic quotient modules are zero is used or obtained.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let G be a countable discrete amenable group. For every right CG-module M and every integer q>0, the N G-von Neumann dimension of Tor_q^{CG}(M,N G) is zero. This dimension-flatness statement does not say that the Tor module itself is zero.

Assume AC. Let $G$ be a discrete group, let $A=\mathcal N G\subseteq\mathcal B(\ell^2(G))$ have its canonical faithful normal trace $\tau$, and give matrices the unnormalized trace $\tau_r((a_{ij}))=\sum_{i=1}^r\tau(a_{ii})$. These dimensions are independent of the projective representation. derivations.claim: First replace the term above degree $n$ by a finite free module if necessary. The image of $d_{n+1}$ after tensoring with $R$ is the kernel of $d_n$ over $R$, a finite-dimensional space. Choose finitely many tensors in $C_{n+1}\otimes R$ whose boundaries span it, and expand each tensor as a finite sum $c\otimes r$. The finitely many resulting elements $c\in C_{n+1}$ define a finite free module $P_{n+1}$ with a map to $C_{n+1}$; compose this map with $d_{n+1}$. Keep $P_i=C_i$ for $l\le i\le n$ and set all other terms to zero. Since $d_nd_{n+1}=0$, this defines a bounded finite-free complex $P_*$ whose $R$-homology vanishes through degree $n$. Below $n$ its $A$-homology is the original one, and in degree $n$ its $A$-homology surjects onto the original one, since it has the same cycles and possibly fewer boundaries. It suffices by [F3] to prove the result for $P_*$.

Over the field $R$, split the exact complex through degree $n$: choose vector-space complements of the kernels in each of its finitely many finite-dimensional terms, and invert each boundary map onto its image on the chosen complement. This gives maps $s_i:P_i\otimes R\to P_{i+1}\otimes R$, $l\le i\le n$, with $ds+sd=I$ through degree $n$. For $R=\mathbb F_p$, lift the finitely many matrix entries to integers and then to constant coefficients in $\mathbb Z\Gamma$, obtaining maps $D_i$. For $R=\mathbb Q$, choose a single positive integer $a$ clearing the denominators of all these finitely many matrices, and lift $a s_i$ instead; in the finite-field case put $a=1$. Set $D_i=0$ outside the indicated range. Then $f=dD+Dd$ is a chain map over $\mathbb Z\Gamma$, chain homotopic to zero, and its augmented matrix in degree $i\le n$ is $aI$, which is injective over $R$.

Apply [F1] to $f_i\otimes_{\mathbb Z}R$ on the free $R\Gamma$-module $P_i\otimes_{\mathbb Z}R$; its augmentation is injective by step 2.1, so this map is injective. Hence $f_i$ is injective over $\mathbb Z\Gamma$. For $R=\mathbb Q$ this follows by viewing a nonzero integral vector as a nonzero rational vector. For $R=\mathbb F_p$, an integral kernel vector has finitely many coefficients; divide them all by the largest common power of $p$. Torsion-freeness of the integral target preserves the kernel equation, and the resulting nonzero vector modulo $p$ contradicts injectivity. Passing to $\mathbb C\Gamma$ preserves this injection: any finite complex relation can be decomposed using a basis of the finite-dimensional rational span of its coefficients into rational relations, each of which clears denominators to an integral one.

Resolve the cokernel of the injective square matrix $f_i$ over $\mathbb C\Gamma$. The degree-one Tor group is the kernel of $f_i:A^{r_i}\to A^{r_i}$ after tensoring, where $r_i$ is the rank of $P_i$; this is the same free-presentation computation used to prove [F2]. Consequently [F2] makes that kernel dimension zero. Its projection has trace zero and is therefore zero by faithfulness in [F3]. Thus $f_i$ is injective on the Hilbert completion. Let $Z_i$ be the Hilbert kernel of $d_i$. The chain identity makes $f_i$ preserve $Z_i$. Its restriction to $Z_i$ has zero kernel, and polar decomposition in [F3] makes its Hilbert-closed image have the same trace dimension as $Z_i$; since that image lies in $Z_i$, faithfulness makes it dense in $Z_i$.

The algebraic $A$-cycle module is the projection module $P_{Z_i}A^{r_i}$ and is Hilbert-dense in $Z_i$ by [F3]. On these cycles, $f_i=d_{i+1}D_i+D_{i-1}d_i=d_{i+1}D_i$, so its image is contained in the algebraic boundary module. Step 4.1 shows that these boundaries are Hilbert-dense in $Z_i$. The dense-quotient assertion in [F3] therefore gives dimension-zero $A$-homology of $P_*$ through degree $n$. The identity/surjection comparison of step 1.1 transfers this conclusion to $C_*$. The proof establishes vanishing of the dimension and does not assert algebraic vanishing of the homology module.
