```tikz
  \draw[->] (0,-1) -- (0,1) node[above] {$v_{\rm under}$};
  \node[above left] at (0,0) {$+1$};
\end{tikzpicture}
```

In the displayed local chart, the over tangent is the positive horizontal
vector and the under tangent is the positive vertical vector, so the determinant
is $+1$. This figure illustrates the determinant rule only; no proof below
depends on a picture.

Let $A$ be an indeterminate, $R_A=\mathbb Z[A^{\pm1},(A^{-4}+1)^{-1}]$,
$q=A^{-2}$, $t=q^2=A^{-4}$, $\delta=-(q+q^{-1})=-A^2-A^{-2}$, and
$z_0=-1/(t+1)$. For a nonempty regular diagram $D$, define
$\langle D\rangle$ by summing its crossing smoothings with weights $A$ and
$A^{-1}$ and the factor $\delta^{k-1}$ for a state with $k$ circles. Let
$B_n$ be the $n$-strand Artin braid group with positive geometric generators
$\sigma_i$ (label $i$ passes below the midpoint and label $i+1$ passes above),
drawn with braid parameter increasing from bottom to top; let
$e:B_n\to\mathbb Z$ be the homomorphism $e(\sigma_i)=1$. Let $H(n)$ be
the type-A Hecke algebra with generators $T_i$, quadratic relation
$T_i^2=(v-1)T_i+v$, braid relations, and distant commutation; let $\pi_n$
send $\sigma_i$ to $T_i$. Its normalized Markov trace $\operatorname{tr}_n$
satisfies $\operatorname{tr}_n(1)=1$, cyclicity, tower restriction, and
$\operatorname{tr}_{n+1}(xT_n)=z\operatorname{tr}_n(x)$. Let
$\mathrm{TL}_n$ be the noncrossing pairing algebra with loop value $\delta$,
and let $\operatorname{Tr}_n(D)=\delta^{c(D)}$ be the unnormalized trace,
where $c(D)$ is the number of circles after joining corresponding top and
bottom endpoints outside the rectangle; set
$\tau_n=\delta^{-n}\operatorname{Tr}_n$. For $\beta\in B_n$,
$n\ge1$, orient its closure in the braid direction. Under the specialization
$v\mapsto t$, $z\mapsto z_0$ of the Hecke tower, one has
$$\langle\widehat\beta\rangle
 =\delta^{n-1}(-A)^{e(\beta)}\operatorname{tr}_n(\pi_n(\beta))\big|_{v=t,\,z=z_0}.$$
The identity gives bracket value $1$ on the one-strand identity closure. Its
positive and negative Markov stabilizations multiply the raw bracket by
$-A^3$ and $-A^{-3}$, respectively.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $B_n=\langle\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_{n-1}\mid\text{Artin
relators}\rangle$ be the braid group of the Artin presentation
([[def-braid-group-by-the-artin-presentation]]); recall that $B_0$ and $B_1$
are trivial. The **exponent sum** is the unique homomorphism

$$e_n:B_n\longrightarrow\mathbb Z,\qquad e_n(\sigma_i)=1\quad(1\le i\le n-1),$$

where $\mathbb Z$ is the additive group of integers. It is well defined because
every defining relator of the Artin presentation has exponent sum $0$: the
braid relator $\sigma_i\sigma_{i+1}\sigma_i=\sigma_{i+1}\sigma_i\sigma_{i+1}$
has both sides of exponent sum $3$, and each far-commutation relator has both
sides of exponent sum $2$, so the assignment $\sigma_i\mapsto1$ kills all
relators, and [[thm-von-dyck]] applies. It is surjective for $n\ge2$ and it is
the trivial map on the trivial group $B_1$. For every Artin word
$\beta=\sigma_{i_1}^{\varepsilon_1}\cdots\sigma_{i_k}^{\varepsilon_k}$ one has
$e_n(\beta)=\sum_{r=1}^k\varepsilon_r$ independently of the word, and
$e_n(\beta^{-1})=-e_n(\beta)$. **Caveat:** $e_n$ is the composite of the
abelianisation $B_n\to B_n^{\mathrm{ab}}$ with a surjection onto the free cyclic
group $\mathbb Z$ (for $n\ge2$): since the target is abelian, every commutator is sent to $0$, so $e_n$ factors through $B_n/[B_n,B_n]$ ([[def-abelianisation-of-a-group]]). No normal form, Garside structure or
faithfulness statement is used anywhere.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\mathcal C$ be a
ribbon category ([[def-twist-and-ribbon-structure]]) with
chosen left duals ([[def-left-dual-and-right-dual-object]]), braiding $c$
([[def-braiding]]) and twist $\theta$, and let $X\in\mathcal C$. Write
$X_{+1}:=X$ and $X_{-1}:=X^{\vee}$. In a strict model of $\mathcal C$
([[thm-every-braided-monoidal-category-is-monoidally-equivalent-to-a-strict-braided-one]])
there is a unique strict monoidal functor

$$F_X\colon\mathcal T\longrightarrow\mathcal C$$

from the framed oriented tangle category $\mathcal T$ with

$$F_X(+)=X,\qquad F_X(-)=X^{\vee},$$

$$F_X\bigl(X^{+}_{\varepsilon,\varepsilon'}\bigr)=c_{X_\varepsilon,X_{\varepsilon'}},\qquad F_X\bigl(X^{-}_{\varepsilon,\varepsilon'}\bigr)=(c_{X_{\varepsilon'},X_\varepsilon})^{-1},\qquad F_X(\cup_{+1})=\operatorname{coev}_X,\qquad F_X(\cap_{+1})=\operatorname{ev}_X,\qquad F_X(\varphi^{\pm1}_{+1})=\theta_X^{\pm1},$$

where the cup and cap are the coevaluation and evaluation maps attached to the
chosen left duals and the signs are the blackboard conventions of
[[def-the-framed-oriented-tangle-category]]. The remaining elementary tangles
of $\mathcal T$, those carrying a negative sign at a cup, cap or twist, receive
the values forced by these data through the relations. Explicitly put
$j_X=u_X\theta_X:X\to X^{\vee\vee}$, with $u$ as in
[[thm-a-braided-rigid-category-has-a-drinfeld-morphism]]. Then

$$F_X(\cup_-)=(1_{X^\vee}\otimes j_X^{-1})\operatorname{coev}_{X^\vee},\qquad F_X(\cap_-)=\operatorname{ev}_{X^\vee}(j_X\otimes1_{X^\vee}),\qquad F_X(\varphi_-^{\pm1})=\theta_{X^\vee}^{\pm1}.$$

These are the right coevaluation and evaluation on $X$ induced by the ribbon
structure; they need no identification $X^{\vee\vee}=X$ on objects. For a general ribbon
category the same assignment determines a strong monoidal functor, unique up to
the canonical coherence isomorphisms of the strictification. Isotopic framed
tangles are equal morphisms of $\mathcal T$, so $F_X$ is an invariant of framed
tangles. Uniqueness needs no choice.
$$t_n(\beta)=F_X(\widehat\beta^{\mathrm{fr}})\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathcal C}(\mathbf 1),$$

derivations.claim: In the ordered basis of [F1], direct subtraction gives $e:=A(c_{V,V}-AI)=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&0&0\\0&-A^2&1&0\\0&1&-A^{-2}&0\\0&0&0&0\end{pmatrix}$. Writing $U(1)=-A^2v_+\otimes v_-+v_-\otimes v_+$ and $B(v_+\otimes v_-)=1$, $B(v_-\otimes v_+)=-A^{-2}$ shows entrywise that $e=UB$. Hence $B(U(1))=-A^2-A^{-2}=\delta$ and $e^2=\delta e$. The explicit snake equalities in [F2] give the adjacent tensor relations: $e_{12}e_{23}e_{12}=UB\otimes1$ because the middle composites $(1\otimes B)(U\otimes1)$ and then $(B\otimes1)(1\otimes U)$ are identities; the reversed calculation gives $e_{23}e_{12}e_{23}=e_{23}$. Distant placements commute because they act on disjoint tensor factors.

In source-chart coordinates $(u,v)$ and braid-box coordinates $(x,t)$, the orientation-preserving quarter-turn $(x,t)=(-v,u)$ sends the source over direction $(1,1)$ to $(-1,1)$. This is the positive-braid over direction: [F5]'s vector $(1,-2h)$ in ordered coordinates $(t,x)$ is $(-2h,1)$ in $(x,t)$. The source chart's top endpoint pair $v=1$ maps to the braid box's left pair $x=-1$, and its bottom pair $v=-1$ maps to the right pair $x=1$; each pair is a through strand at fixed braid position. The source chart's left and right pairs map to the braid box's bottom and top pairs, respectively, so the B-smoothing is the top cap and bottom cup $e_i$. Thus the A/B crossing expansion is $C_i=AI+A^{-1}e_i$. Its inverse is $C_i^{-1}=A^{-1}I+Ae_i$, since their product is $I+(A^2+A^{-2}+\delta)e_i=I$. By [A1] and [F8]–[F9], the categorical ribbon trace is the framed tangle evaluation of this braid closure, and that evaluator is monoidal with the stated crossing and duality maps. Expanding a braid word into the two smoothing choices therefore gives the bracket weights in [F4]. Because the closure has $n\ge1$ strands, each complete smoothing is a nonempty closed 1-manifold, hence a union of at least one circle. Its categorical value is $\delta^{|S|}$ by monoidality in [F8] and the loop value [F2], whereas the bracket state sum uses $\delta^{|S|-1}$; the extra single factor is independent of the state. Thus $t_n(\beta)=\delta\langle\widehat\beta\rangle$.

The matrix trace $t_n$ in [F3] closes the tensor-word braid with the duality maps $B,U$ of [F2]. Substituting each crossing into the trace expansion from step 2.1 therefore gives the first identity in the Statement. The Hecke formula [F6] then yields $t_n(\beta)=\delta^n(-A)^{e(\beta)}\operatorname{tr}_n(\pi_n(\beta))\big|_{v=t,z=z_0}$. By [F7], $e(\beta)=w(\beta)$. The twist in [F1] is $\lambda=-A^3$, so multiplying $t_n=\delta\langle\widehat\beta\rangle$ by $\lambda^{-w(\beta)}$ gives the second displayed identity. The only choice assumption is [A1], used in step 2.1 to invoke the published trace-to-closure identification; no stronger choice principle or division by $\delta$ is used. Since $A$ is indeterminate, the specialization is taken in the rational-function field where $t+1\ne0$.

Let $X$ be absolutely simple, so its twist is $\theta_X=\lambda\operatorname{id}_X$ for a unique $\lambda\in k^\times$. Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\beta,\beta'$ be braids. Then
$\widehat\beta$ and $\widehat{\beta'}$ are equivalent oriented links if and
only if $\beta$ and $\beta'$ are Markov equivalent, that is, related by a finite
sequence of conjugations in a fixed braid group, stabilizations
$\beta\mapsto\beta\sigma_n^{\pm1}$ into the next braid group, and their

Let $(\mathcal C,\otimes,\mathbf 1,\alpha,\lambda,\rho)$ be a monoidal
category ([[def-monoidal-category]]).

A **braiding** on $\mathcal C$ is a natural isomorphism

$$c_{X,Y}:X\otimes Y\longrightarrow Y\otimes X$$

natural in both variables ([[def-natural-isomorphism]]) such that, for all
objects $X,Y,Z$,

$$\alpha_{Y,Z,X}\circ c_{X,Y\otimes Z}\circ\alpha_{X,Y,Z}=(1_Y\otimes c_{X,Z})\circ\alpha_{Y,X,Z}\circ(c_{X,Y}\otimes1_Z),$$

and

$$\alpha_{Z,X,Y}^{-1}\circ c_{X\otimes Y,Z}\circ\alpha_{X,Y,Z}^{-1}=(c_{X,Z}\otimes1_Y)\circ\alpha_{X,Z,Y}^{-1}\circ(1_X\otimes c_{Y,Z}).$$

These are the two **hexagon identities**. The invertibility of each
$c_{X,Y}$ is part of the data, not a consequence of the hexagons.

Let $\mathcal C$ be a braided rigid monoidal category with braiding $c$, and
fix left duals $X^\vee$ for all objects together with the dual-morphism
operation of [[def-the-dual-of-a-morphism]].

A **twist** on $\mathcal C$ is a natural automorphism
$\theta\in\operatorname{Aut}(\operatorname{id}_{\mathcal C})$ such that

$$\theta_{X\otimes Y}=(\theta_X\otimes\theta_Y)\circ c_{Y,X}\circ c_{X,Y}$$

for all objects $X,Y$ and $\theta_{\mathbf 1}=1_{\mathbf 1}$.

A **ribbon structure** is a twist satisfying the dual-compatibility condition

$$(\theta_X)^\vee=\theta_{X^\vee}.$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $(\mathcal C,\otimes,\mathbf 1,\alpha,\lambda,\rho)$ be a monoidal
category and let $X$ be an object of $\mathcal C$.

A **left dual** of $X$ is an object $X^\vee$ together with morphisms

$$\operatorname{ev}_X:X^\vee\otimes X\to\mathbf 1,\qquad \operatorname{coev}_X:\mathbf 1\to X\otimes X^\vee$$

such that the composites

$$X\xrightarrow{\lambda_X^{-1}}\mathbf 1\otimes X\xrightarrow{\operatorname{coev}_X\otimes1_X}(X\otimes X^\vee)\otimes X\xrightarrow{\alpha_{X,X^\vee,X}}X\otimes(X^\vee\otimes X)\xrightarrow{1_X\otimes\operatorname{ev}_X}X\otimes\mathbf 1\xrightarrow{\rho_X}X$$

and

$$X^\vee\xrightarrow{\rho_{X^\vee}^{-1}}X^\vee\otimes\mathbf 1\xrightarrow{1_{X^\vee}\otimes\operatorname{coev}_X}X^\vee\otimes(X\otimes X^\vee)\xrightarrow{\alpha^{-1}_{X^\vee,X,X^\vee}}(X^\vee\otimes X)\otimes X^\vee\xrightarrow{\operatorname{ev}_X\otimes1_{X^\vee}}\mathbf 1\otimes X^\vee\xrightarrow{\lambda_{X^\vee}}X^\vee$$

are identity morphisms.

A **right dual** of $X$ is an object ${}^\vee X$ together with morphisms

$$\operatorname{ev}'_X:X\otimes{}^\vee X\to\mathbf 1,\qquad \operatorname{coev}'_X:\mathbf 1\to{}^\vee X\otimes X$$

such that the mirror composites

$$X\xrightarrow{\rho_X^{-1}}X\otimes\mathbf 1\xrightarrow{1_X\otimes\operatorname{coev}'_X}X\otimes({}^\vee X\otimes X)\xrightarrow{\alpha^{-1}_{X,{}^\vee X,X}}(X\otimes{}^\vee X)\otimes X\xrightarrow{\operatorname{ev}'_X\otimes1_X}\mathbf 1\otimes X\xrightarrow{\lambda_X}X$$

and

$${}^\vee X\xrightarrow{\lambda_{{}^\vee X}^{-1}}\mathbf 1\otimes{}^\vee X\xrightarrow{\operatorname{coev}'_X\otimes1_{{}^\vee X}}({}^\vee X\otimes X)\otimes{}^\vee X\xrightarrow{\alpha_{{}^\vee X,X,{}^\vee X}}{}^\vee X\otimes(X\otimes{}^\vee X)\xrightarrow{1_{{}^\vee X}\otimes\operatorname{ev}'_X}{}^\vee X\otimes\mathbf 1\xrightarrow{\rho_{{}^\vee X}}{}^\vee X$$

are identity morphisms.

This page uses EGNO's convention: the word "left" refers to the side on which
the dual object sits in the evaluation map.

In a braided rigid monoidal category there is a natural isomorphism

$$u_X:X\to X^{\vee\vee},$$

called the **Drinfeld morphism** (or **Drinfeld isomorphism**), defined by

$$X\xrightarrow{1_X\otimes\operatorname{coev}_{X^\vee}}X\otimes X^\vee\otimes X^{\vee\vee}\xrightarrow{c_{X,X^\vee}\otimes1_{X^{\vee\vee}}}X^\vee\otimes X\otimes X^{\vee\vee}\xrightarrow{\operatorname{ev}_X\otimes1_{X^{\vee\vee}}}X^{\vee\vee}.$$

$$d_{X,Y}:X^{\vee\vee}\otimes Y^{\vee\vee}\xrightarrow{\sim}(X\otimes Y)^{\vee\vee}$$

for the monoidal comparison of the double-dual functor. Then

$$d_{X,Y}\circ(u_X\otimes u_Y)=u_{X\otimes Y}\circ c_{Y,X}\circ c_{X,Y}.$$

Thus $u$ need not be monoidal: the double braiding is precisely its
monoidality obstruction.

Use $S_{U\otimes W}=S_U\otimes S_W$, the ordinary flip braiding, standard vector-space duality, and define $\theta_U=S_U$. This is a ribbon category: the twist is natural because every morphism commutes with $S$; its tensor rule is $S_{U\otimes W}=S_U\otimes S_W$ and the double flip is the identity; and on the dual, $S_{U^*}=(S_U^{-1})^T=S_U^T=(\theta_U)^*$, giving ribbon dual compatibility. The unit is $\mathbb Q$ with trivial involution, so $\operatorname{End}(\mathbf1)=\mathbb Q$. By [F7], the Drinfeld morphism in this symmetric vector-space category is the canonical double-dual identification: on $v\in U$ and $f\in U^*$ its evaluation is $u_U(v)(f)=f(v)$. Thus the ribbon-induced pivotal map $j_U=u_U\theta_U$ is the canonical double-dual identification composed with $S_U$.

Take $X=\mathbb Q e_+\oplus\mathbb Q e_-$ with $S_X=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)$. It is decomposable and its twist is invertible but nonscalar. For the identity $e\in B_1$, [F1] gives $t_1(e)=\operatorname{Tr}(S_X)=1+(-1)=0$. For $\sigma_1\in B_2$, the braid action is the flip $P$. By [F8], under the canonical vector-space double-dual comparison, $j_{X\otimes X}$ has matrix $S_X\otimes S_X$, so the trace of $(S_X\otimes S_X)P$ is $2$: the basis tensors $e_+\otimes e_+$ and $e_-\otimes e_-$ contribute diagonal entries $1$, while the two mixed basis tensors are exchanged and contribute no diagonal entries.

The braid $\sigma_1$ is the positive Markov stabilization of the identity braid in $B_1$, so [F3] says their oriented unframed closures are equivalent. Their exponent sums are $w(e)=0$ and $w(\sigma_1)=1$. Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $\mathcal C$ be a ribbon category with chosen left duals and tensor unit $\mathbf 1$. A **finite oriented framed link colored in $\mathcal C$** is a finite disjoint union $L$ of oriented smoothly embedded circles in $S^3$, a homotopy class of nowhere-zero normal vector field on each component, and an assignment of an object of $\mathcal C$ to each component. A framed colored isotopy carries orientations, framings, and component colors. If $F_{\mathcal C}$ is the ribbon-tangle evaluation functor, define
$$\operatorname{RT}_{\mathcal C}(L):=F_{\mathcal C}(L)\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathcal C}(\mathbf 1).$$
This value depends only on the framed colored isotopy class. It is not automatically a field scalar; if $\mathcal C$ is $k$-linear and $\operatorname{End}_{\mathcal C}(\mathbf 1)=k$, it is a scalar in $k$. The empty link is assigned $1_{\mathbf 1}$.

An **effective field** is a field whose elements have finite encodings and whose exact addition, subtraction, multiplication, equality test, and inversion of nonzero elements are terminating procedures. Input a finite-dimensional strict matrix realization of a $k$-linear ribbon category with $\operatorname{End}(\mathbf1)=k$, finite-dimensional color objects with fixed bases, exact matrices for every braiding and inverse braiding used, duality and twist data, and the induced pivotal matrix $J_W$ for the tensor word $W=V_{a_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes V_{a_n}$. Also input a finite braid word $\beta$ on $n\ge1$ strands and the top color tuple $(a_1,\ldots,a_n)$. The matrices are assumed to satisfy the stated ribbon-category axioms; an implementation does not infer those axioms from arbitrary matrices.

Use the strand-position permutation homomorphism $\pi:B_n\to\operatorname{Sym}(\{1,\ldots,n\})$ given by $\pi(\sigma_i)=(i\ i+1)$. Read the braid letters in composition order, updating the current color tuple at each crossing by swapping its adjacent colors. For a positive letter $\sigma_i$, use the matrix of
$$1\otimes\cdots\otimes c_{V_{a_i},V_{a_{i+1}}}\otimes\cdots\otimes1,$$
and for a negative letter use its inverse. Let the blackboard-framed closure join the bottom and top endpoint at each position by the identity pairing. Reject the input if the final color tuple differs from the initial tuple: the tuple records the colors at the paired endpoints, so equality is exactly the condition that the closure carries a consistent color on every component. Starting with the identity matrix, multiply the typed crossing matrices in word order to obtain $M_\beta:W\to W$, then return
$$\operatorname{Tr}(J_WM_\beta)\in k.$$
This is the exact ribbon evaluation of the blackboard-framed colored braid closure in the given matrix realization. No algorithm is asserted for arbitrary abstract ribbon categories without effective finite matrix data.

For every valid input of the colored-braid evaluation algorithm, where the braid word has $m$ letters and the total tensor-product dimension is $D$, the procedure terminates after exactly $m$ crossing-matrix updates and one finite pivotal-trace contraction. It returns the ribbon-category evaluation of that framed colored braid closure in the given matrix realization. The stated bound concerns the number of matrix updates; each update is a finite exact matrix multiplication over the effective field.

Let $X$ be a finite set and let $\sigma\in\operatorname{Sym}(X)$, with cycle
notation and composition as in [[def-symmetric-group]].

The **support** and **fixed-point set** of $\sigma$ are

$$\operatorname{supp}(\sigma):=\{x\in X:\sigma(x)\ne x\},\qquad \operatorname{Fix}(\sigma):=\{x\in X:\sigma(x)=x\}.$$

A cycle $(a_0\,a_1\,\ldots\,a_{k-1})$ has **length** $k$ and support
$\{a_0,\ldots,a_{k-1}\}$. Two cycles are **disjoint** when their supports are
disjoint. A **disjoint-cycle decomposition** of $\sigma$ is an expression for
$\sigma$ as a product of pairwise disjoint cycles of length at least $2$.
One-cycles are omitted, and the empty product is the identity permutation.

When $|X|=n$, the **cycle type** of $\sigma$ is the list of natural numbers
$c_1(\sigma),\ldots,c_n(\sigma)$, where $c_k(\sigma)$ is the number of
$k$-element orbits of the action generated by $\sigma$. Thus $c_1(\sigma)$ is
the number of fixed points. Equivalently, the cycle type records the lengths of
all cycles after each fixed point is inserted as a one-cycle.

In a braided rigid monoidal category there is a natural isomorphism

$$u_X:X\to X^{\vee\vee},$$

called the **Drinfeld morphism** (or **Drinfeld isomorphism**), defined by

$$X\xrightarrow{1_X\otimes\operatorname{coev}_{X^\vee}}X\otimes X^\vee\otimes X^{\vee\vee}\xrightarrow{c_{X,X^\vee}\otimes1_{X^{\vee\vee}}}X^\vee\otimes X\otimes X^{\vee\vee}\xrightarrow{\operatorname{ev}_X\otimes1_{X^{\vee\vee}}}X^{\vee\vee}.$$

Write

$$d_{X,Y}:X^{\vee\vee}\otimes Y^{\vee\vee}\xrightarrow{\sim}(X\otimes Y)^{\vee\vee}$$

for the monoidal comparison of the double-dual functor. Then

$$d_{X,Y}\circ(u_X\otimes u_Y)=u_{X\otimes Y}\circ c_{Y,X}\circ c_{X,Y}.$$

Thus $u$ need not be monoidal: the double braiding is precisely its
monoidality obstruction.

Every permutation of a finite set is a product of pairwise disjoint cycles,
uniquely up to reordering the factors and cyclically rotating the entries within
each cycle. The identity permutation has the empty disjoint-cycle decomposition.

derivations.claim: By [F1], the closed-link value is the ribbon-tangle evaluation, and [F3] identifies the algorithm output with that value. In the flip category, each positive braid generator swaps two adjacent tensor factors and each negative generator does the same swap, so the braid action on $V^{\otimes n}$ is the permutation of factors given by $\pi(\beta)$. The twist is identity. Let $w_1,\ldots,w_{d^n}$ be the tensor basis of $W=V^{\otimes n}$ and $w_1^*,\ldots,w_{d^n}^*$ its ordinary dual basis. Substitution in [F5]'s formula gives $u_W(w_r)(w_s^*)=1$ when $r=s$ and $0$ otherwise, so the ribbon-induced pivotal map is the canonical double-dual identification. Thus [F2]–[F3] reduce the value to the ordinary matrix trace of that permutation operator.

Fix a basis $e_1,\ldots,e_d$ of $V$. A basis tensor $e_{i_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes e_{i_n}$ is fixed by the factor permutation exactly when its indices are constant on each orbit of $\pi(\beta)$; by [F4], these orbits are exactly the cycles counted by $c(\pi(\beta))$, including fixed points. There are $d$ independent choices for each cycle, hence exactly $d^{c(\pi(\beta))}$ fixed basis tensors. A permutation matrix has trace equal to its number of fixed basis vectors, proving the formula.

The identity in $B_1$ has one permutation cycle, the identity in $B_2$ has two, and $\sigma_1$ has the transposition permutation with one cycle. Substitution into the formula gives $d$, $d^2$, and $d$, respectively; the latter closure is a single component because its endpoint permutation has one cycle. These calculations include $d=0$ because every listed cycle count is positive.

Two chords **intersect** if their endpoints alternate around the oriented circle. A chord is **isolated** if it intersects no other chord. The **1T relation** sets every unframed diagram with an isolated chord equal to zero. The framed degree-$n$ chord-diagram module is the free $R$-module on degree-$n$ chord diagrams modulo all 4T relations. The unframed degree-$n$ chord-diagram module is the free $R$-module on degree-$n$ chord diagrams modulo 4T and 1T relations. A framed weight system is an $R$-linear functional on the framed module; an unframed weight system is an $R$-linear functional on the unframed module.

derivations.claim: A degree-$n$ chord diagram is a pairing of $2n$ cyclically ordered endpoints, so only finitely many such diagrams exist. A 4T relation is determined by a background diagram and finitely many endpoint positions, and a 1T relation by one diagram; hence there are finitely many relation vectors. By [F1], each has integer coefficients, so they form the rows of a finite integer matrix $A$. Write $A_n(F):=F^{C_n}/\operatorname{rowspan}_F(A)$ and $W_n(F):=\operatorname{Hom}_F(A_n(F),F)$. Since $k$ has characteristic zero, $\mathbb Q$ embeds in $k$. The rank of $A$ is unchanged by this field extension: a nonzero maximal minor over $\mathbb Q$ remains nonzero in $k$, while every larger minor that vanishes over $\mathbb Q$ still vanishes in $k$. Thus the row space over $k$ is the scalar extension of the rational row space, and $A_n(k)\cong A_n(\mathbb Q)\otimes_{\mathbb Q}k$.

The quotient is finite-dimensional, so extending a rational basis and its dual basis gives $W_n(k)\cong W_n(\mathbb Q)\otimes_{\mathbb Q}k$. If $n=0$, the sole diagram is the empty diagram and any weight system is its value $c\in k$; the constant invariant $V(K)=c$ has top symbol $c$. For $n>0$, choose a finite $\mathbb Q$-basis $\phi_1,\ldots,\phi_d$ of $W_n(\mathbb Q)$; finite-dimensional row reduction chooses this basis without a choice axiom. By [F2], for each $i$ there is a rational-valued finite-type invariant $V_i$ with top symbol $\phi_i$. Write the given weight system as $W=\sum_{i=1}^d a_i\phi_i$ with $a_i\in k$, and define $V=\sum_{i=1}^d a_iV_i$, viewing each rational value in $k$. Linearity of the finite-difference operator gives top symbol $W$. If $W_n(\mathbb Q)=0$, the sum is empty and the zero invariant supplies the zero weight system.

derivations.claim: Form the coefficientwise formal expression $C_D(z)=\sum_{j\ge0}c_j(D)z^j$ from [F1]. It is a diagram invariant, has value $1$ on an unknot, and satisfies $C_{D_+}-C_{D_-}=zC_{D_0}$ coefficientwise. A local positive and negative curl on any component of the $r$-component unlink are both that unlink; the oriented smoothing is the $(r+1)$-component unlink. Thus $c_j(U_r)-c_j(U_r)=c_{j-1}(U_{r+1})$ for every $j\ge1$. All coefficients of $U_{r+1}$ vanish. Therefore the unlink values of the formal expression are $1$ for one component and $0$ for more than one. This is also the forced unlink value for ANY polynomial-valued invariant satisfying the Definition.

Here is the finite argument that the expression is actually in $\mathbb Z[z]$. In a diagram choose finitely many component basepoints and an order. Call a crossing bad when its first encounter in this traversal is the underpass. If none is bad, the first component passes over every later component and has a descending self-diagram. Pull its successive arcs above everything they first encounter to isolate a round circle; repeat for the remaining components. Thus a descending diagram is an unlink. At a bad crossing the skein relation writes its value as the value of the switched diagram, plus or minus $z$ times its oriented smoothing. The switched diagram has one fewer bad crossing and the same number $N$ of crossings; the smoothing has $N-1$ crossings. Reset the finite component data on a smoothing if necessary. The nonnegative integer $N(N+1)/2+b$, with $b$ the number of bad crossings, decreases in each branch. Hence this is a FINITE resolution tree. Its leaves have values $0$ or $1$ by step1.1. Working back through the tree uses only integer addition/subtraction and multiplication by $z$, so $C_D\in\mathbb Z[z]$. In fact every branch has at most $N$ smoothing operations, giving degree at most $N$. This proves finiteness and integrality without assuming an integer-valued formal sequence theorem or making an infinite selection.

Apply the SAME finite tree to any two polynomial-valued invariants satisfying the stated normalization and skein relation. Their unlink leaves agree by step1.1, and each internal skein relation then forces agreement. Their values agree on every diagram. Use coordinates $(z,t)\in\mathbb C\times\mathbb R$ on oriented $\mathbb R^3$, with $t$ increasing upward. A knot is a smooth embedding $K:S^1\hookrightarrow\mathbb C\times\mathbb R$ with the orientation of $S^1$. A strict Morse presentation is one for which $t|_K$ has nondegenerate critical points, meaning its second derivative in a local coordinate is nonzero there, and pairwise distinct critical values. Write $t_{\min}:=\min_{x\in K}t(x)$, $t_{\max}:=\max_{x\in K}t(x)$, and $r(K)$ for the number of local maxima. A parenthesized $q$-braid is a smooth braid with $q$ strands, each strictly increasing in $t$, together with an ordered binary parenthesization of its lower endpoints and an ordered binary parenthesization of its upper endpoints.

For $n\ge0$, a degree-$n$ chord diagram is an oriented circle with $n$ disjoint unordered pairs of distinct points, called chords. Let $\mathcal A_n^{\mathrm{fr}}$ be the rational vector space on these diagrams modulo 4T, and let $\mathcal A_n^{\mathrm{un}}$ be its quotient by 1T as well. A 4T relation fixes one chord $pq$ and another chord endpoint $r$, moves the other endpoint of the second chord to just before or after $p$ and just before or after $q$, and takes the alternating sum of those four diagrams. A chord is isolated when it intersects no other chord, where intersection means that chord endpoints alternate around the circle; 1T sets every such diagram to zero. Put $\widehat{\mathcal A}^{\mathrm{fr/un}}_{\mathbb C}:=\prod_{n\ge0}(\mathcal A_n^{\mathrm{fr/un}}\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb C)$, with multiplication induced by connected sum of diagrams and unit the empty diagram. For $q$ ordered upward strands, let $\widehat{\mathcal A}_{\mathbb C}(q)$ be the completion of the associative algebra generated by $t_{ij}=t_{ji}$ for $1\le i<j\le q$, with relations $[t_{ij},t_{kl}]=0$ when $i,j,k,l$ are distinct and $[t_{ij},t_{ik}+t_{jk}]=0$ when $i,j,k$ are distinct. The generator $t_{ij}$ is a horizontal chord joining strands $i$ and $j$; multiplication stacks diagrams from bottom to top.

More generally, a compact strict Morse tangle $T$ is a compact oriented smooth one-dimensional submanifold of $\mathbb C\times[a,b]$, with distinct boundary points on the planes $t=a$ and $t=b$, transverse to those planes, and with nondegenerate interior critical points of height having distinct critical values. A tangle chord diagram is a finite set of unordered pairs of distinct interior points on the oriented tangle skeleton. Its 4T relation is the same local alternating relation as above on the skeleton. The unframed tangle quotient also sets to zero any chord whose endpoints are consecutive in the order along the same skeleton component; for a circle the order is cyclic and for an arc it is linear. The completed degreewise tangle diagram space is denoted $\widehat{\mathcal A}^{\mathrm{un}}_{\mathbb C}(T)$.

The unframed configuration series of a strict Morse presentation $K$ is the formal degreewise series
$$
Z(K):=\sum_{m\ge0}\frac1{(2\pi i)^m}\int_{t_{\min}<t_m<\cdots<t_1<t_{\max}}\ \sum_{P}(-1)^{\downarrow(P)}[D_P]_{\mathrm{un}}\bigwedge_{j=1}^m\frac{dz_j-dz'_j}{z_j-z'_j}\ \in\widehat{\mathcal A}^{\mathrm{un}}_{\mathbb C}.
$$
The ordered simplex is divided into chambers by the critical values of $t|_K$. In each chamber, $P$ ranges over choices, at each level $t_j$, of an unordered pair of distinct points $(z_j,t_j),(z'_j,t_j)$ of $K$. The diagram $D_P$ joins the corresponding preimages on the oriented parameter circle. The integer $\downarrow(P)$ counts endpoints at which $t$ decreases along the orientation of $K$. The differential form is pulled back to the chamber by the selected local branches. The degree-zero term is the empty diagram with coefficient $1$; the displayed integrals are interpreted as improper integrals on each chamber.

For a compact strict Morse tangle $T$, $Z(T)$ is given by the same formula with $T$ in place of $K$, the interval $(a,b)$ in place of $(t_{\min},t_{\max})$, the chord diagrams on the tangle skeleton in place of circle diagrams, and the corresponding unframed tangle quotient in place of $\widehat{\mathcal A}^{\mathrm{un}}_{\mathbb C}$. A parenthesized braid is a special case with no interior critical points.

For a parenthesized braid path $\gamma$ in the configuration space of $q$ distinct complex points, define its Knizhnik–Zamolodchikov (KZ) series by the degreewise iterated-integral holonomy of
$$\Omega_q=\frac1{2\pi i}\sum_{1\le i<j\le q}t_{ij}\,d\log(z_i-z_j).$$
Explicitly, if $\gamma:[0,1]\to\operatorname{Conf}_q(\mathbb C)$ is an ordinary path with noncolliding endpoints, its holonomy is
$$1+\sum_{m\ge1}\int_{0<t_m<\cdots<t_1<1}\gamma^*\Omega_q(t_1)\cdots\gamma^*\Omega_q(t_m).$$
A tangential endpoint is a limiting collision configuration together with a specified nonzero first-order direction of approach for each colliding cluster. When endpoints have such clusters prescribed by the parenthesizations, the holonomy is the constant term after removing the local logarithmic factors $\exp(t_{ij}\log\varepsilon/(2\pi i))$ at each tangential endpoint. A change between the two parenthesizations of three consecutive strands is encoded by the regularized transport $\Phi_{\mathrm{KZ}}$.

For parenthesized braids the KZ holonomy takes values in the framed strand algebra, where only tangled 4T is imposed; passing from a closed framed strand diagram to an unframed knot applies the quotient by isolated-chord 1T. Fix a standard hump $H$ by starting with the two-critical-point unknot and inserting one local birth of a maximum-minimum pair; thus $H$ has two local maxima. The normalized unframed Kontsevich series of $K$ is
$$
I(K):=Z(K)\,Z(H)^{-r(K)}\in\widehat{\mathcal A}^{\mathrm{un}}_{\mathbb C},
$$
The normalization uses one copy of $Z(H)$ for each local maximum; its degree-zero term is $1$, so its inverse is interpreted in the product completion. This definition makes no assertion that the unnormalized KZ coefficients are rational or that equal Kontsevich series separate knot types.

Fix the round metric and orientation on $S^3$. An **$m$-singular oriented knot** is a smooth immersion $K:S^1\to S^3$ with exactly $m$ distinct transverse double points and no other self-intersections; each double-point image has exactly two preimages with linearly independent tangent vectors, and the preimage pairs are disjoint. The knot has no framing. Choose disjoint small balls around its double points, each containing no other part of the singular knot. At each double point there are two **resolutions**, obtained by separating the two local branches in the ball; label them $+$ and $-$ so the resolved crossing signs are respectively $+1$ and $-1$ under the convention that, in a diagram whose positive viewing normal agrees with the ambient orientation, the sign is $\operatorname{sgn}\det(v_{\mathrm{over}},v_{\mathrm{under}})$ and the positive Artin half twist has sign $+1$.

A **framed oriented knot** is a smooth oriented embedding $K:S^1\hookrightarrow S^3$ together with a homotopy class through nowhere-zero smooth sections of its oriented rank-two normal bundle. For an immersion $K:S^1\to S^3$, including one with double points, define its branchwise normal bundle over the parameter circle by $\nu_K:=K^*TS^3/dK(TS^1)$, oriented so that a positive tangent followed by a positive normal basis gives the ambient orientation. Because $dK$ has rank one at every parameter, its image is locally a smooth line subbundle and this quotient is locally a rank-two bundle. Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the framed clauses below, so these normal quotient bundles have their smooth vector-bundle structures. A **framed $m$-singular knot** has finitely many transverse double points and finitely many simple zeroes of a smooth section of $\nu_K$, all disjoint; its number $m$ of singularities is the number of double points plus the number of zeroes. A simple zero is one at which the derivative of the section in an oriented local trivialization is nonzero. Resolve double points as above, extending the normal section over the local resolution balls; each resulting section determines a framing homotopy class. To resolve a framing zero at parameter $t=0$, choose the oriented normal trivialization so the section is $t e_1$ near $0$, with $e_2$ the positive quarter-turn of $e_1$; replace it by $t e_1+\delta e_2$ or $t e_1-\delta e_2$ for sufficiently small $\delta>0$. These are the $+$ and $-$ resolutions of that zero and determine the framing classes on the resolved knots.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring. For an $R$-valued ambient-isotopy invariant $V$ of unframed oriented knots and an $m$-singular knot $K$, its **finite difference** is
$$
D_mV(K):=\sum_{\epsilon\in\{+1,-1\}^m}\left(\prod_{i=1}^m\epsilon_i\right)V(K_\epsilon),
$$
where $K_\epsilon$ resolves singularity $i$ positively when $\epsilon_i=+1$ and negatively when $\epsilon_i=-1$. For $m=0$, set $D_0V(K)=V(K)$. The same formula defines $D_mV$ for an invariant of framed knots on framed singular knots, counting both double points and framing zeroes among the $m$ singularities. For one double point it reads $V(K_+)-V(K_-)$; the zero resolutions use the local normal-section model just specified. An invariant has **type at most $n$** if $D_{n+1}V$ vanishes on every $(n+1)$-singular object in its category. It has **exact type $n$** if it has type at most $n$ but not type at most $n-1$. Type at most $-1$ means the zero invariant, so a nonzero type-at-most-zero invariant has exact type zero. For an unframed link, replace $S^1$ by a finite disjoint union of oriented circles, allow marked self- or mixed double points, and use the same resolution sum. For a framed link, take a normal section on each component and count its simple zeroes together with all double points.

derivations.claim: The critical points are isolated in the compact one-dimensional skeleton and absent from the tangle boundary, so there are finitely many critical points and critical values. On every open interval between consecutive critical values or boundary levels, the inverse image is a finite union of arcs on which $t$ is a local diffeomorphism. Thus the number of branches, and the finite set of allowed pairs at a level, are constant on each such interval.

At a regular level, each branch is a smooth graph $z=z_\lambda(t)$, so its evaluation extends smoothly to any regular face. Near a critical point, choose a local parameter $x$ with $t(0)=c$, $t'(0)=0$, and $t''(0)\ne0$. The function $h(x)=(t(x)-c)/x^2$ extends smoothly with $h(0)=t''(0)/2\ne0$; after shrinking the coordinate interval, $s=x\sqrt{|h(x)|}$ is a smooth coordinate with nonzero derivative and $t=c+\operatorname{sgn}(h(0))s^2$. Since $z=z(x(s))$ is smooth, the two local branches and their limiting common point extend to the critical face in this coordinate.

Fix a chamber and let $k_r$ be the number of its ordered levels in the $r$th interval between critical or boundary levels. The chamber is a product of open simplices, one for each interval, with $k_r$ ordered coordinates. Its closure is the product of the corresponding closed simplices, hence compact. The facets of a closed simplex are exactly adjacent-coordinate equalities or a coordinate reaching one endpoint of its interval; across the finite family of chambers those endpoints are the knot extrema, tangle boundary levels, or critical values. Thus before resolving endpoint collisions the only faces are level collisions, outer endpoints, and critical-level events.

In a regular-level collision, endpoints on distinct branches remain distinct because $K$ is embedded; endpoints on one branch coalesce along a smooth arc. In the latter case, use local parameters $s_1,\dots,s_k$ for the colliding endpoints, their center $p=k^{-1}\sum s_j$, the radius $r=(\sum_j|s_j-p|^2)^{1/2}$, and the normalized shape $(s_j-p)/r$. Replacing the diagonal $r=0$ by this shape data is the real oriented blow-up of that collision diagonal; its local coordinates are $r\ge0$ and smooth shape coordinates. At a critical point, step 1.2 supplies the same form with the Morse coordinate $s$.

For a cluster of several endpoints, first blow up the full collision diagonal and then each proper collision diagonal in its limiting shape space, from larger clusters to smaller ones. Collision subsets in any limiting configuration are either nested or disjoint, so these blow-ups introduce finitely many nonnegative radii $r_C$ and smooth shape coordinates. Each resulting chart is a product of half-lines $r_C\ge0$ and an open smooth coordinate set; transition maps are smooth because they are changes of center, scale, and unit direction. Hence the resolved cell is a manifold with corners. Each added boundary hypersurface is a collision cluster, and its boundary orientation is determined by the outward vector $-\partial_{r_C}$. The original simplex orientation and the local coordinates $s\ge0$ at critical levels give the stated orientations on all remaining faces.

Each chamber closure is compact by step 2.1, and real oriented blow-up replaces a closed collision diagonal by a compact sphere of limiting directions without losing compactness. Only finitely many chambers, branch pairings, and endpoint subsets occur at fixed $m$, so their resolved union is compact. The boundary labels from steps 2.1 and 3.1 exhaust its boundary faces; no additional face can occur because every boundary coordinate is either a level-gap, a distance to a critical/global endpoint, or one of the finitely many collision radii. The branch evaluations extend by steps 1.2 and 2.2.

Work in the smooth category ([[def-smooth-manifold]]). Fix once and for all the
three-sphere as the one-point compactification

$$S^3:=\mathbb R^3\cup\{\infty\}$$

of Euclidean three-space, carrying its standard smooth structure, and fix the
standard orientation of $S^3$: the orientation induced by the standard
orientation of $\mathbb R^3$ under the one-point compactification, so that the
charts of the standard atlas away from $\infty$ are orientation-preserving and
the orientation is that of a connected oriented $3$-manifold in the sense of
[[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]]. For $r>0$ write
$\overline B_r:=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:\lVert x\rVert_2\le r\}$, the closed ball of
[[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]] with the following restriction convention. Smoothness on a closed ball means
local extension to a smooth map on an open neighborhood in Euclidean space;
smoothness on $M\times I$, for a smooth manifold $M$ without boundary, means
local extension across $t=0,1$ in $M\times\mathbb R$. Thus these closed domains
are not asserted to be manifolds without boundary in the cited definition.

**Links.** The **standard oriented circle** is the circle
$S^1=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ with its standard counterclockwise orientation,
regarded as a smooth $1$-manifold; a
**finite disjoint union of oriented circles** is a smooth manifold
$C=S^1\sqcup\dots\sqcup S^1$ ($k$ summands, $k\in\mathbb N$)
diffeomorphic to the disjoint union of $k$ standard oriented circles. An
**oriented link** (with $k$ components) is a smooth embedding

$$L\colon C\longrightarrow S^3$$

of such a disjoint union in the sense of [[def-smooth-embedding]]. So $L$ is
injective, is an immersion, and is a homeomorphism onto its image with the
subspace topology, and its image $L(C)$ is a finite disjoint union of smoothly
embedded circles. Thus every link considered here is finite and tame: the
smoothness of $L$ is exactly the standing convention, and no polygonal or other
tame model is used. The **components** of $L$ are the images of the individual
summands, and the number of components is $k$.

**Ambient isotopy.** Let $I=[0,1]$. An **ambient isotopy** of $S^3$ is a smooth
map

$$H\colon S^3\times I\longrightarrow S^3$$

such that $H_0=\mathrm{id}_{S^3}$, each $H_t\colon S^3\to S^3$,
$H_t(x):=H(x,t)$, is a diffeomorphism ([[def-diffeomorphism-and-local-diffeomorphism-of-manifolds]]),
and each $H_t$ is orientation-preserving with respect to the fixed orientation.
The last clause is in fact automatic: $t\mapsto H_t$ is continuous in the
$C^\infty$ topology of the diffeomorphism group, the orientation sign is locally
constant in $t$, and $H_0=\mathrm{id}$ is orientation-preserving, so it is kept
only for emphasis.

**Equivalence of links.** Two oriented links $L_0\colon C_0\to S^3$ and
$L_1\colon C_1\to S^3$ are **equivalent** (written $L_0\sim L_1$), or
**ambient isotopic**, when there are an ambient isotopy $H$ and an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism $f:C_0\to C_1$ with
$H_1\circ L_0=L_1\circ f$. Thus parametrizations and component labels are
irrelevant, while the induced orientation of each image component is preserved. The relation is an equivalence relation on links:
it is reflexive with $H=\mathrm{id}$, transitive by composing isotopies, and
symmetric because a smooth family of diffeomorphisms has a smooth family of
inverses. An equivalence class is an **(oriented) link type**.

**Moving off $\infty$.** Because the definition of equivalence allows the
isotopy to move a link through $\infty$, the standard practice of this page is
to first apply an ambient isotopy that carries a given link into the open ball,
and only then to project; every projection and every Reidemeister move below is
read after moving the link off $\infty$ into $\mathbb R^3$ in this way. The
orientation-preserving clause in the definition of ambient isotopy is exactly
what the oriented Reidemeister moves and the oriented closure construction must
respect. The unoriented theory uses the same ambient isotopies but forgets
the orientations of the link components.

**Links in the three-sphere versus links in $\mathbb R^3$.** A link contained in
$\mathbb R^3\subset S^3$ is a link in $S^3$; conversely every link may be
assumed after isotopy to lie in $\mathbb R^3$, by choosing a point outside the compact one-dimensional image and moving that
point to $\infty$ by a smooth rotation of the standard sphere. When comparing
links already in $\mathbb R^3$, an isotopy can also be arranged to avoid
$\infty$ throughout; the track-avoidance argument is given in
[[thm-oriented-reidemeister-equivalence-theorem]].

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\mathcal F:M\times S\to N$ be a smooth family of maps and let $Z\subseteq N$
be an embedded submanifold. If $\mathcal F\pitchfork Z$, then the set of
parameters $s\in S$ for which the slice $\mathcal F_s:M\to N$ fails to be
transverse to $Z$ is a null subset of $S$.

Let $F:M\to N$ be a smooth map and let $p\in M$. If $dF_p:T_pM\to T_{F(p)}N$ is
an isomorphism, then there are open neighbourhoods $U$ of $p$ and $V$ of
$F(p)$ such that $F|_U:U\to V$ is a diffeomorphism.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $M$ be a compact smooth manifold without
boundary, let $N$ be a smooth manifold, and let
$F\colon M\times I\to N$ be a smooth isotopy such that $F_t:=F(\cdot,t)$ is an
embedding for every $t\in I$. Suppose $F$ is constant near the ends of $I$:
there is $\varepsilon\in(0,\tfrac12)$ with $F(x,t)=F(x,0)$ for $t\le\varepsilon$
and $F(x,t)=F(x,1)$ for $t\ge1-\varepsilon$ and all $x\in M$. Then for every
open neighbourhood $W$ of the image $F(M\times I)$ there is an ambient isotopy
$H\colon N\times I\to N$ such that

$$H_t\circ F_0=F_t\quad\text{for every }t\in I,$$

$H_0=\mathrm{id}_N$, each $H_t$ is a diffeomorphism of $N$, and $H_t$ is the
identity outside $W$ for every $t$. Moreover $H_t=\mathrm{id}_N$ for $t\in[0,\tfrac{\varepsilon}{2}]$ and

To verify this for the given compact family, cover $S^1$ by finitely many parameter intervals on which the derivative of each $K_s$ has a uniform positive lower bound; a sufficiently small $C^1$ perturbation remains an immersion there. On the compact complement of a neighborhood of the diagonal in $S^1\times S^1$, injectivity has a uniform positive separation because $(s,x,y)\mapsto\|K_s(x)-K_s(y)\|$ is continuous and positive. A sufficiently small $C^0$ perturbation preserves that separation. Thus a small perturbation of $h$ alone keeps every slice embedded and fixed at the two endpoint collars. The straight interpolation between $h$ and its perturbation is also $C^1$-small, hence stays embedded; [F6] extends this path to ambient isotopy.

For a smooth height family $h$ on $S^1\times[0,1]$, use finitely many coordinate intervals and smooth bump functions supported away from the endpoint collars to form a finite-dimensional perturbation family $h_a=h+\sum_j a_j\phi_j$. Cutoff multiples of $x$, $x^2/2$, $x^3/6$, and $(s-s_0)x$ prescribe, independently, $h_x,h_{xx},h_{xxx},h_{xs}$ at a point; finitely many smaller intervals cover the compact cylinder. The universal maps for $h_x$, $(h_x,h_{xx})$, $(h_x,h_{xx},h_{xxx})$, and $(h_x,h_{xx},h_{xs})$ are transverse to zero because the parameter derivatives span the corresponding target coordinates. By [F4], choose one arbitrarily small parameter for which all four slices are transverse. The zero set of $h_x$ is then a one-manifold; the zero set of $(h_x,h_{xx})$ is zero-dimensional; and the two three-coordinate maps have no zeros because their two-dimensional source has smaller dimension than their target. Thus every degeneracy has $h_x=h_{xx}=0$, $h_{xxx}\ne0$, and $h_{xs}\ne0$. The fold condition is open, so later perturbations can be chosen small enough to preserve it.

Remove small disjoint fold neighborhoods and endpoint collars from the parameter cylinder. On the remaining compact set, distinct critical points have a positive separation in the circle coordinate. Cover it by finitely many charts and add bump functions with disjoint small supports so that, at any two distinct critical points, the parameter derivatives independently span the two derivative values and the difference of the function values. For a pair $(x,y)$, the event map $(s,x,y)\mapsto(h_x(s,x),h_x(s,y),h(s,x)-h(s,y))$ is therefore transverse to zero for generic coefficients by [F4]. Its source and target both have dimension three, so its zeros are isolated. At a zero the derivative matrix has determinant $h_{xx}(s,x)h_{xx}(s,y)(h_s(s,x)-h_s(s,y))$. The first two factors are nonzero because the fold neighborhoods were removed; transversality makes the third nonzero. Thus the two critical values cross transversely. Use further bump functions supported near mutually distinct critical points, so their value and derivative jets can be changed independently. For three distinct critical points, the event map with their three $x$-derivatives and two value differences has five scalar components on a four-dimensional parameter-and-point domain; [F4] makes its zero set empty. For two disjoint value crossings, four critical-point equations and two value differences give six components on a five-dimensional domain, so simultaneous crossings are absent. A birth/death coinciding in height with another critical point imposes $h_x=h_{xx}=0$ at the fold, $h_x=0$ at the other point, and equality of their values: four independent conditions on a three-dimensional domain, so this event is absent. A fold simultaneous with a value crossing at two other critical points imposes five independent conditions on a four-dimensional domain and is absent. Two folds at the same parameter impose four equations on a three-dimensional domain and are absent as well. The same finite-dimensional bump family can impose all these conditions simultaneously: the bad parameter set for each map is null by [F4], their finite union is null, and every coefficient ball contains a point outside that union.

Outside the finite fold and crossing parameters, every critical point is nondegenerate and the critical values are pairwise distinct, so each height slice is strict Morse. Use coordinates $(z,t)\in\mathbb C\times\mathbb R$ on oriented $\mathbb R^3$, with $t$ increasing upward. A knot is a smooth embedding $K:S^1\hookrightarrow\mathbb C\times\mathbb R$ with the orientation of $S^1$. A strict Morse presentation is one for which $t|_K$ has nondegenerate critical points, meaning its second derivative in a local coordinate is nonzero there, and pairwise distinct critical values. Write $t_{\min}:=\min_{x\in K}t(x)$, $t_{\max}:=\max_{x\in K}t(x)$, and $r(K)$ for the number of local maxima. A parenthesized $q$-braid is a smooth braid with $q$ strands, each strictly increasing in $t$, together with an ordered binary parenthesization of its lower endpoints and an ordered binary parenthesization of its upper endpoints.

For $n\ge0$, a degree-$n$ chord diagram is an oriented circle with $n$ disjoint unordered pairs of distinct points, called chords. Let $\mathcal A_n^{\mathrm{fr}}$ be the rational vector space on these diagrams modulo 4T, and let $\mathcal A_n^{\mathrm{un}}$ be its quotient by 1T as well. A 4T relation fixes one chord $pq$ and another chord endpoint $r$, moves the other endpoint of the second chord to just before or after $p$ and just before or after $q$, and takes the alternating sum of those four diagrams. A chord is isolated when it intersects no other chord, where intersection means that chord endpoints alternate around the circle; 1T sets every such diagram to zero. Put $\widehat{\mathcal A}^{\mathrm{fr/un}}_{\mathbb C}:=\prod_{n\ge0}(\mathcal A_n^{\mathrm{fr/un}}\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb C)$, with multiplication induced by connected sum of diagrams and unit the empty diagram. For $q$ ordered upward strands, let $\widehat{\mathcal A}_{\mathbb C}(q)$ be the completion of the associative algebra generated by $t_{ij}=t_{ji}$ for $1\le i<j\le q$, with relations $[t_{ij},t_{kl}]=0$ when $i,j,k,l$ are distinct and $[t_{ij},t_{ik}+t_{jk}]=0$ when $i,j,k$ are distinct. The generator $t_{ij}$ is a horizontal chord joining strands $i$ and $j$; multiplication stacks diagrams from bottom to top.

More generally, a compact strict Morse tangle $T$ is a compact oriented smooth one-dimensional submanifold of $\mathbb C\times[a,b]$, with distinct boundary points on the planes $t=a$ and $t=b$, transverse to those planes, and with nondegenerate interior critical points of height having distinct critical values. A tangle chord diagram is a finite set of unordered pairs of distinct interior points on the oriented tangle skeleton. Its 4T relation is the same local alternating relation as above on the skeleton. The unframed tangle quotient also sets to zero any chord whose endpoints are consecutive in the order along the same skeleton component; for a circle the order is cyclic and for an arc it is linear. The completed degreewise tangle diagram space is denoted $\widehat{\mathcal A}^{\mathrm{un}}_{\mathbb C}(T)$.

The unframed configuration series of a strict Morse presentation $K$ is the formal degreewise series
$$
Z(K):=\sum_{m\ge0}\frac1{(2\pi i)^m}\int_{t_{\min}<t_m<\cdots<t_1<t_{\max}}\ \sum_{P}(-1)^{\downarrow(P)}[D_P]_{\mathrm{un}}\bigwedge_{j=1}^m\frac{dz_j-dz'_j}{z_j-z'_j}\ \in\widehat{\mathcal A}^{\mathrm{un}}_{\mathbb C}.
$$
The ordered simplex is divided into chambers by the critical values of $t|_K$. In each chamber, $P$ ranges over choices, at each level $t_j$, of an unordered pair of distinct points $(z_j,t_j),(z'_j,t_j)$ of $K$. The diagram $D_P$ joins the corresponding preimages on the oriented parameter circle. The integer $\downarrow(P)$ counts endpoints at which $t$ decreases along the orientation of $K$. The differential form is pulled back to the chamber by the selected local branches. The degree-zero term is the empty diagram with coefficient $1$; the displayed integrals are interpreted as improper integrals on each chamber.

For a compact strict Morse tangle $T$, $Z(T)$ is given by the same formula with $T$ in place of $K$, the interval $(a,b)$ in place of $(t_{\min},t_{\max})$, the chord diagrams on the tangle skeleton in place of circle diagrams, and the corresponding unframed tangle quotient in place of $\widehat{\mathcal A}^{\mathrm{un}}_{\mathbb C}$. A parenthesized braid is a special case with no interior critical points.

For a parenthesized braid path $\gamma$ in the configuration space of $q$ distinct complex points, define its Knizhnik–Zamolodchikov (KZ) series by the degreewise iterated-integral holonomy of
$$\Omega_q=\frac1{2\pi i}\sum_{1\le i<j\le q}t_{ij}\,d\log(z_i-z_j).$$
Explicitly, if $\gamma:[0,1]\to\operatorname{Conf}_q(\mathbb C)$ is an ordinary path with noncolliding endpoints, its holonomy is
$$1+\sum_{m\ge1}\int_{0<t_m<\cdots<t_1<1}\gamma^*\Omega_q(t_1)\cdots\gamma^*\Omega_q(t_m).$$

$$
I(K):=Z(K)\,Z(H)^{-r(K)}\in\widehat{\mathcal A}^{\mathrm{un}}_{\mathbb C},

The normalization uses one copy of $Z(H)$ for each local maximum; its degree-zero term is $1$, so its inverse is interpreted in the product completion. This definition makes no assertion that the unnormalized KZ coefficients are rational or that equal Kontsevich series separate knot types.

Height increases upward, the right-bottom strand is the overstrand under the determinant crossing convention, and the labels at the ends record the ordered parenthesizations; no proof below relies on the drawing.

```tikz
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.82,thick]

\end{tikzpicture}
```

Fix the round metric and orientation on $S^3$. An **$m$-singular oriented knot** is a smooth immersion $K:S^1\to S^3$ with exactly $m$ distinct transverse double points and no other self-intersections; each double-point image has exactly two preimages with linearly independent tangent vectors, and the preimage pairs are disjoint. The knot has no framing. Choose disjoint small balls around its double points, each containing no other part of the singular knot. At each double point there are two **resolutions**, obtained by separating the two local branches in the ball; label them $+$ and $-$ so the resolved crossing signs are respectively $+1$ and $-1$ under the convention that, in a diagram whose positive viewing normal agrees with the ambient orientation, the sign is $\operatorname{sgn}\det(v_{\mathrm{over}},v_{\mathrm{under}})$ and the positive Artin half twist has sign $+1$.

A **framed oriented knot** is a smooth oriented embedding $K:S^1\hookrightarrow S^3$ together with a homotopy class through nowhere-zero smooth sections of its oriented rank-two normal bundle. For an immersion $K:S^1\to S^3$, including one with double points, define its branchwise normal bundle over the parameter circle by $\nu_K:=K^*TS^3/dK(TS^1)$, oriented so that a positive tangent followed by a positive normal basis gives the ambient orientation. Because $dK$ has rank one at every parameter, its image is locally a smooth line subbundle and this quotient is locally a rank-two bundle. Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the framed clauses below, so these normal quotient bundles have their smooth vector-bundle structures. A **framed $m$-singular knot** has finitely many transverse double points and finitely many simple zeroes of a smooth section of $\nu_K$, all disjoint; its number $m$ of singularities is the number of double points plus the number of zeroes. A simple zero is one at which the derivative of the section in an oriented local trivialization is nonzero. Resolve double points as above, extending the normal section over the local resolution balls; each resulting section determines a framing homotopy class. To resolve a framing zero at parameter $t=0$, choose the oriented normal trivialization so the section is $t e_1$ near $0$, with $e_2$ the positive quarter-turn of $e_1$; replace it by $t e_1+\delta e_2$ or $t e_1-\delta e_2$ for sufficiently small $\delta>0$. These are the $+$ and $-$ resolutions of that zero and determine the framing classes on the resolved knots.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring. For an $R$-valued ambient-isotopy invariant $V$ of unframed oriented knots and an $m$-singular knot $K$, its **finite difference** is
$$
D_mV(K):=\sum_{\epsilon\in\{+1,-1\}^m}\left(\prod_{i=1}^m\epsilon_i\right)V(K_\epsilon),
$$
where $K_\epsilon$ resolves singularity $i$ positively when $\epsilon_i=+1$ and negatively when $\epsilon_i=-1$. For $m=0$, set $D_0V(K)=V(K)$. The same formula defines $D_mV$ for an invariant of framed knots on framed singular knots, counting both double points and framing zeroes among the $m$ singularities. For one double point it reads $V(K_+)-V(K_-)$; the zero resolutions use the local normal-section model just specified. An invariant has **type at most $n$** if $D_{n+1}V$ vanishes on every $(n+1)$-singular object in its category. It has **exact type $n$** if it has type at most $n$ but not type at most $n-1$. Type at most $-1$ means the zero invariant, so a nonzero type-at-most-zero invariant has exact type zero. For an unframed link, replace $S^1$ by a finite disjoint union of oriented circles, allow marked self- or mixed double points, and use the same resolution sum. For a framed link, take a normal section on each component and count its simple zeroes together with all double points.

derivations.claim: Put $\alpha_{ij}=d\log(z_i-z_j)$. Since $z_i-z_j$ is nonzero on $\operatorname{Conf}_q(\mathbb C)$, in local coordinates $\alpha_{ij}=d(z_i-z_j)/(z_i-z_j)$ and $d\alpha_{ij}=0$ by equality of mixed partial derivatives. Thus $d\Omega_q=0$.

Write $a=t_{ij}$, $b=t_{kl}$ for two distinct chord generators. In the expansion of $\Omega_q\wedge\Omega_q$, the two ordered terms for these generators combine as $[a,b]\alpha_{ij}\wedge\alpha_{kl}$. If the pairs have four distinct indices, $[a,b]=0$ by [F1]; if they are the same pair, $\alpha_{ij}\wedge\alpha_{ij}=0$. Hence only pairs of generators supported on a common triple of strands can contribute.

Fix $i<j<k$ and put $a=t_{ij}$, $b=t_{ik}$, $c=t_{jk}$, $x=\alpha_{ij}$, $y=\alpha_{ik}$, and $z=\alpha_{jk}$. The tangled 4T relation on these three strands is exactly the pair of infinitesimal braid relations $[a,b+c]=0$ and $[b,a+c]=0$. The contribution of this triple is $[a,b]x\wedge y+[a,c]x\wedge z+[b,c]y\wedge z$. The infinitesimal braid relations in [F1] give $[a,c]=-[a,b]$ and $[b,c]=[a,b]$, so this is $[a,b](x\wedge y-x\wedge z+y\wedge z)$. With $u=z_i-z_j$ and $v=z_j-z_k$, we have $x=du/u$, $z=dv/v$, and $y=d(u+v)/(u+v)$. Direct expansion gives $x\wedge z+z\wedge y+y\wedge x=(1/(uv)-1/(v(u+v))-1/(u(u+v)))du\wedge dv=0$, which is equivalent to $x\wedge y-x\wedge z+y\wedge z=0$. Thus every triple contribution vanishes.

The repeated-pair, disjoint-pair, and three-index cases exhaust the expansion of $\Omega_q\wedge\Omega_q$; steps 2.1–3.1 show that each contribution is zero. Together with step 1.1 this gives $d\Omega_q=0$ and $\Omega_q\wedge\Omega_q=0$.

Fix a smooth path $\gamma$ and let $U(t)$ solve $\dot U=A_tU$, $U(0)=1$, where $A_t=\Omega_q(\dot\gamma(t))$. In each degree this is a finite linear ODE system, solved recursively by the iterated-integral formula. For a homotopy $\gamma(s,t)$ with fixed endpoints, set $A_s=\Omega_q(\partial_s\gamma)$ and $W=U^{-1}(\partial_sU-A_sU)$. Differentiating and using $\partial_tU=A_tU$ gives $\partial_tW=U^{-1}(\partial_sA_t-\partial_tA_s+[A_t,A_s])U$. The coefficient in parentheses is the evaluation of the flatness expression from step 4.1, so it is zero. Since the initial endpoint is fixed, $W(s,0)=0$ and hence $W(s,t)=0$; at the fixed terminal endpoint $A_s=0$, so $\partial_sU(s,1)=0$. The holonomy is therefore constant throughout the homotopy.

The KZ form is unchanged by relabeling the strands, since its sum runs over every unordered pair; endpoint strand permutations therefore act on holonomy by the same permutation of the $t_{ij}$. For $|i-j|\ge2$, the paths for $\sigma_i$ and $\sigma_j$ lie in disjoint two-point disks, so exchanging their time intervals is a fixed-endpoint homotopy and step 5.1 gives $\sigma_i\sigma_j=\sigma_j\sigma_i$. For three adjacent points, start at $(-1,0,1)$ and follow the configuration path $(-e^{\pi it},0,e^{\pi it})$, $0\le t\le1$. Its endpoints agree as unordered configurations with the three points reversed, and its pairwise distances stay bounded below by $1$. At $t=1/2$ the three real projections coincide. Small perturbations of the trajectories therefore remain collision-free and can separate the three projected crossing times in either of the two orders; both perturbed paths are homotopic to this rigid half-turn and give respectively $\sigma_i\sigma_{i+1}\sigma_i$ and $\sigma_{i+1}\sigma_i\sigma_{i+1}$. By step 5.1 their transports agree.

derivations.claim: Near a nondegenerate maximum, use the Morse coordinate $s=\sqrt{t_c-t}$ from [F2]. The two local branch functions satisfy $z_+(s)=z_c+a s+O(s^2)$ and $z_-(s)=z_c-a s+O(s^2)$ for some $a\ne0$; this follows because the tangle or knot immersion has nonzero tangent and $dt/ds=0$ at the critical point, so its tangent there is horizontal. Hence $|z_+(s)-z_-(s)|\asymp s$ and the short logarithmic form has absolute size at most $C\,ds/s$. A minimum has the same estimate after reversing $t$.

For a long chord with one endpoint on a needle and one outside it, compactness of the family gives a uniform positive lower bound on its denominator. The two choices that put this endpoint on opposite needle branches have opposite factors $(-1)^{\downarrow(P)}$. Their endpoint positions differ by at most $\varepsilon$, so the mean-value estimate for $\log(z-z')$ away from $z=z'$ bounds the difference of their integrands by $C\varepsilon$ times bounded remaining factors. Integration over the fixed simplex preserves the $O(\varepsilon)$ bound.

Order the chord endpoints on the small oriented component arc between the two branches near the maximum. The endpoints of the level closest to $t_c$ are adjacent on this arc. If their chord joins the two branches, it is isolated under the tangle or circle 1T rule, so its diagram vanishes by [F1, F3]. Thus every nonzero pairing approaching this critical face either has no short chord or has short chords nested below an interrupting long chord.

For a surviving nested chain of $k$ short chords, write their branch separations as $0<\delta_k<\cdots<\delta_1<\varepsilon$. Each short factor is bounded by $C\,d\delta_j/\delta_j$ by step 1.1. The long chord interrupting the short chord nearest the critical point has denominator bounded away from zero; integrating its level variable produces a factor $O(\delta_k)$ because its logarithmic primitive is Lipschitz there and its endpoint limits differ by $O(\delta_k)$. The whole nested contribution is therefore bounded by a constant times $\int_0^\varepsilon \frac{d\delta_1}{\delta_1}\cdots\int_0^{\delta_{k-1}}\frac{d\delta_k}{\delta_k}\,\delta_k=\varepsilon$, by repeated use of $\int_0^a(d\delta/\delta)\delta=a$. This also covers $k=1$. At any noncritical level-collision face, each chord still joins two distinct points of the embedded knot or tangle, so every within-chord denominator remains nonzero and has a positive lower bound locally. If a within-chord denominator tends to zero, the endpoints lie on the two branches meeting at a critical point and are covered by steps 1.1–2.1. There are finitely many faces and pairing types at fixed $m$, so the degree-$m$ chamber integrals converge absolutely.

A short chord joining the two needle branches is killed by 1T when it is the highest such chord; otherwise its nonzero diagram contains an interrupting long chord and the nested estimate of step 3.1 applies. Pairing the long-chord endpoint choices as in step 1.2 supplies an additional $O(\varepsilon)$ factor. There are finitely many pairing types in fixed degree $m$, so their sum is bounded by $C_m\varepsilon$ and tends to zero.

A strict Morse presentation is one for which $t|_K$ has nondegenerate critical points, meaning its second derivative in a local coordinate is nonzero there, and pairwise distinct critical values. Write $t_{\min}:=\min_{x\in K}t(x)$, $t_{\max}:=\max_{x\in K}t(x)$, and $r(K)$ for the number of local maxima. A parenthesized $q$-braid is a smooth braid with $q$ strands, each strictly increasing in $t$, together with an ordered binary parenthesization of its lower endpoints and an ordered binary parenthesization of its upper endpoints.

For $n\ge0$, a degree-$n$ chord diagram is an oriented circle with $n$ disjoint unordered pairs of distinct points, called chords. Let $\mathcal A_n^{\mathrm{fr}}$ be the rational vector space on these diagrams modulo 4T, and let $\mathcal A_n^{\mathrm{un}}$ be its quotient by 1T as well. A 4T relation fixes one chord $pq$ and another chord endpoint $r$, moves the other endpoint of the second chord to just before or after $p$ and just before or after $q$, and takes the alternating sum of those four diagrams. A chord is isolated when it intersects no other chord, where intersection means that chord endpoints alternate around the circle; 1T sets every such diagram to zero. Put $\widehat{\mathcal A}^{\mathrm{fr/un}}_{\mathbb C}:=\prod_{n\ge0}(\mathcal A_n^{\mathrm{fr/un}}\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb C)$, with multiplication induced by connected sum of diagrams and unit the empty diagram. For $q$ ordered upward strands, let $\widehat{\mathcal A}_{\mathbb C}(q)$ be the completion of the associative algebra generated by $t_{ij}=t_{ji}$ for $1\le i<j\le q$, with relations $[t_{ij},t_{kl}]=0$ when $i,j,k,l$ are distinct and $[t_{ij},t_{ik}+t_{jk}]=0$ when $i,j,k$ are distinct. The generator $t_{ij}$ is a horizontal chord joining strands $i$ and $j$; multiplication stacks diagrams from bottom to top.

More generally, a compact strict Morse tangle $T$ is a compact oriented smooth one-dimensional submanifold of $\mathbb C\times[a,b]$, with distinct boundary points on the planes $t=a$ and $t=b$, transverse to those planes, and with nondegenerate interior critical points of height having distinct critical values. A tangle chord diagram is a finite set of unordered pairs of distinct interior points on the oriented tangle skeleton. Its 4T relation is the same local alternating relation as above on the skeleton. The unframed tangle quotient also sets to zero any chord whose endpoints are consecutive in the order along the same skeleton component; for a circle the order is cyclic and for an arc it is linear. The completed degreewise tangle diagram space is denoted $\widehat{\mathcal A}^{\mathrm{un}}_{\mathbb C}(T)$.

The unframed configuration series of a strict Morse presentation $K$ is the formal degreewise series
$$
Z(K):=\sum_{m\ge0}\frac1{(2\pi i)^m}\int_{t_{\min}<t_m<\cdots<t_1<t_{\max}}\ \sum_{P}(-1)^{\downarrow(P)}[D_P]_{\mathrm{un}}\bigwedge_{j=1}^m\frac{dz_j-dz'_j}{z_j-z'_j}\ \in\widehat{\mathcal A}^{\mathrm{un}}_{\mathbb C}.
$$
The ordered simplex is divided into chambers by the critical values of $t|_K$. In each chamber, $P$ ranges over choices, at each level $t_j$, of an unordered pair of distinct points $(z_j,t_j),(z'_j,t_j)$ of $K$. The diagram $D_P$ joins the corresponding preimages on the oriented parameter circle. The integer $\downarrow(P)$ counts endpoints at which $t$ decreases along the orientation of $K$. derivations.claim: First consider a horizontal deformation of a closed strict Morse knot that fixes the height function and a neighborhood of every critical point. On a compactified branch chamber, write the full degree-$m$ form as the finite sum $\omega_m=\sum_P(-1)^{\downarrow(P)}[D_P]\bigwedge_{j=1}^m d\log(z_j-z'_j)$, with each differential taken in the level and deformation variables. Every branch difference is nonzero because the tangle is embedded and has no critical points; hence each logarithmic factor is closed and $d\omega_m=0$. Stokes on the chamber cylinder reduces equality of the two end integrals to vanishing on its codimension-one faces.

The upper and lower closure caps lie in height bands disjoint from $T$ and the return arc. Each cap has exactly two points at every regular level in its band. In a nonempty pairing on an upper cap, the chord at the highest selected level has an empty subarc on the cap side; on a lower cap use the chord at the lowest selected level. In either case that chord is isolated, so [F4] kills the diagram. The return arc has exactly one point at each level of $[a,b]$, so it has no internal pairing. Hence cap and return factors contribute only their degree-zero units.

On an outer-level face, the extreme endpoints are fixed, so the restricted form has no $ds$ component and vanishes. On a face where adjacent levels coincide, if the two chords use the same two branches, their logarithmic forms agree and their wedge is zero. If they use four distinct branches, exchanging the two chord choices preserves the diagram and reverses the wedge sign, so the terms cancel in pairs. If they use exactly three branches, the 4T relation [F4] groups the six choices into one common diagram coefficient times $\alpha_{12}\wedge\alpha_{23}+\alpha_{23}\wedge\alpha_{31}+\alpha_{31}\wedge\alpha_{12}$, where $\alpha_{ij}=d\log(z_i-z_j)$. Setting $f=z_1-z_2$, $g=z_2-z_3$, and $z_3-z_1=-(f+g)$, direct expansion gives the coefficient $1/(fg)-1/(g(f+g))-1/(f(f+g))=0$. Thus every codimension-one face integral vanishes, so Stokes gives equal end integrals. Summing the finitely many chambers and composing the fixed critical pieces proves horizontal-deformation invariance of $Z$.

In $[a,b]$, any pairing using the return arc must join its point $R$ to a point $z$ of $T$, since the return arc has one point per level. For $R>1+\sup_T|z|$, its logarithmic factor is $d\log(z-R)=dz/(z-R)$, with denominator at least $R-\sup_T|z|$. On each compact branch the integral of $|dz|$ is bounded by its finite arc length; after integrating this selected level, the remaining degree-$(m-1)$ pairing integrals are absolutely convergent by [F3]. Hence each mixed term is $O((R-\sup_T|z|)^{-1})$. There are finitely many pairing types, so their total tends to zero. Pairings whose endpoints all lie on $T$ give exactly $\operatorname{cl}(Z(T))$. With the cap and return units from step 1.2, this proves $Z(K_R)\to\operatorname{cl}(Z(T))$ degreewise. Varying $R$ moves only regular horizontal arcs while keeping the height function and cap critical neighborhoods fixed, so step 1.1 makes $Z(K_R)$ independent of $R$. The limit is therefore its value for every sufficiently large $R$.

At the regular joining plane, smoothing the single matched upper and lower endpoints forms the neck in the connected-sum construction. Cutting that neck recovers the closures of $T_2$ and $T_1$, so the closure of their composite is their oriented connected sum as stated. On diagrams, the endpoints from $T_2$ occur before those from $T_1$ around the closure cut; applying $\operatorname{cl}$ to a stacked diagram therefore gives exactly the concatenated circle diagram defining $\#$. Apply [F3] to the tangle composite and close the resulting degreewise identity to obtain the claimed series equality.

Near $z=0$, substitute $G_0(z)=f(z)z^a$ with $f(z)=1+\sum_{n\ge1}f_nz^n$. Comparing coefficients in the differential equation gives $(n-\operatorname{ad}_a)f_n=-b\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}f_j$, where $\operatorname{ad}_a(x)=[a,x]$. On the degree-$N$ quotient, $\operatorname{ad}_a$ raises degree and is nilpotent, so $(n-\operatorname{ad}_a)^{-1}=\sum_{s=0}^{N}(\operatorname{ad}_a)^s/n^{s+1}$ is defined. This determines every $f_n$ uniquely. If $S_n=\sum_{j=0}^n\|f_j\|$ in any norm on the finite-dimensional quotient, the recurrence gives $S_n\le(1+C_N/n)S_{n-1}$ for a constant $C_N$; hence $S_n$ grows at most polynomially, and $f$ converges for $|z|<1$. It solves the equation by termwise differentiation.

Replacing $z$ by $1-z$ and interchanging $a,b$ gives the same recurrence at $z=1$ and uniquely constructs $G_1(z)=g(1-z)(1-z)^b$ with $g(0)=1$. The same coefficient recursion, inductively in the specified nested collision tree, gives a unique regularized transport after removing $\rho^{A_S}$.

For a compact strict Morse tangle $T$, $Z(T)$ is given by the same formula with $T$ in place of $K$, the interval $(a,b)$ in place of $(t_{\min},t_{\max})$, the chord diagrams on the tangle skeleton in place of circle diagrams, and the corresponding unframed tangle quotient in place of $\widehat{\mathcal A}^{\mathrm{un}}_{\mathbb C}$. A parenthesized braid is a special case with no interior critical points.

For a parenthesized braid path $\gamma$ in the configuration space of $q$ distinct complex points, define its Knizhnik–Zamolodchikov (KZ) series by the degreewise iterated-integral holonomy of
$$\Omega_q=\frac1{2\pi i}\sum_{1\le i<j\le q}t_{ij}\,d\log(z_i-z_j).$$
Explicitly, if $\gamma:[0,1]\to\operatorname{Conf}_q(\mathbb C)$ is an ordinary path with noncolliding endpoints, its holonomy is
$$1+\sum_{m\ge1}\int_{0<t_m<\cdots<t_1<1}\gamma^*\Omega_q(t_1)\cdots\gamma^*\Omega_q(t_m).$$
A tangential endpoint is a limiting collision configuration together with a specified nonzero first-order direction of approach for each colliding cluster. When endpoints have such clusters prescribed by the parenthesizations, the holonomy is the constant term after removing the local logarithmic factors $\exp(t_{ij}\log\varepsilon/(2\pi i))$ at each tangential endpoint. A change between the two parenthesizations of three consecutive strands is encoded by the regularized transport $\Phi_{\mathrm{KZ}}$.

For parenthesized braids the KZ holonomy takes values in the framed strand algebra, where only tangled 4T is imposed; passing from a closed framed strand diagram to an unframed knot applies the quotient by isolated-chord 1T. Fix a standard hump $H$ by starting with the two-critical-point unknot and inserting one local birth of a maximum-minimum pair; thus $H$ has two local maxima. The normalized unframed Kontsevich series of $K$ is
$$
I(K):=Z(K)\,Z(H)^{-r(K)}\in\widehat{\mathcal A}^{\mathrm{un}}_{\mathbb C},
$$
The normalization uses one copy of $Z(H)$ for each local maximum; its degree-zero term is $1$, so its inverse is interpreted in the product completion. This definition makes no assertion that the unnormalized KZ coefficients are rational or that equal Kontsevich series separate knot types.
