derivations.claim: If an edge does not meet the basepoint circle, its map is the identity on the basepoint factor and hence commutes with $X_p$. If the edge merges the basepoint circle with another circle, associativity gives $m(Xa\otimes b)=X\,m(a\otimes b)$. If it splits the basepoint circle, the Frobenius identity gives $\Delta(Xa)=(X\otimes1)\Delta(a)=(1\otimes X)\Delta(a)$; on $a=1,X$ these are respectively $X\otimes X$ and $0$ on all three sides. Thus every edge map commutes with $X_p$, so $\operatorname{im}(X_p)$ is a subcomplex.

By [F3], the unreduced differential already squares to zero, and by step 1.1 it preserves $\operatorname{im}(X_p)$; thus the induced quotient differential also squares to zero. In each state the based factor is $\mathcal A=\mathbb Z\{1,X\}$, and $X_p$ has image $\mathbb Z\{X\}$. Therefore the quotient factor is $\mathbb Z\{1\}$, with raw quantum degree $+1$; subtracting one gives reduced degree $0$.

After cutting the based circle, every state has one distinguished interval factor $M$. The quotient identification sends the surviving based label $1$ to $1\in M$. For a merge into that interval, $m(1\otimes1)=1$ and $m(X\otimes1)=0$ in the quotient, exactly the displayed $m_M$; for a split, $\Delta(1)=1\otimes X+X\otimes1$ and the term with $X$ on the distinguished interval is zero in $M$, leaving $X\otimes1$, exactly $\Delta_M(1)$. Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the smooth normal-bundle structure used in the
framing clause. For a knot component $K$, its normal bundle is the fibrewise
quotient $\nu K=TS^3|_K/TK$, and a normal section is a smooth section of this
bundle.

Let $D$ be a regular oriented link diagram in a projection plane $P$ of an
oriented $3$-sphere, after moving the link off the point at infinity. Fix the
unit viewing normal $n$ pointing toward the viewer. Orient $P$ by the rule that
an ordered basis $(u,v)$ of $P$ is positive exactly when $(n,u,v)$ is a positive
basis of the ambient $3$-space. At a crossing $c$, let $v_{\rm over}$ and
$v_{\rm under}$ be the nonzero projected tangent vectors following the
orientations of the overpassing and underpassing strands. Define
$$\operatorname{sgn}(c):=\operatorname{sgn}\det_P(v_{\rm over},v_{\rm under})\in\{+1,-1\}.$$
Reversing the orientation of $P$ reverses every crossing sign.

This convention makes the positive geometric Artin half twist positive. In
the braid chart $(x,y,t)$ with ambient orientation $(x,y,t)$, view along $+y$;
the induced positive orientation of the $(x,t)$ projection plane is the ordered
basis $(\partial_t,\partial_x)$. For the positive half twist, label $i$ moves
from $x=-h$ to $x=h$ below the midpoint, while label $i+1$ moves from $x=h$ to
$x=-h$ above it, with $h>0$. Thus the over and under projected tangent vectors
in coordinates $(t,x)$ are $(1,-2h)$ and $(1,2h)$, whose determinant is
$4h>0$.

The **writhe** of $D$ is
$$\operatorname{wr}(D):=\sum_{c\text{ a crossing of }D}\operatorname{sgn}(c).$$
For a link component $K_i$, its **self-writhe**
$\operatorname{wr}_i(D)$ is the sum over crossings whose two branches belong to
$K_i$; the total writhe also includes all mixed crossings between distinct
components.

The **blackboard framing** of a component of $D$ is the homotopy class of the
normal section represented by the positive quarter-turn in $P$ of the projected
oriented tangent. The projection is an immersion, so this vector never
vanishes; it is perpendicular to the projected tangent, hence also to the
spatial tangent, and therefore represents a nonzero normal section of the
component in the ambient $3$-sphere.

```tikz
  \draw[->] (-1,0) -- (1,0) node[right] {$v_{\rm over}$};
  \draw[->] (0,-1) -- (0,1) node[above] {$v_{\rm under}$};
  \node[above left] at (0,0) {$+1$};
\end{tikzpicture}
```

In the displayed local chart, the over tangent is the positive horizontal
vector and the under tangent is the positive vertical vector, so the determinant
is $+1$. This figure illustrates the determinant rule only; no proof below

Let $D$ be a nonempty finite regular oriented link diagram in an oriented $3$-sphere, with finite crossing set $C(D)$. Fix a unit viewing normal $n$ and orient the projection plane $P$ so $(u,v)$ is positive exactly when $(n,u,v)$ is positive in the ambient $3$-space. At a crossing $c$, define its sign as the sign of $\det_P(v_{\rm over},v_{\rm under})$, where the two nonzero projected tangent vectors follow the oriented over- and under-strands. Let $n_+$ and $n_-$ be the numbers of positive and negative crossings.

Set $\mathcal A=\mathbb Z[X]/(X^2)$, with $\deg(1)=1$ and $\deg(X)=-1$. Its unit, multiplication, counit, and comultiplication are
$$
\eta(1)=1,\qquad m(1\otimes1)=1,\quad m(1\otimes X)=m(X\otimes1)=X,\quad m(X\otimes X)=0,
$$
$$
\epsilon(1)=0,\quad\epsilon(X)=1,\qquad \Delta(1)=1\otimes X+X\otimes1,\quad\Delta(X)=X\otimes X.
$$
Thus $m$ and $\Delta$ have quantum degree $-1$, while $\eta$ and $\epsilon$ have degree $+1$.

Choose a total order $c_1<\cdots<c_n$ on $C(D)$. A resolution state is a function $v:C(D)\to\{0,1\}$; at $v(c)=0$ use the A-smoothing and at $v(c)=1$ use the B-smoothing from the Kauffman source chart. Write $|v|=\sum_c v(c)$, let $D_v$ be the crossingless resolution, and let $k(v)$ be its number of circles. Assign the state module $\mathcal A^{\otimes k(v)}$. For an edge $v\to v+e_j$ changing crossing $c_j$ from $0$ to $1$, use $m$ if the local smoothing merges two circles and $\Delta$ if it splits one circle, tensored with the identity on all other factors, and multiply this map by $(-1)^{\sum_{i<j}v(c_i)}$. The resulting direct sum has cohomological degree
$$i(v)=|v|-n_-$$
and the generator with circle labels $1$ or $X$ has quantum degree
$$j(v)=|v|+n_+-2n_-+\sum_{\text{circle labels }a}\deg(a).$$
This defines the normalized integral Khovanov cube and its candidate degree-zero cochain differential; the assertion that the differential squares to zero is a separate lemma.

```tikzcd

\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal A \arrow[r,"\mathrm{id}\otimes m"'] & \mathcal A\otimes\mathcal A
```

Rank-nullity in this bounded rational complex gives $\dim C^i=\dim H^i+\dim\operatorname{im}d^i+\dim\operatorname{im}d^{i-1}$; alternating over $i$ cancels the image dimensions. Let $D$ be a nonempty finite regular oriented link diagram in an oriented $3$-sphere, with finite crossing set $C(D)$. Fix a unit viewing normal $n$ and orient the projection plane $P$ so $(u,v)$ is positive exactly when $(n,u,v)$ is positive in the ambient $3$-space. At a crossing $c$, define its sign as the sign of $\det_P(v_{\rm over},v_{\rm under})$, where the two nonzero projected tangent vectors follow the oriented over- and under-strands. Let $n_+$ and $n_-$ be the numbers of positive and negative crossings.

Set $\mathcal A=\mathbb Z[X]/(X^2)$, with $\deg(1)=1$ and $\deg(X)=-1$. Its unit, multiplication, counit, and comultiplication are
$$
\eta(1)=1,\qquad m(1\otimes1)=1,\quad m(1\otimes X)=m(X\otimes1)=X,\quad m(X\otimes X)=0,
$$
$$
\epsilon(1)=0,\quad\epsilon(X)=1,\qquad \Delta(1)=1\otimes X+X\otimes1,\quad\Delta(X)=X\otimes X.
$$
Thus $m$ and $\Delta$ have quantum degree $-1$, while $\eta$ and $\epsilon$ have degree $+1$.

Choose a total order $c_1<\cdots<c_n$ on $C(D)$. A resolution state is a function $v:C(D)\to\{0,1\}$; at $v(c)=0$ use the A-smoothing and at $v(c)=1$ use the B-smoothing from the Kauffman source chart. Write $|v|=\sum_c v(c)$, let $D_v$ be the crossingless resolution, and let $k(v)$ be its number of circles. Assign the state module $\mathcal A^{\otimes k(v)}$. For an edge $v\to v+e_j$ changing crossing $c_j$ from $0$ to $1$, use $m$ if the local smoothing merges two circles and $\Delta$ if it splits one circle, tensored with the identity on all other factors, and multiply this map by $(-1)^{\sum_{i<j}v(c_i)}$. The resulting direct sum has cohomological degree
$$i(v)=|v|-n_-$$
and the generator with circle labels $1$ or $X$ has quantum degree
$$j(v)=|v|+n_+-2n_-+\sum_{\text{circle labels }a}\deg(a).$$
This defines the normalized integral Khovanov cube and its candidate degree-zero cochain differential; the assertion that the differential squares to zero is a separate lemma.

The Frobenius identity that controls a merge-split face is represented by the two equal composites below. The diagram records the maps only; the proof verifies the equality on the basis $\{1,X\}^{\otimes2}$ and does not rely on the drawing.

```tikzcd
\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal A \arrow[r,"m"] \arrow[d,"\Delta\otimes\mathrm{id}"'] & \mathcal A \arrow[d,"\Delta"] \\
\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal A \arrow[r,"\mathrm{id}\otimes m"'] & \mathcal A\otimes\mathcal A
```

Let $(D,p)$ be a finite regular oriented diagram of a knot with a basepoint $p$ away from the crossings, and let $C(D)$ be its normalized integral Khovanov cochain complex. At each resolution state, let $X_p$ act by multiplication by $X$ on the tensor factor for the circle containing $p$, and by the identity on every other circle factor. The basepoint action is the direct sum of these statewise maps. Define the reduced cochain complex by
$$\widetilde C(D,p):=C(D)/\operatorname{im}(X_p),$$
with the same cohomological grading and with reduced quantum degree $\widetilde j=j-1$ for the class represented by a state whose basepoint circle is labelled $1$. Its cohomology is the reduced integral Khovanov cohomology $\widetilde{Kh}^{i,\widetilde j}(D,p)$. The unknot is normalized so that its reduced group lies in bidegree $(0,0)$.

Equivalently, cut the based knot at $p$ to a one-interval tangle. Put $M=\mathbb Z$ in quantum degree $0$ with $X\cdot1=0$. A resolution with $k$ closed circles and the distinguished interval is assigned $\mathcal A^{\otimes k}\otimes M$. An edge that merges a circle into the interval uses $m_M(1\otimes1)=1$ and $m_M(X\otimes1)=0$; an edge that splits the interval uses $\Delta_M(1)=X\otimes1$, where the circle factor is written first and the interval factor second. Edges not meeting the interval use $m$ or $\Delta$. This based tangle cube is the quotient complex above, with the stated quantum shift.

The integral signed Khovanov cubes have the local graded cancellation models described below. They are chain homotopy equivalences over every fixed exterior resolution, commute with exterior saddle differentials, and commute with multiplication by $X$ at every marked point outside the local disk. Consequently they also give chain homotopy equivalences after taking the reduced quotient. For the crossing with A-smoothing the identity matching and B-smoothing the cap-cup matching, the two three-crossing braid cubes with words $121$ and $212$ retract to the same three-term complex. The two-crossing inverse-pair cube retracts to the identity matching in local cohomological degree one and quantum shift upward by one. derivations.claim: **Crossing order and planar isotopy.** Reordering adjacent crossing coordinates $a,b$ is corrected by the diagonal state factor $s(v)=(-1)^{v(a)v(b)}$: on an $a$-edge its ratio is $(-1)^{v(b)}$, and on a $b$-edge it is $(-1)^{v(a)}$, exactly the sign change from swapping their order. Thus local crossings can be ordered first, and can be restored to the original order afterward by explicit chain isomorphisms. A planar isotopy bijects labelled resolution circles and saddles, so its factor permutations give a grading-preserving chain isomorphism.

**Both curls, with natural contractions.** For a positive curl the local differential is multiplication from a small circle and a continuing arc. Put the small-circle factor first, denote the dot on the continuing arc by $x$, and use coordinates $1\otimes u+X\otimes v$. The map is $(u,v)\mapsto u+xv$. Its $1$-label component is the identity; cancel it, leaving $v\mapsto X\otimes v-1\otimes xv$ in degree zero. Equivalently this is $j=\Delta-\iota m\Delta$, with $\iota(v)=1\otimes v$; it sends $1$ to $X\otimes1-1\otimes X$ and $X$ to $X\otimes X$. The canceled pair has inverse identity, so its contraction is the explicit cancellation rule of [F5], agreeing with the cochain identity-cone contraction in [F6]. The survivor has quantum shift $\{1\}$. For a negative curl the map is $v\mapsto( xv,v)$ into the circle coordinates; cancel its identity $X$-label component. The remaining $1$-label coordinate is in local degree one and has quantum shift $\{-2\}$, giving $[-1]\{-2\}$. These descriptions commute with exterior saddles because the dot and the local saddle commute with them by the displayed Frobenius identities; they therefore contract the total complexes, including exterior differentials with their totalization signs. The additional normalizations are $\{-1\}$ for a positive curl and $[1]\{2\}$ for a negative curl, canceling the respective raw shifts.

**The signed RII square.** In the four states of the Remark take $U=E$, $V=I$, $W=E\sqcup\bigcirc$, $Z=E$, after ordering the $(I,E)$ crossing first and the $(E,I)$ crossing second as in [F5]. That step gives the exact differential $u\mapsto(su,xu,u)$ and $(v,w_1,w_X)\mapsto tv-w_1-yw_X$, with $ts=x+y$, and the chain maps $i(v)=(v,tv,0)$, $p(v,w_1,w_X)=v-sw_X$, and homotopy $h^1=w_X$, $h^2(z)=(0,-z,0)$. Their checked identity is $1-ip=dh+hd$, $pi=1$. Thus the two canceled pairs are actual contractible summands over the integral exterior cube and the surviving identity matching is in local degree one with quantum increase one. This is precisely the raw shift $[-1]\{-1\}$ in the Statement. An RII pair has one positive and one negative crossing, so its normalization changes by $[1]\{1\}$ and cancels that shift. A quadratic tangency has two branches which are both graphs over their common tangent direction; orienting these graphs temporarily in the same direction puts every underlying RII picture into this model or the opposite crossing order. Reversing either actual strand arrow only changes crossing signs, still one of each, and does not change the A/B maps. Rotation of the local coordinate chart transports the same model; its crossing-order correction was proved in step 1.1.

**The signed RIII model.** Let $P_i$ denote the crossing complex with A-state $I$ and B-state $E_i$; this description fixes the smoothing convention without using a crossing-sign mnemonic. In [F5], both words $P_1P_2P_1$ and $P_2P_1P_2$ are retracted by two explicit cancellations to $I\xrightarrow{\binom{s_1}{s_2}}E_1\oplus E_2\xrightarrow{\begin{pmatrix}-u&v\\ w&-z\end{pmatrix}}E_1E_2\oplus E_2E_1.$ Here $u$ appends $E_2$ below $E_1$, $v$ prepends $E_1$ above $E_2$, $w$ prepends $E_2$ above $E_1$, and $z$ appends $E_1$ below $E_2$; each is the actual ordered-tensor saddle specified there. The canceled maps are the $-1$ from the circle's $1$ coordinate in state $101$ to state $111$, and then the $+1$ from state $001$ to the circle's $X$ coordinate. The remaining cube signs are exactly the displayed matrix on both sides. Inclusion and projection after the coordinate changes of [F5] compose to mutually inverse chain maps up to the given contractions. These maps preserve quantum degree and commute with all exterior differentials by [F5]. This proves the raw, unshifted model RIII equivalence with explicit chain maps and homotopies.

**All height and orientation variants.** The opposite crossing complex $N_i$ has A-state $E_i$ and B-state $I$. Step 2.2 shows that $Q_i=N_i[1]\{1\}$ is a two-sided inverse of $P_i$ up to local chain homotopy; the contractions are natural under adjoining other crossings. Thus the relation $aba\simeq bab$, with $a=P_1,b=P_2$, also gives the relations with exponent triples $---$, $++-$, $-++$, $+--$ and $--+$, interpreting negative exponents by these explicit inverses. The $---$ relation is the inverse relation; $aba^{-1}\simeq b^{-1}ab$ follows by multiplication on the left by $b^{-1}$ and on the right by $a^{-1}$; $a^{-1}ba\simeq bab^{-1}$ follows by multiplication on the left by $a^{-1}$ and on the right by $b^{-1}$; their inverses give $+--$ and $--+$. Each multiplication is stacking a crossing complex and composing the actual chain maps and homotopies, so this is an operation on complexes, not an appeal to a braid-group invariant. A generic transverse triple event can be put in a small rectangle with all three branches monotone in one longitudinal coordinate: choose a direction transverse to their three tangents and use a sufficiently thin rectangle. Their two diagrams have braid words $121$ and $212$. The crossings concern the pairs of strands $AB,AC,BC$, respectively; a strict height order has precisely the six transitive sign patterns just listed, excluding the two cyclic patterns $+-+$ and $-+-$. For any such pattern the counts of $N_i$ agree on both sides, so the extra shifts in $Q_i$ cancel when removed. The actual oriented RIII move retains each of its three crossing signs; hence its normalizing $n_+,n_-$ shifts also agree. Actual strand arrows may be arbitrary because the raw cube depends only on the smoothing chart. This proves every oriented RIII variant.

By the Frobenius formulas it commutes with $X_p$ even if its continuing arc lies on the distinguished resolution component. The same commutation for every RII/RIII map and homotopy, including compositions and inverse-pair cancellations, is proved in [F5]. Consequently all equations $pi=1$ and $1-ip=dh+hd$ descend modulo $\operatorname{im}X_p$. By [F4] this is exactly the reduced quotient, or equivalently the interval-module complex. Steps 1.1–3.1 and the checked shifts therefore prove every unreduced and based assertion of the Statement. All local constructions use finite integral formulas and are choice-free.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $D$ and $D'$ be regular oriented link diagrams.
Then $D$ and $D'$ represent equivalent oriented links if and only if $D'$ can be
obtained from $D$ by a finite sequence of planar isotopies and oriented
Reidemeister moves R1, R2, R3.

Let $D,D'$ be finite regular oriented link diagrams related by a planar isotopy or one oriented Reidemeister move. Let $\bar C(D)$ be the integral signed state cube before the writhe shifts, with cohomological degree $|v|$ and quantum degree $|v|+\sum\deg(a)$, and normalize it by $C(D)=\bar C(D)[n_-]\{2n_--n_+\}$ to obtain the state degrees $i=|v|-n_-$ and $j=|v|+n_+-2n_-+\sum\deg(a)$. Before normalization, a positive type-I curl gives $\bar C(D_+)\simeq\bar C(D)\{1\}$, a negative type-I curl gives $\bar C(D_-)\simeq\bar C(D)[-1]\{-2\}$, a type-II move gives $\bar C(D_{II})\simeq\bar C(D)[-1]\{-1\}$, and a type-III move gives an unshifted equivalence. Consequently the normalized complexes are bigraded chain homotopy equivalent. If $D,D'$ are based knot diagrams and the move disk is disjoint from the basepoint, the same chain homotopy equivalence descends to their reduced quotient complexes, equivalently to the cut-tangle complexes with interval module $M=\mathbb Z$, $X\cdot1=0$.

For a finite regular oriented link diagram $D$ with $n$ ordered crossings, the procedure that enumerates all $2^n$ smoothing states, assigns one copy of $\mathcal A=\mathbb Z[X]/(X^2)$ per resolution circle, places a generator in degrees $i=|v|-n_-$ and $j=|v|+n_+-2n_-+\sum\deg(a)$, and sums the signed merge or split edge maps terminates after finitely many operations. Its output is a finite direct sum of finite-rank free abelian groups with a differential of bidegree $(1,0)$ satisfying $d^2=0$; hence it is a bounded bigraded cochain complex.

A chain map $f:C_\bullet\to D_\bullet$ is a **chain homotopy equivalence** if
there exists a chain map $g:D_\bullet\to C_\bullet$ such that
$$g\circ f\simeq1_C,\qquad f\circ g\simeq1_D.$$

Such a map $g$ is called a **homotopy inverse** of $f$.

derivations.claim: By [F1] and [F2], choose a finite sequence $D=D_0,D_1,\ldots,D_r=D'$ whose successive diagrams differ by planar isotopy or one oriented Reidemeister move. By [F3], each pair has a bigraded chain homotopy equivalence, with chain maps in both directions and homotopies from their composites to the respective identities. The normalization in that supplier cancels the raw shifts, so these maps have bidegree $(0,0)$.

A chain map takes cocycles to cocycles and coboundaries to coboundaries. If two chain maps differ by $dh+hd$, their values on a cocycle differ by a coboundary, so they induce the same cohomology map. Thus each equivalence in step 1.1 gives mutually inverse maps in every bidegree. Composing the finitely many induced isomorphisms identifies the cohomology of $C(D)$ and $C(D')$. It follows that the groups $Kh^{i,j}(L)$ are independent of the chosen diagram up to bigraded isomorphism. The empty sequence gives the identity, and no assertion of a canonical isomorphism for all move sequences is needed.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$.

1. **Compact main case.** Let $M$ be a compact smooth manifold, possibly with boundary, let $N$ be a smooth manifold without boundary, let $F:M\times I\to N$ be a smooth isotopy of embeddings that is constant near the ends of $I$, and let $W$ be an open neighbourhood of $F(M\times I)$ in $N$. Then there is an ambient isotopy $H:N\times I\to N$ with $H_0=\mathrm{id}_N$, every $H_t$ a diffeomorphism, $H_t\circ F_0=F_t$ for all $t\in I$, $H_t=\mathrm{id}_N$ outside $W$ for every $t$, and $H_t$ stationary near the ends; if $F$ is constant near the ends with parameter $\varepsilon$, then $H_t=\mathrm{id}_N$ for $t\le\varepsilon/2$ and $H_t=H_1$ for $t\ge1-\varepsilon/2$.
2. **Relative form.** Let $N$ be boundaryless, $U\subseteq N$ open, $A\subseteq U$ compact, and let $F:U\times I\to N$ be a smooth isotopy of embeddings whose track image is open in $N\times I$. Then there is a compactly supported ambient isotopy $H$ of $N$ with $H_t\circ F_0=F_t$ on a neighbourhood of $A$ for every $t$.
3. **Boundary stratum.** If $N$ has boundary and $F(M\times I)\subseteq\partial N$, then the ambient isotopy of clause 1 can be chosen with every $H_t$ carrying $\partial N$ onto itself; if $F(M\times I)\subseteq N\setminus\partial N$, it can be chosen compactly supported in $N\setminus\partial N$.
4. **General isotopies.** For the same compact source (possibly with boundary) and boundaryless target as in clause 1, every smooth isotopy extends with support in a compact subset of any prescribed neighbourhood $W$ of $F(M\times I)$. The endpoint-constancy hypothesis and the stationary-end conclusion are both omitted; all other conclusions of clause 1 hold.

Assume countable choice. Let $(D,p)$ and $(D',p')$ be finite regular diagrams of the same oriented smooth knot, with marks away from crossings. Remove a small open arc about each mark and regard each complementary diagram as a one-interval tangle diagram in a disk, using the complementary disk in the projection sphere. Identify their two boundary endpoints and short oriented product collars. The resulting proper arcs can be realized in one standard smooth three-ball so that they are smoothly isotopic with those endpoints and collars fixed. Their diagrams are connected by a finite sequence of planar isotopies and oriented Reidemeister moves supported away from those collars. This holds when the two diagrams coincide and only the mark has moved along the knot.

Let $D,D'$ be finite regular oriented link diagrams related by a planar isotopy or one oriented Reidemeister move. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

Let $D$ be a finite regular oriented diagram of a link with $n_+$ positive crossings, $n_-$ negative crossings, writhe $w=n_+-n_-$, and $n=n_++n_-$. For each resolution state $v$, let $k(v)$ be its number of circles and let $D_v$ use the A-smoothing at coordinates $0$ and B-smoothing at coordinates $1$. Put $\delta=-A^2-A^{-2}$ and define the normalized bracket
$$f_D(A):=(-A^3)^{-w}\sum_{v:C(D)\to\{0,1\}} A^{n-2|v|}\delta^{k(v)-1}.$$
For integral unreduced Khovanov cohomology, define $\chi_q(Kh(D))=\sum_{i,j}(-1)^i\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb Z}Kh^{i,j}(D)q^j$. For reduced cohomology use its basepoint quantum grading $\widetilde j$ and define $\widetilde\chi_q=\sum_{i,\widetilde j}(-1)^i\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb Z}\widetilde{Kh}^{i,\widetilde j}(D,p)q^{\widetilde j}$. Under $q=-A^{-2}$ and $t=q^2=A^{-4}$,
$$\chi_q(Kh(D))=(q+q^{-1})f_D(A),\qquad \widetilde\chi_q(D,p)=f_D(A).$$
Thus the unreduced unknot factor is $q+q^{-1}$ and the reduced unknot factor is $1$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $A$ and $t$ be formal variables and $K$ a
nonempty oriented link. At each crossing of a regular diagram $D$ use the
source chart with over-strand southwest-to-northeast: A joins top and bottom
endpoints with coefficient $A$, and B joins left and right endpoints with
coefficient $A^{-1}$. A state $S:C(D)\to\{A,B\}$ assigns one smoothing at every
crossing; let $a(S)$ and $b(S)$ count these choices and $|S|$ count the
resulting circles. Fix a unit viewing normal $n$ and orient the projection
plane $P$ so $(u,v)$ is positive exactly when $(n,u,v)$ is positive in the
ambient oriented $3$-sphere. Define
$$\operatorname{sgn}(c)=\operatorname{sgn}\det_P(v_{\rm over},v_{\rm under}),
\qquad \operatorname{wr}(D)=\sum_c\operatorname{sgn}(c),$$
$$f_K(A)=(-A^3)^{-\operatorname{wr}(D)}
  \sum_{S:C(D)\to\{A,B\}}A^{a(S)-b(S)}(-A^2-A^{-2})^{|S|-1}.$$
For an $n$-strand braid $\beta$ whose oriented closure is $K$, let
$e:B_n\to\mathbb Z$ be the homomorphism $e(\sigma_i)=1$, where $\sigma_i$
is the positive geometric Artin half twist. Let $H(n)$ be the type-A Hecke
algebra with generators $T_i$, quadratic relation $T_i^2=(v-1)T_i+v$, braid
relations, and distant commutation, and let $\pi_n(\sigma_i)=T_i$. Its
normalized Markov trace $\operatorname{tr}_n$ satisfies
$\operatorname{tr}_n(1)=1$, cyclicity, tower restriction, and
$\operatorname{tr}_{n+1}(xT_n)=z\operatorname{tr}_n(x)$. Define the library
Jones value by
$$V_K(t)=s^{e(\beta)}\left(-\frac{s^2+1}{s}\right)^{n-1}
\operatorname{tr}_n(\pi_n(\beta))\Big|_{v=s^2,\,z=-1/(s^2+1),\,t=s^2},$$
where $s=t^{1/2}$. With $A=t^{-1/4}$, these values satisfy
$$V_K(t)=f_K(t^{-1/4}).$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. For every nonempty oriented link $L$, the bigraded integral groups $Kh^{i,j}(L):=H^i(C^{*,j}(D))$, where $D$ is any finite regular oriented diagram of $L$ and $C(D)$ is the normalized Khovanov cochain complex, are independent of the choice of $D$ up to bigraded isomorphism.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $K$ be an oriented knot and let $(D,p)$ and $(D',p')$ be finite regular oriented diagrams of $K$ with basepoints away from all crossings. Then the reduced integral groups $\widetilde{Kh}^{i,\widetilde j}(D,p)$ and $\widetilde{Kh}^{i,\widetilde j}(D',p')$ are isomorphic for every $(i,\widetilde j)$. In particular, they are invariant under Reidemeister moves supported away from the basepoint and under transport of the basepoint along the knot.

Let $D$ be a nonempty finite regular oriented link diagram in an oriented $3$-sphere, with finite crossing set $C(D)$. Fix a unit viewing normal $n$ and orient the projection plane $P$ so $(u,v)$ is positive exactly when $(n,u,v)$ is positive in the ambient $3$-space. At a crossing $c$, define its sign as the sign of $\det_P(v_{\rm over},v_{\rm under})$, where the two nonzero projected tangent vectors follow the oriented over- and under-strands. Let $n_+$ and $n_-$ be the numbers of positive and negative crossings.

Set $\mathcal A=\mathbb Z[X]/(X^2)$, with $\deg(1)=1$ and $\deg(X)=-1$. Its unit, multiplication, counit, and comultiplication are
$$
\eta(1)=1,\qquad m(1\otimes1)=1,\quad m(1\otimes X)=m(X\otimes1)=X,\quad m(X\otimes X)=0,
$$
$$
\epsilon(1)=0,\quad\epsilon(X)=1,\qquad \Delta(1)=1\otimes X+X\otimes1,\quad\Delta(X)=X\otimes X.
$$
Thus $m$ and $\Delta$ have quantum degree $-1$, while $\eta$ and $\epsilon$ have degree $+1$.

Choose a total order $c_1<\cdots<c_n$ on $C(D)$. A resolution state is a function $v:C(D)\to\{0,1\}$; at $v(c)=0$ use the A-smoothing and at $v(c)=1$ use the B-smoothing from the Kauffman source chart. Write $|v|=\sum_c v(c)$, let $D_v$ be the crossingless resolution, and let $k(v)$ be its number of circles. Assign the state module $\mathcal A^{\otimes k(v)}$. For an edge $v\to v+e_j$ changing crossing $c_j$ from $0$ to $1$, use $m$ if the local smoothing merges two circles and $\Delta$ if it splits one circle, tensored with the identity on all other factors, and multiply this map by $(-1)^{\sum_{i<j}v(c_i)}$. The resulting direct sum has cohomological degree
$$i(v)=|v|-n_-$$
and the generator with circle labels $1$ or $X$ has quantum degree
$$j(v)=|v|+n_+-2n_-+\sum_{\text{circle labels }a}\deg(a).$$
This defines the normalized integral Khovanov cube and its candidate degree-zero cochain differential; the assertion that the differential squares to zero is a separate lemma.

The Frobenius identity that controls a merge-split face is represented by the two equal composites below. The diagram records the maps only; the proof verifies the equality on the basis $\{1,X\}^{\otimes2}$ and does not rely on the drawing.

```tikzcd
\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal A \arrow[r,"m"] \arrow[d,"\Delta\otimes\mathrm{id}"'] & \mathcal A \arrow[d,"\Delta"] \\
\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal A \arrow[r,"\mathrm{id}\otimes m"'] & \mathcal A\otimes\mathcal A
```

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the smooth normal-bundle structure used in the
framing clause. For a knot component $K$, its normal bundle is the fibrewise
quotient $\nu K=TS^3|_K/TK$, and a normal section is a smooth section of this
bundle.

Let $D$ be a regular oriented link diagram in a projection plane $P$ of an
oriented $3$-sphere, after moving the link off the point at infinity. Fix the
unit viewing normal $n$ pointing toward the viewer. Orient $P$ by the rule that
an ordered basis $(u,v)$ of $P$ is positive exactly when $(n,u,v)$ is a positive
basis of the ambient $3$-space. At a crossing $c$, let $v_{\rm over}$ and
$v_{\rm under}$ be the nonzero projected tangent vectors following the
orientations of the overpassing and underpassing strands. Define
$$\operatorname{sgn}(c):=\operatorname{sgn}\det_P(v_{\rm over},v_{\rm under})\in\{+1,-1\}.$$
Reversing the orientation of $P$ reverses every crossing sign.

This convention makes the positive geometric Artin half twist positive. In
the braid chart $(x,y,t)$ with ambient orientation $(x,y,t)$, view along $+y$;
the induced positive orientation of the $(x,t)$ projection plane is the ordered
basis $(\partial_t,\partial_x)$. For the positive half twist, label $i$ moves
from $x=-h$ to $x=h$ below the midpoint, while label $i+1$ moves from $x=h$ to
$x=-h$ above it, with $h>0$. Thus the over and under projected tangent vectors
in coordinates $(t,x)$ are $(1,-2h)$ and $(1,2h)$, whose determinant is
$4h>0$.

The **writhe** of $D$ is
$$\operatorname{wr}(D):=\sum_{c\text{ a crossing of }D}\operatorname{sgn}(c).$$
For a link component $K_i$, its **self-writhe**
$\operatorname{wr}_i(D)$ is the sum over crossings whose two branches belong to
$K_i$; the total writhe also includes all mixed crossings between distinct
components.

The **blackboard framing** of a component of $D$ is the homotopy class of the
normal section represented by the positive quarter-turn in $P$ of the projected
oriented tangent. The projection is an immersion, so this vector never
vanishes; it is perpendicular to the projected tangent, hence also to the
spatial tangent, and therefore represents a nonzero normal section of the
component in the ambient $3$-sphere.

```tikz
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.8,>=stealth]
  \draw[->] (-1,0) -- (1,0) node[right] {$v_{\rm over}$};
  \draw[->] (0,-1) -- (0,1) node[above] {$v_{\rm under}$};
  \node[above left] at (0,0) {$+1$};
\end{tikzpicture}
```

In the displayed local chart, the over tangent is the positive horizontal
vector and the under tangent is the positive vertical vector, so the determinant
is $+1$. This figure illustrates the determinant rule only; no proof below
depends on a picture.

An **oriented Reidemeister move** is one of the following local replacements of
a regular oriented link diagram ([[def-regular-oriented-link-diagram]]),
performed inside a small closed disk while the diagram outside the disk is left
unchanged, and understood up to planar isotopy outside the disk
([[def-planar-isotopy-of-link-diagrams]]). All sign and orientation variants of
each local picture are included.

**(R1) Kink creation and deletion.** A single strand is replaced by a small
kink: two arcs crossing once and otherwise disjoint from the strand, with the
over/under datum of the new crossing as in the picture. The move is allowed in
both directions (create or delete the kink) and with both signs of the kink,
the sign being the sign of the crossing created. The orientations of the two
strands of the kink are the two possible consistent orientations through the
crossing, and all of them occur in the move list.

**(R2) Slide of two strands.** Two local arcs belonging to two strands are
replaced so that the number of crossings between those strands changes by two
of opposite signs: the standard picture slides one strand over or under the
other, creating or deleting the pair of crossings, with the two crossings being
the two possible signs in either order. All four orientation patterns of the
two strands at the two crossings are included.

**(R3) Sliding a strand past a crossing.** One strand is moved across an
existing crossing of two other strands, so that the crossing of the two other
strands passes from one side of the moving strand to the other; the three
crossings of the local picture keep their signs and the over/under data are
preserved. The three strands must have a consistent strict height order:
one is above both others, one below both, and the remaining strand is between
them. The cyclic over/under pattern is excluded. Every orientation pattern
and all six height orders of this standard local picture are included.

A local R2 or R3 picture is **braid-like** when, after a local coordinate
change and deformation, all participating strands run in the same positive
longitudinal direction. This is a local condition and does not require a
globally chosen braid axis. R1 is kept as a separate kink move.

The strands keep their orientations throughout every move. The union of the
three move types, together with planar isotopy, generates the equivalence
relation on diagrams used in the Reidemeister equivalence theorem below; the
moves are sometimes called R1, R2, R3 as above. Since every move changes the
diagram only inside a disk, it has a type and a finite list of local
orientation/sign variants, and each variant is realized by an ambient isotopy
as the next items show. The complete list of variants is required because the
Markov and Alexander constructions below act on oriented diagrams and count
signed crossings.

Let $D,D'$ be regular oriented diagrams of links $L,L'$. If the diagrams
differ by one oriented Reidemeister move or a planar isotopy, the links are
equivalent. The local Reidemeister replacement has a realization supported
in a ball over its move disk, after choosing lifts that agree outside that
ball. Comparing arbitrary realizing links may additionally require changing
their heights away from the move disk.

Then the sum $d$ of all edge maps satisfies $d^2=0$.

For a finite regular oriented link diagram $D$ with $n$ ordered crossings, the procedure that enumerates all $2^n$ smoothing states, assigns one copy of $\mathcal A=\mathbb Z[X]/(X^2)$ per resolution circle, places a generator in degrees $i=|v|-n_-$ and $j=|v|+n_+-2n_-+\sum\deg(a)$, and sums the signed merge or split edge maps terminates after finitely many operations. Its output is a finite direct sum of finite-rank free abelian groups with a differential of bidegree $(1,0)$ satisfying $d^2=0$; hence it is a bounded bigraded cochain complex.

In the positive curl, the $0$-state contributes $(q+q^{-1})^2$ and the $1$-state contributes $-q(q+q^{-1})$, because the state coordinate raises quantum degree by one and homological degree by one. Hence $\chi_q^{\mathrm{raw}}(U_+)=(q+q^{-1})^2-q(q+q^{-1})=1+q^{-2}=q^{-1}(q+q^{-1})$. In the negative curl, the $0$-state contributes $q+q^{-1}$ and the $1$-state contributes $-q(q+q^{-1})^2$. For each quantum degree, tensor the bounded finite-rank free complex with $\mathbb Q$. Clearing denominators shows that kernels and images localize to the kernels and images of the rationalized maps; applying the same argument to a kernel modulo the preceding image identifies rationalized cohomology with integral cohomology tensored with $\mathbb Q$. Its dimension is therefore the integral rank of cohomology. In the bounded rational complex, rank-nullity gives $\dim C^i=\dim H^i+\dim\operatorname{im}d^i+\dim\operatorname{im}d^{i-1}$; alternating over $i$ cancels the image terms. Thus the raw cohomology Euler polynomials equal the chain Euler polynomials in steps 1.1–1.2. The distinct Laurent polynomials $q+q^{-1}$, $q^{-1}(q+q^{-1})$, and $-q^2(q+q^{-1})$ come from diagrams of the same unknot by [F4]. The raw groups are consequently not invariant, and the raw unknot factor is not the claimed $q+q^{-1}$.

In $\mathbb R$, associativity, commutativity and the unit law follow from quotient-ring multiplication. On the basis $1,X$, the counit composites $(\epsilon\otimes\mathrm{id})\Delta$ and $(\mathrm{id}\otimes\epsilon)\Delta$ both send $1\mapsto1$ and $X\mapsto X$. Cocommutativity follows from the symmetric formulas for $\Delta(1)$ and $\Delta(X)$. citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $D,D'$ be regular oriented link diagrams
([[def-regular-oriented-link-diagram]]), regarded as decorated immersed oriented
$4$-valent planar graphs. Then $D$ and $D'$ are **planar isotopic** when there
is an orientation-preserving ambient isotopy
$\Phi\colon\mathbb R^2\times I\to\mathbb R^2$, with $\Phi_0=\mathrm{id}$ and
each $\Phi_t$ an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism
([[def-diffeomorphism-and-local-diffeomorphism-of-manifolds]]), such that
$\Phi_1$ carries the decorated graph of $D$ to that of $D'$: it maps the image
curve of $D$ bijectively onto that of $D'$, carries the over/under datum of
every double point to the over/under datum of the corresponding double point,
and preserves the strand orientations. A **planar isotopy of diagrams** is a
family $D_t=\Phi_t(D_0)$ for such a jointly smooth ambient isotopy $\Phi$,
with the decorations transported by $\Phi_t$. The source curves are immersed,
not embedded in the plane at their crossings.

Planar isotopies are admitted as moves in the Reidemeister theorem: they carry
a regular projection between the exceptional times of a general-position
isotopy of the link, and no crossing of the diagram is created or destroyed
along them. They are listed separately from the three local moves
([[def-oriented-reidemeister-moves]]), of which R1 and R2 create or destroy crossings, while R3 rearranges three
existing crossings and preserves their number.
Composing planar isotopies and composing them with the local moves gives the
equivalence relation generated by the moves, and every single move below is
understood up to planar isotopy outside its small disk.

derivations.claim: **Straighten only a crossing-free marked germ.** Translate the mark to $z=0$ and rotate its oriented tangent to the positive real axis, by paths of positive planar similarities. Since the mark is a regular non-double point, there is a small disk meeting the diagram in just one arc. The inverse-function theorem expresses that arc as $y=f(x)$, where $f(0)=f'(0)=0$. It can be straightened by the supported shear $(x,y)\mapsto(x,y-t\chi(x,y)f(x))$, $0\le t\le1$: choose a cutoff equal to one near the smaller graph segment and supported in a rectangle of width and height comparable to a sufficiently small $r$. There $f(x)=O(r^2)$, whereas $\partial_y\chi=O(r^{-1})$. Thus $1-t(\partial_y\chi)f>0$ after shrinking $r$. Each vertical coordinate map is strictly increasing and the identity outside a compact interval, so each shear is a global orientation-preserving diffeomorphism; its inverse is smooth by its positive vertical derivative. Choose nested neighborhoods so that after this shear the diagram in $|z|<2r$ is the real diameter and no other strand meets that disk. Shrink $r<1$ if necessary. The part not in the real interval $|x|<r$ consequently satisfies $|z|\ge r$. All these isotopies merely transport the mark and crossing decorations; their local supports meet no crossing.

**An actual rotation recharting.** Choose $0<\epsilon<\min(r/4,1/4)$ and set $a=i\epsilon$. On the oriented stereographic sphere use the fractional linear coordinate $$w=-\frac{1+\overline a z}{z-a}.$$ The matrix $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}-\overline a&-1\\1&-a\end{smallmatrix}\right)/\sqrt{1+|a|^2}$ is unitary with determinant one: its columns have norm one and scalar product zero, and its unnormalized determinant is $1+|a|^2$. Hence its fractional linear action is the action of an orientation-preserving rotation of the round two-sphere. Its omitted old point is $a$, which lies off the real germ in the marked disk, hence in a face adjacent to the mark and outside all crossing disks. The old omitted point $\infty$ is sent to $-\overline a$, which is an ordinary point of the new chart. The map is smooth on the entire spherical diagram and preserves the oriented local crossing charts and all transported decorations.

**A quantitative exterior closing arc.** For every old diagram point outside the interval $|x|<r$, step 1.1 and the triangle inequality give $$|w|\le\frac{1+\epsilon|z|}{|z|-\epsilon}\le B:=\frac{1+\epsilon r}{r-\epsilon}.$$ The second inequality holds because the rational function has derivative $-(1+\epsilon^2)/(s-\epsilon)^2<0$ for $s\ge r$. The inequality $B<1/\epsilon$ is equivalent to $2\epsilon<r(1-\epsilon^2)$, which follows from $\epsilon<r/4$ and $\epsilon<1/4$. Choose a real $R$ strictly between $B$ and $1/\epsilon$. On the real germ $$|w(x)|^2=\frac{1+\epsilon^2x^2}{x^2+\epsilon^2},$$ whose derivative with respect to $x^2$ is $(\epsilon^4-1)/(x^2+\epsilon^2)^2<0$. Since the value at $x=0$ is $1/\epsilon^2>R^2$ and at $|x|=r$ is at most $B^2<R^2$, the circle $|w|=R$ meets that germ at exactly $x=\pm c$, with $$c^2=\frac{1-R^2\epsilon^2}{R^2-\epsilon^2},\qquad 0<c<r.$$ Both intersections are transverse, since $c\ne0$ and the derivative just computed is nonzero there. The only diagram points outside the closed disk $|w|\le R$ form the single open arc parametrized by $-c<x<c$; its closure contains the mark and has no crossing. The image is a round circular arc, because a fractional linear map sends a circle on the sphere to a circle and its pole $i\epsilon$ is not on the real circle. Every other strand and every crossing is strictly inside the disk. Thus this is the claimed exterior closing arc, with uniform crossing-free neighborhoods of it and of its two cut points.

**Record spatial coordinate identifications.** A planar shear in step 1.1 lifts on a spatial projection chart by $(x,y,h)\mapsto(\Phi_t(x,y),h)$. Its compact planar support can also be cut off in height on a larger box containing the link: use its compactly supported time-dependent planar velocity multiplied by a height cutoff equal to one on that box, with zero height velocity. The flow is complete, agrees with the displayed lift near the link, and extends by the identity to $S^3$. The initial translations and rotations have their usual orientation-preserving similarity lifts and smooth conformal extensions at the point at infinity. For the rechart, realize the projection sphere as the equator of $S^3\subset\mathbb R^3\oplus\mathbb R$. If $Q\in SO(3)$ is the rotation from step 2.1, then $(v,s)\mapsto(Qv,s)$ is an orthogonal determinant-one map of $\mathbb R^4$ preserving $S^3$ and preserving its orientation. On the equatorial collar it transports the projection direction, the signed height, and the over/under datum. The Euclidean projection and the equatorial product projection require an explicit chart identification. Write $q=(0,0,1,0)$ for the spatial stereographic point, $z=x+iy$, $$X(z)=\frac{(2x,2y,|z|^2-1)}{1+|z|^2},\qquad d(z)=\frac{2}{1+|z|^2}.$$ Standard inverse spatial stereographic projection is $$E(z,h)=\frac{(2x,2y,|z|^2+h^2-1,2h)}{1+|z|^2+h^2}.$$ The product-collar chart with the same first normal derivative is $$T(z,h)=\bigl(\sqrt{1-d(z)^2h^2}\,X(z),d(z)h\bigr).$$ On $h=0$ these charts agree and have identical full first derivatives: both normal derivatives are $d(z)e_4$, while their tangential derivatives are those of $X$. On a compact planar neighborhood containing the diagram, the coordinate transition $\Psi=E^{-1}T$ therefore satisfies $\Psi-\mathrm{id}=O(h^2)$ and $D\Psi-I=O(|h|)$ uniformly. Choose a slightly larger compact planar box and cut off this difference there and in a height slab $|h|<\eta$. A height cutoff has derivative $O(\eta^{-1})$, multiplying an error $O(\eta^2)$; thus the resulting global compactly supported displacement $V$ has $\|DV\|<1/2$ for small $\eta$. Every $\mathrm{id}+tV$ is injective by the Lipschitz bound, is a local orientation-preserving diffeomorphism, and is onto: it is proper, its image is closed and open, and the plane-height space is connected. Its inverse is smooth by the inverse-function theorem. This is an actual ambient coordinate isotopy, extending by the identity to $S^3$. First shrink any existing Euclidean height realization by a positive constant so it lies where both cutoffs equal one. Height scaling is an embedding isotopy: at every double point both branch heights are multiplied by the same positive factor. The new spatial representative is then exactly $T(z,h)$, with product-collar base coordinate $z$ and signed height $d(z)h$. Because $d(z)>0$, at a double point it preserves the strict over/under ordering. Hence the displayed Euclidean diagram is identified with the product-collar diagram by this explicit spatial map; they are not assumed literally equal off the equator. These are actual marked link isotopies and coordinate identifications with specified endpoints. Composing these coordinate maps and height isotopies gives the asserted spatial identification; no claim that the rotation is a planar isotopy is used.

**Compatibility with protected long ends.** The exterior arc and two slightly longer joining collars have injective projection and are disjoint in projection from the remaining compact part, except at their adjacent ends. On a narrow planar neighborhood of that arc its spatial height is a smooth function $h(x,y)$, extended from the arc in tubular coordinates. A supported vertical translation $(x,y,z)\mapsto(x,y,z-t\eta(x,y)h(x,y))$ sets its height to zero on a smaller neighborhood; this is a diffeomorphism for every $t$, since its derivative in $z$ is one. It cannot reverse an over/under ordering, and there are no double points in its smaller marked support. Choose the joining neighborhoods slightly longer before cutting, so the resulting cut collars are fixed smooth product collars. The remaining diagram is a compact tangle in the round disk, and the single planar exterior arc is its marked closure. These are precisely endpoint data that may be retained as protected long endpoints in a relative movie construction. Every operation has preserved the transported mark, and none passes it through a crossing. Finite composition proves the assertion, including its recorded spatial coordinate identification. No algebraic comparison of the two charts, no arbitrary mark-slide identity, and no purely planar comparison have been assumed.

Let $D$ be a finite regular oriented knot diagram with ordered crossings $c_1<\cdots<c_n$ and a marked point $p$ away from crossings. Put $\mathbb A=\mathbb Z[X]/(X^2)$ and $\mathbb F_2=\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z$. At a resolution state $v\in\{0,1\}^n$, let $V_v$ be the free abelian group generated by the resolution circles, order its circle generators, and use the exterior algebra $\Lambda^*V_v$ as its state module. A wedge of $r$ distinct circle generators has circle quantum degree $k(v)-2r$, where $k(v)=\operatorname{rank}V_v$; its total normalized degrees are $i(v)=|v|-n_-$ and $q=|v|+n_+-2n_-+k(v)-2r$. For a merge saddle joining circles $C_1,C_2$, let $p:V_v\to V_{v+e}$ be the quotient sending both to the merged circle and fixing the other generators; the edge map is $\Lambda^*p$. For a split saddle replacing $C$ by $C_1,C_2$, let $j:V_v\to V_{v+e}$ send $C$ to $C_1$ and fix the other generators; the unsigned edge map is $z\mapsto(C_1-C_2)\wedge\Lambda^*j(z)$. Choosing $C_2$ instead of $C_1$ gives the same map, while reversing the order of $C_1,C_2$ changes only its sign. Multiply each edge map by a sign $\epsilon(e)\in\{1,-1\}$, incorporating any circle-generator reordering sign. The direct sum of these state modules with the resulting cube differential is the odd Khovanov cochain complex $C_o(D)$. Write $Z_p$ for the circle containing the mark. Use the right action $z\cdot X=z\wedge Z_p$, making $C_o(D)$ a complex of right $\mathbb A$-modules; since $\mathbb A$ is commutative these are also ordinary modules over that ring. The action has quantum degree $-2$.

The square condition is that the sum of the two signed saddle composites around each two-dimensional cube face is zero. An edge sign function satisfying it is called square-compatible; existence and invariance require separate proofs.

Let $\mathbb R=\mathbb Z[h,X]/(X^2-hX)$, with $\deg_q(h)=\deg_q(X)=-2$. Its Frobenius structure has unit $\eta(1)=1$, counit $\epsilon(1)=0,\epsilon(X)=1$, quotient-ring multiplication, and comultiplication
$$ \Delta(1)=1\otimes X+X\otimes1-h\,1\otimes1,\qquad \Delta(X)=X\otimes X. $$
Applying these operations to the same normalized cube gives the Bar–Natan cochain complex $C_h(D)$, with circle labels $1,X$ of quantum degrees $1,-1$ and the same normalized state shifts; it is a complex of free $\mathbb R$-modules, and the marked circle acts by multiplication by $X$.

Put $\mathbb B=\mathbb F_2[X]/(X^2)=\mathbb R/(2,h)$. Modulo $2$, the odd exterior basis vector $C_{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge C_{i_r}$ corresponds to the even tensor state labeling the selected circles $C_{i_j}$ by $X$ and all other circles by $1$. This statewise bijection defines the candidate comparison $f_D:C_o(D)\otimes\mathbb F_2\to C_h(D)\otimes_{\mathbb R}\mathbb B$ after setting $h=0$.

A **local even–odd (LEO) triple** is a triple $(C,D,f)$ consisting of a finitely generated bigraded cochain complex $C$ free over $\mathbb A$, a finitely generated bigraded cochain complex $D$ free over $\mathbb R$, and a bigraded $\mathbb F_2[X]/(X^2)$-linear chain homotopy equivalence
$$ f:C\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb F_2\longrightarrow D\otimes_{\mathbb R}\mathbb B, \qquad \mathbb B=\mathbb R/(2,h)=\mathbb F_2[X]/(X^2), $$
such that $D[h^{-1}]$ is chain homotopy equivalent over $\mathbb R[h^{-1}]$ to one free rank-one module supported in cohomological degree $0$ and odd quantum degree. For a based knot diagram the intended candidate is $(C_o(D),C_h(D),f_D)$, where $f_D$ identifies the reduced edge maps modulo $2$ and $h$; its satisfaction of the homotopy and localization conditions is a separate theorem.

A local map $(C,D,f)\to(C',D',f')$ is a pair of bigraded module chain maps $\alpha:C\to C'$ and $\beta:D\to D'$ such that $\beta[h^{-1}]$ is a chain homotopy equivalence and the square induced by $f,f',\alpha,\beta$ after quotienting by $(2,h)$ commutes up to an $\mathbb F_2[X]/(X^2)$-linear chain homotopy. Two LEO triples are locally equivalent when there is a local map in each direction.

derivations.claim: **The two-saddle calculation.** Quotients commute with quotients. Two split factors anticommute because $u\wedge v=-v\wedge u$. A quotient and a split commute when the quotient carries the split difference to the corresponding output difference. These give $\kappa=1,-1,1$, respectively, for two merges, two splits and a mixed pair whose saddle types are unchanged by interchange. The remaining connected nonzero case starts with two circles and two bands between them: either order first merges and then splits. Both composites factor through the quotient identifying the two input circles. If the two band arrows point towards the same input circle, their final split differences are opposites, giving $\kappa=-1$; if they point towards different circles, the differences agree, giving $\kappa=1$. Finally, alternating endpoints on a single input circle give a split followed by a merge in either order. The quotient kills the split difference, so both composites are zero. These exhaust the cases: discard components missing both arcs, and distinguish whether each arc joins equal or distinct components; if both are self-arcs, their endpoints either alternate or do not. A spectator generator is carried identically throughout, so the computation on the incident generators proves the full exterior-map equation.

**Reversing an arrow is a gauge change.** Reverse the arrow at coordinate $i$. The unsigned edge map changes by $r(e)=-1$ on its split edges and by $r(e)=1$ on its merge edges; other edges have $r(e)=1$. The face coefficient changes by the product of these four $r$'s. For nonzero composites this follows by multiplying the two equations for the edge maps. For a zero face, the $i$-saddle is a split in one ordering and a merge in the other. Reversing its arrow reverses the left/right test defining $\kappa$, so the coefficient changes by $-1$, again the product of the $r$'s. Consequently the product of the six $\kappa$'s on a three-cube is unchanged by reversing any arrow: every edge belongs to exactly two of its faces. It suffices to check one choice of arrows for every unoriented three-saddle configuration.

**Separating a configuration.** Collapse each saddle disk to a four-valent vertex and retain the regular arcs joining its four ports. Discard vertex-free circles. This gives a planar four-valent multigraph with three vertices. If it is disconnected, one component contains just one vertex. If it has a two-edge cut, cut those edges and cap the resulting pair of ports in each piece by an arc. The original diagram is then obtained by joining the two capped marked arcs; one piece again has one vertex and the other two. The caps can be chosen in a thin neighbourhood of the cut, so they preserve the cyclic orders and inside/outside intersection test for every two-saddle face within a piece. Every resolution of the joined diagram has the circle count $k_1+k_2-1$; in the disconnected case it has count $k_1+k_2$. Thus the merge/split status of a saddle is its status in its own capped piece. A face using one saddle from each piece is an ordinary interchange with coefficient $(-1)^{b_i b_j}$ by step 1.1. The two faces using both saddles of the two-vertex piece have equal coefficients and cancel in the boundary product. If the one-vertex piece has split indicator $b_c$, the product from the four remaining faces is $(-1)^{b_c N}$, where $N$ is the sum of the split counts in the two orders of the two saddles in the other piece. Each order has the same split count, namely $(k_{\mathrm{out}}-k_{\mathrm{in}}+2)/2$. Hence $N$ is even and the boundary product is $1$. This also proves the disconnected case, using separate exterior generators rather than the marked connected sum.

**The irreducible list.** Suppose the graph is connected and has no two-edge cut. It has no loop: a loop uses two of the four ports at its vertex, and the remaining two edges would be a cut. Write $m_{ij}$ for the number of edges between vertices $i,j$. The three degree equations give $m_{12}=m_{23}=m_{31}=2$. At each vertex the two parallel edges bound a lens on one side; the remaining edges must lie on the other side, since they must reach the third vertex without crossing. Thus the planar graph has three lens faces and two triangular faces, with its cyclic orders determined up to reflection and permutation of the vertices. Resolving its three vertices gives eight choices. Permuting the vertices identifies choices having the same number of switches from the resolution into three lens circles. The four representatives, obtained by zero, one, two and three switches, have respectively these circle-and-band descriptions: three circles with three bands forming a triangle; two circles joined by two bands, with a self-band on one circle separating their attachment points; one circle with two parallel inside bands and one outside band alternating with each of them; and two circles joined by three parallel bands. This enumeration follows also by doing the switches successively: the first merges two lens circles, the second merges the remaining two circles, and the third splits their common circle. It accounts for all eight choices, without an assumption about the arrows.

**Triangle and three parallel bands.** In the triangle representative direct the three bands cyclically. A face with the third band absent is two successive merges, of coefficient $1$. With the third band performed first, the two remaining arrows point towards different circles, again giving coefficient $1$ by step 1.1. Thus all six coefficients are $1$. In the three-parallel-band representative direct all three arrows from the first circle to the second. The three bottom faces have two arrows towards the same circle and coefficient $-1$. After the third band merges the two circles, the two remaining bands are nonalternating self-bands; their two split factors anticommute, so each top face also has coefficient $-1$. In both representatives the six-face product is $1$.

**Digon with a self-band.** Place the two circles to the left and right, draw the two joining bands above and below, and draw the self-band across the left circle, separating the upper and lower attachment points. Direct both joining bands towards the right circle. The face of the two joining bands before the self-band is a same-head interchange and has coefficient $-1$. After the self-band, those bands form a tree on three circles and the corresponding face has coefficient $1$. The two faces involving the self-band before the other joining band are ordinary mixed interchanges and have coefficient $1$. After a joining band is performed, the other joining band and the self-band have alternating endpoints. The two resulting zero faces are reflections across the horizontal midline, with the self-band arrow retained and the two equally directed joining arrows exchanged. Reflection reverses the inside/outside oriented-intersection test, so their $\kappa$'s are opposite. Their product is $-1$, cancelling the single nonzero coefficient $-1$. The total product is $1$, for either direction of the self-band arrow.

**Two inside bands and an outside band.** List the endpoints clockwise as $c,a,b,c,b,a$, where $a,b$ are the two parallel inside bands and $c$ is outside. Direct $a,b$ upwards. Their bottom face consists of two splits and has coefficient $-1$. After performing $c$, their heads lie on the same one of the two resulting circles; their top face is a same-head interchange and has coefficient $-1$. The faces $(a,c)$ before $b$ and $(b,c)$ before $a$ are zero faces with the same inside-arrow direction and the same outside arrow, hence have equal coefficients. Their product is $1$. In the two remaining faces, performing the other inside band has separated the endpoints of $c$; the two events are an ordinary merge and split with coefficient $1$. Thus the six-face product is again $1$, for either direction of $c$. Steps 3.1–4.3 and arrow reversal in step 2.1 prove that every three-cube has boundary product $\prod\kappa=1$. Consequently $\phi=-\kappa$ also has boundary product $1$, because there are six faces.

**Constructing the signs.** Induct on cube dimension $n$. For $n=0$ there are no signs; for $n=1$ choose the only edge sign $1$. For the induction step construct signs on the lower face $v_n=0$, set every edge in direction $n$ to $1$, and define an upper-face edge in direction $i<n$ by $\epsilon_i(v,1)=\phi_{i,n}(v)\epsilon_i(v,0)$. This enforces each vertical face product. For an upper face in directions $i,j<n$, multiply the six face equations for its three-cube with direction $n$: the lower face and four vertical faces already have their prescribed products, while the six prescribed products multiply to $1$ by step 4.3. Therefore the upper face has its prescribed product too. The resulting differential has square zero: on a nonzero face the two unsigned composites differ by $\kappa$, while their signed coefficient ratio is $-\kappa$; on a zero face both composites vanish. Every operation in this induction is a finite multiplication of signs.

**Comparison.** If $\epsilon,\epsilon'$ realize the same face products, their quotient $\rho(e)=\epsilon'(e)/\epsilon(e)$ has product $1$ around every face. Give the lowest vertex sign $1$, and give any other vertex the product of $\rho$ along a monotone path to it. Two such paths differ by interchanging adjacent coordinate changes; each interchange is a square and leaves the product unchanged. Therefore these vertex signs are well-defined and their ratio across an edge is $\rho(e)$. Multiplying every state module by its vertex sign gives a chain isomorphism. These scalar maps preserve both normalized gradings and commute with the marked action by [F2]. This proves all the assertions.

Proof, 5.1: 5.1 **Constructing the signs.** Induct on cube dimension $n$. For $n=0$ there are no signs; for $n=1$ choose the only edge sign $1$. For the induction step construct signs on the lower face $v_n=0$, set every edge in direction $n$ to $1$, and define an upper-face edge in direction $i<n$ by $\epsilon_i(v,1)=\phi_{i,n}(v)\epsilon_i(v,0)$. This enforces each vertical face product. For an upper face in directions $i,j<n$, multiply the six face equations for its three-cube with direction $n$: the lower face and four vertical faces already have their prescribed products, while the six prescribed products multiply to $1$ by step 4.3. Therefore the upper face has its prescribed product too. The resulting differential has square zero: on a nonzero face the two unsigned composites differ by $\kappa$, while their signed coefficient ratio is $-\kappa$; on a zero face both composites vanish. Every operation in this induction is a finite multiplication of signs. [F1, step 4.3, construct, algebra]

Proof1.1 computes both vanishing split–merge composites on an alternating-endpoint face; Proof4.2–4.3 include those zero faces in the six-face parity calculation. Proof, 1.1: 1.1 **The two-saddle calculation.** Quotients commute with quotients. Two split factors anticommute because $u\wedge v=-v\wedge u$. A quotient and a split commute when the quotient carries the split difference to the corresponding output difference. These give $\kappa=1,-1,1$, respectively, for two merges, two splits and a mixed pair whose saddle types are unchanged by interchange. The remaining connected nonzero case starts with two circles and two bands between them: either order first merges and then splits. Both composites factor through the quotient identifying the two input circles. If the two band arrows point towards the same input circle, their final split differences are opposites, giving $\kappa=-1$; if they point towards different circles, the differences agree, giving $\kappa=1$. Finally, alternating endpoints on a single input circle give a split followed by a merge in either order. The quotient kills the split difference, so both composites are zero. These exhaust the cases: discard components missing both arcs, and distinguish whether each arc joins equal or distinct components; if both are self-arcs, their endpoints either alternate or do not. A spectator generator is carried identically throughout, so the computation on the incident generators proves the full exterior-map equation. [F1, given, algebra]

Proof2.2 treats disconnected configurations and two-edge cuts; Proof3.1 reduces the no-cut three-vertex case to its explicit finite doubled-triangle list. Proof, 2.2: 2.2 **Separating a configuration.** Collapse each saddle disk to a four-valent vertex and retain the regular arcs joining its four ports. Discard vertex-free circles. This gives a planar four-valent multigraph with three vertices. If it is disconnected, one component contains just one vertex. If it has a two-edge cut, cut those edges and cap the resulting pair of ports in each piece by an arc. The original diagram is then obtained by joining the two capped marked arcs; one piece again has one vertex and the other two. The caps can be chosen in a thin neighbourhood of the cut, so they preserve the cyclic orders and inside/outside intersection test for every two-saddle face within a piece. Every resolution of the joined diagram has the circle count $k_1+k_2-1$; in the disconnected case it has count $k_1+k_2$. Thus the merge/split status of a saddle is its status in its own capped piece. A face using one saddle from each piece is an ordinary interchange with coefficient $(-1)^{b_i b_j}$ by step 1.1. The two faces using both saddles of the two-vertex piece have equal coefficients and cancel in the boundary product. If the one-vertex piece has split indicator $b_c$, the product from the four remaining faces is $(-1)^{b_c N}$, where $N$ is the sum of the split counts in the two orders of the two saddles in the other piece. Each order has the same split count, namely $(k_{\mathrm{out}}-k_{\mathrm{in}}+2)/2$. Hence $N$ is even and the boundary product is $1$. This also proves the disconnected case, using separate exterior generators rather than the marked connected sum. [step 1.1, algebra, construct]

boundaries.reason: Statement asserts sign existence and comparison, not an iff predicate; Proof6.1 constructs vertex-sign comparison for the prescribed full face data. Proof, 6.1: 6.1 **Comparison.** If $\epsilon,\epsilon'$ realize the same face products, their quotient $\rho(e)=\epsilon'(e)/\epsilon(e)$ has product $1$ around every face. Give the lowest vertex sign $1$, and give any other vertex the product of $\rho$ along a monotone path to it. Two such paths differ by interchanging adjacent coordinate changes; each interchange is a square and leaves the product unchanged. Therefore these vertex signs are well-defined and their ratio across an edge is $\rho(e)$. Multiplying every state module by its vertex sign gives a chain isomorphism. These scalar maps preserve both normalized gradings and commute with the marked action by [F2]. This proves all the assertions. [F2, step 5.1, algebra, construct] ∎
