citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\mathcal F:M\times S\to N$ be a smooth family of maps and let $Z\subseteq N$
be an embedded submanifold. If $\mathcal F\pitchfork Z$, then the set of
parameters $s\in S$ for which the slice $\mathcal F_s:M\to N$ fails to be
transverse to $Z$ is a null subset of $S$.

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold, let $K\subseteq M$ be compact, and let $W\subseteq M$ be open with $K\subseteq W$. Then there exists a smooth function $\rho:M\to [0,1]$ that equals $1$ on an open neighbourhood of $K$ and satisfies $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)\subseteq W$.

If $M$ is a compact smooth manifold and $f:M\to\mathbb R$ is a Morse function,
then $f$ has only finitely many critical points.

Let $W$ be a compact smooth manifold with boundary and let $f:W\to\mathbb R$ be
a Morse function with finitely many critical points, all interior and none in a
closed neighbourhood $C$ of $\partial W$. Then every $C^\infty$ neighbourhood of
$f$ contains a Morse function $g$ with $g=f$ on $C$, the same critical points and
the same Hessian at each of them, and distinct critical values.

Let $f:M\to\mathbb R$ be smooth, let $p$ be a nondegenerate critical point of
$f$, and let $\lambda$ be the index of $p$. If $n=\dim M$, then there are local
coordinates $(x^1,\dots,x^n)$ centered at $p$ in which

$$f=f(p)-\sum_{i=1}^{\lambda}(x^i)^2+\sum_{i=\lambda+1}^{n}(x^i)^2.$$

For $n=0$, both sums are empty.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $f:M\to\mathbb R$ be smooth on a boundaryless manifold, $a<b$, and let $K=f^{-1}([a,b])$ be compact with $df\ne0$ on $K$. For any Riemannian metric there is a compactly supported smooth field $Y$ agreeing with $\operatorname{grad}f/\|\operatorname{grad}f\|^2$ near $K$. Its complete flow $\Phi$ satisfies $f(\Phi_t(x))=f(x)+t$ for $x\in K$ and $a-f(x)\le t\le b-f(x)$. Thus every intervening level is reached in exactly its value difference.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $F:C\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be a smooth
isotopy of a finite disjoint union of circles, constant near both ends, and
suppose both end projections under the fixed $\pi$ are regular. Arbitrarily
close to $F$ in the strong smooth topology there is such an isotopy $F'$, equal
to $F$ near the ends, whose projected slices have only these exceptional events:

(i) finitely many ordinary cusps, at distinct times; in a source coordinate
$x$, writing $g(x,t)=\pi F'(x,t)$, each satisfies
$g_x=0$, $\det(g_{xx},g_{xt})\ne0$ and
$\det(g_{xx},g_{xxx})\ne0$;

(ii) the **off-diagonal unordered** double-point locus is a smooth
one-dimensional manifold with boundary in the local-extension sense of
[[def-smooth-chart-atlas-and-structure-on-a-manifold-with-boundary]]; its boundary
consists exactly of the double points at $t=0,1$. Its interior is a manifold
without boundary, and its time projection has only finitely many
nondegenerate critical points, each an ordinary quadratic tangency of two
immersed branches;

(iii) finitely many transverse triple events, with all three pairs of
projected tangents independent, and no quadruple points.

No two exceptional events have the same time. All other slices are regular,
and between exceptional times their decorated diagrams vary by planar isotopy.

Let $F'$ satisfy the general-position conditions of
[[lem-a-smooth-isotopy-of-links-can-be-put-in-general-position]], with
exceptional times $t_1<\cdots<t_N$. Immediately before and after each event,
its regular diagrams differ, up to planar isotopy, by one oriented
Reidemeister move: R1 at an ordinary cusp, R2 at a quadratic double tangency,
and R3 at a transverse triple event. The regular intervals contribute planar
isotopies, and the moves preserve the over/under and orientation data of $F'$.
Consequently the end diagrams are connected by a finite sequence of these moves.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. For every oriented link $L$ contained in
$\mathbb R^3$, the directions $u\in S^2$ for which the orthogonal projection
$\pi_u$ is regular are dense in $S^2$. Every such projection has finitely
many double points.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $F:M\to N$ be a smooth map between smooth manifolds. Then the critical value
set of $F$ is a null subset of $N$.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$.

1. **Compact main case.** Let $M$ be a compact smooth manifold, possibly with boundary, let $N$ be a smooth manifold without boundary, let $F:M\times I\to N$ be a smooth isotopy of embeddings that is constant near the ends of $I$, and let $W$ be an open neighbourhood of $F(M\times I)$ in $N$. Then there is an ambient isotopy $H:N\times I\to N$ with $H_0=\mathrm{id}_N$, every $H_t$ a diffeomorphism, $H_t\circ F_0=F_t$ for all $t\in I$, $H_t=\mathrm{id}_N$ outside $W$ for every $t$, and $H_t$ stationary near the ends; if $F$ is constant near the ends with parameter $\varepsilon$, then $H_t=\mathrm{id}_N$ for $t\le\varepsilon/2$ and $H_t=H_1$ for $t\ge1-\varepsilon/2$.
2. **Relative form.** Let $N$ be boundaryless, $U\subseteq N$ open, $A\subseteq U$ compact, and let $F:U\times I\to N$ be a smooth isotopy of embeddings whose track image is open in $N\times I$. Then there is a compactly supported ambient isotopy $H$ of $N$ with $H_t\circ F_0=F_t$ on a neighbourhood of $A$ for every $t$.
3. **Boundary stratum.** If $N$ has boundary and $F(M\times I)\subseteq\partial N$, then the ambient isotopy of clause 1 can be chosen with every $H_t$ carrying $\partial N$ onto itself; if $F(M\times I)\subseteq N\setminus\partial N$, it can be chosen compactly supported in $N\setminus\partial N$.
4. **General isotopies.** For the same compact source (possibly with boundary) and boundaryless target as in clause 1, every smooth isotopy extends with support in a compact subset of any prescribed neighbourhood $W$ of $F(M\times I)$. The endpoint-constancy hypothesis and the stationary-end conclusion are both omitted; all other conclusions of clause 1 hold.

derivations.claim: **A spatial chart and small embedding perturbations.** If $S$ is empty take the empty movie. Extend its spatial projection constantly across appended product collars to a boundaryless surface. Its differential has rank at most two, so [F5] makes its image in $S^3$ null; in particular the original compact spatial image is null. Choose a point outside that compact image and use a spatial stereographic chart, so the entire surface lies in $\mathbb R^3\times I$. If endpoint diagrams use the fixed point at infinity, choose this missing point near infinity, outside the track, and move it to infinity by an ambient point motion in a small ball disjoint from the end links; this fixes smaller end collars, exactly as in the compact-track argument for link isotopies. Write its embedding as $e(x)=(a(x),h(x))$. Small $C^1$ perturbations of $e$ on a fixed compact support in the interior remain embeddings: injectivity of each local differential has a uniform lower bound on finitely many smaller charts, while images of source pairs outside those chart neighbourhoods have positive minimum separation. Interpolating a sufficiently small perturbation with $e$ gives an embedding isotopy fixed on the collars. Its velocity extends by [F5], working in the boundaryless collar extension $S^3\times\mathbb R$ and cutting it off away from the fixed end collars. Thus these perturbations preserve the actual collared surface up to ambient isotopy.

**Morse height realized on the embedded surface.** Cover the complement of a smaller product collar by finitely many chart cores and choose supported bumps equal to one there by [F1]. In each surface chart with coordinates $x_1,x_2$, perturb the height $h$ by finite linear combinations of $\chi x_1,\chi x_2$, extended by zero. At a zero of its differential, the parameter derivatives span the cotangent fiber on at least one core. Thus the evaluation of the differential is transverse to the zero section. [F1] gives arbitrarily small parameters with transverse differential, hence nonsingular critical Hessians. Choose them so small that step 1.1 applies and the height stays strictly between zero and one off the collars. On the collars $h=t$ is unchanged and has no critical point. By [F2] there are finitely many critical points; separate their heights by the supported small perturbation in [F2], still within the embedding neighbourhood. The embedding is now $(a,h')$ with excellent Morse height $h'$, and is ambient isotopic to the original surface relative to the collars.

**Isolating the Morse pictures.** Let $p$ be one of the finitely many critical points, of height $c$. Since $dh'_p=0$ and the surface embedding is immersive, the spatial derivative $da_p$ is injective. Choose planar projection transverse to this tangent plane. In a small source disk the spatial projection is therefore a diffeomorphism onto a planar disk, and [F2] writes the height there as $c+x^2+y^2$, $c-x^2-y^2$, or $c-x^2+y^2$, after a change of its planar disk coordinates. These give respectively one circle born, one circle dying, or the two smoothings of a saddle band. The orientations are the boundary orientations induced from the same oriented surface. We may arrange that the projected critical point misses every other branch at height $c$: equality with a distinct regular-level branch imposes two planar equations on its one source coordinate, so a transverse perturbation has no solution. Likewise regular immersion, transverse double points and absence of triple points on the rest of that slice follow from the one-slice jet conditions in [F4] or [F5]. Here the finite-dimensional families are supported away from the critical source disk and the end collars; on the disk only its projection direction or an arbitrarily small spatial linear perturbation is needed to make its tangent projection invertible. Finitely many disjoint source disks permit these choices simultaneously, with no change in $h'$. Transversality on the remaining slice pieces uses independent chart bumps exactly as in [F4]. All conditions are open away from the selected local critical model. Compactness then gives a small time interval about each $c$, disjoint from the others, in which the critical picture occupies a disk missing all other projected strands, and the complementary diagrams are regular and vary by planar isotopy. Thus there is one isolated birth, saddle or death in each such interval.

**Regular slabs retain the actual isotopy.** Cut at regular levels on the two sides of each critical interval. Extend the height over the product collars when a boundaryless carrier is needed. On every complementary closed slab the normalized-gradient flow [F3] identifies the surface with $C\times[a,b]$ and its embedding with $(F_t(x),t)$, for a finite union of circles $C$. Compactness makes $C$ finite, and each $F_t$ is a spatial embedding. If a slab is empty there is nothing to do. Use slightly extended regular bands at the cuts. Choose a smooth function $\rho$ on each such band, equal to the cut time on a smaller central strip and equal to $t$ near the band's two outer faces. Replace $F_t$ by $F_{\rho(t)}$. This replacement is an isotopy of the traced surfaces, not an assertion that $\rho$ is an ambient time diffeomorphism: the interpolation $(F_{(1-s)t+s\rho(t)}(x),t)$ is an embedding for every $s$, because its time coordinate is still $t$ and its spatial slices are embeddings. It is fixed near the band's outer faces, so it extends by the identity over the rest of the surface and ambiently by [F5]. In particular the traces on both sides of a cut now agree with the same stationary product near it. Bands are chosen disjoint from the critical pictures and the prescribed end collars. The regular slabs, with these smaller product strips at their ends, therefore have stationary regular endpoint projections, while the intervening critical pieces remain unchanged on smaller neighbourhoods of their critical levels. The endpoint diagrams at the cuts are regular by step 3.1.

**Finite projection events on each regular slab.** Apply [F4] to each stationary-ended $F$ of step 4.1. It gives an arbitrarily small smooth perturbation $F'$ fixed near both slab ends, with finitely many mutually distinct cusp, quadratic double-tangency and transverse triple times. Interpolate linearly in the spatial $\mathbb R^3$ chart between $F$ and $F'$; take the perturbation small enough that all intermediate slices are embeddings, using compact local immersion and distant-pair separation as in step 1.1. The traces $(F_{s,t}(x),t)$ are therefore embedding isotopies fixed on the slab ends, and extend ambiently by [F5]. Thus the chosen generic isotopy represents the original traced regular slab up to ambient isotopy relative to its cuts. By [F4] its projected events are precisely oriented R1, R2 and R3 and the intervals between them are planar isotopies. This uses the generic-isotopy supplier on the actual traced family; replacing it merely by an arbitrary Reidemeister sequence between the same endpoint links would not establish the trace assertion.

**Gluing and boundary cases.** There are finitely many critical intervals and regular slabs. All slab perturbations are fixed near their cuts, so their traced surfaces glue smoothly to the unchanged local critical pictures. Their ambient isotopies glue using collars, or compose after extending each by the identity off its support. The resulting finite ordered movie retains all boundary parametrizations and smaller end collars. Critical intervals contain only their one Morse event; the generic projection events are in the complementary slabs, so all exceptional times are distinct. Empty incoming or outgoing links merely omit the respective end cylinders; closed surface components have their own finitely many births and deaths, and are included by the same construction. The empty surface has already been treated. Prescribed regular end diagrams were never perturbed. The orientations and crossing height orders throughout are those of the actual embedded surface. Countable choice has been used only in the named suppliers and countable-chart transversality, not full AC. This proves the stated existence and trace comparison without any movie-move classification.

Let $D$ be a nonempty finite regular oriented link diagram in an oriented $3$-sphere, with finite crossing set $C(D)$. Fix a unit viewing normal $n$ and orient the projection plane $P$ so $(u,v)$ is positive exactly when $(n,u,v)$ is positive in the ambient $3$-space. At a crossing $c$, define its sign as the sign of $\det_P(v_{\rm over},v_{\rm under})$, where the two nonzero projected tangent vectors follow the oriented over- and under-strands. Let $n_+$ and $n_-$ be the numbers of positive and negative crossings.

Set $\mathcal A=\mathbb Z[X]/(X^2)$, with $\deg(1)=1$ and $\deg(X)=-1$. Its unit, multiplication, counit, and comultiplication are
$$
\eta(1)=1,\qquad m(1\otimes1)=1,\quad m(1\otimes X)=m(X\otimes1)=X,\quad m(X\otimes X)=0,
$$
$$
\epsilon(1)=0,\quad\epsilon(X)=1,\qquad \Delta(1)=1\otimes X+X\otimes1,\quad\Delta(X)=X\otimes X.
$$
Thus $m$ and $\Delta$ have quantum degree $-1$, while $\eta$ and $\epsilon$ have degree $+1$.

Choose a total order $c_1<\cdots<c_n$ on $C(D)$. A resolution state is a function $v:C(D)\to\{0,1\}$; at $v(c)=0$ use the A-smoothing and at $v(c)=1$ use the B-smoothing from the Kauffman source chart. Write $|v|=\sum_c v(c)$, let $D_v$ be the crossingless resolution, and let $k(v)$ be its number of circles. Assign the state module $\mathcal A^{\otimes k(v)}$. For an edge $v\to v+e_j$ changing crossing $c_j$ from $0$ to $1$, use $m$ if the local smoothing merges two circles and $\Delta$ if it splits one circle, tensored with the identity on all other factors, and multiply this map by $(-1)^{\sum_{i<j}v(c_i)}$. The resulting direct sum has cohomological degree
$$i(v)=|v|-n_-$$
and the generator with circle labels $1$ or $X$ has quantum degree
$$j(v)=|v|+n_+-2n_-+\sum_{\text{circle labels }a}\deg(a).$$
This defines the normalized integral Khovanov cube and its candidate degree-zero cochain differential; the assertion that the differential squares to zero is a separate lemma.

The Frobenius identity that controls a merge-split face is represented by the two equal composites below. The diagram records the maps only; the proof verifies the equality on the basis $\{1,X\}^{\otimes2}$ and does not rely on the drawing.

```tikzcd
\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal A \arrow[r,"m"] \arrow[d,"\Delta\otimes\mathrm{id}"'] & \mathcal A \arrow[d,"\Delta"] \\
\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal A \arrow[r,"\mathrm{id}\otimes m"'] & \mathcal A\otimes\mathcal A
```

Let $\mathcal A$ be an abelian category. A **cochain complex in $\mathcal A$**
is a family of objects $(C^n)_{n\in\mathbb Z}$ together with morphisms
$$d^n:C^n\to C^{n+1}$$
such that
$$d^{n+1}\circ d^n=0$$
for every $n\in\mathbb Z$.

This page uses the reindexing convention that a cochain complex $C^\bullet$ may
also be read as the chain complex with $(C^\sharp)_n:=C^{-n}$ and
$d^\sharp_n:=d^{-n}$, so that lower and upper indices differ only by the sign
of the grading.

derivations.claim: The quotient $A_L=\mathbb Q[X]/(X^2-1)$ has basis $1,X$, and its multiplication table is the displayed $m_L$. Hence multiplication is associative and commutative with unit $1$. The counit identities follow on $1,X$: $(\epsilon_L\otimes\mathrm{id})\Delta_L(1)=1$, $(\epsilon_L\otimes\mathrm{id})\Delta_L(X)=X$, and the other counit composite gives the same values.

For input $1$, both composites $(\Delta_L\otimes\mathrm{id})\Delta_L$ and $(\mathrm{id}\otimes\Delta_L)\Delta_L$ equal $1\otimes X\otimes X+X\otimes1\otimes X+1\otimes1\otimes1+X\otimes X\otimes1$. For input $X$, both equal $1\otimes1\otimes X+1\otimes X\otimes1+X\otimes1\otimes1+X\otimes X\otimes X$. Thus $\Delta_L$ is coassociative. Cocommutativity follows by swapping tensor factors in its two displayed values.

On the ordered basis $1\otimes1,1\otimes X,X\otimes1,X\otimes X$, each of $(m_L\otimes\mathrm{id})(\mathrm{id}\otimes\Delta_L)$, $\Delta_Lm_L$, and $(\mathrm{id}\otimes m_L)(\Delta_L\otimes\mathrm{id})$ has outputs $1\otimes X+X\otimes1$, $1\otimes1+X\otimes X$, $1\otimes1+X\otimes X$, and $1\otimes X+X\otimes1$. The Frobenius identities therefore hold. On a cube square, two changes on disjoint circles commute by tensor functoriality; two merges give the same composite by associativity of $m_L$; two splits give the same composite by coassociativity of $\Delta_L$; and a merge-split pair gives the same composite by the Frobenius identities just checked. In each case the cube signs on the two routes are opposite, so the square contribution to $d_L^2$ is zero. Every length-two path in the cube lies in one such square, so summing over squares proves $d_L^2=0$.

The terms of $m_L$ and $\Delta_L$ inherited from $\mathbb Q[X]/(X^2)$ have total quantum degree $0$ after the state shift. The new multiplication term $m_L(X\otimes X)=1$ changes the label degree from $-2$ to $1$, and the edge state shift adds $1$, so it raises $q$ by $4$. The new term $1\otimes1$ in $\Delta_L(X)$ changes label degree from $-1$ to $2$, and its edge state shift again adds $1$, so it raises $q$ by $4$. Thus every differential term preserves or raises $q$, making each $F^pC_L$ a subcomplex. The state set and each state module are finite, so only finitely many $q$-degrees occur and the filtration is finite. All algebra and cube checks use finite bases and no choice axiom.

Let $D$ be a finite regular oriented knot diagram with ordered crossings $c_1<\cdots<c_n$ and a marked point $p$ away from crossings. Put $\mathbb A=\mathbb Z[X]/(X^2)$ and $\mathbb F_2=\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z$. At a resolution state $v\in\{0,1\}^n$, let $V_v$ be the free abelian group generated by the resolution circles, order its circle generators, and use the exterior algebra $\Lambda^*V_v$ as its state module. A wedge of $r$ distinct circle generators has circle quantum degree $k(v)-2r$, where $k(v)=\operatorname{rank}V_v$; its total normalized degrees are $i(v)=|v|-n_-$ and $q=|v|+n_+-2n_-+k(v)-2r$. For a merge saddle joining circles $C_1,C_2$, let $p:V_v\to V_{v+e}$ be the quotient sending both to the merged circle and fixing the other generators; the edge map is $\Lambda^*p$. For a split saddle replacing $C$ by $C_1,C_2$, let $j:V_v\to V_{v+e}$ send $C$ to $C_1$ and fix the other generators; the unsigned edge map is $z\mapsto(C_1-C_2)\wedge\Lambda^*j(z)$. Choosing $C_2$ instead of $C_1$ gives the same map, while reversing the order of $C_1,C_2$ changes only its sign. Multiply each edge map by a sign $\epsilon(e)\in\{1,-1\}$, incorporating any circle-generator reordering sign. The direct sum of these state modules with the resulting cube differential is the odd Khovanov cochain complex $C_o(D)$. Write $Z_p$ for the circle containing the mark. Use the right action $z\cdot X=z\wedge Z_p$, making $C_o(D)$ a complex of right $\mathbb A$-modules; since $\mathbb A$ is commutative these are also ordinary modules over that ring. The action has quantum degree $-2$.

The square condition is that the sum of the two signed saddle composites around each two-dimensional cube face is zero. An edge sign function satisfying it is called square-compatible; existence and invariance require separate proofs.

Let $\mathbb R=\mathbb Z[h,X]/(X^2-hX)$, with $\deg_q(h)=\deg_q(X)=-2$. Its Frobenius structure has unit $\eta(1)=1$, counit $\epsilon(1)=0,\epsilon(X)=1$, quotient-ring multiplication, and comultiplication
$$ \Delta(1)=1\otimes X+X\otimes1-h\,1\otimes1,\qquad \Delta(X)=X\otimes X. $$
Applying these operations to the same normalized cube gives the Bar–Natan cochain complex $C_h(D)$, with circle labels $1,X$ of quantum degrees $1,-1$ and the same normalized state shifts; it is a complex of free $\mathbb R$-modules, and the marked circle acts by multiplication by $X$.

Put $\mathbb B=\mathbb F_2[X]/(X^2)=\mathbb R/(2,h)$. Modulo $2$, the odd exterior basis vector $C_{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge C_{i_r}$ corresponds to the even tensor state labeling the selected circles $C_{i_j}$ by $X$ and all other circles by $1$. This statewise bijection defines the candidate comparison $f_D:C_o(D)\otimes\mathbb F_2\to C_h(D)\otimes_{\mathbb R}\mathbb B$ after setting $h=0$.

A **local even–odd (LEO) triple** is a triple $(C,D,f)$ consisting of a finitely generated bigraded cochain complex $C$ free over $\mathbb A$, a finitely generated bigraded cochain complex $D$ free over $\mathbb R$, and a bigraded $\mathbb F_2[X]/(X^2)$-linear chain homotopy equivalence
$$ f:C\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb F_2\longrightarrow D\otimes_{\mathbb R}\mathbb B, \qquad \mathbb B=\mathbb R/(2,h)=\mathbb F_2[X]/(X^2), $$
such that $D[h^{-1}]$ is chain homotopy equivalent over $\mathbb R[h^{-1}]$ to one free rank-one module supported in cohomological degree $0$ and odd quantum degree. For a based knot diagram the intended candidate is $(C_o(D),C_h(D),f_D)$, where $f_D$ identifies the reduced edge maps modulo $2$ and $h$; its satisfaction of the homotopy and localization conditions is a separate theorem.

A local map $(C,D,f)\to(C',D',f')$ is a pair of bigraded module chain maps $\alpha:C\to C'$ and $\beta:D\to D'$ such that $\beta[h^{-1}]$ is a chain homotopy equivalence and the square induced by $f,f',\alpha,\beta$ after quotienting by $(2,h)$ commutes up to an $\mathbb F_2[X]/(X^2)$-linear chain homotopy. Two LEO triples are locally equivalent when there is a local map in each direction.

Let a finite planar resolution cube be equipped with an arrow at each crossing, transported to its saddle edges while resolving the other disjoint crossing disks, and use the odd exterior merge and split maps. There is a function assigning a sign to every edge such that the resulting signed differential squares to zero over the integers. More precisely, one can prescribe the face products on all faces, including faces whose two composites vanish, as follows. On a face with nonzero composites let $\kappa\in\{1,-1\}$ be their relative commutation sign. On a zero-composite face the two saddle arcs have alternating endpoints on one circle, one arc inside and one outside; put them in the standard two-chord picture by an orientation-preserving planar isotopy and rotate so that the inside arrow points upwards and set $\kappa=1$ when the outside arrow points left, and $\kappa=-1$ when it points right. Then the prescribed product of the four edge signs is $-\kappa$. These prescriptions are consistent, and two edge assignments realizing the same prescriptions are related by a vertexwise sign change. All the constructions are finite and choice-free. The vertexwise comparison commutes with the marked right $\mathbb Z[X]/(X^2)$-action.

derivations.claim: **A cancellation identity over any ring.** Suppose a cochain differential $d$ on $M=A\oplus B\oplus R$ has a degree-one block $b:A\to B$ which is an isomorphism. Set $h|_B=b^{-1}$ and $h|_{A\oplus R}=0$. Then $h^2=0$ and $hdh=h$. Consequently $E=1-dh-hd$ is a projection commuting with $d$: expansion using $d^2=h^2=0$ and $hdh=h$ gives $E^2=E$ and $dE=Ed$. Writing $j:R\to M$ and $q:M\to R$ for the direct-sum maps, set $i=Ej=j-hdj$, $p=qE=q-qdh$, and $d_R=q(d-dhd)j$. The $A$-coordinate of a vector in $\operatorname{im}E$ is minus $hd$ of its $R$-coordinate, and its $B$-coordinate is zero; hence $q:\operatorname{im}E\to R$ and $Ej$ are inverse. Thus $pi=1$, $ip=E$, $di=id_R$, $pd=d_Rp$, and $1-ip=dh+hd$. These identities also give $d_R^2=0$. If the blocks and their inverse are right-module maps, so are all these maps. This calculation applies to entire finite exterior cubes at once; their differentials are included in $d$, rather than omitted as spectators.

**The RII four-state model.** Call the straight matching $I$ and the cup-cap matching $U$. Rotate the disk and order the crossing whose smoothing pair is $(I,U)$ first, followed by the crossing whose smoothing pair is $(U,I)$. This order refers to the geometric smoothings; for either orientation of the two strands the pair contains one oriented positive and one oriented negative crossing. The local states $00,01,10,11$ are $U,I,U\sqcup z,U$. In state $10$ label the circle through the upper arc $a$, the small circle $z$, and the circle through the lower arc $c$; the exterior closure may identify $a$ and $c$. These labels therefore denote actual generators, with that equality imposed when applicable. At $00\to10$ the map is the split $(a-z)\wedge(-)$ after choosing its lift; at $10\to11$ the quotient identifies $z$ with $c$. Each edge has its prescribed sign, which is $\pm1$ and may depend on $v$. In $10$ set $Y=z-c$ and write $L=\Lambda W$, $K=Y\wedge\Lambda W$, where $W$ is the circle group of $U$. The quotient $10\to11$ is the identity on $L$ and zero on $K$. The $K$-coefficient of $00\to10$ is minus the identity, because $a-z=(a-c)-Y$. This remains true when $a=c$. Thus both indicated blocks are invertible right-module blocks for every exterior closure.

**The merge curl.** Write $W_v$ for the old circle group and $c_v$ for the circle through the curl's continuing arc. The two local states are $\Lambda(W_v\oplus\mathbb Zz)$ and $\Lambda W_v$, with merge quotient $m(z)=m(c_v)=c_v$. Put $Y=z-c_v$ and decompose the first state as $L_v\oplus K_v$, where $L_v=\Lambda W_v$ and $K_v=Y\wedge\Lambda W_v$. The merge is the identity $L_v\to\Lambda W_v$ and kills $K_v$. External edges preserve both summands. Indeed a merge takes $Y$ to its new $Y$, while a split takes $Y$ to the new $Y$ up to a multiple of its own split difference; that extra term vanishes when wedged with the same difference. On $L$ the external maps are the old maps. On $K$, identifying $Y\wedge w$ with $w$ negates each external split and leaves each merge unchanged. Put $\sigma(v)=(k(v)-k(0)+|v|)/2$. It is an integer, unchanged by a merge and increased by one by a split. Thus $w\mapsto(-1)^{\sigma(v)}Y\wedge w$ identifies $K$ with the old complex. The other two summands cancel by step 1.1, using the signed merge pivot and its inverse. With the ordinary cube ordering its pivot coefficient can be taken $(-1)^{|v|}$. The normalization makes the survivor's cohomological and quantum degrees those of the old diagram: the extra small circle and extra exterior generator change the local quantum degree by $-1$, cancelling the positive-curl shift $+1$.

**The two RII cancellations.** First cancel $L_{10}\to U_{11}$ by step 1.1. Its inverse is the signed inclusion using no $z$. The correction $-dhd$ does not alter the $00\to K_{10}$ block, since external edges preserve $L$ and the local outgoing arrow from $L$ lands only in $11$. That block is still the signed minus identity, so cancel $U_{00}\to K_{10}$. The survivor is $I_{01}$. Its exterior differential is unchanged: after the first cancellation no differential from $I_{01}$ enters $K$, since its only local outgoing edge was to the cancelled $11$ and the correction factors through $L$, which has no $K$-component. Consequently the second cancellation contributes no correction on $I_{01}$. The local height is one, the pair adds one negative and one positive crossing, and hence the homological shift is $1-1=0$ and the quantum shift is $1+(1-2)=0$. This proves the normalized equivalence.

**The split curl.** Here the local arrow is $\Lambda W_v\to\Lambda(W_v\oplus\mathbb Zz)$, $w\mapsto Y\wedge w$, with either overall sign allowed. Use the same decomposition $L\oplus K$. The split is an isomorphism onto $K$; $L$ survives. Choose the crossing-edge coefficient $(-1)^{|v|+\sigma(v)}$ when the external edges have their old coefficients. Across an external merge this coefficient changes sign, and across a split it is unchanged. Since the unsigned curl split commutes with the former and anticommutes with the latter, every mixed square anticommutes. Cancel its isomorphism onto $K$ by step 1.1. The surviving $L$ has its old differential and right action. It is at local height one; the negative crossing increases $n_-$ by one, so its normalized cohomological degree is unchanged. Its additional circle contributes quantum degree $+1$, its local height contributes $+1$, and the negative crossing contributes $-2$, again giving shift zero. The formulas include both directions of the move, since the inclusion and projection are homotopy inverses.

**Module maps, signs and reduction.** The mark is outside the disk, so it is never the small circle $z$. In the displayed decompositions a right multiplication appends an old generator. Coefficient projections in $z$ and $Y=z-c$, the inclusions, and multiplication by a left split difference therefore commute with that right action. All pivots, their signed inverses and the maps in step 1.1 are module-linear. Different admissible edge signs are accommodated by [F2]. Reversing a saddle arrow negates its split map and is absorbed in that edge coefficient; changing strand orientations changes only the normalized crossing shifts, already checked for R1 and RII. Rotations simply relabel the generators and disk ports. Modulo two all displayed signs become one, exterior products become commuting square-zero circle labels, and $z-c$ becomes $z+c$. Merge, split, inclusion, coefficient projection and the formula $d-dhd$ reduce to precisely the even cancellation operations. Thus the maps, inverses and homotopies have the asserted comparison, for every closure and orientation.

Let $D$ be a finite regular oriented knot diagram with ordered crossings $c_1<\cdots<c_n$ and a marked point $p$ away from crossings. Put $\mathbb A=\mathbb Z[X]/(X^2)$ and $\mathbb F_2=\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z$. At a resolution state $v\in\{0,1\}^n$, let $V_v$ be the free abelian group generated by the resolution circles, order its circle generators, and use the exterior algebra $\Lambda^*V_v$ as its state module. A wedge of $r$ distinct circle generators has circle quantum degree $k(v)-2r$, where $k(v)=\operatorname{rank}V_v$; its total normalized degrees are $i(v)=|v|-n_-$ and $q=|v|+n_+-2n_-+k(v)-2r$. For a merge saddle joining circles $C_1,C_2$, let $p:V_v\to V_{v+e}$ be the quotient sending both to the merged circle and fixing the other generators; the edge map is $\Lambda^*p$. For a split saddle replacing $C$ by $C_1,C_2$, let $j:V_v\to V_{v+e}$ send $C$ to $C_1$ and fix the other generators; the unsigned edge map is $z\mapsto(C_1-C_2)\wedge\Lambda^*j(z)$. Choosing $C_2$ instead of $C_1$ gives the same map, while reversing the order of $C_1,C_2$ changes only its sign. Multiply each edge map by a sign $\epsilon(e)\in\{1,-1\}$, incorporating any circle-generator reordering sign. The direct sum of these state modules with the resulting cube differential is the odd Khovanov cochain complex $C_o(D)$. Write $Z_p$ for the circle containing the mark. Use the right action $z\cdot X=z\wedge Z_p$, making $C_o(D)$ a complex of right $\mathbb A$-modules; since $\mathbb A$ is commutative these are also ordinary modules over that ring. The action has quantum degree $-2$.

The square condition is that the sum of the two signed saddle composites around each two-dimensional cube face is zero. An edge sign function satisfying it is called square-compatible; existence and invariance require separate proofs.

Let $\mathbb R=\mathbb Z[h,X]/(X^2-hX)$, with $\deg_q(h)=\deg_q(X)=-2$. Its Frobenius structure has unit $\eta(1)=1$, counit $\epsilon(1)=0,\epsilon(X)=1$, quotient-ring multiplication, and comultiplication
$$ \Delta(1)=1\otimes X+X\otimes1-h\,1\otimes1,\qquad \Delta(X)=X\otimes X. $$
Applying these operations to the same normalized cube gives the Bar–Natan cochain complex $C_h(D)$, with circle labels $1,X$ of quantum degrees $1,-1$ and the same normalized state shifts; it is a complex of free $\mathbb R$-modules, and the marked circle acts by multiplication by $X$.

Put $\mathbb B=\mathbb F_2[X]/(X^2)=\mathbb R/(2,h)$. Modulo $2$, the odd exterior basis vector $C_{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge C_{i_r}$ corresponds to the even tensor state labeling the selected circles $C_{i_j}$ by $X$ and all other circles by $1$. This statewise bijection defines the candidate comparison $f_D:C_o(D)\otimes\mathbb F_2\to C_h(D)\otimes_{\mathbb R}\mathbb B$ after setting $h=0$.

A **local even–odd (LEO) triple** is a triple $(C,D,f)$ consisting of a finitely generated bigraded cochain complex $C$ free over $\mathbb A$, a finitely generated bigraded cochain complex $D$ free over $\mathbb R$, and a bigraded $\mathbb F_2[X]/(X^2)$-linear chain homotopy equivalence
$$ f:C\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb F_2\longrightarrow D\otimes_{\mathbb R}\mathbb B, \qquad \mathbb B=\mathbb R/(2,h)=\mathbb F_2[X]/(X^2), $$
such that $D[h^{-1}]$ is chain homotopy equivalent over $\mathbb R[h^{-1}]$ to one free rank-one module supported in cohomological degree $0$ and odd quantum degree. For a based knot diagram the intended candidate is $(C_o(D),C_h(D),f_D)$, where $f_D$ identifies the reduced edge maps modulo $2$ and $h$; its satisfaction of the homotopy and localization conditions is a separate theorem.

A local map $(C,D,f)\to(C',D',f')$ is a pair of bigraded module chain maps $\alpha:C\to C'$ and $\beta:D\to D'$ such that $\beta[h^{-1}]$ is a chain homotopy equivalence and the square induced by $f,f',\alpha,\beta$ after quotienting by $(2,h)$ commutes up to an $\mathbb F_2[X]/(X^2)$-linear chain homotopy. Two LEO triples are locally equivalent when there is a local map in each direction.

derivations.claim: **A right-linear reduced decomposition.** At each state let $V$ be the circle group, $Z$ its marked generator, and $U=\ker(\operatorname{aug}:V\to\mathbb Z)$, where every circle has augmentation one. The vectors $Y_j=Z_j-Z$ for unmarked circles are a basis of $U$, and $V=U\oplus\mathbb ZZ$. Thus $\Lambda V=\Lambda U\otimes\mathbb A$ as a right module, by $u\otimes1\mapsto u$, $u\otimes X\mapsto u\wedge Z$. A merge preserves augmentation and takes the marked generator to the marked generator. For a split choose the lift of its old marked generator to the new marked generator; if the marked circle is unaffected this is the usual lift. This lift also preserves augmentation, and the split difference belongs to $U$ in the target. Hence in these coordinates every edge acts as its reduced exterior quotient or split on $\Lambda U$, tensored with the identity of $\mathbb A$. This is an equality of maps on both $u$ and $u\wedge Z$, not merely an unmarked abelian-group splitting.

**The map and its exact signs.** For a vertex $v_j$ set $\sigma_j(v_j)=(k_j(v_j)-k_j(0)+|v_j|)/2$. A merge leaves $\sigma_j$ fixed and a split increases it by one. At a joined state the reduced difference group is $U_1\oplus U_2$, by sending every $Z_i-Z_j^{\mathrm{mark}}$ to its difference from the merged marked generator. For $u_j\in\Lambda^{r_j}U_j$ and $a_j\in\mathbb A$, define $\Phi((u_1\otimes a_1)\otimes(u_2\otimes a_2))=(-1)^{r_1\sigma_2(v_2)}(u_1\wedge u_2)\otimes a_1a_2$. The degree $r_1$ here is the reduced exterior degree and excludes the marked $X$-factor. The formula is balanced and right $\mathbb A$-linear because its sign is independent of $a_1,a_2$. Its reduced wedge basis times $1,X$ is exactly the joined basis, so it is bijective. Conjugating the tensor differential gives the following coefficients relative to the joined unsigned saddles: $\epsilon_1$ for a first-diagram merge, $(-1)^{\sigma_2}\epsilon_1$ for a first-diagram split, and $(-1)^{i(v_1)}\epsilon_2$ for either second-diagram saddle. For the last assertion, a second split increases $\sigma_2$ by one, contributing $(-1)^{r_1}$; moving its left split difference past $u_1$ contributes the same sign, and the two cancel. The remaining sign is the tensor cochain sign. A first split increases $r_1$ by one and supplies precisely $(-1)^{\sigma_2}$. Merges preserve reduced exterior degree. These equations prove that $\Phi$ is a chain isomorphism for the induced signs.

**The induced signs are fully admissible.** A two-face within one diagram has the same geometric coefficient as that diagram's face: insertion of the other marked arc and its passive circles changes neither the cyclic order of its saddle endpoints nor the oriented inside/outside test. On a first-diagram face the additional sign in step 2.1 has boundary exponent $\sigma_2$ times the sum of the split counts in its two paths. The counts agree, since each equals $(k_{\mathrm{out}}-k_{\mathrm{in}}+2)/2$, so this exponent is even. On a second-diagram face the common extra sign $(-1)^{i(v_1)}$ occurs four times. Thus all internal face products are unchanged. For a mixed face let $b_j$ be its saddle's split indicator. The joining strip separates the two saddle disks by a two-edge cut. Their unsigned maps commute except for the interchange of two reduced split factors, giving $\kappa=(-1)^{b_1b_2}$; no alternating-endpoint zero face occurs across that cut. The induced coefficient product is $(-1)^{1+b_1b_2}$: changing a first coordinate changes $i(v_1)$ by one, while a second split changes the first split's factor $(-1)^{\sigma_2}$ by $(-1)^{b_1b_2}$. This is exactly $-\kappa$. Hence all prescribed faces, including the internal zero faces, have their required products. By [F2], any other admissible realization is related to this one by a marked vertex-sign isomorphism.

**The Bar–Natan map, gradings and reduction.** At a state multiply the two marked circle factors, leave every unmarked circle factor unchanged, and multiply by $(-1)^{n_-^{(1)}|v_2|}$. Balanced tensoring over $\mathbb R$ identifies its basis with the joined state basis, so this is an isomorphism. Associativity and the Frobenius identity in [F3] show that the unsigned multiplication commutes with every saddle. For first-diagram edges the added vertex sign is unchanged. For second-diagram edges it changes by $(-1)^{n_-^{(1)}}$, converting the tensor cochain sign $(-1)^{i(v_1)}$ into the joined cube sign $(-1)^{|v_1|}$, since $i(v_1)=|v_1|-n_-^{(1)}$. This proves the signed chain equation. Both maps identify two marked circles with one, so their quantum degree before the displayed shift is $-1$. Crossing counts and $n_+,n_-$ add, giving the stated normalized homological and quantum degrees. In characteristic two the odd sign in step 2.1 is one, $Y_j$ corresponds to the even label operator $X_j+X_{\mathrm{mark}}$, and the merged marked generator corresponds to $X_{\mathrm{mark}}$. Thus the reduced wedge product times $a_1a_2$ is exactly the even state-label identification obtained by marked multiplication. Both theories therefore induce the same comparison square after the required quotients. This proves all assertions.

Let $D$ be a finite regular oriented knot diagram with ordered crossings $c_1<\cdots<c_n$ and a marked point $p$ away from crossings. Put $\mathbb A=\mathbb Z[X]/(X^2)$ and $\mathbb F_2=\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z$. At a resolution state $v\in\{0,1\}^n$, let $V_v$ be the free abelian group generated by the resolution circles, order its circle generators, and use the exterior algebra $\Lambda^*V_v$ as its state module. A wedge of $r$ distinct circle generators has circle quantum degree $k(v)-2r$, where $k(v)=\operatorname{rank}V_v$; its total normalized degrees are $i(v)=|v|-n_-$ and $q=|v|+n_+-2n_-+k(v)-2r$. For a merge saddle joining circles $C_1,C_2$, let $p:V_v\to V_{v+e}$ be the quotient sending both to the merged circle and fixing the other generators; the edge map is $\Lambda^*p$. For a split saddle replacing $C$ by $C_1,C_2$, let $j:V_v\to V_{v+e}$ send $C$ to $C_1$ and fix the other generators; the unsigned edge map is $z\mapsto(C_1-C_2)\wedge\Lambda^*j(z)$. Choosing $C_2$ instead of $C_1$ gives the same map, while reversing the order of $C_1,C_2$ changes only its sign. Multiply each edge map by a sign $\epsilon(e)\in\{1,-1\}$, incorporating any circle-generator reordering sign. The direct sum of these state modules with the resulting cube differential is the odd Khovanov cochain complex $C_o(D)$. Write $Z_p$ for the circle containing the mark. Use the right action $z\cdot X=z\wedge Z_p$, making $C_o(D)$ a complex of right $\mathbb A$-modules; since $\mathbb A$ is commutative these are also ordinary modules over that ring. The action has quantum degree $-2$.

The square condition is that the sum of the two signed saddle composites around each two-dimensional cube face is zero. An edge sign function satisfying it is called square-compatible; existence and invariance require separate proofs.

Let $\mathbb R=\mathbb Z[h,X]/(X^2-hX)$, with $\deg_q(h)=\deg_q(X)=-2$. Its Frobenius structure has unit $\eta(1)=1$, counit $\epsilon(1)=0,\epsilon(X)=1$, quotient-ring multiplication, and comultiplication
$$ \Delta(1)=1\otimes X+X\otimes1-h\,1\otimes1,\qquad \Delta(X)=X\otimes X. $$
Applying these operations to the same normalized cube gives the Bar–Natan cochain complex $C_h(D)$, with circle labels $1,X$ of quantum degrees $1,-1$ and the same normalized state shifts; it is a complex of free $\mathbb R$-modules, and the marked circle acts by multiplication by $X$.

Put $\mathbb B=\mathbb F_2[X]/(X^2)=\mathbb R/(2,h)$. Modulo $2$, the odd exterior basis vector $C_{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge C_{i_r}$ corresponds to the even tensor state labeling the selected circles $C_{i_j}$ by $X$ and all other circles by $1$. This statewise bijection defines the candidate comparison $f_D:C_o(D)\otimes\mathbb F_2\to C_h(D)\otimes_{\mathbb R}\mathbb B$ after setting $h=0$.

A **local even–odd (LEO) triple** is a triple $(C,D,f)$ consisting of a finitely generated bigraded cochain complex $C$ free over $\mathbb A$, a finitely generated bigraded cochain complex $D$ free over $\mathbb R$, and a bigraded $\mathbb F_2[X]/(X^2)$-linear chain homotopy equivalence
$$ f:C\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb F_2\longrightarrow D\otimes_{\mathbb R}\mathbb B, \qquad \mathbb B=\mathbb R/(2,h)=\mathbb F_2[X]/(X^2), $$
such that $D[h^{-1}]$ is chain homotopy equivalent over $\mathbb R[h^{-1}]$ to one free rank-one module supported in cohomological degree $0$ and odd quantum degree. For a based knot diagram the intended candidate is $(C_o(D),C_h(D),f_D)$, where $f_D$ identifies the reduced edge maps modulo $2$ and $h$; its satisfaction of the homotopy and localization conditions is a separate theorem.

A local map $(C,D,f)\to(C',D',f')$ is a pair of bigraded module chain maps $\alpha:C\to C'$ and $\beta:D\to D'$ such that $\beta[h^{-1}]$ is a chain homotopy equivalence and the square induced by $f,f',\alpha,\beta$ after quotienting by $(2,h)$ commutes up to an $\mathbb F_2[X]/(X^2)$-linear chain homotopy. Two LEO triples are locally equivalent when there is a local map in each direction.

Let a finite planar resolution cube be equipped with an arrow at each crossing, transported to its saddle edges while resolving the other disjoint crossing disks, and use the odd exterior merge and split maps. There is a function assigning a sign to every edge such that the resulting signed differential squares to zero over the integers. More precisely, one can prescribe the face products on all faces, including faces whose two composites vanish, as follows. On a face with nonzero composites let $\kappa\in\{1,-1\}$ be their relative commutation sign. On a zero-composite face the two saddle arcs have alternating endpoints on one circle, one arc inside and one outside; put them in the standard two-chord picture by an orientation-preserving planar isotopy and rotate so that the inside arrow points upwards and set $\kappa=1$ when the outside arrow points left, and $\kappa=-1$ when it points right. Then the prescribed product of the four edge signs is $-\kappa$. These prescriptions are consistent, and two edge assignments realizing the same prescriptions are related by a vertexwise sign change. All the constructions are finite and choice-free. The vertexwise comparison commutes with the marked right $\mathbb Z[X]/(X^2)$-action.

derivations.claim: **The zero-face cyclic-order test, with both outside placements.** Name the inside arc $a$ and the outside arc $b$, and write their directed endpoints as $a_-,a_+,b_-,b_+$. Give their common circle the positive boundary orientation of its bounded disk. The endpoints alternate, so the two possible cyclic words starting at $a_-$ are $W_+=(a_-,b_-,a_+,b_+)$ and $W_-=(a_-,b_+,a_+,b_-)$. Put $\chi(W_+)=1$ and $\chi(W_-)=-1$. The precise calibration must include both possible placements of the unbounded face on the outside-arc side: they need not be related by a planar isotopy fixing all endpoint labels. Straighten the circle locally at its four endpoints, with inside $a$ directed from South to North, and put the endpoints of $b$ at West and East. Read the outside arrow at an endpoint germ, as in the stipulated standard picture, rather than at a midpoint of its exterior route. There are four cases. If $b$ runs from West to East above the circle, it enters its head at East leftwards, the cyclic word is $W_-$, and $\kappa=1$. If it runs from West to East below the circle, the head germ is still leftwards, its word is still $W_-$, and $\kappa=1$. If $b$ runs from East to West above the circle, it enters West rightwards, its word is $W_+$, and $\kappa=-1$. If it runs from East to West below the circle, its head germ remains rightwards, its word remains $W_+$, and $\kappa=-1$. The same direction is obtained at the tail germ: outgoing at West is leftwards and outgoing at East rightwards. Thus all four placements give the single formula $\kappa=-\chi$. This table also treats the two possible faces on each side of the circle cut by its surgery arc. Straightening an endpoint germ uses only its transverse attachment on the indicated side and does not change which directed endpoint it is; no isotopy exchanging the two outside-face placements is assumed.

**Changing the omitted point.** Consider the same zero-face circle on the oriented sphere. Its two complementary sides contain its two surgery arcs. If the two omitted points are on the same side, both planar boundary orientations agree and both presentations call the same arc inside. Their cyclic word and $\kappa$ agree by step 1.1. If the omitted points are on opposite sides, the inside/outside names are exchanged and the positive bounded-side boundary orientation is reversed: the boundary orientations of the two sides of an oriented surface are opposite. Both changes are necessary. For example, an old word $W_+=(a_-,b_-,a_+,b_+)$, read in the reverse orientation starting at $b_-$, is $(b_-,a_-,b_+,a_+)$, which is the new word $W_+$ when $b$ is the new inside arc and $a$ the new outside arc. An old word $W_-=(a_-,b_+,a_+,b_-)$ becomes $(b_-,a_+,b_+,a_-)$, which is the new word $W_-$. Hence $\chi$, and therefore $\kappa$, is unchanged in this case too. This is the full two-case calculation; exchanging only the names without reversing the boundary orientation would give an incorrect sign. The same argument applies to an arbitrary orientation-preserving spherical change of coordinates by transporting the circle and its two sides first.

**Naturality of every unsigned saddle.** At state $v$ let $P_v$ send each circle generator to that same spherical circle in the other chart. It is a bijection of bases. For a merge quotient $q$, both $P_{v+e}q$ and $q'P_v$ send the two merging generators to the same merged generator and fix every spectator. Thus their exterior extensions agree. For a split, transport the arrow and its ordered output circles. Then $P_{v+e}$ carries the difference $C_1-C_2$ to $C'_1-C'_2$. Choose the transported lift $j'$ of the split input. On every wedge $z$ one has $\Lambda P_{v+e}((C_1-C_2)\wedge\Lambda j(z))=(C'_1-C'_2)\wedge\Lambda j'(\Lambda P_v(z))$. The alternative lift gives the same expression by [F1]. Circle order changes are absorbed by the exterior relabelling, including their actual wedge signs. Thus the two unsigned composites on every face are conjugate by invertible relabellings. On a nonzero face their relative commutation sign $\kappa$ is consequently unchanged. On a zero face it is unchanged by step 2.1. All face products prescribed by [F2] therefore agree in the two charts.

**Odd chain isomorphisms and their actual inverse.** Choose a full admissible assignment in the first chart using [F2] and give each corresponding edge of the second chart the same sign. By step 3.1 these are full admissible signs in the second chart, and $P_o=\bigoplus_v\Lambda P_v$ intertwines their signed differentials. Its inverse is $\bigoplus_v\Lambda(P_v^{-1})$, so both composites are exactly the identity; the chain homotopies for an inverse are zero. If the second chart instead has independently chosen full admissible signs, divide those signs by the transported signs. The quotient has product one on every face, including the zero faces. Fix the lowest vertex sign to be one and assign each other vertex the product of the edge quotients along a monotone path. The square equations make this independent of the path, since adjacent coordinate exchanges connect all monotone paths. Multiplication by the resulting scalar at each vertex conjugates the transported differential to the chosen one. Compose this diagonal map with $P_o$. Its inverse is the inverse relabelling followed by the same scalar signs in the inverse order. This proves the asserted isomorphism for the independently chosen assignments, without claiming independence for arbitrary weak square-compatible assignments.

**Marked linearity and gradings.** Relabelling carries the marked generator $Z_p$ to the marked generator $Z'_p$. Hence $P_o(z\wedge Z_p)=P_o(z)\wedge Z'_p$. Vertexwise scalar signs commute with this right action too. Both the odd map and its inverse are thus $\mathbb A$-linear. An orientation-preserving surface chart preserves the signed crossing, its designated 0/1 smoothing and its over/under information. It consequently preserves $n_+,n_-,|v|,k(v)$; relabelling preserves exterior degree. The formula in [F1] then proves preservation of both normalized gradings. Vertexwise signs have degree zero. There is no semilinear substitution $X\mapsto-X$ in these maps.

**The integral Bar–Natan map.** On each state relabel the tensor factors by their spherical circles and keep the labels $1,X$ and the coefficient $h$ unchanged. Commutativity of multiplication and cocommutativity of comultiplication make this independent of a tensor-factor ordering. For a merge, split, birth or death the relabelling intertwines the operations because their input and output circles and all coefficients in the formulas of [F1] agree. In particular it intertwines every cube edge. The crossing order has been kept, so the ordinary cube edge signs agree as well. This yields a chain isomorphism $P_h$ with inverse the inverse tensor-factor relabelling. It takes multiplication by the marked $X$ to multiplication by the target marked $X$, and fixes $h$, so is $\mathbb R$-linear. The grading check is the same state-shift calculation as in step 5.1, with unchanged circle labels. Both inverse composites are identities with zero homotopies.

**The common reduction and the local maps.** Modulo two all vertex signs and exterior reorder signs are one. The reduced odd map sends a selected subset of circles to exactly the same spherical subset in the other chart. After setting $(2,h)=0$, the Bar–Natan map sends the tensor state with those $X$-labels to that same subset. Under the comparison of [F1] these maps are identical on every basis state, including its marked action. Thus $P_h f=f'P_o$ holds exactly after the specified quotients, not merely up to homotopy. The inverse maps satisfy the same calculation. Since $P_h$ is already an integral marked-module chain isomorphism, localizing at $h$ retains its explicit inverse and zero homotopies. This verifies all local-map conditions, with the full asserted degrees and module structures, whenever the endpoint triples satisfy the LEO-object hypotheses; it does not assert rank-one localization for arbitrary multi-component links. The only sign assignment and comparison constructions used finite cube paths and finite multiplications, so require no choice axiom.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\mathcal F:M\times S\to N$ be a smooth family of maps and let $Z\subseteq N$
be an embedded submanifold. If $\mathcal F\pitchfork Z$, then the set of
parameters $s\in S$ for which the slice $\mathcal F_s:M\to N$ fails to be
transverse to $Z$ is a null subset of $S$.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$.

1. **Compact main case.** Let $M$ be a compact smooth manifold, possibly with boundary, let $N$ be a smooth manifold without boundary, let $F:M\times I\to N$ be a smooth isotopy of embeddings that is constant near the ends of $I$, and let $W$ be an open neighbourhood of $F(M\times I)$ in $N$. Then there is an ambient isotopy $H:N\times I\to N$ with $H_0=\mathrm{id}_N$, every $H_t$ a diffeomorphism, $H_t\circ F_0=F_t$ for all $t\in I$, $H_t=\mathrm{id}_N$ outside $W$ for every $t$, and $H_t$ stationary near the ends; if $F$ is constant near the ends with parameter $\varepsilon$, then $H_t=\mathrm{id}_N$ for $t\le\varepsilon/2$ and $H_t=H_1$ for $t\ge1-\varepsilon/2$.
2. **Relative form.** Let $N$ be boundaryless, $U\subseteq N$ open, $A\subseteq U$ compact, and let $F:U\times I\to N$ be a smooth isotopy of embeddings whose track image is open in $N\times I$. Then there is a compactly supported ambient isotopy $H$ of $N$ with $H_t\circ F_0=F_t$ on a neighbourhood of $A$ for every $t$.
3. **Boundary stratum.** If $N$ has boundary and $F(M\times I)\subseteq\partial N$, then the ambient isotopy of clause 1 can be chosen with every $H_t$ carrying $\partial N$ onto itself; if $F(M\times I)\subseteq N\setminus\partial N$, it can be chosen compactly supported in $N\setminus\partial N$.
4. **General isotopies.** For the same compact source (possibly with boundary) and boundaryless target as in clause 1, every smooth isotopy extends with support in a compact subset of any prescribed neighbourhood $W$ of $F(M\times I)$. The endpoint-constancy hypothesis and the stationary-end conclusion are both omitted; all other conclusions of clause 1 hold.

Assume countable choice. Let $S\subset S^3\times[0,1]$ be a compact smooth properly embedded oriented surface, with product collars and boundary the finite oriented links $-L_0$ and $L_1$ in the two ends. Components of $S$ and either boundary link may be empty. After an ambient isotopy fixed on smaller prescribed end collars, $S$ has a finite movie consisting of planar isotopies, oriented Reidemeister moves R1, R2 and R3, births, oriented saddle band moves, and deaths. All exceptional times are distinct. The movie's actual smoothly embedded trace is ambient isotopic to the given $S$ relative to those collars, with its boundary orientations and parametrizations retained. Prescribed regular endpoint diagrams may be retained. This is movie existence; it asserts no equivalence theorem for two movies.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $F:C\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be a smooth
isotopy of a finite disjoint union of circles, constant near both ends, and
suppose both end projections under the fixed $\pi$ are regular. Arbitrarily
close to $F$ in the strong smooth topology there is such an isotopy $F'$, equal
to $F$ near the ends, whose projected slices have only these exceptional events:

(i) finitely many ordinary cusps, at distinct times; in a source coordinate
$x$, writing $g(x,t)=\pi F'(x,t)$, each satisfies
$g_x=0$, $\det(g_{xx},g_{xt})\ne0$ and
$\det(g_{xx},g_{xxx})\ne0$;

(ii) the **off-diagonal unordered** double-point locus is a smooth
one-dimensional manifold with boundary in the local-extension sense of
[[def-smooth-chart-atlas-and-structure-on-a-manifold-with-boundary]]; its boundary
consists exactly of the double points at $t=0,1$. Its interior is a manifold
without boundary, and its time projection has only finitely many
nondegenerate critical points, each an ordinary quadratic tangency of two
immersed branches;

(iii) finitely many transverse triple events, with all three pairs of
projected tangents independent, and no quadruple points.

No two exceptional events have the same time. All other slices are regular,
and between exceptional times their decorated diagrams vary by planar isotopy.

Let $F'$ satisfy the general-position conditions of
[[lem-a-smooth-isotopy-of-links-can-be-put-in-general-position]], with
exceptional times $t_1<\cdots<t_N$. Immediately before and after each event,
its regular diagrams differ, up to planar isotopy, by one oriented
Reidemeister move: R1 at an ordinary cusp, R2 at a quadratic double tangency,
and R3 at a transverse triple event. The regular intervals contribute planar
isotopies, and the moves preserve the over/under and orientation data of $F'$.
Consequently the end diagrams are connected by a finite sequence of these moves.

The interpolation $G(s,u)=(b(u),(1-s)h(u)+su)$ is a smooth homotopy fixed near the two endpoint collars. Away from those collars its time coordinate stays in $(0,1)$. Its spatial vector field extends and integrates as in [F2], with time $t$ merely a smooth parameter. Hence a level-preserving spatial coordinate family sends the marked track and a surrounding surface strip to a fixed straight model in one small three-ball. Choose the endpoint coordinate identifications to be its endpoint values; compatible prescribed long presentations need no change there. The rest of the surface is a compact collared tangle cobordism in a fixed ball of $\mathbb R^3\times[0,1]$, with two fixed endpoint collars on the spatial ball boundary at every time. All other parts of the surface are disjoint from the retained strip; compactness after taking a slightly smaller strip provides a uniform separation. This closure represents exactly the deleted standard marked interval in its three-ball, with the same endpoint parametrizations. The compact part projects inside the large disk and the closing arc misses its interior. Consequently all later compactly supported projection events can occur inside that disk while the mark and a neighborhood of it remain fixed outside.

**Finite Morse events relative to the strip.** Run the height part of the construction in [F3] on the compact tangle part. All bumps have support outside the fixed tangle-end collars and the removed marked strip. Where those collars are protected, height is the product coordinate and has no critical point. On the remaining finite chart cores the bump-linear perturbations of height span each cotangent fiber exactly as in [F3]; [F1] therefore gives a Morse height. The critical points are finite, their values can be separated by disjoint supported bumps, and sufficiently small perturbations remain embeddings with an actual ambient trace isotopy. Their tangent-plane projections and complementary regular branches can be made generic by spatial bumps on the same compact part. The resulting birth, saddle and death disks lie inside the large projection disk. The long end collars and the marked closing arc are fixed. These are the actual local models of [F3], with a protected regular boundary added, not any assumption that a mark survives an arbitrary unbased movie.

Its flow gives an isotopy of compact tangles fixed near their ends. Glue the finitely many critical intervals and regular slabs along their stationary cuts. Choose their exceptional times distinct as in [F3]. The fixed exterior closing arc supplies the mark in every frame, including any frame with additional circles, and none of its points participates in a birth, saddle or death. Undo the spatial coordinate family of step 3.1 and the marked-strip replacement to compare the trace: all actual perturbations were ambient isotopies relative to the retained collars, and the coordinate family has the explicitly recorded endpoint identifications. Therefore the transported trace is the original marked concordance up to the asserted relative isotopy. The construction preserves the annulus and its orientation. Let $D$ be a finite regular oriented knot diagram with ordered crossings $c_1<\cdots<c_n$ and a marked point $p$ away from crossings. Put $\mathbb A=\mathbb Z[X]/(X^2)$ and $\mathbb F_2=\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z$. At a resolution state $v\in\{0,1\}^n$, let $V_v$ be the free abelian group generated by the resolution circles, order its circle generators, and use the exterior algebra $\Lambda^*V_v$ as its state module. A wedge of $r$ distinct circle generators has circle quantum degree $k(v)-2r$, where $k(v)=\operatorname{rank}V_v$; its total normalized degrees are $i(v)=|v|-n_-$ and $q=|v|+n_+-2n_-+k(v)-2r$. For a merge saddle joining circles $C_1,C_2$, let $p:V_v\to V_{v+e}$ be the quotient sending both to the merged circle and fixing the other generators; the edge map is $\Lambda^*p$. For a split saddle replacing $C$ by $C_1,C_2$, let $j:V_v\to V_{v+e}$ send $C$ to $C_1$ and fix the other generators; the unsigned edge map is $z\mapsto(C_1-C_2)\wedge\Lambda^*j(z)$. Choosing $C_2$ instead of $C_1$ gives the same map, while reversing the order of $C_1,C_2$ changes only its sign. Multiply each edge map by a sign $\epsilon(e)\in\{1,-1\}$, incorporating any circle-generator reordering sign. The direct sum of these state modules with the resulting cube differential is the odd Khovanov cochain complex $C_o(D)$. Write $Z_p$ for the circle containing the mark. Use the right action $z\cdot X=z\wedge Z_p$, making $C_o(D)$ a complex of right $\mathbb A$-modules; since $\mathbb A$ is commutative these are also ordinary modules over that ring. The action has quantum degree $-2$.

The square condition is that the sum of the two signed saddle composites around each two-dimensional cube face is zero. An edge sign function satisfying it is called square-compatible; existence and invariance require separate proofs.

Let $\mathbb R=\mathbb Z[h,X]/(X^2-hX)$, with $\deg_q(h)=\deg_q(X)=-2$. Its Frobenius structure has unit $\eta(1)=1$, counit $\epsilon(1)=0,\epsilon(X)=1$, quotient-ring multiplication, and comultiplication
$$ \Delta(1)=1\otimes X+X\otimes1-h\,1\otimes1,\qquad \Delta(X)=X\otimes X. $$
Applying these operations to the same normalized cube gives the Bar–Natan cochain complex $C_h(D)$, with circle labels $1,X$ of quantum degrees $1,-1$ and the same normalized state shifts; it is a complex of free $\mathbb R$-modules, and the marked circle acts by multiplication by $X$.

Put $\mathbb B=\mathbb F_2[X]/(X^2)=\mathbb R/(2,h)$. Modulo $2$, the odd exterior basis vector $C_{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge C_{i_r}$ corresponds to the even tensor state labeling the selected circles $C_{i_j}$ by $X$ and all other circles by $1$. This statewise bijection defines the candidate comparison $f_D:C_o(D)\otimes\mathbb F_2\to C_h(D)\otimes_{\mathbb R}\mathbb B$ after setting $h=0$.

A **local even–odd (LEO) triple** is a triple $(C,D,f)$ consisting of a finitely generated bigraded cochain complex $C$ free over $\mathbb A$, a finitely generated bigraded cochain complex $D$ free over $\mathbb R$, and a bigraded $\mathbb F_2[X]/(X^2)$-linear chain homotopy equivalence
$$ f:C\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb F_2\longrightarrow D\otimes_{\mathbb R}\mathbb B, \qquad \mathbb B=\mathbb R/(2,h)=\mathbb F_2[X]/(X^2), $$
such that $D[h^{-1}]$ is chain homotopy equivalent over $\mathbb R[h^{-1}]$ to one free rank-one module supported in cohomological degree $0$ and odd quantum degree. For a based knot diagram the intended candidate is $(C_o(D),C_h(D),f_D)$, where $f_D$ identifies the reduced edge maps modulo $2$ and $h$; its satisfaction of the homotopy and localization conditions is a separate theorem.

A local map $(C,D,f)\to(C',D',f')$ is a pair of bigraded module chain maps $\alpha:C\to C'$ and $\beta:D\to D'$ such that $\beta[h^{-1}]$ is a chain homotopy equivalence and the square induced by $f,f',\alpha,\beta$ after quotienting by $(2,h)$ commutes up to an $\mathbb F_2[X]/(X^2)$-linear chain homotopy. Two LEO triples are locally equivalent when there is a local map in each direction.

Let a finite planar resolution cube be equipped with an arrow at each crossing, transported to its saddle edges while resolving the other disjoint crossing disks, and use the odd exterior merge and split maps. There is a function assigning a sign to every edge such that the resulting signed differential squares to zero over the integers. More precisely, one can prescribe the face products on all faces, including faces whose two composites vanish, as follows. On a face with nonzero composites let $\kappa\in\{1,-1\}$ be their relative commutation sign. On a zero-composite face the two saddle arcs have alternating endpoints on one circle, one arc inside and one outside; put them in the standard two-chord picture by an orientation-preserving planar isotopy and rotate so that the inside arrow points upwards and set $\kappa=1$ when the outside arrow points left, and $\kappa=-1$ when it points right. Then the prescribed product of the four edge signs is $-\kappa$. These prescriptions are consistent, and two edge assignments realizing the same prescriptions are related by a vertexwise sign change. All the constructions are finite and choice-free. The vertexwise comparison commutes with the marked right $\mathbb Z[X]/(X^2)$-action.

For a finite planar odd resolution cube with the prescribed full face signs, a Reidemeister I or II move supported away from the marked point induces a normalized bigraded chain homotopy equivalence over the right ring $\mathbb A=\mathbb Z[X]/(X^2)$. The equivalence, inverse and contraction are finite integer matrices in exterior quotients, exterior products, and projections to the two coefficients of a small-circle generator. Their reductions modulo two are the corresponding even Khovanov cancellation maps. The result holds for every exterior closure of the move disk and every orientation of its strands, and is choice-free.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$.

1. **Compact main case.** Let $M$ be a compact smooth manifold, possibly with boundary, let $N$ be a smooth manifold without boundary, let $F:M\times I\to N$ be a smooth isotopy of embeddings that is constant near the ends of $I$, and let $W$ be an open neighbourhood of $F(M\times I)$ in $N$. Then there is an ambient isotopy $H:N\times I\to N$ with $H_0=\mathrm{id}_N$, every $H_t$ a diffeomorphism, $H_t\circ F_0=F_t$ for all $t\in I$, $H_t=\mathrm{id}_N$ outside $W$ for every $t$, and $H_t$ stationary near the ends; if $F$ is constant near the ends with parameter $\varepsilon$, then $H_t=\mathrm{id}_N$ for $t\le\varepsilon/2$ and $H_t=H_1$ for $t\ge1-\varepsilon/2$.
2. **Relative form.** Let $N$ be boundaryless, $U\subseteq N$ open, $A\subseteq U$ compact, and let $F:U\times I\to N$ be a smooth isotopy of embeddings whose track image is open in $N\times I$. Then there is a compactly supported ambient isotopy $H$ of $N$ with $H_t\circ F_0=F_t$ on a neighbourhood of $A$ for every $t$.
3. **Boundary stratum.** If $N$ has boundary and $F(M\times I)\subseteq\partial N$, then the ambient isotopy of clause 1 can be chosen with every $H_t$ carrying $\partial N$ onto itself; if $F(M\times I)\subseteq N\setminus\partial N$, it can be chosen compactly supported in $N\setminus\partial N$.
4. **General isotopies.** For the same compact source (possibly with boundary) and boundaryless target as in clause 1, every smooth isotopy extends with support in a compact subset of any prescribed neighbourhood $W$ of $F(M\times I)$. The endpoint-constancy hypothesis and the stationary-end conclusion are both omitted; all other conclusions of clause 1 hold.

Assume countable choice. Let $S\subset S^3\times[0,1]$ be a compact smooth oriented collared embedded annulus from a knot $K_0$ to a knot $K_1$. Let $\gamma\subset S$ be a smooth properly embedded arc joining their specified marked points and equal to their vertical marked intervals in smaller end collars. There exist based regular diagrams representing these endpoint knots and a finite oriented movie between them, consisting of planar isotopies, R1, R2, R3, births, saddles and deaths, with a marked point in every frame. The marked track is strictly increasing in height, never dies, never lies at a diagram crossing, and misses the closed support disks of every exceptional move. Every regular interval also keeps a neighborhood of the mark fixed in its chosen diagram coordinates.

More precisely, first an ambient isotopy fixed on smaller end collars carries the given marked surface to one with monotone marked arc. A smooth level-preserving change of spatial coordinates then puts a neighborhood of that arc into a fixed exterior closing-arc position. The movie trace, transported back by those same coordinates, is ambient isotopic to the original marked $S$ relative to the smaller end collars. Its endpoint diagrams and their marked parametrizations use the corresponding endpoint coordinate identifications. One may retain prescribed endpoint diagrams already in this compatible long-tangle presentation. The conclusion does not assert a based Reidemeister sequence between arbitrary prescribed planar endpoint diagrams or between arbitrary basepoint presentations, and asserts no movie-independence theorem for algebraic maps.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $F:C\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be a smooth
isotopy of a finite disjoint union of circles, constant near both ends, and
suppose both end projections under the fixed $\pi$ are regular. Arbitrarily
close to $F$ in the strong smooth topology there is such an isotopy $F'$, equal
to $F$ near the ends, whose projected slices have only these exceptional events:

(i) finitely many ordinary cusps, at distinct times; in a source coordinate
$x$, writing $g(x,t)=\pi F'(x,t)$, each satisfies
$g_x=0$, $\det(g_{xx},g_{xt})\ne0$ and
$\det(g_{xx},g_{xxx})\ne0$;

(ii) the **off-diagonal unordered** double-point locus is a smooth
one-dimensional manifold with boundary in the local-extension sense of
[[def-smooth-chart-atlas-and-structure-on-a-manifold-with-boundary]]; its boundary
consists exactly of the double points at $t=0,1$. Its interior is a manifold
without boundary, and its time projection has only finitely many
nondegenerate critical points, each an ordinary quadratic tangency of two
immersed branches;

(iii) finitely many transverse triple events, with all three pairs of
projected tangents independent, and no quadruple points.

No two exceptional events have the same time. All other slices are regular,
and between exceptional times their decorated diagrams vary by planar isotopy.

Let $F'$ satisfy the general-position conditions of
[[lem-a-smooth-isotopy-of-links-can-be-put-in-general-position]], with
exceptional times $t_1<\cdots<t_N$. Immediately before and after each event,
its regular diagrams differ, up to planar isotopy, by one oriented
Reidemeister move: R1 at an ordinary cusp, R2 at a quadratic double tangency,
and R3 at a transverse triple event. The regular intervals contribute planar
isotopies, and the moves preserve the over/under and orientation data of $F'$.
Consequently the end diagrams are connected by a finite sequence of these moves.

derivations.claim: **Small marked arcs and their relative center–tangent data.** Parametrize a uniformly small marked interval by oriented arclength $v$ near zero, smoothly in the isotopy parameter $t$; the resulting reparametrization changes neither knot nor mark and is stationary in the end collars. Let $b(t)=F(0,t)$ and let $u(t)$ be its unit tangent. Identify $S^3$ with unit quaternions. The imaginary unit quaternion $c(t)=b(t)^{-1}u(t)$ lies in $S^2$, and $(b(t),c(t))$ is a smooth loop in $S^3\times S^2$, constant in the end collars. The two endpoint marked arcs are the same by hypothesis. In exponential coordinates at $b(t)$ the small actual arc has the form $vu(t)+O(v^2)$, with derivative $u(t)+O(v)$ uniformly in $t$. Interpolating its error to zero gives a smooth family of embedded intervals for a sufficiently small uniform width: projection onto $u(t)$ has strictly positive derivative. This interpolation is stationary in the end collars if their common model is taken to be the geodesic round arc, as stipulated. Its inverse will later restore the actual marked germ.

**An explicit contraction fixes both parameter ends.** A smooth loop in either $S^d$, $d=2,3$, misses a point. Indeed a derivative bound makes its $n$ equal parameter intervals map into $n$ balls of radius $C/n$; their total spherical $d$-volume is at most $C'n^{1-d}$, which tends to zero. They cannot cover the positive-volume sphere. Choose one omitted point for each of the two loops from step 1.1. Stereographic coordinates from those points send each loop into Euclidean space. The straight interpolation from its constant endpoint value to its value at $t$ contracts it through loops constant on the same end collars; inverse stereographic projection gives smooth loops $b_s(t),c_s(t)$, with $s=0$ constant and $s=1$ the given data. Thus $$A_{s,t}(v)=b_s(t)\bigl(\cos v+c_s(t)\sin v\bigr)$$ is a smooth family of geodesic marked interval embeddings, with $A_{0,t}$ the common standard arc and $A_{s,t}$ equal to it in both end collars. Concatenate with the inverse error interpolation in step 1.1, using stationary smooth parameter joins. This constructs a two-parameter family of embedded intervals from the constant common arc to the actual moving marked arcs; at $t$ in either end collar the entire family is the constant arc.

**Relative ambient coordinates really are identity at both ends.** Extend the velocity in the contraction parameter $s$ of step 2.1 by the actual construction in [F1], with $t$ an additional parameter. To spell out the relative point: the track in $S^3\times[0,1]_s\times[0,1]_t$ is embedded because its last two coordinates retain $s,t$ and each interval slice is embedded. In finite track charts extend the three spatial velocity components constantly in normal coordinates, patch by a smooth partition, and apply a compact cutoff equal to one on the smaller interval track. The prescribed velocity is zero on both $t$ end collars; choose all extended components zero there, using charts of the constant product arc on those collars and a cutoff in $t$ on their complement. Integrate in $s$. Uniqueness of the ODE gives a smooth family $H_t$ of orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms with $H_t(A_{0,t})$ the actual marked interval and $H_t=\mathrm{id}$ on both time end collars. Consequently $H_t^{-1}F_t$ is a knot isotopy retaining exactly the given endpoints and fixing one common marked interval for every $t$. This contraction argument is necessary: simply extending the moving interval in the parameter $t$ would not by itself force the terminal ambient map to be the identity.
