Let a finite oriented based regular link diagram, with its ordered crossing disks and crossing arrows, lie on an oriented two-sphere. Choose any two orientation-preserving planar coordinate presentations whose omitted points miss the diagram and all crossing disks. Transport the diagram, crossing arrows, over/under information and mark by these coordinates; keep the same crossing order. Circle relabelling gives grading-preserving marked-module chain isomorphisms between their integral odd complexes with transported full admissible edge signs, and between their integral Bar–Natan complexes. In particular the full odd face prescription, including zero-composite faces, is unchanged by the choice of omitted point.

For independently chosen edge assignments satisfying that full prescription, compose the odd relabelling with vertexwise signs. The resulting odd and Bar–Natan isomorphisms have inverse maps, are respectively right linear over $\mathbb A=\mathbb Z[X]/(X^2)$ and $\mathbb R=\mathbb Z[h,X]/(X^2-hX)$, and give a strictly commuting square under the statewise reductions modulo $2$ and $(2,h)$. Their inverses give the inverse square. Whenever the endpoint triples satisfy the LEO hypotheses, these maps therefore give local maps in both directions; this applies in particular to knot triples once their separate foundations have been established. The Bar–Natan maps are already chain isomorphisms before localization. The construction is finite and requires no choice axiom. This assertion concerns recharting the same spherical diagram, not transporting a mark through a crossing of a fixed planar diagram.

Assume countable choice. Every prescribed finite regular oriented knot diagram with a specified marked point away from its crossings admits a compatible long endpoint presentation by finitely many planar isotopies and one orientation-preserving spherical rotation recharting. All crossing labels, crossing arrows if specified, strand orientations, over/under data and the mark are transported. No crossing is created, removed, or passed through the mark. The final planar diagram has a round disk containing every crossing and all of the diagram except a single crossing-free exterior closing arc carrying the mark; the disk boundary meets the diagram transversely in exactly two points. A neighborhood of that arc can be used as the protected marked neighborhood in a long-tangle movie.

The recharting omits a point in a face adjacent to the marked germ. Its spherical rotation extends by an explicit orientation-preserving linear map of $S^3$, and the planar normalizations have actual spatial coordinate lifts. Thus the construction records an orientation-preserving spatial identification of the represented marked endpoint knot, rather than declaring its coordinate identifications to be identities. A representative can be chosen with the exterior arc at constant projection height and with product collars at its two cut points. This is a geometric existence assertion. It asserts neither a purely planar protected Reidemeister comparison nor an algebraic invariance theorem. The construction uses only finite selections and explicit maps, so in fact introduces no choice beyond the stated branch.

Assume countable choice. Let $F:S^1\times[0,1]\to S^3$ be a smooth isotopy of oriented knots, stationary in end collars, with a specified marked source point. Suppose its two endpoint diagrams are regular compatible long presentations with the same standard oriented exterior marked arc, parametrized identically on a neighborhood of that point. Use the corresponding spatial endpoint coordinates, in which this common marked arc is a standard small round arc through the stereographic point at infinity; its puncture is closed in the planar diagrams by the same standard exterior arc. Then these prescribed endpoint diagrams are related by a finite sequence of planar isotopies and oriented R1, R2 and R3 moves, whose closed support disks miss the mark. The marked neighborhood remains fixed. There are no births, saddles or deaths. The movie represents the given marked isotopy up to a spatial coordinate family equal to the identity in both end collars and a small isotopy relative those collars.

Here compatible long endpoints include the displayed common oriented arc and its spatial coordinate identifications. This statement does not silently identify arbitrary physical endpoint coordinates. Spherical endpoint recharting may first be used to choose such common compatible presentations; no algebraic invariance of that recharting or of these movies is asserted here.

Assume countable choice. Let $S\subset S^3\times[0,1]$ be a compact smooth oriented collared embedded annulus from a knot $K_0$ to a knot $K_1$. Let $\gamma\subset S$ be a smooth properly embedded arc joining their specified marked points and equal to their vertical marked intervals in smaller end collars. There exist based regular diagrams representing these endpoint knots and a finite oriented movie between them, consisting of planar isotopies, R1, R2, R3, births, saddles and deaths, with a marked point in every frame. The marked track is strictly increasing in height, never dies, never lies at a diagram crossing, and misses the closed support disks of every exceptional move. Every regular interval also keeps a neighborhood of the mark fixed in its chosen diagram coordinates.

More precisely, first an ambient isotopy fixed on smaller end collars carries the given marked surface to one with monotone marked arc. A smooth level-preserving change of spatial coordinates then puts a neighborhood of that arc into a fixed exterior closing-arc position. The movie trace, transported back by those same coordinates, is ambient isotopic to the original marked $S$ relative to the smaller end collars. Its endpoint diagrams and their marked parametrizations use the corresponding endpoint coordinate identifications. One may retain prescribed endpoint diagrams already in this compatible long-tangle presentation. The conclusion does not assert a based Reidemeister sequence between arbitrary prescribed planar endpoint diagrams or between arbitrary basepoint presentations, and asserts no movie-independence theorem for algebraic maps.

Let a finite oriented link-cobordism movie carry a marked point continuously through its regular levels, with its trace disjoint from all elementary move disks, and with the marked component never dying. Use the odd cubes with the prescribed full face signs and the integral Bar–Natan cubes over $\mathbb R=\mathbb Z[h,X]/(X^2-hX)$. This movie admits an integral odd map, linear for the marked right $\mathbb A=\mathbb Z[X]/(X^2)$-action, and an integral marked $\mathbb R$-linear Bar–Natan map. For a connected oriented concordance between knots the localized Bar–Natan map is a chain homotopy equivalence over $\mathbb R[h^{-1}]$. A localized knot complex retracts over that ring onto one free rank-one module in cohomological degree zero and odd quantum parity. and the Bar–Natan complexes admit the corresponding marked $\mathbb R=\mathbb Z[h,X]/(X^2-hX)$-linear chain isomorphism. In the odd case the induced signs realize the full prescribed face products, so admissible sign comparison applies, including zero-composite faces. The two isomorphisms agree after reduction modulo $2$ and $(2,h)$ under the statewise comparison. Their construction is finite and choice-free.

derivations.claim: Local equivalence is reflexive because each triple has its identity local map, symmetric by its definition as maps in both directions, and transitive because the composites of local maps remain module chain maps, their localized Bar–Natan maps are composites of homotopy equivalences, and the two mod-$(2,h)$ squares compose up to the sum of their module-linear homotopies. Thus local equivalence is an equivalence relation.

The tensor product of two LEO triples is again a LEO triple: tensoring finite free complexes preserves finite freeness, tensoring the reductions gives the homotopy equivalence $f\otimes f'$, and tensoring the localized rank-one equivalences gives a rank-one equivalence over the localized coefficient algebra. Tensor products of local maps are local maps because tensor products preserve chain homotopies and homotopy equivalences between these free localized complexes. Hence the shifted tensor product is associative and respects local-equivalence classes. The graded symmetry $u\otimes v\mapsto(-1)^{|u||v|}v\otimes u$ gives commutativity, and the unknot triple is the unit because its complexes are $\mathbb A\{1\}$ and $\mathbb R\{1\}$.

Finite freeness lets dualization commute with reduction and localization; it preserves chain homotopies and chain homotopy equivalences. Thus $T^*$ satisfies the LEO conditions, and dualizing both maps and the module-linear homotopy in a local-map square gives a local map in the reverse direction. The finite-free tensor-Hom isomorphisms identify $T\otimes T^*$ with $(\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb A}(C,C)\{1\},\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb R}(D,D)\{1\},F)$, where on reductions $F(\eta)=f\eta g$. The coevaluation maps from the unknot triple send $1$ to $\mathrm{id}_C$ and $\mathrm{id}_D$. citations.quote:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere and let $B^4$ be the standard four-ball with boundary $S^3$. Let $\mathcal S_{\mathrm{sm}}(K)$ be the set of genera of connected compact orientable smooth properly embedded surfaces $F\subset B^4$ with oriented boundary $K$. Let $\mathcal S_{\mathrm{top}}(K)$ be the set of genera of connected compact orientable locally flat topologically properly embedded surfaces $F\subset B^4$ with oriented boundary $K$. For each such surface, its genus $g(F)$ is the nonnegative integer determined by $\chi(F)=1-2g(F)$. Define the smooth slice genus and the locally flat topological slice genus by

$$
g_4^{\mathrm{sm}}(K):=\min\mathcal S_{\mathrm{sm}}(K),\qquad g_4^{\mathrm{top}}(K):=\min\mathcal S_{\mathrm{top}}(K).
$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. For an oriented knot $K$, let $V_K$ be its two-dimensional rational Lee homology with the diagram-independent induced decreasing quantum filtration $F^pV_K$. For a nonzero class $x\in V_K$, define its filtration level by
$$ \ell(x)=\max\{p\in\mathbb Z:x\in F^pV_K\}. $$
Set
$$ s_{\min}(K)=\min_{x\ne0}\ell(x),\qquad s_{\max}(K)=\max_{x\ne0}\ell(x), \qquad s(K)=s_{\max}(K)-1=s_{\min}(K)+1. $$
The equality of the two formulas is part of the definition’s well-definedness, supplied by the rank-two Lee filtration theorem.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $S\subset S^3\times[0,1]$ be a connected compact oriented smoothly properly embedded surface of genus $g$, with product collars and oriented boundary $(-K_0\times\{0\})\sqcup(K_1\times\{1\})$ for oriented knots $K_0,K_1$ in the standard three-sphere. A **finite movie** for $S$ is a finite ordered sequence of regular-level link diagrams whose changes are planar isotopies, oriented Reidemeister moves, births, saddles or deaths. Such a movie defines a map on rational Lee homology that preserves the induced decreasing filtration with degree $\chi(S)=-2g$. The map is an isomorphism; consequently
$$
|s(K_1)-s(K_0)|\le 2g.
$$

Assume countable choice. Let $F\subset B^4\subset\mathbb R^4$ be a compact connected oriented smoothly properly embedded surface of genus $g$, with its supplied smooth boundary collar and oriented boundary the knot $K\subset S^3$. There is an orientation-preserving ambient diffeomorphism $\Psi:B^4\to B^4$ equal to the identity on a neighborhood of the outer boundary, and $0<\varepsilon<1$, such that $\Psi(F)\cap B^4_\varepsilon$ is exactly a flat two-disk in a plane through $0$. The surface $\Psi(F)\setminus\operatorname{int}B^4_\varepsilon$, in the explicitly round shell $B^4\setminus\operatorname{int}B^4_\varepsilon\cong S^3\times[0,1]$, is a connected smooth oriented knot cobordism between $K$ and a standard unknot, with genus $g$ and Euler characteristic $-2g$. Both boundary components have product collars in a shell identification fixing $K$ and the inner sphere. Over $\mathbb Q$, replace its circle algebra by $A_L=\mathbb Q[X]/(X^2-1)$, with $\deg_q(1)=1$ and $\deg_q(X)=-1$, and structure maps
$$
\eta_L(1)=1,\quad \epsilon_L(1)=0,\quad \epsilon_L(X)=1,
$$
$$
m_L(1\otimes1)=1,\quad m_L(1\otimes X)=m_L(X\otimes1)=X,\quad m_L(X\otimes X)=1,
$$
$$
\Delta_L(1)=1\otimes X+X\otimes1,\quad \Delta_L(X)=1\otimes1+X\otimes X.
$$
For a resolution state $v$ with $k(v)$ circles, assign $A_L^{\otimes k(v)}$ and cohomological degree $i(v)=|v|-n_-$. On a tensor basis element whose circle labels are $a_1,\ldots,a_{k(v)}\in\{1,X\}$, set
$$
q(v;a_1,\ldots,a_{k(v)})=|v|+n_+-2n_-+\sum_{j=1}^{k(v)}\deg_q(a_j).
$$
The differential is the signed sum of the edge maps $m_L$ and $\Delta_L$. The resulting finite cochain complex is the **Lee-deformed Khovanov complex** $C_L(D;\mathbb Q)$. Its decreasing quantum filtration $F^pC_L(D;\mathbb Q)$ is spanned by basis elements of quantum degree at least $p$. Its homology with the induced filtration is the Lee homology of the diagram. The diagram-level definition does not by itself assert invariance under changing $D$.

```tikzcd
A_L\otimes A_L \arrow[r,"m_L"] \arrow[d,"\Delta_L\otimes\mathrm{id}"'] & A_L \arrow[d,"\Delta_L"] \\
A_L\otimes A_L\otimes A_L \arrow[r,"\mathrm{id}\otimes m_L"'] & A_L\otimes A_L
```

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$.

1. **Compact main case.** Let $M$ be a compact smooth manifold, possibly with boundary, let $N$ be a smooth manifold without boundary, let $F:M\times I\to N$ be a smooth isotopy of embeddings that is constant near the ends of $I$, and let $W$ be an open neighbourhood of $F(M\times I)$ in $N$. Then there is an ambient isotopy $H:N\times I\to N$ with $H_0=\mathrm{id}_N$, every $H_t$ a diffeomorphism, $H_t\circ F_0=F_t$ for all $t\in I$, $H_t=\mathrm{id}_N$ outside $W$ for every $t$, and $H_t$ stationary near the ends; if $F$ is constant near the ends with parameter $\varepsilon$, then $H_t=\mathrm{id}_N$ for $t\le\varepsilon/2$ and $H_t=H_1$ for $t\ge1-\varepsilon/2$.
2. **Relative form.** Let $N$ be boundaryless, $U\subseteq N$ open, $A\subseteq U$ compact, and let $F:U\times I\to N$ be a smooth isotopy of embeddings whose track image is open in $N\times I$. Then there is a compactly supported ambient isotopy $H$ of $N$ with $H_t\circ F_0=F_t$ on a neighbourhood of $A$ for every $t$.
3. **Boundary stratum.** If $N$ has boundary and $F(M\times I)\subseteq\partial N$, then the ambient isotopy of clause 1 can be chosen with every $H_t$ carrying $\partial N$ onto itself; if $F(M\times I)\subseteq N\setminus\partial N$, it can be chosen compactly supported in $N\setminus\partial N$.
4. **General isotopies.** For the same compact source (possibly with boundary) and boundaryless target as in clause 1, every smooth isotopy extends with support in a compact subset of any prescribed neighbourhood $W$ of $F(M\times I)$. The endpoint-constancy hypothesis and the stationary-end conclusion are both omitted; all other conclusions of clause 1 hold.

Let $X$ be a four-dimensional manifold with boundary and let $W$ be a compact surface with boundary. An embedding $e:(W,\partial W)\to(X,\partial X)$ is proper when $e^{-1}(\partial X)=\partial W$. It is locally flat at an interior point of $W$ when there are neighborhoods of the point and its image and a homeomorphism of pairs from those neighborhoods to $(\mathbb R^4,\mathbb R^2)$, with the standard linear plane $\mathbb R^2\subset\mathbb R^4$. It is locally flat at a boundary point when there are such neighborhoods and a homeomorphism of pairs to $(\mathbb R^4_+,\mathbb R^2_+)$, where $\mathbb R^4_+=\{x_4\geq0\}$ and $\mathbb R^2_+=\{x_2=x_3=0,\ x_4\geq0\}$; the line $\partial\mathbb R^2_+$ lies in $\partial\mathbb R^4_+$. A collar of a boundary circle of $W$ is an embedding of that circle times $[0,\varepsilon)$ into $W$ that is the identity on the circle at parameter $0$; a concordance collar is required to agree with the corresponding product collar of the ambient end. A smooth proper surface has the analogous smooth charts and collars, which are also topological locally flat charts.

In ZF, let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be smooth, and let $a\in U$. If $Df(a)$ is invertible, then there are open neighbourhoods $a\in V\subseteq U$ and $f(a)\in W$ such that $f|_V:V\to W$ is a diffeomorphism. Writing $g=(f|_V)^{-1}$,
$$Dg(y)=Df(g(y))^{-1}\qquad(y\in W).$$

Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere. Let $F$ be a compact connected oriented Seifert surface with boundary $K$, and let $\mathcal H=(\Sigma,\boldsymbol\alpha,\boldsymbol\beta,w,z)$ be an admissible doubly pointed Heegaard diagram representing $(K,F)$. The associated one-pointed hat chain complex $\widehat{CF}(\mathcal H)$ is the finite-dimensional chain complex over $\mathbb F_2$ obtained from the minus complex by setting its basepoint variable to zero; its differential counts index-one disks with zero multiplicity at $w$. Assume for this specified data that the differential is nonincreasing in the Alexander filtration, that the absolute Alexander formula below takes integer values, and that $H(\widehat{CF}(\mathcal H))\cong\mathbb F_2$. Give a generator $\mathbf x$ its absolute Alexander filtration
$$A_F(\mathbf x)=\frac12\left\langle c_1(\mathfrak s_{w,z}(\mathbf x)),[\widehat F]\right\rangle,$$
where $\mathfrak s_{w,z}(\mathbf x)$ is the homology class of the nowhere-vanishing vector field assigned to $\mathbf x$ by the pointed Morse construction, with its prescribed boundary data near the two basepoints; $c_1$ is the first Chern class of the oriented plane field perpendicular to that vector field. To form the zero-framed surgery, remove a tubular neighborhood of $K$ and glue in a solid torus whose meridian is the longitude induced by $F$. The surface $\widehat F$ is obtained by deleting a boundary collar of $F$ and capping its longitude by the meridian disk of that solid torus. This is the standard integer normalization, with the one-generator diagram of the standard unknot at filtration zero. The subcomplex $F_s\widehat{CF}(\mathcal H)$ is spanned by generators of Alexander filtration at most $s$.

More generally, a finite integer-filtered chain complex is a finite-dimensional chain complex $C$ over $\mathbb F_2$ with subcomplexes $F_sC$ such that $F_sC=0$ for all sufficiently small integers $s$ and $F_sC=C$ for all sufficiently large integers $s$. If $H(C)\cong\mathbb F_2$, define
$$\tau(C):=\min\{s\in\mathbb Z:\operatorname{im}(H(F_sC)\longrightarrow H(C))\ne0\}.$$
For the fixed diagram and surface above, write $\tau_{\mathcal H,F}(K)=\tau(\widehat{CF}(\mathcal H),F_*\widehat{CF}(\mathcal H))$. Once diagram and surface independence is proved, their common value is the knot invariant $\tau(K)$. Until that comparison is proved, $\tau_{\mathcal H,F}(K)$ denotes only the value for the specified data.

$$ \ell(x)=\max\{p\in\mathbb Z:x\in F^pV_K\}. $$
Set
$$ s_{\min}(K)=\min_{x\ne0}\ell(x),\qquad s_{\max}(K)=\max_{x\ne0}\ell(x), \qquad s(K)=s_{\max}(K)-1=s_{\min}(K)+1. $$
The equality of the two formulas is part of the definition’s well-definedness, supplied by the rank-two Lee filtration theorem.

Assume countable choice. Let $K$ be an oriented knot in $S^3$, and let $F$ be a compact connected oriented surface embedded in $S^3$ with boundary $K$ and minimum possible genus; write $g(K)=\operatorname{genus}(F)$. Let $G$ be any toroidal grid diagram for $K$ with grid number $n$. Let $C^-_{\mathrm{grid}}(G)$ be the full filtered minus complex produced by the grid-complex algorithm, and let $C^-_U(G)$ denote this same complex regarded over $\mathbb F_2[U]$ by letting $U$ act as one chosen $U_i$, with the other variables retained independently. For an admissible $2n$-pointed Heegaard diagram $\mathcal H$ compatible with $(K,F)$, define $C^-_U(\mathcal H)$ by the same restriction to a single variable action. Write $CFK^-(K)$ for the full filtered complex of an admissible doubly-pointed diagram. The ordinary fully collapsed quotient, obtained instead by setting all $U_i=U$, has type $CFK^-(K)\otimes V^{\otimes(n-1)}$; the restriction of scalars $C^-_U$ has type $CFK^-(K)$.

For the absolute Alexander normalization, let $\mathcal H_1$ be an admissible doubly-pointed Heegaard diagram for $(K,F)$. For a generator $\mathbf x$ of $\mathcal H_1$, set
$$A_F(\mathbf x)=\frac12\left\langle c_1(\mathfrak s_{w,z}(\mathbf x)),[\widehat F]\right\rangle,$$
where $\mathfrak s_{w,z}(\mathbf x)$ is the relative $\operatorname{Spin}^c$ structure assigned to this generator by the pointed Heegaard construction: it is the homology class of the nowhere-vanishing vector field obtained from the gradient trajectories through $\mathbf x$ and the chosen basepoint pair, after extending the field across small balls around the critical points. Its first Chern class is that of the oriented plane field orthogonal to this vector field. The surface $\widehat F$ is obtained by removing a tubular neighborhood $N(K)$ from $F$ and capping the resulting longitude with the meridian disk of the solid torus attached in zero-framed surgery on $K$. Let $\widehat{HFK}(K)$ be the homology of the Alexander-associated-graded complex obtained from the doubly-pointed complex $C^-_U(\mathcal H_1)$ by quotienting by its sole variable $U$, with this $A_F$ normalization.

Then $C^-_U(G)$ and $C^-_U(\mathcal H)$ are filtered chain homotopy equivalent, preserving relative Maslov grading and the $A_F$ filtration, and their Alexander-associated-graded minus complexes are chain homotopy equivalent. For any two grids of $K$, the resulting normalized filtered complexes are filtered chain homotopy equivalent. If $\widetilde{GH}(G)$ denotes the homology of the tilde grid complex over $\mathbb F_2$, then
$$\widetilde{GH}(G)\cong\widehat{HFK}(K)\otimes V^{\otimes(n-1)},$$
where $V$ is the two-dimensional bigraded vector space with one generator in bidegree $(0,0)$ and one in bidegree $(-1,-1)$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. For every smooth oriented knot $K$ in the standard oriented three-sphere,
$$
|s(K)|\le 2g_4^{\mathrm{sm}}(K),
$$
where $g_4^{\mathrm{sm}}(K)$ is the minimum genus of a connected compact orientable smooth properly embedded surface in the standard four-ball with oriented boundary $K$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $S\subset S^3\times[0,1]$ be a connected compact oriented smoothly properly embedded surface of genus $g$, with product collars and oriented boundary $(-K_0\times\{0\})\sqcup(K_1\times\{1\})$ for oriented knots $K_0,K_1$ in the standard three-sphere. A **finite movie** for $S$ is a finite ordered sequence of regular-level link diagrams whose changes are planar isotopies, oriented Reidemeister moves, births, saddles or deaths. Such a movie defines a map on rational Lee homology that preserves the induced decreasing filtration with degree $\chi(S)=-2g$. The map is an isomorphism; consequently
$$
|s(K_1)-s(K_0)|\le 2g.
$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $D_+(T_{2,3},2)$ be the positive-clasped Whitehead double of the right-handed trefoil in the Hedden–Ording twist convention, with companion-annulus framing two. Equivalently, start with the three-crossing positive trefoil blackboard parallel, add one negative full annulus twist, and attach the positive clasp as in the admitted sixteen-crossing code. Then
$$s(D_+(T_{2,3},2))=2.$$

Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot and let $C(K)=\mathrm{CFK}^{\infty}(K)$ be its normalized bifiltered complex over $\mathbb F_2[U,U^{-1}]$. The complex of the reverse mirror $-K$ is filtered-chain-homotopy equivalent to the dual complex $C(K)^*=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb F_2[U,U^{-1}]}(C(K),\mathbb F_2[U,U^{-1}])$, with dual differential $d\phi(x)=\phi(\partial x)$ and dual basis elements at negated bifiltration coordinates. There is also a Maslov-graded filtered-chain-homotopy equivalence from $C(K)$ to the complex obtained by exchanging the algebraic and Alexander filtrations. These are distinct symmetries: duality negates both filtration coordinates, while conjugation exchanges them.

derivations.claim: Use the admitted cable/clasp diagram of [[lem-explicit-two-twisted-whitehead-double-has-sixteen-crossing-code]]. Its four-strand cable word is $\sigma_1^{-2}(\sigma_2\sigma_1\sigma_3\sigma_2)^3$, with the separate two-crossing clasp and the admitted wiring. The correction to blackboard framing is $-1$ full twist; the trefoil's blackboard framing is $+3$, giving exactly two full twists relative to the zero longitude. Here is a finite grid admission for this same diagram. Draw its sixteen crossing disks and joining orthogonal arrows, scale by $100$, and rotate the drawing by a quarter turn. At a horizontal overcrossing replace its overarc by the ordered vertices $(-10,0),(2,0),(2,4),(10,4),(10,0)$ and its underarc by $(0,-10),(4,-10),(4,2),(0,2),(0,10)$, reversing either order to retain its directed strand. The sole crossing is now $(2,2)$ with the same signed boundary ports. The six required replacements have disjoint supports. Delete straight subdivisions, separate coincident levels by perturbations smaller than $1/100$, and rank the levels. This gives a $33$-grid with exactly the sixteen original signed crossings. Its saved $986$ exchanges, cyclic cuts and three-corner destabilizations give the following $12$-grid, with zero-based rows: $$O=(4,9,6,1,2,11,0,8,5,3,7,10),\qquad X=(8,2,0,7,10,4,5,3,1,9,11,6).$$ Each exchange has nonalternating endpoint intervals or the permitted shared endpoint; each destabilization has three alternating marks in adjacent rows and columns. These conditions verify the individual isotopies and the displayed endpoint. The directed word is the negative reverse of the input traversal: the negative is the orientation-preserving change of viewing direction $(x,y,h)\mapsto(x,-y,-h)$, while the reverse records the independently chosen component orientation. Thus the actual grid is for the reverse of the oriented knot in the Statement, with its positive clasp and two-full-twist framing retained. The complete integer arrows and finite move list are recorded with the computation data below; neither a knot-table name nor a Floer rank identifies this knot.

The orientation junction preserves the normalized filtered invariant without an ambient invertibility assumption. For a doubly-pointed diagram of an oriented knot $J$, swapping only $w,z$ presents $J^r$. The actual disks are unchanged and their two marked degrees exchange, so $I:[x,i,j]\mapsto[x,j,i]$ is a Laurent-linear swap-filtered chain isomorphism to that diagram. The carried zero-Seifert cap gives $A'(x)=-A(x)$. The relative disk index then gives $M'(x)=M(x)-2A(x)+c$ for one integer $c$, so $I$ has constant full Maslov degree $c$. Compose it with the normalized same-oriented-knot conjugation of [F4], whose Maslov degree is zero and which swaps the two filtrations, including its inverse and homotopies. The composite is an ordinary bifiltered equivalence to $J^r$ of degree $c$. Its vertical hat quotient is an isomorphism between the two total three-sphere hat groups, each concentrated in normalized Maslov degree zero; hence $c=0$. This proves equality of the normalized inclusion thresholds for $J,J^r$. It also identifies their normalized bigraded knot Floer homologies. Apply this to the grid in step 1.1. Reflecting its columns, $O_r\mapsto11-O_r$ and $X_r\mapsto11-X_r$, gives a grid for its mirror: $(x,y,h)\mapsto(-x,y,h)$ reverses ambient orientation and keeps vertical strands over horizontal strands. No further knot-recognition premise is needed for this second grid.

Compute the full tilde differential of each of these two explicit grids. For a permutation state $p$, use $M_O(p)=I(p,p)-I(p,O)-I(O,p)+I(O,O)+1$ and $2A(p)=M_O(p)-M_X(p)-11$, with marks at half-integer cell centers and $I$ counting pairs strictly increasing in both coordinates. In the quotient $Q=C/F_0C$ retain exactly the states with $A>0$. Only Maslov degrees $-1,0,1$ enter $H_0(Q)$; discarding the outgoing differential from degree $-1$ does not change that group. The inventory is exhaustive by the following finite assignment recurrence. For used columns $S$ in the first $r=|S|$ rows, choosing $c\notin S$ increments the state-state term by $|\{b\in S:b<c\}|$. Add $-\#\{k\ge r:O_k\ge c\}-\#\{k<r:O_k<c\}$ to obtain the Maslov increment; the Alexander increment is the corresponding $X$ expression minus its $O$ expression. Accumulating the resulting two-variable polynomial over the $4096$ column subsets counts every permutation exactly once. For every retained state and ordered pair of distinct rows, take its southwest/northeast rectangle, reject a rectangle containing an interior state point or $O$, and retain every other rectangle, including those containing $X$. Its output transposes the two chosen columns; discard that output only when its Alexander value is at most zero. Summing modulo two gives the actual quotient matrix. The first grid has $45\,824$ retained states, $159\,685$ rectangle orbits, including $24\,181$ with positive $X$ multiplicity, and $158\,523$ nonzero matrix entries. The reflected grid has $6080$ retained states and $11\,474$ rectangle orbits and nonzero entries. Every term has Maslov drop one and Alexander drop exactly its $X$ multiplicity; actual matrix multiplication gives $d^2=0$ in both quotients. These are the literal rectangle counts of [L1], rather than a formal-domain enumeration.

Exact column elimination over $\mathbb F_2$ gives $$\begin{array}{c|rrrrr}&\dim Q_1&\dim Q_0&\dim Q_{-1}&\operatorname{rank}d_1&\operatorname{rank}d_0\\\hline G&12347&17919&15558&8384&9535\\G^{\mathrm{mirror}}&4385&1463&232&1243&220.\end{array}$$ To specify the finite rank operation, encode a column by its row bits; repeatedly cancel its highest nonzero row with the previously retained pivot column at that row, or retain it as a new pivot if no such column exists. The counts of retained pivots are the displayed ranks. The saved complete columns and pivot-reduction traces give these computations directly. A separate exact verification used the complete joint assignment polynomial, checked every state and both normalized grid gradings, reconstructed every retained rectangle, checked $d^2$, and recomputed both ranks. Thus $$\dim H_0(Q_G)=17919-8384-9535=0,\qquad\dim H_0(Q_{G^{\mathrm{mirror}}})=1463-1243-220=0.$$ This uses the full filtered quotients, including the positive-$X$ terms in the first matrix.

Apply [L1]'s absolutely normalized filtered comparison and specialize all marking variables to zero. The full tilde complex is filtered chain homotopy equivalent to the doubly-pointed full hat complex tensored with $V^{\otimes11}$, where the two degrees of $V$ are $(M,A)=(0,0),(-1,-1)$. Its total Maslov-zero homology is consequently one-dimensional, represented by the normalized three-sphere generator tensored with the sole degree-zero vector of $V^{\otimes11}$. Its filtration threshold is exactly $\tau(J)$: inclusion into that tensor factor and projection onto it are filtered degree-zero chain maps, so they give both threshold inequalities. The exact sequence $0\to F_0C\to C\to Q\to0$ and step 2.2 show that this total Maslov-zero class comes from $H_0(F_0C)$ for each grid. Hence $\tau(J)\le0$ and $\tau(mJ)\le0$, for the actual knot $J$ of step 1.1 and its mirror.

For completeness derive the required threshold sign from [F4]'s normalized reverse-mirror duality. Let $D$ be the finite normalized doubly-pointed full hat complex and write $t$ for its inclusion threshold. Its dual filtration is $F_sD^\vee=\{\lambda:\lambda(F_{-s-1}D)=0\}$. Choose a total generator cycle $z\in F_tD_0$. Then $z\notin\operatorname{im}(d:D_1\to D_0)+F_{t-1}D_0$: any such expression would give a homologous cycle at level $t-1$. Finite-dimensional linear algebra therefore gives a functional $\lambda$ vanishing on that sum and taking value one on $z$. It is a nonzero dual homology class at filtration $-t$. Conversely every functional at level $s<-t$ vanishes on $F_tD$, hence on $z$, and cannot represent the nonzero dual class. Thus the dual threshold is exactly $-t$. The absolute normalization and full duality in [F4], together with the orientation junction of step 1.2, give $\tau(mJ)=-\tau(J)$. Combining the two actual quotient inequalities of step 2.3 forces $\tau(J)=0$. By step 1.2 this is the normalized tau value of the actual two-twisted positive Whitehead trefoil in the Statement.

The admitted diagram and framing in step 1.1 are also those of [F3]. That accepted finite Lee computation gives $s(D_+(T_{2,3},2))=2$. Together with the independently established normalized value in step 3.1 this proves both numerical assertions of the Statement.

derivations.claim: Each $I(P,Q)$ is an integer count. For $P=Q$, $J(P,P)=I(P,P)$, so the two self-pair terms in the formulas for $M_{\mathbb O}$ and $M_{\mathbb X}$ are integers; the cross terms occur doubled. Hence both Maslov functions are integer-valued.

Suppose a rectangle $r$ is contained in the chosen fundamental square. Write its southwest and northeast corners as $x_1,x_2\in\mathbf x$ and its northwest and southeast corners as $y_1,y_2\in\mathbf y$; all other state points are common. In $J(\mathbf x,\mathbf x)-J(\mathbf y,\mathbf y)$ the common-point terms cancel, the ordered corner pair contributes $1$, and each point of $\mathbf x$ strictly inside $r$ contributes twice, once against each changed corner. Thus this difference is $1+2\#(\mathbf x\cap\operatorname{Int}r)$. In $2J(\mathbf x,\mathbb O)-2J(\mathbf y,\mathbb O)$ the same cancellation leaves twice the number of $O$-markings in $r$. Substituting these two counts into [F1] gives $M_{\mathbb O}(\mathbf x)-M_{\mathbb O}(\mathbf y)=1-2n_{\mathbb O}(r)+2\#(\mathbf x\cap\operatorname{Int}r)$. Replacing every $O$ by $X$ gives the stated formula for $M_{\mathbb X}$.

For a marking set $P\in\{\mathbb O,\mathbb X\}$, write $M_P(\mathbf x)=J(\mathbf x-P,\mathbf x-P)+1$ and let $\mathrm{NW}(P_i)$ denote the northwest grid vertex of the cell containing the $i$th mark, read on the bottom edge when that cell is in the top row. Let $\mathbf x_{\mathrm{NW}P}$ be the state consisting of these vertices. Expanding the $J$ formula in [F1] gives $M_P(\mathbf x_{\mathrm{NW}P})=\#\{(i,j):\mathrm{NW}(P_i)<\mathrm{NW}(P_j)\}-\#\{(i,j):\mathrm{NW}(P_i)<P_j\}-\#\{(i,j):P_i<\mathrm{NW}(P_j)\}+\#\{(i,j):P_i<P_j\}+1.$ For distinct $i,j$ with neither mark in the top row, all four inequalities are equivalent and their signed contributions cancel. If $P_j$ is in the top row, the second and fourth inequalities are equivalent and the first and third are false; if $P_i$ is in the top row, the first and second inequalities are equivalent and the third and fourth are false. These contributions also cancel. For $i=j$, the only inequality that can hold is $\mathrm{NW}(P_i)<P_i$, and it holds exactly for the unique mark in the top row. The displayed count is therefore $-1+1=0$, proving $M_{\mathbb O}(\mathbf x_{\mathrm{NW}\mathbb O})=M_{\mathbb X}(\mathbf x_{\mathrm{NW}\mathbb X})=0$.

For two complementary rectangles $r$ and $r'$ with the same vertical edges, let $v$ be their common width, counted in column strips. The one-$O$- and one-$X$-per-column conditions in [F2] give $n_{\mathbb O}(r)+n_{\mathbb O}(r')=v$ and $n_{\mathbb X}(r)+n_{\mathbb X}(r')=v$. The state has one point on each of the $v-1$ vertical circles strictly between those two edges, so $\#(\mathbf x\cap\operatorname{Int}r)+\#(\mathbf x\cap\operatorname{Int}r')=v-1$. If the formula of step 1.2 holds for $r$ from $\mathbf x$ to $\mathbf y$, these three equalities give the formula for $r'$ from $\mathbf y$ to $\mathbf x$ by subtraction. The same argument applies to complementary rectangles sharing horizontal edges, counting rows instead of columns. Of the four torus rectangles for the two states, one lies in the fundamental square; successive horizontal or vertical complementations reach each of the other three, so the formulas hold for every torus rectangle.

Subtract the $M_{\mathbb X}$ change from the $M_{\mathbb O}$ change and divide by two. The constant terms and state-interior terms cancel, giving $\frac{M_{\mathbb O}(\mathbf x)-M_{\mathbb X}(\mathbf x)}2-\frac{M_{\mathbb O}(\mathbf y)-M_{\mathbb X}(\mathbf y)}2=n_{\mathbb X}(r)-n_{\mathbb O}(r)$. The common normalization $-(n-1)/2$ in $A_G$ cancels, proving the rectangle-change formula and that all differences of $A_G$ are integers.

The row and column connections from $O$ to $X$ and back form one $n$-cycle by [F2]. Equivalently, the relative permutation between $\mathbf x_{\mathrm{NW}\mathbb X}$ and $\mathbf x_{\mathrm{NW}\mathbb O}$ is an $n$-cycle. Factor that cycle into $n-1$ transpositions and apply them successively to obtain grid states between the two states. Two states that differ by one transposition have four intersection corners: the two row circles and two column circles cut the torus into four rectangles, and one of those rectangles has the first state at its southwest and northeast corners and the second state at its northwest and southeast corners. Thus each transition is realized by a torus rectangle, whether empty or not. Each rectangle changes $M_{\mathbb X}$ by an odd integer by steps 1.2 and 2.1, so $M_{\mathbb X}(\mathbf x_{\mathrm{NW}\mathbb O})\equiv n-1\pmod 2$, using the zero normalization at $\mathbf x_{\mathrm{NW}\mathbb X}$ from step 1.3. Since $M_{\mathbb O}(\mathbf x_{\mathrm{NW}\mathbb O})=0$, the numerator $M_{\mathbb O}-M_{\mathbb X}-(n-1)$ defining twice $A_G(\mathbf x_{\mathrm{NW}\mathbb O})$ is even. Hence this value is integral.

Any two grid states correspond to permutations, and a finite product of transpositions carries one to the other. Each transposition gives a rectangle transition. Step 3.1 shows that $A_G$ changes by an integer at every transition; since one state has integral Alexander value by step 3.2, all grid states do.

citations.quote:
Work in the smooth category inherited from the oriented-link convention. In particular, an embedded bridge witness disk means the image of a smooth rank-two embedding of a planar disk, with ordinary smooth boundary or smooth transverse corners at its two marked endpoints; smoothness at a boundary or corner means local smooth extension in its charts. Witness parametrizations can be chosen for the finite disk families. This category convention does not require the knot arcs to meet the Heegaard surface transversely: tangential smooth crossings remain permitted.

Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot. Let $\Sigma$ be a closed oriented surface of genus $h$, let $k\ge1$, and put $m=h+k-1$. A **handlebody** is a compact three-manifold that is a regular neighborhood of a finite connected graph. Curves from different systems intersect transversely in finitely many points. Each component of $\Sigma\setminus\boldsymbol\alpha$ and of $\Sigma\setminus\boldsymbol\beta$ contains exactly one $w$-point and exactly one $z$-point. The diagram also includes trivial arc systems in the two handlebodies: the $\alpha$-arcs join $w_i$ to $z_i$, and the $\beta$-arcs join $z_i$ to $w_{i-1}$, with indices modulo $k$. Each system is disjoint from its compression disks and is simultaneously boundary parallel: its arcs cobound pairwise disjoint embedded disks with arcs in the corresponding components of the attaching-system complement on $\Sigma$. Thus each ball obtained by compression contains one unknotted arc. Together the arcs form an oriented knot, oriented from $w_i$ to $z_i$ in $U_{\alpha}$ and from $z_i$ to $w_{i-1}$ in $U_{\beta}$. The diagram is **compatible with $K$** when this knot is orientation-preservingly ambient isotopic to $K$. For a grid diagram, compatibility uses the row and column orientation fixed in the grid definition, with $w$-points at $O$ and $z$-points at $X$. For a grid representing one knot, the basepoint pairs can be numbered cyclically in reverse order of travel along the oriented knot so that $w_i,z_i$ lie in the same component $A_i$ of $\Sigma\setminus\boldsymbol\alpha$ and $w_i,z_{i+1}$ lie in the same component $B_i$ of $\Sigma\setminus\boldsymbol\beta$.

Equivalently one may specify the surface isomorphism together with its compatible collared extensions over both handlebodies carrying those arcs. The attaching systems are carried as systems; reordering their curve factors induces the corresponding product identification. Comparisons also allow **arc normalizations in the fixed splitting**: a smooth isotopy of the represented oriented knot, supported near the ordered marks and fixing each mark, during which every open connecting arc stays in its original handlebody and the two simultaneous boundary-parallel witness systems are retained or replaced by embedded witnesses for those same arcs. The surface, attaching curves, marked points and compression disks stay fixed. Such a normalization may replace a tangential marked crossing by a transverse one; the original data are not required to have neat arcs. This is a change of knot representative relative to the fixed surface, not a diagram isomorphism carrying both objects. Analytic and assigned grading data depending on the fixed surface diagram can be kept identical; the corresponding generator and disk-count identification is then the identity. Existence of normalizations with the required witnesses is a separate geometric assertion, not part of this definition. Such a comparison transports the represented oriented knot and any specified Seifert surface as well. For analytic data, it transports $j$, the surface area form, all chosen divisor neighborhoods and $J_t$ by the induced symmetric-product diffeomorphism. The comparison maps on generators and disk classes are their pushforwards under this map; compatibility with the count differential is a mathematical property to be proved. No identity action is part of this convention, even when the ambient diffeomorphism is isotopic to the identity.

The $m$-fold symmetric product $\operatorname{Sym}^{m}(\Sigma)=\Sigma^m/S_m$ is the space of unordered $m$-tuples of points of $\Sigma$, where $S_m$ permutes coordinates. Let $q:\Sigma^m\to\operatorname{Sym}^{m}(\Sigma)$ be the quotient map. The product tori are the images $\mathbb T_{\alpha}=q(\alpha_1\times\cdots\times\alpha_m)$ and $\mathbb T_{\beta}=q(\beta_1\times\cdots\times\beta_m)$. Their intersection points are the generators. A **Whitney disk class** $\phi\in\pi_2(\mathbf x,\mathbf y)$ is a relative homotopy class of maps from a disk to $\operatorname{Sym}^{m}(\Sigma)$ whose two boundary arcs lie on $\mathbb T_{\alpha}$ and $\mathbb T_{\beta}$ and whose endpoints are $\mathbf x$ and $\mathbf y$. Write $n_{w_i}(\phi)$ and $n_{z_i}(\phi)$ for its local multiplicities at the marked points. An almost complex structure $J$ on $\operatorname{Sym}^{m}(\Sigma)$ is a smooth endomorphism of the tangent bundle with $J^2=-1$. Fix a complex structure $j$ and an area form on $\Sigma$. The path is a sufficiently small perturbation in this class. For $m=0$ the symmetric product is a point. Local multiplicities are intersection numbers with these divisors; positivity is a mathematical property to be proved, not an additional choice of disk counts. A $\mathbb J$-holomorphic strip representative is a smooth map $u:\mathbb R\times[0,1]\to\operatorname{Sym}^{m}(\Sigma)$ satisfying $\partial_{\tau}u+J_t(u)\partial_tu=0$, with $u(\tau,0)\in\mathbb T_{\alpha}$, $u(\tau,1)\in\mathbb T_{\beta}$, and limits $\mathbf x,\mathbf y$ as $\tau\to-\infty,+\infty$. Each $U_i$ lowers Maslov grading by two and Alexander filtration by one. In a grid diagram, $\Sigma=T^2$, $h=1$, $k=n$, and $m=n$; the horizontal circles are the $\alpha$-curves, the vertical circles are the $\beta$-curves, and the $w$-points and $z$-points are the $O$- and $X$-markings respectively.

derivations.claim: Regard the grid torus as the standard Heegaard torus separating the two solid tori of $S^3$, with horizontal circles meridians of the first and vertical circles meridians of the second. The $n$ parallel meridian disks in either solid torus cut it into $n$ balls, one for each row or column annulus. Push the row $O$-to-$X$ arcs into the first solid torus and the column $X$-to-$O$ arcs into the second. Their pushing disks lie in disjoint row or column annuli and are disjoint from the compression disks, so each arc system is simultaneously boundary parallel as required by [F2]. The over/under convention is vertical over horizontal, exactly [F1]'s link. The **grid-complex algorithm** takes a finite encoded grid and a mode from $\{\mathrm{tilde},\mathrm{minus\text{-}associated\text{-}graded},\mathrm{minus\text{-}filtered}\}$. It requires an integer grid number $n\ge2$, disjoint $O$- and $X$-markings with exactly one of each in every row and column, and an induced component permutation that is one $n$-cycle. If $n<2$ or the marking conditions fail, return `invalid-grid`; if the component permutation has more than one cycle, return `link-input-not-supported`. No chain complex is returned on either branch.

For a valid knot grid, number the horizontal and vertical circles $1,\ldots,n$ and enumerate all permutations of $\{1,\ldots,n\}$ in lexicographic order. The state for a permutation $\sigma$ consists of the $n$ intersections $(i,\sigma(i))$. For each ordered pair of states $\mathbf x,\mathbf y$, if they agree in other than exactly $n-2$ points, add no rectangle terms. Otherwise enumerate the at most two torus rectangles with the four nonshared state points as corners, retain those whose interiors contain no point of $\mathbf x$, and apply the selected mode. In the full filtered mode, each term drops filtration by $n_{\mathbb X}(r)$; the associated-graded mode retains precisely the terms with zero drop, which are the rectangles with no $X$-marking:

1. **Tilde mode.** Work over $\mathbb F_2$. Count a retained rectangle with coefficient $1$ exactly when its interior contains no $O$- or $X$-marking.
2. **Associated-graded minus mode.** Work over $\mathbb F_2[U_1,\ldots,U_n]$, with each $U_i$ of Maslov degree $-2$ and Alexander filtration degree $-1$. Count a retained rectangle exactly when its interior contains no $X$-marking, with coefficient $\prod_{i=1}^n U_i^{O_i(r)}$.
3. **Full filtered minus mode.** Work over $\mathbb F_2[U_1,\ldots,U_n]$, with each $U_i$ of Maslov degree $-2$ and Alexander filtration degree $-1$. Count every retained rectangle, regardless of its $X$-markings, with coefficient $\prod_{i=1}^n U_i^{O_i(r)}$. Use the grid Alexander value for each state and assign filtration drop $n_{\mathbb X}(r)$ to this term.

Return the ordered state list, the mode and coefficient ring, the exact differential matrix obtained by summing coefficients modulo two, the state Maslov and Alexander values, and the filtration data for the full filtered mode. The algorithm returns this finite presentation only; its identification with knot Floer homology and its independence of the chosen grid are separate theorems. The factor $V^{\otimes(n-1)}$ is not multiplied into the output.

Let $G$ be a toroidal grid of grid number $n$ representing one oriented knot, and let $M_{\mathbb O}$, $M_{\mathbb X}$, and $A_G$ be the functions defined from its finite point sets and the pair-counting function $J$. Then $M_{\mathbb O}$ and $M_{\mathbb X}$ are integer-valued, and every rectangle $r$ from a grid state $\mathbf x$ to a grid state $\mathbf y$ satisfies $M_{\mathbb O}(\mathbf x)-M_{\mathbb O}(\mathbf y)=1-2n_{\mathbb O}(r)+2\#(\mathbf x\cap\operatorname{Int}r)$ and $M_{\mathbb X}(\mathbf x)-M_{\mathbb X}(\mathbf y)=1-2n_{\mathbb X}(r)+2\#(\mathbf x\cap\operatorname{Int}r)$. Consequently $A_G$ is integer-valued and $A_G(\mathbf x)-A_G(\mathbf y)=n_{\mathbb X}(r)-n_{\mathbb O}(r)$.

derivations.claim: For two successive rectangles $r_1,r_2$, let $\psi=r_1+r_2$ be their cellwise sum as a two-chain, and let $\mathbf x,\mathbf z$ be the initial and terminal states. The state permutation changes by one transposition at each rectangle. If $\mathbf x\ne\mathbf z$, their relative permutation is either a product of two disjoint transpositions, so four points move, or a $3$-cycle, so three points move. These are the only nonidentity products of two transpositions.

For a counted rectangle $r$ the interior contains no state point, so [F3] gives $M_{\mathbb O}(\mathbf x)-M_{\mathbb O}(\mathbf y)=1-2n_{\mathbb O}(r)$. The coefficient $\prod_iU_i^{O_i(r)}$ lowers Maslov degree by $2n_{\mathbb O}(r)$ by [F2]; hence the full term has degree $-1$.

In the four-point case, the two transpositions are disjoint and commute. Exchanging their order gives the alternate intermediate state; the first rectangle in one decomposition has the same support as the second rectangle in the other, and conversely. Thus both decompositions have the same two rectangle interiors and are empty together. No third decomposition is possible, because the four distinct changing corners must be paired into the same two disjoint transpositions fixed by the endpoint permutation and the domain boundary.

In the three-point case, following the boundary of $\psi$ gives a six-corner region with five right-angle corners and one reflex corner of angle $270^\circ$; every cell coefficient is zero or one. At the reflex corner the boundary can be cut in exactly two ways into two rectangles. Each cut gives the required intermediate grid state, and the resulting interiors contain no additional state point because any such point would already lie in the interior of one of the original empty rectangles. The six-corner boundary has no other concave corner at which to make a cut, so these are exactly the two decompositions.

If $\mathbf x=\mathbf z$, the two rectangles reverse the same state transposition and their union is a periodic annulus. If the annulus were not thin, its transverse width would include at least two grid strips; the interior would then contain a state point on an intervening grid circle, contradicting emptiness. Hence every returning domain is one of the $n$ horizontal thin annuli, each occupying one row strip, or one of the $n$ vertical thin annuli, each occupying one column strip. Conversely, the two state points on the boundary circles of any one-row strip split that strip into two empty rectangles, and the same holds for every one-column strip, so all $2n$ listed annuli occur as returning composites. Each contains exactly one $O$ and one $X$ by the row and column marking conditions, so it is excluded in tilde and associated-graded minus modes. In the full filtered minus mode, the horizontal annulus through the row of $O_i$ contributes $U_i$, and the vertical annulus through its column also contributes $U_i$. Every $O_i$ therefore occurs twice among all returning domains, and the total is zero over $\mathbb F_2$.

In either non-annular case the two decompositions have the same cellwise domain $\psi$. A forbidden $O$- or $X$-marking occurs in one rectangle of a decomposition exactly when its cell has positive coefficient in $\psi$; hence a mode excluding that marking accepts either both decompositions or neither. For each $O_i$, the exponent in the product coefficient is its multiplicity in $\psi$, so the two accepted terms have the same monomial. They cancel over $\mathbb F_2$.

The Alexander change in [F3] is $A_G(\mathbf x)-A_G(\mathbf y)=n_{\mathbb X}(r)-n_{\mathbb O}(r)$. Multiplication by the coefficient lowers filtration by $n_{\mathbb O}(r)$, so the output filtration is $A_G(\mathbf x)-n_{\mathbb X}(r)$. Thus the full filtered term drops by exactly $n_{\mathbb X}(r)$, and the tilde and associated-graded modes, which count only rectangles with $n_{\mathbb X}(r)=0$, preserve Alexander grading.

The **grid-complex algorithm** takes a finite encoded grid and a mode from $\{\mathrm{tilde},\mathrm{minus\text{-}associated\text{-}graded},\mathrm{minus\text{-}filtered}\}$. It requires an integer grid number $n\ge2$, disjoint $O$- and $X$-markings with exactly one of each in every row and column, and an induced component permutation that is one $n$-cycle. If $n<2$ or the marking conditions fail, return `invalid-grid`; if the component permutation has more than one cycle, return `link-input-not-supported`. No chain complex is returned on either branch.

For a valid knot grid, number the horizontal and vertical circles $1,\ldots,n$ and enumerate all permutations of $\{1,\ldots,n\}$ in lexicographic order. The state for a permutation $\sigma$ consists of the $n$ intersections $(i,\sigma(i))$. For each ordered pair of states $\mathbf x,\mathbf y$, if they agree in other than exactly $n-2$ points, add no rectangle terms. Otherwise enumerate the at most two torus rectangles with the four nonshared state points as corners, retain those whose interiors contain no point of $\mathbf x$, and apply the selected mode. In the full filtered mode, each term drops filtration by $n_{\mathbb X}(r)$; the associated-graded mode retains precisely the terms with zero drop, which are the rectangles with no $X$-marking:

1. **Tilde mode.** Work over $\mathbb F_2$. Count a retained rectangle with coefficient $1$ exactly when its interior contains no $O$- or $X$-marking.
2. **Associated-graded minus mode.** Work over $\mathbb F_2[U_1,\ldots,U_n]$, with each $U_i$ of Maslov degree $-2$ and Alexander filtration degree $-1$. Count a retained rectangle exactly when its interior contains no $X$-marking, with coefficient $\prod_{i=1}^n U_i^{O_i(r)}$.
3. **Full filtered minus mode.** Work over $\mathbb F_2[U_1,\ldots,U_n]$, with each $U_i$ of Maslov degree $-2$ and Alexander filtration degree $-1$. Count every retained rectangle, regardless of its $X$-markings, with coefficient $\prod_{i=1}^n U_i^{O_i(r)}$. Use the grid Alexander value for each state and assign filtration drop $n_{\mathbb X}(r)$ to this term.

Return the ordered state list, the mode and coefficient ring, the exact differential matrix obtained by summing coefficients modulo two, the state Maslov and Alexander values, and the filtration data for the full filtered mode. The algorithm returns this finite presentation only; its identification with knot Floer homology and its independence of the chosen grid are separate theorems. The factor $V^{\otimes(n-1)}$ is not multiplied into the output.

Let $G$ be a toroidal grid representing a knot, and use the three differentials defined by the grid-complex algorithm. For any fixed source and target states, every non-annular composite of two counted rectangles has exactly two ordered rectangle decompositions; the two decompositions have equal $O$-monomial weights and are either both counted or both excluded in each mode. Returning composites consist of thin annuli, one horizontal annulus for each row and one vertical annulus for each column. Every such annulus contains one $X$ and one $O$, so it is excluded in tilde and associated-graded minus modes. In the full filtered minus mode, each horizontal annulus contributes the variable of its unique $O$-marking, and each vertical annulus contributes the variable of its unique $O$-marking; every $O$-variable occurs once in each family and therefore twice in total. Thus all returning terms cancel over $\mathbb F_2$. Every counted rectangle term has Maslov degree $-1$ and lowers Alexander filtration by exactly the number of $X$-markings in its interior; the modes excluding $X$ preserve Alexander grading.

Let $G$ be a toroidal grid of grid number $n$ representing one oriented knot, and let $M_{\mathbb O}$, $M_{\mathbb X}$, and $A_G$ be the functions defined from its finite point sets and the pair-counting function $J$. Then $M_{\mathbb O}$ and $M_{\mathbb X}$ are integer-valued, and every rectangle $r$ from a grid state $\mathbf x$ to a grid state $\mathbf y$ satisfies $M_{\mathbb O}(\mathbf x)-M_{\mathbb O}(\mathbf y)=1-2n_{\mathbb O}(r)+2\#(\mathbf x\cap\operatorname{Int}r)$ and $M_{\mathbb X}(\mathbf x)-M_{\mathbb X}(\mathbf y)=1-2n_{\mathbb X}(r)+2\#(\mathbf x\cap\operatorname{Int}r)$. Consequently $A_G$ is integer-valued and $A_G(\mathbf x)-A_G(\mathbf y)=n_{\mathbb X}(r)-n_{\mathbb O}(r)$.

For every one-component toroidal grid and each of the tilde, associated-graded minus, and full filtered minus modes, the differential defined by the grid-complex algorithm satisfies $\partial^2=0$ over its stated coefficient ring.

derivations.claim: The sum defining $H_\ell$ is finite because there are finitely many states and at most two torus rectangles for each ordered state pair. It is $\mathbb F_2[U_1,\ldots,U_n]$-linear by its coefficient formula. For each counted rectangle $r$, [F4] gives $M(\mathbf x)-M(\mathbf y)=1-2n_{\mathbb O}(r)$; the coefficient has Maslov degree $-2n_{\mathbb O}(r)$ by [F2]. Therefore each term of $H_\ell(\mathbf x)$ has Maslov degree $M(\mathbf x)-1$. Also [F4] gives $A(\mathbf y)-n_{\mathbb O}(r)=A(\mathbf x)-n_{\mathbb X}(r)$, and $X_\ell\in\operatorname{Int}(r)$ implies $n_{\mathbb X}(r)\ge1$. Thus $H_\ell$ does not raise the Alexander filtration.

Expand $\partial^-H_\ell+H_\ell\partial^-$ and group its terms by their two-rectangle domain $\psi$. If $\psi$ is non-annular, [F3] pairs its two decompositions. In each decomposition, when $X_\ell$ has multiplicity zero neither ordered term is selected; when it has multiplicity one exactly one of the two rectangles contains it and exactly one ordering is selected; when it has multiplicity two both rectangles contain it and the two possible placements of $H_\ell$ cancel in characteristic two. The paired decomposition has the same domain, $O$-weight, and multiplicity at $X_\ell$, so every non-annular contribution cancels.

A returning two-rectangle domain is a thin horizontal or vertical annulus by [F3]. The only thin annuli containing $X_\ell$ are the horizontal one in its row and the vertical one in its column. In the horizontal annulus the unique $O$-marking is $O_i$, so its coefficient is $U_i$; in the vertical annulus the unique $O$-marking is $O_j$, so its coefficient is $U_j$. Each annulus has one decomposition and contributes its coefficient times the input generator. Hence the returning contribution is $(U_i+U_j)\mathbf x$. Together with step 1.2 this proves the chain homotopy identity.

The marking route in [F1] orders the variables cyclically, and each adjacent pair in that cycle is consecutive as defined in the statement. Any two indices are joined by a finite path of adjacent pairs. By [F5], each multiplication map is a chain map for the differential; adding the homotopy maps from step 2.1 along the path gives a filtered chain homotopy between multiplication by $U_i$ and multiplication by $U_j$.

citations.quote: Let $G$ be a finite nonempty planar marked grid with vertical-over crossing convention. A horizontal segment is a cap if its two incident vertical segments both extend above it or both extend below it; otherwise it is monotone. A marked stabilization splits a marked cell into a two-by-two block with the chosen marking type twice at opposite corners, the other type once and one empty corner, preserving one of each type per row and column. A legal column commutation exchanges adjacent columns with disjoint or strictly nested closed vertical marking intervals. There is a finite sequence of marked stabilizations and legal commutations carrying $G$ to a grid in which every cap has no crossing and every monotone horizontal segment has exactly one crossing. Thus the resulting grid is bridge-like: slightly tilt its crossing-containing horizontal segments in the direction of height travel and round its empty caps to obtain a bridge diagram. Every operation respects the oriented $O,X$ convention of the grid-diagram definition, and the number of link components is unchanged. The decorated planar diagram before and after the entire refinement is planar isotopic after rounding corners; in particular no Reidemeister move is needed for this refinement. No global grid-move generation theorem is assumed.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $D$ and $D'$ be regular oriented link diagrams.
Then $D$ and $D'$ represent equivalent oriented links if and only if $D'$ can be
obtained from $D$ by a finite sequence of planar isotopies and oriented
Reidemeister moves R1, R2, R3.

Assume countable choice. Let $D_0,D_1$ be nonempty oriented bridge diagrams that are planar isotopic with crossing decorations transported by the isotopy. Then any bridge-like grid rectification of $D_0$ is connected to any bridge-like grid rectification of $D_1$ by finitely many marked grid stabilizations, legal commutations and destabilizations. Here vertical strands pass over horizontal strands, a legal commutation exchanges adjacent rows or columns with disjoint or strictly nested closed marking intervals, and a stabilization is a three-mark two-by-two split preserving one $O$ and one $X$ per row and column. In particular the grid-move class assigned by bridge rectification depends only on the oriented decorated planar-isotopy class whenever that class is represented by bridge diagrams. No Reidemeister-move or global grid-isotopy generation theorem is used.

Assume countable choice. Suppose two nonempty oriented decorated planar diagrams differ by one Reidemeister move inside a disk, retaining the entire exterior and its boundary incidence. Each endpoint admits a bridge representative in its decorated planar-isotopy class. Let $D_0^\prime,D_1^\prime$ be any bridge diagrams planar isotopic to the respective endpoints. Then any bridge-like grid rectifications of $D_0^\prime,D_1^\prime$ are connected by finitely many marked grid stabilizations, legal commutations and destabilizations. All signs, strand orientations and consistent strict over/under orders of R3 are included. The exterior diagram is arbitrary. A legal commutation exchanges adjacent rows or columns whose closed marking intervals are disjoint or strictly nested; a stabilization is a three-mark two-by-two split preserving one mark of each type in each row and column. No shared-endpoint switch is assumed as a primitive move. The conclusion uses no global grid-isotopy generation theorem.

derivations.claim: A knot grid is nonempty. Apply [F1] to each $G_i$, obtaining a finite grid-move sequence to a bridge-like grid $B_i$. Smooth $B_i$ as in that supplier to a bridge diagram $D_i$. Its crossing decorations and strand orientation agree with the original grid diagram, and the supplier proves planar isotopy after smoothing. Thus $D_0,D_1$ represent the same oriented knot. The three-mark splits and strict interval commutations in [F1] are among those specified here: the retained exterior row and column partners provide the two markings outside the stabilization block in the Statement. No unlisted shared-endpoint switch has been used.

By [F2] choose a finite sequence of planar isotopies and oriented Reidemeister moves from $D_0$ to $D_1$. Compose successive planar isotopies, and regard each remaining Reidemeister move as an edge between its two decorated planar-isotopy classes. The sequence now traverses finitely many such classes, with the first and last represented by $D_0,D_1$. If there is no Reidemeister edge, these two diagrams are planar isotopic. Otherwise each intermediate class is incident to a Reidemeister edge and has a bridge representative by [F4]. Choose one bridge representative for each occurrence of a class in this finite sequence, keeping $D_0,D_1$ at its ends, and choose a bridge rectification there. The choices are finite; no stronger choice principle is invoked.

Across a Reidemeister edge, the chosen bridge representatives need only be planar isotopic to that edge's original endpoint diagrams. This is exactly the relative-representative interface of [F4], so their chosen grid rectifications are joined by actual grid moves, with every exterior strand included. Across an interval with only planar isotopy, [F3] joins the chosen rectifications. This also treats the sequence with no Reidemeister edge. The endpoint rectifications may be taken to be precisely $B_0,B_1$, because both suppliers apply to arbitrary rectifications. Concatenating the finitely many constituent finite sequences gives a sequence of allowed commutations, stabilizations and destabilizations from $B_0$ to $B_1$.

Prepend the refinement from $G_0$ to $B_0$ and append the reversed refinement from $B_1$ to $G_1$. Reversing a stabilization gives a destabilization and reversing a legal commutation gives a legal commutation, so all operations remain allowed. This produces the required finite sequence from $G_0$ to $G_1$. The proof needs no cyclic permutation, but allowing those additional moves in the Statement does not change the conclusion. The local suppliers cover all marking types and strand orientations, so the sequence preserves the prescribed oriented-knot convention throughout.

Let $G,G'$ be knot grids related by exchanging two consecutive columns whose marking-height intervals are disjoint or strictly nested. The same assertion holds for rows, using intervals of marking abscissae, and for a switch, where an $X$ and an $O$ of the exchanged columns share a row. Identify variables by their individual $O$-markings, retaining the full polynomial ring. There are explicit filtered chain maps $P:C^-(G)\to C^-(G')$ and $Q:C^-(G')\to C^-(G)$ given by empty pentagon counts with their $O$-monomial weights, and filtered homotopies $H,H'$ given by empty hexagon counts, satisfying
$$dH+Hd=\operatorname{id}+QP,\qquad d'H'+H'd'=\operatorname{id}+PQ.$$
The maps preserve Maslov grading and do not increase Alexander filtration; the homotopies have Maslov degree $+1$ and do not increase filtration. Taking the associated graded retains precisely the polygons avoiding $X$. Setting all $O$ variables to zero in that associated-graded equivalence gives the tilde equivalence. The maps and homotopies remain valid under any coefficient specialization.

Let $G'$ be an $X$ stabilization of type southwest of a knot grid $G$. In the four cells incident to the new crossing $c$, the northwest cell contains $X_1$, the northeast cell contains the new $O_1$, the southeast cell contains $X_2$, and the southwest cell is empty. Let $O_2$ be the old $O$ in the row of $X_2$. Write $I$ for states containing $c$, and identify such a state $\mathbf y$ with $e(\mathbf y)=\mathbf y\setminus\{c\}$ in $G$. Retain the independent variables of all markings.

An incoming left domain is either the zero domain or a nonnegative domain from $\mathbf x$ to $\mathbf y\in I$ with the following properties. At every state corner other than $c$, at least three adjacent cell multiplicities vanish; near $c$, three multiplicities equal $k$ and the southwest multiplicity is $k-1$; exactly $2k+1$ coordinates of $\mathbf y$ are absent from $\mathbf x$. For an incoming right domain, replace the southwest exception by southeast multiplicity $k+1$, and the number of absent coordinates by $2k+2$; the zero domain is not of right type. Denote these sets by $\pi^{iL},\pi^{iR}$. Define $D^{iL},D^{iR}$ by counting their targets $e(\mathbf y)$, with weight $\prod_{j\ne1}U_j^{O_j(p)}$, omitting the power of the new variable. Then
$$D=(D^{iL},D^{iR}):C^-(G')\longrightarrow\operatorname{Cone}(U_1+U_2:C^-(G)[U_1]\to C^-(G)[U_1])$$
is a finite polynomial-module chain map preserving Maslov degree and not increasing Alexander filtration. The first cone summand is shifted down by one in both degree and filtration. Its associated-graded map counts only domains avoiding $X_1,X_3,\ldots$; these have complexity at most two and give exactly the usual graded destabilization map: deletion of $c$ on $I$ in the first component, and rectangles through $X_2$ on the other states in the second component.

For a southwest $X$ stabilization, the incoming-domain map from the full filtered grid complex to the cone of $U_1+U_2$ on the polynomial extension of the smaller grid complex is a filtered chain homotopy equivalence over the full polynomial ring. Its inverse and both inverse homotopies can be computed by finite polynomial matrix formulas from empty rectangles and incoming domains. Composing with the explicit cone retraction gives filtered equivalence with the smaller complex over any retained old variable action, without imposing relations on its other variables. After simultaneous ordinary collapse of the marking variables, stabilization contributes the zero-differential factor $V$ of bidegrees $(0,0)$ and $(-1,-1)$. The same $V$ factor occurs on tilde homology.

Let $C$ be the full filtered complex of a knot grid with independent marking variables. The same underlying complex, regarded as a module over $\mathbb F_2[U]$ with $U$ acting as $U_i$, has filtered chain homotopy type independent of $i$. This assertion concerns restriction of scalars; no marking variables are identified or set to zero. For consecutive markings the equivalence and its inverse homotopies are explicit polynomial divided-difference formulas and finite weighted rectangle counts.

Let $R=\mathbb F_2[U,Z_1,\ldots,Z_s]$, and let $(C,d)$ be a graded, Alexander-filtered chain complex of free $R$-modules. Every variable has Maslov degree $-2$ and Alexander filtration degree $-1$, and $d$ has Maslov degree $-1$ and does not increase filtration. Extend scalars to $C[T]$, with $T$ having the same degrees. Put $f=T+U$ and form the cone $B=C[T]^{\mathrm{low}}\oplus C[T]$, with differential $D(a,b)=(da,db+fa)$; the first copy is shifted down by one in both Maslov degree and filtration. Regarded over $R$, this cone has an explicit filtered chain deformation retraction onto $C$. Its projection is evaluation of the second component at $T=U$, its inclusion is $c\mapsto(0,c)$, and its homotopy is polynomial divided difference in the second component, placed in the first component.

In contrast, the ordinary scalar quotient $T=U$ taken before homology gives the zero-map cone $C\oplus C^{\mathrm{low}}$, equivalently $C\otimes V$, where $V$ has zero differential and bidegrees $(0,0)$ and $(-1,-1)$. Any further ordinary quotient of the old variables has the same direct-sum description with the corresponding quotient of $C$. Thus an equivalence of a basepoint insertion complex with this cone over the full polynomial ring implies invariance for the chosen single-variable action and an extra $V$ factor after simultaneous collapse. These are different operations.

More generally, let $E$ be free over $R[T]$ on a homogeneous filtered basis, and let its differential $d(T)$ have the same degree and filtration behavior, with polynomial matrix entries. Then $\operatorname{Cone}(T+U:E\to E)$ admits an explicit filtered deformation retraction over $R$ onto the ordinary quotient $(E/(T+U)E,d(U))$. If multiplication by $T+U$ on $E$ has a polynomial-linear homotopy $L$ with $dL+Ld=T+U$, Maslov degree $-1$, and filtration degree at most $-1$, this quotient is filtered chain homotopy equivalent over $R$ to $E\otimes V$. Iterating applies to independent marking variables and survives every earlier scalar quotient. Thus pairwise such homotopies imply that simultaneous collapse of $n$ variables to one has type $E\otimes V^{\otimes(n-1)}$ over the chosen variable action.

derivations.claim: A cyclic permutation is a change of fundamental cut on the same grid torus. It identifies states, rectangles, and marking monomials bijectively. The finite pair-count gradings also agree under this change. To check this directly for a column cut, use the signed set $P=\mathbf x-\mathbb O$ in $M_O=I(P,P)+1$. The wrapping column contains one state point of sign $+1$ and one $O$ of sign $-1$. Only their comparisons with nonwrapping points change. At an integer state height the signed number of all points below is zero, and at the height of a marking in row $r$ it is one, since the states have heights $0,\ldots,n-1$ and the markings have one height in each open row. Thus the signed difference of the below/above counts for either wrapping point, excluding itself, is one. Multiplying by the two signs and adding gives zero; the comparisons between the two wrapping points cancel from this sum and do not change. Hence $I(P,P)$ is unchanged. Apply the same count to $\mathbf x-\mathbb X$, and interchange coordinates for a row cut. Both Maslov functions and the Alexander formula are unchanged. The torus-identification map is therefore a filtered chain isomorphism, with inverse the opposite cut change and zero inverse homotopies.

For a commutation, use the maps and homotopies in [F1]. Their weights retain every $O$ variable separately, and their filtration drop is the number of $X$ in the polygon. Thus they are filtered equivalences over the full ring; restricting the ring action to any chosen marking variable preserves these identities. Their associated-graded maps retain precisely polygons avoiding $X$. Setting the variables to zero gives the tilde equivalence. The identical conclusion holds for the switches used below.

For a southwest $X$ stabilization, [F2] supplies the map to the cone of $U_1+U_2$ on the polynomial extension of the smaller complex. By [F3], it has a finite matrix inverse and both filtered inverse homotopies. Compose with the explicit retraction in [F5]. Its inclusion, divided-difference homotopy, and evaluation are linear over every old variable, so the resulting equivalence and homotopies are over any chosen retained old-variable action. If either grid uses another chosen variable, including the newly inserted one, first or last compose with the chosen-variable equivalences of [F4]. Hence the assertion holds for arbitrary choices of the single variable action, without setting any independent variable equal to another.

The other local stabilization types reduce to this one using the following finite operations. An $O$ stabilization introduces a vertical segment joining marks in consecutive rows. Commute this short segment horizontally toward the next $X$ endpoint; while passing another vertical segment, its length-one interval is either disjoint or nested, since no marking height lies strictly between its two endpoints. At a shared endpoint level the exchange is a switch. Stop at the next $X$, where deleting that short segment is an $X$ destabilization back to the original grid. Tracking the empty corner gives the pairs $O{:}NE$ with $X{:}SW$, $O{:}SE$ with $X{:}NW$, $O{:}NW$ with $X{:}SE$, and $O{:}SW$ with $X{:}NE$. Among the four $X$ types, exchanging the two new adjacent rows moves the empty corner across a horizontal side, and exchanging the two new adjacent columns moves it across a vertical side; these are switches because the central opposite-type marking shares a column or row with the adjacent same-type marking. One or two such switches carry any empty corner to the southwest corner. These operations concern only the added row, added column, and their endpoint segments; after deleting them the original row and column orders are unchanged. Thus every stabilization is a southwest $X$ stabilization followed by finitely many commutations, switches, and cut changes.

Compose the equivalences for that finite sequence, using step 1.2 for commutations and switches and step 1.3 for its sole stabilization. Explicit inverse homotopies compose: for equivalences $f_1,f_2$ with inverses $g_1,g_2$ and homotopies $g_i f_i+1=dH_i+H_id$, a homotopy for $g_1g_2f_2f_1+1$ is $H_1+g_1H_2f_1$. The counterpart on the other complex has the analogous formula. Every summand remains filtered and has degree $+1$. Reversing the roles of the two grids proves the destabilization assertion as well. All map formulas are finite sums of composable grid-domain counts and the explicit polynomial formulas in [F3]–[F5].

The full polynomial equivalence with the stabilization cone in step 1.3 can also be tensored with the simultaneous ordinary coefficient quotient. Its cross map $U_1+U_2$ becomes zero, so [F5] identifies the quotient cone with the collapsed smaller complex tensored with $V$. The first summand's grading and filtration shift is $(-1,-1)$, giving exactly the displayed bidegrees. Taking the associated-graded equivalence first and then setting every variable to zero gives the same direct sum for tilde homology. Commutation and switches preserve tilde homology by step 1.2, and cut changes do by step 1.1. These comparisons prove the tilde and collapsed assertions for every stabilization type.
