Assume full AC. Use the actual based earring $K\cup L\subset S^3$, its normal radius arc $\omega$, the compact exterior $X$ and a supplied $SO(3)$ bundle $P\to X$ with $w_2(P)=PD_{\mathbb F_2}[\omega]$ in the singular-data definition. Both boundary-torus restrictions of $P$ have nonzero $w_2$. The bundle admits a compatible extension to an order-two orbifold bundle over $(S^3,K\cup L)$ whose local isotropy is rotation by $\pi$, whose axis-orientation cover on each link component is nontrivial, and whose ordinary local singular residue is $\frac14\operatorname{diag}(i,-i)d\theta$ up to conjugation. It therefore supplies the compatible finite local data required by the order-two gauge-completion lemma.

For this completed data every connection has determinant-one stabilizer exactly $\{\pm1\}$. The bundle on the exterior also has an actual $U(2)$ lift with a chosen determinant line and determinant connection, as needed for cylinder holonomy functions. These statements concern the topology and analytic input data, not independence of the resulting choices or construction of Floer homology. The supplied-bundle existence clause of the original definition is retained; this result does not classify all singular extensions up to canonical isomorphism.

Assume full AC. Let a compact smooth pair $(M,S)$ without boundary of dimension three or four have $S$ of codimension two, and supply finite branched charts $(y,w)\mapsto(y,w^2)$ with group $\mathbb Z/2$ acting by $w\mapsto-w$, together with their compatible coordinate lifts. Supply a smooth orbifold metric and an $SO(3)$ bundle in these charts with nontrivial isotropy a rotation by $\pi$ about a line. Use its determinant-one gauge transformations: in each local quaternionic lift they obey $u(y,-w)=\rho u(y,w)\rho^{-1}$, where $\rho=\operatorname{diag}(i,-i)$ and $\rho^2=-1$. These conjugation conditions are independent of the sign of the lift.

Finite-chart invariant Sobolev spaces $H^k$ are Hilbert spaces with smooth invariant density, compact $H^{k+1}\hookrightarrow H^k$ inclusion, and the usual dimension-three or dimension-four Sobolev product and embedding estimates. For $k\ge3$, the $H^{k+1}$ determinant-one gauge group is a Banach Lie group acting smoothly on the affine $H^k$ connection space. At an irreducible connection, Coulomb slices give a smooth unbased quotient and equation bundle; arbitrary connecting gauges between converging slice representatives have converging $H^{k+1}$ subsequences, up to their central ambiguity.

Every smooth first-order operator with scalar Clifford square, acting on these bundles and respecting the invariant local conditions, is Fredholm $H^k\to H^{k-1}$ on compact $M$. Its kernel and cokernel are smooth. A formally selfadjoint such operator $H$ has domain $H^1$ in $L^2$, compact resolvent and a complete real discrete spectrum of finite multiplicity. In particular this applies to the extended three-dimensional Hessian $H_B(\phi,b)=(d_B^*b,d_B\phi+*d_Bb)$, and in dimension four to $d_A^*\oplus\sqrt2d_A^+$.

On an infinite cylinder over the compact three-dimensional pair, suppose $H(t)$ has one fixed first-order principal part, shared by $H_\pm$, throughout the cylinder and differs from $H_\pm$ by smooth zero-order coefficients tending to zero with their first $k$ derivatives, while the selfadjoint limiting $H_\pm$ are invertible. The same assertion allows additional possibly nonlocal zero-order operators $R(t)$: every $\partial_t^aR(t)$ is bounded $H^j(Y)\to H^j(Y)$ for the needed integer orders, these bounds are uniform, and they converge on the ends in those operator norms; the two limiting full Hessians are selfadjoint and invertible on their $H^1$ domains. Then $\partial_t+H(t):H^k\to H^{k-1}$, including these additional terms, is Fredholm. The conclusion remains true on spaces weighted by $e^{\delta|t|}$ if $0\le\delta<\min\operatorname{dist}(0,\operatorname{spec}H_\pm)$. No index formula, nonlinear asymptotic convergence, transversality, trajectory compactification or Floer differential is asserted here.

Assume full AC. Supply a compact oriented three-dimensional order-two singular pair $(Y,K)$, compatible orbifold bundle data and determinant-one gauges as in the preceding completion lemma, and a fixed $U(2)$ lift on $Y\setminus K$ with fixed determinant connection. Suppose every connection in this singular configuration space has stabilizer $\{\pm1\}$. Use $H^k/H^{k+1}$, $k\ge3$.

There is a separable Banach space $\mathcal P$ of countable weighted sums of smooth cylinder functions supported away from $K$. For $\pi\in\mathcal P$ its function $f_\pi$ is bounded, smooth and gauge invariant, and its $L^2$ gradient $V_\pi$ is a smooth gauge-equivariant $H^k$ vector field. It is uniformly pointwise bounded by $C\|\pi\|_{\mathcal P}$, independently of the connection; its derivative is bounded on $L^2$ with the same type of uniform bound. Its spatial covariant derivatives have polynomial bounds in lower spatial covariant derivatives of curvature, with constants uniform on bounded perturbation sets.

The critical-point projection for $*F_B+V_\pi(B)=0$ is proper over compact subsets of $\mathcal P$ in the actual $H^k$ quotient. An open dense subset of $\mathcal P$ has only nondegenerate critical points; their set is finite. All critical connections are smooth in orbifold gauges. This result proves the critical set and not transversality, compactness or gluing for nonconstant trajectories. The existence of the stipulated global singular data and $U(2)$ lift is not asserted here.

Assume full AC. Fix the constructed earring data and a holonomy perturbation with finitely many nondegenerate critical points. There is a separable Banach space of further cylinder perturbations whose functions and all connection derivatives vanish at those critical points. Sufficiently small such perturbations retain exactly the same critical points and Hessians. A residual dense set of these perturbations makes every nonconstant finite-energy trajectory in every relative class regular, at every integer Fredholm index. The corresponding translation quotient is a smooth Hausdorff second-countable manifold of dimension $I-1$. In particular there are no nonconstant trajectories with $I\le0$.

Trajectories here are solutions in the actual unweighted cylindrical configuration spaces with critical asymptotics, and finite energy is the flow energy defined above. Establishing that arbitrary finite-flow-energy solutions have those asymptotics, and proving compactifications or gluing collars, remain separate claims. No orientability assertion is made here.

Assume full AC. Use the earring singular data, completed determinant-one gauge group $\mathcal G$, and fixed determinant lift constructed above. The restriction to the two core circles gives an exact sequence of component groups
$$0\longrightarrow\mathbb Z\longrightarrow\pi_0\mathcal G\longrightarrow(\mathbb Z/2)^2\longrightarrow0,$$
where the kernel generator is a degree-one gauge transformation supported in a ball disjoint from the singular link. For a loop in the unbased configuration quotient define $I$ as the index of its cylindrical ASD deformation operator with fixed invertible asymptotic Hessian, and define its topological energy period by twice the Chern–Simons drop, using inner product $-\operatorname{tr}_{\mathbb C^2}$. Then
$$\mathcal E=\pi^2 I,\qquad I\in4\mathbb Z.$$
Both quantities vanish on the central stabilizer and descend to actual quotient loops.

Fix any perturbation in the nondegenerate critical class of the preceding critical-set lemma. For critical endpoints $\alpha,\beta$ and a relative path class $z$, let $I_z$ be the corresponding cylindrical index and $\mathcal E_z$ twice the drop of the perturbed functional. There is a constant $C$ depending on this fixed data, but not on $z,\alpha,\beta$, such that $|\mathcal E_z-\pi^2I_z|\le C$. For every finite upper index bound $D$, only finitely many endpoint pairs and relative classes of nonconstant gradient trajectories with $I_z\le D$ can occur, and their flow energies satisfy $0<\mathcal E_z\le\pi^2D+C$.

Here finite flow energy means $2\int_{\mathbb R}\|\partial_tB\|_2^2dt$ in temporal gauge, equivalently the perturbed topological energy. It does not mean the unrenormalized integral of curvature squared over the whole cylinder when its perturbed critical endpoints are nonflat. No trajectory compactness, regularity or gluing conclusion is part of this result.

Assume full AC. Let $\Gamma=\mathbb Z/2$ act on $S^4=\mathbb R^4\cup\{\infty\}$ by rotation by $\pi$ in one normal two-plane, with fixed two-sphere. Supply a smooth equivariant $SO(3)$ bundle whose isotropy on that fixed sphere is a rotation by $\pi$. If $A$ is any nonflat equivariant anti-self-dual connection, its unbased invariant ASD complex has zero obstruction space and kernel dimension at least three. The corresponding flat reference bundle with constant fiber action has unbased index $-1$. Consequently the relative ASD index of this bubble against that flat reference is at least four.

At an ordinary point the analogous relative index loss is at least eight. These conclusions include every nonflat charge, not just BPST charge one.

More precisely, suppose two Fredholm ASD deformation operators on a compact four-orbifold, or on a cylinder with identical invertible limiting Hessians, have bundles identified away from one standard ball or one such order-two quotient ball. Form the comparison bundle $Q$ on $S^4$ (respectively $S^4/\Gamma$) by gluing their local ball bundles with that boundary identification, and let $Q_0$ be the constant reference. Then their index difference is exactly $\operatorname{ind}D_Q-\operatorname{ind}D_{Q_0}$. Thus when $Q$ is an actual nonflat ASD bubble the preceding lower bounds apply. The result does not assume that every degeneration has such a comparison until point-removal and topological identification have been proved for that degeneration.

Assume full AC. Use the fixed earring orbifold data, metric and an allowed holonomy perturbation in a bounded set of the constructed perturbation space. On every compact subcylinder, a sequence of smooth perturbed ASD trajectories with a common upper bound on flow energy has, after gauges and a subsequence, a limit away from finitely many points. On that punctured subcylinder the convergence is strong $W^{1,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}$ for every finite $p$ in local gauges. The limiting connection extends across those points as a smooth perturbed ASD connection on an actual smooth orbifold bundle. The lost energy at each point is a positive multiple of $8\pi^2$ at an ordinary point and a positive multiple of $4\pi^2$ on the singular surface, in the fundamental trace convention.

All concentrated bundles are accounted for by finitely many nonflat ordinary or order-two invariant ASD sphere bubbles with flat matching collars and no additional clutching contribution on the intervening necks. Thus the cylindrical index difference is the sum of their actual relative indices, at least eight per ordinary bubble and at least four per invariant bubble. In particular every concentration point has index loss at least four. If there are no concentration points, convergence on smaller closed subcylinders is smooth in orbifold gauges. The statement is local in the cylinder direction and does not assert convergence at its infinite ends or any nonlinear gluing collar.

Assume full AC. For the constructed earring data choose one of the all-index regular holonomy perturbations with its finite nondegenerate critical set. Every smooth trajectory of finite flow energy has a single critical orbit at each infinite end and, in actual determinant-one orbifold gauges, converges to representatives exponentially in every Sobolev order. For every fixed integer index bound there are only finitely many possible endpoint pairs and relative classes of nonconstant trajectories.

Sequences of trajectories of index one or two have, modulo translations, subsequences converging to finite broken trajectories without bubbles. The total index is the sum of the positive indices of the nonconstant levels. Thus the index-one translation quotient is a compact finite set; an index-two sequence has either a smooth unbroken limit or precisely two index-one levels. This statement identifies sequential limits and does not yet assert gluing collars or orientations.

Assume full AC and the actual all-index regular earring perturbation. Every ordered broken pair of index-one trajectories has a gluing collar of index-two unparametrized trajectories. Each sufficiently broken index-two trajectory belongs to precisely the collar of its broken limit. The glued relative class is the actual concatenation class. Together with the unbroken moduli, these collars make the index-two compactification a compact one-dimensional manifold with boundary the ordered broken pairs. The smooth structure is its ordinary smooth structure in the interior and the collar smooth structure at its boundary. No assertion of analyticity in an arbitrarily preassigned exponential neck coordinate is made.

Assume full AC and the constructed earring data. The real determinant line of the cylindrical ASD operator is orientable on every fixed-endpoint trajectory configuration component. One can choose rank-one integral orientation modules for the critical points and compatible determinant identifications for every relative trajectory class. They are compatible with concatenation, gauge equivalence and the nonlinear broken-trajectory collars. With the translation orientation removed, the signed boundary of an index-two compactification is the signed sum of its ordered index-one broken pairs. Consequently the integral signed differential defined by those pairs has square zero. Choices of bases in the critical orientation modules change the resulting complex by the corresponding diagonal signs.

Assume full AC. Integral earring instanton complexes formed from any two regular orbifold metrics and allowed regular holonomy perturbations of the fixed based earring data are related by continuation chain maps. A map depends only on its endpoints up to chain homotopy and the declared determinant-orientation sign choices. Continuation maps compose up to chain homotopy, and the maps in reverse directions are inverse chain homotopy equivalences. Transport under an isotopy of the based knot and its earring data gives the corresponding homology isomorphism. This statement concerns the singular instanton complex; it makes no assertion about sutured-closure independence, a knot-detection theorem or an instanton surgery formula.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: By [F1] the prescribed singular data are realized by actual finite-group charts and determinant-one gauges, with no reducible stabilizers. By [F2] the critical points of the perturbed Chern–Simons functional form a finite nondegenerate set, and its genuine singular trajectory equation has the stated Fredholm Sobolev realization. All smooth finite-flow-energy trajectories have the critical asymptotics in those spaces by [F3]. Thus the zero sets used to define the complex are actual smooth finite-dimensional regular moduli, rather than only formal expected-dimensional spaces.

Let $o_\alpha$ be the rank-one integral orientation module of a critical point from [F4] and set $C=\bigoplus_\alpha o_\alpha$. This is finite free. For each ordered critical pair, sum the signed module maps over every relative class of index one. There are only finitely many such classes and finitely many trajectories in each translation quotient by [F3]. Hence this is a well-defined integral homomorphism $d:C\to C$. The index periods are divisible by four, so the relative grading modulo four from [F3] gives this differential degree one in the cochain convention; no unsupported absolute integer grading is claimed. Choosing bases of the modules identifies this complex with the displayed generator convention of the Definition.

For any two endpoint critical points, take all index-two relative classes. Their finite union of compactified translation quotients is a compact oriented one-manifold by [F3]–[F4]. Its boundary consists exactly of all ordered index-one broken pairs, without bubbles, missing collar sheets or constant nonregular limiting levels. The actual signed boundary comparison in [F4] identifies its algebraic boundary sum with one fixed convention sign times the corresponding coefficient of $d^2$. That boundary sum is zero. This holds for every endpoint pair, so $d^2=0$ over $\mathbb Z$, not only modulo two. No surgery or sutured excision theorem is used in this argument.

The continuation theorem [F4] constructs finite signed counts for the actual nonautonomous equation, its chain maps and inverse chain homotopies between any two regular metrics and allowed perturbations. Its finite-parameter energy estimate and low-dimensional compactness supply the composition and homotopy relations, including the constant-continuation identity. Therefore the homology of this finite free cochain complex is independent of those choices with the stipulated determinant-orientation sign convention.

An isotopy of the based knot and its earring data transports the actual branch charts, exterior bundle, holonomy perturbations and gauge-fixed operators. The pullback chain identification and the continuation equivalence of [F4] give the asserted isotopy isomorphism. The sign choices agree with the orientation-module convention in step 2.1. This proves precisely the analytic construction and invariance in the original Statement. Sutured-closure independence, the KHI rank detector, resolution-cube maps, instanton L-space surgery and a distinguished canonical class remain their own separate obligations; none has been inferred from this complex construction.

Step 3.1 proves every coefficient of d squared is zero by the signed compactified one-manifold boundary sum, including zero trajectory counts.
Step 2.1 uses a rank-one integral orientation module for each individual critical point and sums its module maps; singleton indexing requires no separate basis or parity assertion.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K:S^1	o S^3$ be a smooth oriented embedding and write its quotient normal bundle as $
u_K=K^*TS^3/dK(TS^1)$. Choose an orientation-preserving trivialization $
u_K\cong S^1	imes\mathbb R^2$ and a tubular map $\Phi:\Omega	o S^3$, meaning a smooth embedding from an open neighbourhood $\Omega\subseteq
u_K$ of the zero section onto an open neighbourhood of $K(S^1)$ with $\Phi(s,0)=K(s)$, such that in these product coordinates $\Omega$ contains $S^1	imes D^2_{2\epsilon}$ for some $\epsilon>0$. Here $D^2_r=\{z\in\mathbb R^2:\|z\|\le r\}$. Set $N(K)=\Phi(S^1	imes D^2_\epsilon)$, $E_K=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$, $T_K=\partial E_K$, and let $i:T_K\hookrightarrow E_K$ be inclusion, $p:T_K	o S^1$ the product projection, and $\mu$ the positive boundary of a normal disk, using the normal-plane orientation determined by the orientations of $K$ and $S^3$. A class is primitive if it is not $m$ times another class for any integer $|m|>1$. Then $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$ is generated by $[\mu]$. The kernel of $i_*:H_1(T_K;\mathbb Z)	o H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$ is a primitive rank-one direct summand generated by a unique class $[\lambda]$ with $p_*[\lambda]=1\in H_1(S^1;\mathbb Z)$. It has a simple closed representative, is the preferred longitude, and $([\mu],[\lambda])$ is a basis of $H_1(T_K;\mathbb Z)$.

Assume countable choice as in the chosen tubular-neighbourhood data. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot with chosen exterior $E_K$ and boundary torus $T_K=\partial E_K$, and let $p:T_K\to K$ be the projection of the chosen normal-disk tube. Orient each normal disk so that its positive tangent direction followed by its oriented normal basis agrees with the orientation of $S^3$. A **meridian** $\mu$ is the oriented boundary of one such normal disk. A **degree-one parallel curve** is a simple closed curve $\lambda$ in $T_K$ for which $p|_\lambda:\lambda\to K$ has degree $+1$. A **preferred longitude** is a degree-one parallel curve satisfying $i_*[\lambda]=0$ in $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$, where $i:T_K\hookrightarrow E_K$ is inclusion. This is a condition on a curve; this definition alone asserts neither existence nor uniqueness. Reversing the orientation of $K$ reverses the orientations of both $\mu$ and any degree-one parallel curve. If a subgroup $P\le\pi_1(E_K,x)$ is specified using a path from $x$ to $T_K$, record it only up to replacing it by $gPg^{-1}$ for $g\in\pi_1(E_K,x)$.

Let $T=\mathbb R^2/\mathbb Z^2$ be oriented by $dx\wedge dy$, and identify $H_1(T;\mathbb Z)$ with $\mathbb Z^2$ in the standard basis, so the algebraic intersection of classes $v,w$ is $\det(v,w)$. Let $\gamma_0,\gamma_1\subset T$ be smooth embedded circles that are not null-homotopic. Orient them so that their homology classes agree, and suppose their common class $v\in H_1(T;\mathbb Z)$ is primitive, meaning it is not an integer multiple $m u$ with $|m|>1$. Then $\gamma_0$ and $\gamma_1$ are isotopic through embedded circles in $T$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. For every smooth oriented knot $K$ in $S^3$, its Seifert genus is zero if and only if $K$ is ambient isotopic through orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms to the standard unknot.

Let $M$ be a compact smooth three-manifold, possibly nonorientable and with boundary, and let $f:F\to M$ be a smooth embedding of a compact smooth surface with $f^{-1}(\partial M)=\partial F$. Transversality to $\partial M$ is not assumed. Given an open neighborhood $U$ of $C=f(\partial F)$, there is a jointly smooth map $(x,t)\mapsto f_t(x)$ such that each $f_t$ is an embedding, $f_0=f$, every $f_t$ agrees with $f$ on $\partial F$ and outside $f^{-1}(U)$, and $f_t$ is neatly proper for every $t>0$. Time may instead be reparametrized to be stationary near both endpoints; in that version neatness holds after the initial stationary interval.

There is also a jointly continuous ambient isotopy of homeomorphisms $H_t:M\to M$, starting at the identity, supported in $U$, fixing $\partial M$ pointwise, and satisfying $H_t f=f_t$. The construction makes $H_t$ jointly smooth on $(M\setminus C)\times[0,1]$. If $f$ is already neat, the same $f_t$ alternatively admits a jointly smooth ambient extension fixing $\partial M$. No smooth ambient extension at an original tangency is asserted.

derivations.claim: Under the full-AC hypothesis [F1], the supplier in [F2] applies. Since $c$ is essential on the torus, it is nonseparating: a separating simple curve on a genus-one surface cuts off a disk on one side and is null-homotopic. Cutting the torus along $c$ therefore gives a connected orientable surface with two boundary circles and Euler characteristic zero, hence an annulus. An embedded arc joining its two boundary circles closes after regluing to a loop meeting $c$ transversely once. The algebraic intersection is therefore $\pm1$, so $[c]$ is primitive in $H_1(T_K;\mathbb Z)$.

Because $c=\partial D$, its image in $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$ is zero. By [F2], write $[c]=q[\lambda]$ for an integer $q$. Since both $[c]$ and $[\lambda]$ are primitive, $q=\pm1$. Orient $c$ to make $[c]=[\lambda]$. By [F3], $c$ is isotopic on $T_K$ to a chosen simple representative of the preferred longitude.

In product coordinates $N(K)\cong S^1\times D^2$, the curve $c$ has core degree one by [F2], so its torus class is $(1,k)$ for an integer $k$. The graph $\gamma_k(t)=(e^{it},e^{ikt})$ has that class. By [F3], choose a smooth isotopy $c_s(t)=(u_s(t),z_s(t))$ on the boundary torus from $c$ to $\gamma_k$, stationary near its final time after smooth reparametrization. This isotopy need not trace an embedded annulus on the torus itself. Instead choose a smooth strictly decreasing radius $r(s)$ from $1$ to $1/2$ with nonzero derivative, and use $(s,t)\mapsto(u_s(t),r(s)z_s(t))$ in the tube. Distinct $s$ have distinct radii, while each fixed-$s$ curve is embedded; moreover the time derivative has nonzero radial component and is independent of its circle tangent. This gives a smooth embedded annulus with outer boundary exactly $c$ and inner boundary the radius-$1/2$ copy of $\gamma_k$. Continue it inward by $(r,t)\mapsto(e^{it},r e^{ikt})$ for $0\le r\le1/2$. The stationary final curve makes the collars agree; the inward annulus is smooth and regular even at $r=0$ and has core boundary $K$. The resulting annulus lies otherwise in the interior of $N(K)$.

If the given disk is only boundary-preimage embedded, first replace it using [F5] by a neat smooth disk in $E_K$ with the same boundary $c$. The annulus of step 3.1 has nonzero inward radial derivative at $c$ on the tube side. The resulting proper disk $D$ on the exterior side and this annulus on the tube side meet only along $c$. Their union is an embedded disk with boundary $K$; smoothing the corner along $c$ in a product collar leaves that boundary fixed. Thus $K$ bounds a smooth disk, which is a genus-zero Seifert surface. Full AC supplies the countable-choice hypothesis of [F4], so [F4] makes $K$ ambient isotopic to the unknot, contrary to the hypothesis. Therefore no such disk $D$ exists.

Assume full AC. For any smooth based link $L\subset S^3$ with a chosen nonzero normal vector at its marked point, add the small meridional earring on that marked component and its joining arc. With the corresponding determinant-one singular bundle data, finite nondegenerate critical points and all-index regular holonomy perturbations give a finite free integral cochain complex. Its differential counts all index-one classes and has square zero; its homology, denoted $I^\natural(L;\mathbb Z)$, is independent of regular metric and perturbation and invariant under isotopy of the based link data, with the same orientation sign convention as for knots. For a knot it agrees with the singular knot complex already constructed.

For the standard $n$-component unlink with a marked component, $n\ge1$, this group is free of rank $2^{n-1}$. It has a chosen representative complex with zero differential and sphere-pole generators, in the even relative degrees of the unlink model. This theorem does not supply a canonical tensor-product identification under arbitrary cobordisms, saddle maps, an exact triangle or a KHI identification.

Assume full AC. In $[0,m]\times S^3$ take a finite composite of the specified local skein saddles and standard disk births or deaths, with every surface component meeting a temporal boundary and every local ball disjoint from the fixed basepoint earring and its radius arc. Include the vertical earring annulus in the surface $\Sigma$, and put $\Omega=[0,m]\times\omega$. There are actual marked order-two orbifold $SO(3)$ data on this four-dimensional pair, product in the temporal end collars, with surface isotropy rotation by $\pi$ and ordinary residue $\frac14\operatorname{diag}(i,-i)d\theta$. Their sheet cover on $\Sigma$ is dual modulo two to $\partial\Omega\cap\Sigma$. The exterior bundle has $w_2=PD_{\mathbb F_2}[\Omega]$ and an actual $U(2)$ lift with determinant class $PD_{\mathbb Z}[\Omega]$. Every determinant-one connection has central stabilizer only. The endpoint restrictions are admissible based-link earring data, with nontrivial axis cover on the two marked components and trivial axis covers on the other oriented end components.

The assertion is existence of compatible backgrounds for these actual surfaces. It asserts no four-dimensional count, cobordism-map invariance or sutured nonvanishing theorem. Whole end collars may be fixed for a chosen background. Cut pieces of that background retain their actual restriction identifications.

Assume full AC. Fix a marked earring cobordism made from the specified saddles and standard disk births or deaths, initially with every surface component meeting a temporal boundary, or any finite composite of such cobordisms with its actual glued background. Fix the actual orbifold and exterior determinant background, fixed regular nondegenerate critical data on its based-link ends, and a compact finite-dimensional parameter manifold with corners $P$. Boundary faces may prescribe broken metrics only along admissible based-link cuts carrying the same product data. Assume the prescribed face data already have regular counts and collars and agree on their corners. Let $D$ be a nonempty finite regular oriented link diagram in an oriented $3$-sphere, with finite crossing set $C(D)$. Fix a unit viewing normal $n$ and orient the projection plane $P$ so $(u,v)$ is positive exactly when $(n,u,v)$ is positive in the ambient $3$-space. At a crossing $c$, define its sign as the sign of $\det_P(v_{\rm over},v_{\rm under})$, where the two nonzero projected tangent vectors follow the oriented over- and under-strands. Let $n_+$ and $n_-$ be the numbers of positive and negative crossings.

Set $\mathcal A=\mathbb Z[X]/(X^2)$, with $\deg(1)=1$ and $\deg(X)=-1$. Its unit, multiplication, counit, and comultiplication are
$$
\eta(1)=1,\qquad m(1\otimes1)=1,\quad m(1\otimes X)=m(X\otimes1)=X,\quad m(X\otimes X)=0,
$$
$$
\epsilon(1)=0,\quad\epsilon(X)=1,\qquad \Delta(1)=1\otimes X+X\otimes1,\quad\Delta(X)=X\otimes X.
$$
Thus $m$ and $\Delta$ have quantum degree $-1$, while $\eta$ and $\epsilon$ have degree $+1$.

Choose a total order $c_1<\cdots<c_n$ on $C(D)$. A resolution state is a function $v:C(D)\to\{0,1\}$; at $v(c)=0$ use the A-smoothing and at $v(c)=1$ use the B-smoothing from the Kauffman source chart. Write $|v|=\sum_c v(c)$, let $D_v$ be the crossingless resolution, and let $k(v)$ be its number of circles. Assign the state module $\mathcal A^{\otimes k(v)}$. For an edge $v\to v+e_j$ changing crossing $c_j$ from $0$ to $1$, use $m$ if the local smoothing merges two circles and $\Delta$ if it splits one circle, tensored with the identity on all other factors, and multiply this map by $(-1)^{\sum_{i<j}v(c_i)}$. The resulting direct sum has cohomological degree
$$i(v)=|v|-n_-$$
and the generator with circle labels $1$ or $X$ has quantum degree
$$j(v)=|v|+n_+-2n_-+\sum_{\text{circle labels }a}\deg(a).$$
This defines the normalized integral Khovanov cube and its candidate degree-zero cochain differential; the assertion that the differential squares to zero is a separate lemma.

The Frobenius identity that controls a merge-split face is represented by the two equal composites below. The diagram records the maps only; the proof verifies the equality on the basis $\{1,X\}^{\otimes2}$ and does not rely on the drawing.

```tikzcd
\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal A \arrow[r,"m"] \arrow[d,"\Delta\otimes\mathrm{id}"'] & \mathcal A \arrow[d,"\Delta"] \\
\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal A \arrow[r,"\mathrm{id}\otimes m"'] & \mathcal A\otimes\mathcal A
```

**Input:** a nonempty finite regular oriented link diagram $D$ and a total order $c_1<\cdots<c_n$ on its crossing set. A diagram object is supplied as mathematical input; this procedure does not parse a serialized string.

**Output:** the normalized bigraded Khovanov cochain module $C^{i,j}(D)$ and its candidate differential $d:C^{i,j}(D)\to C^{i+1,j}(D)$, constructed by the following finite instructions.

1. Enumerate every state $v:C(D)\to\{0,1\}$ once. Form the crossingless resolution by using the A-smoothing at $v(c)=0$ and the B-smoothing at $v(c)=1$.
2. For each state, create one tensor factor of the integral Frobenius algebra for each resolution circle and place the resulting tensor product in cohomological degree $|v|-n_-$ and quantum degree $|v|+n_+-2n_-+\sum\deg(a)$ for its circle labels $a$.
3. For each state and each crossing $c_j$ with $v(c_j)=0$, create the edge to $v+e_j$. Apply multiplication if that smoothing change merges two circles, comultiplication if it splits one circle, the identity on other tensor factors, and the sign $(-1)^{\sum_{i<j}v(c_i)}$. Sum the edge maps out of every state to obtain $d$.
4. Return the finite direct sum of the state modules with these degrees and maps. The square-zero property is the separate local lemma named by `justified_by`.

Let $(D,p)$ be a finite regular oriented diagram of a knot with a basepoint $p$ away from the crossings, and let $C(D)$ be its normalized integral Khovanov cochain complex. At each resolution state, let $X_p$ act by multiplication by $X$ on the tensor factor for the circle containing $p$, and by the identity on every other circle factor. The basepoint action is the direct sum of these statewise maps. Define the reduced cochain complex by
$$\widetilde C(D,p):=C(D)/\operatorname{im}(X_p),$$
with the same cohomological grading and with reduced quantum degree $\widetilde j=j-1$ for the class represented by a state whose basepoint circle is labelled $1$. Its cohomology is the reduced integral Khovanov cohomology $\widetilde{Kh}^{i,\widetilde j}(D,p)$. The unknot is normalized so that its reduced group lies in bidegree $(0,0)$.

Equivalently, cut the based knot at $p$ to a one-interval tangle. Put $M=\mathbb Z$ in quantum degree $0$ with $X\cdot1=0$. A resolution with $k$ closed circles and the distinguished interval is assigned $\mathcal A^{\otimes k}\otimes M$. An edge that merges a circle into the interval uses $m_M(1\otimes1)=1$ and $m_M(X\otimes1)=0$; an edge that splits the interval uses $\Delta_M(1)=X\otimes1$, where the circle factor is written first and the interval factor second. Edges not meeting the interval use $m$ or $\Delta$. This based tangle cube is the quotient complex above, with the stated quantum shift.

Let $D$ be a finite regular oriented link diagram, order its crossings as $c_1<\cdots<c_n$, and form the direct sum of state modules $\mathcal A^{\otimes k(v)}$ over all functions $v:C(D)\to\{0,1\}$. Here $\mathcal A=\mathbb Z[X]/(X^2)$, each crossing is changed from its A-smoothing at $0$ to its B-smoothing at $1$, and the edge map is the multiplication $m$ for a merge or comultiplication $\Delta$ for a split, multiplied by $(-1)^{\sum_{i<j}v(c_i)}$ on the edge at $c_j$. Then the sum $d$ of all edge maps satisfies $d^2=0$.

derivations.claim: The crossingless diagram has one based circle, hence its reduced state module is $M=\mathbb Z\{1\}$ in degree $0$ by [F2]–[F3]. There are no crossings and therefore no differential, so its cohomology is $\mathbb Z$ in degree $0$.

First compute the auxiliary positive two-strand closure, whose $A$-smoothing is the identity tangle and whose $B$-smoothing is the cap-cup tangle. This is only an auxiliary raw cube; it does not change the specified negative diagram. With zero, one, two, or three cap-cup smoothings, the closure has respectively two, one, two, or three circles: composing cap-cups creates one additional internal circle each time after the first. Thus its four raw cochain degrees $0,1,2,3$ have modules $M\otimes\mathcal A$, $M^3$, $(M\otimes\mathcal A)^3$, and $M\otimes\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal A$, of ranks $2,3,6,4$.

Order crossings from top to bottom. The first differential sends $1\otimes1$ to $(1,1,1)$ and $1\otimes X$ to zero, so its image is the diagonal copy of $\mathbb Z$ and its kernel is $\mathbb Z\{1\otimes X\}$. After suppressing the common based factor $M$, the next differential is the signed incidence matrix
$$
\begin{pmatrix}-1&1&0\\-1&0&1\\0&-1&1\end{pmatrix}
$$
with each integer entry multiplying the label $X$, because each edge splits the based circle and the reduced split sends $1$ to $1\otimes X$. Its image has rank two and its kernel is the diagonal copy of $\mathbb Z$.

Label the three two-circle states in crossing order and identify the two unbased factors in the all-$B$ state from left to right. The last differential is
$$
(a,b,c)\longmapsto a\otimes X-\Delta(b)+X\otimes c.
$$
Here the first and third edges split the based circle, while the middle edge splits the unbased circle; the signs are the cube signs from [F2]. Its image is exactly the subgroup generated by $1\otimes X$, $X\otimes1$, and $X\otimes X$, and its kernel consists of triples with equal coefficients of $1$ and with coefficients of $X$ satisfying $a_X-b_X+c_X=0$.

These auxiliary raw differentials have ranks $1,2,3$. Their images are primitive subgroups of their target free groups: the first image has a coordinate $1$, the incidence matrix in step 1.3 has a $2$ by $2$ minor $1$, and the last image is the coordinate span of $1\otimes X,X\otimes1,X\otimes X$. In each case elementary integral row and column elimination therefore gives only unit nonzero diagonal entries. Hence all auxiliary homology groups are free. The kernel/image calculations in steps 1.3 and 1.4 give raw cohomology $\mathbb Z$ in degrees $0,2,3$ and zero in degree $1$.

Now return to the specified negative diagram. At each crossing its A-smoothing is cap-cup and its B-smoothing is through, so the state $v$ has exactly the same circles as the auxiliary positive state $w=1-v$. Put the perfect integral pairing $\langle a,b\rangle=\epsilon(ab)$ on each unbased circle, with matrix $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$, and pair the based module $M$ with itself by $\langle1,1\rangle=1$. Multiplication and comultiplication are adjoints for these pairings, directly on $1,X$; the reduced merge and split are adjoints too, since $m_M(1\otimes1)=1$, $m_M(X\otimes1)=0$ and $\Delta_M(1)=X\otimes1$. Use the same actual circle order on the two complementary states. For an edge in coordinate $j$, the old transposed sign is $(-1)^{j-1-\sum_{k<j}v_k}$ whereas the negative cube requires $(-1)^{\sum_{k<j}v_k}$. Multiplying vertex $v$ by $J(v)=(-1)^{\sum_j(j-1)v_j}$ corrects this ratio: across that edge its ratio is $(-1)^{j-1}$. Thus the negative raw cube is integrally isomorphic to the degree-reversed transpose of the auxiliary cube, with this explicit diagonal sign correction. No spatial reflection or change to the given negative crossing is used.

The reversed transpose has ranks $4,6,3,2$ in raw degrees $0,1,2,3$, and differential ranks $3,2,1$. Transposition preserves the unit diagonal entries proved in step 2.1, as do the unimodular pairings and $J$ in step 2.2. Each image is therefore primitive; its quotient in the kernel is torsion-free because it is a subgroup of the free quotient of the whole target. Rank-nullity now gives free homology of ranks $1,1,0,1$ in raw degrees $0,1,2,3$. The negative diagram has three negative crossings, so the normalization $i=|v|-3$ gives $\mathbb Z$ exactly in degrees $-3,-2,0$, with zero in degree $-1$. Together with step 1.1 this proves all stated ranks for the actual two diagrams.

citations.quote: Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in the oriented $3$-sphere, let $N(K)$ be a chosen closed tubular solid-torus neighborhood, let $E_K=\overline{S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)}$, and let $T_K=\partial E_K=\partial N(K)$. Let $\mu$ be the positive oriented meridian, meaning the boundary of a positive normal disk in $N(K)$, and let $\lambda$ be a preferred longitude, meaning a degree-one parallel of the core $K$ in $N(K)$ that is null-homologous in $E_K$. Assume that $[\mu],[\lambda]$ are an ordered basis of $H_1(T_K;\mathbb Z)$, with the boundary-orientation convention $\mu\cdot\lambda=-1$. A slope is the unoriented isotopy class of an essential simple closed curve on $T_K$ whose homology class is $p[\mu]+q[\lambda]$ for coprime integers $p,q$ not both zero; $(p,q)$ and $(-p,-q)$ represent the same slope. For a slope represented by $p[\mu]+q[\lambda]$, the Dehn filling $E_K(p/q)$ is obtained by gluing an oriented solid torus $D^2\times S^1$ to $E_K$ by an orientation-reversing boundary homeomorphism that sends $[\partial D^2\times\{1\}]$ to that slope; the filled orientation agrees with the fixed orientation on $E_K$. If $q\ne0$, the coefficient is written $p/q$; the meridional slope is $1/0$, and integer $n$-framed filling means slope $n[\mu]+[\lambda]$. The oriented homeomorphism type is independent of the gluing map once its meridian image is fixed.

Assume countable choice as in the chosen tubular-neighbourhood data. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot with chosen exterior $E_K$ and boundary torus $T_K=\partial E_K$, and let $p:T_K\to K$ be the projection of the chosen normal-disk tube. Orient each normal disk so that its positive tangent direction followed by its oriented normal basis agrees with the orientation of $S^3$. A **meridian** $\mu$ is the oriented boundary of one such normal disk. A **degree-one parallel curve** is a simple closed curve $\lambda$ in $T_K$ for which $p|_\lambda:\lambda\to K$ has degree $+1$. A **preferred longitude** is a degree-one parallel curve satisfying $i_*[\lambda]=0$ in $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$, where $i:T_K\hookrightarrow E_K$ is inclusion. This is a condition on a curve; this definition alone asserts neither existence nor uniqueness. Reversing the orientation of $K$ reverses the orientations of both $\mu$ and any degree-one parallel curve. If a subgroup $P\le\pi_1(E_K,x)$ is specified using a path from $x$ to $T_K$, record it only up to replacing it by $gPg^{-1}$ for $g\in\pi_1(E_K,x)$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

$$S^3:=\mathbb R^3\cup\{\infty\}$$

of Euclidean three-space, carrying its standard smooth structure, and fix the
standard orientation of $S^3$: the orientation induced by the standard
orientation of $\mathbb R^3$ under the one-point compactification, so that the
charts of the standard atlas away from $\infty$ are orientation-preserving and
the orientation is that of a connected oriented $3$-manifold in the sense of
[[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]]. For $r>0$ write
$\overline B_r:=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:\lVert x\rVert_2\le r\}$, the closed ball of
[[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]] with the following restriction convention. Smoothness on a closed ball means
local extension to a smooth map on an open neighborhood in Euclidean space;
smoothness on $M\times I$, for a smooth manifold $M$ without boundary, means
local extension across $t=0,1$ in $M\times\mathbb R$. Thus these closed domains
are not asserted to be manifolds without boundary in the cited definition.

**Links.** The **standard oriented circle** is the circle
$S^1=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ with its standard counterclockwise orientation,
regarded as a smooth $1$-manifold; a
**finite disjoint union of oriented circles** is a smooth manifold
$C=S^1\sqcup\dots\sqcup S^1$ ($k$ summands, $k\in\mathbb N$)
diffeomorphic to the disjoint union of $k$ standard oriented circles. An
**oriented link** (with $k$ components) is a smooth embedding

$$L\colon C\longrightarrow S^3$$

of such a disjoint union in the sense of [[def-smooth-embedding]]. So $L$ is
injective, is an immersion, and is a homeomorphism onto its image with the
subspace topology, and its image $L(C)$ is a finite disjoint union of smoothly
embedded circles. Thus every link considered here is finite and tame: the
smoothness of $L$ is exactly the standing convention, and no polygonal or other
tame model is used. The **components** of $L$ are the images of the individual
summands, and the number of components is $k$.

**Ambient isotopy.** Let $I=[0,1]$. An **ambient isotopy** of $S^3$ is a smooth
map

u(U)	o

The resulting proper disk still has essential boundary. Pull that disk across $h$ or $h^{-1}$ into the other exterior. Its parametrization is a continuous disk map with boundary in the target torus; the boundary class remains nontrivial because the boundary restriction is a homeomorphism. Suppose both knots are nontrivial and let $\gamma$ be the slope represented by $h(\mu_K)$. Let $W,W'$ be the source and target filling solid tori with product coordinates. Order all extensions $\phi:E\to\Omega'$ with $F_0\subseteq E\subseteq\Omega$ by extension. A chain has the union embedding, so Zorn's lemma from [F3] gives a maximal one. If $E\ne\Omega$, choose $\alpha\in\Omega\setminus E$; it is algebraic over $E$. Apply $\phi$ to its minimal polynomial and choose a root $\beta\in\Omega'$. The transported minimal polynomial is irreducible over $\phi(E)$ because $\phi$ is an isomorphism onto its image, so sending $\alpha$ to $\beta$ extends $\phi$ to an embedding of $E(\alpha)$, contradicting maximality. Hence $\phi$ extends to $\Omega$. If $\phi_0$ maps $F$ onto $F$ and both source and target are algebraic closures of $F$, this extension is onto: its image is algebraically closed and contains $F$, so it contains every root of every polynomial over $F$, hence all of $\Omega$.

derivations.claim: Put $R=\mathbb C[M,L]$ and $S=\{M^aL^b:a,b\ge0\}$. The coordinate ring of $(\mathbb C^*)^2$ is $A=S^{-1}R$, a finite-type domain with fraction field $\mathbb C(M,L)$ of transcendence degree two. Each irreducible curve $Y$ in $C$ has prime ideal $P_Y\subset A$, and its quotient coordinate ring has dimension one by [F3]. Thus [F2] gives $\dim A=2$ and $\dim(A/P_Y)=1$; [F4] yields $\operatorname{ht}(P_Y)=1$.

Contract $P_Y$ to $p_Y=P_Y\cap R$. It avoids $S$ because every element of $S$ is a unit in $A$. By [F5], contraction and extension identify all primes below $P_Y$ with primes below $p_Y$, so $p_Y$ has height one. By [F1], $p_Y=(f_Y)$ for an irreducible polynomial $f_Y\in R$. Since $p_Y$ avoids $M$ and $L$, neither variable divides $f_Y$. In the localization of the UFD $R$, an irreducible remains prime unless it divides an inverted element; therefore $f_Y/1$ is a nonunit prime and $P_Y=(f_Y/1)$.

Distinct components have distinct prime ideals, hence their irreducible generators $f_Y$ are pairwise nonassociate in the Laurent ring. A Laurent polynomial belongs to every $(f_Y)$ exactly when each pairwise nonassociate prime factor divides it; unique factorization then makes it divisible by their product. If $C$ is empty, the vanishing ideal is the unit ideal and the empty product is $F_0=1$; otherwise the same product over the components generates the vanishing ideal. In either case the generator is square-free, and any other generator differs by a Laurent unit.

By the stated rational structure, every automorphism of $\mathbb C$ fixing $\mathbb Q$ preserves the vanishing ideal. Shift the finite support of $F_0$ so its lexicographically least exponent pair is $(0,0)$, then scale its coefficient there to $1$. This gives a unique normalized generator: by [F6] any two generators differ by a Laurent unit, and the support shift and specified coefficient remove that unit. Every such field automorphism preserves the normalization, hence fixes each coefficient. By [F7] the coefficients are rational. Clearing denominators and dividing by their integer gcd gives a primitive integer Laurent polynomial. Any two primitive integer-coefficient generators differ by a Laurent unit with rational scalar part; primitivity forces that scalar to be $\pm1$.
Steps 1.1–2.2 prove existence of the square-free primitive integer equation and show that its only ambiguity is $\pm M^aL^b$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K:S^1	o S^3$ be a smooth oriented embedding and write its quotient normal bundle as $
u_K=K^*TS^3/dK(TS^1)$. Choose an orientation-preserving trivialization $
u_K\cong S^1	imes\mathbb R^2$ and a tubular map $\Phi:\Omega	o S^3$, meaning a smooth embedding from an open neighbourhood $\Omega\subseteq
u_K$ of the zero section onto an open neighbourhood of $K(S^1)$ with $\Phi(s,0)=K(s)$, such that in these product coordinates $\Omega$ contains $S^1	imes D^2_{2\epsilon}$ for some $\epsilon>0$. Here $D^2_r=\{z\in\mathbb R^2:\|z\|\le r\}$. Set $N(K)=\Phi(S^1	imes D^2_\epsilon)$, $E_K=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$, $T_K=\partial E_K$, and let $i:T_K\hookrightarrow E_K$ be inclusion, $p:T_K	o S^1$ the product projection, and $\mu$ the positive boundary of a normal disk, using the normal-plane orientation determined by the orientations of $K$ and $S^3$. A class is primitive if it is not $m$ times another class for any integer $|m|>1$. Then $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$ is generated by $[\mu]$. The kernel of $i_*:H_1(T_K;\mathbb Z)	o H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$ is a primitive rank-one direct summand generated by a unique class $[\lambda]$ with $p_*[\lambda]=1\in H_1(S^1;\mathbb Z)$. It has a simple closed representative, is the preferred longitude, and $([\mu],[\lambda])$ is a basis of $H_1(T_K;\mathbb Z)$.

Let $M$ be a compact connected orientable smooth three-manifold, let $F$ be a compact connected smooth subsurface of $\partial M$, and let $N\lhd\pi_1(F)$ be normal. If a continuous disk map into $M$ has its boundary in $\operatorname{Int}F$ with class outside $N$, there is a smoothly properly embedded disk in $M$ whose boundary lies in $\operatorname{Int}F$ and has class outside $N$. No pointwise preservation of the original boundary loop is asserted.

Consequently a compact neatly properly embedded two-sided smooth surface $S$ in such a compact orientable smooth three-manifold is incompressible if and only if its inclusion induces an injection on fundamental groups, component by component. Here incompressibility means absence of a smooth embedded compressing disk, with the conventions of the indicated definition.

Let $M$ be a compact smooth three-manifold, possibly nonorientable and with boundary, and let $f:F\to M$ be a smooth embedding of a compact smooth surface with $f^{-1}(\partial M)=\partial F$. Transversality to $\partial M$ is not assumed. Given an open neighborhood $U$ of $C=f(\partial F)$, there is a jointly smooth map $(x,t)\mapsto f_t(x)$ such that each $f_t$ is an embedding, $f_0=f$, every $f_t$ agrees with $f$ on $\partial F$ and outside $f^{-1}(U)$, and $f_t$ is neatly proper for every $t>0$. Time may instead be reparametrized to be stationary near both endpoints; in that version neatness holds after the initial stationary interval.

There is also a jointly continuous ambient isotopy of homeomorphisms $H_t:M\to M$, starting at the identity, supported in $U$, fixing $\partial M$ pointwise, and satisfying $H_t f=f_t$. The construction makes $H_t$ jointly smooth on $(M\setminus C)\times[0,1]$. If $f$ is already neat, the same $f_t$ alternatively admits a jointly smooth ambient extension fixing $\partial M$. No smooth ambient extension at an original tangency is asserted.

Let $F_0=f(F)$ be a compact two-sided smoothly embedded surface in a compact smooth three-manifold, with $f^{-1}(\partial M)=\partial F$, and let $F_1,H_1$ be its angular neatification from [[lem-compact-smooth-boundary-preimage-surfaces-admit-neat-embedding-isotopies]]. The ambient manifold may be nonorientable. If $F_1$ has a smooth compressing disk or smooth boundary-compressing disk, then $F_0$ has a disk of the same type. Boundary-compressing disks can also be transported in the opposite direction: if $F_0$ has one, then $F_1$ has one. Consequently absence of either kind of smooth disk passes from $F_0$ to $F_1$.

Here the boundary-compressing witness has one boundary arc in the surface and the other in $\partial M$, its interior missing both. The construction allows the broader convention of ordinary smooth disk embeddings with tangential endpoint contact, and also gives smooth corner-disk witnesses with transverse surface arcs when that convention is used. No smooth ambient removal of an original surface tangency is asserted.

An essential smooth embedded circle in the standard torus $T=\mathbb R^2/\mathbb Z^2$ represents a nonzero primitive integral homology class. A finite disjoint family of essential smooth circles can be carried by a jointly smooth ambient isotopy of $T$ to parallel affine circles. Two essential circles with the same primitive unoriented class are smoothly ambient isotopic. The components between disjoint essential circles have smooth annulus parameters, with prescribed product collars on their boundary circles. No choice axiom is assumed.

Likewise two smooth spanning arcs of a parametrized annulus with the same endpoints and relative winding number are smoothly ambient isotopic relative to any collars on which they already agree. When disjoint, they have a smooth disk-strip parameter; disjoint essential circles in a parametrized annulus have smooth annulus-strip parameters. All isotopies may be stationary near their time endpoints.

Assume full AC. Let $A,B$ be compact connected oriented surfaces with supplied finite PL triangulations, let $\pi_1(A)\ne\{1\}$, and let $f:(A,\partial A)\to(B,\partial B)$ be a PL map inducing an injective fundamental-group map. Then $f$ is homotopic as a map of pairs either to a finite-sheeted PL covering $A\to B$, or to a map with image in $\partial B$; in the latter alternative $A$ is an annulus.

If the restriction $f|_{\partial A}$ is a local homeomorphism, the homotopy can be chosen constant on $\partial A$. The alternatives retain all orientation signs and all possible finite covering degrees; no assumption that $A$ or $B$ is closed, hyperbolic, or of negative Euler characteristic is imposed.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $N$ be a compact codimension-zero $C^2$ subsurface of a Hausdorff second-countable boundaryless $C^2$ surface $S$, with $C^2$ boundary. Let $G\subset\operatorname{Int}N$ be a finite embedded graph: its vertices are distinct points, each edge is a regular $C^2$ embedded arc up to its endpoints, and different edge interiors are disjoint and avoid the vertices. Closed regular edges may first be subdivided by inserting finitely many vertices. Then $N$ has a finite triangular cellulation containing $G\cup\partial N$ in its one-skeleton. Each closed triangle is an embedded topological disk, the prescribed graph and original boundary retain their regular $C^2$ arcs, and the cell maps induce a homeomorphism from a finite abstract simplicial complex onto $N$ after finite subdivision. Interior edges have two incident triangles and boundary edges one; vertex links are circles or intervals, respectively.

A cell map is required to be a homeomorphism; the statement does not assert a differentiable straightening of an arbitrary prescribed graph at its vertices. This permits tangencies between prescribed edge germs. The empty $N$ or empty $G$ is allowed.

Let $K$ be finite, $A\subseteq K$ and $B\subseteq L$ subcomplexes, and $f:(|K|,|A|)\to(|L|,|B|)$ continuous. For all sufficiently large integers $r$, there is a simplicial approximation $g:(\operatorname{sd}^rK,\operatorname{sd}^rA)\to(L,B)$, homotopic as a map of pairs to $f b_K^r$. Here $b_K^r$ is the composite barycentric homeomorphism. No pointwise fixing of a positive-dimensional restriction is asserted.

Let $B$ be nonempty, path-connected, locally path-connected, and semilocally simply connected, fix $b_0\in B$, and put $G=\pi_1(B,b_0)$.

1. The assignment $$[p:(E,e_0)\to(B,b_0)]\longmapsto p_*\pi_1(E,e_0)$$ is a bijection from based-isomorphism classes of based connected coverings of $B$ to subgroups of $G$.
2. After forgetting the chosen point in the fibre, the assignment to the conjugacy class of $p_*\pi_1(E,e_0)$ is a bijection from isomorphism classes of connected coverings of $B$ to conjugacy classes of subgroups of $G$.

Let $Y$ be path-connected and locally path-connected, let $f:(Y,y_0)\to(B,b_0)$ be based, and let $p:(E,e_0)\to(B,b_0)$ be a covering. A based lift $\widetilde f:(Y,y_0)\to(E,e_0)$ exists if and only if $f_*\pi_1(Y,y_0)\subseteq p_*\pi_1(E,e_0)$; when it exists it is unique.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice-principle-for-foliation-pair]]). Let $S$ be an oriented Hausdorff $C^2$ surface without boundary, possibly disconnected. Then:

1. Every compact subset $K\subset S$ lies in the interior of a compact finitely cellulated $C^2$ subsurface $N$. If $K$ is contained in one connected component of $S$, $N$ can be chosen connected. A specified finite embedded regular $C^2$ graph contained in $\operatorname{Int}N$ can be included in its one-skeleton.
2. Every connected closed compact subsurface has an oriented genus normal form: the sphere for $g=0$, or the polygon word $\prod_{i=1}^g a_i b_i a_i^{-1}b_i^{-1}$ for $g\ge1$, with $\chi=2-2g$. A connected compact subsurface with $b>0$ boundary circles has a free fundamental group; capping its boundaries defines genus $g$ and gives $\chi=2-2g-b$ and free rank $2g+b-1$.
3. The fundamental group of every connected component of $S$ is torsion-free.
4. Every regular embedded $C^2$ nullhomotopic circle $c$ bounds an embedded compact disk region in $S$. Here a disk region is a compact subsurface homeomorphic to the closed disk, with boundary exactly $c$; its inherited surface structure and boundary are $C^2$. It is unique unless the **connected component containing $c$** is a sphere; in that component the two complementary disk regions are the two possibilities.

The normal forms in clause 2 are homeomorphism normal forms. No general differentiable smoothing theorem or arbitrary-surface triangulation-existence theorem is a premise of this item.
For a CW pair $(X,A)$, the quotient cellular complex $C_*^{\mathrm{cell}}(X;G)/C_*^{\mathrm{cell}}(A;G)$, whose degree-$n$ group is $\bigoplus_{e^n\subseteq X\setminus A}G$, computes $H_*(X,A;G)$.

Assume AC. Let $M$ be the compact exterior of a smooth fibered knot, equipped with a compatible finite PL structure, and let $G$ be its connected fiber, with nonempty connected boundary. Let $S$ be a connected two-sided properly embedded incompressible finite PL surface. Suppose their boundaries have been aligned, with compatible product collars, and that there is a homeomorphism $h:S\to G$ and a homotopy from the inclusion of $S$ to the inclusion of $G$ composed with $h$, fixed on this aligned boundary through maps into $M$. Then $S$ and $G$ are ambient isotopic relative to $\partial M$. This assertion concerns the actual marked original fiber, not just existence of some fibration with fiber $S$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice as an ambient hypothesis; the finite construction and
the ODE interfaces below use no additional choice, so this hypothesis is
dispensable. A smooth manifold with corners here is Hausdorff and second
countable, with charts in relatively open subsets of $[0,\infty)^c\times\mathbb R^{n-c}$
and transition maps smoothly extendible with invertible derivative at corner
points; transitions preserve the local depth and its face germs. Let $M$ be
compact. Then $M$ has a finite corner-adapted whole-star smooth triangulation.
Corner faces are locally subpolyhedra, and any specified finite union of
closed faces is a subpolyhedron.

If the total boundary already has a finite piecewise smooth triangulation
$f:L\to\partial M$ compatible on all local face intersections, with its
differential fan giving a homeomorphism onto the union of boundary faces of the
tangent orthant at each point, the triangulation extends to $M$, pointwise
preserving $f$ with compatible subdivisions allowed. In the resulting finite
union construction all intersections may be made full subcomplexes. The same
relative conclusion applies to a fixed corner-adapted triangulated closed neighbourhood piece
whose smaller protected subcomplex lies in its relative interior: fitting is
performed away from that protected subcomplex. No extension of arbitrary
incompatible boundary data is asserted.

derivations.claim: Use [F2] to take a neat representative, preserving boundary and incompressibility. Nonseparation is preserved by its ambient topological extension. A short oriented transverse segment through $S$ closes through its connected complement to a loop intersecting $S$ once. Thus the intersection-dual cohomology class of $S$ is primitive. By [F1], $[S]=\pm[F]$ in $H_2(E_K,\partial E_K;\mathbb Z)$. Every loop in $S$ may be represented in its interior and pushed slightly into its two-sided normal product, so its intersection with $S$ is zero. Its value under the fiber's meridian homomorphism is consequently zero. Therefore the inclusion lifts to the infinite cyclic fiber cover $\widetilde E_K=F\times\mathbb R$. The lift is an embedding, since equality of two lifted image points would imply equality of their projected points on the embedded $S$.

Align the finitely many longitude boundary curves by [F3] with distinct fiber-boundary levels in the torus, extending across its collar. In the infinite cyclic cover their lifts are horizontal circles in $\partial F\times\mathbb R$. Straighten the neat surface's smaller boundary collars to the product collars using their simultaneous half-space coordinates, fixed on the boundary curves. The projection of the lifted inclusion is now a proper map $p:(S,\partial S)\to(F,\partial F)$ equal to a product near boundary; every boundary restriction is a diffeomorphism. Its fundamental-group map is injective: the lifted inclusion is injective on fundamental groups by [F2] and covering injection, and $F\times\mathbb R\to F$ is a homotopy equivalence. The relative fundamental class of $F\times\{t\}$ generates $H_2(F\times\mathbb R,\partial F\times\mathbb R)$ and pushes to $[F]$ downstairs. Consequently $[S]=\pm[F]$ from step 1.1 makes the relative degree of $p$ equal to $\pm1$.

Give the compact smooth surfaces the finite triangulations of [F4], choosing matched boundary subdivisions through the actual boundary diffeomorphisms. On their product collars retain the boundary map and its linear collar coordinate; relatively approximate the remaining compact map by a finite PL map. Interior compact separation and sufficiently fine approximation keep it in the target interior, so this is a homotopy of pairs fixed on the original boundary. If $\pi_1S\ne1$, apply the full actual classifier [F4]. Its annular-collapse alternative induces zero on relative $H_2$, contrary to the degree $\pm1$ in step 2.1. Its finite covering alternative has absolute relative degree equal to its number of sheets, by summing the lifted oriented triangles. Thus it has one sheet and is a homeomorphism $h:S\to F$, homotopic to $p$ relative to the aligned boundary. If $\pi_1S=1$, [F5] makes $S$ a disk. Lift $p$ to the cover of $F$ for its trivial image subgroup. An infinite-sheeted cover has relative top homology zero: all coefficients of a finite two-cycle on adjacent oriented triangles agree, and connectedness forces a single coefficient on infinitely many triangles, which must vanish by finite support. A finite-sheeted cover pushes its fundamental class to its sheet number times $[F,\partial F]$. Nonzero degree $\pm1$ therefore forces this cover to have one sheet. Hence $F$ is simply connected and also a disk; its boundary map extends to a disk homeomorphism, homotopic to $p$ relative boundary by convex interpolation in disk coordinates. In either case $S$ has one boundary component. The height coordinate of its lifted inclusion can now separately be homotoped linearly to its one constant boundary height, fixed there. Combine these homotopies in $F\times\mathbb R$ and project to get an actual homotopy of the parametrized inclusion of $S$ to the corresponding fiber, relative to the aligned boundary. This asserts a homotopy of maps, not a projection of an arbitrary embedding isotopy.

The homeomorphism and actual boundary-relative homotopy in step 3.1 meet [F6]. Use [F7] on the pair cut along its transverse smooth surface faces and protected product collars, matching paired face subdivisions before regluing; this gives compatible finite structures retaining the already matched boundary triangulations. That theorem constructs an empty embedded product patch in the actual cut fiber product, verifies that the patch meets only one fiber face so embeds downstairs, and reduces the finite intersection system until the patch is the whole surface. Hence its ambient boundary-relative isotopy carries $S$ to the original marked fiber $F$. Restore the preliminary boundary-torus alignment and neatification if necessary. This proves both the isotopy assertion and its relative aligned-boundary refinement under the authorized AC assumptions.

citations.quote: Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot, let $D$ be a valid finite planar code for a regular diagram of $K$, choose a basepoint $b$ in the complement, and designate a starting under-arc. The finite procedure $\mathsf{Wirtinger}(D,a_0)$ terminates and returns a presentation with one positive-meridian generator for each under-arc and one crossing conjugacy relator for each crossing. For the based meridians determined by the diagram's common upper-collar paths from $b$, the homomorphism from the presented group to $\pi_1(S^3\setminus K,b)$ that sends each generator to its corresponding based positive meridian is an isomorphism. Changing the designated starting under-arc only relabels the same finite cyclic arc set and gives an isomorphic presentation. If all basing paths are changed by prepending the same based loop, every generator image is conjugated by the same element, so the isomorphism type is unchanged.

derivations.claim: Work with the fixed finite presentation in the Statement. Fact [F1] ensures the existence of finite presentations for the knot group, but no change from the specified presentation to different Wirtinger generators is presumed here. Write each generator matrix as four coordinate variables and impose the polynomial determinant equation $\det(A_i)=1$. These finitely many equations cut out $SL_2(\mathbb C)^n$ in affine $4n$-space.

Evaluate each relator word by matrix multiplication, replacing each inverse letter by the adjugate matrix from [F2]. Every entry of $r_j(A_1,\ldots,A_n)-I_2$ is therefore a polynomial in the coordinates.

A tuple in $SL_2(\mathbb C)^n$ satisfies all these matrix equations exactly when its generator assignment extends to a homomorphism from the presented group $G$. Hence their common zero set is precisely $\operatorname{Hom}(G,SL_2(\mathbb C))$, a closed algebraic subset of affine space.

citations.quote: Assume full AC and let $G=\pi_1(E_K)=\langle g_1,\ldots,g_n\mid r_1,\ldots,r_m\rangle$ be a finite presentation of a knot-exterior group. The set of homomorphisms $G\to SL_2(\mathbb C)$ is the affine algebraic subset of $SL_2(\mathbb C)^n$ cut out by the matrix-entry equations $r_j(A_1,\ldots,A_n)=I_2$ for $1\le j\le m$. After each inverse letter is replaced by the adjugate of its determinant-one matrix, these equations have integer coefficients in the matrix-entry coordinates.

Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot, let $D$ be a valid finite planar code for a regular diagram of $K$, choose a basepoint $b$ in the complement, and designate a starting under-arc. The finite procedure $\mathsf{Wirtinger}(D,a_0)$ terminates and returns a presentation with one positive-meridian generator for each under-arc and one crossing conjugacy relator for each crossing. For the based meridians determined by the diagram's common upper-collar paths from $b$, the homomorphism from the presented group to $\pi_1(S^3\setminus K,b)$ that sends each generator to its corresponding based positive meridian is an isomorphism. Changing the designated starting under-arc only relabels the same finite cyclic arc set and gives an isomorphic presentation. If all basing paths are changed by prepending the same based loop, every generator image is conjugated by the same element, so the isomorphism type is unchanged.

Assume countable choice as in the chosen tubular-neighbourhood data. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot with chosen exterior $E_K$ and boundary torus $T_K=\partial E_K$, and let $p:T_K\to K$ be the projection of the chosen normal-disk tube. Orient each normal disk so that its positive tangent direction followed by its oriented normal basis agrees with the orientation of $S^3$. A **meridian** $\mu$ is the oriented boundary of one such normal disk. A **degree-one parallel curve** is a simple closed curve $\lambda$ in $T_K$ for which $p|_\lambda:\lambda\to K$ has degree $+1$. A **preferred longitude** is a degree-one parallel curve satisfying $i_*[\lambda]=0$ in $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$, where $i:T_K\hookrightarrow E_K$ is inclusion. This is a condition on a curve; this definition alone asserts neither existence nor uniqueness. Reversing the orientation of $K$ reverses the orientations of both $\mu$ and any degree-one parallel curve. If a subgroup $P\le\pi_1(E_K,x)$ is specified using a path from $x$ to $T_K$, record it only up to replacing it by $gPg^{-1}$ for $g\in\pi_1(E_K,x)$.

Assume full AC. Let $n\ge0$, let $R_{\mathbb Q}=\mathbb Q[z_1^{\pm1},\ldots,z_n^{\pm1}]$ and $R_{\mathbb C}=\mathbb C[z_1^{\pm1},\ldots,z_n^{\pm1}]$, and let $I\subseteq R_{\mathbb C}$ be an ideal invariant under coefficientwise application of every field automorphism of $\mathbb C$ fixing $\mathbb Q$. Then $$I=(I\cap R_{\mathbb Q})R_{\mathbb C}.$$ If $I$ is radical, then $I\cap R_{\mathbb Q}$ is radical as well. In particular, if $S\subseteq(\mathbb C^*)^n$ is preserved by all such coordinatewise automorphisms, the radical vanishing ideal of its Zariski closure is the scalar extension of a radical ideal over $\mathbb Q$. This includes the empty set, the whole torus and zero variables. No algebraicity or closedness of $S$ is assumed.

derivations.claim: Fix an automorphism $\sigma$ of $\mathbb C$ over $\mathbb Q$. If generator matrices $A_1,\ldots,A_n$ define a representation of the given presentation, then their entrywise images $\sigma A_1,\ldots,\sigma A_n$ do too: determinants and all relator equations are integer-polynomial equations by [F1]. Word evaluation commutes with $\sigma$, including inverse letters because their adjugate formulas have integer coefficients. Thus $\sigma\rho$ is again a representation, with peripheral matrices $\sigma(\rho(\mu))$ and $\sigma(\rho(\lambda))$.

Suppose $(M,L)\in\mathcal E_K$. A common eigenline can be represented by one nonzero vector $v\in\mathbb C^2$, with $\rho(\mu)v=Mv$ and $\rho(\lambda)v=Lv$. Applying $\sigma$ gives the same equations for $\sigma\rho$, the nonzero vector $\sigma v$, and nonzero eigenvalues $\sigma M,\sigma L$. Hence $(\sigma M,\sigma L)\in\mathcal E_K$. Applying the inverse automorphism proves equality $\sigma(\mathcal E_K)=\mathcal E_K$. This treats both eigenline charts at once; it does not assume a preferred eigenvector, an algebraic section of eigenlines or a closed projection image.

By [F3], the radical vanishing ideal of the closure of $\mathcal E_K$ is the extension of its rational contraction, and that contraction is radical. This is exactly the stated meaning of being defined over $\mathbb Q$. In particular reduction of the image introduces no unproved field-of-definition step: it is the point-set vanishing ideal to which the finite-dimensional row argument was applied. The statement retains its full-AC branch through [F3]; all matrix and eigenvector operations in steps 1.1–2.1 are finite.

citations.quote: Assume full AC. For any finite $r\ge0$, every polynomial in the entries of $r$ complex $2\times2$ matrices invariant under simultaneous conjugation by $SL_2(\mathbb C)$ is a polynomial in traces of words in those matrices. For each given invariant only finitely many words are needed. If $Z\subseteq M_2(\mathbb C)^r$ is any closed reduced invariant algebraic subset, every invariant regular function on $Z$ is likewise a polynomial in the restricted word traces. In particular this applies to the representation variety of any finitely presented group in $SL_2(\mathbb C)$, with its determinant and relator equations. The assertion does not identify a nonsemisimple representation from its character or assert a generic representation over the character function field.

Assume full AC. For every word $w$ in the generators of a finitely presented group $G$, the function $\rho\mapsto\operatorname{tr}(\rho(w))$ is a regular function on $\operatorname{Hom}(G,SL_2(\mathbb C))$ and is invariant under simultaneous conjugation.

Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the named suppliers. Let $G$ be a
complex reductive affine algebraic group and let $X$ be an affine algebraic set
with an algebraic $G$-action ([[def-rational-action-on-affine-variety]]). Then:
(i) $\mathbb C[X]^G$ is a finitely generated $\mathbb C$-algebra; (ii) for any
finite generating set $f_1,\dots,f_n$ of $\mathbb C[X]^G$ the image of the
morphism $X\to\mathbb C^n$, $x\mapsto(f_1(x),\dots,f_n(x))$, is closed and is
canonically isomorphic to the affine variety with coordinate ring
$\mathbb C[X]^G$, so the quotient is independent of generators up to this
canonical isomorphism; (iii) the resulting surjective $G$-invariant morphism
$\pi:X\to X/\!/G:=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb C[X]^G$ is a categorical quotient
([[def-categorical-and-geometric-quotients-of-classical-varieties]]); (iv) for
every closed $G$-stable subset $Y\subseteq X$ the induced morphism
$Y/\!/G\to X/\!/G$ is a closed immersion, and for closed $G$-stable
$Y,Y'\subseteq X$ one has $\pi(Y\cap Y')=\pi(Y)\cap\pi(Y')$; (v) every fibre of
$\pi$ contains exactly one closed $G$-orbit; (vi) if $X$ is irreducible then so
is $X/\!/G$, and if in addition $X$ is normal then so is $X/\!/G$.

Let $G$ be any group and $\rho,\rho':G\to SL_2(\mathbb C)$ be representations with $$\operatorname{tr}\rho(g)=\operatorname{tr}\rho'(g)\qquad(g\in G).$$ If $\rho$ is irreducible, then $\rho'$ is irreducible and there is $P\in SL_2(\mathbb C)$ such that $\rho'(g)=P\rho(g)P^{-1}$ for every $g$. If $\rho$ is reducible, it has the same trace character as its diagonal semisimplification $g\mapsto\operatorname{diag}(\chi(g),\chi(g)^{-1})$, where $\chi:G\to\mathbb C^*$ is the character on a common invariant line. The two diagonal characters $\chi,\chi^{-1}$ determine the same semisimple conjugacy class. This is a pointwise statement; it does not assert that an irreducible character component admits a tautological representation over its function field or prove rational quotient descent.

derivations.claim: By [F2], choose a finite algebra generating list $f_1,\ldots,f_s$ for the character coordinate algebra. Each $f_j$ is a polynomial in finitely many word traces by [F1]. The union of these finitely many word lists is finite; denote it by $w_1,\ldots,w_N$. Their traces generate an algebra containing all $f_j$, hence the entire coordinate algebra. This establishes one fixed finite list for the quotient, rather than just a separate list for each function.

Send $z_i$ to $t_{w_i}$. Step 1.1 makes this polynomial-ring map onto the reduced invariant coordinate algebra. Its kernel is therefore radical. The actual affine coordinate-ring construction in [F2] identifies the quotient with the closed zero locus of that kernel in $\mathbb C^N$ and its point map with the displayed trace-coordinate map. Thus this is the asserted closed embedding with exactly the stated defining ideal.

Equal listed coordinates give equal values of every element of the coordinate algebra by step 1.1. In particular they give equal traces on every group word. The irreducible claim follows from [F3], including preservation of irreducibility. A reducible representation is triangular in an invariant-line basis, and [F3] gives its diagonal semisimplification with identical traces. Since the listed traces are the quotient coordinates, both have exactly the same quotient point. This records the semisimplified character and does not assert conjugacy of a nonsemisimple triangular representation to that diagonal one. All full-AC hypotheses are retained from [F1] and [F2]; the pointwise conjugacy argument adds no choice axiom.
